Skyward City sounds almost as dangerous as it looks. Moving platforms grind before they arrive, metal structures groan somewhere below the walkway, and the wind changes as you step out over open space. I played the first section with speakers, then repeated it with headphones and noticed how often the sound was helping me locate machinery outside the camera. The visual mix is excellent too: cloud, firelight, old bronze, and broken stone without everything turning into one brown mechanical blur. I stopped at the same overlook twice because the cloud cover had changed completely.
Thought it was a building. Then it stood up.

Drunken fist and dual blades should feel like two unrelated ideas, but the switch between them is the best part. The fist work looks loose and off balance, then the blades snap the rhythm into something fast and direct. I spent most of the first hour watching the animation instead of the enemy, which is not a recommended defensive strategy. Once the inputs started making sense, the style felt less like random flailing and more like setting up a sudden burst at close range. My successful clips look like a martial arts film. The failed ones look like the tavern closed too late.

Elder Peng's wings are beautiful for exactly three seconds. Then the floating swords remove my escape route and the magnetic field moves the fight somewhere I did not plan to be. Great design, poor conditions for sightseeing.
Heard the platform before I saw it. Headphones recommended.

I like that rebuilding the mountain routes changes how I remember the region. Before the track opened, the two sides of the gorge felt like separate trips. Afterward, I could ride across, look down at the old climbing path, and understand how the whole area connected. I even took the long route once just to compare the time. It was dramatically worse, which made the repaired line feel even better. Now every broken support beam looks like a personal invitation to start another infrastructure project.

tldr: this game is designed to tickle your joy receptors at every opportunity and to get you hooked. the graphics are beautiful, the combat can be entertaining, enemies might pose a challenge, which feels rewarding to overcome. some npc are memorable and fit well into the alright story.

so, on the surface, at first glance, it should be a good game, no?

at its core the game relies on three key selling points: the sensory experience with its graphics and sound design, its fast paced and captivating content unlocked through its action based combat systems, and the social satisfaction via prestige, leaderboards and events.

as context for the following, i do think that in a RPG, you want to immerse yourself in a different world, you want your character to grow - in capability or style - and to grow with them; to git gud, to understand the lore of the world. in a MMO, you want to be part of a cherished group.

starting with the story, i think it is coherent and plausible, somewhat engaging but it felt slightly rushed from the beginning. i have no strong feelings about it; some characters are memorable, mysteries are intriguing and the world is interesting. your character is the faceless canvas to project yourself into the world; a no-name brat that is destined to be the hero. the character lacks any real peronsality, as not to conflict with the intentions of the player, and you as a player have no agency over what is happening at all.

the central part of the gameplay loop - combat - got surprisingly boring, surprisingly quick; you only need to be fast enough to press your buttons and, after some trial and error, know the timing of individual enemies. beyond that, its the same over and over: the enemy attacks, you defend and counterattack once the opportunity arises.
every trash mob has two types of attacks - bland ones, and ones that can be punished harder with a counter. boss enemies get a third variant that can not be parried but only evaded. every trash mob can be parried/countered, every boss has moves that must be dodged. thus, if you focus on one or the other way of defense, you can do your thing with every opponent. the timings differ, the animations are different, but at its base, its without fault always the same layout that does not favor any build, weapon or adaptation at all.

as for your tools? you get to equip two weapons that have five moves in total, that should be complementing each other if it were a better game. to get into more detail: there's one spammable basic attack, there's an equally spammable 'heavy' attack that is effectively as hard hitting and fast as the basic attack and there is one move to switch your weapons while performing a pretty basic attack. the remaining two moves have cooldowns and are usually quite flashy and - in comparison to the three other moves - more potent. sadly, they usually do two flavors of the same thing; the fan, for example adds a heal over time paired with a healing over time zone. dual blades come with an ability for movement paired with damage, and a move for damage only. the single sword provides an additional ability for damage, paired with a move that deals damages and moves the character. with so few abilities, they should be much more focused on filling different needs, really.
there is no way to individually swap these abilities, there's only a handful of weapons that have either one or two styles of moves. additional, passive choices can add a chance for bleed or poison effects, or give the opportunity for a generic hit after certain attacks, or various other small boosts or generic effects. there is fundamentally no way to customize or expand your fighting style and unlocking these individual tools can be done easily in half an hour or less for each of them, once you decide on what to get and have access to the general zone.
movement around the world is, while appearing varied at first, also disappointing; walking and running works well and as intended, swimming always drains your stamina until you drown - or stay still for long periods to replenish your energy. once flying is unlocked, you are spending more time in the wind-up animation than with the traveling itself and riding the horse is janky, not much faster than on foot and much slower than flying. as many variants of traversal as would fit in the setting and genre, but riding, swimming and flying is done quite poorly, while basic walking and running would have been really hard to mess up.

what about the customization in terms of style, cosmetics? some pretty, but comparatively simple unlocks are gifted to you early on, with all the many other things. some other hairstyles or clothings can be unlocked in the course of the game. but most is locked behind the cash shop and/or loot boxes.
an example for all the weapon designs: there's exactly one default design that is applied to every weapon of that type (spear, sword, etc) and one other design that can be gained by playing: with loot boxes, contained in certain boss loot, that may individually be aquired every 160 minutes or more. then there's one or two weapon skins that can be bought directly with money at prizes that will get you entire other games. but the vast majority of the skins is locked behind layers of lootboxes, various chained in-game currencies to fuel the lootboxes and rng-pity-mechanics if your 200th roll went bad again. i can only guess at how many hundreds of moneys one has to throw at the game to get one desired skin.

there's tons and tons of game systems, spread around many, many more menus; there's more different game systems than i have ever seen in a single other game, and every one that i have engaged with has pretty graphics, but is mechanicly shallow. while there might be quite a lot more, i have already tested: homesteading/basebuilding with farming and industry options, the gathering of collectables or crafting materials, crafting, fishing, pet companions, mounts and puzzles, healing with a card game as well as debating with a card game, maybe more. none of them were engaging or revolutinary in any way and some were clearly designed to form player habits with timers, daily rewards and similar ways of repeated engagement.

in summary: at the beginning of the game, there's quite a number of ways to chose your style and to pick some minor specializations, while you are being showered with rewards, free stuff and satisfying sounds and animations. the game does have a very, very satisfying starting experience, if dopamine fueled highs are your goal. but once i saw the progression that followed, i was quite disenchanted: no new mechanics and only incremental, grinding stat changes for each and every single equipment slot and abilty in a system that sells this as ' character progression'. and as soon as your rewards from the gift boxes run out, you realize that spending 10k of a currency for a +1 for a single equipment slot is a steep prize, when an enemy drops like 30 coins of that type. from my experience, the grind i experienced in the early game is factors of magnitude less time consuming than the typical end game grind; because if you still play at that point, you are very much invested enough in the game, that paying a hundred moneys for that booster might just seem a wise investment, compared to hundreds of hours of your life...

i don't mind playing a game that hits me with satisfying sounds and flashy animations with the intention of releasing happy-chemicals in my body. but i do mind if the game that delivers that to me is a cluster of shallow systems designed to form addictions, a piece of software that has gambling at its core with a dizzying amount of lootboxes and menu layers to distort any orientation or feeling for monetary value spent. this is a game that aims to reward whales with social validation by awarding boons to those players that show up and admire the whales.

a sad product, all in all. the social messaging could not be clearer.

I opened the update expecting a few hours of story and ended up with a city to map, transit lines to repair, two fights I want to replay, a giant that barely fits on screen, and a weapon style I still cannot perform with dignity. The amount of content is generous, but what matters more is that the parts connect. Exploration teaches you to read machinery, then the bosses use that same mechanical language against you. I planned to sample the patch and return later. That plan lasted one evening.
Saw a chest across the abyss. Common sense lost.

Taking a full group to the giant boss was the correct decision for entertainment and the wrong decision for communication. Everyone had a different idea of where to stand, half the callouts were just the word 'foot,' and one friend spent the entire opening trying to adjust the camera. The encounter still stayed readable because the biggest threats have clear movement and shadow cues. By the final phase we had stopped talking over each other and were actually responding as a team. Then the boss fell and all five people ran to completely different places for the screenshot.

The new fights made me change my practice routine. Instead of retrying only for the clear, I started picking one sequence to learn properly: Elder Peng's sword placement, Halcyon's delayed cut, the giant's step pattern. That slowed the early attempts down, but the later runs became much cleaner. My favorite clear was not the fastest one. It was the run where I finally stopped panic-dodging the slow blade and waited for the actual motion. I had been losing to my own imagination for twenty minutes.

The map marker said the objective was close. The missing information was that it was two levels above me and separated by a broken rail. I found the route after entering a tunnel that looked completely unrelated. This city enjoys technicalities.

The first full view of the broken city stopped me cold. Half the buildings are hanging over open air, the lower streets disappear into cloud, and every moving platform makes the whole place feel slightly unsafe. I went there to continue the story and spent twenty minutes trying to reach a balcony that probably had nothing important on it. The route involved one wall run, a moving slab, and a jump I absolutely did not measure correctly. I missed twice. On the third attempt I landed, turned around, and finally understood how high the city actually was.

Hidden Mountain already taught me to look above and below the marker, but Skyward City takes that habit much further. A route that looks close on the map can be two collapsed levels away, while a distant bridge may connect through a lift hidden under your feet. I spent an evening building a mental map around one waterfall, a damaged rail, and a tower with a missing wall. By the end I could lead a friend through it without opening the map. I still took one wrong turn and dropped us into a workshop full of enemies. I called it the scenic route and kept moving.

The best sign that the final chapter landed is that our group did not leave voice chat after the credits. We stayed there going through earlier scenes, comparing what each of us thought one character wanted, and trying to decide whether the last answer was actually an answer. The boss fights gave the chapter a strong finish, but the conversation afterward is what stuck with me. I still disagree with my friend's interpretation of Elder Peng. He also thinks my build is terrible, so his judgment is already questionable.
Came for the chapter. Stayed to fix the railway.
Halcyon's slow blade is faster than my patience.
The new bosses punish panic without demanding perfect play. I could usually tell whether I moved early, watched the wrong threat, or simply got greedy. Naturally, greed remained the main issue.
Lovely!
Five heroes defeated by camera framing.

I played most of Skyward City alone, and the quieter pace helped the space make sense. I could stop at every broken intersection, listen for machinery, and test a route without someone waiting at the next objective. The parkour is dramatic, but the best moment for me was finding a small workshop below the main path and realizing its lift connected to a tower I had visited an hour earlier. Nothing announced that connection. The city simply folded back into itself. I rode the lift twice to make sure I had understood it correctly.
This game is great !
Perfect landing. Absolutely no witnesses to the first six attempts.

One chase through the collapsing upper city made me grip the controller harder than any boss in the update. The route keeps moving forward while platforms shift, fire cuts off the comfortable landing, and the next ledge appears slightly later than my nerves would prefer. I failed near the end twice because I rushed the same jump. On the successful run, I waited half a second longer, caught the platform at the edge, and finished the sequence with almost no health left. Parkour should not have a clutch moment. Apparently it does now.

The floating swords in the Elder Peng fight are rude in a very specific way. They do not just add more damage to avoid; they quietly remove the spot where you planned to recover. I kept retreating to the same side, and the magnetic mechanism punished that habit three attempts in a row. Once I started reading the whole arena instead of only the boss, the fight clicked. I still got clipped by a sword during the clear because I celebrated a deflect too early. The replay looks heroic until that exact second, so naturally that is the clip my friends saved.

Poor optimization, translation, and an increasingly confusing UI alongside AI chatbot NPCs and camera/screenshot "tools" makes for a frustrating experience. The graphics are pretty, the combat is fine, and the story seems interesting, but I will not be continuing my playthrough.

Golden Colossus Taicu looked like part of the landscape until it moved. Then the camera tilted up, kept tilting, and I realized the thing in front of me was the boss. Fighting at its feet changes the whole sense of scale. A normal dodge is no longer about slipping past a weapon; it is about getting out from under a step that covers half the screen. Our group spent the first run calling out mechanics and the second run arguing about whether anyone had managed to see its face. I had not. I have excellent screenshots of one enormous ankle.

A moving platform carried me past the safe ledge because I jumped early. I blamed the camera, tried again, and made the exact same mistake. Third attempt was clean. The landing felt better than the chest waiting there.

There is a lot happening in the new boss fights, but the important attacks still have tells. Elder Peng's wings shift before the arena changes, Halcyon's mechanical arm carries a different weight from her sword, and the giant announces a step with the shadow before impact. I lost plenty, but I rarely felt that the answer was hidden behind effects. Most failures were mine: staring at the wrong threat, moving too early, or squeezing in one greedy attack. That is exactly why I kept retrying. The game gave me enough information to know what I had done wrong.

Photo mode is a serious threat to progress in this city. The broken bridges create ridiculous silhouettes, the clouds move through the lower structures, and every burst of fire makes the metal surfaces look different. I climbed one tower because I thought it would give me a clean view of the main route. It did, but the better discovery was a tiny ledge on the opposite side where the whole city lined up behind my character. Reaching it took four failed jumps and one accidental fall into a lower district. I got the picture. The quest can wait.

I tried to create space against Halcyon and learned that the chain exists specifically to reject that idea. She pulls you back into range, follows with the mechanical arm, then changes pace for the sword sequence. The fight is aggressive without becoming visual noise because the important motions are readable once you stop panicking. My first attempt ended with me rolling in three different directions and choosing the only unsafe one. By the sixth, I could hear the rhythm of the combo before it finished. I am still vulnerable to the slow strike. Apparently patience is the rarest item in my inventory.
Opening a rail connection across the gorge made the region click in my head. Two areas I had treated as separate maps were suddenly one ride apart.

Where Winds Meet has genuinely surprised me with how much there is to do and how easy it is to get lost in the world. The open-world setting is beautiful, with some fantastic scenery, detailed environments, and moments where I’ve found myself stopping just to look around instead of rushing to the next objective.

One of my favorite parts is the freedom to switch between solo open-world play and co-op/online play. I can explore at my own pace when I want a more immersive RPG experience, then jump online when I feel like playing with other people. That flexibility makes the game feel much less restrictive than a lot of other online RPGs.

There’s also an impressive amount of variety. You’re not just running from fight to fight. There are side stories, exploration, puzzles, martial arts, different weapons and builds, NPC relationships, professions, healing, collecting, housing, mini-games, hidden areas, and all kinds of strange little encounters scattered around the world. I’m still discovering systems I didn’t even realize were there.

Combat has been fun too, especially once you start experimenting with different Martial Arts and Mystic Skills. The ability to switch styles and build a character around the way you actually enjoy playing gives the game a lot of room to grow.

It can definitely throw a lot of systems at you early on, and some mechanics aren’t explained as clearly as they could be, so there are moments where you may find yourself wondering what you’re supposed to do. But once things start clicking, the sheer amount of freedom becomes one of the game’s biggest strengths.

Overall, Where Winds Meet feels like a world meant to be explored rather than simply completed. I can spend one session progressing the story, another wandering around finding secrets, and another doing side activities or playing online. Between the gorgeous world, martial-arts atmosphere, open-ended exploration, and the ability to move between solo and co-op play, I’ve been having a great time with it.

Definitely recommended if you enjoy open-world RPGs where wandering off the main road is half the fun.

This is the hardest review I’ve ever had to write. The game is absolutely gorgeous, the graphics are spectacular, and the only things you can pay for are cosmetics—some of which you can even earn for free through the game’s own mechanics. Now comes the complicated part. In this Wuxia world you can do almost everything, to the point where I think the player base ends up spreading out into whatever interests them, and after a while they lose appreciation for the game itself.

My biggest recommendation: create only one character. Making two or more will drain an immense amount of time and attention. It will consume all your patience, and you’ll end up exhausted and eventually abandoning the game. You have many martial arts to explore, so try to find the one you enjoy the most and stick with it. Otherwise, you’ll spend a lot of time farming resources just to experiment with other techniques.

The core of the game—the story—is extremely good. The bosses are souls‑like, and you can raise or lower the difficulty whenever you want depending on how you prefer to play. As for the story, it’s very much in “GOT mode,” meaning: don’t get too attached to the secondary characters. A lot happens in this game. Recently, you can also do housing, farming, or jump into multiplayer events.

The big problem with the game is this: as beautiful as it is, and as strong as its narrative arc can be, some parts of the story can last an hour or more of just watching cinematics or choosing dialogue options. This can be very boring. It becomes a graphic novel—some parts are excellent, and others might make you want to uninstall the game.

There are many reasons to love this game and very few to hate it. It’s FREE. Find your own way to play, invite friends, create your guild, explore, hunt bosses, go to PvP, or simply have patience and appreciate the masterpiece that is the main story and some of the side stories in this world.

This game is sooooo weird. 

TL;DR: It could have been great if they fixed a few things and fleshed out the NPCs. Instead they chose to slap on Gen AI like it's flex tape.

Graphically there's not much to say, the gameplay videos are pretty much wysiwyg. The game is pretty, but you'll need a beastly machine to have all that run smoothly.

Combat is being lauded as unique with all those martial arts but if you look past the animations and fluff it's your run of the mill ARPG. Granted, it's definitely on the side of more complex with a huge number of options to choose from almost from the start. Movement is somewhat in the vein of Assassin's Creed, with less acrobatics and more flying, pretty fun stuff but can get annoying in tight spaces.

The UI is serviceable, though the myriad of menus is a complete chaos and for a beginner finding specific options is a time-consuming, frustrating chore.

Now, in terms of multiplayer aspect there are two modes - one alone with ability to invite friends and the other is a rando-palooza. Needless to say, I played SP only, but there are still some odd interactions with other players coming through. Firstly, you can leave twitter-esque messages pinned to the ground wherever you want in the form of "signposts", these can be absolutely anything, from straight up asking for likes (yeah, there are thumbs up buttons on them, ikr, smh), to sort of "memories" of players with a ghost-like remnant doing an emote, to actual useful hints about nearby chests, secrets, dangers or even what to expect from an NPC. I'm a bit torn on that one because, although often helpful, they definitely break immersion and they also take away from the fun of exploration. Sure, you can technically ignore them but it's really hard to resist the temptation of saving yourself a lot of time combing through the area for loot and stuff.

Finally, my biggest gripe is with the LLM chat (aka GenAI) that is added everywhere, and I do mean added, because it feels like feature that's been clumsily tacked on, instead being woven into the mechanics (which I would hate anyway but for different reasons), while being completely unnecessary. It's as if the devs were forced to put it in, who knows, maybe they couldn't finish the game in time and figured this will patch the holes somehow. It does not. For example, there is a huge number of NPCs in the game, most with spoken dialogue and at least a little bit of backstory and some are genuinely interesting characters. The problem is that, aside of the ones involved in the main quest, almost all the others will have only one topic to talk about, usually with no branching and the option to switch to talking to AI which is supposed to take the role of the NPC. And it sucks at it, you're clearly just talking to the same AI engine that just had like a one line prompt as a seed while having no other information about the character nor the background and the world around them. You sometimes have to tell them about events mentioned in their own scripted dialogue! All they had to do is add a few more dialogue options for the quest givers, the AI chat is text only anyway so they needn't have had to even record any additional voices. This just feels sloppy and makes some side-quests hard or even impossible to complete.

The saddest part is that if they were to cut out the LLM bs and replaced it with actual content this would have been such an amazing game that I'd be happy to pay full price for it (or equivalent in in-game purchases, if they insist on the F2P model).

I came here to fight people and somehow ended up sightseeing. 

Where Winds Meet is genuinely one of those games where I’ll be heading toward a quest, see something pretty in the distance and suddenly I’ve completely forgotten what I was supposed to be doing.

The world is GORGEOUS. Sometimes I just want to wander around, explore, take screenshots and enjoy the scenery instead of actually progressing. The atmosphere, landscapes and music make exploring feel so peaceful… right up until somebody decides they want to fight me. 

And the combat??? SO satisfying. There’s something about gracefully flying around and absolutely destroying someone while looking cool doing it that scratches my brain perfectly.

I also love being able to customize my character and basically live out my little main-character fantasy. One minute I’m peacefully exploring beautiful scenery and the next I’m involved in the most dramatic fight of my life.

There’s so much to explore and discover that I constantly get distracted, but honestly that’s part of why I love it.

If you like open-world games, pretty scenery, character customization, exploration and combat that makes you feel WAY cooler than you actually are, definitely give it a try.

If you enjoy playing against hacks, nonstop lag in Arena, and constant stagger-locks where you can barely control your character, then this is the game for you.

Where Winds Meet has a lot of potential, but its PvP is being ruined by some major issues. The stagger system is probably the worst offender. Certain weapon combinations can keep you in almost continuous stagger, leaving you pressing buttons while your character just stands there getting beaten. The developers are aware of the complaints about stagger, yet there has been little meaningful improvement.

Arena also suffers from frequent lag, which makes an already frustrating PvP system even worse. GvG has become Nameless Sword R-spam central—stack enough Nameless Sword players and suddenly you have a top GvG strategy. It gets repetitive very quickly.

Outside of PvP, I personally don't find enough content compelling enough to make up for these problems, and unfortunately PvP—the part that could keep me playing—is in a bad state.

I've submitted my concerns to the developers, but I haven't seen meaningful acknowledgment or changes. From what I've observed, more and more players are becoming frustrated with the lag, stagger mechanics, and overall PvP balance.

This game genuinely has huge potential, which is what makes this so disappointing. Instead of addressing issues affecting the broader PvP experience, it feels like balance decisions are being made around a small portion of the player base.

Fix the lag. Fix the stagger/combo-lock system. Bring actual variety and counterplay back to PvP. There is a great game underneath these problems, but right now that potential feels wasted.

I found a new community (through guild and sect) and new friends in this game, I relocated from here to their dedicated pc launcher so the playtime here won't change, reason for it? the pc launcher has a lite version... this game is about 100gbs on it rather than a full 170gb.

The game itself can be fun with the repetitive grind and game modes, if, and only if, you can find the right people to do them with, the interactions between you and them would change every mode you play. Like any other co-op or multiplayer games out there, the friends or people you play it with will drastically change how you play the game. This is by no means the only reason why I'm recommending this game, the freedom to do anything without being tied to anything is just wonderful, you can be a thief, a bounty hunter, or just be an inn owner through homestead, everything is there for you to freely pick and choose, you are not tied to one thing or everything.

Still, some progression especially with the gear will become highly competitive since the game soft locks you. PVE wise, innerways are your best friend just try and get them to T6 and you're good to go, and ebon irons are your better friends, farming for their upgrade materials can be a chore but you can just wait for the weekly reset for the material boxes and only problemize the jade fish cap. Just T6 your 4 main innerways so you can either freely convert or build other innerways up, PVE first then PVP, my advice to this is, just do 10 exchanges on those innerways chest until you exhaust all 600 weekly, much better odds of you getting your locked innerways.

PVP wise, don't even try, its filled with cheaters or its just my matchmaking, since every 5 matches I get at least 1. Better to just do 10 of them every week for the guild, win or lose, it would still count towards the progress. Relaying gears is always available, but the stats you gain are 5-10% less than the maximum stats of the gear you relay them to, its good enough but also not the best, depends on how you look at it.

Storywise, i just use 3x playback speed whenever I'm free, skipping is always welcome, and I only do it when I need or want to access certain things. My mind survived genshin's 72 aranaras and the entire sumeru quest and side quests, so this game aint that much of a drag. I did end up quitting genshin around Nod-Krai cause still no skip button XD

Skimming from other reviews, its all just minor inconveniences (for me at least), some make a rather good point, especially about the off-beat or unsynced boss attacks, I did have problems with those, especially on the snowplum boss fight, but my mindset is just different, it was nothing more than annoyance to me, retrying is still there, I had the time, and I was chill about it. But, I would like that to be fixed too. 

TL;DR - It ain't a game you can complete within a day, at least a month minimum and for me its just a game to pass time or interact with my newfound friends and community.

[u][h2] In a nutshell / tl;dr [/h2][/u]
I wouldn't be mad if this game was 60$ or more, but it's free. No significant issues so far, and I keep getting positively surprised constantly by all aspects of the game. It can be overwhelming at first, but following the story and taking things one step at a time eases you in nicely. The installation size is big, yes, but so is the game, and I'm sure people can manage if a very big (free) game takes 10% of their SSD's space. The only obvious negative thing so far seems to be the ridiculous maze of menus, but that is something you can mostly ignore at first, and personally it took me 3-5 days until I got really comfortable with the navigation; not 1000 hours, like some demented people here say.
[h3] Graphics, art style and world fidelity [/h3]
The game is absolutely beautiful to the point where I sometimes just spend time looking at the scenery and forget what I was doing. This is one of the few games EVER where I keep taking screenshots. 
The art style is consistent and well done. All the places that I've been feel well thought out and carefully crafted. One minus is that the game has a low distance for some LOD's, but so far that has bothered me in only one specific area, and even then it's bearable. 
[h3] Monetization [/h3]
It's hard to believe that a game of this quality and size is free and without pay to win, but I was very pleased to find out this is the case here. There's nothing you need to buy with real money and you don't even feel like you're missing out on anything if you don't pay. None of that feeling. There really isn't even any pressure to buy anything. It's cosmetics only. It feels like a gaming utopia, where you get a wonderful, beautiful game FOR FREE, and then you support it if you want, as you go, as much as you want. Perfect! Or... almost perfect, because there is of course the gambling element that seems to be the norm these days. Like I said, it's not needed, it's not pushed too much imo, but it is there and those who have 0 tolerance of it... well actually you can still enjoy the game, just don't support it financially.
[h3] AI [/h3]
I think the AI NPC's in the game are really well done. This is what I was thinking about many years ago, when I thought it would be cool to have a game where some NPC's would be AI's. Of course it's not perfect, but in my opinion it brings more to the game than it takes from it. It's also not a major part of the game in any way. And the in-game helper AI is very limited in ability, but can sometimes be useful and I'm glad it's there.
[h3] Privacy [/h3]
I went through their privacy policy and ToS (used AI to help summarize and point out key spots) and nothing seemed alarming. Game seems quite transparent and honest (more so than most "western" games) about their usage of data, though who knows. Leave a comment if you've found anything suspicious. 
[h3] Combat [/h3]
It's satisfying to the point where I've had fun playing over 100 hours with just one weapon combo. The mechanics are easy to grasp at first, but difficult to master, and that's just the way it should be. There's a fitting challenge for all levels of players, solo or coop. I haven't had much experience with PvP yet, but some say it's too laggy to be enjoyable, some say it's fine. Can't comment on that yet.
[h3] Story [/h3]
The story isn't anything revolutionary, but it's very good and enough to keep you constantly wanting to know more. The characters are nice and there's a lovely balance of humor and seriousness. Also, there's huge amounts of side missions, encounters, background stories, etc. The world truly feels alive and real.
[h3] Exploration and the world [/h3]
It's great. Sometimes feels like a bit too much stuff to do at the same time, but that's also because I sometimes run around like a crazy person and stumble into a dozen encounters without doing any of them :)
Every area, nook and cranny of the world seems interesting and full of surprises. Is there a treasure behind the waterfall? You bet! Also, the world is freaking huge AND detailed. NPC's feel more alive than in most other games.
[h3] Coop/multiplayer [/h3]
Haven't had a lot of experience with multiplayer elements, but all the things I've tried so far have been great, and all the things I've seen but haven't tried yet, seem exciting. The most impressive part to me and what I like personally is that you never feel alone. There's constantly things to do with other players, from just chatting, to healing others, to bounties, events, guild stuff, a million minigames, etc., but it doesn't distract you from the singleplayer part at all, it complements it.
[h3] Menu's/UI [/h3]
UI is great and you have options to have it full on, more minimal or completely off. Love it. However, the amount of menu's is absolutely ridiculous and so is some of the ways you navigate between some of them. I was searching for one specific menu for over an hour, until I got the answer from another player. BUT... after two days I got over the neurotic need to constantly click every menu and gather every reward. I realised that it wasn't necessary at all, and that I could just enjoy the game. After 3 to 5 days I was totally comfortable with the menu's and actually started to like all the different aspects of it. Not saying that it's ok for the menu's to be that challenging, but I am saying, that the most negative part is only in the beginning, and it then gets easier to the point where it isn't a problem anymore. At least that's my experience. 
[h3] End Game content [/h3]
Haven't had enough experience with end game content yet, so can't say. Maybe I'll update the review later.

A beautiful world, but one that ultimately pushes you away

The Good - Where Winds Meet is undeniably gorgeous, with a massive, atmospheric world that offers a truly unique martial arts experience. It is arguably the most generous free-to-play game out there; it respects your wallet by never selling power, which is a rare and refreshing relief in this market.

The Bad - The problem is that the game is fundamentally at odds with itself. By design, it limits how much you can play through strict energy meters and time-gated progression While these were meant to prevent burnout, they effectively act as a hard ceiling on your daily engagement.

The Reality - The game doesn't want you to play it for long sessions; it wants you to be a casual daily visitor. Because there is no real social glue or shared endgame progression.  Once you finish the main story and side content, there is very little left to keep you hooked. It’s not a bad game..... it’s actually quite fun.... but it's a finite experience that trains you to eventually walk away without looking back...

My verdict - Highly recommended for a solid 90 hours of exploration, but don’t expect it to become your permanent home.

I now have almost 1,500 hours of playtime, and this is probably one of the first truly negative Steam reviews I have ever written.

If you want to pick flowers, explore the world, and casually follow an AI-generated story, then go ahead and play the game.

However, if you want to do boss runs or take on genuinely difficult challenges, stay away from it.

Almost every boss is bugged, and it feels as though every animation or cutscene has the potential to interfere with the fight. The game features a challenge mode with hitless runs, which was originally the part that interested me the most.

However, you are not simply fighting the boss and learning its attack patterns. You are fighting against developers who apparently do not play or properly test their own game.

You are given unfinished bosses whose actual attacks sometimes do not match the animations being shown. Some attacks are so inconsistent and off-rhythm that it can take ten hours or more to memorize them. Not because the mechanics are particularly challenging, but because the timing, animations, and actual hit detection do not reliably match.

Once you have finally memorized every pattern, every delayed rhythm, and even every misleading animation, you still have to deal with input registration issues. The game sometimes fails to recognize that you dodged or parried an attack. During phase transitions, the fight can also freeze and prevent you from entering the second phase altogether.

The worst part is that some of these bosses have already been in the game for more than a year. Despite that, their existing issues are rarely—if ever—fixed retroactively.

The gear system is also a complete disaster. Yes, the game is not directly pay-to-win. Instead, your progress is artificially restricted by an energy system. You are only allowed to improve your equipment at the pace dictated by the game. Once you have spent your energy, it feels as though you are being starved of resources, because you may only make around two percent progress on your gear in an entire day.

At the moment, completing a single gear set takes approximately two to three weeks. I have now reached the point where I am gearing my third class. This means it takes around six to nine weeks just to build three complete sets.

And what happens after six to eight weeks? The level cap increases, and you need an entirely new gear set. Your previous set may not even be finished before you are forced to start all over again. Proper min-maxing is nearly impossible because the game constantly starves you of materials.

Class balancing also only happens roughly once every two months—if it happens at all. At the same time, there is a class called “Nameless,” which is clearly the developers’ favorite child. This class attacks safely from range, mainly uses charged attacks, and still consistently achieves the highest damage. Almost no risk, very little mechanical skill required, yet always the highest DPS.

As I said before: if you simply want to play casually, collect flowers, and explore the world, you may have a good time.

However, if you expect a fair challenge, technically polished boss fights, and reliable mechanics, stay away from this game. You are better off investing your time in a more polished game made by developers with enough experience to properly test their own content.

I will not say much about the gacha system. If someone wants to spend €300–€500 on a legendary skin with generic animations that ultimately does little more than glow slightly brighter, they are free to do so.

That is for everyone to decide for themselves.

Aside from the awkwardness of quickly navigating menus with a controller, I have nothing to complain about regarding the gameplay.
However, if you’re a free-to-play player who likes gacha, I wouldn’t recommend this game because its gacha system sucks. In 2020, Chinese developers invented the so-called “losing the 50/50,” and in this game it has evolved into “losing 50/50 at 90% five times” before you are guaranteed to get the banner item.
(Don’t get me wrong—you can still get it after losing twice by exchanging two Legendary items you receive from losing. The game doesn’t want to drive you away; it just wants to find a different way to humiliate you. A loser is still a loser.)
There’s a Chinese saying, 不過三, meaning that bad luck doesn’t happen more than three times. Clearly, this game has failed to promote Chinese culture because of the publisher’s greed. Why not just get rid of the safety shorts altogether? The game would attract more players that way—after all, profit comes first.
That said, the wuxia style is beautiful and the game is free. Outfits don’t give stats, but without them you look like an NPC in someone else’s game. Even with free outfits, you still look like a homeless guy.
Even if you fully clear the map, the currency you earn cannot buy pulls: 3 pulls per week and 2–4 per event. You need 150 pulls for one failed 50/50 (maybe sooner but they won't add the 20% bad luck point if you get it before 131)—that’s about $340 if you have money to spare.
In short, after all those hours, I only had enough resources to lose three times, and there will not be a fourth (I’m a battle pass player). Somehow, this game makes me feel like a clueless tourist getting ripped off by the locals.

i massively underestimated this game. its great. as if Nio, dark souls, an actual MMORPG and a story-focused RPG had a child. 

pro: 
- its not pay to win and F2P. only real money things you can buy are cosmetics and the ones that are in the game are already pretty decent. you can also get all of them in theory as a F2P just much worse odds obviously. 
- it is incredibly gorgeous. visually its an artform. the wind-effects, the weather effects, the general quality for something you can play as an actual MMORPG, the biomes, the lighting, etc. ; some of the clothes you can get are also reallllly good. 
- the biomes/areas/general map. very good use of verticality. you have some grass-planes which are flat and also beautiful but generally this game has beautiful landmarks to orient by, dungeons and other things have layers upon layers of verticality, and very often things loop back or are visually hinted at the same way you would expect it from good old dark souls. everyting is detailed and filled with life, quests, things to do, things to collect, things to kill. i often scale games by a pseudo-score of how many times they satisfied me when looking behind a waterfall and expecting loot. this game KILLS that score lol. love it. everything feels handcrafted, no generic giant empty world. 
- the dialogues are actually good and quite funny, quests very original and bringing a "fresh wind" pun not intended. i was ready to spam skip and just go collect and kill lik in moost games of this type, but quickly found out they have incredible charm and it would be an insult to skip them. i could tease so many things that would convince you to play it, but they would all spoil the first-time experience. 
- combat is actually very good and satisfying. general game loop is also great. you explore, kill, farm, craft, build, enjoy the scenery, nothing feels wasted, everything gets rewarded with smth you need for smth else. its great. i recommend to enjoy the game in solo mode till you finished campaign, its worth it to go at your own pace and slowly discover/learn everything yourself. also will make you a more skilled fighter later on. 
- so much random stuff you would have never expected from a game like this. i had to laugh out loud multiple times and was flabbergasted even when smth unexpected happened. last time (spoiler) i red a message (people can leave them, they help you a bit) that i missed smth under the elevator. everyone commented how crazy it was and how many chests they missed (rediculous amounts) and that they struggled to get through that incredible content etc. - i thought "fool me once..." like it was one of those "try jump" messages from darksouls xd. was curious though as that part of the dungeon really was kinda bland (still good enough) and went back to check the chest under the elevator. it was there. and i fell through the ground. under there was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ anor londo from dark souls ahahaha im not kidding. i was underleveled too, im not even in that zone yet, just wanted to explore a bit. god it was HARD. and took so LONG. but it was awesome. had many restrictions too, one i never had before that made it so much harder. dont wanna spoil it more than that. the satisfaction when i came back out and commented on that  note lol. it was like a 2h content adventure that you would EASILY miss if you dont check under the elevator. incredible. other games could never. 
- events give good rewards, it doesent feel dead or unsuported.

- you can let your mastery score be translated into "goose". "0,812 goose" for example. let that be a warning lol. 
- they implemented AI as NPCs you have to convince and befriend lol. gets a bit tedious but its smth new. 

con:
it is not perfect. i have two main cons with the game. 
1. the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ menues (UI) xd. menues in menues in menues, its menuesception. finding stuff is hard and you better get used to it over time and dont think to much of it when you start out. just chase the red dots lol. wish they would simplify/overwork these and give us a meta-collect-all-button. 
2. while the synchronization is really good, its a bit odd what is and what isnt synchronized. sometimes it just gives you text, sometimes really great professional voices, sometimes an AI-voice lol. 

conclusion: overall it is an incredible and immensely underrated game/ hidden gem IMO (should be much more popular(hyped). the couple flaws and imperfections it has are easily overshadowed by the massive wins this game has over and over and over. the mine gripe really are the UI/Menues. try it, it is F2P and i would even call it a worthwhile purchase if it was a AAA full price titel.

EDIT: 120 hours in. game is incredible! here some tipps to maximize fun/experience.

1. play solo mode (besides events etc.) in your own pace and enjoy it all, take it in, no one talking over, no one rushing, immerse yourself into the jianghu. 

2. swap between progressing main quest and exploration/outposts/side-quests. main quests are incredible IMO but they are very emotional/dialogue intensive, so some "Mindless" slaughter or collectable run inbetween is a very nice "taste-bud-clenser"-

3. ignore the fact the menues have menues which have menues xd. slowly get used to it. if you leftclick a resource the game tells you where to get it. VERY useful. it also has inbuild "guides" to advance your favourite martial arts/weapons (Which quests to undergo to get your stuff). 

4. pick up and kill everything you can find. it is ALL very useful. exploration also progresses the areas "mobility" for your character. aka how fast you can run, if you can fly through the sky, walk over water, etc. 

5. auto-upgrade is pretty convenient. prob not "optimal" but as a beginner i recommend using it. no need to break your head in the submenues of all the shops to buy the needed resources when you can one-button it.

[h1]Where Winds Meet & My Free Time Leaves (But Still, Time Well Spent) 🗡️🌪️[/h1]

[i]Where Winds Meet[/i] is what happens when you mix [b]wuxia, open-world chaos, ridiculous martial arts, and a healthy amount of grinding…[/b] and somehow end up with a game that makes you forget you have responsibilities.

The good? Combat is flashy, satisfying, and makes you feel like a martial-arts legend. Flying across rooftops, parrying enemies, throwing out ridiculous techniques, [b]tai chi-ing the fishies at the river[/b]… one minute you're a humble wandering swordsman, the next you're basically [b]Jackie Chan with a PhD in kicking people[/b].

The world is beautiful too, and there's [i]so much[/i] to do. Exploring, hunting for secrets, upgrading gear, learning new techniques… and of course, getting distracted by a random side quest that somehow becomes a [b]three-hour career change[/b].

If you're the kind of gamer who enjoys [b]grinding, collecting loot, experimenting with builds, and exploring every suspicious-looking corner of the map[/b], you'll probably feel right at home.

The side effect? There's a LOT going on. Skills, crafting, upgrades, currencies, quests, systems… sometimes you open the menu and feel like you've been handed the [b]employee handbook for becoming a professional swordsman[/b].

And yes, the grind can get repetitive. Eventually, you may find yourself doing the same things again and again just to make a number go up.

But hey… [b]number go up = brain go brrr[/b]. We all know the rules.

And honestly, props to the devs for making such a huge game [b]free-to-play[/b]. The fact that the monetization leans heavily toward cosmetics rather than constantly asking you to open your wallet to become the [i]chosen one[/i] is genuinely refreshing.

You know a game is confident when it basically says:

[i]"Here. Have the whole damn game. If you want to look fabulous while beating people with all the shimmers, that's gonna cost you."[/i]

[h2]TL;DR[/h2]

So, who is this for?

If you enjoy [b]grinding, exploring, collecting, building your character, getting lost in side quests, and slowly turning yourself into an unnecessarily powerful martial-arts menace[/b], you'll probably have a blast.

If you prefer a short, focused experience with a clear objective…

[b]Good luck. There are like 641 quests behind you.[/b]

Jianghu Legacy. Worldly Affairs. Campaign. Exploration. Encounter. Wandering Tales.

And somehow, [b]all of them are calling your name[/b].

But honestly, that's also where [i]Where Winds Meet[/i] deserves some serious praise: [b]the worldbuilding[/b].

The sheer number of different activities and stories makes the world feel like an actual [i]jianghu[/i] rather than just a giant map filled with collectibles. There are always people with their own problems, stories, grudges, secrets, and apparently [b]an unlimited supply of things that somehow become your problem[/b].

Beautiful world, satisfying combat, loads of content, and a surprisingly generous approach to being free-to-play.

Just don't start playing at night thinking,

[i]"I'll only play for an hour."[/i]

[b]That's how they get you.[/b] 😂

What happens when you mix Elden Ring with Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, and Genshin Impact? You get Where Winds Meet. This is easily the best free to play game I've ever played. I'm still really new to the game, but I'm having a blast. It looks great, it runs very smoothly and most importantly, it's fun!  The combat is like eldenring lite, with kung fu. I haven't played the game on legendary or hardcore, but the combat works well and is enjoyable. Exploring the world is really satisfying. There have definitely been times while exploring and during cutscenes that made the hair on my arm stand up, definitely can give you goosebumps. Fantastic art style, and perfect world building execution.

The one thing I thought was really unique is how you can talk to some NPCS. You can talk to them by typing and it uses an AI chatbot to actually have a conversation. Normally I think AI is really lame, but this works quite well. For instance I ran into a lumberjack in the woods and he was lamenting about he didn't have anyone to buy firewood lately. I told him I could go find someone for him, and I ended up running to a town and asking around. It was actually way more fun than most MMORPG fetch quests.

I stopped playing world of warcraft because the community was super toxic but I still wanted to scratch that MMORPG itch. People can leave signposts like in death stranding/eldenring and it is quite helpful. I haven't had a single negative interaction yet. The game is free to play, but I already spent a few dollars just because I was so impressed with the first few hours. Really liking this so far. The only gacha mechanics are for costumes/cosmetics which do not effect combat, so this isn't a pay to win game. But getting the battle pass for like $10-20 will make it a little easier, extra inventory slots and stuff like that. But nothing that gives you a real advantage. The developers make money from the battlepass and gacha costumes, and I'm totally ok with that. It's a great game and I hope they make a ton of money. 

I'm still not max level, (In the 70's) but the game has been fun the entire time. The difficulty definitey goes up, the bosses get harder, but it scales at a reasonable pace. Early on the game is easy while you learn the ropes, now I get to some bosses and die a few times until I learn the attack patterns. I'm still loving this game so much.

I keep updating my review because I'm constantly impressed with new things. The bosses are really awesome and quite challenging, but the community makes it super easy if you need help. I have gotten stuck on a couple of bosses where I got wasted over and over. The second you ask for help, people jump in your game and slay the boss for you. I think some people just wait around town and do this non stop all day. Literally you ask for help and 1 second later someone is there helping you. I prefer to solo anything I can, but having a helpful community makes me want to play with others.

It's if Elden Ring took place in Song Dynasty China and actually had a cohesive story, characters with depth and backstory, and also had crisp, responsive and coherent controls.  Oh and it's free.  Granted, it has some gacha stuff going on in the shop, but also has some cosmetics you can just straight up buy if you want.  Not pay to win at all that I've found.  

Play alone or co-op (or pvp if that suits you).  

It's a lot more fun than I would have thought it would be.  It has beautiful landscapes that are really fun to explore.  Dungeons are also satisfying without being overly frustrating.  Fighting non-boss enemies is fun, satisfying, and challenging without being punishing (there are several difficulty settings you can chose from).  Also quite a few puzzles that are fairly straightforward without being too vague. 

The boss fights can be pretty brutal, and some rely on non-parryable one-shot attacks that you have to just keep your distance from.  Others have long-chain combos that take precise parry timing.  If you love these kinds of boss fights, you'll love these fights.  I personally don't care for them, but I see the boss fights as a sort of minor hurdle for me to get past so I can get back to more map completion/exploration and story progression.  Speaking of which, map traversal is fun, with running up walls/cliffs, triple-jumping, air dashing or even straight up launching yourself into the the air and flinging yourself across the map in spectacular fashion.

The only major criticism I have so far are the way the menus are structured; there are so many menus buried within menus buried within menus.  While there are some shortcuts if you press hotkeys during popup notifications, trying to organically navigate to certain places (or remembering how to do so) can be taxing.  It is a very convoluted menu system.  Truly, the end boss in this game, is mastering navigating the menus.

It's also a pretty large install size (~170Gb at the time of this review).

Highly recommend giving it a try.

Where Winds Meet is a good free to play game. You can spend a lot of time in it, and it looks amazing.
Unfortunately, a lot of that time will be spent ever so slightly frustrated.

Frustrations start right away with menu design. Where even after 1k hours you won't know where all the menus lead as it is an entangeled web of unintuative paths. And that's just the beginning.


First, if you try to play co-op with a friend, you'll quickly realize that only a handful of quests (none of the main quests) actually work in co-op. More often than not, something will break, so even content that should work together suddenly doesn't. And if the host gets too close to certain, seemingly random areas, the other player gets kicked.

So you decide to play solo. Great, except some of the best rewards are locked behind multiplayer activities, especially events.

Fine, you play the events with other people. Except many of them are essentially reskinned versions of popular games (Slay the Spire, Dark and Darker, Resident Evil, TFT, etc) and often don't work properly. Their mechanics often don't ever get looked at again.

You don't have to play the events, though. How about something permanent and core to the game like PvP.
1v1s tend to have one of two outcomes. you combo your opponent, or they combo you. Thankfully, whichever happens, it usually ends quickly.

Is it at least fair? Well money is involved so.. players who can afford better routing to the servers, which the game openly advertises in its launcher have a noticeable advantage. And like in many games new weapons tend to be a little stronger than the old ones, conveniently accompanied by fresh skins.

GvG is an interesting take on large scale MOBA, that is overshadowed by the amout of stutters that 60 shiny skins fighting with special VFX moves brings.

There are other PvP options too. Perception Forest is an extraction (not) shooter with a surprisingly good feel to it... as long as you don't fight near walls, cliffs, trees, or boulders. If you do, the winner may simply be whoever manages to unstuck their character from the vertical surface first. New weapons can dominate here too, sometimes by simply staggering you indefinitely.

And that's really the core problem with PvP in Where Winds Meet: stagger. It's direct interference with your inputs, taking control away from you rather than rewarding your ability to play.

TLDR: The game has a lot of potential, and around the same amount of flaws. There is a genuinely good game buried underneath all of this. but it's constantly fighting against its own design and technical problems.

If you're looking for an open-world RPG this might just be the one for you. The graphics? Stunning. The combat? Awesome. The story? Really cool. Overall this game has just about everything you'd want in an open-world RPG. Tons of exploration, mini-games, side-quests and even the chance to have a partner for some romance. There's so much to do in this game it almost becomes overwhelming! 

The beauty of this game is that it can be played entirely solo OR with other players. You can enable online mode to see other players roaming the world, play together in co-op or even engage in PvP combat. There is also built in voice chat right in the game itself but be careful because there is NO filter when it comes to the types of people you might encounter. 

While this game does have some AI elements to it (specifically when typing to NPCs and a few other things), there is thankfully no AI generated assets as far as I'm aware. There is however a really neat use of AI in that you can upload a photo of yourself to create your character or even record a snippet of your voice for the game to make a character based off of that; which is something I haven't seen in any other games recently. 

The character customizing is where this game really shines though. There are a TON of options and ways to make your character unique. There are also lots of cosmetics and this is where the game might have your wallet in a chokehold because the prettiest stuff is locked behind a gacha system. So if you are easily parted with your money just keep that in mind.  The only other negatives are that the English localization could definitely use some work, there's a lot of translation errors in the subtitles and the lipsync is not the greatest at times. 

Overall I highly recommend this game if you are looking for a unique experience with open-world gaming.

Strong WARNING to those who this is relevant to: Do NOT use macros or any type of software or hardware that will give you "an unfair advantage" in this game. Even in solo mode, you risk getting your account banned! This includes things like setting up combos on M-Buttons on controllers. Don't do it unless your account is disposable. Check the site for details on violations, but if you wonder whether it counts, it probably does. You have been warned.

I am playing primarily on PC at this time because:

A. I prefer a larger screen than my tablet.
B. I like to stream gameplay and PC makes it more convenient.
C. Console failed me too hard, too many times for this game in particular. it is not optimized for console, at all.

This review focus is on the PC experience I've had so far. Steam lists my playtime as 66 hours and that is true on PC. I, however, have around 1k hours on console, and roughly 20 hours on mobile. Therefore, I believe I can give an informed review.

The game itself is wonderful. It is, by far, my favorite game of the year. The graphics are stunningly detailed and beautiful. There is such a vast show of scenery, from beautiful bamboo forests to snow-covered landscapes and mountains, to arid deserts with incredible night skies. If you are a visual person, you will never be disappointed with the maps and exploration in this game. There are plenty of things to find to power up your character, and little gems to make you laugh, smile, and look at your screen in confusion. 

Fighting in PvE is very fluid and there are so many different ways to build out your character. Select from established paths that pair a main and secondary weapon with compatible Inner Ways and gear sets or play around with all of the options to create your own path to suit your playstyle. It can be a bit complex, so if you are starting out, I HIGHLY suggest doing some reading or video watching to learn how the character building system works. Once you have an understanding of the basics though, go ham! The RNG on the best gear drops and stat rolls is kinda... awful. BUT! They've introduced ways to increase the tier and stats on your gear using items you can earn through regular game play (Often purchasing from event shops or weekly shops using In-Game currency, again earned through regular game play). So work hard, play hard, perfect your build!

I don't have much to contribute about the PvP experience, but as it can be an important part of the game for some, I will share what I've noted. I have only ever done a few PvP matches, and they've all taken place on PC. You can review my PC specs and compare with your own, but I typically have approximately 25-60ms ping, which can become a bit more erratic or a little on the higher side in areas where a lot of components are being loaded and/or there are several players nearby, such as the guild arena. 

Side info about internet bandwidth: Playing MMO and co-op games, you really want latency as low as possible. If fiber isn't an option, try to at least be wired to your router/modem. If that is also not an option, then ensure that your signal from your wi-fi router is as unobstructed as possible. Do NOT place it near other electronics, do not place two different routers near each other, do not place wireless extenders near each other, and beware of network crowding (this is when there are too many devices on a single network or network channel for the amount of bandwidth or the routing device itself to support properly). Online gaming typically wants a minimum of 15-20 Mbps down/5 Mbps up for that single gaming device, so if you have low bandwidth you may which to ensure no one else is doing network heavy things while you game.

Back to the game:

My FPS is typically between 58-90 depending, again, primarily on the current graphical load I'm experiencing in an area. I have been able to tweak in-game settings to balance beautiful graphics with fluid, lag-free game play. There are some people who swear by capping their FPS at 60 to increase performance, and others who say to turn off VFX for everyone but you. I have done neither of these things but I also do not PvP regularly, and certainly not competitively. So, my advice is more for the general/casual player, while the aforementioned tips from other players (that DO PvP) may help someone looking to be more competitive.

There is a constant influx of new events that are diverse, non-repetitive (as in the same old events don't pop up every single update), and fun. The story updates are at a slow but steady pace and each map expansion is very detailed and equally as breath-taking as all the others. The bosses are always so unique, both visually and mechanically. And the lore in this game runs SO deep. You can also learn real facts about Chinese history through the game as you collect notes, stories, anecdotes, and artifacts. There's pretty much always something to do!

The online mode offers leisurely activities to partake of, if you crave human connection without the fighting. Visit Revelry Hall online to do an aerial dance with other players or NPCs! Work with fellow healers to diagnose and treat woefully ill patients. Help the needy by giving away coins to beggars. Oh, and don't forget, you can marry the love of your Jianghu life via the partner system, take on or become a disciple, or form a cohort group with your sworn brethren. You can join a guild and/or join a sect that speaks to you. All of these different things have different advantages, including exclusive outfits and other items which can be purchased from the affiliated shops with the relevant in-game currency earned by taking part in the relevant activities.

Which brings me to the fashion. There are so many outfits available, its actually amazing. Usually they have several pieces to them, such as a hairstyle, top, bottom, and an accessory. Some have more or less items. Most outfits and hairstyles can be dyed (you can earn basic and advanced (bright color) clothing dyes through regular game play and in shops with game currency, but hair dye is scarce and advanced hair dye is a premium item) and many also have alternative tailoring. There are dozens of outfits. hairstyles, and accessories available for free, earned via typical game play. But there are premium outfits too...

*Sigh* This game is free. It is not possible to pay to win, either.  That is, unless you are trying to win Best Dressed in the Jianghu. Then all bets are off. 

There are ways to earn free gacha pulls for banners, but with a higher than average hard pity of a whopping 150 pulls, and soft pity starting at 110 pulls, good luck! You'll need it. Unfortunately, fashion aspirations aren't guaranteed either, as legendary item pulls may be the banner outfit, a mount, or harmonic cores - usually only 1. Most premium outfits require 2 cores for exchange. Mounts, premium hairstyles and some weapon skins are 1-2 cores. And don't get me started on the "reforge" system. That requires a whole discussion that we aren't having here. Just know it can be expensive or painfully slow, as the material (taiyi stone) is not often earned via events; They are often bought outright for a value of about $1/ea.

Have I dashed your dreams of hitting the Jianghu runway in style? Fear not, for there are many outfits available for direct purchase ! They can be as low as $1, though typically range between about $10 and $50. You can earn Resonance Vouchers, too, through regular gameplay that discount outfits by 10% per voucher (up to 50% for 5 vouchers). Again, there's so much more to say but this is already a novel so I'll end it there.

Briefly, I'll mention that you can also build houses and other stuff in this game! Solo or co-op and in your guild. The homestead feature is an awesome recent addition.

Happy to answer any questions!

The game is very opaque about what you need to do to clear certain content the correct way. It makes you assume you do not have what you need to do it and often teaches you "guns blazing first" and "these guys are always hostile no matter what," so you clear an outpost that way. Then you later learn that you could have just WALKED UP TO THE FRONT GATE AND TALKED TO THE LEADER and gotten a much more satisfying first-clear, then done murder-hobo on the subsequent clears. But the game DOES NOT LET YOU RESET TO FIX YOUR PERMANENT MISTAKES. If you want to, you have to DELETE YOUR ACCOUNT—that you have likely spent money on. 

(Possible correction: there is a slight possibility that there is an NPC you can visit somewhere and do a side quest for or something to reset your progress, but I am not entirely sure what progress it actually resets, although it's supposed to keep your achievements. Am also not sure if it is real or what it actually does or how far into the story you are required to be to use it. It also might not reset world content, which is the thing that most players would want to reset with some degree of granular control over what exactly you're resetting so they can go back and fix the mistakes the game pushed them into making, such as devaluing and corrupting their playthrough because they assumed they weren't able to clear an outpost the optimal/civilized way and thus locked themselves out of IMPORTANT STORY AND WORLD CONTENT). There is no way to start over without losing everything or reset progress on various things.

What this game needs:

1. Some way to reset your character back to the start of the game and the main story.
2. Multiple characters on international servers.
3. More transparent indicators on the correct way to do things.
4. Stop expecting players to already know what to do and not play like amoebas. 
5. Ability to fully reset outposts to how they were before you first cleared them, easily.
6. Ability to granularly reset world content.

Originally played this at launch at the recommendation of a few people and thought it was fun enough, but it felt pretty unpolished in a lot of areas so I thought I'd give it a while to sort out a lot of those problems.

It's been almost a year now and they still aren't better and if anything it feels like they've been amplified in some areas.

The main draw of the game for me personally is the combat, which when it works it [i] really [/i] works, but it feels like so many bosses have issues that should've been picked up by now. Be that hitboxes that rival Dark Souls 2 (Puppeteer), combos in which the animations for them are completely mismatched (Lucky Seventeen), instances where their AI breaks and the boss just stands there circling you doing nothing for long periods (Also Lucky Seventeen) or where a boss is given a ranged attack that after the black screen that takes you into a boss plays, they can instantly hit you with (Tian Ying Phase One). It feels like every time I encounter a boss that seems like it's really fun, something or other like the examples I've already given ends up just ruining it for me.

Outside of the combat, I think the game is even more unpolished in basically every other area you can think of.

Exploration is at least fine, but often you'll get your character stuck on the terrain or some other edge while you attempt to jump around or other something which kinda just takes you out of it and ends up ruining exploration for me.

The RPG mechanics themselves with gear and stats are kind of a mess, at least without using external resources I feel, the gear is very generic and with the lacklustre explanations the game provides for some info a lot of the stats it shows just feel like complete fluff. This may be in part due to some of the shoddy translation the game has which I think has improved in some areas, but in others I feel like I'm looking at dialogue or menus that make zero sense in English as if they weren't even proofread before being shipped.

Arguably the worst thing the game suffers from though I believe, is it's abhorrent UI. I'm not entirely sure why every game saw what Genshin Impact did for it's UI and decided that it needed to use the exact same thing, but WWM has managed to take that UI and it make it the most unnavigable UI I've seen in gaming to date, with every menu seemingly containing another 3 menus within them so taking any time away from the game and coming back makes it near impossible to figure out where the hell to look for anything.

Clearly by the review score sitting so high I am very much in the minority on not recommending the game, but that's also because there's no middle ground as that's where I'd rather sit this, I think if you want an all round polished game, you're better to look elsewhere even in the free games market. But if you're someone who can handle more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ than even the strongest Eurojank games can dish out, you'll probably at least get a good enough time out of Where Winds Meet.

As soon as I started trying to play with someone else, the experience just went downhill. Only some of the missions have shared progression in coop. Often the host is the only one that can interact with things. Follow your buddy around to new areas and you can't unlock travel points unless you are in multiplayer mode, in which case the world map is almost empty. Outposts can be replayed in multiplayer only if you have already cleared them in solo mode. Teaming up and trying to find something to do everyone could progress on was absolutely painful.

The UI via controller is awful. There were so many times just trying to figure out how to get out of an interaction was a puzzle itself. Trying to figure out where things are in the UI always took effort. Hold RT and press select to exit placement mode? Seriously? Select is used in so many interactions, it's baffling.

The game looks amazing. It doesn't scale well though. No matter what graphical preset I used, I got the same framerate, usually around 80 fps at 4k, and that is on a 4090. The game felt like it had a lot of potential, and I really tried to give it a chance, but the networking just killed it for me.

The game itself is very entertaining. I was surprised at how much the story eventually drew me in, despite dropping a ton of lore and different characters on you. It can be hard to keep up, and sometimes you wonder about the dense nature of your main character — but maybe he’s supposed to suffer with you.

Visually, the game is a knockout. You might find yourself comparing it to AAA titles like Ghost of Tsushima. The map is huge and offers lots of varied landscapes that invite exploration. Many dialogues are fully voiced, and almost all NPCs chatter as you move along, which adds a ton to the immersion. Some voice actors feel a bit stiff, but considering the sheer amount of voices, it’s more than forgivable.

Gameplay-wise, the controls are crisp. Mouse/keyboard and controller both feel good, though I currently prefer controller for couch gameplay. There is so much to do: main quests, random encounters, secrets, mini-games, social games — it feels like an amalgamation of souls-like titles, Assassin’s Creed and RDR2. Solo, raids, PvE, PvP — there’s something for everyone.

The combat system has real depth. You build “paths” by combining two main weapons that synergize with each other. It follows the creed of “easy to learn, hard to master,” and I like that skill can compensate for lack of levels or gear. Higher-tier equipment (“Inner Ways”) adds passive effects and heavily influences your weapons, but leveling them is time-gated and can be tedious depending on your build. Still, combat feels precise and responsive, and losing to a boss often motivates you to try again and get a bit closer.

Now for the big BUT. The devs and art team did an amazing job and deserve recognition — but the monetization system is nothing short of predatory. A standard equipment set costs around 1250 pearls, yet the game sells pearls only in awkward bundles (900 for ~14€, 1800 for ~28€). Above-standard skins cost ~2580 pearls, forcing you into the 3000‑pearl pack for 46€.

You can farm currencies to “draw” items, but drop rates are abysmal, and the soft pity system only helps after many pulls. Shop items cannot be obtained this way. You have a tiny chance to get “Echo Cores,” which unlock some things — and most require two of these extremely rare items.

Then there are timed exclusive pull queues that require pearls. The current “Celestial Glow” set includes a skin set, animations, and a background. If you fall for the FOMO, be ready to pay upwards of 800€ for a statistical chance to get it. The price is wildly disproportionate and preys on gambling addiction. Whales will spam it, and others save for months — only to get shafted when sets release earlier than expected, as happened with the CN vs. EU/US release.

All in all, it’s a great game that gets in its own way. The world, the gameplay, and the presentation deserve praise – but the monetization definitely needs an overhaul. It's doubtful that they will fix it, but if the would,  the game could become something truly exceptional among the F2P-Genre. I’m giving this a negative rating solely because of the monetization.
