[h3]Added context: I primarily played this casually and mostly avoided PvP beyond the early days and casual GvG[/h3] 
[i]+ is good, - is bad, ~ is neutral[/i]


[h2]Visual[/h2]
+ Has great aesthetics for map, character and cosmetic design. caveat below*
- *The female versions of clearly male-intended designs (like full body armor) are lazy (personal gripe)
+ The themes are great. Really good for people who love taking photos of their characters
+ Boss designs are great.

[h2]Audio[/h2]
+ It's pretty good.
~ It's only pretty good. Nothing really sticks.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
+ The core combat design is fun. It's basically Temu Sekiro.
+ Boss designs are pretty fun.
+ PvP is fun. I can't say if it's balanced, but it is fun and has depth to it. RPS mindgames.
~ The way the game is meant to be structured kind of means the progression of difficulty fluctuates.
~ Exploration is mostly just clearing checkmarks, a la Ubisoft, but the world's aesthetics makes it passable, a la Ubisoft.
- There's a lot of minigames and all of them are copy pasted from other popular games without understanding what makes them good, instead of focusing on improving the core of the game.
- You are basically required to join a guild to get the most out of the game's timegates.

[h2]Microtransactions and cosmetics[/h2]
+ Good design philosophy.
- Expensive gacha, as expected.
- Everything is overpriced.
- Rewards for accomplishments are basically nothing. They exist, but are nothing compared to spending money.

[h2]Special mention: PROGRESSION[/h2]
It's awful. The worst in any game I've ever played, including 2005 Maplestory where level cap would take literal years.
There are catch-up mechanics, but they designed the skill system (for your builds) to require EXORBITANT amounts of time to reach the peak capacity of any given build.
It stifles new players and makes getting a second build going on an old account excessively annoying.
At the amount of hours I have, playing since basically the launch, I have only two builds on one character.
Which I cannot even get the right gear for quickly for both with each level update because it's pure RNG rolling on top of RNG rolling.
I've basically only ever played two builds in this game.
The only other way to do different builds is to convert your skill levels, but again, you still only have so many points. So if you wanna keep your original skill points in your build, you're time-gated to it.

[h2]Other Stuff[/h2]
+ Building exists in this game but it's super clunky. It's decent, though? Not worth the headaches for me to maneuver through it.
+ The game is built around chores, mostly weekly, a few easy dailies, but the payoff is pretty bad for most of it.
- UI is bad
- Performance has degraded with each patch
- The game's filesize is 170GB right now. 
- Events are basically all the same thing, monotonous and uninteresting.
~ There's a lot of promo codes to find, all of them give basically nothing and it's actually a nightmare to type them all in.
~ Writing is a hit or miss, with mostly misses for me. It hits when it hits, but the English VA's don't do it well enough. Use CN VAs. Problem is the hits are usually not main story beats. The story is mostly convoluted as hell, but it fits the vibes of the theme it's going for, which also tends to have that, though I'm no expert.

[h1][u]Conclusion[/u][/h1]
I wouldn't recommend the game unless you really vibe with the gameplay loop and just really love the aesthetics.
Also that you don't mind spending some money or acknowledging that people will always look more fly than you.
Or if you do spend money and realize some people will look INFINITELY more fly because there's a lot of ♥♥♥♥ they let you spend money on.

I saw a couple of shorts on youtube, advertising the game and asked the viewers about some of my curiosities regarding it, however i never got a reply… hence i decided to go full on Thanos mode (fine… i’ll do it myself) and thus… here we are.

The game has some very good graphics. The visuals are indeed awesome.
The combat seems quite interesting.
The game gives you a lot of content. It will keep you occupied.
YOU CAN PET ANIMALS!

But now we move to the problems of a casual player’s point of view.

The game is ridiculously convoluted. God help us, everything I did would activate a new system that had systems in its systems with systems and menus in the menu of a menu that was made of menus. Later I was trying to find the same functions and I could not in the mess of so many menus.
I also have a bone to pick with how fake the freedom of picking different fighting styles appeared in this gacha game.
Also very poorly made is the way you experience the story, cause you are not allowed to progress with the story if you don’t play other aspects of the game.
Bad explanations. From prompting you on self healing before that is possible, to telling you that healers are gonna heal you for free for also being a healer (fake)... we have many functions that are not explained correctly. I tried the animal moves training and while it looked like I was doing nothing wrong, the game was failing me constantly. Turns out the instructions were wrong.
You find some special insects that you need to grab and the game tells you, shoot them down… I did… nothing happened. I ran towards them, grabbed it as it was flying around, victory.
You unlock a skill to grab things from a distance, game tells you you can disarm enemies with it and to go practice on some bandits... it does not activate… I tried several times and only days later I found out how to use the snatch skill. Not to mention that the first time I passed by a snake camp I was prompted to use that skill to grab the item in their midst, but I had not unlocked it yet. Due to the game’s explanation I was trying for several minutes to find how the snatch from a distance worked, till I eventually lost my patience and charged on the snakes only to be obliterated.
You see two people stealing horses early on and the game tells you to look for them. I go the way they went and see a dude on a horse with the same model. I get close and try to talk to him, only that this was a different dude and the “talk” was “snach horse”… so i’m now a horse thief. Also the victim would not let me go after trying to steal their horse no matter what and I had to kill them. No consequences.
As for the gacha system. The amount of different currencies used for every pull made it a mess. More about this later.

Now… all the above are a very negative impact to my impression of the game, however i’m sure that by checking media, having enough time/patience to experience in the game and/or with a supportive community you can overcome and as such… the game would have gotten a positive rating from me… but now come the actual bad stuff.

Why i’m NOT recommending this game:

1) The story is bad. The pacing is terrible… Seriously... One of my top listed games for bad passing...You open up with a couple of dudes that show up, act as is a medallion is a big deal, but only mention the medallion and not the MC, making you think that the MC is with them only for sentimentality purposes, but then your name is on it and the MC is important, but nobody cares about them. I mean... There are only two characters I cared about in this game... They both die a hero's death and the story goes: "OH NO... 3) Forced co-op. Game literally forces you to play co-op. For someone that has a terrible experience in co-op such as me, this is a MASSIVE negative. 4) Way too many bugs. At the very start of the game you go down the mountain and see something like a theater troupe or something with dead bodies all around, advertising a great battle.  I go in and a cutscene plays and as soon as it ends it starts playing again... and again... and again. I skip and the battle starts. As soon as I take down the dude, fight resets and i have to fight him again. I beat him and 2 "puppets" show up to fight me. I take them out and i have to fight the dude again, only that as soon as I beat him the first cutscene plays again and i'm back at the beginning of this fight. Eventually i fall and game is like "come back when you are lv.30 n00b". Right... Cause i totally didn't humiliate your champion multiple times right now. And this "reset" happened another couple of times with other bosses. An events of trying to chase a cat launched me to the stratosphere. Cleared a martial arts training quest with the dude resetting every time and when I reloaded my game he was no longer there. My gacha pulls got reset.
Also here i'm gonna talk about bad design of quests/events. You are platforming to get a chest and mid-jump game starts a "cutscene" stopping you, messing you up or straight out killing you. Not to mention areas where you can multi-jump, you are going for a chest only to find out at the last step without warning that you multijump has been sealed away and you fall to your doom, resurrecting in a totally different area and having to walk a long way to get back to your chest. Now these are bad design flaws but they are so random I consider even those bugs.
Speaking of, I used my 10 free pulls and the game reset the pull... only that I no longer had the 10 pulls available.It just went back to the initial pulls page... I checked if i had any new items or presentation looks but there was nothing... and here is my final issue

5) Support inefficiency. I reported that my free 10 pulls got cancelled and waited for a reply... only to never get one. Just to be fair, I waited for a couple of days before giving my final verdict, but no reply came.
Look, the game has great graphics and huge potential. But it really did not click with me. The way the story is portrayed, the confusing systems, the huge amount of time needed to clear dailys and the huge amount of bugs encountered that did not get a reply from the support even after days. I don't think this game is awful, in fact, i think it's a good game that is worthy of a try. But it's also a game where I would hesitate to truly recommend. 

It's a game with an incredible presentation and commitment to its theme. From world design to costume design, done in an extremely masterful and tasteful way. There are some immersion breaking mechanic like the BOTW tears of the kingdom vehicle crafting system, but it's entirely optional and can be totally ignored.

Yet at the same time this game want to be your one and only game due to its long list of things that it want you to do on the daily basis, while does not provide the sufficient amount of content nor variety to justify the amount of commitment you need to make to ensure you are kept up in the endgame. 

The boss fights, while fun for the first time, hell, maybe even the tenth times (mostly carried by the crazy shenanigans that can happen in coop), will stop being so fun on the twentieth. The fight design is also not exactly deep, and often come down to some very simple mechanic that is communicated to the player in a very insufficient way which can cause a lot of trial and error. A mechanic that, when failed, is often result in a full wipe  with little counter play allowed. It's similar to FFXIV in term of fight design. But unlike FFXIV where the fight is fully scripted down to the minute, and a successful clear look like a beautiful and elaborate dance off between the boss and the players, in WWM, it's more of a free style where the both party just hoping for the best. That is to say, the mechanics are clunky and sometimes bug ridden, or so poorly designed that they can overlap which randomly caused an unavoidable wipe.

Where Winds Meet is a gorgeous game with a lot going for it. The world is beautiful, the character customization is fantastic, and there’s a lot of attention to detail that makes the game enjoyable to explore. Honestly, the visuals and customization alone kept me interested for longer than I probably would have otherwise.

However, as someone who leans toward the semi-hardcore side of gaming, the actual gameplay and progression didn't quite scratch the itch for me.

The biggest issue is that the game doesn't demand much time, investment, or skill. Most of the PvE content feels relatively easy, and there isn't much that feels genuinely challenging or mechanically demanding. I still regularly see PUGs struggling with some PvE content, but at the same time, the difficulty itself doesn't feel particularly rewarding. The addition of AI companions also makes it possible to clear content without necessarily relying on other players, which I assume is intended to make the game more accessible.

If you're looking for content that actually tests your mechanical skill, PvP is probably where the game shines the most. Outside of that, I found myself wishing there were more difficult PvE encounters, deeper optimization, and more meaningful reasons to push my character further.

The gacha is also far too expensive for what it offers. For a game that is otherwise so generous with customization, the monetization can feel particularly excessive.

Ultimately, I think Where Winds Meet is a great game for casual players. You don't need to sink huge amounts of time into it, you can progress at your own pace, and there's plenty to explore and customize. But for players who enjoy min-maxing, difficult PvE, optimization, progression, and constantly having something challenging to work toward, I don't think there's quite enough here.

The game is beautiful enough that it kept me around for a while, but eventually I realized I was staying for the aesthetics rather than the gameplay. I have since uninstalled the game at the start of season 4 due to lack of content, and wouldn't recommend this for gamers looking for challenging and engaging gameplay. However, if you do not have too much time on your hand and do not want heavy investments, this game is good for casual gaming.

There is a lot of joy in building or fixing one practical thing and realizing it connects a part of the map you were avoiding.
The vertical layout means I keep seeing places I want to reach instead of only markers I need to clear.
The new combat style feels like someone asked what would happen if a monk got tired of waiting for enemies to come closer.

I like that a simple walk in the new region can turn into route planning without feeling like homework. A bridge leads to a mechanism, the mechanism opens a lower path, and that path brings you back to a view you saw an hour earlier from above. I spent about twenty minutes chasing one platform simply because I had noticed it from the other side of the valley. The reward up there wasn't anything extraordinary, but the shortcut finally made a whole section of the mountain make sense. I'm gradually building a mental picture of how the city fits together, and that has kept me wandering longer than any marker could.
The region is serious about ancient mechanisms, then lets a monkey insult you from a hillside. Correct balance.

The graphics and storytelling are stunning! The combat style is a little complicated, but nothing that isn't easily picked up with practice. The amount of side quests is awesome; always something to do so you don't get bored.

The new mountain is the first place in a while where I have been happy to miss a turn. In most open worlds, getting lost means I'm wasting time. Here it usually means I found another level of the city, a path above a waterfall, or a mechanism that explains why the route looked strange in the first place. The layout has enough visual landmarks that I can recover without feeling punished. More importantly, the detours are interesting. I would rather spend five minutes understanding a mountain than follow a straight line through another empty valley. I missed one turn, found a lower tunnel, and came back above the original path. After that I stopped pretending I had a plan.

The big surprise for me is how often the version turns a simple task into a story. I see a broken route, assume it's a quick interaction, then end up following a mechanism chain through several levels of the mountain. I spot a strange animal, get distracted, and find a view I would have missed. I try a new combat combo and accidentally turn an ordinary encounter into a practice session. That kind of accidental momentum is what makes a new area last longer than its main quest. It gives me reasons to come back after the obvious content is done. A repair that looked like a two-second interaction sent me across three levels, through a cave, and back to the original platform from the opposite side.

The character creator immediately hits you with AI generation options for voice clips and face photos of yourself, and the AI voice acting apparently goes further into the actual game itself as well. Where Winds Meet is a NetEase game, a genuinely huge name at this point, and they somehow still decide to rely on AI for aspects of the game. I truthfully don't care how many NPC's there are, or whether the open world is so large that they can't possibly hire that many voice actors. Liam O' Brien alone makes up 20% of the dialogue you'll hear in The Elder Scrolls, and I'm perfectly fine with that, because he voices so many of the smaller quest givers and random NPC's strewn about the game. He is also, Liam O' Brien.

The engineering sect progression has me pretending I understand what I am building. The confidence is part of the build.
The engineering sect has homework. Naturally.

The construction elements make co-op exploration feel less like everyone following the same route. When a group can stop, solve a practical problem, help with a structure, or argue about how something should be arranged, the map becomes more social. It's not only about who reaches the next objective first. I had more fun discussing a ridiculous idea for a mountain-side build than I expected, mostly because the region gives that idea a place to exist. The scenery helps too. Bad plans always look better near a waterfall. Our group now has one person who solves the mechanism, one who tests every dangerous ledge, and one who contributes absolutely nothing except bad placement advice.

I was skeptical about the vertical map because games love saying a place has depth when they really mean there's one cave under a hill. This one actually earns the description. Surface paths, suspended routes, and lower mechanical areas keep feeding into each other, so I'm constantly changing my idea of where I'm. It makes navigation more active. I'm not just moving toward a marker. I'm choosing whether to climb, drop down, follow water, or inspect something that looks like it might be part of a bigger machine. The first time I dropped from a high walkway into a chamber I knew, the layout finally clicked. It felt like folding two maps together.
I solved the puzzle by finally looking behind me.
New region, new fear of moving platforms.

The new automaton enemies are a good reminder that not every boss needs to feel alive to have personality. The puppet-like movements are unsettling in a way that makes the fights more memorable. I kept trying to predict the attacks as if I were fighting a person, then got caught because the rhythm was wrong. One attack looked graceful until I realized it was baiting an early deflection. The machine fooled me three times before I learned. Once I adjusted, the encounter became much more satisfying. It's a fight about watching closely, not just reacting quickly, and that fits a version built around mechanisms and hidden structure.
The new area is making me take screenshots of infrastructure. I did not know that was a thing I wanted from a wuxia game.

This game is completely and utterly goated. I play a lot of soulslikes and MMO titles and this game is a perfect fusion of all of them. Beyond that, it's done something no other game has managed to do -- get me into Wuxia storytelling. 

I loved Nioh 3's open world. I made love to it. I put the controller in my hands and let it take my pants off on a regular basis. This is the game Nioh wants to be (for Japanese culture, I understand WWM is Chinese). It's got a perfect blend of combat and narrative while not cheapening the experience that I just can't get enough of. Every single area and town I've visited has been pristine, like a painting out of a fairytale. 

I can't get over how much I actually want to do in this game. It shows you how little publishers like Ubisoft can get away with these days, and playing this game and investing seriously into its world and systems will completely ruin open world RPGs for you.

Give this game a try, embrace its rougher edges, and you'll find a compelling story, a deep world that cares about teaching you its language and culture and gives you nuggets of real historical knowledge. You'll find a combat system that's as competitive as you are, and a content schedule that is prepared to engage with you on your terms. You got 10 minutes to play? Cool, we have a kitty cat vs goose auto battler. Got 2 hours? Go solve a mystery quest that popped up as a rotating event. Don't have any attention span? There's a hundred small, fun world activities to dance between which are seriously rewarding. Got 8 hours and want to spend all of it in a deep, single narrative that puts you at the center of events in 10th century Chinese folklore? That's possible.

Judging purely by the game itself, I would give it a 9/10. The game does an excellent job with its wuxia setting, combat system, and overall amount of content. It could even be considered one of the most representative titles to come out of the Chinese gaming industry.

PVP is one of the game’s most distinctive features. The combat is highly action-oriented, and there is plenty of room to improve and experiment with skill combinations, dodging, counters, and matchups between different martial arts styles. At the moment, it is difficult to find another game with a Chinese wuxia setting that offers PVP combat with this level of action and mechanical depth.

However, network latency has a very noticeable impact on PVP. In a combat system that relies heavily on precise timing and quick reactions, even a moderate amount of latency can result in situations where you appear to have dodged an attack but still get hit, or where your inputs and the on-screen response feel out of sync. For international players who are located far away from the servers, latency can seriously affect the overall PVP experience.

The PVE side of the game also contains a large amount of content. New players can spend a considerable amount of time going through the main story, side quests, exploration, puzzles, collectibles, and various smaller activities. Although many of these side activities do not add much to the overall experience and are not particularly memorable, the game still offers a substantial amount of content.

The larger issue is the slow pace of updates. Once players finish the main story, exploration, and activities available in the current phase, the game usually enters a fairly long content drought. During this period, there is not enough meaningful PVE content to keep playing regularly, so players are often left with daily tasks and PVP while waiting for the next major update.

Aside from that, the game’s speech censorship system is also extremely difficult to accept.

The chat system in the international version appears to directly use the same political keyword restrictions as the Chinese version. Normal country or place names such as “Taiwan” and “Hong Kong” may be blocked and cannot be entered or sent properly in the game.

These terms are not profanity, sexual content, hate speech, or personal attacks. A player may simply be trying to mention where they live, find teammates from the same region, or discuss network latency in different locations, yet the chat system may still prevent them from doing so.

Chat moderation should be used to prevent insults, harassment, scams, and hate speech, not to block ordinary country or regional names. An even bigger problem is that the system usually does not clearly indicate which word triggered the restriction, and there is no transparent list or explanation of the filtered terms.

The moderation standards used in the Chinese version are one matter, but an international version aimed at a global audience should not require players around the world to accept the political censorship standards used within China.

Overall, the game itself is of very high quality, and both its PVE and PVP have clear strengths. However, network latency, the slow pace of content updates, and the censorship system in the international version remain major and very noticeable problems.


單純以遊戲內容來說，我會給 9/10。這款遊戲在武俠題材、戰鬥系統與內容規模上都做得相當出色，甚至可以算是中文遊戲市場中具有代表性的作品。

PVP 是我認為最有特色的部分之一。整體動作性很強，招式銜接、閃避、反擊以及不同武學之間的對抗，都有一定的操作與研究空間。目前市面上很難找到另一款同樣採用中國武俠題材，又能提供這種高動作性 PVP 體驗的遊戲。

不過，網路延遲對 PVP 的影響非常明顯。這類需要精準判定與即時反應的戰鬥，只要延遲稍高，就可能出現明明已經閃避卻仍然被命中，或是操作與畫面反應不同步的情況。對距離伺服器較遠的國際玩家來說，延遲問題可能會嚴重影響整體對戰體驗。

PVE 方面的內容非常豐富。新玩家剛加入時，主線、支線、探索、解謎、收集以及各種小活動，確實足以遊玩很長一段時間。雖然其中不少小活動對整體遊戲體驗的影響不大，完成後也不一定會留下深刻印象，但整體內容量仍然相當充足。

比較大的問題是更新速度偏慢。當目前階段的主線、探索與活動內容完成後，遊戲通常會進入一段較長的空窗期。這段時間缺乏足夠的 PVE 內容可以持續遊玩，最後往往只剩下每日任務與 PVP，等待下一個階段更新。

除此之外，這款遊戲的言論審查機制也相當令人難以接受。

國際版的聊天系統似乎直接沿用了中國版本的政治敏感詞標準。像是「台灣（Taiwan）」與「香港（Hong Kong）」這類正常的國家或地名，都可能無法在遊戲中正常輸入或傳送。

這些內容並不是髒話、色情內容、仇恨言論或人身攻擊。玩家可能只是想說明自己的所在地、尋找同地區的隊友，或討論不同地區的網路延遲，卻仍然會受到聊天系統限制。

一般的聊天審查應該用來阻止辱罵、騷擾、詐騙與仇恨言論，而不是封鎖正常的國家或地區名稱。更大的問題是，系統通常不會清楚指出是哪個詞彙觸發限制，也沒有提供透明的敏感詞規則。

中國版本採用什麼樣的聊天管理標準是一回事，但國際版本既然面向全球市場，就不應該要求所有國際玩家共同接受中國境內的政治審查標準。

整體而言，遊戲本身的品質很高，PVE 與 PVP 都有明顯特色，但網路延遲、內容更新速度以及國際版的言論審查制度，仍然是目前非常明顯的問題。

I spent a long time trying to decide whether the mountain is more beautiful from the high paths or the lower mechanical spaces. The answer is probably both, which is annoying because now I keep taking the long route through each area. The high sections have the wind, mist, and broad views. The lower sections have water, machinery, and that feeling that something huge is operating behind the walls. The transition between them is what sells the map for me. It never feels like you are loading into a separate biome. The high paths make me stop for screenshots; the lower rooms make me slow down and inspect everything. I keep switching routes depending on my mood.
I am not lost. I am checking the lower layer.
Rope dart plus gauntlets is pure bad-intentions combat.
I am here for the ancient machinery, but the cat climbing-frame detail is what convinced me this mountain has actual residents.
The mechanical bird stuff has exactly the right amount of ancient-tech weirdness. I want more travel solutions that look like they should not work but do.

The gauntlet combat has made me notice sound design more than I expected. Swords are elegant, but the new weapon has a heavier, more direct rhythm. Every close hit feels like a decision because you have to be near enough to get punished if you guess wrong. When the rope dart pulls someone back into range and the combo actually connects, it feels great. It's not only about damage. The whole style makes the player character look more reckless, and I mean that in a very good way. That learning curve is exactly why I keep going back to it after the novelty should have worn off. The impact sounds also make failed combos obvious. You can hear exactly where the rhythm breaks, which is both useful and a little embarrassing.
The monkey is somehow the most confident NPC here.

I like how the new story brings familiar faces along without turning the opening into a recap. The jokes work because the group already has history, but none of them really knows what they're walking into. One exchange starts with everyone talking over a questionable plan, then the machinery nearby begins moving and the whole conversation gets a little quieter. Nobody stops to announce that the situation is dangerous; you can hear it in the way they talk. That felt much more natural than having each character wait for a turn to explain the mystery. I'm avoiding details, but I was happy to follow this group into another bad idea almost immediately.
One clean deflection against a puppet feels incredible.

The cat-house construction detail is small, but it tells me a lot about the version's tone. The game can give me dangerous puppet bosses, deep underground machinery, and high-mobility martial combat, then ask me to help fix a climbing frame for a cat. That should feel random, but it actually makes the place warmer. It's the same reason I like the construction tasks in general: the mountain is not only a mystery to solve. It's a place people and animals are trying to live in. I stopped beside the finished cat structure longer than I did at some scenic viewpoints. Apparently tiny domestic details are my real endgame.

The new region gives the game a better sense of scale because the city is not spread out in one direction. It's stacked, hidden, and folded into the mountain. I can stand on a high platform, see a waterfall far below, notice a structure behind it, and later discover that the cave near that structure leads into an entirely different level of the city. At one point I saw the same tower from three elevations in ten minutes, and every angle made the route look different. That's much more satisfying than simply seeing a big map full of icons. The space itself becomes the thing I'm trying to understand.

My favorite moment so far wasn't a big boss kill. It was a puzzle where I finally understood why a set of moving parts, water channels, and platforms had been arranged the way they were. For a few minutes I stopped seeing it as a game room designed for me and started seeing it as a broken piece of infrastructure with its own history. I went back through the chamber afterward just to watch the sequence run again without pressure. Seeing the whole mechanism move was its own reward. Then I immediately messed up the timing and fell into the water, so the illusion didn't last long. I left the room feeling like I'd understood a tiny part of the city.
The gauntlets made me stop playing safe. Regret nothing.
The new region makes climbing useful again. Half the time the better route is not forward, it is somewhere above the thing you were already looking at.

I haven't had this much fun with a rope dart in an action game for a while. Pulling enemies out of position, keeping them from escaping, then closing in with the gauntlets makes the combat look much more dramatic than the effort I'm putting in. It has the right kind of showmanship. You can feel the weapon doing its job at range, then switch immediately into something brutal and close. I keep going back to the same encounters just to see whether I can make the transition cleaner the next time. There is something extremely satisfying about pulling one enemy away from a group and deleting their personal space before the others can react.
The mountain keeps hiding paths in plain sight.
The first time I lowered the water and saw a new route appear, I stopped treating the puzzle like a quest task and started poking at everything in the room.

The monkey encounters are silly, but they do useful work for the pacing. After a tense mechanism room or a hard fight, getting mocked by a giant animal on a hillside is a good reminder that the mountain is not only about grand secrets. It has wildlife, weird behavior, and small problems that don't care about the main plot. The best one chased me farther than expected, stopped to make another face, and then got hit by a mechanism meant for me. Perfect encounter. I also like that the region lets you answer that energy instead of treating every creature as a serious combat target. Sometimes the correct response to a monkey throwing rocks is just to laugh and keep walking.

The boss design has made me appreciate deflection practice more than any tutorial ever did. When the puppet sequence starts, I can't rely on panic rolling and hope. I need to watch the order of attacks, react cleanly, and keep enough composure to recognize when the next opening is actually safe. The fight is theatrical without becoming noise. By the third attempt, I was recognizing the opening sequence before the first strike landed. That tiny bit of progress felt better than simply raising my stats. I like that the biggest threat is not just damage, but the way a mistake can change how comfortable the rest of the encounter feels. It makes every good response feel earned.

I was worried the mechanical city aesthetic would feel too clean or too modern for the rest of the game. It doesn't. The best parts look old, patched, weathered, and slightly dangerous, like the machines have been surviving in the mountain for a very long time. The wood, stone, metal, and mist all keep the area grounded. Then you see a structure move or a route open and remember that this place runs on an entirely different logic from the earlier regions. It feels like a real expansion because it changes the texture of exploration, not just the color palette. By the end of the session, I remembered the city through its routes and views, not the icons I'd cleared. That slow understanding makes even a missed turn feel useful, because the detour usually changes how the next route reads. There was a moment where sunlight hit an old gear assembly through the mist, and the whole place looked less like a fantasy city and more like a machine still waking up.

The mechanical bird idea is exactly the kind of thing I want from a wuxia game that's willing to be strange. I'm used to opening doors with a key or finding a hidden lever. Here I'm looking at parts, routes, and old machinery, wondering whether I can turn the local engineering problem into a traveling solution. Watching one of those machines unfold is half the fun. It looks clever, slightly unsafe, and exactly like something I would trust without reading the instructions. It makes the world feel less like historical decoration and more like a place with its own technical imagination. Even when a device is only useful for one route, I remember it because it changes how I approached the area.

The new close-combat style makes ordinary enemy groups more interesting because I can't just stay at a comfortable distance. With a sword, I often play patiently and wait for a safe opening. With the gauntlets, I keep seeing chances to push in, break the rhythm, and stay right on top of someone. The rope dart gives me a way to control the space before I commit, so the combination feels more flexible than pure brawling. I'm not saying it makes every fight easy. It just makes me want to take risks I would normally avoid. I now spend more time thinking about when to stop attacking than when to start. The weapon is basically a very stylish lesson in self-control.

I keep thinking about how much the new region trusts the player to get a little lost. The paths are not always obvious, the layers overlap, and the mechanisms sometimes make you reconsider a room you already walked through. That could be frustrating if the scenery was boring, but every detour has something to look at: a waterfall, a broken machine, a high platform, a cave entrance, or some animal acting like it owns the cliff. I spent more time wandering than progressing for a while, and I mean that as a compliment. I took one wrong turn into a lower chamber, found a shortcut back to the top, and realized the mistake taught me more than the intended route.
The water puzzles are good because the room changes when you solve them. I am tired of switches that only make a door glow.
The invisible walls in boss fight arenas, are the cancer that kills this game for me.

The best construction moments in the new area are not the big buildings. I liked helping with small things that made the mountain feel used: finishing a route, putting together a damaged structure, or making a cat climbing frame where it actually makes sense in the space. It's a small shift from simply discovering a world to leaving a trace inside it. In co-op, these little repairs also give everyone something to argue about. We spent longer choosing where a route should end than actually building it. I don't need every open world to let me build freely, but it's satisfying when a puzzle or construction task changes a place I will pass through again later. I actually remember where those fixes were because I helped put them there.

I didn't expect the giant monkeys to become one of my favorite small details in the mountain. Getting pelted with rocks by something that also makes faces at you is exactly the right amount of disrespect for an exploration game. The fact that some of them are riding boars only makes it better. It breaks up the heavier machinery and ancient-city atmosphere with a little bit of wilderness nonsense. One of them interrupted me while I was lining up a screenshot, threw a rock, and immediately ran uphill. I respected the commitment to being annoying. I went in expecting a serious hidden mountain civilization and came out wondering whether I could become monkey royalty. That range is part of why the region feels memorable. What keeps it from feeling like a feature list is the way the small details support the larger setting. The mountain still has room for accidents, animals, and bad plans.

One thing I appreciate about the new region is that vertical movement actually changes how I travel. In a lot of open worlds, climbing is just the annoying bit before a chest. Here, I started planning routes around whatever I could see above me instead of blindly following the quest marker. A cliff path can lead to a suspended structure, which connects to a cave, which drops you into an older part of the city. I kept recognizing the same landmarks from completely different elevations and feeling weirdly proud whenever the geography clicked. Of course, this also means every “quick trip” now takes an hour because I spot another platform halfway there. The mountain isn't just tall; it keeps making me rethink where I am.
I went sightseeing and became an unpaid engineer.
The new engineering sect has research, construction, and professional paranoia. Basically the most accurate technical job fantasy ever put in a wuxia game.
GOOD

The underground water section made me realize how much I missed puzzles that change the space around you. Raising and lowering water, finding routes through submerged machinery, and watching a previously inaccessible platform become usable feels much better than a standard switch puzzle. It creates the sense that the city has an actual mechanical logic, even when I only understand half of it. I had one room where I changed the water twice, got confused, walked away, then came back and finally noticed the platform moving with it. I kept making bad assumptions about where the route would go, then had to backtrack and look at the room from another angle. That's not something I usually say as praise, but here it made the exploration feel earned.
The rope dart is my new answer to everything.

I joined the engineering-focused sect expecting a novelty system and somehow ended up treating the research applications like real homework. You study components, test elemental combinations, and get weirdly proud when a questionable machine actually works. One promotion task had me reading the requirements twice because I genuinely wasn't sure whether the sect was testing my engineering or my ability to survive paperwork. The funniest part is that useful engineers are valuable enough to get kidnapped, so everyone is supposed to hide their identity while still submitting neat reports about what they built. I logged in to punch things and left worried about deadlines and industrial espionage. Very normal jianghu career path.
Finally, a puzzle that makes pipes interesting.

Where Winds Meet is a visually stunning MMO with genuinely beautiful environments, great cosmetic designs, and one of the best character creators I’ve used in a while. The fantasy aesthetic is strong throughout, and when you’re in the world, it really does feel magical.

That said, the game throws a lot at you. Systems, items, currencies, materials — it all piles up quickly. Bag clutter becomes a real issue, and if you step away for a bit, coming back can feel overwhelming. You end up asking yourself “What does this do again?” far too often. The game doesn’t do much hand-holding, which some players will appreciate, but others may find frustrating.

Cosmetics look fantastic, but most of the best ones sit behind a paywall. It’s understandable for a free MMO to monetize, but it’s still worth mentioning.

Despite the clutter and the learning curve, I’d still recommend Where Winds Meet. It’s gorgeous, atmospheric, and has a lot of potential — just be prepared for a steep re-entry if you take breaks.

On the positive side, the combat is  fun. Very fun. Even compared to paid games, this is one of my favourite combat systems in gaming so far, its simple yet complex, and PvP and PvE has depth because of it. The weapon variety and paths are impressive and its fun that you can mix and match them at certain modes and playstyles so you are not funneled into a single weapon set, but also throughout your playtime you can grow bonded to certain weapons, and I just think its the perfect balance of variety and consistency. For the animations, I like that they received thorough guidance from so many styles of martial artist choreographers and the effort and care they put into it really shows. Each combat movement in the game is quite memorable, and sometimes funny and ridicilous, which adds to its charm. It doesn't take itself too seriously, and it leans onto the comedy, which I appreciate. I particularly enjoy the drunken style animation.

The areas are detailed and there are so many minute details that adds to the fact that real people lived here (historically) and continue living there. Kaifeng and the Imperial Palace are definitely the highlights so far. The social systems need some work, but at the end of the day, is what keeps me coming back to the game. I wish they did deepen the system a bit more though, as the co-op system is somewhat repetitive.

With that I will segwey into the stuff that I find much less satisfying. This game is deeply deeply flawed that I would hesitate to recommend it to people who do not have prior interest in this genre.
One the negative side, most quests are downright incomprehensible jumbles dialogue (without prior knowledge of chinese history and stock characters) but even without prior knowledge, its testament to bad story telling that i do not understand why these characters are here and what they are doing. And I think the sad thing is, the story is amazing. It's this sweeping plot of historic proportions, war, politics, complex intertwining military strategies, with characters full of autonomous desires who think they are doing the right thing in their own way, and its intertwined with the protagonist's personal journey of finding family and dealing with grief. The issue is, you can only understand the full extent of the plot if you watch a youtube video explaining it to you.

Before I get accused of media illiteracy, yes, you can understand this fully in-game, but it is a chore rather than something you have the pleasure of experiencing. You have to read every item description, every note and letter, and listen to poor translations of side missions and some of the wandering tales that have very little in-game guidance to understand its full depth. Yes, the main missions on their own give enough information for you to understand it, but you also miss a lot of things if you ignore the side content. Now, I love the concept of a plot you must work for and piece together on your own, but also the starting point is so illegible that I wish it had communicated the depth it has (especially in English) more accurately, because the plot is lost on so many of the Western fanbase.

 I think the worst thing is, most side missions and adventures basically have no real resolutions, after you defeat the boss you rarely get closure with some rare exceptions (I liked that Zheng E's closure was more in the environmental storytelling than a cutscene for example). There is a reason a lot ppl skip dialogue even if its voice acted (don't get me started on the AI dialogue that they thankfully put a stop to in the new area). 

Maybe I am expecting too much from a free game, but I think if the quests were even 10% more articulate, this would be a 10/10 even with all its flaws, because I like the experience of laughing at this game and then being in awe of some of its best moments. There are many bugs and glitchy experiences but they aren't like gamebreaking and add to the accidental humor. Overall, if you like this genre, and are interested in Chinese history, you are going to like this game. I know I complained about the bad parts for a majority of this review, but I genuinely enjoy playing it, and my complaints emerge from a desire to see it do better and fix its translation issues.

This is a great game, but it's being ruined by the developers' lack of responsibility. The game is full of balance issues and bugs, yet after more than six months, almost none of them have been addressed.

Here's one example of the balance problems. In the bounty mode, what weapon do you think is used the most? A sword? A blade? A spear? No—it's the fan. For some reason, healing is reduced in every other PvP mode, but not in bounty hunts. As a result, you end up with players who have what feels like endless healing.

Some players even deliberately commit crimes just to become wanted and lure bounty hunters to them. They know that if the hunter isn't using a healer build, they'll almost certainly win. If the hunter is also a healer, the fight usually drags on until the timer runs out. It's a toxic and unhealthy gameplay loop.

Then there are the bugs. In the Inheritance Challenge, during the final stage against the Nameless General, the boss turns invisible in roughly 3 out of every 10 attempts. Many players, including myself, have recorded videos and reported the issue, but nothing has been done. It feels like the developers are more interested in selling skins than fixing their game. :)

The homestead update for Where Winds Meet has turned a game I liked into a game I love. I’ve always enjoyed the game’s combat and story, but I never felt like I had a real place in the world—until now. Building my own homestead has given me a sense of belonging in the game’s vast, beautiful world, and it’s added a whole new layer of depth to the gameplay. What I appreciate most is that the homestead system is flexible: you can make it as simple or as elaborate as you want. If you just want a small cottage with a garden and a cat, that’s totally fine. If you want to build a huge, sprawling estate with multiple buildings, a farm, a training yard, and a whole menagerie of pets, you can do that too. I’ve gone all out with mine: I’ve got a main house with a traditional wuxia-style courtyard, a greenhouse for growing rare herbs, a pond with lotus flowers and fish, a bird aviary, and even a small shrine where I can leave offerings for my ancestors. The pet system is also incredibly well-done—each animal has its own unique behaviors and animations, and it’s clear that the developers put a lot of thought into making them feel real. My cats will nap in the sun, play with each other, and even comfort me when I come back from a tough battle. My geese are always up to something, whether they’re chasing insects or splashing in the pond. It’s these small, immersive details that make the homestead feel like a real home, not just a set of buildings. I also love that the update added new quests and content tied to the homestead, so it’s not just a sandbox—there are goals to work towards, like unlocking new furniture recipes, upgrading your homestead, and bonding with your pets and companions. It’s given me a reason to keep playing, even when I’ve finished the main story, and I can’t recommend it enough.

I came back to Where Winds Meet after a few months away, and the homestead update blew my mind. I remember thinking the game was fun but a bit empty when I first played it—great combat, but not much to do outside of fighting and questing. Now, with the homestead and pet systems, the game feels like a whole new experience. I’ve spent the entire weekend building and decorating my homestead, and I’m still not done. I’ve got a main house with a bedroom, a kitchen, and a study, a separate stable for my horses, a big garden where I’m growing all kinds of herbs and vegetables, and a little playground for my pets with toys and scratching posts. The customization options are amazing—you can change everything from the type of wood used for the walls to the color of the roof tiles, and there are so many different furniture options to choose from. I also love that you can invite your friends and companions to your homestead; we’ve had a few little gatherings where we cook food, play with the pets, and just hang out, and it’s made the game feel much more social. The pets are probably my favorite part, though. My cat will bring me little gifts sometimes, like herbs or small stones, and my goose will follow me around and help me collect resources. It’s the little things like that that make the game feel so special, and it’s made me want to keep playing for a long time. I also want to mention how well the update is optimized—even with all the decorations and pets in my homestead, the game runs smoothly, no lag or frame drops, which is a huge plus. If you’re a fan of wuxia games or life sims, you owe it to yourself to check out this update.

Good game with great graphics, great combat, and great story. I love learning about the history of China in a period not many in the West are familiar with (if they're familiar with Chinese history at all), and I think the romantic elements add well to it in places like Hexi and others. 

I play solo mode pretty much only, and as mentioned, I love the combat, it's a great challenge, but I will say this game has a habit of running you into a brick wall in progression for story bosses. If you haven't upgraded your character to a high enough, you will struggle massively to effectively kill these bosses and you're pretty much pushed to having to farm the "Wandering Paths" dailies to get gear upgrades (which of course has an "energy cap"). The story is great, so it definitely makes it worth it to get to the point where you can beat them, but I've had more than one occasion where I've had to quit the game in frustration because a boss just felt unnaturally strong from the natural pace of the combat up to that point. I play on Recommended difficulty with parry assistance off, and yes I know you can turn the difficulty down to Story and you can turn on deflection assist, but I don't think you should have to dumb down combat that much just to get through a boss fight, there's a happy balance between natural feeling progression and a challenge. 

Cosmetic shop also has some insanely crazy prices for some skins, but the game does give you some, and there are nice ones which are cheap. It seems the fantasy skins are the insanely priced ones, so not getting those doesn't matter as much to me as I prefer the more world appropriate clothing, the expensive ones just seem out of place for the story.

Finally, and I would recommend anyone doing this immediately after starting, turn the subtitles on and change the voiceovers to the original Chinese and you will have a much more enjoyable experience. The English voiceover is pretty trash and you will get tired of it quickly, whereas the Chinese voiceover has the passion and immersion you'd associate with the characters, and the localization for the subtitles is good so you will rarely not understand.

Overall, this game is fun, beautiful and a nice challenge combat-wise, and I would recommend it, but if I could give it a more precise score it'd probably be around 80% as it does have some glaring flaws that will take away enjoyment from time-to-time (though not as bad as other gacha-style games), and you will most likely run into scenarios where the natural progression feels unnatural and you're forced to farm and wait for energy to reload, or to buy cash shop items which can help speed that process up. Oh, and as mentioned by some, even in solo you will be exposed to some weirdos via the sign posts that you and other players can leave...there are some sad individuals  on there who know only gooning  and racism.

Where Winds Meet is one of the most beautiful open-world games I've played. The environments are absolutely stunning, and it's easy to spend hours simply exploring, taking in the scenery, or hanging out with friends. The story is intriguing, and there's a surprising amount of content to keep you busy.

The cosmetics are also gorgeous, although I do think they're on the expensive side. One thing I appreciate is that the developers have improved the outfit system since launch. Originally, you had to wear an entire outfit as a set, but now you can mix and match some of the individual pieces. There are still some outfits where you need to buy the whole set just to get the piece you want, but the customization is definitely better than it was before.

For most of my playtime, the game felt very welcoming to casual players. I'm not someone who enjoys spending hours researching optimal gear builds. I like exploring, experiencing the story, and progressing naturally.

Eventually, though, I hit a wall. Progressing further required a much deeper understanding of the gear upgrade systems than I personally wanted to invest in. If you're someone who enjoys optimizing equipment, farming materials, and learning every progression mechanic, you'll probably love this part of the game. If you're a more casual player like me, there's a point where the game starts expecting a level of investment that may not be for everyone.

One thing I'd really like to see improved is the multiplayer experience. While you can play together in many situations, there are still story quests that can't be completed alongside friends. I think allowing players to experience the entire journey together would make an already enjoyable game even better.

Despite eventually reaching the point where I decided not to continue, I still recommend giving Where Winds Meet a try. If you're looking for a gorgeous world to explore, an interesting story, and plenty of content, there's a lot here to enjoy. And if you're the type of player who loves mastering gear progression and character optimization, you'll probably get even more out of it than I did.

I’ve played a lot of wuxia games over the years, and most of them fall into the same trap: they focus entirely on combat and story, with no real way to connect with the world or build a life for your character. Where Winds Meet’s homestead update breaks that mold completely, and it’s one of the best updates I’ve seen in a wuxia game in a long time. What I love most is that the homestead system isn’t just a side activity—it’s a fully fleshed-out part of the game that ties into other systems in meaningful ways. For example, the herbs you grow in your garden can be used to craft better potions and medicines, the food you cook in your kitchen can give you buffs for combat, and spending time with your companions in the homestead increases your bond with them, which unlocks new dialogue and even unique combat abilities. It’s not just about decorating a house; it’s about building a sustainable, fulfilling life for your character in the game’s world, and that’s something I’ve always wanted from a wuxia RPG. The pet system is also a huge highlight—being able to feed, pet, and play with my cats and geese adds such a warm, personal touch to the game, and it’s nice to have a break from all the intense combat every once in a while. I also appreciate that the developers didn’t lock any combat content behind the homestead system; if you just want to focus on fighting and quests, you can totally ignore the homestead, but if you want to take a more relaxed approach, it’s there for you. It’s the perfect example of how to add depth to a game without alienating existing players, and I’m excited to see how they expand on it in the future.

When I first heard about the homestead update, I thought it would be a tiny, throwaway feature—just some extra furniture to craft and a house to decorate. I was so wrong. This update has completely transformed how I play Where Winds Meet, and I’ve spent more time in my homestead than I have in any other part of the game in the past two weeks. I’ve spent hours planning out every corner of my property: I built a herb garden near the front door so I can easily grab ingredients for crafting, a training yard behind the house where I can practice my martial arts forms, a cozy little patio with a fire pit where my companions and I can sit and chat, and even a small pond with fish that my cats love to watch. The pet system is the real star of the show here, though. Each of my cats has their own personality: one is super curious and will follow me everywhere around the homestead, another is more laid-back and will only come over if I bring it treats, and the geese are just hilarious—they’ll chase butterflies around the garden, steal food from the table, and even honk at my companions if they get too close. It’s these little, realistic details that make the homestead feel so alive, and it’s made me care about my character’s world in a way I never did before. I used to rush through quests to get to the next big fight, but now I take my time, enjoying the quiet moments in my home, and it’s made the game feel so much more immersive.

I’ve been playing Where Winds Meet on and off since the early access days, and I have to say the homestead update is exactly what this game needed to feel like a fully realized wuxia world. Before, the game was all about nonstop combat and questing, which was great for a while, but I always felt like there was a missing piece—something that made the world feel like home, not just a battlefield. Now, with the homestead system, I find myself logging in just to tend to my garden, rearrange my furniture, and check in on my cats and geese. The attention to detail is incredible: the cats will curl up on the porch railings when it’s sunny, the geese will wander into the vegetable garden and peck at the crops, and even the way the sunlight filters through the trees in my homestead feels intentional. It’s not just a decoration system; it’s a way to build a life for my character outside of the main story, and it’s made me fall in love with the game all over again. I also love that the Martial Heart Palace is a separate, combat-focused mode that doesn’t interfere with the homestead progression—you can jump into intense duels and boss fights without worrying about your home or pets, and vice versa. It’s the perfect balance between relaxing life sim and high-stakes wuxia combat, and I can’t wait to see what they add next to the homestead system.

[b]The 6-Month Cliff: How Predatory Gacha Burnt Out Where Winds Meet[/b]

When Where Winds Meet first burst onto the scene, it was hailed as a breathtaking fusion of historical Wuxia fiction and high-speed open world action. Its fluid combat, beautiful vistas, and promise of a monetization model free from raw "pay-to-win" stat purchases drew hundreds of thousands of eager players at launch. Yet, mere months later, the game stands as a stark cautionary tale. By the six month mark, the title suffered an staggering population collapse, bleeding roughly 90% of its initial player base. This dramatic "6 Month Cliff" was not a fluke of the market; it was the direct, inevitable result of weaponized gacha mechanics and profound player burnout.

[b] The Cosmetic Gacha Mirage [/b]

The game’s fatal flaw lies in the deception of its "no pay to win" marketing. While it is technically true that players cannot directly purchase raw character power or combat stats to clear content, the developers fundamentally misunderstood or chose to exploit the psychology of the modern multiplayer community. In a shared online world, visual identity, prestige, and custom animations are the endgame currency.
By locking high tier character skins, premium mounts, and unique weapon visual effects behind the predatory "Celestial Echo" gacha banner, the game erected a massive psychological barrier. When the standard cost to guarantee a single elite outfit easily scales between $500 and $600 out of pocket due to a punishing token exchange pity system, casual players are instantly made to feel like second class citizens. The game effectively commodified social status, creating an aggressive disparity between the average player and high-spending "whales."

[b] RNG Layered on RNG [/b]

Compounding the sheer financial exhaustion of the banner system is the game's relentless weapon reforge loop. To fully realize the aesthetic potential of a weapon skin that a player may have already spent hundreds of dollars to acquire, they are funneled into a secondary casino: spending premium real-world currency on Taiyi Stones to randomly roll cosmetic visual slots.
This multi-tiered gambling ecosystem drains the joy out of personalization. Instead of rewarding dedication, exploration, or skill, the game reduces player identity to an expensive slot machine. When a player realizes they must gamble just to fix an mismatched color palette on a skin they already paid a fortune for, the fantasy breaks. The gameplay loop stops feeling like an epic martial arts journey and starts feeling like an exploitative chore.

[b] The Emptiness After the Story [/b]

The ultimate trigger for the 6 Month Cliff occurs when players exhaust the single-player narrative and exploration content. Once the initial wonder of the open world fades, players look to the multiplayer loop for longevity. However, Where Winds Meet fails to sustain a healthy endgame because its ecosystem is built around hunting whales rather than fostering a community.
Unlike peers like Once Human, which offer direct-purchase cosmetics and transparent seasonal loops that respect a player's time and money, Where Winds Meet doubles down on aggressive time gated energy systems and talent limits. Non-spending players hit an agonizing, artificial wall, while being constantly reminded of the $600 gacha banners they are missing out on.

[b] Final Verdict [/b]

Where Winds Meet is a mechanical masterpiece suffocated by its own corporate greed. Gambling in video games sours the player experience at every level, and this title proves that cosmetic-only gacha can be just as toxic and destructive to a community as traditional pay to win mechanics. The 6 Month Cliff was the community’s collective rejection of a casino masquerading as a Wuxia epic. Until publishers realize that player retention requires mutual respect, gorgeous games will continue to hollow out, leaving behind empty servers and a handful of isolated whales.

I really wanted to enjoy Where Winds Meet, especially because the PvP has a lot of potential, but the current balance is honestly frustrating.

Right now, Hengdao and Nameless feel completely overtuned compared to Strategic Sword. These builds keep getting updates, buffs, better cooldowns, stronger damage, and more reliable tools, while Strategic Sword feels ignored. Strategic Sword is supposed to be a technical build that rewards timing, positioning, and smart play, but instead it feels like you are punished for using it.

The biggest issue is that Strategic Sword has serious bugs and hit registration problems. Even in PvE, there are times where bosses move slightly and my attacks just do not connect properly. The charged R skill misses way too often, even when it clearly looks like it should hit. In PvP, this makes the build feel even worse because one missed skill can decide the whole fight.

Meanwhile, Hengdao can pressure people with ridiculous charge light attack stun locks, and Nameless already has strong cooldowns and damage. On top of that, CN server is getting even more Nameless updates, including more charged R damage. Why are already strong builds getting even more attention while Strategic Sword is still left broken?

Strategic Sword also lacks proper PvP tools compared to other builds. It does not have the same kind of reliable yellow attack option, and it cannot stun lock or pressure enemies like Hengdao or Nameless. I ended up using Heavenquaker Spear to climb ranked because it simply feels more practical, which says a lot about how bad Strategic Sword feels right now.

The balance update schedule is also a major problem. If this game wants to have a serious PvP scene, balance changes cannot only happen every season. Broken builds need to be adjusted faster, and bugged builds need to be fixed faster. Players should not be forced to grind all over again just to switch to whatever build is currently meta.

This is why people are leaving. PvP players want fair balance, reliable skills, and builds that actually work. Strategic Sword needs proper fixes, especially hit registration, charged R consistency, and a real yellow attack option.

Until the developers actually fix Strategic Sword and stop allowing Hengdao and Nameless to dominate the meta, I cannot recommend this game.

My biggest criticism of the original release was lack of emotional casual content: no pets, no personal home, no meaningful companion bonding loops. This patch fixes every single complaint without muddling separate gameplay systems together. Watching cats curl up beside you while resting at the manor feels incredibly warm, geese honk happily when you bring wild fruit back from journeys. Maxed tacit unlocks heartfelt companion cutscenes featuring your pets, fully separate from Martial Heart Palace’s combat-focused story fragments. Small interaction bug: pet prompt buttons sometimes fail to pop up when standing directly next to them.

Most wuxia sandbox games tack housing systems on as lazy afterthoughts, and Where Winds Meet nearly fell into that trap before this major update. The homestead and pet systems feel fully polished and standalone from combat content, with smooth tacit bond progression tied only to manor activities. Cats automatically mark uncollected wild resource locations across the map, a great quality of life tweak. Martial Heart Palace exists as a fully separate combat challenge with no reliance on your estate or pets. Minor schedule annoyance: daily homestead refresh timer resets at an awkward hour for EU players.

Where Winds Meet is fairly mind blowing in size and gameplay. It has a little something for everyone here, with cross platform multiplayer and solo worlds. You like Sekiro-like combat and boss fights? They got you. You like PVP and fortnight-like battle royal? Boom, here you go. Want to play on your phone when you are waiting in line for that bubble tea? Ok, sure check out this app that lets you play the full game on iPhone. Like Tomagatchi pet like sim system and talking to Ai pets? Ok, here you go. Like farming life, and social sims? Alright, we got you. Like going around petting cats, and learning how to talk to animals? There are like hundreds of cats, knock yourself out. Like talking to Ai NPCs about the weather and your last relationship? You can actually do that with many NPCs in this game. Like building homes and insane properties you can live in with NPCs? And build almost anywhere, even in many dungeons? It's there. Its quite insane what you get, all in a free game. And it looks beautiful. Environments are well thought out, look gorgeous. Many of the stories and quests pull you in, and are long. And if you like  late Tang, early Song Dynasty era stuff and clothing, you are going to love the style. I think 90% of C-drama are in this type of era, not to mention Japan, Korea, Vietnam etc etc getting most of the beginnings of their now cultural clothing, written language, tradition, government, religions and philosophical ideas etc etc from this era in China. It is like Pursuit of Jade in a game version. Maps are huge. Weapons are many and each have different gameplay. Different martial arts abilities etc etc. You will learn a lot about real places and events in Chinese history around that time, with cities modeled after  the real places around China and Asia. And the game has some really good humor at times, with hilarious side quests, events, and clothing/costumes. Its got tons of Ai NPCs you can converse with about anything, and you can even scan your face and voice to put into your character. You can also load TikTok videos and make your characters do the dances on your video using Ai. I can't think of another game that is able to do this.
  I could go on and on about this game. Its like everything thrown in one game. And its free, the paid stuff is cosmetic. And you'll want to buy it too. Cause the paid stuff is pure Aura farming. You don't need that long flowing $10 hairstyle from the shop, or the armor that looks like it is on fire, but at some point you are gonna look at it and try to chance the gatcha system to get it, or just outright buy cosmetic skins in the shop. I thought, surely a game that throws the kitchen sink of gameplay at you can't do any of it good right? Well, I was wrong. It does most decently well, and some very well.
  The bad stuff: It is pretty limited in my point of view. There are some buggy quests. Occasionally i get some graphical glitches. Like seeing thru a wall. Or a door glitching closed. Getting stuck. But most are solved by using the fast travel to get out, or the unstuck option in settings. Stuck quests I often fix after logging out of game and back in. Occasionally I run into people online, bugging me to PVP etc, but its pretty easy to avoid. 75% of my time in this game is in single player mode. The game interface can be daunting at first. There is just so much going on and so much to do in this game. Lots of mechanism and different windows to understand. Different currencies, chat channels, tabs etc. You eventually get it down, but the learning curve is definitely there.
  If you like martial arts, ancient Chinese history, just petting cats all day, C-dramas or any of the above mentioned, I think you'll find this free game pretty enjoyable. And with people buying $40,000 boats in this game, it seems that it is making enough for continuous unlimited content and updates. I've already met a few fun people to play with on the game as well.

Combat is still solid and responsive like before, but what surprised me is how much the pacing has changed. I used to just chain missions and log out, now I actually take breaks between fights just to go back home and check things. It sounds simple but it completely changes how I experience the game compared to earlier patches.

I remember earlier versions of Where Winds Meet feeling a bit more lonely, like you’re just traveling between fights and cutscenes. This update changes that feeling a lot. The homestead system gives you a base that actually feels like yours, and the pets make the world feel less empty even when you’re not doing anything important.

The goose is honestly ridiculous in the best way possible. I don’t even know why it’s in the game but it just keeps causing chaos around my homestead. It steals things, wanders off, and somehow I ended up treating it like a priority target to protect. I’ve played since earlier versions and this is probably the most unexpected thing they’ve added so far.

I'm sure there is a decent game hidden somewhere under a mountain of ridiculous micro-transactions, horrendous UI and broken English dialogs translated with Google Translate, but it's very hard to find.

Not gonna lie, I was one of those people who thought pet systems were just fluff content, but now I literally care about my cat in-game more than I expected. It follows me around, reacts to things, and sometimes just sits there when I’m doing nothing. It’s small but it changes how I feel about the whole game loop compared to the older version.

The homestead system sounded like a side feature when I first read about it, but it’s way deeper than that. I thought it would just be cosmetic decoration but I ended up spending hours optimizing the layout like it’s some kind of management sim. Compared to earlier builds where I just logged in for combat sessions, now I actually have a routine in-game, like checking home first before anything else.

Pre-June patch the jianghu world felt cold and empty, villages sat abandoned with no personal permanent base to claim as your own. Now my manor acts as my central peaceful hub, every crop planted, pet raised and companion bond built through tacit value feels rewarding and long-lasting. The tacit system unlocks unique dialogue and courtyard events exclusive to home life, with no carryover to Martial Heart Palace challenges. Small layout restriction: training ground buildings cannot be moved after initial placement, limiting creative manor design

Hardcore kung fu main here, I worried the homestead sim would dilute the game’s combat identity, but the two content lines stay completely divided and well-balanced. After grinding brutal high-level Martial Heart Palace trials (a fully independent combat mode), I unwind separately by tending my garden, playing with geese and cats to gradually raise team tacit value. Pet model textures hold up beautifully even at max graphic settings. Minor loot feedback: rare combat skill materials drop slightly too infrequently inside Martial Heart Palace.

I used to rush every side quest just to jump back into fighting, there was zero incentive to slow down and enjoy peaceful world content pre-patch. Now I actively pause main story progress to go home, rearrange my courtyard layout, feed my pets and slowly raise tacit bond with my favorite companions. Martial Heart Palace mixes puzzle mechanics with combat for a totally unique separate challenge mode you can tackle whenever you want. Hope devs add a one-click fast travel shortcut straight to your manor gate from any map area.

The open world scenery was stunning on launch, but there was zero player-owned private land until this homestead patch dropped. I built a secluded bamboo courtyard just for my cats to wander freely, geese splash around the fish pond all day long. Regular team gatherings at home keep tacit value rising steadily. Martial Heart Palace is an independent combat trial zone with its own progression system that doesn’t touch your manor or pets at all. Tiny rendering bug: frame drops occur briefly when loading a full manor with four+ pets roaming at once.

Review written after 1,600 hours of gameplay and having experienced a wide range of situations in the game:

- Several bugs: broken world map textures, glitched interactions, bugged building items...

- Reports and bug reports are ignored: Bugs remain unresolved no matter how many times they are reported, and players reported for violations listed in the report options—including spam, inappropriate audio, cheating, and other disruptive behavior—are never punished.

- Extremely expensive cash shop: Want to look fancy? You have to pay real money to get Pearls. There is absolutely no way to earn premium currency for free (not even a small monthly allowance for F2P players).

- Instead of fixing these structural issues, every new patch just adds more cosmetics to the cash shop and shallow, cash-driven events.

- Terrible PvP system: Horrible balance that forces the player base to use the exact same rigid META builds and weapons.

- Insane lag and terrible optimization.

- Confusing UI: Cluttered menus that lack any proper explanation.

- Boring story quests: Long, tedious conversations and forced slow-walking segments that completely kill the pacing.

- Lack of content variety: Repetitive NPC models and a complete lack of voice acting.

- A Toxic Community: Because it is a free MMORPG, it attracts many toxic, weird, creepy, and attention-seeking players. The community is one of the strangest and most toxic in the MMO genre. Many guilds have an unhealthy, cult-like mindset where defending the game’s flaws matters more than criticism. Leaving a guild feels like being erased — friendships often end instantly. The game revolves around social status, creating endless drama and ego clashes.

- Global chat is constantly flooded with spam: Players beg continuously for shop outfits, Pearls, gallery exhibition votes, and sect rank votes, often repeating the same requests through unsolicited DMs. This creates an endless 24/7 scroll that makes the chat channels annoying, intrusive, and practically useless.

- A special mention goes to the Velvet Shade sect, which is by far the worst offender for community and spam issues. It embodies all of the aforementioned problems and also has a high volume of unsolicited marriage proposals and flirtatious requests that add to the overall annoyance.


Conclusion:

The game constantly tries to hook you into spending money. The shop is updated weekly with new outfits, flashy FX animations, mounts, weapon skins, and limited-time items—often wrapped in fake "special discounts" designed to trigger FOMO.

Before you play, keep this in mind:

They don't care about the community.
They don't care about optimization or stability.
They don't care about balance or fixing game-breaking bugs.
They only care about bleeding your wallet dry.

At this point, it feels less like a martial arts RPG and more like a social status simulator driven by whoever puts on the best show and spends the most money in the cash shop.

Ultimately, many players forget a harsh reality: when this pseudo-MMORPG inevitably shuts down, everything they spent real money on just to look fancy and show off will disappear forever along with the servers.
