[h2]A Stunning Wuxia World That Rewards Patience[/h2]

Where Winds Meet is an absolute visual treat. The landscapes are breathtaking — sweeping mountains, misty rivers, ancient towns, and vibrant seasonal changes that make exploration genuinely feel alive. The art direction and attention to detail in this 10th-century China setting are top-tier. Whether you're gliding through the clouds or simply standing on a cliff overlooking a valley at sunset, the beauty never gets old.
What surprised me most was the storytelling. Even the "normal" questlines have surprising depth, with well-written characters, emotional moments, and that classic wuxia flavor of intrigue, honor, revenge, and personal growth. The main story pulls you in, but side content often feels meaningful too.

I also really enjoyed the use of AI in some NPC interactions. The conversations feel surprisingly natural and responsive, adding a nice layer of immersion. Despite what some people might say, I thought it was rather well done and enhanced the experience rather than breaking it. But, if you really don't like it, you can break it, just like an chat bot. Please don't.

That said, the game throws a lot at you right from the start. The opening hours can feel overwhelming as systems, tutorials, and mechanics pile on without always explaining things clearly. There's a steep learning curve, and the sheer number of currencies, resources, and upgrade paths is honestly excessive — it can get confusing and a bit exhausting trying to keep track of everything. A better onboarding experience would have helped a lot.
Despite those rough early impressions, I'm glad I stuck with it. Once things start to click and you carve out your own path through the world, it becomes very enjoyable. Combat feels fluid and flashy, exploration is rewarding, and there's a ton of content to dive into.
For a free-to-play game, Where Winds Meet delivers an impressive experience with genuine heart and ambition. If you're into wuxia vibes, open-world adventure, and beautiful settings, it's well worth downloading and giving a fair shot. The winds will carry you far if you let them.

I honestly think Where Winds Meet is heading in a bad direction and could end up losing a lot of its player base sooner rather than later if things don't change.

When the game first launched, it was actually enjoyable. The world felt fresh, the combat was interesting, and there was enough content to keep players invested. Like many players, I was willing to overlook some bugs and issues because the game was still new and had plenty of potential.

However, as the game progressed, more problems started to become noticeable. Bugs that have been reported for a long time remain unfixed, while player abuses and exploitative behavior continue to affect the overall experience. Instead of improving over time, it often feels like the same issues are being carried forward from one update to the next.

What makes it more frustrating is that these problems directly impact gameplay. When players can abuse certain mechanics without consequences, it creates an unfair environment that takes away from the fun. A game can survive bugs for a while, but when players start feeling that their concerns are being ignored, that's when people begin to lose interest.

The biggest issue for me is that the game has started to feel boring. The excitement I felt during the early days is mostly gone. New content doesn't feel meaningful enough to keep me engaged, and the core experience isn't improving in ways that matter to long-term players.

A good comparison would be Dota 2. Anyone who has played Dota knows how frustrating it can be. You can get angry, lose multiple games in a row, and swear you're done with it. Yet somehow you still want to queue up for another match because the gameplay itself remains engaging and rewarding. The frustration comes from competition, not from feeling neglected as a player.

With Where Winds Meet, it's different. When I stop playing, I don't feel excited to come back. I don't find myself thinking about the next session or looking forward to future updates. Instead, I feel like the game is wasting its own potential.

Right now, it feels like the developers are putting more attention on gacha systems and monetization rather than addressing the issues that affect the everyday player experience. Of course, every game needs to make money, but a successful live-service game also needs to maintain player trust. If players start believing that monetization is a higher priority than game quality, community concerns, and long-term enjoyment, then the game's future becomes uncertain.

I really want Where Winds Meet to succeed because the foundation is there. The world, combat, and overall concept have a lot of potential. But if the developers continue to ignore bugs, exploits, and player feedback while focusing primarily on gacha content, I wouldn't be surprised to see more players leave over time.

A great game can survive monetization. A great game can survive balance issues. But no game can survive if players stop caring enough to log in.

With over 300 hours played, I definitely got my money's worth out of Where Winds Meet.

The game offers a beautiful world to explore, strong progression, an engaging story, and some of the best character customization I've seen in this type of game. The combat felt fluid, each weapon had its own weight and style, and exploration was consistently rewarding. I also enjoyed collecting outfits, accessories, and creating different looks for my character through the color customization options.

There always seemed to be something to work toward, whether it was progressing the story, exploring new areas, improving my character, or simply seeing what the world had to offer next. For some players, the amount of content will be a huge positive. For others, it may eventually feel overwhelming since the story and progression systems continue expanding over time.

My biggest criticism is the forced PvP and wanted system, as I personally am not a PvP-heavy gamer. There were times when the game seemed to think I had stolen something or committed a crime when I hadn't. If you become wanted, other players can be sent into your world to hunt you down. If you're defeated, you can end up imprisoned, and some of the punishment mechanics felt unnecessarily harsh or humiliating.

Even if you are not defeated, you either have to survive until the timer runs out or defeat the person sent after you. If you defeat them, they can still place a vendetta against you, allowing another player to accept it and spawn into your world to attack you, even while you're in the middle of a mission or conversation. That part could get frustrating. The nice thing is that, since it's your world, you can have a friend join and help you fight back.

While some players might enjoy the system, and while I understand what the developers were going for, it simply wasn't something I personally enjoyed. That said, if this type of gameplay appeals to you, then this will likely be right up your alley. The cosmetic gacha system can also feel grindy unless you're willing to spend money.

Despite those complaints, I still had a great time with the game and found it even more enjoyable when playing with friends. If you enjoy open-world action RPGs with beautiful environments, strong customization, fluid combat, and plenty of content to dive into, I'd definitely recommend giving Where Winds Meet a try.

My opinion is subjective on how you want to play Where Winds Meet. If you're playing it as a single-player Souls-like, you'd probably be fine for the most part until you get to the later bosses. At which point everything is a visual spectacle of "I cannot see anything, but all right". At least until Hexi, I stopped doing the story at some point in Hexi, so I don't know if they fixed it. 

PVE Content (Group play)

If you're hoping to have any variety in class jobs, don't bother. This game has DPS and Healer. It only requires DPS and Healer. Healers are so OP that you can face-tank most of everything in the game without caring about damage-- to the point that it's better to let your highest DPS pure-melee tank instead of the actual tank class because there is no need for any aggro pull and no upsides to letting the tank actually tank the boss unless they're the highest DPS melee in the party. 

Speaking of tank function and why tanks are so useless (in terms of actual tanking) in this game, the raid bosses aren't designed to be kept static. No matter what you do, these bosses will float, jump, run, or displace themselves just because of their move set. MMORPGs can and do have these, but it's usually tied to a party mechanic, such as CCing the boss to prevent movement. Here in Where Winds Meet. NADA. So really, tanks are just DPSes with a different icon.

These bosses are very clearly designed to be single-player bosses. Not raid bosses. Using them as raid bosses is just a cheap way to give multiplayer content without actually committing to creating raid bosses. Sure, they add some mechanics to the boss that makes it feel more like a raid, but the core move set of the boss was never designed for it. None of what they've done, ie. wipe mechanics, will matter in this regard. 

Pushing this issue even further is their attempt to build some classes around buff management, Bellstrike - Umbra in particular. How do you expect a class to maintain their buffs when bosses keep moving around? A boss moving an inch too much could mean the difference between having to restart your rotation or completely missing out on 25% of your damage. 

The gear system is also poorly designed. You NEED to change your gear every level cap. ALL of them. The problem is, your gear stats are gambled. You can get absolutely nothing usable for weeks or months. They recently updated with allowing you to level your gear 1 level higher, with some reduction on effectivity. Unfortunately, having to grind for gear, then grind for stats-- in a game that caps your energy-- basically just means you can never really tell whether you'll have 0 or 8 perfect gear or even usable gear that's better than your last. 

Then, to add insult to injury, they LOVE DPS-scoreboards as events. 

PVP Content

PVP in this game is actually really fun-- but balancing is absolute garbage. Only two classes in this game has stuns. A couple of classes have unblockable attacks. Some classes are extremely strong and end up being used more often in the arena. 70-80% of your matches will either be Hengdao variants, FanBrella, or Twin Blades + Nameless sword.

FanBrella, which was already fairly strong before with its gimmicks-- ie. being the only class that can cancel a guard break-- now has tenacity on knock-up. Hengdao can just nearly perma tenacity themselves with their strongest DPS skills as part of their main rotation. Just grabbing either one of these classes instantly puts you on an advantage in PVP.

Twin Blades + Nameless at least requires some form of skill, but people love to play this because Twin Blades has Rage Mode AKA full tenacity for the whole length of it. There's nothing you can do for that duration. Just run, block, and parry. 

But it's fine of they at least play the game, but a lot of people in this game are incentivized to run away and just keep running (acceptable for ranged classes), then you have Nameless builds that will just run away the whole fight and try to chip down your HP with their range skills and do absolutely nothing else. 

And of course, the best part is, how ping reliant this game's PVP is. You have 30ms to the server? Good luck fighting against anyone that's 20ms and below-- better yet the ping Gods with their 1-8ms ping. Some classes are unplayable when you're above a certain ping because your combos will just drop against anyone with good ping. Never have I ever seen 30ms be considered "unplayable" until I played Where Winds Meet.

Guild vs Guild Content
Could also be fun if it functioned even remotely well. Learned a lot of combos in 1v1? Forget it. None of your combos are going to stick here. LOL. Catch anyone with any skill and they will walk right out of it. The only way you can actually capture anyone is if you actively stun them, ie. Knock them up, use a stun skill, etc. Any normal hit will not keep them stun-locked. 

--------------

This game is otherwise good, but these issues compound until you're just tired of the game.

Game Review: Great Potential Ruined by Network Issues and Shallow Content
This is a great free-to-play Wuxia game with beautiful graphics and tons of activities. However, many of these activities feel quite superficial—there is a lot quantity, but very little depth. The story seems decent, but as a hardcore PvP player, I didn't pay much attention to it. That said, the community seems to have a fair amount of emotional investment in it.

The gear progression system relies on a seasonal reset, forcing you to constantly grind for new gear. I’d rate it as mediocre; it gets repetitive, though the devs have made it a bit easier recently. Eventually, you’ll reach a point where you feel aimless, like your "inner self" is maxed out and the story is fully cleared. Collecting cosmetics and achievements is fine if you're into that sort of completionist pride.

A Narrow Online Experience & Shallow Mechanics
The online aspect feels very narrow. You rarely interact with other players outside of your own guild. You can customize a gorgeous character, but your guild is pretty much the only part of the world that will ever see or interact with it. Other elements—like boss raids, farming, or the healing/injury system—feel incredibly shallow, and players just go through the motions like robots. The most social thing people do is singing, dancing, and using voice chat on boats, but that's just not my style.

The Sect system is completely garbage compared to older games. Joining a sect carries no real consequences or permanent impact on your character. Its main purpose is just to trade for faction items, and there is absolutely nothing stopping you from fulfilling a dream of maxing out every single sect. On the bright side, the PvE boss mechanics are actually fun and scale nicely in intensity—but again, that's not why I'm here.

The PvP: A Masterpiece Ruined by Ping
"The core combat is incredible. The fun comes from the reactions—dodging, parrying, blocking, and the intense back-and-forth slicing. It is so good that it’s almost impossible to find another game that matches it."

However, having played heavily since Season 1, the ping disparity ruins everything. If you have a ping difference of even 20ms, that latency gap will utterly destroy you in high-level play. The developers are clearly aware of this, as they keep announcing that they are working on a fix.

Because of this, you constantly encounter enemies with mismatched animations:

Low-ping players: Their skills and animations register incredibly fast, giving them an unfixable, unfair advantage. Many combos are exclusive to them.

High-ping players: Their animations lag behind and display much slower.

When playing on the SEA server, you literally have to memorize player names just to know what kind of ping you are fighting against. Players from Singapore and Malaysia get the best latency, allowing them to pull off combos that a Thai player like myself simply cannot execute.

There is zero reason for me to stay and suffer through this. Therefore, I cannot recommend this game if you are looking for a competitive PvP experience. I might return if they ever fix the netcode.

What is Left Once the PvE Content Dries Up?
Once you hit the PvE ceiling, you are left with only two real options:

The Casual/Social Route: You play purely for aesthetics and socialization—dressing up, dancing, making trending memes, or trying to find an in-game boyfriend or girlfriend.

The GvG (Guild vs. Guild) Route: This is for people who live for drama, trash-talking, and climbing the ranks with high-tier guilds. The in-game rewards themselves aren't worth it; the game doesn't provide any meaningful item incentives. You have to actively hunt for drama because the only real motivation is the ego trip of wanting to be number one. The 30vs30 battles are highly entertaining, but they come with massive headaches. If you prefer peace and quiet, finding a guild that suits your vibe will be just as challenging as the guild wars themselves.

Bugs, Balancing, and Cash Grabs
None of this even accounts for the bugs—ranging from minor glitches to game-breaking issues—that plague every single patch. Chinese players often say the bugs in this game are like a Hydra: the devs fix one, and three more pop up.

Then there is the weapon balancing. I can tolerate meta shifts, but I'm getting tired of it. The Tang Dao (straight sword) is a prime example of a weapon that is just a bit too overpowered. It makes me wonder if the developers actually understand how to balance a game.

The root cause of all these issues is that this game was originally designed to be an offline title. The developers pivoted it into a semi-online game purely as a cash grab, cramming in bloated content to push microtransactions.

It is such a shame. If they fixed the PvP mode and made it viable, I would gladly dedicate a massive portion of my life to this game. Unfortunately, it is obvious that their development priority is heavily skewed toward PvE and selling skins, which are their main revenue drivers.

But they won't be getting my money. I despise the "Modern Wuxia" style with its blinding, overly vibrant neon colors. I am an old-school Wuxia purist. Since my tastes are in the minority, they rarely get a dime out of me.

One last positive note: the developers seem to be aware of their own game’s limitations. As a result, they adjusted the system so you don't have to spend hours aggressively grinding. This makes it a perfect "side game"—something you boot up just to enjoy the beautiful scenery, run around looking for an in-game marriage partner, or participate in the meme culture that the game desperately tries to push (it’s basically a meme game at this point).

However, that is also a major drawback if you are the type of player who wants to invest serious time into a deep farming loop. If you're expecting to find rare, extraordinary, or prestigious rewards from your grind, you won’t find them here.

Honest Review After 2,000+ Hours

After playing this game for more than 2,000 hours, I want to share my honest feelings.

At first, I really enjoyed the game. The story was interesting, the world felt alive, and there were many activities, events, achievements, and side content to explore. These are the good points, and they are the reason I kept playing for so long.

However, if you are thinking of spending money on this game, I think you should be careful.

The biggest problem is that the game ties your progress too strongly to weekly limits. Important materials for tuning, attuning, upgrading, and improving gear are limited. Once you run out, you cannot really keep progressing properly. You are forced to wait.

The gear system also becomes very frustrating. Farming for better gear takes time and energy, but even after opening many gear chests, you can still end up with nothing useful. It feels like bad rolls happen far more often than good ones. You keep getting stats that do not fit your build, and because farming is limited by energy, every bad roll feels even worse.

What makes it more tiring is that every time a new gear tier comes out, the cycle starts again. You may spend a long time building your character and finally feel strong in one patch, only for the next update to make your progress feel weak or outdated. Then you have to grind, reroll, and rebuild again.

After so many hours, this does not feel rewarding anymore. It feels exhausting. The game has many good ideas, but the progression system makes players feel trapped instead of excited. I wanted to enjoy improving my character, but now it often feels like I am fighting against the system more than enjoying the game.

So my honest advice is: enjoy the story and the activities if you like the game, but think carefully before spending money. The more seriously you care about gear and performance, the more frustrating the weekly limits, RNG rolls, and repeated gear resets may become.

i "bought" this game… oh wait, it's free, my bad. but seriously, for a free game the production values are embarrassing for some AAA studios. the cutscenes are actually directed with a cinematic eye, the voice acting (in Chinese at least) is genuinely good, and the world is packed with hand-crafted content instead of the procedural filler you get in a lot of open world games these days.

started this completely blind, didn't know anything about wuxia or the setting, and i'm obsessed. the game does a good job of letting you discover the world at your own pace — there's a main story to follow but you can completely ignore it for hours and just explore, and the game rewards you for doing so. the combat is genuinely difficult in a fair way
the clothing and character customization options are actually kind of absurd (in a good way). the level of detail you can get with the face sculpting tools is genuinely impressive.
i was skeptical because free-to-play MMO-RPGs have a terrible track record, but this one actually respects your time.

this game is beautiful and i'm tired of pretending it's not. the art direction is so clearly inspired by wuxia cinema — think Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon, House of Flying Daggers — and they've executed it with genuine care. the soundtrack is also underrated, it's not just generic "eastern sounding" filler music, there are actual leitmotifs and the combat music ramps up properly during boss fights. the fact that you can adjust the difficulty on certain bosses if you're stuck is a nice accessibility touch. the gacha system for cosmetics is a bit stingy with drop rates but honestly it's all optional and the base game gives you plenty to work with. if you're on the fence because it's "another chinese MMO," give it a genuine try, it's not what you think.

the narrative design in this game is secretly outstanding and i don't think enough people are talking about it. the main story is told through multiple perspectives — you're not just the hero, you're also seeing snippets of what's happening with other characters in different parts of the world, and it all converges in a way that actually makes you care about the larger conflict, not just your own personal quest. the side content is also way better than it has any right to be for a free game — there are side quests that hit harder emotionally than full-price RPGs i've played this year. the combat has a proper learning curve and doesn't hold your hand, which i appreciate. my one criticism is that the game could do a better job explaining its systems to new players, the tutorial is a bit of an info dump, but push through it and it opens up.

There's always something over the next hill or around the next corner, and the game does a good job of making you feel like the world existed before you showed up and will continue after you leave. the NPC routines, the day/night cycle actually affecting gameplay, the way shops close at night — it's environmental storytelling that most games just don't bother with anymore. combat is challenging but fair, and the fact that you can adjust the difficulty on certain bosses if you're stuck is a nice accessibility touch. negative: the community in global chat is mostly unbearable, just mute it and enjoy your game.

Beautiful. Immersive. Massive.

It's hard to believe Where Winds Meet is free.

The first thing that stands out is the world itself. The graphics are stunning, with beautiful environments that feel detailed, cinematic, and alive. More than once, I found myself stopping just to take in the scenery.

What impressed me even more was the scale. Just when you think you've seen everything, the game opens up with new locations, mechanics, side activities, hidden areas, combat styles, and story moments. There's always something new to discover.

Despite its size, the game never loses its relaxing atmosphere. Exploration feels rewarding, the music fits perfectly, and the world encourages you to slow down and enjoy the journey rather than rush through it.

The story is another pleasant surprise. It gives you a reason to care about the world, while the combat, movement, and exploration all come together to create a polished and engaging experience.

The biggest question I kept asking myself was, "How is this free?" It genuinely feels like a premium AAA title.

If you enjoy open-world RPGs, Where Winds Meet is absolutely worth playing.

1k Steam Hours and similar on official client (around 2k total hours), and i can say this is a good game no doubt, but the flaws are really hard to avoid.

The main issue being that: The Connection is very server based and proximity to the server plays a dramatic role in performance, especially in pvp. 
The Fix: Pay a monthly subsciption to GeForceNow, or move. 

For F2P with overpriced cosmetics, monthy fund, and battlepass, it is expensive to get true quality of life in this game, running about 35$ CAD in monthly expenses, as well as 30$ CAD in battlepasses per season (they do a 2 part, there is no refunding currency to purchase future passes.)

If you want to look good look at spending hundreds because gatcha cosmetics are better but insane. Its a few hundred $ CAD for hair lol, unless youre like really lucky. Even then its like 30-40$ CAD for some of the cosmetics that arent gatcha. Rerolling a weapons color is so expensive we wont talk about it. 

The Content: Great campaign. period. It is well done. Very engaging, good looking world. Well devised combat systems. The bosses can be challenging, as they should be. 

The biggest turn off: The game has tonnes of content pre planned on cn servers. Lazy developement allowed us to experience the same bugs and exploits, which they later fixed in Chinese game version.
 To clarify, they had already worked out and fixed the bugs, but rather than deploying patches to the older game version, they allowed us to play through thier same mistakes, even though they had devised fixes. 
When the player base was eventually bored of waiting for them to step up, assuming they had planned to fix things as we got them, and not later when the next patch came out, majority of the 2-300k daily players stopped waiting for them. 

This game boasts a daily 10-20k players and leans in and out of the top 100, when it could have stayed top 25 if they had just gone through the game and tweaked a few things before releasing it, and updated patches to contain the fixes before they deployed. 

Simply put, we still dont have the game we saw when it was announced. Most gamers looked to the CN version and saw clips and videos of the gauntlets like 5 months ago. We have them now, but we dont have the 200k+ players who saw and waited and waited. 

Xbox support was JUST added.... 8 months later. 
That was a huge mistake, and missed opportunity. 

All together like like a 6.5/10 because of the devs neglect... Could have been an 8.5, and maybe it still has a chance. 

There are just serious flaws that were avoidable, but arent now. Curious how/if the game will recover.

I think what stands out most isn't any single feature.

It's how naturally everything blends together.

The movement encourages exploration.

Exploration leads to stories.

Stories lead to new locations.

New locations make you want to keep moving.

The game has flaws, absolutely.

I've complained about the UI.

I've complained about repetitive content.

I've complained about various design decisions.

But despite all that, I keep finding myself logging back in.

Not because I need to.

Because I want to.

In an era where so many games feel designed around retention metrics, that's a surprisingly refreshing feeling.

The more I play, the less I care about progression.

That's probably the strangest thing about my experience with this game.

Usually I'm chasing levels, gear, upgrades, or some number going up.

Here, some of my favorite sessions involve accomplishing almost nothing.

I'll spend an hour climbing around a city.

Another hour wandering through the countryside.

Maybe stumble into a quest.

Maybe not.

And somehow I still feel like I had a good time.

That's not something I can say about many online games.

Most online games make me feel like I should always be optimizing my time.

This one occasionally reminds me that it's okay to just enjoy being there.

One thing I really appreciate is that exploration rarely feels like a waste of time.

In many open-world games, once you've seen the pattern, you know exactly what you're going to find behind every corner.

Another chest.

Another collectible.

Another icon on the map.

Here, I often explore simply because I'm curious.

Sometimes I find a useful reward.

Sometimes I find a hidden area.

Sometimes I find absolutely nothing.

And weirdly enough, I'm okay with that.

Going into this game as someone who doesn't normally play wuxia games, I expected to feel completely lost.

Instead, what surprised me most was how approachable the world felt.

I don't know every historical reference. I don't know every martial arts term. But I never felt like the game required me to.

What carried the experience for me was the atmosphere.

The villages feel lived in. The roads feel like they connect actual places rather than just points on a map. Even when I'm not actively doing content, I enjoy being in the world.

That's a difficult thing to explain because it doesn't show up on feature lists.

Nobody advertises ""good atmosphere"" as a gameplay mechanic.

But it's the reason I've spent dozens of hours here.

There are better combat systems out there.

There are better stories out there.

Yet somehow this is one of the few games lately that keeps pulling me back.

I think the biggest compliment I can give this game is that it constantly distracts me from whatever I originally logged in to do.

I'll start my session planning to finish a questline, then I'll notice something interesting in the distance, climb over a few rooftops, find a random NPC, get pulled into another story, and completely forget what I was doing in the first place.

That's a feeling I haven't had in many open-world games lately. Too many games are built around checklists and efficiency. This one occasionally feels comfortable letting you waste your own time, and I mean that in the best possible way.

Is everything amazing? Not really. Some activities become repetitive after a while. The interface could be cleaner. There are definitely moments where the game feels rough around the edges.

But when I'm looking back at my time spent here, those aren't the things I remember.

I remember standing on rooftops at night.

I remember getting lost in places I wasn't supposed to be exploring yet.

I remember seeing something weird and deciding to go investigate.

That's what keeps me playing.

The game isn't trying to reinvent open worlds.
It just does a lot of little things well, and together they add up.

There are definitely flaws.
But unlike many games I've dropped this year, this one keeps giving me reasons to come back.

I don't think this game will be for everyone.
If you only care about rushing progression, you'll probably get bored.

After three full playthroughs of the palace area, I want to share some hard-earned exploration tips and a few suggestions for the development team.

The exploration progress system in the palace is more nuanced than it appears. Don't just rush from point A to B — the hidden discovery threshold is tied to how many unique NPC interactions you trigger, not just locations visited. I missed several secret rooms on my first run because I didn't talk to enough servants in the outer court. Talk to everyone, especially the ones that seem like background characters.

For the stealth sections, here's a crucial tip that took me way too long to figure out: guard dogs can be distracted by throwing items into specific directions, but they have a detection cone that most players don't notice. Approaching from their blind spot at a 45-degree angle while crouched gives you a massive window compared to a direct approach. The palace rooftop routes are not just for show either — they connect areas that would otherwise require sneaking through heavily guarded corridors.

Night exploration is genuinely the best time for discovery. Between 11pm and 3am in-game, several NPCs move to different locations and trigger unique dialogue. The court musician near the inner garden plays different melodies at night that hint at hidden quest triggers. Found two secret areas this way that I completely missed during daytime play.

Developer suggestions: first, please add a compass or minimap indicator for incomplete exploration in each palace zone. The current system makes it very hard to tell what you've missed without external guides. Second, the investigation board is great but could use a filter system for different quest lines. When you have 20+ active clues across multiple storylines, it becomes cluttered. Third, consider adding a palace journal that auto-records NPC dialogue summaries — the lore here is incredible and players will want to reference it later.

Cannot recommend this game in good faith to anyone.  It had incredible potential as an open-world exploration title with the immersive elements of the Jianghu in its writing and mechanics.  Character design and opportunities for multiplayer interaction are enjoyable and there is endless exploration potential.

As the game progresses, the level cap increases with live-service updates.  If you take a break, there are useful mechanics to help you catch up, but it does not save this game from its MMO power-scaling system that is bound to strip most of your friendlist due to how grindy the game gets.  Gameplay to improve your builds also gets repetitive after a while, and the new raids that come out are very time consuming.  Worse, they come with a plethora of mechanics bound to make any casual player encounter hours of team wipes without understanding why.  Raids end up being content you have to externally study for like its a dadgum exam.  

The problem is that exploration is endless, with virtually no hope for completion (100% of an area) in sight with the sheer amount of different tasks and interations.  Combat is fun and blends well together, although ping differences make pvp gamemodes some of the least pleasant parts of the game, especially closer to launch when international players were still contained in one server.  There is a nice element of humor in quest writing and events, although after a certain point it starts to come across as quite forced given its similarities to other mobile gacha titles.  On the note of gacha, this game has some of the more predatory monetization with limited banners.  Certain limited gacha outfits can reach prices exceeding $800, which is certainly a relative cost for some who equate it as a luxury purchase for those with the means.

I am not entirely opposed to spending in free to play video games as a way to support developers.  However.  This game continuously and exceedingly relies on AI for its content, which is something I cannot find any significant discussion about online.  Player profile picture options, NPC interactions, content generation for in-game forums, etc.  All of it.  If this was not enough, the game continues to encounter many basic gameplay and visual glitches signifying a lack of polish despite the outrageous monetization pricing metric.  I cannot think of a game deserving of a limited-time spending of $800, but it certainly would not be this game.  Outfit designs are good, but the graphics quality does not necessarily do it justice, ludicrous spending requirements aside.  

While purchases in this game are purely cosmetic, I do not think that remotely qualifies as an excuse for pricing such as this, especially in this economy.  It sets a bad precedent to make players think that $800 for glitched assets with notable overlap to other cosmetics is somehow "reasonable" or "worthwhile."  

Monetization aside, I love open-world exploration.  This game made me hate exploring.

My experience with Where Winds Meet was honestly exhausting, and not for the reasons a PvPvE game should be. I came into the game as a longtime Naraka: Bladepoint player. While Naraka still has some of the best melee combat available, the increasing number of bots has made ranked and competitive play feel less meaningful. Seeing that Where Winds Meet came from the same developer and advertised real-player PvP with ranked progression immediately got my attention. Unfortunately, actually reaching that content turned into one of the most frustrating grinds I've experienced in recent years.

The biggest issue is the sheer amount of story content standing between a new player and competitive PvP. The game constantly interrupts progression with lengthy dialogue scenes, cutscenes, quests, and exposition. Even playing every conversation at 3x speed, I found myself repeatedly staring at dialogue boxes instead of actually playing the game mode I downloaded it for. After a while it felt less like an RPG adventure and more like a series of roadblocks preventing access to the content I was interested in.

What makes this even worse is how important progression is for PvP preparation. Unlike many competitive games that provide equalized loadouts or separate PvP progression systems, Where Winds Meet requires players to unlock and equip various Mystic Skills and abilities through the PvE world. On paper this sounds like it creates a sense of progression, but in practice it means anyone interested primarily in PvP is forced into dozens of hours of PvE content before they can compete effectively.

I tried following multiple YouTube guides from experienced players to speed up the process. The problem is that many of these guides assume you already have large portions of the map unlocked or have progressed significantly further through the main story. Time after time I would find a guide showing a powerful Mystic Skill only to discover the area wasn't accessible yet, requiring several more hours of story progression before I could even attempt to obtain it. Then, once I finally reached the location, I would often be met with additional quests, puzzles, or side objectives before gaining access to the reward.

This creates a particularly frustrating situation for competitive players. The game effectively tells you that PvP is available, but then places a massive PvE grind in front of it. The result is that you're not only learning combat mechanics but also worrying about whether you've unlocked the correct skills, completed the right side quests, found the right collectibles, or progressed far enough into the story to remain competitive.

The strange part is that this problem could be solved if PvP operated as a separate progression environment. If players entered ranked modes with standardized gear, equalized Mystic Skills, or a dedicated PvP progression system, then the lengthy campaign would feel optional and enjoyable for those who want it. Instead, the current design ties competitive viability directly to PvE progression, turning what should be an exciting climb into ranked PvP into a mandatory checklist of story missions, exploration tasks, and unlock hunts.

After roughly 10 hours, I felt like I had barely scratched the surface of what was required to properly prepare for ranked play. Looking at guides and community discussions, it seemed there were still another 20 hours or more of campaign progression, skill hunting, and world exploration ahead of me before I could confidently say my character was fully equipped. At that point I had to ask myself whether I was actually having fun or simply grinding through content to reach the game I wanted to play.

The combat itself shows promise, and the idea of a large-scale martial arts PvPvE experience is genuinely appealing. However, the decision to lock so much player power behind story progression and world exploration severely hurts the experience for anyone whose primary interest is competitive PvP. Instead of feeling excited to queue for ranked matches, I felt trapped in an extended tutorial that refused to end. For players who love RPG progression and exploration, this design may work. For players looking to jump into serious PvP competition, it's one of the game's biggest flaws.

After a long shader compile I got to the main menu with 400+ FPS.  I checked graphics settings and v-sync is on (165hz display).  It's already set on ultra, I have a 5070ti.  Oh well let's go.  The intro starts, and right away it's lagging, choppy.  Impossible to get immersed.  There's no way to go to the main menu, or pause and change settings.  There's not even a way to quit apart from alt-f4 or end task.  So I kill the game and reload it.  v-sync is still not applying.  I turn off v-sync and cap the fps at 60.  It's on fullscreen, so I check for a windowed borderless mode to see if performance is different, no such option there.  I fire up the game again, pickup up where I left off.  Same choppy laggy stuff.  

I get to the part of the game (the very start) where you find out that it's going to be a linear cinematic style game that just tells you to spam some random controller button, or in my case keyboard or mouse button, in order to pass any given obstacle.  Alt-F4.  I'm not looking for a cutscene game sprinkled with cognitive reflex tests.

I will admit I didn't give the game a chance in terms of it's creative content, but it's hard to get past the fact that it fails to be a PC game right out of the gate.  Every option in the main menu is an icon, with no description..no mouseover even.  a box with lines on it, that's the EULA, a globe with arrows on it... internet?  AOL Mail?  who knows....What do all these buttons do...who knows.  The graphics settings consist of presets only, ie: low, medium, high, ultra; along with vsync, motion blur.  No granular control.  vsync doesn't function.  no distinct borderless window and fullscreen settings.  The fact that motion blur is so prominently presented in a void of other typical settings kind of says it all, the game is apologizing for itself early.  Even with ultra settings, the game look like an unbalanced mix of high and low res textures.  Like you won't notice that the ground is just some 8-bit unblended repetitive texture if your attention is on the extreme bump mapped fidelity of the characters clothing.  There's an overwhelming feel of a console game poorly ported to PC here.

Can I keep tinkering?  Lower my preset setting, find config files and make manual adjustments for things not in the menu (like...everything)?  Maybe.  Is it worth my effort to watch anime while testing my reaction time?  Na.  This game might be for you, but it's not for me.

This game is just a well-dressed mobile game, but of the worse kind. When you first start playing Where Winds Meet, everything is incredibly overwhelming. There are menus inside menus, with even more menus inside those. While some parts of the story can be skipped, you can't skip anything else. Even if you just want to let a cutscene play out, it occasionally pauses to make you press a button to continue, forcing the player to pay attention to the mind-numbingly boring dialogue.

If this were the game's only issue, I wouldn't even complain, but the amount of lag and bugs is out of this world.

Interestingly, they managed to fix the latency issues on their own Chinese servers, but they leave global players to suffer. They have promised multiple times to fix things and take action, but what they are actually doing is pushing skin sales at full steam. The game is about nothing else but buying skins; the moment you log in, the latest available skin is thrown right in your face. There isn't really any endgame content either, so all you're left with is dealing with skins, because, well, that's all you see.

The events are also quite short and are always time-gated to control when the next part unlocks, regulating exactly when you can play.

It's rare to see such a massive joke of a game. I was really looking forward to it because it seemed promising, but the devs don't care about anything other than your wallet.

Honestly, I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone. Even though it's free-to-play, the content isn't all that captivating, and the monetization is unbelievably shameless. But they are a Chinese company, so we shouldn't expect anything else—and by this, I mean NetEase Games, because they have multiple games that ended up the exact same way. They get hyped up at the beginning, then they ruin them with their greedy monetization, and then they move on to the next game. This is exactly what happened with Once Human and Fragpunk, and now Where Winds Meet is next.

This is the first time I've tried a game of this type, a free-to-play game, and I didn't really enjoy it. It's just not my genre. I usually only play single-player games, but it was recommended to me, so I decided to give it a try and see what it was like.

The combat seemed good from what I played, although it looks like it's quite deep and offers a lot of different combinations and build options.

I wouldn't recommend this game to someone like me who mainly plays single-player games, but if you're curious about it, I encourage you to give it a try. It's free, after all.

This is easily one of the worst gaming experiences I’ve had. While the game receives a lot of praise for its combat, its monetization model is deeply problematic and feels predatory to a degree that arguably conflicts with Steam’s policies.
A good example illustrates the issue. I’m blonde in real life and wanted to reflect that in-game—something you’d expect to be simple. Instead, the process is buried behind a three-layer currency system, which ultimately feeds into a low-odds, gambling-style mechanic. There’s no direct or transparent way to get what you want—you’re effectively forced to rely on chance.
Realistically, obtaining something as basic as blonde hair would cost in the range of $150–$200. What’s worse is that this isn’t made clear upfront. The multilayered currency system obscures the true costs until you’ve already started spending money. Fortunately, I did some research early and limited my spending to around $30, but even that felt like a loss.
I rarely say this, but the experience left me uncomfortable with how certain options are gated in ways that feel uneven and unnecessarily difficult. Regardless, the broader issue is the lack of transparency and the reliance on exploitative mechanics.
I can’t honestly recommend this game to anyone.

Amazing game with a lot to love—PvP, Guild War, PvE, all of it is great. I genuinely enjoy the PvP even while playing on 150ms+ ping.

The only major issue is that this game is far too dependent on ping. In WWM, even your skill feels tied to your latency, which is a serious problem because not everyone lives near the game server. Players close to the server can get single-digit ping (like 5ms), and that creates a massive advantage. Even a difference between 5ms and 40ms feels like night and day. In many cases, a 5ms player will beat a much better 40ms player simply because of the latency gap. That’s unfair; your location of birth shouldn’t determine the outcome of a competitive match.

I’ve played many online games, and I’ve never seen ping matter this much. Sure, latency matters in every multiplayer game, but not to the extent where such a relatively small difference completely decides matches.

From what I’ve heard, WWM’s netcode is one of the weakest parts of the game. It seems the game was originally designed mainly for the Chinese market, where server proximity made ping less of an issue. But with the global release, this became a major problem. They obviously can’t place servers in every country, so the poor netcode became impossible to ignore.

WWM might have one of the best PvP concepts ever made, but also one of the worst multiplayer networking implementations I’ve seen. Fixing this won’t be easy; rewriting netcode is an enormous task, almost like rebuilding a major part of the game from scratch. But if they want the game to thrive competitively, they need to address it.

They should look into networking solutions used by other top competitive games. For example, Street Fighter 6 uses rollback netcode, Path of Exile and World of Warcraft use client-side prediction, and games like Valorant and Counter-Strike 2 use lag compensation to make online matches feel much fairer for players with different ping.

If they solve this issue, WWM could genuinely become one of the best PvP games ever made.

At first this seemed like a pretty solid game with ARPG elements baked into it, and plenty of things to explore and discover. However, you'll hit a huge brick wall for progression due to the time-gating of currencies and other resources, like daily Energy and Stamina amounts. Once you're in the endgame for farming, you'll only play for a few minutes every few days due to these constraints once they replenish a bit.


The Inner Ways (big damage abilities) will require a significant amount of specific "currencies" but are mostly acquired through gacha mechanics, so if you're unlucky, you're going to take forever to actually gain any real progress in that department.


Also, the overwhelming amount of menus and submenus buried within the (arguably) intentionally confusing UI is just a complete mess. I don't know how many hours it took me to actually get a feel for the menus, because half the time I was navigating through them, I'd forget what the hell I was doing or looking for in the first place.


If you want a game where your time is actually valued and you can make meaningful progression, play ANYTHING else.

Honestly, not a bad game. Gacha game, $50 outfits, yeah. Gacha game. 
Not many games dive into an ancient Chinese world, with the mythology, magic, and culture to match. It's been a really cool and unique experience game-wise for this suburbian American. Now, points are docked for the Gacha, if you want really any cool suits or skins, be ready to pay for them. I prefer games where if there ARE things behind a paywall, they're also reasonably retrievable after some grinding or looting. This game doesn't do that. That aside, The world feels big and expansive, and like people truly live in it. You can really get to understand the Lore of the characters and why this place is here or that person is that way, if you have time to keep track of all that. Honestly, this game feels very similar in structure and style to Genshin Impact in lots of ways, so if you like Genshin, I think you'd like this.

HOWEVER. My goodness, the input lag for no reason sometime. I can forgive random switches or button inputs where I can just re-input or wait. But on the bosses? No, I need frame-perfect inputs. I like games where when I am defeated, I realize that the weakest link in the chain is me (Hollow Knight, Doom, Mario Odyssey, etc)- I just need to improve my skill. This game doesn't make me feel like that. The times I died, I felt like I was cheated. Such as, mashing E at least half-a-dozen times within the obvious "CLICK E TO DEFLECT" prompt you get in fights, and it NOT REGISTERING AS A DEFLECT. Is it my keyboard? Well, the keys have no delay anywhere else, like writing this 'e' filled sentence. Is it my PC lagging? No, It can usually max out a game like Batman: Arkham Knight, raytracing and all. But in case that was it, I was running lowest display settings and STILL the input lag persisted. Seems like the game is just poorly optimized. 
Now, lots of other aspects of this game, are pretty good. the Sound guys did an INCREDIBLE Job. Music is maybe the best I've ever heard in a videogame, really ups the atmosphere, like Helldivers II. The world? Looks phenomenal. The pacing? Slow, but I don't mind it. There's always something going on so it doesn't feel stagnant.
Honestly, without the input lag, this game is a solid 6/10. -4 for being an obvious gacha. WITH the input lag, It makes me want to forgo the 12 hours I've already put in and never play again. Will I? Probably.

TLDR: this game has dailly caps and rng heavy gear grind that leads to it feeling like a job where every day you hop on to do nothing but grind making it a missarable experience

The base game is fine i trully wish i could recomend it since i've been having a blast with hunting bosses on legend difficulty thanks to it having solid combat/great bosses

The real issue is the grind for the gear, you can get around 25 gear pieces a day due to energy cap (+20 from grinding) out of these only a couple will be of the max quality and then even fewer will actually be usefull for your build due to gear type/set, so out of the around 50 drops you will likelly only get 1 thats good for your build, and after days of grinding to finally get a good gear set (not great just good) guess what? now you hit the breakthrough so you can level up and your gear is obsolete This means that its time to go back to the grind what a great experience.

Not only that but you can't even enjoy hunting bosses since they level up to your level, meaning if you level up you will be too weak to beat even the first boss thanks to your ex gear set being a paperweight, so once you get past the level cap you cant fight the bosses anymore until you reach the current level cap and grind the best gear for it which would take ages. 

For reference in my 70 hours i reached lvl 60 (which was the cap) killed half the bosses (had to stop once i reached lvl 50 due to the above issue) and had yet to actually get a single full set of gear, the closest i got(after 2 weeks of dailly gear grinding) was 1 full set and 2 half sets with 2 of the gear pieces being of lower quallity/level for the set bonus.

I was playing the game on max difficulty (Legend) and killed all but 2 bosses i've met (last 2 being Tian Ying and Wolf Maiden who were the hardest of the starting area) when i tried to do the wolf i was struggling a bit and thought that leveling up to 50 would make her easier instead she got a massive stat boost making a gap that could only be closed by min-maxing, maxing out everything except the gear rarity/level and sets still had me doing less than before the level up which is why i quit, this game is like a Sisyphus simulator and every level up is you letting the rock slide down to the start, Meaning this game is either a grind fest or a game where you shouldn't level up

Where Winds Meet is honestly one of the biggest surprises I’ve had in gaming lately. A massive, beautiful, free-to-play open world with great combat, fun exploration, and a mix of solo, co-op, and MMO elements that somehow actually works.

PROS:
+ Free to play, but feels huge and premium
+ Big, beautiful world with tons to explore
+ Exploration is actually fun, not just filler
+ Awesome combat with great bosses and enemy variety
+ Genius mix of solo play, co-op, and MMO-style features
+ Lots of activities, mini-games, quests, side missions, and online content
+ Co-op is integrated really well with matchmaking, direct teleports, and easy grouping
+ Talking to NPCs with typed conversations is very innovative
+ Fun storylines and side quests
+ The first MMO-ish game I’ve genuinely liked in years
+ Western game makers should take notes

CONS:
- Can lag sometimes, especially with cross-server play enabled
- There is almost too much to do, so it’s easy to lose track of your goal
- Personal nitpick: I don’t love the “run around and grab shiny herb/stone nodes” gathering loop; I wish it felt a bit more realistic

Overall: an amazing free-to-play game and easily one of the most impressive open-world experiences I’ve played in a long time.

Okay so off the bat, its like a Red Dead Redemption except set in Medievil China. It has soulslike elements. Its CO-OP + PVP with MMO elements. Theres housing, guild wars, crafting, doctors, ♥♥♥♥ talking (yes a ♥♥♥♥ talking minigame), lots of ways to customize your character. Several playstyles (want to heal? you can be a healer). The monetization is almost entirely gatcha based cosmetics with only a few little "helping" things here and there. Anyone could play this without dropping a buck and access all the content just fine.

The first 2 regions are huge on their own with loads of side quests and little hidden things to discover, sets a nice tone. Then when you get into the 3rd region woah. Its easy to lose yourself exploring, talking to NPCs, finding hidden things to loot/kill. There are quests that trigger at certain times of the day, or from talking to a specific NPC. So much stuff to collect that anyone who likes to 100% a game is going to have a hard time here.

The general vibe of the game is its brutal, silly and doesnt take itself too seriously. There are moments that may capture you, or you may just want to smash that skip button and get to the guts.

You can totally solo the game, and not notice the MMO side. There are things which will draw you into MMO moments, like PVP or needing to be healed, but for the most part its not too invasive and you can opt in and out of the MMO side as you please.

Now as for the network.... I am in Australia and sometimes the game can be a lagfest in PVP. I understand that they are improving the network and adding nodes in more countries to reduce latency. I guess we will see, but I have enjoyed PVP/MMO part of the game a lot. 

I can see this game being one I log into regularly for years. I have had an Elden Ring sized hole in my chest for a while... its nice thats been filled with this game which also has the bonus of being seamlessly online. 

Lets hope its not some flash in the pan cash grab that fades out.

LINUX USERS: enabling NTSYNC helps a lot for running this smoothly. It does require some tweaking based on your system.

I love this game, much more than I initially expected to. The story and characters are intriguing and have substance and no pointless yapping but are still expansive and interesting. The graphics and optimization are top-notch (runs quite well on my mid-range PC from 2017), excluding the size of the game, which is only to be expected, given its size and content density. The gameplay is very fun too, with a plethora of satisfying weapons and martial arts and more fantastical skills you can pull off. Overall, it's a very unique and charming experience that combines Action-RPG elements (e.g. Witcher 3, Ghost of Tsushima, later Assassin's Creed titles), with MMORPG elements (e.g. PSO2/NGS, FFXIV), anchored in Chinese history and Wuxia aesthetic.

And for the elephant in the room, yes, it's free to play. Yes, it has a Gacha system, but it's almost exclusively for cosmetics, and its rates suck. It's hard to complain though, with the actual game being fully free and not pay to win at all. There's some cosmetics that are crazy expensive, though, so aspiring whales beware. It's worth a try, at least. And there's plenty of good reasons to stay. Also the community is very welcoming, which is always a positive for MMO-style games. Another cool option is the ability to play either online or solo; pick and choose as you like, whenever you like.

Note: I haven't played a staggering amount of hours, and I'm pretty early on in the story still, since I'm a busy adult and I started playing recently, but I'll keep updating this review if I find something worth mentioning (e.g. endgame).

I am only reviewing this as a Solo-mode player, and I will say it delivers an amazing single-player experience. I see a lot of the criticisms seem to come from PVP players, so if you are looking for a single player game, do not be discouraged, you can get so much out of this. I genuinely feel like most of the critiques that I’ve seen for this game are form people who don’t actually want to play the story quests or engage with the world, they just want the multiplayer content, which is not the bulk of the game, and are upset that the game doesn’t solely focus on PVP and multiplayer content.

If you are playing a female character, the English audio will often refer to your character as “Him/He,” even if the text will say “She/Her” (or not having a gender pronoun at all, instead having a blank space). If that is something that might be distressing to you, use the Chinese audio (better voice acting too!) or avoid the game. 

My main gripes as a solo-mode player come from decisions that I believe were made to try and attract a PVP audience. Bosses scale with your level, it is therefore impossible to raise your level and come back to a boss fight later and have an easier time beating them. Additionally, all the weapons classes are weighted for multiplayer use. And with all the different elements you need to build a set of a specific type (gear types, gears of various levels with maxed out stats for passive bonuses, leveling up the weapon skills and mystic skills specific to your gear type). That means that if you find a specific playstyle that works for you, and it’s not the weakness of the boss, you will be at a horrible disadvantage for the fight and changing out your gear will involve days, if not weeks, of playtime to build up the right set, let alone getting used to the new fighting style. It takes so much time because the weapons are locked behind progression systems designed for multiplayer games, not solo-player games, which is a bizarre choice given how most of the quests and storyline are solo-mode content to begin with. Lastly, if you want to join a sect as a solo-mode player (not the same a guild which is the multiplayer thing) to get rewards or just because it feels right to your character, you’ll probably be forced into engaging with multiplayer content if you don’t want to get auto-kicked out after a month. There is also a stock market that heavily incentivise going to other players’ worlds to take advantage of their solo-world stock market prices and other things like that which try to force single-players to engage with the multiplayer content in non-meaningful and annoying ways. 

Other than that, I honestly have no complaints. The writing for the main quest lines blew me away. I am so invested in my character’s journey to the point where I am wearing a mask in certain areas after the end of Act I to stay in character and plan outfits around sentimental outfit pieces. When it comes to quests, the only things that’s found a bit annoying as someone who is invested in my character’s story is the fact that it’s very easy to do quests “out of order” so to speak, which leads to confusing moments when the game assumes you know some lore and you don’t, or your character is going around saying their full name and where they’re from when it’s now supposed to be information they’re trying to hide. Or characters will refer to a situation that you have solved or be coy about information that you have already learnt. It is a bit frustrating, but I do understand that it gives the player a lot more freedom to run around and mess about in the world. 

I do not understand all the critiques that the quests do not have good rewards. There is so much lore to uncover in the world, even talking to characters can unlock lore nodes. I also love the Wandering Tales, which rely on you paying attention to what the characters are saying instead of just following quest marker blindly. Additionally, this game implements character stats that go up as you collect oddities (the main secret collectibles of the game). These stats will allow you to use advanced gear better, unlock passive skills, and the collectibles can be exchanged for more health, skill improvements, and some outfit pieces. In most games, they are types of collectibles just exist in a “number go up” type of way, and have no actual value to gameplay, so I find that lack of reward critique absolutely wild. I would assume they mean lack of multiplayer specific rewards. Everything you do in this game will reward you with lore, skill progression, etc. Even running around has the chance of triggering Encounter quests if the right conditions have been met, so it is worth it to travel in map instead of fast travelling. 

One feature I would love to see if taking care of horses. Riding horses is so satisfying, and I love travelling the world on horseback. The main horse that the game gives you is tied to the story and is thankfully protected form being accidentally sold, but it has zero stats for good travelling. Since there is already a house/base building mechanic, I would love to be able to build a stable and make a little home for Clip-Clop, so I know he’s doing well and safe while I am off on adventures with the beefy black horse I tamed in the wilderness (I also LOVE the horse taming feature, so much fun, there is a lot of potential here for a horse game if the devs implement a few things). 

If you are playing on the Steam Deck, the Quinghe area runs okay, but the other two areas (Kaifeng and Hexi) are too much for it.

Lastly, this game is free, so you have nothing to lose trying it out.

It's honestly with a heavy heart that I write this. There are many good things about this game: combat feels great and is a lot of fun, the amount of minigames and paths you can take is astounding, and the world really feels alive. However, ultimately for me what matters the most is storytelling. And this sadly is all over the place so much that ultimately is why I can't recommend this game.

One issue is tonal inconsistencies - moments of epic wuxia cutscenes are often undermined by very goofy stuff. That alone isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it aggregates with other problems. Second thing is pacing - very uneven. Most NPCs important to the main story often say completely inconsequential blabber, that honestly makes you wonder if any thought was put into writing. I honestly think during development most time was spent on designing the world and combat, and there was little thought about the narrative. On top of this, you get terrible localisation: VAs are great, but it always feels like they were never given any direction; subtitles often don't match the voice lines or are swapped; names don't match between subtitles, names appearing over the character, or names in the quest log (this also includes the names of places, mind you). The recent updates completely throw away the main narrative, instead focusing on flashbacks to small side stories of unknown characters (some of them interesting, but mind you, none of it is important to the main story). Oh and some NPCs are AI chatbots, which is another strange choice. This all compounds together to create the most bizarre and confusing storytelling I have seen in years. On the good side though, there are these larger side missions that were honestly more interesting sometimes than the main story of the game.

This game deserves to be treated like a AAA game, and if you play it with that mindset, you'll see how crazy it is that this game is $0. 

  Similar to traditional $60 games like Zelda, GoW, or The Elder Scrolls, you have a massive open world to explore as you please. If you wanted to beeline the story completion, you'll probably get 10 hours of gameplay and you probably won't have very much fun. The world of WWM is massive and highly interactive; stop and smell the roses and you will be pleasantly surprised.

  One aspect of this game that may put people off are the parts similar to old Zelda games where you need to unlock abilities in order to access new areas or to beat puzzles. Many people will be put off by the lack of instant gratification that they've grown addicted to, but I have had no complaints there.

  This is a 100% free game of unprecedented levels. Even Elden Ring and Genshin Impact (games that boast massive open worlds) have aspects of gameplay that are locked behind a paywall. For Elden Ring, the game is not free, and neither is the DLC. For Genshin Impact, playable characters are locked behind Gacha. WWM locks nothing behind a paywall. All playable weapons, all available locations, all fightable bosses, are all free. Sure COSMETICS cost money, and yes, it's expensive. But that's something I'm willing to give up in exchange for free actual game content. 

  Personally, I have not reached end-game yet, but it doesn't matter. The hours I have gotten are hours that I have enjoyed. To me, the end game just gives you things to chase for and a reason to keep playing after the main content is done.

  Even if this game is not your cup of tea, I want this game to be a success so that future games can learn by example and deliver content to gamers without a ridiculous paywall. I want this game to topple the AAA game devs that have grown comfy pumping out the same $10 sparkly pretty slop with a $70 price tag. Call me an idealist, but I'm really just a poor gamer hoping for greener pastures.

9/10 the game ain't perfect, but the devs certainly want it to get there. That's a lot more than what we can say about most devs with a sizable budget supporting them. I truly hope these devs keep up the good work and keep their F2P monetization model.

TLDR - Treat this as a Sekiro-like singleplayer open world game and it's amazing. Treat it like a pure grind MMORPG, and you will probably get bored. If you're the type to chase leaderboard rankings, this may not be the best game for you.

Title: [Urgent Protest] Logical Contradictions Regarding the Recent PvP Matchmaking Rollback and Shared Leaderboards
Dear Where Winds Meet Development Team,
We are writing to strongly protest the sudden rollback of the unified PvP (Matchmaking) system between the KR/JP and TW/HK/MO servers, which occurred less than a week after its implementation. This abrupt decision has completely ruined the PvP experience for players on the KR/JP server.
We request an immediate review of this decision based on the following undeniable issues:
1. Unplayable Matchmaking Environment
You are fully aware that the KR/JP server has a smaller player base, which was the original reason for the server merge. Since the rollback, queue times frequently exceed 20 minutes. Even when a match is found, players are forced to fight the exact same opponent repeatedly for hours. The PvP mode is currently unplayable.
2. Unfair Operational Precedent
It is clear that this rollback was a panicked response to TW players complaining about "ping differences" and threatening a "boycott of in-game purchases." KR/JP players were also playing with ping disadvantages, yet we embraced the merge for the sake of a healthy matchmaking pool. By caving to the financial threats of one specific region, you have set a dangerous precedent. You are sending a clear message that the gameplay experience of regions with smaller populations does not matter to you.
3. The Fundamental Contradiction of the Leaderboard
This is the most illogical part of your recent update. If you separate the matchmaking pool because of ping issues, meaning we can no longer fight against TW/HK/MO players, why are we still sharing the exact same PvP Leaderboard? It makes absolutely no sense to compete for rankings against a group of players we are physically restricted from playing against.
Our Demands:
	• Revert the matchmaking system back to the unified Asia pool so that we can actually play the game without 20-minute queues.
	• OR, if the matchmaking must remain separated, you MUST separate the PvP Leaderboards. Create a dedicated, independent leaderboard exclusively for the KR/JP region.
We expect a logical and prompt resolution to this severely mismanaged situation.

标题：【强烈抗议】关于亚洲服论剑（PvP）匹配回退及排行榜系统矛盾的诉求
致《燕云十六声》开发团队：
对于近期突然取消韩日服与港澳台服论剑（PvP）匹配互通的决定，我们韩日服玩家表示强烈的不解与抗议。这一决定在不到一周的时间内匆忙做出，已经严重破坏了韩日服玩家的正常游戏体验。
以下是我们认为该决定存在严重逻辑漏洞的三个核心原因：
1. 匹配环境恶化，游戏体验极差
开发团队应该很清楚韩日服玩家基数较小，这正是当初合并匹配池的初衷。而在分离匹配之后，现在我们单次排队时间经常超过20分钟，即使好不容易排到人，也是在一小时内反复与同一个对手交战。目前的论剑系统对我们来说已经处于无法正常游玩的状态。
2. 妥协于部分玩家的威胁，有失公允
很明显，这次的匹配回退是因为部分台湾玩家抱怨“延迟（Ping）差距”，甚至以“拒绝充值”作为集体威胁而促成的。事实上，我们在匹配中也同样承受着延迟的影响。如果开发团队仅仅因为害怕某些地区的充值抵制就放弃了保证健康匹配池的初衷，这将开创一个极其恶劣的先例。这让玩家觉得：“只要基数大、会闹事，就能随意改变规则，而玩家数较少国家的体验根本无关紧要。”
3. 排行榜系统存在根本性矛盾
这是最令人无法理解的一点：既然你们以网络延迟为由，在匹配机制上把我们和港澳台玩家完全隔离开来，让我们彼此无法交战，那为什么 PVP 排行榜却依然把我们放在一起竞争？ 让两群根本无法排到彼此的玩家在同一个榜单上争夺排名，这在游戏逻辑上是完全说不通的。
我们的合理诉求：
	• 恢复亚洲服统一匹配机制，以保证玩家能够正常进行游戏，而不是把时间浪费在无尽的排队上。
	• 如果坚持要分离匹配池，请务必分离排行榜。既然无法交战，就请为韩日服玩家设立独立的论剑排行榜。
我们希望开发团队能够正视这一决策带来的严重不公，并迅速做出符合逻辑的调整。

제목: [강력 건의] 아시아 서버 논검(PvP) 매칭 롤백에 대한 항의 및 랭킹 시스템의 모순 해결 촉구
개발진 여러분,
최근 일주일도 채 되지 않아 갑작스럽게 진행된 한국/일본 서버와 대만/홍콩/마카오 서버의 논검(PvP) 매칭 통합 롤백 조치에 대해 강력한 유감을 표합니다. 이 결정은 현재 한국/일본 서버 유저들의 게임 경험을 심각하게 훼손하고 있습니다.
저희가 이 조치에 대해 납득할 수 없는 세 가지 논리적인 이유는 다음과 같습니다.
1. 게임 플레이가 불가능한 수준의 매칭 환경
한국과 일본 서버의 유저 풀이 적다는 것은 개발진이 가장 잘 알고 있을 것입니다. 매칭 분리 이후, 현재 논검 큐를 돌리면 20분 이상 매칭이 잡히지 않는 것이 기본이며, 간신히 잡히더라도 1시간 동안 똑같은 상대만 몇 번씩 반복해서 만나고 있습니다. 이는 정상적인 PvP 콘텐츠로서의 기능을 완전히 상실한 상태입니다.
2. 형평성을 잃은 운영과 선례
이번 매칭 분리는 대만 유저들의 "핑 차이"에 대한 불만과 "과금 보이콧" 등 집단적인 협박에 가까운 항의에 의해 급조된 패치입니다. 핑 차이로 인한 불편함은 우리 역시 감수하며 플레이하고 있었습니다. 일부 유저들의 과금 중단 압박에 굴복하여 서버 통합의 본래 목적(원활한 매칭)을 훼손한다면, 앞으로 개발진은 더 많고 비합리적인 요구들에 계속해서 휘둘리게 될 것입니다. 이는 유저 수가 적은 국가의 플레이어들을 완전히 기만하는 행위입니다.
3. 랭킹 시스템의 근본적인 모순
가장 이해할 수 없는 것은 랭킹 시스템입니다. 핑 문제로 매칭을 분리하여 서로 싸울 수조차 없게 만들었으면서, 도대체 왜 'PVP 랭킹'은 여전히 대만/홍콩/마카오 유저들과 통합된 상태로 경쟁해야 합니까? 교전이 불가능한 집단과 같은 순위표를 공유한다는 것은 시스템적으로 완벽한 모순입니다.
요구 사항:
	• 논검 매칭을 이전의 아시아 통합 매칭 상태로 원상 복구하여 정상적인 게임 플레이가 가능하도록 조치해 주십시오.
	• 만약 대만 유저들의 반발로 인해 매칭 분리를 끝까지 유지해야 한다면, 반드시 한국/일본 서버만의 독립된 논검 랭킹 보드를 신설해 주십시오.
이 문제에 대한 신속하고 납득할 수 있는 조치를 강력히 요구합니다.

This game has beautiful visuals, and is amazing to play thru if you have a good PC. I attached my PC specs to this review for those of you that are curious as to what my PC specs are. I'm using a SkyTech Azure 3 Custom Gaming PC. For best performance, I recommend running 1920x1080 for PvP, but you can run full native 4K for the full experience with good performance on most everything else with a build like mine. This game had a beautifully in depth storyline, with lots of stunning visuals, fun and very different combinations of fight styles and techniques that can be chosen, and it has a lot to offer players to pass time. Most of the content is time gated, so you have to keep leveling up gear and martial arts skills every so often to keep up with current content. This can be frustrating if you are a heavy grinder that likes to dive in to a game head first and try to make as much progress as fast as you can. On the positive side, this allows most people to not have to worry about having to do as much grinding and upkeep non stop to keep from falling behind other competitive players. The game is still expanding and growing, and it definitely has one of the best storylines of any of the games I have ever played thru; I would rate it up there with being on par with as good as the Halo Game Series and Gears of War game series as far as depth and detail of story. The difference in Where Winds Meet is experiencing the rich culture embedded into the game. I love how they really want to pull at their players emotions with the depth of their stories. Some of the gameplay must be done solo which is one of my biggest complaints along with the gotcha high end gambling for cosmetics system, but some of the stuff can also be done in multiplayer with friends or by friends pairing up on solo world content. Not being able to do all of the storyline in co-op I think is one of the biggest let downs in the game for it being a MMORPG, and they they seem to be making less and less content available for co-op as they have progressed. The developers have been doing a decent job of cleaning up frame rates and patching up buggy mechanics at least though. If you are curious about the PvP aspect of the game, there are several different varieties of PvP. There are ranked 1v1s, ranked 3v3s, there is a battle royale mode, there is bounty hunting, there are vendettas, and there are GvGs on Saturdays and Sundays. Saturday and Sunday GvGs start with the clan's ranked placement matches and then can be extended with more non placement matches. As far as GvGs go, there is still lag even for PC users, but they have been improving the lag by quite a bit and I do not recommend doing GvGs in anything other than 1920x1080 with full low graphic settings. When it comes to difficulty in PvE, this game varies based on what starting difficulty you pick. You can only pick the Legendary difficulty if you pick it when you first start the game; there is no new game plus which I would like to see added, and there is no option to increase the difficulty later. Also no that any purchased cosmetic items are character locked, and you will not have access to them if you start a new character to play thru on a harder difficulty later; keep in mind that some of these cosmetic gotcha outfits can cost anywhere between $600-$900 IRL for a single outfit without playing mix and match. The Mirage Boat is the worst gotcha item of all that is character bound costing the average person somewhere between $45,000-$75,000 IRL. Please keep this in mind if you plan to spend money before picking your difficulty because every one of those items will be character bound. For the record the legendary difficulty is absolutely ridiculous for all you try hard gamers out there that want to sweat and rage at the ai while getting demolished. Legendary definitely reminds me of when I 100% got all the achievements for all the Dark Souls games. I would definitely recommend this game to others, but with a caution to look into how much gotcha cosmetics cost and entail before deciding to gamble any money into them, and I would have to overall rate this game a 4 out of 5 stars with it not getting the 5th star only because the multiplayer feels like it should include campaign and include more online as well as I believe that the gotcha system for cosmetics is drastically overpriced and outrageous.
