This is literally the future of MMO gaming, for better or worse. And since it's free, if you're an enthusiast of Exploration/MMO/Open world genres, I recommend to try it. It's far from a perfect game, mind you - but it does try a lot of experimental things, and gets a noticeable number of them right... or almost right. See below.

Some outstanding features:
 [+++] Customizable experience (controls, difficulty, UI, social features)
 |+++] Ridiculous QoL (tooltips tell how to acquire/use all items, filters on map to see enemy or resource spawns, equipment filtering, auto disassembly, etc)
 [ + ] Simple ARPG combat that is actually 80% optional
 [???] AI chatbot NPCs to up relations. It's barebones and only funny 5 minutes.
 [ + ] AI Voice/Appearance import from external media in char creation
 [ + ] Assisted blocking with slowmo - Optional
 [ - ] Mobile slop monetization, mostly cosmetics
 [+++] Heavily exploration centric game with vibes to match
 [+++] I'm not kidding, you can walk in on bandit outposts and play chess with them
 [---] Menu hell, you spend half of the game in menus unlocking things
 [????????????????] Social feature overload: public gifting, chat transcript, voice chat, in-chat voice chat, you can literally level up your relation with other players, partnerships/disciples system, on-map signs for other players, pre-made raidgroups, guilds (yes, separate), bounty system -- there's more than i could even imagine
 [+++] 2 profession (scholar/healer) both for exploration and group content, also as "mercenary" to help other players (cure them, clear their name, etc)
 [???] PvP invade and kill people that did in fact not clear their name 
 [--]  Bounty systems for the above stuff has insane player competition, i could never find a job for it
 [...] Ramping up flashy main story (feels like Warframe, negative for me but...)
 [ + ] Mobile style boss assistance by other players and Coop mode assistance
 [ + ] Actual full-on online MMO mode, although limited
 [???] There's literally a Voice Changer option in Voice Chat
 
Overall this feels like some kind of Ubisoft MMO prototype from 2032, after they came back from the brink of death and made bank on AI and Mobile gaming. This comes with absolutely ALL the bell and whistles associated, both good and bad.

I can't guarantee you'll like it, especially since in some regards it's really not that good, but it's still largely viable. If anything, I recommend to try it out just to get a feel of all the odd takes and experiments in it.

Rating: Mixed

I’m stuck in a love-hate relationship with this game. The combat mechanics are some of the best I’ve ever played, but the actual systems feel like they’re sucking the life out of the experience. The devs are prioritising the shop and new content over fixing the core bugs.

The Death of the Needle Sect:
Leveling is way too fast, which makes progression feel shallow. It’s baffling that healing is open to everyone at Level 13. Being a top healer should be a status symbol—like owning a rare legendary skin—not a default setting for every random player. It should be EXCLUSIVE to the Needle Sect. If everyone can do it, the role loses all its prestige and respect.

The Board is Cancer (We need a Universal Queue):
The Bounty and Physician boards are just a bot-snatching simulator. You stand there for ages while scripts win every time. We need a Universal Matchmaking Queue for Bounties and Healing.
It should work like a dungeon finder: match us and put us in co-op instantly.
For healing, show the Injury Rating (Tier 1-5) before we accept.
Stop making it a social media popularity contest for "likes." It's a medical profession, not a photo op.

The PVP Stun-Fest:
PVP is a laggy mess because the servers are trash. Inputs don't register, turning skill-based fights into a stun-lock simulator. If you get hit once during a lag spike, you’re stuck until you’re dead. We need better dedicated servers, not "routing" excuses.

Walking Simulator:
The story is mostly just walking. You spend 90% of your time running between fetch-quest markers instead of using the combat system. I want to be a warrior, not a courier.

Verdict: 10/10 potential, but 2/10 management. Fix the foundation before you build the roof.

This is an absolutely amazing game both visually and from a gameplay standpoint considering it is a completely and truly free to play title. (Meaning that even paying doesn't give you an edge in this game. Just pretty looks.) It is however quite a complex nut to crack in terms of explanation because it dips its toes in a lot of varied interests.

The game world is separated into Solo World and Online World. Solo is your own world where you can invite other players if you wish to adventure together. It also changes a few aspects as you progress the story. You are also able to build custom structures in nearly the entire game world of your Solo World which is a great creative outlet for builders!
The combat mostly focuses on parrying with some emphasis on dodging. Difficulty can however make these MUCH easier with accessibility options such as parry assist. And if you do not care for “gamer honor” then you can call in assistance from other players who offer to help you beat the boss.

Character customization focuses mainly on the face with body customization being quite lackluster. In terms of cosmetics there is a pretty nice variety of items even for free players with a TON more in an expensive in-game shop. (With earnable in-game items to get discounts up to 50% off.) If you are into fashion, you will likely enjoy the gallery/photo features where you can create lovely photos or short videos for people to see and enjoy.
PvP seems to be a stunlock-fest but some people seem to enjoy it I guess. Group PvE content is mostly centered around doing big damage numbers while healers do even bigger healing numbers because damagers don’t bother to dodge. These raids also have certain objectives to do during them. Refusing to perform these usually leads to death but generally I do find them enjoyable. There is also no reason for a Tank archetype.

There is a good bit of emphasis on inter-character interaction in this game through Friendship, Partnership, Sworn Cohorts or Sects. Progression in these is done through communication in chat, and playing together. Leveling it up can unlock various new items for purchase and possibly build a positive relationship with other players.
The game also has AI NPC characters which you can befriend by chatting with an AI chatbot and once you befriend them successfully, you will receive weekly gifts from them. This AI use might dissuade some people but I do believe the voicing is also done with AI, but I am not entirely sure. Subtitle text pretty often doesn’t align exactly word-for-word with what is being said by the voice.

There are various Sects in the game where each of them is focused on something else but you can join any one you like and even switch at will. (But if you switch you will be forced to play a Battle Royale mode called Perception Forest as punishment.) They each have their own shops which have various different items based on what the Sect itself is about and also has shop "tiers" based on your tier in the sect. You can usually get yourself to the second highest tier by getting points for doing what your Sect is about. (Healing, Co-op, PvP, PvE, Fashion, Relationships, etc.) Every week from Wednesday to Sunday there is a voting going on where on Sunday the top 10 voted players within a Sect are pushed into the top rank of the Sect until next Sunday. There is usually no way you can achieve the top rank and receive the badge that is tied to this achievement without having to engage with the very bad voting system though so you might dismiss the thought.

There are also various “Leisure Activities” in the game, ranging from board games such as Mahjong or Madaio Cards, strategic friendly wrestling, dung collection or a Wuxian guitar hero called Graceful Melody.

There is a LOT of world content to engage with even as a completely free player and you are given quite a good amount of nice items and resources by the game and ongoing event participation. Plus there have been various new very distinctly different maps released.

The one thing though that severely ruins the game for me and gets me fed up is that EVERYTHING has very low caps with very slow recovery:
- You have an energy limit of 550 that limits how many boss rewards you can claim from group PvE: 60 per claim from a boss and 20 per claim on Outpost clearing. This energy refreshes at a rate of 1 per 8 minutes which means from 0 to full it needs over 73 hours.
- Every relationship track has a weekly limit of 2000 points which can easily be reached in an hour of play.
- Sects use Reputation as a resource for their shop and you are limited by 1500 weekly. But only of the shop resource. Any reputation you gain over this limit still counts towards your Merit points to help advance your rank. You can usually have 1500 points by Wednesday without much issue just so you get an idea of how bad it is.

Everyone (Paid or free) is bound by the same low caps as a method of player retention -which seems to be working- ensuring that players are pretty much forced to pause and return to the game more often and can't just lock-in and have everything from an update done in 20 minutes (metaphorically speaking).

All in all, Where Winds Meet has it’s chips on a lot of different numbers and it does so quite well, where you are free to engage with what you want to engage with. I do believe a very large spectrum of players will find something to enjoy within this game and it is truly worth a shot. (Especially if you’re the type of person who can easily sink thousands of hours into a single game.)

This game is honestly just too deep for me. It feels tailor-made for the type of MMORPG player who loves "doing nothing", those who enjoy getting lost in endless side systems and life-sim fluff rather than a focused narrative.

It’s essentially a much prettier, PC-version of KingsRoad. It offers way more to do and hides its gacha mechanics a bit better, but the DNA is the same. If you want a world to live in and don't mind a grindy loop, you'll love it. For me, it's just a bit too much noise.

Where Winds Meet feels like stepping into a living martial arts movie .... but with the freedom of a massive open world.

Visually, the game is stunning. The landscapes, traditional Chinese architecture, and dynamic weather create a very immersive atmosphere. You can literally get lost just exploring forests, villages, and mountains. It has that calm but powerful vibe .... almost poetic at times.

Gameplay-wise, it mixes open-world exploration with wuxia-style combat, meaning fast, fluid fighting with martial arts techniques, special abilities, and movement that feels light and cinematic. It’s not just about fighting .... you also interact with the world, NPCs, and make choices that shape your journey.

What stands out:

Freedom: You’re not locked into one path ...  you create your own story
Combat style: Smooth, stylish, and very satisfying once you get used to it
Atmosphere: Peaceful but intense at the same time

What could be better:

It can feel a bit overwhelming at the start
Some mechanics aren’t explained super clearly
Depending on the version, performance/optimization may vary

Overall:
If you love open-world games and want something different from the usual Western RPGs, Where Winds Meet is definitely worth trying. It’s not just a game .... it’s more like an experience you slowly sink into.

Rating: 8.5/10

After 200 hours of gameplay, I still believe this game is 10/10. With an absolutely gorgeous game with an epic story and journey through bits of history, emotionally-laden human stories, and a glorious way of storytelling. As a gamer for 40 years, I feel this truly is a one-of-a-kind game in a decade. This game is a treasure trove for those who enjoy an immersive, expansive and ever expanding MMORPG deeply rooted in the history and stories around the many peoples and cultures that coexisted and thrived along the Silk Road / 5 Dynasties & 10 Kingdoms history and the people who lived through it. Everything from the symbolism to architecture, local foods and dialects are truly well-thought out and researched. The architecture and landscapes reflect many real world locations starting from Xi'an (Chang'an) past the Hexi Corridor. Beautiful historical (as well as fantastical) costumes, characters, factions, guilds, sects - can easily get lost if you don't have a) time to invest b) familiarity with these types of games. Highly recommend for those with hyperfocus and ability to go slow (vs not speed-running through a game) and enjoy games like Skyrim and or World of Warcraft. Stunning game, highly recommend we teach history this way.

I went into Where Winds Meet already suspicious of it.

Since Genshin Impact made gacha-style open-world games feel unavoidable, I have bounced off most of them quickly. Big map, too many systems, obvious monetization pressure — not for me. I expected to uninstall this after a few hours.

That did not happen.

Where Winds Meet should be much worse than it is. It has all the warning signs: free-to-play structure, giant map, too many systems, too many menus. And then you actually start playing — sprinting up walls, parrying blades, learning martial arts, wandering into strange side problems — and it works anyway.

[H2] The World [/H2]

The best thing here is how the world feels like it has more going on than the main path can explain.

Qinghe is open and great for wandering. Kaifeng is dense, massive, and detailed enough to feel like a real city. Traversal (Lightness + fast travel) makes movement part of the reward instead of a chore.

It is not just map icons. Sects, reputation, and skills create a sense that knowledge exists socially. Your build feels like a history of what you have found and who you have dealt with.

[H2] Combat [/H2]

Combat is the reason the game holds together.

- Parry-focused, readable, and responsive  
- Not brainless, not overly punishing  
- Strong rhythm that fits the wuxia tone  

Weapons and styles actually change how you play (tank, DPS, support, hybrid). The best fights — especially bosses — narrow everything down to timing and understanding the enemy.

[H2] Side Content [/H2]

There is a lot:

Fishing, cooking, guilds, bosses, chess, mahjong, mini-games, long quest lines, and more.

It is excessive, but it also makes the world feel alive. Not everything is equally strong, but the variety works.

[H2] Too Many Systems [/H2]

The biggest problem is that the game does not trust itself to be simple.

There are systems everywhere: currencies, upgrades, menus, tabs, popups. The core loop is straightforward, but the interface makes it harder to see. Sometimes you feel like you are playing the game. Sometimes you feel like you are managing it.

[H2] Free-to-Play [/H2]

The game handles monetization better than expected.

It shows you the battle pass and cosmetics, but it never felt like progress was blocked. I never hit a hard wall. The suspicion is still there, but it is not constantly annoying.

A paid version would probably be cleaner, but also smaller and less strange.

[H2] Verdict [/H2]

Where Winds Meet is a great game with too much game wrapped around it.

The combat works. The world has texture. The systems give exploration a purpose. Qinghe made me want to wander. Kaifeng made the scale feel real. The menus tested my patience.

I expected to bounce off this. Instead, I kept playing.

4.25 / 5

After about 200 hours on this game (most of my time was on the standalone launcher due to connectivity issues), no, I do not recommend this game. While it looks gorgeous, runs great and nails the "live the wuxia life" aspects, it also uses all the dirty tricks free to play games have in their book to milk customers. While this one's monetization is not too bad (arguably, depends on what you like in the cash shop, really), it doesn't respect your time. Make no mistake, the devs are not in the business of making video games, they are in the business of whaling.

So, credits where it's due, first. This game looks amazing, even at low settings, and runs well on a moderately good machine. You can explore freely, build almost anywhere, solve puzzles, fight in a technical and flashy way, and it has all the wuxia clichés you expect. So far so good.

Unfortunately, once you're past the honeymoon phase, it gets less pleasant. The interface is horrible. I mean, there are menus everywhere, most submenus have submenus, you have rewards to collect in each and no "collect all" buttons, some really important upgrades are barely mentionned... Imagine your average mobile crapgame, then cranks its disgusting interface to 11, and you have Where Winds Meet's interface. To make it worse, there are always at least a couple events going on to add clutter.

I hope you like simple, not too fancy clothes. Those are available for really cheap in the cash shop. And I mean real cheap, like 1 buck, maybe up to 10. If, however, you want to look like an envoy of the spirit realm or some such, either you're gonna shell 35+ bucks per costume, or will have to attempt the gacha. It's easily 600+ bucks if you're not super lucky, from what I'm told. I've never had any interest in those over the top costumes, but hey, some had, and reported the cost. And don't even consider dying your hair in anything but black or deep brown. The dyes alone will cost you more than a non-gacha costume.

Then, martial arts are concieved to be paired VERY specifically. Sure, you can run pretty much anything and make do, but it's really subpar. So either pick a pair of martial arts designed to work together and stick to it, or be a lesser martial artist. There is no real freedom in build, and creativity is severy limited here.

Each martial arts group have a specific damage type. Strategic sword does "bellstrike" damage, for exemple. Not a single umbrella style does "bellstrike". So of course you can roll any type of damage on any type of weapons, which means you can end up with "bellstrike" damage on an umbrella. And you can only reroll ONE stat, once per weapon. Which means that if you want a weapon with stats that are actually useful for your playstyle, you might just need to drop a new one. This could have been avoided easily by having one damage type instead of half a dozen types, but it's a design choice made to waste your time purposefully. 

So, you go grind bosses. But of course, energy mechanic. While it's rather generous for a mechanic of that type, you can quickly exhaust it. And as you increase in power, the drop rates seem to lower. But hey, it's not so bad right ? At least once you get your good gear, you're set ?

Nope. There is no horizontal progression, only vertical. Once you're finally set, or maybe even before that, level cap is raised and you need to do it again. Compare with Guild Wars 2, where better gear is available in the long run but your equipment is never obsolete. Here, you need to grind endlessly just to keep up.

On top of that, progression is bad. You never really feel that much more powerful than before. Forget the usual wuxia trope where the MC starts kinda bad but learns fast / gets some secret arts / whatever makes them OP over time. You get stronger, by a bit, then need to breakthrough to a new level, and when you do, [i]so does the whole world[/i]. Which in turn makes you weaker than before in comparison, since your gear is now outdated, enemies are stronger, and you need to grind. Granted, after lvl 50 or so, enemies don't grow stronger anymore, but truth is, neither do you. Which makes me ponder why there is even a vertical progression at this point... Oh, yeah, of course, players like bigger numbers, it keeps people engaged and whatnot.

This game is weird : it tells you to get stronger but lies to you about it, then tells you to grind to get stronger but makes sure you don't get much, and it also says "hey, actually you don't really need to do all that, your old gear kinda works anyway, but... You WANT better gear and better stats right ?".

But hey, at least while you're wasting time, you're exposed to all the multiple new items in the cash shop, the brand new gacha, so maybe you'll spend some more ? You've already invested so much time, good ol' sunk cost fallacy kicks in and you're gonna stay around, right ?

Also, they have a 35 000 dollars ship. No, this is not a typo. Some people actually bought it. I'm not mad at them, if they can afford it and have fun with it, good for them. But that's basically the yearly income of my household, for one single virtual good. I don't know what to make of that, but if this is the direction free to play games are taking, I'm not interested. Neither am I interested in games wasting my time. And sunk cost fallacy no longer works on me, I leveled my "detect BS" skill too high for that.

Actually, after uninstalling this game, I went as far as to look for "free to play" games on Steam and checked "ignore" on most of them. Not because of the boat or the gacha in this game, mind you. But because Where Winds Meet is actually one of the "good" ones as far as monetization is concerned. And I still find it disgusting that it uses all those tricks, those retention strategies and the whaling techniques.

This game served one purpose : it finally put a definitive stop to my interest in games that are concieved as a monetization platform first and foremost, and where the game is just duct-taped on it for incentive. I'd even go as far as to say that it's a whole branch of the videogames industry that needs to disappear. But until then, ignoring everything on that branch will have to make do.

So long, leeches. You won't be missed.

I put 437 hours into Where Winds Meet. The first 250 to 300 hours were genuinely excellent. The game offers a beautiful open world, super fun and stylish martial arts combat, great exploration, and a solid Wuxia atmosphere.
The story was actually pretty interesting with some emotional moments, but it is heavily locked behind time gating. You constantly have to wait for dailies, weeklies, and progression timers, which kills the pacing and turns the story into a chore.

Even collecting oddities, which felt fun early on, quickly turned into a tedious chore. PVP is also terrible due to constant server issues, horrible desync, rubber banding, and disconnects.
On top of all that the game is very poorly optimized. I can barely run it smoothly with my current specs (RTX 4070 Laptop GPU, i7-14700HX, 64GB RAM) even after lowering settings. The monetization is extremely predatory as well. Gorgeous cosmetics are locked behind ultra expensive gacha with awful rates. Even basic hair dye feels like a scam. It really feels like they cared more about milking players than building proper long term content or fixing performance.
This could have been an amazing Wuxia game. The early and mid game are fantastic, but the late game is so empty and boring that it ruined the whole experience for me. If you expect the game to stay fun after the honeymoon phase, look elsewhere.

After about four hours, Where Winds Meet feels like a flashy wuxia sandbox with a gorgeous world and a slightly messy core loop. It’s early days for me, but I can already see both the potential and the rough edges.

World and atmosphere
The open world is the standout so far: sweeping fields, dense villages, and striking vistas that really sell the 10th‑century China setting. Every area I’ve passed through feels handcrafted rather than copy‑pasted, which makes simple exploration surprisingly satisfying. The atmosphere is strong enough that just riding around, doing small side tasks, and watching the weather and lighting change has been a good time on its own.

Combat and gameplay
Combat is fast and flashy, clearly aiming for that martial‑arts‑movie fantasy with air dashes, counters, and a mix of weapons and techniques. Even in the first few hours, the variety of martial arts sets and weapons gives you room to experiment, though it can feel a bit overwhelming and not every system is explained clearly. The game throws a lot of activities and mechanics at you very quickly, and right now it sometimes feels like it’s trying to do too many things at once instead of nailing a few.

Progression and systems
As a free‑to‑play open‑world ARPG, it packs in a ton of content early on—quests, side stories, progression trees, and social/MMO‑style features. The good news is that the early monetization doesn’t feel pay‑to‑win; it’s mostly cosmetics and grindable materials, at least from what I’ve seen and what other players report. On the flip side, the economy and menus are cluttered and a bit confusing, so I’ve spent more time than I’d like just figuring out what all the currencies and systems actually do.

Performance and polish
Visually, the game looks great for a F2P title, with strong lighting and animation work in combat, but character faces and lip‑sync are noticeably weaker. Performance and overall polish feel “okay but not great” so far: serviceable enough to enjoy the world, but you can tell the game is juggling a lot of systems behind the scenes. Voice acting and localization are hit‑or‑miss, which can undercut story moments if you’re paying close attention to the dialogue.

Early verdict (4‑hour take)
Right now, Where Winds Meet feels like a beautiful, content‑rich wuxia playground that’s slightly held back by clunky systems and uneven polish. If you like exploring big worlds and experimenting with stylish martial‑arts combat, it’s already worth trying, but whether it truly sticks long‑term will depend on how much the jank and system overload bother you as you go deeper.

Where Winds Meet (GeForce NOW): A Beautiful World Running Out of Breath
Rating: ★★☆☆☆ (A Disappointing Global Experience)

I have spent hundreds of hours in Where Winds Meet. It was one of my favorite games of all time, and on GeForce NOW, the visuals are absolutely breathtaking. But as a long-term player, I have to be honest: the Global version is a shadow of what we saw in the Chinese release, and the current state of the game is heartbreaking.

The "Global Tax": Content Dripping & Caps
The most frustrating part of the Global experience is how much the developers are holding back. Compared to the Chinese version, we are getting content in tiny, spoon-fed drips. Everything you do feels artificially capped. Whether it’s progression, rewards, or energy, the game constantly puts up walls that stop you from actually playing.

Combat: Bosses vs. Pointless Open World
The combat mechanics are well-made, but the open world has become a chore.
The Bosses: There are a handful of bosses that actually offer a challenge, and they are great. But once you master them, you’re forced to fight them over and over because they are the only thing worth doing.

The Mobs: Open-world enemies are completely pointless. You grind right through them with zero skill required. There’s no tension in exploration when everything outside of a boss arena is just fodder.

The Gimmicks: Some world activities are just annoying. Why am I chasing moons on the water that disappear and reappear in different spots? It feels like busywork designed to pad out playtime rather than offer fun gameplay.

The Story Slog
If you’re here for the action, be prepared to wait. The dialogue is excessive, and the game frequently forces you into "walking simulator" segments where you move at a snail's pace through boring exposition. The lack of a "Skip" button for these sequences is a crime. I find myself wanting to care about the world, but I end up just frantically clicking through menus just to get back to the fighting.

Technical Woes & Declining Population
Playing on GeForce NOW keeps the graphics high, but it can't fix the atrocious PvP ping. Depending on your opponent, matches are often decided by lag rather than martial arts skill.
The most telling sign of the game's health is the social list. My friends list is a graveyard; almost everyone I started with has moved on to "powerhouse" gacha titles like Wuthering Waves. Even when new expansions drop, the player numbers barely move. The world feels empty, and the "community" is bleeding out.

Final Verdict
It’s a shame. Where Winds Meet is a beautiful, well-crafted world held back by developers who seem unwilling to fix the core issues of the Global version.

For New Players: Enjoy the initial magic of the world and maybe buy a cool skin, but don't get too attached.

For Veterans: Like me, you’ll probably find yourself just logging in to collect dailies and logging right back out.
I want to come back. I want this game to be what it used to be. But until the devs stop the "content dripping" and fix the soul-crushing caps and lag, this game is destined to be left in the dust.

[h1]Review?[/h1]
This is only my personnel opinion and how I feel about the game.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Pros:[/h2]
[list]
    [*]Great story telling
    [*]Satisfying combat
    [*]Solo and F2P friendly
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Cons:[/h2]
[list]
    [*]Overwhelming at beginning
    [*]Needs a lot of time to grind for good gears if min maxing
    [*]"Endgame" feels empty
    [*]Really bad anti aliasing and upscaling
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]My Take[/h2]
I am playing on 1440p and the game performs decently with specs like mine, although it is heavily cpu bound, especially on populated area like Kaifeng. Like mentioned in cons, the anti aliasing is pretty bad and shows ghosting enough to be noticeable. For me, xess gave me least ghosting but I am currently not using any sort of anti aliasing or upscaling tech. One thing to note, the frame gen if used have not only input latency but also causes artifacts on the game which is immediately noticeable too.

Yes, there are few bugs here and there which is bound to be in a big game like this one. The endgame like I pointed out feels kinda empty, you get the max gear, farmed for better stats for the gear, upgraded the martial arts, completed the main and side quests, now all that will be left is collectables and it gets pretty boring collecting them all especially aiming for 100% each region.

But I think these all cons cancels out for me with how great the story telling is, how satisfying the combat feels, [i]especially defeating harder bosses[/i], the game environments, the soundtracks, these all combine to make a great experience to me. Sometimes, yes the game control do get bit janky? like when running around the field and passing through the gate, instead of running through it, the game decides to climb on it.

Cosmetics are completely optional, some of the free outfits we can get are good, but not as good as the paid ones.

One thing I have not done yet is PvP. Apart from the "battle royale" type arena that you will have to join when leaving the sect, I haven't done any PvP so I can't say anything about that front.

Not to mention though how solo friendly the game is. Almost everything can be done solo except the group activities which again is completely optional.

The frequent new events are welcomed but it gets quite overwhelming too, which it might just be me. The rewards from the events are bit hit or miss for me, [i]eyy no complain about free pulls though[/i].

Overall, we don't really need to spend a lot of time to enjoy the story and progress but having low gear do make the game bit challenging especially on high difficulties. Other than that a solid 8.5-9/10 for me

Where Winds Meet makes a strong impression with its incredibly well-crafted open world — from landscapes and architecture to the overall atmosphere, everything feels alive and immersive. The soundtrack is absolutely top-tier, elevating the emotional experience throughout. Combat is visually stunning, with smooth, stylish moves and a wide variety of skills that allow for diverse playstyles. The story is another highlight, offering real depth and plenty of tragic, memorable moments, supported by cutscenes that are hard to fault.

That said, the game still has some noticeable issues. PvP is currently quite unbalanced, heavily affected by hardware performance and ping, and Umbrella’s stun abilities feel overtuned. Cosmetic outfits are also priced unreasonably high. While many main quests are interesting in concept, their storytelling often feels dragged out and unnecessarily padded, combined with sluggish movement pacing that can be frustrating. Additionally, the minigames seem heavily tailored to Chinese players, making them less accessible to a broader audience — although the addition of card games is a good step, and hopefully more familiar options like chess will be introduced in the future.

Short sumamry of my experience so far (I like the game but can't recommend after Hexi dropped):

Pros:

TL:DR; (The game killed it's own momentum, coupled with the worst quest design I've seen in the last couple of decades)

Details:

Bad pacing to the point of boredom

Walking simulator - 90% of the quest could have been a cutscene or footnote, rather than dramatically dragging your feed one scene to the next

History "lessons" shoved down your throat - I signed up for action souls-like not chinese history class, however much of this is actual history and not historical fiction

The very definiton of doubling back - to unlock the main quest part 3 you have to go into the area that you are supposedly only now discovering a way into and complete several quests there, before going back and "discovering" the path forward. I truly think this game is a way for China to 1: gather our information and traits, 2: introduce us to their culture/ lore for later population integration 3: show off. There's no other explanation as to why this is free. Like a free Chinese Crimson Desert. A lot of people are complaining about prices in-game but I've yet to come across something i cant do unless i pay for it. the purchases seem mostly cosmetic. 

This game heavily focuses on beauty and style, reminiscent of the ancient Shan Shui art. You can also contribute to the creativity with detailed character/ outfit customization, vast traversable landscapes, and a detailed home building feature that seems to be available anywhere.    

Personally I think this game really shines the most with its world building. The graphics are just a step below what I'd consider the best right now (much like assassin's creed) but, the density in gardens, buildings and cities just blow my mind. I often find myself  running around exploring the different scenery and various allies, rooftops, mountains, and groves.

The exploration will take you to distant lands, to secret underground cities, other worldly dimensions, or just through a flowered meadow next to a stream. You never know what your adventure will entail, where they'll take you, or what story they'll tell. Full of hijinks, treasures, lore, and enemies. 

While combat profiles are complex and the actions very souls-like in style, dodging, and creativity, this game offers a much more relaxed approach where you can revisit bested bosses but don't have them thrust upon you from every corner, where I would normally feel doomed, in Winds I just roam around and get better which definitely breaks up the XP grinding. It's a two weapon based system that can be heavily modified with different focuses, perks, and play styles. I'm learning the hard way that weapon cohesion is very beneficial. 

Winds offers an array of different PvP activities/ mini games and even a cruise ship that seamlessly blends into the world where players can socialize. There is also AI powered NPCs that you have to hit with some key phrases to complete certain quest. They typically talk in circles but, its a interesting feature I haven't seen till now.

All in all you're getting a AAA game for less than an Indie game price

Pros:
- Open world, MASSIVE player base and a good sized map
- Amazing multiplayer/co-op support, doesn't feel unfun or unbearable to play with friends.
- Great for either solo players or multiplayer enjoyers, a great main story with lots of characters and dialogue to learn from. 
- Good mechanics and combat, definitely not many complaints about it at all. 
- Character customization is through the roof, even if it uses AI for some aspects of it.
- Beautiful graphics with a well suited PC.
- Strong optimization with the game, ability to get over 180 fps on high settings in 1080p without dlss4. When you enable dlss4, you gain a near-stable 500 FPS generally all time with next to no compromises on looks nor feel. 
- Voice acting is good, lots of characters with voice acting in the game, so there's no need to worry about silent dialogue unless its from a VERY random person in the town or something similar. 

Cons:
- Character movement is a little finnicky on keyboard and mouse, sometimes your character will move everywhere but where you want it to. 
- Character will climb almost anything you get close to, and it gets a little annoying having to jump off of it all the time.
- Similar to other MMORPG games (a little too similar)
- Face movement is subpar, very weird-looking facial movement for dialogue. 
- The game is absolutely not easy to run on a low-end PC, consoles struggle to run this game, and you definitely wont be seeing a super stable 120 FPS if your monitor supports 120hz on PS5 or Xbox.
- Very minor consequences of multiplayer support such as some looting and other miscellaneous things that only the party host could do, so if you're joining a friend, you cant expect to be picking up any good loot off the floor. 


Overall, this game is very entertaining and fun to play with just a few beta release bugs. You cant expect a game like this to be absolutely perfect considering it came out October 2025. The game reminds me a lot of games such as Genshin, just a lot more engaging than it with less of a push towards P2W. Your character can do almost anything with enough time to level up and play the game, no need for rolling for other "characters" unless you want a different look. The one hunch I have with character customization is the fact that a lot of clothing and accessories will require payment, and I honestly haven't played the game enough to know whether or not you can unlock certain clothing and accessories, but off rip, it will want you to buy a lot of the clothing. Adding onto the similarities of something such as Genshin, the dialogue boxes and reply boxes to those dialogues is near identical to that of Genshin, with the style and mechanics of it. Nothing wrong with that at all, just something I'd noticed while playing. If you're a fan of MMORPG's and you want to try out a newer game, I couldn't recommend this game more. Its a extremely fun and engaging story line for single player and a great support for multiplayer with little to no major consequences of it, almost all basic aspects of the game are more than doable on multiplayer with friends.

The UI is definitely messy at first, not gonna lie, but you get used to it and I actually kind of enjoy clicking around everywhere and randomly unlocking stuff and discovering features I didn't know where there. I know it's probably an unpopular opinion but it works for me!

The game runs super smoothly and I don't have crazy PC specs at all! I haven't even really encountered any major bugs at all, some minor ones here and there but like getting stuck in a rock from time to time and it's really just so minor.

The combat feels really satisfying and lets you build your own style instead of locking you into one way of playing. I didn't try all of the weapons and martial arts and abilities yet but I like the idea that I can switch at any time. 

I also like the social aspect a lot. Playing with a friend and jumping into each other’s world to clear bosses is a lot of fun. Even with random players: you can ask for help with healing, reputation, or fights, and people actually show up. 

The music is great and fits the vibe really well. I especially like those mini games where you gotta play a track to earn the music sheet!

There are indeed a lot of microtransactions but honestly I just ignore them. They’re mostly cosmetic and don’t feel pay-to-win at all, so they never really bothered me.

Overall I just really love this game and the fact that it’s free makes it even better so if you're looking for a good RPG, just go for it and hey if you don't like it, you don't even have to ask for a refund! Isn't that great?

So, after spending over 1000 hours in this game, I feel like I can give it a fair review in its current state.

There are many issues that veteran players who have reached the endgame feel, and I feel them too. But it would be more than unfair to base the entire review on issues experienced by players who have invested hundreds and hundreds of hours into the game. There are many amazing and, from my point of view, revolutionary things this game does extremely well.

THE GOOD:

+ There are hundreds of hours of fun, storylines, and interesting boss fights for single-player RPG fans to enjoy. You don’t have to pay a dime to have a quality experience, whether you prefer a chill or challenging game (depending on the selected difficulty).

+ Character customization offers nearly endless options. You want your character to look like Keanu Reeves? Check. Like Shrek? Check. Or you can make them look like a K-pop star. Almost whatever you can think of is achievable within the character editor. (This does not include fashion, as that is the main source of the game’s monetization. The majority of outfits are paid.)

+ There is little to no pay-to-win. Whether you’re talking about PvP or PvE content, as of today, players who have spent tens of thousands of dollars will be on equal footing with those who spent nothing. Paying players will simply look better while doing whatever they’re doing.

+ All builds are playable. If you invest resources into something, it won’t become useless or irrelevant. Of course, there is a meta, but each build has its own strengths and weaknesses. One may be better suited for 1v1 PvP, while another may perform better in large-scale PvP. Still, every build is viable in any game mode.

+As the game follows a live service model, as long as it remains profitable, new content will continue to be released. You can step away for months, come back, and still have plenty to do: new bosses to defeat, new stories to complete, new achievements to unlock, and new game modes to experience. So far, the developers tend to be quite experimental, so you won’t just get more of the same—you’ll likely return to entirely new gameplay systems as well.
The developers are listening. They encourage feedback, and I’m confident that given enough time, they will address the most pressing issues raised by the community.

+ It’s a very good social game. There are features like marriage, guilds (including guild wars, 5- and 10-player raids, and guild challenges), and systems like Spotlight, where you can upload your own dance moves for others to view and try. The social aspects are already robust and will likely continue to expand.

THE BAD:

I strongly believe the developers will try to fix as much as possible over time and rethink certain systems.

- The most pressing issue, which you’ll only really feel once you reach the endgame, is the energy system. If you’ve played any gacha game before, you know what I’m talking about. I understand why it exists in gacha games—it’s usually used as a time gate to prevent players from progressing too quickly and often serves as a monetization tool. However, here it serves no clear purpose. It’s not monetized (you can’t buy more), and progression is already gated through the breakthrough system.

- It’s not just the energy system. The endgame loop is not very satisfying at this stage, and many activities are time-gated for no clear reason. It’s frustrating to only be able to participate in guild raids once a week to claim rewards. The game needs some optional grind for PvE-focused players.

- The story quality varies significantly between patches. I understand that Hexi was their first major expansion and that they were still experimenting with storytelling, but for most global players, it simply didn’t hit the mark.

- Due to the limited availability of servers in certain regions, the PvP experience can be frustrating due to higher latency. This depends heavily on your location, but at higher ranks, having lower ping provides a significant advantage. That said, 1v1 PvP has a high skill ceiling and can be a very satisfying and complex experience.

Advice for new players:

Take your time and don’t rush into the endgame. The solo experience (bosses, story, and world activities) is one of the strongest aspects of the game and more satisfying than the current endgame. Don’t rob yourself of that experience out of fear of missing out.

I didn’t engage with the social aspects of the game until about four weeks after I started playing, and it was one of the best decisions I made. So take your time and enjoy the game. You’ll always have time to catch up to veteran players later.

Also, don’t let the menus discourage you at the beginning. There are many systems in the game, but early on, you don’t need to worry about most of them.

500 hours in Where Winds Meet and I’m still locked in—but I really need to talk about the translation and historical context.

The game is gorgeous, the wuxia vibe is strong, and the combat still makes me feel like a martial arts legend (right before I get folded by some random NPC named “Hungry Bandit #3”). But the English translation definitely needs work. A lot of dialogue feels awkward or unclear, and important story moments sometimes lose impact because the wording just doesn’t hit right.

The historical references are also interesting but under-explained. For example, when the game touches on regions like the Hexi Region, it clearly expects you to already understand the significance—but for most players, there’s not enough in-game context to connect the dots. I’ve spent nearly 100 hours in Where Winds Meet, and it’s been a unique experience overall.

The game really shines in its world design. The open world feels alive, immersive, and deeply inspired by wuxia culture. Exploration is one of the strongest aspects — you constantly discover new places, secrets, and side activities that don’t feel repetitive.

Combat is another highlight. It offers a mix of fluid martial arts mechanics and strategic depth. Once you understand the system, fights become very satisfying and cinematic.

The story and atmosphere are well-crafted, though at times pacing can feel a bit slow. Some quests could be more polished, but the overall narrative and setting keep you engaged.

That said, the game isn’t perfect. There are occasional bugs, performance drops, and some UI/UX issues that could be improved. Optimization still needs work, especially during large-scale scenes.

**Pros:**

* Beautiful and immersive open world
* Unique wuxia-style combat system
* Tons of exploration and content
* Strong atmosphere and world-building

**Cons:**

* Performance issues in some areas
* Occasional bugs
* UI/UX could be smoother

**Final Verdict:**
If you enjoy open-world RPGs and martial arts themes, this game is definitely worth your time. It still needs some polish, but the core experience is very strong.

**Playtime:** 100+ hours
**Rating:** 8/10

Alright here's a list of what's wrong with this game:
We have quests. But not all quests are the same! There are regular quests and there are hundreds of so called Wandering tales. Example: "Muai hunao met huai moonao and a lone star shone on the morning sky! Do what you must, hero! (quest clue: search western miao for the lost leylao)". Understand anythin? Noone does, welcome to Great Wise Chinese Wisdom. Tons of quests like that and you will not find quest marks on the map so this is getting very tedious very fast. (Solution: youtube guides. Hundreds of quests = hundreds of guides, enjoy)
Want PvP with tons of concealed mechanics? You won't even know what hit ya! (spoiler: it was tangbao triggered by zhao) Such fun! Much WOW! 
By the way, you think this is an MMO? Sure, about 5% of the time. You do most quests ALONE. You explore the storyline ALONE. And you know what? The game gives an ENTIRE WORLD just for yourself! Build, explore! ALONE. Well yeah ok, technically others can join you or you can join others but there is literally NO incentive to do so 95% of the time.
Oh, oh, oh almost forgot! You know what the MMO part looks like? I'll give you some examples: playing cards, standing on a boat until you get reward, standing in guild hall until you get reward, standing in a pool until you get reward, standing in a circle automatically doing some kungfu stuff until you get reward. Not tired of all the exciting standing-around-waiting-for-reward yet? Here, dear player, we have ANOTHER circle you have to stand in while automatically doing some OTHER kungfu staff (that's entirely different type of kunfu staff, not the one you did before, and another circle, you might fail to notice but they are very different, absolutely not the same, that's extremely important, don't confuse the two).
You think this is RPG? Yeah, mostly. Well, usually. I mean not quite. And what I really mean is: NO IT IS NOT. It is a visual novel, walking simulator, soulslike, casino, puzzle, adventure, find hidden objects all-in-one with RPG elements. 
HEED ME! This game is NOT about martial arts and sword swinging. It is about wandering around, gathering herbs, searching for hidden chests and other hidden objects, reading tons of dialogues, watching tons of script videos and lots of standing around waiting for a reward. You will run around talking to grandma Liao who will send you to speak to general Mao so that you find out you have to kill traitor Babao. But not before you learn the full story of his betrayal by speaking to Mamao, Pao, Tao, Kakao and all their friends, family and distant relatives. That will take you roughly half a day (everyone in this game talks for half an hour, giving their brief history, their family history, anciet China history and also local news about aunt Lulao's pregnant donkey). But don't worry, after you're done chatting with all those -aos the game will let you fight some 5 or 10 mobs or even fight a boss! BTW, that's when you learn that this a soulslike and not just some RPG. Prepare to suffer. 
A few words about the interface. Calling it "extremely user unfriendly" would be a rich compliment. I can't say what it really is because it involves lots of F* words to properly describe it. I'll just clue you in. Imagine a car tith a steering wheel in the trunk and you have to press the left turn signal with your right ear and the right turn signal with your elbow. There is absolutely NO system to where find what. Quests are listed in your journal. Logical right? Yes, but not ALL quests can be found in your journal. Try opening a map and there at the bottom left corner you'll find an icon with... quests. Not all of them, just SOME specific quests. What do you mean there is no such icon? You must stand in a certain location for it to appear, stupid. Because this is how it works. I promise you, you will be absolutely amazed by things you find in different parts of the interface. Or rather you will be struck again and again by the same question 'how the hell this ended up here?'. Why do we have 3 types of shops? Why not place them all in one place? Why these skills are here and other skills are illogically in an absolutely different place? And it takes literally several months to get acquainted with the interface enough not to suffer evey time you want to change a weapon or access the skills upgrade menu.

So, I wanted to come back to the review I wrote and give a bit of a spitshine. This is that!
TL;DR: if you like the idea of this game, play it! It's a very fun game and my hours show how much I really do like it. But be prepared to deal with both game-breaking and annoying bugs, a very touchy quest system, a playerbase that's nice and funny as best, & annoying and toxic at worst, insanely expensive fashion, no real tutorials past first 5 hours, shoehorned in generative AI, absolutely no moderation + reporting being pointless, and a very restrictive multiplayer.

-

The good of WWM:
The design of the world overall is wonderful, and it's a very alive place even if you play solo. There's so many NPCs to talk to and learn from at all different in-game times, and you're encouraged to do so so you can collect anecdotes! Love this system. It's also a very pretty game, and the photo mode is pretty good for what it is!

The fashion of this game is both accurate and non-sexualized. Of course, there's gonna be a little bit of slut in any MMO's clothes regardless of what game it is, but overall everything is very appropriate while still looking beautiful. I really appreciate this in an era of eastern gaming where everyone needs to be dressed like a stripper. Outfits are gender locked, but given that WWM is a Chinese game I'll leave that be.

The combat is super fun! I think it's a good mix between Sekiro (which this game is very Souls inspired) and simplicity. There's lots of weapons to pick from, and even more martial art styles (combat styles), though you will have to level up each martial art individually. There's also a good set of accessibility options for people that struggle with things like parrying/countering - but some points get knocked off because that accessibility is NOT available for Martial Fellowship (NPC duels), some event fights, and PVP. PVP I understand, but... the other two being excluded is very, very stupid.

Most minigames are fun! Gift of Gab, most of the Meow Meow puzzles, Archery competitions, NPC healing, Pitch pot, and Graceful melodies are all great little momentary distractions. Chess doesn't have really any tutorial at all, but it's almost the same rules as normal Xiangqi, and besides the fact it's too easy most of the time I really like the idea of the challenge boards they use. Madiao is explained very poorly, but it's also pretty fun. 
To dip a bit back into the bad, Old Friends (the AI chatbots) are stupid and pointless - get rid of them. They're easily cheated and provide NO value to this game; they were shoehorned in to follow a trend, and it's very obvious.

There's an in-game translator, so you can communicate with anybody in the world who's playing! It's not that bad most of the time, though there can be hiccups.

- 

The bad of WWM:
Quests are BUGGY. BUGGIER THAN A BETHESDA GAME AT LAUNCH. I cannae recall all the times that this game has made me rage, feel like I was going ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane, feel like I was missing something, etc. Half of the systems in this game around quests feel like they're designed to be overly confusing and frustrating. The rules around encounter spawns are also unclear, and may include an IRL 30 MINUTE WAIT between them if some comments are to be believed. Most of the bugs I found were THREE MONTHS OLD. This game just got a major update this month and no bug fixes. They don't care.
This is not helped by the fact there's no official guides or anything, just another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI chatbot that's not helpful at all. Game8 is the main resource for guides, and their guides are almost always inaccurate.

Speaking of buggy, this game's movement is janky as all hell. Normal running and walking is fine, but when you get your upgraded sonic run, that thing is going to run you up trees your pinkie toe touched, force you to climb houses because your elbow nudged the edge of the hitbox, and might even get you beat up by NPCs if you screw up badly enough.

Also, the game keeps running out of memory and CTD'ing if you play for too long at one time. Don't know what's going on there. Memory leak?
Also fun fact: there's the option to have dark skin, but half the time the game won't even load the pigment and you'll be white again. What's the point?

Signposts are a great idea on paper, and is trying to emulate messages from the Souls games. The problem is that while there are genuinely kind, helpful, or funny people that leave them, 90% of them are gaudy whale outfits (because there's a pointless "outfit borrow" system), like beggars (most of who spam the same message 500 times all over the map to farm), thirst traps/fetish content, over objectives to grief other players, petty whiners (especially in the story-heavy Hexi), or other more nasty things. Plus, anybody can reinforce a sign for YEARS to make it indestructible. Longest I've seen is 1207 days (3 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ years). Like I said, there is NO moderation in this game - any report you give will NOT be answered and they DO NOT CARE. There's a vague chat filter, but it only seems to work on Chinese and English, and doesn't stop anybody from saying what they want. Plenty of Russian players swearing with no censor.
Downvoting a sign does absolutely nothing, and it just comes back later. There's no punishment for leaving a bad signpost at all.

The translation is very, very poor. NPCs will just straight up speak gibberish, give you wrong directions, ask for items by the wrong name, all that jazz. It gets worse once you leave Qinghe. Actually, almost forgot: if you play fem MC, a good portion of the NPCs will still call you a guy. They misgender each other a lot too.
Side note: the English voice acting is very hit and miss. I'm going to blame this on the voice direction, and not the voice actors. Swap it to Chinese if you want, it's immersive anyways, right-

No true multiplayer. You can't go do MSQ with your buddy, just play all the minigames and sometimes do a quest that lets you do it while the other player stands around doing ♥♥♥♥ all. Voice chat is enabled BY DEFAULT and is VERY LOUD BY DEFAULT. Ugh.

Fashion in this game is INSANELY EXPENSIVE. Outfits not on a "special, limited time discount" cost $50 A POP. I'm not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kidding: an outfit is 2580 pearls at full price, best option is 3000 ($49.99). The 'average' discount will knock outfits down to 2322p, but you'd still want to get the $50 option.. You get some options as a F2P player, but you're going to know if someone is "poor" or not because F2P all get the same selection.
There's also a mostly equally expensive GACHA randomly thrown in as an "alternative", and get this: you can ONLY get vibrant/neon hair dye from said Gacha. It's like they say, in nature poisonous things are brightly colored! (For the record, a lot of WWM's whales are entitled brats who think because they pay money they are above the rules and criticism, part of the toxicity I mentioned before.)

The sects are boring at best, and stupid at worst. As far as I can tell, they're overblown cliques with player leaders - and as someone who spent a lot of time playing a game with player leaders, this is NOT A GOOD IDEA IN THE SLIGHTEST. Some sects encourage you to harass other players (looking at YOU Masked Troupe), & some sects aren't even available, and exist purely to tease you as well. Sects are also a massive contributor to signpost abuse.
I beg of thee to read the rules of a sect you want to join, and if you understand those rules through the bad translation, come to terms with the fact that it will also lock you out of some content or force you into certain combat. And if you don't like the sect you joined? You can leave it... after you're forced to participate in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Fortnite clone game mode where you're just going to get your butthole pushed in by some overtuned whale. Leave the PVP to the people that like it. Sectless is the way to go for most, honestly. I like Nine Mortal Ways, though...

Though this game is interesting initially and has very interesting systems, and deviates from many other MMO's, creating a breath of fresh air in that regard, it ruins it by adding to many tedious flavor systems and other old mechanics in a terrible way.

On top of that unfortunately the developers seem too busy pushing out new content for the "small" playerbase they have left to address most issues and thus pull back players that left because of the issues.

Though very smart things have clearly been done in the game, I feel that adding the issues with the game, clear as day in the feedback section (to see if more people agree or something) rather than just fixing it is extremely ill advised.

The game menus are just absolutely impossible. If you jam this much systems and crap in a game, at least make sure the menus are easily traversable and everything can be found with ease.

My major gripe is also that there is a solo mode and online mode, which is perfect. Unfortunately they decided to borrow ideas on this from famous games, but implementing them unclearly, creating major frustrations when you think you are playing solo because solo mode is on, and others suddenly join your game or vice versa.

Some people also find it P2W, and I kinda see how that can be a thing, but just spending time will get you where you want to go eventually, so that seems partially true, but partially not so much depending on your definition of P2W. With mostly cosmetics and small buffs, pretty much everything can be done for free, and I feel like spending a lot of time in game can get you just as far as paying for all the buffs and stuff.

Unfortunately since the main story quest also seems to go everywhere and nowhere, and isn't finished, the game just feels like early access, rather than a full version, and though combat is interesting, it doesn't feel very intuitive.

Lastly with all the innovative stuff they did, getting hard stuck in a holy trinity system is also a huge dissapointment (specially with the lack of healing and tanking diversity, and only having a lot of DPS diversity). Since Guild Wars 2 has shown us the holy trinity is no longer holy, this dissapointed me in this game big time.

Have you ever dreamed of a truly good Souls-like game - one focused on PvP, with a lively online experience, well-designed PvE activities, and combat systems built around parries, combos, and dodges that actually work the way they’re supposed to? I’m sure many people have. Well, if that’s exactly what you’ve been looking for - let me “congratulate” you: Where Winds Meet is the complete opposite of that kind of game

I’ve been playing since almost the very beginning of the global release - starting on one client and later switching to the official launcher - and over that time I’ve managed to dive pretty deep into the game. That experience has been more than enough to form a clear opinion: if you’re looking for a quality online project, this game simply does not deserve your attention

It’s important to start with a basic understanding: although the first dozens of hours may create the illusion of a single-player adventure, the game is actually built around online systems, and especially PvP. However, before getting into that, it’s worth talking about PvE, because that’s what ultimately leads you into the “endgame”

PvE here is split into two directions: online and solo. Online PvE consists of group activities like 5- or 10-player bosses and clearing outposts. On paper, this sounds fairly standard for the genre, but in practice it falls short: the mechanics are primitive, the difficulty is almost nonexistent, and the activities become repetitive very quickly. On top of that, there are frequent bugs that cause even the few existing mechanics to malfunction

But the core issue is the energy system. Players have a limited pool that regenerates extremely slowly, while a single dungeon run can consume a significant portion of it. As a result, you hit a hard ceiling: a couple of proper runs - and the game simply stops rewarding you. It creates a sense of artificial restriction that doesn’t encourage you to come back, but rather pushes you away

Solo PvE, on the other hand, initially feels much better. Exploring the world, progressing through the story, solving puzzles, fighting bosses - all of this creates a strong first impression. The early regions are genuinely well-designed, the story is engaging, and the cutscenes are solid. At times, the game even starts to feel like the one people were hoping for. However, over time, the quality noticeably drops. In later regions, such as Hexi, quests become dragged out, dialogues are excessively long, and the lack of a skip option only makes things worse. In the end, no matter how enjoyable it feels at first, the solo content runs dry fairly quickly, and after a month or two of regular play, you may simply run out of things to do

Additional open-world activities - like mini-games, competitions, or casual side content - are present, but they’re hard to take seriously. They feel more like short distractions rather than meaningful gameplay. Most players will likely try them once or twice and never return

And this is where the game leads you to its core feature - PvP. This is what the entire progression system revolves around: you farm gear for it, join guilds for it, and participate in large-scale activities for it. The problem is that PvP here doesn’t work the way it should. It’s not about skill, not about precise timing, and not about reaction. It’s about ping

Even the smallest difference in latency between players can completely decide the outcome of a fight. You can press parry - and it won’t register. You can dodge on time - and still take damage. Your attacks may fail to connect, while your opponent’s land consistently. In large-scale modes like guild wars, things get even worse: attacks pass through targets, characters may not display properly or disappear entirely, and what’s happening on screen becomes completely unpredictable

The server-side performance is the game’s biggest weakness. And even compared to problematic titles like Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege, the situation here feels even more disastrous. In a game where core mechanics rely on precision and timing, these issues make PvP fundamentally unviable

As a result, we end up with a paradox: a game built around online systems turns out to be at its weakest precisely in its online component. PvE is restricted by the energy system, PvP suffers from technical issues, and balance is questionable at best. As a single-player experience, it can still offer dozens or even hundreds of hours of enjoyment, but as an online game, it stands as one of the most disappointing experiences in recent years

The most frustrating part is that the developers are clearly aware of these problems, yet they seem in no hurry to fix them. No significant improvements are being made, while the player base continues to decline rapidly. The Chinese version has reportedly lost nearly 80% of its audience over the past six months, while the global version has dropped by around 90%. Online numbers have fallen from roughly 135,000 players to around 16-30 thousand during peak hours. And honestly, that’s not surprising - players can forgive a lot, but not when the core mechanics simply don’t work

In the end, Where Winds Meet is a game with massive potential, a beautiful world, and a strong start that ultimately failed to live up to its own ambitions. And before you decide to dive into it, it’s worth asking yourself one simple question: are you willing to accept that its main feature - the online experience - is also its biggest problem?

[h1] Honest Review After 500+ Hours (Long Read) [/h1]

I have tried every aspect of this game 100% progress in some things, tried both high end pvp and leaderboard rankings. So here's an honest truth about the game. A wuxia styled F2P MMORPG with insane potential, beautiful worldbuilding, very similar to Wukong and Sekiro/Dark souls elements mixed in.

[h2] Customization [/h2]  
The character creator is [b]insanely detailed[/b] easily one of the best parts of the game. You can tweak faces to perfection and create almost any look you want.
However, it’s limited:
• No body customization (height, build, proportions locked)
• Only face + skin tone customization

You can look unique but only from the neck up.

[h2] Animation & Movement [/h2]
Movement is smooth, sprinting, parkour, climbing everything feels fluid.
You can climb trees, mountains, buildings basically anything if you have stamina.

[h2] Photo Mode [/h2]
The photo mode in this game is [b] insanely good [/b] and honestly one of the most underrated features.  
It offers:
• Advanced camera controls  
• Lighting adjustments (intensity, direction, tone)  
• Depth of field and focus tweaks  
• Filters and color grading  
• Pose and angle control
• Also newly added custom poses and dancing by tracing with AI from a source

[h2] Weapons & Combat [/h2]  
Huge variety of weapons:  
• Dual blades  
• Umbrellas  
• Spears  
• Katanas  
• And more  

Each weapon has its own:  
• Unique mechanics  
• Combos  
• Playstyle identity  
• Role in team fights  

[b] No weapon feels useless [/b] but here’s the catch:  
At high end PvP or leaderboard play, the meta becomes extremely narrow.  
If you want to compete, you’re forced into specific builds and weapon combinations. Freedom exists — until you want to be competitive.

[h3] Playstyles [/h3]  
Three main roles:  
• DPS  
• Healer  
• Tank  

These can be mixed depending on your build.  
Each role comes with:  
• Unique abilities  
• Combo systems  
• Team synergy 
You can also freely re-spec your gear if you get tired of 1 playstyle but limited amount of times in a season

[h2] World Building (best part) [/h2]  
The world is:  
• Beautiful
• Deeply inspired by Chinese history, folklore, and legends  
• Filled with handcrafted environments  

You’ll find:  
• Unique dungeons and cave systems  
• Massive mountains to climb  
• Fully interactive NPCs 
• Animals (cats, dogs, etc.)  
• Even AI NPC-chatbots

Every location feels carefully crafted and alive.

[h3] Exploration [/h3]  
Exploration is heavily rewarded so try and reach 100% for each part of the map, you will get:  
• Hidden loot  
• Lore  
• Character progression buffs  

There’s also a compendium system that tracks everything you discover from plants to NPCs, bosses etc.  

[h2] Social Features [/h2]  
This is one of the most social MMOs out there.

You can:  
• Hire players (healers, scholars)  
• Place bounties on players  
• Help others through bounty systems  
• Become a disciple or mentor  
• Form sworn groups  
• Get married/build relationships  
• Break players out of prison or capture them  
• Join guilds and sects  
• Play minigames  
• Dance, play instruments, relax in saunas

The game is designed to reward social interaction heavily with most cosmetics rewards behind it.

[h2] F2P & Monetization [/h2]  
The good 
• No pay to win 
• Gear cannot be bought with real money  
• Cosmetics can be earned in game  
• Free gacha pulls exist with guaranteed rewards over time  

The bad
• Gacha is extremely expensive (150–300$ for premium cosmetics)  
• Strong FOMO elements  
• Global version lacks trading systems (like China's Black Market)  

[h3] Cosmetics [/h3]  
Very different from western MMOs:  
• No oversexualized designs  
• Modest, elegant, wuxia style outfits  
• Unique designs for male/female  
• Full dye system  

[h2] Voice Acting & Translations [/h2]  
This is one of the weakest aspects:  
• Poor English voice acting  
• Missing or broken translations  
• Some things remains in Chinese  

[b] Recommendation: [/b] Play in Chinese with subtitles but even those aren't perfect.

[h2] Now for the bad part [/h2]
Since I mentioned a lot of pros here are the cons and why it's primarily bad and might affect current and future players

[b] 1. Timegated Progression [/b]  
You hit caps and must wait 1-3 weeks for breakthroughs.  
No grinding your way forward you’re forced to wait.

[b] 2. Global vs China Version [/b]  
China gets:  
• Better QoL  
• Better pricing for gacha 
• More features  

[b] 3. Gacha & Pricing [/b]  
• Extremely expensive  
• Worse pricing than Chinese version  
• Encourages FOMO heavily  

[b] 4. No Black market [/b] 
No trading system like China's Black Market less player freedom, more monetization pressure.

[b] 5. Server Issues [/b]  
The game only has 4 dedicated server locations
• Players will lag and affect others gameplay
• Host based sessions

[b] 6. Meta Problems [/b]  
• One dominant meta for PvP/leaderboards  
• Little room for experimentation at high level  

[b] 7. New Player Disadvantage [/b]  
• New players almost have no chance to catch up
• Missed events = fomo and less progression
• New players probably won't find enough people for old activities without looking into discord or other places for help 

[b] 8. UI & Complexity [/b]  
Menus inside menus inside menus.  
Hidden stats everywhere.  
Very overwhelming for new players.

[b] 9. Endgame Difficulty [/b]  
• The late game mechanics are too confusing for new players
• Requires knowledge and coordination  
• You will get the most braindead teammates who won't help you or leave after you failed to do a raid mechanic or failed to heal enough

[b] 10. Sect System [/b]  
If you don't have 10+ friends that will willingly give you a vote your not reaching max rank and staying there
No social circle = no progression.

[h2] Final Verdict [/h2]  
A beautiful, deeply immersive wuxia MMORPG with one of the best social systems in the genre.

But it’s also:  
• Timegated 
• Unbalanced 
• Regionally unfair 
• Overly complex 

If you:  
• Don’t care about meta  
• Don't care about being top tier  
• Enjoy exploration and social gameplay  
You will love this game.

Picked this up out of curiosity and ended up spending way more time in it than I expected.

Where Winds Meet drops you into a huge open world inspired by ancient China where martial arts, exploration, and story all blend together really well. The combat feels smooth and learning different techniques makes fights pretty satisfying.

The world itself is gorgeous and there’s always something happening — wandering NPCs, side activities, random encounters, and a lot of places to explore.

It’s not perfect though. Some systems can feel confusing at first and the UI could definitely be clearer. But once you get into the flow of the game, it becomes a very enjoyable experience.

Pros
✔ Beautiful world
✔ Fun martial arts combat
✔ Lots of exploration

Cons
✖ Some mechanics aren’t explained well
✖ UI could use improvement

Overall, if you like open-world RPGs and martial arts themes, this game is definitely worth trying.

Where Winds Meet is a gorgeous, mist-drenched wuxia RPG that feels, at times, like wandering through a legend half-buried in wind and steel. Its world is beautiful, its combat stylish, and its atmosphere strong enough to keep pulling you back even when the cracks begin to show.

This is not a perfectly polished experience. It can be bloated, uneven, and rough in ways that dull the sharpness of its ambition. But even so, there is something deeply magnetic here. For every frustration, there is another moment where the world opens again and reminds you why you stayed.

Pros
Beautiful open world with strong visual identity
Wuxia atmosphere is genuinely immersive
Combat feels fluid, elegant, and satisfying
Exploration is rewarding and often the best part of the experience
Large amount of content
Ambitious in both scale and style

Cons
Noticeable jank and rough edges
Some systems feel overcomplicated or unnecessary
Pacing can become uneven
Repetition sets in after a while
Polish does not always match the game’s ambition
Certain parts of the experience feel under-refined
What I Liked

The strongest thing Where Winds Meet offers is mood. It knows how to create a sense of wandering beauty, and that alone carries much of the experience. The world has presence. The combat has grace. There are stretches where the game feels genuinely absorbing, not because every mechanic is flawless, but because its atmosphere is strong enough to make even ordinary movement feel cinematic.

What I Didn’t Like

The game often feels heavier than it needs to be. Some mechanics clutter the experience instead of enriching it, and the overall structure can lose momentum. It is the kind of game that aims high, but sometimes you can feel the strain of that ambition in the roughness beneath it.

Performance / Polish

Not disastrous, but definitely not seamless. Expect some rough edges, occasional clumsiness, and a level of inconsistency that may bother players who want a more refined experience.

Final Verdict

Where Winds Meet is not a masterpiece, but it is far more interesting than something merely polished and forgettable. It is a flawed, alluring experience: beautiful enough to enchant, uneven enough to frustrate, and memorable enough to justify the journey.

Worth playing if you care more about atmosphere, exploration, and style than absolute refinement.

After putting more than 120 hours into Where the Winds Meet, I can say the game hooked me with its world almost immediately. The scenery, atmosphere, and overall sense of place are what kept me exploring long after the main story pushed me elsewhere. I constantly found myself stopping just to look around or wandering off simply because something in the distance looked interesting.

Combat has been another highlight for me. The variety of martial arts styles, weapons, and abilities gave me a lot of freedom to experiment, and even after all this time, I’ve still found new combinations that feel fun and fresh. The side quests and small world events also surprised me—many of them felt worthwhile, not just filler.

The game isn’t without its issues, though. Across my playtime, I’ve run into a fair share of bugs, from awkward animations to quest hiccups. Movement and parkour can be inconsistent, and some systems are poorly explained or buried in a cluttered UI. I also noticed some strange difficulty spikes that break the flow.

Even with those flaws, I’ve really enjoyed my time with it. The world is unique, the gameplay is flexible, and the experience stuck with me.
