After spending a good amount of time playing *Where Winds Meet*, I’d say this is a **mixed but mostly positive experience** for me.

The biggest highlight of the game is definitely the **combat**. It feels smooth, satisfying, and really fun once you start learning the different skills and movement options. Every fight feels cinematic, and the martial arts style combat gives it a unique identity that stands out from other open-world RPGs.

The **story** has also been really enjoyable so far. It does a great job pulling you into the world, and I found myself actually wanting to keep progressing to see what happens next. On top of that, the **world feels alive**, which is one of my favorite things about the game. Walking through towns, exploring different areas, and interacting with NPCs makes the game feel immersive rather than empty.

Speaking of NPCs, I genuinely enjoy **talking to them and discovering side stories**. A lot of open-world games have NPCs that feel like background decoration, but here they actually add to the atmosphere and make the world feel lived in.

My main complaint is the **skins/cosmetics pricing**. They are definitely on the expensive side, and I think the prices could be much more reasonable. That said, it doesn’t really ruin the core gameplay for me since it’s mostly cosmetic.

Overall, this game has strong combat, a good story, and an immersive world that keeps me coming back. It’s not perfect, but if you enjoy open-world action RPGs with great atmosphere, it’s definitely worth trying.

As a F2P player, this game delivers everything I’ve had hoped for in a Chinese wuxia game. Previously, I had played other wuxia and xianxia games, and only Gujian 3 truly stood out. Where Winds Meet delivers in spades for its well written storytelling and beautiful settings of ancient China in 962 A.D. Now I know other famous figures like Bao Qingtian (999-1062) didn’t exist until another half a century later of this game’s timeline, I’m still in awe of how awesome Kaifeng city look in the game. Now that’s how I’d imagine what the ancient capital look like.

The single player contents alone are more than 100+ hours. No P2W paywalls to block progress. I have spent the majority of my time playing the single player campaign and side quests. I haven’t touched the online portion much besides helping a few people fight boss battles. 

The game does suffer some bad UI design: too cluttered of menus and submenus. I don’t know if it is because they have a mobile version so they try to make UI between PC and mobile similar or not. Anyway, that’s the main drawback of the game for me.  I wish there is an option to hide most of the UI besides the mini map. 

Overall, I would highly recommend this game. Any fan of old Hong Kong wuxia flicks like me would love what this game aims to achieve. All of the gacha stuffs in the game is for optional cosmetics, and they didn’t hinder the single player portion. Thank you for all the whales financing this game so I could play it for free.

I usually avoid free-to-play games like the plague. 
[h3]But this one (Steam version) has almost none of the fundamental annoyances, if you just wanna play it (as essentially an SP or even MMo-ish MP game). 20 hours, lvl 30+. [/h3].
That MAY may change later.

1. You don't need to make any account, just install and play. 2. It does not at all feel slowed down in progression and access to the story to "encourage" buying microtransactions (Ubisoft). 3. It has no waiting timers or even excessive grind between story bits (SWTOR). At least on lower difficulty.
   It is almost baffling how there is no incentive beyond cosmetics to spend money. Unlike in (very) full-price Ubisoft games, where you can buy literal "booster packs for XP," and where the progress does feel slowed down to encourage that.

[h3]What it has is an incomprehensible jungle of unlocks, upgrades, and (cosmetic) shop mechanics that are so messy and confusing, I literally would not use them even if I wanted to. [/h3] 
And why not, if I play it like a real, solo game? I wouldn't mind paying a little, if it's worth it. But I won't because the whole thing is such a mess.   Maybe worth considering for them.
But as mentioned above, you don't have to spend money; it feels like a real game without it. Unlike, say, SWTOR, where the f2p version is a fancy demo version of the game (massively 
 slowed down, restricted features) .
[b]Just in general, as most reviews mention, the entire menu system ingame (inventory, quests, (12 different...) exploration progress menus) and system options is a MESS! The worst mess I have ever seen in a game's menu. And it's not even close.[/b]

Anyway: I play this (for now) like I play ("modern") Assassin's Creed games: as a single-player story game. Ignoring any online mechanics completely (Ubisoft) or almost completely (WWM). And in both cases that works. You have a normal game. Better, actually, in WMW than in AC Shadows.

[h3]Of course WWM (unlike AC) does have actually a lot of working and interesting actual multiplayer mechanics; you can play it MMO-esque with others. While Ubisoft is just a "service game" with no added value.[/h3]
While I ignore this part of the game for now, that is a massive additional boost for it. I can't talk about how well it works with coordinated boss fights, dungeons, and so on, or how bad lag is. In SP, even though it needs to be online, there are no lag issues. That may change in mp.
I read from others that there is no pay-to-win in the multiplayer system.

Now I have a few issues with it, which are not related to f2p, and that MANY people seem to share.
[h1] Too many, too annoying, too incomprehensible minigames.[/h1] In some cases (the arguing one), it helps to just drop cards at random, press Q and E when prompted, and spam "damage" as fast as possible. But that just proves how pointless it is.
And unlike in modern Ubisoft (and others') games, there are no accessibility options to bypass that stuff. But it also does not seem to happen in the main story quests, so you can usually ignore it.

The other issue comes with f2p: always on. If it loses internet connection, it stops and tries reconnecting. But at least it does that, unlike Ubisoft+ games, which just insta-close. Also, connection handling and servers seem to be a hell of a lot more stable and reliable than the Ubisoft ones.

Why do i mention Ubisoft and AC so much? Let's say it is VERY inspired by it, with a slightly shifted focus (more complex combat, much simpler climbing/movement).   [b] While i would say the story in WWM is actually better! [/b] It's crazy but It feels more connected and written through,  while most recent AC's feel like short stories put together in a lose connection (AC Valhalla! Mirage and Shadows a bit better) ) .

The game being free to play and having no pay to win does not single handedly make the game good and honestly people telling you otherwise are knee deep into a sinking ship fallacy. To give it credit the game does a really good job at getting you hooked for a while until you realize there really isnt much substance to it.

Its the kind of game where if you get it, you get it, and if you don't, you won't. It is inherently catered to the CN market, so it functions quite differently from games most players would be used to. I find the people who are most critical about it are usually unfamiliar with or uninterested in Chinese culture. 

This game is so much more than just fighting and PvP, its also an immersive cinematic experience tying history with the fantastical. Some references might be lost on players who don't know anything about ancient China, especially because the translation work isn't the best. The maps are based on real Chinese cities. There's always something for you to do, and with the number of quests available in game, I find it hard to believe people who say there's nothing else to do after completing the main quests. Like I said, iykyk, and if you don't you just never will.

Where Winds Meet – Steam Review

👍 Recommended

Playtime: 26 hours
Rating: ⭐ 9/10

✔️ Pros:
✔️ Stunning graphics and world design
✔️ Smooth, satisfying combat (great for Souls-like fans)
✔️ Huge open world with rewarding exploration
✔️ Relaxing atmosphere – perfect to just chill
✔️ Includes fun non-combat mini-games
✔️ Its Free to Play

❌ Cons:
❌ Story feels a bit boring at times
❌ Mostly text-based storytelling
❌ Very few cinematic cutscenes

Review:
Where Winds Meet is honestly one of the most visually beautiful games I’ve played in this genre. The environments are detailed, immersive, and just fun to explore—you can easily lose hours just wandering around and taking everything in.

The combat is another major highlight. It feels responsive and skill-based, giving off strong Souls-like vibes. Fights are engaging and require proper timing, which makes every win feel satisfying.

However, the story is where the game falls a bit short. It’s mostly told through text with minimal cutscenes, which can make it feel slow and less engaging compared to more cinematic games. It’s not bad—but it’s definitely not the main reason you’ll keep playing.

That said, the overall experience is still fantastic. The game mixes exploration, combat, and even some unexpected mini-games that add variety and make it stand out. It honestly feels like it can compete with big titles like Ghost of Tsushima in terms of vibe and world design.

And the best part? It’s free. That alone makes it a must-try.

Final Thoughts:
If you’re looking for a beautiful open-world game with challenging combat, lots of exploration, and something you can both grind and relax in—this is absolutely worth your time.

Where Winds Meet feels like stepping straight into a living wuxia novel. The martial arts are fluid, the landscapes are poetic, and the world has this quiet pull that keeps drawing you in. If you’ve ever wanted something that captures the vibe of Ghost of Tsushima but mixes it with classic Chinese martial arts fantasy, this comes pretty close.

The biggest highlight is definitely the combat. It feels stylish and responsive, and it actually rewards good timing instead of just button mashing. Every move has weight to it, especially when you start chaining abilities or countering enemies at the right moment. It doesn’t feel like you’re just fighting, it feels like you’re putting on a performance.

The open world also deserves credit. It’s not just large for the sake of it, it has atmosphere. From misty mountains to quiet villages, everything feels designed to pull you in. Talking to NPCs and exploring side activities makes the world feel alive, like you belong there instead of just passing through.

That said, it’s not perfect. There are moments where the game feels a bit rough around the edges. AI can act strangely, some animations feel clunky, and performance isn’t always consistent. The story has interesting ideas, but the pacing can feel off at times, especially if you’re not already familiar with wuxia themes.

Even with those issues, the potential here is huge.

Final verdict
If you enjoy exploration, martial arts combat, and immersive worlds, this is definitely worth trying. It’s not flawless, but it has that kind of charm that makes you want to keep playing just to see what’s waiting ahead.

Let's be clear, I really like this game and I think it is missjudged by lots of people. 
The first one are the youtuber and the second unemployed people who are looking  for an endless farming game service. 

So let's start to talk about what Where Winds Meet is not. 
It' is not an MMO and it is not a PURE game service because the game is not looking to make you sink Tons of hours inside the game. They want you to come back ofcourse but the stamina system limits what you can do. 

So what is Where Winds meet ? 

It is a ARPG MMO LITE and the lite is really important. 
You have tons of SOLO content, a story which is enhanced and keep on season after season, it's a game novel. 
If you start today, you have at least 150  - 200 hours of pure solo play. 
You have a catch up system which will allow you to improve your equipement faster than people at the edge. 

Yes Chinese UI are bad and overwhelming, you will play the notification game after 5 first hours, although Everstone Studio tried to introduce features slower in order to not lose you in the menus. 
The stamina system is limiting your progression but it also allows workers, Dad or casual to keep up by coming every week to do the solo content and farming some equipement while playing  IARPG season/a competitive game/another mmo lite
There is no pay to win, you can't buy more stamina, you can't buy power and you can only buy style and aura. 

SO you  are only paying for cosmetic if you want. Yes the flashiest cosmetics cost a lot but you can have descent character without using the gacha system. 

At the end, it's a great APRG with good gameplay, good enough story, good characters and Wuxia univers with one of the fairest monetisation in the free to play scene. 
It is worth trying and even staying. 

My playtime is my proof.

Where Winds Meet is a game I can recommend with some clear reservations. The fact that it is free-to-play combined with the sheer amount of content available makes it an easy title to try, especially for players curious about the genre.

The standout feature is, without question, the combat system. It is a solid 10/10 - fluid, engaging, and genuinely addictive. What elevates it even further is the level of build diversity. Experimenting with different playstyles and character setups is, in my opinion, the game’s strongest aspect and the main reason to keep playing.

That said, the experience is not without its flaws. Exploration quickly becomes repetitive and, at times, frustrating. Much of it revolves around performing the same tasks repeatedly. Collecting resources and grinding materials to improve your character. This loop can feel tedious, especially after extended play sessions.

Another major downside is the user interface. The menus are overly complex, cluttered, and reminiscent of a mobile game design. Navigating through numerous windows becomes unnecessarily time-consuming and detracts from the overall experience.

As for the online component, particularly PvP, it feels significantly unbalanced. Personally, I chose not to engage with it and have little interest in doing so unless improvements are made.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is definitely worth playing for its main story and exceptional combat system. However, players should be cautious about rushing into the endgame, as the repetitive nature of its systems can lead to burnout rather quickly. I personally began feeling fatigued around level 40 due to the constant cycle of gathering and exploration. Despite that, the high-quality combat kept me engaged longer than I expected.

Where Winds Meet has ended up being one of those games I didn’t expect to get so attached to. It’s a surprisingly deep open-world RPG that blends exploration, combat, and player freedom in a way that kept me playing all the way to the current level cap. I’ve now fully completed Qinghe, Kaifeng, and the full Hexi region content, including Qinchuan Path, and somehow I’m [i] still [/i] logging in daily just to chase achievements, help guildmates, and wander around looking for secrets I probably missed the first time.

[b] What the Game Does Well: [/b]
The world is huge, lively, and constantly throwing something interesting at you. If you like wandering into random events, side quests, hidden NPC chains, or bizarre achievements, this game rewards curiosity nonstop.

Some achievements are completely unhinged in the best way possible. “Goose Slayer” had me [spoiler] intentionally failing a healing quest just to trigger a demonic goose transformation so I could defeat it using Tai Chi. [/spoiler] Another achievement had me collecting 200 buckets of dung under a timer. The newer Hexi and Qinchuan Path content somehow continues this tradition with hidden martial fellowship chains, secret wells, wandering NPC duels, and entire questlines that only trigger at specific times of day.

The game constantly feels like it’s hiding [i] something [/i] behind every ruined temple, cave entrance, or suspiciously isolated shack.

[b] Solo Content: [/b]
Solo play is still one of WWM’s biggest strengths. You can comfortably experience the full story, exploration, and most activities without needing perfect gear or hardcore optimisation. The game is very good at letting players engage at their own pace.

Main story content remains solo-only, which honestly helps the narrative land better. You still [i] can [/i] invite friends into your world for exploration, bosses, or help with difficult content, but the game never forces constant multiplayer interaction just to progress.

[b] Combat: [/b]
Combat still sits in that sweet spot between flashy wuxia fantasy and Souls-like timing combat. Dodges, parries, counters, and weapon combos feel satisfying without becoming exhausting.

The weapon variety has gotten even better with newer updates and balancing changes, and there’s now a much stronger focus on buildcrafting and skill synergy at endgame. Casual players can still comfortably enjoy the game, but high-level PvE and PvP absolutely reward players who learn mechanics properly.

Difficulty settings continue to be one of the game’s smartest features. You can make combat challenging or relaxed depending on what kind of experience you want.

[b] Exploration: [/b]
The world has expanded massively since launch, and every major region feels distinct.

[b] Qinghe [/b] – The starting region and still one of the largest. Relaxed pacing, huge landscapes, and thousands of collectibles and markers make it the perfect introduction to the game.

[b] Kaifeng [/b] – Dense, crowded, and packed with activity. It feels the most MMO-like, full of NPCs, quests, and vertical exploration. Beautiful, but overwhelming if you’re trying to 100% everything.

[b] Hexi [/b] – The newest major region and currently my favourite overall. The desert landscapes, ruined battlefields, hidden settlements, and open terrain give it a very different atmosphere compared to the earlier regions. Qinchuan Path, which is part of the Hexi content, adds a more atmospheric and story-focused layer to the region with hidden encounters, martial fellowship questlines, and some of the best environmental storytelling in the game so far.

[b] Multiplayer & Online Features: [/b]
WWM still has one of the strangest, and honestly smartest, multiplayer structures I’ve seen in an open-world RPG.

The shared online world functions mostly as a social sandbox. Players hang out, roleplay, gather materials, play minigames, duel, show off outfits, or recruit for instanced content. It’s surprisingly chill.

Meanwhile, all major combat activities remain instanced:
• Dungeons & Raids
• World Bosses
• PvP Arenas (1v1, 3v3, 5v5)
• Massive 30v30 MOBA-style battles
• Bounties & invasions
• Guild activities
• Co-op PvE modes

The invasion/crime system is still hilarious. Commit enough crimes and eventually either the in-game authorities or actual players get sent after you.

Player professions are also still wonderfully weird. You can heal injuries, cure illnesses, provide support services, or even act as a lawyer defending criminal players.

To put it simply:
[b] Online Mode [/b] = social interaction, minigames, professions, roleplay, guild activity, gathering, and non-combat systems.

[b] Solo/Co‑op Mode [/b] = exploration, enemies, bosses, progression, quests, housing/base systems, and most actual gameplay.

[b] Main Story [/b] = solo only.

It sounds strange on paper, but in practice it works extremely well.

[b] Customization: [/b]
Character customisation remains fantastic. You can completely redesign your character whenever you want, from minor tweaks to a full identity crisis.

The playerbase absolutely abuses this freedom in the funniest ways possible. I’ve seen elegant wuxia heroes, anime protagonists, celebrities, demons, cryptids, and yes, SpongeBob is apparently still wandering around Jianghu somewhere.

Fashion remains the true endgame.

[b] Things to Watch Out For: [/b]
The breakthrough/world difficulty system is still the game’s biggest trap for new players. Raising difficulty too quickly can leave you massively undergeared, and suddenly basic enemies start deleting your health bar.

The game also does a poor job explaining just how important gear optimisation, combo flow, and skill synergy become in higher-level multiplayer content. Solo play is forgiving. Endgame group content is significantly less forgiving.

PvP balance also continues to shift pretty frequently with updates and weapon adjustments, so expect metas to change over time.

[b] Verdict: [/b]
Where Winds Meet is one of those games that quietly gets under your skin. It’s atmospheric, flexible, chaotic, and full of personality. Between the massive regions, absurd achievements, hidden questlines, social systems, and genuinely rewarding exploration, it constantly feels like there’s something new waiting around the corner.

What surprised me most is how well it balances freedom with structure. You can spend hours sweating through PvP, optimising builds, and learning boss mechanics,or spend an evening playing music in town, helping random players, and hunting weird hidden achievements.

I’m max level, fully cleared through the current Hexi content including Qinchuan Path, sitting on 100% exploration, and I’m still logging in daily.

This is a game of difficult to swallow comprises. It's wonderful in some areas and sadly outdated in others. Ambition over refinement.  However, if you like to explore and can put up with rigid systems, this game is for you. 

--------------------------------------------------------------
GAMEPLAY

Easily the stand out feature of the game. The combat is just fluid, the abilities are always flashy and fun to look at, they actually change up positioning  effectively.  Each weapon is largely unique thanks to it's abilities even if the basic  attack scheme remains the same. 

The martial arts abilities are a particular stand out since they actively change the flow of combat. You can stun enemies, reposition them, and transport them. You can do next to anything as long as you have the ability unlocked. 

Jumping is fluid but this is where the game starts to feel more rigid. Despite a triple jump being accessible, the animation can lock you into place. 

In fact any ability based combat maneuver will  perform much more like a rigid, stay in one spot, encounter rather than something you can trigger (and move about) dynamically. 

Likewise pushing button to engage in every activity, freezes your character and often throws them into some menu or blocked out animation which takes a long time. These systems are all exciting but they all feel stilted. You really can do so much, cook, fish, eat. side quest, observe skills, learn them, but it can be tough to stomach. 

Not to mention the game is doing that live service thing where the game and story seem sprawling but really there's only so much new content and regions before hitting a sharp end because content has yet to have been released. It's a free game so it does get a pass but beware this game isn't as big as most would have you think. At least in terms of main, polished, story content. 

-------------------------------------------------------------------
GRAPHICS

Gorgeous. It rivals Unreal Engine for detail and pure scale. The environment and ability effects are always stand outs. Their vibrancy lights up the world. 

Generally the lighting is the strongest; you should see this game at night! Especially lanterns or the city, oof, wonderful. 

-------------------------------------------------------------------
MUSIC & UX 

It fits the genre. The music is well orchestrated and paced. It occurs at just the right times to swell with the environment or a particular story beat. Although sometimes the mixing can be a bit off. The music either being too loud or too quiet. 

This game is menus, menus, menus. Each freezing your character and only allowing very specific interactions with them. It can make navigating things frustrating or at the least tedious. While, I wouldn't say anything is unclear, it can be difficult to understand where the game wants you to go given just how many different buttons and clutter between effects and other menus pop ups are on the screen at once. Not horrible but something to note. 

-----------------------------------------------------------------
STORY

Easily the strangest part of this game. Some of the side character voices are most definitely AI and well it may or may not be a step up from non voiced MMO's, it's still jarring. It drags out any emotional resonance of a scene. Also a few characters with absolutely major roles have this AI voices and it's quite confusing as to why. 

Beyond that it's a typical wuxia narrative. Meaning a typical wondering hero searching for quests and living in the world. By and large there, could be, a plot about following the man who raised the character, their special abilities and revenge but it's mostly side lined for random, small, human moments between side characters. The adventurer helping the community. 

If you play this like an adventure game with story instead of a proper narrative game, you'll have a better time. 

--------------------------------------------

Lots of ambition, just could be more fluid. Although lots of fun ideas in here. Good adventure. Treat this like an ambitious Ubisoft game rather than something wholly revolutionary. Plus it is free and that already makes it worth the try.

Where Winds Meet delivers an aggressive level of visual quality—the graphics are genuinely impressive, with a richly detailed world and a strong, immersive atmosphere. Every environment feels intentionally crafted rather than filler content. This is not just “good-looking”; it’s clearly high-effort design.

It’s deep, not unnecessarily complicated. That depth becomes a strength, rewarding players who invest time to understand it.

Combat is another standout element. Enemies are not passive targets—they are challenging and force you to think instead of relying on button-mashing. This makes each encounter feel engaging and dynamic rather than repetitive.

In conclusion, Where Winds Meet is not a casual experience. But once it clicks, it becomes highly satisfying. Strong visuals, deep mechanics, and challenging enemies make it a compelling game to keep playing.

Where Winds Meet is an open-world action RPG inspired by traditional Chinese wuxia culture, developed by Everstone Studio and published by NetEase Games. It was released in 2025 on PC and PlayStation 5, with additional versions available on mobile platforms.  

The game places players in the role of a wandering swordsman during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, offering a vast world filled with political conflict, martial arts, and exploration. Players can shape their own journey by choosing different roles, skills, and combat styles.  

Gameplay focuses heavily on fluid martial arts combat, allowing players to use a variety of weapons such as swords, spears, and even umbrellas, each tied to unique abilities and fighting techniques. The game also features open-world exploration, co-op gameplay, PvP modes, and dynamic activities like quests, dungeons, and guild systems.  

One of the standout elements is its immersive world design, with procedurally rich environments and multiple regions to explore, alongside a progression system that lets players upgrade skills, gear, and abilities over time.  

Overall, Where Winds Meet stands out as a large-scale wuxia experience combining open-world freedom, fast-paced combat, and multiplayer elements. While it offers a huge amount of content and variety, some players may find it overwhelming due to its many systems and mechanics.

The gameplay is where the experience really shines. Combat feels fluid and satisfying, blending martial arts mechanics with strategic depth that keeps encounters engaging rather than repetitive. There’s a strong emphasis on freedom—whether you want to follow the main story, explore hidden locations, or experiment with different playstyles, the game gives you the tools to do so. Progression feels meaningful, and the variety of skills and abilities allows for a personalized approach that keeps things fresh over time.

What really elevates Where the Wind Meets, though, is its storytelling and overall vibe. The narrative unfolds in a way that feels natural and immersive, supported by strong world-building and memorable characters. Combined with an excellent soundtrack and attention to detail, the game creates an experience that feels both relaxing and exciting at the same time. If you enjoy open-world adventures with depth, atmosphere, and freedom, this is definitely worth your time.

1. Some encounters not triggering (despite correct time and weather)

3. As of right now I am trying to clear Tian Ying No Hit but for some reasons this particular boss can attack you right after the loading screen (the moment the black screen is fading away). It wouldnt be really a problem for normal run but sometimes I can control my character and dodge or deflect it and sometimes i cant even move at all and have to restart the run again and again. As a long time fan of wuxia and xianxia MMO style games, I was excited to dive into Where Winds Meet expecting it retain similar fans. The community instead is full of grifters, beggars, sexual harassers, and with every language coming together in the same text channels, it makes it difficult to connect with others in-game itself. While you can find those connections on Discord, it would be easier to find them in-game if there was any development pushed towards the social tools. Being able to filter languages out would be a big boon for every community, but you can't even block someone: blacklisting them still allows their messages to show up on your screen so if someone is spamming for votes or items (which offer nothing of value to conversation), the only way to filter out their message is to simply turn off the chat or go to another channel which is often filled with the same thing. 

Being a member of the Velvet Shade is a cycle of people begging for likes instead of simply doing things that would obtain them naturally because they simply can't compete with the hundreds of other players already spamming channels. 

For a game filled with socializing aspects between the sects and gallery, as well as all of the other features, it's really a shame there's nothing for chat! People will respond "just turn off the chat", but so many features are enriched by a social presence that it's really discouraging to be told that is the primary way of handling the issue when the game is at fault for not allowing players the opportunity of curating their own experience.

3 Months into this game and decided to write a review.

The Good.

1.	Graphics : simply stunning for a f2p game.

2.	Character Creation : Great functionality which enables the player to upload a photo and use that as their characters face. It will still require the player to tweak the features manually in order to achieve the desired look.

3.	Outfit Cosmetics : Very beautiful designs with dyeing functionality built in. There’s at least 1 or 2 new outfits every month so far.

4.	Fight Mechanics : Fairly easy to understand with the usual parry/deflect and attack moves. The fights are fairly smooth and the animations look quite nice.

5.	Quests : Plenty of quests all over the place as you explore the land.

The Bad.

1.	Menus : This one is No.1 on the list. A huge number of menus to click through, as you play through the game, to claim your rewards. And they’re all not always in the most obvious places. Seriously, a LOT of menus to click through.

2.	Locks/Caps : The developers have a reason for the weekly locks on eg coin accumulation but after awhile, it just enforces a lack of interest to play the game since the player may end up thinking “meh why bother playing ? Might as well wait till next week so I can max out the coins”.

3.	Cosmetics : Some come from the in-game gacha system (don’t expect to get the cosmetic in just a few rolls, if ever) and some from the cosmetics shop. Unfortunately, depending on your territory, some of those cosmetics may be very expensive. For myself, 1 cosmetic would on average cost me about 2 weeks worth of lunch & dinner.

4.	Quests : Although there are plenty of side quests all over the place, they are time/distance related, ie if you run out of range or do not click accept, then they may not be there when you next come back as they’re not auto loaded into your quest list. To make matters worse, some are either in-game time related and/or linked to other side quests to be completed first. Some quests also seem to be bugged as even following online guides to the letter, they still won’t trigger.

5.	PvP : There are multiple PvP modes available in the game but I’ve only done what is called ‘Perception Forest’; basically arena style combat. The basic rule seems to be “1st to stun lock the opponent, wins”. 

Overall, it’s not a bad game considering that it is free. There’s no real paywall other than for cosmetics. All in all, it would be worth it to try the game out just to experience it.

I have around 360 hours in this game, and unfortunately, I can’t really recommend it in its current state.

To start with the positives: the game is genuinely f2p friendly. There are no p2w mechanics, and players cannot purchase stronger gear with real money. That’s a big advantage and something more games should strive for.

However, the overall experience is held back by several major issues.

PvP feels unbalanced, and the presence of cheaters further undermines any sense of fair competition. (And no there is no skill issue or anything like that... I am quite good at PvP)
Systems like the bounty mechanic add frustration rather than meaningful engagement. U often get a bounty for no reasons, often you don't even realize when and when that happens... You will get an annoying invasion from a REAL player. Which even when u manage to defeat, u won't get anything and you still gonna have a bounty in ur head. It's better to just log off for a minute then come back to be in jail to get out, because this mechanic is really bad.
The outfit pull system also feels unnecessary and out of place, especially given how much of the social environment revolves around it. You must be very lucky to get an outfit from limited banner.

Speaking of social features, the global chat is rarely used for actual interaction. Instead, it is dominated by guild recruitment spam and players begging for outfits, which makes the game world feel less alive than it should. Even within guilds, activity tends to be inconsistent — many players join briefly, then leave or stop playing altogether. Over time, this makes it difficult to maintain any stable or active community.

While the world itself is large, there isn’t enough engaging content to support it long-term. Many events feel repetitive or uninteresting, which contributes to a gradual loss of motivation to keep playing.

For me personally, the main reason I stayed as long as I did was because I was playing with close friends. Once they lost interest and stopped playing, it became much harder to find reasons to continue. Eventually, I reached the same point.

In summary, *Where Winds Meet* has a strong foundation and a fair monetization model, but it currently struggles with balance issues, weak social systems, and a lack of engaging content. With improvements in these areas, it could become a much better experience — but as it stands now, I cannot recommend it.

A game with very good ideas but ruined with poor execution, terrible predatory monetization mechanics, and an abysmal player community.
I wanted to like this game so much, it has some nice features and looks beautiful, but play long enough and you'll notice the cracks. AI is used for voice acting and in a bizarre feature where you can talk to NPCs to earn their friendship, and while not confirmed it's suspected it's used in graphics too. 
Combat is simplistic to a fault and offers little in ways of playing. It offers multiple martial art styles but most of them are varieties of DPS, and you end up using the same few combos over and over.
The sect system is atrocious and offers little to no real benefit or unique gameplay, instead merely encouraging interacting with a certain feature while providing no real benefit outside of getting certain outfits. You have to earn votes from players in order to achieve the highest rank, which leads to obnoxious spamming for vote requests at best and outright deceit from some people at worse. Some will even spam your DMs begging for votes! Imagine experiencing election season spam calls in your game, and you can picture the experience.
Multiplayer is completely ruined by a terrible community amongst the player base. If you try to do bosses and raids, most will leave after one fight. You can specify you want to do all the bosses but people will queue up for everything to speed up finding a group and completely ignore it. Not only that you will see basic mechanics completely ignored, even after MONTHS of these fights being available, players will leave mid fight if they don't get top DPS. If you want to even remotely finish this content you need friends or a guild.
On top of just being terrible at playing the game, the community is flooded by the worst behavior I have ever seen. People will spam in world chat and even DM you begging to be gifted premium store items, even going as far as to solicit premium instagram accounts and ERP sessions in return. There is tons of racism and harassment, and often in game features will be exploited in order to troll other people in very malicious ways. This also extends into community organization too, as the discords for guilds and sects I have been in are filled with harassment campaigns and group reporting directed towards certain people for petty reasons, often fueled by sect politics. A reminder that being elected for the highest tier in a sect gives zero benefits or new gameplay elements, it is literally only for the prestige.
Then there is the monetization system, which revolves around a Gacha pull that has very little chance to give you anything worthwhile. On top of that they sometimes introduce temporary secondary systems that are even worse, expecting you to spend HUNDREDS of dollars to get anything worthwhile, and three times that to finish it. Where Winds Meet is a solid 7/10 game that offers a unique and visually impressive experience, but it’s held back by some frustrating design choices—especially its confusing UI.

One of the biggest strengths of the game is its setting and atmosphere. The world is beautiful and feels inspired by historical martial arts themes, with fluid combat and interesting abilities that make exploration and fighting enjoyable. There’s a strong sense of style that helps it stand out from other open-world games.

The combat system is fun once you get used to it, offering a mix of skills and techniques that give players different ways to approach fights. There’s also a lot to explore, which adds to the overall experience.

However, the user interface is a major downside. Menus can be confusing, cluttered, and not very intuitive, making it hard to understand certain systems or navigate options smoothly. This can take away from the enjoyment, especially early on.

The game can also feel overwhelming at times due to the number of systems and lack of clear guidance.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a good game with great atmosphere and combat, but the confusing UI and learning curve hold it back from being truly great.

I’ve put 288 hours into Where Winds Meet, and honestly, I’ve loved every minute of it.

For a free to play game, it absolutely overdelivers. It ticks pretty much every box you’d want in an open-world RPG freedom, exploration, combat depth, and a world that actually feels alive. The wuxia inspired setting is a standout it’s not something we get often at this level of quality, and it really pulls you in.

The game doesn’t hold your hand, which I personally appreciate. You’re encouraged to figure things out on your own, experiment with combat styles, and carve your own path. It can feel a bit overwhelming at first, but once it clicks, that’s where the real enjoyment kicks in.

Combat is smooth and satisfying, with a lot of flexibility in how you approach fights. Whether you’re going stealthy, aggressive, or somewhere in between, it gives you room to play your way. Exploration is just as rewarding there’s always something to stumble across, and it never feels like you’re just ticking off a checklist.

What really stands out to me is how much content there is without feeling forced into spending money. For a free to play title, that balance is rare.

Overall, if you’re into immersive RPGs with a bit of a learning curve and a lot of depth, this is 100% worth your time.

A great game, absolutely underrated by Western critics. If it had been made by a well‑known Western developer, people would be talking about it far more. Give it a try: the beginning can feel overwhelming, there are many systems to understand, and the most interesting part of the story (as well as the side quests) only becomes engaging after at least twenty hours of play. At first it may seem simple, but then it opens up into gripping plots and subplots.
The setting is fantastic, the landscapes are stunning. It conveys Eastern culture beautifully and is incredibly polished in many aspects. It’s a game to play slowly, to savor.
Unfortunately, the English translation isn’t very smooth, but the meaning and the moral of each story remain fascinating. Definitely worth trying: don’t give up at the start, if you push through, its strength reveals itself.
If you want something immediate, if you lack patience, or if you don’t appreciate art and atmosphere, this isn’t for you. For everyone else, don’t miss the chance.

Where Winds Meet is one of the most frustratingly brilliant games I’ve played in a long time. It genuinely feels like it could have been one of the best RPGs of the decade—but it’s dragged down hard by mobile-style systems and aggressive monetization.

Let’s start with what it absolutely nails:

The art design from outfits to the environment are both beautiful and immersive. Additionally, some of the combat aspects are phenomenal and satisfying.

Now for the bad—and unfortunately, there’s a lot of it.

The daily game cycle is buried under mobile game mechanics. You’re constantly dealing with energy systems, time-gated content, and progression blocks that exist purely to slow you down. Once you are out of energy or looted a certain amount of drops (whether it's Coin, gear for recycling, or even materials for crafting), you are bound to wait to get at least 20 Energy (for an outpost), daily reset, or 24 hrs from the time you last looted a resource node.

While the monetization is mainly for cosmetics, it is still brutal. Gacha systems, multiple currencies (depending on the event banners), battle passes, and endless cash prompts. You can easily spend hundreds (or far more) and still not get what you want. It doesn’t feel rewarding—it feels predatory.

The UI is a complete mess. For the start of a daily session, you’ll spend more time clearing red notification dots, closing pop-ups, and digging through nested menus than actually playing. It’s overwhelming and kills the pacing. Let's also not forget if it's patched incorrectly, you are stuck trying to figure out if the notification dots are legit or false positives.

Technically, it’s rough. Optimization is poor, with frame drops constant texture pop-in. On top of that, updates are massive and frustrating—expect huge downloads, and if something interrupts them, you might be starting over. 

Additionally good luck IF you want to PvP and you don't live next to the region servers. Enemy movement will be rubber banding, or worse moving faster than supposed to due to their connection being better. Net Codng is just beyond horrible from packet overload and even dropped inputs. And let's not forget the absolute lack of an anti-cheat which allow cheaters to enhance Qi damage, movement speed, auto-parry, etc.

The localization doesn’t help either. From translation errors in quests to overall instruction of what to do completely break immersion in what should be a rich wuxia world.

The endgame loop is also deeply unsatisfying. Because of time-gating, RNG-heavy systems, and seasonal resets, it feels nearly impossible to ever reach a truly optimized gear set before progress is effectively wiped or made irrelevant. It turns what should be long-term progression into a cycle of grinding without meaningful payoff, making the late game feel like a waste of time. Some end-game aspects like Abyss Trials don't even need optimized gear due to Inner-Ways and gear being taken to a base value.

On top of that, the development itself feels stretched thin. The game is trying to support too many versions at once—mobile, PS5, Lite, standard, and even an upcoming “Ultimate” version. Instead of one polished experience, it feels like compromises everywhere. Performance already struggles across existing versions, and considering how resource-heavy the current builds are, it’s hard to imagine the Ultimate version being anything other than a system devourer. It gives the impression that the development cycle is being diluted across too many targets instead of refined into a stable, optimized experience.

Personal note:
I went in wanting to support this game. I've bought numerous battle passes, threw some money at it early, and genuinely believed it would respect my time and investment. Looking back, that was pretty naive. The systems here aren’t designed to reward support—they’re designed to extract as much time and money as possible. That realization hit hard and completely changed how I see the game.

Game immediately slaps you with choices bigger than your grocery list, 20‑plus regions to explore, and combat that feels like someone told me “bro, timing matters” way too late. and yes, it’s free, but the moment you walk out of the starting village you realize this game is one part serene wire‑fu stroll, one part “oh god ten enemies at once why is there EVEN a rope dart umbrella combo?” vibe. movement and combat actually feel good. like, you swing, you parry, you accidentally tumble off a cliff because you bobbed your head at a cute NPC and now you’re dead. honestly, about half my deaths were because I went “oh this scenic view looks peaceful” and then gravity popped in like “nah dude, fall harder.” the world is massive, pretty, and sometimes overwhelming. there’s story quests, co‑op stuff, guild wars, little side activities, collection quests… and you might be like “cool, I want to do everything”—then you realize you don’t even know what half the icons on your map do yet. like, am I supposed to be chasing this tiger or just vibing with NPCs under lanterns? probably both. controls and combat reward you when you actually think about what you’re doing. unlike games where you just mash and pray, here if you dodge at the wrong moment you’re eating dirt and boots. feels fair enough to teach you, but also makes you salty when you wipe on a group of low‑rank enemies because you thought you had that parry.

free‑to‑play? yeah, it’s free, and most monetization is cosmetic, so you don’t get some “pay to win” nonsense in combat (thankfully). the UI can feel like it threw 100 menus at you at once, but once you get used to it, it’s manageable—not great, but it’s not the end of the world either.

and finally, the vibe. being a wandering sword master in a wuxia world is actually cool. wire‑work movement, random moments where you glide across rooftops like you’re suddenly anime protagonist, side quests that hit surprisingly emotional notes… there’s a lot of charm here.

end of the day you’re gonna:

think the world is gorgeous
get lost in the menus once or twice
accidentally fall off things far too often
feel pretty badass when you string together a clean combo
and ultimately feel like you learned something even if you died a bunch

overall: very positive vibes, especially for fans of martial arts RPGs. lots of content, rewarding combat, and surprising depth.

8.8/10 — fun, chaotic, and worth the download (especially for a free‑to‑play game that doesn’t shove paywalls in your face)

Controls are non-local. Meaning they depend on server response, making the game based on strict timings of parries, dodges and attacks unresponsive exactly at critical times. As an overseas Chinese player, I genuinely feel proud and happy to see such a high-quality wuxia game gaining recognition globally. It’s great to see Chinese culture reaching a wider audience in this way.

However, the PvP experience is honestly frustrating. Playing with ~200ms latency against players with ~20ms is simply not fair. Even with tools like ExitLag, you still can’t overcome the physical distance to the server.

The PvP system itself has great potential, the combat feels solid and skill-based, but the latency gap completely undermines it. After finishing ranked matches, I often just feel more frustrated than satisfied.

I really hope the developers can address this (e.g., regional servers or better netcode). Once this issue is resolved, I’d gladly change my review to positive.

EDIT: People keep saying it's free game, actually I believe most of people have spent more than a paid game on it, definitely enough money for adding servers.

This game is actually damn good. Here are my 2 cents for this game:
Pros:
1. Combat is good. Mystic skills are really cool and diverse with a lot of weapons to try out. There are in game guides too to teach you which weapons and mystic arts go well together. But you can do whatever you want.
2. Story is decent. First couple of hours was slow, but it really starts picking up once you reach the end of MQ1.
3. Truly the most open-world experience of all time. This is a huge world. With lots of encounters (sub quests) and sub bosses that trigger when you're just roaming a place. Don't rush wanderers. Take this game slow and explore. Tons of things to do beside the MQ. I spent all this time just exploring the 1st map of the game, and then theres 2 more on the line.
4. Boss Difficulty - Now I'm a DS3 and ER player. So naturally I took the Legend Difficulty. And boy is it rough. Bosses are actually dang tough, and you have learn the patterns to parry, dodge and so on, on Legend difficulty, otherwise the boss will yeet you into outer space. That said the bosses are really cool, unique and fun to learn; Gives me a lot of ER joy if you catch my drift. More casual players should prefer Story or Recommended difficulty though, because it will feel like you're up against a wall. (Secret mechanic: I won't spoil the details, but there is a mechanic by which you can nerf bosses like you do in Sekiro, which was genuinely a pleasant surprise)
5. Exploration mechanics: Horses, Fast running, Wall running and 3 ways to fly across the map like wuxia master you are. Nuff said.......
6. No pay to win mechanic whatsoever. There is a gacha, but that's for the true endgame - Fashion. You'll see when you play in the arena

Cons:
1. The menus: They can get overwhelming at first, but you'll get used to it eventually.
2. There is no skip button to the dialogues of all quests except the MQ. Can get frustrating at times when you just wanna skip.
3. This is a grindy game. To deal Mega Bonk levels of damage, you will need to grind a lot of materials.
4. This is a specific complaint to the devs - Please add a feature to convert lower tuning materials to higher ones.

I was interested in playing this game, after all the good reviews done by many people; and overall I think the game is a good game, but not enough to dedicate time to it, due to its very average combat and interactions overall.

The game does look great; it is very "inspired" in terms of being standard martial arts fantasy/realistic style as seen many times in many other games. Performances are OK; with stuttering here and there but nothing too bad.

Where the game fail in my opinion is in the overall interactions and combat. The story is average; person have a fight; person get adopted, person mystery and so on... And most side quests are also in the same fantasy/kung-fu movie style and tone, which either is your thing or it is not. I didn't mind it and found it pleasant in general.

Ended up playing about 4 hours, to see where the game is going after the initial intro, and sadly it didn't really stick with me. Combat and interactions as mentioned are quite unpleasant. The interactions are done with right trigger holding it; while you have other actions requiring to tap on the right trigger and a face button or the left trigger and the face button. This often end up becoming a pain when you just want to talk to someone or interact with something, and have to hold the trigger. Not sure why they went that way but it is really uninspired. Also some interactions requires only the tap of the right trigger, which end up also starting the action wheel animation and it is a hell of a distraction.

IF this was the only issue, I would say it could be manageable, but then you try the combat and see that it is not that inspired. Very clunky and not that enjoyable. I spent 4 hours walking around, talking to people and clearing a dungeon in a underground temple; and not for a single moment I felt I was having fun. Neither collecting things, with 200 notifications bombarding you about stuff happening; nor with the actual combat, nor talking to people and hearing their quests. Some were fun, like uncover cheaters selling fake remedies or playing drunk games (this game seems to be fixated with alcohol as recurring theme... At one point I got in a scene where there was a watermark on the screen saying "young people should not drink alcohol"... WTH).

One thing that I found interesting is that some quests are done with AI, so you talk with AI agents in real time using your keyboard (or a microphone I guess). If you complete their request you gain something (items, points, whatever) and your relationship with them increases It was fun for few times until I realized I was just wasting time roleplaying with chatgpt-style gameplay, but if you are lonely and have nobody to talk to, there are plenty of these AI NPCs around to be entertained.

It has its moments and walking around is very inspiring, due to the great backgrounds and the map is really well done; but it is really boring to interact with anything and I can find other free games that would entertain me more. As such I am not recommending it but it is not a bad game... If there were no other action RPG games free to play on the market, this would be a great one, but as 2026, it is really not enough for me to keep me busy.

So far, I find this game extremely ... boring. And at the same time supremely overwhelming. There are soooo many menus and screens and screens within screens within screens. The story so far is utterly banal and irritating. Looking at you, Ruby, and yes, this may be very much the start of the journey, but I'm not really invested in following this little spoiled brat around the area all the time. I did some optional tombs, I guess you call them? They were ... not very interesting. I tried fighting a world boss and the game told me to come back at level 30. I'm level 9. Guess, this is the "MMO" aspect.

The game's combat is Sekiro inspired, but Sekiro felt like a rhythm game. I haven't found that rhythm here yet if there is one. The problem here is that deflect and block are on two different buttons, whereas in Sekiro not 100% hitting the deflect would at least net you a partial block. Here you take the brunt of the attack. Which doesn't seem to matter, as long as you're vaguely keeping up with the power level? Every other "boss" so far was a pushover I could almost face-tank, every normal enemy doesn't stand a chance. It feels strangely balanced. Even the lvl 30 boss would be beatable. Got him to his last phase basically on my first try, but you're limited to 1 healing item for this fight, so I'm just going to wait.

Rewards feel unfulfilling. No matter WHAT you do in the game every reward is basically the same. You get gold and materials, just in different quantities. It doesn't really entice me to go explore and find hidden chests, because all I'm going to find in them is going to be more of the same. I know I NEED those materials, but that doesn't make it more interesting, you know?

Traversal around the map is fine, but there is no fall damage and the whole movement feels kinda floaty, like you're not really part of the world, especially when your character just decides to run up on a wall, any wall, in a 90 degree angle. This is supposed to look "cool" and "mystical", but in reality you get stuck on 90% of surfaces, making some weird half-poses, and falling down after you run out of stamina.

The game just has too many systems to really enjoy, to be honest, Block, deflect, but also stamina and Qi as two more separate bars. Then, of course, there's your hit point bar, and your enormous amount of usable skills and items (you have basically 4 skills per Trigger button combination). It's imho an improvement over the Dark Souls approach of slowly cycling through your spells and items, but the way it's implemented here just clutters the screen. Whereas in Souls games you can clearly see what you're using, here there are hundreds of skills that have very indistinct symbols. Maybe there is a better way to implement this, but you better know all your skills by heart, and remember where they are, and then actually press the right button combination in the heat of the battle.

Graphically, it's quite nice-looking. The character creation is obviously where a lot of the motivation for players is supposed to come from in the form of endless amounts of hairstyles, dyes, accessories and clothing articles, which for the most part are behind a Gacha paywall, which is ... fine. It's F2P after all. However, I feel like this game would have been better suited as an actual SP game with co-op for a fixed price. Trim down the open world, get rid of the battle passes, the gacha, the whatever, but that's wishful thinking.

As it stands right now I don't really see this as an actual MMO, it's more a SP open world style game with endless amounts of markers, with optional coop elements. Enemies sometimes just but out and either ignore you, run away, after running at you, or just are indecisive what they wanna do. The camera is another MAJOR point of contention. It spazzes out completely. All the time. But even more so in confined spaces. Since you're constantly moving around relatively fast, and there is a lot of verticality in combat, you don't see ♥♥♥♥ half the time ... and get motion sick.

Parrying feels fine when you connect, but since the parry is basically instant, you really need to condition yourself to not anticipate a hit, but react immediately, which is damn hard, since the game's attacks are often very poorly telegraphed, minus the actual red and yellow attacks, which I found quite fair most of the time, but everything else can be a 15 hit combo with varying speeds and slow downs, which you all need to perfect parry or evade, while the enemy hyper armors through everything you throw at them. Looking at you, Elder what's his name.

But in all seriousness: SO MANY MENUS AND SUBMENUS! I will keep playing until the 1st proper story boss, at the very least, but if the story and boss encounters don't pick up by then, I guess, I'm done. I'm not going to engage in the gacha ♥♥♥♥ anyway, no way. These systems are ALWAYS a scam.

Also, the heavy use of AI in the game is something to be mentioned. Not sure how much they're using for art, voice, etc., but I wouldn't be surprised. As it stands, there are characters in the game you can build a reputation with it seems 0/100 friendship, yay. But they require you to talk to them ... as in talk with a LITERAL chatbot. And you know, who gets all the data from that? And who is going to use that to "train" their stupid LLMs? Right. I wouldn't trust Google or any other company with this ♥♥♥♥, let alone a Chinese company, which is beholden to hand over all data to their government if they demand it.

So, my feelings thus far are mixed. The English translation has some serious flaws, and as is so often the case with Eastern games what is written in the subtitles often doesn't match what is being said. Entire names change, for instance. The voice acting is also, well, not very great, to be honest. Unless they intentionally went for very annoying. Your character's lips move, but half the time they're totally out of sync. Volume randomly changes as well. Speaking of volume: I had to turn the game down to like 50% master volume, otherwise it's just unbearably loud compared to everything else on my system.

Cutscenes are also a major uncanny valley factor. They tried to do a lot here, so everything is over the top, but the animation quality can't really handle this style of action cutscene, so at least it has that in common with other MMORPGs.

I have a feeling that gearing your character will become a chore soon, and inventory management will be the bane of my existence. You also find some weapons early on you can't effectively use, because in order to unlock the martial arts skills for it, you need to do things you can't really do right now ... or you'd have to go out of your way to find somewhere in the world. AND be a certain level. That is ... weird design.

I think there are a lot of other Eastern (and Western) action RPGs out there that are far superior. Be it Nioh or Black Myth Wukong, to name just two. Where Winds Meet is this weird amalgamation of ... menus, kidding, ideas. And I don't think they all meld together nicely.

IMPORTANT: My Steam playtime is wrong because I mostly play this game on mobile (thanks, RAM), but in the hours I have played on PC, I'll share my thoughts on it. My review is based on over one month of playing (I guesstimate I have over 40 hours on this game already as of this review).

The game's premise, stories, and battle system are SO FUN. Gameplay on PC is wonderfully smooth, despite the complex menus. It seems like most people complain about this as well, so I hope the devs really try to streamline things to not make it as complicated as it is now. That being said, you DO get used to it, so please be patient and give the game a chance.

There's a lot of opinions, also, surrounding the gacha mechanic of this game. For people who are new here: this game's entire story, weapons, and ALL GAMEPLAY ASPECTS are FREE. The only thing that costs money is cosmetics (e.g. costumes, skins). There are also such things as Battle Passes, which can help aid your exploration, but none of these purchases actually "make the game easier." Personally, I think this is the BEST "gacha" game I've ever played, in that it's very fair. It's your own choice to want to buy outfits and skins, but even if you don't, the story and gameplay mechanics aren't worse because you choose to remain F2P. 

I also appreciate that some costumes are MUCH cheaper and can be directly bought from the Shop, and not all costumes are locked behind a gacha. The free outfits are perfectly fine, too, and overall, I've spent about $50 on this game so far because I enjoy some of the premium costumes. The devs need to make money somehow, is my logic, and here's my "thank you" payment for the game!

Finally, my biggest "criticisms" of the game are:

1. Please make photo mode easier and allow us to do more poses easier. I have a partner I want to take cute and cool photos with, but BOY is it hard sometimes. Obviously, the game doesn't allow mods, so I'm hoping the devs listen to the fans and make the Photo Mode easier to navigate and use.

2. Co-Op somehow becomes HARDER when we play with a friend, because it scales up the difficulty to the highest level player. This means that unless you REALLY know what you're doing and can deflect on time, etc., you're kind of screwed with the difficult bosses like Tian Ying. (I have a personal vendetta against this man.)

If all of that was too much to read, here's the TL;DR:

Pros:
1. Game story is wonderful, immersive, and fun. There's LOTS to do in Solo Mode. You don't even need to do Co-Op/Online to have a good time.
2. Graphics are incredible, and battles are fun.
3. ALL GAMEPLAY ASPECTS, INCLUDING CHARACTER LEVEL/POWER, IS FREE AND NOT LOCKED BEHIND PAYWALL. This is the best part!
4. Customization options are plentiful even for F2P players

Cons:
1. Menus are way too complex at times and confusing, though you do get used to it after playing for a few days.
2. Gacha is impossibly mean. You typically need to hit hard pity to get the Legendary items.
3. Photo Mode is clunky and limiting. I want to take cute (and hot lol) poses of me and my partner!
4. Co-Op Mode to fight bosses scales UP, which means it's harder to beat. I do not like this aspect but respect people who like a challenge.

I think this is my first-ever review on Steam, so thanks for listening!

The Xianxia scratch for the MMORPG Burnout itch.

Do you want to play as a cultivator dashing through the air and harnessing the power of qi to smite your enemies while wielding traditional and unconventional weapons like an umbrella or fan?  Pick this up. 

I spent maybe a decade total in my younger days in MMOs such as WoW and FF XI, and as much as I fondly recall the nostalgia of those times, the reality is I would rather be skinned alive by a pack of baby murlocs than pick one up again.  Very much a "I miss the idea of it" type things.  

That all being said, this is the perfect game to recapture that feeling with pure solo run-through ability.  The quests are standard MMO fair, and the bosses are somewhat Souls-Like (which is a genre of games I don't particularly care for), but not to an insane degree.  There are always collectables to spot and pickup, and a plethora of factions, weapons, gear, and side-missions to encounter.  The mobs also scale to your level range, which can remain capped where you want or increase it through trials for more abilities, talent points, and challenge levels.  There is also the signpost feature that allows others to pin hints in the game for solo players to interact with, which is a neat feature, even with the occasional troll or poorly placed note.  There is a wide diversity in build styles, the minigames/professions are neat, and best of all it is 100% F2P.  Sure you can drop an insane amount of real cash for a gatcha system with terrible odds, but by and large it is purely cosmetic gains.  Very pretty gains, but unnecessary to enjoy the game.  On that note this game is gorgeous, and even better runs fairly well on the SteamDeck with default settings - baring an occasional frame-rate spike in NPC heavy areas. 

It's not without it's faults, translation errors, or glitches - but overall I'm enjoying the hell out of it.  

Also, don't mess with the Geese.  Trust me on this, those little demons are brutal.  They are this game's version of the Killer Rabbit of Caerbannog.  You have been warned.

Between all the bugs, bad servers and matchmaking, boring story gameplay most of the time a walking sim, cosmetics dropped every week, and broken weapons/abilities in pvp, the game is fun.

This wallpaper generator is also a fast-paced RPG but it's also an interactive lesson in Chinese history however we can't forget that it's also a collection of multiplayer mini-games and an online fashion show. Oh, right, I forgot, it's also tactical PvP fighter with combos and huge build variety.

I've played pretty much since launch and haven't been able to put it down.

Single-player mode reminds me of Wukong and Sekiro mixed in. Beautiful scenes, diverse bosses and great variety. Legendary difficulty (which can only be selected at the start of the game but can be turned down if needed) offers a solid challenge with different approaches being viable. I've struggled early on and called in friends via co-op for some of the bosses but as I've learned my build and got used to the systems the fights transformed into cinematic masterpieces. While some bosses can down you in only a few hits, they are designed very fairy with clear understanding after each loss of where exactly you messed up.

Only PvE Raids with 5 and 10 man groups can be difficult in pick-up groups as there are boss mechanics that players will need to learn and a small level of coordination is required. Running them in a pre-made Guild team is almost trivial but still fun and unlockable talents (achievements) give you something to work towards. From previews of Chinese server it seems like the difficulty of Raids will pick up even more and better teamwork will be required.

PvP - there are currently 4 forms of it in Where Winds Meet. The meatiest and deepest is 1v1 Arena. It's like Black Desert Online and Tekken had a baby. It's very fast but extremely tactical. Spamming gets you nowhere and knowledge rules supreme. 3v3 Arena is a fun, less demanding format. Some builds clearly stand out for it and you're less able to brain your way out of trouble. Perception Forest is a battle royale with all the common systems in-place. Lastly, there's open world PvP via the Bounty system. Fun, but not particularly flashed out. (There's Prison Break PvP as well but that's more of a "For Fun" mode)

Free to Play. It really is. Completely void of any Pay to Win mechanics. All paid content is cosmetic and while Gacha is pretty expensive, you also get plenty of draws for free with guaranteed Legendaries after a certain amount of draws. There's a ton of cosmetics which are earned in-game and you can be the show-stopper without ever spending a dime. Once I passed 600 hours I couldn't stop myself from buying a few skins and as I continue to enjoy this game, I'm sure I'll Pay-to-Slay again. The devs deserve my money.

Lastly let's mention performance. I started playing WWM on a 3060 laptop and was able to run it smoothly over 60FPS except for some very dense areas. I never tried the Lite client which tones visuals more because it was always running well enough to enjoy. Currently I'm on a 5070Ti and I can comfortably max out all settings and still not get any framedrops at 140+ FPS. The game is gorgeous and there's so much eye candy that I spend a few hours per week in Photo Mode.

Highly recommend to try this game out and perhaps I'll see you where winds meet.

Where Winds Meet, a game about a world-like China. You travel the world as if you are a person inside reality. You are in a journey to escape from the poorness of the bamboo abode, wrecked and covered with moss all over. From zero, you progress onward, each and every step on the way. You see the beauty of the environment, the sun, the moon, the light, the ground, the trees. the animals, the vast seas, even the deserts. As you travel around, there shall be company, the poor and the rich. Resources can be gathered in every way possible. You can converse with one another, as if it is a 1-on-1 session, despite it only being an NPC. I am truly thankful for such wonder to be birthed by the hands of god.

I’ve been enjoying Where Winds Meet, and I really appreciate the depth and design of the game. However, I’ve run into a couple of issues that I think could be improved to enhance the player experience:

Character Name Reuse:
Once a character is created, the name is permanently tied to that character. Even if the character is deleted, the name cannot be reused. For players who value customization and consistency (like me, using the name FEENUHKS across games), this feels unnecessarily restrictive. Allowing name reuse for deleted characters would make it easier to restart without feeling like progress or identity is lost.

Legend / Hardcore Mode Visibility:
Legend Mode (legend difficulty) is hidden under another mode at the start, and it’s not explained clearly during character creation. Because of this, I only realized I couldn’t switch to Legend Mode after reaching max level. Making this mode visible and selectable from the beginning would prevent frustration and help players who enjoy a hardcore challenge.

I think these changes would make the game more user-friendly while still keeping its challenge intact. Thank you for your time and for creating such an engaging experience — I hope this feedback is helpful.

Fun game with huge potential, but when spending money in the cash shop, buyers need to be careful.

First, I want to make something very clear so this review is fair.

I have put a LOT of hours into Where Winds Meet already. If the game was not fun, I would not have spent this much time playing it. The combat feels great, the wuxia setting is unique, and the world design has a lot of promise. There is a genuinely good game here.

That said, there are some very concerning issues with monetization and customer support that players should be aware of before spending money.

I am not writing this to attack the developers or to be toxic. I actually spent money on the game because I wanted to support it. I tend to think carefully before spending money in games, which is why this situation is so frustrating.

My main issue comes from purchasing the $199 package.

I bought this package expecting to receive the bonus jade associated with the purchase tier. That bonus jade never appeared.

After looking more closely at the packages, I realized something that made the situation even worse.

If I had simply purchased two $99 packages instead, I would have received more total value.

Two $99 purchases would have given me:

• The same number of beads
• The same extra bead bonuses
• An additional 6000 jade

So despite spending more money on the $199 package, I actually ended up receiving less value than if I had split the purchase into two smaller ones.

That makes the $199 package feel like a complete waste of money, and it is something players should absolutely be aware of before purchasing.

I contacted support hoping to resolve the issue, but unfortunately that experience has also been disappointing. Response times are extremely slow, and the replies I eventually received were vague and not very helpful.

Again, I want to emphasize this: the game itself is fun. I would not have invested this many hours if it was not. The core gameplay has a lot of promise.

But until the developers address the package value inconsistency and improve customer support, I strongly recommend that players be very careful when spending money, especially on the higher priced packages.

Advice to other players:

• Compare the purchase tiers very carefully before buying
• Do not assume the most expensive option gives the best value
• Be prepared for slow support responses if something goes wrong

I genuinely hope these issues get fixed because the game itself deserves to succeed.

Right now though, players should go into the store with their eyes open.

Rarely do I find a game I feel is really engaging. I'd say some of the positives are that you can play it on whatever difficulty you want, side quests are meaningful and you really do get to choose your own path. You can get thru the game and a decent amount of it's content without being an extremely good player though the parry system and dodging is very satisfying and does reward the player's efforts! The side quests themselves can be hilarious, serious and gorgeous, the game definitely does not neglect side quests. Most side quests are quite quick as well and there isn't a sense the game is just trying to waste your time. I was very impressed by the amount of weapons and styles that the game provided, none are paywalled and are all pretty much viable, there isn't really a obvious very meta choice. It is true the free cosmetics can take awhile to get but there are still options that are free and do look good. As a f2p player though, you will pretty much never be able to pull on the limited cosmetics banner as getting free pulls is few and far between especially considering the 120 needed. Personally I do not mind as the very luxurious, flashy and heavenly appearances do not fit a wuxia protagonist quite well anyway. The voice acting for CN is amazing and the English voice acting is underwhelming. Throughout the story, it can confusing as to what is occurring since a lot of the context isn't given in the game but would only be known if you have studied Chinese history. The only gacha is cosmetics which I consider not that predatory for a gacha game as 'looking cool' isn't needed to be a better player. Overall for a game that is free to download, this game is amazing! If you love wuxia, cool combat and a moving story, definitely try this.

The combat is brilliant and feels like Sekiro every time you parry, but the game constantly hits you with energy limits and progress blocks that are very frustrating on PC. The interface is a total mess; for the first few hours, you spend more time fighting pop-ups, notifications, and red dots than actual bosses. Optimization is still bad, so expect frame drops in big cities and textures popping in right in front of you. Also, the English dubbing sounds like a robot, and there are many translation mistakes in quests that ruin the Wuxia atmosphere. Even with the technical mess, terrible UI, and forced grind, I’m giving it a thumbs up because the combat and exploration are just too good to ignore. Just be aware that it’s a beautiful game trapped inside very frustrating mechanics.
