I went into Where Winds Meet thinking I was about to become a legendary wandering swordsman. You know—mysterious hero, cloak blowing dramatically in the wind, villagers whispering my name like I’m the main character in a kung-fu epic.

Instead, I spent the first three hours accidentally parkouring off roofs, getting slapped around by bandits with sticks, and eating mysterious food I found in a basket like a raccoon with a sword.

Don’t get me wrong—this game is gorgeous. The landscapes look like someone took a Chinese watercolor painting and said, “What if you could fall off that mountain?” The wind flows through the grass, the mountains look majestic, and every town feels alive… right up until I start a fight and five dudes jump me like I owe them money.

Combat is slick once you figure it out. At first it feels like the enemies are masters of ancient martial arts while you’re swinging a sword like you just discovered arms yesterday. But after a while you start pulling off moves that make you feel like you’re starring in a lost wuxia movie.

The freedom is wild too. You can sneak, duel, explore, steal stuff you definitely shouldn’t steal, and generally behave like the most chaotic wandering warrior in ancient China.

The only downside? Half the time I have no idea what I’m doing. I’ll be on a noble quest one minute and the next thing I know I’m chasing chickens, learning flute techniques from a stranger, or starting fights I absolutely cannot win.

But honestly… that’s part of the charm.

Final verdict:
A beautiful open-world martial arts adventure where the wind is poetic, the combat is stylish, and I personally spend a suspicious amount of time getting beaten up by people who look like background characters.

10/10 would get wind-slapped again.

My (an ex-hoyo games player) mainly PvE playthrough has primarily three main stages:
1. Get immersed in the world with nothing to expect, learning many new things purely by playing. This is where it hooks you.
2. Set back in progression because you did not do something you should have done along the way (e.g., collecting oddities). So you search up a lot of things since the game tells you just a few from dozens of the game's mechanics and features.
3. Learn things at a significant rate, relying more on external sources rather than the game to teach you. Now you know a lot about the game, and find progression is getting stagnant, and fall to the pit of drip chase (perhaps $$$).

Lessons to be learned:
Limit your playtime sessions (there is an abundance of things for you to do, and you dont need to chase to complete everything). Play at your own pace. Don't search up too deep into the meta and play how you want to play. DO NOT treat it like a j*b.

As previous reviews mentioned, the gacha system is beyond awful... far worse than ANY other gacha game I've ever played (I've played a good amount.) and the content is lackluster. The martial arts is well done in PVE content, but in PVP.. its a mess. There's no actual skill involved in the PVP section of the game, which is just attack attack attack, run, heal, attack again, hope your opponent is lagging worse than you are and win. A lot of powerful gear is tied to stats that force you into horrible exploration mini games, bug hunting, etc instead of any actual stats that you can raise by leveling, forcing you to abandon the main story for exploration for large portions in order to get better gear to actually play the story. Getting better gear and leveling up is also tied into world levels, which are gained by doing awful trials, exploration etc. You are constantly advised to join a "faction" or get a "profession" which does nothing but add a ton more fetch and "repeatedly do this same task every day" missions. Martial arts that are supposed to be faction-specific can be easily "stolen" when not in that faction, making the ONLY reason to even join that faction become getting the cosmetics from the awful faction quests, which take forever to gain even half the currency required. And then there's currency.... currency for this, for that, for dying clothes, for draws, for buying items, oh for buying other items though you need another currency that you can only get by spending actual money to get an item to get an item that gives you a change to get that currency or some useless item you'll never actually know where to use.. OH, dont forget the currency that is used to exchange for loot boxes for gear sets, that themselves are a form of gacha drops because gacha for cosmetics isnt enough, we need it in EVERYTHING! 

In short, the game is amazingly beatiful and just exploring the world for the beauty could be fun, if you didnt have to be pushed into so much lackluster time-wasting "content" filled with currencies, mechanics, and systems to waste every last second of your time so you spend money to get the better things, which quickly become less better. This game is a fashion show-money grab painted pretty.

Will I still play it? Abso-freaking-lutely. Will I spend any money on it? No. Would I recommend it to anyone based on my own experience? Also, no.

It's also not possible to play the game purely in single player, because you constantly get sicknesses and injuries which can only be cured by other players. Very often it's unclear how stuff works or what to do next. For example, I arrived in Kaifeng, but the map is obscured for some reason and I have no idea how to uncover it like in Qinghe. Why?! I'm also in some palace now, wearing some weird golden dress I'm unable to change anymore. Why?! And then you have a horse that's so slow that it makes a snail look like a racer. Why?!

I'm also not too fond of the combat system, since the constant quick time parry events are pretty annoying. It just hurts the combat flow. I also have the impression that combat styles don't really exist and it's just one main combat system with some mostly useless mystic arts added to it. If you compare that to what Lost Ark has to offer in terms of class combat diversity, it's just disappointing.

Overall, it's not really a bad game and it does have its strong points like good graphics and an interesting setting, but it's also so bloated, that if you decide to play this game, you have to fully commit to it and play nothing else anymore.

I’ve been really excited about Where Winds Meet ever since I first saw it. The game just has this incredible atmosphere that immediately pulls you into the world. The landscapes look beautiful and alive, from peaceful villages to vast mountains and forests, and it really feels like stepping into a classic wuxia story. What I love the most is the combat — it looks so smooth and stylish, like something straight out of a martial arts movie, but still seems deep enough to master. It doesn’t just look like another open-world RPG; it feels like a place where you can truly explore, discover stories, and create your own path as a wandering martial artist. Honestly, it’s one of the few upcoming games that genuinely made me stop and think, “Wow, I really want to play this.” If the final game delivers the same feeling we’ve seen so far, I think Where Winds Meet could become something really special for fans of open-world games and wuxia stories.

With about 255 hours in Where Winds Meet, I can confidently say this game feels one of a kind in its own lane.

The combat system is excellent, blending martial arts mechanics with fast, responsive swordplay that makes every fight feel cinematic and rewarding. It really captures that wuxia fantasy style in a way that few games manage to do.

The world is massive and packed with things to explore. There are hidden areas, riddles, side activities, and plenty of content whether you prefer playing solo or jumping into multiplayer. The game does a great job of constantly giving you something new to discover.

My only real complaint is that I wish there was more main story content. The world is so rich and interesting that it sometimes feels like the story could go deeper.

Overall though, Where Winds Meet offers a unique experience with great combat, tons of exploration, and a lot of replay value. If you enjoy open-world martial arts games and discovering things at your own pace, it’s definitely worth the time.

Where Winds Meet is a genuinely free-to-play game with stunning aesthetics. From character creation to the variety of outfits, everything looks beautifully designed. The combat is engaging, especially if you enjoy souls-like mechanics, and the soundtrack fits the atmosphere perfectly. On high graphics settings, the world is absolutely breathtaking.

The open-world activities can feel overwhelming at first due to the sheer number of things to do, but once you get used to it, the game becomes very enjoyable.

There are a few downsides, though. Optimization can be rough in certain areas, particularly in Kaifeng. The UI also takes time to get used to because the menus are extremely layered—it's often a menu inside another menu several times over. Additionally, the gacha system for cosmetics is extremely expensive.

Overall, Where Winds Meet offers a beautiful and expansive experience for a free-to-play game, but it could benefit from better optimization, a more streamlined UI, and fairer cosmetic pricing.

Review at ~500hrs, just after Hexi has released and first bit of the story finished.

Where Winds Meet is an incredible game, that is also free. It's not 'good for a free game', it's a damn good game in it's own right. There is truly something for just about everyone. Coming from WoW, it takes some adjustment with the Western vs Eastern ideology of gaming and leisure time... What I mean by that, is that Where Winds Meet is progression-gated more than I would like at parts, and forces lateral progression, which isn't a bad thing - it means I explore more of the world, level my healing profession, hang out with my Guild, do PVP arenas or one of the probably 20-30 different social minigames that the game has on offer... and if that none of that tickles my fancy, there is still more left to uncover exploring the world, delving into the fantastic photo-mode, or importing your own 3D dance moves for your character to perform in-game, or post to the in-game 'social media' components, etc... and constant rotating, actually kinda fun events to keep things interesting even through everything else the game has on offer for you.

This isn't a game to be rushed, it is truly a game to be enjoyed. I made a second character to replay through the story on Legend difficulty (more of a soulslike experience) after rushing through it on my main, and using parry assist the whole time since I had never played a game where parry-timing was a needed skill... I didn't realize until halfway through the 2nd region that the cutscenes and story that I'd been blowing by at 3x speed because 'free china game' and assuming it wasn't anything special, were actually very well-written (even if oft goofily translated) and deep storylines, with strong emotional ties to characters that become built up and shift your mindset as you play through the first 10 hours or so of the gameplay.

The end-game loop isn't something we can really speak on fully yet as we are still in the process of catching up with the Chinese release of the game which had been out for a year prior to the Global release... However, the raids are fun and have meaningful mechanics that have made PUGs increasingly difficult to do without Excedrin on-hand (join a guild, or get a group from your sect chat, honestly. PUGs can be brutal.) There are 10-man Heroes Realms, 5-man Sword Trials, and outposts on the PVE group-content side, not including guild-specific PVE and PVP events built into the game... For PVP, we have 1v1 arenas, 3v3, 30v30 guild wars, perception forest (Naraka/Fortnite BR gamemode, essentially, surprisingly fun even if you don't like BRs).

I feel as though this is more of a social sandbox game at it's core than something like WoW that rewards constant progression and gearing tiers. The core content of the game might not take you a crazy amount of time to complete and hit max level, it can be rushed, though I wouldn't recommend it - the true value of this game comes from the in-between moments, getting lost in the world and enjoying all of it's parts as an experience vs just focusing on hardcore PVP, or raiding, etc...

Honestly, there's still so much more I haven't even touched on... Like how most of the systems meaningfully link into eachother, where arrests can allow for prison breaks, or hurt your Sect reputation... Where avoiding the law can mean a real player bounty hunter will invade your world and seek you out to take you in, or how there's a whole in-game newspaper that a certain sect manages and writes for...

If what you've read here interests you at all, there's quite literally nothing stopping you from giving it a shot. Worst case scenario, you uninstall it and play something else, but I feel like you'll figure out by level 30-40 if this is your kind of game or not. Enjoy the process, don't rush to the endgame - that's not how this game is supposed to work, though it can if you really want... You might enjoy it more to soak it all in and take your time, there is a lot to uncover.

The game is fun and clearly has a lot of potential, but it also has a lot of frustrating issues that really hold it back.

For starters, the voice lines in quests are a mess sometimes. Some quests don’t have voice lines at all, and other times the dialogue just cuts off and goes silent in the middle of a scene. Cutscenes can also be buggy and don’t always play correctly, which completely ruins the moment. The localization is pretty bad too.. there are times when the subtitles say one thing but the characters are saying something completely different. Because of that, some quests end up being confusing or just don’t make sense.
PvP can also be really laggy and buggy. Combat movement sometimes feels awful, and locking onto enemies or bosses doesn’t always work the way it should, which can make fights way more frustrating than they need to be.
Some quests just aren’t engaging at all and feel more like chores you have to push through. A few of them are so confusing because of the translation and cut voice lines that they honestly make you want to rage quit. Another thing that stands out in a bad way is some of the outfits, especially the newer ones. A lot of them just don’t look good at all.. That being said, the game does have a lot of awesome things going for it, and that’s why it’s frustrating to see these problems. The foundation is there for a really great game, but the developers still need to fix and improve a lot of things for it to truly shine.

If you grow up consuming Wuxia media, this game is a love letter, so do yourself a favor and play this. The story capture the essence of the Wuxia genre, including the way of the Jianghu, the factional drama, the dilemma between honor and survival and of course the beautiful flowing combats. Its like watching or reading all of the classic Wuxia.

It seemed surprisingly good when I started. I could ignore the boring, generic story because who cares? It's an mmo. The buggy movement was fine because when it was working properly it felt serviceable enough to be worth the occasional hiccup. Once you reach the milestone necessary for the enhanced movement skills, exploration feels a lot smoother and more enjoyable. I also really enjoyed the animation and artistic designs of some of the bosses, and some of the pre boss cutscenes did a great job getting me excited for the fight. The horse dancer's cutscene for the Dalang fight reminded me a lot of what I liked about the style of late 90's and early 2000's cutscene animation with emphasis on character and expression over raw graphical fidelity and realism. Others were incredibly generic.

What got to me was the unnecessary grindiness, the poorly implemented difficulty system, and the extremely repetitive exploration.

The thing is that combining a soulsy combat style/exploration loop with an open world MMO serves neither genre. It's like ESO, where combining Elder Scrolls with an MMO just creates a really lame, watered down Elder Scrolls game with a lame, watered down MMO stapled to it. WWM's concept could work, but the combat would need to be exceptionally polished and not be hampered by the MMO grind, leveling systems, and tacked on RPG elements. 

To elaborate on the difficulty system, the base difficulty is unbelievably, ridiculously easy and legendary just makes enemies do slightly more damage and have absurdly more health, leading to every enemy feeling like a damage sponge and every fight feeling like it drags on too long. Both options are mind-numbing in their own way, and I just wish the game was designed around a base difficulty that was actually engaging so they didn't have to clumsily implement a higher difficulty for people who want a genuine challenge.

The overall package feels muddled and pulled in too many conflicting directions for any one element to shine. I think it would take a Warframe-level rework/redesign in order to make this enjoyable long term, and I don't see that happening any time soon. Pass.

As far as free to play games go, Where Winds Meet is definitely worth your time to play. There's genuinely so much to do in the game, so let me share some things I love about the game (as well as some things that could be done a little better)

1)The combat. As someone who's favourite games are Elden ring and in general souls games (Wo long, Dark souls etc), there are a striking number of similarities between WWW and those games. Parrying feels clean and satisfying, If you'd rather focus on dodging you can; and the game even features a parry assist for newcomers who could use the help.

2)Exploration. I didn't realise when I fist started, Just how HUGE the map is. I've sunk maybe 24hrs into the game over a week of playing and have only just reached the second area. WWW is littered with collectibles, landmarks and breath taking scenery wherever you look. As some one who loves to do everything before the story, I really enjoyed how captivating the game has been. There are dungeons, hidden quests, bosses and so much more (that I don't wanna spoil); so much that I can easily see myself sinking many more days into this game.

3)Side activities. So far in my playthrough I have come across the ability to: Get drunk and throw darts, Fish competitively, Play music in a way that makes guitar hero feel easy, Wrestle geese, Perform medical miracles and diffuse situations with "the gift of gap" (yapping).

So far, my only complaints would be the lack of weapon choice and the common evil of all ftp games.... Gacha. Although there is a good list of weapon styles to choose from; I feel it could do with some more playstyles.

Overall, the game is a lovely 8.5/10 from me!!

Initially I thought I was going to play this game for a week but now I'm here for months and already established a very active guild. This game is a hybrid of MMORPG + SINGLE PLAYER experience, its not really a true form of either genre but a Perfect Combo of both. 

If you are a PVE Only player this game is for you, Social Butterfly? It is for you, PVP HARDCORE? It also caters to that audience. In short it does everything all at once and surprisingly they pulled it off. But it does not mean its perfect.

The world is expansive and very rich in lore, if you like that , take time to immerse yourself through the story and read through all of the lore dumps scattered around the Jianghu or do what I did, watched someone on YouTube explain Where WInds Meet lore. 

Overall, I think I found the game that's right for me as a long time fan of MMORPG and Single Player Games. 

So if you are interested in trying out this game well give it 2 Hours, don't be in a rush , take your time and immerse yourself, not much games out there that pulled off what the game did in so many ways. BETTER ENJOYED WITH FRIENDS TOO.

**NOTE: Might add more to this review in the future but for now See ya in the Jianghu!**

This game can be fun. However, it could also be better. Much better.

The story and bossfights are great, and the only thing that would mark them down when I played through is that it's kind of hard to leave bossfights once you get into them, and sometimes the dialogue screws up during the story. 

The open world is simply stunning. It's stupidly detailed and honestly? it is as good, if not better, than Red Dead Redemption 2's open world. That is an achievement worth so much, considering how much I love that game. 

The combat is super fun and that is coming from someone who doesn't really like souls-likes. Calling this game a souls-like is kind of a stretch, but it's the closest example I know of. Most of the abilities are fairly cool, and some can even be chained together with others to act differently. The weapons are super fun and unique, I've never used anything like them. 

All that being said, that is where my praises for this game end. 
This game is insanely grindy. I've spent probably half of my time in this game mindlessly killing the same boss for the drops I need. Are there grindier games? Yes. Does that change the fact that this game is still very grindy for the free to play player? No.

That brings me into my next point, the microtransactions.
Honestly? this game isn't the worst in this department. Far from it. At the same time, however, it's also far from the best monetized game. Most of it is cosmetic, but that's also because of the sheer amount of it that is cosmetic. The cosmetic microtransactions also stop the game from giving you many options as a free to play player (without an insane grind behind them). 

Then, there's the most irritating negative, but not the biggest. The menus.
There's a solid 12 menus as a conservative estimate, most of which lead to even more menus, which lead to more, and so on. It is a NIGHTMARE to navigate, especially when you top it off with the fact that the notifications it gives you don't tell you exactly what it's trying to tell you about. I had a notification that never went away, and it was just constantly irritating me. There's no way to fully disable notifications, or to auto-claim rewards. Then there's also cutscene menus that play music even if you have music off which, if you can believe it, also can't be turned off. 

And last but certainly not least, my biggest gripe with this game; the drip-feeding of content. 
I stopped playing for about 3-4 months, and came back recently to see what changed. Ultimately, they added a few new side-quests, some new story, and they added 2 more weapon styles/martial arts. Obviously there were some events during that but those annoyed me more than anything. That, for context, is practically nothing, in my eyes. ESPECIALLY when you consider that the Chinese version of the game already has 2+ more weapon types and 5+ weapon styles/martial arts coded into the game.

TLDR: Game can be fun, but has a lot of problems that outweigh the good parts in my eyes.

My honest review after 73 hours in less than 2 weeks.

[h2] Pros [/h2] 

- Incredibly beautiful graphics. The most immersive open world experience. Comparing to similar games like WoW it feels like a huge step ahead. No place in the world feels shallow or the same. Sometimes you just want to stand and take the atmosphere in.

- No exploring restrictions. In games similar by mechanics it often felt frustrating when you could not cut the path by passing through mountains, when you were blocked by world design, limiting you to a certain prewritten path. Here you can travel however you want.

- Immersive atmosphere of old China, traditions, art, music. It feels very unique.

- Very good optimisation. Game always feels fluid and crisp even on weaker devices.

- Absolutely unique mechanics with AI chats, real time prison, healing and diplomacy through mini-games. I mastered almost every mini-game including chess, cards, pitchpot and each feels very interesting.

[h2] Cons [/h2] 

- Huge amount of content feels overwhelming at first steps into the game. Especially if someone didn`t play anything of such genre. Dozens of types of currency, dozens of reward tabs, not quite intuitive controls for combat. It took me several days to figure some of them out.

- Multiplayer is a bit laggy. Also celectial seize, stealth attack and some objectives are unavailable if I join someone`s world which is frustrating, since it is a core mechanics of combat for me.

- Fishing seems a bit pointless, since you can get the fish just by tai chi and not spend your time reeling the fish in. It was also a bit dissapointing that the type of fish does not matter, since it all just turns into "river fish". I would love to see more diversity in it, gems and herbs. I was sad when I first found beautiful gem stones, but when I pick them up they turn into just "ore".

- It is not necesserily a con, but I get the feeling that my chosen path of splitstone is quite useless in pvp. I get the feeling that the mere speed of attacks wins pvp.

- It is also not a con, but I personally would prefer a slower character development. Just under two weeks I reached maximum world and character lvl. It would be more engaging to receive less experience, money and gear. 18 gold chests after one boss is too much.

This game is absolutely 10/10 for me and I look forward to all updates!

WWM is an ambitious blend of open-world wuxia and MMORPG elements that manages to stand tall as a solo experiencem even when its technical foundations feel a bit shaky. After 66 hrs, the game reveals itself as a masterpiece of storytelling trapped in a somewhat unpolished shell.

[h2]Storytelling[/h2]
The absolute crown jewel of this experience is the narrative. Set during the turbulent era of 10th-century China, the game moves away from generic fantasy tropes to deliver a grounded, politically charged epic.
 
In term of atmosphere, the "lone wolf" experience is highly effective here, the game honors the wanderer tradition, making you feel like a pivotal figure in a world that doesn't just resolve around you, but reacts to you.

[h2]The world & Visuals[/h2]
While the art direction is inspired-capturing the sweeping vistas and melancholic beauty of ancient China- the technical execution holds it back.
 
 - [h3]The highs[/h3]: Sunsets over the bamboo forests and the scale of cities are breathtaking at first glance.
 - [h3]The lows[/h3]: Optimization issues, aggressive pop-in(s), and a cluttered UI often distract from the immersion.

[h2]Combat[/h2]
Combat is perhaps the most divisive element, while it boasts a variety of martial arts, it often lacks the visceral "crunch" found in dedicated action titles.

[h2]The MMORPG Factor: Gameplay[/h2]
The "MMO-lite" structure is surprisingly flexible.

 - [h3]Solo Friendly[/h3]: It is rare to find an MMO that feels this rewarding for a solo player. You can ignore the social hubs and massive raids to focus on being a hermit doctor or a wandering merhcant.
- [h3]Interactivity[/h3]: The world is dense with puzzles and life skills. However, the gameplay loop can occasionally feel like a "checklist" due to the overwhelming number of icons and markers on the map.

WWM is a 10/10 story struggling against 5/10 mechanics. If you value narrative depth and historical atmosphere above else, this game definitely a jackpot for you. If you're looking for the next revolution in action combat, you may find the blade a bit dull. Overall, this is not a Pay-To-Win game but definitely can give a try on this Free-To-Play game, you may or may not discover an element(s) that surprise you.

This is the first free to play game in a long time that doesn’t feel like it’s trying to rob you.
I’m 128 hours in and I’m still messing with builds and not bored.

> Combat

It’s souls inspired, but not punishing like Elden Ring or Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. You’ll manage durability and health, but it’s not trying to break you unless you turn the difficulty up.

Combat feels grounded but still has that flashy Wuxia movement. Stats matter, but skill absolutely matters too. The more you understand your build and tweak it to your playstyle, the smoother everything feels. PvP is balanced and fun, but if you don’t learn parries or you’re playing on bad internet, you’re going to get annoyed.

> World and Exploration

Big Ghost of Tsushima energy in the atmosphere and flow. The world actually feels alive. There are hidden stories, dungeons, and exploration rewards that feed back into your build. It doesn’t feel like empty open world filler.

> Monetization

Windows (adds) don’t pop up consistently. 
Not pay to win. Cosmetics only.
Some outfits are overpriced, sure, but you are not buying power. I’ve never felt pressured to spend money.

> Pros

Combat feels unique and rewarding
Real build depth and mastery
Beautiful, immersive world
Exploration actually matters
PvP is skill based
No pay to win mechanics

> Cons

UI is overwhelming at first
English voice acting needs work
Some cosmetics are overpriced
Can feel complex if you want something simple

There is grind, but nothing even close to World of Warcraft levels.

This game won’t be for everyone. It doesn’t hold your hand.

But if you like Wuxia themes, souls style combat without the constant punishment, and getting lost in a world, this is absolutely worth trying.

Take your time with it. If it clicks, you’ll sink 100 plus hours into it without realizing it.

Mixed feelings on this one, leaning heavily negative.

The good stuff: The narrative content is serviceable. Some main story arcs and side content have decent moments, though nothing memorable. Visually it's competent without being a standout. Solid mid-tier presentation, not the jaw-dropper marketing implies.

The problems pile up fast. Localization is rough enough that meaningful chunks of the writing get mangled in translation. English voice work is also weak (around Infinity Nikki tier, for anyone who endured that), which drags down every cutscene.

Even the bits that work get buried under monetization. Progress requires energy, energy runs out, and conveniently the Battle Pass has more. Playing "optimally" means maxing every Battle Pass plus the monthly subscription, before you even start untangling the dozen-plus in-game currencies. I genuinely lost count of them.

Cosmetics go beyond greedy into absurd. Hair colors are gacha pulls. Not store purchases, not gameplay unlocks: lootbox rolls. Gear upgrade materials? Monthly pass again.
Mechanically the UI is a mess. Power progression (Goose Level) has so many overlapping layers it becomes incoherent. Combat customization (martial arts, attunement, Inner Ways, item sets) looks deep on paper but collapses in practice. Pick one setup, it works, nothing ever shifts.

Group content is borderline broken. Matchmaking will throw five DPS into a dungeon that needs a tank and healer, then watch you fail. Older content like Hero's Realm and Sword Trial is dead. I queued for hours across multiple days and got nothing. PVP and other multiplayer queues just time out after 20 minutes because nobody's there. Real co-op barely exists anyway, just one weekly run you can solo.

A handful of decent moments doesn't justify the friction. The player retention numbers speak loud enough.

No, I Do Not Recommend This Game

I really wanted to recommend Where Winds Meet.

When I first started playing, I fell in love with it fast. The world is beautiful, atmospheric, and full of personality. Character creation felt personal, the combat was smooth and satisfying, and early on the game felt very rewarding. Opening chests, exploring, and doing activities gave me the feeling that my time mattered. For a while, it honestly felt like one of those rare free to play games that respected the player.

That is what makes this review frustrating to write.

There is a lot here that I genuinely like. The world has strong mood, the combat is simple but fun, and the game has a huge amount of content on paper. Exploration, professions, martial arts, mini games, side content, and story all make it feel ambitious. I also appreciate how it mixes wuxia fantasy with historical inspiration. Even when some of the references felt overwhelming to me at first, I could still tell the world had identity and care put into it.

But the longer I played, the more the systems started working against everything I liked.

My biggest issue with this game is that it constantly limits the player. Almost every important progression system feels capped, time gated, slowed down, or buried under layers of RNG. The more invested I became, the more I started hitting walls.

The energy system is one of the biggest reasons I cannot recommend this game. I actually like grinding when I enjoy a game. If the gameplay is fun and the rewards feel worth it, I want to farm more. But this game constantly tells me to stop. Energy comes back too slowly, and the amount you can spend on meaningful activities each day feels too limited. If I want to farm outposts, bosses, or other key content, I get cut off very quickly.

And it is not just energy. Open loot rewards are capped. Healing rewards are capped. Sect rewards are capped. Battle pass XP is capped. Certain currencies are capped. Event rewards are capped. It feels like every time I want to engage with the game more deeply, another system steps in and says I have hit the limit.

That would already be frustrating, but it is made worse by how demanding the progression systems are. The game wants you to improve martial arts, gear, inner ways, mystic skills, professions, and sometimes appearances too. But if all of those systems take so much time and materials, why does the game keep restricting how much I can actually work on them?

RNG is another major problem. Too much of this game feels like feeding resources into slot machines. Challenge rewards often give tickets instead of the item you want. Appearance systems feel heavily luck based. Gear perks are random. Inner Way notes are random. Box openings are random. Even when the game lets you pick a category, there is often another layer of RNG underneath it.

Inner Ways are one of the most frustrating examples because they are so important for making builds stronger, but upgrading them takes a huge amount of duplicate notes. Even when you finally get the boxes you need, opening them is still random. So first you farm the boxes with limited energy, then you hope the game gives you what you need. That is not satisfying progression.

Mystic skills have a similar problem. Common materials are easy enough to get, but the rarer resources are painfully slow to gather. Farming them around the map becomes tedious fast, and the game does not make that process smooth enough to justify how much of it you need.

Because so much is capped, weekly reset starts feeling like the only time meaningful progress happens. That is one of the saddest parts of the game for me. Reset day should feel exciting, but it should not feel like the only day the game is really alive. Too much of the progression is packed into that one cycle, and the rest of the week can feel dry.

This also hurts build experimentation. On paper, a game with this many martial arts should make trying new builds exciting. Instead, it makes it feel risky and exhausting. Leveling a new martial art takes a lot. Getting the right tips takes a lot. Getting the right inner ways takes a lot. Getting the right gear set takes a lot. Getting the right perks on that gear is more RNG. Even with refund systems, not getting everything back still makes experimenting feel punishing.

The cosmetic side is also hard to defend. I think the game has beautiful outfits and customization, but the gacha side of it feels absurdly expensive. I do not mind paying directly for a normal skin at a fair price, but the luck based premium systems feel way too aggressive. Even the battle pass, which has decent value overall, is dragged down by filler style chests that mostly give common rewards instead of the rarer things they tease.

There are also smaller issues that add up. The English localization could be better. I play as a female character, and it is immersion breaking when the game still refers to my character incorrectly. Co-op also feels more limited than it should be for a game with such a large and beautiful world.

That is what makes Where Winds Meet so disappointing to me. There is so much here that is genuinely good. The world is beautiful. The combat is fun. The lore is interesting. The game has real charm and ambition. I understand exactly why I fell in love with it at first.

But I also cannot ignore how badly the systems drag it down over time.

At some point, the beauty of the world and the strength of the combat are not enough to make up for the energy restrictions, reward caps, excessive RNG, and progression systems that make farming and experimentation feel more exhausting than fun.

So no, I do not recommend Where Winds Meet right now.

Not because it has no good qualities. Honestly, the opposite is true. I do not recommend it because there is a genuinely good game in here, maybe even a great one, but too much of it is buried under systems that constantly limit the player and drain the long term enjoyment out of it.

The idea of this game is great.  Some of the choices seem a little suspect.  

Lets start with the pros.  
First, it is beautiful.  It is fluid and the open world does feel open.  You can triple jump, wall run, and swim.  
Second, there's alot of stuff to explore and you can advance doing other activities besides fighting.  You can pick herbs or catch bugs if you don't want to fight.  That covers most of the good stuff

Now start with the cons.  
1.  Your awesome movement skills just stop working in certain places.  A jump you could have made effortlessly now becomes a deathtrap or insurmountable obstacle.  You want to wall run over a pit?  No, you have to follow the narrow beam.  Your legs just don't work how they used to.  One of my pet peeves is removing abilities in order to create artificial difficulty.
2.  The Healing system is frustrating.  I spent 29 levels afflicted with bee venom.  I did go looking for a doctor or to pick up a skill to heal myself but was unable to find either.  It eventually went away, after 29 levels.  There's also more dangerous ailments that can ONLY be healed by a player doctor.  Even the in game provided doctor can only deal with minor ailments.  That's a massive hard NOPE for someone who plays mostly solo.
3. The Combat.  I wanted to like it, but even though it looked smooth, it didn't feel impactful.  It was missing something.  Even the finishers weren't carrying the weight I expected.  Finishers go from fight enders to just another move very quickly.  The deflection assist starts off helpful but quickly becomes frustrating with enemy archers.  Your focus is eaten up on arrows and you can't do anything while focus assist is "assisting" you.
4. The skill system.  This includes inner arts, weapon forms and mystic skills.  It's so scattered and haphazard.  I felt like i was just picking up random skills with no rhyme or reason.  I got a stealth skill hours after i did a stealth mission where the character used that stealth skill extensively.  I got a weapon form needed for the third part of a chain quest before I even encountered the the second form.  It feels janky and disappointing.
5.  Your character doesn't feel powerful in terms of the world.  I'm not sure how to explain this but seeing some of these bandits and the attacks they use along with how much damage they do makes it seem like you are the underdog.  Going through my full cycle of moves three times on an archer (complete with finisher) at the same level just feels bad when at lower levels you did once cycle and a finisher just feels annoying and unfulfilling.  Mooks should be mooks, not approaching boss levels of sword sponginess.

I want to like it, but the jankiness and lacking hero fantasy pull me out of the game.  I don't want to spend literal hours afflicted with an illness because the Doctor is out meditating.

Several hours into this game, I gave it a glowing review. I praised its combat, world, exploration, bosses, and accessibility, which are all still positives that I believe make Where Winds Meet a great game. However, I did mention one issue I had with the game that was only a minor annoyance at the time. The more I played after my review, the more that issue affected my experience, and now it's too the point where I'm not answering "is this game good?" and instead "would I recommend it?" This is a still a great game, perhaps the best game that I would not recommend to anyone. It has so much going for it. The combat is a satisfying blend of Soulslike and spectacle fighter elements with a high skill ceiling and tons of build diversity, the world feels engaging and alive, and the bosses are awesome and cinematic. Here's the thing, though: 

This game has the single worst progression and development system I've ever had the displeasure of grinding through in a video game. 

I've played and tolerated a variety of MMOs, gachas, and live-service looter-shooters. Progression in Where Winds Meet wraps together all the most tedious and miserable aspects of all those genres while ditching almost all the quality-of-life that makes other games enjoyable in spite of how progression works. Building a character in this game is like air traffic control in slow motion. Here's a detailed list of everything you are expected to upgrade: 

- Your solo level
- Your online level
- Your Mastery level
- Your trait levels 
- Your gear quality
- Your gear stats (these are separate)
- Your gear [i]slots[/i] (as in, the slots to which you equip your gear to have their own scaling separate from the gear itself)
- Gear maintenance 
- Inner Ways
- Mystic Arts
- Martial Arts
- Skill tree 
- Other skill tree
- Other [i]other[/i] skill tree 
- A fourth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ skill tree 
- Exploration level
- Crafting level
- Cooking level
- Healing level
- Healing effectiveness
- Healing flask limit 
- Scholar level 
And more that I probably haven't even discovered. 

Each and every one of these requires at least one completely different currency obtained from a different source, many of which are rare random drops or heavily RNG-based. And if you fail to max out even one of these, you'll fall behind so much that you'll get one-shot by every grunt enemy and your attacks will hit like a wet noodle. This is because enemy strength is determined by your solo level, which progresses naturally and significantly faster than anything else. Not only are some resources extremely scarce and dependent on very slim RNG, but grinding is time-gated by a weekly stamina system. This creates a situation where the game itself progresses significantly faster than you do and leaves your epic wuxia hero behind to rot unless you play the game like a job AND have godlike luck. Even after farming every source of Inner Way upgrade materials for several weeks, I haven't upgraded a single one to Tier 2 and I'm barely even close. At my current level, I'm expected to have multiple Inner Ways at Tier 4. 

I really want to keep enjoying this game, but it feels like the devs have made that impossible with the character development system. There's so much fun to be had in this world that was designed with care, but there's no real way to experience it unless you're unemployed and have enough time to grind for hours upon hours [i]and[/i] complete the rest of the content. It's sad, really. The hardest time I've ever had recommending an 8/10 game.

Edit: The more this game goes on, the more I realize it's bogged down by layers and layers of Black Desert-esque nonsense. Sometimes it wants to be a Witcher-style "walk around and talk to people" game, but without any branching questlines or decent writing, so you're just running around and mashing the "talk" button. Quests feel pointless because they reward you with fifty different random "currencies" that are all used for specific different things, none of which seem particularly important. The game contains an impenetrable mass of systems and menus that make Genshin Impact look like an example of clean UI/UX. The minigames are boring. Having conversations with the "AI" NPCs is interesting for about five seconds until you realize they're running off a Temu version of GPT-3 and will constantly repeat the same catchphrases over and over again. The storyline is convoluted wuxia nonsense that is not done any favors by the translation, which varies between boring and broken. You can't ignore this terrible story because you are constantly assaulted with cutscenes and dialogues. Combat is decent, graphics look nice, and the martial arts choreography in the cutscenes is actually really good, but there is so much tedious garbage in this game that I can't justify playing it anymore. I really want to like this game, but it would have been better as a pared-down action game than this bastard child of Black Desert and Genshin Impact.

Where Winds Meet is a game I love mainly for its exploration, combat, and visuals rather than any deep story or lore. The world feels alive and full of hidden corners, with dungeons and environments that are packed with things to discover. The teleportation animation is especially stylish and fun to use, making traversal feel like part of the spectacle instead of just a menu option.

Combat is flashy and satisfying, with a wide variety of weapons and moves to collect and experiment with. As a casual gamer, I enjoy just roaming around, opening chests, trying new builds, and feeling the flow of fights without worrying too much about optimization. Some bosses are fine more about spectacle and spectacle than pure difficulty and that suits my playstyle well.

The only downside is that the game offers so many systems and options that it can feel overwhelming. Some menus and features are hard to find, and as a casual player I often just follow the red‑marked prompts instead of digging through everything. I haven’t replayed much after the newer updates, but the dungeons still stand out as some of the best parts there’s always more to explore, and that sense of discovery is what keeps me coming back.

This game has been a bit of a complicated experience for me. The game itself looked incredible, the fact that it was free was astonishing, though they do make up for it in other ways in-game. It didn't have (that I saw) any sketchy DRM attached to it, didn't have previous history of failed games. As some people have mentioned, it is attached to Gaijin and they alleged that it will be milked for money. The one big gripe that I had with the game that prevents this from being a Recommended is that it has various AI-based things incorporated into the game. Some(though few that I saw) activities require it, to complete an interaction with an NPC, some appeared to just be optional things where you could speak to an NPC AI-chatbot though I believe that it does have some effect in the game. There was also the ability to use an AI to create your character, and I'm not 100% convinced that some of the voicework for NPCs wasn't AI as well. I am against the tidal wave of AI-involvement in absolutely everything that has been flooding everywhere - and this game, genuinely, did not need the incorporation of AI - it is otherwise an amazing experience, that could stand entirely on its own as incredible.

The graphics and soundscape both were very good, the game is beautiful, and they have some photo mode features that let you capture some really good shots, and you can share them with others. The world feels vast and full of things to do, it is easy to wander around and lose yourself in the game, meeting all kinds of NPCs and hearing what they have to say or doing things for them. The wuxia atmosphere feels done well, and things are immersive. I only did a little bit of co-op activities but there were lots more to do, and the bits that I did were fun, and helpful. I did not do anything PVP-related, but there were options for that as well. I made it up to level 55 in my time played and still have plenty of world to see. If you want to focus on one particular thing, questline or whatever, you can do that, or if you want to explore and find all kinds of cool things, that is very rewarding as well. There is no shortage of activities.

There are many ways that the Devs earn money in-game as well, between various timed events to fuel FOMO, a battle-pass, cosmetic releases and things like that, I am sure they are doing well for themselves - It honestly does not feel too invasive or anything like that, the game is free, can't really complain too much there. 

So yeah. The game itself feels great, but as someone who cares about AI involvement in things as it does not need to be in everything, I think the AI features should be disabled or taken out of the game, and if that were the case, I would have recommended it in a heartbeat and played it a lot more.

It’s not often I play a free game and don’t feel like it’s quietly checking my credit score in the background. But Where Winds Meet? It actually feels… generous. Which is wild. Most “free-to-play” games start friendly and then slowly turn into a toll booth. This one honestly feels better than a bunch of $60 AAA titles I’ve bought, played for a week, and then quietly uninstalled.

Now, if you’re anything like me and the word “multiplayer” makes your blood pressure tick up a little, you’ll get this. I love big, living worlds. I do not love the idea of being the guy who wipes a 10-person raid and gets that long, awkward silence in chat. Instant alt-F4 energy.

This game fixes that.

The absolute MVP feature for me is Solo Mode. You can do almost everything in your own private instance. Just you, the scenery, and whatever poor boss is about to catch a sword to the face. For tougher fights, you bring AI companions. Are they elite esports champions? No. Do they stand in fire sometimes? Yep. But they get the job done and, more importantly, they don’t judge you. No pressure. No random stranger sighing into their mic. It makes the whole experience feel way more welcoming than most MMOs for someone like me.

What surprised me is that the game still gently nudges you toward other players without shoving you off a cliff. When I finally dipped a toe into multiplayer, it was… chill. Like, suspiciously chill.

Guilds are actually built around different playstyles. Want to explore? Fight other players? LARP as a traveling musician or doctor? There’s a lane for that. Honestly, the rewards alone make joining worth joining a guild (or even switching between them for the unique rewards in each). And co-op is another sweet spot. One or two other humans exploring together is manageable. Ten is a committee meeting. Small group content feels relaxed, and it makes special events way easier without turning the game into a part-time job.

There’s also always something going on. Daily and weekly stuff keeps you moving, and it feels like there’s constantly some event happening. The world never really feels dead.

And let me be clear: this is not pay-to-win. You don’t need to spend money to compete or succeed. Most of the paid stuff is cosmetic, which is fine. If someone wants to spend money to look like a legendary silk-robed demigod, good for them. There’s a monthly pass that speeds up materials a bit, but it’s optional. If you’ve got patience, you can earn everything (that matters for play) just by playing.

I haven’t run into toxicity or cheating, though I also avoid the ultra-hardcore PvP and multiplayer stuff, so your mileage may vary. But if you want a gorgeous, sprawling martial arts epic and you’re allergic to forced social chaos, this is absolutely worth a try.

Where Winds Meet is honestly one of the most complete open-world RPGs I’ve played in years. It checks every box a true gamer could want — no exaggeration.

The graphics are a straight 10/10.
From the environmental detail to the lighting and weather effects, the world feels cinematic. Mountains look massive, cities feel lived-in, and the architecture captures that authentic wuxia atmosphere perfectly.

The gameplay? 10/10.
Combat feels fluid and skill-based. You’re not just button mashing — positioning, timing, internal skills, weapon choices, and martial arts styles actually matter. You can build your character around speed, heavy pressure, internal damage, stealth, status effects — whatever fits your playstyle. It rewards creativity instead of forcing one “meta” path.

Story immersion? 10/10.
The narrative doesn’t feel like background noise. The dialogue, character motivations, and faction politics pull you in. Side quests aren’t just filler either — many of them feel like mini story arcs with real emotional weight.

World-building? 10/10.
The world feels alive. NPCs have routines. Random encounters happen. Hidden martial arts manuals and secret areas reward exploration. It’s the kind of game where you wander off the main quest and end up discovering something insane two hours later.

Now, let’s be real about one thing — the UI.

At first? The UI is a nightmare. There are menus inside menus, systems layered on systems, and it can feel overwhelming in your first few hours. But honestly, that’s just because the game is deep. Once you stick with it, watch a couple YouTube guides, and start understanding how everything connects, it clicks. And when it does, you realize how much freedom the system actually gives you.

It has true open-world freedom.
You can focus on PvE, dive into PvP, explore, roleplay, grind skills, experiment with builds — the choice is yours.

And most importantly: it isn’t pay-to-win.
Progress comes from learning mechanics, mastering combat, and investing time — not swiping a card.

This is what a modern wuxia RPG should feel like — ambitious, immersive, skill-based, and rewarding.

---{ Summary }---
Overall, Where Winds Meet delivers a very satisfying experience in terms of gameplay, music, story, and especially visuals. The world design and artistic direction are genuinely impressive and help the game stand out in the MMORPG genre.

Despite being an MMORPG, it avoids pay-to-win mechanics. All purchases are purely cosmetic, which is a model I genuinely think other games in the genre should follow. It creates a fair environment where progression depends on your time and skill rather than your wallet.

The large open world and the typical in-game energy system can naturally push you toward extended play sessions and a fairly intense grind loop. However, thanks to the separate PvE mode and the currently available main story questline, players who are mainly interested in the narrative can get around 40–50 hours of satisfying content in its current state.

At the moment, the biggest downside is that the main story is not yet fully completed. That said, the game is actively updated with new regions, weapons, combat styles, and additional main story quests. If you are planning to play purely for the story and don’t enjoy returning to games later, I would recommend waiting until the narrative is more complete.

On the other hand, I can confidently say that the online elements are highly enjoyable and immersive.

Considering that the game is free, what we have here is a rare gem. If you’re looking to have a great time and enjoy an immersive world—especially with friends—Where Winds Meet is definitely worth checking out.

- non-kernel anti cheat

- a no-p2w cashshop of mainly cosmetics

Cons:
- horrible localization that makes understanding the story more confusing than it needs to be
- there a specific type of quests that require passing some item you find in the world to a specific npc. No quest marker, NPC can be so vague in telling you where the item is, and/or the item is very hard to find among the environment objects (e.g., grasses)
- some non-game breaking bugs with combat and map traversing
- world is huge (which arguably can be a pro)
- RIP Ruby

A Revolutionary Open World Diamond!

After logging over 150 hours, I can confidently say: Where Winds Meet is not just a game; it is a world you live in. It creates a gravitational pull I haven’t experienced since The Witcher 3 or Skyrim. It is massive, complex, and initially overwhelming—but that very depth is what makes it a "black hole" that completely sucks you in. If you are willing to master its systems, you are rewarded with an experience that is currently unparalleled in the industry.


What makes this title truly groundbreaking is its sheer density of content without sacrificing quality. It feels like the perfect symbiosis of everything the modern gaming industry has to offer:

- Genre Fusion: It captures the atmosphere and the combat fluidity of Ghost of Tsushima, Assasssins Creed, Wuthering Waves and Elden Ring.
- Infinite Variety: From hardcore PvP and integrated Battle Royale to single-player and innovative social features and events.
- A Living World: In-game social media (similar to Instagram/TikTok), a trading registry with dynamic market rates, and deep professions like the healer system elevate the immersion to a new level.

Absolute Freedom: Between Solitude and Community
The game perfectly masters the balance between a single-player epic and a multiplayer hub. You can enjoy the breathtaking world in complete peace or dive into a deep social web: join sects, form guilds, get married, or take on a mentor-student relationship etc..

The "Scratch" on the Diamond: Gacha Pricing!
Despite its brilliance, there is one undeniable flaw: the Gacha pricing. The costs for cosmetic content are currently extreme and stand in sharp contrast to the rest of the game’s excellence. It is the only scratch on an otherwise perfect diamond. To ensure long-term player loyalty, the developers must address this and implement a fairer system.


Final Verdict:
Where Winds Meet is already a Top 5 game of all time for me. It is bold, innovative, and visually stunning. With the massive map expansion coming in two weeks, the scale is only going to get more impressive. If the developers fix the Gacha pricing, this game will undisputedly sit at the #1 spot.

Pros:
- Incredible depth and complexity
- A stunning, constantly evolving open world
- Unique blend of single-player and multiplayer freedom
- Social and economic systems
- Deeply satisfying and versatile combat system

Cons:
- Exorbitant Gacha prices!!
- High entry barrier due to complex menus.

Well for a free game it's great, especially in the beginning and seems like it's made for those who appreciate graphics first and foremost, to sell cosmetics obviously :),

There is much to explore and I can definitely I say that I prefer the first area that focuses on small villages over the second area which is focused on the big city, maybe because it's also what I prefer in real life.

The game tries to include as many mechanics as it can, like free world solo/co-op exploration, various mini-games, some crafting and construction, guilds and multiplayer activities, PvP, stealth, puzzles, AI based conversations with NPC's and hidden quests, Chinese lore (Wuxia), with added humour that often gets you into absurd situations.

Personally I don't like the combat system at all, partly because it's made so it would work even on mobile, and therefore also more inclined towards console than PC which makes it a bit buggy and unintuitive at times, especially in PvP, while it's heavily based on Parry mechanics, so not the best thing in an online game. There are also some quick time events but at least you can try everything once again without doing the whole thing all over again.

Despite it being a free game, at least for now, it's very easy to switch between weapon styles and sects if you wish to try something else from time to time.

But in the end, after finishing the main quests, I've found myself focusing on timed events which I can't say I liked too much because even if they might be very casual, you have to repeat them many times in a short time to get rewards. So it feels like it's too forced, trying to play on FOMO effect. Also, there seem to be some problems with automatic match-making so I guess it's better to play it mostly with friends where possible.

Oh, also when it started the signposts where mostly helpful info for those who beat the content first, but then there were too many trolls appearing as the game got more popular (partly devs' fault for having daily quest to put signposts) so this also started to be very annoying at some point, making you ignore them altogether.

Do not build tank if your going to PVP in the arena. Blacklist Mo Blade and Heavensquaker Spear from your mind!

There is a system in arena that, if you run the clock out, whoever did the most damage wins the game. It doesn't matter if you have half of your health vs your opponents seemingly non-existent health-bar. 

As long as at the end of the match the score screen says they tripled your damage they win by default. 

Now you might ask "what if you won using the health system? Wouldn't that be unfair against people who build glass cannons or who aren't tanks?" and I would respond YES, I AGREE!

Which is why i'm complaining in a review so people can help bring this to the dev's attention. 

If you have 1 system and not the other than you shouldn't have either system period.

How could you solve this problem you ask?

Running out the clock either results in a draw (both players lose their win-streak) or a loss (both players lose their win-streak AND lose arena points). If the object of fairness was to promote a high intensity player versus player arena where skill is key then having a system that is by design AGAINST slow moving, high health characters. I believe this would be the proper fix. FORCE PLAYERS TO FIGHT! THERE IS NO WINNER UNTIL SOMEONE FALLS!

I don't mind being kited but if the win condition is "I did more damage than you" then to build a tank for player vs player is pointless. Id like all builds to be viable. Not restricted or hindered by game systems thank you.

If you are looking for a fun and free MMORPG that is Wuxia, I truly and highly recommend Where Winds Meet. 

The maps are incredibly expansive, the lore is very rich following along the Song Dynasty historically, and adding in a lot of history from Ancient China. Bringing in cultural elements you may not have known about before and providing insight on folklore- and battling it out quite literally. 

The combat is extremely fluid and easy to grasp, with a wide variety on DPS. Healing and Tank builds. Not to mention it offers a fairly comprehensive guide on starting out your builds and when ranking up before you can find what works best for your character. There's always an event or fun activities to do where you can mostly do solo so you aren't really required to have to run around with other people. 

It's a nice change of pace from where most MMO's force you to have to wait on and work with other players for a lot of things like World Bosses. You can call upon others for assistance if needed with the other NPC's in the game if necessary. 

You even have the option on solo mode to play in story or abyss, etc. if you are looking for something easy and go with the flow or with something that offers a good challenge.

Not to mention it is NOT pay to win. Yes some resources are a little more finite but events, new maps, regions, etc. allow for re-collection of it all and spending your Echo Jade wisely. 

The game does have micro-transactions, but just for cosmetics (and yes that 40k irl boat you may have heard about). 

The amount of stuff you can get for free in this game in my opinion can make it rather obsolete if you're wanting to avoid spending any money. For every one of the events there's a new cosmetic to collect, there's community motivated things, there is in game currencies to get new cosmetics. 

I don't play much PVP- but there is an Arena to do 1v1, there is group fights to unlock certain things like bows and many random players will join you.

I don’t normally write long reviews, but this game had me stumped after 4 hours of gameplay. To sum up this game in one word I’d use ‘confusing’. Even though this game was free, I still felt like I was robbed of my time. There isn’t much good to say about this game, but I will give credit where it’s due. However, some of its flaws are so flagrant it’s almost inexcusable for such a hyped game.

Pros:
It isn’t an understatement to say that the character customization was the best part of this game. The fact that you can use your voice to generate the look of your character is a really cool mechanic and then being able to work off it is a nice feature. 
A really funny thing this game offers are the signposts that allow you to add a message for other passerby players (kind of like in a souls game). 
I will say, the developers absolutely nailed the graphics and art style of this game. The intro was epic and was so nice to watch and play through. I truly felt like I was in for a fun and challenging experience. However, like many false advertisements, you’re promised a delectable chocolate bar but what you’re really getting is ♥♥♥♥ in a candy wrapper.

Cons:
As soon as you load in with your character, the most obvious and criminal flaw of this game is shown. The UI in this game is a confusing mess of menus within menus, endless tutorials and a mountain of items that don’t seem like they do anything. The fact that there are also 3 different currencies in the game adds to the already growing confusion of the god-awful UI. 
That being said, I never know what items to pick up but does it really matter when my inventory has no limit and can hold everything in the universe? So just grab everything you see… This just makes it so that it doesn’t feel rewarding when you find a chest or take down a boss. 
The combat was fine but nothing I’d write home about. No real challenge to it but maybe I just didn’t get deep into it enough.
Now, I don’t have the highest IQ by any standard but there is no way I am so stupid as to not know what to do at any given moment. In many similar style games, you can venture off the main story path and stumble upon something interesting that would give you an advantage later in the game. This game feels so full yet so empty.  Another review said it best: This game feels like it lacks a soul.

While I would like to recommend this game to practically anyone, it's a matter of taste and personal preference, I can't in good faith tell anyone to play a live service Gacha Game. While the Sekiro inspired combat and Wuxia elements are fantastic, the underdeveloped MMO aspect of the game will likely wear a lot of players down over time. Three month long seasons, weak battlepass offerings, month-long stretches of time with nothing to do made up of time gated, drip fed, and buggy content that largely is comprised of mini games and weekly/daily runs of the same thing. Nearly every resource or incremental point of progress you make towards unlocking a free cosmetic/accessory is capped out. The resource farming is capped daily, coins are capped, everyday drops from monsters, crafting. I don't think there is a single system that doesn't have an internal limit to progression, even if it has no direct impact on PVE or PVP combat. I think the biggest killer of this title, for me, is the fact you run out of engaging solo content pretty early on, so you resort to trying PVP, Raids, and Abyss challenges. The raids can only be completed once per week, PVP is laggy and inconsistent (filled with bots), and the abyss trials are a fun challenge with little to no reward. Worst of all, outside of drip fed, time gated, energy capped content, is the abysmal integration of the Gacha system and no end-game trading system. I do appreciate it isn't explicitly pay-to-win, but the fact that it is so disconnected from the main gameplay loop makes it feel tacked on. Once again, you're capped to purchasing 3 premium pulls a week without forking over hundreds of dollars to get a single skin. The shop skins are 3x the price of CN servers, the Gacha is also wildly over priced (30 dollars for a single 10 pull btw) and a hard pity set at 150 which means virtually nothing. Hard pity doesn't guarantee the outfit, hitting hard pity then hitting pity again doesn't guarantee the banner reward. You have to spend on average around 400 dollars for a single item and there is no other way to purchase the premium currency without spending your college fund and selling your kidney. Here's my advice, play Sekiro, or Elden ring, Dark souls, or an actual MMO if you're into that. While I appreciate some of the potential depth of combat and the aesthetics, don't play aggressively monetized live service games like this. The lack of content, end game systems, and repetitive boring grind isn't worth it when the chance to get something good is less than .014% and the free outfits pale in comparison and take months to grind for (only because of hard caps.) I'll still revisit this game from time to time, and am willing to change my mind if the developers adapt, but I don't see that happening considering we aren't the main player-base. Until then, I'll be treating this game as if it's in maintenance mode for the next couple months (at least until Hengdao comes out.)

Alright...stick with me! I promise it's worth your time! I'm 200 hours in now, and I have some good thoughts!

So, if you’ve ever wished an open-world game could feel like a playable wuxia film and a screenshot playground, this is that game.

From the moment you step into the world, it’s stunning — not just “pretty” pretty, but walk-two-steps-and-you’ll-stop-to-take-a-photo pretty. Lighting, scenery, mood, architecture… it all feels handcrafted for adventuring and for players who love capturing moments. I’ve taken more pictures here than I have in most dedicated photo-mode games. But taking pictures isn't the important part!

What surprised me most: it’s fun and easy to sink into

The gameplay hits a sweet spot: engaging without being exhausting. Quests don’t feel like a confusing spreadsheet or a “go here, do chores” simulator. Instead, they’re approachable, readable, and still give you that “okay one more mission” momentum. The challenge feels fair — enough to stay interesting, not enough to feel punishing. Menu's take a little getting used to, but once you've got the grip - you are cruising without issue.

Story + tone: movie-level, with humor that doesn’t ruin the vibe (honestly!)

The story genuinely feels cinematic. It has that “I’m in a living epic” pacing, and it actually made me want to follow what’s happening instead of skipping dialogue. And the humor? Perfectly placed. It adds warmth without turning everything into a nonstop meme. It respects the world, which makes the big moments land harder- and it also has a personal feel to many of the stories as well, making it relatable for so many other gamers out there no matter what walk of life you come from.

Community: shockingly wholesome (in the best way)

I expected the usual online game chaos/trolling/memery… and instead found one of the most helpful, positive communities I’ve seen in this kind of game. Players actually answer questions, point you in the right direction, and don’t treat new folks like an inconvenience. That energy and support matters more than people think — it makes the whole experience feel welcoming - whether you're an extroverted group play person, or more of an individual contributor who prefers to venture by yourself.

Quick notes for new players

If you love exploration and atmosphere, take your time. This world rewards wandering - and please enjoy the beautiful environment! Did I mention "take your time"? TAKE. YOUR. TIME. Enjoy the game - I beg you!

If you enjoy photos/screenshots, you’re going to eat very well here.

Don’t be afraid to ask for help — people are genuinely kind and helpful!

Verdict: Beautiful, fun, well-paced, and surprisingly heartfelt — with a community that makes you want to stick around. If you like story-rich adventuring with style, this is an easy recommendation. If you just like to run around a DPS the heck out of everything - there's a seat for you on this bus as well.

⭐ Recommended. And yeah… I boot it up “to do one quest” and suddenly it’s.....hours.....later. LOL (and don't forget to drink water, and go outside and touch grass. Take breaks!)

Suggestions for the Devs: Please add more men’s outfit options that let you show off the chest (open-front robes, deep V tunics, sleeveless wraps, dare I ask for a harness?, etc.). A simple layer toggle (hide inner shirt/outer robe) and more mix-and-match clothing pieces would also go a long way. The options available now are as stunning as the world itself, but just some more customization across the board would be *chefs kiss!

Where Winds Meet is nothing short of a revelation in gaming , a massive, breathtaking journey through a richly detailed world inspired by ancient Chinese history and wuxia tradition. This isn’t just another game , it’s an experience that stays with you long after you put down the controller. 
From the moment you step into its expansive open world, every direction invites awe. Ancient cities bustle with life. Hidden temples whisper secrets beneath mossy stone. Lush forests sway with the wind. Every region feels lovingly crafted, with no two landscapes the same , and together they create one of the largest, most involved RPG worlds you’ll ever explore. 
The story in Where Winds Meet is deep, layered, and moving. Set during China’s turbulent Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, the narrative unfolds like a sweeping wuxia epic , filled with honour, betrayal, destiny, and the longing for identity and justice. Legends aren’t just told here; you live them. 
What makes this game truly special is how China’s rich cultural heritage is on full display. Every corner of the world is woven with folklore, philosophical depth, and aesthetics drawn from real traditions and artistic themes. From poetic landscapes inspired by traditional lore to the martial arts that shape every battle, Where Winds Meet captures the soul of Chinese storytelling like nothing else. 
This isn’t a short diversion , it’s a huge, life,devouring adventure. Whether you’re chasing the main plot, chasing secrets hidden across the map, or just wandering among rivers and rooftops as the wind carries your legend, there’s so much to do and feel that players often spend well over 100+ hours absorbed in its mysteries. 
In short?
✨ Epic.
✨ Emotionally powerful.
✨ Culturally rich.
✨ Absolutely unforgettable.
If you’re hungry for a game that blends deep storytelling, jaw,dropping exploration, and authentic cultural immersion, Where Winds Meet delivers on every level , and then some.
