[h2] Review after ~3k hours [/h2]

[url=https://i.postimg.cc/52YFDVH8/image.png] -> Proof of me actively playing <- [/url]

So, It's time I tell my honest straightforward opinion about the game. It is a game i easily spent 3k hours in. Since may im playing through netease launcher (predownload option mostly and my slower download bcs i dont want to wait for the game to update when i finaly get home from work)
Before I bother you with details I'm going to say one sentence.

[h2] Before reading further. This game is worth playing. [/h2]

Before spewing a ton of problems here's...

[h2] PROS [/h2]
- For the cost of waiting for the game to download you're getting a massive openworld set in early medieval china.
- Game runs on funding from cosmetics, no paying for power, energy or anything that makes you stronger
- Story is good and engaging with mythos influence
- Graphics are pretty
- Combat feels good
- 'Most' of the time theres stuff to do
- Social element
- Good raids
- Ton of exploration to do and bosses to fight

[h2] CONS [/h2]
I will need to split this into sections.

[b] 1. Technical issues [/b]
- Heavily ping reliant PVP, difference between 15ms and 60ms makes you feel it a lot in higher ranked PVP. Comboes not chaining properly, desyncs, worse escapes from comboes
- Ocassional stutters on native frames in demanding bossfights with a lot of effects

[b] 2. Multiplayer side of the game [/b]
- Insanely long queues on lower Swordtrial bosses, not worth queueing without premade team
- Social element
- Players leaving Swordtrial after 1st try without even attempting to do mechanics
- Restricted Coop
- Thining/silent/empty online mode (mostly ppl enter it only bcs they need to do one particular thing and then afk around in it/leave it)

[b] 3. Gacha, outfits, etc [/b]
Note: I understand that the game is PURELY funded from those and ppl are willing to pay it but lets face it, it is a lot to pay for what you get.
- Prices on outfits are quite high (2580 pearl outfits you can get with 50% discount occassionaly for ~20$, ~40$ full price)
- Gacha has horrible chances even with pitty system on average you can get 1 Harmonic core (you need 2 for a outfit) every 3-4 months, sinlgle core is approx 300-400$ if you decide to pull for money
- All free outfits cannot be recoloured
- if you want a good outfit for free just play for approx half a year and save up 2 cores

[b] 5. World design [/b]
- Side quests (wandering tales): 
Most feel unimpactful reward and world wise, they are there just to exist mostly being trivial thing to do with bunch of text instead of voicelines. Wandering tales are mostly only for completionists that want to see that 100% exploration.
- Hidden mountain region:
I was excited about this one what we got felt empty, half cooked and time gated. Dont get me wrong it looks good, cutscenes are fine but the amount of times i ran into misplaced textures. This is not referencing main story that was done well but the region itself felt filled with bunch of clutter only "to fill it up" rather than making it feel alive
- Hexi Campaign:
I highly recommend studying upfront basics of chinese history or you wont understand a single thing as i did. Whole Hexi campaign was pretty "self discovery journey" for our MC without any major plot progress. Just dont get me started on death of the Governor quest (genuinely fell asleep during it).

[b] 6. Caps, caps, caps + Energy system [/b]
Everything is either capped, time gated or both. This made sense maybe first two months of the game only to slow down people who would rush everything to max asap rn this system is pointless and straight ridiculous. Capped retuning, innerway boxes exchange, Capped conversions, time gated resets of gear and much more. All of this while employing purely luck based gear system is conflicting each other and only thing this results to right now is preventing never players from reaching the endgame their f.e. guild peers might already be in. If the energy system is to be kept even doubling the energy recharge rate might not be enough.

I know that the game tries to push you away from trying to grind for better gear, level up your weapon passives (inner ways). But when the gear is luck based, you can go whole breakthrough (2 months atm) without being satisfied with your gear. If you start now and want to compete in late game content and actually progress you get soft locked by not having higher level innerways. To get the largest number of them you need to do bosses in raids with other players. Bosses you dont have the appropriate gear for which locks you in a weird "pre-endgame" phase of the game where you have barely anything to do to make meaningful progress. For people already at the endgame the energy system only enforces longer wait times to level up new builds, get better gear etc. You dont get anything from doing the bosses/outposts without energy making you wait for days. On average you got about 1-3 pieces of usable endgame gear per week turning something that would take you 4 hours to do all together into a multiple week spanning waiting game only for your energy to refill. 

[h2] Summary: [/h2]
Now, this is a long list of cons i understand that... Hope i didnt scare you off as a new player but at its current state this is a point you will reach after at least spending about 100-150hours in the game. And that being considered is a ton of content for a free game. 

If youre a new player barely starting and plan to dump hours of hours into this game like i did best tip i can give you is to play at your own pace, explore the vast world of jianghu and once you hit a wall or decide that this is a game worth your time find a fine guild you will feel good being a part of. Get help from fellow guildies on your build because most of them will help you or at least direct you to someone who will give you an idea about what to do. It can be a solo game for only so long. Never be content with some guild you feel like you have inner conflict with bcs the guild is what will shape most of your experience going forward and effectivelly is one of the few things keeping this game alive. 


[b] And the most important tip: Do what you enjoy bcs most of the things will at some point give you meaningles rewards anyway so... Enjoy your time and trust me theres quite a bunch of things to do however negative this review might sound. [/b]

Let's look at the headline: this is a [b]free game[/b] that at times feels like it should have cost $50+. I cannot speak for the multiplayer side of things, so this review will be exclusively about the singleplayer (or as they call it in-game, "solo mode") campaign.

At ~7 hours in, I still keep coming back to that feeling of "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this game was free?" The game is densely packed with characters, side quests, hidden dungeons, and bears performing Tai Chi, while the main campaign (as of 7 hours) is more than interesting enough to keep me invested. The main thing you will be doing is using your martial arts skills to dispatch enemies. The fighting style is similar to most games in the same vein: you have a couple of weapons you can switch between, each with their own unique skills and specialized martial arts styles. You can parry and stance-break enemies (deplete their qi) to deal loads of damage. On top of this, you can learn additional martial arts skills to deploy in combat. There are also armor/talismans which offer defense.

This ties into one of my main complaints: this game is complex. More complex than it should be. There are so many things to keep track of. Here is a shotgun blast of examples: You have a base character level, which upgrades on its own as you do things. You can equip a variety of weapons. You can upgrade your armor/weapons/talismans alongside your character level. You can also upgrade the base strength of these item slots (still a bit confused about this myself). Once you reach a level threshold, you have to complete a "breakthrough" to progress to higher levels. You can equip a variety of martial arts for each weapon type. You can equip a variety of special martial skills which are one-off flashy attacks. You have a talent tree that unlocks skills/abilities/more martial arts slots. You can develop an "inner path." You can use consumables in combat many of which have important effects. You can join a sect to gain benefits/martial arts associated with them (or you can be "sectless"). You can join a guild. You can find a master/be a master who accepts multiple disciples of your own. You can form a "partnership" (as I've been playing singleplayer I'm not really sure what this is but it is heavily implied to be a romantic relationship between two actual players so I guess this game is also a dating app?). There are special events, gacha-style grabs, calligraphy, healing/medicine practice, construction (yes you can build things), musical performance, art, fashion (with a leaderboard for people whose fits are the best), and bounty hunting. There's a battle pass and a cosmetic shop and even more beyond this that I haven't even scratched the surface of. There's just so so so so so much.

I say this like it's a bad thing, but I respect the ambition. There's something here for everyone, and you don't often see that in games. But at times it feels as though there is a lack of direction as a result. And the free-to-play mechanics can sometimes be a little in-your-face. Despite this, I wholeheartedly recommend at least giving WWM a shot. The world is beautiful, vast, and feels triple-A (in a good way) more often than not. The combat is fun, the aesthetics are impeccable if you like Jianghu stories. What's the worst that can happen? It's a free game. Stop reading reviews and try it already.

TL;DR: It's a free game that feels like it should cost money. Play it. Have some fun. If you don't like it, uninstall. But you'll probably like it.

TLDR: I have not had this much fun in an MMORPG type game in a long time! Fun, immersive, interactive, with beautiful sceneries and enjoyable combat mechanics.

The world and setting of WWM is absolutely stunning and feels incredibly immersive, with grand vistas, hidden secrets and lots of NPCs that are just doing their own thing. It feels like you become part of a living and breathing world in this game.

The combat is nice, with a selection of interesting weapons that all have their own special traits. I haven't tried all of them yet, but all of the ones I've played around with feel good. 

If you like to play with others, great! There is a big variety of content you can play with others, you can co-op, join multiplayer, do mini-games, hunt bosses, pvp, etc. There is also a large social aspect to the game in the form of sects, guilds and the social bonds you can have. (Partnership, master disciple, sworn cohort, etc.)

If you don't like socializing too much, that's also cool! You spend a lot of time in your own solo world, especially when going through the story. You can play most content without touching multiplayer whatsoever.

The only part that I am not a huge fan of is the poor localisation in the EN version, but the devs are actively working on improving this aspect of the game. For now I simply play with CN voice acting, instead of EN, and that works like a charm for me.

Altogether, I would 100% recommend you to try out this game if you're on the fence about it. The game is F2P with no P2W, so you do not lose anything (other than some time) if you don't end up liking it... BUT if you do like it, you get to enjoy a great game for no fee (I do encourage you to support the devs though if you like it and can afford doing so...)

In its essence, WWM is a costume gacha game. Visually stunning, you can tell a lot of work went into its presentation to give you one of the best Wuxia experiences you can ever have in the game. Well, for the first 100 hours.

Once you reach the end of the story, you start to realize this is designed just like Genshin but the gacha/cosmetics are amped up to 20. There are people that spend more money on in-game clothing than their entire wardrobe IRL in this game. You can spend upward of $600 just to get an outfit that seems irresistible because it ticks the FOMO in your brain. And expect this to happen weekly or bi-monthly. Make no mistake: This game is designed to rein in whales.

This game is not an MMO. It is designed for short co-operative incursions in PVE and PVP form that gets old quickly. Expect to grind heavily to upkeep your gear score every week until a new level cap is dropped and the process starts over again. There are no magical adventures in the jianghu with your friends. Just trials and battles that you have to do weekly for gear. If you're pugging, good luck.

There are a lot of unique systems and minigames that at first, seem like novelties but they're never very well thought-out and designed. The election system is an egregious example of this. The voting menu is bugged and you'll see nothing but spam until the election period is over -- and this lasts for most of the week when you just want to socialize with your sect or global channels. There's no working spam or blacklist filter on PC WWM, despite the many feedback submissions to the devs. Nothing has been fixed regarding its social systems and it's most likely intentional.

Conflict is central to the game's design as PVP is one of its selling points and money farms. Never have I seen so much drama around wanting to be top 10 among your sect through popularity contests. Are there people you hate in game because they spammed 24H for 6 days straight to exploit vote gathering in chat channels? Yes, you can spend real money to send a bounty after them. Some dude spent too much time with your e-wife at the bathhouse and you want him to stop? You can spend real money and hope a skilled PvP player causes him grief in his own instance.

UI design is also a bunch of clunk. Because it's designed to have crossplay with Mobile players in the same instances as PC and Console players, there is an undeniable performance issue and jank with the menus. It has remained the same in the CN version that is a year ahead. Don't expect it to improve. You're given so much currency, you're your own world trade center and you don't remember what half of them are used for.

While I enjoyed the game for the first 286.2 hours socializing and killing people and getting killed, it took that long to realize I tried to like this game and in the end, I disliked what it stood for and what potential it has but will never reach. It's just a gacha game that looked really pretty and everyone enjoyed at launch but in the end, there was nothing different about it compared to Mihoyo style games except visually. Your FOMO is fashion and not characters. You're given a promise that it can't fulfill because that's just how NetEase games are.

Currently sitting at 140 some hours in game, and I've finished the main storyline up until Feb 2026's season. Absolutely gorgeous artwork, fantastic music soundtrack, and a pretty engaging storyline. Side quests also have their own interesting lore, and a lot of it is linked, so if you're story-type of player, you'll have a great time. 

Coming from Ghost of Yotei + Tsushima, this game carries a lot of the same mechanics and at times, feels eerily like a copy of the gameplay. But then again, why reinvent the wheel? If you've ever played any of those types of games, you'll feel at home with the game mechanics. 

The biggest difference obviously is that this is one of the most fleshed out Chinese wuxia mmorpg games where you can also play solo as a single player without ever touching a multiplayer mechanic. It's everything anyone has ever wanted from a wuxia c-drama and more, especially where you act as the "hero" of the whole game.

NPCs are believable and at times, even charming-- but there is a weird AI mechanic inserted in some of the optional conversational dialogue you can have with NPCs. It doesn't detract from the game, but it's definitely an interesting choice. The biggest issue with localization comes with the "riddle" games when you unlock further pieces of the game -- it simply gives you a word or two and expects that you make crazy assumptions to get to the final answer. For example, "holes" = "lotus root", which without cultural and cuisine knowledge, you might never have gotten there. 

Other pieces of note: WWM is cross-platform, and albeit the linking instructions are confusing, this game works great between my PS5, Steam, and its native launcher. I assume you can also play mobile but I haven't tried.

Overall I would say for a F2P, this game gives a lot of value and is wildly fascinating. The global version is a bit behind the CN version, but that also means all the kinks and issues are ironed out before it lands on our side.

they've really perfected the genre. this one reminds me of fable and some old pirates game i used to play, with some soulslike elements

but first of all i want to address the llm/genai allegations, the game does have an actual llm as an ingame mechanic, as in some npcs in addition to fixed storyline dialogs also have "chat" option which lets you use your own keyboard input like i know some of you weirdos do on char dot ai. i haven't interacted with this mechanic at all, but judging from the experience of others it is ass, it's a small model, same for every npc, but it's also dumbed down even further than regular llms because an average f2p rpg player can't solve regular puzzles so from game developer's perspective it doesn't make sense to ask for anything more than a few cliche phrases for the llm to go along with you. what else did you expect?

all of that is completely optional and i didn't have to do that at all during any quests or at any stage of the game. it's just there to test the waters and to give you the ability to rizz npcs for some minor rewards. some roleplayers who have little respect for themselves may utilize that. personally i don't think it has a place in any art or storytelling medium, it also draws a lot of (deserved) hate hence it's optional and implemented to be out of sight

another genai application is in character creation. the game has an AMAZING character creation tool where you can materialize all your eugenics fantasies down to single digits of nose tilt angle and glabella shape. do you even know what glabella is?
all is done by hand, or you can draw inspiration from other players' showcases in the same character creation screen, there's really creative stuff out there and almost too many options, which is great, however you can also choose to vibe-create a character using "ai", which is just randomizer with extra steps so it's not a big deal, but wait there's more - you can actually send your personal data to china by using mic or webcam and it will try to generate a character based on your voice or likeness. as far as i can tell it does so pretty poorly

i couldn't find any obvious signs of other gen ai usage, in particular for assets. the world design is really compelling; even though the game is in a fantasy setting it is still medieval china loosely based on folklore stories, and i'm willing to believe they wouldn't want to misrepresent it with sloppiness. i'm also trusting my own eyes: a significant part of the game relies on its visuals, exploration is offered as a complete activity, even for guilds. kaifeng (it's a real city) is greatly designed. players seem to love taking screenshots of landscapes, weather effects and reflections, and the sight of the milky way in the night sky, and posting them in the game (more on that later) - i can see that a lot of good work was put into that. during some quests it becomes clear that things were arranged in such a way for the player to appreciate the surroundings while listening to the dialog - that requires good camerawork and hands-on direction. overall i can clearly see that the game was made with extreme care. proving something like ai-assisted texture design is a whole different story, but until something of substance comes up i'm willing to trust them

the game has an easy and seamless switch between solo and online modes. online mode is sandboxy and is meant for social activities, guilds and arena, and in the solo mode you're doing the main story and you don't have other players running around, however one feature i particularly like is other players' notes/signposts. i don't play a lot of games released in recent years so i don't know if this is a new and unique feature, but basically players can plant signposts in the world with helpful tips for puzzles, directions, resource locations, or just their drip [spoiler]or begging for likes[/spoiler]. signposts can contain a screenshot in addition to text, and there are even comments right there in the interface, with built-in translation tool, so there's a lot of memeing going on there. upvoting a signpost prolongs its lifetime, downvoting hides it. it's really one of the better ways of interacting with others while staying in singleplayer mode, with this you don't have to alt-tab to online communities in a browser

the game is pretty handholdy, so if you're some kind of dark souls veteran - don't hesitate to choose harder difficulty level. you can change it at any time

i won't attempt to list all the positives because overall the game is great and it's a hard recommend from me, especially if you've watched as many cdramas as i have. it really has more rpg mechanics than i can remember (or can be bothered with), the game actually wants you to pet every cat you encounter for a stat increase, there's trading, there's crafting, there's housing, there's bounty placing and bounty hunting, there're tiered trials similar to genshin's spiral abyss, there's mahjong (which was invented in the 19th century but the game setting is in 10th... immersion-breaking...), there's healing as an actual profession (you can restore hp but you will have to reach out to others if you catch serious illnesses and ailments), there are craftable weapon buffs probably similar to soulslikes, the class i've chosen requires me to use at least 10 buttons in combat not counting movement, and there's also mogging other players because oh hell somebody take it away from me - garment design and dyeing is a big thing in the game and i can spend hours not progressing or interacting with anything else...

however i will mention a couple of downsides

• performance. it's at 2015 rust level, when near the end of the wipe cycle you're surrounded with tons of player constructions away from the map's edge, if you know what i mean. the game does offer unrestricted (above 120) fps option and i think that's cute, because i haven't seen anything close to three digits even in a dungeon

...i'm not a very demanding player in that regard, but there doesn't seem to be a lot of bugs - there's a horse drowning in textures every now and then, there are occasional visual glitches and clipping, but so far the game is very stable. granted, the bar is set very low, but i was never logged out or crashed, the game does not memory leak when played for many hours, there's only one loading screen at the very beginning. it's just kinda poorly optimized probably because of mobile

• confusing, clunky interface. okay it's not rocket science, but there's clearly a degree of artificial complexity. there was no need for so many types of currencies, there was no need to give them all fantasy names instead of naming them after what they're actually for. there's no need for so many menu levels too. the game will give you tips for navigating this mess, but... didn't they already meaningfully simplify lots of other tedious and time consuming rpg mechanics? you don't have to mash spacebar when climbing, you don't have to vendor trash, typically if something doesn't need extra clicks it can be done without them... so why this then?

• top tier gacha is prohibitively expensive, compared to hoyo games for example. you're looking at something like $1000 before you reach hard pity o_o i mean sure, i'm being picky - it's a free game with plenty of content, and i said "top tier" because you do get a lot of stuff for free or as seasonal rewards and there's also lower tier gacha for peasants, but the main banner is exclusively for whales. the stuff there is pretty cool, but i don't think any ingame attire (in any game) is worth $1000, however i know whales who do think that, and so do the developers... whatever i guess, let them get the money. it's worth mentioning that expensive purchases don't seem to be related to player power, only cosmetics, which is great

• llms and generative ai should be gone in any shape or form. fortunately, if this game is anything to go by, they won't find much use

Runs well even on lower end systems. Unique open world gameplay and responsive online experience. UI has a somewhat steep learning curve, but one can progress far enough without utilizing all the features of the game. There are some bugs in the 2nd region (Kaifeng), but the first region (Qinghe) seems to be more polished. The story seemed mid at first but it draws you in slowly and delivers some emotional moments (no spoilers!). There are also some real world Buddhist and Taoist concepts mixed in with ancient Chinese mythology. These mix in well with the story and does not feel like religious propaganda. The game shows the positive and potential negative sides of organized religion (like corrupt monks). It is very neutral in its representation of sensitive topics. I learned a lot about some aspects of philosophy while playing the game, some of it was profound, others unrealistic, and some I did not agree with on a personal level. There are some areas of the game where the English translation does not make much sense, but inferences can be made. Overall it is a good game, with room for improvement. It has received regular updates so far and I hope they prioritize fixing existing issues over constantly introducing new content.

I’ve played my fair share of oriental-inspired MMOs over the years (shoutout to the KalOnline veterans), but Where Winds Meet is on a completely different level. It is, hands down, one of the smoothest experiences I’ve had in the genre.
Why you should play it:

    Silky Smooth Combat: The movement and combat are incredibly fluid. Coming from older "clunky" MMOs, the responsiveness here is a breath of fresh air. Once you switch to ARPG Mode, the game truly shines—parrying and dodging feel impactful and precise.

    A Living, Breathing World: This isn't just a world of static NPCs. The interaction system is deep. Whether you're debating a drunkard to get him back on his feet or helping a local woodcutter with a bandit problem, the world feels alive. And watch out for the geese—they are more dangerous than they look!

    Infinite Freedom (Identity System): You aren't locked into a single class. The "Identity" system lets you be a Physician, an Architect, a Musician, or even a Beggar. You can build your own dynasty, recruit NPCs to your base, and automate your empire.

    The Aesthetic: The Wuxia/Oriental theme is handled with so much respect and detail. From running on water to the way the wind moves the trees, the immersion is 10/10.

Technical Performance (Linux/Steam Deck):

For my fellow Linux users, I’m running this on CachyOS with an RTX 3060, and it runs like a dream on Ultra settings. If you’re looking for a modern AAA experience that respects your hardware and your time, this is it.

Final Verdict: It’s Free-to-Play, but it feels like a premium AAA title. It captures that classic "oriental mystery" vibe and brings it into 2026 with flawless execution.

Where Winds Meet is an absolutely breathtaking experience and one of the most immersive open-world RPGs I’ve played in recent years. Set in a beautifully recreated world inspired by ancient China, the game immediately stands out with its stunning art direction, atmospheric landscapes, and remarkable attention to historical detail.

The combat system feels fluid, dynamic, and deeply satisfying. Blending martial arts techniques with elegant swordplay, every encounter feels cinematic yet skill-based. I especially appreciated the freedom to approach battles in different ways — whether through stealth, agility, or direct confrontation. The mechanics are intuitive but still offer enough depth to stay engaging for hours.

Exploration is another major highlight. The world feels alive, filled with meaningful side quests, memorable characters, and hidden secrets that reward curiosity. Traveling across mountains, forests, and villages never feels repetitive thanks to the game’s rich environmental storytelling and dynamic weather system.

The narrative is equally impressive. The story unfolds naturally, allowing players to shape their own journey while still delivering emotionally powerful moments. The writing is thoughtful, and the character development adds real weight to your decisions.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a masterfully crafted adventure that successfully combines beauty, freedom, and compelling gameplay. It’s a must-play for fans of open-world RPGs and anyone who appreciates a well-designed, atmospheric experience.

A Beautiful Epic with Untapped Potential

In my initial review-in-progress of Where Winds Meet, I was cautiously optimistic. I hoped its early issues were simply the result of its unfinished state and would be resolved by launch. While the full release improves certain aspects and delivers an impressive amount of content, many core problems remain. What emerges is a free-to-play MMO that offers remarkable value and ambition, yet struggles with refinement and long-term engagement.

At its best, Where Winds Meet is breathtaking. Set in 10th-century China during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, the game delivers a vast, Wuxia-inspired world filled with lush fields, ancient cities, and scenic wilderness. Exploration is consistently rewarding, supported by excellent music and strong environmental design. Simply wandering through Kaifeng, Qinghe, and surrounding regions is one of the game’s greatest pleasures, capturing the romantic solitude and freedom central to the Wuxia fantasy.

The narrative follows a wandering sword master whose journey begins with the theft of a treasured jade pendant and gradually expands into a larger, darker conflict. The story shows real promise early on, introducing intriguing characters and compelling themes. However, while the opening chapter is engaging and memorable, later portions lose narrative momentum. Technical shortcomings such as lip-sync issues, missing audio, and awkward localization further weaken immersion.

Gameplay is where Where Winds Meet both shines and stumbles. Combat is initially excellent, offering fast, reactive encounters built around Martial Arts sets, Mystic Arts abilities, and weapon specialization. The lack of traditional classes gives players freedom to shape their own playstyle through weapons, factions, and skill progression. Abilities range from elegant swordplay to fantastical techniques like summoning giant bells or charging enemies atop flaming mounts. PvP, in particular, stands out as a highlight, rewarding timing, positioning, and player skill rather than raw gear advantage.

However, this depth comes with limitations. Weapon balance feels uneven, stealth systems are underdeveloped, and over time combat encounters begin to feel repetitive. While the progression systems are extensive and rewarding, only a handful of weapons and builds remain consistently effective, which discourages experimentation.

Beyond combat, the sheer volume of content is impressive. The campaign is supported by meaningful side quests, world bosses, guild systems like the Hundred Industries, and exploration-driven activities that reward curiosity. These systems create a satisfying gameplay loop, encouraging players to explore and improve their abilities. Importantly, monetization is fair. Microtransactions are largely cosmetic, and the game avoids aggressive pay-to-win mechanics, making its free-to-play model feel surprisingly respectful of the player’s time.

Multiplayer adds both strengths and weaknesses. Exploring with friends enhances the experience, reinforcing the sense of shared adventure. PvP modes are especially enjoyable, offering balanced and competitive encounters. However, cooperative PvE can feel chaotic, and technical issues such as lag, bugs, crashes, and unresponsive controls frequently disrupt gameplay. AI-driven NPC interactions also feel hollow and undermine immersion.

Technically, Where Winds Meet presents a mixed picture. Its open world is visually stunning, with excellent lighting, animations, and environmental detail. Yet persistent bugs, localization problems, missing audio, and interface issues make the experience feel unpolished. These flaws highlight the gap between the game’s ambition and its execution.

Ultimately, Where Winds Meet is a paradox. It offers tremendous value, a vast and beautiful world, deep progression systems, and fair monetization—qualities that make it stand out among free-to-play titles. Yet repetitive combat, technical instability, and inconsistent narrative execution prevent it from reaching its full potential.

There is something truly special here. The world, atmosphere, and early gameplay demonstrate what Where Winds Meet could become with continued support and refinement. For now, it remains a generous and ambitious MMO that is easy to admire, occasionally thrilling to play, but not yet polished enough to fully recommend as a long-term commitment. With future updates, however, it could evolve into one of the defining Wuxia games of its generation.

Best Persistant Multiplayer Dungeon game.

MMORPG WORLD SYSTEM (8/10): EXCELLENT, but too many menus

"Where wind meet" is a hybrid Multiplayer game with a game lobby and a interactive world, that have character progression based on a Single Player mode. Your quests/level progression mainly happens in a single player world. It is here the narrative and plot unfold, where you fights the soul-like bosses. Combat is fluid and smooth, comparable with the likes of BDO. 

The game lobby is a series of menus that open up various activities where you can join queues to fight dungeons, bosses (5man and 10man), or engages in PVP contest (1v1 and multiple player groups). The interactive world is just like a MMORPG, you can travel around, kill stuffs, collect resources and see everyone else.  This world allows open world PVP and all manners of freedom.

COMBAT SYSTEM (9/10):
Combo based combat similar to most soullike/action combat game. Each character can equip 2 weapon, each with 4-6 moves. With around 10 odd weapons to choose, you can work out various combi. In addition, you can obtain various universal moves known as Mystic Arts (I see them as a series of addons, with some skills to improve combat mobility/durability/CC/counters). You can only equip 8 of these skills to your arsenal to further expand your combat option.

PAY TO WIN/GRIND TO WIN/GROVEL TO WIN (10/10): BEST in MARKET
Probably the best feature of this game. Any poor dude will get close to the whales. So no way to pay for power.
No excessive grinding will gain you overwhelming resources, that will give you super distinct advantage. No grovel to your guild leaders to get first dips on loots, and maneuver in guild politics.

GEARING
Gearing is casual, just play 30min-1hr daily, you should get to level cap and gear cap in no time.

DEATH PENALTY
Close to nil, since everytime you die u lose 1 durability for each gear. Each gear has 100 durability and the repair is cheap. 

COSMETIC (10/10 or 0/10): Depends if you get jealous over someone else outfit
They have quite detailed and beautiful free outfits, with a few dollars you can get some outfits. These are pretty cool too. Then you suddenly goes from few tens of dollars to whale class. These are outfits that cost till $800, and weapons close to $2k. Then again, since it is just to "Pay to Look Beautiful", I am fine, since they are paying the server uptime.

Chinese mobile slop lovingly squeezed out on to a plate by a squatting man for your enjoyment. This is the type of game where you create a character at the start of the game and when you start playing you don't look like that because every cosmetic requires gacha.

There is one good element. The combat is fine. It feels a lot like Black Myth Wukong, a type of Dark Souls combat where parrying is heavily rewarded like Sekiro. The higher difficulties would genuinely challenge anyone who likes Sekiro. However, in higher difficulty, the parry reliance means it wont appeal directly to souls players. Absolutely nothing new to add here. We've seen basically everything here, a lot, with the possible exception of the Rope Dart weapon, a totally ineffectual chinese dancing aid that might allow you to kill one unarmoured man if you attack from behind. Mind you we don't get and Guandao, Tiger Hooks, Crescent Fists, Axes, Polearms, Staffs or many weapons that are effective at killing, nor do we get any of the other made up weapons that look cool while dancing like Nunchuk, which I believe is Japanese but Bruce Lee made it sexy. However we do get some expected gimmick weapons, the hidden blade in the umbrella and a fan. Both fun ideas.

Speaking of Wukong he's just not in this Wuxia story for some reason. There is a reference to just about every Chinese character from the three kingdoms era to modern day except the most famous one. Its seems pretty weird because he's also the best character. Like every culture has a fat man who acts very happy and friendly but is actually greedy. Not every culture has a wise cracking monkey who rides a cloud and can make his shaft bigger. Seems like a bit of a missed opportunity.

The localization is pretty bad. If I had to guess a lot of it is translated by AI. There are repeated voicelines and incorrect translations in the closed captions. The voice actors they have hired are about the worst in the industry besides a few very notable exceptions that just seem to pop up. Their performance comes across like they recorded a script in a booth and didnt really know what the scene was about but they stand out a lot whenever one of them is talking.

For a role playing game the main character is extremely boring. They're just generic hero person. Everyone spends so much time praising you and telling you how amazing you are that it starts coming across as disingenuous. Your character can't really have any flaws, you can't make any choices in the story, even to just change a voice line and how your character reacts to the same situation. Have you read any Chinese story written since 1770? Do you know what Divine Virtues are? Then you know exactly what your character is. This is juxtaposed against a character creator where you can make the most sinister looking snake human alive. It just doesnt work. Like a lot of Wuxia stories, the main character just comes across as a weak self insert of whichever artist had to re write every single story when they burned down the confuscian libraries. He is a peerless beacon of morality as it's beaten into the Chinese population and as a result is extremely monodimensional. This is especially obvious when compared to other very well written characters who are flawed but still good people, such as Killerblade.

Everything else is FINE. The art is fine. The music is fine. The environments are fine. The puzzles and side activities often include chinese characters and games like Majong which nobody else on the earth is going to care about which is why no westen MMOs have chess. With no way to set or even tell what the difficulty of the activity is, these side activities can range from brainlessly easy to basically impossible, and the minigame quality ranges is scale immensely. The archery minigame involes just using your bow to shoot stuff like youve been doing the whole game and the Music minigame involves you playing Guitar Hero at expert difficulty to off-beat anicent chinese gobbledygook on the Guqin. Again, lets look at all the good western RPGs that make you play Beethoven's entire catalogue in guitar hero format for some experience. Not a good system. Not fun at all.

Overall for the price of free this title is above average. The story is... Alright. It's got some decent twists and turns, especially at the end, and I genuinely didn't expect some of the character developments. This game is essentially 3 games in one.

The first is a single player action combat game:

This is mostly great, great bosses, good story. Sometimes heavy with the dialogue and can slow down a bit. But over all a great game play experience for an any Sekiro fan. A boss replay mechanic with rewards for no hit runs and increased difficulty. There's probably about over 30 bosses at this point. And there is a lot of quests and constant dlc sized updates with new areas, full stories, new weapons, and mystics (magic) and new unique bosses. The game came out in fall of last year, there's already been 4 or 5 of these dlc sized updates. There's another one coming in late July. 

The second is pvp. There are 4 main types:

1v1s this is where you'll find most of the rage reviews are coming from. Mythic players dominate this area and are everywhere all over the ranks. They'll make you feel like you can't do anything and honestly theres a lot of builds that can just exploit stuns and heals. For 90% of players I wouldn't reccomend this. You can also just do private 1v1s with your friends or open lobbies for randoms to join, so you don't have to play ranked all the time. You can even just 1v1 in your guild hall.

Group Strategy: A tourament style pvp match (3v3, 4v3 or 5v5). Is actually really fun but under played feature. Starts with you selecting of your players to engage in two separate 1v1s at the same time. If one of your players lose and the other wins, those two have to fight with their current health. Winner wins the round. Next round is a 3v3 or 4v4 or 5v5 team death match. Can be fun but also chaotic allows for some clutch 2v1s. If the score card is even, then their is once final 1v1. Players usually save their best player for this one (as you cannot use one of the two players who fought in the first round).

Perception Forest (battle royale): Can be fun, but often you get paired with people with very high ping, which ruins the experience. 

Guild vs Guild: Actually a well done feature. Though there isn't a cap or a minimum number of people you can bring from your guild. Most fights are between 20-30 people on each team. You have to take nodes and kill the enemy's goose and bring back their tree thing. Theres bosses that provide buffs if killed. And a 1v1 match everyone has to watch where the winner gets a huge buff for their team. Depending on your guild can be very fun.  

Finally there is the social style of play: This includes hanging out with your boys playing minigames, or base building. and romances etc. Theres group pve too but honestly its not great imo. Not for me but I know theres a lot of mmo players who like that sort of thing.

Honestly most of fall off of players, comes from the single player styles people. They "finish" a game and move on, and you can see this drop off with most single player games. The other part comes from people raging the game from 1v1s. I've raged from 1v1s myself.

A must play in my opinion as the combat is unmatched. I have trouble playing other games because Im lacking combat depth and responsiveness. And its not at all pay to win. Has something for literally everyone.

This is my first review on Steam, so I’ll focus on what stood out to me the most.
I decided to try WWM because of the very positive feedback from players and not so-called “experts”. I was hooked almost immediately. The sheer amount of content is mind-blowing. There’s so much to do that, combined with the online features, it took me at least 20 hours just to learn the basics. I felt overwhelmed at first—especially since I jumped straight into multiplayer—but if you focus on single-player early on, the experience feels much more balanced.
I rarely spend over 100 hours in a game, so the fact that I’m now close to 120 hours says a lot. It’s genuinely addictive. I’m about 50% through both regions, and after finishing the main story plus most of the major quests, it does start to feel a bit grindy (though there are still dozens of smaller quests and encounters left). These days, I log in mostly for weekly tasks, to spend energy, and to explore a bit more. The developers keep adding new content, which definitely helps maintain long-term engagement.
One thing I noticed after going back to other open-world games is how empty they feel in comparison. In WWM, villages feel alive—NPCs are everywhere, and many of them are interactive with AI features. The world feels populated and dynamic. There were a few mechanics I didn’t enjoy at first, but as I learned the systems better, most of those concerns faded.
I also appreciate how balanced the game is between paying and non-paying players. Those who buy passes mainly progress a bit faster with upgrade materials, but ultimately everyone reaches the same point. Most monetization seems focused on cosmetics and visual upgrades rather than power advantages.
My biggest issue—though partly personal—was the heavy emphasis on parrying. I’ve completed many Souls-like games, but I usually rely on dodging rather than parrying. I started on Legendary difficulty to fully test myself, but after about 30 hours, I realized I wasn’t enjoying it. I couldn’t consistently beat bosses without mastering parries, and since enemy levels scale with your gear (if you break through), leveling up didn’t help much. I also encountered some frustrating bugs—during certain campaign boss fights, my healing flasks were stuck at first level and one use, even though I had unlocked three and upgraded them to level two. That made things even more punishing.
Since I had so much left to explore and learn, I didn’t want to spend hours memorizing every boss pattern and parry window. I eventually lowered the difficulty to the recommended setting, which still provided a solid challenge but made the experience much more enjoyable. Playing via a cloud gaming platform didn’t help either—even a tiny bit of input lag makes precise parrying noticeably harder. Later, I realized that Legendary difficulty mainly rewards you with a flashy health bar and a profile badge, so I didn’t feel like I was missing much.
Overall, I’d rate the game a 9/10. Despite a few frustrations, it’s one of the most engaging open-world experiences I’ve played recently, and I’m genuinely excited for the massive upcoming content.

A Masterpiece of Wuxia Artistry – We Need This as a Full MMO!
After spending dozens of hours in Where Winds Meet, I can confidently say this is one of the most refreshing open-world experiences I’ve played in years. It’s a love letter to martial arts cinema and historical RPGs.
Technical Performance:
I played this on an RTX 4070 Super at 1440p (2K), and the experience was excellent. The framerate remained consistently above 60 FPS, even in more demanding areas, making the fast-paced combat feel incredibly smooth and responsive.
What makes this game incredible:
The Combat System: This isn't just "button mashing." The combat is tactical and heavily reliant on timing and parries. Switching between different weapon styles feels fluid, and the boss fights are genuinely cinematic.
A Stunning World: The world-building is top-notch. From the bustling ancient cities to the serene bamboo forests, the attention to detail is breathtaking. The "Qinggong" movement (running on water and walls) makes exploration feel magical.
The "Wuxia" Spirit: The game captures the philosophy of martial arts perfectly. You aren't just a fighter; you are part of a living world where you can learn medicine, architecture, or even trade.
My Personal Wish:
While the single-player and co-op elements are fantastic, the world is so rich and the mechanics are so polished that I would absolutely love to see a true, full-scale MMORPG built on this exact engine and style.
The social potential is massive. Imagine a persistent world where thousands of players belong to different martial arts sects, competing for territory or interacting in these beautiful cities. The foundation is already perfect; turning this into a "true MMO" would be a dream come true!
Conclusion:
It’s a high-quality journey through ancient China that sets a new standard for the genre.
Rating: 9/10

Where Winds Meet has great potential to be a completely different gacha game than others. The PvE is great, and guild wars are extremely fun. However, the PvP aspect in 1v1s has got to be one of the most absolute garbage systems I have seen across any type of online game in the history of all gaming. You could be a level one within your first hour of the game and get paired with a max level, max goose (power level), player and have a 0% chance of winning. In my first experience, I had won maybe 2 matches, and was immediately paired with someone at max level with a goose level multiple times higher than mine. At the beginning of the last update, ranks for PvP were reset, and again, you could be paired with someone significantly higher skill/power/rank than you. If you enjoy PvP, this is not the game for you. Every other aspect of this game has potential. It is not pay-to-win, the gacha system is primarily cosmetic. PvE with friends is entertaining, but can be repetitive. Resource grinding is heavy, and limited with resets required for energy, and specific upgrade materials. If you start this game, expect to be significantly behind everyone else, with a very slow upstart to get caught up. Attaining materials should be made a little more available, in order for new players to catch up with the current players. PvP needs a significant revamp if they want to retain people in that mode. Weapons need rebalance, the Vernal Umbrella is extremely overpowered and is not balanced with any other weapon in the game. Overall, again, this game has the potential to do something very different as a gacha. I'm happy to say that it is not pay-to-win, even though cosmetics take several hundred dollars to obtain from the gacha rolls. Where Winds Meet has plenty of room to grow, and it will need to do so.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted wuxia game. If I focus purely on the main storyline and the most important quests, it easily delivers the quality of a strong single-player experience. Story depth, atmosphere, mysticism, the philosophical subtlety typical of wuxia, and character progression all perform remarkably well. I’d confidently call it a top-tier RPG capable of providing 60 hours or more of engaging content.

However, it’s important to remember that this is a free-to-play live service game. What does that mean in practice? The game offers cosmetic skins for real money. “Who cares about skins?” one might ask. In a traditional 60-hour RPG, probably very few players.

Free-to-play games, though, are designed differently. Progression is intentionally paced more slowly. You can gather herbs and flowers, pet cats, heal or argue with NPCs, go fishing, hunt for hidden quests, and engage in countless other side activities. The catch is that these are not truly optional — they are tied directly to character advancement, such as earning talent points. If a player aims to maximise their talents, then every minor task, every collectible, every trivial interaction becomes mandatory. Even the last hidden cat must be found and petted.

At this point, the consequences become difficult to ignore. Sixty to eighty hours of exceptional narrative and handcrafted content only retain their value when experienced within a comparable timeframe. When that same content is diluted across hundreds or thousands of hours, its perceived quality inevitably changes.

If a cup of fine tea is diluted with a hundred litres of water, it not only loses its richness — it ceases to be recognisable as tea at all.

Everything I ever wanted in a game: cats, food, and beautiful characters, what else do you need?
On a more serious note, I love how many things there are to do and how many quests the game offers. The story is really interesting and complex, with many elements interconnected. I’d recommend watching a lore video, though, since it’s based on the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era and can get pretty confusing due to how quickly things changed in such a short period of time. The Chinese voice acting is beautifully done, but the English localization still needs some work.

It’s rare that a free-to-play game delivers this level of polish, immersion, and pure fun, but Where Winds Meet absolutely does.

      I've been playing since 2 weeks after launch, and I've found the experience to not only be smooth and bug free, but also breathtaking, and captivating, with satisfying combat. Since the very beginning, the level of quality in this free to play game has absolutely blown me away. 
     For starters, the world is so incredibly well done. The art, the atmosphere, the characters (YingYing is my favorite), and the ambiance, to include the music. All of it is superb. There are moments within the story that, for me, a lifetime gamer, are next level. There's a running 6/10 joke in the community. You can post signs in the ground with a photo and comment for others to see (like in Elden Ring and Once Human). People will post a sign next to the most breathtaking scenery or story event, and comment 6/10. We all love the joke, because we all see it as 10/10, but IGN gave it a 6/10 at launch. I haven't met a single player that would dream of rating the game that low. 
    Speaking of the signposts. This is another part of WWM that I think is so well done. They've managed to merge MMO and single-player action-RPG into something that's on the next level for both genres. You get this truly immersive world all of your own. You're not competing for kills, you're not seeing people wearing some comical cash shop outfit bunny hopping around after your absolutely epic cutscene. You're truly immersed. That said, I often forget that it's a single player game. It feels like an MMO to me. I get group dungeons. I get guild dungeons. I get active guild parties every night and an active guild chat. I get GVG on weekends. There is active PVP around the clock. There are weekly guild boss fights that you can get credit for fighting or observing. There are weekly 1v1 "showdowns" for the guild that you can get credit for fighting in or observicng. There are some recreational activities that you can totally skip if you want, but I often do them, and they're full of players. There was a player in our guild base this past weekend (not from our guild) that was making everyone in the guild itchy. Everyone was walking around scratching themselves. Everyone was having a good laugh from it in voice chat. Things like this make you really enjoy how much it feels like an MMO. It's like it took all of the good from both worlds, and none of the bad. There is an incredibly well-done video by Dhalfang that discusses this, and I highly recommend checking it out. The title is something about Where Winds Meet being the next generation of MMORPG. 
     On the subject of guilds, I have heard that it can be hard to get into the full and active guilds. I didn't have any trouble at all myself, but someone said it's challening. I know that my guild leader, dearcindyphan, regularly removes inactives and recruits fresh members for our guild, Trashpandas. We always have  a roster of around 100 very friendly and helpful players. The guild is officially casual, but we have so many players excited about the game that you wouldn't realize it by performance alone. Events and GVG go super smooth but we all have a great time, and some relaxed fun while we go about it. Can't make it? No worries. Anyways, just catch one of dearcindyphan's streams if you want to catch a glimpse of daily end-game gameplay or if you want to see if the guild is a good fit for you. She streams multiple times/week. 
     I can't review this game without mentioning how fun the combat and movement are. I absolutely love the freedom and versatility of the two-weapon system. You aren't pigeon-holed into some exact build like in other games. Many find benefits in using two weapons from the same category, but other options are viable. I've fallen in love with strategic sword (bellstrike umbra path) and vernal umbrella (silkbind jade path). I love the versatility of melee and ranged viability. The rotation for me is so fluid too, like they were made to be paired together. Movement adds so much to the fun, with double jumps, mid-air dashes, dives, etc. You can even basically fly after you unlock it with enough zone activity. 
      For a free to play game, it's probably important that I mention that there is no P2W, not  at all. Players call it "pay to slay", because the only thing in the cash shop is fashion. That said, you can get a lot of really great outfits for free or really cheap. I have a nice looking dyable outfit that I bought from a temporary battle pass that was one dollar. The battle pass had some other nice things, like I believe maybe some dye, and other outfit things. The outfit cash shop can definitely get VERY expensive, but it's all fashion, and even the starter outfit looks cool imo. Everything looks nice, so spend money where it feels good, and nothing more. 
      I've been a long-time gamer, since the 90s. I've had my share of MMORPGS, and action RPGs, and I've definitely chalked up enough experience to make myself a harsh critic, but I honestly don't see where this game is lacking. I'm going to have to say this is 10/10 for me, and if it were selling for 59 dollars instead of free to play, I'd say this game is 10/10 and I would highly recommend. 
     The level of quality for this game at launch and for the first few months has been top-notch, and after 213 hours of gameplay, I can't wait to see where this game goes in the future.

The Bad:

          - The AI character creation seems cool at a surface level but it is pretty much equivalent to pressing the "generate random character" button, it would have been far better implamented if it was prompt driven

Massive design problems, I'm just going to list them. If you've played real MMO's back in the day and have been searching for the good ole' days, much like me you see the same problems and why we can't seem to get back to that place. 

- Boring Gear
- Menus, menus, menus of menus, in menus of menus. Menus that point to gear, that point to skills, that point to menus, that point to gear, that point back to skills, only to point to items. Just stop.
- GACHA GACHA GACHA!!! 50k for a boat?! Want to simp for hot Asian characters played by dudes. There's literally a friendship/dating mechanic! Who doesn't want to blow $500 on their fake girlfriend lying about their gender? Me that's who.
- Choices, but you don't choose anything. The exact skills for that class are mandatory unless you want to gimp your progression. Sure, use 2 weapons that don't mix, but it won't work because if you don't the animations and combat flow get janky and the abilities have no synergy.
- A real economy where farming and items matter. Everything is disposable. You never build equity in the character, so it feels soulless. The gear treadmill is so severe and disjointed, you could cap at epic gear at 65, miss one breakthrough update, wait for the next, breakthrough, then entirely skip the fact you had to regear at the 70 cap and go straight to 75. It's a game you could play once every three months, for a week, and somehow not fall behind.
- Why are there professions? You created problems that don't really matter in the grand scheme of the game, and things you can grind to fix them. Oh boy, I'm a scholar (lawyer). Now I can play ridiculously easy mini games that also play like a phone game. Have your skill number be within 10% of the targets and you win. The healer profession lets you skip the entire mini game if your skill is higher than the targets. I love knowing my decisions truly matter. 

That's 6, and i could go on for quite a while. While this review is negative, I will say the experience is enjoyable. Take it for what it is. A fun romp through old world China. Once you get end game you realize there's really nothing there and you're just stuck waiting for something with meaning to do. It's a single player game with a new game+ worth actually playing, but once you get to the that end, you're just waiting for them to move the carrot on the stick down the road. Play it free, enjoy it for what it is, give them a little cash if you enjoyed it (20-30), and maybe revisit it a few times a year when the content piles up and you actually have a weeks worth of new stuff to do.

Why It Stands Out:
Deep, Elaborated Stories: Unlike many open worlds, the narrative here isn't filler. The lore is rich and cinematic, treating every side quest with the weight of a main campaign.

Unpredictable Mechanics: The game is a "beautiful mess" of genres. One moment you’re in a high-stakes duel, the next you’re building structures, practicing medicine, or using "Lightness Skills" to run across water. This unorthodox mix makes every session feel fresh and exciting.

True Versatility: The customization is staggering. Beyond just looks, you customize your life—choosing professions and martial arts styles that actually change how the world reacts to you.

Solo-Friendly Design: Perhaps its best feature is the lack of "online pressure." You can ignore the co-op entirely and enjoy it as a pure single-player experience. It offers the scale of an MMO with the intimacy of a solo journey.

The Verdict
It is a rare, versatile masterpiece for fans of Wuxia and open-world exploration with vast versatility and fun weird experiences unlike any other "MMO" out there

For a free-to-play title, Where Winds Meet is visually stunning. The landscapes are breathtaking, the character designs are detailed, and the overall atmosphere gives you a genuine sense of wonder. There’s a lot to do in the game—exploration, quests, and combat all feel rich and engaging. The storyline is tight and well-crafted, pulling you in while also making you reflect on our planet and our people in a different light. It’s a game that doesn’t just entertain; it inspires.
That said, there are some drawbacks that hold it back from being flawless:
• 	Co-op performance: Multiplayer is plagued by severe lag. Joining friends often results in the game freezing to the point where neither you nor your teammates can move.
• 	Chat system: World and sect chats are extremely spammy. The inability to fully switch them off makes the experience frustrating.
• 	Server availability: Not having servers closer to certain regions means players are stuck with pings over 300, which hurts gameplay fluidity.
• 	Shop pricing: While shop items aren’t mandatory, the costs are excessive. A single mount priced as high as an entire new game feels unreasonable, especially for a free-to-play experience.
Verdict: Where Winds Meet is a beautiful, thought-provoking game with immense potential. Its artistry and depth make it worth experiencing, but technical issues and monetization choices need serious improvement to match the brilliance of its design.

I don't like MMOs. They so often run the risk of being hollow when it comes to story and personality since they gotta fit in all sorts of classes. I also don't like having 1000 people who are all better than me run around all over the place and spamming me with invites to their guild or whatever. Additionally don't like gacha games because I don't like the way the mechanics prey on people's weaknesses. So why am I here? 

Well because when it comes to the first point, this game sidesteps that beautifully and gives us a fully fledged character with human connections and attitudes. Certainly the PC isn't the deepest well in the courtyard, but they're a full person at least. I feel invested in this person's adventures. The game also has no shortage of story to it, with beautiful cutscenes  (Including one in Kaifeng, the second big area) that left me outright speechless, with people actually doing stuff instead of gormlessly standing around dispensing quests, and countless characters ranging from the epic to the hilarious (Brother "Toss Roosters At Guards" is my spirit animal). It reminds me of Star Wars: The Old Republic in the best way possible. There's even a "Solo" mode where I can be left alone and don't need to have others intruding on my fun! 

The gacha mechanict meanwhile are certainly there, and I'm jumping around menus designed by the bloody Riddler to figure out where everything is and what I'm supposed to click to get what after getting achiements in twelve different places. This is ANNOYING, but the base game seems at time of writing solid enough that I'm still enjoying myself just oing the F2P stuff. Most currencies can be earned in-game, even if it's at a glacial pace, and one must make one's own evaluation of whether one has the kind of addictive personality that could get suckered into dumping money into this. If that's the case, don't play this game. Yet for me, it's not bad enough to ruin my fun. 

Other than that, the action feels awesome and responsive, with selectable difficulty levels that let even a casual trash goblin like me can get to feel like Li Mu Bai. The character and world design is properly fantastical - with everyone having the face of a K-pop star admittedly because that's what they're into over in China -  and the quests feel varied enough that I haven't yet had to have too many "bring me 12 bear butts" quests. Even the use of AI for various NPCs is not too egregious. Unimportant NPCs can be chatted with via an AI bot that pretends to be them, and admittedly that makes the conversations flow a little better in some cases. (I still hate AI, but this was as good as it gets in terms of usage of the damn thing) 

Overall, this game is a genuine delight, and I will be continuing to Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon my way over the rooftops and fight epic wuxia battles here for a long time ahead.

The game is great, I found it quite addictive, I won't lie. The open world and both solo and online modes are nice. The monetization is good and definitely not pay-to-win.

But this review will be one that highlights the annoying things within something that is so beloved.

*The game frequently lags in multiplayer mode. 
*There's not much you can do in the end-game, other than group dungeons or PVP.

*Peer-to-peer gameplay is used. In some arena PVPs (at least half of them), lag makes it unplayable. There are weapons that can be spammed (like dual blades), and those who spam with them win. This renders the game's ultimate weapon useless, despite its excellent dodge/kite/deflect mechanics. Lag makes skillful moves pointless. In other words, when there's lag, a good and skillful player will almost certainly lose to an unskilled teenager. And this happens A LOT!

*The ranged and melee classes in the game are incredibly unbalanced. If you're melee, a ranged guy who knows his stuff will definitely beat you. You have no chance against him. Because the people who coded these mechanics didn't really account for variables like mana, gap closing, and kiting. You'll chase him until dawn, and he'll take you down with a kite. And he'll think he's so skilled (the harsh truth).

PVP is full of these idiots.

Adding ranked mode to such a poorly designed PVP system, and the game running like this for so long, unfortunately gives a clear idea about the future of the game. If I had such a masterpiece, I could balance it with a night's work; these things aren't that difficult. The developers are indifferent.

I hope this review helps you.

It's FREE. That is the first and most important part. Now, lets get to the good parts.

Stick with the sub. The English dub for this game is really crap. Just play it in Chinese. There are other languages though for voices at least. 

The worst part of this game at the moment I can say for sure, is the advertisement. It doesn't seem to be an MMO in the traditional sense. I will update as I go further in. But, all the videos I saw made it seem like a traditional MMO. 

This game is a good entrance into learning more about Chinese culture, history and mythology. I have always felt that we didn't really get to see good representations of this in more popular media. It seems a bit harder to digest, as the names of a lot of things over there just do not roll off the English tongue as well as something that's Japanese. I can say the same about Korean things as well.

The game is beautiful. The art style is great and it's very smooth. I haven't noticed any performance issues atm. Combat is very similar to soulsbourne games. Blocking, Parry, Dodges, Lock on, Bows with varied ammo, cooking, harvesting materials. Upgrade gear for each typical slot and then each weapon can have a different art attached to it. I'm not sure about how many arts there are, but each one gives like 5 different abilities on a weapon and you have 2 melee and your bow equipped. Swapping between them all is very fluid. 

Then, you have these mystical art type things which are special abilities with short cooldowns. One lets you become a spirit frog form and jump around doing aoe. 

I haven't done too much, and it seems there are actually settings to allow you to get more to the classic MMO vibe, but I will update later. Story seems interesting so far and I haven't found myself bored.

One big thing is the puzzles from exploration. Typically, these are braindead easy to do. Now, they aren't crazy in this game, but it's a combination of fun with a bit of thought. I feel like they had the wrong people advertise this game, because I'm seeing stuff in the first few hours that just weren't show on average.

Also, what I saw on Youtube reminded me a lot of Hogwarts Legacy with a few grains of Avatar-combat, two games which are chill and nice casual gaming experiences. But that is where the good things end.

Which brings me to the bad stuff. So, for one I wouldn't call this a game for casual gamers. The combat difficulty in boss fights, even in the simplest mode, is too crass for that (and you have to tank them most of the time, long range is for hunting chicken...). Let me elaborate a bit: any attack has a counter intuitive rhythm, feeling like it starts in slow-mo and suddenly going beyond comprehension speed. You have about two seconds to breathe between being clobbert even if you are at the other end of the arena, because the range of any attack is always far enough to reach you, even if that means that the boss is glitching ten meters through the air. I like to play smart, not hard, trying to find the rhythm of an opponent and doge away from any attack until I get it, and you just can't do that here because you lose too much life while watching and trying to understand. It's also a complete visual overload.

Apart from that, the amount of AI that is being used can be off-putting and the conversations with characters are a bit boring, the menu is hell (I have never seen such a badly designed UI), and some of the mini games like the one where you spew random rudeness at your opponent without rhyme and reason, is just unnecessary.

I'm curious how long this game will be hot stuff. My guess is, they are training some AI with this and that's why it's free. If you read this, try the game, and come to the same conclusion, leave me a comment :D

Where Winds Meet is a GREAT game for boss rushes, has in-depth combat, looks and runs beautifully, but does it offer much else? Read on to find out! I'll give my take and honest impressions after 260+ hours. 
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I want to preface this brief review by simply stating that Where Winds Meet is a stellar achievement, especially for a free game -- from the visual fidelity and artistic arrangement, to the in-depth systems underpinning the invigorating and often adrenaline-pumping boss battles; the overworld, lore, and storytelling are no slouch either. Kaifeng, the Imperial city, feels like a living, breathing character in its own right. I am often marveling at the craftsmanship that went into this game in terms of the visuals, minute details, collectible costumes, and this makes exploring the overworld all the more immersive. 
Exploration is another gameplay element this game does fairly well, offering ample rewards for more inquisitive or discerning players. All of this having been said, you may have read that Where Winds Meet is a feature-rich game, with many other ways of playing the game on offer, including joining various sects with unique themes, and participating in mini games. On paper, this all sounds incredible, however, almost all of these additional features are rather shallow, and not fleshed out in the slightest. If you are looking for anything additional from these aspects of the game, you will surely be disappointed. Sects, for example, do not serve any purpose, aside from allowing you to unlock an outfit. Even the "missions" you can do for your sect are exactly identical to every other sect in the game, offering almost zero meaningful variance in gameplay. 

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a fantastic game for you if you enjoy world exploration and boss battles, but may find yourself a tad disappointed if you arrived for anything else.

I put some thought into this before I decided to write out this review. I am not recommending Where Winds Meet, for a number of reasons, that I felt, outweighed its strong showing as a great game. My opinion on this game is very much mixed. It is both an excellent game, and an insidious one. 

First off, "F2P" is a fallacy. There is no such thing as a free lunch. People want to throw out that "its a great game and its free". When its not, your access to the game is a transactional contract. You give your information, your data, which can be sold to third parties or given to the CCP for "reasons". If you feel its worth that price, then by all means, indulge yourself. 

Secondly, this game's true nature is simple: its a whale game. Everything about this game is driven about the collection of cosmetic items to be applied to your character, which you can then show off when you interact in the game's social game modes. It's so overt, the game literally tracks your cosmetic collection as a stat known as "elegance", and its tracked on global leaderboards. Whaling is literally the lifeblood of this game. 

If you can accept the fact, this game is designed to social engineer you into buying the ludicrously overpriced cosmetics, and engage with the predatory gacha systems (its pity pull system requires $300 USD to trigger). then you may be able to enjoy this game without much issues. If you however, have OCD and collection obsessive urges. I strongly urge you, to stop here, and *DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME*. You simply will not be able to afford it, most of the legendary gacha-only skins cost upward of $600 dollars investment to even have a CHANCE of getting one without incredible luck that beats less then 1% drop rates. You have better chances at casinos, then with this game's gacha. It's not worth it unless you have money to waste. 

If you can past these shortcomings, then you have to deal with a phenomenal game that will eventually whiplash you with its F2P nature. 

MY experience with Where Winds Meets began great. It's story, its accessibility, its world building, all exceptional. Then you hit the F2P wall. The developers have put in, internal daily hard caps on drops so efficient grinding is punished. This is on top of the weekly hard caps. 

This game is fantastic until you realize its on rails dictated by the developers. Then it becomes frustrating, as leveling requires that you log in and play the game like a daily chore. It's no longer a game you play at your pace, but by weekly and daily activity caps. I played Destiny 2 and enjoyed it until I realized it did exactly this. One has to basically play or FOMO. This game is full of FOMO. Miss an event? Too bad, that cosmetic is permanently delisted. Missed a week during an event? You missed the event's final reward milestone, too bad. 

When a game has to constantly bait you with another piece of candy to keep you engaged because it will not let you enjoy it if you outpace the activity cap. Then you see why a great game gets not recommended. 

I noticed alot of people drop this game because of this. Most of the game basically is daily activity grinding and going into social hubs to see how many people are willing to throw their money into a black hole. 

So if you can overlook its nature as a game, and deal with its frustrating handicaps as a F2P game. You will get your time's worth out of this game. But always understand, this game is literally a whale game. It's designed around whales and getting people to convince themselves its worth it, when its not.
