The newest update, Version 1.3, introduces a new feature called "Spotlight Mode." The update states that you can "Upload your photos or videos in the Spotlight Mode and let intelligent (lmao) AI generate character emotes, poses, audio, and camera movements for you." Yeah, generative AI is an automatic "no" from me. Like, cool, you're plagiarizing people's work by using your Gen AI models to scrape data to make ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ versions of existing work. I prefer real humans' art over robots, thanks.

Most of the visually stunning and interesting outfits are locked behind premium currency (you can only buy it with real money, there's no grinding it for free). Many of the outfits in the shop that you can buy outright are overpriced to ♥♥♥♥. Gacha is also an automatic "no" (sorry, I don't support gambling). The outfits you get through the free gambling section are underwhelming and there's a very limited amount of them. In the previous updates, they never added more outfits to the free gambling section, and I didn't see any mention of the devs putting more outfits in the free gacha in the newest update.

Also, let's be real, the game isn't that fun. I stopped playing around the end of version 1.1 because there really wasn't anything genuinely interesting or fleshed out. I really tried, but the game has too much and yet nothing at all. Everything feels so surface-level, from Gift of Gab to medicine to building to crime to exploration. Nothing this game does is particularly creative, intriguing, or just *different*. I don't think I'll list all complaints here, but just the ones that stood out to me the most when I played.

Building is clunky and buggy. There's honestly not much else to say. There's some items that have no blueprints and give almost no hints as to where you would obtain them (why have them in the building inventory if I can't craft them??). For example, there's a bathtub that only says you can get it through "house rental" but then doesn't elaborate further. The way you can get a bathtub is by renting the Compound in Kaifeng and then just.... deconstructing the bathtub. You can't actually craft it. You kind of steal it. You can do this in the Mansion, too. Also, it's just very annoying to build. It doesn't follow a grid system and you can't enable one either, the snapping tends to be very illogical and tries to put an item inside of walls??? Instead of just snapping to a different spot?? The game also had an issue where some variants of items just straight up never loaded and you couldn't place them down, so you had to pick another variant. I don't know if the devs ever fixed that.

Even the story is kind of dull. Like, why should I care about pretty much anything that happens outside of chapter 1's primary story quests? Why does it matter to me or my character? I thought I was looking for my family and trying to help the people of my hometown? Why am I trying to save a country that I have zero connections to and don't give a ♥♥♥♥ about? I just want to find Aunt Han?? Hello??? Why am I now a wanted criminal????

It's also kind of difficult to understand what the hell is happening *in general*. Wuxia and xianxia are already difficult enough for westerners like me to understand, but it's even worse when the game does the absolute bare minimum to actually explain the concepts used in the world. I don't know what these martial arts techniques are, I don't understand their significance, I know nothing about any of the sects in the Jianghu, I don't understand many of the cultural references, and the game does not do ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to explain anything. Qianye is the one singular character I thought was interesting, if only because she's mysterious and I desperately want to know her backstory, and why she's working with the Aureate Pavilion (and what the ♥♥♥♥ the Pavilion's goals even are as a whole), and why she even cared about our hometown and attacking our family and friends, and I want to know exactly how she developed her abilities and if they're like, supernatural or something. IDK, she was the only interesting character in the story. Aunt Han wasn't bad either, but her lore is so scattered throughout the game and there's like, no clues on where to find anything about her that isn't told to you in the main story quests, so.....

The puzzles are worse, because they were NOT translated or intended for western players. ♥♥♥♥♥, what do I know about elements in Chinese mythology?? How am I supposed to know how they interact with each other for this puzzle??? What do I know about Chinese astrology (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nothing)??? And they are barely explained before you do the puzzle????? Thanks, I guess?? Almost every puzzle I either brute-forced or read a handy in-game signpost someone left that just tells you the solution. You guys are the GOAT, btw.

The game's optimization isn't great. Even on medium settings, there's plenty of areas in the game that I really shouldn't be dropping below 60 FPS and yet I still do, even when there's barely any NPCs or buildings around, just foliage and trees. Character movement is clunky; it's difficult to precisely position myself without shuffling to the side constantly. 

Combat is very lackluster; it's very deflect-heavy to where I can barely get through one sequence of basic attacks without getting destroyed. It advertises that martial arts are diverse and allow for different playstyles, but the best way to get through every single fight is just bring Panacea Fan and hold block until you can time your deflects. When I first heard about this game, what came to mind was my years playing worthless Chinese-developed mobile MMORPGs. So that's what came to mind when people started talking about it. I wasn't interested.

Then I saw some clips of the combat and the game mechanics and it made me interested a bit. It's free. Why not? I need a new game anyway. So i download it, against my gut feeling.

I have to say... After 150+ hours, i'm hopelessly hooked. Like Frank in Hellraiser.

The pros:

-Amazing graphics.
-Amazing character customization
-RIdiculously detailed world jam packed with lively characters and things to do that are actually fun
-Combat is easy to learn, ridiculously hard to master
-Choice of playing solo/hosted co-op/MMO mode and switching between them is about as seamless as it can be.
-The content is beautiful and the game engine is extremely well-optimized. You get a lot for what the game takes in hardware resources.
-I never feel bored. It's almost like Witcher 3 in that regard.
-The boss fights are all difficult and unique and feel tied in to your story
-There's tons of secret and hidden things packed into every zone. 
-Not pay2win, but "Pay2Advance" and "Pay2LookCool"
-Free to play and completely still playable even if you go f2p 100%
-I feel like im playing a character in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. Seriously. This is about as close to that as you'll ever get. 

The cons:

-As a westerner and English speaker, the story, in typical Chinese fashion, feels very ambiguous and a bit disjointed at times. You can tell there's a story there, but, nothing is explained, characters are rarely properly introduced, you just seem to magically know everyone you run into as if you've been friends for years.
-It's hard to play together with your friends at times because every play mode (Solo/Co-op/MMO) has different rules about what content can and cant be done and by whom. It's definitely not a dealbreaker and you eventually figure it out through trial and error, but this could be improved upon, IMO
-The updates are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ huge and often. Limited data gamers, this isnt your game.
-The gacha draws are expensive and it's rare to ever get anything actually cool. There's a system that guarantees a top tier draw after so many pulls, but it resets the counter if you get anything better than blue-grade (meaning mid-grade purple draws reset your guaranteed counter, which strikes me as false advertisement..)

Overall score: 8.5/10

It certainly helps that exploration is actually really very rewarding, there are tons of secrets to find and beautiful views to pose in front of for that perfect screenshot. The combat is engaging, challenging, and just pure fun. It's also easy to pick up for those that don't enjoy being challenged at every turn. The story isn't anything super special, but I did actually greatly enjoy most of it. There were even parts of it that had me on the edge of my seat. The best part is the game really does a good job of making you feel like you're actually part of the story, which at times can be pretty exciting if you let yourself get sucked in. All in all, I simply love almost everything about this game and would definitely recommend it to just about anyone who enjoys a good game.

This game starts off amazingly and then rapidly runs off a cliff. 

The character progression begins smoothly and then hits a completely invisible wall around 60 where if you keep pressing "level-up" the enemies become incredibly deadly. You have to work on many other aspects of character progression if you want to keep progressing and just *guess* when you can level up again. I assume this is where the original endgame was? For new players this is just a hard, totally random wall.

The game has a bunch of fun weapons but you can only pick two. The amount of resources you have to put into weapons is incredibly high. If you want to switch and experiment with new weapons, it takes weeks of boring farming per new weapon.

The appearance customization is basic. There are no options for customizing separate pants, shirts, coats, etc. like you'd see in AC: Odyssey, Guild Wars, even 20-year-old WoW. While there are slots for boots, there are only a total of three boots in the entire game.

"But the story!" people cry. The story is the biggest disappointment. It starts off really well in the first area - a classic Wuxia tale of a missing master, hidden identities and an attack on your home. But then the second area has a totally incomprehensible story that is completely disconnected from everything in the first zone! For some reason you end up helping rat children steal coins - or return coins? - but only some coins, not all coins, because the government - or not really the government? or only some parts of the government - is taking the coins to make weapons, or pay their soldiers, maybe. Meanwhile you have classic videogame moments (tm) of beating up 100 soldiers only to be captured by the next two identical ones, etc. Ugh, what a letdown.

Like the cliche saying goes, it does get better after around 3 hours. This review was made through the perspective of a solo player who doesn't PvP or co-op.

-The opening is very weak compared to when the game fully opens up. It can 100% cause you to leave the game, and I won't blame you. When it does open up, the fun I feel in regards to exploring the world is like a mix between Far Cry, Ghost of Tsushima, and Genshin Impact.

-Localization has been improved compared to 2 months ago, but it still could be better. Voice-acting is decent enough. Story is serviceable so far, some good moments here and there, nothing that I can say I dislike/hate (yet).

-Solo players like me can find tons of fun in combat and exploration, and most of the content can be enjoyed without needing to interact with other players. Even some of the online activities don't really need you to interact with others.

-Min-maxing is entirely optional and is aimed towards co-op boss raiders/PvP players. You can enjoy the game without thinking about gear too much, but with each "breakthrough" (increasing the level cap), you need to at least gain equipment that is in your level, which is very easy to do through solo boss battles.

In short, you'll have fun if you ever wished Assassin's Creed 2 had a wuxia cousin. Enjoy!

This is just a genuinely good game, free-to-play or not. The kind that respects your time so well that spending money on it feels less like a transaction and more like supporting good design.

The game clearly assumes players have a life. Progress feels meaningful without demanding endless grinding or daily obligation. You’re not pressured to play, yet the story and combat are engaging enough that you want to log in more. That pull comes from solid writing, satisfying gameplay, and good pacing, not artificial timers or FOMO.

What’s especially refreshing is how monetization stays out of the way of “winning.” Most purchases are cosmetic, and the few things that could be labeled P2W are really just quality-of-life touches. Mounts that auto-collect loot, gather herbs within a range, point you toward nearby treasure, or minor conveniences like extra potion slots for PvE only, --none of these give real competitive advantages, especially not in PvP. They save time, not skill checks.

It’s rare to see a game--free or paid--that balances respect for the player with enough depth to keep you engaged. This one manages both.

The only notable weak point is localization, which could use improvement. Switching the voice language to Chinese with English subtitles mostly fixes it, but it’s still something that could be polished further.

Overall, this isn’t “good for a free game.” It’s a good game, full stop.

Why It’s Worth Your Time:
Atmosphere: The world is drenched in mood. Whether you are walking through a rain-slicked village or standing atop a mountain peak, the visual storytelling is top-tier. It captures that specific "Wuxia" feeling of being a lone wanderer in a vast, beautiful, and dangerous land.

Insane Depth: The "sandbox" label actually means something here. You can focus on mastering intricate martial arts, or you can pivot into being a doctor or a merchant. The sheer number of systems—from building structures to healing NPCs—is staggering.

True Asian Style: The game avoids the "generic fantasy" trap. Everything from the architecture to the flow of combat feels culturally authentic. The movement is like poetry; sprinting across water and wall-running feels fluid and impactful.

Unique Identity: It manages to feel different from the "Souls-likes" or standard RPGs. It’s a simulation of a martial arts life, giving you the freedom to engage with the world on your own terms.

Where Winds Meet – Great atmosphere, but frustrating systems

Where Winds Meet has an amazing presentation. The graphics are beautiful, the world feels alive, and exploring the environment is genuinely fun. Wandering through the landscapes and discovering new areas is easily the strongest part of the game.

Unfortunately, several major issues drag the experience down hard.

The public chat is extremely toxic and feels like it's full of little children; there's also constant guild spam. This is especially frustrating because there is a dedicated guild recruitment channel. Even worse, the block and report functions don’t work, which makes dealing with toxic behavior almost impossible.

Another big problem is the lack of meaningful endgame content. I play for 5 minutes a day. Progression becomes painfully slow because gear crafting is entirely RNG-based. Getting the equipment you want can take literal years unless you’re insanely lucky, which feels more frustrating than rewarding.

In short:
✔ Beautiful graphics
✔ Fun exploration and world design
✘ Toxic public chat and broken moderation
✘ No real endgame
✘ Extremely grindy, RNG-heavy gear progression

Where Winds Meet has a lot of potential, but right now it feels like a gorgeous world held back by poor systems and community management. With proper fixes, this could be great — but in its current state, it’s hard to recommend.

Where Winds Meet – a quick review

+ Positives

Free to Play & no Pay-to-Win (most microtransactions are cosmetic)
Large, open world with visually appealing locations (matters of taste)
Varied quests (puzzles, exploration, action)
Story is interesting but can feel a bit sustained
Good introduction to gameplay; controls work well with mouse & keyboard or controller but it's habitual


- Negatives

Menus can feel overwhelming at first
Multiplayer/Co-Op is limited (main story is mostly solo; co-op feels like a side feature)
Gametrailer. Wish, they would've show more gameplay footage (2nd gametrailer is better)


~ Conclusion

A strong Free-to-Play action RPG for solo players and explorers. Good amount of content, fair monetization but not a full MMO or co-op experience.

A review definitely needs to be given here.

The game's fantastic. Beyond what I expected.

It's an Open-World RPG. You explore, quest, play and fight in ancient China. It's as intense, or casual, as you want from it.

I've played many games with Appearance Customisation, and this one's easily the strongest for Facial Features.

You can play a plethora of minigames, Solo with NPCs, Co-Op with Friends, or Matchmade Online.

The Dungeons and their puzzles are really fun and diverse. Some involve water flood levels, some involve stealth, shooting multiple targets, at once, in specific angles...

Photography's very fun, you can take time out of your day to just make in-game Photos, adjusting Zoom, Contrast, Bloom, Wind-Direction, Time of the Day, adding Poses...

Everything that's 'Casual' feeds into your progress, and isn't a waste of time. Whether it's rewards from Photography, or your Character's Stats from the Minigames you play: Archery, Wrestling, Cards, Mahjong...

There's absolutely zero pay-to-win. Only optional cosmetics.

The tone of the game's extremely dynamic, you've got light-hearted silly humour throughout, contrasted against very dark and serious topics.

Gear doesn't just become obsolete. When you get higher levelled gear, as you naturally progress, that old gear can be stored in your arsenal, which still contributes to your overall power.

A huge game-changer for people on the fence about playing with others is you're never forced to play the endgame with random people. The game has a next-generation, progressive approach to AI, and integrates it into the gameplay almost without fault or issue. Smart Assist allows you to tackle both World Bosses and 10-Player Raids with Bot Assistance. They'll do the Mechanics, DPS and Healing with you, without the tantrums or nasty PMs you would typically come across. 

The AI is also present when chatting to certain NPCs. It's natural, and very much grounded in the game world. They know their names, the region they're in, and what they're doing. Talking to the AI's fun, and you're given weekly rewards for befriending them. There are also minigames with the AI, such as Riddles, where you must guess the subject in a given topic. Sometimes it's very easy, sometimes incredibly tricky. It's fun, and once again, you also get rewards.

You can have relationships with other players, in-game, and I've been playing this with my real-life partner, daily. Master-Student, or Intimacy, are all available, and yield their respective rewards.

Finally, the game's optimised extremely well.

This game's a whole big leap into the future of gaming, and entertainment, and everything about it has been a pleasure to experience.

Where Winds Meet is one of the most ambitious Wuxia action RPGs of recent years and delivers exactly what this genre needs: a huge, vibrant open world, a fast skill-based combat system, and an atmosphere that takes Chinese martial arts fantasy quite seriously and consistently pursues it.


Map/World:
The game world is its biggest strength. Exploring it is consistently enjoyable, not just because of its size but also because of its intricate details. There's something to discover almost everywhere: side quests, secrets, and optional activities. You practically never get the feeling that even a side quest is pointless, because it seems like everything is geared towards other NPCs or quests that also offer rewards. You can enjoy the game in solo mode, in co-op or team mode with friends, and online.

The sheer number of quests and other tasks seems endless. Of course, there's a main storyline, but countless other quests are waiting to be discovered, whether by completing various tasks or by manipulating time to trigger new encounters and quests. The activities and gameplay systems are extensive. The boss fights are particularly well-designed. Yes, the whole thing is quite complex, but it offers depth rather than superficiality. 


Combat:
The combat system is surprisingly challenging and clearly designed to require skill. Parrying, countering, positioning, and timing are crucial. The combat controls are somewhat comparable to "Souls like games” even though Where Winds Meet maintains its own unique identity. Battles feel dynamic, fluid, and satisfying. 


Menu:
Menus are very complex and translations aren't perfect, but they're functional and clearly trending towards improvement. Most importantly, though: none of this ruins the gameplay experience. These are minor issues, not fundamental problems.


Pay to win:
There's no pay-to-win requirement; progress depends on playing, not spending money. For a free-to-play open-world RPG, this is a strong signal and one of the reasons why the game is taken seriously by many players. Even if you're willing to spend money, you don't get any advantages, only cosmetic items for characters, mounts, etc.


Update´s:
Each major update brings new game content, tasks, and features that continue to provide plenty of entertainment. 

Conclusion:
Current game rating: 9/10
Fun and gameplay experience: 10/10

Cons: Post-story content is a FOMO-driven treadmill. The transition to a "daily chore" system is jarring, and the gacha rates for premium items are some of the worst in the genre.

Recommendation: Enjoy the story for what it is, but don't get invested in the endgame. Treat it like a single-player game, finish the narrative, and move on to your back-log before the "daily grind" habit sets in.

TL;DR: Looks dope, plays like a cash grab

Review:
I wanted to like this game. The world is gorgeous, some fights are flashy, and the story has okay writing. But honestly? Underneath all the shininess, it’s just a glorified grindy cash trap.

Story mode fights? Can’t lose. Legend mode? You either memorize attack patterns perfectly or grind forever. No skill, no fun, just repetition. PvP is broken. You can get stuck in attack chains that you can’t dodge or counter.

Triple jumps, mid-air dashes? Fun until you enter any area that actually matters. Then the game slaps invisible walls and limits your mobility.

Weapons all look the same by default. Want something cool? Pay or grind forever. Rewards don’t feel earned.

Semi-cutscenes are stiff and weird. Often your main character is swapped or disguised, which is clever for rendering, but it kills immersion.

The game constantly overloads you with events, limited-time rewards, and FOMO pushes. It’s exhausting, overstimulating, and constantly trying to make you spend or grind.

Looks pretty but it’s hollow, grindy, and monetized to the point where fun takes a back seat. Fun concept buried under bad execution. Thumbs down.

I really wanted to like this game. And at over 250 hours played, I feel like I gave it a pretty good try.

The graphics are very pretty, if thats your thing. The problem is that everything else is kinda crap, and it gets worse the more you dig beneath the surface.

The much-vaunted combat system is basically an excuse to watch the pretty combat sequences the devs want you to watch. It is entirely bult around putting yourself in harms way, standing stupidly where the enemy is going to hit with its ridiculously telegraphed attack sequence, and then hitting the appropriate "dodge" or "block" button when the devs want you to. Any other approach to combat is at best incredibly time consuming and inefficient. 

The writing sometimes reaches the heights of sophistication seen in a Naruto filler episode.

The support and technical optimization are everything that should be expected from a NetEase property.

All of this I was wiling to look past for the sake of finding something fun hidden in the wreckage.

Unfortunately, the recurring "emotional motivation" wielded by the writers is the torture and slaughter of children.

After the 5th drawn out, gratuitous torture of a kid, I had enough. 

I suppose if you never read the game text, and just want to see flashy lights as you mindlessly pound the food pellet button, this game may be for you. But be prepared to be sneered at by a lot of cringy cartoony villains... and then do absolutely nothing about it.

Honestly way much more than you would expect for a free to play title. The character customization is deep, the combat is fluid and reminiscent of Soulslike games, and the story is enthralling. A must play if you are also into Chinese inspired aesthetics.

This is a beautiful open world 10th century China themed game designed with just about every single type of gamer in mind.  I personally am mostly a PVE player because a lot of the PVP games I've played have had very toxically competitive communities, but the community in this game has been so welcoming and all they're looking for is to enjoy the fun side of competition.

Esse é um jogo incrível. Melhor que vários jogos por ai. Como single player ele não deixa nada a desejar, é um excelente hack and slash, com combos muito fodas e combinações maneiras de builds. O mundo é realmente vivo e tem muita coisa acontecendo, você sempre é surpreendido. Os NPCs tem um sistema de IA que permite conversas interativas em tempo real. Tem muitos colecionaveis, puzzles, eventos dinâmicos, bosses de mundo aberto, montarias, sistema de voo e várias outras coisas. É um mundo aberto muito mais completo que os jogos pagos por ai. Até hoje só vi essa qualidade em jogos AAA da franquia Dark and Souls.
Ele supera os hack and slashs comuns pq também te dá liberdade no sentido de escolhas e ações no mundo aberto, como um GTA ou Skyrim. Você pode ser um vilão, atacar NPCs, roubar estranhos (como roubar o cavalo de um andarilho ou as moedas de um comerciante), barganhar, discutir com alguem (o jogo tem um IA para isso), ser amigo ou inimigo de uma pessoa ou grupo, entrar em guildas, se tornar médico e várias outras coisas. Essa liberdade é fundamental para um RPG se tornar mais divertido, é isso que um bom RPG deve ser, não só progredir niveis.

OBS.: Mesmo que você vá jogar sozinho, ative o modo multiplayer no seu mundo solo, para ver as dicas que a comunidade deixa pelo caminho. Fica muito divertido.

Ainda não testei o multplayer, mas aparentemente aqui também teremos elementos de MMO.

A monetização fica por conta da loja, que é bem maneira e as skins valem a pena, são realmente bonitas.

The game itself is genuinely good. The core gameplay, systems, and community features are solid, and I would otherwise recommend it.

Unfortunately, the moderation and customer support experience severely undermines that quality.

I received a 30-day chat ban for an alleged first-time offense. I reviewed my chat history and could not identify any clear rule violation. When I appealed, I received no meaningful explanation of what rule was broken, only automated denials in-game and a vague email response stating my case was “in follow-up actions.”

As of writing this, I have been banned for multiple days with no human review, no clarification, and no estimated timeline. The review delay itself has already exceeded what many first-time chat penalties normally last, which makes the process feel punitive even before a decision is made.

The in-game appeal system appears to be fully automated and instantly denies submissions without review. This leaves email support as the only option, but responses are slow, non-specific, and provide no actionable feedback. There is no transparency, no accountability, and no way to understand or correct alleged behavior.

This system also seems vulnerable to abuse through mass reporting, especially for players with visible online or in-game presence. Without timely human moderation, report volume appears to matter more than verified context.

To be clear: this is not a complaint about being moderated. Rules are necessary. This is a complaint about a lack of meaningful review, unclear enforcement, and extremely slow support responses for severe penalties.

The game deserves better support systems than this. Until moderation and appeals are handled with clearer communication and faster human review, I cannot recommend it.

So I jumped into Where Winds Meet and came away mostly impressed but definitely mixed, especially for a free-to-play RPG. It’s got this beautiful, sprawling wuxia open world full of ancient Chinese landscapes, lore, and exploration that really feels alive — whether you’re roaming bustling cities, uncovering hidden temples, or just wandering riversides with the wind in your hair.

Here’s what stood out for me:
🔥 Combat and movement are addictively fun. The martial arts-inspired fighting feels like you’re actually wielding skill, with dodges, parries, and weapon combos that keep fights engaging instead of button-mashing.
🔥 Open world exploration really shines. You can climb, glide, and explore lots of varied regions — and there’s always something cool waiting around the next hill or hidden in a cave.
🔥 Free-to-play without heavy pay-to-win pressure. Most of the monetization leans cosmetic or seasonal — so you can put in serious time without feeling nickel-and-dimed (even though menus and systems are a bit overwhelming at first).
🔥 Co-op and multiplayer add replay value. You can team up with friends or jump into shared world activities once you’ve made some progress, which keeps it feeling social and dynamic.

What dragged it down a bit:
⚠️ Story and pacing aren’t always great. While there are interesting moments, many quests and cutscenes can feel cliché or slow, and the narrative doesn’t always hit emotionally.
⚠️ UI and menus feel clunky and confusing. There’s so much going on that it takes time to get comfortable navigating everything, and new players might feel overwhelmed.
⚠️ Technical rough edges show up now and then. Things like localization issues, stiff animations, and occasional performance hiccups remind you it’s ambitious but not polished like big-budget single-player RPGs.
⚠️ Combat and progression can be time-sinky. Some players (and I sorta felt this too) will end up spending tons of hours grinding quests, puzzles, and exploration — which is fun, but occasionally feels like work.

Overall vibe:
Where Winds Meet feels like a huge, ambitious adventure — the kind of game that pulls you into its world and keeps you coming back, even if some parts are rough around the edges. If you love open-world exploration, wuxia combat, and deep RPG systems, this is easily one of the most unique experiences you can play right now — especially for free.

It’s not perfect, but when the combat clicks and you’re roaming that beautifully crafted world? It’s seriously satisfying.

Would I recommend it?
Yes — especially if you enjoy deep RPGs with lots to explore. Just be ready to spend time learning the systems and forgiving a few rough parts along the way.

[h1]Where Winds Meet, soft, quiet, kind of addictive... [/h1]

Honestly, I didn’t expect this game to hook me, but it surprised me.

Where Winds Meet is one of those games where you get so many storylines that, at some point, you might stop caring too much about the main story. That said, there are moments where it pulls you back in, mainly because of the cinematics. They are really well done and kind of hypnotic.
The world boss stories also deserve a mention. Being honest, some of them genuinely caught my attention when following their quests from start to finish. The ones that impressed me the most were The Void King and Lucky Seventeen.

Combat isn’t anything completely out of the ordinary, except for the parry system, which feels a bit more interesting in this kind of game, at least from my point of view. If you have never played a game with this mechanic before, it is basically about blocking an attack at the exact right moment to completely avoid the damage. If you miss it, you take full damage. If you play it safe and just block, you will receive reduced damage instead.
The idea, though, is to land the parry, especially when you are low on healing, because it can literally save you. If you are not used to parrying, it can feel very hard at first. I struggled a lot too. But with time, you get used to it, since before each attack there is a small visual shine that helps you time it.

[b]Note[/b]:
If it feels too difficult, the game has an option you can enable to show you the exact moment you need to press the parry button. This only works in single-player mode. It is disabled in multiplayer.

As for weapons, the game offers a good variety that can match different playstyles. In the Global version, not the Chinese one, there are 12 weapons you can try until you find what fits you best. You have classic melee swords, dual blades, spears, and also more unusual options like umbrellas and fans for ranged damage.
Each weapon has its own martial art, meaning different abilities. Everything depends on what you want to focus on, whether it is dealing damage, tanking bosses, or healing.

[b]Recommendation[/b]:
If you are like me and enjoy playing as support or healer, first of all, great taste. Secondly, sadly, in single-player mode you should probably forget about going full support. Otherwise, bosses and enemies will take forever to kill. My advice is to carry one weapon for damage, whatever you like most, and another for healing. That way, even if your damage is not very high, your healing will still be solid.
Personally, I use the support healer umbrella because it has an ability that boosts your damage and heals you instantly. For damage, I use the fan. It attacks very fast and has a wall ability that increases your damage when you attack from behind it. That is my recommendation. ♥

About the world and atmosphere of Where Winds Meet, honestly, the only thing I can say is that it is BEAUTIFUL. The landscapes make you want to turn off the HUD and just walk around. Villages are detailed, the structures look amazing, and each boss area has its own distinct environment. It is the kind of game where you will want to take screenshots in almost every corner of the map.

To finish, let’s talk about multiplayer content. If you enjoy playing with others, there are dungeons and raids for groups of up to 5 players, and larger group activities with up to 10 players. You can complete missions in co-op, join another player’s world to help with a boss, or simply keep them company.
There are also small activities you can do together, like Meridian card games, playing musical notes, or even sumo-style fights. And if you are into PvP, you can aim to reach Mythic rank and try to become Top 1 on the leaderboard. (Hi Averse)

[h3]Note:[/h3]
The Chinese version currently has more weapons than the Global version, six more to be exact. However, the Global version is slowly catching up, and those missing weapons are expected to be added over time. For now, we just have to wait.

Where Winds Meet is one of those rare games that quietly pulls you in… and then suddenly you realize you’re completely hooked.

From the very first hours, the gameplay feels incredibly satisfying—whether you’re playing on keyboard and mouse or on a controller, the controls are smooth, responsive, and intuitive. Every movement, every strike, every dodge feels deliberate and polished. The visuals are simply stunning, creating a world that feels alive, atmospheric, and worth getting lost in for hours.

Combat is where the game truly shines. It’s extremely well balanced, and the way mystic skills and martial arts blend into your playstyle adds a layer of depth that constantly keeps things fresh. You’re not just mashing buttons—you’re shaping a fighting style that feels uniquely your own, which really helps immerse you in the world.

Character customization is another standout. The amount of detail and freedom you’re given lets you create a character that actually feels personal, not just another generic hero. And when you step into multiplayer, the experience only gets better. The player base is genuinely amazing—there are so many people willing to help, guide, and team up, which makes the world feel welcoming rather than intimidating.

The sect system adds even more enjoyment, giving you goals to work toward and communities to belong to within the game itself. Every new layer you uncover just makes you want to keep playing.

I could honestly go on and on.

And here’s the biggest compliment I can give: I typically do not like RPG-style games. At all.

But Where Winds Meet has me completely HOOKED.

This is truly a game worth playing.

The story is actually nice, though I noticed a lot of NPCs are reused in different clothes to make "new" characters. Game looks really "pretty," and I have zero complaints about the graphics; but it's definitely taking inspiration from the "Ghost of..." series. 

Great performance on 11700KF and 3080 combo, 32GB RAM, 1440p, everything set to ultra. 80-100+ fps.

Combat can be challenging if these games aren't your go-to (like me) or if you refuse to play on "story/recc" mode, but it's also rewarding in the sense of accomplishment. At first it seems like enemies/bosses have the same attack patterns post death, but I've come to notice at least 2 more attack patterns for enemies that can randomly occur, making combat more about paying attention in the now, then "what'd we learn last time," and I 100% love/hate that.

Surprisingly good game for the low low cost of free.99, but do keep in mind that the vast majority of cosmetics are locked behind paywalls; even things like hair color. 

Character creation is a wet-dream, I don't think I've seen that many options on a creation start without using mods. Think Fallout 4 creation but on steroids. Even allowing people to use images that AI then creates a character from. Kinda cool actually. 

Overall I actually think it's worth the time to get into, it's no where near a "bad game," It 100% caught me off guard with how good it is so far.

BIGGEST ISSUES/CONS:

Again that paywall stuff makes me sick. I won't give into it - but damn are the cosmetics actually kinda cool. KINDA.

Very limited combat controls that 100% need to be remapped. Who in the right mind makes any kind of attacks: ~, q, tab, and 1?? I'm lucky lucky I have an MMO mouse.

YOU CANNOT PROGRESS THE MAIN STORY IN CO-OP. So be prepared for insane level gaps if buddies had it before you, and enemies level to the co-op hosts level. 

BUGS, from having to restart quests, to having to restart my PC. This game doesn't like Discord being opened, and used if the game is already started, so fair warning.

Solid 8/10 game. Worth it for that free.99

I clicked Not Recommend on this game for one reason only: to make the review more noticeable. Below is my honest opinion after 500 hours of playing WWM.

1. Open World

Credit where it’s due. This is one of the most detailed and well-crafted open worlds, especially considering it’s a free game. I’ve completed 100% of both Kaifeng and Qinghe maps.

I really like how the game integrates medieval culture into the world, with small stories hidden in NPC interactions. There isn’t much to complain about overall, but most of the open-world minigames are genuinely bad and lack any real challenge.

2. Gameplay
PvE

Blatantly copied from Sekiro, and I actually like it. The combat gives you many tools to deal with bosses, the pace is fast, and there’s a wide variety of martial arts styles to use with mystic skills.

That said, 5-man and 10-man boss instances are far too easy. They don’t feel challenging at all and are designed more like daily chores. Killing the boss brings zero sense of satisfaction.

PvP

Heavily dependent on ping and extremely unbalanced. It’s a boring loop:
queue > drink wine > breathe fire > try not to get comboed for 10 seconds and lose your entire HP bar.

Sometimes it’s just endless chasing between two players, waiting to see who gets stunned first, which is honestly stupid.

At the time of writing this review, I’m at Mythic rank ~1200, and I almost never win because my ping to the Southeast Asia server is too high (150ms). Deflecting usually only works for the first hit, and that’s basically all the PvP depth the devs put in.

The current meta is Twinblade and Nameless Spear ,no surprise there. One weapon allows brain-dead combos, the other stuns and breaks stagger easily.

3. UI

Overly cluttered and poorly designed, which is typical for many Chinese games. The game constantly suggests you to claim rewards for trivial things like 1–2 Echo Jades, and you’re endlessly interrupted by reward pop-ups.

It’s a design meant to make players feel like they’re being rewarded nonstop, but in reality it’s just annoying and dumb. I completely understand why Western players hate this kind of UI design.

4. English Translation

The English translation and voice acting are genuinely rough. It’s not even acceptable, let alone good enough to convey what’s actually interesting about the game.

Some lines are translated word-for-word, others completely change the original meaning. Overall, the localization is bad and does the game no favors at all.

5. Cosmetics

The outfit selection is very diverse, sometimes even ridiculous. Aside from the intentionally funny items, many paid outfits feel over-the-top and completely out of place in a wuxia setting. That said, this is clearly a monetization tool, so I can understand why the developers do it.

This game is one of the great surprises of 2025 for me. It is really fun to play, to explore the world and the story.

The big point is exploration and quests. The game offers a lot of those, with a huge, beautiful world, with really great background music. And exploration is really rewarding, you get gear, skills, talents, materials, skins, and stats from it, so it is important if you want to be strong. I have to emphasize it: the world of the game is really beautiful and immersive. You don't even need to have knowledge about Chinese culture and mythology to feel this.

One of the big positives of the game is the monetization system. The game is not pay-to-win. You can't buy power, only skins and mounts. Some are expensive, but there are some good-looking ones that cost around 1 €. Well, yeah, there is a ship that costs 50k and you can take the server on a boat ride on it, so if you buy it, thank you for keeping the servers online.

The game has one of the most fun ways to introduce AI to a game world. There are NPCs you can befriend via a chat with an AI. It is a lot of fun, since you can gaslight them into anything. For example, I convinced one that he is Neo and the game world is the Matrix.

Now to the negatives. There are four big negative things about this game.

First, the localization. It is terrible. One of the worst in existence. For starters, the translation was made by unsupervised AI, this makes the whole game confusing. You will have trouble understanding the main story and the regional campaign, which can be especially confusing since you can play it out of order. And if you have no understanding of Chinese culture and/or mythology, it will be way worse. Thank you to the Chinese bros who make YouTube videos on the lore, helping us understand what the hell is happening. 
But the issue is not just the story. The description of skills is also badly translated, so you'll have to Google what they do. 
And the voice acting... there are some AI voices used, but they sound better than the actual voice actors, since most of the voices sound uninterested and bored. The quality is just abysmal. And the subs and the dubs are not even in sync a lot of the time.

Then the menus. The game has 123123 different systems you have to understand, each with its own menus, submenus, and sub-sub-sub menus. It is really confusing until you learn what is where, and the bad translation does not help.

The weekly caps. The game has 42424 different currencies, and each has a weekly cap. These weekly caps are extremely low; you can max them out just by playing casually by Tuesday. 
And the worst is money. While you explore and do quests, you will not notice the cap. But you need a lot more money than what you get from there. And when you run out and start doing daily activities, well, you are limited to 175k/week. Which is extremely low, especially since you have no reliable way to actually farm money from anything else. So you'll have to wait a week until you can. But without money, you can't upgrade your character, so this slows down progression extremely. 
You can get some from bosses, though. So time to farm bosses, yeah? Well, you are limited by an extremely slowly recharging energy pool on that front. You can get around three boss kills/day.

And the last one is the progression.
In this game enemies level up with you. This should be fine, but the issue is, because of this, you feel that progression is completly meaningless. You put a lot of resources and time, to level up your character, gear it up nicely, max out talents and skills, but fighting regular mobs, still feels like you are level one. All the progression feel completly meaningless with this system.

So basically: exploration fun, combat mid, endgame abysmal.
[b]10/7[/b]

The game has a lot of needless friction and poor design that ultimately leaves the experience more frustrating than satisfying.
- Atrocious UI and clunky controls.
- Deflection-based combat with terrible telegraphing and wonky timings.
- When you progress, it scales the world as well, so you often feel weaker as you progress instead of stronger.
- Most stuff isn't voice acted, and much of what is uses terrible AI voices. You can't control the speed at which dialogue progresses, so it will often hang on single words or rush past a paragraph you barely had time to start with no way to go back. At some point, I had to give up on caring about story or the world.
- Boss battles are serviceable, but the open world combat is just terrible. Trying to deflect 6 different enemies while half of them are pelting you from range is just an exercise in frustration. What makes it worse is that ranged attacks hit like a truck. If they were glass cannons, I could understand the design. But no, they're just cannons.
- Healing (both in and out of combat) uses items that you have to farm or buy, and gear loses durability every time you die. This makes learning bosses and recovering between open world encounters more draining than it ought to be.
- The game is free, but only if you consider your time worthless. There are too many good entries in the genre to spend time on a mediocre option just because it has no upfront cost.

- Plenty of F2P rewards and generous BP offers, and all purchases are purely cosmetics so not much FOMO.

Cons:
- Although its F2P, there are /slim/ rewards for BP-owners that let whales get outfits and a little gear /slightly/ quicker. Not a super big deal.
- Some quests/puzzles are a little difficult to navigate, mostly because translation issues.

After 169 hours, I’m still utterly hooked — and that says everything.
Where Winds Meet isn’t just a game, it’s a full-blown wuxia fever dream wrapped in mist, moonlight, and quiet magic. From the moment you step into its world, it sinks its claws in and refuses to let go — and honestly? I’m grateful.

You can pet cats (instant 100/10), encounter Tai Chi bears that radiate ancient balance, and deal with demon geese that feel like they crawled straight out of a cursed folktale. It’s whimsical, eerie, serene, and unhinged in the best possible way. Every corner feels alive, like the land itself is watching you — judging you — but also kind of rooting for you.

The combat and skill variety are absolutely intoxicating. There are so many epic skills to choose from that you genuinely feel like you’re carving your own legend. No two builds feel the same, and experimenting feels rewarding rather than punishing. You don’t just play a martial artist — you become one. This is pure wuxia fantasy: flowing movement, devastating precision, and moments where everything clicks and you feel untouchable (then you get smacked in the face by a goose and die).

And the atmosphere? Chef’s kiss. 🌙
It has that quiet, witchy energy — like old magic humming beneath the surface. The kind of world where spirits could be watching from the tree line and destiny feels just one bad (or brilliant) decision away.

What excites me most is that this is only the beginning. If the foundation is already this strong, I cannot wait to see what’s coming next. More stories, more skills, more secrets hidden in the wind.

If you’ve ever wanted to live your wuxia dream — not just play it — Where Winds Meet is it.
I came for the combat.
I stayed for the Wuxia magic and cats... 
And I’m not leaving anytime soon.

I want to like this game. I really do. But Where Winds Meet just isn’t that good beyond being Pretty. Like an itchy wedding dress. There, you did it, congratulations. Now take it off and burn it so you never have to do it again because even if this ends poorly you’ll never wear it again anyway. I’ve jokingly started calling it Where A.I. Meets thanks to the atrocious English “Voice Acting” and the Uncanny A.I. NPC interaction. I’ve had more cohesive conversations with someone enduring a bad crossfade. 

The combat is passable so long as you  leave it on the hardest difficulty. Otherwise any indicators regarding timings are going to ruin you because the difficulty setting seems to only affect how long your enemy winds up an attack and it is not consistent across modes or bosses meaning you are going to get hit by poor indications and confusing triggers across the board due to inconsistency. Do not use the parry assist, it’s a trap because it doesn’t work in all modes and has a limiter after a few enemy swings. You’re going to do better just panic smashing the parry button. 

I cannot freely change keybinds. If it’s a keyboard input I have to use a keyboard input. So I can’t put dodge on my middle mouse click where I like it to be without using my hardware to circumvent the limitation. Also, why is it that in a game where NPC get mad at you for running into them to the point they will attack you, you can’t consistently walk? It turns off constantly and I have to hold a button to turn it on. What?

There’s too many currencies. I need pearls to draw for lingering melodies to win Harmonic Cores to trade for Hairdye Giftboxes to color my hair. There’s Echo, Trade Currency, Jade Fish, Echo Jade, Pearls, at least six special trade in items from the draw shop and a couple others I can’t be bothered to remember.

Menus. Holy Menus Batman I can’t find anything in here. When I’m not being pestered by the “Claim” icon for something 5 menus deep in a direction I thought was correct and isn’t, I just can’t find anything at all. I’ve been less lost in a stranger’s house after a night terror. There’s lore in here somewhere, but I’ll need divine intervention to find it and what I did find is apparently interactive because apparently figuring out this game’s trope-laden, painfully predictable, shallow excuse for a Main story. I was going to call it a Plot, but Clip Clop has more lore than your PC’s whole family. Also, why does Clip Clop Suck? You put all that woomph behind a horse and don’t even give it the ability to swim? Excuse me? RIP Clip Clop, you can live in my inventory I guess.

I can’t locate that one menu about increasing my constitution through wrestling so I can more easily tame useless horses any more than I can navigate my quest menu to figure out why/how I have a quest for a weapon I can’t get because it’s in the next zone and locked behind another quest. Also, why didn’t my character say something? I have skills for weapons I don’t own, I have quests to upgrade skills for weapons I can’t get and I have quests that require a weapon I don’t have to complete. Cool.

Upgrade system is a redundant redundancy of redundant upgrades of stacking systems. You have overall gear upgrades, weapon type upgrades, you have to eventually ‘tune’ your gear piece by piece, a skill upgrade system and a bunch of unlocks and level systems for every other stat from horse-taming to swimming and fall damage. Which are tied to your Elegance rating, because dressing nice is key to taming horses you won’t use because you can fly and Spirited Courser is the only one you’re ever gonna need because AoE flower picking is OP. 

I threw some money at the game to make myself more comfortable and I don’t regret it. I played the game for 30+ hours, no AFK, just exploring, doing quests, fighting. Tried the Co-Op and found it lacking because I think the disparity between my strength and the strength of my friends was killing them (It’s 2026 you can do better than that with level sync systems). The characters have no personality. Just opinions and tropes and “oooh mysterious” vibes that would only keep you guessing if you’d never read a single good book in your life. The only people worth your time in this game are apparently you Uncle and Ruby because one you spend time with and the other is just a kid. 

The whole game is incredibly shallow and very pretty, with lots of minigame modes, fighting and not much else. If you like that sort of thing, cool. This is the game for you, no judgement from me. I play Monster Hunter and Ranch of Rivershine. But right now? I’m gonna get my money’s worth out of this game, shrug, say I did it and give it a pass.

4.something/5, highly recommended for fans of: ARPG (could be "souls-like"), gorgeous worlds, character progression, in depth and varied combat, difficult and fun boss fights, Sekiro-style deflect system, build customization, distinct weapons/movesets, open world exploration, Solo/Coop experience (also PvP), Wuxia, constant rewards. EDIT: 1/26/26 WE HAVE MULTIPLE CHARACTERS NOW!

Incredible free to play game

BOSSES/COMBAT:
I have enjoyed some of these boss fights as much or more than FromSoft bosses, Lies of P, and other similar titles. I haven't found a boss yet that has obscenely varied/delayed or cocaine-required deflect windows. Really awesome to experience gameplay like this for free. I downloaded Sekiro again because I'm enjoying these deflects so much, but haven't actually gone back to play more because I'm getting my fill here.
Legend difficulty makes every encounter something to pay attention to, and the boss fights are very enjoyable to "git gud" at.
I have only played on legend because I'm a masochist and enjoy tough fights over feeling like I am a god amongst mortals, but even that has been very enjoyable. I'd assume the lower difficulties allow most people to enjoy this content, which is AMAZING, considering there is a beautiful Wuxia world to explore as well.

EDIT: I literally just ran into the worst varied and delayed timing boss who also requires cracked out reaction after writing this... aaaand I learned more about the game mechanics, figured out I was severely underleveled, upgraded a bit and applied my new understanding, on to more bullsh.... *ohhhh okay, I get it* moments.

WORLD DESIGN/VISUALS:
Awesome, stunning, and a joy to explore.
The visuals are beautiful *chefs kiss*, and there are plenty of opportunities for amazing photos if that's your thing. It's not mine, and I've found myself using the photo function anyway. There are plenty of secrets to find throughout the already gorgeous world. It's a joy to explore this world from the start, and it only gets quicker and gives access to more viewpoints and ways to explore as you continue your journey.

CHARACTER DESIGN:
 EDIT: 1/26/26 WE HAVE MULTIPLE CHARACTERS NOW!
Wow. I am a hideous monster, but I love it. I'm sure you could create your ultimate waifu or chad equivalent, but I can't stop making ridiculous creatures.
My only gripe with the character design as of now is that you only get one character per account. Apparently the Chinese version (about 1 year ahead) has multiples characters which will be great, but pick your name wisely or you will be stuck with it unless you want to spend some real $ (I think it's about $5 USD for a name change).

F2P:
I haven't run into any timelocks, or premium only content and have been enjoying at least a couple hours a day over the past couple weeks. This is the style of free to play content I fully enjoy. There is a free battlepass, as well as options to pay (upto I believe $15 USD/month) for additional rewards. I haven't paid any attention to what I have been missing from not having the premium, and have not felt like I need to pay to get anything.
GACHA:
This game has a gacha system for appearances, cosmetics, boats, and idk what else, but it's there. If you're prone to gambling addiction and can't stay away from inappropriate spending, maybe steer clear of this one. That said, the cosmetics available in game are still cool, and you get some free "rolls" of the gacha system just from playing.

PUZZLES:
Most of the puzzles are fairly simple so far, but a couple have made me think about what I'm doing. The signpost system can be a great aid if you just want the solution (built in translation feature allows worldwide communication which is lovely).

MENUS:
There are too many "hidden" menus. Once you start clicking through everything that's flashing you'll eventually end up with a ton of free stuff, but finding it can be a bit difficult at times, and finding that same menu again can be tough.

OVERALL:
Sick game, beautiful visuals, fun combat. Definitely give it a try if you enjoy a selection of the tags at the top, and avoid if you can't stop spending your money for cool waifu skins. Unless you are truly a gacha addict, I can't see any reason to not give this game a try.

It is a cool game, nice visuals and fun mechanics, and really good in terms of a free to play game. However given the complexity of it, it has a steep learning curve, and there is a lot of information you need to gather even before you start the game. 
For one: you have to choose certain settings when you create your character and there is little to no information about what they do or what they mean. 
You would, more than likely think "that is ok, I'll fix it later, or try it with a different character". 
If you want to play a different characte, or you do not like the one you made, tough luck, you are stuck with the one you made unless you make another account or go through a convoluted process that may or may not delete the character so you can start another one when you have learned more about it.

I have no problem with difficult games. 
I have no problem with steep learning curves
I have no problem with insuficiant information when you create your character
I have no problem with loads of different options
I have no problem with a game that uses a third party account system
I have no problem with transactions as they have in this game

I do have an issue with a game that demands in depth research on character generation before you even start the game, because you will more than likley not be able to delete the character and start over when you understand more.
I do have an issue with a game that does not inform you at the start of character generation that you are only allowed one character per account.
I do have an issue with a game where you are not informed that deleting that one character is a convoluted process involving customer support and another account system then that of Steam.
I do have an issue with a game that demands you use a third party account to unbind your game account so that you can, possibly, delete your character, a third party account that has not much of any information on how to link your game to it and neither does the game itself, yet it locks your Steam account to it.

In short, until they make it

1. easier to delete a character 
or 
2. add more character slots 
or 
3. Inform the potential player implicitly that you will not be allowed more than one character, and they add extensive information about the choices you make during character generation

I cannot in good conscience recommend this game, which is sad, for the game does look nice, and is fun to play once you start to understand it, but you will have to continue with that 1st character, and the choices you made before you even started play, even if that charcter does not fit your play style, or that your character ended up being something far different than what you thought it would be.

So thumbs down from me

/Edit
One more thing. 
Tried co-op with a friend after the above review. 
This game is not a co-op game, it is a "bring a friend to make it easy for YOU", and your friend will not get quest progress when assissting you, more or less all of the progression your friend helps you with is canceled the moment s/he leaves your realm to enter their own. 
They should have dropped the whole co-op thing altogether rather than making a half-ar*** and annoying feature like what they call co-op. 

Short and sweet about co-op: It is not, and it is so close to false advertisement as you can possibly get, without it being a false advertisement, to call it co-op. With that in mind, I dread what what they call MMO entails.
I've unistalled it now, will never return.

TL:DR Summary: Menus are more Menus making it annoying, Connection in Multiplayer is playing CS with McDonald's Internet, Combat is that of a Temu Sekiro, and the Gacha System is only for whales, so no cool anime looks for you!!! Stamina system is so bad I rather be swallowing Legos.
---
The cons of Where Winds Meet or WWM (going to use the abbreviation for the rest of the review) that I'm going to talk about consist of the UI, CO-OP connection, PvP connection pretty much the whole multiplayer experience being bad, the gacha system of this game (Now I'll get into that part before getting told it is optional which I agree it is 100%) and combat.
---
Starting with the UI it is absolutely horrendous, as took me a few weeks to finally get a hang of the menu to open another menu to get to this menu to upgrade or put a skill point into the talents tree which is absolutely annoying, and is that of a mobile game which is funny because they had their big mobile release back in December. You get used to, but all the menu hopping gets old really quick and the names they put for the editing your gear as "Develop" I do not understand why they chose the word "Develop" instead of Gear, but you can get to it quickly by pressing the "H" Key.

Now, onto the connection in multiplayer, it is atrocious and it is a complaint that has been many, many, many times by players for them to fix it, yet that haven't. I convinced a few friends to get the game after I've sunk 100+ plus hours into WWM because thought it would be a fun time playing with them and it was, when we weren't having the worse connection I've ever seen. On top of it too you aren't even able to play the story at all with your friends, you can only do the dungeons. mini games, and open world with them, but not the story quests making it just an co-op grinding session. 

PvP in this game is ridiculous from the obvious latency issue and players having an obvious advantage when they live near the host of the servers. I watched a stream of the rank 1 PvPer and for the few minutes I watched and saw his opponent lagging around I just laughed and closed his stream because it is just absolutely ridiculous. Top it off too PvPers will deny the fact there is a clear latency issue and just say you need to adapt, git gud, or just D ride the game and say it is your problem you have bad internet, etc. 

PvE content like the raid bosses is just as bad always feeling like you are under da water with how your movement feels unresponsive making for it to be unfun, especially when you are doing your rotation of your abilities and not coming out the instant you press the button and taking a second instead throwing you off rotation, being a healer makes this even worse I can vouch for that.
---
Onto the Gacha System now I understand you don't have to use it, it is only cosmetics, etc. etc. I completely get it don't get me wrong, but it has a predatory practice with how insanely ridiculous the buying pearls cost to purchase the currency to pull on that banner that has the cool, kawaii, waifu clothing or husbando clothing for your character you have that you want to make them look super cute or badass whatever look you are trying to go for. The chance to get the outfits you want seem to be non-existent and from looking at streamers who are whales spending hundreds of dollars on the banners and getting nothing until the very, very end before the pity comes is always when there is only single digits before pity happens or 10-20 pulls left before pity. Only time I've seen it proven wrong when not doing 10 pulls at a time is when these streams are doing the 50 pull which makes sense because you are pulling more, meaning get more of a chance to get the Gold, Gold, Gold, but it happens rarely. Even with the 50 pulls they do, they still don't get the gold even with doing the 50 two times in a row and start doing 10 at a time to try and save money when they have the last 50 remaining. 

The pity resets once you hit a gold which makes sense from the business side as you don't want to lose money if you let the player base get the gold before the pity and then let get the pity. So you keep dumping more and more money into the banner till you get enough of that limited banner currency to buy the outfit you want. Sounds like a big complaint about nothing, but the drop rate for golds in WWM seems extremely low and leans more to the "House" winning more and more money from you till you finally get what you want.

Onto the super gacha weapons that only a select people have because they are the most ridiculous money grabbing system I have ever seen in my life. If you ever seen some WWM youtube videos of streamers spending thousands of dollars on a weapon you have the jist of what exactly they're doing and how ridiculously expensive it is to constantly reforge those weapons till you get the look and color you want for it. being cheap at first being 1 reforge stone, then 2 when you start locking the parts you want, then 5, then finally 10. The price of these stones costs pearls and you have to spend 30 dollars to enough pearls to buy a few rolls, to not even get what you want because there are so many possibilities in each category of the weapon that you could be spending 400-800 dollars getting unlucky trying to get the exact look you are going for from the available options. They have catered this system to the whales who will spend 400, 800, and 1000s of dollars making the F2Ps not able to get the sick looking cosmetics, and the statement can be made again, "It's cosmetics, you don't have to spend money and you are stupid, a clown, a troll" etc. for talking about the gacha system, but there are some people like myself who would like the super cool outfits, but don't want to have to take out a second mortgage on a house to be able to get a single cool outfit or make one of the gacha weapon skins look super cool.
---
We are onto the combat now, and oh boy this is gonna be a fun one. I think it is fun yea, but it is not good the enemies are literal sponges like any MMO game with the higher levels you go, they scale with you and just become more and more sponge like. Doing any side quests or bounties makes you fight sponges instead of having areas that are leveled based making it so you never feel like you are actually getting stronger, better gear, or improving abilities. The gear is a big issue with the drop rate being for legendary or gold gear from chests being dog water and spending days farming trying to get gold gear, because of the STAMINA system. It feels like a mobile game when you get to the end game and you log in, do 1-2 raids depending on if you use more stamina to get more rewards from the bosses then after your stamina is depleted you get to log out and wait 3 days for it to refill and redo it all over again. It makes grinding for better gear take longer than it needs to and the horrible drop rates extend it further. The real mobile game experience if I say. The boss fights are cool with having the red deflectable attacks and the gold dodge only attacks taking somewhat of a sekiro route (with sekiro only having the kanji above your head) Bosses do unrealistic delayed attacks looking at Wolf Maiden who loves to do quick flurry of attacks then decides to stop and charge up her attack like she is an anime protagonist messing up the flow of combat and the effects in combat are so flashy that it literally makes it difficult to see the attacks that are coming at you. I don't get this at all either, but when your character deflects they move to the left instead of standing in position after you deflect. It is stupid that your character moves to the side after a deflect. If you have sekiro I recommend you play this and then go back to sekiro and feel and see the difference in the responsiveness as it is night and day of a difference.

To conclude this review, just play Sekiro as it is just a better game.

Where Winds Meet is the first game I have actually really played in over 6 months or more. I have a gigantic library on Steam, and can never get the motivation to put time into most games these days. This game caught my attention with the sprawling, lush open world. I am running this game on an RTX 3080, and the graphics are still jaw dropping, and it runs surprisingly well at that. It is very easy to get immersed in this game, and lose hours without even realizing. I can barely recall the last time that I was pulled into a game the way Where Winds Meet has. Thankfully the game is playable and enjoyable, even with gacha mechanics available. Being someone who's been a fan of novels of the same genre, Where Winds Meet blew me away with its quality. As for cosmetics, we were given some free ones, and some cheap, 1$ ones. There are more expensive costumes, of course, but the game gives vouchers that grant up to 50% off the original price.

The most expensive of course, are the gacha ones. While I do not recommend grabbing these for the average player (averaging hundreds of dollars just to get one),  we get a few pulls on the regular to slowly build to pity at 150.

Overall, while not completely without gacha, I find WWM to be a game I'll stick to for a long time.

[i][From ~8 hours of play in Dec 2025]
Recommendation based on whether the game is worth the time investment for gamers with limited time.[/i]

Where Winds Meet is an [b]incredibly impressive[/b] game. It feels like a culmination of the past 20+ years of progress in game mechanics, design, and graphics. The game is visually stunning and includes nearly every imaginable game mechanic and system: MMO-style progression, open-world exploration, action RPG combat, stealth systems, climbing and traversal mechanics, skill trees, job-style roles, crafting and resource gathering, and multiple combat disciplines layered on top of one another. You can even play the entire experience in a solo story mode and skip the MMO elements altogether.

As an aside, this game has the best (fun, intuitive and extensive) character creation system I've ever used. 

However, the game is also exactly that: a [b]massive mishmash of ideas with limited cohesion[/b] between them, leaving players feeling confused and overwhelmed. The world is large but sparsely populated, with key NPCs, events, and even early tutorial content spread so far apart that they are easy to miss entirely. Interesting ideas, such as building relationships with AI-driven NPCs or gaining early access to mounts exist, but they are poorly explained or underdeveloped, making them feel more like disconnected experiments than integrated systems.

The game does a poor job of ramping players up the learning curve, and it is difficult to play without frequently searching online for basic explanations.

While Where Winds Meet could be the [i]inception of a new paradigm for large-scale MMORPGs[/i], its current lack of cohesion and polish is too jarring to recommend, consistently breaking immersion rather than reinforcing it.

-------
Additional Note
-------
While I don’t recommend the game for someone looking for a new long-term commitment, it is free and worth satisfying your curiosity for a few hours. There are genuinely interesting ideas here, and the sheer amount of different ideas stitched together makes it fascinating to explore briefly.

The game has 2 very strong points:

1. Graphics are very good, not your typical UE5 garbage. Everything is crystal clear and well-optimized. Overall, the game is beautifully made, the art direction is top tier.

2. Single player Bosses. There are 24 of them ATM, they are very diverse and memorable. The gameplay is heavily parry-focused. If you dislike gear grinding component of the game, you can fight them in trials which normalizes your stats so you don't have to worry about RNG, but you have to kill them at least once in solo mode before that.

BUT, there are many problems there, like broken animations, weird hitboxes, some bosses having strange behaviour (I got hit by a bird the moment I finished execution animation on 2nd phase Murong Yang).
And people still very much want to play and even do no-hit Abyss trials (me included) despite all those problems because these fights provide challenge, allow multiple approaches and are a fun experience.

Every other activity, at least for me, is below average and is just there to waste time. Side story content is really boring and repetitive, Raid mode bosses are slowed down, have inflated HP and party wipe mechanics, also your gear matters there. PvP content has the same problem, there are people alrealy with Tier6 Sword Morph (400 legendary tips) that you have 0 chance of winning against until you grind tf out this mobile-like energy system which everybody dislikes.

I am currently playing this game with friends, and will likely continue to do so as long as they like playing it, but..
as much as I like the setting and as pretty as it is, as someone who is a rather infrequent player of MMOs, I already found a lot of things to hate about Where Winds Meet.

1. Having exclusive costumes that you can't just outright buy or win in game. I'm a completionist at heart, but I imagine like many people... when it becomes impossible to collect everything, I don't want to bother at all. I'd rather delete the game and just not play. If WWM expects me to fork over $500+ every month just get every special looking outfit, they are delusional. Since there's that lack of attainability, I feel like it's all or nothing. Either I have the option to attain them at some future date, or I won't spend a single dime on any of it. That whole fear of missing out vibe is a joy sucker and I'm not a sucker.

2. Making it impossible to redo certain quests that other players exploit indefinitely for farming gear. This sort of stuff makes playing organically feel completely frustrating and pointless. If I have to research every story line and have the plot spoiled for me just to remain competitive, this isn't a game anymore. "Beauty in the Shade" is apparently closed forever if you get too close to the NPC that ends the objective. Other players have learned how to farm this place indefinitely by avoiding completion, but if you're not reading player guides to know this cheat, you end up locked out forever. That becomes a deep disadvantage for anyone who wants to play normally.

3. Due to the one above, this creates another irritating factor. The inability to create a new character and transfer purchased items to the new character in order to remedy the inequality of the missed exploits and opportunities. I also find it supremely irritating that they try to make it okay by saying you can completely start a new account by unlinking this one, but you can't transfer all the purchases you made, which means that you should just NEVER BUY ANYTHING on an account if you are intending to play organically, because starting over is destructive.

4. Trying to claim that these won't affect your gameplay experience... A fat lie. That is like saying they don't care about your gameplay experience. It's such a DOWNER. If you want to feel like you're late to a party, all the food is gone, your friends have left, while you're just there to stand by yourself and watch other people have a good time, then this game is for you. It's specifically designed to make you feel like you're wasting your time.

As such, though I would have wanted to love this game, it has become a game I hate more than like. The only reason to continue is on the premise and optimism that they will remedy the inequalities that make it completely biased towards people who know everything ahead of time.

Before going into the game, I knew about Wuxia, the tropes, the style, the aesthetic. Sometimes overdone, I hoped this game, with its monetization model, generally positive ratings, and a certain confidence in its presentation, would be a good modern adaptation of the genre.

Unfortunately, it turned out to be exactly that - a 'Modern adaptation', in the worst way possible, ruining every aspect of the experience in a way only modern corporations can.

The over-the-top introduction, overdramatization, and cramming as many relevant tropes into the experience is cringe, but something I can stomach, as this has been plaguing any attempted adaptation of a previously niche genre (look at lovecraftian and cosmic horror: many people think that if it has tentacles and 'madness', it is lovecraftian, while missrepresenting the trope completely. Just because a setting has dwarves and elves, doesn't make it the Lord of the Rings).

But then the gameplay - it starts with a long cutscene and a bunch of quicktime events. Ok - not ideal, not something I like, but fine. Then the tutorial boss: my game is paused 15 times to tell me about the different UI elements, and game mechanics. It tells me I can adjust keybindings, it lets me select the level of 'assisstance' the game will provide. Ok - I got it, I read it, let's go. But wait - there's a problem. One of the crucial abilities is bound to a key I already use for something outside of the game. No big deal, let's go into the menu, and change the keybinding. Keybindings can't be changed during the tutorial. Amazing. Get me out.

Good Wuxia was Jackie Chan, Steven Chow, but not this. From the presentation, to the controls and the flow of gameplay - the game feels condescending. Nuh uh.

Within the first 10 minutes, I knew I would never boot this game up again.
