WWM impressed me with its beautiful graphics, fair monetization model, great customization options and massive amount of content. It definitely sets a new standard for free-to-play games. It takes a bit of time to wrap your head around all the pop-ups, sub-menus and different currencies, but it's well worth it once you do. 
At its core, the game is single-player and is packed with a solid main story and varied side quests. Right from level 10, you unlock two new modes: Co-op and MMO. The latter acts more like a social lobby, with both modes dedicated for group content, including dungeons and raids.
Is it a Souls-like experience? Not really, but it's close enough. The combat revolves around parries and dodges, yet it remains fast-paced thanks to the martial arts and various weapon combinations. The world map is immense and exploration is engaging with lots of minigames and secrets to discover. 
Gear progression follows a mobile-style energy system, with the energy refill not being a daily thing: this is definitely a blessing for anyone with a busy schedule since it lets you play at your own pace and still keep up. There are gacha elements in the game, but they are all focused on cosmetics items that offer no gameplay advantages.
If you're looking for a free MMO-ish game with lots of options, including both PvE and PvP, this might be your next game to try.

Where Winds Meet is free, and somehow I still feel overcharged.

The game desperately wants you to believe you’re on an epic Wuxia journey—ancient China, poetic dialogue, legendary sword master, destiny in the wind, etc. In reality, you’re just jogging across a massive, empty map listening to NPCs talk like fortune cookies while nothing interesting happens.

Combat looks flashy but feels weightless. Sword strikes have no impact, enemies politely wait their turn to die, and the skill system exists mostly to give you the illusion of depth. It’s less “master swordsman” and more “stylish leaf blower.”

The open world is huge and pretty, which is great until you realize it’s mostly filler. Same activities, same enemies, same animations, repeated endlessly. Exploration quickly turns into busywork designed to inflate playtime rather than provide actual content.

Performance issues are the real final boss: stutters, pop-in, clunky UI, and animations that look like they’re still buffering. For a game that leans so hard on immersion, it does everything possible to break it.

Yes, it’s free—but free doesn’t mean fun. Time is still a currency, and this game spends it poorly.

I'm very conflicted over this review but have decided to go for positive. I'll just list the pros and cons and summarise.
Pros:
*Beautiful Graphics. Everywhere you look is a work of art, especially at certain times of day. I'm very excited for the ultimate "Natural" Graphics mode.
*The combat with the different martial arts, mystic arts and gear really flows nicely. The game really lets you feel like a boss as you style your way through fights. 
*Exploration is fun and interesting, it really feels like a living world. You can just pick any direction and you'll come across some kind of activity, quest or reward. the design of all the villages and everything in between has been so carefully placed.
*The developers have tried to fit in so many different elements and most of them really work well. 
*The story is pretty good in the single player mode, and most side quests of varying types actually have meaning, not just fetch quests like most games rely on.
*There's lots of online modes. you can play a lot of the single player game in co op with friends for smaller quests and boss fights (main story quests are single only so friends will have to wait in the world or get kicked until you're done). There is various chill hangout modes to receive rewards while chatting to everyone, big group boss fights, prison break, pvp arena, group healing, guild war etc. I've never really been an online player but this game has made me actually want to join online activities.

Now for the negatives that have ruined the experience for me having gotten through the single play content and played with the online features:
*THE BIG ONE - Limits, limits everywhere! everything has a limit that's easily reached from minimal play. Energy needed to claim rewards, a triple claim after a group boss takes 180 energy. At the current level cap you now, after the update increasing it by 50 points (woohoo -.-), have 550. so expect 3 online group boss fights before running out. this regenerates 1 point every 9 minutes. About 3 days for energy to refill... yeah it sucks. Then there's limits to how much of every resource you can get, that includes playing the single player story too. Can't farm weapon drops for long before waiting a day for it to reset.
*The Servers are awful, I have 1.6Gb/s Fibre, 4-5ms ping. Playing in any online activity can be so frustrating from the lag. Everything will just stop during group boss fights for extended amounts of time, player and enemy locations will just change suddenly where its lagged and caught up. You have to time deflecting perfectly to survive in this, but in co op with friends, online boss's or pvp it's impossible when what is happening on your screen actually happed 1-2 seconds ago. I have to give up trying sometimes as I cant predict deflecting before something actually happens. 
*The Gacha pricing and value in this is extorsion. It's a complete cash grab for the global market. Buying the pearl things needed for just 10 draws costs about £30, and all the drops are like single food, scroll or health items that are worth nothing. you have to draw 150 times to get a guaranteed rare skin or draw shop currency to purchase rare accessories. And the chances of naturally drawing something good seem unreasonably low. This accompanied with how much content is missing from the China version just seems like a slap in the face.

I have loved playing this game but have struggled to continue enjoying it now that I've played through it. As it's a free game the story is very much worth a play through and brings a lot of enjoyment, just be prepared to be disappointed at times especially as you reach the end of the current content waiting for future updates.

WWM delivers top‑tier story, visuals, and characters, but the real highlight is the boss fights. They’re tough, intense, and incredibly satisfying to beat. Every encounter feels like a true test of skill.
And the fact that all of this is free makes it even more impressive.
Final score: 100 out of 10.

I’m probably in the minority when I say I really dislike [i]Dark Souls[/i]–style combat. My only real exposure was about 38 minutes of [i]Bloodborne[/i], and that was more than enough of my time wasted.

I came into [i]Where Winds Meet[/i] expecting something closer to [i]Ghost of Tsushima[/i].[spoiler](Not sure why I didn't watch any gameplay footage before downloading the game)[/spoiler] I loved parrying in [i]GoT[/i], even on Lethal difficulty, so I was hoping for a similar feel here.

The game [i]is[/i] somewhat comparable to [i]GoT[/i] in a few ways. You have side abilities with cooldowns, and exploration feels familiar. And that's where the similarities end.. Combat here can be pretty fast, enemies are even faster than [i]GoT[/i] and give you much less time to react. Telegraphs rely more on visual effects than clear UI cues. Groups of enemies can kill you very quickly, especially archers using fire arrows.

The game also doesn’t explain much beyond the basics of combat. There are several systems that would be good to understand but the game never introduces them.

[h3]Bad:[/h3]
* [i]Souls[/i]-like combat. It feels okay early on, then the difficulty ramps up fast. I still pushed to level 60 despite the frustration.
* Enemies feel increasingly spongey at higher levels.
* Fighting groups of enemies can be deadlier than boss fights.
* The world feels emptier than an [i]Assassin’s Creed[/i] game.
* Clunky UI. Important menus are hidden behind obscure buttons in equipment, discoveries, and character stats.

[h3]Meh:[/h3]
* Main story quest is serviceable.
* Tasks get repetitive.
* Crafting feels basic.
* Riddles and lore sometimes suffer from localization issues.

[h3]Good:[/h3]
* Music.
* World design.
* Lore.
* Voice acting.
* Beautiful graphics.
* Character customization.
* Outfits.

[h2]Score: 5/10[/h2]

I really don’t enjoy [i]Souls[/i]-style combat, but the visuals, lore, and overall presentation were enough to keep me me playing longer than I expected, despite the ongoing combat frustrations. 
Players who enjoy [i]Souls[/i]-like combat may find more to appreciate here than I did.

[b]P.S.[/b]

For an MMO, it has quite a lot to do. The quality for a free game is immense although you are being subsidized by the gacha mechanics. Luckily, there's no pay2win elements here, so this game doesn't fall into the trap some other MMOs have. Gameplay is Sekiro-like with loads of deflecting, and you can engage it like a souls game if you amp up the difficulty. Yakuza levels of minigames where most can be played with friends. Way too many little systems to engage with, including a bounty system, being accused of crimes, going to jail and jailing your closest friend via intimacy system crime by association, then some co-op jail break fun. Collectathon style exploring, danganrompa style lawyering/trolling minigame, list genuinely goes on.

Not only that, but this is one of the first few games to really engage the west with the Wuxia/Xanxia genre, an extremely popular novel genre in the east. It's an extremely specific fantasy genre involving chinese alchemy/cultivation and the pursuit of immortality. So it's actually pretty exciting to have something like that. Of course, the game follow suit with it's mechanics and story as well. You don't get stronger simply by leveling up, but doing random things, collecting random stuff, and engaging with different development systems. There's very little you do in this game that doesn't contribute to your strength in some way.

It's pretty cool. It obviously has translation issues and globalization catchup pacing going on, and some aspects of the game can be annoying. (The UI makes me want to commit extra special self caring) But overall a really really good package. It's hard to beat "decent to good game for the price of free."

After having played my fair share of MMORPGs (Warframe, Lost Ark, etc.) and Action RPGs (Dark Souls, Sekiro, Elden Ring, etc.), I will say that Where Winds Meet is a beautiful product for someone looking for a bit of both. As if that wasn't enough, the storytelling, music, and atmosphere in this game are immaculate. 

So just for ease of reading, here are my pros and cons about the game:
[PROS]
+ Beautiful game/atmosphere
+ Engaging combat
+ Amazing cosmetics
+ No P2W; completely F2P
+ Huge amounts of content
+ Very unique setting of Wuxia

[CONS]
- Localisation is a little rough; as both a chinese and english speaker myself, some of the translations are rather messy, which is a shame for the english-speaking audience
- Bugs are quite rampant; from some bosses, to exploration, to NPC interactions
- Premium skins are EXTREMELY expensive; we're talking about premium price-gated skins that are >USD400
- Communication between Devs and playbase could be improved imo; patch notes are sometimes delayed or not even shared sometimes. This makes periodic content droughts difficult to go through
- There are many time gated elements in the game (i.e. endgame gear grind [energy system], level cap breakthrough, currency farming, etc.)

Despite the seemingly long list of CONS, I must say that this game must be looked at with the right lens; it's a game meant to be played casually and stress-free, perfect for someone who plays an average of 2-4 hours a day. If you are someone like that, this game will absolutely suit you being a nice winding down game after a long, tiring day at work. But if you have much time to spare, playing anywhere from 6-12 hours a day, this game may not offer enough for you. 

All-in-all, I cannot ignore the work of art created here, and it is truly a masterpiece worthy of recognition, and I would recommend anyone from any walks of life to give this a go. After all, it is completely free :)

Where Winds Meet was a very pleasant surprise to me. I haven't been hooked to any MMORPG in over 10 years, because I found them all lacking any interesting gameplay or narrative compared to solo games. But [b]WWM is built different[/b]...

First the [b]Art[/b]... It's absurdly beautiful, like "I'm never going out again" beautiful. So often during exploration I paused and admired the view. Character are also very well modelled, and the character creation has way too many features and detailed modelling options it's insane.
And finally on the art, the bosses... They're Elden Ring level of epic, gorgeous cutscenes, incredible style,  it's a spectacle. 

[b]Gameplay[/b] is so varied I'm still dizzy from all you can do. Exploration is dense with lots of activities and questing. So many quests and varied encounters, and the quests are so interesting! It's never "go kill X wolves", but quests like The Witcher 3: Stories, that are solved in multiple ways. Crafting, building bases, joining guilds & sects, dungeons, outposts, trading, (multiplayer) mini games. 
And you don't need to do all of that, the game can also be played chill on Story mode so you don't need to optimize your character and do all activities.

And while there are tons of mechanics in this game, [b]combat[/b] is still very important in WWM... And it's better than any MMO I've touched or seen. Incredibly dynamic, bosses are truly epic with gorgeous cutscenes, and very cool moves. Instead of classes you just swap martial arts so you try out any style of gameplay with one character. 

[b]Movement[/b] in Where Winds Meet is also an amazingly well designed mechanic. You don't just run jump and ride horses, there's a whole skill tree of movement abilities that you unlock as you progress in the game. And it's so cool, to learn how to ride the wind, jump on water, soar in the sky, ... Something I've also never seen anywhere else and renders exploration really fun. 

Finally, I'll touch on the [b]Systems[/b]. Where Winds Meet has so many systems, including tons of ways to upgrade your character. But it's so well designed, that's it's not confusing at all. You unlock the different systems bit by bit, and the interface has tons of elements to help you find your way and take advantage of the right mechanic when you need it. 

The only aspect of the game that I'm not very found of is [b]progression[/b]. both that of our character and difficulty escalation. 
On one hand, I felt like for the first 40 levels, I didn't really become more powerful: Damage was increasing in single units and changing a full set of gear had no noticeable effect. 
But suddenly above level 40 and particularly 50, some features unlocked give a massive power spike - but require farming resources, which wasn't necessary before. 
And you have to farm, because it ties in with the difficulty progression: For the first 40 levels it's extremely easy, you can face-tank bosses and still win. But at level 50 enemies also get an enormous power spike (I've checked and some bosses hit 4x harder than the previous difficulty level) So you're suddenly stuck in a grind to catch up on these newly very powerful enemies who can kill you in a little more than one combo and can tank hits for days. 

But still a solid 9.5/10, free game, haven't spent a cent yet, but I think I'll take that battle pass to support the development.

After around 150 hours in this game, i think I'm qualified to write an actual review here.

First things first. As a souls player who loves the challenge, is this game worth your time? No.
Don't get me wrong. It DOES have challenging parts and challenges, but it isn't a souls game. Even as a souls-like, it's definitely on the easier side of games, which makes sense since it's ment to attract casual gamers who want to play with their friends as well. So, if you're a souls veteran who wants the hardest challenges there are, you'll be disappointed with this. Anyone else - Come in!

It also isn't your typical MMORPG. Yes, it does have MMO aspects, but for like 90% of your progress, you stay offline and explore your world, do story quests etc. You CAN play with friends to boost your exploration progress together, at the same time, which is huge. But, story missions are the ones you can not play in co-op, sorry guys. The "online mode" also isn't like a big open map with enemies everywhere for people to slay, no. It's more of a hub. Like, a lobby for players to meet and make up parties who then go into someones individual world together, or to form up for raids.

It's also not your typical F2P game. Buying the battlepass DOES grant you a small advantage, yes. But, it's basically almost meaningless, and all you can truly do with real money is buying cosmetics. This game isn't Pay 2 Win, it's essentially Pay 2 Flex. I am F2P with a 0.90€ cosmetic, not a single battlepass, and my power level is close to 20k at this point, which puts me above basically 99% of the players at the point of writing this. Individual skill also matters a lot more than gear in most cases, unless the difference in gear is extreme.

Progression is quite fast. A friend of mine who started just 2 weeks ago caught up with us day 1 endgame players already, currently at 17k power, and max level on their account. The game is time efficient, beginner friendly and honestly optimized pretty well.

Now, the negatives. As long as you're offline, everything is fine, crisp, and responsive. As soon as you play with others, however, expect massive desync and input lag. Me and my friends live close to each other, we all have a ping of between 5 and 20 - and still, no matter who's world we join, there's massive delays. The servers definitely are on the lower end of things I've seen within 20+ years of gaming, but that's something that could always change in the future.

All in all, the game is a solid 8/10. It's a F2P game that doesn't offer huge advantages from spending money. The gameplay is satisfactory and the progression is very good. However, there's negatives, like the poor server performance and a pretty weak main story plot (as of now). All fixable, of course. If you like souls like games but aren't one of these basement dwellers who need it to be the be-all end-all of souls likes, you'll love this game, especially with friends to play with. Even if you're a casual player who can't get their footing into souls games, this game might be for you. It's easier than most of them, it's online meaning your friends can help you get into it, and the only difficult part is learning and understanding the stats system of this game. But, YouTube is your friend, and with the willingness to look things up here and there, it won't be too much of an issue.

I have to say though, the translation is terrible in some places, but that does lead to some funny moments. "Look, so many money!"

This game GENUINELY surprised me in the best way!

From the moment I stepped into its world it felt calm, beautiful, and deeply connected to its culture. Everything from the look of the towns/cities and clothing to the music and martial arts carries a strong sense of identity. It doesn’t feel like culture was added just for style. It feels naturally intertwined with the world, which made exploring it feel meaningful (I really love exploration in games)

What really stood out to me was how alive everything feels. The NPCs don’t feel like they’re just standing around waiting for you. They feel like people who actually live there. They have routines, they interact with each other, and they exist whether or not you’re involved. Towns feel lived in and that immersion was really wonderful.

Also there's always something to do, no matter how you feel like playing. If you want to explore solo, the world constantly rewards curiosity with hidden details, side activities, and secret quiet places that feel just as important as the bigger story quests and areas. If you’re in the mood for combat, there's pvp and even a battle royal PvP option that is interesting for those who like it. There's an online mode as well that has fun events and shared activities, even random PvP "payload" type events where you have to help or prevent a prison break.

The game gives you space to breathe without ever feeling empty. You’re never rushed, but you’re also never bored. Combat is fluid and elegant, cinematic without feeling overwhelming, and learning it has felt genuinely satisfying.

Overall this game feels like a world with a soul. It’s immersive, thoughtful, and clearly made with care. Whether you prefer peaceful exploration, competitive moments, or engaging with others online, there’s always something for you. And if you value atmosphere, culture, and a truly lived-in world, this game is absolutely worth your time.

I've put in 300 hours into this game in two months. I think it's pretty obvious that I *really* like it.

TL;DR: Give it a shot. You might like it, you might not. It's very overwhelming at the start, but there's a lot of different ways to play and things to enjoy. There is gacha. Don't expect to have an exclusively single-player experience, even if you avoid online mode, as there are mechanics that force you to interact with other players (i.e., healing, bounty hunters, etc).

What hooked me right off the bat is the atmosphere and scenery, as it is utterly gorgeous. It can be deeply immersive, and there are some views that stop you in your tracks. There are a lot of little details to it that make it satisfying to adventure through. Truly stunning. You can tell that the studio is very proud of their culture and history and put real effort into trying to offer an engaging, mostly authentic experience that feels very alive.

Movement in this game is very fun, and it makes exploring the open world a blast. I personally enjoy the game's combat, both PvE and PvP, and find it fun and satisfying with a somewhat decent variety and plenty of room to optimize and customize. There is RNG when it comes to loot and your gear's stats, and there is an "energy" system wherein farming bosses for loot costs energy that takes time to replenish on its own.

The character customization is a mixed bag. The actual character creation when it comes to faces is fantastic, and you can create some unique and beautiful characters easily. However, the cosmetics -- hairstyles, clothing, etc -- are very, very limited. The game is a gacha game, with cosmetics being the prize. The gacha mechanics are brutal, and while there are plenty of outfits you can simply buy rather than gamble for, those are pretty expensive as well. If you want an appealing, cohesive outfit, as things stand currently, you most likely need to spend real money.

I would not recommend this game if you have a history of ill-advised impulse purchases or a past gacha addiction.

A downside to the character customization is that if you wish to edit your character's facial structure, there is a cost. The item required for this costs one of the special in-game currencies used for one of the gacha pools, though it's the more "free-to-play" one that you earn plenty of throughout. Still, super annoying that you can't do it freely. Moreover, if you wish to change your character's gender -- "body type," as the game calls it -- then you *must* spend some amount of real money. There's a limited number of slots for saved appearances and makeup schemes, with additional slots (of which there is still only a limited amount) costing more of that "free-to-play" currency.

Clothing and hair can be dyed, and players can upload their dye schemes to a gallery for other players to use. I like this, but the issue is that dyeing things requires items. Some are basic that are handed out like candy, some are more limited, and one costs real money and is only obtainable through gacha.

PvP is something I have always avoided like the plague; too intimidating. However, I got roped into something that required me to play PvP in this game, and now I'm ranked Legend II with over 150 matches in under a month. I don't know what it is, but I really, really enjoy PvP in this game. It's infuriating, frustrating, and deeply unbalanced, but damn, it hits my monkey brain just right sometimes. My build isn't meta at all -- it's literally just the basic Nameless Sword/Nameless Spear build that's recommended by the game -- but I invested a lot into it, and it's working for me. So you don't necessarily need to worry about meta, which is nice.

The story is... unbelievably confusing. I don't think it's just localization issues either, though those are still abundant in the game at this point. Something my friend who plays the game said, and with which I entirely agree, is that it is very hard to understand "cause and effect" in the game's story, both in regards to the main quests and side quests. I suspect this is partly due to it being written for a Chinese audience who are familiar with a whole host of genre tropes that a Western audience isn't, so they're able to fill in the gaps with context we simply don't have.

Or maybe the writing is just bad. I really can't tell.

The English voice acting is... eugh. The audio quality is wack, and I'm positive that some NPCs are just AI-generated voicelines. The subtitles don't always match what's said. The Chinese voice acting, however, is exceptional. There are plenty of smaller quests that aren't voiced, but having played god knows how many hours of Genshin Impact, I'm used to that; others may find it off-putting. If possible, I would recommend switching the audio language to Chinese. There are going to be some throwaway lines from enemies and bosses that don't have subtitles, but I've found the tradeoff worth it.

Oh, also: the game is loud as hell. I have the master volume set to 20. When you boot up the game for the first time, brace yourself.

The music is beautiful, though it's repetitive in the open world. It does well to set the tone and add tension and excitement, but I don't find myself wanting to listen to the OST on its own.

There is *a lot* going on in this game. Like, *a lot*. So many different game modes. There's no way I'd be able to cover everything in a single review, not least of all because I still have yet to actually try everything. It's overwhelming, honestly, especially at the start. Guilds, discipleships, sworn cohorts, partnerships, sects, co-op, online mode, mini-games, 1v1 PvP, battle royale PvP, boss trials, building, commerce, professions, open world challenges, mystic skills, inner ways, martial arts, bounties, vendettas, photo mode, a newspaper, path trials, sword trials, hero trials, events, battle pass, rhythm game/musical instruments, injuries/illnesses, sect elections, hero titles, scenarios, a bonkers amount of different currencies... Even *healing* has a leaderboard.

It's hard to have a true single-player experience. There are a lot of things -- including crafting recipes for bows -- that require you to do multiplayer. (It does have a "Smart Assist" option that pairs you with AI rather than real players, but even so.) Some in-game currencies that can be used to unlock items or cosmetics require you to interact with other players.

If you break the law and successful evade the guards, a bounty will be placed on you that another player will accept, allowing them to enter your world to engage in PvP without your consent. If they win, you're thrown into prison in online mode for 15 minutes to perhaps much longer. There are things you can do to decrease your sentence and get out sooner, but still. Now you might also be punished if a friend or partner committed a crime. (Which I personally kind of love, but I'd be fuming if I were still trying to play this as a single-player game.)

Additionally, there are some injuries and illnesses that *cannot* be healed by the NPC healer and require another player to heal you. Healing is super competitive, so there will always be an abundance of players eager to heal you, but again, that's just another instance of being forced to interact with other players.

With recent updates, the game has improved QoL and clarity when it comes to certain mechanics, but there are still things that are simply under-explained or aren't actually accessible in the game yet with no indication that that's the case. (I'm looking at you, furniture recipes supposedly at Feng's Tradehall.) As I mentioned earlier, localization is still an ongoing issue in some aspects, with some instances of Chinese text remaining unlocalized. Much of the game is optimized for Chinese, so the character limit for names and even bug reports is absurdly low.

The game has its strengths and weaknesses. Overall I recommend most people try it out, but it certainly is not for everyone.

I'm very torn on this game, it has a lot of good qualities and a lot of bad qualities. In the end your enjoyment will probably hinge on what you're looking to get out of the game.

First, as someone who is playing completely solo, I think its big open world with tons of random stuff to do is where it shines, you can run around for hours doings side quest, collecting things, fishing, catching horses, fighting bosses, arguing with people, healing injuries, there's really quite a lot to do.

I think if this was a strictly single player/co-op game we'd be talking about it as one of the best of the year, and though at times it feels like it was closely copying Ghost of Tsushima's homework, it often goes much further into the details than GoT.

However there are problems, for one, the game is buggy as hell, not generally game breaking, but still annoying. Like if you commit crimes you can be thrown in jail, cool idea, but something as simple as accidently breaking some pots can be considered a crime and the only option to make amends is to repair the pots, no big deal right? Except one of the pots fell through the world and can't be repaired, so now you have to look at the crime warning on your screen for 24 hours.

Other annoyances like if you push open a door and then try to immediately go through it, your character freezes until you stop moving forward and let them reset and this happens basically 100% of the time, getting stuck in the terrain is also a normal occurrence, luckily they included a "unstuck" button that is gonna see some use.

Also the other big problem with the game, that many have pointed out, comes from it's F2P MMO half and it unfortunately affects everyone, there are so many menus, none of their placement or organization makes any sense, seemingly connected information can be broken up between multiple menus and it seems like every grouping of menus was made by a different person, they all look and work differently and are spread all over the UI.

Also if you decide to play with a controller like I did, do yourself a favor and have your mouse ready at all times, because the menus are not controller friendly and you'll save yourself a lot of time and sanity by just clicking what you want. There were many scenarios where I genuinely couldn't figure out how to reach certain parts of the menus with a controller and the battle pass is a complete nightmare without a mouse.

As for the story, I know people will be split, I've completed the first campaign, I wasn't a huge fan, the English VA isn't particularly good, the translation isn't great either often leading to moments of just nonsense dialogue. They use heavy handed plot devices that seem unnecessary and mess the game world up in a way that takes away from the overall experience. If it was a single player game like GoT I think it would work better, but as it's intended to be a more persistent world that you're in long term, as apposed to a game you'll finish in a week and put down, non-reversible changes to the world feel like a really odd and out of place decision in a game that I'd assume they want you to play indefinitely.  

Ultimately I think this is a game worth playing, it's free after all, so why not. Despite being janky and difficult to sift through, it's really ambitious, there's plenty of fun to be had, and I'd say it rivals any of the modern AAA titles being released these days, as the bar isn't very high. 

If you don't care about all the flashy cosmetics that honestly often feel out of place and ignore the gatcha, then you get to play one of the best open world games released in the last several years for free. I think this is probably the best current example of F2P where you could spend no money and still get the full experience.

This game targets 10% of gamers, which is why the Population of the game has already dropped by about 90%. That's because only Hardcore gamers are left, the ones they actually built this game for.

PvP: Stun-Lock or be Stun-Locked in 1v1. 
In Guild Wars be prepared to either fight no-one, or be outnumbered 4 to 1.

PvE: This 100% tailors to a minority of gamers, people who like hardcore combat with over the top punishment for missing a 0.01 second deflect window. The deflect window is not exaggerated...it is legit, a few rendered frames wide. 

We actually have someone in our guild, who has never beat a single boss because they are so over the top difficult....and you can't progress the story line without beating them...and yes they have the difficulty as low as it will go.

It's important to know that the Bosses scale with you, because the devs don't want you to be able to come back later when your stronger, they want you to "Get Good". Well I could say the same about them after realizing they have lost 90% of their player base in only a few months.

Campaign Bosses are a real challenge, and they nerf your healing by about 50%, not that it would matter, because the first ones you come across...you won't have but 1 or 2 health pots anyway...and they will heal less then half your health....and you will run empty within the first 60 seconds.

Fighting a Boss in this game is comprised of you deflecting and dodging for 1-2 minutes at a time about 5-10 deflects a second on average, sometimes up to 20 deflects a second. If you miss more then 3 or 4 deflects your basically guaranteed to be done, and have to start completely over again. 

The deflect windows are about 0.02 to 0.1 seconds long...yes your window is in microseconds and varies on attack. This goes on until they finally get drained, at this point you are given about 10-15 seconds to try and get as many hits as you can in on them, each hit does about 1% to 5% damage. After you finally kill them....congratulations....now you get to fight him 1-2 more times, each time he will get significantly more difficult. Some bosses you have to go for 3 rounds, and on the 3rd round you will be deflecting dozens of times a second for minutes at a time, and the attacks intervals will vary, to ensure you get thrown off, this makes spamming deflect pointless.....because deflect has a cooldown, so you have to be intentionally deflecting at precise moments, you can't simply mindlessly spam it.

if you happen to die...you get to start all over again...some of the bosses do not have nearby spawns...so if you do come back later, you get to travel halfway across the world on foot at a jog.....just to get back to him so that you can try again..

If you liked New World from Amazon, you'd probably like this. Since there's really nothing quite like New World to begin with...

The world itself is very pretty. They know how to do the most with what they're given. The NPCs have very Basic AI Chat bots so you can kinda chat them up for extra items or even avoiding battles/starting them/etc. If you're naughty, like breaking wine jars, being caught stealing, beating up people in town, etc - you can be chased by constables... And if you escape, other players can step in to kick your butt and bring you to jail (don't worry, it's cheap to leave jail and you get achievements for it). Just don't attack the Geese. Never attack the Geese. Never.
Combat is easy to get and hard to master. Most player animations can be stopped by blocking, dodging, or hitting the deflect/parry button. There's more than 1 way to mitigate damage, deflect being the hardest, followed by dodge, with block being the easiest - each balanced so one isn't better than the other AND there's more than 1 option to protect yourself. There are plenty of weapons and they're all decently balanced and players can mix the weapons without penalties. Each weapon itself has its own defined playstyle, rarely is there a useless option on a weapon and weapons aren't locked into one strict way of playing either.

Cash Shop is Pay2Pretty, but even then, they offer a great amount of outfits for free. Then they offer plenty of pretty outfits that cost just 1 dollar (60 pearls). The Gacha Pay2Pretty portion on the other hand is quite obviously the Whale Pit. 

Story wise is OK. The voice acting is OK. The voiced lines aren't consistent either. The Story's translation is functional but not great. There's plenty of little encounters throughout the world. There's plenty of lore.

Boss Fights are actually fun and tough. Even Easy Mode can be challenging to some for later bosses. Thankfully you can ask friends or randoms for help. Multiplayer Boss Fights introduce even more mechanics. With the game TELLING YOU what big-bad-mechanic is coming next via a scrolling message, great for players who get lost in the sauce. 10v1 fights have the most mechanics to deal with, 5v1 is tamer but more than solo fights. 

Multiplayer World is pretty barebones, with easy to do Daily Quests. It's good enough for what it is, as a sort of chat hub/doctor waiting room or other leisurely activities like playing instruments.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
[b]3/5[/b]
[list]
[*][h3]Single player[/h3]
[b]4/5[/b] 

It is great to play single player. Puzzles are fun. For combat difficulty, I haven't played any games like this one, the closest I can say I played is probably MHW doing no damage runs and clear times. It is the same, just learn the enemy's movements and you are set. If the game bosses aren't level locked, you can probably kill it with whatever you got. (I play on Legend difficulty)

-1 from this is because of the Mobile game style limits so you get limited key binds. Energy style gameplay therefore time locked activities and farming. After you 100% almost everything, you are stuck to online activities...

[*][h3]Multiplayer[/h3]
[b]2/5[/b]

Co-op - Can't do everything in coop. Some important interactions with NPCs are missing unless you go Solo. My experience, my friend can't learn Taichi as it is not there in coop. idk if that was fixed or really intended. But if you want to have a full Co-op experience of the game. You won't get it. A lot of things you still need to do in solo.

Online - Server latency is bad. 200ms - 300ms is a bad online latency. I'm in Oceana server. idk where it is but it isn't Singapore or Hong Kong. I played games with servers there and I get 35 - 50 ms on those. This also applies to [u]Arena[/u]. Lag is your enemy, not the player. Oh, and there are videos too showing that people can [i]cheat[/i] in this game. Tons of auto-scripters doing online farming. Online is really bad unless you are just hanging out.
[/list]
[h1]Graphics[/h1]
[b]4/5[/b]

Only thing I can say here is that, a lot of side quest people's faces are too copy pasted, like aren't you the one from the other quest? just without a mole? hahaha. And come on, "Grandpa this, Grandma that", those NPCs are way too young to be. I've only seen probably Turtle Grandma as the only old one here.. If there's another.... sorry, I might have missed him/her. 

[h1]System[/h1]
[b]2/5[/b]

Took this out of Gameplay part as it is necessary.

This game is way too [u]MOBILE[/u]. What I meant is, it feels like it is designed directly for mobile phones and consoles. Lots of the items in the menus needs to be scrolled by "touch" and can't be scroll by a mouse wheel specially the descriptions.

All textbox for quantity input are not even optimized. Some you can straight up click and type, some you can't, and some even has an in-game number pad to pick numbers with like 3 different developers are working on 3 different text boxes. 

Lastly is this game is still way too far from being optimized even though it is 2 years old (CN server). Almost every time you start the game, client is repairing itself. Every update, in my case 1.1 and 1.2, bugs for QoL, Gameplay and minor seems to not be disappearing and more seems to be added. And also, of all my steam games, this is the only game I experienced updating the whole game itself. 80gb update? no, it's a new game.

To add, some bugs are actually fixed by closing and opening the game.. Like what is that? Hahaha.

[h1]Monetary[/h1]
[b]3/5[/b]

As the game endorse, it is free to play.

-1 here is for a game that has a lot of time gated farming, whales are always ahead on others as they get more resources from like battle passes. No negative if the farming has no limit.

Another -1 is from a specific mount. It has a skill that can pick up resources in a press of a button. This my friends is a part of pay to win. As long as an item bought by money, whether there's a lot or in case here, 1, and it affects gameplay, It is pay to win :) I'll remove this if the devs' integrity can ban those who paid this horse and sit in online mode to farm spots. :)

If I'm going to compare this, Warframe is still up top 1 for me in terms of Free2Play. Farm all you want(No energy limit), trade farmables for microtransaction money, buy skins, accessories, etc with it. The only thing you can't get free there are tennogens (Player made designs & prime launch specific skins) and Limited (Events from previous years that has no specific date return or never will again)

[h1]Overall[/h1]
[b]3/5[/b]

The only reason as of now as to why I'm recommending it is because it is still Free2Play and still a young game to be judged too highly. Bugs here and there. Still very low optimization. Playable.

I will probably update this if I ever make it to 1k hours :)

I went into Where Winds Meet mostly for the wuxia vibes and honestly, that’s where the game shines the most.

The world is beautiful. Exploring feels relaxing but also exciting, with mountains, towns and little details everywhere. Just walking around and soaking in the atmosphere is genuinely enjoyable. If you like open-world games that let you wander without constantly telling you what to do, this one does that well.

Combat is fun and flashy. The martial arts movement, weapons, and skills feel smooth, and fights look cinematic. That said, combat can start to feel a bit repetitive after a while unless you switch up weapons or playstyles.

The story is interesting but a bit slow at times. It leans more into political drama and character moments, so it might not instantly hook everyone. Some side quests actually surprised me and ended up being more engaging than expected.

There are a few rough spots, some mechanics aren’t explained very clearly and pacing can feel uneven but nothing that completely ruined the experience for me.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a solid game if you enjoy wuxia aesthetics, open-world exploration and stylish combat. Not perfect, but definitely worth checking out if that’s your thing.

TLDR:  If you  haven't been finding  anything that  draws you in, with a crisp captivating  world, great stories, and just an all around  ORIGINAL feel - just download and get ready for a JOURNEY!

This game scratches an itch that  very  few have been  able to.    The world, expansive,  well thought out - I haven't seen any moderate graphical glitches  or cracks in the landscape plane.  Not  even an odd decorative model that's placed upside-down/backwards that catches you off guard.  The  level design  crew were clearly miticulous and passionate.   I can spend hours just exploring and petting every cat along  the way!   With a  world so wonderously captivating - I find myself accidentally discovering side quests.  There are a couple of side quests that are so well storey-boarded, detailed, relevant to the main plot - even if merely suggestive or by what seems coincidence.   The  main story has the  WWM community traumatized, mourning,  missing a proverbial gem lost.  A tale as old as time, but NOT cliche, and I find  a  hard time predicting what's  next.  Then comes the  detail of the voice acting.  BROTHERS AND  SISTERS GATHER ROUND, HEAR MY HARK; The actors instill and support the emotion of the story.  As if there is PRIDE in the project and staff is treated with the utmost respect.  This is a tripple A game, GIFTED to us, and the only thing  that may frustrate you is navigating the HUD/menus because there is A LOT - and for a new player like myself, it was overwhelming to learn.  Where Winds Meet gently guides you, but not  in the gentle of  today's  parenting.  It's light, not intrusive or distracting with major dialogue    windows that are overly decorated, trying to boast elegance.  What's more, it's available for mobile!  For the optimum experience a controller (PC/Phone) is recommended.   With all that said. must I recommend the game?  It is evident I'm an immedaite fan, haven't felt this drawn to an RPG since I first loaded my  LOZ: Ocarina of Time cartridge into  my Nintendo  64,  Download it, find kitty - pet kitty, feed the  doggo's,  swim, fish, explore, MURDER, AVENGE!  you can even terrorize a civilian if  you like, but there is a jailing system.

This game is a surprise from head to toe ! The economy system is insanely expensive but it's only for cosmetics and this is the only true negative point I can find to be honest. The settings menu allows you to fully customize your experience, from casual explorers to full dark souls masochism, mouse toggle camera or not, bright colors, moody ambient light or even foggy mysterious world.

Walking in villages and cities feels real as you easily can tell how people lives. Horse field? The village nearby has more horse tamers. The empire is digging a new canal? The village nearby is full of workers, officials sharing rations, and army soldiers.

The story, and the past me wouldn't believe me because it's a free game, but the story is written with golden hands. Your character being fully dubbed in main quests (and to me it adds a lot of immersion (Yes I stare at you Baldur's Gate)), movie-like cutscenes, lively characters with their own personnalities and motives. Each campaign stories left me jaw open drying some tears and I really hope you could believe me when I say that because as I said: I wouldn't have few months ago. This is a very decent free-to-play open world game...that I bounced off of after about 8 hours.

The good:
It's a pretty environment to explore. Beautiful traditional Chinese vibes throughout.
Good character creator, though don't expect curves.
There are some interesting NPCs and side quests.
Combat is decent.  There are some truly challenging mini-bosses as well.
You have a lot of choices, and you'll never be without some goal or quest to keep you moving forward.
You can play solo or like an MMORPG (at least eventually).

The meh:
Progression systems, currencies, items, weapon upgrades, and basically every system in the game is cryptic and poorly explained. You're going to have to hit some YouTube guides.
Stick with the Chinese voice acting. Trust me.
The translation is...maybe literally correct, but almost every interaction feels a bit unnatural. Not sure if this is because of cultural differences or simply bad translation.
Some weird AI NPCs.  F*ck AI, seriously.
You're eventually going to get pushed into typical MMORPG style guilds, so if you prefer solo play, be warned.

The bad:
It is now over 100GB of memory, and shows no sign of slowing down.  I just don't have that much spare memory, to be honest.

The verdict: If you have a computer with loads of memory and a good internet connection, enjoy Chinese culture and appreciate Yakuza style mini-games, give WWM a try. It's pretty good, and you can definitely lose yourself in it.  But I prefer offline games with a bit more focus, and if you do too, you'll probably bounce off pretty quickly, too.

Where Winds Meet is a beautiful and ambitious game that delivers a rich world paired with genuinely challenging, skill-based combat. The environments are visually striking, exploration feels rewarding, and the combat system demands timing, positioning, and mastery rather than mindless button-mashing. What makes it even more impressive is that the game is completely free while avoiding any pay-to-win mechanics. Monetization is limited to cosmetic items, which keeps progression fair and competitive for all players. Taken as a whole, Where Winds Meet stands out as one of the best free-to-play games available and sets a high standard for how free games should be made.

I’m leaving a negative review in the hope that this reaches the developers and gets fixed.

No matter how many times I launch the game, it always starts in DirectX 11. I have explicitly configured my system and launch options so that only DirectX 12 should be used, yet the game keeps loading DX11.

I’ve tried forcing DX12 from outside the game, but the result is inconsistent - sometimes it works, most of the time it doesn’t. This is a serious issue because without DirectX 12, DLSS is unavailable, which results in noticeably lower FPS and worse performance overall.

I really hope the developers address this problem, because it significantly affects the experience, especially for RTX GPU users. If this issue gets resolved and DX12/DLSS work properly, I will gladly change this review to a positive one.

Positives:
     The story is nice and the scenery is epic.  If you're a mid/ casual player that enjoys a relaxing game then this is definitely for you.  The character creation system is insanely detailed.  You can use voice samples or pictures to automatically seed/ produce your characters appearance.  The cosmetic items are so over the top in detail and are mind blowing.  The game is free to play and the only pay element is their cosmetic items.

Up in the air:
     Not exactly sure how I feel about their lottery systems.  Yes you can spend money for chances to acquire an epic piece of cosmetic loot but there are so many different lottery systems in the game.

     Skill acquisition/ advancement In this game you have to really spend time studying the various skills/ inner ways etc in order to get the most out of them.  Often the process by which you acquire a new skill is hidden in a random encounter or the like.  It's not a negative but it does get cumbersome at times.

     Story:  The various story elements are good in some places and not so in others.  The main questline starts out like a shaw brothers film which is great then becomes rather vanilla.  There are side stories which reference various films and for those that have seen them it is a real treat.

     Like to see:  It would be nice to see more weapons choices in the game.  Currently there are just a handful and it would be cool to have other weapons to add modifiers to the core skill sets.  

     Sailing / river/ocean going missions on ships.  Having ships/ boats floating along the waterways going about their various tasks would be nice.  Being able to partake in a quests to support or perform tasks on those vessels would be nice as well.
     Would be nice to streamline the menu system. (And that leads me to the cons section)

Cons:
     The biggest con is the convoluted menu system in the game.  If you decide to play then be prepared to have to spend a lot of time rummaging through multiple menus in an attempt to find what you're after.  The multiple lottery systems add to this confusion.

     Being restricted to a single character is a big issue for players similar to myself.  If you're the type of player that likes to RP different characters then this isn't a great game for that.  

     Open world.  This is a minor complaint.  If you're claiming a world is fully open then why close off an area until you hit a specific point in the main story?  Once you unlock the "Flight" ability having an invisible wall that drops you into the river is just lazy.  The main story characters could have an available/ unavailable flag that's set depending on where you're at in the story.  Keeping players out of an area until the story is at a certain point.

The reason I've brought this up is because I've intentionally kept my main story arc at a specific point while I work on developing my character.  Several skills are currently locked behind the next zone which is forcing me to advance the main story.  This isn't a total deal breaker though.

Overall rating:
      3.2 out of 5
Reason for the rating?  The game has so much potential.  It's absolutely breathtaking in many ways.  The daily grind to acquire lottery materials and the convoluted menu heavily detract from enjoyment of the game.  It offers so much but the combat and bosses appear to not have much to do with the story.  The MMO element doesn't feel polished/ complete.  There should be a defining reason you're forming a clan outside of because you can.  Some games have group based side quests where you can earn epic loot and need to coordinate and unlock the event.  The MMO element is definitely something that needs some work.

I have essentially completed "the beginning of the hero's journey" chapter, and it was fairly long. From what I have played, I did feel that what I got out of a free game so far was excellent.

For a more concrete reference, at the time of writing this it says I have 17 hours and I have only beaten then first chapter (in reality, half the game at it's current point in development, but that's the nature of the beast of live service GameDev) and I finished the story of Space Marine II in around the same time. I would say my enjoyment of time spent with both is about the same.

So far, I am really enjoying the GAME side of it. The combat is MMO ARPG styled, you're not going to learn 50 different things and use them in sequences, I think you can only have a total of 8 "Special skills" alongside your base weapon moveset. Which I actually love because other games *cough* RIP Sword of Legends *cough* in Wuxia settings had A LOT of bloat when it came to rotations. Here it's dead simple. I'd say it's got more in common with something like Code Vein (Which I did like!) than Dark Souls if you need a non MMO example. I have only done solo stuff, no pvp or any real multiplayer experience as of yet.

Visually, and a lot of people have said this already so no real reason to add to it, but it's incredible that a free game looks this good. The dedicated photo mode is fantastic as well. 

The Gacha and cosmetic grind is a bit much but given that you can just switch off and grind for stuff and get pseudo-premium currency alongside is nice.  But you can ignore it a lot of the time, I never felt pressured to get anything.
That being said, if you want instant appearance options, the battlepass is only $10usd and you can easily get the main outfit by just playing the game - for reference, I started the game about 4 or 5 days ago, played maybe 3-4 hours a day, and got the unlock level for the appearance set at the end of my third day - and then I bought the pass.

The main gripe I have is the menus. There. are. so. many. menus.
While I understand the need to have a different menu for upgrades and stuff, it feels like 8 people worked on UI/UX and just mashed their work together. Very strange how some menus make sense, and others are just, press something with a red dot and then press space to get rewards for some reason, then forget about it for 4 hours, the find it again an press space and get more rewards. I think it may just be an unfamiliarity thing, but if you told me how to get to the "Character Improvement" section where it explicity tells you how to improve your character (mind you, this is not in the actual character upgrade section) I'd be entirely lost on where to start.

I'd give it an 8/10 so far, I am very keen to do more in it and to see future developments of it.

During a simple quest in Kaifeng to protect a healer from some thugs, we get jumped by a group of guys while fighting the thugs. Naturally, we defend ourselves and fight off a number of them. Later while digging through the development menu I hear noises and wonder what is going on. I cancel out of the menu right as I die. Someone has been allowed to invade my supposedly solo game and kill me with no notice and no warning. No notice of being attacked, no chance to do anything. Thanks a lot. Where Winds Meet is one of those rare games where I honestly struggle to understand how someone could walk away with a truly negative impression.

The world is gorgeous, the atmosphere is incredibly strong, the combat looks and feels stylish, and the whole game has this beautiful martial-arts fantasy identity that makes it stand out immediately.

What I love most is how much freedom it gives you. You can explore, fight, discover hidden places, learn different skills, interact with the world, and simply get lost in the setting. It doesn’t feel like a game that constantly pushes you in one direction — it lets you enjoy the journey.

The visual style is amazing, the environments are beautiful, and the movement and combat have that elegant wuxia feeling that makes even simple encounters enjoyable to watch.

Of course, no game is literally flawless. There will always be things someone can criticize. But with Where Winds Meet, I genuinely feel like the overall experience is so strong that the positives completely dominate.

Honestly, when I read a really bad review of this game, part of me wonders if the person was even playing the same game. 😄

Beautiful world, great combat, strong atmosphere, a lot of freedom, and a unique identity.

For me, this is easily one of those games you can sink a lot of hours into without even realizing it.

Absolutely recommended.

This game is difficult to adequately describe.

If you're the type of person who's offended by the presence of microtransactions, that shouldn't be a huge problem for you here.  This game isn't predatory.  Actually I've only glanced at the paid items because this game (like many) will mark things you haven't seen with a little dot, and those were things I hadn't seen.

In fact, like a lot of things in this game, I didn't even know that's what was in the given menu.  So many menus.  This thing has more menus-within-menus than Visual Studio, except with something like an IDE you can be reasonably sure that if you aren't familiar with a thing, that's because you don't need it.  Here it's unclear.

I just finished a mission and, as things often do in WWM, it popped something on the screen asking me to hit the menu button to open up... something.  So I did, and I stared with no comprehension at seas of text and selectable things with no discernable usage.  This was minutes ago and I can't even remember what it was.  Do I get something in here?  Dunno, and I can't tell that I even need anything.  I'm not struggling to win fights.  If I'm missing something I'd like to have, it beats me.  In fact, I'm not even sure why a new feature revealed itself at that point - I just stumbled into a map marker and did a thing in some puzzle dungeon, why is there a whole new concept in play now, especially since I'm still in the middle of shrugging at the last new feature that was introduced?

In these same menus you'll find tons of bits and bobs as rewards for doing things you forgot you did, whose purpose is unclear, and that you weren't looking for.  You might not find these until days after unlocking them and think, "I don't care that I missed this, and I don't care that I found it either."

So I guess "directionless" is the best word.  In an RPG I like tangible progress.  I get no sense of any sort of progress here.  There are a millions things to do, but what do I do [i]next[/i], and [i]why[/i]?  You never feel like you're getting stronger either (enemies level with you, but other games manage to do that without making you feel like you're on a treadmill).

The game does look good.  Combat is fine, if not great - it lacks impact.  I don't expect a miracle for $0, and I'd give this a thumbs up if it wasn't constantly trying to distract me from whatever I'm doing, which was already something I wasn't sure I should be doing.  Even then I'd be satisfied if I was having fun, but I'm just sorta... not.

But hey, it's free, so there's no harm in giving it a shot.

This game scratches so many of my wuxia itches. I didn't think I'd ever care much for the social aspect but it's not bad at all. I've found a relatively decent guild.  I've finished most of the Kaifeng story with much less encounters/side stories.

Things to know: The combat is action RPG. It can be quite simple and low difficulty if you choose Story Difficulty or Recommended. If you do like the sweaty hard fights, legendary difficulty must be chosen at the start and not lowered. I admit I'm still trying to learn my rotation. In 10 mans I'm only reaching less than 10% dps while some others are much higher. It's a lot harder to pull off the rotation than when I played FF14 lol

The game is f2p with very very very minor pay 2 win if your definition includes having more stamina regenerating items to possibly get better gear faster. The more energy spent, the more tips and gear you can grind from campaign bosses/trials. Having paid for the battlepass does not inherently mean you have better gear. The cash shop is pretty much all cosmetics. You can't buy additional stamina pills outside the ones from the battlepass.  Be forewarned. The cosmetics can be pricey though they do have low cost ones as well as coupons. The gacha for cosmetics is NOT friendly to wallets. If you have a cosmetic addiction or so, please note that you are incredibly likely to be spending $200-$400 or more on the costume set. If you can control yourself and your wallet, you can spend much less.

The story is vast and hidden in little notes, little quest items, little encounters all around the map and at different times of the day.  Petting every cat, looking for anything to interact with, and being wary of the GOOSE OVERLORD. Surprises hidden in cups of wine, behind other faces, and etched in statues. 

There are definitely some poor optimizations but when having to consider all the different models of phones, PC hardware configurations, and consoles I'm not too surprised. The visuals are amazing. It's absolute peak cinema. I don't regret picking up the game I've had my eyes on since at least August 2022.

3- you get punished for not playing. lets say you run out of stuff to do( you will quickly). well, if you stop playing for a extended period of time, you start to lose things. that clan you made and cost to build up, gone due to inactivity. that sect you joined to try and unlock some cool abilities and items, oh no you de ranked and possibly got kicked and have to restart. that cool battle pass you are trying to grind, oh you missed a day, guess you gota restart or pay to continue.

overall, you get punished for playing too much by losing rewards, and you get punished for not playing enough by losing things you already earned or worked for. this games seems to be trying to force ride the line of "play every day, but only play 2 hours"

[h1]GER[/h1]

Zusammenfassung:

Das Spiel ist ein Mix aus viel zu vielen Games wie WoW, Final Fantasy, SoulsLike, Black Desert, Gacha, macht aber nichts davon wirklich gut. Durch die vielen verschiedenen Inhalte im Game, hat es vieles aber nichts vollständig gereift. Ich wollte es zwar mögen, jedoch überwiegt das negative und trübt den Spaß. Angefangen schon bei der grauenhaften Übersetzung und den vielen CS die ohne Lipsync auskommen (gesprochenes kommt nicht durch Lippen, geschlossene lippen und co.. eventuell ein Grafikbug der häufig vorkommt?). Ebenso ist es so, dass man absolut kein Gefühl dafür hat, dass man stärker wird. Sobald man aufsteigt, tuen es auch die Gegner und sind meistens auch stärker als einen, wobei es dann zu Gegnern kommt, bei denen man durchgehend draufeinschlagen muss, ohne dass man jemals mehr schaden als zuvor macht. Dann hätten wir noch die schlechte Questführung, die einen bei Sidequests zu Bossfights führt, die locker mal 30 level über einem sein können - das erfährt man natürlich erst im nachhinein wenn man dabei stirbt und gewarnt wird, nicht davor. Der Ingameshop ist ebenso sehr unübersichtlich und auch extrem teuer im vergleich zu anderen Gacha Games. Da ich mit dem Controller spiele, habe ich auch einige Bugs und Fehler was die anzeige der Tasten angeht (Rechte Tasten sind mit linken tasten im Tutorialfenster vertauscht, wie RB, RT...)

Fazit: Ein unfertiges Spiel das vieles sein möchte, aber nichts ist. Es ist ein überteuertes Gacha mit viel zu vielen Elementen die unausgereift sind und mehr Verwirrung als spaß bringen. Da gibt es definitiv bessere alternativen zu diesem hier... PS - Der Spieler wird immer als Männlich bezeichnet, das ist kein Übersetzungsfehler, da man als "Junger Herr" und co angeredet wird. Immer. Nicht sehr toll.

[h1]ENG[/h1]

The game is a mix of far too many games like WoW, Final Fantasy, SoulsLike, Black Desert, and Gacha, but it doesn't do any of them really well. Due to the many different elements in the game, it has a lot going for it, but nothing is fully developed. I wanted to like it, but the negatives outweigh the positives and spoil the fun. Starting with the terrible translation and the many CS that don't have lip sync (spoken words don't come through lips, closed lips, etc... possibly a graphics bug that occurs frequently?). It's also the case that you have absolutely no sense of getting stronger. As soon as you level up, so do your enemies, and they are usually stronger than you, which leads to enemies that you have to keep hitting without ever doing more damage than before. Then there's the poor quest guidance, which leads you to boss fights in side quests that can easily be 30 levels above you – of course, you only find this out after you die and are warned, not before. The in-game shop is also very confusing and extremely expensive compared to other gacha games. Since I play with a controller, I also have some bugs and errors regarding the button display (right buttons are swapped with left buttons in the tutorial window, such as RB, RT...).

Conclusion: An unfinished game that wants to be many things but is nothing. It's an overpriced gacha with far too many elements that are underdeveloped and cause more confusion than fun. There are definitely better alternatives to this one... PS - The player is always referred to as male; this is not a translation error, as you are addressed as “young man” and so on. Always. I never thought that I would find a game where my knowledge of Dao, Buddhism, Xianggi and general Chinese culture would have any effect on my results.  This is that game.

It cannot be defined by the easy, pre-defined categories.  It's some of this, some of that, and a lot of great artistry.

I am currently at the maximum character level, 95.  Lately, I've spent time in teams.

The keyboard combinations are difficult at times, but it is possible to make progress.  In deed, at 400+ hours, I still struggle with the keyboard combinations from time-to-time.  I don't rely on macros.  I've tried an Xbox controller and it has advantages, but perhaps, for me, the disadvantages are more than the advantages.

The open world is smaller than Genshin Impact, but it is also more realistic.  Puzzles are not entirely difficult but sometimes require speciality knowledge of Tao, Buddhism, or general Chinese culture.

The artwork is impressive, and art and music play a huge role in the latest expansion.  To enter a painting is to understand the lives of those in the painting.

There are many paths to take or you can just wander.  Collecting items early to build your armoury is important.  At higher levels, you could regret not taking great care in the early times.

The combat is good.  The testing of combat skills to elevate can be difficult, especially with the keyboard.  Profession is important.  Alliances with NPCs can also make your journey more worthwhile.

Since the game isn't just a game of one category, there are many focuses.  They don't charge you real money to play, but the Battle Pass can be enhanced.  It is truly a most interesting game with few limits.

I’ve been diving into Where Winds Meet lately, and wow—this game is something else. Imagine stepping into a living martial arts epic where every rooftop, every duel, and every whispered legend feels like it’s waiting for you to discover.
🎮 Gameplay
Combat is fluid and cinematic. You’re not just button-mashing—you’re stringing together sword strikes, mystical abilities, and acrobatic moves that make you feel like you’re starring in your own Wuxia movie. One moment you’re dueling on a cliffside, the next you’re sprinting across rooftops chasing down a rival.
🌐 Multiplayer Magic
Here’s the part that really hooked me: the world isn’t just yours. Other players are constantly around—sometimes allies, sometimes rivals. I’ve had moments where strangers jumped in to help me finish a tough boss fight, and other times where I got challenged to a duel in the middle of a bustling town square. It makes the game feel alive, unpredictable, and social in the best way.
You can join guilds, form bonds, or just wander together. There’s even a friendship system that tracks how close you get with other players, which adds a surprisingly personal touch.
🏮 The World
The setting is gorgeous—lush valleys, ancient temples, misty mountains. It’s the kind of world you want to explore slowly, but it’s also packed with quests, secrets, and random encounters that keep you moving.
⚖️ Pros & Cons
Pros:
- Stunning visuals and atmosphere
- Deep, stylish combat
- Multiplayer that feels organic and fun
- Tons of side activities and social features
Cons:
- Some quests feel uneven in quality
- Occasional bugs and audio hiccups
- Requires a stable connection (not great if your internet drops)
⭐ Final Thoughts
Where Winds Meet isn’t just a game—it’s a shared adventure. Whether you’re dueling strangers, teaming up with friends, or just soaking in the beauty of its world, it feels like you’re part of a living martial arts legend. If you’re looking for a game where other players can truly join your journey, this one delivers.

There really is no real sense of progression.

new era for co op gaming

- Visuals:
First of all, the game is very beautifully staged.
However the graphics are lacking a bit in terms of fidelity and consitency. The Level of details range is very narrow, therefore taking away from a smooth visual experience.
You should be able to change the detail range to your individual needs.
If you have a strong PC, then you shouldn't be locked into 5m Lod...

The Animations for the characters are pretty good, especially the fighting moves from the player character.
Classic chinese martial arts, stylish and effectively choreographed together.

- Audio:
I'm playing the game in chinese, and hearing the citizens in the streets talk, argue or fight makes the enviroment authentic and lively. In addition to that, is the relaxing music in the background which is a good contrast from the action in the game.

- Coop:
You will be able to cooperate with a friend or with an NPC in certain scenarios, but most of the game you will only be able to play solo.
The coop play in this game is rather restrictive, as in most MMOs.
You can travel around the map in coop, or go through some side quests.
Other than that, your friends are locked out of coop which is mind boggeling for me.
This descision is a great cause of frustration, for me and friends at least.
So if you are planning to play with a friend, then this game may not be the best one for that.

- The fighting system is a big topic:
It takes much from the Lies of P fighting System, where you are forced to parry the enemies attacks ( blocking at the moment of impact ) to reduce a poise meter, in order to cause a stagger when reduced completely, which then gives the player a relatively big opening window to unleash attacks.
You can also just block an attack, but it will still damage the character, so it is not a reliable option.
Dodging is also possible, as well as dodging in the last moment, basically in the same way as blocking and parrying,
but with the difference that dodging will not reduce the enemies poise.

The player is forced to parry because the enemies have gigantic health pools, coupled with the ability to just attack back at will while they are being hit, an ability that is exclusive to NPCs.
So dodging and counter attacking is not a successful tactic. You may do some damage, but it is negligible and not effective, especially when there is more than one enemy.
In addition to that, enemies have tracking hits, which can hit you even after moving out of the line of attack, by turning while striking, as if on ice.
There are also only a few moves which can stagger enemies, especially bosses. Usually you will get a small stagger after a 4 or 5 hit combo on a small enemy, but only a few moves work on bosses.
This results in the players inablillity to interrupt a potential attack from the opponent or in other words, you are not able to go on the offensive because it will be punished, which is what it ultimately comes down to with this kind of fighting system. Therefore you are expected to learn the whole moveset of an enemy, so you can parry it and then win.
This method means, that you will eventually fail to beat an enemy immediately, most of the time, especially when you are not experienced in these kind of games.

- Rant:
In my opinion, this was a very bad descision to just copy paste the "fighting system" from Lies of P.
I sill completed that game, and still consider it a very good game, but I wouldn't play it again.
Many aspects about it are good, but the main thing, the fighting system is the opposite of what I find fun.
Being passive and waiting for your turn is just frustrating.
On the other hand there are many people who love this game for said system, so shouldn't be a problem for too many.

- Conclusion:
I'm not through the story yet, but I have experienced the game enough to be able to come to a fair conclusion, which of course is just my own conclusion.
All in all the game is nice, when I look at it from a more objective perspective, but when I don't, the game sucks and it is a shame that so much potential seems to be going to waste, because of bad descisions.
It is a perfect mix of very positive aspects, and very negative ones.
But in every game there are  core aspects, which decide wheter or not the game will be a success or not.
The completely backwards fighting system and the restrictions for coop play are the biggest problems I see.
So is it worth playing?
It is when you are not like me and still enjoy the game despite all the criticism I have for it.
I'd give it a solid 5/10 points. Halve of it is beautiful, the other half is garbage.

I hope I could deliver an overview of the game, in a way that is informative and not too biased around my feelings towards it. If you are somebody who enjoys this game in its entirety, then don't bother and keep enjoying it.

As far as I can tell, the game itself is great — but I can’t recommend it because of one unbelievably simple design flaw: the game only allows [b]one[/b] character per account and you are [b]not[/b] allowed to delete your character 🤡.

I started on [i]Veteran[/i] difficulty to learn the basics — mechanics, combat, world, and systems. After a few hours, once I had gained enough confidence, I discovered that you cannot change the difficulty to [i]Legendary[/i]. Ever.

That means I’m permanently locked out of Legendary difficulty with that character. Well, fair enough, I thought. I’ll just delete my character and start over… except that’s also [b]not[/b] possible 🤡.

The only “solution” I’ve found is to create a brand-new [i]NetEase[/i] account, start over, and then contact customer support to rebind it to my [i]Steam[/i] account — which would also inevitably mean losing everything I got from the cash shop.

This is a bafflingly stupid restriction for a high-budget game that completely undermines the game's core design: its difficulty. And this issue is especially stupid since, according to people online, accounts in China have 6 character slots.

Until this is fixed, this game will sit on my digital shelf gathering digital dust.

[b]Update: More character slots are now available, and accounts are no longer difficulty locked.[/b]

From a mostly-solo POV:
Pros: 
Incredible story, great mission structure. You really get into your character as a person - they have a strong personality and great ties to the world. I cried several times during the main story. When my character was struggling emotionally so was I. Highly improved by the excellent voice-acting in Chinese.
Combat offers very fun options. In solo-play, mixing and matching styles is perfectly fine (e.g. both DPS and Healer). Be careful if you queue group dungeons - you may be slotted as something you're unprepared to actually play.
Only monetization is cosmetic. Character customization is excellent even without spending egregious amounts of money, or spending at all. 
Huge variety of content. The minigames are fun and help naturalize the setting.
Highly recommend for people who are fans of the Wuxia genre. The world feels just like stepping into your favourite cultivation novel/drama.

Cons:
Sects feel a little pointless at the moment, but the 1.2 update has already expanded sect and guild gameplay to incentivise more rolelplaying and multiplayer. 
Localization in the Kaifeng region is still a bit messy in places, but the Qinghe region is essentially flawless.
Menus take a while to understand. The UI is not particularly intuitive, especially if you haven't played an eastern mmo before. If you want to check your Exploration Skills, click on 'more details' under your combat score in the Develop tab. Took me forever to figure this out (not a searchable section).

Optimization on PC is still terrible. People with older devices (me) have to play multiplayer sections on mobile for proper performance. QOL options like limiting number of players loaded in/simpler map styles available on mobile/forcing simple outfits in co-op to reduce load are non-existent. Solo play is mostly still doable, and well worth it for the much better graphics on PC. Players with stronger setups complain that their visuals are heavily nerfed by comparison. No solid middleground or proper options for players yet.
