Overview:
I do absolutely love what they are trying to do but if it isn't one thing it's another with more bug's than Skyrim could hope to achieve. It feels behind on the times with clumsy camera & over saturated menu's but it's a world that needs living to go beyond the flaws.

Pros:
*Huge amount of customization (when it works properly).
*World: There is so much to explore & It's only early days. (English version is a joke, reasons below).
*Combat is very fast paced & almost souls like. The boss's are punishing & there are difficulty modes to try the Buddha's patience.
*Story (Was better in Chinese but the subtitles have no size option)
*Huge amount of things to do: Crafting, Building, Adventure, Fishing, Treasure hunting, Solo campaign, Co-op modes, MMO options, Trials, Challenges, PvP/PvE Grind grind grind.

Cons:
*The English version is a joke (The main quest's are great but anything outside of that is very sporadic & makes the world feel empty with lack of voicing. The AI is even worse as it does most of the work in the world for voicing & it just never sounds like it fit's in the game, maybe in some futuristic game like Cyberpunk with AI everywhere but in this world it spoils the game completely. (One of the most useless English Dub's I have ever played).
*Settings: There are no sliders/options for screen text/subtitles size, which makes it hard to keep up with when you play with a controller from further away. Also a few other things in the menu for optimization like an FOV slider would be nice.
**It's a 12+ game with a dating/marriage system? So that's stuff I avoid. (Won't go recommended until this changes).
*This game just like any game from NETEASE is a whale farm. Constantly cycling through very expensive cosmetics & has 2x paid passes, 1 for in game currency & one battle pass but they removed all the re-purchase currency so you need real world money every time.
*That brings me to one of my major hates of the game & that is the capping. There are daily, weekly, monthly & season caps for XP, currency, PvE rewards, exploration, level, gear, skills. You name it, they capped it. So in all the game rewards the metered play but anything after that is 0%!
*The lag in multiplayer, especially with the cross server option selected is so bad you are in a battle of who does the most DMG while the other is frozen (In smaller modes this manifest's through interaction lag & combat/skill delay).
*The co-op as a whole is From Soft vibe rather than being easy & accessible, so this is an invite system for certain tasks which then disband after completion instead of any kind of full co-op. Works but could be so much better.
*The menu's are so vast that there are menus in menus in menus in menus & to make it worse the translations can be a bit off. It works but is not well thought out & can be too much for some people.
*The AI chat in the game is I suppose something to expand on player interaction/roleplay but it is garbage when there is a mission held by a chat gpt character that needs to be prompted correctly. To be fair it makes you miss selectable options & shows how AI is making developers lazy & game content bland. (Note I have no problem with this system on all general non interactive NPC's so you get conversation out of 100% of the worlds inhabitant's but any quest related stuff should still follow the tried & tested method of dialogue selection options rather that random chat prompt's which are not guaranteed to generate the quest/content).

Conclusion:
I'm going to be playing. It's F2P so it's always worth trying but because of the deep rooted issue in the game age rating with marriage I absolutely can not recommend this game right now but I'll be hoping in future updates that might change.

It's a great game. It's beautiful and interesting, which makes it all the more sad that after a couple of months of playing, there's literally nothing to do. The map is cleared, the quests are completed, the equipment is polished to perfection, and the bosses fall at a glance. What's next? 
1) I believe that the developers should focus more on interesting multiplayer activities like Guild Wars. The current format of guild wars is not very viable. Firstly, why is there so little???? Why only on Saturday and Sunday, and so late??? There's nothing to do in your game, and the online player count is already low, but you're literally shooting yourself in the foot with this restriction. WHY???? 

The proposed solution is to redesign the game. Instead of a personalized activity for guilds, it should be a general activity for all players. In this case, something needs to be done to manage the large number of players. Currently, this responsibility lies with the guild leaders. To expand the scope of battles to other players, consider implementing a "role-based" system similar to other moba games. This would allow players to choose their roles and form separate teams responsible for specific areas. People who break the rules of their role for no reason get a penalty and a rank down. Your like and dislike system is perfect for this. 
This is about PvP, now let's talk about PvE.

2) The energy-based system is an anachronism that should be removed from games and forgotten like a bad dream. People only come in once every three days to drain their energy on the boss, and that's it. Again, there's a lack of online presence. Okay, if you like the concept of energy, fine, keep it. But make sure it's not the primary reason for people to log in. Allow them to earn rewards for defeating bosses without expending energy. What's the point? Let the reward for energy be immeasurably high, compared to the rewards for killing bosses without spending energy. For example, the chance of getting gold equipment from bosses by spending energy is 30%. However, the chance of getting the same gold equipment without spending energy is only 3%. What does this smell like? Grind! You got it right. If you want top-notch online gaming, you need to force people to perform in-game activities endlessly to reach higher levels. Speaking for myself, I truly enjoy farming bosses in multiplayer. However, it's sad to do it for no reason. So give me and the other players a reason to farm these bosses for days on end and improve their equipment. Increase the number of bosses for farming, let the players have more choice.

Unfortunately, I'm not good at game development, and I may not know some fundamental points. All of the above is a concept, an idea. And I want to believe that my ideas will be at least partially implemented in the games. The odds are near zero, but still...

I guess I'll write my review now. So, for the cost, it's hard to find a meaningful reason to avoid this game. I would definitely recommend playing.

My main comments on the game are as follows:
I would only recommend the solo content. The quests, exploration, and story are all A+ and I would absolutely love to experience more. I would even pay for it. There's easily 200+ hours of content you get in solo for absolute free, as almost all of the microtransactions are cosmetics. You can enjoy coop if you want, as well as make yourself miserable playing legend mode. I'm sticking to legend, as painful as it is, because I just couldn't live with myself knowing other people are playing a harder difficulty. Even if I've died 600 times already.

This leads to the complaints I have on the game. For starters, legend difficulty (and maybe the easier ones? I'm not sure) is just not enjoyable. Every boss fight is essentially the same thing, sit and wait to parry. There is absolutely no point trying to attack, there's no reason to level up skills or talents or arts. The only thing you do in every boss fight is parry. In my opinion, this is just stupid. I know plenty of people are having fun with it and to each their own, though. 

Online content is unbearable. As plenty of others have said, if you're not playing with a group or with friends, playing with randoms is awful. PVP is awful, mostly because you're likely playing with 200+ms ping in a game where millisecond parries are half the gameplay. You're forced into several online things regardless of if you want to be or not, with no way out for some reason. I just want to play for the story but I got arrested and had to sit in online jail with other people because someone falsely accused me of poaching? What? 

Lastly the bane of all these gacha games. Energy. There is just simply no defense for it whatsoever, it has never, ever, ever been a positive point of any game it has ever been included in. It was only ever started to sell energy through microtransactions, but this game doesn't even let you buy it if you wanted to. You just have to wait for your energy to come back to farm equipment. Completely insane. Tons of other online games let you farm gear as much as you want with absolutely no drawback, why even bother putting an energy system in when no one enjoys it and you're not even trying to make money off of it?

I could go on with complaints. There's a hundred things to nitpick, but honestly if you go in expecting to play the story and campaigns and quests on a reasonable difficulty, it really is a fabulous game. 

TLDR; The gear system is awful, online is awful, farming is awful. The story, quests, and world are great.

I came into this wanting to love the game, largely due to the review defining the character arc of a healer in the making coming full-circle. <chef's kiss> Any review that begins "My first hours in this game were an unhinged sitcom starring me, a bear, and several medical emergencies," surely heralds a fanTAStic gaming experience!

However.
A few scant minutes into the tutorial, I was faced with my first boss fight and about a dozen different combat instructions to keep track of. I am not a fan of this kind of combat, but OK, there's more than just combat to the game - surely. I asked my GPT "is there more to this game than fighting," and I was assured there is plenty to keep me coming back.

Killed off the Void King (only because I was literally not allowed to die any of the 87 hectobazillion times I should have - and the six times I deliberately tried to die just to end it) --  only to immediately find another combat tutorial with even more to keep track of. NOPE. Not for me. Wiped hands, walked away.

A note for the devs: If there is significantly more to this game than combat, you're alienating a lot of people like me who Just Aren't That Into Fighting by throwing a frustrating boss fight at us a few moments into the game. Get us hooked a little first, show us what the game is about - THEN make us endure the combat if we like what we've seen. 

Although, if fighting is the backbone of the game, it's good to get that right out of the way up-front so we can move on. Well done.

This may be the best free to play game I've ever played or that has been released. With that said, you really need to know exactly what you're getting. Yes, it does have some multiplayer features but it's not really a true MMO. There isn't a very strong "end game" at all. It's just a few bosses you can fight and that's about it. 

Once you've exhausted all of the games content (I still haven't with close to 200 hours played) you're basically left with about 10 to 20 minutes of content a day due to an energy system. The only point of this is to get better gear or rolls but honestly it's not needed. It's just to see numbers go up when you're out of other stuff to do. I suppose you can grind the PvP arena if you'd like. That requires no energy what so ever. 

To me the game is basically a mix up of Assassin Creed or Ghost of X games with some Dark Souls type combat (though more forgiving with aids you can enable if you choose). 

There are so many different mini games you can play throughout the game. A lot of social features and puzzle type dungeons you can run. Literally thousands of chests scattered about the world to find as well as numerous other things.

There is of course a main story you can follow and then numerous side quests with their own stories. The world is very expansive and beautiful. 

It's just a very unique game and one that is easy to get sucked into. 

As stated though, just have the mind set that it's a AAA single player game with the ability to see others online at times. If you look at it that way you won't be upset that the content will eventually dry up while you wait for the devs to release more. 

I should mention the one con the game has imo. That's the UI. While it's not impossible to navigate it IS very intimidating as a new player. There are menus beyond menus, beyond menus. It can really take a bit before you get used to it and understand everything there is on offer. I was discovering new menus 100+ hours into the game. 

To end, I just can't believe this game is free. I really can't. It's truly given me an Assassin Creed type game with Dark Souls light combat that has hundreds and hundreds of hours of fleshed out content. ALL for free. Yes, there is a cash shop but every single thing you can buy is 100% cosmetic. There isn't a single thing that's remotely pay to win in it.
Hard to complain about a FREE game with this much depth, story-telling, and AAA-game level graphics.

This is my first review of a game on Steam that I want to comment on.

This game surprised me in a very positive way. I installed the game just to test it — it’s free to play, so why not?
I had never played games in this genre before, but with this game I discovered that this genre actually suits me very well and lets me have a lot of fun in soulslike games.

The game looks very beautiful. The map has a lot of hidden spots, quests, and stunning areas. It doesn’t feel empty at all — in every corner you may find something. There are many NPCs running around, living their lives and making the world feel alive. The quests are interesting, and both side quests and main quests are enjoyable.

For a free-to-play game, the amount of time I could spend just playing solo is amazing, without the need to buy anything. Of course, you can buy premium items and bonuses if you like, but it isn’t necessary for solo play. If you just want a story-driven game with the option of multiplayer or co-op, it’s totally doable and enjoyable without paying.

I recommend the game and I’m grateful to be a part of it. I already had many great hours in the game, and I’m sure there will be many more. I believe there is potential for everyone to find something they can enjoy because of all the different things you can do in this game.

Give it a try — it’s free, nothing to lose! ♥

TL;DR: The GAMEplay, the meat of the game, is genuinely amazing & incredibly solid, same with the graphics. HOWEVER the way how they monetize their game is incredibly scummy; they monetize gambling, scummy prices where you have to buy 1 tier higher worth of premium currency cuz the items are a tad too expensive, and they also utilize FOMO (Fear Of MIssing Out). I HAVE NO QUALMS ON OTHER PEOPLE ENGAGING WITH THE SYSTEM, I JUST BOTH PERSONALLY & ON PRINCIPLE WISH THESE PRACTICES OUTRIGHT DIDN'T EXIST IN THEIR GAMES.

If I could I'd give this a "Mixed" review. It does a lot of things right, but also a lot of things wrong.

I'll start off with what it does right: The combat is very enjoyable, there's quite a lot to do in the open world such as fishing & drunken minigames, resources to farm & collectibles to find, mini-quests you find as you explore, and you can even build wherever you want! The story is fairly solid too! No comment about thr graphics tho, cuz my PC is out of spec, so I have to play at lowest setting to play LOL.

Also its Free & No Pay-2-Win soiling the fun.

Now with the negatives.

First off its a Chinese NetEase game, so no surprise there's gambling (I'm calling it for what it is) and scummy pricing where Dress A costs 680 Pearls but oop! You can buy 600 pearls for $5, which is a few pearls short, making me have to buy $10 amount of Pearls. Also has FOMO, or items you can either gamble or purchase for a limited time. IM NOT INHERENTLY AGAINST MICROTRANSACTIONS, I'M SPECIFICALLY AGAINST SCUMMY MONETIZATION PRACTICES, AND THEY CROSSED EVERY LINE.

Second, the UI is atrocious. Just like any other "Gotcha" games, there's so many different menus everywhere, its a damn maze. Figuring out where to reach one of the many shops was a maze & a half. Sure they do give pop-ups that take you there, but that's IF they appear cuz you either need an item or it popped up due to an event. The fact there's several different premium currencies & shops for each of them isn't helping either.

Third, there ARE issues with the gameplay despite my praises, but not many fortunately.

1. There's a Legend difficulty that you can select, but only at the beginning and downgrading to any easier difficultly PERMANENTLY locks you out of Legend. This would've made sense if we had multiple characters, but we don't.
1a. Also according to public info, higher difficultlies have enemies with higher HP, and Legend scales their HP between 200% to 400%! I love difficult challenges, but this isn't one of them. I played on Legend and all the enemies & bosses felt alright, until I started facing bosses post-Qiyang content. Bosses from that point had SO much health, that it felt like my abilities & weapons stopped mattering & the only way to meaningfully do anything against them was to constantly parry them to drain their Qi to EVENTUALLY open them up to finishers. Parrying is cool, but I don't want that to be the only way to play against bosses.
2. For some reason YOU CAN'T ACCESS SETTINGS UNTIL YOU BEAT THE TUTORIAL. WHY?!?
3. Movement feels like I'm controlling a tank, so its sometimes difficult to do precise movement.

A great game with a lot of potential hindered by some technical issues and bugs.

It is, quite frankly, one of the best adaptations of the wuxia genre to video game form. If you are looking for a game that captures the essence of Chinese martial arts fiction, this is the game for you. Even if you are unfamiliar with the genre, it is generally well done fantasy action game. The singleplayer and multiplayer are  fairly seperate, in that nothing in the singleplayer experience is specifically locked behind the multiplayer. Multiplayer leans more towards an mmo-style game, with boss raids and team PvE experiences, but the rewards can still be obtained in the singleplayer modes.

Where it falls short is on the technical side of things. The game has issues with rendering, pop-ins and loading textures that has the potential to break immersion. The game looks good and area can look downright gorgeous at times, but that comes at the cost of optimization.

Navigating the UI and the various mechanics of the game (i.e., stats) is unintuitive for newer players, and an external guide is recommended to have a less confusing experience.

As a free game, microtransactions are expected, though they are thankfully mainly relegated for cosmetics. There is both a gacha/gambling system where you can roll for outfits, as well as a way to directly purchase outfits with paid-for in-game currencies.

Overall, I would still recommend the game since it is free and the only thing you would be investing is your time. If it piques your interest and you've got the hardware, I would suggest giving it a try.

Besides the 16 miles of menus that need endlessly slipping through just to find basic things, the game itself is extremely well crafted. There's a brilliant balance of difficulty for different kinds of players and I don't mean the token difference you get in most games where 'story mode' is just as much fighting but a bit less difficult - this game adds layers of assists and lower difficulty that ensures that those who want a real Storymode *actually get one*. No being forced into PvP even for 'tutorials' either - You pick story mode, get used to spending your time hunting for butterflies and plants, helping sick geese, reading historical explanations of life in ancient China and enjoying those dopamine hits as you tally up all the menus that have little red markers of joy attached to them.

Not to mention the music is perfect - not too repetitive that you notice the drone after 5 hours but not so energetic you feel like you ran a marathon after 2. And the visuals are absolutely stunning, even on a laptop (although I'm running a 5070 but still). I can't recall how many times I just stopped and spent time staring at the screen as the sunlight moved across landscapes and shadows moved with it, changing the way the whole area looks.

If you ever played Age of Wushu or Age of Kung Fu, you’ll feel right at home. This is that experience—fully modernized and clearly trained by a grandmaster who min-maxed polish. Chinese wuxia (Kung Fu era) lore is my all-time favorite genre, and this game doesn’t just hit the mark—it roundhouse-kicks it into the next server. 9.7/10 for a modern MMO.

The AI-driven NPC conversations are the first thing that stand out. These characters don’t just idle until you press “Accept Quest.” They talk, react, and carry on whether you’re watching or not—because yes, it’s an MMO and the world absolutely keeps spinning without you. Genius design. Even better, there’s a ton to do beyond the usual gear grind and PvP hamster wheel.

The world itself is immersive, beautiful, and alive. And not in a “pretending to be alive” way—this thing is living its own life while you’re offline. Side stories range from genuinely hilarious to full-on emotional damage, sometimes back-to-back. Laugh, cry, then check your inventory in silence.

Now let’s talk about the part that feels illegal: this game is free on Steam. Free. As in “Did I miss a catch?” No. It belongs in the same quality tier as some of the industry’s biggest names. While it doesn’t quite reach the universally familiar, near-perfect status of GTA V, Red Dead Redemption 2, or Skyrim V, it comfortably sits alongside Horizon Forbidden West, Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag, The Witcher 3, SWTOR, and The Elder Scrolls Online.

Here’s the shocker: I usually don’t like Asian MMOs. They tend to be grindy enough to qualify as a long-term relationship. Somehow, the devs avoided that trap and delivered something that respects your time. The only reason this isn’t a full 10 is that it’s rooted in a period-specific genre that’s culturally foreign to many Western players. Meanwhile, GTA lets you cause traffic accidents, Red Dead lets you be depressed on a horse, and Skyrim lets you yell at dragons—comfortably familiar experiences.

The main storyline is a roller coaster. Boss fights and raids are challenging, short, and sweet—no bloated encounters that overstay their welcome. As the story unfolds, you genuinely feel like an integral part of it, which is rare for MMOs and rarer in real life.

Solo players are well covered too. With AI companions and adjustable difficulty, you can raid entirely on your own or tackle everything with friends and guildmates. Whether you’re in the mood for teamwork or peaceful monk energy, the game accommodates you.

All things considered, this game has a very strong year ahead—though it’s hard to imagine how the developers will top what they’ve already accomplished. That’s a good problem to have.

Where Winds Meet is a strong showing overall, offering a solid amount of content and an experience that feels worthwhile if you enjoy action RPGs with a cinematic flair. From a South African perspective, the game largely holds up, though a few technical realities do affect how it plays locally.

The gameplay itself is good, with enough content to keep you busy and engaged. Combat feels satisfying, exploration is rewarding, and there’s a clear sense of care put into the world and its systems.

That said, co-op is unfortunately buggy. Playing with friends revealed issues tied to a non peer-to-peer connection, which can lead to instability and occasional frustration—something that’s especially noticeable when connecting over long distances.

PvP is manageable, but South African players should expect 180ms+ ping in most cases. It’s playable and not a total dealbreaker, but it does put you at a disadvantage in tighter encounters and competitive moments.

Where the game truly shines is in its visuals and music. The environments are stunning, richly detailed, and atmospheric, while the soundtrack complements the world beautifully and elevates the overall experience.

Final Verdict:
Where Winds Meet is an enjoyable game with strong presentation and decent depth, held back slightly by co-op instability and latency challenges for SA players.

Score: 7/10

This game is not for the faint of heart and feels more like a second Job then something fun.  I am quitting this game.  The game is for Hardcore gamers.  If you are a Casual gamer (and want to keep your sanity/have fun) you will want to avoid this game.
1.  The boss fights take several hours/days to learn and are in multiple stages.  Stages in which if you die in stage 2 or 3 will be sent back to stage 1 to start all over again.
2.  There is the poor implementation of the parrying mechanic where you hope it will work.
3.  The Story bosses (and even some enemies) scale with your level which is not usually a bad thing. In this game it is.  At around Level 50+, they scale way beyond anything I have ever seen.  If you miss the parry/dodge/deflection you will get one shotted.  NOTE:  I tested the Trial Boss which I can beat.  Then move to the same Story Boss and get one shotted.  Definitely a coding/scaling issue.  Even people in China are complaining about this issue (a year ago till today) and they still have not fixed it. 
4.  Another issue is the interface is very disorganized.  You have shops all over the place.   The multiple Journal interfaces and multiple "gated" sects (bad concept how they implemented it.  Just have guilds and/or the ability to join multiple sects).  Very confusing.
5.  Gated areas are also a very bad idea.  MMOs don't have gated areas and are open world.  Video games are gated.
6.  As you guessed I want to talk about the Gotcha (Gambling) shop.  Having such a concept in-game is bad business.  You have the whales spending thousands of dollars (Yes, you heard me right.  Look it up) on special cosmetics for the game.  People (which is most of us) who can not spend that type of money will have FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out) and quit due to lack of respect.  NOTE:  I always like to support a game and buy their subscription, cosmetics, etc.  It is disappointing that the "Worthy" cosmetics people want cost thousands of dollars.

First 4 hours in this world and I’m already questioning reality:

1) Spend 20 minutes in character creation, make a creature that looks like it crawled out of the wrong dynasty
2) Immediately thrown into a gorgeous cutscene next to NPCs who look like they stepped out of a wuxia drama
3) Decide to “politely” test my martial arts on wildlife
4) Get bodied by a tiger, sprain my ankle, bruise three ribs and somehow poison myself with flowers
5) Try to do a heroic escape, accidentally roll down a hill and land on a fisherman’s rice pot
6) Apologize by catching fish for him, instead pull out a boot and a wooden bucket
7) Wander into a village doctor who tells me my blood pressure is “concerning for someone my age”
8) Learn basic martial healing and immediately try it on random townsfolk
9) Accidentally cure a guy’s cold and gain EXP like I meant to do it
10) Meet a player who introduces himself as “Silent Monk,” heals my injuries, then asks for a duel
11) He turns out to be anything BUT silent and beats me so badly I contemplated uninstalling
12) He bows respectfully, leaves, and I swear I heard him laugh through the wind
13) Decide right there that I’m becoming the greatest healer the world has ever seen
14) Grind every herb, every quest, every poor injured NPC unlucky enough to cross my path
15) Eventually able to cure poison, fever, anxiety, and probably heartbreak
16) Start joining random sessions: heal → bow → duel → exit
17) People in world chat start calling me “that guy in green who hits hard AFTER healing you”
18) Begin receiving invites every few minutes
19) Finally get a whisper from Silent Monk asking for treatment
20) Cure his disease in record time… and we duel again
21) After the closest fight of my life, I win with 2 HP and a dream
22) He bows once more and disappears into the mountains

I am now the Wind-touched wandering doctor-warrior I always dreamed of.

Great world building and main story, but the side stories are where it really shines. The world feels alive, but it also means you are not spoon fed all the information, you have to piece things together and pay attention to actually know what is going on. Combat is mostly fluid, though the parry mechanic does feel a bit confusing at times.  Also, this game really is built for those who like to explore, the map is chock full of stuff to do or explore. While it does get repetitive eventually, it took me well over 70 hours to feel anything like that, and by that point I think it is fine, you can only bring in so much variation. Even God of War got pretty repetitive by the time I finished it, and I played it for a lot less time. You always have something else to do in this game if you look for it. 
The game also runs pretty well on my 14 inch laptop with RTX 3060 mobile, and I can still play at a reasonable fps for most parts of the map at 1440p. The city in Kaifeng is where it really struggles, but it is also the largest of all cities with a living population that i have seen in any game so far. Most games make their cities either as a ruin/decaying structure, or the population is just there as ghosts, you can't interact with them. This city sets itself apart, it is full of stuff to do, though it may be a bit boring at times, It makes sense considering the activities for the time period. 


Some problems - 
For now, a lot of the dialogues are muted, or AI made for English version, so I would recomment the chinese voice instead. The muted part is understandable as a cost cutting/time saving measure for small side missions. 
The second problem is the weirdly designed menu. It has menues inside a menu inside a menu, and if you want to find it again, good luck. You do get used to it after some time, but even after 100+ hours in the game, I still sometimes find there is another hiding somewhere for something. 
The game is great as a solo game, but the MMO part of it feels weirdly dated. I guess it's mostly there for showing off skins you have unlocked. It also means you can mostly ignore the MMO part if you don't like it. 

Overall, Where Winds Meet has insane quality considering it is a free to play game. The paid gacha parts of it are not needed to play the game, they are cosmetic only. They do have some nice skins though, so maybe worth it for all the whales out there.

I went into Where Winds Meet expecting another flashy wuxia MMO that looks great and then quietly falls apart once the honeymoon ends. That did not happen.

This game rewards curiosity and patience in a way most modern games do not. Exploration actually matters. The world feels intentional, not just big for the sake of being big. Where Winds Meet is an action RPG with online and multiplayer elements. In my opinion, it’s a very good game with a few serious flaws that keep it from reaching its full potential.

[b]The good[/b]
The story, atmosphere, and open world are extremely impressive - arguably better than most AAA open-world games we’ve seen in recent years. The gameplay and combat system are easy to learn but hard to master. There are many different weapon types and martial arts styles, each of which plays differently - and you can learn them all (if you have the resources and time to grind). The boss fights are particularly memorable, each boss is unique, many have multiple phases, and several encounters feel very cinematic. There are also plenty of well-designed side quests, challenges, dungeons, and enemy camps to clear. Overall, the solo experience is awesome.

[b]What could and should be better[/b]
Weapon and level progression are generally confusing and heavily dependent on RNG. With enough time and some online tutorials, you can learn how to build your character effectively, but you really shouldn’t need external guides to understand basic systems. A big part of this confusion comes from the user interface. The game is jokingly called “Where Menus Meet,” and that description is unfortunately accurate - this game desperately needs a cleaner UI design. 
On top of that, certain UI translations are vague or unclear, meaning you often have to click something just to see what it does and hope the action can be undone. Speaking of translation: the English voice lines are terrible. Many lines are missing, some don’t match the subtitles, and others sound clearly AI-generated, sometimes even using the wrong voice pack so it doesn’t even sound like English. This ruins many cutscenes and makes the story difficult, and sometimes impossible, to follow. If you truly want to understand the narrative, you’ll probably need to watch an explanation on YouTube.
Next, the online modes (like Perception Forest, Arena, Guild Wars, etc.) is full of exploiters, cheaters, bot farmers and smurf accounts. If you are a hardcore PvP player, you might like it, but for casual or PvE players it's one of the worst places to be and many of the isses, that plagued this modes since the beginning, are still present almost a year later.

[b]The questionable (and somewhat shady) things[/b]
The game is free to play, and right now the only things you have to pay for are cosmetics. There are a few free outfits you unlock naturally through the story, and if those are enough for you, you never need to spend any money.
However, the moment you engage with paid cosmetics, things become questionable. The gacha system feels outright predatory, with extremely low chances of obtaining useful or desirable items. The listed rates for pulling a legendary (the featured outfit) are incredibly low, meaning that unless you get unbelievably lucky, you may need to spend $200 or more - and for limited outfits, potentially up to $700.
Directly purchasable outfits are better, but still expensive, ranging from $10 to $50. To be fair, you can earn vouchers to reduce the price and even stack them for up to a 50% discount, but these vouchers are rare and usually require daily logins and some gacha participation to obtain.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Where Winds Meet is a fantastic game that could be truly outstanding if its bugs and translation issues were fixed. It surpasses many recent AAA titles, it’s free to play, and currently there is no pay-to-win aspect. However, I strongly recommend staying away from the gacha system—it’s clearly predatory and an enormous money sink.

[h1]Where Winds Meet — I Didn’t Expect This to Pull Me In Like It Did[/h1]

I went into [b]Where Winds Meet[/b] blind and curious, having played similar genre games but not fully sure what to expect. A few hours later, I realized I was completely absorbed, not just playing the game, but in the world. It's been a long time since I pulled some degen hours to keep playing a game.

This is one of those rare games that slows you down in the best way and makes you want to explore, listen, and actually exist in the setting. Which makes you lose track of time 100%.

I will list some of my favourite parts of the game as well as interesting unique things that I haven't seen in a while when it comes down to online, mmorpg/coop games.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The World Feels Alive[/h2]

The first thing that really hit me was the atmosphere. The landscapes are genuinely beautiful, but more importantly, they feel [i]intentional[/i].

[list]
[*]Quiet villages that feel lived-in
[*]Wide variety of NPC's and side quests that feel refreshing
[*]Mountains and fields that make you want to wander off the path and explore
[*]Weather and lighting that completely change how places feel
[/list]

I caught myself stopping just to look around more than once, not because the game told me to with a cutscene or an obvious marker, but because it felt right.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Combat That Feels Like Martial Arts, Not Button-Mashing[/h2]

Combat is easily one of my favorite parts of the game. Feels a lot like souls-like games, or even akin (very slightly) to Sifu, time your dodges, blocks or parries. Make sure you utilize your attack windows properly and dont get too greedy in a fight because you will get shot down.

It’s fluid, stylish, and incredibly satisfying once it clicks. Every fight feels like a small duel rather than a button smasher.

[list]
[*]Martial arts styles feel distinct
[*]Movement and positioning actually matter
[*]Fights look and feel cinematic without being overwhelming
[*]The learning curve is quite easy to catch but hard to master
[*]There is lots of tutorials both in game and outside that help you incredibly
[/list]

Winning a fight feels earned, and losing usually feels like my own fault, which I honestly appreciate. Although it might be frustrating to lose bossfights, you learn to adapt and it feels rewarding when you just get it right.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Story & Quests That Respect Your Time[/h2]

The story doesn’t shove itself down your throat, and I mean that as a compliment. It unfolds naturally as you explore, talk to people, and take on quests. Even side content often feels meaningful instead of filler. You move to next areas of the map and it feels tied in with the previous 'chapter' the main story line is not dreadful or long and you can skip most of it if its not your style of play.

[list]
[*]Strong themes around identity, honor, and choice
[*]Side quests that feel grounded and human
[*]A world that reacts in subtle ways to what you do
[*]Avaliable interactive map that shows you everything that you can do to complete an 'area'
[*]Characters that feel likeable/dislikeable which brings meaning to the story
[*]AI NPC that you can literally ROLEPLAY with and (most of the time) reply in comprehensive manners that feel truthful to the world around them
[/list]

I found myself paying attention to dialogue instead of skipping it, which says a lot with these kinds of games.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Sound & Mood[/h2]

The soundtrack deserves a mention because it does so much heavy lifting emotionally.

[list]
[*]Calm, traditional-inspired music that fits the setting perfectly
[*]Ambient sounds that make exploration feel peaceful and immersive
[*]Combat audio that adds weight without being noisy
[/list]

This is absolutely a “wear headphones and get lost” kind of game.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Freedom & Exploration[/h2]

What I love most is how little the game tries to rush you. You can wander, climb, fight, investigate, or just exist in the world at your own pace. It really captures the feeling of being a wandering martial artist forging your own path.

[list]
[*]Exploration feels rewarding
[*]Plenty of hidden moments and quiet discoveries
[*]Multiple ways to approach situations
[*]It doesn't waste your time and rewards feel hefty
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

[b]Where Winds Meet[/b] feels like a game made with genuine care for its world and genre. It’s beautiful without being forceful, deep without being exhausting, and immersive without trying too hard.

If you enjoy open-world RPGs, wuxia themes, or games that let you slow down and sink in, this is an easy recommendation from me.

[h3]Score: 9/10[/h3]

I don't usually bother writing reviews, but this game is one that is worthy of a good review to help spread the word. 

The highlight of this game is the immersion into the Wuxia/Jianghu world which it did pretty well on. It's a very popular and mainstream entertainment genre across multiple media in China, such as novel, movies, and now games. This also leads to a weakness of the game if you will, in that if you aren't Chinese, or aren't familiar with this culture/backdrop, you are likely to miss out on half if not more of what the game has to offer, it really is a integral part of the game. Even translation will not be able to convey the meaning/cultural significance of a lot of the dialogues and story. Keep that in mind.

The graphics/cinematics are also nice, but do realize that it could use a bit more polishing compared to some of the top notch AAA games. It's by no means a bad game, but you will see a bit of rusty graphic/cinematic scenes and weird renderings here and there throughout the game.

Combat is pretty satisfying for the most part, it's fast paced and somewhat Sekiro/Soul like, it's definitely not as difficult as those games, but it's got some elements and style similar to those games. After learning a certain boss's moves and timing on parry, it's a fulfilling achievement to defeat them with fluid moves and gameplay.

There is a bit of grinding to it, it's what recent Chinese games have adopted in a lot of their online games, especially in the Gacha scene. It's made popular by the Mihoyo series of games, and there's a bit of it here in this game as well. You don't have to grind though, you can take it slow. The grind affects your skills and gears etc, so it does make a difference in your overall combat effectiveness, but if you are playing PvE/teaming up with other players to fight bosses, it's not a big deal, just take your time and enjoy the journey.

Overall this game is really good, deserves to be way more popular than it is known right now, and some of the stories will make you tear up and reflect on life in general. It's got philosophical concepts that might be harder to understand not played in Chinese, and it's got touching/sad moments that make you really think and ponder. It's a game built with actual effort and heart that's not your typical assembly line AAA games like AC etc.

And lastly, it is FREE! Can you imagine? Getting a AAA like action RPG game with lot of exploration, content, side quests, dialogues, characters, beautiful world with significant historical/cultural backdrop from around 10th-11th century ancient China, all for FREE!

Let me end the review with this, IGN gave this game a 6/10, and indeed, you can't spell ignorant without IGN. GG, GL and HF!

OK so i have played a couple of hours and I am mixed in my feeling towards this game, do not get me wrong I am having fun so far and as such I DO recommend you try this game for yourself it is free after all. 
Below I have tried my best to compile my thoughts on this game in a pros and cons.


Pros: 
Great looking game - a little on the intense side for a low end PC but my laptop manages.

Lots of content for the early game but not so much your overwhelmed too badly.
Really fun solo experiance so far.

Solo and multiplayer options to play the game, this is amazing and i wish all MMO style games had a option like this, Solo play is very story driven but is also such an amazing experience that you will want to actually play it, as for online multiplayer content there seems to be a open world aspect otherwise its dungeons and events mostly at least for the early game I am in.

Combat, this i a chinese martial art game done right, the fights are visually amazing and super easy to learn yet its seems that mastering it will be difficult (which is a good thing) there is a level of focus and practice needed to get the timings and flow of battle just right but once you got it it feels so damn rewarding.

Armor and weapons - firstly the designs, they look amazing from the starter gear to end game the game devs spent so much effort and care when designing everything that it all feels right and natural, no tiny metal bikinis on females (OMG thank you devs for this I really appreciate this aspect), everything looks like it belongs in the most natural way i have ever seen in a MMO.

---

Cons:
Story is very confusing at times, i honestly believe its mostly because i play with english translated scenes and they feel like they are missing context/content and I feel these issues are not there in the localized version but im having to fill in alot of gaps with my imagination to the point that i just simply checked out of the story all together, its simpler and easier to just follow the quest markers and the cutscenes have been so buggy that i know im missing almost half of the dialog lines. (this could very much be a me thing)

Online.... holy hell... i have been on the online part of this game for at MOST a hour so far and well, My personal opinion is just avoid it, 90% of players good people that will enhance the game for you but you still get the players that cant help but abuse the open Mic that is in all public areas, thats right when your in a public space anyone can say anything they want to you over open mic anywhere, if your streaming DO NOT enter a open play zone or room unless your willing to risk a platform ban, in the first 10 mins on being in a multiplayer room i heard enough players screaming out slurs and words that will get your twitch or youtube account banned a thousand times over, you have been warned.

Online combat ... if you live somewhere that suffers from high ping in most games (im australian, you dont get worse than our internet) then simply DO NOT bother trying to fight anything, i have never had a attack trigger faster than 5 seconds AFTER i hit the button, the lag WILL ruin your game, anywhere with decent internet and you should be good to fight all you want but this remains a con for me due to how laggy it is.

---

Conclusion - for me personally I really like the game so far its a bummer about the online side being so unplayable but the Solo content has more than made up for it for me even without the online parts its a freaking fun game, i have a few mates that play this game online together and they have a absolute blast with each other so the online side is also super fun just not for myself due to my ping but hey thats fine, its free.

A Beautiful Journey into Chinese Martial Arts and Culture

"Where Winds Meet" is an exceptional role-playing game that truly captures the essence of Chinese martial arts and cultural heritage. From the moment you step into its beautifully crafted world, you're immersed in a rich tapestry of legends, history, and breathtaking landscapes.

The game's storytelling is compelling and deeply engaging, offering a perfect blend of character development, intriguing quests, and meaningful choices. The combat system is fluid and satisfying, rewarding strategic thinking and mastery of martial arts techniques. The visuals are stunning, with detailed character designs and vibrant environments that bring ancient China to life.

What sets "Where Winds Meet" apart is its dedication to authenticity and depth. It thoughtfully explores themes of honor, loyalty, and self-discovery, resonating with fans of martial arts and historical fiction alike. The soundtrack complements the experience perfectly, enhancing the atmosphere and emotional impact.

One area that could use some improvement is the menus. Currently, they can be a bit cumbersome, making it challenging for newer players to find everything quickly. A more streamlined interface would definitely help new adventurers dive into the action without frustration.

Of course, one of the most exciting aspects of the game is its multiplayer mode. Playing with friends adds a whole new layer of fun and excitement, allowing you to team up for epic battles, share strategies, and explore the world together. The multiplayer experience is smooth and engaging, making every session a memorable social adventure.

Overall, "Where Winds Meet" is a must-play for anyone who loves immersive role-playing adventures, beautiful art, and stories rooted in Chinese culture. Its engaging multiplayer mode makes it even better to enjoy with friends. With a few tweaks to the menus, it could be perfect — but even now, it’s a game that leaves a lasting impression and invites players to embark on a memorable journey of self-discovery and heroism.

This game tries to do allot of different things, but it has a consistent theme across all its systems. Imagine you’re a famous painter, you’ve painted a masterpiece. A work of art. A mere glance at it dazzles the eyes. And then you draw a gigantic red line through the painting. Why? Who knows. Now, instead of trying to paint over that red line and fix the drawing, you offer people temporary glasses that hide the color red every time they view it. A band-aid solution to something you’ve done intentionally, with no benefit to you, only harm.
This is Where the Winds Meet.

Let me break down the systems of the game, as well as its pros and cons, to show you the marred painting I mean. I’ll try to keep it organized into systems and subsystems.

The Combat:
At a glance, combat seems very fun in WWM. It’s flashy, parry-based, all weapons have their own playstyle and combinations, and you can mix and match! Not really.
As you go deeper, you realize every “combo” is a reskin of the same style, with very few exceptions. Almost every available combination boils down to “this is your main weapon, use it 24/7” and “this is your secondary weapon, used only for a single ability or buff/debuff.”

You’re not really using both. Every build boils down to a 10–15 second buff/debuff window while spamming 1–2 attacks. Your combat rotation is 1–3 abilities, chained or spammed every 10–15 seconds. Any weapon effects that significantly change how a weapon looks or feels are locked behind a €300 pity gacha, with awful rewards that make it a money sink.
Thematically, many weapon combinations don’t make sense or have boring playstyles. Demonic twin blades that push you into rage paired with… rats? And actively using two weapons from different paths is shooting yourself in the foot.

PvE:
For some reason, the devs looked at Genshin Impact and said “that energy system limiting players from playing looks fun.”
You have an energy system that takes 3 days and 3 hours to fully charge. It caps at 500, with ~1 energy every 9 minutes. There are three forms of group PvE:

• 10-man raids: On paper, fun. In reality, rewards are capped once per week. With 9 people you know, it’s surprisingly fun to coordinate. Bosses are repetitive, sometimes buggy, and can outright kill you regardless of execution.
Don’t have 9 people? Welcome to gambling.

A large portion of players don’t read mechanics. Before fights, during fights, ever. So 10-man (and 5-man) becomes gambling on randoms knowing how to read. My success rate was about 20%. You’ll spend hours queuing, watching people die to mechanics that could be read in 30 seconds, and leaving. Rinse, repeat.

• 5-man raids: Energy-limited. Each reward claim costs 60 energy, or 180 for triple rewards, once every 20 hours.

PvE boils down to a raid every day or two, allot of gambling, and mediocre rewards.

Progression:
Probably the worst system I’ve seen in a very long time. Progression in WWM is multilayered, with each layer locked behind something more inane than the last.

Mystic skills—some of your hardest-hitting abilities—are leveled by picking flowers. Each flower has a very low chance to give 1 rare material. You need around 108 to max a skill. No markers. You just search greenery for tiny petals. The game then offers limited weekly chests and food buffs to increase drop rates. Red line painting once more.

You also need to run outposts—the third PvE mode—which offer almost no rewards besides iron for mystic skills and random gear. They scale, so you can’t prefarm. You use around 10–12 skills total, each requiring a different plant, meaning you’re farming multiple rare materials in some of the most boring content I’ve played.

Then comes gearing. You open random gear chests hoping for legendary gear with usable stats (many don’t make sense). You can spend months not getting one. Then you gamble again tuning it, needing good rolls on 6 random stat slots. Bad roll? Start over.

Lastly, Inner Ways. You can equip up to 4. They require escalating amounts of notes, awarded randomly from content chests. You constantly reroll instead of the system just not being random. They’re integral to player power, and falling behind cripples your character.

PvP:
If you’re not near central Europe, don’t bother. Above ~40 ping, input delay kills animation cancels, reactions, parries, and combos. Opponents fall out of combos due to ping differences, and you’re playing with a 1–2 second delay.

PvP also uses a separate upgrade system and Inner Ways, meaning you’re maintaining two characters and halving your progression speed.

The Story:
The story is surprisingly good—if you understand it. It follows Dark Souls-style storytelling while relying heavily on ancient Chinese history. Between awful localization and obscure references even many Chinese players don’t know, you’ll probably skip it and watch it on YouTube later.

The Content:
Global releases are slower than China’s. Level caps and progression are drip-fed every 15 days, forcing you to repeat the same progression grind. New content arrives even slower, so once you’re done, you mostly log in to dump energy every few days.

Most systems are weekly-limited. Finish them in a few hours and that’s it. Need upgrades? Too bad—weekly coin cap.
Co-op is limited, laggy, and often only counts for the host. Online presence has little point outside of dailies. This isn’t even touching on shop pricing, gacha odds, or reward quality.

The game had an insane amount of potential, but the devs keep designing great systems and then crippling them. Maybe this design works better in China, but it clearly doesn’t hit the same mark here.

Ok. So I gave the game a negative review because of some gripes I had.

It seems they fixed making purchases when using the Steam version although I did make an account and try to link it which was a pain. I think that is a bad system. If we buy on Steam then that's all we should need. But that is my opinion.

Character creation: 
I still think "body type" is dumb in a character creation. There is only male and female in reality. Anyway, my character which was female looked better in the character creation than when in game. I used the Ai feature to help create her.  Overall, the character creation was full featured. You can customize quite a bit but you can't do much for the chest and butt unfortunately.

Now my thoughts on the game:

1. Free to Play: You can play the whole game as far as I know. But...

This is a typical free to play Asian game with fairly high in game store prices which supports the game's longevity. But it seems that these companies are at least yielding some to the players by giving heavy discounts on some things and allowing people to buy some decent stuff with currency you earn through the game. That is a move in the right direction. If you at least give people a chance to buy then the game is getting support. But locking a majority out of the store because of high prices then you just get the rich people or gamblers. Making things more accessible for all is better.
 
"Loot boxes" are still in the game though. If you want the real premium stuff you will pay dearly. Oh well, you can't have everything.

Note: There are still many things behind pay walls. Like being able to change the outfit color which I think is kind of dumb. But as I said already they do have sales on many things frequently.
The Battle-pass will get you currency and some free stuff which is not too bad. I'd start with that if you are on the poorer side. Don't be ashamed. You are alive. Life is better than money.

2. Open World: 
The game is primarily open world which I love. You run from point to point in a region and pick up quests, talk to Ai, find chests, puzzles, and dungeons, practice arenas, and other interesting things as you travel. There are big bosses here and there but just be sure you are high enough to fight them or they will squash you. I went a little too far off region and a duck almost killed me. Therefore, there is a limit to your exploration. Stick with the main quest and region for your level.

3. Combat: 
The combat I don't have much to say about. I am in stpry-mode with assistance. I really don't like complexity in games. I just want to shoot, kick or whack with easy dodge. As of this writing the assistance is making combat rather easy as it is telling me when to dodge and knock down. But that might change when i have my challenge or whatever to get to the next uptick in being a master. Some people like hard challenge. I do not. I just want to play and have fun running around. But that is me. I am glad at least for now I can enjoy the game on easy mode just to chill. When I get much higher I'll give my thoughts on the higher challenges.

4. Graphics:
If you have a good graphics card the game will look very nice at Ultra settings with high fps. As you turn settings down though the game looks worse and worse. Note: I play at 4k or Ultra Wide usually. I noticed too when restarting the game it sometimes puts everything back to default and then FSR. I had to put the ( -dx12 ) command in the steam command line of the game settings. I am not sure about FSR quality. I only have NVIDIA gpus.

I am using an RTX 5070. Intel 13700k, with 64 GB RAM playing the game right now at 5120x2880. 
I will post my settings here:

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3639936522

I am not sure about FSR quality. I only have NVIDIA gpus.

Overall, I am enjoying the game as I am free to roam and engage who and what I want but if that changes then I may just drop the game altogether. For now I am happy.

For now I give the game a 7/10.

Where Winds Meet offers a rich world and a strong atmosphere, but it can be overwhelming at first. The game has a lot of systems and mechanics that aren’t explained very clearly, which makes it hard for beginners to get into.

Well, I've got nearly 30 hours in this things now, and I still have no idea wtf I'm actually playing, because frankly, it's so much. I feel like somewhere out there, in some tiny building, they're, they, them, are holding a night school to teach people what they're playing, and how to play it. God knows I could use those courses right about now. As I've said, nearly 30 hours in and I'm still cursing like a sailor when I'm navigating the menu in this thing, because the menu's, menu's have a menu. It feels like your cruising the internet with 20 tabs open. I do things in this menu and then completely forget how to navigate back to it when I need it later because there is ... just so much menu. There is so much of that mobile game clutter involved with a dozen currency's and all the various ways in which you earn them. I mean on the plus side, the answers you seek are somewhere in that menu, because it has everything, except how to properly navigate the menu. ...anyways.

You get lost in this thing. No, I'm not talking about the menu anymore. I'm over that ... for the moment. I mean gameplay. It's beautiful, responsive, fast paced, with more options than you can fathom. You can go fight badguys in an insanely large world map, that eventually you'll be able to fly across in spectacular style. You can play songs on an instrument. You can go fishing, with a fishing pole, or by smacking the water with your fancy Tai Chi skills that you got via animal abuse. You can go on a date. You can fight bosses with friends and strangers. You can go around healing the sick (If you're looking to become a healer, like I was, be prepared to be angry ... all the time. No, not some of the time, all of the time. Trying to heal people for your progression is like pulling teeth, with butter knife and rubbing alcohol.) You can go for a run with some NPC's as an activity, and have a wolf agro you and try to bite your @ss while you're unable to move on your own accord. You can do some quests who's mood and tone shift as violently as a bear being thrown into a boulder so you can steal his martial art move. You can just take in the incredible sights. You can ... do so many many more things. That's why I have no idea what I'm playing.

Other than the menu ... yeah, sorry, back on that train, and the shop stuff, you can completely forget that this is a game that can be played on mobile, because what's here feels like an actual game. No, not feels, it is. It's an actual, feature complete, or I mean god I hope so, because I got enough to do and figure out as it is, game. Character creator is crazy in depth, some of the quests are really, really great, the combat feels really really nice. 

I'm actually kind of sad there isn't any real jank in this game. With it's bonkers mood and tone shifts, I know I could be getting massive laughs with some bugs and whatnot, but those are not here. I have had nothing go wrong save for getting stuck behind a wall once ......... sadly while I was under water. That's it. It is SOLID in it's design. 

I would whole heartedly recommend this to anyone and everyone, because there is something here for anyone and everyone. And if you're a sucker for Chinese atmosphere, marital arts, and beautiful music, than it is a must play. To anyone who has figured out all of the in's an outs of this game, and understands it in it's entirety, well ... I hate to be this guy, but I got to say it. GET SOME SLEEP!

If you’re a solo player trying to clear raid bosses, expect most runs to fail. In my experience, around 9 out of 10 pickup-group raids fall apart.

PUGs almost always include one or two players who intentionally sabotage the run, either through griefing or reckless behavior. A lot of players at the current level cap seem bored, and that boredom has turned into toxic play rather than teamwork.

I’m taking a break from the game. Before I do, here’s a genuine tip for solo players who still want to make raid progress, though it may not stay viable for long.

Drop the raid difficulty down by one tier.

At the slightly lower difficulty, I consistently found groups that actually want to clear the boss instead of wasting everyone’s time. Yes, the rewards aren’t as good, but you still progress the boss menu, which is far better than failing endlessly at max difficulty.

I am not sure how I feel about the game.  If you are just running around, the scenery is beautiful and the story is fantastic with it's depth.  I see a lot of potential for the game down the road but in it's current form I am at a stopping point.  I have several concerns/complaints for the game: 
1. It is poorly optimized for m/kb players.  There are so many different abilities that come up in the middle of play that while in mid battle you will be pressing at times 4 different buttons at once, which is distracting as hell when you are trying to defend and attack and that window is almost non-existent.  
2. Leveling is incredibly unrewarding.  When enhancing weapons and gear, there is little in the way of noticeable difference.  Even after attuning gear, nothing feels better or stronger.  
3. Boss fights and in general open world battles aren't fun.  Half the time is spent parrying the 6+ enemies that will inevitably surround you, and when healing is necessary there is no way to cleanly evade for a heal (primarily in boss battles) as the moment the game finally registers that you are attempting to heal, you are forced to parry.  Boss fights feel like playing a souls style game and as someone who is not interested in that type of experience, it's a little off putting, especially when getting hit once in battle means losing half my health bar.
4. Difficulty scaling doesn't seem to make a difference.  I always play new games on the most basic story mode, so I can learn the mechanics and dive into the story, which is what I enjoy about these types of games.  One would think that when playing in story mode I would take half a health bar of damage, when the game stops registering the parry that I have hit 20 times in the last 30 seconds.  Story mode should be a story, not a ulcer.  
I would love to see them improve on  things such as gear leveling materials, with providing a way for us to combine lower level material into higher level item.  Having so much tuning material for lvl 61 and below with no way to sell it or use it, and yet I am somehow still getting these things when playing in Solo lvl 8.  Here's to hoping that the future brings some much needed balancing and optimizations.  Still fun to just run around.

Where Winds Meet is a game that honestly surprised me a lot. I didn’t expect it at all and didn’t even know it existed. A story set in ancient China is quite uncommon nowadays, especially for open-world games, which often fall into the same repetitive fantasy themes. Here, it’s different – the atmosphere of historical China with a slight touch of fiction feels fresh and original.

The game is often compared to Genshin Impact, which makes sense since it also features gacha elements. However, the key difference lies in its visual style and overall approach. It’s not a copy of Genshin nor a typical “anime” game. Where Winds Meet doesn’t feel like a title aimed only at anime fans or gooners, but rather a more mature and stylistically refined experience.

A big plus is the character customization – you can upload your own face, use your voice, and create an avatar exactly how you want (or go completely crazy with it). This level of freedom isn’t something you see very often in similar games, and it definitely adds to the fun.

At first, the controls felt a bit unusual and somewhat clunky, but over time I got used to them and adapted. After a few hours, they no longer felt like an issue.

Honestly, I have to say I haven’t had this much fun with an open-world experience since the release of Once Human. On top of that, the option to play with a friend makes a huge difference – without it, it wouldn’t be nearly as enjoyable.

Where Winds Meet is a surprisingly original, atmospheric, and fun game that I can confidently recommend. And I say that with genuine enthusiasm.

TLDR : Not Recommended 

- Not for for PvE / ARPG-focused players (fun for some hours I cant deny it, but past a certain point youre left with nothing to do if combat is what you enjoy most. Some annoyance in needlessly delayed attacks by some bosses, and some being parry-simulators.)
- Insanely long time gates AND weekly caps on almost every reward
- Excruciatingly slow energy system ; more than 3 days to fully recharge energy for about 30-60 mins of bossing
- Co-op mode almost nonexistent
- Horrible AI translations AND voice acting (which is absolutely terrible)
- Global shop items more expensive than chinese version
- Clunky fast movement mechanics
- No endgame loop
- If you enjoy looking cool, youre out of luck because none of the armor you equip ingame change how your character looks.



Where Winds Meet has strong atmosphere and an enjoyable combat foundation, but its systems (energy system, currency cap, fish cap, cap for this, cap for that, cap for basically every single thing that will make you progress your account EXCEPT non-combat stuff; i.e. playing cards, wrestling, catching insects, etc.) actively discourage long-term play.
Some boss fights rely more on artificial slowdowns and memorization than reflex or mastery which is annoying sometimes. Technical issues like poor collision (try running fast in a straight line almost anywhere and youll end up triple jumping at literally any obstacle ; staying in place, or youll end up running up a tree doing 360s) and clunky menus further disrupt the experience (with obvious garbage gacha predatory mechanics).

Progression is heavily fragmented: too many currencies, limits on every single possible reward, world-level scaling feels lazy (you never feel powerful; enemies in first zone will always be as strong as they were when you start), and extremely limited (if not almost non existent) co-op content. All in all, past a certain point, with the limits and timegates you will be restricted to meaningful play of about 30–60 minutes, followed by multi-day recharge timers. If I want to play chess, Ill play with my friends irl. Same with cards. And chatting with an AI bot to befriend them is utterly uninteresting to me. 

Endgame lacks a real loop. After brief bossing sessions for loot or mystic upgrades, you’re pushed into filler activities (collectibles, puzzles, oddities) that quickly become the majority of “rewarding” content. These can be fun as side activities, but not as the core of the game. You simply dont have the endgame loop of other ARPGs and MMORPGs of fighting bosses/raiding/dungeons for loot and to upgrade your character.

If you like action-heavy PvE and have a lot of free time, this game paradoxically isn’t for you. It’s enjoyable until you finish the story/upgrade your character to a certain point, after that, the game seems designed to tell you to stop playing.

Good potential, but restrictive systems and time gates kill long-term engagement. This game is basically a f you to anyone who prioritizes combat and loot/upgrades (the core of any RPG).

I rarely write reviews, but I have to write a scathing one for this steaming pile of trash. That is important because I have been a fan of Wuxia and Cultivation themed novels and games for a very long time, before it really entered the western sphere at all. I genuinely thought this game was exactly what I'd been searching for, for maybe the first 2 hours, but probably more like 45 minutes.

First of all, this game has approximately ten thousand settings except for the things that will drive you the most insane. The bow has aim assist you cannot disable. There is a chat that spams you anytime you pick up an item or gain experience (which will happen a LOT, there is a chest every 15 feet that gives you 5-10 items). You will not be able to see any of the chats you actually want to. The other chats can be disabled but not this one.
The fight mechanics are janky. It makes genshin look like a fluid game, but you end up just getting animation locked and ♥♥♥♥ on by the npcs. Half of the boss fights you will run out of stamina because they attack nonstop and you can only dodge so many times.
There will be boss fights it locks you into or start randomly when you get close to them. They do not warn you, you do not get an option, and it will mock you and tell you to lower the difficulty after forcing you into a boss fight that is 10+ levels above where you are at.
The breaking point for me is a boss fight thats part of the story with this witch lady you can see in the steam page's cniematic trailers with the big scythe. You fight her once earlier in the game which is fairly easy, but the second time you encounter her is different. The first phase you get a companion that mostly does the work for you. For the second part of the fight you're on your own and deal almost no damage to her. You don't have enough healing, they let you lower the difficulty and then it literally does not make it any easier. After you die 3 or 4 times you can skip the fight, which is actually worse. They force you into this fight in the main story, you can't leave it, and you have to skip it. I don't think any game ever should have the option to skip a fight like that, you should just be able to beat it. They let you do this fight at level 25 (which is when you can enter this narrative instance that you cannot leave) and the boss is level 39. 
The only good part of the game is it doesnt seem to be P2W, but just like any genshin clone, there are 1000000000 tabs (this is only a mild exaggeration) and anytime you do anything, you have 15 new notifications that require you to go into 7 different windows to find and claim your 1 jade as a reward. This is not a joke or exaggeration, and you will immediately see what I mean if you look at the UI. 
Like I said early the fighting is janky. Fighting more than one enemy is annoying, they give you a stealth kill skill and the most lacklust stealth mechanics ever.
I was excited for the professions. I like "life skills" in games like this, but the healer and scholar (only two professsions available) are literally just card games, and as far as I know for the healer eventually you just skip the game entirely. These are not interesting in any way shape or form. They have put so much into this game that is literally nothing. If you want a card game go play Slay the Spire.
Didn't get to the sects at all, because the one I was interested in isn't available right now. I'm not sure why you can even see this sect if you cannot join it.
This is at its core a mobile game. A lot of the movement puzzles look challenging but then you just hold W and it takes your character through it, doing all the jumping and pathing. 
The keybinds are awful. They put skills on just about every key so rebinding seemed really really inconvenient and one of your core skills is on the ` key (to the left of the 1 key). I have NEVER EVER EVER seen a game EVER use this key as an important keybind, and the reason for that is obvious, its inconvenient and often you end up hitting TAB instead which switches your weapon.
If you dislike AI this is not the game for you. A lot of NPCs have mini missions where you talk with an AI chatbot that you have some sort of goal like to praise them or give them details about an enemy or something. ALL OF THESE MISSIONS CAN BE DONE BY SAYING SOMETHING ALONG THE LINE OF "Here is [whatever NPC wants)" I did not authentically do a single one of these missions, they are a waste of time but they "befriend" the npc forever and apparently they are supposed to send you a gift once a week. One of the NPCs literally asks for a plan to infiltrate a city and I told it "here is a plan I spent three months making" and he was like "but what about contingencies" and I literally just told the AI chatbot that I'd thought of all contingencies and it was satisfied. Its actually so dumb I hope no game ever ever ever ever does anything like this ever again.
Oh also immediately after this they make you run somewhere as a horse which takes a little less than 10 minutes. No idea why. You're literally a horse. You go to a tree. Then you're back to your character. I'm not the best at paying attention to game lore, but not sure why this is. You don't get turned into a horse or anything, you just take the perspective of a horse briefly.

Chinese mythology and culture and cultivation style lore is SOOOOOOOOOOOO interesting to me. This game is such a disappointment. There is tons to explore and learn about and you will get distracted every 5 minutes and that isn't a bad thing but its the same 5 puzzles (follow a blue butterfly, follow a red butterfly, follow a yellow butterfly, follow a purple cricket, shoot a purple butterfly, etc). over and over and over. It gets old fast. All the other puzzles have a note from a player telling you how to do it which is nice at first and then it also gets old. They aren't that complex in the first place.

I have so much more to say about this game and little of it is positive. They have put a lot of work into 100000 mechanics and details and none of them are particularly compelling.

Outside of that, progression is just kind of jank. Basically you have to regrind for gear every 5 levels when you increase your "world level", and all the bosses scale up to a certain point. The problem is, if the bosses and everything scale, why would I want to increase world level? It makes you feel like you're on some kind of treadmill. 

This FOMO feeling is driven home by basically every mechanic being an activity mechanism in some way, including most ways of getting Jade for items like appearance changes. It's nice that you can get this stuff for free by just being active, but the best ways all tie into some kind of multiplayer system where you gain a social pressure to continue playing. Personally I like to play games for fun, and while I find the combat and boss design extremely engaging, I'm basically forced into a corner where I'm either going to stop my character progression by not increasing world level and abandoning keeping up with friends or I'm going to have to grind for effectively very little difference in actual gameplay.

I mean it's significantly better than a game like BDO where they make you pay for everything after paying for the game, and BDO is kinda crap compared nowadays as well.

I can recommend playing it casually for a bit, but I ask you do not get caught up in the social trap mechanisms.

When I play Where Winds Meet I feel like I have stepped into a living cultivation world where exploration matters more than being rushed from quest 2 quest.  and as I move through cities, villages, and open landscapes the game constantly impresses me with how alive it feels through NPC routines environmental details and hidden activities, yet at the same time I often feel overwhelmed by the sheer number of systems menus and mechanics that demand my attention. combat is one of the parts I enjoy most because switching weapons and martial arts makes me feel like a true wandering swordsman and some fights genuinely feel cinematic even though rough animations and inconsistent hit feedback sometimes pull me out of the experience. and also the story does not strongly push me forward through a clear narrative path and instead relies on atmosphere lore and personal discovery which I find immersive but occasionally unfocused. as a free to play game I appreciate that progression does not feel locked behind payments although the constant presence of cosmetic options is always noticeable. overall, imo Where Winds Meet is a mix of admiration and frustration because it offers a beautiful culturally rich and expansive world that rewards patience and curiosity while asking me to tolerate complexity and uneven polish in return.

Netease, please either make a proper MMO or a proper singleplayer xianxia, don't half ass both, it's pitiful and annoying, and just because you make it free does not mean I am going to give you any clemency.
