I'm currently loving this game but rating it as NOT recommended. Why? the game is flawed but I see a ton of people that do not recommend this game, do so in a very bias and inaccurate way. In my review I want to point out the flaws harshly BUT fairly. instead of just hating the game and nitpicking it.

1. P2W.
This game is P2W. BUT the scale of P2W is minor. PVP aside, this game is VERY skill based and even with good gear, if you suck ass, being a whale doesnt matter as you will still suck. even then, its a non issue as theres no penatly for playing the game on story mode which has very lenient parry assists. you cant directly buy equipment upgrades from store, nor do you need to fully maximize your gear. you CAN get a lot of extra materials but the gap between a paying and non paying player actually does not matter as long as you dont PVP. 

If you care about PVP, a good player can outskill whales, and even as a free player you can upgrade all your equipment to a very competitive level without spending a cent.

One MAJOR P2W issue is there's a horse that allows players to farm materials in a very unethical way, You can also issue bounties on other players using in game cash shop items which can be used to kill other players (for example the ones using the p2w horses). but you really dont need the materials too much as you're still strong without em.

TLDR: its p2w but to an extent that MOST players dont even consider it P2W or deem it as acceptable. The amount of FOMO from not engaging in the P2W aspects are almost zero. me personally?  totally zero. tho i admittedly am pissed that the people using the unethical horses are a thing. the devs created something that made the experience worse for other players. BUT its still something i can turn a blind eye.

2. Predatory Gacha mechanics
There is a LOT of hidden gacha mechanics that are not obvious. they have a variety of different ways to pull/draw and one of them starts of cheap but gets more expensive the more you pull. another could use limited time currency which heavily incentivizes players to get all they want in one shot or else leftover currencies would just get converted. this would reset all progress should you decide to get the mtx if it ever returns to the store for purchase.

A huge lot of FOMO limited time to purchase and a lot of hidden costs that they DO explain but can be confusing or intentionally hidden behind an info button. This is annoying as they get to pretend that they did explain clearly. but the way it is, most players wiould not click on the button instinctively and assume the devs have "got your back" only to realize later that its not as straightforward as it first seemed.

some people may even need to resort to gacha guides.

TLDR: WWM gacha system IS predatory. BUT everything players want from it is GACHA only. almost never do people pull with the hopes of getting non gacha drops. and since its all COSMETICS, most people give it a pass. and if i  m being honest, WHY ARE YOU COMPLAINING ABOUT COSMETIC PRICES? its cosmetic! you can play the entire game without a single paid cosmetic. in fact, there are many in game cosmetics earnable in game without spending a cent that look REALLY GOOD.  and if youre being anal, there are some paid cosmetics that are tailored for low spenders, costing about 1 USD each. the next tier of cosmetics is around 10-30 USD. then for the whales its 100-2000 USD depending on luck. 

3. Buggy and some parts are unpolished

Agreed. they can do better and they should do better. But that said, lets not pretend triple A games are any different. Elder scrolls is a huge buggy mess but when the devs re-re-rerelease the game 100 times with the same bugs that modders have actually fixed, their fans still buy and play the game.

TLDR: yes there will be bugs. but its normally not too much nor not too game breaking.

4. Time gated progression/leveling system
You cannot just keep grinding non stop. you will reach a level cap that is based on the game server's age. this allows newer players to catch up to older players.

this also encourages players to TAKE THEIR SWEET TIME enjoying their game. i've played POE over a decade. played tons of their temporary seasons/leagues which literally puts your game on a timer (3-4 months to complete all challenges). i really liked the feeling of actuallly reading/listening and watching cutscenes play out. i enjoy NOT feeling FOMO that my friend is 10-20 levels ahead of me.\

TLDR: timegating level caps can be annoying but if you change your expectations, there is a huge lot you can do in the game, such as exploring all locations and doing all content. theres TONS of content.

5. Energy/time based especial encounters
This forces players to login at least once every 2-3 days. energy based encounters give the best loot. farming regular mobs outside of energy based content tend to be kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as theres a hidden lock which makes enemies drop ♥♥♥♥♥♥ items if you've been farming them a lot. so the best way to get upgrades is by doing energy based events.

TLDR: if you've done ALL content that you like, grinding for gear can be a big pain in the ass to farm unless you spend energy. spending energy is a hassle as you need time for to generate enough energy to actually run said content.

6. Governed by CHINESE RULES
there are things you will never see in the game as it is prohibited by chhinese laws. but that said, its something people should learn to ignore. 

7. "forced" multiplayer
there are multiplayer events that give good rewards, you can play 99% of the game solo and are encouraged to do so but in the end, MP content can be more rewarding. technically you COULD run raids with bots, but you will get a penalty against your rewards. you're still not strictly forced to go MP, me personally i HATE having to play MP as i dont like commitment. i dont want demand commitment from others so i dont expect people to demand commitment from me. i play when i want, how i want. the option to play with bots is AMAZING. as long as you're not actively trying to lose and sufficiently geared, you can actually learn the raid mechanics. albeit with lesser rewards. 

TLDR: multiplayer content exists and is rewarding, but not necessary. you can team up with bots for lesser rewards

8. PVP can feel unfair
some people say it fair. but to me, i just choose not to participate so i cant judge. on the higher levels, people who pvp constantly do tell others that there is a lot of counterplay, so it could be a skill issue.  so this can be a very subjective opinion.

NITPICKS:

1. Male characters sometimes tend to have better costumes than female ones
you'd be amazed at how cool you can look using a male character. BUT the females ones look pretty/elegant. 

2. Male and female costumes can share the same motif but can be very visually different such as the male one have 2 long sleeves while the female one is sleeveless. you cannot choose and you're stuck with the design based on your character's gender

3. you only have ONE character per account. this might change in the future, but for some reason the devs force you to only have one character per account. 

4. changing your characters "facial" appearance/ fine tuning colours/changing gender IS possible but requires real money shop items.

5. MENUS. TONS OF MENUS EVERYWHERE. tho once you get used to it, you wont really care about em.

6. FOMO daily login rewards/tasks. Any game with daily rewards preys on FOMO. simple as that. it also has consecutive day login rewards if you really want to nitpick but it does give you ways to "earn" missed daily rewards to a small extent.

Thats all i can think of. there are things that i find horribly annoying. like timegating. but on the flipside. its a hit or miss sort of thing. if you have more time, then you might run out of things to do in the game.

As for the positives, read the positive reviews. i myself am loving the game to bits.

From a purely gameplay perspective, this is a great game. If you're interested in story, this game is difficult to recommend to people without some background knowledge of Chinese culture or wuxia purely because of how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the translation quality is, especially after you leave the first area, and how little effort has been put into translating basic menus and tutorials to English. So much of the exploration is incomprehensible without a video guide to follow, and they only started slowly rolling out translation updates after the game's release on global. Unfortunately this is also a game that conveys a lot of story and lore through documents found in through exploration, so if you're a player who wants to put together the deeper untold parts of the game's lore, you're kind of SOL and reliant on Chinese players who have access to the original text to help interpret the story since Netease couldn't be assed to invest more money in the global server.
From a gacha perspective, there are specific parts of the game that are pay to win. The battle pass helps immensely with giving "free" materials (tomes, battle pass currency, etc.) and you can either get the 10 dollar or 20 dollar version. Energy also caps and can be purchased with real money, and you spend energy for loot drops. There are also mounts with some utility, but not game-breaking in any way. Other than that, most of your money will be spent on skins/cosmetics, which are where you get your 40k usd boats and 2k weapon skins from. There's plenty of mid-tier (30-50 usd) and free cosmetics that look great. Be aware that the game tried to cheat the global players recently by making one of the popular direct buy skins a gacha banner instead. Aesthetically the skins tend to draw inspiration from Chinese historical art (however loosely is dependent on the skin) but the game is currently facing controversy in China because one of its latest skins that was released simultaneously in global as well seems skimpy to appease gooner tastes for both body types. Not sure what Netease means by this when we have to wait for an unknown amount of time for plenty of other gorgeous skins that the Chinese server already has, but somehow the skimpy one was released on global ahead of them all, but they're not exactly immersive if you're looking for an immersive wuxia experience.

Overall, if you can accept these things (especially the translation quality) like I have for the most part, then I would recommend checking the game out since it is free. I would also recommend playing with the Chinese audio over the English one since there was 0 effort (lines not matching sub, AI voices, terrible VA quality overall with cut parts left in) put in there.

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.

Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The Learning Curve When you first start, expect to feel a bit overwhelmed. I was definitely confused at the beginning, but as the story unfolds, you start to understand the rhythm of the game and how it’s meant to be played. It’s a game that requires you to pay attention; you’ll need to do some reading regarding your abilities, as certain quests require specific skills to complete. If you haven't unlocked a particular skill yet, you'll have to go grab it before you can move forward with the mission.

Helpful Guidance The game doesn’t just toss you into the deep end and walk away. It offers a surprising amount of support; even after 60 hours of playtime, I was still seeing new tips and tricks pop up that taught me things I didn't know. It’s great that the game continues to coach you even when you’re deep into the endgame.

Life Beyond Combat Even though fighting is the core of the game, there is so much more to do. I spent a lot of time on "main tasks" that didn't involve a sword, like hunting for rare bugs and flowers to unlock special skills. There are also great mini-games like fishing competitions and drinking games with NPCs. The drinking games can be pretty stressful, but they are honestly a lot of fun.

Technical Reliability I did run into one glitch where I got physically stuck in a room. I was worried I was going to lose all my progress on a special mission and be forced to restart, which would have been incredibly frustrating. Luckily, I was able to just open my map and teleport out. I was so relieved to find that all my mission progress stayed intact—it turned a potentially "pissed off" moment into a really pleasant surprise.

- Plenty of free outfit from sects, pvp, events.

After 34 hours of playtime as south-east asia/non-china player, I feel like I've gotten a good grasp of the game .

Pros :

Free-to-play for the most part

Can be played solo- or co-op

Visuals are stunning for something that can be played on mobile

There's much to do most of it does not feel like busywork or generic mmo fetchquests there's plenty of things to  do and  dungeon designs are very well made ranging from beautiful scenery to creepy dungeons full of undead.

Combat works for the most part excluding a tad bit of clunkiness here and there

Plenty of freedom to play in whatever way you choose to do so

Gacha system is purely cosmetic

Cons:

Progression is softcapped by a time limit and gear grinding activities are hard capped by an "Energy" system much like typical gacha games  which may discourage players who like gear grinding arpgs etc Diablo , Poe .

Side activities are not very well explained if explained at all leading to confusion and mistakes

Online play is garbage for non-china players , ridiculous lag and poor netcode to the point where even hunting wildlife was impossible (deer would phase right through my attacks) which made me avoid online play for the most part .

Some progression systems are infuriatingly mind drainingly tedious (oddities, mystic art upgrades requiring materials that are ridiculously rare drops from weeds that only spawn one or 2 in a spot eg: beauty's plume.

Gacha pull rates are ridiculously bad to the point that id stay away unless you're that desperate to bling out your character.

Overwhelmingly ridiculous amount of menus which will lead to a ♥♥♥♥ ton of confusion as to "click where to do what" 

Enemy difficulty scales with your level so it makes progression seem a bit less impactful.

Story falls victim to typical chinese storytelling tropes which is plenty of exposition but not a lot of coherence.. I could'nt tell you what the main point of the story is nor where its going..

Final Thoughts :

If you want a  free pve arpg to play solo or co-op  casually by all means it is a good time but for online play diehards who enjoy pvp id stay clear unless you are somehow based in china.

Where Winds Meet punches well above its weight for a free-to-play title. While it has its rough edges, it’s one of the most impressive free-to-play experiences available today, and I wholeheartedly recommend diving in. 

The story starts slowly, taking its time to establish the world and its stakes, but patience pays off. Once it gains momentum, the narrative delivers intriguing plot hooks and thought-provoking themes, weaving personal growth with grand, wuxia-inspired drama. It’s not perfect, but the depth and ambition keep you invested. 

Visually, Where Winds Meet is great. The game’s environments—lush forests, misty mountains, and vibrant towns—are gorgeous, far surpassing what you’d expect from a free-to-play title. The boss fights are a particular highlight, with stunning choreography and effects that make each encounter feel like a cinematic spectacle. 

Combat is really fun, and it’s a blast when it clicks. Blending fast-paced martial arts with elemental abilities, it’s satisfying to chain combos and unleash devastating moves. However, the controls can be a hurdle. Inputs aren’t always tight, and a misclick can lead to frustrating moments—prepare to wrestle with the system until you find your rhythm. 

Monetization follows the standard Chinese free-to-play model, leaning heavily on cosmetics. The Battle Pass offers some crafting materials, but progression is largely tied to gameplay. You’ll need to grind to improve, which could turn some players off. 

The multiplayer and social features are a surprisingly delightful. From intense raids that demand coordination to silly, lighthearted antics in hub areas, there’s a vibrant community vibe that adds replayability. Whether you’re teaming up for a tough boss or messing around with friends, multiplayer is a blast.

My biggest gripe is the game’s complexity and lack of guidance. Where Winds Meet throws a lot at you—crafting, skill trees, factions—and doesn’t explain enough. Expect to Google core mechanics frequently (my search history is proof). This learning curve can feel overwhelming. 

It’s not flawless, but in my opinion its ambition and heart make up for it's short-comings.

Game has various early game issues that may put people off:
1. Too long before you have access to a variety of abilities.
2. Too much alt-content grind (aka, the sheer number of oddities & chests to gather and that is just considering what's needed for character progression).
3. The PvE is too focused on parries as your main source of damage at the start of the game, which makes the slow "tank" weapon feel particularly bad and can make combat feel same-y.
4. The campaign stories have too many filler segments + cutscenes and the characters aren't particularly likeable (especially your own). That said, the boss fights are good & both campaigns end well.
5. Navigating the menus is a learning curve & honestly there are just too many different menus from which you have to collect the currency you've earned.

It also has some lingering issues:
1. Healing weapons are too strong for non-world-boss PvE, while potions and Out of Combat healing without the weapons are needlessly relatively weak crafted consumables.
2. Passive skill progression (inner ways) is very RNG heavy with no real way to catch up if you get bad rolls (you can destroy some you don't want to make more chests for a chance at the ones you want, but not all inner ways have the same 'destroy' value and inner ways you destroy in high volumes get lower 'destroy' value overtime).
3. Limited key binding options (no rebinding alt+, cntrl+, etc.).
4. Illness & honor system are more annoying than interesting.
5. Playing with friends is actually pretty limited for an online game (especially if 3-4).

Recommended, but heavily held back by time-gating

Where Winds Meet is a good game. I like playing it, the combat and world are enjoyable, and while the optimization still needs work, it’s okay for now and playable.

That said, the biggest problem by far is the insane amount of time-gating, especially the energy system.

I understand time-gating breakthroughs — that’s fine. But why does the game also need an energy system? It completely messes with the experience. Once you’ve finished the story mode and weekly content, you’re basically done. You can only play around 2–3 hours every 3 days, because energy takes roughly 3 days to fully refill.

So the loop becomes:

Play for 2–3 hours

Energy is gone

Go offline for 3 days

Come back, energy is full

Play another 2–3 hours

Then wait another 3–4 days for weeklies to reset

Repeat

That’s not a game you can really commit to. Personally, I’m the type of player who wants to hop on and play 8 hours or more if I feel like it — not be “done” with the game for the entire week after 6 hours total. This system feels artificial and frustrating, especially because I actually like the game and the story is decent.

At the very least, increase the energy cap (for example from 500 to 600) and make it refill in 12–13 hours so you can play again the next day. Or better yet, remove the energy system entirely and let players play the game they enjoy.

Right now, the time-gating holds this game back way more than it should.

An Action RPG with Massively Multiplayer Online elements. First the part that f2p MMO gamers are going to care about the most-: There is NO Pay2Win element in this game. You cannot, in any way, purchase an advantage over another player in PvP or PvE. All cash shop is cosmetic. That said, they do have old school "premium" subscription services that give you things like extra energy (more on that later) and extra EXP. 

*Action RPG*
The combat in this game players similar to a Souls-like with multiple difficulties. At the lowest difficulty the game guides you with parry timings and you can get away with button mashing. At the highest difficulty some of these bosses are like Dark Soul's 3, you mess up once and you're dead. Your healing potions are limited to 2 uses per combat session. You can upgrade this to 3 per session.

*Massively Multiplayer Online*
Unlike a traditional MMO, you spend majority of your time in a Single Player instance. You can invite up to 4 other players into your instance for a Co-op session. There is a persistent global chat across all instances to give the game an MMO social feel. Players are dumped into a random global channel and you can then either manually or randomly change to another channel if you're not vibing with the people in your chat. 

Contrary to many articles online, there does exist a Multiplayer Mode which puts you into an open instance with any and all online players who have selected the same mode. This is where players congregate for events, raids, and guild content. You cannot progress the story in this mode and there aren't any major enemies to fight. 

*Story*
This game has some poorly done acting in some elements, perhaps due to the nature of localization, but, at its core, the story is pure cinema. You are in for a treat. I would personally have played $60 for just the single player experience in this game if it had been sold as such. That said, as a $60-90 game it would only rate a 7/10. As a FREE story? this is a 10/10 game. 

*The Negatives*
- This game sometimes feels like Menu Simulator. There are menus ontop of menus ontop of menus. I'm almost 200 hours into the game and I still sometimes get lost in the menu. 
- ENERGY, you consume energy to do raids and boss fights just like in a gacha game. You do get plenty of energy, in my opinion, for a casual playthru. You can buy *some* extra energy and you get a little extra energy from the subscription but we're talking 3-5 extra runs worth, nothing to really cry about. 
- GACHA, while the cash shop *is* purely cosmetic, including the gacha system, it does still feel predatory to say things like "5000% return" and also to have time limited RNG systems that you spend real money on. But that's just me, personally, I simply don't like to gamble. 
- VSYNC <- disable this setting immediately. For some reason that nobody has been able to explain to me, vsync makes the game feel very sluggish. It most definitely does not give you the FPS that your rig can put out. 
- Voice Chat exists in the game and it is awful, it's like being in an xbox live party. Thankfully, you can opt out of it. By default the game does not autoplay voice messages EXCEPT when you get on the big multi-thousand dollar boat. Then you're dumped into a persistent voice chat and have to choose to leave. 
- You read that right. Average of $50,000 USD for the big Mirage Boat. Believe it or not, people are spending it. I don't know why, I see no real benefit to it. You can't even choose what instance of the boat you go on so it's not like you're hanging out with people you know. People buy this thing multiple times a day and I cannot fathom how or why. I'm grateful, though, because if it keeps the game free then spend as much as you want I guess. 

Overall, as  someone that loves MMORPGs more than any other genre, I give this game a solid 9/10. I want to see more games like this. I would love this game more if it were a fully persistent MMORPG. The entire gaming industry needs to learn from Where Winds Meet and Helldivers 2 when it comes to monetization because I promise you this, I'm gonna spend a ♥♥♥♥ ton more money on Where Winds Meet than I ever spent on Black Desert Online, Elder Scrolls Online, or Star Wars The Old Republic.

Had a suspicion about this game and I was right, the game was TOO high of quality, I would have a constant use of my GPU with random spikes of how much it is using, and the INSTANT I deleted Where Winds Meet the GPU usage flatlined, and my CPU usage went down a little too.

"Nothing comes free"-Lyndon B. Johnson.

Where Winds Meet sets an exceptionally high standard for modern RPGs and free-to-play design.

From a technical and artistic standpoint, the game excels across all core pillars. Visual presentation is outstanding, with a beautifully crafted world that feels alive and immersive. Gameplay is fluid, responsive, and skill-driven, while the narrative and world-building provide strong motivation to explore and progress rather than serving as simple background content.

The PvE experience is deep, challenging, and consistently engaging, offering meaningful progression without artificial grind. At the same time, PvP is remarkably well balanced, rewarding mastery of mechanics, timing, and decision-making instead of raw numerical advantages.

What truly distinguishes Where Winds Meet from most contemporary titles is its monetization philosophy. Despite being fully free-to-play, microtransactions are limited strictly to cosmetic customization. There is no pay-to-win design, no ability to buy overwhelming power, and no scenario where players who choose not to spend money are placed at a competitive disadvantage. Progression remains fair, transparent, and entirely dependent on player skill and engagement.

In an industry increasingly dominated by aggressive monetization and artificial progression barriers, Where Winds Meet demonstrates how a game can be both financially sustainable and genuinely respectful toward its player base. This should be the blueprint for future games, particularly free-to-play titles.

A rare example of excellent gameplay design, fair systems, and strong creative vision working in complete harmony. Highly recommended.

Bosses kinda suck with telegraphing, dodging is inconsistent for me but that's largely just a skill issue, one that could be remedied with time, but I just can't be assed to do it in this game due to a plethora of other, far more damaging issues I have with this game.

The combat wants to be interesting and engaging, but... it's mainly focused around parries/deflects and breaking enemy stamina to do a large chunk of damage all at once, which can be fun, and gets some people really excited, but I didn't like sekiro or grounded for this exact same reason, so, unfortunately, I ended up not liking it as much as I did the beautiful environments and the music. Also, the peculiar classification for weapons in "tank, dps, healer" archetypes don't really make a lot of sense.

Unfortunately, after spending a little bit of time in the game I invited a few of my higher level friends into my game to play together, and due to there not being a level attenuation system (mainly for story/co-op mode) that I could perceive, a couple of key bosses were completely trivialized, where as when I joined my friends, the opposite was true, very hard boss for them, impossible for me because I die in one hit, neither of these things encourage me to play in co op because I want to be challenged and fight bosses, not play a broken sword playthrough in darksouls, or to bring my max level friend (trained attack minion) in and have him wipe the boss in one slap, that's not fun.

On that note:

I specifically downloaded this game to play it with my friends, I play games with my friends because I like playing games with my friends, many games get this right, very few do not, and this is one of those that fails miserably, worse than most, it actively discourages you from playing with them, either by kicking everyone out during quests, straight locking some quests out of co op or the aforementioned lack of a level adjusting system to avoid situations where you get a max level toon coming in to a lower level area and turning everything in a 10 mile radius into paste.

I also don't like the time gating system that's tied to levelling up, I don't like the energy system which I didn't even perceive until I looked at the energy stat and saw I had used half of it up... somehow, this stuff isn't really explained when you kinda just go to quest markers and talk to people, like one does in a game like this, so when I hit the "no more loot for you until your 'generic mobile game energy resource' comes back" wall it was very discouraging. While I understand it to some degree to avoid bot accounts joining in and max levelling instantly, waiting (from what I've read) up to 10 days to  get to do one of your challenges again to rank up your world tier is kinda awful, and doesn't make me want to come back, combine that with the some... sixteen bajillion menus and buttons and confusing interface options and it just leaves a bad taste in my mouth.

All in all, it's got some decent bones, if these issues I listed get ironed out over time I may come back and try again, but for right now I cannot recommend it.

The Art Design is a chef's kiss! The outfit, amazing, The character creation, pretty solid. The in-game locations, Breathtaking! 

The game is literally the peak of a free to play game! 

10/10 would recommend!

That is a game that you'd want to be good, as foundamentally it took inspiration from other successful and popular games - souls-like, mmo-rpg's, stealth games, and have foundamentally fun mechanics in place with good visuals, but this game is only meant to leave an impression and not made to last, as all it's foundamentals breaks to technical debt and poor design choices.

It has some fun fights, it starts off really good, but more you play it - more you notice it's flaws, worse it gets.


[Visuals & World Design]
[+] Visually appealing environment.

[-] Late-loading NPCs and objects popping into view.
[-] Exploration feels like chores rather than discovery.
[-] Some invironmental interactions which "should just work" often does not, not going to list them all there.


[Combat System]
[+] Foundamentally souls-like fights are fun.

[-] Latency directly affects attack speed and parry timing, even during solo play.
[-] Camera and targeting is often taking control from player, focusing what it should not.
[-] Auto-aim makes it annoying to aim if you have a mouse and know how to use it.


[Multiplayer Elements]
[+] Foundamentally similar multiplayer raid model as in mmo-rpg's.

[-] Most multiplayer features are barebones, very minimal, basic. No depth to PvP or boss fights. 
[-] Raids and PvP suffer from severe latency and desync.
[-] Coop is incomplete, barely functioning - no proper progress sharing.
[-] Progression affects PvP arena.

[+-] Not an MMO - Don’t expect large-scale raids or massive open world fights. It has missleading mmo user steam tag.


[Progression & Time Gating]
[-] Daily and weekly caps restricting progress.
[-] Energy system restricts amount of loot obtainable from boss fights.
[-] Stamina system restricts crafting.
[-] New players are behind due to upgrade materials being limited by weekly timegates.
[-] Progression is artificial due to "breakthrough" mechanics - each new breakthrough you throw your old gear away, farm and upgrade new. There is no meaningful content that comes with it, all bosses and mobs scale with you.
[-] Leveling ("breakthrough" mechanic) is also timegated - a day at first, then turns into weeks.

[Monetization]
[+] Can't buy everything you want directly.
[+] Can buy cosmetics


[-] Gatcha banner crap.
[-] Battle pass provides additional resources - additional energy you can spend to get more loot from bosses, additional upgrade materials, additional potion slots.
[-] Paid mounts with auto-loot and auto-collect affect farming efficiency.
[-] Monthly subscription with additional in-game currency.
[-] Can put bounties on other players to be hunted until they die.
[-] Can buy trial hitless run completion.

[-] Above features could be classified as p2w, despite it being advertised otherwise.


[Stability & Performance]
[+] For the most part playable.
[-] Frequent crashes, freezes, stutters, most notable in second act.



[Movement & Physics]
[-] Movement is unreliable.
[-] Character frequently misinterprets terrain, backflipping all over the place, failing to climb or climbing where it should not.
[-] Incorrect objects geometry in the world - climbing or standing on top of invisible objects.
[-] Traditional invisible walls.
[-] Parkour quests \ dungeons are misarable.

[Story & Presentation]
[+] Some cutsecenes looks cool.

[-] Unskippable dialogues.
[-] Some quests lack voice acting, some voice lines incorrectly placed or repeated.
[-] AI generated voicelines.
[-] Often presents a choice which does not affect anything, just a button to press.

This game is great imo! 
There's a ton of different gameplay mechanics, and they're all based on daoism, wuxia tales, and the beliefs and lives led in the dynasty the game takes place in. You have a healing minigame to heal npcs and other players, a debate mechanic to help npcs deal with conflict, sects you can join that each have their own ranking system, rules, and daily tasks, you can get in trouble with the law by stealing horses, pickpocketing, disguising yourself, just attacking random people, and then get hunted down and go to jail if the law enforcers beat you, a bounty mechanic where you can hunt down npcs or other players, profession mechanics, a really complex, detailed, and fun combat system, etc. There's A TON of different things to do, and every single one is insanely well thought out and designed. 

The world itself you explore freely is also done really well! Its a gorgeous game, and was made with so much care. To me, some open world games can be really jarring with geographical changes, like how one second you're in a comfortably warm area and then all of a sudden like two steps later you're somewhere where you could freeze to death in 5 seconds, but this game doesn't have that issue. Every area makes geographical sense to me. Each area feels distinct yet interconnected, and each area always feels like it has some story to tell, like people have walked these lands before. The npcs are all also very well designed; they all feel like they have real lives, and everyone is also fully voiced, no matter their story importance. There's also a lot of them, with villages and cities being crowded as you overhear all the peoples conversations. Also, you can ride a horse and pet cats. 

The combat is so detailed. You have all sorts of mechanics, and it makes you feel like you're actually fighting and not just button mashing, even if you actually are because you're new and don't know how to fight because the movements of your Mc are so cool and fluid. You have a bunch of different weapons you can switch between, plus skills and talent things, so you can customize combat to how you wanna play. Fighting people just feels so smooth and satisfying, and the different weapons are so fun. You can beat people up with a paper fan and umbrella. 

The story is amazing! Its very detailed, as all wuxia tales are,  and full of complicated plotlines and past connections between characters. The side stories are also amazing. Some of them really will have you just sitting there thinking about what you witnessed and what it all means. To get the full idea, you really need to look at the details, and a lot of character connections are hidden throughout the rest of the game, if you want lore, you really need to work for it, and also pay attention to how everyone lives in the different areas as it will provide some much needed context. I get that thats not everyones thing, and the game will tell you important bits either through character logs or in the finished quests menu, but really, you won't get everything if you don't look at the details.

In my opinion, there's only two real issues with the game. 

First, the tutorials are, honestly, kind of bad. They don't tend to explain everything about the new mechanic, and the game as a whole operates under a 'learn as you go' model. I've been finding myself going to the reddit community a lot to figure out how things works. It also sometimes just, won't explain things to you. In some cases I like it like that because it honestly is hilarious, like figuring out you can get into legal trouble for the first time. I was so confused the first time I was caught disguising; One moment im vibing, the next im beating up and chasing strangers as the police come after me and random civilians begin throwing rocks, then im in a prison cell looking like ive been in there for 10 years. A hilarious experience and one I would not change. However other mechanics, like the stock market, don't explain at all how they work, and you need to use it at least a little bit, so I had to look up how it works. Thankfully, the reddit community is very helpful, so it isn't too hard to find an outside source.

Second, it assumes you have some knowledge of how wuxia stories work, and therefore, an idea on daoism, which is what wuxia tales are based on. Concepts like qi, the existence of sects, the idea of cultivation, the jiangzhu, etc are never explained. I think you can pick up on context clues, but honestly, especially in the beginning, its just really confusing. This didn't really affect me, but I was also already aware of all these concepts before playing this because I myself have been a fan of wuxia type stories for a bit, so I can't say too much on how much worse your game experience is if you don't know these.

TLDR; Amazing game, super detailed super fun, just have google at the ready to figure out some mechanics and what some terms or concepts are.

I'm not really sure how to describe this game, or star this review. I've played the game for coming up on 40 hours...I still don't really know what's going on.

It's an MMO, that can be played completely single player, where you the most you interact with other players is via signposts that people can place. Or you can play it like a traditional MMO, group activities and the like.

In the 40 hours, I've not set foot into the Co-Op/MMO side of things, not once.

It's a bit of a hybrid game. At it's core, an action RPG akin to Dark Souls, timing your parries and dodging correctly is key, but it's the collectibles from something like Warframe, and the sheer amount of skills to develop like Runescape...oh and there is building too...I've not touched that yet either...

I've no real idea what the story is about, but I think that might be more a translation issue, from the bits I've seen of the story, it's not bad, nothing amazing. But it's an MMO...not many MMO's have amazing stories...

There's so much to do, and you're actively encourage to explore, whether that's to collect things, talk to people (AI bots based...), fish, throw sticks in a pot, talk to cats who give you magical bells...it's a real random mix of a game and I didn't expect to be playing it for more than an hour, let alone 40...

Yes there are microtransactions, they aren't a case of buying power, just cosmetics and items every now and again, but all the items are achievable in game.

My only real complaint is...I don't really know half the systems, the affinity between different weapon sets, how upgrading gear really works, how to get to certain areas of the menus. You get bombarded with so much stuff all at once especially when you level up or finish a quest, even looting chests...it can get real overwhelming.

That being said, it's free, looks beautiful, runs amazing and its a real time sink of a game if you give it a few hours to hook you in.

So, this is almost a game that meets all my personal requirements, however has gone downhill rather fast. I’ll cover as many aspects as I can think of in a long overly drawn out review.

It starts off almost perfect and keeps you going for a good while before personal preference disputes begin to kick in.

Character creation is good, but could have some more individuality, like adjusting the height and weight, etc. It focuses mostly on facial features, in which is done well, but seemed to leave off other physical character traits. Perhaps some RPG character stat choices in character creation would have also been interesting, giving it a little bit more individuality.

The quest and story-line are engaging up until a point, and then the long drawn out quirky NPC dialogues begin to get annoying and I find myself skipping through some of them. This is usually a bad sign for quest, as skipping through too much dialogue causes the game to loose some of its immersion. Though a user decided option, skipping through quest usually originates from some sort of over-extended quest dialogue.

Though the overall mechanics of the character are done very well (skills, movement, battle, etc.), there is some little things I noticed. Underwater is only available in a quest related underwater scene, and swimming will cause the character to drown after a short time. Mining isn’t a craft, you just jump on a rock to crack it open (though this does make ore gathering faster, it is less realistic). 

Puzzle quest and dungeons. These are great and keep your brain intellectually engaged instead of mindless constant killings. There is allot of aspects like this to give the player choices on how to play, and this is good. Other aspects include card playing, drinking games, chess, and other ways to loose game money.

Skills and character development: This aspect seems endless, and there is too many options to get started with. So I will leave at that. Overall, very good.

Cats, bears, ducks, (and dogs, oh my!). The excess amount of skills will however occasionally cause accidental killings of wild animals, innocent bystander aggro, and even killing a villagers dog. There is so much cat interaction in the game that it makes me wonder why dogs were left out, dogs are our friends too. The cat interaction and cat quest aspect is great, but, let’s not leave out our intelligent canine companions. Add in some Dog quest/skill bonuses, for talking with and befriending dogs as well. Perhaps even some other animal faction quest. Why not? And why do I have to literally ‘throw a bear’ in order to repair my gear. Forced animal killings is not a plus in my opinion, it is more of a redundant game aspect (let’s just throw in some rats there, some wolves over there, and make the player toss a bear to repair their gear). :/ Hmmm, ok ….. at least there isn’t an overabundance of laughing skeletons attacking you.

AI NPC conversion: this could have been left out, doesn’t really do anything for me, but perhaps the developers have plans for that. Unless it is doing something in the background to individualize a players NPC interactions, I don’t see the point of the ‘chat with NPC’ option.

Class diversity: So I feel 50/50 on this. I think allot more could have been done, but at the same time, there is some very unique styles incorporated. For someone that plays healer type classes, the fan/umbrella Silkbind-Deluge path is very engaging. The rope dart is another very interesting choice. There could have been more range type choices included however, more archery focus for those that like ranged combat, and perhaps even throw in some throwing weapons. Overall I like the play style, at least for my chosen class of Silkbind-Deluge.

Trials and leveling: this gets overly redundant. I feel that the leveling trials should be different, based on your class. For example, if you are a healer, then your trials should consist of keeping other NPC’s alive while they fight. Currently however, all healers must hack and slash their way through the trials.

Professions: Good, and very engaging, however there should be more professions. And currently the healer profession I feel is slightly exploited. Lot’s of click bait time wasting. Which is sad, because the healing profession aspect of the game is very well done. However, when there are no more NPC’s to heal, and there gets to be too many players in the healing profession, then what?

Sects: (Updated) A waste of time.

Guilds: Not for sure about guild aspect yet.

Crashes, glitches, and other buggy anomalies: At first none. Then… well there has been some glitchy things that happen. Perhaps just me, perhaps others, not sure. CTD during combat while hitting ALT key, can’t open chest and menu options disappearing during teams and co-ops. I only fell through the game world once, but it did happen (common hole in the world mesh somewhere that got unfilled). Overall, for a less than recommended PC I am using, I can play it very smoothly. But lot's of lag.

Last but not least, the Online versus Solo game aspect: So the solo game quest aspect I think is good, and you have the option to invite others to your personal game-world. That is very interesting. However the online world where everyone just hangs out and jumps around like monkeys is just not my thing, and I think it is kind of silly. But each to there own, I do see how this solves allot of issues of game lag and players, so I see the purpose, and it seems to work.

Arena, and PVP by choice? Ok I guess, I think the hardcore PVP'er may be able to give more opinion about this. Leaving the PVP out of my quest world is good however. Let me do my quest in peace please, thank you. However, arenas seem kind of a standard boring way of doing PVP. This is mostly a PVE game, for those that wonder.

Where is your character going? As with most games, it is still a DPS based game, regardless of class, hack, slash, stab, kill. That is what it boils down to, fighting and killing mobs. And at level 70 healer, it is starting to get down to the same old grindy game leveling. However, overall, there is still allot to explore, allot of quest to do, and allot to engage in with the character. Hopefully the game will be expanded further to incorporate allot of the aspects I feel are missing, and keep someone as picky as me going.

So far though, it has been engaging enough to keep me occupied and level a healer to 70 in about two weeks. However it has turned into a grind like other games.

For most people however, I think this game will be enjoyable, depending on their personal preferences. It does have plenty of aspects to cater towards different play styles, developers just need to fill in all the gaps in my opinion.

8/10. Overall, a good game, but with some of the usual live service limitations.

The upsides:
1) Game runs great, nicely optimized.
2) Lots of different weapons to play with.
3) Has a good feel to it, in terms of setting. If you are a fan of "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon", "Hero", or other such movies, you might appreciate this game. And if you're just playing the game and haven't ever seen those movies, check them out.
4) The macro-transactions are mostly cosmetic, with no pay-to-win, even very little in terms of quality of life/speed impact.
5) Lots of things to do, between mini-games, various achievements, hard modes, and such.
6) While the game has daily log in rewards and a battlepass, as well as a energy system, it isn't as "log-in every day" as most live service games. The log in offers lots of "make up a day" tokens, the BP is easy to max, and the energy system has a cap in excess of two days of energy regen.
7) Solo, co-op, and PvP stuff, so whatever floats your boat.

The downsides:
1) if you aren't into hard modes, achievement hunting, or just lazing around in game, you will run out of things you find worth doing. As is typically the case for most live service games.
2) Some time gated leveling stuff. It doesn't serve any useful purpose, but it is there. On the plus side, only a day delay, so not a big deal.
3) Clunky main UI for certain things. Can make finding what you want in the whole system a bit painful, plus a lack of some useful things like conveniently placed "claim all" style buttons.
4) Balance and/or UI for certain mini-games is bad. Pitch Pot has bad mouse+keyboard controls, plus the streak bonus makes it very hard to come back from behind. The music mini-game UI draws from Genshin Impact, rather than actual rhythm games, so poorly designed. And so on.
5) Some annoying "might as well go AFK" elements to daily/weekly activities, like Blessed Land or "spend time in your guild hall".
6) The prices on cosmetics can be pretty silly. Like $40... that's just nuts.
7) While you can do stuff like outposts with others, there's no point, as it is just trivial/boring.
8) The rules the sects have make them less, rather than more, fun.

Overall, if the setting or the style of game interest you, worth giving it a shot. And if you reach a point where you find you aren't as interested anymore, well, then just drop it until when/if you feel like playing it again. You'll have gotten your money's worth, because it is free ;)

This is my first foray into the world of "Gatcha" games, I've stayed away from them primarily because I'm not down for luck based loot acquisition. Whilst WWM does indeed have a Gatcha system, it primary reason for existence is to offer outlandish costumes and weapon skins, although some of the more grounded costume options can be obtained for free.

The game itself is essentially an an open world RPG with BOTW-esque puzzle dungeons and Souls-like combat, with heavy emphasis on deflection and countering. There's a huge amount to do in the current release, with various side-quests that range between some of the best content the game has to offer, to standard fetch quests. In favour of all of the content is the writing, the storylines are well fleshed out and have gravitas, although unfortunately the translation and particularly the mismatch between vocalised lines and accompanying subtitles break the immersion from time to time.

The main storyline is a definite highlight, the pacing is wonderful and it is genuinely engrossing, it isn't perfect by any means, the aforementioned issues with translation are present and there are awkward moments when being guided by NPCs that feel way too slow, but these are footnotes in an otherwise epic adventure.

The world itself feels just alive enough without being either sparsely inhabited or overcrowded, you're never far from something to do or something to fight. The movement options available are also varied and work well with the terrain, you have traversal on foot or mounted, three jumps and a midair dash and a super-jump or sorts that allows you to cover large distances easily. You can also teleport between waypoints once discovered.

The combat is going to be the main draw for a lot of people, and for good reason. It feels tight, fair and well balanced, the sort of thing you'd expect from a AAA Souls-like, you have various skills, some tied to the handful of weapons available, some learned as you level up or observe things in the world. The weapons are perfect as they are, you chose two weapons, each of which have a certain "path" attached to them, they all work best with another weapon within the same path. I can't help but want more weapon types or just an incentive to stray from the pre-matched weapon combinations. I began using the standard sword and spear you begin, which turns out are some of the best in the game, but later switched to using the sword and other weapons depending on the mode just to mix things up. Negatives aside, the boss battles are amazing, I've had more fun with some of these than I have from similar titles from AAA studios, the fact you are rewarded for repeating the epic fights is the icing on the cake.

The main grief of the game is the menu system, there are too many currencies that can only be used in shops buried away under one of the many, many menus. I know where they are now, but it's taken 60 hours of play to get there. That's the real battle. The second negative is an understandable one, the level cap only increases every two weeks at the moment. I've managed to hit the cap the day it has been released, meaning I've got the full two weeks gaining "stored experience" which will only make the next rush to the cap even easier - now, this is understandable, the team is working on translating the material between level caps, so fresh content is released at a steady pace. I just hope this doesn't cause the fan base to stagnate once their maps are completed. The multiplayer is great but outside of PVP it has the same issue as the single player content.

Overall 10/10. Will continue playing for as long as it holds my interest, and I don't mind buying the battlepass for £9 each month to support development, it's definitely value for money.

Great game. 8/10.
It has fulfilled the Wuxia dream I've had for so long. Nothing else even comes close to what this game has to offer. There is tons of content, even if it is only 20% of what has been released in the Asian market.

Pros:
Length: 20 hours of gameplay with side quests gets you to Lv30, covering only about 15% of the first map's exploration.

Variety: There is so much to focus on. You can talk to NPCs to discover side quests, collect materials, enjoy a sunset on the mountain, fish by the beach, or play Chinese Chess with random people.

AI Integration: The AI system is deeply integrated into NPCs. Unlike traditional games where you just give gifts to make them like you, here you have to properly chat with them and complete side quests for them.

Multiplayer: The online mode allows you to raid dungeons with other players, play card games, or just do random weird stuff for the lolz.

Achievements: There are a lot of achievements to unlock, making it suitable for grinders.

Freedom: You can kill villagers and become a criminal—it's a bit of a blend of Red Dead Redemption 2, lol.

Potential: This is only the release version, so it will only get better.

Cons:
World Style: If you come from WoW, know that this isn't your traditional MMORPG. It is a GTA-style sandbox but with a bit less depth (though this may change with updates).

Combat: The combat system is good, but not great. Do NOT expect Souls-like complexity. However, it isn't simple either; it features parrying, counter-hits, blocks, and a mix-and-match of spells and martial arts styles.

Monetization: It is a bit 'pay-to-progress,' but not 'pay-to-win.' To look properly cool, you have to buy skins—but games have to make money somehow, right?

Open World: The world is beautiful but feels a little empty. There aren't enough mobs for grinding in the open. This game is a weird, beautiful experiment mixing WoW, GTA, and Red Dead. Because it tries to do everything, it results in a just slightly above-average experience in some areas.

Overall: I think it is a beautiful and exciting game for what it is and what is to come. And it is FREE. I would say even if they started charging a ~£8 ($10) subscription per month, I would still be playing it."

I was first drawn to this game for it's wuxia aesthetics, but I wasn't sure if I'd like the gameplay loop (you never really know from trailers). To my great pleasure and surprise, this game managed to achieve more than I could have ever hoped for. And then some. The simplest way to describe the gameplay, think Sekiro combat + Genshin Impact open world + MMO-lite features. In other words, WWM is an open world action RPG, like Elden Ring, with a bit more social components connected.

Pros:
- Combat > Action-packed, well animated, just as good as Sekiro and other Souls games = 10/10 
- Open World > Large, varied biomes, well-designed, feels hand-crafted = 8/10
- Incentivises Exploration > Rewards are peppered around everywhere, and everything is useful,. You will look forward to being side-tracked = 9/10
- Minigames > Half of these are decent to legitimately fun (e.g. madiao cards, wrestling, chess) with more to come in the future = 8/10
- FREE. GAME.

Cons:
- Excessive Menus > As others have said, this is an area that can definitely be improved. Not the biggest deal in the world as you will become familiar over time.
- Subtitles too quick > Half the time the text disappears before you've even read it, so you need to pay attention and fast

This game is jam-packed with content, and 90-95% of it is very enjoyable. People say 'Jack of all trades but master of none', but this game is an exception to this rule. IMHO, many of the systems and features are very polished, with a handful that are a little forgettable and lacklustre (e.g. Gift of the Gab minigame), but these are such minor elements that it really doesn't matter. This game does so much right and offers so much more than many AAA games, that it is easy to overlook the few downsides it has.

Verdict: 
Give this game a shot, you have nothing to lose. The best part is that we KNOW there is a tonne of content lined up because the Chinese version is 1 year ahead in terms of updates, so the roadmap is clear for us western players. It will take you about 20hrs to fully comprehend and understand all the systems, because the game gradually introduces them to the player so it's not overwhelming, but the entire journey along the way is memorable and enjoyable. I haven't had this much fun in an immersive open-world game since Witcher 3/Red Dead Redemption 2/Cyberpunk. Chinese game devs are coming through hot with a streak of banger titles. A lot of the old western triple A studios could learn a thing or two (cough Ubisoft, Bethesda, Blizzard etc).

Despite having absolutely no p2w, this game is still somehow ruined by monetization. The premium hair dyes, the only way to unlock white hair, costs about 600-700 dollars because you have to gacha for them essentially have to rely on hitting full pity ($350), twice ($700). That is just to dye a single hair. Premium outfits are around $350 each as well relying on the same gacha system. I dont even care about the $40,000 boat for ultra whales that virtually does nothing. Even when I'm locked onto a specific target right in front of me, my character will often do a 90 degree turn to attack/aim a mob that I'M NOT EVEN LOCKED ONTO. This ranges from mildly inconvenient for most of the the game, to completely game breaking at certain points. Nothing more annoying than doing a 180 to miss the Sleep Daoist roots you're trying your use Mystic Fire, or jumping into a mechanic/attack against your will because of an auto aim that essentially cannot be turned off. Only a setting that reduces the auto-aim and its not even 100% consistent and worse, it seemingly doesn't work on Mystic Skills. This drastically reduces player agency for no reason making this game more frustrating rather than fun. 

There are a lot of great things about this game, but having a character consistently turn away from my target to attack an enemy that I'm not even locked onto is just unacceptable. I could not possibly recommend a game that takes that player agency away and charges $700 dollars for each premium hair dye.

Superb Gameplay and Story

Some games try really hard to impress you. Where Winds Meet doesn’t. It just drops you into its world, hands you a sword, and quietly lets you figure things out—and honestly, that’s what makes it special.

The world is beautiful in a calm, almost old-school way. Misty mountains, small villages, abandoned temples… it all feels peaceful but slightly dangerous at the same time. Exploring never feels like a checklist. You wander because you want to, not because the game is yelling at you with markers and pop-ups.

Combat is where I really got hooked. It’s smooth, fast, and incredibly satisfying once it clicks. You can’t just mash buttons and hope for the best—you have to pay attention, time your moves, and actually think. When you win a fight, it feels deserved. When you lose, you usually know it was your fault (and yeah, that stings a bit).

The RPG side is handled nicely. You’re not forced into one “correct” build. You can shape your character around how you like to play, and experimenting never feels punishing. Progress feels steady and meaningful, not bloated with useless skills.
Overall 10/10 game although story is quite complicated :}

[h3] ENDS OF THE EARTH, NEAR AT HEART [/h3] 

You may have heard much to the contrary in general conversations surrounding this game, but Where Winds Meet is not an MMO, Where Winds Meet is an open world single player ARPG with optional* co-op and multiplayer. It is a hybrid of many genres and in being so brings a unique assortment of gameplay opportunities to the table.

Set in the aftermath of the turbulent Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period in China, which bridges the Tang and Song Dynasties, Where Winds Meet is an historically inspired romance and cultural love letter. In classic Wuxia fashion, your journey begins as a young aspiring hero who is pining for adventure and to follow in their uncle’s footsteps. Your origins are a mystery to unfold and uncover, as are the complicated relationships with your protecting uncle and aunt.

At the time of this review, your adventure will take you across two distinct regions, the rolling natural wonders of Qinghe and the sprawling city of Kaifeng. The main story begins in Qinghe and progresses to Kaifeng, while additional major narrative mysteries permutate throughout everything you do.

As someone who loves Chinese history, culture, and Wuxia stories, I did not expect a free to play game to finally scratch the long standing itch to satisfy the want for an open world Wuxia adventure, but here we are - I had a lot of skepticism on the obvious concern points going in, but I feel confident in saying that it has many paid games beat on style, content, and passion. You have nothing to lose and everything to gain giving this one a shot. When I said this was a love letter to the culture, I meant it. The price of entry is nothing, but there’s a high chance you’ll fall in love enough to spend some money.

I strongly recommend that you use the Chinese Voice Over, because while the subtitles translation aren’t always perfect, the emotion in the performance is crucial, and the English VO lacks that, being thoroughly bland and doing a genuine disservice to the story and atmosphere.

Much like Dynasty Warriors did for me in my younger days, Where Winds Meet is going to inspire a lot of people to take an interest and look into Chinese history - and that is special.


[h3] * ON OPTIONAL CO-OP AND MULTIPLAYER [/h3] 

If you commit enough crimes in your world and resist the NPC law enforcement enough, you can be invaded and arrested by bounty hunter players.

And if you suffer one of few severe enough injuries or ailments you may require other players for healing - be comforted that there are no shortage of healers looking for patients and it's a very quick interaction.


[h3] ON MONETISATION [/h3] 

Actually free to play. Your own will and desire is the only thing stopping it from being so, and even if you do give into the want, you're only buying cosmetics.

Not pay to win. You cannot buy power and level cap intervals keep everyone on the same playing field. Everything that you need to develop is acquired at a steady pace through just playing the game. Some in-game currencies are capped week-to-week and an energy system is in place to restrict the need to grind - while some of the more MMO-minded players could view this as a negative, personally, I find the way these gates are implemented to be more respectful of your time as a player, as you don’t have to dedicate your life to the game to maintain relevancy.

Paid content. Fashion. You can buy some cosmetics outright or you can gamble for [sometimes limited] cosmetics, but there are a plethora of non-paid cosmetics that are earnable through just playing the game. The toughest grind in this game are cosmetic drops from the bosses.

Battle passes. There are free and paid tiers. You can get additional fashion through the paid version, but the paid version doesn't offer a big advantage over the free version otherwise, other than netting you some extra in-game currency gain that is not otherwise hard to acquire anyway.

                                                               Where Winds Meet — 9/10

A Stunning Wuxia Adventure I Recommend to Everyone

Where Winds Meet is one of the most impressive wuxia action RPGs released in recent years. It blends open‑world exploration, MMO depth, and fast, skill‑based combat into an experience that feels both ambitious and genuinely fun. Despite a few rough edges, the overall package is strong enough that I confidently recommend it to players of all backgrounds.

Gameplay

Combat is responsive, stylish, and rewarding, built around parries, dodges, and weapon mastery. Each weapon supports a different role—Tank, DPS, or Healer—giving players meaningful flexibility in how they approach encounters. Beyond combat, the game offers a huge variety of activities: martial arts duels, medicine, housing, sumo wrestling, raids, and more. This breadth makes the world feel alive and gives players countless ways to engage.

Leveling & Progression

Progression is satisfying and steady. Breakthrough tests add challenge without feeling unfair, and the MMO‑style gear and stat systems give players room to experiment with builds. Whether you prefer focused combat progression or exploring side activities, the game supports both approaches without forcing a rigid path.

Graphics

The visuals are a standout feature. Powered by Unreal Engine 5, the world is breathtaking—lush forests, ancient cities, sweeping mountains, and cinematic wuxia movement that feels straight out of a martial arts epic. Animations are fluid, environments are richly detailed, and the overall presentation is consistently impressive.

Storytelling

The narrative is serviceable and occasionally emotional, following a young swordsman on a personal journey. While localization can be uneven at times, the story still provides enough momentum to keep players engaged, and the worldbuilding helps fill in the gaps. It’s not the strongest part of the game, but it’s far from a deal‑breaker.

Conclusion — 9/10

Where Winds Meet delivers a visually stunning, content‑rich, and highly enjoyable wuxia RPG experience. Its combat is engaging, its world is beautiful, and its variety of systems ensures there’s always something new to discover. While the story and localization could be stronger, the overall experience is excellent.
I fully recommend this game to all players—whether you’re here for the action, the exploration, or the sheer beauty of the world.

To be honest the game looks and feels nice. But if after playing for less than 2 weeks I’ve already run into several problems. 
Firstly, they constantly restrict you in how much you can level, well if they didn’t most players would have maxed out after two days. But after less than 2 weeks I’m at the stage; Quest, explore, grind bosses, harvest stuff, level my gear, and so on. All while I cannot level above level 70 until some time in ten days. The exp is not wasted though, it is put into stored EXP. So, when I’m finally allowed to level up it will happen in an instant. Sounds nice, but frankly it ruins the experience of progression.
There are quite the few glitches all over the game, invisible buildings, holes that you fall into, and so on. 
The game uses a lot of AI, some of it makes perfect sense for instance talking to certain npc's. But they clearly used AI to translate casual NPC conversation, and that did not go well so it sticks out (they do want real money when you buy things, in the gatcha shop).
All of the above would be ok if there was more volume to the game. Already I feel like I’m getting bored, the multiplayer content is really limited and most of what you can do is just goof around and act like a 12-year-old. Beside the more or less boring boss fights and limited pvp. options. It also feels like the dev team never played an MMO, if you go into multiplayer most npc’s disappear leaving the world devoid of life, players just gather at certain spots trying to do the daily music, giving money to beggars, and exchanging emote, thing. 
There are some nice, dungeons and puzzle dungeons to explore around the world but most are clearly built for single player, and puzzles are just way to easy. I get that everyone (even me) should be able to do them, but what is the point of gathering clues if they have no real function in solving the puzzles.
All in all, though the above could sound like a rant, I think the game has potential, I’m just afraid that players will have run away to greener fields by the time they make it great. 
I do recommend people to try it out but only because its free, if not I would leave it to ripen for a year or so.

Where Winds Meet is a beautiful game with solid mechanics and a promising start, but it is heavily undermined by aggressive monetization and exploitative RNG systems.

For free-to-play players, the RNG is punishing to the point of absurdity. Grinding in-game currencies to obtain a single cosmetic through draws requires treating the game like a second job—and even then, success isn’t guaranteed. Many of the better-looking cosmetics are time-limited, meaning that even if you grind consistently, you can still come up short when the timer expires.

The game constantly pushes monetization. Questionnaires are sent out asking for feedback, yet the RNG issues are routinely glossed over. Near every RNG-related system, you’re met with mobile-style ads encouraging you to spend money. The message is clear: pay, or fall behind.

I started playing to enjoy the game with friends, not to engage with a cash grab. I won’t invest money into a system that doesn’t respect my time, and I won’t treat a game like a job—especially when the rewards are functionally out of reach. While the world is visually stunning and the core mechanics feel good, the story also loses focus after a strong start.

After countless hours and hundreds of appearance coupons—amounting to nothing unless you have thousands—the progression simply stops feeling meaningful. This model may work for some players, but for me, the monetization overshadows everything the game does right.

[h1] Where Winds Meet [/h1]

Where Winds Meet is one of those rare games that immediately signals ambition. From the moment players step into its world, it’s clear that the developers aimed to craft more than just another open-world action RPG. The game’s greatest strength lies in its atmosphere and artistic direction. Drawing from wuxia, the environments feel alive with sweeping landscapes, elegant architecture, and a sense of cultural identity that sets it apart from most mainstream releases. Combat, deserves praise: fluid, stylish, and expressive, it captures the fantasy of being a martial arts master without feeling overly stiff. When the systems click, battles feel cinematic, rewarding experimentation with movement, skills, and timing.

[h1] Discover your world [/h1]

Narratively, Where Winds Meet shows promise. Its world-building hints at political intrigue, personal honor, and philosophical tension, themes that resonate strongly with the genre it draws from. Even when the story doesn’t fully unfold yet, the tone and presentation suggest depth waiting beneath the surface. Exploration is similarly engaging at first. The map encourages wandering, verticality, and discovery, and early gameplay creates the illusion of a living world filled with opportunity. In its opening hours, the game feels fresh, confident, and full of potential—exactly the kind of experience that can hook a dedicated player base.

[h1] Content gate, the Death of all games [/h1]

However, that early promise is precisely what makes the game’s long-term outlook feel so precarious. Where Winds Meet appears to be fundamentally undermined by its pacing and content strategy. Progression quickly becomes constrained by aggressive gating, forcing players to wait, grind, or disengage rather than continue naturally. Instead of rewarding curiosity and momentum, the game often places artificial barriers in the way of enjoyment. This creates a sharp contrast between what the game wants to be—a free-flowing martial arts epic—and how it actually plays over time.

The issue is compounded by content dripping.

Where Winds Meet feels doomed not by lack of talent or vision, but by structural decisions that erode goodwill. Unless the developers significantly rethink gating, accelerate meaningful content delivery, and trust players to engage at their own pace, the game risks becoming a cautionary tale: a beautiful, mechanically promising world gradually emptied by design choices that suffocate its momentum.

I jumped into Where Winds Meet because my cuzzo put me on and I’m glad he did. I’ve played with him a little but I’ve been mostly running solo, the game still feels like it has plenty to offer either way. I’ve been playing a lot over the last three days and it’s one of those games where you hop on “for a bit” and suddenly hours are gone. The first thing that hits you is the scale of the game, this is a big open world with a lot to explore. It doesn’t feel like a tiny map with copy-paste areas, it actually feels like a world you can get lost in which I have lol. I catch myself roaming, getting distracted by side stuff, checking out new areas and constantly feeling like there’s something around many different corners.

Combat-wise, it’s challenging in a good way. It’s not just button mashing, you actually have to pay attention, pick your moments and learn how fights flow. When you start improving and landing things clean, it feels rewarding. The difficulty adds to the satisfaction because you earn your progress.

The atmosphere is also a spectacular vibe to though. Between the open world design and the overall classic type feel, it’s easy to sink deeply into it. It gives you that “escape from reality” feeling for sure, especially when you’re exploring and just locked in.

The only real downside so far for me is the game could definitely use some bug fixes and polish. Nothing that made me quit but you can tell it’s got some rough edges here and there especially when I have to add this game to my VPN bypass list you know, it makes me feel like they are trying to invade on my privacy in some type of way real talk. If they tighten that up amongst other things then this game could be even better.

But look, overall, I’m having a great time with it. If you like open-world exploration and you don’t mind a game that can be a little challenging, this is definitely worth jumping into, especially if you’ve got a friend to run with sometimes but it’s still solid even when you’re mostly solo without a doubt.

Pros:

1. Huge open world that’s fun to explore

2. Combat feels rewarding and has a real challenge to it

3. Easy to get immersed and lose track of time

4. Very fun solo, it's even good with a friend companion here and there

Cons:

1. Needs bug fixes / extra polish here and there.

I've been trying to put some real effort into this game but it is just bad, first I'll explain what the devs did right.

The map is big, and there is plenty to explore. The amount of activities to do or collect are pretty robust and can keep you occupied for a while.

And that is all I feel they did good on, now the bad:

The entire game feels like it was made using AI, there is absolutely so much content and half of it doesn't play into the main story at all, not to mention trying to keep track of so much content with an over cluttered and complicated UI doesn't help.

The main quest has nothing to do with the main character which was an instant turn off from what the bio stated.

Side quests, while plentiful are horribly tracked with the UI, half the activities available cannot be tracked at all which can make it difficult to try to complete the simplest of encounters.

The interactive map is actually too simple, having to zoom in to try to find a specific quest or activity when I forgot where it was has me constantly zooming in and out like this is the 1990's. Poor terrain relief on the map and half of the quests or just important areas to the game are not marked, nothing becomes marked when you discover it either. The devs found a way to over complicate and over simplify the game.

graphics are bush league, they look great at first glance but try to climb a tree, a cliff, look at a body of water. Slowly I realized the clipping, the boxy edges on a non-boxy rock.

The build leveling is as well so packed with options whereas half of these can be easily consolidated. Over complicating a leveling system and locking end game material behind multiplayer.

The combat system is bad, the most basic attack options with a weapon but you can use eight different mystic skills you don't have the time for when fighting a boss or multiple enemies. So the focus is placed on deflecting attacks. A predictable and poorly thought out system.

You can become ill doing numerous activities in the game but the devs force you to use a broken multiplayer system to try to get healed for the more extreme illnesses.

The game is free and the *Quality* of the content shows, the devs have released a new cosmetic nearly everyday and only one small update. There is a lot of content, but it is not well thought out and we must not reward a company that uses AI to make a half-assed game while capitalizing on microtransactions.
