Where Winds Meet is an outstanding experience and easily one of the most immersive games I’ve played in a long time. It’s rare for a game to pull me in this deeply, but this one truly does.

The visuals are breathtaking—every region of the open world feels handcrafted and alive. Instead of rushing through quests, I found myself exploring purely out of curiosity, which speaks volumes about the world design. The environments, lighting, and overall atmosphere create a sense of calm, mystery, and adventure all at once. The storyline is engaging and well-paced, complemented by NPCs and characters that feel surprisingly real. The AI-driven interaction system is a standout feature—your dialogue choices genuinely matter, influencing relationships and friendliness. This makes every conversation feel meaningful and encourages thoughtful decision-making rather than mindless clicking. Combat is another major highlight. The system is fluid, responsive, and highly diverse. The freedom to choose different weapons and combat styles allows players to shape their own playstyle, keeping battles fresh and rewarding and well as the freedom to either choose a sect or choose to remain sectless is a wonder option they gave.  Whether you prefer strategy, aggression, or adaptability, the game accommodates it smoothly. Overall, Where Winds Meet excels in world-building, storytelling, AI interaction, and combat depth. It’s a game that respects the player’s curiosity and rewards exploration and choice. I would strongly recommend it to anyone who enjoys open-world RPGs with rich visuals, meaningful interactions, and flexible combat mechanics.

Where Winds Meet feels like stepping into a living wuxia painting, one that isn’t afraid to punish you if you get careless. The world is stunning. Mist-covered mountains, quiet villages, and sweeping landscapes feel handcrafted rather than copied-and-pasted. Exploration is slow, deliberate, and rewarding, encouraging you to wander off the main path just to see what’s there. I regularly stopped just to take in the scenery, which says ALOT. Combat is where the game truly shines, especially for fans of Souls-like systems. Fights are deliberate and skill-based, with an emphasis on timing, positioning, stamina management, and learning enemy patterns. Button-mashing will get you punished, but mastery feels incredibly satisfying. The blend of Souls-inspired challenge with fluid wuxia martial arts gives combat a unique identity that feels both cinematic and demanding. The storytelling is subtle and mature. Instead of long exposition dumps, the game lets the world, characters, and small moments do the heavy lifting. There’s a quiet melancholy running through the narrative that makes it feel grounded and emotionally resonant. From a technical standpoint, performance is solid. The game feels well-optimized, animations are smooth, and the overall level of polish is impressive for a world of this size and detail.
it stands out as more than just another open-world action RPG. It’s atmospheric, challenging, and confident in its design. If you enjoy Souls-like combat, immersive worlds, and experiences that respect the player’s skill and curiosity, this is an easy recommendation.

Highly recommended.

Common enemies are pretty boring, 1 on 1 they are no threat as you can pretty much stun-lock them through basic combos and such.
Large groups end up being more about placing yourself and the camera so nothing can attack you from somewhere you can't see.

While the game pretty much advertises the multiple weapons and martial arts, they end up being relatively similar since you use the basic attacks most of the time.
Worse still is that two martial arts are based on healing but bosses cut down healing by 80%, making it absolutely useless in solo and at best somewhat useful in multiplayer (instead of being something that can in theory save the whole team if used properly).

Boss fights end up being hyper-focused on deflecting every single attacks (except the yellow ones that you must dodge, many of them with a pretty strict timing), even when said attacks are in quick successions.
It is a bit reminiscent of Sekiro to me and what you gain by deflecting is also similar, which is putting the enemy in a state where they won't react for a short time, allowing you to attack then trigger a more powerful attack before the timer ends.
You can throw a few basic attacks between deflections in most cases, but never at the cost of not deflecting as missing a deflection against a boss removes a big chunk of your health.
Thankfully deflections cancel most other actions so it's not a monster hunter style where you need to commit to every attack as well.
But still, the boss fights revolve near exclusively around deflecting as your only way to survive.
And that is something I am not a big fan of, I like when there is an option to use timing-sensitive (player-skill-based) actions but less so when it is the only viable way.
For example I like parries in souls-like games because it is something I can opt to do but not something I absolutely need to do in every single real fight.

To add to that, the whole "NPCs use AI chats" is super boring as you have a goal to make them say something (the AI allucinates and says it on its own quite often out of nowhere as well) but the entire possibility of role-playing through it is lost because they "forget" all about it between sessions.
So even if you take the long route to get a NPC to admit that stealing was bad because you want to enjoy the RP, as soon as the goal is reached it is all forgotten and the NPC is reset either as "not a friend yet" if you didn't reach the goal yet or "friend already" if you did, but nothing else is ever kept.
This seems like a massive oversight as this could have gotten a decent amount of players that enjoy role-playing in games to be interested but instead it is another example of "we use AI chat bots" that adds little to nothing.

It sucks, because the concept of different martial arts, sects and weapons was interesting, most bosses look fairly interesting, the game overall is not bad looking (even if a bit generic), but it falls flat on most points and the boss fights (the only thing that can realistically grab players) was a big miss for me due to the deflections being mandatory and so important that everything else takes the second row seats at best.


So if timing chains of deflections and such is your thing, the game is probably enjoyable for the boss fights, it just wasn't for me.

Where Winds Meet is an impressive open-world action RPG that really shines in its combat and presentation, especially considering that it’s free to play. The combat feels fluid and stylish, blending fast-paced martial arts with cinematic swordplay that makes every encounter feel dynamic and rewarding. Different weapons and abilities encourage experimentation, and fights stay engaging rather than repetitive. personally my favorite weapon is the thundercry blade
Visually, the game is stunning. The graphics and art direction do an excellent job bringing its world to life, with detailed environments, smooth animations, and dramatic lighting that make exploration just as enjoyable as combat. The landscapes feel immersive and atmospheric, helping the game stand out among other free titles.

That said, the game isn’t without flaws. The menu layout can feel cluttered and unintuitive, especially for new players. Important options are sometimes buried in submenus, and navigating between systems like inventory, skills, and quests can interrupt the overall flow of the experience.

Overall, Where Winds Meet delivers high-quality combat and visuals that rival paid games, making its free-to-play model especially impressive. With a cleaner, more user-friendly menu design, it could be even better.

Where Winds Meet has a very rich and engaging storyline from what I’ve experienced so far. I’m only about two hours in, but the world already feels carefully crafted, with strong atmosphere, lore, and a sense that there’s a lot more depth waiting to be uncovered. The developers clearly put real thought into how the story unfolds and how the world presents itself, and it shows.

That said, there are a couple of things holding it back for me. First, using a controller feels unnecessarily complicated. There are a LOT of buttons and inputs to remember, and it can feel overwhelming at times, especially early on when you’re still learning the systems. A more streamlined control scheme or better onboarding would go an extremely long way. Second, I really wish there were selectable dialogue options when talking to characters. Being able to choose responses would make conversations feel more alive and immersive, and would help the player feel more connected to the world and their role in it, similar to something like Skyrim or assassins Creed Odyssey. 

Honestly, though, that’s about all I have to complain about. There are some genuinely impressive features here, and the developers do an excellent job implementing them in a way that feels intentional rather than gimmicky. With a bit more polish in a few areas, this could easily become something special. Definitely worth checking out if you enjoy deep worlds and story-driven experiences. 

Overall, I feel like if there were an update in the future to revamp the controls to simplify it for controllers and add dialogue options, I could definitely see myself recommending the game to others. Dialogue choices/options should have different effects on the world around you as well

[h2]Where Winds Meet Review[/h2]

[h1]Where Gravity Is Optional[/h1]
As a fresh entrant into the open-world RPG space, Where Winds Meet attempts a broad ambition: mix cinematic Wuxia-style martial arts, a sprawling open world, deep character customization, a large variety of weapons/styles, and an MMO-lite social/live service structure. Let’s see how well it pulls off those ambitions; where it shines, and where it feels overstretched. Also, keep in mind that this game is Free to Play.

[h1]About This Game[/h1]

[h2]Storyline[/h2]
[b][u]A Wandering Swordsman in a Turbulent Era[/u][/b]
Where Winds Meet places you in the chaotic period of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, a time marked by political collapse, rival warlords, and constant regional conflict. You play as a youxia, a wandering martial artist with a mysterious past, navigating a land struggling to rebuild itself while factions compete for power.

[b][u]Themes of Choice and Identity[/u][/b]
The story leans heavily into classic Wuxia themes. You’re free to approach situations as a compassionate protector, a pragmatic survivor, or something morally grey. Instead of forcing a single heroic archetype on you, the game lets your actions define how NPCs react and how the overall tone of your journey unfolds. I feel that this freedom is something a lot of modern games lack.

[b][u]Personal Tales Within a Massive Conflict[/u][/b]
While the overarching plot deals with political unrest, much of the emotional heart comes from smaller character-driven stories scattered across the open world. Villagers, rebels, scholars, soldiers, and wanderers each have their own struggles shaped by the era’s instability. These quests help the world feel lived-in and meaningful, something I really appreciate.

[h2]Gameplay Mechanics[/h2]
[b][u]Combat & Movement[/u][/b]
[list][*] Combat is a major highlight. The game offers multiple weapon types: swords, dual blades, spears, rope darts, fans, umbrellas, mo-blades; and each weapon type supports different martial arts styles. Players can equip two weapons at a time.
[*] There are also “mystic arts” which are special skills that have both combat and non-combat utility (movement, interaction, special moves).
[*] The combat system is actually really fluid and cinematic. It’s easy to draw parallels to high-quality martial arts fighting from wuxia cinema since the fights genuinely look as amazing as they feel to play.
[*] I was impressed by the emphasis on movement and traversal; the game truly brings the Wuxia fantasy to life not just through combat, but with the fluid mobility, including leaps, dodges, and some parkour-style movements.[/list]

So when it comes to combat + movement, Where Winds Meet strongly leans into the “feel like a wuxia hero” fantasy.

[b][u]Content Variety: Quests, Exploration & Activities[/u][/b]
[list][*] There’s a large variety of content beyond main-story combat: side quests, exploration, customization, mystic arts, crafting or character/weapon progression, and many ways to build and style your character.
[*] The sandbox open-world pulled me in immediately: I’d start a main quest with full determination, but five minutes later I’d be off wandering somewhere completely unrelated, poking into hidden corners or chatting up random NPCs just because the world kept tempting me to explore.
[*] The game supports both solo and multiplayer/social/online features (it’s described as an action-adventure + MMO elements), which means that you can play it more casually or go deeper, depending on your preferences.[/list]

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list][*][b]Fluid, spectacular combat & movement:[/b] The variety of weapons and martial arts, plus mystic arts and mobility, make combat engaging and satisfying. For fans of action-oriented, martial-arts-style gameplay, this is surely the standout feature.
[*][b]Stunning, varied open world:[/b] From dense bamboo forests to snowy peaks to tranquil streams to busy cities, the world is rich and atmospheric. For an online/free-to-play game, the scale and polish are impressive.
[*][b]Freedom and variety of playstyles:[/b] Whether you like to mainline the story, wander and explore, test different weapon/skill builds, or play with friends; the game supports multiple approaches.
[*][b]Strong value for a free-to-play game:[/b] I was pleasantly surprised by the monetization. It actually feels fair, and I never once felt pushed to spend money. You can enjoy pretty much the whole experience without paying, which is honestly rare for a big open-world game.
[*][b]A compelling Wuxia-inspired fantasy:[/b] The blend of historical/cultural inspiration, fantasy martial arts, and open-world RPG structure gives it a distinctive identity as not just another fantasy RPG, but a Wuxia RPG.[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list][*][b]Content overload/dilution:[/b] Because there’s so much: open world, MMO-lite elements, many mechanics, many quest types; some systems feel less polished than others. I’ve seen many players argue that while combat and world shine, many side systems (quests, exploration markers, UI, menus) can feel “bloated” or overly complicated.
[*][b]Quality inconsistency in non-core features:[/b] While combat and visuals are strong, other elements (dialogue animations, NPC behaviour, some idle/clipping issues) feel a bit weak. For example, lip-sync problems, occasional texture/animation glitches, or menu clutter.
[*][b]Sheer scale can be overwhelming:[/b] For players new to large open-world MMOs or those who prefer tight, focused experiences, the sheer volume of systems, side-content, progression paths can be dizzying. It demands time and attention to really get into, which can be daunting.
[*][b]Jack-of-all-trades, master-of-none feel (in parts):[/b] In trying to do a lot: open world, action, customization, MMO, social, exploration; some parts necessarily feel less deep or less refined compared to specialized titles.[/list]

[/table]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Where Winds Meet is a bold, grand experiment; a free-to-play open-world Wuxia RPG that tries to do it all: deep combat, vast world, customization, MMO-lite elements, freedom, and cinematic flair. It’s not perfect. Some systems are less polished. It can feel overwhelming. But the moments when it clicks…when you land a fighting move that feels dramatic, when you discover a hidden corner of the world, when visuals + ambiance + audio combine just right…those moments make it worthwhile.

Rating: 9/10
If the winds keep meeting like this, I might just stay lost in this world forever.

For full review head over to our [url=https://www.united-critics.com/post/where-winds-meet]website[/url]

Free to play with no pay to win (so far) that I've noticed. Very vast open world and many systems within the game to enjoy however you want. Pay systems are in the form of Battle Pass and 2 baseline Cosmetic gacha system. Be warned though the rates are pretty bad. 

Meat and Potatoes:
Combat is clunky. Bad hitboxes, inconsistent parry windows, and poorly telegraphed attacks. Sometimes the attack animations will either be too slow or too fast and you end up missing your dodges or parries. To top it all off there are no distinct audio cues to these attacks. It's just a generic noise with a little red or yellow glow on the enemy. But again, sometimes the visuals don't even match the actual hit of the attack so those ques become useless pretty quickly. All you really know is if it's a deflectable attack or not.

The fights themselves are pretty good though. The level design and the atmosphere, and just the overall general feel to the boss arena. I could see what the Devs were trying to go for and they probably hit those marks, but they missed when actual combat gameplay is considered in tandem. It gives of the feel of style over substance. Although I've overcome a lot of the bosses so far, it doesn't change the fact that the combat gameplay is lacking. Other games with similar gameplay style had great fights and smooth combat, so I think it's a pretty fair expectation for this game is also meet both style and substance criteria.

Menus in this game is atrocious. It's just ridiculous how many you have to navigate through to find what you're looking for. Seems like every pixel of your character has some sort of upgrade system attached to them. But really a lot of these systems feels nonsensical and it's busy farm work to keep me playing.

Your progression is time gated. Just another nonsense thing to have in the game to pad out play time.

Personally, I'm not too pressed about the menus or the time gate. But I sincerely hope the combat gets fixed up a bit, although seeing how people are spending $500+ on 1 costume or $30000+ on a boat mount, I wouldn't be surprised if nothing really changes.

This is not a game I care to play long term but it has a lot going for it. It has combat largely akin to what you'd expect in a single-player action-rpg, the fundamental gameplay design of an MMO, and it monetized largely though a pretty large system of cosmetics/outfits (including an outfit gacha) which are generally quite nice. Perhaps more impressively, the game is set in a (Wuxia-esque) meticulously constructed medieval China during the Tang-Song transition that is really quite stunning to explore and see. The interplay between the Liao('Khitans'), Song, and other forces is really quite fascinating for the historically minded. Aesthetically, the game looks very good as well. The story itself is unfortunately only mediocre in my opinion: like much of Wuxia it seems more focused on creating a moment-to-moment fascination in the consumer rather than in the construction of strong characters and plotlines - which it does with mixed success. There is also just a lot of jank in the game with AI, 'voice acting' and some bugs. A lot to like if you can bear it.

This game, for me, essentially hit like a truck coming out of nowhere. 

I'd seen ads for it, and kept seeing it pop up in the top sellers list. But after a quick glance, I disregarded it: "great, another "free" to play, low quality, pay to win microtransaction *##!-fest. I bet you even have to constantly group with randos to get anything done!" I thought.

I was so, so, SO wrong. 

-----Gameplay-----
OK, let's make a goulash. 

Add a cup of Red Dead Redemption. A serving of Ghost of Tsushima. A light helping of Elden Ring. A dash of God of War. And a largely optional side of Elder Scrolls Online. 

Assuming you are even vaguely interested in the genre (historical fiction+wuxia fantasy), and you liked any of those games, there's probably something here for you to really enjoy (with the caveat that the amount of multiplayer-specific content is relatively light compared to what's built to play and enjoy solo - for me, that's actually a plus, but ymmv).

-----Story/Setting-----
WWM delivers the fantasy of living the life of a wandering martial artist in a Wuxia version of China, ~ 960 CE. 

And I truly mean that. You're not just wandering around fighting (though you do, and the combat is fun). You're learning about competing sects, all with their own martial arts. You're fishing, cooking, crafting. Maybe you've taken up medicine, and are taking requests from players to heal their ailments. Perhaps you're known as a scholar/lawyer, and you enter into debates - sometimes as part of a quest, or maybe you have a friend who plays the game and got arrested for blatant jerk-ery and they need you to represent them to the authorities. 

I feel like my character is the star of a grand epic, with a detailed story of love, loss, betrayal and growth. 

-----Quality-----
With two unfortunate, but (so far) tolerable, exceptions, the level of quality is extremely high. 

The client is very stable. Several times, I've just alt-tabbed away and let it run while I took care of other things. Hours of runtime, no crashes. (TBH, the electricity use is irresponsible of me - and it's not like it's a big loss of time to start the client. It loads very, very fast, and you spawn in right in the middle of what you were doing, *even if it was a multi-step quest*.)

Rock solid frame rate; I'm running at a stable 4k60fps with almost all the graphical settings maxed out. 

(Edit) I don't know how I forgot to mention it. THE GAME IS BEAUTIFUL. It's one of those games where you just stop and stare periodically. 

I look at the size and complexity of this game (which is also cross-platform, cross-progression, including mobile), and compare it with the size/complexity of a lot of 2024/2025's Western AAA games...and frankly, I feel deeply embarrassed for some of those companies. 

-----Respect for my time-----
I work a full time job and have a family. I can't game whenever I want and just ignore time. So, it's a deal-breaker for me when a game needs me to treat it as more important than RL stuff to really enjoy the best parts. 

WWM respects my time. I can jump in, wonder around a little, and do something meaningful in a 30m session (collect parts of a side/flavor story, gather up some supplies that I need to level up some of my martial arts skills, explore someplace new, play some side games that give other rewards, or progress the main story). Then I can log out. 

Are there things that take longer than that? Well, yes, obviously. But I never log off after a short gaming session feeling like, "I just gave this game 30m and nothing meaningful happened." That's freakin' rare, these days. 

-----But what about microtransactions?-----
Yes, they are there. However: 

1. Nothing is pay to win. 

2. The vaaaast majority are cosmetics.
Many of these are, frankly, expensive. However:
   a) they have to make money somehow,
   b) you still have a lot of free options you pick up during play to make your character look unique (when I swap to multiplayer mode, I've seen characters with similar clothing, but I've never seen someone who looked like a clone, even from a distance)
   c) the buyable cosmetics are FREAKING BEAUTIFUL. I haven't bought anything yet, but it's mainly because there's so many frakkin' great looking options - once I decide what I want, I will happily spend some cash to support this game

-----Not all roses-----
Ok, I mentioned there were a couple of issues. Both are a bit unfortunate. 

1 - There is A LOT going on in this game. 
For the most part, it works great! But they haven't solved the riddle of how to make the menus flow well. To be clear: The UI itself (during actual gameplay) is fine. You can even hide it for immersion and I very often play that way. However, you do need to do things in the menus to manage stuff like character progression, items/gear, etc. And on a frequent basis, I can't find something I've seen before and have to hunt around through nested menus for it. I'm hoping they can improve this in 2026 - it's an example of "bad friction" from a game design perspective. 

2 - English translations (both subtitles and fully voiced) are a let down. 
I'm typically playing with Chinese audio (the majority of NPCs you run into are voiced) with English subtitles because, as is often the case, the English dub is really just terrible. Unfortunately, the text localization is also pretty bad. A few examples: 
  a) In settings, as with most games, there are things you can Disable/Enable. Here we have the option to Enable them, or..."Close" them. (Like, seriously? Someone did a blatantly literal translation here with no thought for, or awareness of, the context.)
  b) Some of the story beats have been over-simplified/literalized to the point that it's really hard to get traction in understanding the main story. This is one of the times I'm glad I'm stubborn - the story is actually pretty frakkin' amazing, and the poor translations are deeply unfortunate. I'm really glad I stuck with it, though - I feel like I'm in the middle of a war between secret societies fighting for influence over the nascent Empire, with deep personal histories for some of the major players who want you to take their side. 

-----In summary-----
Download free game. Play free game. Be confused about whether you are misremembering game was free because it's better than many expensive AAA games.

After playing for too many hours, I can't recommend the game. Here's the TL:DR version. 
The story so far was good but has been in filler for 3 months. The combat is very fun, the multiplayer latency issues are insane. People warp around, and combo chains that should work, may not. GvG is quite fun and is region locked, so the latency isn't as bad, but still could really use some work. The gacha system is way predatory with around 3 - maybe 4 premium currencies. I should mention i live in US:West so that may be a location issue. Then you hit endgame and all of the good basically goes out the window.

THE GOOD:
- The combat is really fun. It's closer to code vein than dark souls I would say, but the core combat gameplay is very engaging.
- The world feels very much alive. Don't hate my for saying this, but the AI friendship system is pretty cool and makes npcs feel more real?
- It's definitely a wuxia game. If you know anything about the world, everything from movement to martial arts to inner ways are very much in tune with everything I've read and watched. 
- The world is very well made. Verticality is very much explored.
- 30v30 combat is very fun, if you can find the right group of people to do it with.

THE BAD
- The story has been suddenly and without explanation completely de-railed. Suddenly its less low-fantasy in the newest region.
- Character development is a mess. If you're familiar with resin from genshin, It's many times worse than trying to farm even a set of reasonable artifacts. Imagine genshin had 8 slots for artifacts, 3x in the sub-stat spread and RNG that makes diablo 2 feel reasonable. Though as been remedied somewhat when you can reroll exactly one slot and the final stat.
- The energy system also kind of locks you into one "class." You can't realistically experiment with different martial arts without gimping yourself in either inner ways, gear or weaponry. Probably all 3.
- The game very much limits you in nearly everyway from a weekly standpoint. I imagine once I finish the different campaigns, story and encounters, it becomes a login for 10 minutes and do your dailies then log out for the day kind of game. I will say it doesn't force you to log in every day or you miss out on x reward, mostly.
- There's the practice of multi banner different currency monstrosity. The hoyo made systems feature a singlar premium currency that was fairly farmable. WWM has one free always around banner that you can farm currency for. A semi-premium currency banner that you can get a few pulls. Then there's the premium premium banner that you can only spend money to get pulls for. Granted all of this is cosmetics only. Then there's the monthly thing you buy. Genshin's hands you premium currency, WWM hands you 5 dollars of premium currency and nothing else.
- The multiplayer is kind of laggy. Whether it's online or co-op everything seems to have a weird delay once you enter multiplayer, and bosses will not be where they should.
- Exploration is repetetive. I feel like I'm playing assassin's creed running after the random feathers and doing side content as a 2nd job. 
- I started the game with a friend, and there's many things where we can't do together. It's not so much an optional mmo as it's like fromsoft multiplayer pre night-rein. Somethings you can do together, many things you can't.

FINAL THOUGHTS
At this point, if you're playing from NA the game is dead. Be prepared to play out of region in EU or Asia if you want consistent team play. Solo is as good as ever.

I'm gonna be up-front and say I'm pretty much this game's target audience. 

That being said, I'm writing the review because this game deserves more recognition-- what it has done is extremely impressive and isn't being talked about enough. Many "reviews" online from youtubers and the like do the game a gross disservice. Only showing janky parts or the worst parts of the game possible, for example. 

The TLDR version is: the game is great because it sets out to "gameify" an entire genre of fiction, in this case Chinese Wuxia. That's obviously super hard to do, and yet it pulls it off to an impressive degree. Imagine a Lord of the Rings game that just by playing it, someone totally new to the West's high fantasy can understand the themes and grow to care about them. Extremely tough to do!

Anyways:

The graphics are great

The story is decent (mainly held back by localization and translation)
If you do not know anything about Chinese fantasy (in this case, Wuxia) you should absolutely look up a video or read a little about it. Just like someone from China would be scratching their head if a game about King Arthur showed up on their steam page, the same applies here-- the story is written for people with some understanding of the genre. 

The characters are numerous so you're going to find ones you like and don't like, it's just a massive game with lots of NPCs to talk to and interact with. 

The gameplay is better than any other MMO on the market right now because everything you do to get stronger is tied to the world and its characters. That's heavily influenced by the genre I mentioned above, which focuses often on the society and connections the characters in those types of stories have with each other. But those connections don't have to be sunshine and rainbows: You can go straight to a warrior sect, sneak in, and learn actual abilities from observing them. It makes you actually care about exploring-- you get real stat buffs and unlock a variety of items and resources by simply getting collectibles. You also can unlock very impressive and fun "lightness" skills where you basically fly across the map if you've gotten enough collectibles in a region.

Localization / translations and minor jank are the only real issues with the game, and those don't take away from the experience at all.

I think there's a lot of copium in the West regarding the East's game capabilities. But if you take this game and compare it to literally any Western AAA action RPG (yes, even ghost of tsushima) it comes out on top.

This will be long. Grab a drink, have a smoke and sit back. I have a lot to say about this game. If you want to read about the high and low of this game from my perspective, then hang out with me. If not, I will provide a TL;DR at the end with some prominent points.

I will just get right at it. I do recommend this game. It plays very well, the environment is immersive and expansive and the story is not bad. Not great, but FAR from bad. At the time of writing this, I have about 56 hours in and have burned through a lot of the main storyline. Combat mechanics are rewarding and allow for learning. Low floor, mid ceiling. 

PvE is fun and there is a plethora of stuff to find and interact with. The landscape is gorgeous. I often find myself just taking a minute to appreciate it. The character creator is... Ok? What you can make is amazing. The attention to specific details is also amazing. However, I do feel slightly limited. Roughly speaking you have two options. Abomination or cookie-cutter beautiful Chinese super model with slight variations in lip thickness. Beyond that, I have seen extremely little in the way of variation in the end result. And this is coming from a player who has done extensive time in titles like: Dragon's Dogma, Souls/Borne, Nioh 2, Cyberpunk and Soul Caliber Fighting game franchise from 2 forward. All of these had from ok, to outstanding character creators. Where Winds Meet falls on the middle area of this. As stated above, what you can make is amazing. But lacks variation in my opinion.

Co-op PvE is fun. Just that simple. Base raids, interactive and fun things to do that are not like a lot of other games like the yoga thing. Forgive me for not knowing the proper name of the event. The one where you input some commands and inevitably turn into an animal briefly. I laughed, I didn't know the first time and it was a pleasant surprise. The music making is cool. Hard to master, but as a piano and guitar dabbler, I greatly enjoy messing around with what I can try to make or cover from outside the game. Boss mode with randos is also a blast. I was expecting a ♥♥♥♥ show, but everyone I have queued with has been helpful and played their roles well. Reminds me of the earlier days of Final Fantasy XIV A Realm Reborn (That was when I last played that title).

PvP. Well... It is there. You can do it. And it is... kind of... OK. I like it, don't get me wrong. But. BUT... Dual blades is the only weapon that is truly viable. Others work. Don't shred me over how YOU can make the parasol stomp ass. I KNOW. What I am saying is, the dual blades are, and by a landslide, much too easy to ♥♥♥♥-stomp noobs and unskilled players. If a player is savvy with them the onslaught is near endless. Basically, do not let the blender-bros hit you. It becomes quite difficult to get out once you are being shredded. Yes, there are ways to counter them. Yes, parry is a thing. But, lag can make parry... unreliable. It is not as bad as some games, but lag is still lag no matter where you play. Overall, do not let this deter you from playing PvP. It IS fun and it IS worth playing. Just know that there IS a meta, unfortunately.

Now the bad part. The Gacha...
I am relatively new to the gacha space. I have now hundreds of hours in Wuthering Waves, about 30-50 hours in Duet Night Abyss, the time in this one and probably about 60+ in Zenless Zone Zero. I have a fair idea of good and bad gacha systems, I think. This one is god awful. I get it. A game with this kind of polish being free MANDATES a way to make some money to keep it good and keep it going. However, the prices for cosmetics is insane. Some potentially costing thousands of real dollars to get depending on the alignment of the stars and gacha god's graces. We all know that gacha IS. It's a roll of the proverbial dice, it is a game in and of itself. But this one borders on predatory in my opinion. YOU DO NOT NEED ANYTHING THAT COSTS MONEY. There, I said it. Happy? But we all know what FOMO is, and we are playing a gacha game because we WANT the cool goodies that come from a lucky pull. It detracts from the overall feel-good of this game to see the best gear locked behind a minimum $30 USD paywall. And I said MINIMUM. Take what you see online with a grain of salt. But, I have done a little digging, NOT JUST REDDIT, to find that there are numerous claims of whales and dolphins spending what I would call ridiculous money to get GOODIES. Again, thousands of real moneys. If you can do that, then I am happy for you. Most of us cannot. What the game gives you for free is... OK. But you likely won't be getting the wedding set, boat and horse on an F2P budget. Not impossible, I suppose. Just like me hitting the lottery without ever buying a ticket. There is a non-zero chance the wind will one day blow the winning ticket, dropped by someone accidentally, into my lap. So, it is possible. I just wouldn't count on it. 

Final thoughts TL;DR
Good game
Fun combat
Amazing graphic quality for a free game. Looks AAA
Terrible gacha, predatory and without a single thought about players who are not independently wealthy
PVP, co-op, PVE: fun, enjoyable, able to sink countless hours in for free.

If you stayed, Thank you. I didn't write this for me. I know what I think of the game. I wrote this to hopefully help someone who is unsure become more sure about what they are getting into.

The game was interesting for the first few hours. Character creation was fun. The game looks nice. I didn't like how combat progression was though. If you aren't invested in japanese swordsman style games you probably won't like this much. It's a game with a lot of potential but as it is now you will have a lot of annoying things to ignore in order to derive any fun from the game. 

COMBAT: 
I didn't like the mystic arts and weapon skills system. It just wasn't fun for me. Gaining new skills is a unintuitive, confusing endeavor. You learn your first martial art by watching a bear and copying it's movements. Later I thought I could steal regular human NPC skills and (you can't for some reason) I wondered if i was missing something. The first competition where you fight Elder Gongsun just felt terrible. It's a character that seems much cooler than your own character. I wanted to learn how to get his unarmed weapon style and skills but I didn't see any way. He's very fast and strong and really makes your own character's combat flow feel underwhelming. 

MENUS AND TRANSLATION ISSUES: 
Then there's the obvious low effort translation mistakes like graphics settings being labled 'Close' instead of 'Off'. Menus were scattered around and hard to navigate. Menus in menus in menus. A couple menus like for the mtx loot boxes literally lead to a cutscene. Just clicking the menu starts a low quality gaudy cutscene, then yet another cutscene plays when you open a loot box. It just feels cheap like the sparkles and flashy colors you see on a mobile game reward screen. You can look to Warframe to see a high class f2p game. This isn't it. 

THE DISAPPOINTING INTRO TO THE GAME: 
The game starts really slow and boring. It doesn't hook you. For the first few minutes you play as a completely different character who is much stronger and it's pretty engaging gameplay for a while. Then suddenly that's over and you make your own character. You are then attacked by a ninja like person and he takes your coin and then you name the coin. It's strange. The coin determines your characters own name. I named it 'Jade Coin' at first because I just thought it was a cool token i was naming. 

After that, for the first hour, it's a huge switch from the high action gameplay from earlier before character creation. There's a little girl who you pretty much babysit and who acts really whiny. She was annoying. There's a letter at the beginning you find that feels like a serious call to action mentioning some new threat but then the game continues from there really slow, casual, and uneventful. I was more interested in exploration but it seemed like a lot of things were locked behind doing the main quests.

GRAPHICS:
The game graphics are crisp, detailed, and seem well optimized. They are uninspired though. I just feel like I'm exploring a generic Asian grasslands environment. There's supposed to be a very large city in the game but it seems like they preferred to start with the most boring content and lost my interest. In games I play, the feeling of ambience and atmosphere is really important to me. I need to feel like I'm actually there and get the feeling of; this is really scary/amazing/beautiful/dark/mysterious. Examples of games with great ambience and atmosphere are Metro Exodus, Fallout 4, Elden Ring, and WoW (with its build up of lore and connection to the land, a handcrafted environment, environmental sounds, and zone music). Look up 'WoW Teldrassil OST' to see how well made inspired music changes a game. Look at the comments on the video

The game isn't terrible, but like many of these goofy companies, they find themselves doing the dumbest things I've ever seen and calling it content as usual. When will these companies learn that doing the same stuff over and over will not keep a player base. Making your game into a fulltime job isn't a smart business practice. One day maybe there'll be a company who isn't trying to hijack gamer's lives, but instead they just make a regular video game for once. 

Not every games needs to piggy-back off FromSoftware. The biggest drawback to my continuation of playing this game is the clunky movement and combat system. If feels like they copy-pasta'd DS's combat and movement systems.

In my opinion, players will have a harder time adjusting to those 2 systems more than they will with the parrying, difficulty, economy, or even the repetitive stuff to do in the game-world like collecting things, competition mini-games, and the "forts" and outposts they make the player fight through for level progress.

Player level doesn't seam to matter though, seeing as all enemies scale to the player and it feels like they're just for "talent" points to unlock skills. The leveling system also feels like it's meant to slow the players progress if they're progressing too fast in a certain area. Every 10 levels the player has to compete in a trial to have the ability to progress through the next 10 levels.

With this, it looks like there's a lot in the game, but what I've seen is that there are more menus, windows, and things to click on than actual things to do. That means you'll spend more time standing still flipping through menus and screens than you will be doing anything else (they're competing with MMOs here).

There are also quite a lot of microtransaction options and the only positive being that most of the cash-shop items appear to be cosmetic, with some being progression based. My review will stay because it's not for the faint of heart and even though it's F2P, it'll still steal people's time.

Summary: A frustrating and incomplete game, poorly optimised, with issues in basic game design and map layout.
----------------------------------------------------------------
I'm pretty sure that every section I played had problems.

The first section was quick-time events. These do not work effectively if the UI does not disply the input required. The game displayed an empty timer ticking to zero.

The second section was combat. This does not work effectively for the same reasons. The UI consistently failed to provide the button required to press. 'Press _ to attack' is not helpful.

The third section was overworld traversal. The game does not tell you that you have a triple jump available, but it does tell you about the air dash. Why it doesn't tell you, I do not know.

The fourth section was skills, skill swapping and equipment swapping. However, the tutorial does it automatically for each skill you learn, and doesn't teach you how to swap the skills yourself. If you want to change them outside of a tutorial shortcut, you need to navigate the confusing and disorienting menu system. Also, there are so many skills to learn and few skill slots available, so there's a lot of moving in and out of menus to change weapons, fighting styles, skills and several RPG upgrade trees. Some of these trees are only accessible by interacting with an NPC.

Also your arrows home in on targets, but only if you have the crosshair on them when you fire. This is another thing the game does not tell you.

At some point I ended up in an arena section where I could challenge other villagers. On of those villagers was nigh unbeatable until I turned off auto-deflect, because the only way to get through one of his combo strings is the parry every hit in the 10sec combo sequence.

I gave up with the game when I got to the debating minigame. I gave up because the tutorial mission for the game was very unhelpfully placed after several unwinnable examples of the minigame. They are unwinnable because you have no way to upgrade your ability to play the minigame, unless there is and the game refused to give it to me. It was especially galling to realise I was debating with characters that had 3-4 times the health of the tutorial example. Especially because one of those examples was someone pretending to be the player character, and judging by the signposts around the area indicating immediate death, it was also a boss fight of some kind.

I haven't even talked about the visual glitches and bugs where people don't have faces, or T-pose and rotate on their horses. Or that textures pop in and out on the lowest graphics settings. Or the fact I almost played the game for 5 hours and didn't reach a main plot point. 

Also, play as a male character. Some dialogue is poorly translated, and refers to the player character as 'he' regardless of gender.

Good game overall, but co-op and online features need serious improvement.

The world, combat, exploration, and overall soul of Where Winds Meet are genuinely great. The atmosphere and gameplay feel strong, and the single-player experience shines.

That said, the co-op and online systems feel very limiting. Online mode is basically just a lobby with minigames, which feels underwhelming. There’s no real sense of a shared world. World boss content technically exists, but joining it is awkward—you either have to constantly scan chat or dig through menus to find someone to join, which feels clunky and outdated.

The only meaningful online activities right now are the sword trials and raids, but even those drop you straight into combat. There’s no buildup, no social space, and no opportunity to actually interact with other players or form connections. It all feels very transactional.

Overall, this is a strong game with a great foundation, but it lacks long-term social systems that encourage player bonding and community. I’d love to see improvements in co-op, shared-world events (like proper world bosses), and social features that make playing together feel more meaningful over time.

[h1]Really Great F2P Game, Could Be Better[/h1]

It's a free-to-play that doesn't feel like a free-to-play game at all, in fact it plays and feels like an actual 60$ game with an impressive amount of content and things to do while also being quite generous with free outfits and accessories. It's also primarily single-player, with a integrated online mode allowing you to seamlessly socialize for events or play solo.

If you're looking to play this without ever wanting to spend a penny, you can definitely do so while looking incredibly elegant with all the free cosmetics obtainable. Naturally some things will not be available, such as the more extravagant and flashy cosmetics that steer more into magical fantasy than actual grounded Chinese appearances, but as someone who loves grounded Chinese appearances it's fantastic.

There are however unfortunately some notable negatives with the game:
[list][*][b]Extensive AI Usage[/b] - One of the most immediately obvious things one can notice is that AI is used for English localization. As usual with Google translate errors trying to translate Chinese; females are referred to as [b]HE[/b]. [b]HER[/b] is translated as [b]SHE[/b], so you end up with sentences like [i]"Are you serious about SHE (her)? What is HE (she) talking about?"[/i]. Lots of things are poorly and incorrectly translated, make zero sense in actual language use and end up making an otherwise interesting story/setting extremely confusing and appearing as low-quality.

[i]It's sad to see such a great game with excellent visual representation, soundtrack and gameplay, massively tank in the story department due to terrible AI translation. And the same goes for English voice-overs, which are also AI. Good luck trying to cohesively understand the story with AI English trying to hold it all together while every quest overwhelms the player with names of NPCs that haven't even entered a scene yet, while sounding like [b]Zhing Zhou Yu, the Flaming Meteor of the Heavenly Stars[/b], searching for his [b]Jing-a-ling of the Seventh Shade[/b], riding [b]Anu, the Jade Serpent of the Nine Clouds[/b].
[*][b]The Performance[/b] - Unfortunately not very well optimized, as anytime the player has to go where larger groups of NPCs are the FPS just massively tanks. Especially in Kaifeng with 3000 pointless flavor NPCs sprinkled all over. I have two main gripes however. The limited energy system, and once you've cleared the majority of the map points, the time gates waiting to either level up, or get more content. The online events are pretty fun. The online boss runs can be pretty entertaining. It can be frustrating when you don't get a team with synergy (sorry to say it, but this is down to healers not performing their role)

BUT! There is a ton of time-walls built in many game mechanics and you will not be able to get as much items as you want as quickly as possible. Which makes the game really time consuming, be warned.
The reason I quit the game is because of all those time-walls, it was making playing the game too time consuming.

For example one mechanic is jail, if you commit in-game crimes, you will be sent to jail for 30 minutes and you can't do anything other than wait in prison for all that time doing nothing (or you can pay your way out with in-game currency).
Waste player time system: There is those multiplayer events that increase your stats that is basically waiting 10 minutes doing nothing until the animation ends, sometimes a bit more time like 20 minutes doing nothing.
Energy timewall system: There is crafting time-wall points and combat time-wall points needed to redeem rewards needed to upgrade your character, each refill one point per several minutes.
Lootbox system: There is certain lootboxes needed to upgrade your character that only happen once every week or you have to be end-game to farm them weekly lootbox to obtain better gear.

All of this is somewhat bearable if you are ok with the game wasting a lot of your time.

Have you ever watched one of those old martial arts movies with Shaolin monks, leaps across rooftops, and flying heroes and been completely blown away?

Then this is the game for you.

You can create your own hero or heroine and explore the world as an adventurer. You'll learn skills and how to use weapons.
The world is beautifully designed. There's so much to explore. In addition to the main quest, you'll discover many side quests over time, all equally beautiful and lovingly crafted. You'll have some minigames, a bit of detective work, puzzles, stealth and of course, combat. 
Sneaking across the rooftops and delivering a killing blow from above, Assassin's Creed style? You can. You can easily spend hours experiencing things without having to fight. 
The difficulty of the battles can be adjusted at any time. From manageable to a real challenge, there's something for everyone. But fighting always feels fantastic, and every mistake punishes you at least as hard. 
So boss fights shouldn't be underestimated, especially on higher difficulties.

The game currently uses about 100 GB, but it offers quite a lot in return. Graphically, I really like the game, and it runs smoothly. The options basically offer everything you could want and freely adjustable.

For fans of single-player games, yes, you can play it alone.
For co-op fans, you can play with friends or strangers anytime.
For multiplayer, guilds? Same here. 
For PVP, yepp. 

Purchasing items in the shop is not necessary. You can play the game without making any transactions. Some of the skins look really good, but the price is sometimes quite high. 
I've never seen a free-to-play game with so much content.
In the end, all I can say is: download it and try it out for yourself, it's free.

At the current moment I really don't recommend this game until they clean things up. It's not a horrid game by any means and it has alot of potential but there are some glaring issues that need to be addressed.

This game is extremely unfriendly to new players. If I wasn't a brianrot gacha loser I wouldn't have understood even 1/4 of the systems. I cannot imagine a very fresh player to this genre jumping on this for the first time and enjoying it.  There are so many different currencies in this game, different skills for the player and the weapons, unlocks for levels and unlocks for menus but the game doesn't do a good job of introducing a new player to those systems. One of my biggest gripes also is the menus are terrible because some tabs are just under so many layers which makes it so infuriating find things.

Another major turn off to me is the performance and strange audio issues. I don't understand why but when I went through 2-3 caves the sound audio just explodes some how. Like a dying robot trying to make noises. The game also seems to struggle alot with the environment loading and textures. Like I will walk into a town and it just takes forever to load things in. Sometimes the game literally just freezes and sits there and loads. Some textures also take forever to load, like signs and stuff look groggy until after a few seconds of waiting.

The overall feel of character movement and combat are fine. But the physics of the game are janky and lead to really weird interactions. I was fighting a bandit and we collided and somehow he ended up on my head and just spinning in circles. Some enemies just straight up have bad AI. They are coded to react from certain distances and if you attack from outside that range they straight up do nothing but circle you and you hit them for free.

The AI chat is 50/50. It is a cool idea but has a ton of issues. Their chats essentially have 0 substance and you can just mess around. One time I just kept talking about uma musume to them. They said they didn't understand and wanted get back on topic but I didn't stop messing around. Then, somehow I became revered with them without even mentioning a single thing about the topic at hand.  

The English DUB is terrible and I'm almost certain it is AI generated. Chinese dub is good though.

These are just some of the complaints I have with the game currently, this isn't to say the game isn't enjoyable. I get good laughs with my friends messing around and combat feel pretty fun overall. It's just, I feel like they are so close to something good but have a far ways to go still. I will still hop the game here and there to play with my friends (They hardcore love this game) but I hope this game gets better.

I went in with doubts, as I'm generally skeptical of f2p titles. I gotta say, well done. So far the game is a ton of fun, even if there are a few bugs here and there. Exploration feels rewarding. Not the biggest fan of time-gated progress, but that might be my fault for getting sucked in for about 10 hours - I doubt most would notice it. Damn me and my vacation time. I'm playing on Legend, the current hardest difficulty, and the result is a grand old time. Soulslike in difficulty, but incredibly diverse in gameplay elements.

EDIT - So this game is pretty good for story, and you can get quite a lot of adventure out of it, but it really starts to stagnate at level cap - the endgame grinding is based around an "Energy" system. On one hand, it helps since you can keep up if you've got limited time, but on the other, it means that extended play sessions start to lose their meaning. A huge negative is that progression materials are capped weekly, which means that if you miss a week, you have no reasonable way to catch up to those playing consistently. It's a pretty painful treadmill at the endgame, and I'd prefer not to make the game a permanent fixture in my life to stay competitive.

I'd caution against the PVP game mode - It's basically just a competition of who can cheese and stunlock better, and some weapons are just awful to play against. Additionally, the mode is heavily padded with braindead-easy bots, making win-rate percentages and rankings practically worthless. That game mode is what made me decide to put the game down for the foreseeable future. And honestly? Once I decided to drop it, it was a weight off my chest.

This game is two games. Highly recommend one; Avoid the other.

On the one hand this is an incredible single-player open world rpg. Think Chinese Elden Ring in terms of scope, exploration, and challenging (on legend difficulty anyway) boss fights. Beautiful, vast world with tons to do. The parry-heavy combat is reminiscent of Sekiro, which feels great if you're a fan of that style. Only real negatives here are a needlessly convoluted menu system and occasionally weird english localization. But the boss fights alone are well worth it. 

On the other side of the coin is the live-service aspect. There are co-op dungeons, outposts, and "raids" you can run. Sects and guilds you can join. Lots of stuff that could have made this a great long-term game. Sadly almost everything is hard gated by "energy" which is spent running activities and refreshes over time. You literally cannot get gear, skill upgrades, etc. without energy. If your rng is poor, sucks to suck, try again next week. Super cringe mobile game vibes. I like your game, dummies, let me play it.

All-in-all it's definitely worth playing through the campaign. The world is incredible and the boss fights are sick. Such a shame everything else is so heavily time-gated. This could have been a worthwhile game to invest time/money into long term, but sadly... I'm not interested. If you're a fan of mobile games or just not bothered by ridiculous time gates then more power to you. Either way, it's free. Check it out

A typical soulless free-to-play Chinese grindfest.
There are supposedly a lot of features, but they’re implemented very clumsily. Even basic fast sprinting with parkour: you already took your hands off the keyboard, but instead of running through an arch, your character suddenly does 500 jumps on his own and you end up on a rooftop. Was this even tested at all? And this kind of clunkiness is everywhere.

It’s nice that the whole gacha system is purely cosmetic, but do I actually like any of it? No. Someone probably does — I don’t. Typical Chinese over-the-top pathos like in their movies from that era. It’s strange there’s no flying while standing on a sword yet, but they’ll probably add it sooner or later.

Boss fights are fun solo, but there are way too many parries. In multiplayer, netcode often ruins part of your parries, though this is somewhat fixed by having a healer in the team. ))) There’s no point in doing raid bosses with randoms, because they leave the raid after the very first hit, so you absolutely need a guild.

Fighting groups of enemies is not fun. Again, too many parries. They should’ve added more crowd control, because when there are around six enemies — especially if half of them are ranged — you just stand in place spamming E and F from time to time.

Visuals? Beautiful. Those panoramic views are pure eye candy. But these days it’s nothing impressive — almost every grind-heavy game like this has visuals on that level.

Everything else is complete garbage.
For example, to get a costume from the “sect without a sect”, you need to do online activities 4–5 days a week, where you literally spend half an hour in real life watching your character sleep or something like that. And you need to do this for several weeks. Wow, so fun, I can’t wait to do that every day.

Another example: a bounty hunting costume. To buy literally anything, you first need to save up 50k. That’s an insane grind. Even PvP bounty hunting gets exhausting farming that much, and the income isn’t stable. The fastest and most stable income is lawyering, because you stay in your own world — if your profession level is high enough, you just click a few buttons and in 10 seconds you get 50–70 points. Is it fun? No.

Who the hell came up with all of this? Why? Who actually likes this? Is this just grind for the sake of grind?

Alright, I’ve already written more than I usually do.
I don’t recommend it. There are projects that are much more enjoyable both in terms of content and overall grind — better go play those.

[h1]Review: Where Winds Meet – An Unexpected Masterpiece[/h1]

[b]Rating: 10/10[/b]

[i]Where Winds Meet[/i] is not just a game; it is a sprawling, breathing world that completely defied my expectations. As a Free-to-Play title, I expected compromises, but instead, I found one of the most visually stunning and content-rich open-world experiences I have ever played. It strikes a perfect balance between solo immersion and social interaction.

[h2]Visuals, Audio & Technical Performance[/h2]
From the moment you step into this historical Chinese setting, the production value is evident. The graphics are top-tier, the world is beautifully detailed, and the soundtrack perfectly sets the mood.

Technically, the game runs surprisingly well. On my [b]RTX 3080[/b], the experience has been smooth with no major technical hiccups, which is refreshing for a game of this scale.

[h2]Gameplay: The Dance of Blades and Wind[/h2]
The combat is the heart of the experience. It is fast, responsive, and deeply satisfying. It’s not just about button mashing; it’s reaction-based, rewarding you for perfectly timing blocks and counters against enemies.

The movement system (Qinggong) deserves special praise. While it starts simple, it opens up significantly as you level up. Unlocking triple jumps and the ability to practically fly across the map makes traversing the open world a joy in itself.

[h2]A New Standard for Social Gaming[/h2]
This is where the game truly shines for me. [i]Where Winds Meet[/i] masters the balance between being a solo player and an MMO participant.
[list]
[*] [b]Flexible Modes:[/b] You can easily switch between PvP, Solo, and Co-Op.
[*] [b]Organic Socializing:[/b] The game rewards you for being "a little" social without forcing it. Mechanics like healing others or running dungeons create natural opportunities to meet new friends online. It feels like a safe space where solo play can naturally evolve into group play at your own pace.
[/list]

[h2]The World & Content[/h2]
The story is above average, featuring decent English voice acting and cinematic cutscenes. However, the real star is the game loop. The freedom to explore this incredible world at your own tempo, accompanied by great music, is the best part of the experience.

[h2]The Nitpicks (It’s not perfect, but I don't care)[/h2]
Even a 10/10 experience has flaws, and fairness requires mentioning them:
[list]
[*] [b]UI Clutter:[/b] The menus are messy. There are simply too many of them, and it can be overwhelming to navigate.
[*] [b]Completionist Struggles:[/b] For those of us who like to see "100% Completed" in our journals, the game can be frustrating. Many side quests do not appear on the map, forcing me to rely on YouTube guides to find them.
[*] [b]Specific Mini-games:[/b] Personally, I did not enjoy the "Riddle" quests, card games, or the "Facemask" events. However, I understand that other players might enjoy this variety, so it’s not a dealbreaker.
[/list]

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
Despite the cluttered menus and hidden quests, I cannot give this game anything less than a perfect score. It exceeds expectations in every way that matters. It offers the best open-world balance of solo, co-op, and online play I have ever experienced—and it does so for free.

[b]Highly recommended.[/b]

[h1]Personal Rating 7/10[/h1]

The game has a lot of good things going for it. The stories are done very well. The visuals look very good for a free game. There's amazing scenery and freedom to traverse it all. There's a robust array of various progression features in the game. There are TONS of unlockables and a huge map to enjoy, and because this is a live service game, I'm sure there is much more to come.

Overall I like the game, and I can ignore a number of its flaws in terms of keeping me motivated to play.  I can get past some of sect daily quests not triggering complete after you perform the required action. When so much of the game is voiced, I can get past some of the vocals cutting in on top of others from time to time. Getting randomly transported by to Uncle Jiang's house from time to time isn't that bad either. The PVP isn't that good, and in my experience, it often comes down to who gets hit first. Players with some weapons can chain their opponents into an inescapable combo, but because I look at this like an extra, optional part of the game, I won't grade it too bad.

[b]However,[/b] the lack of responsiveness from the controls... This is key to the main gameplay loop. I don't know if this is only a problem for controller users or if it's also applicable to keyboard, but the issue centers around time sensitive inputs, namely the parrying/deflection mechanic. It works very inconsistently at best, but its a major part of the game. 80% of the difficulty concerning bosses and mobs is whether or not the game will allow you to parry after input. The option to auto-parry is there, but I prefer to actually play a game rather than have it play itself. This takes away a lot of the enjoyment from my experience. I don't have a problem dying if I mess up, I'll just get good. However, if the game intermittingly decides if I'm good, arbitrarily, that's a problem. Gameplay is a big part of a game. For that reason, I'd give this game a 7/10. It has enough going for it that it's definitely worth a try, but the above issue will annoy you from time to time.

Where Winds Meet is likely my favorite game this year overall, and it had some stiff competition. 

It's free, not pay to win(only pay to pretty), and easy to drop in and out of without hassle. I find myself gravitating towards it after work, and can always find something to do. Sometimes it's farming resources, other times its hunting collectables, and of course doing quests. There's always something to do, even if it's minor.

Very few games truly encapsulate a genre, but WWM is Wuxia to the core. I've always enjoyed both Wuxia and Xianxia, and while I prefer the latter WWM is just the chefs kiss at making you feel like a martial arts master. 

It's not without flaws, though. 

The translation can be rough in some spots, but I'm used to poor translations(in fact, I had a college course on it). If you're used to rough translations, like the old fan translations in manga, you'll probably be fine. Additionally, while the cosmetic shop has something for most price ranges, the upper end is truly egregiously priced. Luckily, none of that really impacts the gameplay. There's also a limit on weekly resources, limited both by hard caps(like income) and energy. While it can be frustrating at times, I often find myself using it as an excuse to just go out and hunt collectables or other side activities that aren't impacted by it. 

I have my issues with WWM, like I would any game. But for a free to play title, it's phenomenal. It has so much you can do, and the story is enjoyable. The world is stunning, and the combat is both gorgeous and fluid. 

Even with its flaws, I give it a 10/10. None of the flaws have truly gotten in the way. Cash shop is overpriced, but it's a free game and it's purely cosmetic. Translation is rough in spots, but Chinese is a hard language to translate on a good day. And the weekly limits just encourage you to do other things instead of the same activity over and over. In the end, these are barely flaws, and it has so, so much going for it that they're just a drop of water in a sea of positive things.

[h1]This game has to be one of the best games to just sit down and play in 2025.[/h1] 

[h3]There's really good Vertical and horizontal progression.[/h3] In terms of horizontal progression The number of things you can do in this game is pretty vast. You can Travel the map doing Archery contests, you can do Wrestling, you can play a drinking game where you try to throw arrows into a pot as you get more and more progressively drunk, you can write news articles that are voted on by other players and will be featured in the game. Looking at Vertical Progression you have a ton of different systems to interact with and use. You have your normal stats, you have your martial Arts which are the proficiency by which you use the chosen weapons you use. you have Mystic Skills which are part of your over all rotation along with your weapons. Your also have your normal Gear and later on you have the Arsenal Which Honestly for all the years I've spend playing MMOs of all kinds is a great way to still get value out of the old gear your not currently using. That chest piece you farmed for? Yeah your still going to use it which is great. Because all of those systems feed into your Mastery Score. The game itself also doesn't take itself too seriously either Your Mastery Score also doubles as your indicator of how many Geese you could fight and win against in a fight( [u]pro tip: Geese will beat you[/u]!) 

Another thing to look forward to in this game is the stories, the overall and smaller stories for this game are very well done. and they all have a believable amount of Depth and intrigue. When it comes to the Main story its very well done and if i had to choose a side story, One leaf one life would have to one of my favorites. 

I think a final point that needs to be said is that this game does its combat very well in my opinion. I am very new to the soulslike and Sekiro like style of games where the gameplay revolves around stamina dodging parries and a posture like system. But with the way the game introduces a lot of its systems and lets you experience the game at your own pace I felt right at home and was having a blast fighting new bosses. Its to the point that even if i don't need gear or something I will still help out someone with a fight because I like the combat and the fights in this game that much.

[h2] If I had to Choose A bad thing.. [/h2] To say the game does terribly, It would have to be its in game menus. Coming from a vast selection of games with different and confusing menus I thought I had seen it all but even with 244 hours at the time of writing this review I still get lost in this game's menus. The other things that are sorta iffy.. The battle pass love them or hate them, its in this game along with the energy system that has its own paint points. When it comes to the battle pass I don't particularly enjoy that the Battle pass gives you more energy pills that will help you regain energy but at the same time You genuinely get gear and are able to do what you need to do without interacting with any of these systems if you don't want to. Case and point After 244 hours I've not had to use one of the energy pills that the game gives you via the Battle pass and via the break through or level progression system. 
The other sort of annoying thing.. But this isn't even really a complaint just a preference, But I would coming from games like WoW and FFXIV and other MMOs like this I would rather do all the levels at once going from level 1 to 100 or whatever the max is going to be. I can fully understand why they didn't go that route but its just a difference of preference in this case.

TLDR:

“Gorgeous wuxia, mobile MMO soul – 5/10”

Where Winds Meet is the definition of “looks better than it plays.” The first impression is strong: flashy combat, slick animations, and very fluid movement that nails the wuxia fantasy of darting around, juggling enemies, and doing stylish finishers. Some of the core mechanics are genuinely cool, with interesting martial skills and movement options that make just running around and fighting feel satisfying at a surface level.

The problem is everything wrapped around that combat feels like a mobile game awkwardly dumped onto PC. The UI is straight‑up mobile‑first: cluttered, unintuitive menus, layers of tabs and submenus, pop‑ups everywhere, and a general “gacha MMO” layout that absolutely kills immersion on mouse and keyboard. It never feels like a PC‑native UX; it feels like you’re remote‑controlling a phone game with a cursor.

Progression is where it really falls apart if you care about builds. There are upgrades everywhere, but they mostly feel like shallow stat bumps spread across a dozen overlapping systems instead of a coherent build fantasy. Early on there’s no strong sense of crafting a unique playstyle; you’re mostly following what the game expects, and any “depth” tends to be buried behind grindy, menu‑driven systems rather than meaningful choices. It plays more like a single‑player MMO checklist than a focused action RPG.

On top of that, level progression is time‑gated in a way that feels patronizing. You slam into caps and have to wait for real‑time “breakthroughs” before you’re allowed to level again, with XP just being stored in the meantime. Main story quests, new areas, and systems are often locked behind those levels, so the game ends up drip‑feeding your progression by the calendar instead of rewarding your effort when you’re actually in the mood to play. It’s a terrible feeling to be told “come back tomorrow” in what is marketed as an action RPG.

The monetization and endgame structure don’t help. There’s an energy‑style system that limits premium rewards from repeatable endgame content, with passes and paid tracks giving you more ways to refill and accelerate that loop. On top of that are multiple premium currencies, escalating‑cost gachas, and outfits that were cheaper and directly purchasable on the CN version but are now locked behind more expensive scratches for global players. Even some positive reviews and long‑time players are basically saying “read the fine print” before you spend, which should tell you everything.

Community and support aren’t exactly reassuring either. There are reports of players catching long bans just for joining the wrong co‑op lobby, with slow or opaque appeal processes, and negative reviews often get dogpiled by very defensive accounts. It doesn’t inspire much confidence to invest time (or money) in a live service game when the systems, support, and atmosphere around it all feel this fragile.

If you just want a free, pretty wuxia playground with flashy combat, some goofy moments, and don’t mind mobile DNA all over the systems and UI, you might genuinely have fun for the first 10–20 hours. As a PC gamer who cares about buildcraft, fair progression, and sane monetization, this ends up feeling like a mobile MMO template with high‑end graphics pasted on top. That’s why it lands at a 5/10 for me.

It’s sad to admit this, but Where Winds Meet is simply not for me.

I genuinely enjoyed exploring the open world — sometimes alone, sometimes with friends. The world itself is beautiful, and doing activities together can be fun. However, the biggest downside for me is the intrusive social focus of the game.

“Join a guild. Find a healer. Heal a stranger. Play multiplayer. Play PvP. Share a photo.”
At some point, all of this starts to feel exhausting rather than engaging. The satisfaction from the short — though genuinely impressive — story slowly fades away. The same feeling applies to the open world itself.

This is not a full MMORPG, but it’s also not a proper single-player action RPG. It’s another service game trying to combine every currently popular gameplay element at once — and because of that, it never truly feels whole. 😔

That said, I still had a lot of fun spending time in this game, which I affectionately call Wuxia Impact. And I do recommend giving it a try, especially if you enjoy frequent interaction with other players.
