Hey! I don't normally write reviews, but for once i've decided to give it a go. I'm going to give my genuine thoughts with the pros and cons. In the end i'm going to give a rating X/10.

Pros:
✅Good story: It takes some time to get into properly, but i genuine think it's up there with one of the greats when you get in to the lore. It is a bit "here and there" in how you pick up on the lore, and it does have some downsides too which i will get to on the cons. But i think the game has a very good story once it actually get's going.

✅ Decent combat: Some people consider this a souls like. I don't actually agree to this, as to me it's more like a souls lite. Having said that, when it comes to fighting ads, it's just super satisfying and you feel like you're a powerful fighter in a way that's just done right. Then you got boss fights which humbles you and shows you that there is complexity to the game too. It's not always easy, but it's done in a satisfying way.

✅ Humor: The humor in this game is done in a way that i really enjoy in video games. It does have some funny moments but it doesn't take away from the overall story and the serious moments in games. 

✅ Graphics: It's not going to win the category of "Best" or "Smoothest" graphics ever in any video game. But i personally think it got some decent graphics.

✅ Cross platform: This game can be played on Playstation, PC and phone if i'm not mistaken? Which i personally think it a very good thing.

✅ Content: There is so much content in this game, and so many different activities. Ranging from weird chess variant to card games, to fishing, to story, to combat, to throwing salads at people who's jailed in the game, to BEING jailed in the game. There is enough content in this game to have you playing for hours even if you don't want to do the story for all the time you spend playing.

✅ Free-to-play: Here is where this game scores the best in my opinion. This game is very good if you consider everything you get as a free-to-play title. I'd argue there isn't really any pay-to-win aspects in the game (as of 13.desember.2024) mainly focusing on cosmetic things in the shop, and maybe some "pay to speed up" things that's genuenly not nessesary.

Middle ground: (These are things you're either going to love or hate, which i couldn't place in neither pros nor cons).
✔️ AI chatbots: This is a piece of content you're either going to love or hate. Some of the NPCs you'll encounter in the game are AI chatbots. These you can write too, and try to befriend through texting. What you write also matters, as some of them might get angry or annoyed at you and attack you if you write the wrong thing. If you befriend them though, then you might get gifts etc.

✔️ PvP: PvP is always a hit or miss type of situation. I've personally not had the chance to explore this in the game that much as of yet, but i've heard some people say they really like it, and some hate it. I don't have enough information about the PvP in this game to either put it in the pros or the cons. 

✔️ Weapon system: The weapon system in this game is what determines rather or not you're a DPS, Support or Tank. In the beginning it seems like you've got plenty of options, and for DPS you do! but for Support and Tanks the options get very limited. You do have some variety but it's not the great. However, as the game continues to be developed this can change with the inclution of new weapon types etc. (if we get them obviously)

Cons:
❌ Bugs: It's a bit buggy still. Considering how new the game is as of writing the review, i completely understand that it can have bugs. This game is massive and has a lot of things happening at ones. Being bug free would surprise me. It's definently not bad, and i as far as i'm aware, they are working hard to fix the bugs as they go. That said, i feel like i should mention it here.

❌ UI: The user interface of this game leaves a lot to be desired. It's clunky, and requires a lot of thought. It doesn't take up all of your screen like in other games, but the issue lies in how you have to navigate through it to get to what you want.

❌ Voice: The dialogues in this game often get's cut out. It's not the end of the world since you have text in the dialogues too, but when you're in the moment and enjoying the story, then suddenly your character forgets how to speak, it kinda takes away from the moment.

Final score?
9/10. As it stands now, (13. desember 2025) it's a very good game, which i absolutely recommend people to download. It's free to play and well worth checking out in my humble opinion.

Where Winds Meet – A Wuxia Hybrid with Highs and Lows

Rating: 7/10 Verdict: A visually stunning martial arts game that blurs the line between single-player narrative and multiplayer action. Great combat freedom, but technical issues hold it back.

Introduction
I’ve been diving into Where Winds Meet, and it’s a fascinating experiment. It’s not quite a traditional MMORPG, but it’s not just a single-player game either—it tries to do both. Since it’s Free-to-Play, it’s easy to jump in, but the experience is a bit of a rollercoaster.

✅ The Good Stuff
1. Flexible Gameplay (Solo & Multiplayer Hybrid) This is a huge plus. The game allows for a Single-player experience if you just want to follow the story and explore the world alone, but it seamlessly integrates Online Co-op and PvP. You get the immersion of a solo RPG without the forced crowding of an MMO, but you can still group up when you want to.

2. No Class System = Total Freedom You aren't locked into a specific "class" forever. The gameplay relies on weapon sets and skills.

You can switch weapons to adapt to different fights.

It feels liberating not to be forced into a "tank" or "healer" role permanently.

3. Beautiful Art & Graphics Visually, the game is a treat. The Wuxia art style is gorgeous, the environments are detailed, and the skill effects look incredibly cool. It really sells the fantasy of being a martial arts master.

4. It’s Free For a game that looks this good and offers this much content, the fact that it costs nothing to try is a major advantage.

❌ The Bad Stuff
1. Optimization is Rough (Low FPS) Despite the beautiful graphics, the performance is disappointing.

FPS drops are frequent, even on good hardware.

The game feels unoptimized, which ruins the fluidity of the combat.

2. Buggy Movement & World Collision The movement system (parkour/gliding) is ambitious but buggy. I constantly found myself getting stuck in buildings, clipping through walls, or freezing in weird geometry. It breaks the immersion when you have to fight the terrain more than the enemies.

3. Cosmetic Prices are Too High Since it is F2P, they make money on cosmetics, but the costumes are incredibly expensive. The pricing feels aggressive and out of reach for many players who just want a cool outfit.

4. Identity Crisis? (Added point) Sometimes the game feels like it doesn't know what it wants to be. The switch between single-player story and multiplayer modes can sometimes feel a bit disjointed.

📝 Conclusion
Where Winds Meet offers a great combat system and the flexibility to play solo or with friends. It looks amazing, but the technical jankiness (low FPS, bugs) and the expensive cash shop are hard to ignore.

It’s worth a download since it’s free, just don't expect a perfectly polished experience yet.

Don't let free to play fool you, the game is premium (special thanks to whales for funding this game).
First and most importantly of all, Where Winds Meet effectively sells the wuxia fantasy. The environment successfully immerses the player in the world of legendary heroes, martial prowess, and mysticism.

There are, however, a few flaws that may be offputting to some.
As many have referenced, the menu interface is extremely cluttered and could do with streamlining.
Also, as it is a F2P game, there are aspects of the game here and there that push for purchase of in game currency.
Finally, there is a lot of miscellaneous minigames that bloat up the game experience. That said, all this can be skipped with no major effect to character progression.

Ultimately, as a free to play title, Where Winds meet exceeds expectations (and perhaps redefines it). 
For most, this is a game worth trying out, especially when the price is free.

A game that completely went under my radar, did not hear about it until a friend recommended it to me, and I have to say, what a great game.

Content:
There is so much content in this game, from the the large quests to the hidden chests in a mountain, basically everything has details to it. Tiny things like following butterflies actually matter since it increases a certain stat some equipment needs. Fully optional and avoidable side bosses, which are all extremely unique, and interactions with situations you would think the developers ignored. Go to anywhere on the map, you'll probably find something.

Main quests / chapters are super interesting and enjoyable, there are great cutscene, lore and of course very unique gameplay in each. Sidequests are where it gets kind of crazy. You can accidently sway too far to the right, and enter a no less optional line, where you can leave at anytime, that fits in the story, but isn't required at the same time. There are also the mini-sidequests which are very short, normally just interactions and helping some strangers for a bit of reward. Overall, very packed game.

Combat:
The combat consists of many styles from different types of games. If you are not much of a souls player and just want to chill, you have options to make things like parrying more visual and doable. If you are on the opposite end of the spectrum, and want to make the game extremely difficult, you have difficulties like legend and hardcore, which takes the game to a whole other level. In legend difficulty, you get boss badges whenever you beat one, showing the hard work you put in to beat some of these. 

The game has a variety of different martial art styles to choose from, whether you want to be a healer, or a close ranged DPS, there is something for you. The game itself recommends builds for you to use and combos that they already have. Of course, it is not necessary to use these, you are absolutely in your right to make your own builds. Apart from the normal health bar, stamina bar, you also have a Qi bar, and this mechanic is very important to the combat. Dodging like a normal souls game, grants invincibility like normal, however a perfect dodge, grants a moment's of time-slow. The parry mechanic is where the real damage lies. When you attack or parry, the enemy's Qi bar decreases. When it is fully depleted, they enter a stunned state, and gives you a take-down option, which does a ton of damage, and afterwards, they return to normal with a full Qi bar.

The mythical arts is also something not to gloss over. There are many special abilities lying around the map, optional, that you are able to get, and changes how you play the combat in this game. Some help roaming gameplay, others help in fights. There are just a lot of possibilities.

Online:
This is my favourite part of the game. I am usually not a big singleplayer story mode player, however with the co-op system in this game, it has become one of my most played games. You are able to complete lots of missions with up to five friends in someone's world, where all players within the group getting the rewards. Doing outposts (sort of like dungeons for grinding) has a limit, however you can always hop into a friend's world and do double the amount of dungeons, while your own dungeons are on cooldown. This actually makes co-op useful, not only to play with friends, you benefit from it as well. There are many different relationship systems in the game as well, like partnership (sort of like marriage), mentorship, guilds and others I haven't mentioned. There are also professions, scholar and doctor. You can get injuries like a fractured bone, or a stroke, which needs a doctor to come and treat you for. Some can be treated by the singleplayer doctor, however others, you can call in an actual doctor to fix for you. Sometimes you will get falsely accused of theft or similar, which you will need a scholar to defend you for. The online server is where a lot of players stay and play around in. PvP is something I myself haven't done too much of, however is a fully working online combat experience, with rankings.

Where Winds Meet totally caught me off guard—in the best way. From the moment I started playing the game set in the 5 Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era, I felt like I’d been dropped into a living painting. The art design is stunning: golden fields bending in the wind, towering mountains wrapped in mist, and towns packed with tiny details that make the world feel alive. I kept stopping just to take screenshots.

Gameplay is where the fun really kicks in. The combat feels smooth and stylish, letting you pull off flashy wuxia moves without needing superhuman reflexes. One minute I’m sprinting across rooftops, the next I’m parrying a sword strike in slow motion, and then I’m switching to a bow or using mystical abilities because—why not? The variety keeps things interesting, and the game never pushes you into a single playstyle. It really lets you experiment.

What surprised me most is how interesting the historical touches are. The game sprinkles in real figures, events, and cultural details, and it gives the world a sense of depth without feeling like a history lesson. Even side quests often come with a bit of meaning, whether it’s a moral choice or a glimpse into everyday life during that time.

There’s also a ton to do. Exploration is addictive—every time I think I’m heading to the next main quest, I get distracted by a hidden shrine, a random duel challenge, or some environmental puzzle that makes me wander off the path. The variety keeps the whole experience fresh.

If you love gorgeous worlds, stylish combat, and open-world adventures that constantly reward curiosity, *Where Winds Meet* is absolutely worth diving into. I’m having a blast with it, and I highly recommend giving it a try.

My personal Game of the Year. It has been ages since there was a good Wuxia style game to play, and this is really a quality game. The story is very good, even side quests are well made and tie together with the main story. The graphics are beautiful, map looks gorgeous and character customization / cosmetics are very nice and there won't be a shortage of them. 

For me it has everything. Exploration is huge, there is always something to collect and explore when im not feeling like doing any quests, bossing or pvp. The martial arts are fun and movement skills are nice and fluid. Social aspect is also pretty good, you can do bosses together, pvp, collect things in co-op mode or just join the online mode and do random leisure activities with others.

The only game that ever gave me similar feelings was Age of Wushu back in the day, and ever since playing that i've longed for another game like that and this one fits perfectly.

Lastly, it's Free to play and what's the harm of trying it out for yourself? The various menus can probably scare off some people at the start but they're not too bad, i didn't like them myself but got used to very quickly.

Devastatingly mid. I first heard about this game after the GotY awards when friends recommended it to me so I decided to hop in. It starts off great, love the tutorial which immediately throws you into this Song Dynasty era horse chase. Right after a fantastic intro, you get thrown into the character creator and that's where the first issues arise. I have never seen such incredibly undercooked customization. There's like 3-dozen sliders for the face but you can't change your hair color? The two so-called 'body types' are apparently 'porcelain doll' and 'femboy' with no in-between. Want to play a dude? Too bad, have these 4 indistinguishable beard options you needy ♥♥♥♥♥. Want blonde hair? No problem, it's guaranteed after 140 gacha rolls; that's just upwards of 415 USD (no, I'm not making the number up, that's what blonde hair costs). 

Let's move on to the combat. Have you played Mulan from Smite? Yes? Good, now add a parry and take away the complexity of projectile travel times and needing to lead your shots. Add in a couple weapons like a parasol. There you go, that's the combat. Yes it's as simple as it sounds. 

How about the story and the world? Well, like I said, it starts off beautifully with that horse chase! Then you get to town and NPCs start despawning. Oh yeah and there's AI chatbots in the background because poor little Everstone Studio can't afford actual writers with their blonde hair millions. Anyway, be careful on that first arena fight in the story. The guy you're fighting can jump out of the ring but if you follow him you lose the match. Oh and he can just stun you midair which hardlocks your game and forces you to relog. Glad to see that the $415 blonde hair funds are going to quality control. In lieu of wasting any more time on this game, I'll recommend the following, higher-quality wuxia experiences:

-watch Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
-watch the sequel to Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
-watch Hero featuring well-known Chinese man Jet Li 
-find an actual sifu and go practice real wuxia choreography
-play Jade Empire
-play Mortal Kombat Deadly Alliance
-play the new Avatar fighting game that's coming out
-play every single Dynasty Warriors game
-play Hyrule Warriors just because
-play a monk in World of Warcraft
-play Mists of Panderia in World of Warcraft

Where Wind Meets offers a strong action-RPG experience, standing out with its impressive art design and detailed open world. The combat system, built on fluid animations, gains depth through various fighting styles and abilities, while the game’s atmospheric world keeps the motivation to explore consistently high.

The story successfully blends political intrigue with a personal journey, keeping the player engaged throughout. Thanks to the broad sense of freedom, both the main narrative and side content progress in a balanced and satisfying manner.

In short, Where Wind Meets is a strong recommendation for fans of the genre, with its visual quality, gameplay fluidity, and world-building.

The only negative aspect worth mentioning is the language support. A story-driven game of this scale needs proper local language translation—even if AI-assisted. Many players struggle with the language barrier and cannot fully immerse themselves in the narrative, causing them to lose interest and leave the game early.

I truly love this game, it's a breath of fresh air in the MMO scene. The game play is spontaneous, hilarious, even eccentric. The world is gorgeous, the story is astounding.

But, because of Steam's limited review length, I will start with the bad things. If these things feel unbearable to you, the game might not be for you.

But remember: the game itself great enough that these flaws are acceptable for a huge amount of people.

[h1]The cons[/h1]


[h2]Mobile game approach of monetization.[/h2]

This is possibly the biggest gate blocking PC players. The game is *not* pay to win, all paid items are cosmetic.

But it has RMT gacha, banners, battle pass AND monthly pass. Terms familiar with mobile game players but might be a big no-no to PC players.

Yes, you can spend 9$ a month to get new monthly outfit; or 20$ to get currency to buy outfits.

And yes, no one force you to buy those outfits, nor do they give you any advantage at all in this game.

... I have spent 50$ on this free game in 1 month. So did my friends.

Oh, and you can spend 60000$ to buy a grandeur ship that can board everyone in the server around the river on an all-night party.

Be forewarned.


[h2]Pretty bad UX especially in relation to English language and controller support.[/h2]

It is very clear that this game was designed to be a Chinese Mobile/PC game.

- English text is too long comparing to Chinese text, so very commonly the text are truncated. Sometimes even important texts.
- There are a ton of buttons in the menu at various angles on the screen. Looks good but it's a huge chore to navigate with a controller. Occasionally you will have overlapping button using the same controller hotkey appearing on the screen. In their defense they've been improving a bit lately, but tbh, at the rate they've been improving it, probably you won't have a navigatable menu until the year after next.
- Dialogues autoplay too fast and very commonly go to the next line before you finished reading. And there's no way to disable autoplay.


[h2]Not the best soul-like combat.[/h2]

If you're looking for a great soul-like combat, this game is not it. There are quite a lot of little issues that make the combat frustrating:

- What bug me the most is the frequency of bosses hopping backward or leaping around the map in this game. Although it's theme-fitting for an wuxia game, the bosses keep hoping back until they hit the edge of the arena, causing either camera issues like camera view blocked by wall/pillar, camera stuck underground etc. Sometime it's even worse: for world bosses, sometimes they jump out of the arena and reset combat on their own even if you yourself is still inside the arena.

- In multiplayer instances, there's a delay occurring in the combat, so it's significantly harder to parry, and parry is the main defensive mechanic in this game (dodging endurance cost is too costly comparing to e.g. Dark Souls)

- The 2 weapons system is pretty confusing and hard to pull off. If in theory you can do 100% dmg by rotating 2 weapon regularly, in reality you will never have the chance to do a perfect rotation, and just keep on dealing like 60% of optimal dps even if you parry everything perfectly (because of buff time limit, boss lengthy animations etc). It leaves a bad taste in my mouth seeing the difference between hitting dummy and hitting boss.

[h2]Bad optimization[/h2]

As you can see I have only around 40h of gameplay on Steam. That's because I had to switch to the Lite version (downloadable from their main website). Lite version gives me 60fps with undistinguishable graphical difference versus the "main" version, yet this "full" version on Stream I struggle to reach 40fps. 

Funny thing is when I download the lite version, the game tell me "you have beast-like specs, why don't you play full version instead?" Oh no thank you, just give me the lite please.

===

[h1]The pros[/h1]

[h2]Hilarious, eccentric wuxia experience[/h2]

IMO this is the greatest part of this game. While the single player experience is a serious, mildly sad wuxia world. The multiplayer experience is hilarious and full of... unexpected things.

There's a sect (a player faction) that give its member a daily task of swindling other players.

Your combat prowess is calculated in Goose power. I think it's based on a Chinese internet belief that most adult men can't handle a goose on their own, and have a combat power of about 0.5 Goose.

The latest mount of this game is - instead of horse or dragon - your 2 legs spinning in a Tom & Jerry style.

There's a multiplayer hub zone where you can do various daily kind of... eccentric exercises. like mimicking animals, or doing laps around the town chanting questionable lines.

[h2]Immersive world & story telling[/h2]

The game world is a copy of Ghost of Tsushima style, and it also copy the idea of many other games e.g. Zelda-style puzzle dungeons. But they do deliver as *one* package of experience, not a bundle of patchworks, and - imo - it surpass Ghost of Tsushima by leagues (even though I love GoT a lot).

You really *feel* like you're in a real Wuxia world, you are a daxia doing heroic deeds, not just doing repetitive camp-clearing like GoT endgame. Almost every single NPC has a story of their own, a deep network of relationship with other NPCs spawning many unique stories that you can help or solve.

[h2]Impressive boss design[/h2]

Hey what I hate the most about FromSoftware is that they just create epic-looking bosses with some vague story, and the internet spend half their life conjuring some epic fanfic for those bosses.

Not here. Each zone in WWM has several bosses that are either:
- Big figure in the storyline, with dozen hours of story leading up to why you need to fight them (but actually you usually already fought them long before you figure our those story, open world lol)
- Impressively designed cultural bosses with absolute cinema fight. Man I love the Shadow Puppeteer boss, such a cool fight.

A real treat for fans of Wuxia, Chinese culture and Action-RPGs. 
I try to keep it limited to the most important points so my review is helpful since I could go on and on about this game for hours. 

The good: 
+ it is FREE 
+ no P2W, only cosmetic items in the shop 
+ no tons of blinking ads in your face like some of those f2p games do 
+ very atmospheric, the world feels alive and immersive 
+ combat is fun, a range of different weapons and playstyles 
+ bosses can be a challenge, but not unfair (different difficulty settings and helps to activate)
+ amazing cinematics and high quality writing, lots of lore also in the world or side quests
+ tons of stuff to explore, minigames, treasures, dungeons etc. 
+ a neat Journal to follow up with the tons of characters and their relationships 
+ MMO elements - but optional - guilds, trials, co-op and more 
+ solo world and multiplayer separated so you can immerse to your liking
+ no pressure on farming this or grinding that each day like in other MMOs
+ runs super smooth, no major bugs so far, no lags or delays 
+ very detailed character creation and customization 
+ everyone is super hot

now to the BAD
- confusing menues and upgrade mechanics 
- takes some time to understand story and character progression
-  timegating on progress (for everyone though) 
- quite a few translation and localization errors that make a riddle or 2 difficult to solve 
- lots and lots of currencies and upgrade material, needs some work to get into 
- cosmetic items in shop mostly expensive or gatcha 
- lots of different battle passes, season progress and stuff that piles up fast and is hard to keep track of (but you can easily ignore it and collect everything at once later) 
- some (side) quests annoyingly timegated (wait 2 days to talk to dude A...) 

For me a very good experience so far with lots of amazing characters and fights, no pressure to socialize or grind and a very well done and immersive Wuxia world. 

It is free, just give it a try and don't get discouraged by some bad reviews and tests, it is really worth it.

"As wide as an ocean, and as deep as a puddle." 
Where Winds Meet has an incredibly gorgeous veneer of polish that has exactly half a heartbeat amount of depth. There is no system that is explored in depth at all, and every mechanic gets broken almost immediately after interacting with it for longer than ten minutes. Every challenge or depth is artificially conflated. Collecting hundreds of items for progression isn't fun, it's a chore and a mindless one. Bosses aren't difficult, they follow the exact same pattern of a dark-souls fight, and anything different borderlines on completely annoying that takes you away from the fight. Everything is truly under-baked that is not comfortable with any amount of interaction, but EverStone Studio/NetEase expects you to interact with it for dozens of hours. Two prime examples is both the Bounty and Healing system. Once you look at the healing system mini-game and get a good combo, congratulations, you can heal anything outside of something that is just stats prohibitive. A level 5 could heal a level 70 quest. And nothing changes as you grind from 5-70, and judging from CN timelines, its the exact same from 70+. EVERY mechanic is like this, breaking with just a small amount of thought, and just sits there, forgotten while Everstone/NetEase continues more content, more half-baked ideas  and it just becomes a chore that the devolopers expects you to repeat ad nauseam, leaving the players clamoring for anything slightly fresh that wasn't repeated.

PVP is just a stunlock fest that turns into whoever can get their 15 second cutscene to start first that looks complicated but ends up being incredibly easy, there is rare (or no) counter-play and the entire PvP meta revolves around baiting out the 1-2 counterplays available so you can start your stun-lock cutscene. If you want to be "good" there is no training, just go copy what everyone else is doing and crush anyone who hasn't figure out the "secret of sameness" or did not conform and then feel good at the top with hundreds of others that play and look the EXACT same way. 

Unless you spend money. 
In which you may rise to the top of the pay-pig leaderboards, while looking the exact same.
Thousands of dollars will get you special boat, and then spend more thousands of dollars for it to be "gold."

Ultimately, Where Winds Meet is the video-game equivalent of a Chinese All-You-Can-Eat buffet, there is no real depth or talent, its a hodgepodge of everything else, and maybe the average player won't notice that the food actually kind of sucks if they just keep cramming it into you.

Currently I can not recommend this game despite its pretty enjoyable gameplay for 2 reasons. The UI and the localisation.


The gameplay is good, and the visuals are pretty, but dear god just playing the game is exhausting because of the damn UI. I can genuinely say without exageration that Where Winds Meet has the worst UI I have ever experienced in a video game. Its layers and layers of menus with sub-menus inside sub-menus and somewhere there will be a notification that nags at you constantly buried deep within a menu you wont be able to find.

The localisation varies from just barely understandable to incomprehensible. I genuinely was trying to follow the story, but when half the things npcs say don't make sense, it becomes very difficult to keep up.
These Localisation issues spread to the UI as well, making that even worse. Grammatical errors and completely incorrect text is very frequent.

Just to talk about the positive things, the gameplay was genuinely enjoyable, not perfect, but pretty good.
The world is well designed and very dense with a large variety things to do. Though that is almost not a good thing as a lot of the minigames and little collectables are frankly just annoying and a lot of it seems pretty underbaked.
The visuals are good and the game runs decently well.

I have heard that refighting bosses or doing other endgame stuff does use an energy system which is very stingy, but I have not experienced that myself so i cant say how bad it is.
The microtransactions are also pretty damn bad unsurprisngly. 

If they manage to improve the UI and localisation issues, I may come back to this game. But after 10 hours I am just tired of it.

An anomaly in the gaming industry.

While every publisher is pushing for the standard price of AAA games to be 70€, this Chinese-made experience is given to you for free. All available content is shown to the free player, and the only purchases to be made are purely cosmetic.

First of all, this game is drawn beautifully. Every design is carefully crafted and detailed, and the animations complement them well by being fluid and well implemented. The main areas have soul and are able to properly convey the desired environment, while the other secondary areas of exploration are mostly forgettable with the exception of some locations tied to the story. Boss's designs are memorable and invoke a range of different emotions. You are able to customize pretty deeply your character if you are looking for that level of customization. The only flaw that can be pointed out is in most NPCs' designs, which become repetitive pretty quickly and feel massively overlooked compared to the rest of the game.

The main story is passable and shone in some moments but was brutally sabotaged by the various sound bugs in innumerable cutscenes, at least in this version of the game. The writing is witty, but most of it feels bland and confusing, but that can also maybe be attributed to localization; it's really not where the game shines the most. On the other hand, there are plenty of side stories, and some of them are well written. 

Combat, although not the hardest, is still challenging and rewarding. The game offers a lot of gameplay options, letting the player dictate how they wish to experience it. This feature lets everyone, from people getting into the genre to experienced gamers, focus on different aspects that they wish to spend their time on while not feeling left out. There's a vast variety of builds, and each one can be tweaked to personal preference, giving birth to some wild playstyles. The current state of this system is a little complex but not overbearing, and I fear that in the future when more content is available, it will become too much. For now, I think they did well managing the progression by locking it recurrently behind a wait wall, giving the players time to enjoy the current version while providing more and more content as time passes. I have not tried PVP but was surprised by the bounty system, where a player entered my world when I accidentally tai-chi'd an NPC off a cliff.

Exploration is heavily implied since it's through it that you are able to upgrade your build by taking advantage of the many systems to increment your stats. There are plenty of activities to go around, and most of them are fun to try to complete. Signposts are a great addition and, when used with good intent, give a little touch of personality to some areas/situations. The game also aids you here by giving some great movement options, making traversing areas quite easy, although a little bit buggy at times. The number of currencies and different items is a bit too much; as you progress through the game, you will forget the use of most or not even remember that they exist.

The soundtrack was well chosen and pairs correctly most times with the gameplay and world built. The sound design is nothing exceptional, but it's also not a detriment to the game. The English voice acting is rough and is accompanied by horrible translation errors.

One thing I have to point out is the horrible UI, specifically the menus. The HUD is not bad, and there's room to customize it how you want it portrayed, but the navigation menus are terrible. You often loop through them to find the menu you want, but you forget how to access it again.

In sum, this game provides a little bit for everyone, and it's free. Give it a try and see it for yourself!

Wish reviews were binary cause uh... this is an extremely broad but shallow Wuxia sandbox with tons of features and minigames, that takes a surprising amount of inspiration from Star Citizen of all things, including tens of thousands of dollar microtransactions, and a criminal justice system that forces you into PVP and then imprisons you for a certain amount of time if you lose, AND also has the possibility of you randomly being framed for things.  All while also including gacha style daily and weekly resource limits and fomo mechanics.

Aesthetically the game is quite nice, with beautiful graphics and all sorts of nice costumes for character customization, most of which can only be acquired for money.  The music is not super memorable, but is pleasant to listen to, and fits with the action most of the time.  Voice acting ranges from solid to terrible, and lots of it is simply missing entirely in weird inconsistent ways, like having only none side of a conversation voiced, or even just a single line.  They've also included GenAI content in the form of chatbot NPCs who you chat with to "befriend," which just means you get can occasionally get gifts from them every weekly reset.

The story is extremely generic naive hero call to adventure stuff in the first chapter, then in the second chapter it shifts to mostly incoherent economic espionage that seems to be based on the assumption that money is literally a mystical force of nature.  Very weird and stupid, but the action is cool and the characters are fairly likable.

EDIT: It turns out that the criminal justice system is even more annoying than Star Citizen's because the prison timer doesn't go down while you're offline.  You have to be online for the entire time or else succeed in escaping, which is also a mandatory PVP event.  Ironically, all of this can be bypassed completely by paying a small fine, which just makes the whole thing seem pointless.

Where Winds Meet really manages to capture a beautiful, immersive, Wuxia-inspired open world. The game world is highly detailed, featuring realistic environments, numerous secret places to discover, puzzles to solve, and even a massive city, Kaifeng, that feels lived-in (plus you get different traversal abilities like double jump, dash, and even sky soar). The combat's pretty decent, requiring dodging, parrying, and timing your attacks, and you also have different weapon combinations that create a 'class' and allow different playstyles (on lower difficulties you can win fights just bv spamming though, so it's not a very demanding game). There are tons of quests and activities you can do solo or in co-op. The game also has asynchronous multiplayer (you’ll run into messages from other players, some actually trying to help with puzzles, and others just trolling or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around). On top of that, you can summon other players or even NPCs to help out with boss fights, similar to what you’d see in Soulsborne games. The community also seems extra helpful and offers its services, such as regularly healing wounds or clearing your name when NPCs accuse you of stealing. The world also offers pretty high interactivity, as you can interact with NPCs in different ways (play mini-games, help them when attacked, heal them, rob them, or even murder them, and there's even a police system). And the biggest plus is that the game isn't pay-to-win, as you can only purchase cosmetics from the cash shop (there’s also a battle pass with both free and paid tiers and gacha draws for costumes and other cosmetics, which are a bit predatory as getting the best rewards is not going to be cheap, but still no direct way to buy power).

But like many Chinese F2P games, it has some common pitfalls: the localization is pretty bad, especially the English voice acting (most likely they lacked proper directing), so I'd recommend playing using the Chinese VAs (the English subtitles are ok-ish, but I've noticed some grammatical errors and some translated sentences that didn't make much sense); the game suffers from FPS dips and drops, so you'll need a beefier rig to run it at a decent frame rate, especially in heavily populated areas like Kaifeng City; the UI is pretty bad, as there are a million different menus and you need multiple clicks to get where you want (sometimes I even got lost and I couldn't remember how to access some specific menus, which was really annoying); there are also AI-driven NPCs you can chat with, but they feel rough/unpolished - sometimes they get stuck repeating the same lines, don’t understand your inputs, and are pretty easy to exploit.

There are also some aspects of the game that I haven't even touched, like PvP or the battle royale mode, as they don't really appeal to me, but they are there for anyone interested. At times, WWM feels like it tries to be a game for everybody, with a lot of different systems, and it can get a bit confusing with all the menus, trying to navigate them and trying to understand everything the game has to offer. In general, most of these features feel polished, and hopefully they'll manage to update everything.

Overall, WWM is a very compelling F2P RPG that finally offers an interesting ancient China–inspired world to explore and doesn't feel like just another cash grab/mobile slop released for a quick buck. I'm waiting for the next content updates to continue the story, as it is a fairly enjoyable experience.

Menu simulator with a lacklustre multiplayer. Would be a decent game if co-op actually worked, but it's dreadfully middling otherwise. WWM is certainly ambitious by casting an extremely wide net, but that comes at the cost of losing focus. They're putting too much effort in trying to appeal to as large an audience as possible which ensures that it only ever scratches the surface of all of the genres it encompasses. That way, if you're looking for any one specific type of gameplay, you'll likely find it here, but it's never going to be as good as any other game that has that type of gameplay as its focal point.

Combat is clunky and not refined. Mechanically speaking, combat is comparable to Elden Ring. So to run with that comparison, think about how awkwardly choreographed some of the lower quality FromSoft bosses' attacks are, because that's the bar by which I measured WWM's bosses, which I think is a pretty generous standard for a F2P game that has such a wealth of competitors to draw inspiration from. And yet, that's a bar WWM simply doesn't seem capable of jumping over. 

It's certainly not without its moments but, all-in-all, you could lay your FOMO to rest and pass on this in peace. It's really average.

The game itself is fun. Exploration is great, there's a ton of content, and combat is enjoyable. Bosses are well-designed, the art style is fantastic, and the game looks amazing on a good PC. The music is good, too.

You can expect a lot of grind in this game. Like, a lot. You can't buy your way around it, which is great - the game is not P2W. But if you want to upgrade your combat styles, mystic arts, and all that, be prepared to grind. That's OK, though. It's not really a downside, because if you enjoy the game you'll enjoy the grind, too. It’s important to note that most of the grind is supposed to be done in Co-op (multiplayer mode) - it's just significantly more rewarding. Which brings me to why I'm writing a negative review.

The reason I'm writing a negative review is the absolutely terrible ping, which makes Co-op and PvP unplayable for me. I want to highlight that this issue has nothing to do with my internet connection. This is literally the only game where I have this problem. My average ping to EU servers in other games is usually between 50 and 70. VPNs do not fix the issue. This problem has been present since launch, and not much has been done about it. There’s a thread with, at the moment of writing, 4.2k messages on the official Discord about this exact issue.

A lot of people are being directed to the wrong server, which results in an average ping of around 300. This creates terrible input delays for any online action, which not only tanks your DPS if you play a DPS class, but also makes parrying enemy and boss attacks nearly impossible. Yesterday’s update bumped my online ping to 600, which is just insane. There are no official workarounds or solutions in sight. And the only workaround the community has found is to create a new account (a new Steam account if you play via Steam) - this does fix the ping problem. But I’m not creating a new account after spending 100 hours on my current character.

I’ve patiently waited for three weeks for them to solve the issue, but I’m just tired. So I'm leaving a negative review - I really can't do anything else at this point.

Where Winds Meet: A World You Don’t Just Play, You Live In

Where Winds Meet is one of those rare games that feels like stepping into another world. It’s atmospheric, beautiful, and surprisingly emotional, especially if you play with the original Chinese audio and English subtitles. The characters feel more real, their performances land better, and the tone of the story becomes far more authentic.

Yes, there are audio bugs right now, and yes, the menus need serious work. But none of that takes away from how genuinely impressive this game is.

Music & Sound Design

This is the part that deserves real praise.

The music in Where Winds Meet is easily one of its greatest strengths. You can tell immediately how much custom work went into the soundtrack. The amount of unique virtual instruments and culturally accurate sound choices is honestly shocking. The score doesn’t feel stitched together or reused from libraries—it feels crafted.

As a composer, I can hear the layers in every track: the plucked strings, bowed Chinese instruments, woodwinds, percussion textures, ambient pads… it all blends into a living soundscape that elevates the entire experience. The music doesn’t overpower the game; it complements it. It guides the emotional tone of exploration, combat, quiet moments, and story scenes in a way very few games manage to achieve.

If I were ever to join a game development team, this is the kind of team I’d want to be on: one that clearly respects music and uses it as a fundamental storytelling tool.

Exploration and Worldbuilding

The game encourages exploration in a natural, rewarding way. There’s so much to learn, discover, and interact with. Even staying in the early areas for dozens of hours doesn’t feel like a waste—you’re constantly finding quests, puzzles, systems, and small stories that make the world feel alive.

You can move completely at your own pace. Nothing rushes you. Nothing forces you into content you don’t want to do. You can simply enjoy being in the world, which is a rare design choice in modern games.

Combat, Bosses, and Difficulty

The combat feels fantastic, especially if you enjoy a parry-heavy playstyle. Good builds actually matter, and you can feel the difference as your character becomes more refined.

The boss fights are a highlight. They’re skill-based, memorable, and extremely satisfying to learn. The fact that you can repeat bosses freely is a huge plus—you can practice, improve, and really master the encounters. And if you enjoy a proper challenge, you can scale difficulty and chase harder versions of these fights, which keeps the gameplay fresh.

Visuals

The game is visually stunning. Landscapes, lighting, architecture, atmosphere—everything comes together in a way that looks almost painterly. Even simple exploration feels cinematic.

Solo Experience

Playing solo works perfectly. I’ve only played solo, and it feels like the intended experience. You can progress, explore, and fight bosses without needing anyone else. The game feels complete even if you never touch multiplayer content.

Technical Polish

The audio bugs are noticeable. The menus can be frustrating. The UI feels clunky. These are the weakest parts of the game right now, but they are fixable, and they don’t overshadow what the game does exceptionally well.

Final Score: 9.2/10

Where Winds Meet is a gorgeous, ambitious, deeply immersive Wuxia world with one of the best soundtracks I’ve heard in years. It respects the player’s pace, rewards skill, and offers an enormous amount of content and creativity.

If you enjoy powerful music, atmospheric worlds, meaningful exploration, or skill-based combat, this game is absolutely worth your time.

TLDR: It's been some time since I've been this addicted to a game. At this time my enthusiasm has waned but I'm still enjoying the game and will likely continue to play it for some time. The plethora of nested menus continues to be a UI/UX nightmare though.
    
Random thoughts below:
    As a westerner, WWM really hits the fantasy of a martial-arts game set in a universe that reminds me of "Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon". It's also one of the most aesthetic games I've played, often I'll travel the world just taking screenshots (camera mode is decently robust too). It's a content rich game you can sink your teeth into, with more to come. I recommend WWM if you want a martial-arts hack-and-slash plus a gorgeous open world to explore. 
    
    The biggest turn-off for co-op is ping issues (OCE player here) - good luck parrying even a 3-hit string on 350ms. That said, the game can be played solo which I'm grateful for, the AI even knows raid mechanics (albeit with terrible DPS) but you are incentivised to do group content with other players for increased rewards. I'm not too thrilled with the mmo mechanics, definitely not the worst for dailies/checklists but some things [i]really suck[/i]. For example, most sects (think in-universe faction, ffxiv GC) have you competing against other players each week to rank up by having the most merit points for that week and if you're at the bottom of the bracket you'll be demoted. The highest rank is decided by player votes but instead of competing in brackets of 50-100 players - like the ranks leading up to it - it's against the global population for that sect. End result is chat being spammed by vote begging and degenerate gameplay to even earn the privilige of running for top rank.
     
    Combat is hack and slash with deflect(parry)/dodge mechanics. I've played DS3/Elden Ring and find WWM's parry system to be very forgiving and approachable. There's also assist deflect/dodge in solo with no penalty to rewards - higher difficulty is for clout only. Personally I found the combat-system to be similar to Vindictus: DF (deflect reds, dodge yellows). So far I've managed Legend 40 and completed the Master of Jianghu title but will not be farming any no-hit challenges.

Combat looks pretty from videos but the parry system that is mandatory to use is inconsistent and leads to awkward combat when playing against bosses. Normal human mobs seem okay with many others being janky like all the unstaggerable animals that have no downtime on active hitboxes but most don't stay alive long enough to show the flaws or get frustrating.

The actual parry command is actually consistent, if you press parry before an attack hits, you will parry and it's a fairly large window, the problem I feel being that you need to press it early compared to other games and because of that, many boss attack animations are designed in a way that you can't really react to any normal attack chain unless you know its coming and know the timing on the whole chain like a rhythm game and not a reaction based game. Red flashing attack can be fairly easy to parry with some terrible exceptions but normal attacks from bosses which are usually a chain of many attacks needs rote memorization on every boss to parry. You can't just block everything either because blocking increases your own stagger meter and bosses attack at a rate that you wont get it back in time to keep blocking, forcing you to parry at some point and because bosses link different attack strings at random, if you get unlucky you will have to parry an incredibly hard attack chain or block it and get opened up. 

Bosses who are actual threats show how inconsistent the main parry mechanic of the game is. Desynced parry windows from attack animations, short and bait telegraphs, inconsistent parrying attack chains, short openings after many attacks and parrying building up stagger over time like Sekiro instead of just opening up the boss like Darksouls forcing you to engage with the inconsistent parry system mandatory.

The worst part of the parry mechanic is that parrying certain attack chains from bosses seems to parry the whole attack chain but the 2nd attack chain the boss starts wont be parried but the animations make it look like its one whole chain, So you parry the first hit so the 2nd and 3rd hit are auto parried but now you need to parry the 4th because its technically a new attack even if the bosses animation flowed directly into it. And then the worst sin is that this does not feel consistent between different attack chains on the same boss and other bosses whole attack chains will need to be parried each hit. I can't tell if its latency, a huge parry window blocking multiple attacks, or intended design, but this was the most frustrating part of parrying and combat in general in this game.

My Hot Take

Combat System & Boss Design
The combat in Where Winds Meet is genuinely fun, fluid, and responsive. Boss design stands out as one of the strongest parts of the game, with encounters that are fast, stylish, and mechanically rewarding. Some bosses can feel a bit too aggressive or fast-paced early on, but overall the experience remains engaging. AI-controlled instances provide a helpful way to practice mechanics while still earning solid rewards, making the combat loop one of the game’s most consistently enjoyable features.

PVP Is Forced
PvP is heavily forced onto the player, even if you have no interest in it. Bounty hunters can invade or capture you regardless of your preference, and the only “options” to avoid it involve dying to AI bounty hunters or being dragged into a co-op invasion that leads to forced online gameplay. This disrupts the single-player flow the game initially teaches and encourages, especially since progression relies on quests, exploration, and even theft, systems the game then punishes with PvP consequences.

Edit: There are no options to avoid it as soon as AI kills you it goes from Singleplayer > Online

PVP Balance & Bugs
Even when you willingly engage in PvP, balance issues are immediately noticeable. Early on, Twin Swords allow players to stun-lock opponents with little or no counterplay. A skilled player can lock you down completely, making most encounters feel one-sided. PvP needs further balancing and bug fixing before it feels competitive or fair.

Online Play
When you choose to play online with others, the experience is surprisingly smooth and enjoyable. Co-op exploration, teaming up for bosses, and general open-world interaction feel fluid and well-implemented. The problem is not the quality of online play itself; it is that the game forces online systems into single-player content instead of letting players opt in naturally.

Guild System
The guild system is a major highlight. It responds well to player activity, feels rewarding to engage with, and actually supports community participation. It is refreshing to see a guild feature with this level of responsiveness and incentive.

Community
Unfortunately, the general community is extremely discouraging. Asking questions or discussing mechanics often leads to mockery, deflection, or hostility. Many players seem more interested in defending the game than helping others understand it. Discussions frequently devolve into trolling, misinformation, or being told not to play. This creates an unnecessarily hostile learning environment.

Forced Co-Op & Online Integration
Single-player content is frequently interrupted by mandatory co-op outcomes, PvP invasions, and online dependencies. This breaks immersion and makes the experience frustrating for players who want a traditional solo wuxia adventure. A better model would allow players to fully opt out of online systems, similar to how other games handle offline modes. Instead, online elements are integrated into core progression whether players want them or not.

Overall Rating: 6/10
Strong combat and boss design, a great guild system, and smooth co-op are held back by forced PvP, balance issues, and a hostile community culture.

Despite playing this game for fifty hours, I would be hard pressed to really recommend this game to anyone. To summarize the bulk of my feelings on Where Winds Meet, it's a mile wide and about an inch deep, and while I'm aware these words have probably been said before about it, I can't help but feel as though it rings true. There is a lot of things to occupy your time in WWM, from the guilds and sects to the exploration and secrets littered around the map. However, once you start interacting with these systems, the limitations of the design of this game begin to show. I would be lying if I said the thought didn't cross my mind the moment I really began to explore the utterly labyrinthian UI, as everything is hidden within a different submenu or sub-section of a menu. The combat while simple can be made fun by utilizing the various martial arts throughout the game, but I still would not call it engaging or really even difficult? Parry attacks and hit whatever enemy  you down before their timer runs out and time the finishing sequence. Maybe the game is different for healers, but with how slow the game is to really bring people to larger PVE encounters I can't imagine most people actually getting to large-scale battles and raids. Please tell me if I'm wrong here however, as I would love to hear back from the community and see what the consensus is overall on late-game PVE. This to me was the crux of why Where Winds Meet didn't really work for me, your weapons are static. Sure, you can learn new techniques for your weapons, but without spending hundreds of dollars of lucking out on boss-drops, they will ultimately look the same and  fight the same. Your combos are very, very simple for each weapon, and for a wuxia game I just don't think that's very exciting, with the bulk of the difficulty residing in your ability to parry attacks. Again, not very interesting to do the same thing over and over again as a means to tire out a boss. It's monotonous and boring and feels like a very lazy way to make combat difficult. 

Now, one thing I did actually enjoy was the story, I think overall exploring QInghe, the first map of the game is fairly fun and has a strong story. I cannot speak for Kaifeng, as I have barely played through that part of the story. If you are interested in the story of Where Winds Meet, I would highly recommend checking out some of the Chinese translations of the games story rather than trying to ascertain the fragmented and ill-fitting English translations. Oh, and the voices are AI? And AI is all over this game. Head to toe, there is just generative AI giving stale, awful performances! There is even a """""""mini"""""" game in which, in order to befriend certain random NPCs, you must talk to them in an AI chatroom! And by talk, I mean just repeat the last sentence they said and it will work 90% without fail because this isn't a game, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI. 

To end this review that I really have spent too much time on than this game really warrants (sorta like my playtime), Where Winds Meet is a bloated game with no real gameplay focus other than exploration. I sincerely think that you would get the same amount of enjoyment out of this that you would any modern 3rd person open world game. Which is probably the most offensive thing in this review. 

5/10, it needs better combat and that isn't going to happen.

So in general this game is... ok.  The controls are a bit clunky, but manageable.  The story is terrible, but I'll chalk at least some of that up to cultural differences and translation problems.  And the game loves artificial lengthening with things like tying the level cap to how long you've been playing.  But where this game goes to complete ♥♥♥♥ is the multiplayer.  For one thing it's just tacked on, the game keeps encouraging you to go into co-op, but you can't do any quests there, so what's the point.  Much of the player interaction just seems to be forcing you to interact with others in places where most games would use an NPC.  There are maladies you'll get, sometimes pretty randomly, and many of them can ONLY be healed by another player.  You can usually easily find someone to do it for free, but it's still pointless and time consuming vs. just talking to an NPC doctor like any reasonable game would allow.

Where the game really goes from "poorly designed" to "hot garbage" is the bounty system.  After a glitchy sequence of encounters I was reported for a crime and shook the guards.  What the game doesn't tell you is this opens a bounty that other players can take to jump in attack you.  A Chinese player, who has had access to the game for over a year longer than the US crowd and so was significantly higher level and better geared, dropped on my head, with no need to actually find me, and proceeded to start kicking my ass.  I still figured I had a chance to shake them if I could run, but somehow my stamina, stamina recovery, and stamina usage were all significantly worse, so I couldn't even evade this person that I literally couldn't hurt.  After getting wrecked by someone the game has ensured I would have no chance against I get to be locked down for at least 15 minutes, unable to play the game at all.  So I spent over half an hour trying to get myself out of a situation where the game glitched me into a crime I didn't commit, reported me even after I "won" the gift of gab mini game to convince them not to, and then dropped a player with massive advantages on my heads so I could lose another 15+ minutes.  I say plus because I don't know how long it would actually take, I logged out and uninstalled.

The only thing I've got to say about this game is that you SHOULD NOT under ANY CIRCUMSTANCES play on Legend difficulty. You don't get anything, you're not missing anything, it doesn't mean anything.

What you ARE doing is EXPONENTIALLY increasing both enemy HP pools and Damage Taken. For reference, a SINGLE basic NPC will do a two-step combo attack where they kick you really fast and then follow up with a sword strike. On Legend Difficulty the *kick* part of this attack was dealing ~10,000 damage. Short, difficult to react, mostly there to interrupt you, so that you'll focus on parrying the follow-up swing that could deal anywhere from 14-17K damage. A boss attack could range anywhere from that 14-17K figure all the way up to the 25-30K range. This is out of a pool of what I'm GUESSING is ~66K health, the game is really cagey about giving you hard numbers that aren't abstractions. For an example, it'll tell me I have XX Constitution, and that this "factors in" to my final health score, but not HOW MUCH health I actually have. Healing was ~8K, and you get ~3 unless you go hunt down every single side-story right away and then you max out at 5 and I'm just gonna ballpark that you heal maybe in the realm of 10-15K fully upgraded. It's not a lot, and it's Bloodborne Vials. Only restocked SPECIFICALLY at checkpoints and only if the game feels like you've sufficiently traveled far enough away from one to trigger again when you come back. Also, if you lose to certain encounters and boss fights it WILL NOT restock fully when you respawn.

The issue I'm getting at, that I'm trying to prevent for you, is that you will be 1 or 2-shot by every boss, and you can be 3-hit by ANY MOB.

I have beaten Sekhiro with the bell charm, I have beaten Elden Ring + DLC, Every DS game, and I guess I've basically no-hit (or close to it, or cheesed through with Panacea Fan when all else failed) all the current story bosses. It ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SUCKS. I was NOT HAVING FUN. You grind for gear, you grind for armor, you grind for upgrade material to buff up your Mystic Arts and your Weapon Arts and your base stats and it's ALL FOR NOTHING because you will STILL need to hit EVERY SINGLE BASIC NPC 30+ times and you will only survive ~3-5 hits OR Arrows from offscreen enemies. There is no stacking, there's no encounter design, there's no "pull just a couple guys". These are MMO Mobs and you'll be bending over backwards to try to fight each individual one like they're non-respawning Elite mobs from a Dark Souls game. It's not easy, it's not very fun, and in most cases the encounters are NOT designed for it.

This game is beautiful, it runs great, there's a wide variety of stuff to do, and the basic combat feels awesome. But you CANNOT treat this ♥♥♥♥ like Sekhiro, like I did, and have a good time. It's barely Ghost of Tsushima on a GOOD day, and that assumes you've got a very solid connection to the server and IT is keeping up with YOU. You WILL hit parry and the attacks will connect anyway. You WILL be mashing the button combo that initiates finishers and instead do EITHER a dodge or a parry whenever you are connected to other players for Instances and Raids.

I'm gonna tell you right now, if you think like I did that it's exactly the badge of honor it claims to be.... Nah, not really. The game's not too hard. The parry windows are extremely forgiving, most attacks are telegraphed with a giant literal glowing red orb telling you when to press the button even when it's NOT pausing time to make sure it's impossible to miss. The bosses are fair and still deal high damage and have decent health pools regardless of difficulty. Even as it's presented, the Legendary Difficulty doesn't really change much of anything but the scaling and you're not *allowed* to turn on the Time-Pausing Deflect Assist (which I didn't and still don't use). But what it DOES tell me is that you hate yourself more than I hate myself (and buddy, that's a LOT).

I finally hit my wall and turned it down, bashed it straight to story because I was so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sick of dying over and over to ~5 random-ass mobs throwing attacks over one another so it was impossible to parry everything. It's not precise enough to take seriously; it's like playing the Ghost of- games with the mega-hardcore 1-hit-kill deletes-your-save mode on. I'm just like... "why?" No one cares; most people here are playing for the dress-up and to button-mash on some mobs Dynasty Warriors style. Nothing that is in the game or is coming up is going to be so hard or so sweaty that it necessitates this kind of self-harm. Most people I got matched with online for the Raids couldn't figure out not to stand in the giant glowing flame paths, to move the explosive barrels apart from one another, or to run with the donkeys. I joined the button-mashers, and I'm SO glad I did. Kinda mad I waited this long; I said a LOT of swears.

Anyways, the Nine Mortal Ways is the best faction, don't @ me. The social stuff is really neat and the building mode kicks ass, and there's all sorts of neat random crap coming in future updates so those are really the only other things I'd say that everyone else isn't already gushing over. I was on the fence about dropping this game because I was frustrating myself trying to play perfectly in an extremely loose system and now that I've dropped that element I'm having a blast just chopping up Bad Guys and flying around doing Wuxia Stuff.

There is something for everyone in this game: fun fighting, lots of minigames and collectibles, amazing sceneries, some hit or miss side quests, a lot of exploration, a little bit of grinding and gacha, but as a F2P player I never felt the need to spend seeing that it is exclusively for cosmetics. Community is good and helpful.

Here to update my review, since now I have 5x the number of hours as before.

If you like games like 
Shenmue, 
Hitman, 
Shadow Hearts, 
Devil May Cry,
Tomb Raider
Final Fantasy X,
V-Rising

This game will be right down your alley.
--------------------------------------------------------
This game has made me laugh, cry, and feel a sense of child-like wonder more than
2-dozen times.

I get that feeling that I used to have when I was a kid, playing Final Fantasy X.

I have even put the FFX soundtrack on in the background while playing, causing a few glorious moments of  gaming.
--------------------------------------------------------
However, there were certain aspects of the game I was completely blind to 
being a 99% solo player:

Gatchya-reinforcement,
Pandering to whales,
The headaches of managing PvP is like running two characters worth of stuff 
(I understand from only the perspective of others on that one, I don't PvP)

What I mean by that is Kind of like the "Black Mirror" episode
where everyone can rate everyone for anything? Its a little like that in the social spaces;
Players can instantly tell when someone is a "whale" (deep pockets, heavy spender)
because the nature of the Elegance score, Like system, and popularity scores in the game.

So items earned in-game give 120ish, upwards of 210, 
but all the items acquired with real-life-currency give 1200 and some 4000,
so one or two items might give someone 8000+ score, but those that have 100% everything in the game might have a score of around 3500. (mind you you can have 12-13 items in the game. so a whale would have ~ 52,000 vs a gameplay vet at 3500-5000. Just seems odd.

Also, have to talk about this boat.
so there is an item in the game you get, harmonic core. or something.
with the elite battle pass you get a couple chances at getting one a month. 
these cores are used to buy the rotating stuff in the shop. So if you want any of the cool stuff, have to have the $20/month ELITE battle pass. 
Those cores can also be spent to buy 1 page of a construction manual. 
after 140 you can trade them for a boat.
There are only I think 4 boat owners? And every week there is events that get announced to all players, even those in solo mode. That those boats are having their voyage.
Suddenly you have a bunch of essentially naked people on this boat that has cost
in-game estimate in real dollars, around $40,0000. 
How can anyone justify this being pandered to?

I do feel a bit strange about that fact, so   I stick to solo mode
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

What I don't like is the energy system.
I used to play in the Pantheon a LONG time ago.
An online game, where you could build your stats, take part in olympic games,
try to become the best, but only had 20 energy per 24 hours. 
Eventually once the two storylines are completed its all you focus on. 
Sure there are a handful of things you can do that don't require energy, 
a few guild/sect to-do-lists, the handful of rotating events, and the daily things
like blessing the land, and other things in the "wandering paths casual co-op" mode 
they just added this patch (which is cool). 

I get it, they want their citizens to become something in life,
But the energy system prevents me from just completing the game and moving on with my life. Has me coming back every 1-3 days to use my energy so I can get legendary tunings stacked up before I tune my gear etc. Then its suddenly feeling less fun, and more like trying to remember If I have clothes in the washing machine or something. 
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Things I think they should change:
1) The Color-rarity system; Me being red-green colorblind 
I can only tell when something is gold, I can't tell the others apart.
2) The building mode:
When you snap an object down, its like your mouse becomes detached from the camera for a second, it slows down the building process
2) The building mode part 2:
What is the purpose of building a home or anything? 
Can't sleep in your bed, cant pet your horse, and doing multi-level buildings is a headache
3) Waypoints:
Please give me the ability to name waypoints I put down (also give me the option to turn them off and on , instead of deleting and re-placing them (for instance, I have a building in a great area, but its not super close to a waypoint, but it gets annoying when they are all visible during meteor flight etc. 
4) GUI scaling
you have sooo much stuff, that its kind of a headache trying to figure out what is what,
then with the update 1/07 or whatever it reduced the size of everything even further randomly.
I would like to be able to scale everything in my inventory so I only see 6-10 items at once.
(this is partially because I cannot tell the rarities apart, and now its more frustrating trying to find the gear that has improvements for tuning. (the new auto recycle feature helps, but if all I get is low-tier pulls for an extended period, it would be MORE apparent that my wheels are spinning, and I'm not making progress.

I would like the ability to favorite things in both the wandering tales/sentient beings etc, so when I come back 2-3 days later I'm not completely lost.
6) it Costs ~ $35.00 to change your gender(transformation) and name in the game(badge ~$5.00), and you can't have more than one character per account, so be sure you like your name and gender 
7) BLOCKING. I'm sick of going on the Blessed Voyage or whatever its called, Only to have 3-4 people absolutely destroying the lobby with nonsense. Can I please get a mute icon on everyone so I can easily mute them? (without going to their profile and blocking them)
8) Red Envelopes.
