[h1] Harmless, Hilarious Fun [/h1] 

[h2] TL;DR [/h2]
I wanna start this off by saying that, objectively speaking, WWM is NOT a bad game. At the very core of the maelstrom of poorly thought out mechanics, half-baked ideas, and hilarious bugs is a great immersive experience that I could easily get lost in for hours on end, and having put almost 25 hours into the game, I think I'm finally ready to give my thoughts on it. Lemme be very clear: what this game does right, it does so in all the best ways, and ALMOST everything this game gets wrong, it does so in all the BEST ways. However, it's held back by terrible localization, laughably bad and predatory game mechanics, and a very toxic community. 

So let's list the pros and cons, shall we? 

[h2] PROS [/h2] 

[h3] - Graphics [/h3] 
Starting with the most obvious choice, the graphics in this game are truly amazing. The way light falls over blades of grass flowing in the wind, the incredible views you get from meditating atop a mountain, watching the water shimmer as you stroll along the riverside, this game is a visual FEAST, and a MUST HAVE for photo-mode enjoyers. I'm genuinely shocked at how well it runs at times. 10/10

[h3] - Open World [/h3] 
The reviews aren't lying: this game's open world is vast, and you can easily get lost in exploration for hours on end. Personally, I wish there were more POI's, as there is a LOT of just empty space, but honestly? The graphics and beautiful scenery make up for that. 

[h3] - Combat [/h3] 
Combat is everything you want it to be: fast, fluid, fun. A very entertaining take on souls-like combat. 

[h3] - F2P [/h3]
It should go without saying, but this is a huge plus. The amount of content in this game feels like you're robbing someone every time you're reminded that you got this game for free. You literally lose nothing by trying it. On top of this, there's plenty of free earnable cosmetics in the game, so don't feel pressured to open your wallet just to look good! 

[h3] - Comedy [/h3] 
Weird to see this here, huh? WWM is a game that doesn't take itself seriously at all, in a way that's genuinely refreshing. Wanna learn Tai-Chi from a bear? You can do that. Meet a homeless man who wants you to collect flowers and bugs for him? You can do that too. Cosmetics range from traditional Chinese garments to a comically large stuffed goose head. On the topic of geese, they are canonically the strongest beings in the game, to the point that your power level is rated comparatively to them. This game is a fever dream at the best of times and I adore it. 

[h2] CONS [/h2] 

[h3] - Localization [/h3]
It's as bad as you hear it is. This game has some of the worst localization I've ever seen in any game, to the point of straight up laziness. English VA's deliver their lines with all the passion of High School Drama Nerds, and the game is riddled with TERRIBLE syntax and grammar errors. You will frequently encounter tutorials and dialogue that make absolutely no sense whatsoever, and it makes progression quite frustrating and confusing at times. 

[h3] - UI [/h3]
It's a pain to navigate and it sucks. Enough said. 

[h3] - Story [/h3] 
It's boring at the best of times and utter nonsense at the worst of times. Half the time it doesn't even make sense, and that's not just because of poor localization like some glazers will have you believe. It's just bad.

[h3] - AI [/h3] 
I wanna be very clear here. I don't necessarily despise AI. While I personally refuse to use it, I understand it's potential as a tool. However, you cannot deny the overwhelming amount of laziness it has brought, and that really shines through here. By the time you reach Kaifeng, most of the characters and NPC's are very clearly voiced by AI, with some of them literally reading off punctuation marks in their words. Hell, half the dialogue isn't voiced at all. This wouldn't be so bad, normally, but this game doesn't adhere to Steam's policy of listing AI usage in their game. Not cool. 

[h3] - Kaifeng [/h3] 
Yeah, it's bad. By the time you reach Kaifeng, just about everything good in this game disappears. Localization is worse than ever, half the dialogue is either AI or not voice acted at all, the performance drops from 60 fps down to 30-40fps, it stutters, the QoL disappears. It's just a mess. This entire half of the game really feels like a lazy, rushed afterthought. 

[h3] - Time Gates [/h3] 
Now I will admit, I'm extremely biased here: I DESPISE time gates. Nothing pisses me off more than an already grindy game telling me I need to wait 36 hours for my energy to recharge in order to continue progressing. This doesn't necessarily get in the way of story progression, but it does eventually come around to blocking all other progression. Repeatable dungeons, outposts, boss battles, hell, even CRAFTING and levelling up is all time gated. It's all in an effort to encourage you to spend money on the game, which leads me to the next con... 

[h3] - Predatory Microtransactions [/h3] 
Contrary to popular belief, the microtransactions in this game SUCK. The vast majority of cosmetics fall around the $30 mark at a MINIMUM for like, 4 items. Additionally, there's the increasingly popular practice among Chinese developers of absolutely screwing over global release players. Cosmetics are more expensive for us, and a lot of direct purchase cosmetics are instead funneled into step-up gachas, resulting in a 3x price increase where you're easily spending $150 for one outfit. Not cool. Battle Passes are a thing too, of course, and buying them gives you access to otherwise locked gameplay features like the ability to access traders from anywhere. There's no way for global players to earn premium currency, unlike CN players, and we get screwed over by this system in just about every way imaginable. 

[h3] - PvP [/h3]
It revolves entirely around stunlocking. That's it. It sucks. Glazers will say it's a "skill issue" and that there's a skill in the game (Serene Breeze) that lets you break a stunlock. What they don't mention is that it has an absurdly long cooldown, meaning that once you and your opponent have both used it, it's right back to stunlocking each other. It's boring, it's monotonous, and it's made worse by the fact that some gameplay elements like sects REQUIRE it. Compounding the issue is the utter LACK of balancing. The gear you have in solo mode is the gear you bring in PvP, meaning 90% of the time you're going up against some no-lifer with 50-100 more hours than you: they have more health, more skills, and objectively better equipment. If you don't wanna spend 100 hours grinding for good equipment, just steer clear of PvP. 

[h3] - The Community [/h3] 
I hate saying this, because I have met some really nice people in it, but this game's community sucks, man. It's so full of toxic positivity. Make one criticism about the game, and you get dogpiled. The simple fact is, the only reason this game is such a "breakout success" is because of this toxic positivity---any real criticisms made get bullied into the ground by these copium-huffing glazers. Don't like PvP? You're just unskilled and stupid. Don't like the bad netcode? Get better Wifi. Performance issues? Must have a potato PC. Don't like how CN gets better treatment than Global? Just play on the CN servers. Don't like how expensive the cosmetics are? Lol, what are you, broke? It's exhausting and frankly I'm getting so tired of these kinds of communities. 

[h2] CONCLUSION [/h2] 
Hey! You've made it to the end! Thanks for taking the time to read all that, and I hope I was able to answer some of your questions about this game! All in all, I really do enjoy WWM, despite all it's glaring flaws. I can't necessarily see myself sinking 200 hours into this game, but if you're looking for something fun to play, or a good time full of genuine cry laughing at a fever dream experience, I can strongly recommend this game. Maybe I'll catch you around sometime!

The graphics are simply gorgeous. The amount of content you can get for free is exceptional, including the main storylines, side quests, clothing, and in game currency. The paid content is not game breaking and the balance of it not feeling like pay to win, pay to avoid grinding, or pay to play are absolutely worthwhile. The available skins in the shop are exquisite and not very cost inhibitive. 

If you want a visually pleasing, engaging solo storyline, enjoy pvp and socializing, this game is great.

I REALLY liked this game, and thought it was going to be my main game for the foreseeable future. The graphics are great, the world is nice, and the combat is really fun if you like Sekiro and parry mechanics. The only problem I had with the first 80 hours was that the menus were obnoxious, and getting various rewards was annoying. But over time, you get less of them, and you get more used to quickly getting them and moving on. And for a free to play game, most of the cosmetic items in the cash store seemed reasonable to me. 

Then I got to whatever world level lets you get 55, and suddenly the experience got a lot worse. The scaling of the monsters in the world gets absolutely out of hand, and it gets to the point that even when your mastery rating is more than enough for the content (your gearscore essentially) monsters are quite damage spongey, and will kill you in 2-4 hits depending on the monster.  The scaling on the boss monsters was also pretty bad, to the point where the vast majority of the damage you do is from exhausting enemies with parries and executing them. The Chapter 1 boss at 55 was about as challenging as Malenia in Elden Ring, which felt really out of place this early in the game. But I beat it, and ended up with 15 or so of the legend badges for killing bosses on the hardest difficulty, and was still enjoying the game, even if the scaling was annoying. I will say at this point I did enjoy doing the group content with random people. The fights had an MMO vibe to them, and trying to heal a group in an action combat game was a novel experience. 

Now I'm 60th level, and 2 days from the level cap going up again, and I'm absolutely dreading it. It honestly just feels like there are entire power-up mechanics that I must be missing, or that the game doesn't explain, because now even simple things like bounty missions require me to approach them like a boss fight. And because a lot of the progression that I am aware of in the game is locked behind the time gated energy content, I feel like I'm screwed if I level up more, but I'm screwed if I don't and fall behind and waste the resources. 

If you asked me a week ago, I would have given this game a resounding yes on the recommendation. Now, I'm leaning no, because if the experience is going to continue to get worse until we hit a level cap that actually sticks for a while, it feels like the game will just feel even worse as time goes on, and it'll constantly be on a one-week treadmill of needing new gear and feeling really weak, then finally catching up and becoming weaker when the cap goes up again. It's like the raid cycle experience of an MMO, except it's happening weekly instead of a few times a year.

Where Winds Meet has the exact opposite problem Monster Hunter Wilds does. In MH:W, pretty much everything was too easy, and the one actual challenge they added to the game wasn't really designed to be done solo, so it felt bad. In WWM, enemies have such bloated HP and damage numbers that everything feels like a boss fight, which makes everything outside of a boss fight feel like an obnoxious waste of time. I'll probably maintain things for a while and cut back on playtime in the hopes that eventually the game hits an equilibrium where the number scaling is satisfying again like it was around level 40. But if it just continues in this direction, I don't think this is the game I'll devote my time to.

The combat is easily one of its best parts: you can mix all kinds of combos and strategies, switching styles on the fly, which makes every fight feel different and actually fun instead of repetitive.

The movement is just as good. Running on walls, gliding through the air, jumping between rooftops—it all feels super smooth and gives you this awesome sense of freedom while exploring the world.

What really blows your mind is that the game is free to play. Despite that, it comes with a story that’s surprisingly deep and way more emotional than it first looks. You start thinking it’s simple, and then it pulls you into a much richer plot.

And if that’s not enough, there are tons of online activities—literally something for every mood. Coop missions, events, challenges, exploration with friends… you’ll always find something fun to do.
The graphics are the cherry on top: beautiful environments, detailed characters, and a world that feels alive and vibrant.

In short, Where Winds Meet is a great mix of fun combat, smooth movement, a surprisingly solid story, tons of content, and stunning visuals—all without paying a cent. Totally worth diving into.

TL;DR: A near-perfect open-world wuxia game where I can chill after a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ day at work, with a slight Soulsborne feel in the combat.

After ages, I’m finally writing another Steam review because this game deserves it. Before the FreeFire crowd jumps in, here’s my take on its current state.

The Good:

• The world is filled with loot and collectibles that you can grab immediately or return to later, and either way you’re rewarded. As a loot addict, I really appreciate this. Doing this will reward you, doing that will reward you. its perfect for a loot ♥♥♥♥♥ like me.
• Conversation speed system lets you fast-forward those low-res dialogue scenes without skipping the actual content. Super convenient.
• AI-generated NPC chats are fun to play around with. Easy to exploit, but still a new cool feature.
• Gear farming feels fair and not overly grindy. We’re level-gated for now, but so far RNG is fine.
• Paid content is mostly cosmetic, and nothing feels pay-to-win.
• Every moveset, item, or currency shows exactly where to get it in the Inspect menu of that particular item or moveset. Super helpful for an old guy like me.
• Graphics look beautiful even on the lowest settings.
• Tons of content: main quests, side quests, minigames, challenges, caves, dungeons, customization—always something to do.
• Optimization is surprisingly good. My potato PC still hits around 60 FPS most of the time.

The Bad:

• Ping/hosting system feels terrible. I don’t know how it works, but whatever it’s doing right now is hurting PvP a lot.
• Combat still feels shallow. It’s not close to Soulsborne depth (obviously), but PvP especially needs more counterplay. Stunlock is too easy and too common.
• Audio didn’t feel that good to me or maybe I’m just new to Chinese games.

The Ugly:

• Menus are all over the place and can be very confusing. They really need to fix this—I keep getting lost in the interface.

Conclusion:
I had tons more stuff to say to praise this game, but to keep this review from getting even longer, I’ll stop here. If they keep this up and continue dropping content like this in the years to come, this game will be a landmark for the F2P game industry.

If you enjoy martial arts RPGs, it's certainly worth a download—just be sure to use a controller.

Verdict: A surprisingly polished and engaging free game, best played with a controller.

So where do I even start? I'm probably going with "Not Recommended," but that's not because the game is bad. Far from it. If you have time to invest and don't have some monstrous backlog or too many online games you're already stuck in (or gacha and their ilk), this game will become your main one. But what if you're looking for something with less FOMO, less daily logins, less grinding for ENERGY/STAMINA, less timegating, and less RPG/character/system building that would make gridny Lootershooters and MMORPGs blush? Well... yeah. That's my issue. The game nails a ton of things—impressive graphics, an open-world traversal system that's just plain fun to explore, especially once you unlock that special movement that lets you devour distances with an animation that's never boring to watch on repeat. The combat system offers tons of room for personal flair and how you choose to play... a COOP system, PVP system, and on top of that BATTLE ROYALE—what the hell isn't there?—all wrapped in a Wuxia vibe and atmosphere that's truly one-of-a-kind.
But at the same time, the game leans hard into all those MOBILE and GACHA tropes that are just exhausting, burdensome, convoluted, and turn it into a second job. It also has plenty of JANK, and the voice acting and translation... could use some work. But all that's forgivable.
I can't recommend the game to myself—I just don't have the time I'd want to give it. Maybe I'll dip back in for the campaign and exploration as they keep expanding it. But if everything this great game offers sounds like something worth sinking your teeth into (and probably drowning in), then yeah, it might just be for you.

**“Where Winds Meet: A Gorgeous Game That Plays Like It Forgot What It Wanted To Be Halfway Through Development”**

Where Winds Meet is one of the most confusing gaming experiences I’ve ever had.
One moment I’m stunned by the visuals — beautiful landscapes, amazing lighting, characters posing like they’re in a wuxia movie poster — and the next moment I’m fighting the camera more than the actual enemies.

This game is basically:
**“What if we made a breathtaking world… and then sprinkled jank all over it like parmesan cheese?”**

---

## 🥋 **THE COMBAT: BEAUTIFUL CHAOS WITH EXTRA CHAOS**

Combat LOOKS incredible.
You feel like you’re in a martial arts epic.
You jump, flip, spin, deflect arrows — it’s cinematic perfection.

But actually controlling it?
Feels like trying to play Mozart on a broken piano in a windstorm.

Dodging doesn’t dodge.
Parrying sometimes parries and sometimes decides you deserve death.
And half the bosses swing like they’re lagging even if YOU aren’t.

---

## 🗺️ **THE OPEN WORLD: STUNNING BUT EMPTY ENOUGH TO HEAR YOUR OWN REGRET**

The world is massive and genuinely gorgeous…
but almost too big for how little there is to actually *do*.

Lots of running.
LOTS of running.
Mountains look nice. Trees look nice.
NPCs talk like they’ve never met a human before.

It’s like someone made a breathtaking wallpaper pack and then remembered they needed to build a game around it 10 minutes before launch.

---

## 🧭 **THE STORY: I HAVE NO IDEA WHAT’S GOING ON AND I’M 90% SURE THE GAME DOESN’T EITHER**

There are plot twists.
There is drama.
There is ancient mystery.

There is also absolutely zero explanation for half of it.

I talked to one NPC and they dumped three paragraphs of poetic dialogue on me like I was taking a college philosophy exam.

I walked away more confused than enlightened.

---

## 🐉 **THE PERFORMANCE: YOUR PC WORKS HARDER THAN YOUR CHARACTER**

I swear this game turns my GPU into a space heater.
It sounds like it’s about to lift off and join NASA every time a cutscene plays.

---

## 💬 **THE FINAL VERDICT: PRETTY GAME, MID EXPERIENCE, MAXIMUM BAIT**

Where Winds Meet is gorgeous.
Stunning.
Aesthetic perfection.

But the gameplay feels like a prototype that wandered into public by accident.

If you want:

* Style over substance
* A world prettier than your future
* Combat animations that look cool even when they don’t work
* A story that makes you question your literacy
  …this is your game.

Otherwise?
Even *Genshin Impact* feels deeper — and I can already hear people foaming at the mouth reading that sentence.

[h2]Where Winds Meet * 10/10[/h2]
[b]This game absolutely should not be free. If I've ever seen a game that justifies a $70 price tag, this game is it.[/b]

[h2]Story[/h2]
[b]The story is decent, but it's likely the least impressive aspect of the entire game. Despite the narrative being extensive and supported by many coherent side-quests, the overall plot quality falls short compared to the game's other outstanding features. I am still interested to see the direction the developers take the story in future updates.[/b]

[h2]Graphics[/h2]
[b]There isn't much to say about this game beyond how absolutely stunning it is. Every aspect of the visuals is beautiful. Even when the graphics are set to low, the game still looks quite good, but at Max settings, it is truly beautiful. The visuals beautifully showcase the Chinese culture, creating stunning, lively scenes.
Crucially, the detail is perfectly balanced; it is rich and amazing without ever feeling cluttered or overwhelming. The more you play, the more beautiful scenes you will discover.[/b]

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
[b]The game's combat is not overly difficult to pick up, but it presents a difficult system to truly master. There is immense depth due to the variety of weapons and play styles available, allowing you to customize your builds for countless possibilities. Based on the latest updates, this depth is only set to increase.

PvE For standard play, you can generally create one or two solid builds and progress through the game with relative ease. However, reaching the Legendary difficulty demands that you truly perfect your understanding of boss mechanics and enemy attack patterns.

PvP This is a whole different challenge. You must master intricacies like weapon swing timings, deflecting, and opponent anticipation.

The combat contains many Dark Souls elements, though it is not a one-to-one copy. It can be frustrating at times, but it is ultimately a very enjoyable and highly rewarding system when you finally succeed.

The map for this game's adventure is immense. Initially, you must rely on foot or horseback for travel, but you later unlock options for fast travel or flying. Flying is a very cool, fast option that makes traversing the massive world a joy, even if it's not quite as instant as fast travel.
The map is diverse, featuring numerous different biomes, beautiful sceneries, and a wealth of items to find and collect. You could easily spend countless hours just exploring and continuously discovering new areas and secrets. You can enjoy this exploration either solo by yourself, in co-op with friends, or by playing online with random strangers. No matter your choice, exploring the expansive world is a very fun experience.

This game excels in its unique and varied playstyles. Whether you prefer a dedicated single-player experience, a co-op session, or playing online like an MMO, there are countless ways to approach the content.
To truly get the most out of this game, playing online is essential. You'll want to join guilds, get married, and take on disciples to unlock even more rewards, cosmetics, and benefits.
Fun Fact: If you establish both a marriage and a disciple relationship with a single person, you can double the benefits when playing together![/b]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
[b]I could easily talk about this game for much longer, but I'll end it here: just try this game out! Since it's free, there is genuinely no reason not to. While it has a few minor issues, it is, for the most part, a wonderful game and one of the best releases we've seen in a while. I think many people will be surprised by its quality; unlike many games in this category, this one is actually really good.[/b]

I just started and this game is amazing. It has a lot of a lot of content. What I really enjoy is the combat. The parry assist is so cool, that you can tailor it what you want. Want it on all attacks, OK. Want it only on major attacks, OK. Want it just on boss fights, OK.  It literally allows you to step into combat and get use to the mechanics and then go all Elden Ring on the game.  The story is interesting and there are a ton of side quests which on not just go fetch quests.  There are puzzles, which are not terribly challenging, but break up the constant let's go kill a bunch of enemies to the end for a boss fight. The level progression is also good, in that the as you move up in level, everything else moves up to. So you can't just go back to a beginning area and destroy everything as they leveled up also.  The rewards are on par with your level too, so you don't get trash from killing NPCs which is nice too.  The cons are just small things. For example the menus and amount of exploration rewards.  There is a reward for almost everything you do, which is a little over the top. They are trying to hit your dopamine button, but they are smashing it like crazy. It gets tiring to go through all the crazy menus and hit claim all over and over again.  Or to see what you need to 100% an area.  The voice acting needs help and they need a team to go through and clean up the translations/voice acting.  Some things are voiced and others not. Some times the voice doesn't even match the intent, most likely because it was AI generated.  Which is not a bad thing. They just need a English speaking test team to review and clean it up. But it's a free to play game, so it's hard to nit-pick when they give you a AAA experience for free.  Which I guess is not saying much, when the AAA games have fallen off really bad lately.  But if you are looking for something to play over the winter break or to have fun with after work, I would give this a try. It's free, nothing to lose.

Where Winds Meet is the first RPG in a long time that actually grabbed me and refused to let go. Normally I play an hour or two of an RPG per week (or I drop it for months), but this game legit made me want to stay home and just play it all day. It’s been a while since a game gave me that “one more quest” feeling until I look up and hours are gone.

The graphics are stunning, the world feels alive, and the cinematics honestly look better than a lot of Netflix shows. The story keeps pulling me in, and the pacing doesn’t waste your time. Combat is smooth, responsive, and just fun! I never felt like I was fighting the controls.

Exploring the world actually feels rewarding, side quests aren’t boring filler, and every new area makes me wanna push further. Even with only 13 hours in, it’s hitting that perfect mix of chill exploration and hype moments.

If you’ve been bored of modern RPGs, this one might surprise you. I’m hooked.

I recommend this game to all my friends and anyone looking for something new to play. This game rivals Warframe when it comes to F2P content. I get the same question from all of my friends when I ask them to try this, "What's the catch?" So far, I've yet to find one. This game puts almost all other F2P's to shame.

     I will try to summarize this by saying this has been the most impressive F2P game I have ever played. It is a really fresh take compared to most MMOs I play. What I like the most, is I can play all of this like a solo souls-like campaign with occasional co-op with friends. The music is amazing. The graphics are absolutely beautiful. The UI was a little confusing at first, but after some time it's actually become quite useful when it comes to finding the items I need to collect/purchase. If I'm missing a material for a craft, I can simply mark all sources and the game will guide me to the nearest one. 

     Bosses are really fun, while most souls-like games would focus on dodging this game primarily focuses on parries which makes it really flashy and satisfying to master. Don't let the difficulty scare you away, as there's lots of options to make the game more accessible if having quick reflexes doesn't sound like fun. The game is really good about progressing at your own pace. Most of the leveling is based on exploration, and by doing as much as I could within just the first few areas on the map I was able to get to level 50 really fast within the story. It rewards the exploration more than the grind.

     The only issue I've really had with this game is stuttering. I really like good frametimes and I like the smoothest experience I can get but right now the game hitches and stutters a lot in the open world and in menus. Online mode will absolutely crush your frames when it has to render everyone else's cosmetics and effects, which is pretty typical of an MMO but this game stutters really hard in some of the more active parades and events I've joined. Playing with friends can be fun, but the game's servers are limited and the latency will make the combat feel worse if you're playing with friends from across the world, so I've mostly stuck to solo play and even then the game still stutters a lot.

     Overall I recommend this to all gamers. I think anyone will be surprised by how much this game offers while keeping the microtransactions focused on cosmetics. I haven't had this much fun with an MMO since Warframe, and I'm really excited to see this game grow.

[h1]Where Winds Meet is an awesome single player experience and a pretty good multiplayer experience[/h1]

[h2]The Core Mechanics[/h2]

[h3] + Main story, Campaign stories, and Jianghu Legacy.[/h3]
These quests are all engaging, sometimes jaw dropping and/or emotional. Maybe the best I've played in an MMO.

[h3] + Bosses[/h3]
These are both challenging, creative and a lot of fun in single player. Of course your miles will vary depending on difficulty selected and skill. In Multiplayer they're still fun and they change up the mechanics of the fights to make sense for 5man or 10man content. I wouldn't say they're hard but still engaging.

[h3] + The Obligatory Grind[/h3]
It's really not bad in Where Winds Meet, for a f2p Asian MMO it's really good. Biggest grinds will be mats for Mystic Skills and Inner Ways. Professions can be a bit of a grind but are honestly fun to do. Gear so far is really easy to farm, along with enhancing and divine craft. 

[h3] - Time Gated Content[/h3]
While leveling you will run into time gates, usually a day to wait to get to the next level breakthrough. this happens starting at 30-31 and (I could be wrong) every 10 levels after that. a couple of quests also have 24hr timers but not many. These 24hr time gates are pretty minor though and there is so much other content to do like professions, odditys, and quests that it's doesn't feel to restrictive. The one that can feel restrictive is the energy needed to do 5 man content. Now this doesn't mean you can't still do the content but it does mean you can't get loot from the content. Honestly not much different then a mythic dungoen lockout from wow but handled different. I don't mind it but it does suck running out. 

[h3] + or - The Social Aspects[/h3]
The social aspect totally depends on you. I enjoy it for the most part but overall I don't feel like it's right to fully call this an MMO, and the co-op is limited. Most of the quests are single player only, you can switch to online and see plenty of people, beg, heal, make music for, pose with others that you see and more but it doesn't feel as MMO as say a wow player or ff14 player would expect. If you like guilds there are plenty to find and most are active with a discord. you can also pvp but I haven't done much of that yet. 

[h3]Is this F2P game P2W?[/h3] 
I would say no... BUT. Honestly there is no buying gold, gear or meaningful power from the cash shop. It's the least egregious f2p MMO I think I've ever seen. where one could argue there is some. potions, with leveling up your medicine you can get 5 healing potions per encounter. if you pay for the battle pass you can get 2 more. This basically has no bonus for multiplayer combat. the potions are severely nerfed and not worth using. You can't use potions at all in pvp. It does help in solo boss encounters especially early when you only have 1 or 2 potion slots unlocked. the paid portion of the battle pass does also have echoing jade which you can use to buy from a couple vendors that sell Inner Ways. it's not a lot of jade and you will get that jade from doing everything else in game. The $20 dollar mount, this is probably the biggest pay for convenience in the game. It allows you to gather all resources with an aoe ability that are in however many yards from your player and makes farming mats way easier. It's by no means required but after purchasing it I can't say it isn't really helpful either. 

Overall I think Where Winds Meets is a great game. I've really enjoyed my time. I've topped many dps meters, maxed out my character until the next breakthrough opens up, completed all the main story, campaigns and a ton of quests but I still have a lot of content left to do while I wait for the next breakthrough. I would recommend everyone give the game a shot. It's f2p with very minor p2w aspects, almost exclusively cosmetic.

A game with an atrocious UI and terrible game mechanics covered with a thick layer of pretty graphics. This game has so much potential, but the multitude of problems it has are not things that can be easily fixed.

What's good:

It's free so spend a few hours walking around drinking in the wonderful sights and soaking in the atmosphere. These are the best parts of the game. I love the music-playing minigame. The combat is serviceable when you are still at low levels fighting the mobs you find in the open world.


What's terrible:

1. UI. You see the red dots telling you that you have something to claim, but where is it??? You can click all over the place and still can't find what is it you're supposed to collect. You can switch between two weapons, but quick, which weapon do you have equipped? You can't tell because the weapon HUD disappears after some time and there is no way make it permanent. This lack of thoughtful design is apparent in most aspects of the game.

2. Parry system. This game uses the terrible Elden Ring style where you parry at the start of an attack, but since some boss attacks take seconds to wind up, the combat flow feels very inconsistent. This game, with its life-life animations, would have benefited greatly from using the parry system from Sekiro, where you parry based on when the attack will hit you.

3. Terrible quest designs. Do you like QTEs? No? Too bad! The main quest is way too draggy and preachy.

4. Floaty, inaccurate movements. Your character will slip off surfaces for no reason when you need to just stand still on a moving platform. And vault over things when you need your character to keep in cover. The camera movement can give sudden motion sickness.

5. Super grindy. Yes, there are no classes. But leveling a martial art beyond the early levels requires intense farming for mats from gathering plants so you can't really experiment playstyles freely due to lack of resources. The map can show you where the plants you need to farm are, but you will be running all over the map for them. This is grind for the sake of grind, and not fun.

6. Bad English localization. Are you Body Type 1 or Body Type 2? Yes, this is in the character creation, and the devs doubled down on the woke by asking this again in a survey.  The English voiceovers often do not match the subtitles, and both aren't very good, with nuances that seem lost in translation. The Chinese voice acting is so much better, so be sure to use this if you understand Chinese.

Honestly, it's pretty fun, I haven't felt obligated to spend any money and I feel like the game generally respects my time as someone who works a 9-5. Someone who wants to play 8 hours a day would probably run into some frustration with the resource caps/timers (jade fish, energy caps, level breakthroughs etc.), but if you have a job I think you'll be happy to feel like you're not "falling behind" other players with more free time, at least not by much, and still have a bunch of opportunities to keep up with the daily sign-in bonuses (including make-ups for missed days) and other events. That, and I think it's a really fun ARPG gameplay experience.

Plus, it's free! The barrier to entry is your hardware. The game runs pretty well on a 7900x/4080, but I had some weird freezing/dips in the Kaifeng area during some cutscenes, which will hopefully be addressed in a future patch. The game does need some more "MMO" staples like being able to have multiple characters though. It is my understanding some of these enhancements got implemented in later versions of the game that are running on Chinese servers, and the international release is approximately a year behind in updates, so I'm looking forward to the future updates for both fixes and content.

You play as a young wanderer, who dreams of one day going out into the wide world to explore and become something more than a backwater wine server. TLDR:IGNORE THE MENUS AT THE START AND PLAY THE GAME FOR ATLEAST A FEW HOURS. IT'S REALLY GOOD AND IT'S FREE. GOOD PVP, GOOD GEAR PROGRESSION, GOOD CO OP, GOOD STORY, GOOD SOULSLIKE, GOOD BASE BUILDING, BAD MENUS, EXPENSIVE SKINS

Alright let's break down what this game has to offer. I originally quit the game because there were so many notifications and menus that I thought it was a free pay to win gacha game. Oh how wrong I was. This game is easily over $60 worth in value in its main story alone. The game has something for everyone, well designed pvp, mmo gear farming and raids, soulslike boss content, base/town building, single player campaigns or co op gameplay. And somehow everything feels meaningful in making your character stronger in some way. ALL FOR FREE.

Popular concerns/questions:

Is it co-op?
 
KIND OF. Theres a large mix of solo missions which is a lot of the main story campaign as well as individual dungeons. There's also a lot of co op campaigns and world bosses which you can tackle together. In terms of what the experience is like, I would say it feels like both people playing through their own game and world and when you want or need help you can ask your friends to join your world to help fight a boss, explore your world or complete a dungeon. All exploration and quests done in one world is solely tied to that players world. You share chests and drops for gear but that's about it. It's much more about helping your friend complete their world versus completing one together. 

Is the game pay-to-win? 
NOT REALLY. There's almost no pay to win aspects, the only thing that may be considered pay to win is when you buy the battle pass you gain some upgrade materials which can save some time on farming but it's nothing significant enough that any person would consider pay to win imo.

How's the PVP?
As someone who grinded the Pvp to the highest rank, Mythic, in this game, I can confidently say it was some of the most fun and best designed pvp I've ever seen in an MMO. The pvp is very fighting game-esque. Learning combos, how to break out of combos, spacing your character and playing neutral, all wrapped up in an mmo action combat style. Very satisfying to learn. PRO TIP FOR MATCHMAKING: The game will try and pair you against players of similar gear score to you but after 1 minute spent in queue it will ask you if you want to expand matchmaking: even if you say no it will still put you against someone significantly higher in gear score. To avoid this simply leave queue and requeue before it hits 1 minute. You wait longer queues but the games will likely be better. 

How's the story?
REALLY GOOD. Again, the solo campaign alone is worth $60 imo, go play it go enjoy.

How's the endgame?
DECENT. There's raids, dungeons, bosses to farm, equipment to grind and stats to roll for. The classic, and it's really fun in the soulslike action combat style. One complaint is the energy system which only lets you claim a certain amount of rewards daily. This is a big complaint for people but I would say this is only affecting the absolute GRINDERS. The game is very generous with your time and there's so much to do to improve your character I don't even feel like I have time to use all my energy everyday. Anyone complaining about this is just clocking in a ridiculous amount of time in the game (obviously that means the game is good.)

How's exploring and the world itself?
VERY REWARDING, everything you do contributes to either characters strength or some sort of quality of life like faster travel, more healing potions, new abilities. The world is very full and everything you do feels like it was meaningful.

If you've made it this far hopefully this helped you decide and understand the game a bit more. This game is insane for how many things it tried to mix together and somehow it works pretty damn well. I think it's insane not to try this game. ITS FREE. GO HAVE FUN.

Ok after 200 hours of playing, getting all of the steam achievements available, I can safely say that the game is not worth the price of..... ohhh no, wait, it's free, than sure, you should play it. "Jokes" aside, 

Combat (Good) - Brilliant, very quick souls game, or if you want to go easier, you can change difficulty, so it is for everyone. Martial arts combat is fun, all different builds are fun, it does give out the true fighting experience.

Story/Characters (Bad) - This is a massive downside to me, outside of 3 characters, not a single one is memorable. They are all bland AI slop, Story is simply boring and unimpactful, million of things going on, while nothing is happening really. Also only few moments of interesting story telling, but most is just low effort.

World/Exploration (So,So) - World is fine, nothing different that you would see in Witcher for example or so many other games like this. They really tried to make the world as "lived in", but failed completely. All the random NPC's are just stale, repeat one thing constantly, despawn at night, respawn in the morning and just exist there.
Exploration is fun, there is lots to explore, from caves, to dungeons, to puzzles, to stealing martial arts, to outposts, to towns and villages, to high peaks and deep holes, this is probably explorers dream.

AI (Bad) - AI in this game is just bad, and it's very simplified one! It's an interesting concept, but done as poorly as it could've been.

UI (Extremely Bad) - This is my biggest gripe with this game! The interface is just abominable! Not as bad as in Bethesda games, but this is not how you do the UI. There are million of things when you open the menu, and you have to go through million different menus to get to where you need to be, and than exit the same way, there is no search bar for anything in the menus, so when you enter late game, with million different items in the bag, you can't find anything.... I could go on forever, but it's just absolute sewage.

Graphics (Phenomenal) - Graphics are just brilliant, and the game is optimized quite well amazingly, there is nothing bad to say here, only good things!

Translations/Dialogs (So,So) - Translations are ok for the most part, than they break completely on some, and dialogs are mostly in English, and than it breaks and changes to Chinese, or there are no dialogs at all, and the scene plays in silence, but it's very uncommon, so it's mostly fine.

Replayability (Good) - You can revisit all of the campaigns, all of the bosses, and all of the outposts, with higher challenge, with lower challenge, with impossible challenge, you are simply allowed to play everything over and over again in different ways, different build, difficulties, with teams, in co-op, there are even raids for some bosses, all in all, quite good.
--Will add achievements here. This games is a heaven for achievement hunters!

Minigames (Ok) - There are lots of minigames in this game, from madio cards, to mahjong, to chess (not a normal, but puzzle chess), to riddles (AI slop ones, very bad), to music/instrument playing (which is good as an idea, but bad in the execution), to pitch pot (which is meeh), to archery (also meeh), to wrestling (which is generally bad). Generally it's all ok, but nothing game changing.

Social (??) - I am broken on this one, there is a lots to do in the social aspect, you can just play instruments with other people, take pictures, play all minigames, do healing together, chase bounties. But I must say that all of it, is just plain boring, as I've seen barely anyone is doing any social thing for the sake of socializing, or role-playing, it's just for rewards, and if there are not rewards it's not being done. There is lots to do, but all is just lame really. There are also Partnerships, masters and disciples, also romantic  partnerships, that again are there only for the sake of role-playing, and have no real function, and no one is really doing them....
--I will add guilds here, that are also generally useless, beside getting rewards for activities that are mostly outside of the guild, and most guilds just sit empty even tho they have built in lots of leisure stuff for role-playing (same failure as Warframe has with clans).

Factions/Reputations (Ok) - There are lots of sects with interesting aspects to them, there are rules to be followed if you are in one, voting systems, leaders, builds you need to abide to, it changes your gameplay deeply and interestingly and they are worth checking out later on in game, by then you can just stay sectless and run on your own.

Solo/Multiplayer (Ok) - There is no real solo in this game, it's an online game, solo is just a mask, you can have your world invaded at any point if you get a bounty, so there is no single-player, just lesser multiplayer. It's nice to be able to play with whomever you want, and you can go into another players world and if they have not explored as much as you did, you can reexperience everything all over again without starting anew. All in all, it's ok.

Bugs (Good) - There are no real bug, let alone game breaking bugs, the only thing I've seen are some glitches here and there and few quests and wandering tales bugging out, but it's fixable with reddit guides generally, so you will not miss out on anything.

Servers (Hmmmm?) - For co-op ("private" one) everything works fine, for raids and dungeons through matchmaking also all is fine. But than you hit other matchmaking co-op activities and everything breaks, the lags go through the roof, and can't parry anymore generally, and you play with 1+ second of delay.

IMPORTANT - It's a Chinese game, and it will as I checked, send you connection details to some very sketchy Chinese sites and routing relays. Your operating system and antivirus will generally block them, but with wireshard for example you can see your firewall going haywire while the game is on. No need to go into politics, so that is for you to check yourself if you want to, you get the idea.

Monetization (Good) - It boils down to cosmetics only, and you can play through the whole came without spending a dime in it, which is commendable in this day and age. You can still get most of the cosmetics through gameplay, so if you don't want to pay you don't have to, if you do want to, well, for the part where you do want to give money to the game/developers, everything is so STUPIDLY expensive! It's just ridiculously expensive to buy anything in this game, so if you are not a whale, you will most likely just play the game as it is.

Conclusion - Games is trying to be everything, and failing in most of those things, but still fun to play and worth giving it a shot, you will most likely, like it! I am personally not in awe with this games as lots of people are, but it's worth a shot, since it's free, you can try it out, if you don't like it, you'll just uninstall it and that is it. If you do like it, you will probably have a grand time with it. So I generally do recommend it ^_^

[h1] Almost 300 Hours In: It’s… Mixed. [/h1]

The Bad:
1) Buggy across the board.

2) Arena is basically Ping2Win.

3) Arena when you win you get +15points but -31pts if you loose. 

4) Bounty system a mess. Forced PvP.

5) Profession system is a mess. You can never get a contract.

6) Weapon “variety” doesn’t matter when everyone just uses swords. You don't even need a tank or a healer in group content.

7) Exploration mode is hours of doing the exact same task. Its fun and first and then you're over it.

8) Raids and bosses have fun mechanics, but even on Legendary there’s zero real strategy—just parry and you’re done.

9)Menus feel scattered and unintuitive.

10) English localization is serviceable but rough; voices often sound AI-generated.

11) Gacha feels predatory—especially compared to the CN version.

12) Dev communication is nearly nonexistent; no clear updates or acknowledgment of feedback. This is one of the main things that makes me want to stop playing because of this lack of communication I can't justify that it will get better and thus doesn't make me want to stick around in hopes that they fix these things. 

13) Inner Ways is grindy and takes up to three hours or more. 

14) The game touts co-op, it's not really co-op. Your friends can help you with bosses, but they wont get rewards or receive progress points. 

15) the mmo part is basically you just doing yoga in a forced area. 

16) The restriction of energy limits how much you can play pve content. Which after that there is nothing to do once you complete everything. So then you end up in arena and it is a terrible experience for the reasons above. 

The Good:
Gorgeous visuals.
Interesting story.
You can chat with so many NPC (yay i guess.)
Immersive Wuxia vibes.
And… that’s about it.

[h1]Глубокая, честная игра в эпоху «кликабельного контента»[/h1]

40 часов за три дня — и ни минуты ощущения, что «выполняю задания». [i]Where the Winds Meet[/i] не просто наполнена — она [b]живёт[/b]. Каждый холм, храм, рынок и даже заброшенная хибара несут смысл, историю, деталь. [b]Пустоты? Нет.[/b] Даже «сайд-квесты» здесь — маленькие новеллы с личностями, мотивами и последствиями. Никаких «принеси 10 шкур».

[list]
[*][b]Боёвка[/b] — хирургическая, требовательная, но честная.
[*][b]Атмосфера[/b] — как будто шагнул в свиток древнего художника.
[*][b]Сюжет[/b] не давит, но ведёт — и даёт право выбирать не только действия, но и этику.
[/list]

Да, в игре есть [b]пропуски заданий[/b] — но они [b]абсолютно опциональны[/b], нужны лишь тем, кто хочет экономить время, а не опыт. При этом игра [b]поощряет[/b] внимательность и вовлечённость: за исследование, диалоги и изящные победы дают не «опыт +10», а [b]уникальные предметы, способности, связи[/b].

[h2]Главное — никакого P2W[/h2]

Донат (если он вообще есть) — [b]чисто косметический[/b]. Всё ценное — заработано вами. Это игра [b]для игроков[/b], а не кошельков. [strike]Не для казуалов[/strike] — но для тех, кто помнит, зачем мы вообще в это играем.

[hr][/hr]
Если ты устал от «открытых миров» с картой, заклеенной маркерами… пришло время отправиться туда, где ветер всё ещё несёт смысл.
[hr][/hr]

[h1]A Deep, Player-First Game in an Age of Clickbait Content[/h1]

40 hours in three days—and not a single moment felt like “grinding.” [i]Where the Winds Meet[/i] doesn’t just fill its world—it [b]breathes[/b]. Every hill, temple, marketplace, and abandoned hut has purpose, story, and detail. [b]Empty zones? None.[/b] Even side quests are handcrafted mini-narratives with real characters, motives, and consequences—no “fetch 10 hides” filler here.

[list]
[*][b]Combat[/b] is surgical: demanding, precise, but fair.
[*][b]Atmosphere[/b] feels like stepping into a classical ink painting.
[*][b]Story[/b] doesn’t force morals—it invites you to shape your own path and ethics.
[/list]

Yes, the game offers [b]quest skips[/b]—but they’re [b]entirely optional[/b], meant only for those short on time, not experience. And it actively [b]rewards engagement[/b]: exploration, thoughtful dialogue, and elegant victories grant [b]unique items, abilities, and relationships[/b], not just XP.

[h2]Most importantly—zero pay-to-win[/h2]

Any monetization (if it even exists) is [b]purely cosmetic[/b]. Everything meaningful is [b]earned, not bought[/b]. This is a game made [b]for players[/b], not wallets. [strike]Not for casuals[/strike]—but for those who remember why we play at all.

[hr][/hr]

Where Winds Meet – A Masterpiece That Redefines Open-World Wuxia Gaming

Where Winds Meet isn’t just another open-world action RPG, it’s a love letter to Wuxia, a technical marvel, and a bold reminder of what games can achieve when developers combine artistic ambition with world-class gameplay design.

From the moment you step into its richly detailed ancient Chinese setting, the game proves itself to be levels above most recent open-world titles in both depth and execution.

Worldbuilding: An Open World That Actually Feels Alive

Unlike the copy-paste maps you see in many AAA games today, Where Winds Meet offers a world that feels handcrafted, alive, and reactive. Every village has personality. Every region carries its own history, lore, and atmosphere. NPCs behave naturally; their routines and micro-stories make the world feel lived-in. This is worldbuilding done right — immersive, dense, and emotionally engaging.

Combat: Elegance and Power in Perfect Balance

Combat is easily one of the game's strongest triumphs. Using classic martial-arts philosophy blended with modern action design, fights feel like cinematic duels straight out of legendary Wuxia films. Fluid swordplay. Air-dashing and acrobatic maneuvers. Qi-based abilities. Perfect parries and precise counter techniques. Every battle becomes a dances, stylish yet strategic.

RPG Depth: Choices That Actually Matter

The game respects player agency. Your choices affect alliances, outcomes, and even world perception. The branching storytelling gives replayability that most games only claim to have. Whether you walk the path of righteousness or choose a morally grey journey, the game responds in meaningful ways.

Visuals & Art Direction: Beyond Beautiful

The art direction is breathtaking. From mist-covered mountains to bustling ancient cities, every environment is postcard-worthy. Lighting, animations, and particle effects feel next-gen, not recycled, this is a world you want to get lost in.

Music & Atmosphere: Pure Cinematic Luxury

The OST is nothing short of enchanting. Traditional instruments mixed with emotional orchestration make every moment feel like a scene from an epic Wuxia opera.

Why It Stands Above the Competition

While many games rely on hype, Where Winds Meet delivers on: Superior world design, Deeper combat systems, Stronger storytelling choices, Aesthetic excellence, Unmatched martial-arts immersion. It doesn’t try to be a generic Western open-world game. It embraces its cultural roots boldly and gives players something fresh, exciting, and soulfully crafted.

Verdict: A Game That Deserves Global Recognition

Where Winds Meet is not just one of the most impressive open-world games in recent years, it is a benchmark title that pushes the Wuxia genre into the global spotlight. For players who crave storytelling, combat mastery, and a world worth exploring, this is an absolute must-play.

Where Winds Meet, Çin/Asya temalı açık dünya RPG’lerine karşı olan önyargımı ilk dakikada kırmayı başardı. Görsel dünya muhteşem: sisli dağlar, yansımalar, mimariler… her şey “ben bu manzaranın içinde yaşıyorum” hissi veriyor. Üstelik oyun ücretsiz ve pay to win değil; mikro ödemeler tamamen kozmetik odaklı.

Savaş sistemi şaşırtıcı derecede akıcı ve tatmin edici. Animasyonlar stilize, tepkiler tutarlı ve refleks odaklı yapı, her karşılaşmayı hem eğlenceli hem de öğretici kılıyor. Solo oynamak istediğinizde yeterince sürükleyici bir macera sunarken, co-op tarafı da arkadaşlarla beraber oynamayı gerçekten keyifli hale getiriyor. Zorluk seviyesi genelde adil, ancak bazı mini boss’lar beklenmedik derecede sert vurabiliyor – özellikle meydan okumayı seven oyuncuları memnun edecek bir yapı var.

Eğer açık dünyada dolaşmayı, keşif yapmayı ve refleks odaklı dövüş sistemlerini seviyorsanız, WWM sizi uzun saatler meşgul edecek potansiyele sahip. “Uzak Doğu temalı oyunlara pek ısınamam” diyenler bile bu atmosferin içinde kaybolabilir; ben de tam olarak bunu yaşadım. Where Winds Meet is a far better game than I expected it to be. The story could be more fleshed out, but what's there is immersive and frankly the game world itself  as well as the myths and history they've got to work with in the setting, is so pretty and interesting, that it doesn't matter that much.

I wish the character models were a little more varied. All the males look like they belong in a KPop band and the females all have that child-like anime look, although thankfully they didn't lean too far into the childs-head-on-a-curvy-woman's-body thing. I also wish you could vary your character's voice a little, but I understand why that was not possible given how much of the dialogue was recorded. I also love the costumes - the historically-friendly ones; they're really pretty and fun to collect. It's really nice to see these beautiful cultural costumes on your character!

What I don't love is the convoluted menus, the very many layered activities, expeditions, events, scenarios etc - it gets pretty confusing which ones are important or not and it's a lot of clicking thru menus. Also, while it's not pay-to-win, the shop system is fairly assertive about trying to get you to buy cosmetic stuff, usually by giving you pieces of outfits, or hair or whatever and then relentlessly showing you how you'd look in the whole thing lol. You CAN however, earn many, if not most (?) of the clothes in game with some work and no IRL money. Considering the game is FREE, and runs really well I can easily put up with this, and even spend a few bucks in the store now and again quite happily.

I've only played Solo and once on two player Co-op so can't speak to the MMO aspect at all. In Co-OP only the host's story progresses so bear that in mind. Also, I think it might ruin the lovely immersive aspect to see a crap-ton of people dancing, spamming dumb stuff etc like people do....but either way, WWM is absolutely worth putting in your library!

I'm coming from New World, thus far enjoying this game. Graphics and Exploration are this game's strength. There's always things to find and to farm, which is essentially a requirement in order to maintain your upgrades. So as such, I believe there's still purpose to the level gating that keeps you engaged long term. You're pretty unlikely to get cosmetics if you're not spending putting more into the gacha system, but long term  pity will eventually get you a random legendary reward. Menus are pretty substantial, but honestly after playing Destiny 2 in recent history I don't feel like there's much difference once you get used to where things are that you care about. I've maxed the Battlepass, so there's no longer that flashing alert. I've not paid for any cosmetics thus far, and didn't purchase the Premium Battlepass. I've also not used any of my consumables to refill my energy. Saving those for a rainy day. 

Combat is really good here, with a lot of room for skill expression. Bosses have some fairly intricate mechanics and phases. Group mechanics around these bosses are also rather fun, at larger scale. However, there's a marked benefit for players capable of grinding materials consistently to surpass players not able to put in the time. This shows in pvp, and will effect the sort of player that only wants to log on during pvp hours. You can stack days of points for when the future perk points unlock which is a huge plus. Let me be clear: I’m not here to convince you this game is good. I’m here to tell you it will likely exceed your expectations. Where Winds Meet is a profound journey where the virtues of might, loyalty, bravery, sacrifice, and courage are woven into a world that feels truly alive. Bustling cities hum with activity, NPCs follow their own routines, and every quiet corner of the wilderness holds another mystery, creating an atmosphere that is both immense and intimately detailed.

The solo experience is phenomenal, with a gripping main story and side content polished with clear passion. The PvP offers intense, skill-based duels, while the co-op mini-games provide delightful social fun. And for true warriors, the combat on Legend difficulty is a masterclass in challenge and satisfaction.

Here’s the part that will make you pause: you will find yourself asking, "Is this really free? I don't think I've played a true AAA experience like this in years." Let me assure you, it is. And not by the slightest, not by a single minuscule piece is it pay-to-win. Your skill and dedication are the only currencies that matter here.

To be fully transparent, the game launched with some expected growing pains for a project of this scale—translation quirks, audio glitches, some bugs, and network desync. The developers, however, have shown incredible dedication, rapidly fixing major issues and steadily polishing the experience with each patch. Given the sheer scale and detail of this massive world, their responsive support has been both understandable and commendable.

Ultimately, this game is a testament to passion. It shows what is possible when a project is driven by the palpable love of its creators. If you seek an immersive, expansive, and genuinely fair wuxia adventure that truly feels alive, this is your destination. Highly recommended.

- Puzzles are quite fun, from easy to hard
- Challenges are there to make you improve yourself, though not "a must" to play the game
- Like FF14, you only have 1 character, where the class changes depending on weapon(s)
- PvP has from 1v1 to arenas of "Many VS Many"
- Guilds
- Buildings you can create, though I haven't gotten into that yet
Now for the new things that I loved
- AI conversation with NPCs that can result from friendships to lifelong enemies
- NOTES from other players near objectives to help and guide you. Anyone can leave them and comment on them

I’ve been playing Where Winds Meet for a while now and wanted to share my experience — especially about PvE, PvP, and whether the game forces you to spend money.

🎮 Gameplay & World – 9/10

The world is huge, beautiful, and full of Wuxia fantasy vibes. Parkour, martial arts powers, swordplay, gliding — it feels like a true Chinese martial-arts freedom game. Lots of different weapons and skills to explore, each with its own style.

Exploration is rewarding: hidden bosses, puzzles, treasures, side quests… there’s always something new around the corner.

🗡 PvE Combat – 8/10

Boss fights and elite mobs are skill-based, not gear-based. Dodging, timing, counters — if you play well, you win.
No “must pay” items to progress. If you enjoy mastering combat systems, this game feels very satisfying.

Sometimes the combat animation can feel a bit floaty, but still fun and dynamic.

⚔ PvP – 8.5/10

The game proudly promotes “Your legend is written by skill and choice, never by wallet size.”
And yes — PvP really depends on your own skill, builds, and reaction. No overpowered paid equipment.

Low-level PvP can feel chaotic, but once you unlock more skills, the duels get really intense and strategic.

💰 Monetization – 10/10 (Truly NOT Pay-to-Win)

Cash shop = Mostly cosmetics and visual items.
You don’t need to pay to get stronger. No damage boosts, no pay-only equipment, no pay-wall content.

You can look cooler if you spend… but you will not fight better.

I am living my own wuxia world in 100++ hours of gameplay

Honestly I thought I enjoyed this game at the start but the more I played it the more I realized I hated this game.
It started out fun in the beginning but it slowly devolved into this awful experience of waiting to do daily chores that had little to no impact on the gameplay. It was a major time sync for nothing, and the grind only gets worse the longer you play.

This combined with the gameplay feeling halfway between rpg and mmo made the game incredibly clunky and awkward.

The game feels trapped between multiple worlds and it feels like it does so many different things half-assed. It doesn't feel commited to any one thing enough for me to enjoy it. Everything had major flaws that take away and ruin it for me. And the current late game content doesn't exist as the game was launched without the biggest draw of guild vs guild PvP and that didn't release until February.

The current 1v1 PvP sucks as it's entirely network based and it's pray you have better ping so you can 100-0 hit string your opponent.

And the single player experience is hard gated by time gates preventing you from playing the game as a solo souls like experience.

I think the tell tale sign that this game was not it, was the fact that in all of my hours spent in this game in the 3/4th ranked guild was all spent wishing I was playing something else. Something more fleshed out with more content. Where the game doesn't feel in a half complete state. I'm also tired of MMOs or MMO-lites releasing without half of the late game content that would make the game interesting. It's an mmo game yet there's no multiplayer PvP. Can't do 2v2 or 3v3. No guild vs guild. It's like they had 1 million ideas and executed on only half of them.

Not to mention the horrendously predatory cosmetic gacha. 300 dollars for a single pity when most of the rare items cost two pities to get in the first place. Then after you get your 300$ pity there's thousands more dollars worth of ROLLING to get the correct skin you want.

The game feels super hollow too. When you realize 90% of the available gameplay has minimal effect on growth or progression and you can ignore 90% of all content unless you enjoy exploring and doing the tedious dungeons. There's no point in doing the 30th divinecraft dungeon if I get the same garbage loot and currency I'd get if I did any other content in the game and that is all of the currently released meat and potatoes.

All other content is still gated behind a time gate, in my SINGLEPLAYER EXPERIENCE BTW. This part is also super frustrating. Like why is there an irl time game on my single player experience. This part makes it feel like an MMO yet there is no MMO style content besides the raids. As I mentioned there is no GVG there is no 2v2 or 3v3. There are no guild dungeons. There are only "guild raids" where you fight two bosses. No Dungeon, no puzzle mechanics, just two bosses that you fight in single player. Amazing "MMO" content for sure...

The single player game is time gated because of the game being mmo-like. So you can't even enjoy a full single player experience and ignore the MMO portion. And the main story is only like maybe 10 hours long so far. After that it's the same repetitive exploration missions to find chests that give you currency and gear that is going to be replaced in 10 days when the next time gate opens.

This is the entire gameplay loop. Grind single player, hit gear cap. Get bored. Wait for time gated to open. grind single player, hit gear cap. Get bored. Rinse and repeat.

Where good graphics meet mediocre gameplay.

This game adopted a fair few things from various games, to good effect:
- Sekiro's parry/posture gameplay
- Elder Scrolls' extensive and varied quest lines with incredible background lore
- Genshin's progression (energy as opposed to daily resets as per usual MMO) pacing plus monetization (monthly pass and Battle Pass), minus character gacha (cosmetic gacha only, no P2W).

On top of all that, there's a huge variety of optional online interactions, including PVE and PVP content, casual PVE events, guilds, chat systems (including AI chat systems, they even use AI for some mini-games).

Its all packed together with modern 3D semi-realistic visuals, and all for a grand price of free. Even after 80 hrs I barely feel the need to really spend anything, though the Battle Pass looks to be fairly worth while.

Its also worth noting that after 80 hrs I have only really cleared about 50% of the two areas in the current version. I have also encountered no showstopper bugs or even any real technical issues.

My main points of criticisms are:
- Too many menus nested in each other, with no quick access to those nested menus (apparently devs are working on this as a priority)
- The translation is quite spotty.
- You need some knowledge of Wuxia and Song Dynasty history to appreciate the incredible lore. A number of the named characters are actual historical figures.
- There are places where players can leave a comment on lore tidbits, and it is not filtered for spam or spoilers.
- The treasures located in the open world do not have an organized tracking system like with Wuthering Waves (2.0 onwards), instead opting for Genshin's annoying "place a treasure randomly" strategy.

In summary, this is pretty much the first Chinese Wuxia game I would recommend to anyone. Casuals and sweaty soulslike gamers all will find a home here.

Hello everyone,

Speaking personally, I’ve always been a huge fan of MMOs and raid-based games, and adding an open-world structure on top of that makes this game quite enjoyable for me. It feels like the game has some sort of story—every now and then emotional pieces of text pop up but considering the combat system and weapon variety, I think the game is good for now. However, there are definitely areas that need improvement, and here are the points I personally feel the devs should address:

--The build and weapon system definitely needs a few more weapons added. At certain points, the game lacks clear explanations or the existing preset systems feel insufficient. In some raid missions, our healer dealing more damage than the DPS is both funny and tragic at the same time—especially when the healer isn’t even using a set bonus.

--I don’t know how important cosmetics are to everyone, but I strongly believe this area needs attention. Having to pull rare items from gacha ''twice'' just to change your hair color or using two separate items for a one-time color choice is honestly borderline insane and ridiculous.

--Some cosmetics also feel overpriced or overly niche, although they’ve already stated they’ll release an update addressing this. (But seriously, the hair system is ABSURD.)

--Occasionally, PvP has lag spikes. I literally saw myself kill the same player three times in a row.

--Sects especially the Healer Sect absolutely need a rework! For the first time in my life, I witnessed around 100 healers PvPing each other just to decide who gets to heal someone afterward. Some sect missions and requirements feel extremely low-quality or incomplete. (I tried leveling Healer, but gave up. At least playing a killer/PK role gives you the feeling that you're progressing and contributing something.)

Overall, the game is good, but the AI voiceovers and certain performance issues hold it back a bit. Still, these are things that can definitely be fixed over time. After playing Destiny for years a game that felt like pure suffering at times, this one honestly feels like therapy. And the fact that it doesn’t have BDO-level ridiculous weapon or trading systems is another huge plus in my opinion.

The lore, story, and world building are GREAT in this game. The amount of different activities you can do is also really nice. Things WWM has to offer:

-Souls-like combat (you have to be able to read mobs body language queues to properly dodge/deflect attacks. Real time combat with the option to lock onto targets)
- Chess (Xiangqi - Not wester chest - Singleplayer)
- Mahjong (Single & Multiplayer)
- Madiao Cards (Single & Multiplayer)
- Wrestling (Basically Sumo - Multiplayer)
- Playing Music (Can write your own songs, or learn from NPC's. There's even programs to auto-play songs you upload to said program)
- Dancing (Single / Multiplayer - a couple different outlets for this)
- Riddles (Single or Multiplayer, exactly as the name entails)
- Trivia (Single/Multiplayer)
- Path to Riches (Literally Multiplayer Stock Market simulator)
- Spring Wave Pavilion (Multiplayer - Hot springs that also have mini games)
- Group Diagnosis (Doctor Specific - fellow doctors come together as a group to cure rare diseases)
- Prison Break (Multiplayer - literally as the name entails)
- Bounty Boards (Players place bounty rewards for things such as: (Scholar) - Basically being their lawyer so they don't go to in game jail, Hunting other players, completing trials, etc)
- 1 vs 1 Arena (As the name entails)
- Perception Forest (Multiplayer - Literally Fortnite--but in a Wuxia world)
- Tons of discoverable quests
- Ton's of side quests
- Lots of puzzle solving dungeons/activities
- World Bosses
- Raid Bosses
- Outpost Raids (Multiplayer - join players as you clear out bandits from a series of different outposts)
- Tons of achievements locked behind exploration/lore discovery
- 2 Regions - Qinghe (1st story arc area - can literally spend hundreds of hours 100% everthing if you want), Kaifeng (2nd story arc area)
- More updates coming very soon!

All I can say, is you just need to experience it yourself. It can be overwhelming at first. But if you just follow the main story, and do content that you encounter along the way, you will get your footing <3.

2300 hours later:

This game holds a special place in my heart. I became a guild master and ran an active guild that blasted through endgame content, built a community, and we regularly participated in GvG content and won pretty often. I put a lot of time in here and we had a lot of good times.

Now the game feels.. empty. Not just within my guild (which has seen many core players leave the game), but within the entire community. Sword Trials and Hero's Realms face long queues and you're lucky if the team even makes it through the first fight before people drop out and you have to wait another 10 minutes to run content. Recruiting for guilds has been more challenging as well since most players seem to log in for an hour every day or every other day simply to check boxes and do their daily things. There isn't much of an active player base and now I fear my guild will eventually fall into disbandment as time goes on.

The Pros:
The game is fun.
The combat is fun.
The visuals and music are good.
The story is pretty captivating once you understand what's happening.
The plethora of game systems give you a lot of things to choose from.

The Cons:
The game can get repetitive.
The population is dwindling.
The time-gated content gets old.
The slow drip of main story content is painful and when there is new content, the quests are either so brief it barely feels like a main story, or its so painfully long with cutscenes or odd walking sim mechanics, it feels pointless and most just want to spam click through it all.

I still play regularly. I try to log in at least once a day so I can maintain active status as a guild master, since after 5 days of inactivity, it passes on GM to the Vice GM or an active player if there isn't one (which is honestly a stupid mechanic and whoever on the dev team baked it up should be banned from making games). I do enjoy the quests when they release them and exploring the world is fun to me still, but it's become increasingly difficult to find active players that can run endgame content unless you're in a strict top tier guild and the game just feels a lot more empty all around than it was a few months ago.

I still recommend this game since it's free, there's a lot to do and experience, and at the end of the day it's fun, but a word of advice: treat it like a single-player RPG. This game IS NOT an MMORPG and shouldn't be treated like one. If you want an MMORPG, skip this one. Play ESO, BDO, Final Fantasy or something else. It's a single-player RPG with multiplayer characteristics and cosmetic gacha mechanics.

Absolute Cinema. Best boss fights I've encountered in a game before. There isn't extra clutter on the screen, you know exactly what is going on and which move the boss is doing if you pay attention to the boss. Combat is fluid and you aren't ever animation locked by your own moves, you can cancel them to dodge, parry, or use a different attack and aren't ever just stuck locked in place. Game went from a 8/10 to a 9.5/10 after fighting the final boss in the first act on legend. That boss had me stuck for a good 3 days until I got good and learned the combat system.

My only complaint is the "stamina" system. My favorite content is the multiplayer boss raids, but it takes 60 energy per chest and you only get 1 energy every 9 minutes, meaning I can only raid once every 9 hours. I get that there is a bunch of other stuff to do, but none of the other content is time-gated as hard as the raids, and raids/campaign challenge are the only way to grind gear at a decent amount. What I wish they'd do is make it so doing anything that currently requires energy lets you still get the normal rewards, but if you want to claim twice or three times, make that still consume energy. That way the players who only have time to hop on for a raid every so often can still triple claim and burn their energy to get a bunch of loot at once, and those who have more time and want to grind out a godrolled set of gear can raid repeatedly and earn the standard amount of loot. Timegating acquisition of loot that is rng based and that is required to make your build work is ass, especially if you get bad roles, and even moreso on legend where you want to squeeze every advantage you can out of your gear.

This is a boss battle game. 
The bosses have 2 health bars. 
The first health bar (the chi bar) can only be dropped by deflecting attacks. 
If a boss attacks and you dodge you wasted an opportunity to do damage increasing your chances of being hit by an attack. Boss attacks are almost a 1 hit kill each time.
The second health bar (actual health) basically cannot be touched unless you drop the first health bar (chi bar) by blocking attacks.

In order to do any kind of significant damage to the actual health bar, you have to drop the chi health bar completely.
Typically each boss requires you to block around 11 attacks. Once you blocked those 11 attacks you can do what is called an execution attack. Which drops a small portion of its actual health bar. 

So basically you have to block around 11 attacks to drop the chi bar so that you can damage the actual health bar 1 time. 
After you damage the actual health bar, the chi bar refills. lmao
So then you just keep doing that over and over again. Drop the chi bar so that you can damage the health bar, chi bar refills, drop the chi bar again, do some more damage to the health bar, over and over. 

Typically you have to drop the bosses chi bar around 9 or 10 times in order to fully drop the actual health bar.
So you will be blocking around 11, 1 hit kill attacks. You will block those 11, 1 hit kill attacks another 9-10 times in order to fully drop the actual health bar of the boss.

HOWEVER. you are not done. Because, every boss has multiple stages. Most have 2 stages some have 3 stages. What i mean is. You fully drop the health bar and think you killed the boss, but then it transforms into another stage. And you just do it all over again. Dropping the chi so you can damage the health, dropping the chi so you can damage the health. All while desperately trying to not get killed by the ridiculous nearly 1 hit kill attacks the bosses have.

And every time you die the gear that you have reduces durability making it even more difficult. 

SUMMARY
It takes around 11 blocks to drop the health 1 time. You have to drop the health 8-10 times. Then the boss transforms into its 2nd or 3rd stage. And you do it all over again while trying to not get hit by some cheesy 1 hit kill.
