I honestly can’t remember the last time I left a review, if I ever have, but this game really deserves one. Everyone should give it a try, both for themselves and to support the devs. The amount of content already available is impressive, and even more is on the way. The Chinese servers are much further ahead, with a lot of additional areas, bosses, and features that haven’t released globally yet.

My only real complaint is that the translation still needs some work, especially later in the story and in some side quests. The team is actively improving it though, with frequent small fixes, patches, and the occasional compensation mail that includes a bit of free currency when server issues happen. I personally haven’t had any noticeable connection problems, but I don’t use cross server matchmaking and I mostly play solo.

The world is gorgeous, exploration is very fun, and the combat feels great whether you prefer fast paced action or a slower, more deliberate style. The game doesn’t lock you into strict classes, since your class is basically defined by whatever weapons you choose. There are recommended weapon combinations, but you are completely free to mix and match whatever feels right to you.

Legendary mode has been a great addition for me. The early boss challenges were tough but very satisfying, and learning each fight as I improved at the game has been one of my favorite parts of playing. At the time of writing, I am sitting at 37 Legendary bosses defeated, with a current max of 40 until the new content arrives in a few days.

[h1][b] TLDR: A triple-A gaming experience for free without pay-to-win. Worth it alone for the excellent game world and superb graphics. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Graphics
➕Amazing exploration
➕Lots of minigames


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Bad UI can make it very difficult to locate specific menus
➖Combat is rather shallow
➖Translation issues

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [8/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world is set in a vast and beautiful Chinese land with a heavy Wuxia inspired setting. The world is a massive focus of the game itself, and exploration is king here, both in progressing your character and as a player interacting within the world. It seems like in every direction there is something for the player to engage in, whether it's combat, a minigame, or exploration/lore, there is SO MUCH to explore and find.
As a point of reference, Elden Ring comes to mind as having awesome exploration, and in my opinion, this is even better here. This might be the best exploration-focused game I have ever played. 

The game also advertises its narrative as a core element. Right from the start, there is a strong focus on the story. As I progressed, I felt the story get a bit weaker, but still above average, especially for an online “MMO”-esque game. I think it's a solid story, but the hardest part might be the Chinese influence - names can be very hard to follow. I should mention, In my 40+ hours, I did not finish the story fully, but I did catch up almost to the end of the gated content (the story is time-gated as they release new content frequently).

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay entirely revolves around exploration. Everything is connected to exploration. Exploring progresses your character, and gives you various currencies through things like chests, combat, gathering, and hunting. There are frequent minigames, puzzles, and collectables as you traverse the area. If you walk in a single direction, it wouldn’t take more than 30 seconds before you find something of interest. 

Let’s talk about the combat. I found it interesting, but a bit shallow. There are around ~10 different weapons, that act as classes. Most weapons are tagged as DPS, like swords and spears. There are a few that are classified as tank and healers, using large heavy weapons, or fans, respectively. 
At its core, the combat only consists of using 5 skills from weapons and 4(+4) skills that anyone can use. The 5 weapons I played around with, I found all fairly simple and consisted mostly of building up resources and then dumping them via a spender. 
To expand on the RPG aspects slightly, there are various systems that improve your stats as you level and builds you can create using passive abilities. 

The difficulty in this game can range from easy to very hard, and when you are doing solo content, like the story, you can set the difficulty level to what you are comfortable with. I found it to be close to something like Sekiro or Dark Souls on the higher difficulties, but lower was much easier. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [9/10] [/b] [/h1]
Amazing. This game looks obscenely good many times. By far one of the best looking games I’ve ever seen.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3616375757
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3619889886
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3619889804

There surprisingly isn’t a lot of graphical options, maybe ~15ish, but I was able to max it and get around ~100 FPS with occasional dips. Ironically, I experienced the worst performance with indoor dungeon-like environments, not the outdoor world with the draw distance. Seems backwards, I know. Still, it runs good on a technical side. 

I did run into a few bugs with getting stuck in walls, but was able to get out via teleporting. 
My biggest complaint graphically is the menu UI. Often times I’ll find a screen and then will never be able to find it again if I need to access it. Super frustrating, but the menu is just awful. There are waaaay too many menus. The gameplay HUD is fine, and the top-level menu is good, but its when you start digging you really notice the issues.

[h1] [b] Audio – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
Good audio, very reminiscent of the Wuxia era. All the music is from that period. 
There are instruments that players can play and even compose their own music (mostly using programs). 
There is voice acting, but in English, it's often not very good and doesn’t match the subtitles a good portion of the time. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
There is a LOT to do here and more content is releasing frequently. I haven’t gotten deep into the end game grind yet, so I can’t say if it is worth it dumping hundreds of hours into this, but I’ll say that with the content I’ve played, I haven’t gotten bored yet. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [8/10] [/b] [/h1]
Where Winds Meet (WWM) is a Chinese action RPG game with a heavily inspired Wuxia setting. This is a sort of “Lobby-based’ MMO-lite where you can play solo or online with others. This is not a true Massively Multiplayer Online game - you won’t see hundreds of people at once. Instead, you have the option to complete PVE content with players, like boss fights, or play solo player, where the majority of the game is focused on. 
Despite the single player focus, I really like how WWM incorporates online aspects into the game. Whether it's through world chat, Dark Souls-like sign posts, or joining groups for healing/cultivation, there’s enough of a community focus where I never really felt alone. 

WWM is built around exploration, which greatly appealed to me. I found myself taking much longer to get from point A to B due to being constantly distracted by the amazing world and exploration. There are frequent mini-games and rewards for exploring that not only give you currency, but also develop your character by providing stat bonuses and improvements. 

Overall, I do recommend WWM. Despite some translation issues, this is a bona fide AAA-game that is free, respects players time, and is not P2W. I can see some issues in getting past the Chinese culture, translations, and I do question the longevity of the end game, but this is an experience and world absolutely worth spending some (free!) time in.

Energy limits, coin caps, jade fish caps, gear drop limits… every core progression system is locked behind daily or weekly restrictions. Once you reach endgame. It completely kills the endgame natrual flow. Instead of letting you grind at your own pace, the game forces you to log in, do your little ration of progression, then get out. It turns a genuinely fun open-world experience into a “come back tomorrow” simulator. The foundation is amazing, but these time gated systems hold it back more than anything else. Yes. 7/10, needed more story on launch.

I would suggest playing this as a side game, but you can rush it like an MMO if you want. There's no real reason to hurry towards your end game gearset. The game is as difficult as you would like it to be with a nice assortment of options to lower or enhance it per your whims. 

This is the best performing game in a graphical fidelity to framerate ratio that I have seen released in a long time. At least a year, maybe more and it doesn't even have DLSS. To my knowledge it uses some basic FSR if you enable upscaling. I am running this at 1080p60fps on High settings with an i7-4790k and an RTX 2060. Small dips below 60 during heavily populated areas of Kaifeng, that's it. 

Story is excellent and certain parts of it made me genuinely emotional. However, the introductory act of the game is dreadful. It provides zero reason for you, the player, to care about a single thing going on or any character that you're introduced to. If you push through that however, the game rectifies this and it does so quickly. Excellent writing. The side content and exploration quests are equally engaging.

Graphics are beautiful, on par with Ghosts of Tsushima/Yotei. Not much else to say, it's simply stunning.

Combat is OK, depends on the weapon. The developers would benefit from making the weapons feel less clunky, the fans in particular. Using the well-tuned weapons, such as the sword, spear and dual blades however and you have yourself a top-tier experience comparable to that of genre-defining combat games like Sekiro. I, however, could not get past the clunk and elected to play the game on Story mode so I will end my review of the combat here.

This game is monetised through a gacha system for cosmetics. It does not impact your gameplay whatsoever. 

Sects are awesome but I do wish they impacted gameplay a little more than they do.

Cons you should know about:
- There is an energy/stamina system that restricts your content.
- You must do exploration, regardless of your desire, or you will be unable to equip gear. 
- The inner path is a false choice system, you will only equip your primary weapon, morale chant, which costs 5,000 freemium currency to unlock, and two other paths that benefit said primary weapon. There is zero build diversity here outside of the weapon pairing you choose to run.

Overall, great game.

Very fun game, But it has some fundamental things that are gonna make or break the game for you.


Here is a very short list of things i love and what ultimately ruins the game for me.

The Good :

Beautiful Open World with things to do all over the place, There are no empty places that are there just to increase the size and brag about how big the world is, There lots of secrets and hidden things and stuff to do that makes it worth exploring. 
I spent most of my time played getting distracted from the main quests to do a bunch of random **** i ran into whilst on the way to do the main quest. You will get completely lost in a good way :) 

The NPCs are also very interesting, there are lots of whacky characters you will run into and it really makes the world feel alive .

Fantastic Combat, this is my favorite part of the game, the combat, It feels amazing, looks amazing and has so much variety and all of them feel so good to play. They really nailed it here !

Bosses, There are so many bosses, Most of them are unique interesting and engaging, Some of them are just a dude and a chick with a sword but even those bosses have mechanics that make them stand out from others.

Music is also good, its not Path of Exile, Dark souls or BloodBorne levels of good but its enjoyable and fits the artstyle.

THE BAD

There is one thing that ruins the game for me, Some of you wont mind this but for me it makes me not want to play more even tho there is sooo much i enjoy about the game.
Enemies scaling, this ruins the game for me. 
Here is an example, So at the very very start of the game you will see a boss wandering a field, I think his name is the Puppeteer or something. This boss is very difficult if you actually try and fight him at the very start of the game so naturally after i got my *** beat a few times i decided to leave and come back later after i got more powerful.
So after around 6-7 hours i got some massive upgrades in gear and tons of levels and felt i now was strong enough to go back and fight this dude, I go back to the starting area leaking confidence from every hole in my body just to engage in a fight with this guy and get my **** kicked in. 
I was BARELY doing any more damage then what i did 6 hours earlier and was still taking a TON of damage .
This just ruined my excitement and enjoyment of the game and this is where is stopped playing to write this review.
What is the point in progressing, questing, leveling, getting new improved gear, new moves and upgrading everything  and when you go back to an area where you were struggling before just so you can continue to struggle and not feel any more powerful ? :/
It really feels like my character progression is irrelevant. 
I know that this does get a little bit better as you progress but from what i understand and what i have heard and read, the enemies will continue to scale up.
You may not mind this but for me this is where i stop playing the game, i dont wanna have to dump 30-40+ hours just to get to a point where my character feels more powerful. Its just not worth it to me but i do recommend everyone giving this a try. Its a very fun game and if i wasnt bothered by the enemies scaling then i could easily see myself putting hundreds or even thousands of hours into this game :)

[h2]A genuinely fun free-to-play experience in 2025 that, despite famously expensive boats being sold, is definitely going to make a lot of its revenue through harvesting its players biometric data.[/h2]

This is a good game. There's no easy way to describe it but maybe something like... Ancient Chinese MMO Easy-Mode Elden Ring gets close to it? It's that, plus all the regular free-to-play tropes you've come to know and love. There is a ton of content already but geographically as of right now as far as I can tell there's only Qinghe county in southern Hebei and the very northern bit of Henan that includes Kaifeng so hopefully we get a bit more of the lands south and east in the future. I'm sure more than a few players are anxious to visit a certain wetlands area in Shandong... It's also cool to me that a big step for players moving forward in the game is crossing the Yellow River and arriving in Kaifeng, like so many fictional heroes of old.

The fighting is pretty good. It's going for a very souls-like quality and I think it hits most of the important points of what makes those boss fights exciting for most players.

The co-op mode is also good and there's quite a bit to do together. I hope they keep adding content to it. 

So far it's following in Warframe's footsteps of generating revenue by creating fun content for a purposefully cultivated community of players who see the monetary transactions between themselves and the developers as voluntary, maybe even donative. That's probably the best case scenario for a free-to-play model, but Warframe is also a rare example. Right now, only cosmetics are locked behind a pay-wall but who knows what the future will bring?

If this game isn't popular enough over the coming months or year, it will likely go full pay-to-win like so many other free-to-play games. I expect I'll be playing this until that happens and I'll keep this review updated if anything changes. I don't know how many $40k boats they need to sell per year to keep this going, and who knows what the market for biometric data will be like in 2026 and beyond?

That brings up a very important point about this software: There is NO WAY this game is not harvesting your biometric data, especially from the voice chats and uploaded images. Just, be aware of that and if you care about that stuff just stay away. I mean, the data harvesting in this game is so ubiquitous that I'm sure they're selling statistics about you just from the fact you browsed it in the Steam store and didn't install it.

This game also has AI chat bots RP'ing as characters, and it's pretty fresh honestly. They don't try to pretend they're real players and it's kind of neat to RP being a haohan with a chat bot that's playing along since probably 70% of people playing don't care about or have any interest in the jianghu even though it's expressed so thoughtfully in this game's lore and setting.

See you in the jianghu!

The reviews for this game are booming and friends began to play it - so I did too! 
Unfortunately, despite all the praise I have seen it get, the game just did not do it for me. 
I really enjoy open world games and MMOs, and the setting intrigued me! I played with a few friends and one thing was clear from the start: this is NOT an MMO, no matter how many people and outlets keep labelling it as such. I don't know where that claim comes from, because you are limited to small parties with friends. You are also rather limited in what you can do when you play with friends, as you cannot do quests together or interact with many overworld things when you do so (probably because they are quest related)
The character creater is very flexible and in depth, which was honestly the main reason I decided to get it - I find making a character and seeing them go through things to be extremely satisfying. Sadly, this alone could not keep me. 
'Free to play' sounded to good to be true, and it felt like it, much like some eastern MMOs that came out with a big booming "free and flashy graphics!" only to turn out to be shallow and boring. This is the same thing, just that 'mmo' is misplaced here. Sure the graphics are.. nice if you don't look too hard. Sure the combat feels somewhat flashy at first. Sure it's free.. but what lies beyond that? Not much, not a single person I know has any idea of what the story is about, including myself. It's generic, bland and exposition heavy. Nothing new here. The combat feels okay to me, someone who doesn't really understand much about combat mechanics and stats as deeply as others do, I am just a 'casual combatant', but it feels not nearly fun enough to make me want to seek out battle and just go at it for entertainment. The loot is plentiful and worthless, showering you with a whole lot of nothing to get your dopamine receptors going. There are.. what.. 12 currencies? I can keep track of those about as much as I can keep track of the messy UI - hardly. 
As one might expect, this game is monetized through a premium shop, which notably does not include anything P2W, at least. However since the game relies HEAVILY on you enjoying your character and customizing them as a source of entertainment (as the gameplay is too bland) therein lies the crux of the issue.. 'fahsion is the true endgame' is often echoed here, and that rings very true, honestly I'd even argue it's not just the endgame. And if you want some nice glams, you'll need to either spend cash on outfits, or gacha for the real good ones. And we all know what happens when we go gambling...aw dangit.

Game quality overall is above average ( 6.5/10 ), but there is a lot of stinkers aka TIME GATES, battlepasses, super expensive skins/outfits, gambling.
Once you complete some exploration and story then you can basicly uninstall, because there will be barely anything to do there.

Where Winds Meet is one of the most refreshing open-world Wuxia RPG experiences I’ve played in recent years. It captures the feeling of ancient China beautifully, blending martial arts fantasy, deep storytelling, and sandbox freedom in a way that keeps the game interesting for hours.

What I love most is how the game never forces you into just one playstyle. You can progress through the main storyline, explore the world casually, or simply enjoy the countless side activities. The RPG levelling system feels rewarding, giving you access to new combat techniques and martial arts as you grow stronger. Whether you prefer fast DPS melee, long-range combat, or using internal energy abilities, every style feels unique and satisfying.

The world is filled with things to do — and not just fetch quests. You can play mini-games, take on detective-style missions, hunt animals, tame horses, solve riddles, duel other martial artists, and even meditate to gain skills. The amount of freedom is insane; sometimes I stop progressing the main quest and simply enjoy exploring villages, mountains, and forests.

The environment design is stunning. Every location shows a lot of love — from calm bamboo forests to bustling cities and peaceful temples. The music and atmosphere make the whole world feel alive.

Combat is one of the strongest points of the game. It’s fast, responsive, and cinematic, especially when chaining Wuxia moves, dodges, counters, and finishing attacks. Boss fights require timing and skill but are never unfair.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is an amazing game for people who love martial arts, open world exploration, and Chinese historical fantasy. It’s fun, creative, and full of content — the type of game that keeps surprising you the more you play.

Tried this game at launch and honestly, the amount of content blew me away, leisure stuff, story, boss fights, minigames, all of it. The map is massive. The boss fights and single-player PVE content are absolute fire. There's a ton to do here, though some of the minigames and matchmaking queues are ghost towns. And the fact and ITS NOT PAY TO WIN, EXCUSE ME?? like damn, but yea one thing is, its the time gating and energy system, i understand why they did that but its fine? not until competitive content 

Then I sank 1000+ hours in and touched the endgame content, which is PVP, and yes it was HORRIBLE AS ♥♥♥♥.

Doesn't matter if they slap in server selection or battle groups, the netcode is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to its core, because all the combat logic runs server-side ONLY!. I ranked Mythic every single season, but only by suffering through latency that never should've existed. Some instances and matches characters be blinking and bugging when executing a skill. And it's not just "the netcode is bad," it's that combos and dodges need 8-50 ping to even execute properly. Good luck landing a full true combo unless you're rocking wheelchair builds like umbrella weapons or whatever the current meta crutch is. 

And CLEARLY the devs have some bias and favoritism with these weapons like the Nameless and umbrella other wheelchair broken weapon builds. have 0 effort of balancing the combat system. but if they do it usually takes 3 or so months to do a minor change.

Also about that time gating and energy thing you can farm fast enough to be a the same stat level as some of the players who started the game early. don't even think of touching PVP. its nearly impossible to compete with players the same level as you are. NO MATTER how good you are at PVP, if your inner ways and gears are low, you'll get obliterated.

The only PVP content that you can actually actually play is that Naraka style battle royal gameplay they have. which honestly is fun and other balanced PVP game modes like 5v5 which takes longer to queue.

Region locked? Yes and no, and somehow both answers are infuriating. Single-player mode will auto-route you to your nearest region after a few days if you travel, fine, whatever. But the bounty hunting system's routing is an actual dumpster fire: your bounty list is permanently chained to whatever region you FIRST created your account in, forever, no matter where you actually are now. I don't know if the devs have even looked at this, but it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ server handling. Naraka, a game running the same server-side model, still manages to feel better because at least their inputs execute client-side.

Multiplayer PVE? its a "Meh". No traditional dungeon system like literally every other game in the genre, instead you get "outposts," which is a fancy word for less content wearing a trench coat.

And don't even get me started on the UI. Some menus are buried so deep you need to tunnel through three other unrelated menus just to find them. Black Desert has bad UI too, sure, but at least BDO lets you customize it and has one all-in-one menu where everything actually lives. This game just makes you suffer.

Bottom line: this was built as a single-player game wearing a multiplayer costume, and it shows the second you touch anything competitive.

[h1] An unexpected but good surprise. [/h1]
I enjoyed the game quite a bit so far and recently, not many games can give me the excitement to play and immerse myself in its world. 

[b] TLDR [/b] Personal take so far : 9/10

[h3] Pros [/h3]
+ Graphic (very beautiful Wuxia world and graphic design, i was truly immersed in the world)
+ Combat (in most cases, it is pretty fluid. Variety of difficulty for all skill levels)
+ Combat style/class (not a class per say aside the Tank-Dps-Heal trinity, but there are various martial art style for each weapon, and many martial art techniques to complement your playstyle such as the oh so famous Buddha Palm)
+ Exploration (Although so far only two Main areas to explore, Qing He and Kaifeng, it felt truly big with each sub areas and the nice immersive world while we explore.)
+ Co-op/Online mode (can be enjoyed with friends, guildies or even strangers)
+ Mini games (lots of different mini games if you are into that)
+ Dress your waifus (You can dress up your Main Character in many different ways although there is a big caveat which will be in the Cons section)

[h3] Cons [/h3]
- Performance (i have quite an okay setup but i still suffer some frame rate drops and performance issues here and there, especially in Kaifeng. Hope they will do something to alleviate this. -Ryzen 5 3600x + 32GB Ram + RTX2080 - sure an older gen but still, shouldn't be too big of an issue supposedly on paper)
- Costume (Big red flag here especially with the recent pricing debacle VS CN servers. It is not necessarily cheap. They also have gacha ones so it might deter some players understandably)
- Menus (way too many menus to find something. Bad for OCD people who needs the red dot to go away.)
- Combat (while generally fun, some parts can get clunky and should be improved as time goes by)
-  Co-op/online (if you are expecting a free Dark Souls, this may not be 100% it. It has optional co-op stuff but if you want to face some of the toughest boss, the raids and trials are in co-op, there is a smart Ai mode but i am not sure if its everyone's cup of tea)
- Too early to tell (in general, game is very new and take every praise and insult with a grain of salt. it could still go either way so play and enjoy while you can. I certainly am doing so, so far)

All in all, i definitely recommend it to everyone as it wasn't even in my radar prior to this. I was actually pulled into trying Sword of Justice first before this game but that one is too mobile-ish for me, but who knows maybe they will improve later. Where Winds Meet definitely came out of nowhere for me and is currently my most played game in the past two weeks.

The single player mode, world exploration and character build are my favorite aspects of the game. You have to be strategic with the gameplay.

The mechanics and Ui would take time to get used to. It gets confusing at times though.

For a free-to-play game, this so much worth playing. The game is rich in lore, theme and immersive gameplay. The graphics, too, is amazing although it is a little heavy on PC specs.

It's not my cup of tea, but I'll give it credit where credit is due-- WWM is a beautiful and surprisingly well polished title. The world is amazingly detailed in a way i haven't seen since Blade and Soul with content spinkled everywhere. NPCs voiceovers are competent and the game has no problem giving you action from the outset. No 20 level tutorials here. You get the cutscene, a boss to introduce you to some basics and bam, you're on your way.

What kills it for me is the combat system. For a game that leans so heavily into the action, movement feels incredibly clunky. Even TERA did a better job at the action style fighting system, let alone Blade and Soul, Dynasty Warriors, Soul Edge and others. Getting in and out of attack radius' is a tedious chore and you take hits for no good reason other than the sluggish controls. There's a block and parry system, but anything above a foot soldier has at least some form of unblockable attack that, when combined with the half-assed controls, feels more like punishment than fair play. Obviously there's a lot of people here that can slog through that and you might be one of them. If you can, there's a lot to be had outside of combat. I simply *hate* the combat. In fact, the first introduction boss embodies everything I hate about it.


Like most F2P, Pay-to-Win, or convenience-to-win, WWM is layered and caked with an obnoxious number of menus that ensure you never have things quite at your fingertips and getting basic information is much harder than it needs to be. Supposedly the gatcha is only for appearance and I can almost live with that as a business practice... Except that it usually handicaps your visual progression, and WWM is no different. Expect your char to look the same for a long, long time. I live for my game carrot-on-a-stick dopamine hits. I love gearing characters and watching them advance. Winds makes that common F2P mistake of sacrificing that concept to the cash shop.  You can do both, devs-- Give me incremental appearance upgrades based on gear and have the real flashy stuff at the shop. Not that you really ever look horrible, to be fair.

Character customization is mainly limited to the face and hair. While it does a competent job within that realm, dont expect any sort of body adjustment and do you like black hair? Everybody gets black hair. You can't change your hair color in the char generation setup. You can dye it later, but I'm told it will cost you A LOT of cash shop moneys... TO DYE YOUR HAIR. I mean, come on.

Another constant splinter is the community markers littered all over the landscape. They're meant to have some superficial attempt at community like a real world, if not real-time chat to convey information and hints in that specific area. Sometimes it's actually helpful. Often its just other players spamming deez nuts posts. Worse, it breaks emersion to see these waypoints littered all over what is an otherwise beautiful landscape while simutaneously competing for quest markers and other actually relevant information. I'm sure there's a way to turn them off, but did I mention the menu system?

Naw bro. I just can't. There's a lot of value in this game which is why I can't just slam it with a negative.  It comes close but doesn't quite scratch that wuhan itch for me.

"Where Winds Meet" is an absolute gem of a game that checks all the boxes for what I look for in a modern open-world RPG. From the moment you step into the world, it's clear this is a visual masterpiece. The landscapes are absolutely stunning, with breathtaking vistas that make you want to just stop and take in the scenery.

The combat is fluid and satisfying, offering a great mix of strategy and action. Whether you're slicing through enemies in epic sword fights or using magical abilities, every encounter feels impactful. The skill progression and customization are deep enough to keep you engaged as you build your character in different ways.

The main story quests are some of the best I've experienced in recent memory—full of twists, memorable characters, and emotional depth. But what really sets "Where Winds Meet" apart is the quality of its side quests. These aren't throwaway tasks like in some other games. Each side quest feels like its own little adventure, with compelling narratives and rewarding outcomes that actually make the world feel alive.

There’s no shortage of things to do in this game. Whether it’s exploring the open world, engaging in PvP duels, or teaming up with friends in coop mode, you’ll always find something to keep you busy. The variety of activities is impressive and adds so much replayability to the game.

If you’re a fan of immersive worlds, solid combat, and tons of content, “Where Winds Meet” should absolutely be on your radar. The level of polish and attention to detail is exceptional, and it’s clear the developers put a lot of love into creating this experience. Highly recommend!

On the one hand, it's a beautiful game with loads to do. On the other hand, the core gameplay itself is, in my opinion, bad. Why? Fundamentally because I disagree with the the games design choice of having the world level with the player. Especially in the context of a wuxia game. It's also an odd idea for an MMO if I'm being honest.

Because  the enemies level and scale with the player, despite there being new skills/etc unlocked as the player progresses, the game always feels the same. Skill aside, and this is a heavily skill based game, apparently even on "story" mode, I've put 160 hours into the game and it's all felt the same. You can change your playstyle in terms of the weapons you choose, but the enemies are always the same no matter where you go or what level you are. 

Don't get me wrong, different areas have different enemies, but the experience is the same for the player pretty much at all times. Basic enemies are always the same difficulty with a few elite mobs here and there. On legendary, the elite mobs scaling is insane though. You go from having your generic mobs to, is this a random no named boss? But outside of that, enemies are basically the same everywhere. So once you know what you're doing, get a good set of gear and keep it "enhanced" as you level, you can basically roll all the random enemies but have to watch out for that 1 that's basically a mini boss. 

I do like the boss fights though. Some more so than others, but in general I found all the bosses I encountered to be fun. But the fact that random elite mobs are basically bosses on legendary, coupled with the fact that I as the player can never get OP, kills the game for me. I don't like games where I can't progressively get more powerful than the world/enemies. That's just my personal preference though.

Also, the gacha is seriously frustrating. I get it with cosmetics but when it comes to gear enhancing, tuning needs to be reworked. The devs seem to think that people are going to be ok with farming gear, especially end game gear but even early set gear, tuning it and then being ok with getting terrible stats just to have to farm the gear all over again in hopes that tunning it the next time will give better stats. That is not cool. A core feature for enhancing gear should not be left to irreversible chance. Absurd.

But the game IS free, so... While I wouldn't buy the game, it's free so try it and see for yourself if you like it.

⭐ Professional Game Review — 7/10

After investing more than 47 hours into the game, it is clear that the title offers an impressive level of depth, worldbuilding, and visual quality. However, several structural and monetization issues prevent it from reaching its full potential. Overall, the game earns a 7/10.

🌄 Visual Presentation & Worldbuilding

The game’s visual fidelity is undeniably one of its strongest attributes. The environments are highly detailed, immersive, and consistently spectacular, creating a world that feels both authentic and atmospheric. The setting appears to draw inspiration from the historical period prior to the formation of the Song Dynasty, adding a distinctive cultural backdrop.

The world itself is expansive, featuring two large regions filled with towns, villages, caves, dungeons, and numerous points of interest. A standout feature is the sheer number of interior spaces that players can freely enter, contributing to a sense of realism rarely seen at this scale.

⚔️ Gameplay Experience, Combat, and Exploration

Functioning as both an MMO and a single-player experience, the game offers robust PvE and PvP options. Interactivity is notably high, with most NPCs offering meaningful dialogue or engagement.

The combat system is exceptionally well designed. Boss encounters—whether part of dungeons or open-world events—are engaging, mechanically demanding, and rewarding. Success relies on strong familiarity with parrying, blocking, boss patterns, and proper utilization of Mystic Skills and Inner Ways, ensuring that encounters feel skill-based rather than trivial.

Exploration remains dynamic thanks to random encounters, side quests, oddities, chests, and resource nodes, creating a world that feels reactive and alive.

📚 Complexity & User Experience

One of the notable drawbacks is the game’s overwhelming amount of systems and menus. New players may find the onboarding process difficult due to the sheer density of mechanics introduced early on. Although this becomes manageable over time, the initial learning curve is unnecessarily steep and could benefit from clearer guidance or gradual progression.

👚 Cosmetics & Monetization Concerns

The game’s monetization model is where its issues become most apparent.

Free cosmetic options are limited, especially in solo mode.

Many desirable outfits cost $40–$60, a price point that feels excessive for cosmetic items.

High-end cosmetics are locked behind gacha systems with extremely low acquisition rates, with some rumored to cost up to $600 to obtain depending on luck.

After more than 100 attempts at defeating the dungeon boss HeartSeeker—including the use of draw x3, 60 energy per attempt, and all season pass energy orbs—no outfit or hair cosmetic dropped. This highlights a significant problem in drop rate balance and reward fairness.

The monetization approach appears aggressive and risks undermining long-term player satisfaction.

🔋 Resource Economy & Energy System

The game’s resource economy becomes increasingly restrictive at higher levels. Several concerns stand out:

Commerce Coins are difficult to obtain in meaningful quantities.

Dungeon access is tied to energy points, which regenerate over time, forcing players to wait before continuing PvE progression.

Material gathering becomes tedious once available chests and world resources are depleted.

This system disrupts gameplay flow and contradicts the intent of offering a free-form PvE environment.

🎯 Final Verdict — 7/10

The game delivers an engaging and visually impressive experience with strong combat design, rich worldbuilding, and a substantial amount of content. However, issues with onboarding complexity, resource scarcity, restrictive energy mechanics, and a highly monetized cosmetic system significantly detract from the overall experience.

With improvements to character progression, resource management, and dungeon accessibility, the game has the potential to become a standout title in its genre. As it stands, it remains a compelling yet flawed experience, earning a solid 7/10.

I’ve downvoted this game mainly because, coming from the OCE (NZ) region, online play is practically unplayable. The latency is so high that any form of online interaction becomes frustrating.

The amount of gacha and monetisation is honestly extreme. The outfit draw system starting at 60 pearls and then tripling each time—with only a 1.5% chance of getting the rare—is borderline predatory. It doesn’t feel good, and it doesn’t feel fair. The menus are overly complicated, cluttered with unnecessary systems, and overall make the game feel bloated and unpolished. Some voice lines are even missing, which just reinforces that lack of polish.

But credit where it’s due: Where Winds Meet shines when you’re actually out in the world. The puzzles, dungeon-style encounters for skills, healing NPCs, chatting with AI characters, and general exploration are all genuinely fun. The world is beautiful, and once I turned off most of the UI pop-ups, the game actually began to feel like a true AAA experience. With some care and refinement, this game could be an incredible way to showcase Chinese lore and storytelling. Unfortunately, the aggressive monetisation overshadows that potential and creates a constant sense of FOMO.

I really hope the developers tone down the gacha prices and introduce more affordable cosmetics. I would love to support the game, but I just can’t justify paying $500+ for a single skin—it makes no rational sense.

I’m giving the game a 5/10. The world design and creativity deserve praise, and the foundation is strong. With cleaner menus, fewer bugs, and a more reasonable monetisation system, this could easily be an 8–10/10 experience. The potential is absolutely there—it just needs fixing.

Where winds meet is a very well made game that I have really learned to enjoy with massive potential to it. The game is really well done but does have quite a few downsides. 

The menu can be very convoluted at first, the Energy limitation mechanic can be annoying but it's not a huge deal as they've started to ease up on it. The delayed level cap that happens was one of the reasons a coupole of my friendsd stopped play but it did let me enjoy the story and actually get every tier upgraded properly so that's more a matter of personal preference. 

The content is being timegated pretty poorly but there is pletty of story and exploration to do in the meantime. I've seen people rush the story to get to max level and skip the side quests but part of the enjoyment I get from this game comes from the story and how rich the world building (and the world in general) is. If you’re the type of player who doesn’t care about exploration and always wants to be fighting or doing something then yes it is going to feel like a lot of point A to point B because you’re not stopping for exploration in between those things. 

The story seems the be the main thing they are going for a long side the combat.

There is coop but all the main quests are SOLO only which kinda killed it at first for me as the main reason I got the game was to play with my friends but the game can sstill hold you in if you enjoy single player story games. The pricing for outfits can be pretty bad amd the Gatcha for some outfits is terrible, however with the entire game being free aside from the cosmetics and a few outfits that look preety good for a low price, I'd say it's an alright trade off. 

The combat is a huge plus for me as it's souls-like without the bosses bending you over (Though you can have that if you REALLY want it). 

The world is beautiful and if you stop and really care about the exploration you will find yourself in locations that you really have no business being in other than trying to increase your exploration.

What REALLY shines in this game is the Social aspect of the game. As much as I enjoy the story and the combat, it's just nice building a guild compound and just meeting new people and relaxing with your friends. I think that's what's really going to keep me in this for a long while. Logging on and talking to my friends.

I'd highly recommend this game if you like games like the Witcher 3 or cyberpunk but also want a social side to the game that you can take your time with. The game is had for me to recommend to those who like playing the story with their friends as they have not mentioned plans to add coop to the story at the time of this review. Until then, I can only mention co-op as a very small part of the game and a disappointing one at that. It mighty take a good week or more to learn the menus put once you do it’s not bad at all.

After spending over a hundred hours in Where Winds Meet, I can honestly say this game completely surprised me in the best way. I went in curious, and ended up absolutely hooked.

The first thing that grabbed me was the combat. It’s fast, stylish, and feels genuinely skill-based. Every duel has weight. You can parry, dodge, counter, switch styles… it just feels good. The animations are smooth and the game rewards timing instead of button-mashing, which kept me on my toes the entire time.

The world is the real star here. It’s huge, alive, and filled with NPCs going about their lives. I constantly found myself just stopping to watch the scenery or listening to random conversations. There’s a sense of life in the world that most open-world games completely miss. The devs clearly spent an insane amount of time crafting villages, cities, markets, forests, temples — everything feels handcrafted instead of copy-pasted.

Add to that the graphics and scenery, and wow… some moments honestly look like concept art. Sunsets, foggy mountains, bamboo forests, rivers — it’s the perfect mix of wuxia beauty and atmospheric detail.

And I have to mention the outfits. They absolutely nailed the style. Elegant, stylish, dramatic — perfect for a wuxia setting. Half my time was spent taking screenshots or swapping outfits just because everything looks so good.

What really impressed me though is the interaction and the way the world reacts. You’re never just a ghost moving through empty space. There’s always something happening — street performances, fights, travelers, merchants, monks, thieves, random events… the amount of work behind all this must have been crazy. Huge respect to the team for building a world that feels genuinely alive instead of static.

In short:
✔ Amazing combat
✔ Beautiful graphics & atmosphere
✔ Tons of outfits and customization
✔ A world full of life and memorable NPCs
✔ Strong sense of Chinese culture, wuxia and jianghu vibes
✔ Gives that “one more hour” feeling again and again

If you like wuxia, open-world RPGs, or just want to lose yourself in a living world, this game delivers.
107 hours in, and I still want more.

I've loved my time in this game. Really awesome Sekiro style combat, absolutely beautiful locales with stunning graphics, a fantastic story that's gut-wrenching, dramatic, and humorous. The art design is fantastic, starting in sweeping bamboo forests and taking you through all kinds of beautiful blossom-filled villages and interesting locales such as the sprawling city of Kaifeng. You can play in either Solo or MMO mode, with the MMO side featuring lots of community building events and spots for chatting with other players. Even though you don't have to interact with the community, WWM has a lot of fun people always dropping hilarious Signposts with advice to every puzzle and funny jokes to lighten up the experience.

There are some scenes with mismatched subtitles and a bit of the newest content isn't voiced yet, but overall the game has a ton of polish. It runs extremely well for an MMO with over 9 million players and I've only experienced a couple of crashes in my 50 hours of gameplay. My experience with the community has been nice and I haven't encountered any toxicity or problems with other players. If you enjoy Souls combat and open world exploration then this game is a no brainer, give it a try!

Where Winds Meet is a beautiful game with an interesting and involved combat system. Unfortunately, as an RPG, it is dead on arrival. Even though you do not see other players running around, it feels more like an MMO game with the sheer amount of clutter that immediately gets dumped on the player. There are dozens of menus, skills, quests, inventories, and events that constantly vie for the player's attention with a non-stop barrage of popups and notifications while the skill tree is more or less just a linear string of minor damage boosts.

As in any RPG, all I really wanted to do was to get on the road and begin my quest, but even though the game begins with a weird boss fight before you even get to the main menu, it then jumps forward in time and dumps you in a remote hut with the main story objective of getting back home to your aunt who lives on the other end of China. Two hours in I was still listening to boring, poorly translated yapping of every NPC I met along the way and serving tea to customers in my aunt's inn. And this so called aunt looked more like a sister to my teenage-girl-looking excuse of a male character.

While I did manage to find some bandits to fight on the road and in a hidden side quest dungeon in the first village, they were mostly just complete pushovers who posed no real threat. Meanwhile, every villager, merchant, fisherman, cat and dog along the way jumps up and down trying to get your attention just to have a chat, teach you kung fu, or give you quests and even free gifts. And that's in addition to all the flowers, minerals, and treasure chests littering the ground everywhere you look. Before I knew it, I somehow accumulated 80k in coins and was able to max out all my weapons.

If you are an MMO-enjoyer, streamer, or just have nothing to do all day, then you may enjoy this game. There are countless meaningless conversations, side quests, and other distractions to keep you occupied indefinitely. But if you are looking for a story-rich RPG, Where Winds Meet is not it.

How this game is free, I will never know. The sheer amount of quality content on offer is staggering. I am 18 hours in and I have not played any other game as soon as I started playing this. It got me hooked straight away.

To manage your expectations, I would state the following as a heads up and just look past them and you have a quality game underneath.

1. Localisation - in voice and text - mis-translations most likely due to direct translation from mandarin - you can easily overlook this.
2. In your face pop-ups typical of a F2P game - also can be ignored.
3. UI takes a while to get used to - too much is on screen at one time and it can be overwhelming - I would say give it time and learn what you need to know and the rest becomes just background noise.
4. The appearance/customisation things to buy from are there but can be ignored. So can the battlepass.

Now, those caveats out of the way. Lets talk about the game. The graphics are very good given the amount of free roam you have access to. I would say this is easily Ghost of Tsuhima level and better in some cases when it came on the PS4. The vistas, the sunsets, the rain - they all look incredible and play into the aesthetics of the game.

The solo mode of the game is where I find my self completely absorbed in. I think I got into multiplayer mode once to get healing and then popped out again. The main story is slow to start but the fact the side-quests are so well done and are almost equivalent of a main storyline themselves, i have yet to advance the main story on the first island.

The combat is excellent with simple to learn but difficult to master, with lots of different playstyles and builds. The mocap and movement feels so natural and being able to pull off some difficult combos is a sight to behold.

One unique feature - which I think will quickly catch on in other games - is the use of AI chat with NPCs - i think this is really good. Although restrictive for obvious reasons, all NPCs feel unique to chat to and considering that you can pretty much chat to most NPCs in the game, having AI do the lifting in chat does add to the immersion.

All in all, this game rivals, if not betters, most AAA studio RPG games out there. The production values are incredible and I just can't wrap my head around the fact that this is a free game. I would happily fork out a premium price for a game like this.

Those new to Wuxia genre - it may not be for everyone but if you like RPGs then this is a solid option.

From some of the negative reviews I have read, I am not sure where all are coming from. Its not perfect, I get it but its a breath of fresh air that a studio has put in so much effort into a game and then made it free for all to get into. I am just baffled that searching every nook and cranny on the map has something at the end of it. You are constantly rewarded for going down the beaten path. 

Highly recommended!

You always encounter the typical honorific leftovers in the text, like "aunt, uncle, older sister", so unless you are familiar with manhwa, donghua, anime, or manga, you might be left wondering how large a family MC has. It's possible to localise it properly, but it takes time and effort, which is missing here.

Some spoken dialogues differ from the subtitles, which again shows that someone hasn't done their work correctly. On top of that, you sometimes can hear the Chinese lines between the English ones for some reason.

Dialogues progress too fast, as they are linked to the Chinese language pacing; you often hear lines cut in the middle because they were too long. 

The next thing is that some items, abilities, and even NPCs get different names depending on the place or UI window. The easiest example would be the "Wine-scented Jade" that magically turns into "Fragrant Jade" in your inventory.

And while we are at the UI, this atrocious mobile-like UI makes everything overly complicated. Making you wonder where some of the menus that tutorial opened for you are hidden. 

The "AI-chats" with the NPCs work depending on how lucky you are; some are just bugged to the point where people are leaving signs that tell you to change the language of the game to Chinese and then use Google Translate to progress it.

[h1] "Where Winds Meet is an ambitious exercise in maximalism" - IGN. [/h1]

That opening line from the now infamous IGN review for this game is actually something I agree with; This game has everything, and I mean that.
It has an actual campaign with a pretty damn good story and enough gameplay variety that you WILL find something you like, you have chess, card games, drinking games (not actual drinking, of course), word guessing games, jumping puzzles, AI NPCs, a fully kitted screenshot suite (I'd like to see a few more features here like lens distortions), competently designed boss fights, ubisoft-style collectables, fishing, building, horse taming, trading or you can sit down for a spell and watch a shadow puppet exhibition, enjoy some fireworks or go to a bath house and get a full course service? Sure why not, and that's if you only play solo, if you go online or co-op it turns into a fully functional multiplayer game with even more to do and that's only if you wish to, you can play this game like a singleplayer title and NEVER engage with it's online elements, and it all takes place in the vibrant world of Wuxia fantasy.

It all sounds like it's barely holding itself together but it all works, at no point does the sheer amount of stuff you can do feel like it's out of place, minus of course, the dissonance that takes place because of player agency taking priority.

[h2] So is it perfect? [/h2]
No, it has some performance issues, framerates take a dip especially in towns when looking from certain angles, sometimes your character's channeling skills get interrupted for seemingly no reason, sometimes items straight up don't work, sometimes they do work but they are delayed, the UI can be a bit of a labyrinth at first, which is inevitable considering the amount of features and stats you can keep track of but it is a flaw nonetheless. There are improvements that can be made, of course, but the cohesiveness of the whole is impressive as is from the get go and it's to be commended.

[h2]It's free so how does it make it's money? [/h2]
There are enough posts that explain how they make the big bucks but, on the bright side, they don't seem to be selling power (for now) and there is also a standard cash shop where you can buy what you want, also the "standard" outfits are more believable while the gacha items often times make your character look more like a god with VFX and ornaments everywhere which hey, if that's your cup of tea, I'm not judging (I am though).

P.S. If you're one of those millenials that played Chinese F2P mmos in 2005-2015 when they were getting pumped out seemingly every 2-3 months, especially people who played PWE games or Age of Wushu, if you were looking for a "new" AoW in particular, this is pretty much the closest it's gonna get to a modern itteration of those, and it is fantastic.

Where Winds Meet is a game heavily inspired by Ghost of Tsushima, but with a wuxia setting in China. Combat is swapped to a more soulslike system, which I dislike, but even those who dislike soulslike shouldn't have an issue with the game, as there is a story difficulty mode and parry assists built into the game. But if you do like soulslike combat, I find that the combo systems, buff and debuff application, and camera work, all seem a little clunky and hard to work with. Not the most satisfying, I would say. 

Open world exploration is pretty fulfilling, as there are a lot of collectibles to obtain. Movement offers a lot of freedom with triple jumps, wall running, and air dashing. 

There is a lot to do in the game. Find chests, play chess, gamble, do puzzles, write news articles, wrestle, debate, heal others as a doctor, the list goes on. However note that these are all optional mini-games and can be compared to toppings on top of an ice cream.

The game has a very rough start. It's overwhelming with poor tutorials, and the instructions are really bad and lacking for most things. Menus galore. If you've played any chinese MMOs before, then you'll know what kind of menus to expect. Fortunately, as with these things, it gets better the more you play it, by virtue of just learning and getting used to it.

Graphics are a treat, and you'll see how they tried to emulate the feel of Ghost of Tsushima here. Landscapes are vast, with large flower or grass fields, and brightly coloured trees can be seen from a distance. Cutscenes are also pretty cinematic, but there's a lack of sync between the lips and speech on the english dub. Sometimes, the cutscenes also bug out with repeated dialogue, or a mismatch between the subtitles and speech. Ever since the 1.2 patch, graphics quality and texture pop-in has become a big problem.

There is also quite a bit of jank in this game. Expect bugs and strange issues here and there. It gets worse when playing in multiplayer. The best experience that I recommend for this game is the single player main quest and side quests. All of the main quests and "lost chapters" (smaller side stories) are pretty well done. They're not generic quests with a story just for the sake of it. The quality of the writing is impressive.

The battle against the first major boss in the starting area was a memorable experience. I was at level 5 and he was at level 30. So you know how it turned out. I have no problem with bosses being overpowered or appearing somewhere in the world that you discover through exploration. It's just that the rest of the game has seemed rather mediocre so far. I tried the boss several times at level 5 and level 15. It was fun, but still futile. 

If I were to focus solely on combat progression, [b]the game seems so unfocused[/b] that I would have to take a few, if not many, detours (without fighting) to reach the level required to fight the boss on equal terms. Yes, there are bases that you can locate on the map and simply fight to level up through combat. I have to disagree with that, as it would lead to an Ubi-style game, which is often criticized for that very reason. Fighting the bases is mediocre and, when repeated countless times, becomes less and less fun. 

Fortunately, there is Wand (wemod), which has a map that allows you to filter out the bosses. The standard map in the game does not (if I'm not mistaken) have the function of marking on the map where bosses were found and at what level. Wand's map can do both. So you can play the game and wait for your character to reach the appropriate level, if you wanted to. 

At that point I would like to mention that [b]the game is a time sink[/b]. It's pretty and it's filled to the brim with whatever, but time*value ratio seems off to me. You spend a lot of time doing something and the game would make you believe you are gaining constantly in loot and in progression, but after two session a 5 hours the only purposeful and focused experience was fighting that first boss over and over. 

And if you were to make it all just about the fighting and forget the rest, I already know a game that does mostly that but somewhat better. Wayfinder. Not the combat RPG, mind you, or the fighting animations and style. Both games do excel in that. No. What you do in Wayfinder is combat focused experience. No distractions. 

PS: The UI is getting used to as convoluted as it is, it does serve a purpose, just not as in a user friendly manner as Western games seem to be able to.

I downloaded this game just to prove it was bad. I failed.

I went in thinking, "Okay, it's free. I'll play for 20 minutes, get mad at the Pay-to-Win mechanics and realize it's just another cash-grab mobile port, and then write a scathing review about how these devs only care about money."

I was half-wrong. (They do care about money, but hang on).

Here is my actual timeline:
1. Created a character significantly hotter than I will ever be.
2. Stared at a sunset so nice my jaw actually dropped.
3. Saw a bear trying to get honey.
4. Learned Tai Chi from the bear.
5. Immediately got stung by bees.
6. Ran up a wall, stole a horse, fell into a hole in the ground, and accidentally explored an entire dungeon.
7. Realized I had completely forgotten the main story.
8. Looked at the clock: 4 hours had passed.

This happens every single time I log in. It’s basically GTA meets Dark Souls, which sounds like a fever dream, but it works.

The Money Stuff: Are the cosmetics in the store expensive? Yes. Is it Pay-to-Win? No. Not even a little bit. It proves you can have microtransactions without ruining the game.

Major Con: The menus and UI. Please for the love of all that is holy in this world and the next! Fix the Menu and UI! I want to play the game not play chase the red diamond through 12 Menu's! Streamline this!

The Verdict: Ironically, I'm actually grateful for the time-gating mechanics. If they didn't stop me from playing, I would probably starve to death.

The most fun I had was playing with friends, collecting and exploring zones to reach 100% completion together. The only flaw is that some things aren’t compatible with co-op, which makes it tedious to separate and then rejoin your friends again.
Player invasions aren’t very polished, but I still had a lot of fun defending my friends when we were suddenly attacked by bounty hunters while exploring together. (some players can find it annoying because you cant leave your character afk and safe even in single player world)
Bosses are nice, and mastering them feels rewarding, even though at first parrying everything is hard because some attack animations aren’t predictable (maybe that’s intentional), and parry is on a different button than block. (I wish parrying worked more like in Sekiro)
Some social activities like pardon parade will probably give you a good laugh
Often in the game you'll find yourself admiring the atmosphere because of how beautiful it is (I did, even though I'm not particularly a fan of Asian-themed settings)
Menù UI  and Controls  are bad and some cannot be changed (many skill moves  and less buttons is better than many different keys to do the same thing)
Playing more and grinding feels unrewarding once you finish the one-time activities of your single payer world because rewards get outscaled completely by Time-Gated  weekly 10 min activities rewards

Personally i was enjoying the game and was about to buy the pass, but then I discovered that to progress my character’s skill levels I have to gather a lot of time-gated resources (flowers). I found out that all the gathering spots are camped by AFK players with  p2w mount with an instant wide radius auto-loot function. There are also energy pills in the paid battlepasses that can be saved for later and give you an advantage in end game gearing, and a bounty system where you can just pay to get the hardest archivements/challenges making them feel meaningless... I'm surprised i heard people say  it's not pay to win when something like that exists in the game. Its also used with macro and bots to farm materials like minerals to craft items to keep rolling bonus stats on gear.

In conclusion, if you are looking for a single player co-op casual adventure quality-price of this game is hard to beat, if you are looking for a more long term rewarding gameplay loop better looking elsewhere for now.

This is a super ambitious roleplaying game set within the world of Chinese martial arts fiction (Wuxia/武侠). On top of your usual combat mechanics, skill trees and character levels, there are the all the wuxia elements such as martial arts (武学), inner skills (心法), acupoint technique (点穴), lightness skill (轻功) et cetera. There are also tons of things to do like chess, mahjong and music. You can even rent or construct dwellings and decorate it to your heart’s desire. For those into MMO, the game also have social/multiplayer elements for PvP and co-op play. But far more impressive than the remarkable scope of the game is the fact that it draws heavily on the rich treasure trove of Chinese history and culture to create an engaging and immersive world for players.

[h1]I rate this game a solid [b]7.5/10[/b][/h1]
I’m currently 108 hours in, level 60 and experienced pretty much everything the game has to offer at this stage. Instead of repeating what everyone already knows about its pros, I want to highlight the reasons why it does not deserve a 10/10 from me.

[h3]Multiplayer Server Issues (MMO, 1v1, Co-op)[/h3]
The game offers a wide range of multiplayer modes like combat, exploration, survival, you name it. However, the server distribution (especially in SEA) is simply not enough to ensure smooth play. Ping is consistently 200+, making fast-paced combat frustrating. Basic attacks don’t register in quick succession the way they do in solo mode. 1v1 duels and bounty hunts often feel one-sided due to latency issues. For a game this fast-paced, reliable servers are a must, and right now they’re not delivering.

[h3]Visual Problems[/h3]
The world is undeniably beautiful. Their attention to detail and artistry deserve praise. But the lighting balance needs serious work. Dark areas are too dark and increasing brightness ruins the visual fidelity. Meanwhile, daytime lighting especially around the sun is blinding. Looking near the sun feels like getting hit with a flashbang. If you lower the brightness to fix this, the dark areas become pitch black. A proper rebalance between dark/bright zones and sky lighting is needed.

[h3]Audio Bugs in Quests and Boss Cutscenes[/h3]
Missing audio has been a known issue and although patches have improved things, the problem isn’t fully resolved. Many quests still lose audio (especially after pressing "Space" to skip dialogue). Some bosses have missing voice lines or sound effects during phase-transition cutscenes. For a game that has a focus on atmosphere and storytelling, this is a major immersion breaker.

[h3]Gatekeeping of Game Mechanics[/h3]
It’s disappointing that many modes, gears, abilities, and other features available in the Chinese version are delayed or locked in the global version. Players outside China are spending money too and they deserve equal access to content, not a watered-down or slow-drip version of the game.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]
These issues prevent me from giving the game a higher score, but despite everything, I still recommend trying it. The sheer amount of quality content and experiences you get is genuinely impressive. I just hope the developers listen to community feedback and continue refining the game.

Where Winds Meet is absolutely a 10/10 game, which is precisely why I can’t recommend it to anyone who still values things like friends, sunlight, or knowing what day it is. Not that it matters, the in-game chat is so lively you basically get a brand-new social life full of strangers who greet you more than your real friends ever did.

I’ve been playing for four days. Four. And in that time, the game has quietly taken over my entire existence like a beautifully rendered young master with perfect hair.

I now wake up early — not because I’m suddenly disciplined or spiritually enlightened, but because I need to check whether I can climb another suspiciously tall mountain or get ambushed by more bandits who clearly train harder than I do.
And i go to bed late, because the game whispers, “Just one more quest.” Which is, of course, a lie. That one quest turns into three side quests, a detour through a bamboo forest, crafting tea for a stranger, and an existential crisis on a cliff at sunset.

The world is gorgeous, the combat is flashy, and the freedom is dangerous. Not dangerous for your character!, dangerous for your free time, your sleep schedule, and possibly your friend/relationships.

Where Limits Meet

This game could’ve been incredible… but the devs went out of their way to sabotage their own work.

Graphics? Awesome.
World? Beautiful.
Story? Good.
Combat? Decent.
P2W? None.

And yet somehow, the game still manages to piss me off every time I play.

The Trash Parts

Everything is capped.
Yes—everything.  “Let me farm this real qu— oh look, weekly/daily limit.”
Who thought this was a good idea? Seriously.

Stamina system is a joke.
Full refresh in 3 days. Basically enter game every 3 day and enter the boss claim triple boom 3 day stamina gone in 10 min, stamina system already worst thing in games yet this game refresh it fully every 3 day and takes 10 min to spend all, at least all others games do this daily not 3 day..
1 stamina every 10 minutes like it’s some cheap mobile game.
Absolutely kills the fun.

Nothing left to do after the campaign.
I’ve done exploration, side quests, everything.
After ~100–150 hours, the game just… dies.

Online content is embarrassing.
One of the worse daily quests in online game genre
Run in circles, dance like an idiot and meditate
This is not “content,” it’s punishment.

Balance? Never heard of it.
The whole game is just SWORDS everywhere. Other weapons might as well not exist.

Skill system is painfully shallow.
Two active weapon skills, and 1 hold R charged attacks… and then a flood of pointless mystical-art skills nobody asked for.
Where are the real martial-arts combos? Where is the depth? I’d rather have deeper martial-arts weapon skills or even combo inputs (e.g., LMB+LMB+RMB).

Final Verdict

Amazing potential. Beautiful world.
And then completely destroyed by some of the worst design choices I’ve seen in years.

After sinking 60+ hours into the game, my initial enthusiasm has been completely overshadowed by critical technical and design flaws. Where Winds Meet is a stunning example of ambition over stability, and its current state is actively undermining its own excellent ideas.

1. The WWM Paradox: Beauty vs. Functionality
The game is visually spectacular, and the scale of the Wuxia world is breathtaking. The core systems—the multi-weapon combat, the deep Martial Arts, and the Inner Way customization—are genuinely inspired. However, this amazing foundation is built on quicksand. The deeper you go into the content, the more the game fights against you.

2. The Core Combat is Fundamentally Broken
The issues are not minor bugs; they corrupt the moment-to-moment gameplay, which is essential for an action RPG:

Unresponsive Controls / Input Lag: There is a noticeable delay in input registration, making the game feel sluggish and "floaty" even in solo play. This is the single biggest issue that invalidates all high-level combat.

Broken Parry Windows: Parry timing is inconsistent and unreliable. Attacks often clip through the window, or the required timing feels arbitrary and disconnected from the visual animation.

Dodging and I-Frames: Dodges are unreliable, and attacks frequently pass through the supposed frames of invulnerability (i-frames). This forces players to rely on brute-force stats rather than skill.

3. Monetization Over Quality
The perception within the community is that the developers are prioritizing revenue over core stability.

Daily Cosmetics: The rapid, daily introduction of new skins and store items while fundamental bugs and input issues persist sends a clear message that fixing the game’s technical core is not the top priority.

Endgame Unplayable: When the Sword Trial and high-level bosses require perfect execution, the technical flaws make content completion an exercise in frustration and luck, not skill.

I cannot recommend this game in its current state, as the frustrations of the combat mechanics actively fight against the beautiful world and deep systems. Please fix the controls.

This a strange one for me, because even though it's giving off a lot of gacha alarm bells, it does not seem like they affect gameplay (for now at least). It's also mired in way too many menus, and the localization requires a LOT of polish. But despite these things, there's a lot about the game I find myself loving. Exploration, combat, and story are satisfying and fun to explore. I really enjoy exploring the world, which has a little more serious wuxia vibe, rather than just being anime again. The way the game makes it easy to hop between solo, co-op, and mmo modes is aIso really nice. It also has novel gameplay systems that I don't really see elsewhere, like their crime system with imprisonment, or getting affected by illnesses that can only be healed by another player through a minigame. I want to say it feels reminiscent of Genshin Impact, but that also feels inaccurate - Where Winds Meet manages to stand on its own in that comparison. It also comes with difficulty modes, so if you want a Fromsoft-like experience, then you can. Players can even leave messages on the ground in a similar way. 
Overall, despite it's flaws, I love the game so far. But I also have this distinct feeling that surely this is too good to be true, and the monetization will clamp down and become more aggressive eventually.

Where Winds Meet is one of the most ambitious Wuxia RPGs I’ve played. Its world is breathtaking, filled with bamboo forests, ancient cities, and martial arts legends that make exploration a joy. Combat is stylish and rewarding, blending tactical depth with cinematic flair. However, the game’s free-to-play grind and overwhelming systems sometimes get in the way of the adventure. Despite these flaws, it’s a unique and memorable journey that fans of open world RPGs should experience.

I was concerned that playing this game as a free to play and not participating in the money pit of rolling for cosmetics was going to feel disappointing, but that has been the complete opposite of the case. Even paying exclusively for the battle pass which costs less than any monthly subscription to any other MMO feels like it gives you more access to cosmetics and rewards than you ever felt yourself needing for.
This game is immersive with rewarding combat that feels like all of your favorite elements of so many other games, and allows you to personalize your play style to what feels the most comfortable to you. Want to play a ranged dps that feels like your aiming a weapon through a reticle? Love FromSoftware games and want to parry and dodge and exploit vulnerabilities? However you like to play your favorite games you can play this game and have a rewarding experience doing so.
Ready to take your playstyle into the matchmaking system and fight a boss with a random team? Load times are instant. No waiting 15-30 minutes to load into a dungeon as a DPS like WoW or other MMOs. Find yourself with a particularly strong team fighting a boss? Add them as friends and join up with them when they're online.
I had the smoothest boss fight I had encountered in this game and joined the other player's guild and now have a group that I play with regularly.
I have been skeptical since the very beginning keeping my expectations low and anticipate running out of content and getting bored, but instead I continue to be blown away by this game and feel like I have only scratched the surface of world to explore and story to watch and experience.

Where Winds Meet is the only game where I can be fighting for my life against a boss, performing peak martial arts, and suddenly get a polite little pop-up at the bottom of my screen saying:
“Join our guild? Press Y or N.”
Several times.
Thanks to that distraction, I was being folded like laundry during a world boss fight.
(Thankfully, I later learned how to disable this.)

What really hooked me, though, was how utterly unhinged the world becomes once you add friends and the bounty system.

The first time an NPC slapped a bounty on my head, a real player bounty hunter materialized next to me like he crawled out of the loading screen specifically to ruin my day. I got yanked into my friend’s world to help heal his injury, which temporarily saved me. The moment I came back to my world, the bounty hunter was still there, waiting like a disappointed parent.

I survived by panic-healing and sprinting for my life while yelling at my friend to come help. He showed up, we 2v1’d the guy, and the bounty hunter rage quit.
Beautiful teamwork.
Definitely balanced.

This kept happening even though I hadn’t committed any crimes. Some unknown player was burning through Echo Beads (premium currency from real money) just to throw more bounties on me.
More bounties, and more chaos. I never lost to a single one.

Then I met Asian John Wick with the username JOHN-WlCK who decided he would be the one to claim my bounty. I used my signature survival technique: panic healing + sprinting in random directions, eventually straight into a giant bear. The bear helped me… and also almost killed me.
It mauled John Wick so hard that I literally tapped him once to finish the job. I’m sensing a pattern.

To confirm whether he was the real Asian John Wick, I had my friend duel him later. First to five wins.
My friend beat him five times with only one loss.
Conclusion: Impostor. Not a certified John Wick.

From there, I became a professional bounty-evader:
– One hunter got tired of chasing me and left before even starting the vendetta.
– Another got tricked into attacking an entire army of royal guards in front of Kaifeng Castle. The guards deleted him instantly. He came back a second time… and the guards deleted him again. Then he rage quit.

Between stealing horses, fighting insane bosses, outsmarting bounty hunters, weaponizing wildlife, and watching whole armies erase my problems for me, this game has completely taken over my life.

10/10 Wuxia chaos, questionable decisions, unintentional war crimes. Would evade hunters again.
