Where the Winds Meet shouldn't exist.

It is everything they tell you doesn't work when you learn game design and development. And, in truth, it never does. But this is a game for Almost everyone. The only genres missing are 2D platformer, 4X, And FPS. And if they wanted to they could probably shoe horn in a DLC for it and make it work.

Any other game would be absolutely panned by critics and gamers alike for "lacking direction" or "Trying to do everything" 

But Where Winds Meet isn't trying to do everything -- it does.

Kingdom Come Red Dead Hogwarts Guild Wars matchless Kung Fu Souls is an alternative title. And while it doesn't do any one thing as good as those games do them, it does what all of them do to a certain degree... And... All free.

And let me just say this: it is all free. There's an entire Single player game here. You never have to touch online. Honestly the online is probably the smallest part of the game. But even saying that this is the only the second F2P videogame I've ever spent money on. Not because I felt I had to but because by-God they deserved it for giving me this experience and I felt like I was ripping them off.


Now that's not to say it's perfect. Chinese games still have that problem Japanese games once had back in the nineties and early oughta --- terrible Localization.

The UI is cluttered and all the different modes, and passes , currencies, and menus are a labyrinth. That being said, I never even felt encouraged to spend the money I did. I almost had to look for it.

Related to the Localization, the Voice Acting is clearly AI, as are , I believe the translations themselves. And idk why but sometimes you'll have voice acting, sometimes you won't, and it can be both in the same interaction randomly.

The AI chatbot NPCs are a good addition, but after awhile they do become a bit of a chore and a bit of a... Disappointment? It's not the dev teams fault.  But when you first meet an NPC the conversation is damnear limitless and feels amazing... But the next time you speak to them it will be as if nothing ever happened.

Like for example, I convinced an NPC that he should pour his money into restoring the General's shrine. The next time we speak it's as if it's the first he's ever heard of it. Of course there's no way the team could predict every possible suggestion and have the NPC actually act on those suggestions. So it's not the fault of the developer that the AI NPCs are disappointing, it's simply an unfortunate side effect of using the chat bots over the finite choices of a dialogue tree.


Finally, the martial arts themselves are, pretty static. As you get stronger they seem to remain the same. I feel like this could be remedied by having more powerful variations of moves occur the more you level them up. But they are fine as is and this is really just a nit pick.

Overall though 9/10

This game honestly shocked me with how good it is. I expected something decent for a free title, but this world feels like it was built with the kind of budget and care you only see in big releases. The first moments in the open world hit you hard. Everything from the sky to the tiny details in the ground feels handcrafted. The lighting changes the entire personality of each region. Sunrise warms the whole landscape in golden light, and by evening the shadows stretch long and give the world this soft cinematic feel. It is beautiful in a way that pulls you in even when nothing is happening.

**Pros**
The world itself is the biggest star. It feels endless in the best way. You wander into forests where the trees sway like real weight is behind them, then you step into quiet villages full of life and tiny interactions. Every corner feels like it has a purpose. There are markets with people shouting, musicians playing, boats drifting along rivers, and even little animals that react to you. Nothing feels empty.

The detail is wild. Clothing moves with your character instead of sticking to them. Hair shifts when the wind picks up. Buildings look aged and worn in a way that makes them feel lived in. Even the food in the game looks so real you almost want to sit your character down and let them eat.

Combat is a whole experience. When it clicks, it feels like you are starring in your own martial arts film. You can switch stances and techniques on the fly and everything flows together like choreography. You can run across rooftops, slow down time for perfect strikes, launch enemies into the air, and respond to attacks with smooth counters that feel earned. It is stylish without being complicated, and powerful without feeling cheap.

The freedom you get is one of the things I love most. You are not pushed into one path. You can explore, fight, role play, make choices, build relationships, or completely ignore the main story and go wander for hours. The game always gives you something interesting to stumble into. You might be climbing a cliff just to see what is up there and suddenly find a hidden shrine or a character who changes the direction of your story.

One of the coolest surprises is how the AI bot NPCs work. They feel alive in a way I did not expect. You can actually talk to them, build friendships, give them gifts, and even bring them along as helpers. It feels like the world gives you companions without forcing anything. Some of them are funny, some are emotional, some are weird in the best way. They make the game feel fuller, almost like you are forming a little chosen family inside this giant world.

The cut scenes are next level. They do not feel like filler or something you skip through. They feel like short films. The detail in the clothing, the lighting, the expressions, the way the camera moves, everything looks so cinematic that you end up watching them more than once because there is always something new to notice. They are rich with emotion and art in a way that makes you pause and appreciate how much work went into them. It is rare for a game to make you want to rewatch its scenes like you would rewatch a favorite movie moment.

Co op is a huge plus. Running around with someone else changes the whole vibe. You share the world together and deal with chaos, quests, and random events as a team. Some of the best moments come from unscripted stuff you and your partner pull off just because the world gives you the freedom to do it.

The soundtrack deserves its own shout out. The music is calm when you explore, intense during battles, and emotional during story moments. It ties the whole world together and gives the game this warm, cinematic feel that stays with you long after you stop playing.

Another thing I appreciate is how alive the story feels. It does not spoon feed you. Instead, it treats you like someone who can handle depth. The characters feel layered and the romance and partnership systems add a surprising amount of heart to the experience. Anything tied to fate feels meaningful because it actually changes how people see you and what paths open up.

**Cons**
The UI is the biggest problem. It slows you down. Menus feel like they were designed by five different people who never talked to each other. You click one thing and suddenly you are somewhere else without a clear idea of how to get back. It is not game breaking, but it pulls you out of the experience more often than it should.

The boss fights can also be inconsistent. Some are perfect, fair, and challenging. Then you get the ones where you know you hit block, yet it still lets the attack land. It feels like the game ignores your input on certain fights. When the combat is this good, those moments stand out even more because everything else flows so smoothly.

Even with those issues, the game is unbelievable for a free release. The scale, the polish, the visuals, the music, the movement, the creativity, the quests, the role playing options, all of it has the weight of something that should have cost money. You can easily lose hours exploring and still feel like you are only scratching the surface. (Obviously I have)

My Journey so far...

After spending over 204 hours in Where Wind Meets, I can confidently say this game is a remarkable adventure. Playing alongside friends in the “Here Be Monster” guild has made the journey even more rewarding, turning every quest into a shared story. The graphics are truly top‑notch, bringing ancient landscapes, bustling towns, and mystical battlefields to life with stunning detail.
Combat feels fluid and engaging, blending martial arts flair with tactical depth. Whether dueling in intense one‑on‑one fights or clashing against waves of enemies, the mechanics remain satisfying. The storyline is equally compelling, weaving personal drama with larger world events, and the worldwide quest hunts add endless variety. Each mission feels like a step deeper into a living, breathing world.
Of course, the game has its quirks. At times, navigating through countless tags and systems feels like “Where Manual Meets,” a playful reminder of the complexity behind its design. Yet even with these layers, the experience remains enjoyable. The balance of exploration, combat, and narrative keeps players invested, and the sense of community elevates it further.
For me, Where Wind Meets isn’t just a game—it’s a world worth inhabiting, one that rewards time, patience, and camaraderie.

[h1][i]“Next-Gen WoW Killer!”[/i] - 9/10[/h1]
Where Winds Meet as a true AAA Free-to-Play, with souls-like action combat & open-world RPG game set in a low-fantasy Martial Arts world (Wuxia) during the Imperial China's Song Dynasty era in 962 C.E.

The game [u]is NOT P2W[/u] and they even promise that in a mail on the main menu. The only monetization with shops and gacha cosmetics is built around the Fashion mechanic the game has and it's optional with no effect on gameplay.

[h2]Maximalism at its finest![/h2]
The world map is huge to explore and immerse yourself in the region and its story. There are three ways to play the game: Solo, Co-Op mode, and Online which basically is the MMO side of WWM. You can either play it for its story only, or PVE group activities like dungeons and raids, or if you like PVP then you can either 1v1, 2v2, 5v5 and there is even a Battle Royale mode with 100-players. 30v30 Guild battles are also on the way!

On the world map, there are tons of side activites you can do from farming materials and grinding stuff to mini-games. There is also crafting and house building features as well as house renting. Vehicle building feature is also on the way, along with many different martial art styles (weapon types) from unarmed combat to various melee weapons.

[h2]My new main MMO, even main game![/h2]
Don't even think if its too spread out so it must be jack of all trades, master of none. No! They actually managed to pull it off. The game has everything included to appeal to everyone, and every single of these systems are their own game inside the game. Just go and figure out the stuff you enjoy the most. I'm at 100 hours of playtime, and didn't finish the main questline let alone the side quests.

The Chinese version of the game has been out for about a year by now. We didn't get their current version, but will be getting their updates one after another, and it's so promising. The upcoming maps are beautiful, a desert map in Yumen Pass and a snow map, as well as a third new addition which is just a masterpiece! They will keep bringing us new features, stories, bosses, and of course new types of cosmetics which is the only thing they are making for money. Every single upcoming update is going to be free.

[h2]Many Versions of WWM[/h2]
There is also a Lite version on their website if your build is low-end so you can play it on basically any computer. We are going to get a better 4K version for high-end builds as well. The mobile version is going to be released at 12 December 2025 for both Android and iOS. Mind that the game on PC is not a mobile port flop, and there is cross-progression meaning you can keep playing on any platform including PS5 any time you want. We can only have one character per account at this moment but multi-character feature is coming up to 6 character slots per account.

[h2]Now for the downsides, otherwise it would be a 9.5/10 game...[/h2]
Translation from Mandarin to English is no easy task so there are some mistakes here and there. The translation quality overall could be better and they are working on it anyway.

The UI is okay-ish but needs to be improved, the menus however are nightmare! They don't call it Where Menus Meet for nothing. But they're working on it too. You'll get used to navigating after a hundred hours like me anyway but it will be a welcoming improvement.

Game is no where like a beta nor early-access but it still needs to get some fixes. Nothing game breaking so far but they can, and did polish more on CN version. We didn't get them because of complications as we will get them in time. If they did the game at their current version it would take another year to fully translate and bring everything to global version, so they will keep doing it while bringing us the already fixed things and hopefully we can catch up to match both versions.

Originally I thought this was a pretty good game but the deeper I get into it the more I realise it's just a cosmetics casino with a pretty skin. 

Don't even get me started on the DAMN MENUS. Menus, menus and more menus. All of them designed to give you a tiny hit of dopamine without really giving you anything except wasted time. You shouldn't have to skim through literally hundreds of menus to 'Claim Reward' on every single page just to progress. It's predatory and lazy design. It wouldn't even be so bad if the menus were easy to find and then navigate but it genuinely feels like they intentionally designed it to be a maze UI. I've played thousands of games in my life and I can't think of a single one with more egregious menus than this one.

The only cool feature this game has going for it is the ability to speak to NPCs using AI where you convince them of certain things. For example I had to convince a woodsman that stealing was bad. Some people will like the combat but to me it felt very unbalanced. You have two weapons and can switch between them at will but there's almost never a reason to do so. They really should've studied how a 2 weapon system can be done well (see: Guild Wars 2 and New World) instead of this. It really felt like they tacked on the ability to use 2 weapons at once as an afterthought rather than making it an integral part of combat.

The story also had potential to be good because the cutscenes are high quality but the translated writing just isn't good at all which ultimately ruins the story and makes it dull to get through.

It's free, so try it if you want. If you do I really do recommend checking out the whole 'speaking to the AIs' thing. It's a really cool feature and felt like a taste of what is to come in the future of gaming. Outside of that though, there really isn't a lot here. There's a lot of 'features', yes, but none of them have depth.

This game is actually pretty good, and it’s clear a lot of work went into it. But there are countless bugs. Once at least the majority of them are patched, it’s going to be a decent experience. Just to mention a few: tracking issues in quests, ghost enemies in co-op, and the most annoying one—bosses start attacking during phase changes while the screen is still black (I guess the game is loading). It’s pretty frustrating to lose half my health every boss attempt. And then there are the little annoyances, like how your walking speed isn’t lined up with NPCs—especially in quests where you’re forced to walk, and you have to stop every few seconds because you’re just slightly faster than them. It’s a tiny thing, but also the kind of tiny thing developers should pay attention to.

The exploration is quite fun, and the story—while boring or silly in some parts—is still pretty good overall. The puzzle sections are also solid, but they feel inconsistent. Sometimes you just pull a lever, other times the game straight up tells you what to do, but most puzzles are not too hard and fun to solve.

The game actually runs well on my GTX 1650, and the visuals are solid even on low settings, so no real complaints there, except for a few graphical glitches. Hopefully future patches will fix them.

Combat is really fun for the most part. There’s a decent challenge on higher difficulties, but most bosses are learnable and enjoyable to fight—except for a few that throw some ridiculous true-combo at you that takes half your health if you don’t dodge or parry in time. The practice mode is a good solution, but it’s weird that I have more health and deal more damage in that mode. Not a huge problem, but it makes it harder to compare my actual skills to the boss.

I’ve played for more than 50 hours now, and if you love open-world exploration games, you’ll probably love this. Otherwise, the game still feels unpolished to me—almost like an early access title with the bugs and co-op issues. I can’t really recommend it unless you’re already into this type of game.

If you look at this game and see something that you think you might like, then just try it. It's free, and I can assure you that you will not ever be required to spend money to enjoy what the game has to offer. 

The developers insist that there is no pay2win, and they're not lying. Yes, you can technically get a few consumable items that temporarily buff your stats in a very minor way from the draw shop (the gacha shop), but I never used any of these, and I played on the hardest difficulty (Legend) and beat most of the bosses at the time of writing. I only spent some money because I felt obligated to give back to the devs after all the time I've spent enjoying it for free, plus I got a pretty dress out of it.

Time investment is a slightly different story. There's a lot of mechanics related to character progression that are tied to grinding, whether its grinding upgrade materials, gear, upgrades to "Inner Way" techniques (playstyle-dictating passives), etc. There's a lot to work towards, but that's not necessarily a bad thing for those that like always having something to build up. Even after beating nearly every boss, it still feels like my character is nowhere near at peak power, and I don't know if I'll ever reach total mastery. The grind fits the themes of the game, too, making you truly feel like a student of martial arts that must practice a single punch a thousand times or what have you. 

This is a live-service game, though, so there are things that try to get you to commit time to this game across weeks, if not months. The are some mechanics that arbitrarily limit how much grinding and progress you can achieve in a week (mostly Jade Fish and weekly shop stock). Global level caps keep everyone from leveling up too quickly, forcing you to wait a week or more before being allowed to unlock the next set of levels. Materials for upgrading gear only apply to the specific tier of gear its designed for, making you grind for different materials each time you reach a new level cap. Claiming rewards for doing boss or outpost challenges requires Stamina, which you have a limited amount of, and it can take several days for it to fully regenerate naturally (though, again, you CANNOT pay to skip the wait, which is ultimately a good thing). All these things are meant to get you to come back to this game every so often, even if its for just a couple hours a day. I personally don't love it, but I also don't hate it. It's a good thing for those looking for a game they can fall back on, and it only really matters to those looking to min/max. If you're just looking to enjoy the game casually, then these systems don't really affect you, thankfully.

There are a few other "meh" things about this game that are consequences of the game's business model, but these have less to do with the time/money investment and more to do with the general quality of the experience. 

The game bombards you with menus hidden in menus hidden in menus, and each of these menus is associated with different claimable rewards that you get from doing just about anything. In the early game especially, you'll complete a quest or something and you'll get like 10 different notifications for rewards you can claim, each taking you to a different menu meant to display your progress in one of the game's many systems. It's overwhelming and honestly turned me off from the game the first few days I tried it, but eventually you get used to it, the notifications become less and less frequent, and you'll eventually get a handle on it. I think the reason these menus exist is to guide the player towards the content that has rewards so the player always knows what to do to get what they want. I don't really like this approach, I appreciate when a game keeps things hidden and isn't scared of the player missing content, but whatever, you can ignore most of it.

The other consequence of this game's live-service nature is that it is essentially a perpetual "work in progress." The early parts of the game will feel pretty feature-complete and decently polished, but the further along you go the more incomplete the game will feel. Characters will go from having detailed backstories to having placeholder text for descriptions. You'll walk towards an ominous looking building before the game teleports you away and says the area is still under development. You'll finish the main quest and be told to wait 3 months before you can start the next part of it because they're not done making it yet. If this was a single-purchase game, it would be labelled Early Access. I wish the game was a complete package with a beginning, middle, and end, but that's not the case, and it will likely continue to not be the case for quite some time yet. It makes me look forward to future content updates, but in a sort of bittersweet kind of way.

What I've said up till now has been to give you an overview of the game's free to play model and its consequences so you can set your expectations accordingly. I haven't talked about what I actually like about the game itself yet, and that's honestly because it may not even be relevant to you. There's SO many things to do in this game, that what you get out of it is likely to be very different from what I got out of it. You could spend all your time exploring the world, or spend it hunting bosses, or spend it playing minigames, or spend it taking pictures of the pretty scenery, or spend it doing player bounties, or spend it competing in the arena, or...you get it. The game has a little bit of everything for every type of player, so my only advice to you is to focus on the parts of the game that you personally find enjoyable. For me, that was dungeon crawling, fighting bosses, playing madiao, and spending way too much time in photo mode.

For me, this game was exciting, beautiful, charming, emotional, challenging, and rewarding. It's epic scope and cinematic flair are juxtaposed by somber quiet and a sincere appreciation for the beauty of the natural world and the human spirit. Its AAA grandiosity stands in stark contrast to its goofy little quirks, oddball sense of humor, and its fanboyish commitment to wuxia fantasy. It doesn't nail everything it attempts to do absolutely flawlessly, but I honestly think its daring that they even made such a grand attempt in the first place and provide it for free.

I can only hope that things don't get any worse with future updates. I'm cautiously optimistic, but we'll see.

I generally hate pay to win/buying power, but given that the only avenue for this was the battle pass which caps the power buying at a relatively low monetary number, I stomached it. I figured worse case scenario it's a free single player game of surprisingly good quality, given the graphics, storyline, cutscenes, boss design, etc.

However, the story quests are mostly boring, many of the puzzles are contrived, the menu and systems bloat is ridiculous, bugs aren't game breaking but ubiquitous, the localization is terrible, and the gear progression is full of chores that don't actually reward your time investment. Despite all of this, I was still kind of enjoying the game for awhile there. I put about 70 hours in the game and it didn't start feeling to stale until the last 10. Yet, I kept pushing. That is, until my encounter with the bounty system.

I got a bounty bc an npc I disguised myself as saw me. This caused me to be invaded, wasting my 2nd disguise (which aren't cheap) btw. I fought the invader for HALF AN HOUR before they gave up and left. I was frustrated at this point and logged off for a few days. I logged back on after my break only to be immediately invaded again. I nearly beat this invader, after a 10 minute fight, only to be killed by some geese I accidently agro'd during the fight. This caused me to be put in prison, where I have to wait 15 minutes in game without doing anything, or buying my way out, or crafting a bunch of stuff to "get on the warden's good side." The crafts would probably have taken me most of the 15 minutes to complete, but I didn't even get time to test that theory because you have to compete for access to a small number of workbenches that other players will want to use. You can not opt out of the bounty system btw.

So to recap, about 55 minutes of my time was wasted because I got caught wearing a disguise. I don't even know if winning the bounty fight would have ended the invades, because my fight was interrupted by a geese swarm. Where Winds Meet is a beautifully crafted wuxia open-world RPG that mixes cinematic martial arts, exploration, and absolute chaos in the best way possible.

My first half hour vanished inside character customization, and the second half hour disappeared while I tried naming my hero. I tested more than fifty names, every single one was taken, and in the end I had to add a prefix just to start my journey. For my second hour, I spent most of it dying repeatedly to the Puppeteer’s spear. And somehow, the next five hours slipped away as I wandered through the beautiful wuxia world, completely absorbed by its landscapes and atmosphere.
The game is fully free-to-play and monetized only through cosmetics and battle passes—no pay-to-win, no predatory gacha. Performance can vary, and the menu system is so complicated it feels like the real final boss, but once you understand it, everything flows.

Combat is “Souls-light,” rewarding good timing without punishing you too hard. The world is packed with bosses, puzzles, treasures, side quests, and a surprisingly deep social system—raids, PvP, sects and more (I have to explore that). You also get odd but heroic jobs, like removing someone’s itchy back, immobilizing a molester, or healing ducks… though never fight the ducks. They are secretly boss-level enemies. And Elder Gongsun—please, Let me hit You. And there is some Shaming Prisoner Activity with Special Time Limit.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a stylish, chaotic, and surprisingly heartwarming wuxia adventure. Between the stunning open world, flexible playstyles, cinematic combat, and the absurd stories it creates, it’s easily one of the most memorable free RPG experiences available.

I would be another of those, "Wow, I can't believe this game is free!" type of people. Honestly, when I first saw this game, I dismissed it. It just, didn't look like the type of game I'd play. Wuxia isn't a genre I typically go crazy about.

However, as I kept getting invited by friends of mine, I decided to give it a shot anyways. And I haven't regretted it.

A lot of people compare the game to Dark Souls, and that is honestly valid. But, it's probably closer to something like Warframe, if I had to evaluate it. It's a sort of mix between the two. Fast, fluid combat, brief parry windows, a simple, but robust system that has more depth than it first lets on. From how crime and punishment works, to just, having so many minigames. Being able to have a live conversation with various NPCs, and writing your own songs. There's a lot here.

This should really be how MMOARPGs should be handled going forward. Warframe, Elden Ring, and Where Winds Meet are three really solid games that, I really hope help to shape the gaming landscape in the future. The fact that there's a lot here that I didn't care for, but was still sucked into so deeply despite that, all from a small nudge?

Seriously, give it a try and you'll be surprised.

As someone who has variable time to spend on games as of now. Where winds meet is an experience im still questioning as to why it's free. Just the amount of things you can do within this world is insane. nearly sixty hours in and I can confidently say i'll be playing this game for a while. I HIGHLY suggest you take your time with this game as opposed to brute forcing to the higher end of difficulty.

 Exploration after all is key towards your progression naturally, and overall.  It's like if Sekiro woke up and decided. "How about we become breath of the wild but utterly insane."  Combat flows very nicely, does have it's moments where you'd be questioning "how hell the did that hit me? "But as a whole it has depth that's unseen for a game that may I remind you is F R E E.  The PVE content is the real star of the show, the story being a nicely added treat on-top of it all and the lore spread throughout the world will surely keep you engaged.

 If you don't care for the lore, the game has a plentiful amount of  things to do outside of following the main story and unlike most free games  where there's a system in place to halt progression; this game  allows you continue playing even when your maximum quota is met. You can steal meat from bears, get jumped by geese, force people into poses for the sake of their betterment, throw on disguises to fool people,- literally too many things to list..

The game does have it's shortcomings, the bounty/vendetta system being the weakest part in my opinion. If you're not huge on PVP all the time, you'll find yourself repeating the same bounties daily. Which is repetitive, but I assure you. You'll want to rather do that than deal with actual player bounties in the world. Unless you're stun lock , and ping Jesus, himself.  You are not killing a soul in this game due to how healing is handled within the open areas. I literally had to message a guy and ask for a fair fight simply cause of how the healing works. The reward for killing them is not really worth it for the amount of effort you may need to put in (It is, albeit if you get a fair fight..) , even with the things that reduce healing. The amount of running one can do is not to be understated and you will be stressed out. 

The only other gripe a few seem to have is the fact that the outfits are like, dumb expensive. This is one of those games where you'd have to find that one combination if you plan on buying an outfit. It get's very expensive real fast, though this is truly the only thing that costs money in this game.  The advantages of being paid to a free user are really nothing. (Battle pass I believe gives you some benefits, but nothing that'll boost your prowess against others or the world.)  Someone could have the dankest fit and be totally garbage at the game, so don't be discouraged by the 50 dollar outfit peeps! 

Overall, if you've got friends and want to experience a world of unfiltered chaos. Tell them to give this game a go, though co-op for the main story missions aren't a thing unfortunately. Meaning they'll have to do those given missions on their own, but exploration wise you can ball out all you'd like! 

This game solo is also a treat, as that's been my whole journey and still as of now!

It's a free game and there's a lot going on. Though I want to point out some major issues that harms the experience for me.

Firstly, english localization for the UI and menus is really, really poor; misleading at best, incomprehensible at worst.

Secondly, despite being free to play, it is absolutely loaded with gacha mechanics. All microtransactions are purely cosmetic but there's just so many of them, and the game pushes it on you every chance it gets, it's really obnoxious.

And finally, the amount of reward schemes and progression tracks you have to go into an obscure segment of the menu to claim is truly ridiculous. I played for barely 3 hours and I felt like I had to stop every 15 seconds just to click away a marker indicating I've earned an award. Maybe it slows down later on, but that is not a newbie friendly system.

Overall the game feels purposefully designed to appeal to brainless checklist completioning, it has the look and feel of an MMO even though you can play entirely solo. But therein lies the problem; Classical MMO models are just objectively bad.

I don't want to hate on this game, it offers a ton of content and is extraordinarily well polished while not [i]technically[/i] costing you a damn thing. But underneath that too-good-to-be-true layer lies a predatory whale-catching system that is almost as sinister as Diablo IV.

You can argue that it's all optional and therefore no one is harming anyone but themselves by buying into it. But that's true of real life gambling too, nobody [i]has[/i] to go to a casino, but we all know they still do. It is no longer a valid excuse to leave the responsibility entirely on the consumer.

IMO, best Wuxia game since the MSDOS and PS1 era, with the best F2P monetization model of all time and what I consider the most ideal. That said, the gacha is absolutely not worth it for most players (at least currently) it's more of an excuse to donate money to the devs.

This open-world souls-like MMO-lite action RPG is one big culmination of all the good ideas & systems from several good games put into one. The ambition here is unfathomably huge, but I think they pulled it off very well.
There are a lot of fun references and ingenuity baked into the game which I certainly appreciate. 
Although it must also be said that a good deal of them and also the overall flavour of interactions & story will be lost to western audiences due to translation and differing cultures.
However, localizing this game is extremely difficult - and at times even downright impossible. That's because the original language used here is very old and is akin to Old English or Shakespearean English.

As far as online RPGs go, WWM has managed to place itself into my personal top 1 or 2.
I'm excited to see more and I hope they keep this monetization model going forward.

PRO's:
- No pay to win
- Can switch between solo, co-op and multiplayer mode
- Adjustable difficulty in solo mode (except for Legendary difficulty, which has to be selected from the start) 
- Character appearance can be changed later anytime with in-game currency (not sure about being able to swap gender)
- Exploring the vast open world is amazing, filled with stuff to do
- Story and questing feels fun, dynamic and overall very lively
- Combat feels rewarding (although very parry-heavy) 
- Challenging boss fights
- Side activities and games, incl. fishing & mahjong
- There are some good looking outfits for free or there are some nice 1$ ones
- Authentic wuxia feel


CON's:
- Lagspikes and performance issues, especially during co-op
- Missing basic features: Can't access game options before the tutorial, like changing volume or keybinds until the tutorial is done. No pause-option even during SOLO mode. No disabling / slowing text auto-advance, or pausing cutscenes. Get ready to have the story continue with or without you
- Tons of menus within menus, within menus
- Gacha is mostly super expensive, dolphins are basically left out - which sucks for those, who want to support the game outside of monthly (battle-)passes, but aren't able to mindlessly dump money into cosmetics like whales can. Example: Dying your hair white or other "unnatural" hair colours for just one hairstyle only can cost a few hundred bucks (requires gacha)


REVIEW: 
Fun and free no pay to win game with a big AND very lively open world. Exploration is the best part of the game, traversing the world is fun and doesn't feel tedious. It has a solo and multiplayer mode, and you can play co-op too, although the options to progress together are very limited. Combat feels quite good, but the timing of the parry-system requires some getting used to. 

The game could do with a lot more performance optimisations, and more quality of life features, some basic options are straight up not existent at this point (like pressing ESC to pause the game in solo mode). If you are a story-enjoyer, get ready for the story to continue without you. There is no pause button during cutscenes, and text auto-advancing can't be turned off or slowed down. In other games, you press X or click for the next text line to show up... here, it just does its own thing. Good luck if you have to look away for a second and finding that dialogue written somewhere in the 100s of menus. 

The game has a solo and a multiplayer mode, which is nice. Most of the progression like quests and story are mainly solo though, which deviates from regular MMO's, where you can quest together with a buddy. In my opinion, the social aspects don't feel too MMO-like, it rather feels like a weird mix of Dark Souls signposts, mobile game multiplayer interactions and an online hub. You can invite friends to your session and play co-op, but the lagspikes, not registered inputs (sucks during combat) and the performance issues during co-op are abysmal. Would be great, if they would fix that for the few things where you can actually progress together.

Overall a very enjoyable game, I sank over 100 hours into it already and still haven't discovered everything there is to do. You can tell how much passion went into developing this game, and even after release, that the devs really care. You can easily send your feedback from within the game and actively help, to make the game better over time.


HEADS UP:
Before you start playing, adjust the system volume already at the start, if you don't want to get blasted. Character creation will very likely be a buggy mess. If you just wanna jump in, at least make sure to select the right bodytype you actually want to play with, as you might not be able to change that later in game yet. Face and hair can be changed in game anytime with in-game currency after, and you get one face-change for free from the start. The menus are overwhelming at the start, but you'll get used to it.


CRITIQUES:
- Make game options available BEFORE the tutorial. Not being able to adjust the volume, keybinds or other settings until the tutorial is finished is insane and really off putting.
- Please add the BASIC features which CN already has, to global asap. The code is already written for the CN-version anyways, might as well copy-and-paste it over? I'm not speaking of features like the multi-character feature option etc., but the BASICS, like having the option to PAUSE the game in solo mode. Never saw a game in which the text just moves on without you being able to read it all, good luck if you have to sneeze during the MSQ, get the door, or go to the toilet wtf (yes, some cutscenes are long, and there's no warning that the cutscene will take forever). I read that some people EVEN RECORDED their game, because there was no way to slow / pause the story and there is no other way to read it at your own convenience.
- Please remove the ID number on the screen, it doesn't have to be visible all the time and could easily be put it  one of the 100 menus... does it really have to be burned INTO the screen?

the UI is somewhat clunky, and the translations don't always line up, but the game itself is really fun.  Perhaps in some cases a bit TOO broad of scope.  I'm personally not sure what the MMO mode actually does as I've literally never found an enemy in it, but maybe that's due to sheer population.

Playing Where Winds Meet honestly surprised me in the best way. From the moment I stepped into its version of ancient China, I felt like I was actually exploring a living world instead of just following markers on a map. The landscapes are stunning—wide open fields, quiet villages, misty mountains—and every place I visited made me want to keep going just to see what was next.

What hooked me the most was the combat. It’s fast, fluid, and really makes you feel like a true wuxia hero. Dodging, countering, jumping off rooftops, chaining abilities—everything flows so well that even regular fights feel cinematic. It’s the kind of combat system that makes you want to fight just because it feels good.

The story pulled me in too. It gives you freedom to play things your own way while still offering characters and quests that feel meaningful. Even the smaller side missions are interesting and add to the world instead of feeling like filler.

Yeah, there are a few rough edges here and there, but nothing that took away from my experience. Overall, Where Winds Meet gave me that rare feeling of actually being on an adventure—not just playing a game.

If you love open-world games, martial-arts combat, or just exploring beautiful environments, I’d definitely recommend giving it a try.

A game I expected to be absolute slop but is actually a ton of fun, it's F2P and blows a ton of paid AAA titles out of the water. I had to admittedly rough out some areas, and get accustomed to some of the games quirks. It took me a few hours till the game clicked once it did it got its hooks into me. Note I'm reviewing this game on the basis of playing on "Legend" difficulty.

Pros
- Satisfying parry centric gameplay that provides a nice challenge. Difficulty options and parry assists are available for players if you want.
- Varied dungeon mechanics, bosses
- Challenging
- Not P2W with the cash shop being for glamour
- Lovely visuals, setting and some nice storylines.
- Multiple progression points with a surprising emphasis on horizontal progression (I prefer horizontal over vertical).
- The map is well populated with something to do or find that helps with overall progression.
- Various activities to do that give stat gains/desirable rewards. Chinese Chess, Drunk Darts, Fishing, Playing Music, Archery Contests, Drinking Contests, Sumo, Mahjong, Cards, Dancing.
- Faction system with various rules and playstyles to progress in.
- Lots of player build customization with varied playstyles. Sword, Large Swords, Dual Blades, Spears, Fans, Umbrellas, Rope Dart, some weapons having multiple styles that change their playstyle.
- Tons of player freedom after scripted opening.
- Shared open world co-op. Up to you and 4 other players only limitation being story quests are NOT co-op capable.
- The game is well optimized with me being able to maintain a constant 120fps.

Cons
- Inexcusable UI that needs to be reworked. This is easily the worst part of this game and if the game wasn't so damn fun I would have quit because of it.

- Controller navigation in some mini games and menus is questionable to the point that I use my mouse instead.

- Horrible player onloading, the game dumps you in after the intro and quickly starts to pile on elements often without giving the player any context other than that a thing exists. It makes it difficult especially early on to discern if something is important or not and where to focus. This specific issue is made worse with the game having various currencies, early on it's hard to know what does what and how to earn each one. (I don't have an issue with multiple currencies but it took a while to hash out what was what).

- Gear progression trappings. When you uncap levels the game provides a starter set of gear to onload you to that level range as the game world syncs to your uncaps. This puts it into the players head that they just equip this set and forget because early on this is perfectly fine, but falling into this habit is a mistake. For example when I uncapped to level 50, my prior level range set was much better than the provided because the set bonus synergy to my kit along with the bonus effects I rolled on the pieces. The game makes it easy to fall into equip X item because highest number, and you see many players doing it because of this. Because of this players slap on equipment without thinking about the set effects, stat rolls, etc. which can make you get one shotted or have horrid damage output. One could blame the player for not critically thinking about this scenario but honestly the developers instill this mentality into the players head from their design so I'd fault them for it over the player.

- Cases of bad translation and untranslated text.

Your mileage may vary aspects
- Progression style. If you prefer vertical progression this game has aspects that could be a dealbreaker for you. The are time gates on level uncaps (You still gain exp it's stored for the next uncap) which eventually roll into taking days before you can uncap, a stamina system which takes about 3 IRL days to fully recharge (You can use any accumulated stamina at any time along with stamina regen items if you have any.) for getting rewards from multiplayer boss fights, raids, etc. You don't run out of things to do because of these limiters despite what others may state as the game gives various stats, passives, skills and what not from doing the open world content not leveling/stamina activities. With this being a large part of the game if you dislike doing various types of content and only like leveling this will likely be an issue.

- AI chat bot NPCs you can interact with to befriend and earn weekly rewards. Essentially you converse with NPCs that have a certain set personality and scenario you need to resolve for them, once you do this you befriend them and they'll send weekly gifts with the more you befriend the better weekly rewards. Personally I've had some interesting interactions that I think gives some justification to this interaction such as angering the NPC in the chat that they end it and just outright attack me, or using absurd methods to resolve the chat situation. If you're completely anti-AI then I guess this would be the deal breaker.

- Mobage aspects. The game has dailies, weeklies, battle pass (free and paid tracks), multiple currencies, stamina, gatcha for cosmetics, menus designed like a mobage.

You can buy costumes for your character, if you like, and they run from reasonably cheap to very expensive- but they are simply skins and don't change the game by adding power etc. Be aware that there are also 'free' costumes you can find, and earn through questing, etc., in the game and they are absolutely cool too. So, yeah, no PTW. 

My only hang up, at the beginning when the game launched, was feeling overwhelmed by the amount of content and information being tossed at me…I felt like I couldn’t keep up with the menus (clunky, but the devs are working on that issue) and I'm one of those player types who likes to 'do'—teach me, let me actually practice for a bit to start some muscle memory, then throw me in the deep end lol. That and the terrain sometimes grabbing my character are my only gripes.

The various ways you can play Where Winds Meet is really interesting. Currently I'm playing the game solo, like a single player RPG. But I can easily group up with r/l friends who are playing for co-op. I could play it like an MMO too if I choose. I love the fact I have choice and am not being forced to play any particular way.

The questing (main, side) are actually interesting, not filled with agenda white noise, and many of them are actually fun to progress. I've yet to run into something I consider tedious. I also don't find the game grindy and I've played some grinders in the past (Lineage II anyone?). Getting materials to upgrade gear slots isn't difficult—the menu will tell you what you need and can show you the ways to obtain it, and even mark your map for you.

There is a crafting system that seems to work smoothly but I haven't spent much time with it, other than to make some potions and cook some meals.

Where Winds Meet is vast game. There is a lot to take in, a lot to learn, for sure. The best part is, this game really brings Wuxia and the Jiang hu world to life. Well worth the time. YMMV.

Where winds?

After spending around 60 hours in Where Winds Meet, I can confidently say it’s one of the most engaging new releases I’ve played in a while. The world is vibrant, full of life, and constantly pulling you toward something fun or surprising. Whether you’re exploring, fighting, crafting, or just wandering into trouble, there’s always something to keep you busy.

One of the standout features is the character design. The customization options are incredibly detailed and expansive, giving you the freedom to shape a character that genuinely feels like your own. The clothing and appearance choices are beautifully crafted, offering a huge range of styles—elegant, rugged, traditional, or flashy—so creating your perfect character never feels limiting. It’s clear a lot of care went into the designs, and it pays off every time you step into the world.

The main story is decent—good enough to keep you moving forward—but it’s the side stories that really shine. Some of them have so much depth and personality that they overshadow the main plot entirely, making exploration feel genuinely rewarding.

Gameplay-wise, the experience is smooth and exciting, and the sheer amount of content makes every hour feel worthwhile. You can easily lose track of time just drifting through its world and stumbling into new adventures.

If there’s one downside, it’s the progression system tied to the early-game time locks. Players who started on day one had to wait real-time days to achieve certain breakthroughs, which added a sense of pacing and immersion. New players, however, don’t experience those waits because the system isn’t client-sided. It would feel more balanced—and more fair—if everyone had to go through the same timed progression, giving newer players that same sense of anticipation and world wandering that the early players enjoyed.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a fun, content-packed experience with tons of heart. A few progression inconsistencies aside, it’s absolutely worth diving into.

At 36 hours, this game has been unexpectedly good. A mix between Sekiro, Witcher  3, and Genshin Impact, this one provides a breathtaking world that feels alive, clean combat, an entertaining story, solid crafting and collection, in-depth skill progression across multiple systems, and a VAST amount of exploration/ side content that can easily keep you busy for hundreds of hours but doesn't feel like a list of chores. 

The game does a good job of making most things simple to grasp at a glance while having a high skill ceiling. You can have a very chill, laid back experience just running around collecting and killing baddies, or if you're feeling confident, ratchet up the difficulty and sweat against some REALLY tough bosses and Skillful side NPC's. You can live you're best Isekai Slow-Life by becoming a doctor and just running to other people healing them.

Where Winds Meet starts you out in single player mode and gives you some time to familiarize yourself before allowing you to get involved in multi-player, of which there are 2 modes, Co-op and Online. Co-op is essentially the single player experience with the ability to only Invite friends to a private version of your single player game mode that tracks progress for all players helping out. While Online lets you experience a more community centered MMO-like version of the game world, letting you tackle more complex content with guilds (IE; Raid's). This game will often times feel like 3 different games at the same time, while still feeling balanced and whole. For a Free 2 Play game, there is WAAAY more here than expected.

The game has a few bugs, most of which in my opinion are incredibly minor and can be overlooked as annoying but not game/ immersion breaking. It's well optimized, considering my potato can run it fairly easily with minimal struggle. The main large city pushes the specs of my PC, but in general if you have a mid-tier PC you should be able to run it on low-med graphics with little issue. Even on lower settings, the games art direction carries, its a beautiful world with many amazing locations.

All in all, I recommend that if you have a decent PC, you should give this one at least a try. 8.5/10

[h1]One of the most ambitious games I've ever played[/h1]
Where Winds Meet is a wild game. I don't think I've ever seen a game where you can roleplay as a villain and go around killing NPCs, have bounties placed on you, get hunted by other players, get jailed if you get caught, and then to cut your sentence short, get paraded around town while other players hurl cabbages and eggs at you.
Oh, and this game also has raids, pvp, and a whole ass battle royale system built into it. This game tries to do a bit of everything and amazingly, it kinda pulls it off!

There's enough content packed into this one game that anyone should be able to find something they like. Don't want to fight? Just explore, take screenshots, play musical instruments (players have figured out Linkin Park on the Guzheng), heal NPCs or other players, dance, wrestle, play chess, quiz, wrestle, [b]build houses[/b]... the list goes on. 
Want hardcore fights? Fight challenging bosses solo or co-op (Legend difficulty is no joke), take out enemy camps head on or stealthily, tune your gear, experiment with different builds, join raids etc...

You get the idea. There is a ridiculous number of things you can do in this game. And it's all [b]free[/b], so what's there to lose by giving it a try?

There's a lot to love in this game. It's an open world which is extremely pretty, engaging and full of cultural references. Just exploring has helped me understand better various Chinese films which drew on those references without ever explaining them.

Combat is solid. Bosses are hard and unforgiving but they're a tiny part of the game (and some people enjoy the challenge, and I haven't turned down difficulty).

It's free to play so there are various mechanics which constrain your progress, but I'm already 'max' level and I still haven't done half the story. The story is.. well, there are a lot of stories. Side quests are interesting, standalone campaigns (within the broader world) are nice but quick, the main campaign is well enough written and fine - until you reach Kaifeng. Then it feels they switched game designer and instead of a lot of doing with minimal cutscenes it becomes a lot of cutscenes and minimal doing. Really don't need exposition while walking slowly through a city bored senseless.

But that's again a small part of the game. There's lots to do and see, and even now, having not explored a third of the map, there's a long list of things I want to go back and do in the parts I've already seen.

Then there's the online element. I'm in pseudo-online; signposts (messages) left by players are visible but I'm in a solo gameworld. I can if I choose switch to a populated world, and also join specific co-op missions. Apparently there's PVP but I'm avoiding that.

The biggest issue is the multitude of game mechanics, 'currencies', etc. You need to gather dozens of different components to progress, and there's minimal guidance on this, and the game translation is somewhat janky. But I play with Chinese voices which really adds to the sense of place the game offers, and the story translations are good enough.

So overall there's an awful lot to enjoy in this game; I'd have happily paid full price for it; being free to play makes me guilty that I'm getting this much enjoyment without giving the developers any money. I guess I should buy some cosmetics..

Skins are all gacha and weapon skin customization has the most atrocious money scam system ever without prior warning. (basically youre forced to reforge your weapon for 200 bucks and the colors and effects are randomized unless you lock an attribute, which also makes you have to pay more money.
The UI is absolutely horrendous to learn at first and there are a ton of systems to learn. Even with 100 hours I struggle to remember some of the buttons entirely correctly. 
Theres an AI customization feature, and its really bad.
In my experience the fps drops as you keep playing the game but you can simply restart it and it'll be fine.
I've only had 1 bug, which happened in the main quest and made me struggle to open a door (the one where you open it together).

Putting all of this aside tho, the game is absolute PEAK. The crazy UI design is part of the idea that this game is everything at once. The game functions like a souls-like genshin while also HAVING end-game and really good online functions and gameplay. The game gives a lot of appearances out for free and has a lot of good customization options even with the lack of some features, and a lackluster AI feature. I think the AI concept itself will eventually be a really good idea that will make the customization even better. Even now tho we already have spongebob in game which i have yet to see in any other game. 

The combat system in the game is pretty much flawless, besides the fact i think its easier than other souls-likes even at the hardest difficulty, and with some attacks dealing damage when they shouldn't. Besides this the combat is super fun and parries are satisfying to do. Dodges feel less useful and more buggy but feel good when you pull them off as well. The weapons and weapon types in the game are amazing and even the first weapon arts you learn are beyond goated. Martial arts are also varied and super fun.

The exploration in this game feels worthwhile as you get super good buffs from oddities and can find cool and fun quests with good rewards. The world itself is beautiful and definitely has an identity i like a lot. You also have lightless skills that help traverse much faster and make the exploration easier to get through if you get a bit bored of collecting oddities or running around the beautiful scenery. 

The story is quite good with a few bad translations, but i think its quite coherent and easy to understand. I enjoy the storytelling and how the characters are connected. I also really like the name of the main quest (chpt 1) as its well thought-out and you only really realize how good it is after youve completed the first chapter (in qhinhe).

Finally, I'd say the game has a lot of rough sides but the concept and the design of both the combat and the aesthetics really make the game a strong 9.9/10 for me and probably gotta be the best free game ive ever laid my hands on, with only a few paid games being as good or better. The only thing keeping it off of being a 10 is the expensive appearances (especially the weapons, to which i cant afford it and theyre really good) and the technical flaws that objectively take away from the game, but honestly don't really bother me enough to be a major issue, which is why the game still stays at a super strong rating. Overall though I can't recommend this game enough. 

side note: you can also yeet bears, turn your weapons ablaze, spew fire out of your mouth, literally fly, pet kitties and theres a MEOW MEOW temple.

At first glance this seems like the next big thing. However after a few hours of gameplay, it quickly materializes as derivative AI slop. AI was clearly used in many of the development processes. It feels fast and loose, poorly QA'd, and somewhat cheap. i really really want to like this game. For the first hour I was genuinely engrossed and thought I had found my next "thing". But at the General's Shrine basement level (the first dungeon) I could see cracks in the hull. Alot of the textures and models seem AI generated and the enemy logistics is simply not on par with other 2025 games, leading me to believe that at least some of the coding was AI derived as well. This is all but confirmed when you encounter several AI NPCs that act as chatbots that you have to pass a conversation with to earn their favor. It seems like a shiny new use for AI and honestly it is a unique idea. But in practice it adds to the feeling that the game was made as a gacha mill. This brings me to my next big gripe. Looking at the store and at other reviews, the cosmetic purchases are ridiculously convoluted to obtain, requiring multiple currencies that total an astronomical real world amount. I get that a dev has to make money from a F2P game and from what I can see these are only cosmetics, but this is simply ridiculous. Not to mention the UI is all over the place. Menus upon menus and different shiny things to click on to make the notification dots go away all to obfuscate the lack of actual depth. 
The IDEA, the framework of this game, is VERY solid. It's a good concept, and done differently, properly, over a couple of years without AI with a solid team of devs and a concrete price tag without the fremium gacha model (Maybe even $60 range) I would buy it. As it is now, I can't escape the feeling that this is held together by glue and tape and that if I spend much longer in the game I'm going to regret it. 

I had forgot to mention earlier: I encountered a bug in the General's Shrine arena combatant roster and the subquest from the man sitting next to the rock that simply didn't make sense logistically. I had already fought each of the beginning 4 contestants before speaking to the man, then it acted like I hadn't been in any fights and asked me to fight each of them to size them up. Then I fought each of them again one by one and it only checked off 3, then after I went back to the man I was given the quest reward despite not checking off the 4th. Then that checklist stayed in my active quests until I fought the boss, then went back to the man, 4th contestant still unchecked, and it marked the quest as complete and cleared the list, despite already receiving the reward.

TL;DR: Don't be fooled. For the first hour I thought I found my next time sink that I would spent countless hours on. However that quickly faded as the game was quickly revealed to be held together by duct tape and glue. AI seems to have been used heavily in development and there's so many small details that just feel off. Gacha mechanics are astronomically priced (yes even though you don't need them to play). This EXACT same concept, made without AI and without the gacha model, could easily sell for $60. Until that happens, don't waste your time.

if i had to sum this game up in a sentence, it would be: this game is all gravy, no meat... or in other words, another visit from our friendly neighborhood hero, Potential Man.

it has a lot going on, almost too much going on, but nothing holding it together. it mixes soulslike combat, "fluid" parkour, stealth elements, and a ghost of tsushima-stype open world, but none of those systems have any real substance behind them.

what do i mean by this? the combat looks soulslike, but it doesn't feel deliberate. the movement is smooth, until you're too close to certain geometry, then it becomes sticky and frustrating. stealth technically exists, but it feels like something included because the genre demanded it, not because the game could use it.

the open world is easily one of the biggest strong points for this game, but like most ambitious open worlds, it's empty. there are things to do, puzzles, exploration, points of interest, but it all feels hollow with little meaningful interactions inbetween.

so, yeah. it has a checklist of cool features, but none of them land with an impact. everything looks good, nothing feels great. some people will love this game, but i'm not one of them.

Where Winds Meet – Feedback So Far

I’m absolutely loving Where Winds Meet so far. The story is fantastic, the visuals are a straight 10/10 and the character models and customization options are some of the best I’ve seen in any game. Weapon designs are incredibly well done and the variety keeps combat interesting. Overall gameplay feels smooth, steady and consistently engaging.

That said, there are a few areas that could make the experience even better:

Energy Costs for Bosses and POIs: The current energy system can feel a bit restrictive. Either reducing the energy required or offering more frequent or accessible ways to earn energy would make exploration and boss encounters flow more naturally.*

Healing in PvP Bounties: Healing feels a little overtuned in PvP bounty fights. Either lowering the effectiveness or adding a mechanic that allows players to interrupt or temporarily disable healing would help keep battles fair and skill-based.*

RNG on Weapon and Armor Rolls: The RNG system can feel punishing. While god rolls shouldn’t be easy, having gear roll poorly 99 out of 100 times makes progression feel more frustrating than rewarding. Slightly improving the balance here would go a long way without removing the challenge.*

Overall, the foundation of the game is amazing and refining these systems would help it reach its full potential. Looking forward to seeing how the game evolves!

Honestly, it deserves Game Of The Year as a free game.

Where Winds Meet is a great combination of various game mechanics intertwined into one. The "Pay-To-Win" mechanics are soft in this entry and are only available for energy, materials, and cosmetics, via Battle Pass, Monthly Pass, and its in-game currency via real life purchases, pearls (I'm pretty sure that's the name, don't quote me on that one).

The energy is a significant purchase as it can be used to acquire valuable materials that enhance your "Power Level" in-game - or what this game refers to as "Martial Mastery". Each day the energy is renewed, but through purchasing additional energy, you may continue to obtain further rewards.

The open-world is satisfying to explore, where there are literally events happening around every nook-and-cranny. From platforming mechanics, to card games, to even Sumo Wrestling! Collect-Them-All gameplay as well, and various other achievements one may strive to acquire. The game even features countless leaderboards for a multitude of activities.

And although this game has a lot to offer. It falls short with the time-gated mechanics and the drip-feeding that they provide us.

Personally, I like to think the Battle Pass, and the Monthly Pass cover a full-fledged games price, so that diffuses the Free-To-Play entry that this has. So I can't just simple appreciate it through the lens of a Free-To-Play player. Instead, I feel that this game as having some form of "Membership". The Gacha mechanics in this are purely for cosmetics things and the Boat that you can purchase is obscene, but nonetheless it is there (I have heard people are welcome to buy it, for a whopping 44K US dollars!).

I firmly believe that this game will have you engulfed for countless hours on-end. You will definitely be getting your "moneys worth".

I recommend this game, 7.5/10, good game.

          This is not just a game. it’s a master piece a work of art that stands as a monument to the boundless creativity and vision of its developers. From the very first moment you step into its world, you are greeted by a universe that feels alive. It’s a creation so beautiful, so thoughtfully designed, that it feels like each moment was painted onto the canvas of the game world with the precision and care of a master artist wielding a paintbrush.
    Many of the most AMAZING!!! features of this game is the character creation system. Which is I think is just so cleverly designed. The level of customization is insane it offers an incredible array of choices that allow you to shape a character who feels completely unique. What makes it even more impressive is the blend of A.I Tech that allows for in-depth character creation based on your own voice or a simple picture( or pictures I had to get the right angle :P )). The different variations really helps break down barriers in the gaming experience. Creating a personal connection to the character in ways that most games could only dream of. The possibilities are endless...going to say this again ENDLESSSS!!! ......and no two characters feel the same, giving every player the chance to create their own distinct "identity" in this Amazing world.
    And then there’s the story, oh, the story!!!! While the main Story is flavorful all on its own right, it’s the depth and richness of the world building and side story's that truly sets this game apart!! Every character you encounter has a life, a history, and motivations (( sometimes even forceful at times)) that extend far beyond the main storyline. The developers have poured incredible attention to detail into crafting side quests that are not mere quests *cough go kill some orcs Cough* but many layered experiences in their own right. These quests don’t just serve as filler  they offer meaningful, emotional moments that can sometimes pull you so deeply into their world that you forget about the main plot altogether. It’s easy to get lost in the lives of the NPCs, building connections and friendships that feel real and earned, which is a rare feat in open-world games.
   The game world itself is a true open world experience. The term "open-world" gets tossed.....tossed...toss a coin to your..... hero?...... around a lot, but "Where the Winds Meet" redefines the genree...geraa..gerne..bleh.. There are no invisible walls, no areas blocked off by the limitations of a game engine. At least I havent found yet, I guess if your not supposed to go there I can understand. *tangent* You can literally go anywhere and do anything. The sense of freedom is exhilarating,..makes me a bit hyper especially when i am running from bounty hunters!!! and it’s backed by a level of immersion that makes each area feel alive with possibilitys. From crafting in all its forms to playing music in a tavern or even engaging in common labor, there’s always something to do, something to explore. Every corner of the world feels rich with opportunity, inviting you to live within it rather than simply pass through.
     In the end, "Where the Winds Meet" is more than just a game. It’s a living, breathing masterpiece that pushes the boundaries of what we think is possible in the world of open-world RPGs. It’s a celebration of creativity, freedom, and storytelling that will leave you coming back for more, long after the credits roll.

While the game has really nice visuals, there is a lot about the game that generally just irks me. 

1. This game is heavy on AI. I can tell that at least some NPCs use AI voicing, and it sounds horrible. 
2. This game has a really bad issue with translation/localization. There are parts of the game in Mandarin/Cantonese, without any way of translating it. Some text things have a built-in translation function, but not all... so some aspects of the game you just kind of have to guess.
3. The first day I played, everything loaded/rendered in very well. Every day after, my character T-poses while running and falling. I walk into an area and it takes a minute or two for assets to render in. I click "F" to interact with something and it takes like 5 seconds for the interaction to start.
4. The game does a really poor job of explaining aspects of the game. After nearly a week, there's still so much of the game, including combat mechanics, that are/were never alluded to at any point, especially in the "tutorial" in the beginning, so I guess you're expected to find out things on your own? This also speaks to how convoluted this game is combat-wise. Sometimes less is more. 
Overall, it feels like the developers did the bare minimum to create the game and overutilized AI. At the very least, the game is free, or I'd probably want to get my money back. Honestly, if this game is a representation of using AI in video games moving forward, the future is B L E A K.

I avoid gacha games, and games with cosmetic dlc, because 'it's just cosmetic' is just not valid for me since I care more about cosmetic things than I do about power or anything.
that all said, I love the cosmetics in this game, because I'm a fan of the wuxia stuff in general.
I'm also a big fan that the 140 dollar skin, and the 50 dollar skins, and the 1000 dollar gacha pull skins are so full of themselves that I don't find them aesthetic. Genuinely, the gacha is filled with potions and other things you can easily make yourself, and you never ever get anything that isn't that. So it's so much better at decentivising me from actually trying. Other games would offer an emote, or subpar outfits that I can take as a silver medal and enjoy my wasted money via sunk cost, but this game is good enough to not do that.

gacha stuff aside, I've pulled almost 40 times on the gacha, and paid nothing to it because they have them available for an echo, there is anotehr in game currency only gacha that I do all the time too, but it doesn't keep count of that one. Again, you get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ nothing from doing it, but potions and ♥♥♥♥.
I got the battle pass, because it gives me little battle pass tickets I use to buy stuff, and I got the monthy allowance, because it's 15 bucks all told a month, which is still less than I spent on ffxiv.

♥♥♥♥♥♥ great game, great game play, great systems. Love fighting, love healing, love the mini games, love that the mini games are used to improve passive stats, so if you've got a build you want you'll have minigames you'll have to get good at so you can increase your power.
Love the weapons, finally a game where I can use an umbrella and fan, and it's not just a reskin of the sword moves.
Love the wuxia fantasy
Love the little npc ai that lets you convince them to be your friends.
Love just about everything, 
THey have a reward system for playing with your friends
the reward system also rewards you for marriage
and there is another reward system for playing with guild mates
and yet another for making a regular party that you play with
so with one person you can get 4 different kinds of rewards with regular play!
and again, I don't have my usual instinct to just try the gacha
I think part of that is they put out outfits that are aesthetic as ♥♥♥♥, and cost 1 dollar.

Where Winds Meet is honestly a breath of fresh air. The combat is insanely smooth and cinematic — every fight feels like a wuxia scene you’re directing. Movement, combos, and weapon skills just click in a way most MMOs never manage, and I feel like I have way more control over my character compared to other games.

What makes it even better is how polished it is. I’ve run into almost no bugs at all, which is crazy for a huge open-world RPG. And after playing Guild Wars 2 for about eight years, it’s shocking how much better this feels. GW2 is outdated, full of issues and constant patch clutter… meanwhile WWM just slaps. It’s smoother, cleaner, and way more satisfying.

I also love that I can play completely solo without being punished, or switch to multiplayer whenever I want. That freedom makes the whole world feel alive and flexible.

And going forward, I’m really looking forward to more fashion, more difficult encounters, and new content to push the game even further. It already feels amazing — I just want to see it grow.

Overall? Huge surprise, super fun, barely any bugs, and easily one of the best new RPGs I’ve touched in years. I’m absolutely sticking with WWM!

At the bottom i have some good things to say but the next point after this update here is why i stop playing, eventho the game itself is fun and has a lot of love put into it. If you dont care about challenges, ignore that point:

Ok update after playing 98 more hours: You can officially buy no-hit runs for 78 beads (60 beads = 1€). To me thats completely pathetic to even defend in any way while calling it challenges and achievements.
