Pretty disheartening to see after im 6/10 no-hits run deep.
Do i need an official badge? No. Do i want integrity of an official challenge? Yes.

The latest update brought quite the good performance upgrade and all. Some other QoL, its nice.
But the p2w through challenges that even autocompletes after some time is just insane to me... Which i decided to just vote with me not playing it.

Multiplayer Co-op is insanely buggy too (but not the group bossfights for high levels))
Some optional NPCs are AI voiced (i guess) and their audio quality varies wildly. Its okay but its immersion breaking to me. 
Especially there are so many weird things like a whole area becomes invisible in certain angles. 
Underground you can often just run out of bounds, maybe fall too.
Voiced dialogues sometimes just repeat itself or overlap.

Cutscenes can also sometimes break, especially in multiplayer players would not get the cutscene... scene... so they can move freely and see the scene play out. Maybe even run into the view of other players.
This is actually pretty hilarious.

The movement is also super janky. Your character will take a step to slow down, even if you tap forward once. That makes precise movement or just turning around a nightmare. Often i see myself jumping over the same thing 3x because my character decided to walk off of it or climb back over.
It gets even worse when you unlock the anime style sprint where your character gets pretty fast and can jump over big obstacles... but you can not run through gates anymore because your character will leap to the gate left and right and if you try to guide it back to the ground to walk through that gate where like 6 people next to eachother can walk through, it will just jump back again.

its so silly to me because your character is this super human fantasy whatever where you can blink after your sword and all but you get all these damn slow climbing animations and fall-recoveries that sometimes youre just faster running the roads than actually jump over houses where you often have to jump over or get into climbing animations when going over the top of the roof.

Some skills dont work at all in multiplayer. Its stated in their descriptions that only the host may use them, but even the host cant successfully use them most of the time which is super janky.

Often you see floating objects too. Very much so actually.

Mainstory can be somehow played together until you just automatically kick your co-op players at which point your friends have to do the same thing by themselves just now. However once you get to the bossfight you can somehow do get assistances... but its weird and i dunno how it really works. I wanna play with my friends but its just so damn weird.

Its fun when it works though.
also pretty chill just roaming around sometimes and just yap in voice chat while we try find all the collectibles together. Which are shared and often someone finds something in areas i already was but i didnt find that one thing or did that puzzle so they completed it for me.
Sounds weird but theres a collectible every minute of playtime basically. The game has a map and shows things on the minimap. You also get a button to check your surroundings and sort of show you the directions to complete certain things. 
Which is nice, sometimes i just dont wanna use my brain too much. Mostly played without all the assistances and sometimes refrain from viewing player made signposts to not spoil the puzzle. Some puzzles i dont like and often theres someone who wrote down the solution. 

Now that brings me to the greatest part of the game: The signposts.
You know the soulsgame where "Finger but hole" or all that silly crap. Now this game just lets you type out 60 letters freely. And you can attach an ingame made screenshot (even lets you select pics you made recently... they get deleted after a while, not just 30 days) and that just makes this so creative and entertaining.

You have your usual subjects that are very deprived of sensations. Then theres someone like me who just uses all of my signpost slots to tag every statue with the comment "Dog" or show off out of bounds pictures with a little guide on how to get there.

its even more insane when you are out of bounds and find someones signpost there.
Getting somewhere completely useless just to find someones signpost and you see other people talking a whole lotta brainrot is just peak internet to me.

This feature alone is just awesome.

Then theres combat, which is another thing getting me nostalgic. It reminds me of GunZ the duel.
I love bosses here and i feel like its how i wanted them to be in the Dark Souls 3 DLCs and Elden Ring. Maybe i should have played Sekiro too but i never did.
Theyre not a pushover in legendary, although due to too many menus and upgrade layers i leveled up too quickly and made the game insanely damn hard. But once you find the rythmn to the bosses movesets, its very satisfying.
You can deflect out of almost every animation you do, that means you can be super damn aggressive and still live through it.

The game has a bunch of assistances outside legendary mode where you can apparently slow time to help you deflect or dodge. Inside all modes you also get some passives where you get invincible for a bit if you would die and it has a rather short cooldown, but the bosses are so aggressive that this wont help you all too much even if you play around it too much. But knowing its there allows you to be aggressive until its on cooldown.

You can also play a healer and its fun. Most quest bosses do reduce your healing done by 90% though so you have to learn them or just ask friends to help you.

Theres additional challenges you can put onto your profile if you complete them all for a boss. I think all of the challenges contain that you cant take any damage from a boss though. But its really great that you can show off.

Its another thing i like, showing off personal achievements like that. Sadly there arent too many of those and i wish there were more little achievement rewards to wear and show off too.
(now after i learned you can just buy them defeats the point to me)

Monetary wise i dont see a reason to pay up at all (yet).
The levels are capped but theyre increasing it over time which introduces more content as well.
People cry over it, i dont see the point. All progress between these batches are tied to another upgrade system so everyone has to go through the brackets and upgrade their gear anyways so you get stronger for higher content.

Take a look though, especially if you enjoy a challenge pick the legendary mode!

I was very on the fence on whether or not I liked this game. But the more I played the more depth I found, and the more fun I had. There is still a lot of work to be done on this game, but if the chinese version is any indication a lot of my complaints will disappear when the global version catches up.

There is one undeniable positive about WWM - it is massive and pretty beautiful. Looking over Kaifeng from the city walls produces one of the best vistas in games ever.

Unfortunately, this is where the positives end and what you're left with is shallow slop. It might take you a while because of the sheer amount of different types of content, but you will eventually realise there is absolutely 0 depth in any of the systems. 
Combat? Sure, you get 10 different styles, but they all only have 2 abilities with 0 meaningful synergy between them. 
Gearing? You get 10 different systems, but every piece of gear is just a stat stick (which you don't even see since you only see the equipped costume), and every one of these systems does nothing except increase stats. 
Mini-games? You get 20 of them, but (aside of music, which is admittedly decent), they all consist of 2-clicks gameplay that you "master" on the first attempt.

Even then it might be somewhat enjoyable or have some potential if not for the absolute ungodly amount of jank and bugs. From the technical standpoint, it feels like the game is barely in early alpha. I'm not even going to elaborate on that part, the jank basically hits you right as you log into the game and never lets go - there is no system that simply plays smoothly and the UI is definitely the worst I've seen in games ever.
When IGN says it's bad, you know it's a MUST play.

The time gating is as annoying as it gets and the main complaint I have about the game.  At first it wasn't that bad, a day or two.  However, once you start hitting 50+ that gate goes to 9+ days.  Absolutely horrible design decision.  While I can understand the need to slow content clears by speed runners, putting a time gate in what is essentially a single player RPG is flat out ridiculous!  As if that wasn't bad enough, you also get a weekly cap on how much you can earn for coin, jade fish, and other currency.  But wait, there's even more gated content!  10-man raids - only one a week.  New story?  Wait another week.

The scenery is beautiful, the story in engaging, combat needs a little work but is pretty solid.  Each area has had a great amount of thought put into it, that much is evident.  

With all the different martial arts, compendium entries, trials, lost lore, etc you'll spend a great amount of time just trying to complete a single area of a given region.  Unlocking everything will definitely fall into the 150+ hour mark unless you look everything up with little to no exploration on your own.

With the game being playable in solo, co-op, and online modes you have the freedom to play how you like.

Overall, a decent experience so far with much more to explore.  As a free-to-play game, you can't really complain too much.  However at the current pace of the game, the constant time gating, and the one character limitation I don't see many players continuing to play WWM after finishing the main story arc.  

The cosmetics available without buying anything in their shop, which is absurdly overpriced, more than suffice to get the job done.  Be smart and don't sink a single dime into this game until you reach level cap and have an actual desire to continue playing.  Games like this work off of impulse purchases and with random chance boxes for the gambling addicts trying to get that super rare cosmetic with the 0.00001% chance to get it.

TLDR: Gud game 8ish/10, it's free give it a try, and don't skip story cutscenes ffs.

Alright so now that I have played this game for 2 weeks and put in a lot of time (mostly on epic launcher hence only 32 here) I feel like I can rate this game fairly well. It is a very well crafted game that spans multiple genres, it has some genshin type exploration and world difficulty, some souls like bosses, a sprinkling of sekiro (parry is extremely forgiving here btw), some naraka, and some other games that slip my mind right now. I am going to first talk about the story.

The main campaigns (only 2 atm) are in my opinion well done, a lot of the player-npc interactions feel a bit off due to either ai voicing (they chose a trash voice) or a bad chinese translation. But the overarching story for the first and especially second campaign left me thinking about it for a while which is a good sign that it was thought out. Both also have a few plot twists that were very interesting and certainly unexpected to see, which is refreshing. For side campaigns, I find myself still interested in them enough to read or watch the cutscenes, and don't forget item descriptions.

The Combat in WWM is pretty good, it could use some minor polishing here or there but overall its well made, I would say it's not as fluid as say Naraka, but it is more complex. On the PvE side the enemies dont have many move sets and are mainly just sponges, but I suppose that is to be expected of open world fodder enemies. The bosses on the other hand are really comparable to souls bosses, they make sense in their own niche area of the map (for the most part). On the PvP side it is IMO a bit boring. Either you fight a guy that can combo out the wazoo, or like in my case, you spend 15 minutes fighting a guy with 2 healing weapons that just out heals the dmg you do, at which point you either choke on your own healing or give up. But at least there is a battle royale mode and bounty system to make it interesting to some degree. 

The progression is fairly easy as you are given items of your corresponding level by just opening boxes/crates. And it's really just a matter of unlocking the right to use weapons or skills then tuning them.

The monetization in this game is relatively fair, as skins range from ~$0.60 - $25, then of course there is the $500 skins which you gamble for and the $40,000 whale skin. This games is entirely free to play and anything you get from the shop that has an impact on your gameplay is very minor.

The multiplayer aspect of this game is interesting, if you have heard that it is an mmo lite let me explain. There is a coop mode where (i think up to 3) friends can join your world, and do most everything with you, from (including some campaign) bosses to dungeons, to open world exploration. Then there is the online mode where the world switches to a slightly different version and everyone can play together (mostly sit afk in cities). There are also a lot of (mostly) fun activities that can be done, rythym games, running track, some board games, and other mini games, and some coop special missions and stuff. And I cant forget there is marriage to players here, so you get rewarded for edating and stuff...

But yeah it's a good game overall, I probably glazed the story mode, and it's not like this game is the holy grail, and honestly I am surprised it got so much attention. It's a "pretty good" type game, so like an 8ish / 10 its free so give it a try.

I have to sadly give this game a negative review, it starts off very strong, despite the incredibly generic and painful to hear main character and their hero story. The gameplay in the beginning is really fun, it's fair and square but:

When you get any further into the game, you can see the
- excessive grinding
   - you need to do so many repetetive, mindless tasks, to slightly upgrade yourself so you can progress in the storyline 
      to unlock new areas and fighting styles
    - if you want proper healing items, that are by base kept to a max of 3 per Rest at a Hero's tomb, which is the 
       equivalent of a site of grace from eldenring, you need to GRIND the healing item by leveling up a entirely seperate 
       skill, just so you can craft the item to use it. And then they aren't even unlimited
       - Furthermore, healing in this game is incredibly stupid, as you can't even rest at a hero's tomb all the time, until 
          your HP is critically low

- luck embued into EVERYTHING in this game
   - Obtaining equipment rarity is RNG, getting the right, useful equipment upgrades is INCREDIBLY rare
   - the damage output you deal is by base RNG

- The game is filled to the brim with gambling microtransactions everywhere, which are insanely expensive and are by 
   nature predatory

- Region Locked gameplay and store mechanics
   - If you are playing on the global, non-china servers, then you are unfortunately going to be behind a new update for 
      serveral days, if not weeks
   - You are also out of luck on cosmetics, because some of the cosmetics can be gambled for, costing an expected 
      amount of 130 EURO, which if you were in china, you could buy straight away for the equivalent of 30 EURO

- Severe gameplay quality drop the further you progress
   - In the beginning of the game, you rarely fight strong enemies and get introduced into the game slowly, over time 
      you fight a few bosses with well spaced time inbetween. Later in the game, you will have 5 incredibly poorly made 
      bosses with terribly high stats thrown at you, that have barely reactable attacks, simply because the animations are 
      so terrible
    - the narrative also takes a drastic turn, strangely getting incredibly serious for a game where you play as a 16 year 
       old child and are happy about your adventures as a hero just before
       - the pacing also is incredibly inconsistant. At the start you can follow the story very well, but later on, it just gets 
          so chaotic because everything is paced so fast and you cannot really follow, especially since some things that 
          are crucial never get elaborated on and then suddenly are phased out
          - Later on, you also kill very lore relevant characters and nothing happens.
    - Map quality also worsens if you get far enough into the game, as in some late game mission areas, you can easily 
       go out of bounds, by walking a path which is incredibly easy to unintentionally walk into

- Poor optimization
   - It takes a pretty beefy PC to run this game, it takes aeons to load in everything and if you happen to change a 
      major area during a TP, then you are out of luck and need to wait an estimated amount of ~5 Minutes before you 
      can play again.
    - Atleast for me the game atleast runs smoothly, once it finished loading, I have had people tell me otherwise 
       however

- The PvP is in a terrible state as of right now
      I personally like PvP, however there is such a terrible imbalance in everything, because there are very few weapons, 
      of which their light attacks can trigger a true stun chain combo, allowing to true stun more combo extending 
      moves into one another, and so on. There are many weapons in the game, which lack this M1 True stun, which is 
      horrendously bad, as the move to break out of these true stun combos has a 35 second cooldown, making these 
      true stun combos devastating and the damage output of weapons which do not feature true stun m1 chains cannot 
      come close to the damage done by these combo weapons

      Spamming skills instead of actually parrying and having a regular fight in PvP  is also something that is very much 
      encouraged, as most of the skills in game can autotrack on a very large distance and set you up for a combo 
      starter, as the defender actually punishes themselves by parrying your attack most of the time, as parrying has no 
      effect besides reducing the QI(Posture) of the enemy

      The matchmaking system is also far from ideal, as most of the time there will be a strong imablance in equipment 
      strength between two players, as it is entirely up to RNG how strong your equipment is.
      Half of the time the matchmaking system doesn't even find anyone for you in under a minute, so it just throws you 
       into a match with a very easy to defeat bot and still award you ranked points in a competitive gamemode
      The other half of the time, you will be put into servers that have very poor ping performance for yourself, despite

It's safe to say that I gave it a very fair chance, considering the fact that I completed the whole game in under 60~70 hours. I really tried to like this game. It's beautiful, but it has way too many shortcomings. 

The documentation in this game is really poor, even for a Chinese people like me. I've dealt with many confusing interface across the games and irl too, but this game really tops it off for me. The most important settings are hidden behind 7~8 pages of interfaces and I have to really look where I need to click to find it, and the help function is useless, it doesn't let you type more than a handful of characters in, probably because it's made with Chinese character limits in mind. The inventory section is poorly sorted and the icons are hard to decipher, and a lot of the things I've collected either serve no purpose or doesn't have a clear purpose, clogging up inventory and making it hard to read. I don't know. There are three main classes namely tank, DPS, healer, but the definition of the classes in this game is extremely blurry or nonexistent because anyone can be a healer and do an absurdly high amount of damage and take a lot of damage, it does not reward you and make you feel that you're getting better at any role, in fact it gets more punishing as the enemy balance continues to worsen the more bosses you encounter. If I have to search the Internet for "how-to" videos / wiki articles just to manage the basics, this is an entirely fundamental problem in this game. Even if I had the privilege to understand Chinese, I looked up multiple sites to find what I need help with, but there are either no guides, or anything relevant to this game's topic, even though this game has been out for more than a year at this point.

It feels the developers were so busy pouring in all of these "cool" features that they overlooked providing information to players about how to use / manage those features. And there are endless screens of stuff - constantly presented with new screens. Impossible to keep track of so much data.

The game feigns complexity by adding a bunch of jargon and word salad, even hard for a Chinese to understand. - it's just frustrating when there doesn't appear to be any path to understanding the complexity. Also the sickness system doesn't really do anything, it's just a bunch of added jargon to scare the players and all you need to do is either visit a clinic or have a player heal it for you, this system in particular lacks a lot of depth.

I play games for an obvious reason, either the gameplay is good, or the story presented is good, this game fails to achieve in both fronts. Everyone is very familiar with how buggy this game is and I'll skip over this part. The story however...not a lot talk about it, because it is genuinely not interesting, and there really isn't a character worth getting attached to nor remember about because they all act like an npc and act upon a very stupid reason, for each and every one of them, including the main character of this game. 

I'm not a quitter, but if the game continues to disappoint me since then, and I see no improvement, I'll drop this game at once.



可以说，我已经给了这个游戏很多的机会，我用了不到60~70个小时就通关了。我真的很想想喜欢这款游戏。它画面很美，但缺点实在太多了。

这款游戏的文档实在太差劲了，即使像我这样的中国人也难以理解。我在游戏和现实生活中都遇到过很多令人困惑的界面，但这款游戏绝对是其中最混乱的一个。最重要的设置竟然藏在七八页的界面后面，我必须仔细查找才能找到，而且帮助功能也形同虚设，输入的字数限制非常严格，可能是因为它是按照中文的字数限制设计的。物品栏的分类也很混乱，图标难以辨认，很多我收集到的东西要么毫无用处，或者用途不明，堆满了物品栏，很难阅读。我真是无语了。游戏里有三大职业：坦克、输出和治疗。但这些职业的定义极其模糊，甚至可以说是不存在的，因为任何人都可以治疗，而且输出伤害高得离谱，也能够承受很多伤害，一个火车砸下去都不会死的那种。这种设计既不会让你觉得自己在任何角色上有所进步，反而会随着遇到越多的怪平衡越来越差，觉得自己在游戏里没什么成长。如果我需要上网搜索教程视频/维基百科才能掌握基本操作，这绝对是游戏的一个根本性问题。即使我懂中文，我也查了很多网站，但要么找不到攻略，要么找不到任何与游戏相关的资料，而这款游戏已经上线一年多了。

感觉开发者们忙着堆砌各种炫酷的功能，却忽略了向玩家提供如何使用/管理这些功能的信息。而且游戏里充斥着无穷无尽的界面——新的界面层出不穷。根本无法追踪如此庞大的数据量。

这款游戏试图通过堆砌大量术语和晦涩难懂的文字来营造复杂性，就连中国人也难以理解。最令人沮丧的是，玩家似乎找不到任何理解这种复杂性的方法。此外，疾病系统也没有意思，只是用一堆术语吓唬玩家，玩家只需要去诊所或让其他玩家帮忙治疗即可。这个系统尤其缺乏深度。

我玩游戏的理由很明确：要么游戏性好，要么剧情好。而这款游戏在这两方面都表现不佳。大家都知道这款游戏漏洞百出，我就不赘述了。然而，剧情嘛……没什么好说的，因为它实在乏味，没有一个角色值得让人产生感情或印象深刻，因为他们都像NPC一样，而且每个人的哲学和缘由都愚蠢至极，包括游戏的主角在内。

我不是一遇到什么就退坑的人，但如果游戏之后继续让我失望，而且没有任何改进，我会立刻弃坑。

As someone in my 40s and a seasoned MMO vet with not much time on my hands, I'm enjoying myself thoroughly with WWM after New World's shutdown. I am amazed that this game combines so many ARPG, Multiplayer, MMO, PVP, and Co-op features into one solid, seemingly hyper performant package. It's also very refreshing to experience chinese culture and history as part of gameplay.

Pros:
- Awesome graphics and buttery smooth gameplay
- Very refreshing storyline
- Every quest is unique, every MSG is thoughtfully designed
- There's very little cookie cutter / cut and paste
- The gameplay loops are very enjoyable because the game plays really well
- I like the limits set on levelling speed, so that I don't tunnel and actually get to explore all the content it offers before the breaking through to new levels.
- They don't shy away from convenience, no making your life difficult here, focus on the game/immersion.
- No pay to win

Cons
- The stories are deep, and can be hard to follow, i use youtube to help round out the lore
- The localisation is ok, but can be better, it contributes to the above problem
- For how huge the game and numerous the quests are, some quests and even some bits of the MSQ sometimes come across unpolished, although i'm still impressed

I have thoroughly enjoyed every minute of the game I have played. Though, I can recommend this game to anyone at all there are a few quirks that I am not a fan of but those are mostly nitpicks and nothing major. 
I will go ahead and break down my experience in the following points.
Like: 
1. Visuals: These are absolutely breathtaking from the long expanse of grassy lands and tall mountains of Qinghe or the densly packed city of kaifeng the visuals are simply stunning. Its quite obvious that the artists have put in a lot of time and efforts creating the various assets used in the game and the environmental setup is simply next level as well.

2. Story: The main story is simply incredible: the destruction caused by war and thousands of sacrifices that go unheard of seem to be the main points of the story and overall I am loving it. The entire story of Tian Ying was heart wrenching to read, the way he shed off a piece of him every mission and in every act until all that existed were his shattered dreams and the echoes of what was. He by far outshined every other character till now [spoiler] and I can't wait to see him next with his new identity[/spoiler].

3. World: The world of this game genuinely feels alive. The encounters that I cam across were so random yet also so natural that I felt immersed in the Jianghu. Every time I would think that I want to progress the main story I would get side tracked by really interesting encounters and those would somehow lead me to campaigns or jainghu legacies till the point I completely forget my original purpose. I love when open world games do this, I would rather have a dense open world than a vast one and somehow they have achieved both in this title.

4. Multiplayer elements: The amount of stuff you can do online blew my mind when I first switched over to that mode. At first, I thought that the online elements will be constrained to guilds, raids, pvp and chat but nah they out here giving us everything. From mini games like wrestiling or archery contests to chess and mahjong, there is so much to do with you friends. With these many hours I haven't even tried everything that this game allows me to do. 

Dislikes: 
From here on out these are my personal preference and they may or may not affect the one who reads this. 
1. Object colliders: At first there are no issues but once you unlock wallstride from the oddities guy you will realize that some of the colliders are just not good. Specifically, running on the walls or passing through narrow passages like gates. Its clear that my character should just breeze past but he just starts doing backflips and climbing up nothing which also overall affects the sense of speed. This ability works phenomenally on straight plains or bodies of water but gets any aneurism on the slightest verticality of any sorts.

2. Oddities: At first I thoroughly enjoyed collecting odities but at this point when I have completely finished Qinghe I am still a few odities short and I cant find them for the life of me. What was once abundant is now scarce and there is no way for me to track the remaining ones so all I can do is just run aimlessly and hope I spot one on the minimap. Maybe there is a way to find and I dont know about it in which case this point is void. 

3. Long distance travel: Abilities like the thousand mile travel look flashy and all but actually travel 700 - 800 meters in-game max. I hope this distance is increased to around 1.5 so that it actually is viable because at this point its just not good enough to be used. I use it to travel only if the destination is around 500 and anything beyond 600 I just pull out the fast travel. 

Overall, it's a great game and in a world where AAA market is serving us straight ♥♥♥♥ this game stands as a beacon of quality and its free. 

To anyone who reads this I hope you enjoy the game just as much as me and I hope we come across each other in the Jianghu.

Been some time since i saw these many features and ideas flushed out in a single game.
Now do they all work well together? Sometimes.
The concept for a lot of the gameplay and progression is "Unique" for sure.
Do i like and recommend this game?
Hell yeah 9/10

I very much like a majority of the game. If you ever got into Genshin, Honkai Star Rail, or similar games you'll understand a lot of the upgrade mechanics. If you like souls-like bosses, you will also enjoy the game. Similarly, if you enjoy wuxia media, I think this is going to be fun for you. There is a clear sense of storytelling that aligns with the genre.

[h3]Things I liked:[/h3]
- [b]Bosses are similar to dark souls combat.[/b] I haven't attempted to fight them with friends yet, but taking them on as a solo player means they're very challenging in that way. (possibly even slightly more challenging than some dark souls bosses)
- [b]Puzzles are fun[/b] and the rewards are worth it once you find the shop needed to use them.
- [b]Exploration feels fun[/b] with lots of areas to go to, and everything you can spot can be reached (pretty much). No real areas of dead, lifeless world. There's something to see and do almost everywhere. There are a ton of movement mechanics so you never feel unable to reach things. Also each area is beautiful and unique. I can't wait for more!
- [b]Story releases periodically, and quickly.[/b] As global play catches up to the original this might slow, but I don't expect this to be a game where I need to play for 8 years and still be nowhere near the end of the story. 
- [b]Martial arts are fun to learn and use.[/b]
- [b]Wuxia storytelling is right on the money with tone and writing.[/b] I liked a lot of the cut scenes for the main story and enjoyed how over the top they were. I do think there are some areas where it jumps and it's a little jarring, but mostly they're really well done. 

[h3]Things I disliked:[/h3]
- [b]AI use in the game.[/b] Chat bots are present, but they aren't mandatory. However, it's clear when an npc starts out with a voice actor and they forgot to record a single line so their voice changes mid-conversation to the bot. Hate that.
- [b]Free to Play saving for skins is intense.[/b] The basic wish skins aren't as fun as the golden wish or paid ones. There are ways to obtain and save up your better wishes if you choose to remain free to play, but it's a long wait cause you can only purchase maybe 4 a week, assuming you have the currency to do so. Even then, a lot of the fancy skins that aren't banner pulls are paid. I do wish there was more of a way to wish as a free player, even if it means saving for longer?
- [b]Some of the mini games like "Gift of Gab" are extremely confusing[/b] when you first start, and the game initiates when you're still reading the tutorial text. Unknown if you're meant to read anything on the screen while playing but its a lot of text for no time (and I'm a fairly speedy reader)

This is my first ever Steam review. Writing this after 103.9 hours into the game. Let me tell you this, I have not finished the main story quests. I have played video games for 30 years or more and I absolutely love video games. I am a sucker for especially open world game and role playing game as well. This game has it all, it checked all the boxes for the type of game I like.

Okay, enough about my gaming history and let's get to it. First lets talk about the technical stuffs, this game engine is something, it looks beautiful and also stable. I have never experience any crashes or inconsistency in frame rate. I play this game on 2 devices, ASUS G14 2024 RTX 4060 with 32gb and ASUS ROG Ally X. Both runs smoothly, on my Ally X the small screen and put it on Medium with 900p with Frame Generation gets around 55-60 frames per second, if you want more FPS you need to drop it to 720p to get more. I play 1080p on my laptop and connect it to an external monitor, and it is amazing and stable. I am an abomination of a PC gamer, I use controller just to let you know.

In terms of bugs or glitches, I mostly encountered it on the map, especially tracking mob for materials. Other than that, everything else are smooth sailing. The fact that so minimal loading screen even when go to underground or discover dungeons is amazing, the game never tried to pull you away from the game with loading screen (looking at you Starfield).

Let's talk about the experience. On how I play this game, I just explore, run around, collect things, and thanks to playing Death's Stranding I barely do any fast travel, I walk and run. No mount. Exploring and curiousity are rewarded well in this game, I stumbled upon the Qinghe "campaign bosses" mostly by accidents. I explore, found quests explore a dungeon and then BOOM! THere is a boss at the end. I absolutely love it. I get wrecked most of the time, but that is the experience. Talking about getting wrecked by bosses, I play on recommended difficulty. I by no means a person that dabble into souls-borne game. In fact the only souls-borne game I finished was Elden Ring. The difficulty for me is fair, i do rage quit and stop fighting the boss and go do something else. That is the beauty, I can stop doing what I am doing and still enjoy the game. So in short, my experience so far is exploring, stumble upon bosses, dungeons, or quests. I think I need to finish the main story soon but I get distracted very easily. after 103 hours, I am only at 63% in Qinghe exploration. I just barely arrived in Kaifeng. 

So are there any bad things with this game, plenty. I am sure there are plenty of reviews pointing out the herendous UI and menus to keep track of everything. Especially when trying to get that RED NOTIFICATION AND YOU DON'T KNOW WHERE THE REWARDS ARE! Trying to know and upgrade skills and weapon took me almost a week to remember where there are. I am sure in the future if the devs really care about global audience they will fix this, but time will tell.

The gacha? All cosmetics and I have no idea what the rate are. I bought the Battlepass, just to see what is there to offered. I think the devs need to give better rewards after level 50 of the Battlepass. There are controversial decision that the devs made with prices on global version are more expensive than the China version. If you play this game you should voice out this concern, about us the global version players are not treated equally in terms of the pricing. Personally, I would not buy any of the 2k above cosmetics. Each of us choose to spend or not it is up to you.

Speaking of spending money or not, this game is still awesome if you don't buy cosmetic. i randomly finished a quest and it gave me a set of cosmetics! I'm like what? Really?! The cosmetic that was part of the reward from a quest looks good as well. The amount of content for a free-to-play game in this game is epicly HUGE!

Overall, this game is amazing. I love spending time in the world. Run around, explore, help people (I play healer) in the Multiplayer mode. I cannot even imagine the amount of content that are still not released to us yet. This is my main game now. Sacrificed a lot of games just to give space for this. I will keep on playing and hopefully the enthusiasm I have for exploring still burns bright like the Morning Star for time to comes. 

Hopefully this review makes you feel the same way as how I enjoyed the game. If you disagree, well, you are right. This is just my humble opinion. Nothing more, nothing less. Those that are on the fence give it a try. Those still playing and enjoying it, keep playing. This game respect your time, though it have been sucking the sleep out of me. But that is completely my fault. Well that's it, see you in the game.

“A Beautiful Chaos of Kung-Fu, Myth… and Bear-Throwing” — ★★★★☆ (9/10)

Where Winds Meet is an absolute blast — a gorgeous, chaotic wuxia playground where every cliff, village, and battlefield feels alive. The combat is fast, flashy, and packed with style, and the world begs you to explore every inch of it. But let’s be honest: none of that compares to the game’s greatest achievement…

You can throw a bear.

Yes. A full-sized, roaring, fur-covered beast — launched into the air by the sheer power of martial arts. That alone is worth at least 9 stars.

So why only a 9/10 and not a perfect score?

Because for some reason… you can’t throw wolves.
How do you let me grab a bear by the scruff and yeet it into the horizon but deny me the joy of wolf-launching? It's a tragedy of game design.

And while we’re on the topic…

Let me throw the bosses.

If I can hurl a bear into orbit, why can’t I pick up a towering armored warlord and send him flying with peak wuxia energy? The game’s already wild — just go all the way. Give me boss-yeeting.

Final Verdict:

9/10 — A spectacular, stylish wuxia adventure filled with freedom, flair, and unforgettable moments. Add wolf-throwing, boss-throwing, and it’s an easy 10/10 legend.

Important Survival Tip:

Do NOT fight the goose.
He is a martial god. You are but a wandering mortal. Respect him and walk away.

Where Winds Meet implements both tried and true mechanics while also exploring new ideas. 

It took me a while to like the title as I am not a fan of Wuxia films. The flying combat and 1 vs 1000 style of martial arts films don’t really appeal to me, yet they work really well for a video game. Couple that with a high combat difficulty (when playing on harder modes) and you can get a lot of enjoyment from this title.

If combat does not appeal to you, there are other MMO lifeskill-like elements to this game that might pique your interest. For example, you can make friends with a lot of NPC’s. Not all of them, but a fair number of them. To do this requires getting on their good side. How? Through an AI chat bot. Yes, you have to befriend NPC’s by chatting with them and encouraging them to do certain things. Each one is unique and can only discuss what they know. They are not ‘all knowing’ as most modern AI chatbots can be.

If you have a craving for a good MMO, this could be it. You can switch between solo mode and online mode which displays dozens of players at a time in the world. Each mode has their pros and cons and if you want the full experience, you’ll have to play through both modes. 

The only other game I can think of that does something similar is Elite: Dangerous. I’m glad the feature is picking up.

All in all, this game gets a 10/10 - it’s a solid MMO that tries a lot of new things (too much to list), so I suggest you give it a shot. It is free, after all.

Amazing Game. Fantastic. Oh my god. I downloaded it a week ago, I think, and it is the single greatest game I've played this year, and probably for the last couple of years too. I'm not a huge gamer, and by that I mean there aren't many games that truly grasp my attention enough for me to put in more than 10 hours of gameplay. The last game that held me like this was Undertale, and I played it almost three years ago so that's saying something. Usually not an MMO guy either, but I've always been into Wuxia after reading books like Legend of the Condor Heroes and Sword of Sorrow.

Anyway, I would 100% recommend it to anyone. It's free to play, there's no real Gacha system in the game, it runs really well despite the fact that I have a really crappy laptop, and the solo exploration mode by itself, is in my opinion good enough to warrant playing it. I have heard from a few people that it's really complicated for beginners and that the menu is overwhelming. I didn't really have that issue, and that's coming from a guy who's basically never played an MMO before, but be warned I guess.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Combat:
For a free-to-play game, the combat system is surprisingly decent, but it doesn’t come close to the depth or challenge of something like Elden Ring. Most boss fights can be beaten by simply standing your ground, timing attacks, and parrying without needing much movement or strategy. I haven’t tried the harder difficulties yet, so maybe they improve the experience, but I personally wish the game had a single fixed difficulty setting (with the exception of a dedicated hardcore mode).

Stealth, puzzles, and side activities:
The game really shines in its variety of side content. Stealth missions, puzzles, and other unique activities are creative and fun, adding a lot more playable hours and making the world feel more alive.

[b]Story[/b]
Side dialogues:
These are often dull and filled with unnecessary lines that don’t add to the lore or the main narrative. The worst part is when the game uses dialogue just to explain gameplay mechanics—there should be simpler, cleaner ways to teach the player without forcing them to read through long, pointless conversations.

Main story:
It can be hard to follow, mainly because the excessive dialogue makes it confusing to figure out what’s actually important. The story lacks strong character development, and many plot points feel predictable.

[b]Interface (UI/UX)[/b]
The interface is overwhelming when you first start. It’s cluttered with too many menus, tabs, and features that could easily be grouped together. All players really need is a clean inventory tab and a simple skill section. I want to play the game—not spend hours digging through menus.

[b]Graphics & Environment[/b]
This is one of the game’s strongest points. The visual quality is very good, and the world is huge and detailed. It’s genuinely impressive that a free-to-play game can deliver such a massive and visually appealing environment.
Latency issues aside, I feel guilty experience a game of this quality for free. If you don't care much for multiplayer its amazing.

Where Winds Meet has completely changed how I feel about MMOs, and it has exceeded every expectation for both me and my boyfriend. Ironically, this is actually the third game we’ve played from these developers — we started with Once Human and Naraka: Bladepoint but this one feels truly special.

The open-world Wuxia setting is gorgeous, the character creation is amazing, and the outfits, skins, and customization options are incredible. Mounts, movement, and mobility are smooth and stylish, making exploring and playing together so fun. The quests, story, and lore are engaging, and the multiplayer interactions are so fun, especially since you can form relationships and even get married in-game!

And… the cats. Being able to pet them, do Meow Meow puzzles, and earn buffs from them is just adorable. I hope future updates let us adopt animals because that would be perfect.

Combat is unique and exciting, and the ability to dye outfits adds so much personalization. I do hope cosmetic prices become more affordable and that future updates expand leveling progression and quests, but I’m genuinely excited to see where the game goes next.

Overall, Where Winds Meet brought me back to loving MMOs. It’s beautiful, interactive, cozy, and full of heart. I can’t wait to see what’s next!

Pros:
- gorgeous, large open world
- decent character creator
- an absolute boatload of things to do - collections, gathering, tons of lengthy side quests, puzzles, games
- unique healing system
- interesting weapons with enough variability in skills and animations
- free to play model is good so far, there's a good amount of cosmetics to earn in game by playing and participating, and there are also low-spending options.. for an example I got an outfit for $1

Cons:
- game modes (solo, co-op, multiplayer) are separate and confusing.  you play solo to quest and develop your character.  you can bring in a handful of friends to help with some things.  sometimes.  but only the party leader gets credit and loot.  sometimes.  the campaign is not available in co-op or multiplayer mode.  multiplayer activities are not available in solo mode.  you can fall off a cliff and break your ankle and you are forced into multiplayer mode to find a doctor (in the form of other players) to heal you.  but you have to switch all these modes manually.  and everything exists on the same map but you just can't interact with it if you aren't in the right game mode.
- combat rules also changes between game modes.  if you suck at action combat, like me, there is some dodge-assist mode that's available but only in solo mode.  co-op and multiplayer modes both have different combat rules.  it's hard to keep up and it makes combat overall feel very clunky because you're expecting something to work in one mode but it actually only works in a different mode.
- English voice overs are hilariously bad, make sure to switch to Chinese voices
- you will learn a bunch of terrain traversal skills that are not quickly or easily turned off and make it aggravating to move.  you learn how to run up walls and fly and stuff.. but they are skills you slot so you can't just turn it off, you have to go into a menu and manually unequip them.. but you need them for stuff so it's a pain to keep doing this.. so if you get too close to literally anything, be it a lamp post, a house, a tree.. you are going to run up it and leap into the air and fly off into the sunset even though all you wanted to do was talk to an npc standing nearby

I had a good time while I played it but the more advanced it got, the more skills I learned, the more I did.. the more it was getting to a point where the jankiness was outshining the fun parts so I think I'm done for now.  I do absolutely think the game is worth a try, just needs some more time in the oven.

WWM delivers a captivating, visually stunning open-world martial arts epic that feels less like a game and more like a journey through a living painting. Wherever you set foot, you’re met with an immersive scene that begs to be admired, making exploration not just a pastime, but a genuine pleasure.
The open world is rich with possibilities. You’re free to pursue what you enjoy most: engage in challenging combats (either PvE or PvP), or simply lose yourself in leisure activities.
Performance is another strong suit. The game is well optimized, running smoothly even on modest PC setups without sacrificing visual fidelity. 

That said, the game isn’t without its flaws. The menu interface presents a significant learning for beginners, with layered UI that can feel unintuitive at first. Furthermore, some boss fights suffer from awkward camera angles that can frustrate rather than challenge, for example: can't see shjt whenever the bosses jump up and land hit. Another downside is the bad netcode in PvP, where intermittent lag and latency issues can disrupt the precise timing required for competitive combat. Funny that I even had one player directly messaged me after a PvP match telling me to fix my ping whereas the issue is not on my end. Still, the game is incredibly good for a F2P title.

*Note for challenge seekers: start the game on Legend mode, it is fun. You can't switch to Legend once you choose to play on lower difficulty, don't know if devs are working on fixing this.

THE GOOD:
-Stellar story, if the story telling holds to the standard set by what we have now it will be sizing up to be in my top 5 story wise. The game does a fantastic job on easing you into the world and ramping up the tension as you progress. -No P2W, all gacha and items and sold in store items that can be bought with paid currency are purely cosmetic. (This is a double sided blade, see; THE BAD)

-Beautiful scenery and choreography, the animations and every step of the world is picture worthy.

-Character and Outfit Customization, this game features one of the most in depth character creators I've seen to date, you can view the creations of other players ranging from beautiful model characters to spongebob. -Raid mechanics, in depth and fun mechanics to keep boss fights interesting in the 10 man raids.

THE BAD:

-AI voice acting, very distracting during some points in the game. I finally switched to Chinese voice actors (which are fantastic) but I understand that not everyone wants to have to read everything the characters are saying.

THOUGHTS:

Overall I would highly recommend this game to just about every kind of player. I missed a lot of things in this review (both good and bad) but I hope I hit most of the high highs and the low lows. To me this game is a MUST PLAY.

I cannot in good conscience give this game a positive review until the LLM chatbot NPCs are removed unfortunately

EDIT:
having played more of the game now I feel like I'm in a place to give a more comprehensive review, and it's only fair that I do so. There's a lot to like here, even as someone who isn't all that into open world MMO type stuff: I'm a sucker for a good wuxia story, and it's a woefully underpopulated genre(at least among the games I've seen). The parry/deflection mechanic is decently satisfying, and it feels fantastic to hit that counterattack when you do it right, but outside of that I find myself underwhelmed by the combat. The moves feel airy and insubstantial, it's impossible to bind deflect to a mouse button(which is an issue on top of how weird and unintuitive it feels to have a deflect key separate from the block key), parries not interrupting enemy attack patterns is INCREDIBLY unsatisfying, and I often find my fights ending in a protracted sequence of clicking on one baddie over and over again until I break his qi and do a finisher, usually more than once. The exploration is engaging, and I enjoy the mobility whenever the game lets me use it, which I wish were slightly more often. There are, quite frankly, far too many menus, and I get the sense that figuring them out would eventually feel pretty rewarding but it strikes me first and foremost as a way to squeeze dopamine out of the player by letting them clear notifications over and over again. I wish there were a way to earn free draws somehow, but I guess a free game has to get its monetization where it can. I'm sure there's other stuff that I'll end up coming back to at some point, but the main problem I have with the game at this point really is just the LLM chatbots. 

When I play a game, I want everything in that game to be the way it is because a human being wanted it to be that way. I want intentionality! I want dialogue that exists for a purpose! An infinite well of conversation does nothing for me if it's procedurally generated filler extruded by an algorithm that has no way of knowing whether it's telling the truth, or whether anything it's saying has any bearing on the game. And even outside of the creative implications, the environmental impact of the technology means I wouldn't want to play a game that made use of it. 

TLDR: It's a pretty neat game. I like the themes, the setting is cool, and when the combat works it REALLY WORKS. The various mechanics and currencies seem cool and probably would feel rewarding to master, but they also come off as very skinner-box-y. The use of large language models is an unfortunate Achilles heel and in all honesty I'd probably give it a mildly reserved thumbs up if they were removed

Where Winds Meet isn’t a game — it’s a social experiment to see how fast you’ll question your intelligence. You load in thinking you’re a wuxia legend, but the game immediately clocks your skill level and goes,
“Ah yes… a disappointment has arrived.”
You think you’re a wuxia prodigy? Cute. The game takes one look at your button-mashing and says, “aw… adorable… now perish.”

Story? Honestly… I’m still not sure. NPCs talk like they’re dropping ancient wisdom, but half the time I’m too busy chasing butterflies or trying not to fall off cliffs. Priorities, right?

Parkour? Chef’s kiss. The climbing system makes you feel like Spider-Man got reincarnated as a martial artist. You will fall. You will scream. You will climb again. Growth mindset.

Performance? Depends. Some days it runs like a smooth kung-fu movie. Other days it feels like your GPU is writing its resignation letter.

Everything kills you.
Everything.
Even your own decisions.

Animals? They hate you.
Bandits? They mock you.
Gravity? It has a personal vendetta.

At this point, you’re not playing the game.
You’re performing cosmic slapstick for the universe’s amusement.

50/10 — your dignity will not survive, but at least the scenery is nice.

Game of the year. A pleasant blend of Ghost of Tsushima and Elden Ring.

Overwhelming. Mobile users come first. Essentially feels like a "Chinese super app"
There are literally hundreds of features, buttons, incremental rewards. It feels like they want you to play the menu, instead of the game.

Half of my playtime is repeating the same chinese chess mini-game, and trying to cure a rabid goose that is somehow more powerful than the tutorial boss. When I wanted to test out a gameplay feature, I was told I need to complete up to a hundred different quests before I could access the so called "choose how you want to experience the game" feature labeled across various sponsored videos.

I was told the game had incredible combat mechanics, yet when I tried it out, I could immediately recognize that it wasn't designed for controller or mouse & keyboard input in mind. Here's what it feels like:
You want to jump? Too bad, you are forced to block the attack.
You want to dash? Too bad, you are forced to block the attack.
You want to do a charged attack? Too bad, you are forced to... play an instrumental rythm game..?
The game's combat system is essentially a copy of Genshin Impact, but with better graphics.

It uses generative AI, which Steam failed to disclose, but I actually found it to be one of the more immersive features that the game had to offer. You're basically told to talk to NPCs, given a short description of what troubles them, and then have to talk to them in your own way (you write everything yourself).

The game is very optimized, so much so that even mediocre integrated graphics cards (780m) can run it at High settings, 900p, 60fps stable with some fsr frame gen. The graphics will however appear quite sharp to some players, but I like it that way.

I’m honestly surprised that Where Winds Meet is F2P. The amount of content in this game feels like something you’d normally pay full price for. Yeah there’s the time-gated level cap mechanic but I actually don’t mind it here because there’s so much to do in the meantime. Plus all the XP you earn gets saved and applied later anyway so nothing feels wasted.

I also really appreciate that the game isn’t pay-to-win. The gacha system being only for cosmetics is totally fine by me especially since the game hands out a bunch of dope looking outfits for free.

My only real complaint is the health potion system. I wish pots would refill automatically at camps or safe spots instead of actually being consumed. I’m fine with upgrading the amount you can carry but if I burn through 20 pots trying to learn a boss fight I end up having to craft or buy more. It makes dying feel like I’m losing real progress and it pushes me toward over-leveling just so I don’t waste resources. Same with gear durability dropping every time you die it doesn’t really add anything to the experience it just discourages me from learning tough fights by trial and error. 

Regardless I’m really enjoying the game overall and I’m excited to see where it goes in the future.

Here is my first impressions of this game:

The game visuals are rather good, even on lower end systems... It appears to try and do a bit of everything, from tons of exploration based content, to a somewhat linear main story, lots of side content busy work, and so forth... I found the whole Body Type 1 and 2 non-sense to be annoying when it is clearly male and female... A first for me was the inclusion of an import system that tries to take a photo and AI an in-game character face to match it somewhat... Didn't really feel like it did all that great of a job, but it is something new... Same with an import feature for altering the voice to try and match your own... Didn't experiment with that feature, so do not know how well it actually matches up...

The game's English translations seem to be done rather well, as it doesn't sound like broken-English, but the voice acting itself seems a bit over the top, which is not totally unsurprising... The combat system is simple at first, but becomes more and more complex as you progress... Combat style is based mostly on how you mix a total of 2 weapons together, as well as Martial Arts moves you actively choose to go with... I do have to say that combat flows very well, and does take some getting used to with so many variations... The world itself looks beautiful and well produced, and is filled with all sorts of collecting and exploration busy work... Enemies vary in difficulty, with a mixture of trash mobs all the way to boss mobs, with varying bullet sponge styled health bars... Your DPS varies based on your weapon combos as each weapon is designed with either Healing/Utility, DPS, and/or Tanking in mind...

This is a action based game even though it can take on some MMORPG styled content and game play now and then... You can either play it solo with the option of Co-Op in certain fights, or play it in a more traditional Co-Op MMO setting... In Solo, I did find lots and lots of player placed Sign Posts all over the place, with mostly useless snippets of text on them... The world is littered with them, and not all were in English... 

The game is Free To Play with a cash shop, but all items thus far seem to be cosmetic in nature... The developer has promised it has no future plans to monetize in such a way as to be P2W or give any sort of in-game advantages beyond visuals... Only time will tell if that stays true...

Overall, the game appears to be trying to do lots and lots of things, and includes a rather dense menu system with several different RPG styled progression systems... While I think the game has a bit more mass-appeal then other Wushu style games, there does seem to be a desire to be a jack-of-all-trades style game... The jury is still out if it is a master of all things it tries to accomplish, or just a master of some things and alright in others... The combat is a little more complex then more casual games while not trying to be as difficult as souls-like systems you see in other more recent games... Of course, difficulty is always a matter of perspective and experience, and will be influenced by your weapon and styles choices...

You could call it a [b]historical costume drama[/b].
Whether it's the main campaign or the side stories, the writers keep hitting you with emotional gut punches—you might want to keep some tissues nearby. And somehow, along the way, you actually end up brushing up on your Chinese history.

I often set out to finish a specific quest, only to get completely sidetracked by the breathtaking scenery or some random encounter. The sense of freedom is real, and with more regions on the horizon, it’s only going to get bigger.

[b]One pro tip:[/b] Don’t go around killing NPCs. You never know when you might actually need them later.

Either way, it’s free to try. And if I ever do open my wallet, it’ll probably just be to buy some new outfits for my [i]in-game wife[/i].

Where Winds Meet absolutely blew me away. As someone who spent years playing Age of Wushu, this game feels like a dream come true—like Age of Wushu on steroids, but without all the pay-to-win baggage that eventually dragged that game down.

The world is gorgeous, alive, and incredibly immersive. Every region feels handcrafted, and exploring never gets old. The freeform movement—wall-running, gliding, leaping across rooftops—captures that perfect wuxia fantasy without feeling clunky or restricted. Combat is fast, fluid, and stylish, striking that perfect balance between classic martial arts and modern action design.

What really sets Where Winds Meet apart is the freedom. You can play how you want, wander where you want, and experiment with builds and martial arts without your wallet ever being the deciding factor. For a free game, it feels shockingly premium. The attention to detail, the quality of the animations, the combat system—it all feels like something I should have had to pay for… but didn’t.

If you’re a fan of open-world wuxia, martial-arts sandboxes, or just miss the golden era of Age of Wushu, Where Winds Meet is the evolution we’ve been waiting for. It respects your time, it respects your playstyle, and best of all, it doesn’t nickel-and-dime you for power.

I really, really love this game, and if it keeps growing the way it has so far, it’s going to become a new classic in the genre.

1. The story is truly captivating. It presents the charm of the wuxia world very well. I enjoyed the contrast and integration between the detailed character portrayals and the grand Jianghu setting.

2. The visuals are stunning. Every corner feels like a beautiful landscape, and I often could not resist stopping to take screenshots.

3. The gameplay is diverse, with a good balance between single-player and multiplayer so it never feels overwhelming.

4. The martial arts system is rich, allowing players to try many different move sets and combat styles.

Areas for improvement and suggestions

1. The menu interface is too complex, and it would be great to see it simplified or improved.

2. Multiplayer content, including team-based dungeons, still feels too basic at the moment. More content would be appreciated.

3. There are quite a few strange bugs, such as characters clipping through the environment or falling outside the map. Fixes are needed.

4. Network latency can be very high when teaming up with others, especially in PvP content.

5. The Mo Blade cannot perform double jump or triple jump. It would be great if this could be fixed.

Where Winds Meet is not your normal game. It is a world for you to live in.

Yup that is my first impression I had when I started the game and could not stop playing it. 

I can't stop thinking about it when I am working, resting, eating, walking, you name it, I most likely am doing that activity while thinking about this game; be it the world, the combat, the skills, the music, the lore, just anything.

And now, why is that so? Lemme explain it to you.

WWM is not any ARPG or MMO that was ever in the PC domain up until now. I am not sure they (Netease) decided to have two of their 'Wuxia' games launching in the same period (Month of November 2025), but that did not help the launch of WWM at all. 

You see, people, players make comparisons. They see the launch of SOJ, a Wuxia game ported over from Mobile to PC platform, and see all the cluttered UIs and disconnects from the mobile porting, and assume: 'Ah this is the reality of an Wuxia game, too complicated, too social, too whatever~'. 

Then WWM launches, and casual gamers (or actually tourists) will launch the game, play for 1 or 2 hours (LOOKING AT YOU USELESS IGN), and say: 'Oh damn, nothing unexpected, we already had an previous example launched' and put scathing reviews. 

But what is the true intention and framework of this game? 

For all my readers reading up till now, thank you and I will make it short and clear. WWM has three modes in total, Solo / Coop / Online. The main story is played entirely in Solo mode. The Coop mode lets you and 4 other friends explore the world together. The Online mode is similar to that of other MMOs, where you can see other players, do daily online activities for currencies (For Emotes / Oufits / Housing Items etc), even although currently at V1.0 it may feel abit barebones.

For the intention of the game itself, the story is no Rags to Riches story, where you (the Hero / Wanderer) beats obstacles one by one and triumphs as the 'Savior of the World' whatsoever. WWM bring you to a fractured world, where you leave the comforts and security of a guarded paradise after a series of mournful tragedies, and aim to seek answers from your lost foster Uncle ♥♥♥ Master. 

The world is beautiful, the characters are intriguing, the plots are in motion, and it is up to you to become a part of these stories, not being a 'Main Character' energy whack in this game. If you are an attention-soaking narcissist, this is not the game for you. If you want to explore the stories of ancient martial traditions in a far flung land from your own, do try out this game, it is FREE and all transactions are for cosmetics that does not add any stats to your character. 

All the best, aspiring Wanderers, and may you find light at the end of your path. Farewell~（保重）

I really want to love this game, and there is a lot in it I do love. There's lots to explore, the art and animation is great. Everything is surface level fantastic. But mechanically the combat is just untuned. Playing on legend difficulty, so ymmv with these points as I don't know how the lower difficulty experience feels with assisted parries.

- Timing for parries is way early and really short. Because you can not time it with when the attack is actually hitting your hitbox, you have to guess at when the moment is somewhere before the swing is actually going to hit you, but not where you would naturally parry in say Sekiro, or Ghost of Tsushima. Its super awkward and instead of it getting you into a rhythm it makes you guess constantly. Which leads into the second point;
- Many enemy attacks either hover FOREVER, or come out INSTANTLY - there is very few times that are in between and most attacks have perfect tracking (mid air turntables included) and insane 2 frame gap close. 
- the enemy damage scaling is insane. like forget bosses, trash mobs 2-3 shots you even at level cap because the game scales up every trash mob faster than you gain power, so you are always fighting a losing battle and never actually get to feel powerful against anyone or anything.
- Even blocking you take obscene damage amd block is a different button to parry, so you find yourself having to tie up a keypress on block constantly because the parry is so inconsistently timed between boss attacks. On top of this, blocking also eats chunks out of whatever they call your stagger bar. It needs to pick a lane.
- There is a reason bloodborne is the only fromsoft game that had you farm for healing pots. It is bad. Having to run around for ages farming mats, or alternatively dumping a mountain of coins on buying them meant I had to do most bosses without healing to conserve resources unless I was close to victory.
- You will spend most of your time in game with access to only 2-3 pots for a fight at most because the collect-a-thon for improving your pot supply on hand is frankly, kinda obscene.

Is it impossible? No, I've certainly level capped and beaten a few bosses a bunch of times in solo and often underleveled. But I never once came away from a fight thinking it was fun or fair; even on the genuinely cool looking bosses with neat ideas behind them. It was always thank ♥♥♥♥ that absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is over, and until that mechanically changes, I just can not recommend this game.

Okay, fine. I would recommend this game. Not wholeheartedly, because it has flaws. However, it costs nothing to try, and it is actually packed with content. It had me in a chokehold for two weeks straight after launch, and judging from the numbers, I was not the only one.

Where Winds Meet is like this weird chimera that resembles many different games in many different ways, but to put it succinctly, it is as if Genshin Impact got thrown into a blender with old Chinese MMORPGs, then garnished with combat from parry-centric soulslikes. But to be clear, this does not really fit the bill for an MMORPG, at least not in the traditional sense. The game shines more when played as a single-player action RPG.

In that regard, I think many aspects of the game are fantastic. I find it quite difficult to actually describe why, because there's actually just... [i]a lot[/i]. Of stuff. To go over. The environment design is beautiful, and encourages the player to spend hours running off into the wilderness to explore. The story is actually fairly compelling, especially given the free-to-play label. And the side stories also do a lot of heavy lifting, which took me by even greater surprise. While the dialogue translations sometimes fall short, the in-game compendium and journal features a lot of lore about various factions and characters. Even the food stall NPCs sometimes feature backstories with multiple pages to read. 

The combat is pretty fun and quite accessible given various difficulty settings for players who would like parry assistance, while also providing a decent challenge for those who want it. Some of the bosses are part of "campaigns" that elaborate more on the events in the world, while other bosses are surprise encounters you may run into while chasing an oddity on the map. Honestly, this game could have passed off as a fully-priced singleplayer title with more polish and a lot less jank...which brings me to my next point.

There's quite a lot of jank, for lack of a better word. Movement feels "sticky" at times (seriously, why is walking a toggle on a gamepad?). The AI runs itself in rhetorical circles a lot with the NPC friendship system. The localization is often fraught with errors, missing lines during dialogue, and inconsistent syntax in the game menus. And oh my goodness - the menus. They are overwhelming, and not in a good way. I feel like the biggest learning curve at the beginning of the game is literally learning how to navigate all the systems and learning where to find information. People will argue that this is the norm for gacha games, but I will argue that developers can endeavor to simply put more thought into designing their interfaces rather than leaning into a genre that is often looked down upon in greater gaming spaces. 

The jank is amplified for the multiplayer systems. While I would not go so far as to say that the multiplayer systems feel like they were tacked on like an afterthought, it certainly feels that way sometimes. Co-op, even when paired with other Americans, is quite laggy. When publicly queueing for the Hero & Sword Trials and Hero's Realm, there does not to seem to be any criteria for how many DPS, healers, or tanks end up in your group (which almost always ends in disaster). The text describing mechanics just flies across the screen with no regard for the chaos unfolding at the same time. Notifications about multiplayer requests (joining co-op worlds, healing, trading, etc.) only lasts for a few seconds instead of putting them somewhere accessible in case players are away. The chat box is not customizable and is yet another learning curve to navigate in the same way the menus are. Basically, the multiplayer side of things is where my comparison to "old Chinese MMORPGs" come from.

The game is a bit all-over-the-place in a way I cannot comprehensively evaluate as "good" - but it is, in my opinion, more good than bad. Some parts of it seem very well developed and polished, and other parts of it feel super outdated, janky, and/or barely functional. But ultimately, it is completely free to try [i]and[/i] free to play, as the gacha mechanics are exclusively cosmetic (it was not something I felt that I needed to expound on, since it does not impact the gameplay or progression meaningfully). On a more personal note, it is especially worthwhile to try for those who like wuxia, or take an interest in the one of the biggest fictional genres in China.

"How the hell is this game free???"

This is the question I keep asking myself every time I complete a main quest or side quest, beat a boss I was stuck on for hours, discover a new beautiful location, interact with NPCs and more. This game is, put simply, one of the best titles released globally this year.

When I saw that it was free to play, I initially thought it was yet another gacha game with pay to win monetization schemes that use FOMO to bait players into pulling for stronger items. But this is not the case at all. The monetization is 99% purely cosmetic, and the items you get from the gacha are not essential to the gameplay.

This game is monstrous in terms of content. Despite having around 100 hours of things to do, I wish I were joking, everything is executed nicely and thoughtfully. So far, there are only two regions, and they are huge. The crazy part is that they do not feel empty either. There are tons of collectibles across the vast map, enemy outposts to clear, NPCs to talk to, minor and major side stories to discover, and dungeons to explore.

The combat feels fantastic. The game heavily emphasizes perfect dodging, like Black Myth: Wukong, and parrying, like Sekiro and Wo Long: Fallen Dynasty. If you have played these games, you will feel right at home. You can also choose two weapon types that suit your playstyle, and more will come in future updates. Some weapon combinations can also synergize with one another. Combat is fast paced and smooth as butter once it clicks.

So far, the main story has been great. The first region felt like the calm before the storm. In the second region, you enter a bustling mega city full of life, where the rich enjoy everything and the poor suffer and eat dirt every day. The cutscenes and environmental storytelling pull you right in. Out in the world, something always catches your eye every few seconds. The side quests, called Lost Chapters, are very involved and usually end with a big boss fight. Combine all of this with beautiful graphics, strong sound design, voice acting and amazing Chinese style music, absolute cinema.

Now let us talk bosses. I have fought most of the bosses currently available, and they are all great and well executed. Each one is distinct, with different mechanics and identities. They are not pushovers you can mindlessly unga bunga your way through. They are certainly not easy, and some are genuinely difficult, even for me as someone who goes all in on Souls likes. I am playing on Expert difficulty because I did not know the Legend option could only be chosen during character creation, which is really stupid. Honestly, after hearing that Legend mode is only slightly harder than Expert and not as insane as people make it sound, I do not mind sticking to Expert.

Oh, right, multiplayer. Did I mention this game is somehow an MMO too? The multiplayer aspect is pretty crazy but completely optional. It ranges from mini games to casual exploration to full MMO style raid bosses. There is a lot you can do with other players, and you can even buy outfits for your character if you collect enough points from social activities.

Of course, a game this big and ambitious is bound to have flaws. First, the menus. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the menus in this game are ridiculous. There is a menu for everything. Even after 80 hours, I still struggle to navigate the sea of menus and the messy UI. I really hope this gets improved. Second, the lag in multiplayer content like PVP and raid bosses needs fixing. It was pretty bad in my experience, though still manageable. There are also issues like odd localization and some lines missing voice acting in voiced cutscenes. And I absolutely hate that I cannot switch to Legend difficulty because I did not choose it at the start.

Overall, this game is phenomenal and has definitely raised the standard for free to play games. It genuinely feels like a full priced AAA game, and I have not had this much fun since The Witcher 3, Baldur’s Gate 3 and Elden Ring. I feel like I have barely scratched the surface, and I literally cannot put this game down. And when I do put it down, I am itching to play again. That is how good it is.

After 120 hours in Where Winds Meet, I can confidently say this is one of the most rewarding open-world RPG experiences I’ve had on Steam. The game’s depth, atmosphere, and sheer variety of things to do kept me hooked far beyond the usual playtime for similar titles.

🌬️ World & Atmosphere
- The ancient China setting is breathtaking. Every village, mountain, and temple feels alive, with meticulous attention to detail that makes exploration endlessly satisfying.
- The Wuxia-inspired storytelling blends martial arts fantasy with historical intrigue, creating a narrative that feels both epic and personal.
⚔️ Combat & Gameplay
- Combat is fluid, challenging, and deeply rewarding. The mix of Soulslike mechanics with martial arts flair makes every duel memorable.
- After 120 hours, I still find new techniques and weapon styles to master. The progression system encourages experimentation without punishing mistakes.
- Boss fights are cinematic and demand strategy, but never feel unfair.
🏯 Variety & Freedom
- Beyond combat, the game offers sandbox-style freedom: you can build, trade, explore, or simply immerse yourself in the social aspects of the world.
- The MMO elements add a layer of community without overwhelming the solo experience. I enjoyed teaming up for large-scale battles but also found peace wandering alone.
- Side quests are surprisingly rich, often touching on themes of honor, loyalty, and identity.
🎨 Longevity & Replayability
- Even after 120 hours, I feel like I’ve only scratched the surface. The 150-hour campaign plus online content ensures there’s always something new to discover.
- The game rewards curiosity—hidden areas, secret martial arts techniques, and lore-rich encounters make exploration endlessly engaging.
⭐ Final Thoughts
Where Winds Meet is more than just a game—it’s an immersive journey into Wuxia culture and philosophy, wrapped in a modern RPG framework. For players who love exploration, deep combat, and a living world, this is a must-play. My 120 hours felt like a blink, and I’m excited to see where the winds carry me next.

Where Winds Meet is one of the most refreshing open-world RPG experiences I’ve played in a long time.
The game beautifully combines storytelling, combat, and world-building into something that feels both familiar and completely new. The world is absolutely stunning. Every village, bamboo forest, mountain peak, and ancient ruin feels alive. The lighting, landscapes, and small environmental details make exploration genuinely enjoyable. It’s the kind of game where you stop moving just to admire the scenery. The story is surprisingly emotional and engaging. The characters you meet along the way feel human — some funny, some tragic, some inspiring. Combat feels fast, fluid, and satisfying. You can mix martial arts, weapons, stealth, acrobatics, and even supernatural abilities. Every encounter feels like a small dance of timing and positioning. Whether you’re fighting bandits, assassins, or roaming bosses, the combat always feels stylish. This is where the game truly shines. You can climb almost anything, glide through valleys, sprint across rooftops, ride horses, hunt, solve puzzles, play minigames, or just wander and discover hidden stories. The world rewards curiosity. The visuals are simply gorgeous. The costumes, animations, and environments all carry a strong Wuxia spirit. It’s a constant screenshot-worthy experience. Where Winds Meet is a beautifully crafted open-world Wuxia adventure that delivers on story, style, combat, and exploration.
