TLDR: This is literally the best video game i have played in 35 years, period. It has pretty much everything i ever wanted from a game. Its also free. You should stop reading reviews and just play it, you have nothing to lose.

But for those who care about reviews, or are skeptical like i once was, let me put my 2 cents in: I've been gaming for over 30 years. Where winds meet is, BY FAR, the best video game i have ever played, period. Granted I'm a little biased; I'm into kung fu movies and Chinese culture to some degree, wouldn't say I'm a fanatic about either, and wuxia definitely isn't my favorite genre, but i do enjoy it.

But to me, the game is just everything i ever wanted. Its like if Jade Empire was new, or if Nioh 3 was Chinese and multiplayer co-op and had 20+ mini games.

If you have ANY interest in action games, MMOs, ARPGs, soulslike/soulsLITE, or just enjoy good storytelling, world building, or beautiful scenery, there really is something for everyone. I was involved with both rounds of beta testing, and was incredibly impressed but had some minor issues, BUT, here is the REAL kicker to play the game: the developers not only listened and implemented player feedback (not just fixed bugs, but added whole new weapons and fighting styles, a dozen new mini games, the ability to BUILD HOUSES AND BOATS AND ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ROLLERCOASTERS *WITH YOUR FRIENDS*) but actively encourage our feedback by giving us premium currency for our surveys.

Now add to that that it was $60 cheaper than my SECOND favorite recently released game, 100% free, with literally 0 pay to win BS. Yes, you can spend 10,000$ on cosmetic items if you want. You can do that in a lot of games. But the difference here is that none of these will make you better at combat, they're purely appearances, and the game gives you SO MANY awesome free costumes that its not like 'spend $40 or wear a potato sack', its like you can have 20 ftp outfits or pay $1-$23 for a specific outfit you like, which is pretty standard for games nowadays, except most games like that also make it miserable to advance without spending real money or at least buying a monthly plan.

Basically it puts literally EVERY SINGLE MMO game to shame, and if you're not into multi-player, you can play it as a single player like Ghost of Tsushima but Chinese with a difficulty setting, and 100% character customization, AI NPCs whose convictions feel real, immersive systems, over a dozen different weapons and fighting styles (we have 8 now but chinese server has like 18 and we'll get 3-4 per quarter until we catch up) 

And most importantly, the gameplay itself is actually fun. Thats an issue ive had with a lot of MMOs like WoW, which for me, i liked some aspects but just didn't find the gameplay to actually feel 'fun', it felt very chore-ish, and with WWM it literally feels just as fun as playing Ocarina of Time on my N64 as a kid when it first came out.


Basically, whats NOT to love? Where Winds Meet is a MASTERPIECE that will change the gaming industry forever and show game companies that they CAN in fact give us an amazing AAA game without an $80 price tag, or even a price tag at all (though i would have happily paid $100 for this game)

Editing this review after 127 hours.

When I first started this game, I was amazed by how big and rich the world felt. You’ve got a bear teaching you martial arts, a goose ready to kick your ass, and NPCs begging for mercy only to stab you the second you turn around. It all felt fresh (at least for me). I also loved the minigames, they actually add to the experience. You run into NPCs who challenge you to their own game, and if you beat them, you get rewards. The variety is great too, everything from Guitar Hero-style rhythm games to card battles.

The scenery and graphics are awesome. They nail the wuxia vibe perfectly. Since I read a lot of manhua and manhwa, I immediately got the references, themes, and direction they were going for. They also did a great job making the world feel deep, every area has meaning, lore, and unique hidden quests.

What I didn’t like was the overuse of the same NPC models and outfits. Yeah, it’s a free-to-play game so I get it, but it still breaks immersion when you see the same guy you killed two zones ago suddenly alive with a new name.

Combat is great. The game perfectly captures that flowy martial-arts feel, and I really like the deflect system. Dodge, though, feels underused. Sure, some attacks can’t be deflected, but 70% of the time dodge feels useless (I didn’t try PvP so don’t crucify me). Builds are somewhat varied, but of course there’s a meta DoT DPS build and everything else right now feels like a cope build. Tanking is fun and takes skill in my opinion, but the whole point of being a tank gets ruined when a random matchmaking leader decides to give the aggro buff to the DPS or healer. I’ve literally tanked as a DPS in some runs, which sucks. Tanks should automatically get that buff.

The menus and UI are just awful. I keep discovering new systems and features I didn’t even know existed. And the chat system? Straight-up terrible. They really need to overhaul this.

One thing I liked, but others might absolutely hate, is that many events basically force you to go online and socialize. Weirdly enough, I ended up having a lot of fun with those. It brought back old-school MMO vibes that I’ve been missing for years.

Now for the controversial part: people say the game is free-to-play and funded mainly by cosmetics through a gacha system. That’s fine, but the gacha rates are insanely low right now. You basically have to hit pity. At least release the actual rates so players can decide if they want to pull or not.

TL;DR: Great game with huge potential to become one of the legends in the genre

Where Winds Meet: The Wuxia Open-World Masterpiece

Recommendation: Highly Recommended (34 hours on record)

If you have any interest in Wuxia (martial arts fantasy), vast open worlds, or deep, customizable action combat, this is a must-play.

Where Winds Meet is easily the most ambitious Wuxia RPG ever made, successfully blending an enormous, living historical world with gravity-defying martial arts action.

⚔️ The Good:

Fluid, Cinematic Combat: The Wuxia combat is incredible. You can master multiple weapon styles (swords, fans, spears, etc.) and seamlessly switch between them. The parry system is satisfying, and chaining together aerial and ground combos feels straight out of a movie.

The World is a Character: The world of the Northern Song Dynasty is stunningly beautiful and massive, built with incredible detail and dynamic weather. Exploration isn't just checking map markers—it's using parkour, gliding, and wall-running to discover hidden martial arts schools, side quests, and secrets.

True Player Freedom: You aren't locked into a class. You can be a wandering swordsman, yes, but you can also become a Master Chef, a traveling Physician with unique healing mini-games, or an Assassin with your own bounty system. Your choices genuinely shape your character's reputation and destiny.

Surprisingly Generous F2P Model: For a free-to-play game, the core experience is massive and rewarding, with monetization focused primarily on cosmetics.

⚠️ The Caveat:

The only real friction point is the system complexity. There are a lot of systems—Martial Arts, Mystic Arts, Inner Ways, multiple professions, co-op/MMO mechanics—and the UI can feel overwhelming at first. Stick with it; once you find your preferred playstyle and adjust the settings, the core game shines.

Verdict: An epic, beautiful, and endlessly deep martial arts sandbox. Install it now and let the wind carry your legend! Love this game.

I'm going to be honest when I say, I didn't approach this game with much hope or belief I'd actually enjoy it. I've played numerous F2P games over the years, and most of them have seen me quit after like a week or two, and other MMO's haven't seen me stay past the first month past the initial subscription fee like with FF or SWTOR. But this game? Honestly, it shocked the heck out of me. Why? Simply put, the graphics and story.

For a game that's free, you get a story and graphic heavy game that's something you'd only see from a AAA type of release, not a F2P game. It was honestly wild to start the game up and just see such breathtaking sights and imagery from a game I didn't need to spend $80 on. What's more, the story is actually pretty good... I'll admit, it's stale and a little odd at the start, but it does quickly start getting good and there's a good few parts in it that start showing you go from a young man/woman to a powerful warrior. Now, mind you, I've only completed the second region so far, and the game is still adding a bunch of content that the CN version already has out, so... here's hoping we get to see some more awesome stuff!

Would I recommend this game to people to try out? 100%
Would I recommend this game to anyone looking for time to kill and have a fun time? 100%
Would I recommend to MMO player veterans? eh... 60% if I'm being honest. The reason? The game's MMO aspect is where it really struggles, as the coop is fine, it just... well, there's hardly a point in it aside from some forced mechanics based on daily quests, boss raids, and Sect missions. None of which are very unique compared to other MMO's out there. I mean, it's fine, but if you're looking for your bog standard MMO, this ain't it. This is more of a Solo exploration, Martial Arts, and coop focused experience, with a heavy focus on solo play. 

Either way, I do highly recommend giving the game a try, and no I haven't seen any P2W stuff... it's mostly just been cosmetics and profile stuff. So, all good on that front too XD.

---Original Review:---

Tl;dr - It's hard to beat a price of free, and you'll get dozens of hours out of this without spending a dime.  The question is whether or not that will be enough to hook you for the later game.  PS: It's not a gacha, but it does have plenty of cash shop emphasis even if there is nothing that is P2W.

Full Review: WWM is a wuxia game straight out of mainland China.  Wuxia is basically Chinese-flavored fantasy that has a lot of roots in ancient (literally 2000 years) Chinese history and folk stories.  Without getting into a full explanation of wuxia, it's really important to know this heading in because the writing has almost every wuxia trope in it.

What this means is that there is going to be a lot of nonsensical ♥♥♥♥ happening at almost all times as it concerns the story.  Logical plot sequence, foreshadowing, or what the average western mind might think is a cohesive sequence of events is basically an afterthought in wuxia and it takes a backseat to nonstop flood of "♥♥♥♥ just happens."  If you've read any wuxia, this probably isn't a big surprise to you, but if you've never really gotten into the genre, you need to do more than suspend your disbelief and instead you basically need to turn off your brain entirely because the amount of absolute un-logic present in the story will drive you insane if you try to think about it too hard.

Story aside, the game is fun.  The major focus is singleplayer, although there's some light multiplayer elements with shared lobbies or online mode.  The gameplay is a mix between something like Breath of the Wild and Sekiro / Wukong.  There's a lot of emphasis on timing and reading bosses, but if you're like me and the spray of particle effects and animation locks make it difficult to cancel out of your swing and hit that Meridian Touch in time to NOT die to the boss' instant-death attack 4 minutes into the fight, then there's always settings for parry assist and story mode difficulty.

Tech-wise, the performance is good.  On a 3080, I only really began to chug in downtown Kaifeng.  Otherwise my frames were pretty good the whole time, even on high+ settings.  You should know however there are a plenthora of small bugs you'll encounter.  Stuck on or in terrain, positional desync, quick menus bugging, quick actions bugging.  You get used to some of the jank, but it works most of the time.

As for the cash shop - everything in there is cosmetic.  All the cool stuff of course.  You can't even so much as change hair color without a cosmetic item.  Game still looks good, but if you want to actually look cool, you'll either be achievement farming a very long time or paying some kind of actual money.  None of it REALLY effects gameplay, although there is stuff in there that can speed up a few progression paths, even if they don't affect power outright.

Overall I think the question someone has to ask when they pick this up is whether or not they're gonna be in it for the long haul or if you're just gonna play through to where the story cuts off.  I say cuts off because this is the global release, and not all the content is available ATM.  Dunno when it will be, but you also need to know that wuxia stories notoriously don't really end, or at least they don't end remotely in the same way you'd see elsewhere.  Guess that makes a great forever game so long as you  can tolerate the endless tide of disposable characters who will be discarded as soon as the chapter's over.

That's just how wuxia works.

Honestly I was a bit disappointed with this game. It sounded really exciting, a sort of Wuxia themed combination of souls-like combat, RPG elements, MMO elements, and more. For context, I'm someone who loves souls-like games, and I've read Wuxia novels since I was in middle school, so it seemed perfect for me. The skeleton of a good game is definitely present, but I think its muddled by many small issues, which when together, strip a lot of the enjoyability of the game for me. Starting with the translations, while they weren't horrible, at times they definitely felt awkward in some spots of the game, along with some very odd voice acting quality. Some of the characters had good voice acting, some had none, some had extremely obvious AI voices that sounded terrible, sometimes random lines would have no voiceover, while later lines in the same dialogue would have a voiceover. It just feels very messy and rushed. On the topic of AI, some of the NPC's in this game are AI powered, meaning they have AI voiceovers, and you can chat to an AI chatbot acting like the character. Its an interesting idea, but I think the execution in the end is pretty poor. The AI has no integration with the game environment besides attacking you if you're too rude to them, so it can be pretty immersion breaking when they mention taking certain actions which they can't actually do in game. It just ends up feeling lazy to me, like they couldn't be bothered to create dialogue for some of the less important characters around the world or actually voice act them out. Moving on, the menus are quite convoluted in this game. After a while you can mostly understand what to do, but it certainly doesn't make it easy to enjoy the game, with many UI elements and stats having next to no explanation of what they actually do. I think the last straw for me was some of the minigames around the map. For example, Gift of Gab is genuinely one of the most awful things I've seen in a game. It's a debate minigame where you get inspiration, and can then use that inspiration to play cards that "do damage" to the opponents psyche, while they do the same. Each one of the cards do different things, and there are some more mechanics that I won't go in detail about. It sounds nice on the surface, but during the tutorial for it, the game just starts playing in the background, so you can't really read anything, and honestly, you can't even read anything anyway. The game moves so quickly you genuinely cannot even read the cards. Most people I've seen just button mash, spamming cards until they win or lose. Its actually braindead design. In the end, the game just comes off as sloppy to me, which is a shame, because the core aspects of the game are quite good. The combat feels nice, the world is fun to explore, and there are some cool bosses, but ultimately I think whether you'll like this game or not comes down to how much of the small flaws you can tolerate.

It's pretty fun, especially considering that it's free/

The pros:
+ Great performance on an Ultrawide monitor (6750XT, 7500F, 32 RAM).
+ The visuals are great, there are some minor issues here and there but it's on par with most AAA titles these days and doesn't require fake frames to stay above 60.
+ Fun story and characters, the translation is spotty at times but not bad enough to miss crucial details.

The meh:
= The combat is "meh", it tries to be soulsy + DMC at the same time, but it's an online game and sometimes it just doesn't work right. If you only care about the combat then Rise of the Ronin does it better imo.
= The gear doesn't change on your character when you equip something new. I think the weapons do change, but things like helmets and what not don't affect how your character looks like. It's easy to make a character that actually looks good, but mixing the fashion-souls aspect is definitely missing here.

The cons:
- The game is an absolute UI hell, even after +20h I can't remember where stuff is, new stuff gets added all the time and trying to upgrade everything on your character is a nightmare. Thankfully there is an "upgrade everything" button, but they could have done it properly from the start. The closest menu I can think of that is close is Genshin Impact, but I feel like it's much more intuitive there.
- The "english" VO is atrocious, poor sound mixing and the overall performance is bad, just stick to the Chinese VO, it's much better. 
- The overall multiplayer aspect is not great. The "solo" experience is superb, but joining  public matchmaking for raids or boss fights is a lagfest and actually summoning someone to fight with is a chore. Stick to Solo.

Also some words about the MTX model, at lvl 45 it still seems to be like progress is not gated by money, their main profit comes from visuals it seems. I think you can get some item upgrades from the cash shop, but I bought them all with the currency I got while playing, so it doesn't seem to be a problem +20h in at least. Still, it's a free Chinese F2P game, so some issues may arise eventually after you play for 300h.

Overall I would have much preferred if this was just a $60 title, but as it stands I am having a great time as is.

Then I was left to wonder how much of what I was reading and seeing was AI, and I quickly could not bring myself to play any more. 

It's a shame. There are other design flaws, like needlessly obtuse UI, and occasionally unresponsive controls, but I was having fun exploring the charming world and Sekiro-like combat. These devs have talent, but the work they put in was ruined by the work they didn't want to do themselves.

If you're looking for a game with a clear beginning, middle, and satisfying end — a complete story — this one will disappoint you. On the other hand, it’s perfect for players who feel secure only when the game keeps getting regular updates.
The game offers endless progression: chasing the absolute highest level and best gear with no real ceiling, plus a massive open world and countless collectibles that can feel overwhelming (or even terrifying) to casual players.
No matter what, this is genuinely a free-to-play title. You can try it yourself anytime and see if it fits you.

[quote][b][u]Quick Summary[/u][/b]
[b]Story:[/b] Surprisingly emotional and engaging for a free game. Some moments genuinely caught me off guard.
[b]Gameplay & Mechanics:[/b] Smooth combat with a mix of Ghost of Tsushima, Assassin’s Creed, and a bit of Sekiro-like learning (even though I never played Sekiro). Boss fights are visually impressive and satisfying once you learn the patterns.
[b]Exploration:[/b] Beautiful world with strong visual style, especially if you enjoyed Ghost of Tsushima’s art direction.
[b]Atmosphere:[/b] Strong presentation, memorable characters, and a story that lands harder than expected.
[b]Monetisation:[/b] Mostly cosmetic. You can play the full story and progress without spending anything.
[b]Overall:[/b] A surprisingly polished experience for a free-to-play title. One of those hidden gems worth trying at least once.
[/quote]

[b][u]Important Notes Before You Start[/u][/b]

Remember when the game asks you to set your character’s name:  
[b]it must be unique and it is permanent.[/b] You cannot change it later, so choose carefully.

The game has multiple difficulty modes. You can switch freely between Story and Expert at any time.  But the highest difficulty, [b]Legend[/b], can only be selected at the very beginning when you create your username. If you lower the difficulty later, you can never return to Legend unless you make a new account.
  
I chose Story to enjoy everything peacefully and switched to Expert for some bosses when I wanted a challenge.

[h1]Where Winds Meet – A Free Game That Surprised Me in the Best Way[/h1]

I went in with the mindset of avoiding online free games, mainly because many of them end up turning into pay-to-win or heavy grind traps. But after seeing a few reviews saying “just try it, it is free,” I gave it a chance.  
And honestly, I was shocked by how good it turned out.

People compare it to Ghost of Tsushima, Assassin’s Creed, Black Myth, and Sekiro.  
I only know the first two, but even then the comparisons make sense.  
The visuals instantly reminded me of Ghost of Tsushima’s atmosphere, especially during key story moments.

[h2]Story and Emotional Moments[/h2]

I did not expect a free game to hit this hard, especially so early on.

[spoiler]The ending of Chapter 1 genuinely caught me emotionally. It set the tone for the rest of the journey and felt far better than many paid games I played this year.
[/spoiler]

Chapter 2 also had one of my favourite twists:

[spoiler]Little Fu saying “I’m the Dao Lord,” then switching to “I work for the Dao Lord,” had everyone confused. And when the truth came out at the end, I laughed so hard because the community reaction online was exactly the same as mine.
[/spoiler]

Only two chapters are available right now, but both have solid closure and feel complete on their own.

[h2]Gameplay, UI, and World Feel[/h2]

Combat feels smooth once you learn enemy patterns. Some boss fights look incredible, especially for a free game.  
One side-boss took me hours, but once I learned everything, beating it felt extremely satisfying.

The UI can look busy at first, especially if you prefer clean single-player setups.  
Thankfully, you can hide almost everything in the settings and even turn off world chat on the side.

The world itself looks beautiful. The colours, animations, and overall presentation reminded me of modern AAA titles.

[h2]Online System and Why Everything Is Connected[/h2]

The game is always online, but the reason seems to be tied to how saves and progression work.  
From what I understand, saves are on the server possibly to prevent people from modifying files and skipping progression.  
At the same time, it looks like the developers wanted all modes — solo, co-op, and multiplayer — to share one character with the same stats.

I personally do not know the full technical reason, but that feels like the intention.  
It also means maintenance time can stop you from playing, which might feel odd if you prefer purely offline story games.

[h2]Progression, Resources, and Level Gates[/h2]

There are level gates. For example, to begin Chapter 2 you need to be level thirty.  
At first, I thought it would feel like a wall, but by the time I finished Chapter 1 I was already level twenty-eight.  
Doing two side missions pushed me to thirty, so it did not waste my time.

The only thing that bothered me slightly is how healing items and resources do not reset when you reload a save, since everything is online.  
If you run out of medicine, you have to go farm more and come back.  
Not a dealbreaker, but something to be aware of.

[h2]Monetisation and What You Actually Need[/h2]

The game mainly sells skins and a battle pass. The cosmetics do not give big stat advantages, and you can play smoothly without spending.  
Grinding is enough to keep up with main story requirements.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Even though only two chapters exist at the moment, both are strong and enjoyable.  
The world looks beautiful, the story has emotion and twists, and the combat impressed me far more than I expected from a free title.

It is one of those games where the phrase “just try it, love or hate, up to you” actually fits perfectly.

[b]Where Winds Meet[/b] is a wild mix of wuxia power fantasy, MMO sandbox and single-player ARPG. It’s messy, overloaded with systems, sometimes janky – and also one of the most memorable open worlds I’ve played in years.

[b]Pros[/b]

[list]
[*][b]Stunning Wuxia world[/b] – Huge open map inspired by ancient China, from misty mountains and rice fields to crowded cities and haunted ruins. Great use of weather, time of day and vistas; just riding or rooftop-hopping around is fun on its own.

[*][b]Traversal feels like a martial-arts movie[/b] – Wall-running, water-running, air dashes, gliding, wire-fu jumps, using trees, rooftops and even enemies as platforms. Movement is fast, stylish and lets you approach almost any area in multiple ways.

[*][b]Satisfying, parry-focused combat[/b] – Timed blocks, counters and stagger bars give fights a Sekiro-lite feel, but with more room for mistakes. Perfect deflects and counters are very rewarding, and different enemy types force you to actually learn patterns instead of face-tanking.

[*][b]Tons of weapon variety[/b] – Swords, dual blades, spears, bows, fans, umbrellas and more, each with their own move sets and animations. Swapping between two equipped weapons mid-fight keeps combat dynamic.

[*][b]Powerful Wuxia abilities[/b] – Time-slow, telekinetic pulls, pressure-point strikes, mobility skills etc. Synergies between Inner Ways (passives), Mystic Arts (special skills) and weapon builds give a lot of room for theory-crafting.

[*][b]Sandbox professions & life skills[/b] – You’re not just a wandering swordsman; you can lean into careers like doctor/healer, merchant, architect/builder, performer, scholar, bounty hunter and more. They come with their own progression, perks and side content, not just “+5% stat” buttons.

[*][b]Housing & customization[/b] – Player housing with actual decorating and building, plus detailed character creator, outfits, dyes and fashion options for full wuxia drip.

[*][b]Dense side content[/b] – Dungeons, world bosses, bounty hunts, puzzles, hidden caves, secret quests, mini-games (instruments, board games, races, duels, etc.). The world rewards wandering off the main quest.

[*][b]Multiplayer options[/b] – Seamless co-op for a lot of PvE content, guilds with group activities, and several PvP modes (duels, more chaotic modes, open-world PvP spots). You can treat it like a co-op ARPG or like an MMO-lite.

[*][b]AI-driven NPCs are genuinely interesting (when they work)[/b] – Some NPCs can hold actual conversations, remember what you say and react in surprising ways, which adds a unique role-play flavor compared to typical static dialogue trees.

[*][b]Big, cinematic main story[/b] – Fully voiced, lots of cutscenes, setpieces and dramatic wuxia melodrama. If you enjoy classic martial-arts dramas and tangled political intrigue, the vibe is very on point.

[*][b]No hard pay-to-win so far[/b] – The core combat power comes from playing the game, not from swiping a card. The shop is mostly cosmetics and convenience, so you can enjoy the story and combat without spending.
[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]

[list]
[*][b]Overloaded and sometimes confusing systems[/b] – The game throws an absurd number of currencies, upgrade trees, menus and tutorials at you. New players will feel overwhelmed and the UI doesn’t always help.

[*][b]Tone is all over the place[/b] – One minute you’re in a tragic historical drama, the next you’re yeeting animals off cliffs or doing goofy mini-games. Fun, but not exactly coherent.

[*][b]Story pacing can be uneven[/b] – Strong arcs and cutscenes are mixed with filler quests, slow stretches and occasionally awkward writing/translation.

[*][b]AI NPCs can break immersion[/b] – As cool as they are, the LLM-style NPCs sometimes spit out nonsense, modern references or out-of-place dialogue that clash with the historical setting.

[*][b]Performance is inconsistent[/b] – Even on decent hardware you can hit stutters, frame-time spikes and random hitching, especially in big cities or large fights. Expect to spend time tweaking settings, drivers and upscalers. Console performance in particular needs more optimization.

[*][b]Jank and bugs[/b] – Floating NPCs, broken pathing, weird hitboxes, desync in co-op, quest triggers not firing, etc. It’s playable, but you will encounter rough edges regularly.

[*][b]Camera & lock-on issues[/b] – In busy fights the camera can fight you, lock-on swaps targets randomly, and visibility can get messy when particle effects fill the screen.

[*][b]Multiplayer quirks[/b] – Co-op progression is not perfectly shared, some rewards only go to the host, and matchmaking/UIs aren’t always intuitive.

[*][b]Grind walls[/b] – Later progression can slow down hard, pushing you toward repeating certain activities, daily/weekly routines, or “efficient” farming routes instead of just doing whatever looks fun.

[*][b]Monetization noise, even if not pure P2W[/b] – While the game doesn’t sell raw power, there are a lot of cosmetic bundles, gacha elements and layered currencies. Some ultra-premium cosmetics reach absurd prices and the constant shop pop-ups can be annoying.

[*][b]Cluttered UI[/b] – Pop-ups, alerts, limited-time events, tiny icons and sub-menus everywhere. It feels more like an MMO launcher than a clean single-player HUD at times.
[/list]

[b]Overall[/b]

If you want a tight, focused, no-nonsense action game, this will probably feel bloated and chaotic. If you like giant experimental sandboxes where you can parkour across rooftops, duel swordmasters, run a clinic, build a house, role-play with NPCs and then jump into a raid with friends – all in one place – [i]Where Winds Meet[/i] is absolutely worth your time, flaws and all.

Running underneath lanterns? Not for long. You will dry-hump them for a few seconds.

The story is… okay? I’m not that invested, but I also didn’t skip. We get a lot of stuff to do, but sometimes they feel more like a chore than something to do to pass the time.

The game is good and annoying at the same time, but it’s free, so I think it’s worth giving it a try.

All in all, solid game, but certainly not for everyone.

The bounty-hunting system in Where Winds Meet is completely broken and unfair. I accepted a bounty while having zero bounty on myself, found the target, and the moment I engaged him inside a Co-op Room, he was constantly healed by another player. I kept losing health while he instantly recovered everything, making it impossible to kill anyone who has even one teammate healing them. This makes the entire bounty system pointless.

It gets even worse. When I attacked the target, the game treated me as the criminal and instantly allowed another player to invade me instead. The bounty hunter is punished for doing the bounty. This is terrible design and makes no sense.

On top of that, some bounty targets cannot be tracked or invaded even though the timer is running. They can hide inside Co-op Rooms or bugged areas where the system refuses to let me invade, which wastes my time while the target escapes. The system feels inconsistent, exploitable, and unreliable.

Arena mode already shows that the developers understand healing needs nerfs in PvP situations, but bounty hunting has no reduction at all, so anyone with a healer becomes unkillable. If this is the intended design, bounty hunting might as well not exist. Right now, it does not work, it is not balanced, and it punishes players who try to participate in it.

For now, I am downvoting this and cannot recommend it to anyone, because the main content in the current patch is finished, and the remaining content for players like me is PvP, Arena, and bounty hunting. If bounty hunting is not functional or playable, it becomes a crippled system, and there is nothing left to enjoy. I will gladly change my review and switch to an upvote if this rigged and broken bounty system is fixed.

If you are looking for a single player open world game with plenty to explore, this should scratch your itch. You will have to cope though with a million of things to upgrade and progress using plenty of different currencies. Many of them do so mostly automatically. I made it a habit to every once in a while navigate the labyrinthine menus and click everything that says "Upgrade".

Some of the mini-games were indiscernible to me. But you can skip most of them, or just find a YouTube video tutorial.

Coop for roaming is fine, but pointless to do story or dungeons because only one player gets the rewards. The other would have to replay the content.

Performance was decent enough on my RX6700XT, though in cities the frame rate noticeable drops, especially in busy streets during the night. The game ran stable for the most part, I had it crashing about every 10 to 15 hours.

Monetization so far is fine. You can explore the entire game. I'm at level 55 and did not notice any grind, just playing the game is enough. On every launch you get to see something shiny and a "Purchase" button, which is only fair. You can buy some cosmetics and some boosts, but nothing game changing. Prices are in USD, which is nice at the current EUR exchange rate.

Of note are the female outfits. While most western games either do "slutty" or "ugly", in this game they are elegant and make the characters look appealing with only little skin exposed. I found that refreshing.

This game is overwhelmingly positive experience

This game is genuinely spectacular and sets a new benchmark for the wuxia genre. From the moment you step into its vast, ancient Chinese setting, the sheer amount of content and the freedom of exploration can feel overwhelming in the best possible way. The level of detail in the world building, combined with a truly fluid movement system, makes every moment very enjoyable.

The core gameplay loop, especially the combat, is deeply engaging. Mastering the various martial arts styles and weapon forms is incredibly rewarding, providing countless hours of satisfying progression. It’s genuinely fun and accessible, but still offers enough depth for veterans of action RPGs.

If you’re looking for a massive, beautiful world to lose yourself in, look no further. It is balanced brilliantly, making it excellent to play solo or with friends. Whether you prefer progressing through the cinematic main questline on your own, or teaming up for cooperative challenges, this title is a must play. It’s an easy thumbs up and deserves its positive reception.

Fighting is smooth and you are not limited to just one martial arts technique. It offers full control on how you wish to play the game. In-game currency can be spent on outfits or their draw system; however, unlike other games with a gacha system, it doesn't feel like a pay to win. You aren't missing out on meta characters, and how powerful your character gets is based on leveling up your gear and equipment. 

The only downside I have noticed is that, at least on my end, the co-op function sometimes makes the game lag. WWM combines open world exploration with a perfect parry style combat. 
I am bad at this kind of gameplay but loves the world of WWM. I've been sucked in 114 hours deep just discovering a portion of the game and for a free to play game I haven't hit any paywall. The shop seems mostly cosmetic.
Its solo mode gives you a complex story set in an alternate 10th century China, where historical figures are transposed into a wuxia setting with martial arts, cultivation and sorcery. Your hero runs on water and walls, jumps over a vast expanse of land by throwing his spear and catching up to it. It is the mythical jianghu that your character lives in, served by a mesmerizing soundtrack and a captivating art direction. I've never made so many screenshots in a game.
The social mode gives off MMO vibes with hubs with multiple activities such as minigames, boss battles, guilds and PVP arenas. 
It is an ambitious game that hits many marks, and misses a few. Some game mechanics are hidden behind layers upon layers of menu, and bad translations or missing context will make the storylines difficult to piece together. But WWM is overall a great game and a good surprise so far.

I was fully expecting this game to be yet another p2w game that would be fun for a week tops and then move on to something else. I must say i was wrong. This game truly does not have any p2w elements in it at all and the absolute closest thing it has to pay for convenience is the paid battle pass includes remote access to 4 shopkeepers. That's barely a convenience with all the fast travel points this game has and low loading times.

Everything in the store is cosmetic only. You can outright buy full outfits for a listed amount, there is also a gacha for cosmetics, but in my opinion the "legendary/SSR" outfit from the gacha looks worse than majority of stuff you find in game but that's just me personally. You can also buy cosmetics for your martial arts (you can equip up to 2 martial arts at a time which makes the basis of all your attacks and combat). There's also cosmetic mounts you can get of course as well.

This game has been an absolute delight and is a must play if you are interested/like the wuxia genre of stories at all. The combat in this game is quite fun and the only slight against it is the parry window on some enemy attacks could use some polishing, but this is a non issue if you're playing on non-legend difficulty. (Legend difficulty is the only one that doesn't have the slow-mo parry time option)

The graphics aren't top of the line, but they're as good as you could ask for and this game runs without issues on my nearly 10 year old pc. The story is fine, not an Expedition 33 masterpiece by any stretch, but again if you like wuxia genre, you'll have fun with it. The default controls are pretty solid as well though you might want to change one or two hotkeys to your liking.

The music and atmosphere are really great and they nailed the wuxia atmosphere perfectly. Some localization definitely could be better but you shouldn't have much trouble understanding what it is the game wants to convey outside of a couple more egregious examples.

I'd give this game a solid 8.5 out of 10. 
9.5 out of 10 if you know what wuxia is and like it.

One thing that really took me out of the experience is the mouse cursor always being visible on the screen. It’s distracting, especially during fights.
Also, the camera controls are not very intuitive. Having to use both mouse buttons to control the camera doesn’t feel natural. I wish the basic attack was simply on left-click, and abilities like the one on Q added extra effects instead of forcing awkward controls.

Final Thoughts

Where Winds Meet has a beautiful world, great visuals, and nice animations. The combat has potential, and the three skill types are fun to try. But some control choices and UI issues made it less enjoyable for me.
If these things get polished, it could become a much better experience.

Where Winds Meet — A Stunning Journey of Freedom and Style 
───────── 🎨 Graphics & Atmosphere ─────────
Where Winds Meet impresses from the very first moments. The detailed landscapes, lush vegetation, soft lighting, and realistic weather effects are breathtaking 😍.  
The animation work—combat stances, martial arts moves, parkour—is incredibly polished.

Game dev perspective:  
High-quality post-processing, volumetric fog, and dense textures create an AAA-level feel. And the fact that this is *free* is unbelievable.

───────── 🧭 Open World & Exploration ─────────
Freedom is the core theme here. Run across hills, climb rooftops, glide through the air, engage in sword fights, or meditate by the river.  
The world isn't just big—it's *alive* 💚: reactive NPCs, random events, hidden temples, and valleys full of stories.

───────── ⚔️ Combat System ─────────
Combat is dynamic, stylish, and varied.  
Wall running, acrobatics, precise timing—every fight feels like a wuxia movie 🎬.

Developer insights:  
Smooth animation transitions, clean collision work, and responsive controls. Root motion and hitboxes are handled exceptionally well.

───────── 📖 Story & Presentation ─────────
The story is surprisingly engaging, with philosophical tones, memorable characters, and meaningful choices.  
Cutscenes are cinematic, and the soundtrack elevates every scene 🎶.

───────── 🧩 Gameplay Mechanics ─────────
- 🐎 Horse riding — smooth and satisfying  
- 🏃 Parkour & rooftop movement — fast and fluid  
- 🥷 Stealth — works better than expected  
- 🛠️ Crafting & progression — deep but not overwhelming  

Dev angle:  
A well-balanced blend of mechanics shows the team's careful iteration and testing.

───────── 💸 Free-to-Play ─────────
This is one of those rare F2P games that *feels* like a premium title.  
Monetization is non-intrusive, and progression feels fair 🙌.

───────── 🎉 Final Verdict ─────────
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  5 / 5
Where Winds Meet is a powerful, stylish, atmospheric adventure  
that delivers freedom, beauty, and cinematic storytelling.

As a player — I’m impressed.  
As a developer — I’m inspired by the craftsmanship.

Where Winds Meet hits different. The world breathes: wind bends the grass in real waves, lanterns flicker in village alleys, and when you sprint across moonlit rooftops the valley below glows like spilled honey. Movement feels shamelessly good; wall-run up a cliff, kick off into a glide, land in a silent roll—it’s the kind of flow that makes you forget you’re holding a controller. Combat is straight-up intoxicating. That tiny metallic “cling” on a perfect parry, the way a counter lets you steal an enemy’s move and turn it back on them, the moment you unlock mid-air style switching and start flipping between spear thrusts and fan flutters while a boss screams… yeah, it’s hot. The story takes its time, but the side stuff is where the game really gets weird is gold: following a drunk goose for acupuncture lessons, raising a bear cub that grows up to teach you Tai Chi, stumbling into hidden manuals in caves that feel genuinely secret. Menus are a disaster and the English dub is rough, but none of that stops me from booting it up and losing another evening to it. If you ever wanted to live inside one of those over-the-top wuxia dramas and actually feel untouchable, this is it.

Honestly really enjoying this game despite entering with low expectations. Very janky but I never thought I would see a wuxia single player / mmo-lite sort of game that is essentially The Witcher 3. Fairly polished and heavy in content too, with occasionally extremely cinematic presentation of a lot of classic genre wuxia genre tropes. I've really loved the Puppeteer bosses in particular 

Things I think they could improve short or medium term to make it way more appealing to non-Chinese markets: 

1) They DESPERATELY need to improve the localization in later patches, or at the very least the English subtitling for the Chinese language version. Both the English dub and the subtitling are absolutely terrible, to the point where it will absolutely deter a very large portion of their potential Western player-base from playing the game because they simply do not understand what is happening.

2) The game really needs some more enemy variety among regular mobs on the world map. Where Winds Meet has been fun so far because your player character is constantly getting new moves and martial arts so fights still feel varied in spite of the limited non-boss enemy variety, but this will only last for so long. Once that thrill of discovery and experimentation is over, you'll just be beating down on the same small handful of enemies that you've been beating down on the whole game. 

3) Along with improving the language localization, it might be worth putting in an in-game wiki or database that explains some of the references that regular non-Chinese players who have had limited or no previous exposure to wuxia/xianxia as a genre are not liable to understand the context of, like Ruby's Chinese name being 'Red Thread' or the references to Legend of the Condor Heroes or other wuxia classics. 

4) If they can trim down or at least consolidate the vast array of different menus and currencies and claimable rewards to make the UX experience a little less tortuous that would be fantastic, because I'm 30 hours into the game and still find myself regularly confused at which menu I should be in to get what I want and how to get there. 

5) The subtitle scroll is INSANELY fast, the subtitles themselves are very small, and there's no option to change either. It's genuinely very difficult to even read all of the text flashing by if there are multiple conversations happening in one area, which compounds the issue of the terrible localization substantially since you don't even have time to try parsing it.

I want to like this game, but I'm having difficulty doing so. It's beautiful graphically, and I find that there are a lot of small details that make it immersive - characters actually interact with objects around them when you're talking to them or getting quest items, for example, rather than items in the world being static. Wuxia isn't necessarily my thing, but I'm not opposed to a good game based on it. 

It definitely has major problems, though. IMO, the combat does not feel good. I love a good parry-based game - Sekiro and Nine Sols come to mind, both of which I've beaten. In this game, the parry doesn't feel responsive, I think partially because of short parry windows, attacks that are sometimes poorly choreographed, long enemy attack windups, and a parry that takes you out of your combos. Enemies have multi-hit combo attacks that will stagger you in the middle of each hit, meaning that if you get hit by one, you often are locked into getting hit by much of the combo. All of this made it feel to me like it was optimal to play very safely, staying back when I could not to get stunlocked. One boss allowed me to switch weapons to ones I hadn't tried, and the ranged weapon (an umbrella) felt trivial in difficulty compared to the melee weapons because of this.

The localization also isn't great. Sentences often feel stilted, sometimes the voice acting doesn't match the text, and notably, some of the minigames don't have in-depth explanations of how to play (i.e. Mahjong). It's understandable for a local audience not to have tutorials for common games, but as someone who is not familiar, having to look up the rules of multiple different minigames takes me out of the game.

Where Winds Meet could have been something, but almost every part of it feels designed to waste your time. The story and side quests are mind numbing. You follow slow NPCs who talk about nothing, and even though you can skip dialogue line by line or speed it up to x3, it still feels endless and pointless.

Quests force you into slow walking, carrying useless items, or staring at your character’s face because the camera zooms in for no reason. Exploration is hollow. You collect bugs and honey, repeat the same small set of activities and clear identical camps until your brain shuts off.

Combat is just as dull. Bosses look great but the fights are empty. You mostly stand still, parry and dodge while bosses spin around the arena in nonstop attack loops. There is barely any room for actual combat, and the whole thing becomes a boring cycle.

The UI is a complete trainwreck. It is ugly, chaotic and painful to navigate. Menus are stuffed with random icons and walls of useless text. The map is clunky and its filters barely work. Important info is hidden deep inside submenus, while irrelevant junk sits in plain sight. The inventory is a nightmare with messy categories, endless lists and zero clarity. Using the interface feels slow and outdated, like a bad mobile port.

Overall the game is full of wasted ideas buried under terrible design, boring content and one of the worst interfaces in the genre. It frustrates more than it entertains.

Mediocre at best during rare moments, a buggy mess the rest of the way.

Let's get the mediocre moments out of the way first: stunlocking 2 bosses with friends was fun. That's all.

Now the negatives:
* When you start the game, you instantly receive a reward! Permanent hearing damage!
* During the tutorial, almost all your settings are locked. Because of my specs, I had to fight the tutorial boss on Legend difficulty with a max. of 30 fps and controls I could not get used to nor change.
Things didn't get much better after the tutorial.
* Some graphics settings reset every time the game exits.
* You can speed up cutscenes, but this setting is not remembered when you restart the game.
* The camera defaults to behind you: if you're fighting a smaller sized boss or your teammate runs between your camera and your character, you can't see much.
* Horrible optimization. Example: the red world boss near where you start creates smoke during the fight. This drops my fps from a playable 45~50 to a horrible 20~30.
* The 'chat with a LLM AI NPC for rewards' system is broken: 3/5 times I interacted with AI NPCs, they kept repeating the same thing no matter what my prompt was
* Some enemies teleport. The 2 most memorable examples:
  1. A youkai with dive attacks you had to perfect dodge. They teleported DURING the dive attack... (it did NOT look intentional)
  2. Alligators that phased in and out of existence when I was near. One also teleported onto me for seconds at a time when I was on the other side of the instance...
* Cutscenes are broken. E.g.: My character tried jumping onto a horse Assassins Creed style for some reason, but missed... Then teleported onto the horse 2 seconds later.
* The English translation is bad. Most text I cared to read felt machine translated.

Some co-op specific bugs I encountered:
* Enemies teleport
* Enemies & bosses duplicate.
* Boss fights start while your team is stuck outside of the arena.
* Boss fights start while most of your time is stuck outside the arena. Good luck friend!
* Bosses starts outside of the arena while you're inside...

I don't even want to write any final words. Don't waste your time here. Touching grass is definitely a better use of your time.

I am very torn about this game. On the one hand it is fun and a joy to play and on top of all free, but on the other it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by design in many areas. I'll give a recommendation due to the unbeatable pricetag, but I want to elaborate on all the issues players have to overcome.

[h2]UI[/h2]
This game has the worst UI in the history of video games. There are about 50 menu screens, partially hidden within other menus or only accessible when the cursor is on a certain part of the map, etc. I have played for almost 80 hours and still struggle to find some of the menus. On top of that I'm playing on gamepad and the menus have the worst navigation ever. Want to go to another section of the screen? Maybe you have to press RT or RB. Maybe you have to click RS instead. Or should you use the controlpad? The answer is: all of them at some point, but only one works in the menu you are currently in. And sometimes neither of them get you to where you want to go, so you put down the gamepad and use the mouse instead. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This UI was not designed for gamepads at all.

[h2]Timegating[/h2]
There is almost nothing in this game that is not timegated. Max level increases every few days, though the time between also increases with every step. Main story is blocked as well, though on a separate timer. Then there's a bunch of stuff you need to do daily, but there is of course a limit to how much you can do every day. Same goes for pretty much anything that rewards loot. The game has an energy-system so you can only get a set amount of random loot per X hours. The game very much wants you to come back every day and only play for a short time. On the other hand it has hundreds and thousands of collectibles that are also tied to character progression, so you can technically play almost forever, but only with the most mundane, boring, repetitive tasks.

[h2]Monetization[/h2]
It's a free game and it has to make money. Everyone understands that. Where Winds Meet is fortunately not P2W, but it takes every other predatory monetization tactic and applies it. Gacha with horrendously low chances? Check. Season-Pass with daily login rewards? Check. Battle-Pass? Check. Cosmetic items up to 40 or 50€ with FOMO? Check. Ingame currencies that obfuscate the real cost of shop items and can only be bought in pack sizes that never really match what the store has on offer? Check.
I would like to support the developers at a reasonable price. That is unfortunately only possible by waiting for certain items to get the 90% discount because everything is so overpriced.

[h2]World Scaling[/h2]
The progression by levelling is absolutely unnecessary. The world is capped and the moment you unlock the next capstone, the entire world scales to the new level. At the same time you get access to gear of the next bracket, so overall everything stays the same. Also talents, active and passive abilities, etc. are not unlocked by levelling. There is absolutely no point to having levels in this game. The other 50 progression systems are more than enough.

[h2]That being said...[/h2]
The game is fun. It has decent combat, great graphics, interesting stories and a nice soundtrack. Traversal is cool once unlocked in the respective regions. There are many options to customize the combat with two out of 10 (iirc) weapons, a bunch of passives and weapon-independant mystic skills. Unfortunately levelling more than 1 or 2 sets of weapons is a chore, so the theoretical variety is shrunken a lot in practice. I never got bored of my weapon sets, though.
Unfortuantely I have hit a point where the time-gating is really getting to me. You like those glowy weapons that you can exchange one harmonic core for? [h1] TL;DR [/h1]
Very fun game with flashy combat, plenty to explore, and more ways to (optionally) interact with other players than most modern mmos out there. Give it a couple hours and see if you like it- You'll know pretty quick.

[h2] Pros [/h2]
- It's free.
- Combat is buttery smooth with nice weapon variety.
- Excellent character creation. From Tim Burton Spongebob to supermodel; the game's got you covered.
- LOADS to explore, interact, and engage with. All of it feels worth doing, but not so much that it feels mandatory.
- Performance is decent, but frames will sometimes drop during longer play sessions. (Fixed on restart.)
- Progression is intuitive, with multiple ways to get the gear you need.
- A surprising amount of puzzles that go hand-in-hand with quests that require you to read.
- The signpost system (player-written messages a la Soulsborne games) is excellent, and was not something I knew I wanted until now. Use it as a hint system, use it to s**tpost, use it to share screenshots of your character.

[h2] Cons [/h2]
- You can pay for optional cosmetics (that have a fairly high price-tag).
- There are two optional subscriptions (Monthly Pass + Premium Battlepass).
- Sometimes the menu you need is inside a specific menu which is inside another menu which is inside ANOTHER menu.
- English dub is laughably bad, I'd recommend using Chinese voice with English subs.

Where Winds Meet (WWM) is an open world RPG set in a Chinese martial arts world with light fantasy elements. The game offers a huge map with many activities, such as mobs, bosses, treasures, puzzles, mini games, side quests and obviously also a main story. The combat is souls-light with a focus on getting parries and dodges right to counter for massive damage. While WWM feels to me like a fully-fledged single player game, it also has several multi-player features, such as dungeon and boss raids, pvp or social aspects (join a sect, perform daily tasks, get married, post a bounty on another random player, etc.).

WWM is "free to play" and currently entirely financed through battle passes and cosmetics. So far my anti-virus software has not yet detected any suspicious data mining activities ... The battle pass speeds up progression and grants some usually "no luck"-gatcha pulls for mid-tier cosmetics. The online features are meant to incentivize people to spend serious cash for the more "extravagant cosmetics".

I recommend this game to people who enjoy exploring beautiful open worlds with a broad range of activities. I am having fun playing WWM and it looks amazing! Not all is perfect though, as in order to manage your character and catch up on your next endeavour, you will have to navigate an impressively complex menu system. I am not exaggerating when I say, that it took me several hours to understand what I need to click and in which order to get things done. In a way it is somehow the boss I struggle most so far. I also seem to have a bit more of a hard time in this game to get the parries right. For the time being, I shall not blame network code as it is certainly a "me problem" ...

PvP is straight-up awful right now. A tiny 5–10 ms ping difference completely decides matches, which is ridiculous. You can’t properly combo lower-ping players, while they can lock you into true combos with no way out. That’s not competitive—it’s broken.

Class balance is just as bad. Some classes dominate while others feel useless, so a lot of fights are decided before they even start.

What makes this even more frustrating is that the game actually had an amazing start. The first 20–30 hours of story content were genuinely great and engaging. But now? The way new story content is being handled is unbelievably disappointing.

After keeping players waiting for 2–3 months, the latest “update” added what feels like 30 minutes of slow walking with almost no action, mostly just following NPCs around empty areas. That’s it. No meaningful gameplay, no real progression—just filler.

It’s honestly hard not to feel frustrated with the direction the game is going. The potential is clearly there, but the current decisions around PvP, balance, and content updates make it feel like that potential is being completely wasted.

I gotta be honest... It's fine. 
It looks amazing, the vibes are incredible. And that's what first caught my eye and keeps me coming back every so often. I like the genre and this scratches that itch. 

Everything else though.... no. The story makes little to no sense half of the time. I don't know if this is a translation issue or an AI issue (given that they have AI chatbot npcs in the game... it's not off the table). I haven't played the whole story yet, but far enough to notice that half of what is said or 'explained' makes no sense. I'm just confused half of the time, despite being accustomed to the genre. 
And that's alright. I've seen some people praise the story which is... good for them I guess? Maybe this really is more of a me issue. 

The more glaring problem is the cosmetics. I'm not saying they shouldn't be allowed to make some money of this game or anything like that, what I am bothered by is just how expensive they are. There are some that you can buy for 60 pearls, which is about 1$, and that's a really good price. There's some for closer to ten and all that, that's fine. But why the hell are some of the 'basic' cosmetic sets about 50$?? Don't even think about how expensive the gacha cosmetics are, you're easily in the thousands for those. And then they have the gall to charge you for dyeing them. (I don't know if dyeing the gacha legendary stuff costs anything, because I don't have any of those for obvious reasons, but I honestly assume that it does cost something.) It's really cool that you can dye your stuff, the costumization is nice to see. But if you're asking me to pay 50$ for a pretty basic outfit and then still charge for dyeing? No thank you.

Personally, I also dislike the bounty and jail system. I've never experienced them, but just hearing about it put me off and made me not want to play for a bit. Especially after seeing some people report that they were wanted for things they didn't do or for accidentally breaking a pot just by walking by it. Gotta say, not thrilled by the idea that some op player can come into my world and beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of me. Feels like it's feeding power fantasies for them and trying to convince me to buy something to stop being a loser. Like I said, I never experienced the system myself because I started playing like I'm walking on egg shells once I found out, so I can't say that this is for certain what it's like.

The combat is also very overstimulating, but that could totally be a skill issue.

I really only recommend this if you're purely in it for some vibes and cool looking places and don't mind a somewhat nonsensical story (imo).

Where Winds Meet is a game that truly deserves your attention.
Many people might assume it’s just another gacha title like Genshin Impact - and skip it. That would be a crucial mistake. The developers have created an incredibly engaging game packed with familiar and beloved mechanics from other iconic titles. While playing, you’ll notice influences from the Souls games, Ghost of Tsushima, Death Stranding, The Legend of Zelda, and Genshin Impact.
Where other studios might believe that combining so many different gameplay elements would result in something broken or chaotic, Everstone Studio has managed to turn it into a masterpiece.
As for the gacha aspect - it is almost entirely cosmetic and doesn’t interfere with the gameplay experience at all.
The story, combat system, and freedom of gameplay options are genuinely impressive. The character creation system allows you to design anything from a stunning beauty to the most hideous creature imaginable - completely your choice. It’s also great to see that the developers are actively communicating with the community and paying attention to player feedback.
So, I’ll say this: you simply need to try it for yourself. The further you progress, the more you’ll want to keep playing.
And of course - we’re eagerly waiting for more localization support!

Where Winds Meet is shaping up to be one of the most visually and atmospherically compelling wuxia RPGs in years. With its rich setting, fluid martial-arts combat, and deep role-playing freedom, it captures the magic of classic Eastern epics while offering modern open-world exploration.

If you’ve ever wanted to live inside a wuxia legend — to roam wild landscapes, master graceful combat, and write your own destiny — this game is a dream waiting to unfold.

Game itself is good.
World feels alive, NPCs feel human, battle system is okay, many interesting activities. I give credit, where credit is due. this could had been a positive review if not for the part that everyone seems to be afraid to talk about - business model.

I wish to make two things very clear:
Firstly, NO service provider is entitled to understanding of intricacies of their business or any sort of good will. Good will (and wish to repay or buy services) is at sole disgression of consumer based on value provided. In other words argument "game dev wants to eat" does not work if said dev is asking for too much for too little and I (or anyone else for the matter) have no obligation to care how many people work at their company and how high salaries they need to keep their things running.

Secondly, I am aware, that this game is NOT P2W in a strict sense of a word. When people say that "Game is not P2W" as an argument to defend this game's business model, I consider it a bad faith argument, since it is made on a false assumption, that microtransaction based model can be evil or unfair when and only when game becomes unplayable without utilizing paid options. Knowing video game player psychology, it is plain obvious that player wants to look good and/or express himself no less than he wants to see big numbers in his stat sheet. Therefore the distinction between monetizing good looks or stats is superficial.

Any Gamedev studio needs to make money to function, it is understandable. True question is how much money is it fair to demand in return for the value they offer and how the offer is made?

In-game purchases in this game start from 1$ and go beyond 50$.
and then, this game utilizes the full arsenal of marketing practices: convoluted system of multiple currencies to 
 obfuscate the true price of a lot of items, limited time offers, battlepass etc. And then we get to a heavy emphasis on social interaction to increase pressure on potential buyers to spend more. It does not quite matter if lower bar for in-game purchases is 1$ if anyone and their horse will have the cheap stuff and good old "oh, that guy/gal has that hair, I want too" or "my neighbor made his character look in a certain way, I must make mine look even better" sentiments kick in. Stakes will inevitably be raised.

I can imagine, there could be people in this world, for whom anything below 1000$ is a pocket change, but for an average person (a teacher, firefighter, man from the factory etc) in Japan, US or gods forbid, places like Indochina or East Europe 40-50$ is significant spending for one little nothing in a video game (especially considering you very likely can't keep it in any shape or form when one day in future the game dies and servers will have to be shut off). But it will not be just 50$ for an item. It will be hair from one purchase, dress from other and horse from third.

To sum it up, business model of this game is far from innocent and comes as dangerously close to what happens in gambling as possible even if it is not P2W. 40-50$ is a fair price for a full game, not for a little dress or a hairstyle in the game. In a healthy society, a person who claims otherwise should be perceived as speaking utter and complete nonsense.

Where Winds Meet is the kind of game that hands you a straightforward “go talk to this guy” quest, and sixty minutes later you’re perched on a misty peak you have no memory of scaling, your gallery full of artsy photos of the same gnarled pine tree, quietly questioning your life choices. The world is so ridiculously gorgeous that getting distracted feels like part of the design document.
The story and NPCs have real heart, too. I once had an old sage drop some profound wisdom on me about the impermanence of rivers or whatever, and my only internal monologue was: “That’s beautiful, grandpa, truly moving—now which way is the damn village again? I’ve been wandering since the prologue.”
Exploration is the real star here. You take one innocent step off the path to inspect a suspiciously glowing pebble, spot a hidden waterfall, decide to follow a deer “just for a second,” and suddenly you’re somewhere the devs clearly didn’t expect you to reach until act three. The game doesn’t scold you; it just nods like a proud parent watching you cause chaos.
You can pet the cats. Sometimes they even let you. On rare, magical occasions they rub against your leg like you’re not a complete stranger carrying three swords and a moral crisis. Other times they stare at you with dignified contempt while you’re mid-battle with bandits. Ten out of ten, immersive feline behavior.
It’s not flawless—the pacing takes a nap now and then, quest markers are explained with the clarity of a sleepy tour guide, and I hit a few minor frame hiccups that felt like the game pausing to admire its own scenery.
But honestly? It’s a stunning, chill masterpiece. If you like gorgeous open worlds that reward aimless wandering, regularly forgetting what you were doing, and writing your own accidental epic, this one will steal dozens of hours without you even noticing.

I´ve earnestly wanted to give this game a try since I have mutuals who play and recommended Where winds meet to me, especially since its Free2Play. Now that I´m about 4 hours into the game I figured I´d sum up my thoughts. I have only been playing the Solo Mode for now.

The most jaring thing first: This game seems to use AI in some way, theres NPCs you can "befriend" by texting with a chat bot, and some smaller graphic elements look alot like AI "art". Personally, that alone is usually enough for me to drop a game, and its not marked as such from what I´ve seen. The chat function especially does not seem to add much to the overall gameplay experience and feels more like bloating than anything to me.

Visually the environment is absolutely gorgeous, and despite the detail I´ve personally not experienced any performance issues, so thats a big plus.

The controls overall feel a little clunky to me, and you cant change the keybinds on the PC version. The imputs for movement are quite sensitive and running into NPCs will have them become potentially hostile towards the player.
The Sound balancing is.....a mess, sometimes it blows out your ears, other times it cuts out entirely and the UI is quite hard to navigate, Menues over menues and sub menues hidden behind more menues.....

I cant say much about the Story, and perhaps being ESL adds to the problems but I have yet to figure out what the overarching story is, and the overall sentencing structure can get quite convoluted/confusing to follow.

If you can look past the Controls/Sound issues and dont mind AI, Where Winds Meet can definitelys be fun but I personally avoid games that use AI and as such its not for me.

Where Winds Meet is the best free to play game I've played. Where Winds Meet is also the best MMO I've played. A positive and negative: There is so much content, you will not be able to find it all because it's buried in tunnels of menus. They have done the genius design decision to start players in their own instanced world, where they can unfold a compelling story, explore a vast land, and interact with hundreds of npc characters without being de-immersed by the chaos other players would present running around as well.
But everything is interconnected. As a healer, you can join another player at any time in their world to cure their illnesses in a full mini-game, and then return to your own. You can join groups of players to fight bosses, or play music, or raid enemy forts, or dance. Your interaction with npcs goes beyond taking quests as well. Cleverly designed AI chatting responds to conversation, making them your friend or enemy depending on what you say. Crime does not go unpunished. Theft or physical harm flags attention by local law, and continued infractions puts a bounty on your head and even jail time. Moreover, bounties can be claimed by other players, and allows them to invade your world as consequence. If you're in jail, you can call other players to help you escape.
Everything is interconnected. You are awarded currencies for anything you complete. From exploring, to completing questlines, collecting resources, etc. The developers knew all of their systems-- skill-based action combat, fast traversal, interactive cutscenes-- could only work with players running the world in their own instance. And that's why it works.
Some cons: Framerate does take a huge hit in the second area, as well as well as environmental pop-in even on low settings. CPU and GPU runs hot at all times. People have complaints about other things that never really bothered me. Free or not, if I don't like it, I wouldn't play it.

It does have a gacha system (Banners) that lets you get a small number of skins. The skins change every few weeks. Every 150 gacha pulls will trigger the "pity system," which will either give you a gacha skin or an orb that you can exchange for skins (armors require two of these orbs).

If you don't want to spend money on the gacha, you can still get 3 gacha pulls for free every week using in-game currency. You can also earn some pulls by fighting random NPCs across the map, but those are one-time rewards. We might also get some from holiday events. Even as a F2P player, you will still be able to get 150 pulls every 10-11 months to trigger the pity system. The pity doesn’t reset when the banner (skins) changes, so as long as you’re patient, you’ll eventually get those gacha-type skins.

My only complaint is the "Transformation Pill," which lets you change your gender, costing 20 euros/dollars per use. From what I understand, in the Chinese version players can buy it using in-game currency from a special shop that unlocks after purchasing the 5-euro/dollar "Monthly Pass." I assume that shop will release in the global version too, in a few months or sooner.

Story? I have no idea what’s going on — not because it’s bad, but because I keep getting distracted by rocks, ponds, cats, cliffs, butterflies, and every sparkly thing within a 500-meter radius.

This game is basically:

After around 30 hours, Where Winds Meet has been a surprisingly refreshing and enjoyable experience. Set in a beautifully crafted world inspired by ancient China, the game captures the feeling of wandering through a living wuxia landscape filled with mystery, combat, and exploration.

What I Enjoyed

World & Atmosphere: The open world is stunning. From quiet villages to wide grasslands and towering mountains, every area feels alive and worth exploring. The environmental design is honestly one of the strongest parts of the game.

Combat: Fast-paced and stylish. The combat system blends martial arts with unique weapon styles, and it feels smooth once you get used to the timing.

Movement & Freedom: Parkour, gliding, horseback riding — moving around the world is genuinely fun. Exploration feels natural and rewarding.

Story & Characters: The main story has an interesting foundation, and several side quests are surprisingly well-written, adding personality to the world.

Things That Could Improve

Optimization: Performance can be unstable at times. Some stutters and frame drops happen during busy areas or cutscenes.

Bugs: A few visual glitches and minor quest issues still appear. Nothing game-breaking, but noticeable.

UI & Menus: Some menus feel cluttered and could use better organization.

Overall

Despite its flaws, Where Winds Meet delivers a wonderful mix of exploration, martial arts action, and immersive world-building. If you enjoy open-world wuxia adventures, this game is definitely worth trying — and I’m excited to see how it improves with future updates.

Where Winds Meet has great potential, but, sadly, its atrocious localization ruins the experience — and that alone is enough to make me drop the game.

Still, let's start with the positives:
- WWM is gorgeous. I was drawn in by the Chinese aesthetics and wasn’t disappointed. Honestly, just walking around to enjoy the scenery and architecture is a good enough reason to download it.
- Performance is quite solid for the picture you get.
- The combat system is pretty fun and fluid, with a wide variety of weapons and skills to experiment with.
- It’s free, and the monetization is cosmetics-only.

Now for the glaring issue. Most of the English translation was done by AI, and it seems no one bothered to edit any of it. I don’t care much about the voice acting, since you can just switch to Chinese, which is handled fairly well. But if I’m playing a large, story-driven game set in a foreign country, with tons of dialogue and lore, the text has to be of decent quality. Right now, it’s nowhere close. To make matters worse, subtitles are not properly formatted and often poorly synchronized, giving you about a second to read two lines of text. With English not being my native language, you can imagine how frustrating all that becomes.

Some minor issues:
- Progression and menus are convoluted. There’s just way too much unnecessary stuff.
- Even with upscalers turned off, there’s ghosting around the character whenever the camera moves.
- Ubisoft-esque open world activities and collectibles, many of which feel shallow.
- The NPC AI-chatbot system is extremely primitive. Even if you try to roleplay and take it seriously, it breaks too easily.

I’d be happy to give WWM another shot, but only after major improvements to the localization.
