It's a definite yes... I wasn't sure. I wasn't convinced by the videos I saw. But then I tried it.
It's honestly, if not one of the best MMORPGs ever, at least the most original and innovative for it's mixed solo and mmo gameplay in one game.

The world building is MMO level, the plot is a very good single player experience.
The action combat works great in single player and multiplayer PvE, would be pretty good for PvP too if latency didn't mess it up this much.

Environments and scenery are gorgeous to the point of just enjoying the view and moving around the world with moments when one just had to stop and take it in for how beautiful it is.

Bosses are simply amazing. Original. Diverse. Challenging. And they make you want to go fight them again after the first win.

The combat heavily relies on deflections, pretty much what we all know as "parries", except they are not exactly parries in the way that they do not immediately stun a boss and trigger a counter attack.
Instead deflections drain the boss' "QI bar", consider it like a shield, and when it goes to 0 the boss is stunned and can be hit for a lot of damage.
The window for deflections is much longer and much more forgiving than parries in souls games but you also have to deflect barrages of repeated attacks so the two things compensate each other making it challenging to the right point.

Leveling up the character is very fast and easy and requires absolutely no amount of grinding.
However, what does require an amount of grinding at higher levels is leveling up skills.

The absence of a classic character class system opens the way to a variety of weapons and skills that can be mixed to one's heart's content in the way that they find most fitting their playstyle.
Now, the more experienced of us know any game will eventually turn down to a few min-maxed top builds, however I feel like there is a fair variety of options in this one.

The most challenging content is found in solo mode at the moment, with online bosses being just way too simple and reduced to a spam of attacks and healing from the party.
The first sort of challenging group activity you will find is the 10 players Hero Realm raids you'll unlock at lvl 51.
This is the first fight that will have actual party wiping mechanics and will require coordination, but for anyone with any raiding experience in any classic MMORPG they will still feel like child's play.

At the moment of this review the level cap is temporarily set at lvl 55 and the plan is to raise it by 5 every 7 days up to the final cap of, I believe, 80.
With each increase of the lvl cap new content will become available so probably something more challenging will turn up in the next weeks.

Finally, let me say something about monetisation and microtransactions.
Yes, the game will bombard you with a billion different menus and shops and currencies as in typical asian mmo style. We all hate it.
BUT. Everything that can't be obtained for free is purely cosmetic.
The only form of advantage you can obtain with money is one extra healing charge by purchasing the battle pass for 4.19 euros or whatever your equivalent is.
This is not a big advantage as you will quickly reach 3 heals by upgrading your medicine chest and at this time I have 4 without counting the extra one from the pass.

The game is a lot of fun and a seemingly endless mountain of content for both solo play and online play.
And the eastern version, which is one year in front of the western one, has an insane amount of extra stuff that will eventually get to us as well and is much worth looking forward to.
Such as a mechanisms crafting system straight out of Zelda, flying mounts, new fighting styles, bosses, story and areas.

I warmly recommend this game and encourage you to enjoy it for free without falling into the cosmetics gacha because it is absolutely useless.

One of the first things that hit me was the visual style. You create your own character and explore a world that feels grounded and cinematic. It feels like a world built for players.

The combat is another massive reason I’m hooked. It feels like a combination of Code Vein, Nioh, Black Myth: Wukong and Sekiro, but the strongest influence is definitely Sekiro. Parrying is one of the most important mechanics in the entire game. Timing matters, and you can’t just spam dodge and survive. You just have to actually get good, and the game rewards you for it.

What really shocked me is how much content is in the game. There are 1v1 arenas, guild arenas, and even a battle royale mode that feels similar to Naraka Bladepoint. There are raids and bigger MMO-style challenges. You can build structures and decorate your own world. There is a huge open world filled with things to do. And one of my favorite features is the bounty system, where you can check a bounty board and hunt down real players for rewards. It’s like the Dark Souls invasion system but with an actual purpose, not just chaos for the sake of chaos.

Everything together makes the game feel incredibly packed for something that costs nothing to play.

Overall, Where Winds Meet isn’t a perfect game, because nothing truly is. But it comes really close in a lot of areas. The combat is skill-based and satisfying, the visuals are beautiful and mature, and the amount of content is insane for a free title. With the way it’s designed and the amount of features already in place, I genuinely believe this game has the potential to grow into one of the biggest online titles. This is the first game in years that made me feel addicted again, and honestly, I’m glad I gave it a chance.

Where Winds Meet may very well be the best f2p game to date and it's better than a lot of the AAA slop that has a $70 price tag. While the gacha element is expensive, it is all purely cosmetic with no pay to win elements. At 48 hours I've still only scratched the surface of what the game has to offer, and it's only going to get bigger. Looking at what players in China have gotten since the game launched there a year ago, it's going to be much bigger with additional story content for new regions similar to Genshin and Wuthering Waves. 

The game does have it's flaws like confusing menu navigation, dozens of different currencies to keep track of and occasional performance issues, but the performance issues seem to be mitigated quite a bit by launching with DirectX12, at least for me. 

Despite it's issues, the game has been fun for me from the beginning and has an unbelievable amount of content. It's basically several games in one and the fact that this game has taken so many genres, mashed them together, and retained this level of quality while being free to play with no pay to win is unbelievable. 

If you like Sekiro-like combat, base building, unrestricted exploration, martial arts, or role playing do yourself a favor and try this game. It has something to offer for everyone. Just don't get too tempted by the cosmetics because they will take your kidney for it. On second thought, do get tempted by it and give these devs more money so they can keep releasing banger content for free.

This is an incredibly fun game, with or without friends. It has a ton of cool little mechanics and I love helping heal other players' injuries. The community of the game feels really wholesome so far, great game to play with my gf.

Game is overall fun.

Combat is decent for most weaker enemies. For bosses it can get annoying with trying to block/parry/dodge attacks and needing to use certain abilities in order to prevent very powerful attacks where you can have little to no time to prevent those attacks. Plus the parry windows get super small or basically nonexistent on some bosses. PvP is basically whoever has the most attacks that stun or are unblockable wins. If you get like below 50% health while the other player is near 100% (lets say 65%+) they'll probably win the fight.

Story is pretty good only a few annoying things here and there (using English audio and subtitles). Like subtitles being wrong in some spots. Dialogue in English being a little wrong (like I chose a female character and every once in a while they call me a guy, sometimes the text/audio doesn't match or rarely just some dialogue is in Chinese I believe). Or some times the Dialogue in English repeats (something like: "The dog went to the park and played with it's friends" for text but the dialogue will be "The dog went to the park The dog went to the park). Also for side quests and other random stuff it will just be talking with text with no audio and the text can go by super fast and there is no way to redo most of them (if you don't do the main option to complete the task you can keep selecting the same dialogue).

Movement is fun but can get annoying with the upgrade of going super fast. I am used to holding Shift to sprint. Which I think it technically does (might be press to sprint and hold for the other ability). But there is an ability you can get to make you go super fast that activates from holding Shift where you will climb up walls, fly over stuff and it's kinda hard to control at points. 

I feel like my main issue with the game is the currencies where you need a lot to do stuff and there are limits. Like in order to get an outfit for one Sect is like 6000 of the currency but you can only get like 1200 per week. Or there's like cats on the map that give you challenges to do and they'll give you bells in one area or coins in the other. I believe there are only a certain amount of those challenges on the map and more stuff in their store than there are coins/bells (they have a few cosmetics, another currency and other stuff). Playing with other people you get Adventure Slips but of course again there's a cap to how many you can earn each week.

I mostly play solo and with 1 other person. The main issue is I do a bunch of stuff in my game and when I join someone else's everything I got (chests on the map, the cat challenges, other collectables which are currency) is there but I get nothing for doing/collecting them again. I feel like every currency's shop they are used in has consumable items like I think Commerce Coins which are used for playing minigames with NPCs, renting properties or doing certain activities, or dyes (hair and clothing) which are only usable on certain cosmetics most of which you have to buy with real money.

Sects are kinda annoying. You can join one at a time and every day you get 6 quest from them to get a currency to buy sect items. The problem I have is you need to do a bunch of stuff to get from level 1 to level 2 to actually get anything good from a sect (their outfit/hair cosmetic). I believe I joined the Midnight Blades (PvP focused... I just want their cosmetics because I like them the most out of every free one you can get) which was talk to a guy and do a few things for him. I worked on them for a bit and their story. At the end of the story it wanted me to talk to their leader to join the Midnight Blades.... issue was I was already part of them. SO I had to leave and rejoin them. Which when you leave most sects you have to do the one PvPvE mode (basically a battle royal mode), didn't really realize this just out of nowhere when playing I was playing that mode and was super confused on how I got there from playing solo mode. I think between this (I believe there might have been a cooldown to rejoin them) I joined another Sect and then went and rejoined the Midnight Blades. I then later somehow started another sects story mission to join them... which I don't think I ever did join them. But my quest was talk to a guy and heal him to work towards joining the sect. But I can't heal him it doesn't give me the correct option for the quest. Apparently I need to leave the sect I am in and join the sect related to the quest to join that sect but there is nothing saying you must be part of that sect to do the quest so I thought it was bugged (logic missing on how am I supposed to be in the sect I want to join to do a quest to join that sect). But if I leave my sect I go from rank 2 back to rank 1 to my knowledge which was a pain because I needed 20 kills in the 1V1 PvP mode which took I think a few hours of get 1 kill, die, get 1 kill, die, etc. (a lot of obliterate an opponent, get obliterated with the very rare close match).


But again overall I do enjoy the game but eventually I feel like it's going to get stale with all the limits on what you can earn and what happens once I collect everything and complete all the stories. It will be play maybe once/twice a week until I hit all the currency limits then wait for the limit to reset the next week? I am starting to get there. Like I don't have enough Commerce Coins to buy certain things to do certain quests/activities, I collected a ton of stuff and I believe I am nearing the end of the current story (I have 1 area of the 2nd/last region blocked off I believe until I get a little further into the story. Not sure how much story is left after that.).

There are still a few rough edges like optimization and some minor bugs, but nothing that ruins the experience. Overall, it’s a refreshing open-world wuxia game that pulls you in and keeps you there.

In my experience so far this game is actually 'free to play'. You only pay for cosmetics. And you can also play the way you want. It can be hard for good players, but also very forgiving for casual players. You can change the games difficulty on the fly and there is an assistance-feature you can turn on or off for deflecting/parrying in battle. And I don't think you miss out on anything when you play it on easier difficulties. 

Also finally a mmorpg that doesn't force you into anything group-related! At least I haven't encountered any obligated grouping with other players yet. As a solo player who likes to be 'a lone wolf in an online world' this is fantastic.

Well, mmorpg... It's sort of an mmorpg? Maybe more a crossover between rpg, arpg, soulslike and mmorpg. To be honest, I don't really know how to label it properly. But that's part of the appeal for me. It takes a lot of good stuff out of different games I like and blend it together. 

The UI may take some time to get used to. The game is released in winter 2024 in China, so they had time to optimise things. Maybe it feels intuitive for players in China? For me it felt weird and confusing at first. But it's not as bad as it seems and I got used to it over time.

UPDATE: I've completed the story and sidequests, which were fantastic. Now I'm hunting encounters I've missed and completing some remaining taiping mausoleum stuff. But after that... I don't know. I'm not much of an achievements-hunter. And character progression is locked behind a timegate. I'm level 60 now and have to wait 10 days to be able to get to level 65. So there is no point in farming for better gear because it will be obsolete in 10 days. 

Also, as a solo non-PVP player, I don't think there is much endgame content at the moment that I'm interested in. For players like me the only endgame content I've seen so far is clearing outposts again, doing bounties or repeatable boss encounters. Bounties and outposts are short and repetitive, not a lot of fun. And those boss encounters are not much better. You only fight a boss (or two bosses). There is no dungeon or story around them. Also short and not very engaging... There is also no way to play the story again. And you can't make an alt (1 character only). 

So I am a bit afraid that soon there is not much left to keep me engaged until they release new story-content. Don't get me wrong, it's still a fantastic game. I definitely recommend doing the story and explore the beautiful world. And new story-content is probably coming soon. Hopefully they will also add more engaging endgame stuff for players like me, so it remains fun to play in between story-content releases.

Immersive, beautiful, breathtaking.  If you have an itch to play an MMORPG, but you want something special and fresh, PLEASE TRY THIS ONE. The world is highly developed, with NPC characters full of personality. There's even AI chatbots you can converse with, which does a lot for immersion. Numerous minigames and puzzles that are fun against both the AI and friends, including Majong, Chess, Rhythm Gaming, Slay the Spire, etc. The character customization is extremely advanced, comparing to any of the top tier character customizations you can think of. The story is also incredible and does tug at the heartstrings. It reminds me a lot of Red Dead Redemption 2. There is really so much to explore! As far as complaints, there are waaaaaay tooo many menus, you get lost in the UI easily. Also some of the voice acting is gooby.

انطباعي عن لعبة Where Winds Meet بعد 31 ساعة لعب
بصراحة، الألعاب الصينية بدأت تثبت حضور قوي في سوق الألعاب، و Where Winds Meet كانت واحدة من التجارب اللي فعلاً حسستني بهذا التطور. اللعبة تقدم مزيج جميل من الحضارة الصينية، سواء في القصة أو أسلوب التقديم.
القصة والمهام الرئيسية كانت ممتعة، والمهام الجانبية أعطتني دافع دائم للاستكشاف. عالم اللعبة واسع، جميل، ومليان تفاصيل تشجعك تغوص فيه أكثر.
أكثر شي شدّني هو أسلوب القتال: تنوّع الأسلحة، استخدام العناصر، مزج الفنون القتالية مع الأسلحة البيضاء… كله يقدم تجربة قتالية متقنة وممتعة. ومع كون اللعبة مجانية رغم حجمها الكبير، فهذا شيء يُحسب لهم.
واجهة المستخدم بالبداية حسّيتها معقدة، وتحتاج وقت بسيط لفهمها، لكن بعدها الأمور تمشي بسلاسة. أيضاً أعجبتني ميزة نقاط الإيضاح اللي تبيّن تحركات اللاعبين اللي سبقوك—فعلاً كانت مفيدة.
والشي اللي يميز اللعبة أكثر هو طور الأونلاين: تقدر تلعبها منفرد أو مع ناس آخرين، وهذا يعطي اللعبة عمر أطول ومتعة أكبر.
باختصار… Where Winds Meet لعبة جميلة وقدمت تجربة تستحق الوقت. أتمنى يضيفون خريطة أو محتوى جديد لأنها لعبة ما ودي تنتهي.

My Impressions of Where Winds Meet After 31 Hours of Gameplay

Honestly, Chinese games have been making a strong presence in the gaming market, and Where Winds Meet truly shows that. The game offers a beautiful touch of Chinese culture, both in its story and presentation.

The main story and quests are engaging, while the side quests give a constant incentive to explore. The game world is vast, detailed, and encourages deep exploration.

What impressed me the most is the combat system: the variety of weapons, elemental use, and the blend of martial arts with melee weapons create a polished and enjoyable combat experience. Considering the game is free and yet has a large storage size, it’s definitely commendable.

The user interface felt a bit complex at first and requires some time to get used to, but once familiar, it becomes intuitive. I also really liked the feature that shows progress points of players ahead of you in the story—it’s both fun and helpful.

Another standout feature is the online mode: you can play solo or with others, which adds longevity and extra enjoyment to the game.
In short, Where Winds Meet is a beautiful game that offers a rewarding experience. I hope they add new maps or content because it’s a game I definitely don’t want to end.

Where Menus Meet!

Some traversal animations for the player character and horse are stiff and abrupt. The key bindings are restrictive under certain circumstances, and it is not possible to rearrange all of them. The story is promising, and it features animated cinematics, but there's a boring curve before it picks up again. The Wuxia is a powerful concept in this game, but the game has certain daily and weekly activities which are tedious, such as spending 20 minutes inside the guild hall. 

There is an excessive number of screens and menus required to access "rewards." That's a very weak system for making the player spend time in the game. This is a significant drawback and it takes away from the game itself when I have to visit 4-5 different menus for the trial activities, the bounty activities, the exploration rewards, the realm rewards, the achievement unlocks, the gallery rewards, the social screen, the guild rewards menu, the event menu, the season pass one and the inventory that has 6 tabs in it. I'm certain I missed some still. 

Combat in the videogame is not lethal. The enemies feel like sponges soaking damage. I don't like that. Combat should be short and lethal, for both the player character and the NPCs. That can be an exception for the bosses under the pretence or circumstance that lore wise they are affected by magical or enhancement elements.

There's a lack of blend of environmental design, robust world-building, and player agency. The player character feels like he/she just exists in the world, along with the secret chest butterflies. There's no dynamic/radial events except for the 2 scnarios of catching a thief each time. The community and social dynamics are only done through matchmaking screens, instead of meeting in the game world first. The quest-driven engagement is minimum. There's almost no way for players to interact with the world's problems and daily life. And lastly, because a choice was made for AI generation, certain NPCs feel alive but oftentimes that costs the absence of organic lore and dialogue. Missing a great opportunity and strength for the game's world's lore to be delivered through a variety of methods beyond simple quest tracking markers, including in-game books (there are some letters), ocassionally overhearing NPC rumors (some inconsequential flair dialogue sometimes), and rarely environmental storytelling (e.g., diaries in a cave, scarce human remains or evidence of a struggle or other event), missing out on rewarding exploration and curiosity. A big exception to that is the Dark Surge side stories.

The doctors healing injured strangers in the world for a fee, bounty hunters chasing player criminals, and community-run spa mini-games that give buffs all are enjoyable and give life to the game. The ability to choose a profession (like a healer or scholar) and interact with other players in meaningful, non-combat ways makes the world feel alive and provides a sense of purpose. More meaningful professions would have been nice. Progress is not always shared seamlessly in co-op. Only the host often gets rewards for certain side quests, and non-host players can't interact with certain NPCs needed to unlock abilities, forcing players to repeat content solo. The inability to play the main story campaign with friends is a significant disappointment. The most critical suggestion is to fix the underlying technical issues causing lag and desync, especially for the PvP community. Allow all party members to receive rewards and progress the story or side quests simultaneously when in a group. Ensure all players can interact with key NPCs, with a group vote and a time-out timer. Developers could implement larger, multi-party raids or dynamic boss encounters to offer more complex cooperative challenges. Add an optional co-op mode for the main campaign to allow friends to experience the core narrative together. 

The developer could also offer color palettes in the cash shop and allow for more outfits to be color-able. Some player character and horse animations are stiff and don't blend together well. The horse feels stiff in general. Red Dead Redemption 2 and Guild Wars 2 mounts are more natural and fluid in their animations. it's a decent reference.

The combat and exploration blend seamlessly with themes of honor, balance, and personal destiny, giving players a sense of connection to classical Chinese values. Overall, it’s a captivating and respectful celebration of Chinese cultural heritage presented through an engaging open-world adventure.

This game has so much to offer, and it is free. You get tons of content to explore. I uncover something new about the game each day. And its free to play, you don't need to pay money to be good at the game. The gacha system is only for cosmetics. 

The game is very immersive, I feel like I am in a real world, especially when using that AI system for talking with NPCs trying to get them to like you or do something. Where Winds Meet has beautiful graphics and a well-designed world of Chinese lore. The movement is very fluent and breathtaking when you use lightskills. Furthermore, the game is challenging (at least for those who are not well-versed in souls like games) and makes you wanna play more to get better at it. 

Some say that the game wants to do too much at the same time, but for me it is an advantage. Everyone will find something for themselves and a lot of things doesn't require you to do them if you don't want to. 

However, there are some disadvantages. The interface is kinda confusing and requires a lot of patience from the player when looking for certain aspect of the game. Another minus, some puzzles require knowing Chinese language, eg. the one with pushing buttons having Chinese characters written on them that form a certain phrase/sentence or the puzzle game where you get a clue and sometimes the answer if a Chinese word or Asian type of thing that Europeans have no idea about. 

But apart from that, I highly recommend at least trying this game, especially as it is free and doesn't require a PC with strong equipment.

Updated: As a further con, the concurrent player numbers are not to be trusted. The game is rife with spambots, automated ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, world chat is utter cancer because the "Events" are just low-effort engagement bait that encourages the "players" to spam. Many folks utilize automated bots to spam said trash into the various WorldChannels of the chat, so good luck finding actual players, they're all going to be drowned out by the endless cavalcade of spam and bots.

It also suffers several online safety issues, key of which is the fact that the blacklist does not function properly on PC, so you can neither ignore nor block such spammers, stalkers, or harassment from your feed. This is all detrimental to the longevity of the game, since when new players can't get help, and just see walls of cancerous spam in every chat, they'll leave; with the inevitable decline in vets, because of burn out, locusting, or what have you, the lack of new players will detrimentally affect them, leading to their departure; and then where are the Whales at, with no one to flex on with their car-priced boats (side note: literally. Everstone has shown no interest in fixing any of these issues, even though the Blacklist not properly working has been an issue since the game launched. The fundamentals, gameplay wise, of the game are still solid, with some great story beats, fun mechanics, and a nice mix of content, however these above issues pose significant risks to any longevity the game might have. Community, in an online game, is what keeps folks coming back and staying around. Attempting to build any sense of community in the cancerous trashfire that is chat in this game is next to impossible: several channels are literally just bots.

Playtime: 90 hours

Review: Very Positive

Where Winds Meet is a genuinely great experience that has sunk its hooks into me for 90 hours so far. The visual art style is appealing, creating a beautiful and immersive ancient China that is a treat to explore.

The game truly excels in its combat. The boss fights are challenging but fun, demanding mechanical skill and making each victory feel like an achievement. It's a game that rewards practice and learning its deep martial arts systems.

The divide between the solo and online portions is amazing and a major strength. You can enjoy a complete, narrative-driven single-player RPG experience, or jump into the extensive online "MMO mode" for group activities, raid bosses, and community features whenever you want. This flexibility means you can play the game exactly how you prefer.

While some elements like the UI can be a bit clunky, the core gameplay, stunning world, and rewarding combat make it one of my favorite games this year.

The game is amazing. Very immersive, fun, and beautiful game. I can't count how many times my jaw dropped at how beautiful the world design is. The combat is what really stands out in this game. Combat is very tight, responsive, and lots of attack/skill variety that one can combine to create sick combos. The boss battles are really challenging and fun. Furthermore, the sense of exploration in this game is really satisfying. One instance you're trying to follow a side quest then suddenly you see something interesting from a distance that side tracks you for hours on end. Finally, for a free-to-play game, it's got awesome cinematics and cutscenes that compliment the storytelling, making it feel like you are watching a great movie.

The major cons I saw in the game are the bloated UI/Menus, missing English voice overs, and very linear talent tree. The UI in the game has been criticized by many players as being very bloated with menus that one can easily get lost to, which I confirm to be true. As for the English voice overs, a lot of dialogues are not voiced in English (hopefully the devs fill in more of the missing voice overs in the future) and subtitles are displayed way too fast most of the time that one sometimes misses vital info. Finally, the talent tree could have been improved by providing more branching options that allow players to have more character build customization in their chosen build archetypes (tank, DPS, or healer).

Overall, It is a very fun game. I'll rate it an 8.5/10, for now. With more updates coming to the game soon, It'll definitely become a 10/10.

I selected "no" because the controls were extremely awkward for me, can't change some keybinds, and the default is really really screwed up compared to normal games. Never ran across keybinds this... weird and odd. That being said, if you have the patience to go through all the menus, changing everything from the backwards upside down default keybinds to the normal ones every other game uses, this could be the game for you. Graphically it's beautiful, grass and trees flow with the wind etc. Everything seems like this is a good game, just really don't want to spend an hour changing keybinds to what I'm used to.

Came back and decided to give it another try, maybe they made some improvements to the game. Nope, still very awkward keybinds, but can manage, still beautiful, but for the love of GOD stop with the plethora of systems. Systems for the sake of systems is ALWAYS a fail strategy, as is listening to the elitists on how a game should be made. Stop trying to reinvent the wheel, there is decades of games that have done everything and you can see what works and what doesn't. I played for 4 hours or so and was still confused on how to equip skills, how to get weapon skills... even though I have the weapons? Huh? My counter button was the "e" key, I spam it on one guy, it works and I counter, do it on another the NPC beats the crap out of me. So, I try timing it, hitting the key right before the NPC ability lands, same thing, works for some mobs and fails for others without any apparent rhyme of reason other than when the NPC attacks.

This game isn't "bad" perse, just a lot poor choices in design trying to come up with the next big thing. Quite simply... the acronym K.I.S.S. ... Keep It Simple Stupid... decades of companies and thousands of games trying new things, go with what works, focus on the Casual PvE players they are the VAST majority of players in almost all games (PvP only games the exception). Going with what works and focusing on PvE with tight game loops (not 16 thousand systems & trying to redesign combat... again) is the winning formula, proven, garaunteed... if you want lots of profit which is the whole idea in the first place right? Such a shame, gorgeous game, not-fun or boring/confusing gameplay ruins it.

I have complicated feelings about this game. 

For me it scratches a certain itch, a new open world to explore, a wide array of different activities and minigames to play, a character to create and customise, beautiful visuals and, so far, I felt no need to use any of the monetisation options. For a f2p title it is undeniably impressive. It also has accessibility features I have yet to see adopted in other games and I greatly appreciate all the options you have to customise your experience and preferred playstyle.

It is however not a title I have any desire to interact with in a meaningful manner and it is not a title I would recommend if this is what you are looking for. The best I can describe it is to play this instead of doomscrolling whilst watching your second screen Netflix show. The moment you give this any kind of scrutiny it falls apart at the seams. The story (at least the parts I have played so far) and especially interactions between characters do not make sense, half of the game is following notification pop ups to claim rewards and get lost in menu screens, the translation is atrocious, hard to understand and the prevalent use of AI is frustrating more than fun. The world and mechanics are unfocused, overwhelming and shallow at the same time. 

In many ways this feels like slop, very pretty slop, but still mainly that, like the developers overcooked a pot of pasta, threw it at the wall to see what sticks, and well... since it's overcooked pasta, all of it sticks. It sadly drowns out the genuinely interesting, albeit unpolished, moments this game has to offer every once in a while.

I don't do a lot of these but I'll try to make it helpful. First, overall, this is the most fun I've had in any semblance of a RPG game in a long time and I know that's not even its main focus. Heck, I don't know what it's main focus is other than being fun and kinda out there. 

Things that stick out to me: 
- The game is free? Like forreal free and not pay to do more than 5 things in one day free?

- [Edited] You used to only get ONE character but now you can have more than one. TBH I've just kept going with my original because there's so much I don't have any way to be bored with this game, I think the only reason I'd go back to making another character would be to try a different weapon main

- The menu UI is...kind of overwhelming tbh [EDITED -- MUCH IMPROVED! Still a lot]. Good thing is you have access to like a million different things, bad thing is you have access to A MILLION different things. Yeah I'm serious on that, you think there's only 20 things? Oh no, homeboy, you click on one button there's 10 more behind that lol Also I'm constantly finding I've completed some kind of little daily or task marker for something I've clicked on at random and getting rewards for it? So it's a bit like finding tiny Christmas presents around your house constantly, fun, exciting, a little confusing. I have about 17 hours in the game so far at the time of this and I've kind of figured out the main aspects of the UI but it probably took me like 12-15 hours of intermittent gameplay to feel any kind of certainty where I was going when I clicked on something lol

- The combat is AWESOME, also hard. I'm playing on essentially easy because I'm not about that Hard life style but I've done a little combat on Hard and as difficult as it was, it was also fun. The actions make sense and the timing response in combat is cool to get a hang of even when I was doing it on Hard. Also, the combat animation is Dope AF

- The story so far is kind of interesting, love good Wuxia/Xianxia drama stuff. I can't speak for English voice acting but I have Chinese voices on and it's not janky sounding to me at least, feels like I'm in a drama

- I've done a little co-op with a friend which was also fun if not a little wonky to figure out at first on how to pair up in co-op (mainly just had to figure out which button it hid behind in the menu screen). But we both get EXP and loot when doing things and that is what I want

- The game is GORGEOUS, and the world feels HUGE even though the map doesn't look big. It's like every corner they could think to stick something in, they did it. Even so! It doesn't feel crowded or like you're tripping over NPC's constantly even with all the stuff in it. It's been a ton of fun to explore the map and see different places and it's just absolutely stunning visually

- Got thrown in jail for who knows what but ya know, 15 minutes only in prison on first go isn't bad. Reminded me to get water (some people got hours, seems to depend on what you did, I think maybe it was for property damage for me lol)

- Did I mention it's FREE!!!?????

Honestly, there's some rough bits but overall I've found both the game and the gameplay far beyond any expectations I could have of it. It's absolutely top notch fun getting to live and explore life as a Wuxia up-and-coming hero. The storyline is at least interesting and the characters entertaining and the combat is so cool and immersive to me.

For a free-to-play game, this is phenomenal. Honestly, even compared to full-priced games, it holds its own. I encountered little to no bugs, the world is absolutely stunning, and almost everywhere you go presents a screenshot worthy scene (got 60 already). The whole experience feels like Ghost of Tsushima, but set in China, with less seriousness and more mythic flair.

The music isn’t anything extraordinary, but it fits the mood perfectly. More than once I found myself wanting to put on a classic Chinese martial arts film or an epic period drama while playing, because the atmosphere hits that same nostalgic note.

There is a lot to do, and most of it can be enjoyed “offline” without engaging with the MMO side. One of the coolest features is the AI powered NPCs that you literally have to type to in conversation. Winning them over through dialogue to gain friendship is a surprisingly clever and immersive use of AI in gaming.

The game is packed with mini-games, exploration, and freedom. You can pretty much kill anyone you meet. The gameplay is very much a blend of Ghost of Tsushima and Dark Souls, borrowing elements from both. The world feels alive, the characters can be charming, and there’s always something happening around you.

I’ve played around 20 hours so far. I got distracted constantly and only recently pushed through the main questline. The epic cutscenes at the end genuinely got me excited to see what comes next. The combat system isn’t revolutionary, but many fights are challenging, especially on higher difficulties. Normal enemies aren’t much of a threat unless you’re playing on the hardest setting.

My only real criticism is the menu system. There are too many menus, they’re all over the place, and it takes a long time to figure out where everything is. Even now I’m not convinced I know what half of them do.

Aside from that, this game has been an awesome experience. It’s fully free, with no obligation to spend money. You could play the main story, explore the open world, mess around with the systems, and walk away with 10–20 hours of genuinely high quality gameplay at no cost. It puts many so-called “triple-A” games to shame.

Highly recommend.

[h1] Stunning Game, Great Gameplay (but with a few caveats) [/h1]

[b]TL;DR:[/b] A gorgeous Chinese wuxia action RPG with excellent solo gameplay, but crippled by multiplayer latency and expensive cosmetic gacha.

[h2] What This Game Actually Is [/h2]

Let me clarify what Where Winds Meet is, since I jumped in after hearing it described as "Witcher 3 meets MMO meets Chinese culture." That's not quite accurate. If you've played Genshin Impact, you know how it takes heavy inspiration from Zelda: Breath of the Wild; Where Winds Meet does the same thing with action RPGs like The Witcher 3. It's ARPG-inspired and MMO-lite: you'll find combat and progression elements reminiscent of action RPGs, and some multiplayer features, but it lacks the depth of either genre. If you're expecting a full-fledged ARPG or MMO experience, you'll be disappointed. Think of it more as an open-world action-adventure game with Chinese wuxia flavor and optional co-op elements.

[h3] The Major Caveats [/h3]

[b]First: The latency is terrible. [/b] This is the biggest issue and makes multiplayer basically unplayable. Even doing co-op with someone in the same room creates massive delays for the visitor, making it impossible to parry or dodge correctly, mechanics that are essential for any challenging content. This kills both co-op and PVP. Some feedback suggests this only affects cross-region matching, but that's not true in my experience. I'm unsure why NetEase doesn't use Steam servers to resolve this.

[b] Second: It's a gacha game.[/b] To be fair, it's not as predatory as many others, you don't need to pay anything to be strong, as the gacha is purely cosmetic (aside from minor QoL items like extra health potions and inventory space, which aren't gacha-locked or expensive; I see these as optional subscriptions). However, they went heavy on cosmetic monetization. Want a different hair color? You have a cheaper but less appealing option, or you can pay $400-600 for ONE color with ONE hairstyle. That's right, you pay that much and can't even use it with other hairstyles or switch back without paying more. I've also seen comments that some items with fixed prices on Chinese servers are gacha-locked for Global.

[h3] The Good Stuff (And There's A Lot) [/h3]

It's gorgeous. The Chinese-inspired lore, the fluid combat animations, the humor woven into quests (learning Tai Chi from a bear, getting utterly destroyed by a goose) it's all on point. The multiplayer integration is genuinely clever: you might catch a disease and need a healer, or get framed and need to lawyer up. The character customization is impressive, especially for facial details (though makeup, hair, and piercings are limited, mostly due to the aforementioned paywall).

It's a free game with beautiful scenery, engaging quests, and rewarding exploration. You can play it casually on story mode, or if you're a soulslike fan, crank up the difficulty but good luck with the Puppeteer boss early on!

[b] Final Veredict [/b]

A over and underrated game at the same time. Is it worth your time? Sure, it's free and a perfectly fine game. Only costs your time and that could be spent worse.

What this game is not
- A MMO
- A revolutionary game
- Polished 
- P2W
- Slop

This is not an mmo, this is Genshin Impact with more realistic textures. Exploration, puzzles, item gear/upgrades and general open world content is 1 to 1 Genshin/Wuwa. Unlike those games, the multiplayer features have slightly more focus. It's actually about the same amount of features as those games but you are made to interface with them more. It amounts to doing daily multiplayer outposts and multiplayer mini-games that can be done afk.

This game is not revolutionary. All it does is copy features and mechanics from other games without understanding why they are that way. The open world is all copied from Genshin/Wuwa. The combat is souls-like but a lot more scuffed. It is hard, like a souls-like but in a more frustrating way than engagding. It does deserve props for presenting actually hard content but hard doesn't mean good. The core of it is parries. It's not told to you, but every attack except gold flashes is parriable and doing so does break bar damage. It is the main source of break bar damage and most bosses wont let you do real damage without a break. So the combat is more a rhythm game of parrying everything till you can do a dps rotation. 

 It's even stranger in the multiplayer bosses where the game suddenly stops trying to be a souls like and instead a holy trinity mmo fight but changes nothing except healing numbers. The more you play, the more scuffed everything feels.

It is not polished. The localization and voice acting is scuffed. There is a ton of mistranslated or untranslated text. Some quests are done with AI voice acting while some are not voiced at all. I fell through the map at least 10 different times, 1 time was in a cutscene. The is a floatiness and clunk to just about everything. There is a ton of mini-games and features thrown in that are not complete systems and more at a barely functioning level. 

What is polished is the graphics and performance. It looks genuinely amazing and it runs perfectly on a potato. I have no idea what witchcraft they used to make it run like this.

This game is not P2W, despite copying everything from Genshin/Wuwa. There is a gacha for skins that you can ignore ( they don't even look good ) but nothing to gain power. The is a strange trend among chinese mobile games to suddenly pivot away from gacha entirely. Maybe regulation is coming and they are trying to get ahead of it.

It is not slop. I spent this entire post knocking the game down, but it does try to refine the forumla. Open world puzzles have a point beyond farming 5 pull currency like other games. Each puzzle grants a exploration stat, that is needed for skill unlocks and to use some gear. Collecting all the things gives power and skill, noticable ones too. The quests are interesting. They are not afraid to make a unique one off mini-game for a quest or transform a zone to tell a story. The writing is lost in the bad translation and if you look closely at it you can see the smoke and mirrors but it is still more effort than most games give.

I would rate it 7/10, about the same level as Ghosts of Yotei or AC:Shadows, but seeing as those games are $70 and this is free. I'd pick this one over those any time.

What I loved about this game:

- Combat is spectacular. Motion-captured martial arts make every fight fluid and cinematic, with multiple weapon styles (sword, spear, fan, even umbrella) that each feel unique. Perfect parries and combos are satisfying without being punishing.

- Exploration is rewarding. The world is packed with puzzles, mini-games, and side quests. You’ll stumble across hidden scrolls, sect abilities, and rare techniques that shape your personal combat style.

- Freedom of choice. You can join one of several sects, become a healer, a fighter, or even a wanderer. NPCs react dynamically—sometimes accusing you of crimes or requesting your help—which makes the world feel unpredictable.

- Visuals are stunning. From bamboo forests to snowy peaks, the landscapes are breathtaking. It looks and feels like a premium title despite being free-to-play.

What could be better:

- The UI is clunky and overloaded with menus, currencies, and systems. It takes time to learn, and early hours can feel overwhelming.

- Some puzzles lack creativity, offering only one solution path, which limits player ingenuity.

- Technical hiccups like pop-in, odd menu layouts, and occasional animation quirks break immersion.

- The game is massive—100GB install size—so be prepared for the storage hit.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a joyous, content-rich martial arts adventure that delivers far more than expected from a free-to-play game. It’s not perfect, but if you’re a fan of wuxia, open-world exploration, or stylish combat, this is absolutely worth diving into. The community is already buzzing, and I can’t wait to see how future updates expand this world.

Where Winds Meet is a stunning achievement—an open-world RPG that shines with exceptional beauty, creativity, and emotional depth. From the moment you enter its vast world, the game overwhelms with breathtaking landscapes: misty mountains, serene villages, and vibrant cities that feel alive at every step. The visual artistry is spectacular, making exploration endlessly rewarding.

Movement across the world is wonderfully fluid. Parkour, elegant leaps, and thrilling glides give you a sense of true freedom, turning even simple travel into an exhilarating experience. Combat is equally impressive: fast, graceful, and intensely cinematic. Sword clashes flare with energy, special abilities burst with dramatic flair, and every fight feels both challenging and immensely satisfying.

The story adds remarkable weight to the adventure. Filled with political intrigue, emotional twists, and memorable characters, it draws you in with surprising richness. Choices matter, and even small encounters feel meaningful and deeply personal.

The soundtrack elevates everything further. Sweeping orchestral themes blend beautifully with traditional instruments, creating a soundscape that enhances each moment with striking emotion.

Technically, the game is outstanding—polished, smooth, and crafted with unmistakable care.

In short, Where Winds Meet is a captivating masterpiece that sets a new standard for the genre. It is a game that dazzles at every turn and remains unforgettable long after you stop playing.

My first hours in this game were an unhinged sitcom starring me, a bear, and several medical emergencies. 

I began by crafting a character so horrifying the character creator begged for mercy and the game politely pretended he was normal. Cutscenes paired my goblin-faced mess with perfect K-pop angel NPCs like a before-and-after skincare ad. It only got worse from there.

I witnessed a bear practicing tai chi to steal a beehive, copied the move like a shameless tourist, and immediately punted the bear into the sky like a furry space program. Bees then proceeded to dismantle my will to live, leaving me bruised, poisoned, and looking like expired fruit.

I accidentally stole a horse, got clotheslined by its previous owner, and realized I was one more injury away from becoming medically classified as soup.

Then salvation arrived, a stranger joined my session. His name might as well have been Asian John Wick. He rolled in, healed my collection of crippling ailments, bowed politely and then beat me into paste. Never took a scratch. Left like Batman.

I was humbled. Enlightened. Traumatized. And inspired.

Thus began my medical career.

I healed geese. I cured villagers. I stress-tested guildmates by practicing chakra healing on them at random intervals like an overly enthusiastic chiropractor. Eventually, I was curing depression, bone fractures, and probably childhood trauma.

Requests poured in endlessly. World chat named me The Green-Faced Duelist Doctor, the healer who cures first and challenges later. A legend with 100 flawless medical-violence house calls.

Then he returned.
The one who birthed my journey... Asian John Wick.

He asked me to cure a Soul Bind. I succeeded. We fought. I won with a single HP left and the spirit of every goose I ever healed behind me. He bowed one final time and vanished.

I sat there realizing: I have become the monster healer I feared.

Best free game ever.

One of if not the worst combat system in actions games I've played. 

Terrible stamina system where you're constantly running out of stamina from running in combat, dodge, parry, and guard, yet you still need stamina for heavy attack to do any meaningful damage outside of skill. Other games you only get punished by stamina when you overcommit or spam dodge, but in this game running out of stamina is just the norm, and you must do a ton of exploration to increase stamina limit. 

Bosses have terrible movesets, every new boss you must memorize the entire pattern because they're counterintuitive and combos have zero windup, unlike other action games where you can rely on your instincts build up throughout the game. This means, you don't ever "get better" at the game, you just end up memorizing combos. Most bosses also have two phases, but early on you only 1 or 2 potions so you just have to no hit a phase. There is also a 3 phase boss in the story, terrible experience.

Perfect dodge time stop has no invuln, meaning you can still take damage during time stop. This is especially annoying because of the horrendous lingering hitbox of attacks, and some bosses have double hit from shockwaves, you will ALWAYS get hit by the shockwave if you perfect dodge the stomp. This also means you can't comfortably deal damage during time stop, completely dismissing the point of it. Dodging also doesn't have follow up attacks, this would normally be fine but paired with the horrible stamina, you have no stamina to run towards time stopped enemies and end up walking up slowly. Could've learned from FF16

Parry timing is ♥♥♥♥. Period. It's an extremely short frame if you play without assist, paired with bosses' unrecognizable attacks, it's straight up infuriating. This is taken from straight Wolong yet it's nowhere as good. 

On top of that, no matter what you do to nullify boss attacks, they will continue to combo you, so you must nullify the entire combo. Failing a single one will result in you getting hit by ALL attacks that follow because of stun lock. 

Outside of combat it's okayish, story was fine until they killed characters pointlessly without any meaningful development, exploration is vast but from playing many open world exploration games it's just the same formula. Asset loading is horribly done as you can see things loading in and out on screen so it breaks immersion.

Ehhh, let me just keep this simple.

:Pros:
- Looks great
- Movement/Traversal is fun
- Neat looking cosmetics
- Combat is fun. It's not perfect and takes some getting used to but it's got a good foundation.
- You can bodyslam a bear.
- Stealth is better than Assassins Creed, not joking
- World doesn't feel empty
- A random cave turns into a 2 hour exploration that pops you out 2 miles away from where you started
- There are animals that you can pet
- It feels like you get lots of options for weapons and skill combinations which is great.
- See a mountain? Screw following the trail, run up it. Hang off the side of the cliff. Take a screenshot.
- The sky is gorgeous.
- Runs extremely smooth, in my case anyway.

:Cons:
- First and foremost the in-game shop is INSANELY priced. We're talking $40 on the low end and as high as you can imagine on the high end. I'm completely fine with a game having a shop in a free game, that's totally fine. But when the cost of a back accessory is the same price as a full game, that's absolutely absurd and I feel bad for anyone who pays those prices because they want a cape or something. I'll never understand why companies don't price cosmetics lower and encourage >more< people to purchase them than bank on people being whales while driving the typical, every day, player towards never making a purchase because the shop feels incredibly predatory. But that's this type of game, I suppose.
- Your progress is time gated. Your levels are locked behind 'breakthroughs' so you are limited to how many levels you can get per day. Once you hit the daily cap, your EXP appears to be stored for when you can breakthrough after a daily reset but in reality it just feels like "welp, I'm done for the day" and you close the game.
- Typos all over the place. Even in the in-game survey they specifically ask if you have seen multiple text issues and the question itself is a text issue.
- NPCs have voiced dialog which is fine, but they will repeat it over and over, or sometimes say an action such as "sigh." Not like they audibly sigh, they say "sigh."
- The chat in the UI is eh. At the left side you have player chat. And then if an NPC starts having a conversation is spams the middle of your screen and doesn't stop until they stop talking, even if by the time they started you have ran a mile away.
- People drop messages right on top of objects you need to interact with leading you to need to block the message to interact with the object.
- There is So. Much. Unskippable. Yapping. I get that people enjoy the story, and the game even offers a neat feature in the things you can skip by giving you a quick overview of what you're skipping. But the first hour of the game is just Talk to NPC, yap yap yap, Talk to NPC, yap yap yap. It's >A LOT< of dialog and at least 70% of it is unskippable.
- Menu Hell is all I can say. There are so many menus, sub menus, and 'you got something new! It was a TWIG!' alert dots all over the place that if you have any sort of OCD it's absolutely going to set it off every 60 seconds.
- No Borderless Fullscreen.

Basically - It's a decent enough game especially being Free to Play, but I sincerely wish the cons were handled. I can't say 'don't play this!' because I've been having fun with the hours I put into it but... Man I just hate when games drip-feed me content with time gating so unsure if I'll keep playing it. But you do you and if you enjoy the game, play it. But if you hate the cons listed above, maybe give the game some time to cook.

No propaganda to suffer through.

TLDR; if you wanted the short version: 
Good game, good story, good combat, 9/10, could be 10/10 if the UI was not horrible and confusing at first. 

Single player aspect: 
- this game's story line and animations beat paid AAA games for the low, low price of FREE. 
- the visuals are nice, there was so many moments where I just slowed down for a bit to appreciate the world building. 
- the combat is genuinely fun, blocks, parries, different skills to learn, ITS GREAT! outside of traditional combat weapons and skills they even have goofy ones like using a goose to scream for you mid combat, turn into a frog, tai-chi a bear into a pile of rocks, the list goes on. 
- character customization is peak, you can make it look like yourself using the camera function, or edit it manually by hand, and if you are like me who is extra lazy, just copy from the catalogue of user-made beautiful presets. 

Multiplayer aspect: 
- there is genuinely so much stuff to do in multiplayer ranging from chill, fun activities to sweatlord, maidenless activities. 
- there are things to do if you love socializing, you can do group activities like in game pop quizzes, get drunk, get arrested and paraded, open bath houses, play as a doctor or a lawyer, etc. 
- there is also A LOT more activities if you love combat content, such as solo/group boss raids, outpost raids, battle royale, 1v1 duels, 5v5 fights, guild boss raids, and probably so much more that I just haven't seen yet. 
- no pay2win as the only thing you can buy in this game are cosmetics. 

downsides: 
- menu within menu within menu within menu within menu with- okay need I say more? 
- English voice over SUCKS outside of main quest, the quality goes from good voice acting in msq to straight up AI voiced npcs, the Chinese voice over is definitely better. 
- some of the paid cosmetics are EXPENSIVE, and also GACHA-based. Like 40k USD for a decorative boat expensive, or 20k USD for a specific glowing effect for your weapon expensive. Luckily, these are optional cosmetics only, and the normal priced and free cosmetics are actually good looking so you are not required to whale or even pay at all if you wanted to look good.

    [*]The breakthrough system is flawed because, being mostly single-player, enemies level with you and remain just as annoying.
    [*]To have a chance, you need at least fully slotted purple gear, which can only be obtained by fighting bosses and is [b] randomly [/b] dropped.
    [*]Gear durability is lost if you die, which is frustrating.
    [*]All heals are consumables, so if you're stuck on a boss, good luck.
    [*]There is no level requirement stated for quests, so you'll need to postpone them if you find out you're underleveled while taking the quest, breaking immersion.

I don't write reviews, I don't care to do so, but for those on the fence, here is some insight. I've played Rise of Ronin, and Ghost of Tsushima. This game gets easily compared with having similar styles. I feel like this game combines the concepts of RoR and GoT, with it's own blend. It has a unique style, and scratches my itch for this sort of thing. It feels very immersive to explore the world. The towns and cities you visit, are very busy, and looks very lived in. It feels very believable for the experience it offers, at the price of FREE.  I have spent money on this game, because I have expendable income. After playing approximately 60hours at the time of this review. I can say the gameplay/combat feels very good, especially with different combos with weapons you can choose.  The dodging/parrying, and abilities feel really good.  I like the customization of your character, however, I'm not a total fan of all the clothing options, but that's personal taste. Particularly, everything seems it's robe based in appearance and really sticking with the theme of traditional Chinese attire. Which isn't bad, just purely isn't my taste. I prefer options that would include hakama's, or jackets of sorts, to be nitpicky.  However, my character FEELS like my character. You can unlock clothing rather than purchase from the shop, in which case I would prefer more of. I understand this game is free, so I guess it's acceptable to show support with the shop.  Even with the game being free, the graphics I find to be amazing for what's offered. It runs better than other AAA games that were released this year.  I find the optimization here simply, amazing. As of right now, the graphic options offer FSR, and not DLSS for NVidia users. I use an RTX 5070, and the game still runs super well. The multiplayer is simple enough, and isn't a feature I have explored a ton of, but have participated in. The boss battles change mechanics up enough, and simple enough to understand. There is still challenge enough to fail, but not to be impossible.  The story, is better than I expected, with the characters and relationships you encounter, and can occasionally tug at your heart strings. It's not crazy good, but it's not just passable either. There's effort with the writing, that's appreciated.  I would recommend this game to others who appreciate this sort of style and time period. I'm excited for what's to be upcoming in the future months, and what else there is to offer.

"The Swords of the Sixteen States": Unlock Boundless Freedom in a Turbulent Martial Arts World
If you yearn for a "unshackled, do-as-you-please" martial arts realm, The Swords of the Sixteen States is hands down the most authentically romantic domestic open-world gem on Steam. Breaking free from traditional sect-based frameworks, this game uses its raw, distinctive aesthetics, high degree of freedom, and profound Eastern heritage to let me truly live as the swordsman I’ve always imagined in the chaotic Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.
Martial Arts Freedom Beyond Sects: Forge Your Unique Jianghu Path
The game’s most stunning core lies in completely shattering the rigid "sect-bound martial arts" stereotype. You can join unique sects like the "Three Watch Clan" or "Nine Streams Sect," abiding by their rules to master exclusive skills. Or you can roam as an independent warrior, absorbing strengths from all schools through learning secretly, chance encounters, and exploration. Chinese martial arts tricks like acupressure subdual, Tai Chi’s power redirection, and wall-climbing are at your fingertips. Swords, spears, fans, umbrellas—switch and combine weapons freely; even an unconventional pairing of Tang sword and umbrella can carve out a distinctive combat style. It’s true "my martial arts, my rules."
Immersive Realism: Authenticity in Every Detail
The game’s realistic mechanics breathe life into the jianghu. Suffering heatstroke leaves you weak, eating raw meat might cause diarrhea, a broken leg makes you limp, and reckless martial arts combinations can lead to qi deviation. Different injuries require targeted treatment—you can even choose to play as a healer, gaining reputation by curing others. The "harmony between heaven and humanity" natural chain adds extra fun: use deer meat to lure wolves and bears into fighting, then reap the rewards. Day-night cycles, rain, snow, and wind, paired with scene-fitting ancient melodies, make every exploration feel like stepping into the millennium-old Yanyun land in person.
Both Single and Multiplayer Modes: Rich Gameplay Depth
The single-player mode is a complete standalone masterpiece—just the Qinghe map offers over 60 hours of content, with more than 700 random exploration points, dozens of puzzle levels, and over thirty uniquely mechanized bosses. The main story and hidden plots weave together, revealing the human struggles amid chaos. The multiplayer mode supports thousands of players online in the same server: team up to challenge guardian levels, practice martial arts together, or engage in large-scale roleplay. The 2-3 player squad mode offers exclusive cooperative content, and folk activities like pitch-pot and cuju add warmth to social interactions.
Minor Flaws Can’t Diminish Its Charm
Admittedly, the game has room for improvement. Some dungeons lean toward "sect binding," affecting rewards for cross-sect teams, and certain bosses have slightly imbalanced stats. But the developers consistently release patches—lowering boss difficulty and boosting cross-sect rewards. This willingness to listen to player feedback makes the game’s future incredibly promising.
The Swords of the Sixteen States uses the imagery of "wind" to interpret the free-spirited nature of martial arts. There are no right or wrong answers here—only your unique jianghu story. If you’re tired of repetitive sect-based settings and crave pure martial arts romance in an open world, this game is absolutely worth diving into.

Where Winds Meet is an unforgettable game. Not only is it free to play, and runs on relatively low system  requirements even with the full install (there is a smaller install available; not on Steam) but it manages to look amazing while doing so. I have noticed the odd occasional graphical glitch, and some low res rendering of my character in  cut scenes (but its still the costume and appearance I set up) but these are only occasional and despite this flaw, are subsidiary issues compared to the incredible atmosphere the game manages to create.

Being an RPG the game is expansive with many hours of content to explore. Although there is your standard increase in exp to level you, there are additional ways to customise your character and their traits, through playing various minigames or completing exploration tasks. Your character essentially becomes what they do, which feels like the very essence of roleplaying. For instance petting cats raises your charisma whilst running and training with disciples increases your endurance. 
Additionally,, interactions with NPCs include interactions with individualised chatbots for each NPC this harkens back to the days of MUDs where you were able to freely enter info and receive responses. The chatbot then processes the info and after hitting dialogue points increases your acquaintance with that character. Likewise regularly buying form merchants also increases your friendliness with them. It's a fun way to puzzle through and engage with freefrom dialogue.
The story itself is phenomenal and ranges from the absurd (rabid geese, kung-fu chickens), to tragic (a love never spoken for an entire lifetime, past losses) and sometimes switches between these abruptly to keep the audience engaged and lighten or tone down the mood to create moments of contrast. Its well worth playing, and there is lots of lore to discover...

Combat is incredible for a wuxia game. Not only is each attack beautifully choreographed making you feel like a skilled professional from the get go ,but the souls light combat is fun to play (if you're ping isn't killing you). Most of combat consists of parrying and dodging and counterattacking when enemies are in a weak or vulnerable state. To press them you have a plethora of weapon options (linked to your RP within the sect you choose, or steal the skills ,or be disloyal and leave and join sects). This is further expanded on with passive Inner Way customization. The game does rely on the tank/healer/dps setup. But a skilled DD good at dodging and parrying can still carry a group with a tank unable to taunt properly. Co-op includes running through Outposts killing mobs until the boss arrives ,specific Boss fights with fleshed out mechanics that rely on awareness and co-operation between team mates. There is also a PVP mode in the Arena which I haven't attempted. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3608216465
Exploration is an absolute joy,,, with things that you stumble over at every corner from amusing encounters with a lonely child who is being bullied (til she gets a doll) to enraged bears that you can lure into an enemy camp, and even a mystical deer. I can barely scratch the surface in this short review. 
The multiple mini games are fun and offer a variety so if becoming frustrated in one area, ,hope over to another activity for a bit, ,these games also allow you to level them up such as levelling healing skills, or dialogue cards for the argument minigame. 

There are issues here though, most likely browsing other reviews youll see complaints over the menu complexity ,which is a large issue,, once you have started to figure them out there are some neat tricks to quickly jump around, and the map also is quite complex but once youve figured out the way to set waypoints and track items it becomes a lot easier... it is ridiculous that this can take so many hours of play to figure out.
Upgrading weapons and abilities is also unintuitive, there is a lot to upgrade and this can also become confusing. The game offers tutorials but they are bareboned and dont offer a lot of guidance or help. Especially if you are uncertain what each weapon and ability does (they do have tooltips to start figuring things out though but again this might take a while to master). 
The netcode also seems quite patchy when joining co-op with friends or strangers I noticed massive lag spikes and unresponsive controls so be aware if switching out of solo mode). 

As a free game (that so far is not P2W) and only really raking in cash from cosmetics, I'd advise anyone to download this, it has the best elements of exploration, combat and social, and offers something for everyone. Just be aware you may need to invest time in learning... menus!

Probably the most surprising hit of 2025 so far. Where Winds Meet manages to combine a plethora of different systems into a Wuxia MMO(-lite) that not only feels genuinly alive with its huge open-world design but also encourages multiplayer interaction in creative ways, if one wants to interact with it. It really gives you the choice of playing it entirely solo as an action RPG with a great story and boss fights or more like an MMO with dailies, gear progression and multiplayer dungeons and raids. It's also one of the best looking MMOs I've played to date, while still offering good performance on mid-tier hardware and even a separate version of the game that's meant for even less powerful PCs, though exclusive to their own launcher and not on Steam.

And all of that offered for free with very little P2W, or none at all depending on your definition. It's Pay-To-Flex with dozens of cosmetics, mounts, animations and literal yachts to purchase for those with enough expendable income, yet none of it will make them top the charts in raids or win arena matches.

That said, the game isn't perfect. My 2 biggest pain points with the game are the UI and localisation. While I understand that creating a UI for a multifaceted game such as this is extremely challenging, its mobile-style design with red notification dots, minor rewards for dozens of different reward tracks and general tile-based design makes it much more convoluted than it would have to be, although already improved compared to the Chinese version from what I've seen. Eventually you get used to the parts you need to interact with regularly, but that's just living with the disease, not curing it.

And the localisation, if you want to call it that, is the one thing I hope doesn't set precedent for other games in the future. The Chinese voice acting is great, but they use primarily AI generated voices for the English voiceover, which is grating to listen to. And while the English text is generally understandable, it appears like this too was at least heavily assisted through machine translation, since there are many instances where the translations make little to no sense at all, especially when they reference Chinese characters in puzzles.

So overall, I highly recommend giving the game a shot even if you think the setting or style of the game might not be for you.

(PLAY IN CHINESE DUB FOR OPTIMAL EXPERIENCE) I've only played for a week (don't mind the 111 hours, rookie numbers I know) in Legend difficulty. All I can say is - If this game wasn't released this year, it would be nominated GOTY. Here are the reasons why: (May contain spoilers)

1. Story
The writing of the Main Quest and the Side Quests is almost at the same level as CO:Exp33. As someone who loves Wuxia and a writer myself, the amount of times I nearly cried (or have, cuz I did) just from playing this game exceeded the times I did when reading novels. If you immersed yourself so much into this world, which happens quite quickly as it unconsciously does it to you, you're in for a wild ride. And since the game will continue to keep updating, there will almost always be no end to the content. I have played for 111 hours and I just started with the 2nd country Kaifeng. I have just completed 76% of the 1st Country Qinghe. That's how much content there is.

2. Graphics, Core Gameplay, Optimization
Need I say more? It took the aspects of what I (or most of us) enjoyed from Breath of the Wild's (or Genshin's) exploration, Elden Ring's combat and the artstyle of Donghuas/Manhuas. The exploration type is similar to Breath of the Wild with multiple traversing mechanics (like sword flying, fast travels, dashing with style, walking on walls, etc.) and even underwater exploration. If played on Legend Difficulty, you will basically have the same experience as to when you played Elden Ring when it comes to battles - dodging/parrying on the exact frames, having limited healing items in boss fights, 1 shot combo from bosses if mechanics of the boss weren't properly studied, etc. All these, and I'm only playing with a mid PC while my online friends are using consoles and laptops, We never had any issues running the game at High-Ultra Quality @ 60-120 FPS.

3. Free-to-play live service game with no pay-to-win aspect
All these can be experienced by just downloading the game since it's free to play. But, unlike Wuthering Waves, Genshin, and similar type of games, this doesn't have pay to win. All of the things that can be bought with real money are either cosmetics or items you can farm in the game. Even if one whales, that person cannot outcap a person who never used any money in the game. Unlike previously stated titles where you can use money to overpower anyone (Character powercreep, Constellation, Eidolon, and whatever bs pay-to-win aspect there is), you cannot outskill a person who's just better than you (there's PvP, which is why this is important).

4. Only Acceptable Use of AI
While a controversial take, I know for a fact that AI will become part of games we will be playing in the future. In my opinion, this game uses it in a more fun and acceptable way - we can converse with NPCs who respond through AI, but each NPC AI is different from another, to befriend them and have them send us gifts weekly. If you're tired of real life interactions, you can just talk to whichever NPC you like here, then boom.

5. Multiplayer Aspects
This is definitely better than Arc Raider's multiplayer, and other well-received games with multiplayer. If you go into online mode, you will see people from all over the world. Enter any area with an open chat room, it's like VR chat with its proximity voice chat. There's also multiple ways to enjoy the multiplayer aspect of the game - either you do co-op with close friends, make guilds with a bunch of people you are friends with, be betrothed in game with your IRL lover, or play minigames with anyone with stakes.

There are multiple other funny interactions that I didn't include here since I don't want to spoil any further. I want others to experience it for themselves, so I'll stop yapping now. Am I passionate about the game? Absolutely. Do I recommend this game to others? Definitely. Does it need better soundtrack? Yes please, make it on the level of Exp33 and you'll have forever players.

Where Winds Meet is one of those games that instantly sells you on vibes. The world feels like a living wuxia painting – misty mountains, busy towns, and enough random encounters that just wandering around is fun on its own. The movement and combat are the highlight: running across water, dashing up walls, chaining martial arts skills together – it really makes you feel like you’re in a classic wuxia movie rather than just another open world RPG.

Combat is fast and flashy, with a good mix of weapon skills and martial arts techniques. It isn’t super complicated at first, but once you start unlocking more abilities, there’s a nice depth to how you can approach fights and bosses. The side content is also surprisingly varied: exploration, mini-games, social systems, and random events that make the world feel busy instead of empty.

It’s not perfect – the UI can be clunky at times, and some systems aren’t explained very well. There are also a few rough edges and bugs that remind you this isn’t a big Western AAA title. But the core of the game – the atmosphere, traversal, and combat – is strong enough that I keep wanting to log back in “just for a bit” and end up playing for hours.

If you like wuxia, open worlds, or just the idea of flying around ancient China as a martial arts hero, Where Winds Meet is absolutely worth your time. I’m excited to see how it improves with future updates.
