When I started this game, I had no idea what to expect but as I played and went further forward I was absolutely stunned by what the devs of this game were trying to do.

Unlike other MMORPG's this game let's you play solo so if you want to experience the game as a stand alone RPG you can. If you want other players you can go online or alternatively keep your session close to a close group of friends with their co-op mode. They have a lot of options when it comes to how you play, but the most important is your ability to choose between 'MMORPG' controls or 'ARPG' controls. So if you favour one over the other you can do it.

Customization is absolutely crazy, with the ability to collect different weapons, outfits and hairstyles you can clearly define what you martial artist looks like.

Combat is smooth and while I think there is a lot to keep in mind, there is nothing stoping you from just wailing on an enemy untill they are dust.

Now, I think there are things that some may want to know before going in. Not a biggie to start off with, there are still typo's and translations errors here and there, just something to keep in mind. There is a lot of microtransactions, battlepass stuff and the like but to be honest it never felt more than cosmetic but I understand people don't like microtransactions at all. The big one in my opinion and perhaps it is something that I have the most trouble with is the use of generative AI. The use of it in the game is solely for a 'friendship' mechanic in that you roleplay with different NPC's so they can become friends, I have been surprised by how it has been used and it does make NPC's more interesting (also they give you free stuff if you succeed in them becoming friends with you) but it is still very weird to me. It is intriguing to me that they have used it in a way that it doesn't feel like it takes away but adds to the game and honestly the art and rest of the gameplay is fantastic and doesn't use it, but I would be remiss if I didn't mention it.

So far it is 8/10 and I look forward to playing more and I do recommend giving it a go for yourself if you want a fun Wuxia action game.

Objective review: 8/10
Honest review: 7/10

Objectivist standpoint
For a free to play game, this game looks amazing. Combat feels good with multiple weapon styles to choose from. You can play however you want - want to deal damage while having sustain bring a healing weapon and bring a dps weapon or you can do a meme build and apply DoT to enemies and run around waiting for them to die. This game is a souls-like but not really a souls-like, I would say it has the combat of souls-like but being very forgiving in terms of difficulty. If you want to play souls-like game but do not have the skills for normal souls experience, this game is the perfect introduction. This game does have PvP but it sucks because of weird hit reg, latency and gameplay loop (1 in 5 times you get to see someone playing something else). HOWEVER, just a nitpick from me, the game is not new, it is actually translated from it's original Chinese counterpart. It's translation is not the best and sometimes it gets really confusing what you're supposed to do and the UI can be very overwhelming. If you're willing to overlook these points you will have a good time.

My 1 cent take on the game
VERY AGGRESSIVE MONETIZATION. The game offers a gacha system for cosmetics that doesn't impact the game other than looking good and the rates are atrocious. DO NOT SPEND TO PULL, it can be very costly up to over hundreds for a guaranteed legendary. You will also get greeted with a battle pass that offer some benefits and ugrade materials to expedite your progress while not a lot it's adds up overtime. (Of course there is a battlepass in 2025). Another point regarding UI design, the menu is convoluted AF. In the in game menu, there are so many different options that opens into another menu. Let me explain, for example I want to claim a reward for exploration, instinctively you will filter out to 4 options, journal/map/wandering paths/season. While indicated with a red dot for a notification on the icon, when you open either one of it there are so many sub tabs in each option you want to sift through. It is not intuitive at all, a jank/mess/whatever you call it. Technically you can just ignore them all and claim everything in every single menu. Who doesn't like free reward right? Well it kinda ruins the user experience which can be a big turn off for some and overtime feels like a hassle. I should also mention there are 99 different currencies in game and they all have different uses. (99 is an exaggeration, it's more like 8 or 9 different currencies each having their different shop menu and the methods to obtain them differes too). At this point you should just make a spreadsheet to keep track of all of them, I didn't know excel skills actually came in handy while playing a game.

Amazing overall design, easily up there for F2P games, PvP PvE and gear stuff :) fairy intriguing story, 10 player raids, 5 player raids, co-op, decent share of multiplayer content and some  reason the game has no performance issues for me lol. 

PvP is latency dependant so its not going to be very fun for quite a few people, cross region matchmaking is 50/50 at best, we are not caught up to CN in game version so we haven't gotten the peak experience yet. Players can drop out of combos (True combos), parry windows are also latency dependant and so on, you get the gist. Its still a decent experience, but don't expect to have a smooth experience VS someone in another region :D, other aspects such as GvG  which is a 30 vs 30 mode, it is a lag fest as there are many people in a space all using attacks and AoEs which contribute even with DLSS/Frame-gen, but also network lag as well is huge at times. Do not expect a smooth experience at all times in this mode. Overall PvP is a decent experience, can be fun or can be daunting but it is not a important aspect of the game in terms of progression, sure you get exp and coins but your gear is mainly from PvE content. In addition, there is a mode called Perception Forest which has Solo, Duo and Flex (5v5) modes which tbh works quite well, takes some time to get used to but a well rounded game mode with balancing, but is also cross server so again do not expect a smooth and seamless experience. 

PvE is great, story is genuinely engaging for a F2P title, lots of bosses and world bosses, as well as being able to fight bosses in Trial mode for rewards, you have sword trials, which is a 5 member squad boss fight with very easy mechanics and  you get rewards ofc :D, in addition you also have 10 player raids which grant even more rewards but also have very easy mechanics. Overall if you want challenges, fight bosses in the Trial mode for that almost souls like experience. There are a huge number of puzzles and secrets to uncover which also grant worthy rewards for your character to make them stronger.  There are many ways to make your character stronger, you will see things called oddities which you collect in game and are visible on the mini map, these grant permanent stats which is great. The gear progression is based on a few things, Energy system, you gain a set amount of energy per set time, 550 energy cap, which you can burn really fast and at the same time gain a lot of gear/resources for your build. You can also use a Season shop which uses in game earned currency to buy gear and resources for your build. 

Social aspects are 50/50 at best, I think the way its designed doesn't resonate well with many people, the UI for the social aspects are overdone, and lacks features to make the game feel more engaging with other players and guild. It 100% is not console friendly XD, the social aspect works 10/10 for us PC goats, and with this game being cross platform, communicating with console players is rough unless they join your discord. GG!!! 

The cash shop is where this game shines XD, be prepared to splash TF out in the store if you want the FOMO outfits / special outfits (limited time). Most of the drip in game is decently well designed and looks great on both male and female characters. This also applies to weapon skins and weapon effects, however there are some affordable options which do not shine as well as the highly expensive ones :D

Overall, the game is actually good, PvE is well rounded as well as the PvE group content, PvP is a mixed bag due to it being latency dependant as well as being able to fight people from other regions therefore adding to latency and making the experience worse, people with better ping will have an advantage, the guild events are engaging if you are in or create and active guild, feels a little like an MMO but this game is NOT an MMO, it has some aspects of one but does not engage like one. 

Its a slow paced game tbh, and at some point when you are caught up to the content and have decently min maxed gear it turns into a game you play a few times a week, unless you are a hardcore completionist then I could see players, playing this everyday or hardcore PvPers. The time gating for content is rough but nothing we can do about it sadly, I would love to see faster content roll out so the game stays consistently engaging for me as I am curious about the story and the future game modes coming soon.

A lot of the best parts of a lot of really good games snipped out and combined into this strange unique format. Instead of being just an MMO or just an open world soulslike, it's got MODES for once in both of these genres' lives. This improves so...so much.

Most of the story part of the game (which is really good in my opinion) uses Dark Souls systems. If you don't know, this means it's mostly zones where one person is the host and can bring friends along to help them progress, but the joining friends can't get the same progress. A few quests and stories actually do have co-op synchronization. I found it was about maybe ~30% of the quests? The ones that are able to be progressed together will usually say so on their map marker. Most other quests can be done with other players in your world, and they can help you progress up to certain points but will get teleported away for some scenes.

I play on 'Expert' difficulty which is more co-op player friendly than the highest 'Legend' difficulty. But my friends can play on Legend and I can join them for the co-op sync-available quests. There is also a Story mode and a slightly tougher Recommended mode, and these have some easier combat mechanics.

Most of the progression and exploration is able to be enjoyed together in co-op mode though. I found almost all the bosses, world bosses, arenas, and open world bases/outposts to clear have rewards claimable by everyone in the same world. All open world collectibles, chests, and puzzles share the rewards to everyone in the world as well, so just running from place to place with your friends will dump rewards on you. Some rare puzzles are only able to be done by the host of the world, but rewards are still shared.

Add on the traditional MMO queue-in content like dungeons and raids and pvp (which I haven't tried) and you have a lot of things worth loot and treasure available to do every week. I like the rest of it more though, which is...

Sekiro-like or Wo Long-like combat (deflect through attacks then punish instead of rolling away in the correct direction and resetting)
Player help required for the worst illnesses and afflictions
So many social interactions that they didn't need to put into the game, but did anyways
Ancient China
Ancient China fashion

I highly recommend playing through the tutorial, and then taking it veeeery easy or taking a break instantly to let the background timer build up that slows down progression. I accidentally did this by playing through the tutorial and waiting a week to try it out, and then I was free to try everything and all of a sudden I have 60 hrs in game.

I’ve spent about 29 hours in Where Winds Meet, and honestly, it’s been one of the most enjoyable surprises I’ve had on Steam in a while. I went in not expecting much since it’s free, but the game completely won me over. The story is actually engaging, not just filler, and it pulls you into the world right from the start. The way the world blends history, fantasy, and martial arts feels really unique. It makes exploration feel meaningful instead of just running from point to point...The visuals thoo.. the visuals are another big highlight for me. The world is gorgeous, from the landscapes to the character models, and it gives off this calm but adventurous vibe that makes me want to keep wandering around even when I’m not doing quests. The freedom in movement and traversal is one of my favorite parts too. You can climb, fly, run across rooftops, walk on water and move around in a way that feels smooth and fun, which really brings the “wuxia” feeling to life.

Character creation and customization are also worth pointing out. You can tell the devs put care into the options, and it really helps you feel connected to your character. Even small things like outfits and animations add to that feeling of being part of this world.

Now, it’s definitely not perfect. The game isn’t fully polished yet, and you can feel that right away. I get some stutters and occasional bugs, especially in busy areas or during certain cutscenes. It’s clear the optimization still needs work. But for me, the issues never hit the point where it ruins the fun. If anything, it just reminds me the game is still in a phase where it’s being improved. Even with these rough edges, I genuinely think this game has a lot of potential. The foundation is already strong...great story, great world, great freedom, and a fun sense of adventure. And the fact that all of this is completely free makes it even more impressive. I’ve paid for games that had way less heart put into them.

So yes, I absolutely recommend Where Winds Meet. If you enjoy open world RPGs, Chinese fantasy, martial arts themes, or just exploring a beautifully crafted world at your own pace, this game is worth downloading. I’m excited to see how it improves over time, and I’ll definitely be sticking around for future updates.

Where Winds Meet — 139 Hours Later… and Still Wandering ⭐
Story – 9/10

The story is phenomenal. Fulfiling, rich, and genuinely captivating. Quests are challenging without being repetitive, and even the mini-games are fun… well, except the chess one, which is pure nonsense if you ask me 😅. But overall, the narrative constantly pulls you forward and feels worth your time.

Combat – 10/10

Combat is an absolute blast. It’s intuitive, beginner-friendly (especially in Solo Mode), and packed with amazing weapons and martial arts that nail that medieval Chinese vibe. The weapon progression is simple… well, “Chinese-style simple,” which means there are about 20 different ways to upgrade things 🤣. But it works, and it feels rewarding.

Visuals – 11/10

“Amazing” doesn’t even cover 5% of what this game looks like. The visuals are jaw-dropping, especially when you remember this is a FREE GAME. Yes, FREE. And it has over 200k active Steam players — which is insane for a game of this type.

Interface – 6.5–7/10

Okay, here’s the challenging part. The interface is… confusing. Very confusing at the start. There are 101 different coins, items, and menus, each tied to some specific system. BUT — once you push past the first 5 hours, everything slowly starts to make sense. The UI itself is clean and fully adjustable, which is something most games don’t even offer anymore.

Co-op / Online Experience – 9/10

Whether you want to play it like an ARPG or an MMORPG, the game gives you the choice instantly — which is brilliant. The community is also surprisingly helpful; lots of friendly players who will answer your questions or jump in to help with bosses or dungeons.

Shop – 10/10

Believe it or not: THIS IS NOT A PAY-TO-WIN GAME.
The shop is 99% cosmetics — skins, outfits, emotes, that’s it. There is a special currency for some items, but you earn it just by playing and exploring. Zero pressure, zero stat-boost purchases. Beautiful.

Advice from a 139-Hour Wanderer

Give the game 5 to 20 hours before judging it. The early confusion is normal — the game simply has a LOT of systems, but everything clicks naturally as you play. And if you ever get stuck, the community is super helpful.

I even made my own guild after 130 hours (yes, I was too busy questing and exploring 🤣):
Guild: BadAtEverythin
If you want to join, hit Apply — I’m always online and happy to help newcomers.

Final Verdict

This game is absolutely worth your time.
For a free title, it delivers high-quality storytelling, gorgeous visuals, fun combat, and a shockingly fair business model. I’ll definitely continue playing it.

Good luck, Wanderers — enjoy your journey through Qinghe and Kaifeng!

I'm struggling to understand just how a free game can be THIS good.

Just go for it. If you like games like Sekiro, Ghost of Tsushima, or even just funky indy ones with minigames and fun stuff, you'll find what you want. Hell, you even got housing, card games and turn based weird dialogue combats/rap battles in there. I just had a "guitar hero" segment in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ random quest.

Now to address the elephant in the room tho : YES it is a free to play but NO it is not pay-to-win. The shop is 100% cosmetics, or some ressources that you can get by just playing the game.

As of right now, I'm lvl 50+, got a banger build, good weapons, armors, yaddi yadda, and I didn't have to pay for any of this. It wasn't even a big deal to get. I just play, and progression comes naturally. The only moment I decided (and I emphasize on 'decided', not 'HAD TO') to spent money was when I went "Ok they deserve this, I'm having tons of fun and it doesn't feel tedious, let's throw some money to get a banger cosmetic and call it a day". 

If you are like me and don't really want to "collect all the glams" and can be perfectly happy with just one or two good cosmetic sets forever, you will vibe a lot with this game. If however, your goal is to absolutely collect as many cosmetics as possible, beware, THIS is where the wallet comes into action.

So if you just care about the pure gameplay, story, visuals, and maybe wanna treat yourself with one or two cosmetic along the way for the funzies (and if you can go past the very convoluted menus because yes, there is a LOT to decipher to navigate this game if you are not used to asian games), this game is S tier.

For me, it goes straight into the "hall of fame of free games" like Warframe for exemple. You can't lose here, it's a damn good game, it's free, what else to say.

In short : 

Pros
- Peak gameplay
- Peak visuals
- Solid story, fun characters
- Insane variety of things to do, this is kinda nuts
- Game runs smooth af
- Not very grindy, progression feels okay to achieve
- Some decent cosmetics can even be earned directly in game, but just not a bunch
- NOT P2W

Cons
- Menus are a mess to understand you'll need a PhD
- All the insane banger cosmetics are from the shop
- There is some GAMBA (oh oh) involved, but again, purely cosmetic. Just look away and it won't be a problem if you can resist the temptation.

Can't think of other cons so far tho, I'm having a fcking blast, that's about it.

Where Winds Meet is a boring game.

Don't misunderstand, the game is beautiful and the gameplay is well choreographed.  However, it tries to be Dark Souls and ends up being Wo Long.  Gear is a pointless numbers-go-up grind and character development is simply a matter of higher levels giving you access to gear with bigger numbers. It's an infuriatingly reactive system and ultimately led me to quit the game with half the time still left on my battle pass because I was sick of standing there mashing parry until I was allowed to win.

Where Winds Meet é uma surpresa extremamente agradável, especialmente por ser Free-to-Play. Ele entrega uma experiência de mundo aberto visualmente impactante e um combate que não deve nada a títulos AAA de preço cheio, embora sofra com menus confusos e uma tentativa de abraçar mecânicas demais ao mesmo tempo.

✅ O que brilha (Prós):

Combate Excelente: A mistura de artes marciais com mecânicas de parry/deflexão é satisfatória e fluida. A movimentação (correr pelas paredes, andar sobre a água) faz você se sentir um verdadeiro mestre Wuxia.

Ambientação e Gráficos: O mundo é denso, vivo e tecnicamente impressionante. A recriação da China do século X (Dinastia das Dez Reinos) é imersiva.

Modelo F2P Justo: Dá para jogar dezenas de horas e aproveitar a campanha sem sentir que precisa abrir a carteira. A monetização parece focada em cosméticos, sem barreiras agressivas de progresso ("pay-to-win").

Liberdade: O sistema de profissões (médico, arquiteto, guarda-costas) e a interação com o mundo oferecem uma profundidade rara para o gênero.

⚠️ O que precisa melhorar (Contras):

Interface (UI) Caótica: O jogo sofre do clássico problema de MMOs asiáticos: excesso de menus, submenus, notificações e poluição visual que podem confundir novatos.

Crise de Identidade: O jogo tenta ser tudo ao mesmo tempo (RPG Single-player, MMO, jogo de ritmo, construção). Às vezes, menos seria mais.

Localização: A tradução (inglês/português) ainda apresenta inconsistências e faltam áudios em alguns diálogos, o que quebra a imersão.

Performance: Em áreas muito povoadas ou transições rápidas, ocorrem quedas de FPS e stuttering, mesmo em máquinas potentes.

Veredito: Se você gosta de Ghost of Tsushima, filmes de Kung Fu ou RPGs de mundo aberto e tem paciência para aprender sistemas complexos de menu, o download é obrigatório. É um jogo com "alma" de AAA disfarçado de F2P.

I would rather have just paid for the game than endure any of this.

The best part of the game is certainly the narrative, in both the main story and many sidequests. The writing and visuals are quite a bit better than the passable combat and exploration, though I do wonder how much of that is carried over through the translation for a western audience.

The game is also very experimental, with a lot of interesting features that don't currently have much meat in them. I include in this both forms of "speech check," the card game and the AI chat, as well as a slew of other things, none of which are really fleshed out, but the game is still being very actively developed.

When I first saw the early trailers for Where Winds Meet, I honestly wasn’t interested at all. It looked like another flashy open world game trying too hard, so I ignored it. Then the full game released and the biggest surprise hit me immediately: it’s free. Not only free, but it plays like this strange single player and co-op MMO hybrid. The closest comparison is something like Genshin Impact, except I actually dislike Genshin. But despite that, I decided to give this one a chance.

The moment I started playing, I got hooked. I haven’t felt this addicted to a game since Elden Ring came out. There’s something about it that just pulls you in instantly.

One of the first things that hit me was the visual style. It doesn’t have that anime look like Genshin or Wuthering Waves. It’s not a gacha game, there are no character rolls, and no waifu collecting system. You create your own character and explore a world that feels grounded and cinematic instead of cartoonish. It feels like a world built for players, not a marketplace built for gacha pity pulls.

The combat is another massive reason I’m hooked. It feels like a combination of Code Vein, Nioh, and Sekiro, but the strongest influence is definitely Sekiro. Parrying is one of the most important mechanics in the entire game. Timing matters, and you can’t just spam dodge and survive. And honestly, the best part about this game’s combat is that there are no elemental reaction gimmicks like in Genshin or Wuthering Waves. You don’t rely on some random element combo to deal damage. You just have to actually get good, and the game rewards you for it.

What really shocked me is how much content is in the game. There are 1v1 arenas, guild arenas, and even a battle royale mode that feels similar to Naraka Bladepoint. There are raids and bigger MMO-style challenges. You can build structures and decorate your own world. There is a huge open world filled with things to do. And one of my favorite features is the bounty system, where you can check a bounty board and hunt down real players for rewards. It’s like the Dark Souls invasion system but with an actual purpose, not just chaos for the sake of chaos.

Everything together makes the game feel incredibly packed for something that costs nothing to play.

Overall, Where Winds Meet isn’t a perfect game, because nothing truly is. But it comes really close in a lot of areas. The combat is skill-based and satisfying, the visuals are beautiful and mature, and the amount of content is insane for a free title. With the way it’s designed and the amount of features already in place, I genuinely believe this game has the potential to grow into one of the biggest online titles, right alongside games like Warframe and other successful MMOs.

This is the first game in years that made me feel addicted again, and honestly, I’m glad I gave it a chance.

Where Winds Meet throws everything at you and somehow makes it all work. It is a proper maximist game in the best way. Issues first:

There are a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the game relating to the English voices, specifically lines repeating, or disappearing mid conversation. Some translations are correct in the voice lines but off in the subtitles and that sort of thing.

The menu system is a nightmare to navigate and learn to start with and completely unintuitive. For example, if you have commited a crime your misdeeds show up on the Honor page, but to get to that you have to go to the develop menu then the details menu which is semi-hidden and from there to the honor page.

The crime system is a little annoying, especially as I got a bounty for trying to pick up a grasshopper at the same moment a guy on a horse rode past and then more bounty because two guys randomly attacked me without saying they were police. Then I had to fight off players who came to kill me which I could do because I had a healing fan and they couldn't kill me until finially I got sick with people randomly attacking me and just let them kill me and take me to prison for 15mins.

The game has energy which restricts how many dungeons etc you do, a little annoying but you seem to get enough of it to do 1-2 dungeons a day and get the double rewards at the end.

The gear system is random (to a point) in what you can get as prefixes on the item and what quality they are (although you can get other items to ensure purple/gold prefixes).

The Good Stuff,

The game is visually beautiful. Lots of ancient China scenery with great looking towns, villages, monestries etc around you. The city you reach in the second zone is amazingly huge with so much to do any see. 

It runs extremely well. I normally play through GforceNow, but it wasn't out there for a while and I played on my PC instead and it was able to run smoothly and look great on my old computer. So far have had lot latency issues (play from Australia but able to PvP, block enemy attacks etc).

The combat is good and the bosses appropriately difficult even on recommended difficultly. I imagine those playing on Legend are having a good challenge.

The quests are excellent, even what look like minor side quests have have long puzzles, exploration and history to explore and some quests are truly amazing in visuals and story. I won't go into details here because that would spoil the story. There are no "kill 10 rats" quests I've encountered so far. The only annoying quest type are the encounters where you have to trail and stop a thief, but mainly because they are a bit buggy and it took me ages to work out you have to hit him as he is stealing, not following him after he flees with the goods.

The game is free-2-play with the cash shop for cosmetics primarily. There are a couple of "play 2 win" elements that may help out in the early game, but will have no influence at end game. One is the horsey that picks up stuff for you as you ride past (instead of you spamming F). Eventually you are going to have so much stuff that you don't need to collect anything so the horse eventually becomes useless and I haven't spend much time on horseback and never really had to farm much because you can buy stuff from the shops to do your gear improving. The other is the +1 / +2 potions with the battle pass which can give you a boost early on until you build up your potions in game.

As for cosmetics, the game does have a large number that are free to collect and actually look good unlike some other free-2-play games which have you in a ugly sack the whole time. You can also mix and match parts of each set (clothes, hairstyle, back item, attachments, etc) to get a unique look. The free items I have got so far can't be dyed though, whereas the cash shop items can.

The game can be played entirely free without spending a dollar with no downside, but if you do want to spend money there are a lot of ways to do so in the shop. There are multiple gacha systems (the main one, the free one, the limited time one), three passes (battle pass, premium battle pass and monthly pass) and the cosmetics shop itself. The shiniest glowing items come from the gacha system while the cash shop are nice outfits at a fixed price. There are some cheap discounted items (5 outfits with one added since release) that are 60 pearls each and you get a 10% discount card from login rewards or one of the passes) which you can stack 5x so eventually get a 50% discount if you wait a while. 

All in all a great game with lots of updates to come to catch up with the Chinese version.

This game is a huge experiment in how gullible the world is.  Hidden behind incredible graphics, animations, sound design, and level design, is the most convoluted Gacha game structure I've ever messed with.  From the multiple currencies used, to the favoritism of the non international version, it's a big NeverEndingTEASE! (Netease  *wink)

The combat is overrated considering how spongy the enemies are.  (Wolves look like pincushions before they die if you try to kill them with arrows, and for the love of all things holy don't mess with the geese.)  Almost all fights are dodge simulations nullifying any meaningful use of those beautifully animated combat combos.  The stories are filled with non-essential dialoge, and the AI NPC chat interactions feel like they would work better if I spoke Chinese.  Typing in broken, simplistic english will significantly improve these interactions, but It's annoying to the point I now just try typing "yes" or "no" to anything said to me. 

The convolution doesn't just extend to the online gambling system, it is embraced throughout the entire interface, menus, and skill management.  "You just onlocked a new skill from watching that goose be a bully!  Equip it now! But you can't use it because you don't have enough of something."  "Would you like to heal this goose from it's affliction?  You can sure try! Go pick up some herbs to help it heal! Oh wait you aren't a high level physician so you just wasted your time."  GACHA!  Sometimes talking to a quest NPC signs you up for something you literally don't have enough time for.  Things like being able to equip gear from multiple menu locations, etc.  It's truly confusing.

Even if you find the NPC chatter to be annoying the quests are typically quite fun and interesting.  The characters are beautifully animated, and the world is extremely immersive, and It's FREE.  However the scratching your head and wondering what you should be doing with currency, items, gear, skills, is a real problem.  Maybe some people love playing with non intuitive interfaces to prove they are proficient at menu navigation but I don't think it's that hard to make things easy to understand in a menu.  It doesn't feel like the menus favor the player, but rather the developers desire to cram as much Gacha into their game as the interface can handle.

"Lets fool the player into spending too much."

Even some of the initial NPC interactions feel like an AI data mining my gullibility.
  "Pay me for this object!  Oh you want to barter?  NO pay me for this object, I deserve it!  You aren't going to?  Ok never mind, here you can have it for free." 

Game looks like a AAA title on the surface, but it's Gacha level is somewhere around AAAAAAHG!!  I truly wish I could recommend it because of the art and atmosphere, but I don't support games that favor their origin country with exclusive stores and discounts.  This is simply because I hate racism in all it's forms.  I've watched some Chinese streamers fight bosses that don't use the same attacks as the bosses I fought, but can't tell if that is an update issue or they are making the game harder for international players.

That being said I'm willing to pay money for cosmetics if the company obviously isn't trying to trick me into making mistakes with my money.  If the store feels dishonest I'm not opening my wallet.
I will immediately give this game a thumbs up if they turn their store into a place worth spending money.  ATM it feels like gambler based economics, preying on the uneducated, young, and indirectly anyone not Chinese.

A strong recommendation for people looking for a Third Person Action Combat MMORPG-lite , this game separate out the best aspect of solo and mmo and blend it together for and enjoyable time to play. 

It's a third person action adventure where you are the lone wolf and get to see the world progress through the story. Followed by interesting story and lore, a world that encourages you to explore or side track from main ones. Play it like dark soul, parry or dodge like hell your way to victory or call for help and play with friends*. 

It's also a mmo lite, it consist of socials activities, raids and pvp todo together or npc with not much bloat, all optional, your only energy gated from collecting gears. It's online mode is more for social activity, while its raid and pvp are queue into separate dungeon/shard, raids can be done with npc bots so you can be alone or social when you want. 

Lastly if your a fan of MMORPG but feel that the genre of tab-targeing has been stale lately, Definitely give this game a try. This feels like a MMO 1.5v or 2.0v moment, it may not be perfect or for everyone, but maybe a glimse into the future of mmo could be.

In its current state it's a 7/10 game. Very strong core that's a blend of Sekiro, Nioh, Genshin and Elden Ring, but it's held back by less than stellar localization that borders on lazyness at times, an overly F2P unfriendly gacha system (thankfully only cosmetic for now), and frustrating arbitrary timegates. 

The Good

- The game wears the influences cited above on its face, but they're well executed, don't feel like a knock off version, and more importantly they mix very well together.
- All the content except cosmetics is free, and there is a lot of it.
- Very good character creation, with a seemless social aspect that allows you to easily share your designs and import other people's. 
- Gameplay loop is very addicting, you see numbers go up, things complete, rewards pop up, perfect for your dopamine addicted zoomer brain. 
- Performance is good given the visuals (no UE5 slop yay), but suffers from drops in the second chapter city, presumably due to the mass of NPCs. 
- Adjustable difficulty that doesn't affect the rewards, and comes in the form of increased or decreased assists. So the game is friendly towards most types of players.
- A Dark Souls type message system, but with complete freedom to type anything, which proves very useful when stuck in a puzzle. 

The Bad

- Localisation is very questionable. While it's not google translate level of bad, you frequently see issues with the audio dialogue (AI voiced btw) not lining up with the subtitles, the same audio repeating over the following line of dialogue, some inconsistent translations (Nameless Sword is referred to as Noname Sword several times), there doesn't seem to be any audio gendered for Female characters, as even though the text says "Her" the audio will say "Him", and worst of all, at least one instance of a puzzle revolving around a wordplay that was translated literally and makes strictly zero sense in english. It's not too uncommon to see chinese games struggle with english translations, but for a game with NetEase's backing, I expected better.  
- Arbitrary timegating. It's one thing to have a finite game with updates down the line, it's another to have the content in the game right in front of you, only for it to say "you have to wait x days to access it". It's especially terrible with the campaign, as the current one gives you a narrative with an urgency, but the game arbitrarily drip feeds the mission to you, despite the content being already there in the game.
- Awfully unfriendly gacha. You have three banners. One is paid only, no way around it. One requires paid currency for the ressource but you can technically get a pitiful amount for free each month that will currently maybe get you  *one* pity every few months. The last one is the permanent one that uses F2P ressources, but the rate at which you get pulls feels more like a limited banner in every other gacha. Furthermore, the "exclusive" outfits you get from it are the same one with four different textures. The fact it's only for outfits is the only saving grace, if it was anything with an impact on gameplay it would instantly turn this review into a negative one.
Where Winds Meet is a sublime intersection where souls-like mastery is demanded, gacha's boundless horizons are offered, and true immersion is achieved through a densely woven social sphere.

Game: Where and Wind Meet is a Wuxia genre (Chinese martial arts) open world, that allows you to play co-op up to 5 players in one world. With a lot of weapons to choose from. Umbrella, fan, spear, rope and so on with different class depends on weapon you choose. You can use two different weapons at same time, or different class if you want. There is so many stuff you can do on this game, exploration, dancing, playing instrument, be in a sect/guild or make one, make disciple/accept other players are your disciple, build your own house.
And most interesting part is that you can get married with other player, works both with different gender or same gender marriage.

I can see that developers really put their passion into this game, and they sure had fun making this game. Since this game is filled with goofy moments and stuff. Riding a goose as a mount, huskie on a leash that drags you, a chetah chasing you as a mount and many more upcoming mounts that haven't released in Global server yet. The Chinese server has been realized longer than Global server so it will take some time for us to catch up to most of the contents of this game. But even right now the game itself have a lot of stuff to do. Even while waiting for the capacity of level limit to increase, you won't get bored waiting.
The only thing they could imrpove is their UI, as it's a bit confusing and overwhelming.
So yea, definitely give this game a try. It's free anyway, you don't really lose much from giving it a try ^^

This is not a game for the regular westerner.  This is not a walk in the park that takes you by the hand and tells you what to do at every corner and expects you to be happy and satisficed every 7 seconds.  This is not a game that aims to constant gratification for altering your dumbed down senses.  

This game is to digest hundreds of years of culture and stories slowly, and surely. It's a game that forces you to adapt. It's a game with a different kind of grind. It's a game that tries to teach you something as you go... and that's a bold move these days. As bold as adding an AI driven conversational system to cultivate rapport with NPCs. Or as bold as forcing you to do a series of quests to be able to use a different weapon. 

Yes, it has a plethora of systems and mechanics the makes you go all over the place... and dares you to focus on your goals, and push you to excel to reach them.  How dare he this game?   How is it possible that a game makes you WORK to achieve something?   That's not possible today right?  

40 hours of this game feels like barely scratching the surface of something amazing.   Something that didn't happen since Warframe... or RDR2.   This game is a gem... bastardized by the current western media, afraid of everything that comes from Asia in general.    

For me, as a game developer, this game is a lesson. A lesson that there's still hope for an industry that's imploding from years and years of neglected behaviorism and poor decision making. 

Let yourself go... and embrace what this piece of art has to offer. If you truly submerge into it, you'll enjoy it more than you think... for a whole kind of different reasons.

Where Winds Meet is a captivating open-world action-adventure RPG set in tenth-century China, where players become a young sword master uncovering mysteries and forging their own path in a world filled with political intrigue, epic battles, and deep Wuxia culture. The game offers an expansive, living world with over 20 diverse regions, dynamic weather, and a wealth of activities including exploration, mini-games, and combat that blend seamlessly for a rich experience.

The game stands out with its freedom and depth: players can choose to cause chaos or be heroes, engage in parkour to climb any cliffside, and interact with every building in cities without artificial barriers. Mini-games such as puzzle-solving and bow challenges add fun variety, while the immersive narrative and side stories bring personality and warmth to the vast game world. Combat is praised for its wuxia flair, though some reviews note the game tries to incorporate many gameplay styles, making it feel ambitious but sometimes unfocused.

Where Winds Meet visually impresses with fluid animations and a reactive environment that changes with time and weather, enhancing the immersive experience. Its intricate open world rewards curiosity without overwhelming players with UI clutter. For fans of martial arts and Wuxia lore, this game is a unique blend of action, exploration, and story that invites players to become legends in a beautifully crafted ancient Chinese world.

EDIT:
I have changed my stance on the game after a recent update has significantly impacted the experience of this game. What once was a beautifully rendered open world with stunning environments to explore has become a horrendous mixture of textures not loading, assets popping in and popping out to an extreme degree, and reflection quality dropped to the lowest spec. I had enjoyed the game for over 100 hours with Ultra settings, never experiencing a hint of visual bugs. Then the mobile release came and the following update dropped Ultra to something meaningless. I can no longer discern a difference between Ultra and Low settings, as it all looks terrible. 
Furthermore, I have come to realize that this game introduces vulnerabilities to the client's PC I can not ignore, such as downloading every image viewed by the player into a temporary folder that never purges. Should a malicious actor embed malware or perhaps upload illicit and illegal imagery, it could be downloaded onto every PC who inadvertently views those images while browsing in game menus (Specifically the investigation menus). 

For these reasons, I can no longer recommend this game. 
::EDIT END::

WWM combines a series of genres and world design philosophies effectively. 

They allow the players to play at their own pace and with whomever they please whether that is alone, with some friends, with strangers, or as part of a guild. 

You are able to play in a single player world or join the online world for an MMORPG experience. 

The combat resembles what one would expect from a polished Souls-like. It is fluid and demanding, and respects the player. You can go as far as you wish based on skill alone, or upgrade your gear as you would expect in any ARPG.

There are various levels of difficulty for you to pick from, which flawlessly provides evidence that Souls-like games can be enjoyable, challenging, and accessible without taking away from the player experience. The 5 levels of difficulty available give a wide range of options to allow anyone to pick up and play this game. There are also rewards to those of us who like to fight through the highest difficulty settings, and these rewards do not give an advantage to the player over other players.

Monetization is entirely cosmetic. There is no 'Pay to Win' here, and the developer is quite generous with cosmetics for Free to Play players. The feeling of being compelled to make any microtransaction purchases is entirely dependent on how much the player is interested in cosmetics. 

On cosmetics, this game has the most in-depth customization system I have ever experienced. If you want to create a Bethesda style monster, you are able. If you would like to recreate Willham Dafoe, you are able. Do you live in a pineapple under the sea? Your head can be Sponge Bob. What's more, you are able to make adjustments to the cosmetic accessories you equip. Tilt, rotate, lift, and resize much of the cosmetic items to create your own look.

Open world exploration is a joy, the world is beautifully hand-crafted and very clearly displays a passion for world building by the developer. There are many side stories and quests that flesh out the world's lore, and often strikes as hard as you should expect a main campaign should. That is to say, it is very well written and executed. 

There are puzzles and minigames, world bosses and dungeons, wildlife and a population of NPCs that makes this world feel full and alive everywhere you go. The immersive design and integration of these elements into the world makes every moment feel worthwhile.

You are able to be a criminal, a bounty hunter, a healer, or a gambler. It is all available and accessible. 

I very much recommend Where Winds Meet to anyone who enjoys ARPG, MMORPG, Mahjong, or even those of who like to build your dream home in the game world. WWM really does attempt to do it all, and as far as I have experienced, none of it was done half-assed.

Oh my god, I seriously thought we finally reached the point where we could properly min-max our gear without losing everything. I was actually excited thinking we could upgrade the same gear from 86 → 91 while keeping our hard-earned stats intact, and later continue progressing even further. But nope… once again: Where Caps Meet.

Another 7-day cooldown.
Another restriction.
Another unnecessary limitation.

Now even upgrading gear from level 86 to 91 comes with capped attributes. BRO… WHAT?! So yes, NO POINT in upgrading from 86 to 91 if you aim min-max. Instead, farm lvl 91 stuff AGAIN.

At this point, forget it. I genuinely thought I could finally start enjoying the game after these updates, but they just keep adding more caps, more limits, more restrictions. Then there’s the level 91 attunement system, once per week again or whatever they decided to call it.

They removed parts from the Hexi Shop, yet the entire system is STILL heavily RNG-based. And the funniest part? You upgrade fully optimized gold-stat gear from 86 to 91… and it comes back PURPLE. Absolutely ridiculous design. Still, I tried to stay optimistic and thought, “Alright, maybe this is manageable.”

But then the caps hit AGAIN.

Every single attribute on upgraded 86 → 91 gear is capped, meaning you literally cannot fully maximize your stats anymore like you normally could through tuning. So what’s even the point of grinding, theorycrafting, and min-maxing?

Honestly, this has become Where Caps & Limits Meet.

I’m officially done with this nonsense. Permanently done with NetEase-style systems. They ruined Once Human with endless restrictions, and now they’re doing the exact same thing to Where Winds Meet.

Or whatever studio is behind it, I genuinely don’t care anymore. It’s the exact same pattern all over again:

- Overcomplicated systems.
- Unnecessary mechanics.
- Thousands of menus.
- Millions of layered RNG tuning systems.
- Daily, Weekly limitations everywhere.

At some point, it stops feeling like a game and starts feeling like a second job where you spend more time trying to understand gear systems than actually enjoying combat, exploration, or PvE.

And yes, that criticism is completely valid. People can deny it all they want, but it’s true.

PS: Feel free to reply with “cry more,” “skill issue,” or whatever else. I genuinely don’t care. I’m pointing out the same exhausting developer limitations all over again because this design philosophy is becoming ridiculous.

The best way to describe this game is honestly like this:

They give players eggs… but no fire to cook them with.

Then after 20 breakthroughs, endless grinding, RNG, and timegates, they finally hand you a spoon and act like it’s some massive reward. After that they go, “Hmmmm… maybe now we should let them have a pan so they can actually cook.”

But wait!!!!!! The pan is locked behind an event.
- And that event has daily caps.
- And weekly caps.
- And RNG rewards.
- And the event lasts an entire month.

So after all that suffering, congratulations! You finally obtained the pan and the eggs.

Then the devs suddenly go:
“Hmmmm maybe now we should give them an oven so they can finally cook the food.”

And right when you think you’re finally about to enjoy the game…

BOOM. Another limitation.

Now the eggs are capped at 5%, so you can only eat 5% of what you spent weeks grinding for.

That’s literally what these systems feel like.

Every single progression path in this game feels artificially stretched with restrictions stacked on top of restrictions. Nothing is ever straightforward. Nothing is ever simply rewarding. There’s always another hidden limitation, another cooldown, another RNG layer, another weekly lock, another unnecessary mechanic designed to slow you down.

And the worst part is that the core game itself is actually GOOD.
- The combat? Good.
- The atmosphere? Beautiful.
- The world? Incredible.

That's about it....

But instead of letting players enjoy that naturally, they bury everything under layers of overengineered progression systems and endless caps.

Honestly, I could probably write an entire book about these issues, but I think people already get the point.

Amazing story, exploration, character customization and online experience!!!

Free Game BTW. It has a little bit of everything for everyone.

If you play MMOs/Light RPGs and just care about exploration and story - play on "Recommended" - aka Normal mode. 

If you're a Dark Souls / Elden Ring / Ghost of Tsushima player - Play on "Expert" - game will be tough but enjoyable.

If you're a Sekiro player - play on Legend mode - everyone hits like a truck in almost every move > get rid of (unbind it) your stupid "defend" button and only worry about deflect/parry. "Defending where you take less damage" will get you killed.

- Story: After you get through the first few sets of main story mission, it starts ramping up and the story line gets a lot better. The voice acting with voice anime can be better but again - free game - and the developers are working to do better - it doesn't take away from the core lore. 

- Combat: Absolutely cinema. Very impressed by how varied the major bosses are and unique approaches.

- Meta Progression: It looks simple at first, but then you started hitting levels 41, 51+ respectively and then tuning gets involved - this game's version of RNG rolls for gearing like Path of Exile loot drop attribute rolls. THEN you also have your passive unlocks - SQUIRREL EVERYTHING - you need those random critters in the world. THEN you have your core (4) inner passives to try leveling up. 

- World building: very pretty and lots of great vistas. After you get through the first areas few quests the lore starts coming together. **Note for Eastern Asian drama watchers: very much does feel like the adventure drama series Legends of the Condor Heroes. - Free Game BTW. I think some areas can use a little more verticality but then again this is still early stages of releases so I can't complain. 

- MMO aspects: Main Story missions - solo only. Everything else can be do via co-op/online mode with your friends. There are a lot of mini-games and as the game continues to unlock I noticed there are more weekly boss-raids. 

- Gacha: most of the skins are ok, but the rate between Echo Beads and Real Money are slightly high. I also think it can do pulls like Wuthering Waves with x-multiplier increase for whichever theme they are trying to promote. Right now pulls feels bad.

Enjoying it so far and very excited to see its progression as Global catches up to China's version, seems like there will be an endless amount of things to do. 

All in all - it's a Free Game, why would you not give it a chance when the content and quality is on par with AAAA nowadays.

Honestly, I'm surprised at how quickly Where Winds Meet got me hooked after about three hours of playing.  The world feels alive and full of life, even in the beginning areas. The scenery is so beautiful that it makes you want to stop and take it all in.  I ended up exploring more than I had planned to because every path looked like it would be fun to follow.

 Combat started up faster than I thought it would.  You can parry, dodge, and use weapons in a way that feels good and responsive. Even at a low level, the fights are fun because they have a sense of style and fluidity.  Moving around is fun on its own—running across rooftops, climbing cliffs, and gliding between areas are all fun ways to get around without having to learn any new skills.

 It's not perfect.  You can tell that this game has a lot of systems that will be revealed later because the UI gives you a lot to think about right away.  Some of the NPC animations in cutscenes seem a little stiff, but so far nothing has broken the game.  It looks a lot better than I thought it would for a free-to-play game.

 In general, my first impression is very good.  Even though I've only played for a few hours, the game already gives me that martial arts fantasy feeling—fast, stylish, and full of atmosphere.  If the rest of the experience stays this good, it could turn into something really special.  I'm impressed and excited to keep going for now.

I recently maxed out all the quests and gatherables on all maps available at this moment in time and somehow it is still not enough. I walk around looking for more, maybe one small talk I missed or just to gather some materials, take in the breathtakingly beautiful scenery. It is not an MMO, but I definitely feel what I have not in a really long time, since I left all the MMOs I used to play. I don't like Live Service games and the directions these things are going, but I know how much more content is still ahead of us for FREE and I can't wait to have more.

This game seriously earned a special place in my heart and I hope I can keep it there for a really long time.

#1 Terrible English translation! Everything in the game is terribly translated. I have no fkin idea what's going on or what anything means. It's like simple words are replaced by old English poetry, why? Everything from the story to checking your gear out is a mystery of translation. NPC dialogue is also way too fast to read it all and understand.

#2 Infinite menus! Still as bad as when the game came out. Ten thousand menus and sub menus infest the game and you never know where you're at within them or where to find a single thing. But as long as you're giving them money I bet it's all right! Also when menus or HUD elements matter, they fly by way too fast for you to grasp what just happened. e.g. You just collected something and the "collection menu" flashes by way too fast to realize what you just gathered.

#3 Infinite currencies! It's like everything you touch out in the world is a new currency for some randomly generated old English translation whatever thingamagic.

#4 Gameplay! The game throws you in before you can access the settings (which I already absolutely despise) to make them yours and at LEAST before you reach the "end" of the prologue, prevents you from changing controller keybindings, which of COURSE are very different from everything else in the genre. Besides all that the gameplay is alright. The gameplay is what I was in for, wanting to go for bosses "souls-like" style and exploration and completionism.

#5 Graphics! They're alright but I expected them to have implemented FSR 4.1 by now. The FSR they got is sub-par at least for me.

Overall I think China needs to rethink how they bring out games to the western audiences. The menu hell and the inability to understand what the FK is going on and what your gear is, has to be improved.

Wanted to play for quite a bit before judging the game to try to give a more fair review. 

Where do i even begin? This game has so many things going on that reading about them almost feels like the dev is just trying to fit as many checkboxes as possible. But surprisingly, they are done to a degree where it feels satisfying and fits well the world and gameplay. 

The closest thing to describe combat is Sekiro, since theres a heavy emphasis on parrying (which the game calls deflecting here, but no one does) but also a lot more forgiving. That doesn't mean that the game is easy though, legend difficulty can be quite challenging. Theres a decent weapon variety and the game uses the trinity system for group content, which means i can have a good time playing as a healer while getting destroyed with solo bosses :p

The worldbuilding and setting are phenomenal, as its inspired by real events that happened in China during the 10 kingdoms era. Everywhere you go is absolutely screenshot worthy and we players make very good use of it through signposts. A lot of times using this dark souls inspired system to leave helpful tips for other wanderers but also sometimes simply sharing a photo that looked nice. In a way, signposts also work like small enclosed forum threads, often being a hub to post our sentiments towards the current quest and characters. It always feels like you are playing the game together with other people, even in your solo world. Its a very similar feeling to what Death stranding did a few years before and i hope that more games lean into that social aspect. 

The story is also universally praised, we see the highs of a Wuxia themed story which also has a very serious tone. Many quests are sad or bittersweet, they show you the reality of what it means to be a commoner at that time and they do a really good job at getting you to grow attached to the characters. A lot of the side content has its lore scattered across letters, item descriptions, dialogues and unrelated questlines in a way where it feels like you are uncovering traces of a legendary hero or much bigger story. That said, the EN Voicework and localization aren't perfect. A lot of context and depth of the writing is lost between translating, which unfortunately is very difficult to prevent. I've learned a lot from kind users who post summaries and and essays about characters on reddit while the game itself worked as a complementary tool to visualize what im reading afterwards. Pros:

- Tons of hilarious references to "Kung Fu Hustle", IYKYK.
- Absolutely 0 pay-to-win (the gacha and premium shops are exclusively cosmetics and the upgraded battlepass is essentially "Quality of Life" upgrades via a remote shop for materials and a couple of extra potions to carry.
- PVP feels amazing. There's Arena mode for queueing up for pvp, or if you've been bad and get reported by NPC's for a crime, another player can actually hunt you down for a "bounty" - the invasion is very similar to Souls series invasions without the limitation of being locked into wherever you currently are (want a bigger place to fight? just run away til you find a spot you like lol)
- Farming can be entirely what you want it to be. If you prefer farming solo, do that. If you like playing with friends, co-op worlds can host up to 5 people. The exception is progressing the main story quests (these are entirely solo).
- The world is BEAUTIFUL.

Cons:
- In it's current state, online mode *can* experience very high ping
- Most free outfits/hairstyles are currently not dyable. (i hope this changes)
- THE BIGGEST CON: the absolute clutter of menus. (it's very "mobile game" with rewards to claim in 99 different places, but you get used to it over time and eventually know what you're clicking on and why)

TLDR:

A Wuxia Masterpiece that Runs on Potatoes (Yes, even a 1050 Ti!)

I honestly went into "Where Winds Meet" with cautious expectations. A massive, open-world martial arts RPG with this level of visual fidelity usually demands a NASA supercomputer. However, after sinking hours into this 10th-century China setting, I am genuinely blown away—not just by the game itself, but by how accessible it is.

Here is the breakdown:

--- PERFORMANCE & OPTIMIZATION (The Real Surprise) ---
This is the most important part for my fellow budget gamers: I am playing this on an old NVIDIA GTX 1050 Ti.

I expected a slideshow, but the optimization here is some kind of black magic. The game actually runs smoothly for me. You obviously won't be maxing out 4K ray-tracing settings on older cards, but at 1080p with a mix of Low/Medium settings (and FSR enabled), the framerate is stable and the combat feels responsive.

It’s rare to see a modern title this ambitious respect older hardware. If you’re hesitating because you don't have an RTX 40-series card, don't worry. It is very playable.

--- ART STYLE & VISUALS ---
Even on lower settings, the art direction does the heavy lifting. The game is gorgeous. The developers have nailed the romantic "Wuxia" aesthetic—misty bamboo forests, bustling ancient cities, and cloth physics that make every jump and glide feel cinematic. The world feels alive, not just like a static backdrop for fights. The transition from peaceful exploration to chaotic martial arts battles is visually seamless.

--- STORY & CHARACTERS ---
The narrative is set during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, which is a refreshing change from the usual fantasy tropes. You play as a young sword master searching for their identity, and while the "amnesiac hero" is a classic trope, the execution here is strong.

The characters you meet have distinct personalities and motivations. The writing manages to balance the grand political intrigue of the era with personal, smaller stories. It feels like playing through a high-budget martial arts drama.

--- GAMEPLAY ---

Combat: It’s fast, fluid, and relies heavily on parries, dodges, and using your environment (running up walls, gliding, etc.).

Freedom: You can choose to be a hero, a villain, or just a wanderer. The freedom to engage with the world—even taking up different jobs/identities—adds a layer of immersion I didn't expect.

--- VERDICT ---
"Where Winds Meet" is a breath of fresh air. It’s a stunningly beautiful open-world game that doesn't leave low-spec gamers behind. Whether you are here for the deep Wuxia story or just to run across rooftops like a legend, it is absolutely worth your time.

That said, the progression system is frustrating. Waiting 10 real days to gain just 5 levels, only to then reset all your gear back to square one, is a terrible loop. And all that without new content, most of the players have  complete the game 100% already. It kills any sense of growth and makes your time investment feel wasted instead of rewarded. Upgrading existing gear would make far more sense than forcing constant resets.

On top of that, the cash shop is overpriced, especially for a game that realistically offers around 100 hours of actual gameplay max in its current state. The pricing just doesn’t match the content available right now.

And to be clear:
I’m judging the game as it exists today, not on promises or future updates. What might happen later doesn’t matter — players are paying and playing now, and right now these systems feel badly thought out.

Bottom line:
Good combat and world design can’t carry a game with this kind of time-gating, forced resets, and overpriced shop. Maybe it’ll be better in the future — but that doesn’t help the experience you get today.

I approached **Where Winds Meet** with some skepticism due to its free-to-play model (cough* Diablo Immortal). However, after investing over 95 hours, I can confidently say the game exceeded my expectations. The gameplay, combat system, and narrative are exceptionally well-crafted, to the point where it feels almost unreal that an experience of this quality is free. It genuinely encourages you to support the developers. My friends and I purchased the battle passes and daily rewards, and the value they provide is more than worth the modest cost.

One of the standout strengths of Where Winds Meet is its world-building. The game offers a beautifully realized interpretation of ancient China, blending Wuxia-inspired martial arts with a rich historical atmosphere. Exploration feels fluid and engaging—whether you are traversing rooftops, gliding through mountain ranges, or discovering hidden paths in dense forests, the world consistently rewards curiosity. The attention to environmental detail and cultural authenticity further enhances immersion.

Additionally, the AI-driven NPC interaction system deserves special mention. Being able to hold dynamic conversations with characters and earn their trust is both innovative and impressive. This level of interaction feels far ahead of what most modern games offer and hints at the future of NPC design in open-world RPGs.

Overall, Where Winds Meet delivers a premium, triple-A experience. I fully intend to continue supporting the game, and I believe the monthly battle pass alone provides solid value for players who enjoy ongoing content.

❌The only criticism I have concerns the disparity in cosmetic pricing between the global servers and the Chinese servers. Cosmetics appear significantly more affordable in the Chinese version, and this imbalance feels unfair to global players. Addressing this issue would greatly improve the overall player experience.

A fantastic open-world action-adventure RPG that is genuinely free-to-play friendly. The monetization (Battle Pass, Monthly Sub, Gacha) is strictly for cosmetics; while some prices are high, it avoids pay-to-win mechanics entirely. Optimization is solid, looking great in its Wuxia style while remaining accessible for lower-end hardware. There are no forced dailies, giving you total agency to play how and when you want. The combat is a highlight, offering satisfying Sekiro-like parry mechanics and challenging weekly 10-man raids. You can seamlessly switch between solo exploration and online co-op in a lively open world filled with unique NPCs and deep character customization. Best of all, the developers are active and listens to the community, making it a rare gem in the free-to-play space. Currently it still has some UI localization issues since it was originally released in China but the devs listened and has already made plans for better localization in future updates.

WWM started out as a great game offering unique experience with high potential in becoming something even greater, it was a breath of fresh air in AAA and MMO genre. But of course it doesn't take more than a fool to guess what went wrong; nothing can escape the curse of corporate greed from big company like Netease after all.

Many bugs and balancing issues were ignored despite pleas from the community. What's worse is that with each new update, the devs managed to introduce new bugs into the game without even fixing older ones properly. New game modes and events introduced lately are irrelevant to the game progression. Most of the event rewards are purely cosmetic, some of which are time-limited. Even the newest pet system and homestead system were badly thought out. They do not offer any usefulness to base game progression apart from forcing people to grind through them for rewards tied to their limited-time event, and after that there's no point interacting with them anymore. Every aspect such as gameplay, economy, and even microtransaction have been made solely for the purpose of exploiting the fear-of-missing-out, all just to milk those last drops of your play time and money, and they are doing it more aggressively with every new update.

It is sad to see that, in a span of 6 months, such an amazing game gets ruined to the point where the initial enjoyment is almost unrecognizable. Exploration has become a boring chore, PvE grind has nothing new, PvP balance is non-existent, and the devs are force feeding you stuff nobody really needs. The game itself no longer offers you any notable satisfaction in playing, so what's the point anymore? Rest in peace WWM, it was fun while it lasted.

⭐ Review: Where Winds Meet – 8/10
Where Winds Meet is a beautiful blend of martial arts combat, exploration, and social systems that really shine when played with friends. The game’s world feels alive, and teaming up with others makes quests, duels, and exploration far more engaging than going solo. There’s a strong sense of camaraderie that elevates the experience, especially when you’re coordinating strategies or simply enjoying the scenery together.
That said, the time caps can be frustrating. They sometimes break the flow of play, especially when you’re in the middle of a fun session with friends. While understandable from a design perspective, they can feel restrictive and occasionally dampen the momentum of group play.
On the positive side, the marriage system is a standout feature. It adds a unique social layer that goes beyond typical multiplayer mechanics, allowing players to form deeper bonds in-game. Whether it’s symbolic or just for fun, it creates memorable moments and reinforces the community-driven spirit of the game.
Overall, Where Winds Meet earns a solid 8/10. It’s a game best enjoyed with friends, offering rewarding social systems and immersive gameplay, even if the time restrictions sometimes get in the way.

if you are prepared for a STUNNING, steal your breath, awe inspiring level of depth and visual beauty in a game, for free no less than look no further. The level of story depth that has gone into this game is astounding. they give you every ability to carve your own path in any way you want whether thats as a dancer, an assassin, or a carpenter. This game is both open world rpg and sandbox, but with consequences. The world reacts to you and what you do and who you interact with. You can interact with NPC's in a way that has lasting value. While the UI is a little choppy and the english localization is...awkward, anytime i've given feedback on a word correction/translation its been changed within 24 hours. 

The biggest setback is how many menus there are for various paths of progression, but they are in fact necessesary for you to not be entirely stuck on a linear path , as a result, this gives building your character some real weight of choice. That said, the linear rpg, lvl what you get right out the gate path is also still available, but you can just as easily run off and go be a villain, or wander the land hunting down bandits and catching thieves, or setting up performances.

keybinds, menu awkwardness, and a LOT of upgrade systems to micromanage aside, the amount of voice acting in this game is incredible, i've been playing through as an English speaker with Chinese Audio and it's AWESOME. i love walking through a town and overhearing NPC's having conversations. Where Winds Meet is a surprisingly enjoyable open-world action RPG, especially considering it’s completely free to play. The game has a calm, relaxing atmosphere mixed with moments of intense combat, which makes it easy to play for both casual sessions and long hours of exploration.

One of the best parts of the game is the freedom. The world encourages exploration, and you’re rewarded for going off the main path. Hidden areas, secret encounters, and side activities make the map feel alive. How much you enjoy the game really depends on how much you’re willing to explore the more you roam, the better the experience becomes.

The combat and boss fights are another strong point. Bosses are challenging, but the difficulty can be adjusted, which makes the game accessible for both beginners and experienced players. Online co-op is a nice feature too, letting you team up with others for missions or just explore together. There are also plenty of features to keep things interesting, from character progression to different fighting styles and abilities.

However, the game isn’t perfect.

The menu system feels clunky and unintuitive, and navigating through it can be annoying. PvP is also underwhelming it doesn’t feel as polished or balanced as it should be. Boss raids can feel repetitive, and some mechanics start to become boring after extended playtime, especially if you grind the same content too often.

The game also includes a cosmetic gacha system. Thankfully, it doesn’t impact gameplay or give any combat advantage, but personally it didn’t interest me much and feels more like an optional side feature than something essential.

As for monetization overall, the game is not pay to win in any meaningful way. While the Ultimate Battle Pass gives some benefits, it doesn’t provide a serious advantage and doesn’t seem to affect PvP either. Progress mostly depends on skill and how much you explore rather than how much money you spend.

If you enjoy exploring large worlds, fighting challenging bosses, and playing co-op with friends, Where Winds Meet is definitely worth trying especially since it’s free. Its flaws exist, but they don’t ruin the experience, and what it does well easily outweighs what it doesn’t.

This is a game that may not fully resonate with everyone... there are some definite con's, but overall the pro's may vastly outshine the con's for most people; especially being Free to Play.

Let's get the con's out of the way, as if you can look passed these I see a lot of enjoyment in your future.
1) There are many layers of menus and screens... it's overwhelming, and you will lose and have to hunt for certain details from time to time... eventually once you get into a ryhthm things become more familiar.. but it'll take time
2) There are bugs.  Thankfully I have not run into many thus far, but things like having no issues with elevators for days, then running into a diagonally moving one that's not treating it's floor like "ground you stick to" so it'll slide away from under you if you don't manage to move at the correct speed to stay on.
3) Know you will get stuck and/or float on things... thankfully I haven't run into too many, but when it happens it breaks your momentum and becomes super annoying.  So far I have been able to eventually unstuck myself by spamming, jump, croutch, twerk, and various button mashing.
4) Prepare for time gating.  Apparently this is a known thing for gatcha-type games, so this may roll off of you... but be aware that while the world is open, as you progress through the story you will get ever increasing wait periods before you can advance.  I was okay with waits under 2 days... but 8+?  Perhaps it's just the way they frame the rollout of new content and/or level cap increased.
5) There is no mage... there can be mystical/chi/energy/elemental themes and influences one some skills/arts, but if you were hoping for a spellcaster focused build... it's absent here.
6) Some voice overs / dialogue mismatch and seem drawn out / repetitious / "richard" and Jane.  I'm not sure if this was a translation thing or if the dialogue was pumped out by AI
7) Part of zone completion (if you're a completionist) is making friends with AI chatbot NPC's... the game does give you hints one how the conversation should be steered for success, but if you don't trip on the right words it's looking for... it can be an excrsize in frustration.
8) Profession Bouties have an issue in the way they are handled... seems folks pick them up, horde them, and perhaps never complete them... as when you work though this list it is a miracle if you ever find one you are able to pick up.
9) Male and female replaced with Body Type 1/2 ... thankfully this is as for as they went with the ideology that expects it.

If you've read this far and haven't been scared off, here are some pro's
1) $0 cost for the game.  There is a cash shop, but it's mostly for cosmetics.  There is also a battle pass that some argue approaches pay-to-win in that someone may get a few more resources earlier than you to advance their gear enhancing... but with all the time gates, you'll have time to get them yourself manually if you choose to.
2) The graphics, variety of environments, and overall atmosphere are incredible.  You will have lots of WOW moments as you explore the world... and ask yourself how you're playng a game this beatiful for free.
3) The story is pretty good and the variety of ways the quests unfold, are found, and are completed never feel repeticious or like "fetch quests".
4) The game supports pure solo-mode (in fact is the only way to do some quests), co-op so you and your friend(s) can explore the world together, and online where you'll find folks playing that mode lumped together.  And you can freely switch between these mode seemleessly.  Need a malidy cured?  Put out a call for a healer (chat is always online), they'll send a co-op invite, teleport right beside you, heal you, then go back to whatever they were doing.
5) Even though the menus/pages are varied and layered.... they were very good at providing links on items/enhancements... for example, while upgrading your item you can out of "course hide"... click the course hide requirement and it'll tell you which shops/merchants you can buy it at and which animals you can farm for it... and those animals can be show on the map via the resource options... very helpful!
6) There are Sects (factions) to join if you want to... they can be a source for daily tasks, but they can also at times feel more like a burden/chore... Sectless is an option too
7) There are 3 types of guilds to join... combat/pvp, exploration, and casual... these cana lso be a source for daily/weekly tasks, raids, parties, etc...
8) There are also casual events that people can join as part of daily/weekly tasks... or just to chill out... some tie into the professions whereas others include various games, wrestling, etc... or start a PUG for a RAID
9) While much of what I've mention so far can be considered PVE, there are arena' choices for the PVP'ers too... and if you like to play as a criminal you can get your PVP thrills too fending off bounty hunters.

All this to say there are many ways you can spend your time in this game while being totally inpressed by the graphics/visuals... yes there are some issues/con's but which ones really matter to you and do the Pro's outway them?  If so, you'll have lots of fun!
