So, my input on this game:

I will make this most known right now is that I prefer to play the game on the easiest difficulty, as I'm focused moreso on storywriting and lore and less on combat difficulty and challenge, but I'll still talk about that later.

First off: ANIMALS! Do not try to fight them like you would in any other game. For some reason animals are extremely resistant to regular attacks, they take 99% reduced damage from all attacks unless you're apparently max level with the best gear and all of your skills unlocked. If you need to deal with them, use the Tai Chi ability or try to single them out.

But everything else--bosses, humanoid enemies and such are easily handable on the story difficulty which I played on. You can parry, dodge and counter enemies. You can also turn on settings to slow the game down and tell you when to use the abilities to counter enemies or when to dodge; however, the game turns this feature off automatically whenever you are fighting bosses or other extremely powerful enemies. Which is annoying--and makes no sense to me personally, but I guess you could see it as being 'challenged' but I do not. I see it as them pulling the rug out from under your feet in a moment when you need it the most.

Story-wise this game makes me greatly enjoy it and it definitely gives me Ghost of Tsushima vibes (minus the grimdark nature of the story of that game). Though the morally idealistic nature of the protagonist (which calls to mind the aspect of LAWFUL STUPID) greatly irritates me. It fits with the thematic of the story, I just hate heroes who put their morales above even common sense.

As someone who is a stupid american who doesn't know crap about chinese folklore or mythology, I found my time in this entire game to be a treat in terms of the storyline--even though I personally don't care for a fair few issues in it..

Such as:

* If you break the law? You can be arrested. If you are arrested? You are put into a cage, paraded through town whilst NPCs and other PCs throw ♥♥♥♥ at you and forced to do manual labor until your sentence is over. This is honestly a stupid concept and I greatly despise it. Why? Because it railroads player agency.

* You can randomly obtain various 'illnesses' in the game from any kind of activity. Drink too much? Alcohol poisoning. Drop from a far enough height? Break or sprain your bones.

* If you DO suffer from any illness you have to find a NPC Doctor or let another player healer heal you. It is VERY expensive for a doctor. I get why this exists, but I personally hate this mechanic/restriction. Its forcing me to take time away from the game just to sit through a stupid animation.

* Excessive focus on Mini-Games for actual player growth. You HAVE to do the mini-games if you want to improve your primary/secondary stats. Primaries like Strength, Constitution are resolved by beating mini-games. Secondaries like perception and the like through the same.

* Leveling seemingly doesn't nothing other than make enemies 'slightly' weaker, and puts you behind the curve if you rush through it too quickly. Also it scales the enemies accordingly. So it feels like a punishment--not a reward--to level up.

Leveling up causes you to have to undergo something called a 'Breakthrough'. I'm not going to sugar coat it. Breakthroughs are basically just a concept taken from Warframe where you have to accomplish a test within a limited timeframe in order to advance to the next level. The only redeeming factor of this is its only for solo-play. I still find this concept kind of dumb in a game that is primarily marketed as an MMO Action RPG.

The game has two settings: Online/Co-Op Play and Solo. The game is primarily designed for a SOLO experience, so the online/co-op features are.. honestly? Vastly limited and if you were hoping to be able to have your friend assist you with that boss you've been struggling with? The good news is that they can... the bad news is that they themselves won't get credit for it unless they do the same quest themselves and have you as their co-op ally. I hate this--it reminds me of Monster Hunter World where only the quest poster got credit. Its arbitrary restriction that legitimately serves ZERO purpose.

Next I will talk about difficulty in this game: Honestly? This is where my biggest gripe comes from. There are different difficulty levels in this game, and I played on "Story", which is misleading. Typically, when you play a game on story difficulty (a difficulty that has been used as the easiest difficulty in any game) you expect the enemies to have lower hit points, lower defenses, and lower damage. In this game? It lowers those stats, yes.. but it does not do that in boss encounters. Bosses feel as if they were exempted from this rule. If I am fighting a boss on story difficulty then I expect the boss to be EASY, not slightly downtuned.

The microtransactions in this game are honestly how the game stays 'free to play', but they're only and purely cosmetic--and do not provide any sort of benefit to the rest of the game at all. That's it. You can get by the rest of the game without touching the store even -once-.

Alright, so with all of that out of the way would I recommend this game to other players? Short answer: Yes*. But with an asterisk.

I recommend this game to other players, but be mindful this game is not for those who prefer casual difficulty, gameplay, and such. This game will FORCE you to enjoy difficulty, force you to suffer failure in order to find success. If that's something you enjoy? You'll enjoy this game. But for me? Not so much.

I probably won't be playing this game often--if at all--after this review. And if I do? I will limit my time on it. I was expecting better--and got less than I expected.

There are a lot of really good things about this game from the nearly 4 hours I played. The character creation is amazing, the graphics are stunning, and I really did enjoy the combat and what I did manage to get from the story. 

Where it really fell flat for me was that I feel like the game doesn't know what it wants to be. It's very overwhelming. It puts in a lot of little mechanics and systems and things to keep track of and it's a lot for me to handle. Maybe that would change if I stuck with it for longer, maybe I'd get used to it, but I think if I'm still overwhelmed by the 4 hour mark then I'm probably going to continue to be overwhelmed. The game feels to me like a combination of Genshin Impact, MMOs like FFXIV or WoW, a bit of Elden Ring, and maybe some Infinity Nikki in there too. It results in something that is very confused and unsure of what it actually wants to be. For some people, the complexity might be a thing they enjoy, but it's not really for me. 

The other thing that kind of gives me a bit of hesitation to continue with is the use of a ChatGPT like system when conversing with some NPCs, and it's even a major use of a minigame. I'm not wholly opposed to the use of AI in video games, procedural AI and other such things have been used in games for years. I just personally don't feel like I want to converse with a ChatGPT NPC in the game. I'd like to get to know the NPCs as individuals, rather than teach a chatbot NPC to sound more authentic. The other concern I have with that is, I don't know how much leeway the game will give with people teaching the AI NPCs. If they're not rejecting certain words/phrases/etc that could be offensive or toxic (and you know there's a lot of toxicity in MMOs sometimes ...), those AI bots are just going to spout that kind of stuff back and it's not exactly a good look. It's not something that is present in those AI NPCs at the moment, but it is a possibility I'm concerned about. 

Overall, NOT a bad game. Just not a game for me. I really do wish the game the best in its future.

Finally at the 100 hours mark and I must say this has been an absolutely fabulous game. Albeit with great timing as university in America is on Thanksgiving break so I have a wealth of freetime.

I absolutely adore the intricate detail in the cosmetics, story, NPCs, cinematics and questlines. For people looking to expand their horizons beyond their current MMOs, WWM is a great option especially as it is free with zero subscription services beyond a battle pass if you use it. 

There are some localization issues such as translations but NetEase from my knowledge did not expect the global release to be doing as well as it has so it did not prepare for this as much which is understandable. Luckily the devs have shown to be quite receptive to feedback so I expect with time as the teams catch up on work that issue will be fixed.

The only issue I have had is lag depending on what I'm doing but this is purely a me problem as obviously running a vtuber model with obs AND wwm is bound to cause some lag! 

I recommend everyone gives this game a chance and properly give it a chance, do not be IGN and don't force this game to be what it was never intended to be and instead indulge in the wonderful feast that Everstone Studios prepared for us!

Added notes:
I do wish the cosmetics, especially the gacha, were more affordable but I have accepted this mostly while playing knowing I won't partake in the gacha but it is a loss for the fashion girlies. There is zero pay to win but sometimes you do need to pay to slay.

Where winds meet delivers an experience that feels both engaging and memorable from start to finish. The game stands out with its impressive world design, polished visuals, and smooth gameplay mechanics that keep you invested throughout your playtime.

One of the strongest points is its graphics and environment. The scenery is beautifully crafted, with attention to detail that makes every location feel alive and immersive. Whether you’re exploring open landscapes or navigating tight spaces, the game consistently presents stunning visuals.

When it comes to gameplay, the controls are intuitive and responsive, making each action feel satisfying. The combat/system/mission style is well-designed and offers a good balance of challenge and enjoyment. New players can adapt easily, while experienced players will appreciate the depth.

The storyline also adds weight to the experience. The characters are well-written, and the progression keeps you curious about what comes next. Combined with a fitting soundtrack, the atmosphere is strong and emotionally engaging.

Personally I'm addicted to it. I've been playing it everyday for hours and hours, and the game is just visually stunning if you can run it at max settings and native resolution. I've taken so many in-game photos just because of how beautiful the locations throughout the game are, and you can go just about anywhere. The game's movement system is really fun once you unlock certain techniques. You quite literally can fly through the sky and cover large sections of the map, which makes getting around even easier. The game has a fast travel system as well, but that's not as fun. I enjoy just walking around discovering new things. The maps are massive with lots to find/do, and it's always neat to come across some kind of temple, dungeon, city, statues, etc. You really never know what you might come across. Some people might think I'm blowing this out of proportion, but the game really does have some insane visuals. We're talking like Ghost of Tsushima level details in a massive open world game. 

I know some people don't care for the combat because it's "souls-like" but the game has an assist parry system you can turn on if you really don't think you can get the timing down on parries. The timing seems quite large/fair from my experience, so it's hard to constantly miss. Combat will be hit or miss for a lot of people, but I've been having fun with it. It is a "Wuxia" style game so you'll get a lot of neat martial arts cinematics and techniques that make it seem like you  basically have super-human abilities. You will feel like a walking demi-god at times. I also want to touch on the INSANE CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION SYSTEM. This game probably has one of THE MOST in-depth character creators I have ever seen. You can literally spend HOURS styling your character down to the most minute details in their appearance. I wasn't very good at it, so I just picked a preset, but the other neat thing is you can actually use other characters presets if you don't feel like customizing one yourself and a lot of them are really quite nice looking. You can also dye armor sets and hairstyles in the game as well, which is really neat. There are TONS of hairstyles to obtain and outfits as well, so you can really go all out on dress-up and make your own designs, or even use other player's designs as well that have been posted publicly. The game really does a great job with customization in general and making your character feel unique. I really like that aspect.

I haven't even gotten very far in the story because I've just been exploring the map and having a lot of fun just doing that. The story does look interesting and has been holding my attention so far, granted it's only the first chapter still. There are a lot mini-games as well, like you can play chess, mahjong, a card game, pitch pot (which is like getting drunk and throwing arrows into a pot, so like darts in a way?) fishing is in the game as well, and even a musical mini game that functions like Stepmania. You also have dungeons, jumping puzzles, and just puzzles in general to solve to get rewards. 

The game is a bit strange to define. It's not really an MMORPG, but it has elements of an MMORPG. You can play "solo mode" which is just like a private server where it's just you and nobody else. The "online mode" will let you partner up/matchmake with up to four other players and you can explore the world/do things together, like a "co-op mode" there is also a guild system. You can make a guild and have people join, and there are "sects" which are basically factions in the game that have different principals they follow and use specific weapons/martial arts. As of right now there are only four sects, I believe? But more I assume will be added with future updates. I believe there are actually a total of 8-9 sects right now. You have one faction that focuses on trickery, one that focuses on helping others, one that believes in love/romance, one that is focused entirely on healing, one that focuses on killing others (PVP), etc. There is really something for everyone, or eventually there will be. Each sect has rules that must be followed, and you can be punished for not following them, so that's a neat system. Each sect is unique with specific outfits that can be obtained and items. There are even professions in this game, though as of right now it's just two. Scholar and Healer. The healing system in the game is honestly very fun. You can heal NPC's with specific illnesses/issues, and the healing system functions as a card game, with cards having different effects. Other players can also be invited into your game world to heal you if you become sick/ill. The game has quite a lot of illnesses that people can develop everything from mental breakdowns to bone sprains if you follow from a high drop. Scholar is more like the "lawyer" type of profession. It also functions as a card mini-game where you'll debate NPC's to convince them of something and if you win you get rewards. You can even upgrade these professions with special items and make them stronger to heal stronger illnesses or debate harder NPC's. I really think it's neat, and there are more professions that will be added in future updates as well to expand it. There is even a construction function where you can BUILD a house and personalize it. You can craft and buy furniture for it. You can even craft medicine, weapons, carpentry, blacksmithing. It's all in the game. The game is just a massive expansive world and there is just so much to do and so much to make you feel like you really are living a second life. It's almost like some Wuxia open world Second Life style game. You can even get date and get married in the game and it has it's own system for that where you get points and special abilities with your partner in combat. 

There is just SO MUCH in this game to unpack and it's only going to get bigger. I just really can't stress enough how beautiful this game is. Everywhere you look will just be another photogenic spot to pose your character and take cool pictures, and you also can share those images with other players and they can like them. There is even a "signpost" system similar to Elden Ring/Dark Souls where you can leave hints/messages for other players, which is fun. It can help you solve a quest/puzzle or tell you where to go. I really enjoy that feature as well. Truth be told there really isn't much here that I personally hate, possibly the menus/UI, which can be very overwhelming to navigate but that's because there are so many systems and things to keep track of it in the game. If that sounds unappealing to you then you might not like the game. You might find it "overwhelming" which I suppose it can be if you just aren't into games like this. I'm just really excited to see the game grow and get more and more content, and the biggest shocker is you're getting a game like this FOR FREE. It's mind-boggling because they could have easily charged money for something like this. Oh, sure the game has a "gacha" system but it's not like you HAVE to participate in it. The game gives you outfits and hairstyles for free in some instances, and it's really only there if you want to engage with it. Some outfits aren't even that expensive. Some can be as cheap as $1 or $5, and it's not a P2W system either. Everything you buy is purely aesthetic, so you don't have to worry about people getting exclusive benefits because they're spending money on the game. They might just look "cooler" than your character, but it's not that big of a deal. There is also a battle pass, but it is FREE. You CAN upgrade to their version of the "elite/premium" battlepass and get bonus rewards, like other games have used as well. I didn't really care for Genshin Impact and Wuthering Waves, but this just BLOWS both of them out of the water, and it's not using "anime" visuals, but actual detailed/high quality visuals, and you can even see that in the screenshots on the home page.

Where Winds Meet is an ARPG where you make your own legend. Right from the start, you’re thrown into a world full of adventure, exploration, and intense combat. Feel the wind brushing against your skin as you dive into this epic journey.Some NPCs in the game have artificial intelligence too, which makes the world feel more alive and realistic. 

Then story At first, it might seem difficult to connect with the narrative, but that’s only because many of us aren't familiar with Chinese culture and history, something that’s not taught in Western schools and that is normal. However, once you take the time to explore the world and learn its foundations, the story will appear in a completely new light. It’s not pure fiction: it’s an intricate tale rooted in historical and mythological events that adds deep, rich layers to the game. It’s like opening a history book, but one that knows how to engage you, move you, and make you want to learn more.In the game, you’ll also have the chance to cause some chaos, much like in GTA. You can steal horses, rob merchants, and if you get caught, you’ll end up in prison. But that’s not all: you can join mysterious sects, choose a profession, and embark on a myriad of activities that go far beyond the usual quests. The world of Where Winds Meet is vast, full of possibilities, offering you incredible freedom of action. And all this could easily go wrong in a poorly balanced game, with too many things thrown together without a sense of logic. But here, surprisingly, everything works. Not only does it never feel overwhelming, but it’s all managed with great lightness. You’ll spend hours enjoying yourself without ever feeling bogged down. It’s all “chill” and well-balanced, like a pleasant discovery that will keep you engaged without stress.

One thing to note is the monetization system. The gacha might seem a bit worrying at first, but it’s handled well and doesn’t affect gameplay. It’s just pure cosmetics, and there’s no advantage in pve or pvp You can even get discounts of up to 50% for skins, and some can be farmed. So it’s not P2W, and you can enjoy the game without needing to spend money to progress or get better.

Then option to play in cooperative mode or multiplayer, with MMO elements, further enhances the offering. Whether you want to face the world alone or join a group, Where Winds Meet gives you both options. You can join a guild, participate in events, or explore freely without any pressure. The game world is vast, full of stuff to do, secrets to discover, and the variety of content will keep you busy for hours. Every corner hides something interesting: a small camp, an enemy to face, a quest to complete etc.

One important note: don’t worry too much about the initial menus, they may seem a bit complicated, but don’t fret, you’ll get used to them soon. Where Winds Meet has a lot of content, and learning to navigate through the options and menus is part of the experience. It’s nothing you can’t get the hang of with a little patience, and in the end, you’ll find yourself enjoying the game with the same serenity you would have while exploring a new world.

To truly enjoy the game, take it easy, explore, dive into the story, and try out every available mode: PvP, cooperative activities, main and side quests, and everything else the game has to offer. The experience is all the more rewarding when you approach it with a calm mindset. Let yourself go, there’s no rush. Feel the wind .
Simply immerse yourself in the game’s flow and let yourself be carried away.

Ultimately, Where Winds Meet offers everything you want in an ARPG: adventure, combat, and an engaging story. And what else? It’s free,why not give it a go? You’ve got nothing to lose, and who knows, you might just find your next favorite game

[h2]A Testament to Wuxia's Unbound Spirit[/h2]

Where Winds Meet is not merely an action RPG; it is an audacious love letter to the Wuxia and Xianxia genres, promising a scope that stretches the very definition of an open-world experience. From the moment the game plunges you into the tumultuous final years of the Northern Song dynasty, it sets a tone of majestic desolation and philosophical weight. This is the Jianghu—the world of rivers and lakes—rendered with astonishing fidelity, a land where every bamboo forest whispers of ancient grudges and every bustling city street hides a master swordsman. The visual artistry alone justifies the anticipation; it’s a breathtaking canvas of classical Chinese aesthetics, transitioning seamlessly between serene, mist-shrouded peaks and the gritty realism of historical life, establishing an atmospheric foundation for the epic journey that awaits.

[h2]The Dance of the Unseen Blade[/h2]

At the heart of this colossal undertaking lies a combat system that is less about button-mashing and more about choreography, instinct, and unparalleled freedom. Where Winds Meet delivers on the fantasy of being an authentic martial arts master. The combat is fluid, allowing players to weave together countless styles, from the lightning-fast precision of Jian (straight sword) to the brute force of a massive Greatsword, and even the esoteric movements of unarmed internal arts. The ability to deflect projectiles, counter incoming strikes with cinematic grace, and harness Qinggong—light-body skill—to fight on the walls or skim across water elevates the encounters from simple fights to kinetic, almost unbelievable duels. The player’s identity is not prescribed; it is forged in the crucible of battle, constantly evolving with every new school of martial arts discovered and mastered, truly making the fight a dance of the unseen blade.

[h2]A Thousand Ways to Exist[/h2]

What separates this title from its contemporaries is its almost revolutionary commitment to player agency beyond the main questline. Where Winds Meet proposes a world that reacts, not just with branching dialogue, but with systems that allow the player to adopt a thousand professions. You are not just a hero; you can be a wandering physician, an architect, a street performer, a ferryman, or even a simple innkeeper. This isn't flavor text; these are deep, interactive mechanics that influence the game world and its economy. Should you fail your destiny as a warrior, you can still survive, thrive, and affect the narrative as a humble merchant. This colossal ambition to blend a historical RPG with a sandbox life-simulator suggests a world of unprecedented depth, where the player's choices, both grand and minute, fundamentally determine their path in the vast, unforgiving, and beautiful Jianghu.

[h2]The Verdict: Setting a New Horizon[/h2]

Where Winds Meet is poised to be more than just a great game; it holds the potential to be a watershed moment for the open-world action genre. Its combination of deeply satisfying, highly-customizable Wuxia combat, alongside an unparalleled level of freedom in professional and social roles, hints at a landmark achievement. It is a promise of an immersive world where the player can truly live a second life, navigating the moral ambiguities and breathtaking spectacles of ancient China. This is an essential title for anyone seeking a true, uncompromised Wuxia epic—a powerful reminder that the greatest adventures lie where the winds meet.

A surprisingly complex but ultimately very flawed game.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]1. DEI Injected.[/h2]
For the western release of this game, Genders (Male / Female) has been removed and replaced with "Body types". [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Slistingservice/discussions/0/4307201374342406741/]Read why that is bad here.[/url]

[hr][/hr]
[h2]2. User Interface.[/h2]
Oh dear god the UI. Layers inside other layers that are inside other layers.. A map that is borderline completely unusable because if you are not almost FULLY zoomed in, icons and POI's disappear and then there's the 10+ different pages to collect "rewards". Waypoint markers? Yeah those are still in Chinese. You have to experience it for yourself to understand just how bad it is.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]3. Co-op / Multiplayer.[/h2]
It basically doesn't exist. Same, if not worse draconic restrictions than on Dark Souls. 90% of the content is Single-Player only.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]4. AI Generated Content.[/h2]
Undisclosed on the store page for some reason. It's used when creating character faces, voices and generating dialogue for NPC chatting in the game. Most if not all of the English voices are AI generated as well. There's dozens of times (especially later) where they literally bug out.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]5. Fake Progression.[/h2]
The devs unfortunately decided to implement the bane of all RPG's: "Level Scaling" into this game. Meaning, mobs and bosses scale to your level constantly, making the whole "leveling up" and "getting gear" aspect of this game completely pointless and a 100% artificial grind. When i started out, i fought a bear. Learning combat, i took 5+ hits but ultimately won. Came back to the area much later as a higher level with new, fully upgraded gear, fought the same bear and he killed me in 2 shots.

Want to dive towards something in your talents? Sorry, that's level locked. Want to explore the world or go get upgrades important to your build outside of the starting area? Nope, progression AND strictly time-locked, get teleported back dummy. All the "content" in the world? It's 5000x copy-pasted garbage served on a Ubisoft style plate but with even more pointless minigames. Won a hard battle and excited to get better gear? Sorry but all the loot in the world is pretty much just money and gear upgrade currencies. You get all the gear at once for free whenever you "breakthrough" (remove your level cap with a small trial.. Why is there a level cap? I don't know.)

[hr][/hr]
[h2]6. Boss Designs.[/h2]
A few are good (hard but fair), an overwhelming majority are not. Imagine fighting through a tough boss, having mastered all of their moves. You get through the first stage without taking a hit. Then the second stage starts. You get him down to 25% hp and then oops, you slipped up for 0.1 seconds and now you're dead in a insta-kill combo regardless of gear. Back to the first stage! [b]Yup,[/b] that kind of design becomes the norm after the opening.

Want to practice against a specific stage? Too bad, gotta kill that lengthy first one first, every single time. Later on, some bosses even have 3 phases which is utterly laughable. All the boss arenas are also really claustrophobic, including ones with invisible borders such as with Qianye and i don't know why. Some are also made by complete morons, featuring white-clothed bosses fighting on white backgrounds & terrain, firing white attacks. (Sleeping Daoist)

For those that have played Elden Ring, most bosses unfortunately suffer from a mixture of Godrick and Pontiff syndrome. [b]AKA:[/b] Attacks are artificially staggered, delayed with tons of "oh i'm holding my weapon up here but am i going to swing it?... wait for it.." and Pontiff's 5+ second long combos that you pretty much just have to sit there and wait through. Obnoxious, artificially difficult (learning moves > reactive gameplay) and ultimately incredibly unfun. They also just throw you into bosses at the beginning without letting you do any settings or choose your weapon which is.. A strange choice. Devs seem very confused in general.

Want to call in a NPC companion to help you during the boss fight? That'll be 10,000 coins each attempt. Yes, people (casuals) that struggle will literally run out of money.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]7. Combat.[/h2]
On the surface, it's quite solid and definitely stands out. Unfortunately, due to all the enemy designs being what they are, the core of it boils down to having the same crippling problems that Sekiro had which is a 99% emphasis being placed upon parrying above all else. 100% damage negation + you stun them (including bosses), can be used on pretty much all attacks, including AoE's? That is going to completely dictate everyone's playstyle in a game supposedly offering multiple different ones through different weapons, which ends up being a lie.

Once combined with the previously mentioned Godrick syndrome on most enemies, combat boils down to learning patterns above all else. You can negate SOME of this as the game lets you bring two weapon types and due to the sheer length of boss fights (+ finite amount of healing items that needs to be grinded + crafted, yes really), people pretty much always opt to bringing the self-healing fans but ultimately, you're just drowning slightly slower if you don't parry (deflect) or simply cheese bosses using long-range attacks while running away.

If you're fighting regular human-sized opponents or smaller, you get no warnings for their attacks and can't realistically see them coming at all if you're hitting them due to flashy effects that can't be turned off, especially if it's dark. The camera is also quite awful, being extremely close to the point where you're 100% blind to enemies behind you and has some clunky mouse smoothing thing going on which can't be turned off.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]8. Bugs.[/h2]
There's a bunch. I got soft-locked about 4-5 times up to level 25, having to restart the game because of a mix of getting stuck inside solid terrain (there's no unstuck feature, open a chest at the wrong angle and you're screwed), quest objectives not spawning or letting you interact with them, mobs not dying even if you throw them off 500 foot cliffs, etc. This game was NOT ready for release.

The scaling is also clearly completely broken & all over the place, both for bosses that can go from being easy to complete mountain HP sponges depending on your level and for certain mobs, like the Aureate Pavilion that can 1-2 shot you (depending on level) with their fire throwing combos and appear in groups of 5+.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]9. China Owned.[/h2]
Due to this game company being located in China, all your private info is being beamed straight back to the Chinese government with a reckless disregard for US & EU data privacy laws. [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Slistingservice/discussions/0/3828666283445210026/]Read why that is bad here.[/url]

Game is good and recommended with a few caveats:

Pros:
Looks pretty good, combat loop is generally pretty fun. (Parry and dodge based)
Good amount of weapons to choose from + Can use 2 at once.
Character customization is decent - expected of asian mmos
Chinese dubbing is good, and story is pretty interesting.
Lots of side stories that are good.
Lots of "content" and exploration.
Bosses are visually cool, and are engaging.
Lots of memes + references to chinese movies.
If you dont care for outfits - Then the rest of the game is totally free. There is no progression that is really tied to p2w.

Cons:
Ui + Menu - Way too much things hidden inside like 20 menus.
Currencies - Too many to keep track of.
Not a true MMO experience - it's mostly just drop in coop for certain content + a multiplayer overworld where you can't really do mainline quests together.
Eng translation / Voice overs are pretty ♥♥♥♥ (Ai likely)
AI use - if thats something you care about for some reason.
Unable to change game settings right off the bat - forced to play 20 mins before you can even enter settings.
Monetization - The game relies on whales to keep the game free for the casual player. However that means that prices for cosmetics are absurdly high. It is also noted that the prices are not the same as in CN. So you would be paying 3x what you would be paying if you played in CN.
PvP is pretty laggy.


Overall Thoughts:

If you don't care for spending money on cosmetics + you have capability to run the game: Give it a go. Focus more on the main line quest and play it in chinese Dub. Branch out to other things if you end up enjoying it.

If you want a true mmo experience or really want to spend money to look pretty - then ignore this game.

[h1]Tips and Tricks for Janghu Wanderers[/h1]
[b]Some notes and insights to help fellow heroes out there![/b]


[h2]Map Exploration Highlights[/h2]
Collect as you go: Focus on rare curiosities, boundary markers (+50 Exploration), and Meow-Meow’s treasure (+30). Everything else is optional.

At 4000 Exploration: You’ll get the “Cloudveil Pendant” – it unlocks major movement and roof-leaping skills. No need to grind hard; it’ll happen naturally.

Finish the “Explorer” questline first: It’s basically the game’s official tutorial and gives solid rewards.

Pick your martial combo early: Try to decide on your main build early on — having 2–3 fully leveled martial arts will keep things manageable long-term.

[h2]Newbie Pitfalls to Avoid[/h2]
Don’t rush the main quest! Explore the starter village first and collect everything. When you meet the traveler, gift 50 Jades to earn the “Kindest Soul in Qinghe” title.

Lock your found relics. Items marked as “Past Relics” are valuable for collection progress and easy to melt by accident.

Save your "Stamina Pills". Don’t use it early — wait until you’re farming level 61 gear. Before level 40, spend your stamina on outposts for rare materials.

Save your Jades. Other than gifting 50, save the rest for golden manuals like Morale Chant. They’re incredibly useful. Don't gamble on banner cosmetics.

Farm monsters strategically. Leave one alive in an area so the node resets — infinite farming loop!

Buy your fishing gear early. Check general stores (large and small rods). You can also trigger a hidden brewing encounter.

Loot all treasure chests during the "Golden Pool" storyline — you can’t re-enter afterward!

[h2]Daily Routine[/h2]
Check the Daily Sign-In tab under “Activities.”

Always use your stamina — if it’s full, go farm strongholds or zone bosses.

Play one Leisure Game a day (like pitch-pot). It often doubles as a guild/sect order task.

Want every hairstyle? Head home and brush your hair daily!

Don’t skip Hero’s Walk check-ins — free items just for logging in.

Do Guild Quests if you’ve joined one.

Pop open world chests and harvest plants, ores, and minerals along the way.

Recycle spare gear, but keep any with golden-text descriptions, especially level 41+ for tuning materials.

Building 100% exploration means clearing bosses, tasks, and conversations with unique NPCs. “All Things Known” requires patience (time-based clues), so skip it if you’re not into sleuthing.

[h2]Weekly Routine[/h2]
Open “Companionship” and finish Sword Trials, Hero Realms, Adventures, and Leisure Games at least once. You can skip PvP if not your thing.

Spend your Jades in the Shop on Gleam Stones (essential for power-ups) and Art Manuals.

Each map’s shop sells ore and fur for crafting — buy them weekly.

Complete your Battle Pass and Sect Orders. Maxing out reputation lets you trade for exclusive outfits and consumables.


That’s it, fellow martial wanderers — explore at your own pace, experiment with builds, and don’t forget to enjoy the world instead of grinding mindlessly!

Where Winds Meet delivers a surprisingly strong experience from the very beginning, showcasing a confident combination of artistry, mechanical depth, and narrative ambition.

Strengths
- Innovative Combat System. The game’s combat is one of its standout elements, blending fluid martial-arts movement with tactical decision-making. Encounters feel dynamic and expressive, giving players room to experiment with numerous styles and abilities.
- Exceptional Visual Presentation. The world is crafted with remarkable attention to detail. Environments, character animations, and overall art direction consistently create striking, memorable scenes that elevate the experience far above the average free-to-play title.
- Engaging Storyline. The narrative develops steadily and keeps the player invested throughout. Its pacing and variety of story beats ensure that exploration and progression feel meaningful.
- One of the most notable advantages is that the game is entirely free to play, and it offers a complete experience without requiring any monetary investment.

Weaknesses
- Occasional Co-op Instability. The cooperative mode can be inconsistent at times, with minor glitches that may require reconnecting or restarting a session.

Additional Note
There is ongoing criticism from some players regarding the game’s monetization system. However, it is difficult to justify the negativity when Where Winds Meet can be played comfortably without spending anything. The presence of optional purchases does not impede progress, nor does it create a pay-to-win environment.

Where Winds Meet is easily one of the most impressive games I have played in years. It delivers a huge, living wuxia world that constantly rewards exploration, and it does all of this as a free-to-play title without feeling pay-to-win. Every time I log in, it genuinely feels like stepping into a living historical drama where I am the main character.

The world is the first thing that completely hooked me. The recreation of 10th-century China is stunning: busy markets, quiet villages, misty mountains, hidden temples, ghostly swamps, and massive cities – all packed with side stories, secrets, and environmental details that make the world feel alive. NPCs are not just background decorations; they gossip, move around, and often lead you into small stories or hidden quests if you pay attention. Dynamic weather and day–night cycles change the mood of each area so much that I often find myself just riding around or parkouring across rooftops, enjoying the scenery.

Combat is another huge highlight. It has clear soulslike DNA with a big focus on timing, dodging, and parrying, but it is more accessible and flexible than a traditional soulsgame. Running a dual-weapon setup like Nameless Spear plus Strategic Sword feels incredibly fluid – swapping mid-combo, launching enemies into the air, then slamming them down with flashy martial arts looks and feels amazing. On top of that, the Mystic Arts and Inner Ways systems give you dozens of different playstyles and passive synergies to experiment with. There is a real sense of depth: you can build for agile glass-cannon, bruiser, crowd control, support, or anything in between, and the game gives you plenty of tools to theorycraft and fine-tune your build.

Content-wise, Where Winds Meet is ridiculously generous. There are story arcs, sect questlines, Jianghu “legend” quests, puzzle dungeons, hidden bosses, life skills, housing and base building, guild features, social activities, and countless side quests – enough to keep you busy for a very long time. What I really appreciate is how often the game reacts to my choices: relationships with NPCs, small decisions in dialogue, and how I solve certain quests can all come back later in surprising ways, making the world feel reactive rather than static.

The monetization deserves special mention because it is much better than many other big online games. The core of the game is fully playable for free; you can progress, unlock systems, and clear all major content without spending money. Paid elements are heavily focused on cosmetics, fashion, mounts, emotes, and other visual extras. There are some extremely premium skins aimed at whales, but they do not give raw power. As a regular player, it feels more like a style shop than a paywall, and the game hands out plenty of free rewards, currencies, and events so that free players are not left behind.

Overall, Where Winds Meet feels like a dream come true for fans of wuxia, open worlds, and action RPGs. It combines a beautiful and atmospheric setting with satisfying, skill-based combat and a ridiculous amount of content, all wrapped in a surprisingly fair free-to-play model. It is one of those games where “I’ll just do one more quest” easily turns into several hours, and even after long sessions I still discover new systems, hidden stories, and small touches that show how much care went into its design.

[h2]Fantastic game; rough around the edges[/h2]

Where Winds Meet is impressive and ambitious for a free-to-play game. The world is sprawling, offering a multitude of activities to engage in. The combat is flashy, albeit stiff-feeling at times, and the variety of weapons is great. While the game's main narrative feels mediocre, its writing and delivery shines through several side quests. And despite the graphics being low fidelity in some areas, the art style and visual direction paints stunning visuals, and its photomode contains a nice array of options to fiddle with. Moreover, the solo mode, weekly gating, and monetization are refreshing -- I don't feel like I need to spend money or grind daily just to keep up. 

However, its convoluting system is further bogged down by its menus-within-menus UI, poorly explained tutorials, and low quality localization. Odd translations, missing voicelines, and floaty movements add to the roughness. 

WWM is brilliant and full of potential, but its lack of polish holds back the overall presentation. Even so, the devs seem receptive to feedback, and with continued support, the game could reach a point where its rough edges fade and its strengths really shine.

Where Winds Meet surprised me in the best way possible. It’s an open-world action RPG that blends classic wuxia energy with stunning visuals and a huge world full of life. The atmosphere hits immediately — villages feel real, forests feel alive, and every mountain peak feels like it has a story waiting for you.

The combat is fast, flashy, and super satisfying. You can pull off crazy parkour moves, slow-motion strikes, and wild martial arts combos that make every fight feel like you’re in a wuxia movie. The movement system is one of the game’s strongest parts; running across rooftops or gliding through the air never gets old.

Story-wise, it leans into mystery, political tension, and ancient legends. It won’t be for everyone, but if you like wandering through a world and uncovering secrets at your own pace, it’s a vibe. There’s also a ton of freedom — you can fight, explore, talk your way out of things, or just chill and take in the scenery.

The game isn’t perfect. There are some rough edges, occasional bugs, and moments where the pacing drags. But the world and combat are so fun that those issues don’t ruin the experience.

Final Verdict:
If you love wuxia, open-world exploration, or fast martial arts combat, Where Winds Meet is absolutely worth playing. It’s beautiful, atmospheric, and full of personality — a really refreshing take on the genre.

Where Winds Meet is a game that genuinely surprised me. While it definitely has some quirks, especially with its overwhelming number of menus, it still manages to be fun, intense, relaxing, and everything in between. The game packs in an impressive number of features and systems, and there’s far more depth here than you might expect from a typical action or fighting game.

The world is rich, atmospheric, and full of things to do. Exploration feels rewarding, combat is satisfying, and there’s always something new to uncover. It’s one of those games where you can jump in without a plan and easily lose a few hours just wandering, fighting, or following side stories that pull you in without warning.

That said, it’s not without flaws.
- There are a lot of different currencies, and keeping track of what everything does can feel confusing or - - unnecessary at times.
- The menu system can be clunky and overwhelming, especially for new players.
- Because there’s so much content, it’s easy to accidentally skip storylines or features if you rush.

And that leads to one of my biggest recommendations: you don’t need to rush through this game. You can push forward quickly if you really want to, but doing so means you’ll likely miss a lot of narrative depth, worldbuilding, and useful mechanics that the game doesn’t always put front and center. Some of the best features are tucked behind side quests, exploration moments, or optional storylines that are easy to overlook if you’re speeding through the main path.

Despite these rough edges, Where Winds Meet is worth playing. The depth, the atmosphere, and the sheer variety of things to do make it a standout experience, one that rewards patience, curiosity, and exploration. If you take your time with it, you’ll find an enjoyable and surprisingly rich adventure.

Its a F2P game themed with Chinese fantasy. If you enjoy From Software games, Nioh or other action games like that. Visually the game looks stunning and has a wonderful score to boot.

For the Fromsoft vets; enjoy the bosses which will challenge you in both direct campaign progression but on top of the fact there are trails to test your abilities even more. Including challenges like going hitless on Abyss difficulty and Legend mode for the campaign.

For the more casual sided; the difficulty options are fair and allow you to dial things back. There is plenty to explore and also learn from progression items to minigames. Pitch Pot, Xaingqi (Chinese Chess), Sichuan mahjong, Madiao Cards (akin to something like Lairs Bar), and so on.

For those wanting to play with others; there is plenty of guild related tasks along with both 5 and 10 man boss fights. Most of the mini games can also be played with others. Performing instruments, healing others and even the ability to pardon crimes.

For those wanting to be competitive; the trails do have leaderboards for PVE speed runs. But on top of that the game does support *currently* is 1v1 arena, a BR mode with solo, duo and flex queue up to five people with ladders. And for those wanting to do good, you can bounty hunt other players or join the Midnight Blades to try and fight for your elder slot.

Now the main drawbacks; this game does lean in a bit with the AI chat bots and some of them can be very annoying. Talking to NPCs can just get very repetitive as if you want to make them like you for rewards and looking at the Velvet Shade fills me with dread. The riddles are also annoying and hair pulling as the AI chat bot can give false information, making that riddle impossible.
Honestly I came in expecting nothing and it turned out to be the best game ive played in years.

Even weirder - not only good. 

This beautiful abomination has combined, Sandboxing(You can build throuought Your whole world), crafting and seemingly infinite content, non-p2w gameplay, combat with very high skill ceiling both in PvE and PvP, comparable to Souls-Likes, with potentialy Pro-level PvP, with rich story capable of making a depressed, grown man feel again.
 
It is almost entirely dependant on players skill, rather than infinite grind and items, Souls-like combat and story of quality often comparable to famous Witcher 3 Blood and Wine masterpiece. 

Although items power will gate You from going further by slowing the fights by A LOT, You can still win every fight with 0 gear if You want to take that time and focus for so long, but the gear itself is easly obtained by doing 1-5 boss dungeons or on getting to a level milestone(so far it was around 10 levels).

The maximum level is capped, and being uncapped every x days to assure that players can catch up at least somewhat and to keep players at levels making it possible for more players to enjoy current ''lategame'' together. 
It is actualy genious. Finding a person to play with takes a second.   

You don't farm for that +9 weapon for 2 months, just to sell it off later, You can get it in 2hours, and although You can spend 2 weeks upgrading these items to have perfect affixes and grind it to the max( and it will make You stronger), these 2hours items are more than enough to compete with ultra-geared player if You got gaming skill adventage.

Abilities are a total mix and match. There are no classes. You can learn it all if You grind it all up. 
Instead of skills, there are weapon skills tied to martial arts. 
This gives You 2 skills per martial art, and a weapon type can have multiple of these.
You can equip 2 weapons at once. And a bow on top of that.
On top of that You can equip up to 4 passive, evolvable abilities with a lot of variety.
On top of THAT, You get to equip up to 8 active ablities - mystic arts, that are functioning like spells of sorts.
Some are used for puzzles, some for combat, thieving, some for everything.

Where Winds Meet is genuinely a phenomenal game. The combat feels sharp, fluid, and responsive, and the open world is absolutely gorgeous—easily one of the most visually striking settings I’ve stepped into recently. Even the early quests feel engaging, and I’m curious to see how much deeper they get as the story unfolds.

That said, there’s one thing that really soured my initial experience: the lack of shared progression in co-op. For me, that’s a crucial feature. I want to group up with friends, run quests, explore the world, and have everyone’s progress count—no matter who’s hosting the session.

Right now, if you’re not the host, the quests you do together barely matter for your own story. It feels punishing, especially when you look at how seamlessly games like Destiny or World of Warcraft handle shared progression. I really hope that as development continues, the game adopts a more fluid, unified progression system so co-op feels rewarding for everyone involved.

Aside from that issue, the game is amazing. If shared progression isn’t a dealbreaker for you, Where Winds Meet is absolutely worth playing.

Phew, what a game! You emerge into a huge and very open world overflowing with flair and immersion. It's really beautiful and conveys that "wuxia feeling" really well. The character creator is pretty decent, so your own character can mirror that, too. Pile many clothing, style, and coloring options on top to really drive that point home! It's quite dazzling and let's you immerse yourself in the world if you want.
The story, as far as I have followed it, is also decent. Nothing new under the sun, but steadfastly in the "good enough" territory.
And this is where I have nothing more to praise and have to start critiquing:
Combat is pretty boring and kind of clunky. If you expected something that plays souls-y, you will be disappointed. In theory that would work. You have your blocks, dodges, and parries after all. In practice combat devolves quickly into furballs with so many attacks flying around that you can not block, dodge, or parry all of them. Your skills have cooldowns and cost some stamina-adjacent resource, severely limiting a lot of them. Oh and it's not one stamina-adjacent resource. It's multiple. Your mystic skills drain one, your weapon skills drain another, dodging and the like drain a third. Add your health and your "stance" bar and that's a lot of bars to keep an eye on. The animations are cool at least.
Your role is heavily dependent on your weapon of choice. If you want to be able to heal, yourself or others, you'll have to use a fan or umbrella. Some other weapons are supposed to be for tanking, but I haven't tried those. Sooo yeah, it's not your skills that define your role, but your weapons. That's certainly a design choice one could make.
Leveling and upgrading feels scattered and arbitrary. You have your regular levels you gain from XP, then every ten levels there's a breakthrough to open up the next ten levels and new features. Then there's skill points on a very straight and narrow skill tree with a branch here or there one node deep. And like three additional skill trees drawing from other sources. You upgrade your gear, which differs only by it's level and what set it belongs to (so no cool weapon finds, it's all the same), to the point you don't really upgrade your *gear* but your gear *slots*. But you can also tune your gear. And upgrade your mystic skills. And inner ways (these sort of work like passives). You have attributes which get raised by exploration goals, too.
As you progress, you will very frequently receive rewards for one of the what, half a dozen or more in-game currencies? Which you have to dig out of a variety of menus before you can click the claim button.
And all that upgrading and leveling? Does very little. Because enemies level with you as you tier up. Fun!
There's a ton of minigames, ranging from a cat giving you environmental puzzles (love the guy! There's a lot of cats in the game and you can pet most them!), to chess, fishing, drunkenly tossing darts into a pot, rhythm games to make music, a confusing "card game" about talking to people, and probably a few more I haven't even encountered yet, like doctoring or trading or boat painting or whatever.
There's a superfluous injury system put in so doctors have something to do. Sometime when you get hit, the enemy hits your noggin and gives you a concussion or hurts your tummy. Some of these injuries heal over time, some require you to pay a lot of coin to get fixed or force you into multiplayer to get healed. Though my favorite are sprains and broken legs. Because the game does fall damage like that. But you also have an ability that lets you land quickly and safely. So if you fall from the top of a mountain and forget to press Q? There go your legs. But if you remembered the Q button? You're A-okay!  Or Q-okay? Either way, it serves basically no purpose other than being annoying.
Bosses tend to have questionable hurtboxes and attack sequences that are, let's say difficult to react to. And sometimes they like to pull the rug out from under you by, for example, reducing your healing by 80%. For the entire fight. And there's nothing you can do about it. Again some of the design choices of all time.
Exploration is nice enough, but sadly you never find anything exciting. Treasure chests always have the same contents, differing only in quantity: XP, like four different kinds of in-game currency, some upgrade materials, and of course the exploration-resource itself. Because as outlined above, there is not really any gear to loot.

So all in all: I really want to like this game, but it is so bloated, overloaded, confusing, badly explained, and most importantly inconsistent in what it wants to be that I really can't. On the topic of bugs I will only say: there are many, but they are all minor, nothing disqualifying.

If you have the time, you might as well check it out. It's FREE after all (and not P2W at that)! Maybe the things that annoy me are no deal-breaker for you. Or you might even enjoy them, who knows. But if you don't have a lot of time for gaming, you're probably better served elsewhere.

Pros:
The game is very pretty. Some of the world mechanics and puzzles are neat like healing random NPCs with a slay the spire like mechanic. The dungeon puzzles are also fun to figure out. It seems like most of the currency in the game will give you a button to go to where to spend said currency.

Cons:
There are dozens of menus and it's often hard to know where your cursor is on them so you're thinking you're selecting one option but you're not. The tutorials also aren't helpful because they often take you directly to a menu without showing you how to get there. There's really just "too much stuff" that it isn't intuitive. Tack on all of the gacha/store like stuff, journals, achievements, and so on and it's just awful to deal with.

This may be unpopular but I don't really enjoy the combat either. The general pattern is that you have to learn to parry everything to reduce a blue meter so that you can deal real damage to a red meter. There are already a ton of games that do this. On the plus side they give you a practice mode for this purpose but I personally don't find that game play to be particularly fun. It's made worse by learning a pattern just to have the enemy miss an attack, which messed up your own parry timing causing you to get hit by the rest of the combo. I've also had my own parry counters miss which animation locks you and allows the boss to get behind you. This was most noticeable on the sleepy Taoist boss.

Powering up is spread out across a bunch of menus. Level up your gear slots. Find better gear itself. Level up your stance. Level up your mystic arts. Level up your oddities. So on and so on. Despite all of that, I never actually felt stronger.

Progression makes very little sense. I upgraded an oddity that was supposed to give me faster travel speed and found out through a friend that you can't do that without a special item that you don't get until exploration level 4. Finding exploration level requires you to navigate through the dozens of menus, and it's not even on the main menu. It's on a sub menu that requires you to hit a special button to get to. AND you only learn that you need that in game if you happen upon an NPC that teaches you about it.

---

TLDR;
Where Winds Meet does some really cool stuff, but I think it's held back by menus and combat. Unfortunately you interact with both of those systems a ton so unless you're at the very least, "okay" with them you won't have a good time.

I am obsessed with this game.

POSITIVES

+ A massive amount of exploration!
+ You can pet almost all the cats.
+ Creative and beautifully designed boss fights.
+ Stunning vistas and environments, especially the ones underground.
+ A lot of lore and story, with actual Chinese history as a backdrop as well.
+ You can basically fly, and very quickly over long distances.
+ F2P, even the free outfits can look just as good (if not better) than a lot of the paid ones.
+ Whether you're attracted to men or women (or both), this game knows how to cater to both.

NEGATIVES

- Localisation could be better, and a lot of NPCs will refer to you as the opposite sex of what you play as.
- Menus can be overwhelming and takes a little time getting used to.
- You only have one character slot, and have to spend money if you regret your choice and want to change sex (like I did). But they will add more slots later it seems, so this should be a non-issue later (hopefully).
- Did not find Hua Cheng at the ghost market (yet).

Another game for which I wish there was an option in-between thumbs up and thumbs down. In many ways this is a straightforward gacha game and a blatant ripoff of Genshin Impact and Ghost of Tsushima. It also happens that ripping those two games off makes a really fun game in its own right. 

No one should accuse NetEase of being original here, but its free and its fun.

[h1]ABSOLUTELY AMAZING! [/h1]

There are amazing music, beautiful views, engaging story quests, various social activities, and awesome boss fights! 

You want to play like in Assassin Creed? You can do that. There are skills for that. Going stealth and one hit enemies or jumps from the roof and subdues them feels amazing.

You want to enjoy Lara Croft's thrill on exploring dangerous dungeons? You got it. Each dungeons feel different and amazingly designed. It doesn't feel like copy and paste. 

You want to play mini games like chess, mahjong, musical tools? You got it. Hang back, relaxing with other players, co-op with your friends and guild mates while doing these mini games together. Guild activities are interesting and there isn't dailies on guild activities. All of the are weekly which allows you to be able to finish them within a week and not forcing you to do them everyday and gives you chance to explore more.

You want to play similar like Elden ring? You got it. Not quite like souls like, but pretty close. The bosses fight are amazing and some of them feels fresh. 

You want to fly? You got it. There are different kind of traversal options in this game . The fly effect is cool and allows you to enjoy beautiful view at the same time! 

You want to build house? You got it. The creativity of some players on the way you can design and build house are beyond outstanding! Some of the quests even incorporate building tool into it and some of the oddities need to utilize building mode to be able to collect. 

You want to enjoy great story like single player right? Absolutely! Stories here are amazing. Both main story quest and side story quest are engaging and I highly recommend not to skip them. Go with your pace and enjoy some of the best cinematic stories you will see. Explore more on this open world and you will always encounter these little side quests that may rewards you with something special.

You want to do coop or dungeon or raid? There's spot for ya. Dungeons and raid uses energy but the fight are engaging and some of them interesting. Queue seems fast. You don't really need the traditional tank-healer-dps if you know the bosses mechanics and parry their attacks. 

You want gacha? Be prepared to spend some cause outfits are very well done. These outfits are very well designed and beautiful. Weapon effects and the mounts (based on CN one) looks amazing. Can't wait for them to come to global launch.

Your want a sophisticated character look? Say no more. You may spend hours in creating characters alone and you can customize it in many different ways: using voice input, photo input and let AI figure it out your character or just go the old fashioned way to create your unique looks.

There is GTA Wanted system! You can steal horse, destroy properties, even kill NPCs. However, you will be issued bounty where other player can invade your solo world and may be jailed for x amount of real time hours.

BEST OF ALL? You will not believe that this is FREE TO PLAY with no P2W elements!

CON: 
- Some of them still have a bug
- One of the weapons, Vernal Umbrella doesn't work too well with controller input 
- Guild application list seems buggy sometimes where if new applicant will see it full but it doesn't say full on guild. 
- Some graphic settings may have minor graphical glitches.
- NPCs can be chatted using AI (not a CON) but some of the chat seems to show the level of AI (less than ChatGPT) and can makes things repeatable and makes you decides to ignore that npc conversation.

Give it a try! You may like it. I know friends who weren't interested when I told them this game months before global launch and now they are all playing this. There much more elements than what I have mentioned above that I feel it's best for you to experience it yourself.

Where Winds Meet brings a strong experience at launch. It genuinely captures the excitement I had during the early days of Lost Ark. The visuals, gameplay, and initial content are all engaging. However, the similarities to Lost Ark continue. The heavy time-gating in its content design raises concerns about long-term player retention.

While the game is fun during the initial phase, the overall depth of content feels limited for prolonged grinding. The energy system refreshes slowly, which can make progression feel constrained. If you approach the game like a mobile gacha title, Where Winds Meet succeeds; it’s polished, enjoyable, and provides satisfying short-session gameplay.

Just manage your expectations. Outside of PvP and social features, there isn’t much end-game content at this point, and the pacing still resembles that of a typical mobile game with a limiting stamina system. Despite these issues, the game remains enjoyable overall, especially for players who appreciate its style and relaxed progression loop.

For a free to play game this is really impressive.

1) Single Player story mode is quite good. Going for the chinese hero arc and all that jazz.
2) Online and Co-Op are optional modes. You can do PVE and PVP with/against others. But you can also just stay in solo mode and tackle the game like a Ghost of Tsushima.
3) Gameplay is an odd hybrid of Ghost of Tsushima, Assassin's Creed, Elden Ring etc.
4) Combat is good. For dirty old casuals like me you can play on easy with help deflecting. But you can go really difficult as well. Basically you can play as you want.
5) The games purchases are all cosmetic except a battlepass which i got to support the game finding the game deserving of my money.
6) More provinces are already in the pipeline, previously released in China.

So far... quite fun, quite good! Only negatives:
- The UI takes ages to get used to with screens upon screens, tons of collectibles, development/leveling mechanisms, gamemodes etc. Might be a good idea to tackle some beginner tips about leveling as you might not quite realize how the leveling works.
- The mini games are hit and miss. Some i avoid like the plague, others are great. Your mileage may vary.

Together with Dispatch this may be the most pleasant surprise i had this year gaming wise.

Anyway, somehow this free-to-play game outperforms most Western triple-A titles from the past few years and actually delivers something that's becoming increasingly rare from them - a fun game. Sure, it’s not perfect (menus within menus, some localization/translation issues), but it does enough right that it’s hard not to appreciate what it does well. Though I have some issues with certain aspects, the sheer amount of content you get for free, puts a lot of triple-A titles to shame. Since many of them don’t offer half of what this one does.

This game offers:
[list]
[*] Wuxia theme (think Blade and Soul)
[*] Combat and bosses like Souls games
[*] World exploration packed with things to do like Shenmue, Witcher 3...
[*] GTA-style roleplay (yep, you can go to prison)
[*] You can throw stuff at prisoners during their walk of shame for rewards
[*] Some martial skills you learn by copying animals (geese are the real bosses here)
[*] Funny NPC AI interactions (I had a 20-minute DnD session with one of them lol)
[*] An interesting story with cool cinematic moments
[*] PvP 1v1, battle royale modes (ping can be an issue)
[*] MMO-style social activities (kinda like the FF14’s Golden Saucer... kinda)
[*] Co-op mode (some things are solo-only)
[*] Become a full time doctor and heal other players
[*] Debating NPCs (yes, it's a card game mini-game)
[*] Raids
[*] And more... all for FREE! Like, what?
[/list]

Yes, it’s a gacha game with a cash shop, battle pass, and optional monthly subscription, but everything you need to enjoy the game is 100% free. The paid content is mostly cosmetic (you can still get cool outfits without spending money) or things like name/gender changes - nothing that gives you an edge or power. No pay-to-win here, which is surprising but very welcoming, especially considering all the content it offers.

If you enjoy games like Elden Ring, Witcher 3, or even Genshin Impact, give this one a try.

Originally, I had this at a neutral, but have since moved over to cautiously positive.

I'll go straight to the negatives because I can only really think of 2:

The latency problem in all multiplayer modes.
There's a random latency problem that appears sometimes in multiplayer modes; most commonly in PvP or Guild events. We're seeing the actual latency multiplied several times in input delay. 130 ms latency often has over 1,000 ms of actual input latency which, as you may imagine, makes the game unplayable. This makes the single player aspect currently the only stable one.

The UI. The UI currently is atrocious and extremely confusing. Apparently this gets a lot better in future updates, but for some reason they used this old version everyone also hated in China so for now, this is a noticeable negative. Prepare to miss events you weren't notified of, rewards you can't find the page to claim them, etc.

The neutrals are only 2:

The monetization is pretty whale-centric. Meaning a LOT of the greatest stuff you see for cosmetics are behind rather massive paywalls. There are a few that are through cheaper routes like battle pass or just a straight-up exchange of the currency rather than a gacha, but even so its usually $30-50 for those and well into $600-800+ range at the highest end for the really good ones with lots of effects. Its fine because its only cosmetic, but some may care about not being able to buy into anything truly next-level-looking, so I have to mention it. Not really a concern in my personal opinion.

The timegating. As of right now, our version lacks a massive amount of content to do outside of claiming energy-restricted rewards that the Chinese version has. While it IS assumed to be coming to global version eventually, the fact is for now and for many months to come, there is very little to do outside of the highly restrictive mobile game energy system. It also refills incredibly slowly even compared to other systems of a similar design, taking 75 hours to fully charge up, and approximately 12-15 minutes to use all of. Eventually, this should get better from what we see from China's version, so this receives a neutral for now until we get those future updates (presumably after season 2 starts).

Everything else about the game is great. In instances where the lag isn't present, the combat feels pretty good, story is solid, and all-in-all, I see all the foundation work laid decently for a really top-notch game. Right now, though, a lot of its aspects need updates that we already know from the Chinese version, are coming, but aren't here yet so its just a matter of waiting.

The devs have also given us a pretty big preview of what's ahead and from what we can see, even though the game right now feels honestly like a hoyoverse/mihoyo or similar clone game with a different aesthetic over it, it LOOKS like after several major updates, the game really will be hard to tell from a full MMORPG with all the bells and whistles you'd expect from one.

Its at that phase that we'll truly see if this one can etch its name into long-term history as one of the best you could be playing.

This is a very addictive game, and the bonus is that it's free and not p2w. You should play it. I'm sure you'll see why from the other reviews. That doesn't mean it doesn't have flaws, just that because it is a free game, it's easier to overlook those flaws.

My main critique is the UI. There are SO MANY systems in this game. So many menus. So many different rewards to accept from different UIs. Every time I think I've finally unlocked the last one, there's another. It's not always clear how to get to the menu you're looking for. Changing equipment and skills is a hassle, which is especially noticeable when you encounter puzzles that require a certain weapon or techniques. Often there will be a red dot on the menu icon indicating that something needs to be checked, but the game doesn't always indicate what that is or in which menu. And so you end up hunting around for ten minutes until you give up and learn to live with the dot. It can be especially confusing for new players and put them off to the game. My husband, for instance, who I recommended the game to, got overwhelmed trying to find his way through the menus and many systems with confusing tutorials and gave up.

Once you get into the game, it's easy to overlook, but I imagine there are other people like my husband who won't get that far. So I hope the devs improve it so more people can enjoy the game.

You'll see arguments about whether this is an MMO or not. I'd say it's up to you. It's similar to live service games like Wuwa and Genshin Impact in that you play mostly solo but with multiplayer elements. However, I would argue it feels much more like an MMO because of the world chat and messages left by other players. It feels like you are surrounded by people even if you can't see them. I play MMOs mostly solo myself, and it's the same experience as that. There is also an online mode and a lot of multiplayer activities such as pvp and stuff. Keeping the main game solo also allows much more freedom for choosing your difficulty. Some people like to play with a challenge, and some people like to take things easy, and this way both of those types can enjoy the same content.

The game makes money mostly through cosmetic items. There is a gacha system with three different gachas that I've seen. One uses pearls which can only be obtained by paying real world money, one uses a currency that can be obtained very rarely in game, and then there is a standard banner that uses a currency that can be exchanged for with in-game currency. This means that there is almost no way to get the premium clothing items from the gacha without paying real world money and taking the risk of not getting them anyway. Because it's cosmetic, you can safely avoid the gacha system completely, unless you want to fill out your clothing compendium (it does the Infinity Nikki thing of including premium costumes in the stuff you need to collect if you're a completionist).

The English voice acting isn't great, but it's passable. I chose to use it anyway because dialogue auto-progresses, and my adhd butt gets distracted too easily when having to focus on reading.

Outfit styles change depending on the male or female body type, which unfortunately means you can't play a male character and still wear the pretty dresses or be a female character and wear the masculine style. The male character creator also doesn't have as many makeup options. It costs real world money to change your gender in game, so keep that in mind when making your character. The character creator is super in-depth, though, so you can go crazy with the sliders. Also know that your character is canonically 16, so even if you make them look older, their cutscene voice will still sound young and everyone will treat them like a kid, which can be jarring. 

AI features are rampant in this game. There is a weird feature in the character creator that generates an appearance based on the sound of your voice. There is also one that generates an appearance based on a picture, but I found it didn't work well and just made a generic looking person who didn't match the pics. A feature of the game is to befriend NPCs using chats with an AI chat bot based on that character, where you have a goal to convince them of something. These chats can either be really quick or go on forever and be agonizingly slow. It really becomes a chore after awhile. I'm pretty sure you can skip that content, and you should, but I'm stubborn and like to do everything and unlock everything.  

Anyway, yes, that sounds like a lot of critiques. But you should still play. It's not the perfect game, but it's free and addicting and there's a lot to do.

If you’ve ever wanted to sprint up walls, duel with swords under cherry blossoms, or meditate by a river after a boss fight, Where Winds Meet delivers that fantasy in style. Set in 10th-century China’s Five Dynasties era, the game blends history with Wuxia flair, letting you shape your path as a wandering martial artist.

Combat: Stylish and tactical, with flowing swordplay and mystical abilities that make every fight cinematic.

World: Vast and vibrant, packed with mini-games, collectibles, and factions to influence. It’s easy to lose hours just exploring.

Story: Begins with a stolen pendant and grows into a saga of politics, rival clans, and personal growth. While engaging, it leaves room for future updates and expansions.

Pros: Gorgeous visuals, creative freedom, and a mix of serious quests with lighthearted diversions (like chess battles or drunken poetry challenges).

Cons: The sheer scale can feel scattered, and the free-to-play grind may test your patience.

✨ Final Take
Where Winds Meet is like stepping into a living martial arts epic—equal parts thrilling, chaotic, and beautiful. If you enjoy games like Elden Ring or Genshin Impact but want a distinctly Chinese Wuxia twist, this one’s worth the ride.
