As a casual player, while the beginning of the game takes some time to learn with the endless amount of menus, lore & cutscenes. Once you get out into the world and start to explore, the realization hits of how in depth and well this game has been designed. As a player coming from a background of other MMOs like WoW, FF, Blade and Soul & AION. This game is breath of fresh air. As an older player, the action based combat with options to control difficultly and enable parry assist is letting me really enjoy learning the fights (I am almost nervous to go online with my internet connection being lacking at the moment). I look forward to running across challenges that force me to disable that feature and see how I have progressed. While the cash shop and gatcha system is not appealing to me in any way, I like how the monthly "subscriptions" simply allow players to earn cosmetic rewards easier. With the ability for those that want to grind out everything for free still an option in the game. The way this game treats multiplayer is also an amazing system. If I want to simply enjoy the story and progress my player alone I can, and with 84 hours in I have barely started stepping into the co-op or online modes of the game. While this type of fantasy setting may not be for everyone, I cannot recommend exploring this world enough. The game lets you interact with the world however you want, from exploring the world and finding hidden quests & treasures to learning the lore of the different sects or factions. Every-time I log in I feel I stumble across new hidden features. While the translations are not perfect, and some parts of the story feel disjointed as I have no idea at times what the reason I am doing a quest is, my only gripes about this game for now stem from the sheer amount of menus you have to learn to navigate. While the menus and different ways to progress the character seemed a bit over the top at first, the more I play I find myself simply impressed with how all this is tied together for a F2P experience.

I never play any souls-like and have gone out of my way to avoid them because I don't enjoy the combat. However, I had to give them game a try and can genuinely say I'm addicted. The story is great (don't skip through it), The available side quests are equally on par or even sometimes better than some of the main story. The combat is very punishing yet rewarding and smooth, I'm blown away that this free game has so much content compared to $70 games these days. The story is long and bosses are very memorable, and the open world bosses are equally or more challenging. You can rechallenge boss fights to farm certain gear and even get a chance at a boss specific cosmetic. There's group content like raids and trials that somehow manage to introduce new mechanics that require teamwork that weren't in the original fight. There's a very healthy amount of content out at the moment and seeing the success it has, we're bound to get a lot more!

To add on, The open world exploration is honestly one of the best parts, it's one of those situations where you set out to do 1 thing then keep getting distracted by roaming around on your route. You're rewarded nicely with currencies to improve your character and there's collectibles that you can turn in to further increase your strength. The available side quests are equally on par or even sometimes better than some of the main story. The RP in this game is one of the best for an MMORPG as well, you can join sects such as the silver needle and become a full on healer/doctor. You can cure afflictions and injuries on other players in the online on top of healing NPCs. You can become a wanted criminal and have others hunt down your bounty for a massive reward payout too. You learn new weapon masteries by invading these dojos and killing guards, then you have to observe and steal these weapon arts to gain mastery. The amount of things that you can do outside the main game actually makes it that much more addicting as you immerse yourself.

Lastly, There's mystical arts and a bit of magic in this game but it def feels like a great balance of being grounded in martial arts with some mystical forces. I do have to note that the gacha in this game is ass compared to all the other gacha I've played (Honkai Star Rail, Genshin, Wuwa). However, the gacha and gambling is purely cosmetic and honestly is a hinderance in a game like this where you actually need to see the attacks coming at you. Everything that you can buy and gamble for is purely for looks. Thankfully none of these give you an advantage over another player and the pvp comes down to actually being better and getting those parries down. All in all, very satisfied and it's genuinely criminal that this game is free.

There are a lot of positive reviews that drown out the negative ones, 
be sure to inform yourself before you get invested, and I mean both, your time and money.

If you want any vibrant hair color for example, or simply pure white hair for a hairstyle that doesn't have it already, you have to pay absurd amounts of money.
You can calculate on average that a one-time use dye on a premium hair (base hairstyles cannot be dyed) costs $250 and if you're unlucky even $500 and more because you have to use the gacha system to obtain the necessary items to exchange for the premium dye. And that is only for one hairstyle, if you want another in a vibrant color, you have to spend the same amount again.

Yes, the game does have a lot of appeal in many regards.
However, the western version and monetization for cosmetics can be extremely expensive and is by no means consumer friendly. There are sets that are quite cheap, and some you can acquire by simply playing the game, but they pale in comparison to the sets that will release in the future.

If you don't care too much how you look and you're content with an undyeable cosmetic set, basic black hairstyle and just want to enjoy gameplay for free, it's a good deal. No question.
If you like to express yourself through your character with fashion and other cosmetics, emotes etc - I advise you to stay away. It will cost you a small fortune.

And I'm not even mentioning the wild use of AI and other issues many people point out rightfully, from performance issues over to latency and ping issues that make aspects of the game unplayable.
They may not apply to you, and you may not care about them, but please do not disregard or deny issues that are very apparent and need to be fixed or should be changed for a healthier game and industry.

I've been enjoying the game. Like all games it has good and bad things. Its like Ghosts of Tsushima and Genshin impact had a baby.

The good:
Its free to play. Nice graphics, interesting story, fun mini games and puzzles/ riddles to solve. Can play almost completely solo, but have the options to switch to co-op or multiplayer whenever. You don't have to buy the costumes to enjoy the game and story content. There are a few free costumes, you just have to work for them and earn them. Or you can get free melody tickets every week and rely on luck. It is open world and the world is HUGE. Lots of things to collect and explore. Tons of quests to finish.

If you selected easy, medium or hard difficulty, you can switch between them if needed down the road. But you wont be able to change it to Legendary. If you want a Dark Souls like experience, play it on Legendary. Then it comes down to your reflexes and timing your parry.

The game isn't too difficult in solo mode. It starts off super easy. To the point you are laughing, use this time to figure out what martial arts fit you best. 

Also, just pet all the cats. 

The bad:
Multiplayer servers can be terrible. You're possibly going to get a lot of missmatching and lag, with guild events or group bosses etc.

I went into Where Winds Meet expecting “pretty martial-arts game with some sword twirls,” and instead I got a whole mythos buffet: sweeping landscapes, wuxia drama, combat that can feel like a ballet performed by someone who absolutely has beef with gravity and a UI that sometimes looks like it was designed by a committee of caffeinated squirrels.

This is a free-to-play open-world action RPG set in 10th-century China, built around the wuxia fantasy of wandering heroes, secret techniques, and the kind of stylish movement that makes normal jogging in real life feel embarrassing.


What it nails (the “okay wow” section):

1) The world is gorgeous in that “stop-and-stare” way.
Exploration is the main dopamine loop here. Mountains, rivers, villages, and those cinematic vistas that make photo mode feel like a second job (a joyful one). 

2) Combat: stylish, flexible, and occasionally pure katharsis.
When it clicks, it clicks. There’s a satisfying rhythm to swapping weapons/skills and chaining moves into something that feels choreographed like a wuxia TV series, but with fewer commercial breaks. The game leans into variety (including flashy weapon styles like fans and umbrellas), which keeps fights from turning into one-note button mashing.

3) “There’s always something to do” energy (sometimes a blessing).
If the main story isn’t hitting right that day, the game throws distractions like it’s trying to keep you from texting your ex: mini-games and side activities pile up fast (fishing, puzzles, table-game vibes, odd jobs, etc.). It’s chaotic, but it’s content-rich chaos.

4) Cross-play/cross-progression makes it easy to keep the momentum.
Progress carrying across platforms is a big deal for a time-sink game like this. Less “starting over,” more “continuing the saga.”



What doesn’t (the “prosopon of pain” section):

1) The onboarding can feel like being hit with a textbook.
The early hours can be overwhelming: systems, menus, currencies, pop-ups—chronos stops being time and becomes a blur. Some players bounce not because it’s “hard,” but because it’s a lot.

2) The UI sometimes fights the vibe.
This is a game that wants to be elegant and cinematic… and then it shows you three notifications, two tutorial panels, and a reminder about a reward track. Wuxia fantasy meets modern app design. Not always harmonious.

3) Free-to-play friction: mostly manageable, but always present.
It’s not constantly slapping your hand, but the store-and-progression scaffolding is there, quietly clearing its throat in the background. It didn’t ruin my time, but it did make me occasionally side-eye the screen like, “So… are we friends, or are you a salesperson?” (Both. The answer is both.)

4) Some design choices can feel… uncanny.
There’s been chatter around certain AI-ish NPC behaviors/presentation elements feeling immersion-breaking for some players. It’s not everyone’s deal-breaker, but it’s worth knowing going in.



Who this is for:
- Anyone who wants a big open world with wuxia flavor, flashy combat, and a lot of side content to snack on.
- Anyone who enjoys “learn the systems, then feel powerful” arcs—because the early confusion can pay off later.


Who might bounce off:
- Anyone allergic to busy menus, layered progression systems, or free-to-play “gentle pressure.”
- Anyone who wants a tight, minimal, single-path story with zero clutter.


Bottom line:
Where Winds Meet is beautiful, ambitious, and sometimes too ambitious, like it tried to be an action RPG, a social game, a wuxia epic, and a relaxing life-sim on the side… and then decided sleep was optional. When it’s good, it’s great: the aesthetic is strong, the combat can feel incredible, and exploration has real pull. When it’s messy, it’s mostly because it throws too much at you at once and occasionally breaks its own mood with modern F2P noise.
If there’s patience for a slightly chaotic learning curve, this one can be a surprisingly fun (and frequently stunning) ride, equal parts pathos and “wait, why do I suddenly have 14 new tabs open?”

For the past three to five years, I have been searching for a game that truly aligns with my preferences. During this time, I played numerous titles across various genres—many of them enjoyable, some still part of my current rotation—but none of them fully captured what I was looking for.

Where Winds Meet has finally done that. The game is not only visually stunning but also immersive in its world-building and gameplay experience. From the very first session, it felt refreshingly different—engaging, atmospheric, and crafted with a remarkable level of detail that instantly drew me in.

Another point worth mentioning is that I usually play games for only about two to three hours at a time. Even within such short sessions, Where Winds Meet delivers an experience that feels rich, meaningful, and consistently rewarding. Its pacing allows me to enjoy steady progress without needing long play periods.

Additionally, the Legend Mode deserves special praise. It is undeniably challenging—sometimes intensely difficult—but that difficulty makes every victory feel earned and incredibly satisfying. The mode’s design strikes a balance between toughness and enjoyment, making it one of the most exciting aspects of the game.

Where Winds Meet is a wuxia MMO-lite with Dark Souls-style action combat and open world exploration elements. One of its most interesting features is the Solo Mode, which allows you to play pretty much the entire game single-player, never really seeing other players (except for the messages they leave on the ground everywhere). I would recommend it to anyone looking for a new MMO to try, or a fun open-world wuxia game to experiment with.

The combat is fast, flowing, and feels good to master, and for those who don't want to grind out parry timings, there's a parry helper that you can toggle to make things a little more doable (it runs on a meter that builds when you attack enemies, so you can't just lean on it to auto-win fights).

Monetization is your typical MMO fare- cosmetic items available through direct purchase and gacha, as well as a battlepass, but there's also a fair amount of cosmetic items available through grinding or the completion of ingame secrets, so you won't be hurting for customization if you don't want to pay.

Overall, I've enjoyed my time with WWM, and while the content does seem a little thin for now (there's only a handful of map areas, and while they are VERY dense, I can see the game failing to hold up after 50 hours), I can't wait to see where the developers take this game.

Where Winds Meet is a free-to-play third person hack-n-slash. I'm having fun with it, but there is a lot about it that I don't understand.

Like many open world games, wandering around is some of the fun. It does have a story but I've barely played it 27 hours in. I think the point involves becoming a hero or fighting master, but that's open to interpretation.

WWM throws a lot at you. I haven't had issues with monetization, but it's not hard to miss either. Want cosmetics? This game has them. Want to rename your character? That can be purchased. Stuff like that.

So who should play this? Anyone who wants to! It's free! If you ever wanted to pretend to be an ancient Asian fight master, this game is for you. Want to fight world bosses? You can! Want to run into a dungeon to fight and find treasure? I've got good news! Want to have the ability to upgrade a weapon, unlock a different weapon, upgrade that weapon, upgrade your armor, upgrade your level, upgrade your hair, and maybe get a horse? It's in this game!

Sure, there are issues. It's complex. Some things don't make sense. There are player hints all over the world that are visually annoying. Can they be turned off? Probably. Somewhere there's a click box in a sub-menu in a setting screen I've yet to stumble across. In spite of how wonky this game can be, though, I'm having fun with it - and for that reason I recommend trying it out.

I’m really enjoying Where Winds Meet. The world feels relaxing to explore, the atmosphere is beautiful, and it’s the kind of game I’m happy to come back to after a long day. It’s not trying too hard. It’s just a lovely experience, and I’m glad I started playing it.

There is a lot of game here for free. And that's free, not "free". Everything you can spend real money on is cosmetic, there's zero pay-to-win here. 

Exploration of the open world is where this game absolutely shines. It's an absolute blast to just run around, picking stuff up, and doing random quests. There's almost always something to find or do, where ever you go. Game reminds me of Elden Ring in that regard, in that exploration is always rewarded. This is the main reason to play this game.

Combat and overall gameplay are solid. The different weapon types all feel unique enough, that switching between them is a noticeable change in style. The combat/gameplay are solid and polished to the point that they never detract from the gameplay.

Story and plot is where this game absolutely drops the ball. There are some good bits here and there, but it's marred by poor execution. More often than less often, the storyline for both the main quest and also side quests just jumps forward, like skipping over a chapter of a book and wondering what happened in it. Lastly, some lines are voiced, some aren't (ENG), and subtitles often don't match up with what's being said.
The game also does a lot of the "your character loses in a cutscene" thing. You can expect to be kidnapped/defeated in basically every cutscene-- it's a rule, rather than an exception. Fight a boss and win? Chances are it'll defeat you in the cutscene after. Fight some grunts? Good chance you'll get surrounded and kidnapped/imprisoned/beaten. For a Wuxia game, they really ignored the part where your character should be a badass. Where Winds Meet excels at portraying your character as a weakling, that usually has to run away.

Finally, WWM looks absolutely gorgeous, and plays smoothly. It's actually quite impressive just how well optimized this game is, in a time when nearly every game releases in a broken mess. Part of why the world is such a blast to explore, is because it's so damned beautiful.

I tried Lost Ark, Throne and Liberty, ESO and more. I stopped playing them for various reasons.  
Ex-Vanilla WoW player here that has all but given up on MMOs. Until now.


SOLO-MODE = Amazing 
CO-OP = Still Needs Work
SOCIAL = Best yet

Amazing game full of interesting interactions and lore. Whether it's randomly curing someone's broken head, or debating on their behalf to keep them out of jail because they became "falsely accused", the surprises never end. You can be anything you want to be in this world. Scholar, doctor, carpenter etc. Your main existence doesn't have to be "hero".

AI is used for translation, since it is in Chinese, and the world is so packed with lore that it is no wonder it still needs work.  
Combat is very souls-like. The solo mode allows you to adjust the difficulty and even have block prompts, but the lower difficulties don't sacrifice the creativity of combat, it just means it is a little slower so you have time to react to the prompts. It's still difficult. 

SOLO-PLAY (Reviewed)
- The solo play is out of this world. Literally, I forget reality. I keep getting side-tracked from the main mission by random environment and running off to explore. I find it fulfilling, and way better than multiplayer mode, since you are not entirely cut off from interactions with other players. 
- The approach to NPCs is refreshing and so many of them are memorable.
- The side-characters get main character treatment and exploration is massively rewarded.
- The right amount of social; you can theory-craft and share ideas in comment sections in your exploration journal as you uncover more of the lore. For me, this is the sweet-spot between solo play and too much social interactions happening. 
- Aesthetics are phenomenal. Animation, clothing, environment (The scenery <3) oh my.
- Lvl progression; I appreciate the cap and time-limit they put, since my main gripes with MMOS are all the overlvled p2w no-lifers that are there on literally day 1. It makes it near impossible to find people to lvl with or explore with. This is a much appreciated unique approach (at least for me). And I think it is healthier for the gamers too. 
- Skill acquisition and progression; most MMOs turn these into a soulless grind. Not here. If you like exploring you end up stumbling on most things you need in a decent enough pace. 
- Fast-travel; YES. The beauty, the grace, the bad-assery! but also, you can use waypoints and a horse. I like the options.
- Economy-locks and currency; constructed to prevent p2w and the majority of the aesthetics cannot be obtained by paying or buying in-game currency. Most are campaign and achievement based, some are even simple encounters, exploration and co-op activity based. 


CO-OP
- The chat interface can be set to exploration mode or social mode, which is great. 
- The bounties are impossible to get to on time. I don't know if it is because there are too many of a certain profession, or too few bounties. Either way, a bounty-cap per player might be a good idea. You need these for certain currency and physician/scholar skills.
- Teleporting to someone else's instance for a boss-fight or coop exploration puts you at the mercy of their latency. (haven't investigated the specifics of this, but it is worth mentioning I did allow cross-server match-ups in the options)
- The first time I joined a ferry ride my ears exploded with the voice-chat. Feedback has been sent. 
- The difficulty of boss-fights really does give dark souls a serious run for its money with the way it ramps up. 
- buggy teleportation; I have both accepted and sent requests that were accepted repeatedly, only to be randomly teleported some place else first, presumably this is caused by the leap from solo-mode to coop, and then to the player. Maybe.  But at least it puts you back when you reenter solo mode.
- Awesome multiplayer activities. This is great for me who finds it a drag to socialize for the sake of being social. This is extra incentive to seek out other players for things that don't directly involve campaigns or combat.
- you can become a disciple, a master and even get married to other players. This is awkward if your partner doesn't want to play but you really want the skin that comes with the interactions. -.-


There is a lot more, but this would be too long if I were to include everything. So, GO FORTH, AND FIGHT GEESE AND BEARS AND MONKS. You are not the main character. More like a fart in the middle of hurricane season.

Recommended (👍)

Hours Played: 40+ (approx.) Status: Early Access / Open Beta feel (Free-to-Play)

If you've ever wanted to play Elden Ring but with the movement of Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon and the cluttered UI of a mobile MMO, you are in the right place.

The Short Version: It is genuinely ambitious and surprisingly generous for a Free-to-Play title. The combat is the star of the show—fluid, complex, and flashy. The world is gorgeous and fun to traverse (you can literally run up walls and walk on water). However, the menus are a nightmare, and the game throws 100 tutorials at you in the first hour.

The Good

    Combat is King: This isn't a button masher. It feels like a mix of Sekiro and Naraka: Bladepoint. You have parries, dodges, martial arts skills, and weapon swapping. Pulling off a perfect parry and countering with a flashy Wuxia move feels incredible.

    Movement Freedom: You don't just ride a horse; you glide, wall-run, and sprint across water. Exploring the map is actually fun because moving feels so good.

    Visuals & Atmosphere: The 10th-century China setting is stunning. Fields of flowers, rainy villages, and bustling cities. It’s a screenshot factory.

    Monetization: Surprisingly fair. It’s F2P, but the cash shop is almost entirely cosmetics (skins, mounts). No pay-to-win walls have been found yet.

    Profession System: You can be a doctor, an architect, or an orator. It adds a weird but cool social layer to the game where you can actually heal other players or build structures.

The Bad

    UI/UX from Hell: The interface is cluttered with red dots, sub-menus, and mobile-style notifications. It takes time to learn where everything is.

    Notification Spam: The game constantly wants to tell you about a new event, a new currency, or a new reward. It breaks immersion.

The Ugly

    The "MMO" Identity Crisis: It doesn't know if it wants to be a single-player story RPG or an MMO. You’ll be deeply immersed in a cutscene, and then suddenly a generic "Kill 10 bandits" quest pops up, or you'll see xX_DragonSlayer_Xx bunny-hopping in the background.

Where Winds Meet is an amazing breath of fresh (eastern) air. 
If you're a fan of Age of Wushu-like games, Chinese atmosphere, kung-fu themed combat & a little absurdity, just like in movies e.g. Shaolin Soccer or Kung Pow, then you're in for a treat!
Pros:
* For a game with such graphics, it is pretty well optimized. Both me and my partner with a bit weaker PCs are shocked that we're only getting minor framerates in packed areas like Kaifeng 

* Amazing exploration, that feels rewarding whenever you find a new critter, challenge NPC for an archery contest or open another chest

* Stunning Visuals for bosses. Although there are no towering bosses like in Dark Souls (looking at you Tower Knight), the idea and scenery of most of the boss fights is very appealing. When you meet the final boss of the story in 1st Map, you'll know what I mean

* Build variety - not only you have a wide selection of weapons (I believe it's 7 or 8 weapons on western servers), some of these weapons have different fighting styles (For Tanks, for DoT dmg, for healing, tanking, for ranged dmg, etc.) Not only that, you also can select 4 out of many passive skills which can benefit your playstyle AND YOU CAN ALSO GET 8 MORE ACTIVE SKILLS (called Mystic Arts), which you can use in combat or during world exploration.

* The combat is very fluid and enjoyable. Similar to that of Sekiro but with way, way more variety. The controls might be a bit confusing at first, but once you get the hang of it, it'll feel very rewarding.

* Interesting COOP featues - when you join your friends world you can both benefit from the exploration. Your friend picked up a chest you haven't spotted? Well you're getting its' contents too!. You found a mantis that your friend has not yet gotten? Well, now he has it too!. The performance in combat seems pretty solid (there are some minor lags here & there but it's not game breaking even during coop boss fights)

* Now hear me out as this will definitely be controversial - Clever use of AI in the game. The game puts in some special NPCs that you can actually chat with & "befriend". It can lead to some whacky shenanigans. For example, an NPC said that he feels his village has been forgotten by Buddha. You can tell him you're Buddha in the flesh and you lay 1000 blessings upon his town. It is very silly but it allows you to be more interactive with the world, which for me is actually quite a clever feature to have.

* The game itself costs a reasonable price of 0 AND It's not P2W! Although there is a store with microtransactions, the developers stated they don't want to include any items that might benefit you in any other way than looking fab. But with that...

Mixed feelings (subjective to each person):
*...the prices on the store are horrendous. They've recently allowed a Boat Skin with an outfit that, if you're unlucky, costs around 40k$. It's just cosmetics though but if you want to glow-up your character, prepare your wallet. Keeping it as mixed as I know some people couldn't care less about skins, but I know it's a big let down for my partner.

*Time gating your level cap. Again - some people might hate it, some people might love it. Whenever you level to a specific Level e.g. 30, you reach a cap & you have to follow through a mechanic called "Breakthrough". Now this Breakthrough is time-gated. At first, it's not a big gap (it's around a day at lower levels) but with me being at Solo Level 6 (Char level 55), I have to wait 9 days till being able to Breakthrough and unlock a higher cap. 
I myself find this feature cool as it does not force you to sit through the game each & every day. And also you are not getting flooded with new mechanics on higher levels. But I know there are some hardcore gamers that would like to reach the max level within 3 days and this mechanic blocks them from doing so.

* World levels up with you. Remember those breakthroughs I mentioned? Whenever you do those, the enemies level up with you. So the bosses still stay challenging, the trash mobs are still just trash mobs and you don't have a possibility to massively outlevel and steamroll through open world bosses or substory bosses.

Cons:
*The Menus.... my God. The Menu has families of its' own. If you tried to draw a family tree of it, its' roots would reach the 5 Dynasties era. I myself (after 70 hours) still find myself looking through posts on Reddit with people who entered a menu I have not seen with my own eyes. It's definitely to packed & really counterintuitive to find things here.

*Localization - now, I am just a filthy westerner. I don't speak Chinese. But I'd still like to know what's being said in that language. Sadly... the translation of the game doesn't allow me to. And I'm not talking about minor mistakes like "a player LEAVED your world", but sometimes during the mainstory, the chosen worlds for translation seem a bit random and out of context. I heard rumours that the studio is looking for new people for the Localization Team in order to correct the english translation and I really hope it's true.
BTW don't bother with English dubbing... it's really mehh compared to the Chinese one. 

*The Wester servers are far behind in content compared to Chinese servers. Now I know the game was released for China a year earlier but I really hope that the 2 servers will eventually catch up with each other. I know that in the East, they already have at least 2 new weapon types (fist weapons and sabers) and I'm guessing the main story is far more developed already.

All in all, it is a very good game. And it being free, really doesn't cost you anything to try out.
Even with all the minuses and mixed opinions above, I still say that it's a very enjoyable game that you can try out with your friends!

A breathtaking wuxia world that completely won me over

Where Winds Meet has been a full dopamine booster for me. I started it out of curiosity and somehow ended up deep-diving into ancient China, wuxia history, and every bit of lore I could find. I haven’t been this obsessed with a game in a long time.

The visuals are unreal. The environments, the fabric movement, the lighting, the way the world breathes and reacts… it genuinely feels handcrafted. It might be the most beautiful game I’ve ever played.

The story surprised me in the best ways. Side quests actually matter and some of them hit harder than main quests in other RPGs. A couple of moments even made me cry. There were scenes I absolutely did not see coming, and the game threw me into emotional, strange, poetic situations that stayed with me.

Gameplay feels stylish and fluid. No pay-to-win elements at all. The gacha system is purely cosmetic and never affects progression, which I deeply appreciate.

If I had to point out a few flaws: the game is huge and the amount of menus, systems and icons felt overwhelming during my first two or three days. It’s a lot to process at once. But after playing a bit longer, everything slowly started to click and I’m already way more comfortable navigating everything. Some players might still find the overall structure a bit messy or unfocused, and there are occasional small visual glitches, like clipping or stiff dialogue animations. Nothing game-breaking, just moments that remind you the world is so big that not every corner is perfectly polished.

But honestly, none of these take away from how special the experience feels. Where Winds Meet blends martial arts fantasy, emotional storytelling and stunning world-building in a way that feels both calming and thrilling. It became my comfort game without me even realizing it.

Highly recommended if you want to disappear into a beautiful world for a while.
Very good

Where Winds Meet is one of those rare open-world action RPGs that immediately stands out not because it reinvents everything, but because it delivers its ideas with style, confidence, and a surprising amount of heart. Set in a beautifully realized late-Song–dynasty China, it blends wuxia fantasy with grounded historical flavor, creating a world that feels both mythical and lived-in.

World & Exploration – 10/10 Atmosphere

The environment is the star of the show. Mountains layered in mist, old temples clinging to cliffs, bustling villages, bamboo forests that sway in the wind—every area begs you to stop and take it in. The world feels handcrafted rather than procedurally stitched together.

Exploration is enriched by the wuxia movement system. Dashing across rooftops, running on water, leaping between treetops, or drifting mid-air with qi techniques gives traversal a fluid, cinematic feel. It’s the first game in a long time that made me go “I’m not fast traveling—walking is too much fun.”

Combat – Stylish, Fast, and Deep

Combat is very wuxia-focused: fast strikes, mid-air dodges, martial-arts counters, weapon stances, and flashy finishers. Every weapon class feels distinct, and your martial skills open the door for expressive playstyles. Battles are quick and elegant, more about precision and timing than raw damage trading.

Boss fights are a highlight—dramatic intros, unique mechanics, and arenas that fit their lore and personality.

Story & Quests – A Blend of History and Wuxia

The narrative leans heavily into political tension, wandering-swordsman themes, and moral choices. It’s not afraid to slow down for quieter moments—helping townsfolk, investigating rumors, mediating disputes.

Side quests often feel like short wuxia tales rather than simple errands. Some are funny, some tragic, some philosophical, and most have a twist that adds personality to the world.

Characters – Memorable and Human

The cast is varied: stubborn martial-arts masters, struggling villagers, eccentric hermits, loyal allies, treacherous nobles. Even minor NPCs have touches of detail that make them feel real. Voice acting (where available) is strong, and character animations during story scenes are expressive and cinematic.

RPG Systems – Flexible and Rewarding

The game encourages experimentation.

Skill trees let you mix wuxia abilities and weapon mastery.

Crafting is meaningful without being grindy.

Reputation systems influence how certain factions or towns treat you.

Choices often have consequences, even in side content.

Performance & Technical Notes

On a good setup, the game looks stunning and runs smoothly, though it’s clearly pushing a lot of detail. Expect some occasional pop-in or animation quirks, but nothing game-breaking. Optimization feels solid and patches seem frequent.

Overall

Where Winds Meet is a love letter to wuxia adventures—beautifully atmospheric, mechanically satisfying, and rich with personality. If you enjoy games like Ghost of Tsushima, Sekiro, or classic wuxia films, this scratches that same itch while carving out its own identity.

Pros:
✔ Gorgeous world design
✔ Fluid wuxia movement and combat
✔ Strong atmosphere and storytelling
✔ Memorable side quests
✔ Great sense of adventure and discovery

Cons:
✘ Occasional visual/animation quirks
✘ Some early pacing stumbles depending on your exploration style

Verdict:
If you want a martial-arts open world that feels alive, expressive, and genuinely fun to explore, Where Winds Meet is absolutely worth your time.

Not an offline game. Requires internet connection to play.

There is a Solo mode and 2 online modes available, where you can play with up to 5 friends anyone's world or mmo style server populated by players doing activities together. 

Story rich Gacha Solo/MMO like game. Exploration similar to games like Genshin, Wuthering Waves, where there are different regions and a lot of mini games / puzzles available both in solo and co-op mode. Beware however there are limitations as to what you can do in CO-OP mode. Certain quests cannot be played together like mini cave dungeon unlocks, certain side quests. For the Online mode, you cannot do oddities collection as it limits you to mostly doing activites like sumo wrestling, going around killing mobs to grind materials and stuff. Recommend looking up what can you do in SOLO/CO-OP/online modes to make sure you dont miss out on things.
*CO-OP* If you are playing with a friend in another region, EXPECT HEAVY PING ISSUES. ASIA to EU has like a second ish delay for everything. Jumping, attacking and dont bother parrying unless you know the enemy's moveset so you can predict parry like you are playing in the future. HOPE THIS GETS FIXED ASAP.

Combat wise its fluid ish. 2 active set of weapons to use from, ranging from swords to polearms, to fans, umbrella and dual blades, with some of them having a healer varient of it. Blocking reduces incoming damage, dodge in SOLO mode grants you a slow time effect and parrying allows you to nullifiy damage. Sometimes the parrying window is jank like fighting Lord dao? This red attack feels inconsistent to parry.

Exploration is fun. You can run around, ride a horse or even use skills to traverse the world. Every corner as a story. Talk to Npcs, read documents or books lying around for local lore, puzzles every where so won't feel empty in its lush environment.

Gacha elements are like ONCE HUMAN (same publisher btw). Skins and more skins and more skins! with guaranted pity at 150 rolls. Now thats really expensive when you arent a whale. Pure barbie simulator with those fancy pretty chinese clothings and stuff. Nothing that makes you more powerful except the fancy drip you can flex on poor and unlucky people.

Voice over wise, its typical with chinese games, where what they say and what the subtitles show doesn't match. and the timing for it is jank. [h1]IT'S REALLY GOOD[/h1]
[h3]Note: This review is my honest opinion, based on what I experienced so far[/h3]

First of all, I have to say that this game really really exceeded my expectations! An online game at that! It's really game first, transactions later, meaning they don't shove those stuff down our throats. I've also been soloing so far, so I have yet to have any reviews for multiplayer and CO-OP mode.

[h2]THE GAME ITSELF[/h2]
I was also really surprised to how good the story of the game is, note that it ISN'T the greatest or a really good story but knowing it's an online game with micro-transactions, it's still has a good story. Plus, not many online games have that. Combat, traversal, world, visuals, are all amazing. I really enjoyed it. Though there a few experiences that I would love for this game to have and improve, like walking with controllers without having to toggle, AND I'M SURE THEY CAN DO MORE WITH THE OUTRAGEOUS UI. I know it's a lot of stuff but please, I know this game can do better on managing it. While it's not hard for me as a seasonal gamer to understand, but I know for sure newcomers will 100% get overwhelmed and they might just stop playing because of this.

[h2]USAGE OF AI IN THE GAME[/h2]
Although I don't know if they use any form of generative AI in the game as in art made by AI. The usage of AI in this game is still really smart, whether it's the character customization or the NPC within the game. I really enjoyed talking, making my own scenarios to befriend every NPC I met. 

[h3]FINAL WORDS[/h3]
Love it, hate it, I don't care. But give this game a go and decide yourself whether this game is worth your time or not. It sure is worth it for me :D

​🤯 Where Winds Meet - A Groundbreaking Wuxia Masterpiece (AND IT'S FREE!)
​Verdict: HIGHLY RECOMMENDED
​I cannot believe a game of this quality, with this level of content and polish, is FREE TO PLAY. If you’re a fan of immersive open-world action-RPGs, you have absolutely nothing to lose by downloading this right now.
​🌟 What Makes It a Must-Play:
​Breathtaking Wuxia Combat: The fighting is fluid, incredibly fast, and captures the impossible grace and power of martial arts masters. Mastering parries and combos is a thrilling and rewarding core loop.
​Unmatched Player Freedom: Beyond the main quest, the level of player freedom is astounding. I loved being able to take on non-combat roles like a Doctor, Architect, or Merchant. The game rewards exploration and allows you to truly live in the Song Dynasty.
​A World That Breathes: The visuals are stunning, and the world feels historically rich and massive. This is a gorgeous sandbox to get lost in for hundreds of hours.
​I even came to appreciate the time gates. They wisely encourage slowing down, preventing burnout, and truly committing to the vastness of the world, enhancing the long-term journey!
​💰 F2P Done Right: No Pay-to-Win!
​Crucially, this is a very fair F2P model. The developers promise and deliver on the motto: "Your legend is written by skill and choice, never by wallet size." Monetization focuses almost entirely on cosmetics, a battle pass, and optional subscriptions, meaning you can experience the entire epic 150+ hour story and all the gameplay without spending a penny.
​📝 A Quick Note
​The interface can be a little overwhelming at first due to the sheer amount of systems, but this minor complexity is a small price to pay for the incredible depth the game offers.
​Conclusion: This is an ambitious game that absolutely delivers an amazing, unforgettable experience. Where Winds Meet is a triumph of combat, freedom, and world-building, and the fact that it's free makes it an instant classic. Download it now!

Btw, don't waste your golden pulls unless you know you're getting something good because pity doesn't carry over the banners that use them.

2 rly stupid things tho.
First is that there's this stamina system that is consumed everytime you do an outpost or boss for gear, so there's only so many times you can farm for gear in a week and there's a limit of how much you can store it up. That's one way they make you play every so often.
Second is that at the earlier lvls you gotta get these daily check ins to be able to unlock the earlier lvl caps. Later you just need to do like 2 combat challenges per lvl cap. And as of the current update everyone is locked at lvl 55 until they unlock the next 2 challenges. People say its not that much of a problem because you start storing exp once you hit a cap, but honestly idk how good stored exp rly helps because I always felt like I got more from doing stuff at my lvl.

But yeah, overall for a free game its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy how much you can do in it. It might be a turn off if you don't like collecting stuff in a big open world map or if you don't rly like how wack the localization is, but its honestly worth a shot just for its combat and bosses and maybe pvp for some people.

[h1]Gameplay Highlights & Initial Thoughts[h1]

I've sunk about three hours into Where Winds Meet and honestly, the game is already overwhelming me—in mostly a good way. The sheer volume of content and the beauty of the world are its biggest immediate strengths, but be prepared for a rocky start, especially around the user interface.

[h2]The Good:[h2]

[h3]Breathtaking Graphics:[h3] Right from the jump, the visual fidelity is gorgeous. The Wuxia world is vibrant, the lighting is excellent, and the character animations during combat are stunning. This is a genuinely beautiful game that begs to be explored.

[h3]Pretty Good Mechanics & Combat:[h3] The actual combat feels fluid and responsive. The martial arts style, parrying, and weapon swapping mechanics are the bread and butter of this game, and they are solid. It feels like a high-octane blend of action RPGs, and I’m looking forward to mastering the different weapon styles.

[h3]So Much Exploration (and Freedom):[h3] The open world is vast, and the sheer number of activities available is staggering. Whether it’s flying across rooftops with your lightness skills or simply running through the detailed landscapes, the sense of exploration is huge. I barely scratched the main story because I kept getting distracted by secrets and side activities.

[h2]The Bad:[h2]

[h3]Clunky/Unintuitive UI: [h3]This is my biggest complaint so far. The menus are an absolute nightmare. There are menus inside of menus, multiple currencies, and red dots everywhere, often leading nowhere. The game dumps far too many systems on you in the first hour with little explanation. It makes managing your inventory and skills feel like a chore.

[h3]The Card Mechanics (Gift of Gab): [h3]While I appreciate the attempt at unique dialogue or debate minigames, the card system tied to the "Gift of Gab" is confusing and breaks the immersion. It feels completely separate from the rest of the game's mechanics and I actively dread running into these encounters. I wish the game relied on its excellent combat or dialogue choices instead.

[h2]Final Verdict[h2]

[b]Where Winds Meet is a massive, ambitious title that provides an incredible amount of gameplay, especially for a free-to-play title. It successfully captures the feeling of being a Wuxia hero. If you can push past the horrible UI/menu systems and ignore the confusing card mechanics, you will find a beautifully rendered world with satisfying combat that offers so much to do.[b]

[h2]Recommend to:[h2] Fans of open-world martial arts games who are patient with complex systems and menu navigation.
[h3]Avoid if:[h3] You demand polished UI/UX or hate having dozens of progression systems thrown at you instantly.

Recommended, but with caution

Where Winds Meet surprised me in the best way. The game looks and plays like a full triple A title and it is honestly hard to believe it is basically free to play. The world is stunning, the combat feels great, the character creator is outstanding and there is a huge amount of exploration and side content.

Let me point out the big things though.

First, it is not pay to win. The shop is cosmetics only. The problem is the gacha. The rates are terrible and it feels like a very old school mobile system. Some costumes have fixed prices, which is fine, but the random pulls are rough.

Second, the game throws a ton of menus, systems and features at you at the beginning. It feels overwhelming to the point of confusion. The good part is that once you get used to it, everything becomes easy to navigate. The onboarding could be much better, but you do get over that hurdle.

Now for the biggest issue I have. The leveling gatekeeping is awful. At the time of writing, I have to wait six more days to go from 55 to 60. I do not understand the logic behind this. You keep earning XP anyway, so when the gate is lifted you blast through the next levels in about twenty minutes. It makes the gate pointless. During this forced downtime I fully cleared almost the entire first zone. 98 % of all quests, exploration and objectives done. That is when it hit me. At this pace I will probably clear most of the game before I even reach max level.

After that, all that is left is a short list of activities. Five bosses per zone - Qinghe and Kaifeng, one trial, a pseudo battleground and one arena. PVP is terrible. It is a stunlock fiesta. It could have been fun, but right now it is just frustrating, although I still play it for the rewards.

I already maxed out my mastery at this level, reached almost thirteen thousand power, started collecting books for inner ways and I can already see the long term loop forming. If you remove the mini games, the game becomes three repeating activities. Farm the same bosses, farm the same arena, farm the same outpost. That is basically it.

After checking the CN version I am honestly not sure how long the game will stay alive in the West. It feels like the time gating was brought over for retention, not for any creative reason. I expected proper dungeons and raids, not just straight boss fights. The game needs engaging endgame content, not repetitive farming.

Overall I am still satisfied and I enjoy my time with it. The world and the presentation are that good. But unless the endgame improves, I worry the game will fade as fast as it appeared.

Edit: My first thoughts seem spot on when looking back at them. Despite putting many more hours into the game it still feels lost in what it's trying to do. 
Story- Very hit or miss, some quests feel like chores and others are a dream to play through. Majority of them lately, feel like you need a guide to understand what's going on or how events are tied into each other. This is primarily a problem in the second region though.
Combat- I compare this most to Wo Long, it's close enough mechanically but lacks some of the feedback I experienced from that game. 
Map- Expansive and nice to look at not as much going on though. There's plenty of things to roam and around and complete and while some are nice a lit of it feels shallow. If you've ever played AC: Valhalla you'd understand the complaint that there's too much going on.
Mechanics/U.I.- Again, very busy. Hard to remember every single piece of the games mechanics or layouts. 
Social- Depends on your connection, could be good could be bad. PVP feels reliant on ping, group content is fun but you run out of energy (time gate) so it's not something that can be done all day. GvG can be fun as well...again depends on the connection at the time.

There's a lot to talk about in this game and most of all it's easy to tailor to the type of experience of your choice. If you only want to play a single player action adventure game you can do that. If you want a wuxia social sim you can do that. If you want a melee battle royal game you can do that. Because this game wanted to meet all of these needs well it doesn't hit any of them great. Very few people can enjoy all aspects of the game, 
Picking and choosing what you engage with is great but I personally feel like so much of the content is a "so what" engagement farm.  So far I've gone from exploring one game mode as much as possible before moving on to another. This has extended the longevity of the game for, but much of the content is becoming a chore not an experience for me. For this reason I don't recommend the game to most players because there is most certainly a game that does the aspects you may be interested in better. It is free though...but also gacha.

Where Winds Meet (WWM) is groundbreaking. It has singlehandedly brought about a reimagining of the MMO/ Open World RPG/ Action RPG genre AND Freemium business model. Allow me to elaborate:

What the PROS? 
- WWM is a FULL FEATURE game at the grand price of $0. In fact, you will be overwhelmed by the content available to you. The ONLY thing you pay for is cosmetics and some in-game currency that may save you time. You are free to ignore it and grind it out on your own. Frankly, I like the way that WHALES, big spenders, subsidize the games for others .
- The Graphics are top notch, well-optimized and holds its own in 2025. 
- The combat is smooth, rewarding and accommodates different play styles. Tank, DPS, Healer; Burst DPS, DOTS, Ranged, Melee
- The open world is vast and fun to explore. It is loaded with mini-games which are fun and varied. 
- Leveling and progression is even and rewarding. It leaves you with the feeling of always wanting to improve, seeking out new weapons styles, passive boosts and enhancements. 

So what's GROUNDBREAKING? 
- WWM is genre defining. It is Skyrim, Guild Wars 2, Diablo, FF 14 and other games mashed together. 
- NPCs are brought to life with AI Chat, breathing in personality and real conversation into NPC engagement. 
- There is an in-game translator that enables you to translate hints and advice left to you by other players in Chinese, Spanish, Polish, Russian and French! 
- The toggle between Solo and Co-Op mode isn't just a gimmick, they are full game modes you lean into for hours at a time and for full progression. 


What are the CONS? 
- When we say cosmetics cost a premium, we mean it. The cosmetics are the MOST EXPENSIVE of any game I've played. Regular mounts and outfits can cost $500. The infamous mirage boat costs $40,000. None of it is evident upfront and they lure you into it by raising the price for each random chance at a currency like Harmonic Cores.

- The English voice acting is atrocious, to the point of immersion breaking. I recommend switching audio to Mandarin as soon as you are allowed to and read in English Subtitles. 

- Matchmaking for things like Bounty Hunting and Healing need to be improved. 

- Certain tooltips for game modes are baffling and not well explained.

Finally, I understand there is a lot of negative sentiment regarding Netease. However, I would urge you to judge WWM on its on merits alone. Perhaps Netease has run bad business models in other games. However, I have not encountered it in WWM.

Alright, I’m done with this game. The limitations on absolutely everything are just too much.

Progression makes no sense. Enhancing and tuning gear costs over 1,000,000, yet after a new breakthrough my stats are actually worse than before. Regular mobs now take forever to kill, which completely undermines any sense of advancement.

I’ve already completed most quests, looted nearly every chest, and even resorted to stealing the few money bags available. And still, there’s no meaningful way to progress. I genuinely don’t understand how this system is supposed to work.

Co-op has almost nothing to offer. There are very few co-op quests, and multiplayer provides no real enjoyment beyond whales showing off expensive cosmetics and a handful of unfun mini-games.

Farming and gathering are among the most boring systems I’ve ever experienced. The game clearly wants you to log in for about 20 minutes a day, hit your caps, and then wait until tomorrow. After that, there’s simply nothing to do.

The battle pass offers virtually no value, the menus are a nightmare to navigate, and the targeting system is atrocious. Blocking and parrying feel clunky, inconsistent, and completely unrewarding. Any genuinely good content is locked behind progression walls or systems designed purely to slow you down.

The only part of the game I actually enjoyed was the 5-man and 10-man content—but even that is heavily restricted. You can only earn loot every couple of days due to the painfully slow energy regeneration.

The story is dull, and nearly all content is locked, capped, or time-gated in every way possible. Now I understand why the game is free. I’m just glad I didn’t fall into the spending trap some players do. I bought the battle pass, and it honestly felt like it gave me nothing in return.

Yes, there’s no pay-to-win, and I respect that—but there’s also no real way to play to win either, which kills any motivation for me.

And finally, the menus… honestly unbearable. Spending 30 minutes every few hours digging through layers of menus just to “claim” meaningless rewards is not fun.

I’m moving on.

TL:DR; It's a F2P game with combat similar to the modern action games you're used to, such as Black Myth: Wukong. The monetization is 90% for cosmetics and the rest for small bonuses like the Battle Pass. It has a stunning amount of content to do, and on Legend difficulty can even present itself a brutal challenge at times. Solo play is relatively smooth, but expect high latency for any online gameplay.

The first thing that needs mentioning is the amount of content in this game. Besides core gameplay elements like combat and story, there's over a dozen minigames to distract you from regular combat gameplay, ranging from Chess (with a twist), debating NPCs, turn-based combat (spiritual healing), drunken arrow tossing, mahjong, 20 questions with an AI (yes, really), playing music etc, etc. It's got alot to do, and it all leads to rewards that benefit your overall progression and experience. These small events are scattered throughout the world and will help pace out the feeling of constant grinding.

The combat is similar to Black Myth: Wukong, in that it's an action soulslike style with skills on cooldowns. There's a variety of skills to unlock and upgrade, including skills used outside of combat to solve puzzles aswell. Bosses, especially on Legend difficulty, present a significant challenge in the genre, so there's been little disappointment there. Alot of mob fights can be very messy, but with the right tools aren't that oppressive to deal with. There is also a basic stealth system for back-stabbing unaware enemies too. So long as you're playing Solo with no latency, the combat is pretty clean and fluid, with boss fights being the natural highlight. Online play has been a mixed experience, as latency in an action game with parries and reaction timings becomes alot harder, but with help...also easier? Since it's not mandatory I don't consider it a big deal.

The monetization in this game is pretty unreal, and it does concern me for the future of this game. I really want it to succeed and make more and more content for the future, but I'm worried that cosmetics being the main driving force for profits (besides small things like battle passes) the game won't make the kind of cash something like Genshin Impact 'waifu' type games do, but I'm hopeful since this is the kind of customer-favored model I want to see work.

There is definitely use of 'AI' tech in this game. I feel fairly certain the voice acting is all done by AI, but it's not atrocious, and for an Eastern made game it doesn't really bother me. some NPCS can be spoken to like real people, and after building up friendship from chatting can even give you gifts. There is also 1 minigame that's basically '20 questions' where you need to try and guess the word. These small uses of new AI innovations is the kind of thing that really enhances player experiences, and I'm all in favor of it. It can only get better from here.

The overall experience has been great and I'm still playing the game constantly, which is a good sign in general. It's pretty mind-blowing to have all of this content, effort and development end up becoming a F2P experience. The future is bright for gaming, so long as it's coming from the East.

Where Winds Meet is an absolute blast. From the moment I stepped into its beautifully crafted world, I knew I was in for something special. The graphics are downright stunning—lush landscapes, intricate architecture, and gorgeous lighting that make just wandering around feel like its own reward.

The sword-fighting gameplay is seriously awesome. It’s fast, flashy, and packed with style, but still requires enough timing and strategy to stay engaging. It hits that sweet spot between accessible and skill-based in a way that kept me wanting just one more duel… then another… then ten more.

The story is surprisingly good too, with interesting characters and a sense of mystery that kept pulling me forward. Between major story beats, there are plenty of fun puzzles woven into the world—nothing too punishing, but clever enough to make exploration feel meaningful.

Honestly, the game feels like a wild and wonderful mix of Elden Ring, Assassin’s Creed, and a dash of classic wuxia adventures. Open-world exploration, stylish parkour, tough-but-fair combat, cinematic storytelling—you can feel the inspirations, but the game still manages to carve out its own identity.

If you’re looking for an immersive world to lose yourself in with great gameplay and tons of style, Where Winds Meet is absolutely worth your time. I had a fantastic experience with it.

The time gate criticism isn't that valid. Even if you spend more hours than me it is unlikely you have finished all the content. There are too many events and the open world is very big. It's not a game you can play for 1 week to get the "full experience", it's a game you're supposed to stick with regularly or casually over a long time

it is a mobile game similar to genshin impact but with some better quality of life improvements. The player base seems to be an older, more mature audience than genshin, kind of non toxic. Probably the average age is around 21-30, whereas similar mobile gacha style cartoon style games may have younger averages.

Most content is optional like PvP or all the events so it's more relaxing than a traditional mobile game where you might feel pressure to do everything and log in every day or week. There are optional "dailies" but the rewards are basically nothing. So playing very casually like once a week or so, you wouldn't really miss much. What i like is that it doesn't force you to play PvP or be competitive or do all the quests or events - you can play at your own pace and choose what you want or not want to do without feeling left behind at all

The core "content" are the boss fights, exploration, PvP, story, online raids. The social content is primarily around guilds and there are many active ones, both competitive and casual. There is a lot of focus on the cosmetics and many people do seem to spend a bit of money. But no money is really needed to get the strongest character in PvE or PvP, as money is only really for appearances (the gacha system is expensive)

★★★★★ A Masterpiece of Freedom and Fury

Where Winds Meet is not just a game; it's an invitation to live out your most cherished Wuxia fantasies. From the moment you step into its breathtaking rendition of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era, it’s clear this is a landmark title that understands the soul of the genre. It is an ambitious, beautiful, and deeply immersive experience that stands tall among the giants of action RPGs.

An Unforgettable, Living World

The first thing that will strike you is the game's stunning artistry. The Wuxia setting is profoundly immersive, built with an incredible attention to detail that makes the world feel both ancient and alive. From mist-shrouded mountain peaks to bustling ancient cities, the world design is gorgeous. This is enhanced by a poetic art direction where every element—from the architecture to the flowing garments of your character—contributes to a seamless, moving painting. The atmosphere is so potent that you can almost feel the breeze and hear the whispers of the jianghu. The story matches this quality, weaving a tale of destiny, brotherhood, and sacrifice that is genuinely immersive and, at times, tear-jerking.

Combat That Rivals the Best

Let's be clear: the combat in Where Winds Meet is a top-tier system that confidently earns its place in conversations alongside titans like Sekiro, Elden Ring, and Black Myth: Wukong. It’s fast, fluid, and demands skill, offering a satisfying clash of steel and qi. But where it truly shines is in its huge build diversity. The game doesn't force you into a single style. You are free to master and mix techniques from different martial arts schools, finding and refining your favorite weapon and armor combo to create a truly unique warrior. This customization extends to the beautifully designed bosses, who are not only visually spectacular but also provide thrilling, strategic challenges. Impressively, even many side quests feature their own unique boss encounters, making exploration constantly rewarding.

A Revolution in Player Choice and Multiplayer

One of the game's most brilliant design decisions is its approach to multiplayer. By offering separate single-player and multiplayer worlds, it solves the biggest problem of balance that plagues games like Black Desert Online. You can enjoy a perfectly curated, narrative-driven experience without worrying about PvP metas, or you can jump into a shared world for co-op adventures. This freedom is foundational to the game's philosophy. There are so many different activities to take part in, solo or co-op, allowing you to play as you like. Whether you want to be a righteous healer aiding allies, a shadowy thief mastering stealth, or a simple merchant, your path is valid and richly developed.

Flawless Execution

All this ambition would be for nothing without solid technical performance, and Where Winds Meet delivers. On a capable PC, the experience is silky smooth, with great game performance and no stuttering to break the immersion. The beautiful graphics are allowed to shine at their full potential, making every moment a screenshot-worthy masterpiece.

The Verdict

Where Winds Meet is a triumphant achievement. It masterfully blends a poignant, immersive narrative with world-class combat and an unprecedented level of player freedom, all wrapped in a technically flawless and visually stunning package. It respects your time, your choices, and your desire to craft a personal Wuxia legend. This isn't just a great game; it's an essential play for any fan of open-world RPGs and martial arts epics.

So I went into this hoping to go through the campaign and then calling it a day. The first part of the game has some pretty cool things going on, but holy crap is it overwhelming! Upgrade this, upgrade that, enhance this, enhance that, learn this, learn that, all in like the first 30 seconds. I'm over 18 hours in now and I'm still probably missing about 80% of what I could be doing because there's just way too much going on.

The map has an insane amount of things to do as well. You'll be exploring and there's some fairy looking things you can follow, and while you're following it there'll just be a sick dude you can heal, and then you'll come across a quest giver accidentally, and while you're trying to go talk to that quest giver, another quest giver will appear. There's definitely always something to do, but it really just beats it into you.

Every once in a while though, you'll come across an actual quest. A mini puzzle that opens a path to a mysterious cave with with a satisfying conclusion. A mountain top with an abundance of enemies with a hidden passage that leads to an epic boss fight. These moments so far are a little bit far apart, but they are worth it. The boss fights are actually really really cool, and very well designed considering how much other crazy stuff this game has going on to still be able to have quality boss fights.

After the first major story boss fight, the quality of the main story seems to go down hill. Lots of repeating dialogue (like literally, it will repeat itself a few times in one cutscene), conversations with missing voice lines, buggy interactions with objects and NPC's, it's kind of a hot mess, but It's a free to play hot mess with some cool mechanics, tons of exploration, microtransactions that I haven't felt were pushed a single time, but one of the most horrible UI's ever imagined. Do yourself a favor and if you play this game with a controller, use a mouse and keyboard at least when navigating the menu!

TL;DR - Good free to play time sink, look up a guide on how to do things because there is way too much.

A sweeping Wuxia epic carried by wind, steel, and unforgettable atmosphere

Where Winds Meet is a stunningly realized Wuxia open-world action-adventure RPG set in 10th-century China, and it delivers almost everything fans of the genre could hope for. You step into the role of a young sword master searching for the truth behind their mysterious past—an excellent narrative hook that steadily deepens as you explore its vast, beautifully crafted world.

World & Atmosphere

The moment you enter its landscape of bamboo forests, mist-wrapped mountains, and bustling Song Dynasty towns, it’s clear how much attention has gone into worldbuilding. The game captures the heart of classic Wuxia cinema—every rooftop feels like an invitation to run across it, every cliff edge like a place to take flight. Dynamic weather, fluid traversal, and stylized combat all work together to make exploration feel alive.

Combat & Gameplay

Combat is fast, elegant, and expressive. Sword techniques feel weighty yet graceful, with a wide range of martial arts abilities that encourage experimentation. Whether you prefer counterattacks, acrobatics, stealth approaches, or open duels, the game adapts well to different playstyles. Boss encounters are memorable and often cinematic, offering a satisfying balance of challenge and flair.

Story & Characters

The narrative is strongest when it leans into personal identity, moral choices, and classic Wuxia themes of honor and destiny. Side characters, even minor ones, often feel grounded in the setting rather than filler. Choices throughout the journey allow you to shape your legend in meaningful ways.

Performance & Polish

Though the game is ambitious, performance is generally solid. Some minor bugs and occasional pacing dips prevent it from feeling perfect, but none of these issues overshadow the experience.

Final Verdict

Where Winds Meet is a beautifully crafted Wuxia adventure that succeeds in capturing the magic, mystique, and emotional weight of the genre. With its engaging story, fluid combat, and spectacular world, it stands out as one of the most atmospheric open-world RPGs in recent years.

Final Rating: 9/10 — Let the wind carry your legend.

Expect to be ripped away from the main story like you are playing skyrim. Talk to NPCs via an AI chat bot that is truly immersive if you actually rp it. This game almost feels like a wuxia simulator sometimes. A f2p has no business being this good. The bosses are frankly approaching elden ring level of quality and the world is believable and a love letter to wuxia. 

Inevitably you will enjoy the game more if you are into wuxia and/or anime. Eastern philosophy and mindset are woven directly into the game and without respect for those things, some of it may fall flat. Spamming to skip the story with these requirements met will rob you from some really heart jerking moments.

Gameplay wise, think elden ring meets red dead/gta online, meets a gacha game.. kind of? The thing is that ALL of the gacha is for cosmetics. There is close to NO p2w beyond a battle pass which barely gives an advantage and in itself is mostly cosmetic.

I HIGHLY recommend this game.

This game has very very many pros to it. Its amazing from a million different perspectives. Fun movement, Amazing graphics, forgiving combat in singleplayer and a ton of interesting mechanics never done in a video game before. 

So why am I giving it a bad review?

Primarily because literally EVERYTHING has a WEEKLY LIMIT which bars you from making ANY significant progress on anything in one time. If you have a day off from work, rest assured you will NOT be using that time to grind out that outfit piece you've been wanting. 

To put this into perspective for you:

The bounty system gives you 1000 "fourfold acclaim" for killing a player. You are capped at 1400 a week. You can kill one and a half players through the bounty system before it becomes entirely pointless to do so. And thats not all. If you want one of the only four capes in the game, albiet an ugly brown color, you first need to accumulate 50,000 Fourfold Acclaim to buy it. Yes, you read that right. Fifty Thousand. That means in order to get a brown cape in this game, you need to play the game consistently for a mandatory minimum of EIGHT MONTHS. EIGHT MONTHS IT TAKES TO GET A CAPE.

This is insane. Most of the gameplay is fine if not for the fact you are only allowed to enjoy it at a snails pace, lest you be forced to afk and stare at the wall while you wait for your limits to reset. Its only wednesday and i've hit all the limits. I guess you guys don't want people to play your game?

Beyond that, theres actually a decent amount wrong with the game. The bounty system is broken as hell. It shows you how powerful the player is before you take a bounty on them, which means you will NEVER be invaded by somebody you can just win against. Nobody is going to take a bounty against somebody significantly higher than them. Bounties can be taken no matter what you are doing and will stop you from doing anything in both online and solo mode. I was locked into an emote for a sect mission and i got raided and the guy took a golden opportunity to get a free bounty and killed me while i couldn't fight back. And if you do fight back and kill them, they can literally just jump into some water, teleport away, and then teleport back to you and get all their health back. Me personally, i have avoided the last 10 bounties on my head by building a box in the mud that easily wins against any bounty hunter.

Most of the weapons feel like they are missing something. Only a few of them have heavy attacks. The Dual swords which are supposed to be the assassin weapon dont feel like an assassin weapon, all you do is left click. Theres no heavy attack, the heavy attack was replaced with... a self buff? Pros:

-Story is what Wuxia fans dream of (without the bs secret mentor hiding in the mountains or underground, or their martial will or soul hiding in an accessory, or their fiancé dumping mc for a low tier villain, or something else mainstream)

Cons:
-Like many new games now, they require admin access.
-Like many F2P games, they want microtransactions. (not mandatory but if you wanna look the part, yk what to do -$$$)
-Gacha. (you gacha people have lost your minds, but thats your problem in a few years)
-It is not optimized for low end PCs, I get frequent lag spikes when using attacks or getting attacked. 
-Many (if not all) dialogues are working. Some characters speak, many do not. I feel like they should, considering how many of their voices just cut off mid sentence.

IDK's (stuff thats just odd for me, in other words its just my nitpicks):
-Friendship system for NPCs (they use an AI to generate responses but they are mostly preset, so it isn't really a literal conversation, just telling the npc what it wants. I would know, I have already got 50+ NPCs at 'Revered")
-Matchmaking. Its definitely an issue if you are getting a ping over 300 when doing some stuff like Joint Battle or PvP. Input lag is a big problem for many. But strangely enough online mode is working fine with no input lag at all.
-Localization. The english VAs are amazing, not dogging them at all here. I'm only saying that the locations are being properly said by them, just the subtitles are just basically translated. No scrub work to match what they say at all.
-Signposts. Try finger but whole. I swore that joke died, but here we are lmao.

tldr: Game is good. Game is meh. Game needs more polishing work. Wo Cao!

A pretty solid soulslike MMO overall.
Combat feels great, weighty and satisfying, though it can feel a bit stiff or clunky here and there. Bosses are varied, with interesting movesets that keep fights engaging.
Exploration is genuinely fun, and the more movement tools you unlock, the better it gets. Once everything opens up, traversing the map starts to feel really smooth.
One standout feature are the NPCs. They’re AI-driven chatbots, and as long as you don’t go out of your way to break them (which is admittedly easy), they add a surprising amount of immersion. The main story and side quests are solid and often very cinematic.
I haven’t done a ton of co-op yet, but the dungeons and bosses I did try were well designed. Just be prepared for the usual MMO chaos...there will always be players who ignore mechanics or prompts. x]
The social aspect is excellent. There aren’t many minigames, but the ones available are varied enough, and the emotes/interactions are extremely expressive, which is very typical of Chinese MMORPGs, and sometimes pretty bold.
If you don't care about cosmetics you might as well ignore what I'm gonna say next. One downside, which could be the main reason why some people won't bother with this game, is that the outfits are quite expensive and the game has a costume gacha. Whilst you do get some pulls here and there you will need to hold onto them for a long time in order to guarantee you get what you want. There is a list you can find on the internet with the order these are going to be released in so you can check if you fancy some of them.
If you plan to jump in, I’d recommend taking it slow early on.
Leveling is staggered during the first few days, so pacing yourself makes the experience smoother.
