I'll probably end up rambling, so let me start this review by saying WWM is a solid 8-9/10 game.

When I first got into WWM, the initial introduction is very jam-packed and seems like it's just another f2p gacha game with little else going for it. However, that couldn't be any further from the truth.

WWM has an incredibly vibrant and fun to explore world. There's a bit of dialogue issues, being translated from Chinese to English, but the story is still easily followable and digestible on your first pass. The reward for going and exploring random parts of the world isn't met with disappointing barren wastelands that we've come to see from other AAA companies (Not insinuating that this is a AAA company, just making the comparison), and is instead met with handcrafted areas with depth to them. Every location has a story, even if just small, for you to uncover and explore. Sometimes this will be through items you'll find in the area, or it can be from eavesdropping on NPC's conversations, or even just from talking to them outright. So much TLC was put into making the world feel real and alive.

If you're looking for a fun solo/friend game to play through with plenty of content for you to sink your teeth into, this is 100% worth a try. To list just a *few* of the things you're able to do--

- Fully interact with the world, close to a BG3 level, but it's just scaled bigger. No building destruction, obviously, but you are able to steal, murder, lie, cheat, whatever you can think of. Your playthrough is fully unique to you.
- Interact with NPC's (Powered by AI, but limited enough to basically just be chat bots ((No mecha H, nor gooner bs.)) with stories/personalities) and progress a relationship with them. Having real rewards as well, such as merchants preferring you.
- Standard 3 main roles (Tank, DPS, Heal) while being able to multi-class into them anyway you want.
- "Jobs" that you're able to progress as well, such as a true healer (Doctor), or a Scholar.
- 8 different weapons to choose from, and able to mix/match them freely.
- Plenty of side quests/stories that are fully replayable.
- Your character also has the chance to become injured (The injuries can vastly vary) and you'll require a healer to heal you. There's a bounty board where you'll be able to post and ask help from someone in the community, or you can go and pay for an NPC doctor (Totally free, no premium currency).

There are a *few* issues. As I said earlier, the dialogue can leave a bit to be desired with the lip-sync/timing in some of the cutscenes. But it's never enough to break that level of immersion, nor ruin the moment of a quest that it happens in. A few other complaints I have are--

- Guilds are based around finishing "Activities" to remain active, so if you're looking to just be in a guild with yourself and a few friends, you will have to go out of your way in order to not have it disbanded. (The maintenance cost is 9000, and each person can probably do about 7-8k by themselves while working a normal job, so not impossible to maintain)
- Why don't the animal enemies have stamina bars? >_> Just an endless cycle of being aggro, no matter how much I parry.
- Menus... Menus... And oh, more menus!
- The bounty board is constantly being hawked by however many active players at a time, so trying to get specific bounties, like healing as I said earlier, will be very rng on if you're fast enough to grab it. There are VARIOUS types of bounties, so it's not like that for them all, but it is something that will be noticeable if you enjoy the idea of playing a doctor.

If you made it to the bottom of my rant, I truly encourage you to try the game. It's got so much to offer, and these are the f2p games we, as a community, should be supporting. They delivered a phenomenal experience, one that rivals any AAA company releasing games today, all for free. There's 0 pay-wall restriction on your ability to fully play and enjoy this game for free-- And that, to me, is worth supporting.

If you’ve been waiting for that one Chinese martial-arts fantasy game to finally scratch the Wuxia itch… yeah, this is the one.

I went in not expecting much, and wow—this game grabbed me way harder than I thought it would. The story is surprisingly rich, and the characters feel super likeable right from the start. There’s always something to do: exploring the world, chasing down side missions, stumbling into secret quests, or just messing around and seeing what weird stuff you can find.

And the world… holy crap. It’s beautiful. Like, actually breathtaking. Everything feels alive—NPCs have daily cycles where they eat, sleep, wander around, and react to things. It really makes you feel like you’re in an actual place, not some empty open world.

Combat is a blast, too. I wouldn’t call it souls-like—more like an action hack-and-slash with a martial-arts twist. You get tons of weapons and flashy skills.
Want to breathe fire like a dragon?
Try the drunken fist?
Or just slash the sky and fly around like a maniac?
Yeah, this game lets you do all of that.

If you want to play solo, no problem. Solo basically feels like a single-player ARPG campaign—you can go at your own pace and enjoy the story without needing anyone.

But the co-op stuff is surprisingly great too. There are loads of minigames, co-op missions, and even raid-style bosses. And these raids aren’t baby mode either—they’re closer to MMO raids where you actually need to learn attack patterns and mechanics instead of just smashing buttons.

Ratings & Final Thoughts

Combat: 8/10
Story (so far): 8/10
World: 10/10
Stuff to do: 7/10
Voice acting: 7/10 — main cast is good, but some side characters using AI voices are… kinda iffy.

For players who love going for 100% completion, side quests, and collectibles: just know the game is still in early stages, and new content gets added periodically. Right now we’re about a year behind the Chinese version in terms of content, so expect the world to expand over time.

But the good news: it’s NOT pay-to-win. Monetization is purely cosmetic. After about two weeks of playing, I’m basically at the point where I’m just min-maxing my build waiting for them to raise the cap.

Still, if you’re into Wuxia, martial arts fantasy, or just flying around punching dudes with fire fists—this game is absolutely worth a try.

9/10 – A Stunning Wuxia Adventure That Keeps Getting Better

Where Winds Meet has completely exceeded my expectations. It’s rare to find an open world game that blends exploration, combat depth, storytelling, and freedom this well. The world feels alive, every region has its own secrets, puzzles, hidden caves, and a whole lot of side quests.

Combat is fast, stylish, and extremely satisfying. Switching between stances, countering, dodging, and weaving in martial abilities feels fluid and skill based. Playing on Expert difficulty is tough, But incredibly rewarding once you master your build. For does who dare challange Legendary difficulty, may fate be whit you.

The RPG systems go way beyond simple stats. Joining a sect, taking disciples (who does that?), learning martial arts, and even things like cooking, hunting, or shaping your character’s personality it all makes your journey feel like your story. (beware of the goose, they are relentless)

Performance has been smooth-"ish", the art style is gorgeous, and the atmosphere of ancient China is beautifully captured. The Ghostlight Market, Crimson Cliff, Moonveil, the hidden temples… everything looks and feels handcrafted. Events and encounters feel dynamic rather than repetitive. Kaifeng is a really well carfted city,

Yes, there are a few rough edges and some systems can use clearer explanations, but the developers are actively improving the game and listening to feedback, which is rare nowadays.

If you love Wuxia, open-world exploration, deep combat systems, and games that reward curiosity, this is absolutely worth playing. I didn’t expect to get this hooked but here we are.

Highly recommended.

What Makes it Great:
Amazing Scenarios & Performance: The world design is breathtaking, and the best part is that the game runs with great performance. It is a smooth, visually-stunning experience that lets you truly appreciate the expansive environments.

Great Storyline: The narrative is deeply engaging and memorable, drawing you in with compelling characters and high-stakes mystery.

Dynamic & Varied Playstyle: The combat system is phenomenal. It’s fast-paced, highly responsive, and incredibly varied, allowing for creative skill combinations.

Absolutely Fair F2P: There are absolutely NO pay-to-win mechanics that I encountered, making it a truly rewarding experience for all players.

The Only Con So Far:
The one area that needs refinement is the user interface. There are too many persistent red dot notifications that clutter the screen and menu, requiring excessive clicking to clear them whenever you do anything new in the game.

Verdict: An unmissable F2P title that nails the core gameplay, story, and performance. The "red dot" issue is a minor quality-of-life.

It's astounding how great this game looks and plays for a free release; really one of the best-looking F2P titles out there with a huge open world and Sekiro-inspired combat combined with Chinese MMO flair for a truly fresh feel. The technical state at launch was rough, though, bogging the experience down: expect glitches galore, missing voice lines, crashes, and random lag spikes or stuttering. Another negative is the recycled gameplay; outside of the great multiplayer modes, you will likely find yourself doing the same quests and exploring similar designs over and over. The main story is surprisingly long for a free-to-play game-the community estimates it's 150+ hours with time-gated progress-but starts out pretty boring, with some sections dragging on. The game has tons of mechanics, like the fun gliding/flying skills to get across the map, but you will probably just fast travel everywhere by the end. Honestly, the single and online modes feel disjointed and confusing—with story progression locked to solo, with optional private co-op for bosses, while online is mostly a social hub for PvP, guilds, raids, and endgame grinding without quests or mobs in the open world. It'd be a much better choice to have a fully seamless MMORPG with integrated persistent multiplayer.

Where Winds Meet stands out as one of the most impressive open-world titles rooted in traditional Chinese culture. Its strongest points are undeniably the story and exploration. The narrative is layered, emotional, and heavily inspired by Chinese historical themes and philosophies. If you enjoy plot-driven games, you’ll find its storytelling rich and rewarding.

Exploration is where the game truly shines. The world feels alive—dense bamboo forests, ancient towns, misty mountains, and mythical landscapes all invite you to wander. Every corner feels handcrafted with cultural detail, and discovering hidden locations or lore pieces is consistently satisfying.

That said, the game is very Chinese culture-heavy. Many references, idioms, and historical nuances come directly from Chinese literature, martial-arts traditions (武侠), and folklore. Players without some background in Chinese culture can still enjoy the adventure, but understanding these details will definitely enhance the experience and make the world feel even more immersive.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is an excellent choice for players who appreciate strong storytelling, deep world-building, and culturally rich adventures.

I’ve had a genuinely great time playing this game. The world is incredibly vivid, and exploring it has been one of the most enjoyable parts of the experience. Whether I’m wandering through wide, open fields or diving into dark, atmospheric dungeons, every location feels thoughtfully designed and full of personality. The sense of adventure is strong, and the world constantly rewards curiosity.

The graphics are stunning rich colors, detailed textures, and great lighting all work together to create an immersive atmosphere. Character customization is surprisingly good too, offering plenty of options to shape your character exactly how you want, which makes the journey feel even more personal. The combat mechanics are friendly and easy to grasp, making the battles accessible without sacrificing fun. On top of that, the upgrade mechanics are very user-friendly, which makes progression smooth and satisfying rather than overwhelming.

That said, the game could still use a bit of optimization. Some interactions were noticeably bugged, and there were moments where objects or elements didn’t load quickly enough. It’s hard to tell if it’s a loading issue or just a glitch I’m not recognizing, but it does break immersion here and there.

Despite those technical issues, this is still an amazing RPG. The world is worth exploring, the gameplay is engaging, and the overall experience is full of charm. With a little more polish and bug fixing, this could easily become a standout title. As it is, though, it’s already a fun and memorable game that I’m happy to recommend to anyone who enjoys RPGs or open-world adventures.

I'll start by asking: How can this game possibly be free-to-play?

Imagine blending the core combat elements of a Souls game with the directional fighting mechanics of Naraka Bladepoint, wrapping it all in an open world reminiscent of Ghost of Tsushima, and then adding comprehensive MMO elements as the cherry on top. This game truly has it all, and what's most impressive is how seamlessly it's implemented.

Players can choose their difficulty, ranging from a "Very Hard" mode that truly captures that Souls-like challenge, down to a more beginner-friendly setting with parry assist. There's a wide variety of weapons to choose from, each offering a unique feel, special abilities, and satisfying combo potential. Beyond the combat, the world is beautiful, the NPC interactions feel unique, and the sounds, weather, and overall atmosphere blend together exceptionally well.

However, there are a few areas that need improvement, particularly for players looking to commit long-term. Currently, the game implements weekly caps on nearly all forms of progression. Once you hit these limits, there's little incentive to continue playing for character power. Furthermore, while the fighting system is generally good, it lacks necessary punishment or tactical feedback in PvP. This makes competitive play feel less strategic and more reliant on spamming a basic rotation—I'd prefer to see a depth closer to what's found in games like Naraka Bladepoint.

Overall, the game offers a rich array of activities to keep players occupied, from casual pursuits like playing cards, to co-op 'healing a plague' missions, massive raid-style boss fights, and dedicated PvP. This is all underpinned by a great single-player story and plenty of sidequests that genuinely fit into the main narrative.

For players searching for a quality game to keep them occupied for around 70 hours, this is easily a 9 out of 10. For those seeking a long-term commitment who dedicate five hours a day to progression, the current state of the game feels closer to a 7 out of 10.

★ ★ ★ ★ ★ — “Come for the Wuxia, Stay Because People Keep Paying Me to Patch Them Up”

I booted up Where Wind Meets expecting high-flying martial arts, dramatic cutscenes, maybe some philosophical monk telling me to touch grass.
What I didn’t expect was becoming the medieval UberEats of healing.

This game straight-up lets you be a healer for hire—and people will PAY YOU for fixing the injuries they earned by parkouring off cliffs like diet wuxia superheroes. I’m out here throwing medicine, slapping on buffs, and getting tipped like a fantasy surgeon with questionable certifications.

The healer system is honestly genius:

You heal strangers → you get paid.

You heal friends → you get paid.

You heal someone who immediately sprints into danger again → you STILL get paid, plus a good laugh.

Combat feels crispy, the world is stupidly pretty, and half the community plays like they’re reenacting a wuxia drama while the other half injures themselves right in front of me just so I’ll heal them again. Peak entertainment.

If you’re looking for:
✔️ Gorgeous world
✔️ Chaos with strangers
✔️ Accidental side gig as a traveling doctor
✔️ The most fun you can have being underqualified but overpaid

Then yeah download it. Play it. Heal people. Get rich

Behold, AAA studios -- THIS is FTP done RIGHT (and how rare is it to see a FTP game on steam w/ Very Positive reviews). I'm deeply grateful and I dare say enamoured to discover a game of such high quality pushing the FTP category to the center stage. 

I've been saying it for awhile now -- A free to play game, done right, is by far the best model.
No monetary barrier to entry, with effectively limitless revenue potential for the studio if the MTX are provisioned correctly (not PTW). A very nice balance for both consumer and business, and a true win win.

The mission statement on the start menu says "We will never sell power. We will never be PTW." 

If they stay true to this mission -- Winds will not only have met the FTP gold standard, they'll have redefined it.

It's been encouraging to see the industry recognize that PVE w/ coop potential is more desirable than forced PVP, and I've quietly been hoping to see more titles exactly like this. Bravo, Netease and Everstone Studio! A job well done.

Now, my complaints. I want to preface by saying I understand this game is free (Idk how honestly, it's amazing lol) BUT-

1.) The skill buttons and layout take a second to get used to. For someone with ADHD like myself, it can feel a little overwhelming and I still hit the wrong button some times. But the battle effects and unique weapons are fun to play!

2.) The pricing. WTF is up with the pricing. Again, I understand Gatcha games, but $40 for ONE outfit? Robbery. Especially when a lot of people are struggling to even buy food right now. Again, I understand the store is how you make money, but even a $10 outfit with over 1M players will make you BANK. Stop being greedy. 3.) Co Op is still a little wonky, but I love the fact you can have a solo mode and play in peace, then switch to online mode for boss battles with friends. I normally come here for the story and don't do well in PVP areas, so the solo is a blessing to me. 

4.) We are being spoon fed the MSQ, and each 'release' only takes 15 mins to play through. The graphics are beautiful and the story is pretty good, but the pricing needs tweaked asap lol We want to support, but 40 for a skin is bonkers xD Def play this game and stick around, and hopefully they will listen to their community and fix a few things. Where Winds Meet: Kung Fu Assasin's Creed with a Side of Jackie Chan

Listen. I thought I was signing up for a chill wuxia stroll through ancient China, maybe sip some tea, pet a cat, vibe with the scenery. Next thing I know, I’m sprinting across rooftops like Assassin’s Creed met Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, drop-kicking bandits so hard they reincarnate as background NPCs.

The campaign? Bro, it’s basically Red Cliff directed by Zack Snyder if Snyder had just binged Kung Fu Hustle. Every dialogue cutscene feels like it’s about to slow-mo into a 300-style monologue, except instead of “THIS IS SPARTA” it’s “WELCOME TO THE SONG DYNASTY, PLEASE TAKE A NUMBER.” And while I’m busy yeeting dudes off cliffs with a bamboo spear, the game suddenly hits me with storytelling so good I felt like I’d accidentally enrolled in a historical drama. Not the Netflix kind, the good kind. 

The combat? Absolute martial arts fever dream. Imagine Sekiro, Ghost of Tsushima, and Jet Li’s Fearless all got drunk together and decided to choreograph a fight scene. One second I’m parrying arrows with a sword, the next I’m roundhouse-kicking a warlord into a rice paddy. I wasn’t part of a squad—I was basically the Fast & Furious family condensed into one confused protagonist. Except instead of cars I had a horse that kept ignoring traffic laws, and instead of Vin Diesel I had Confucius whispering “family” in Mandarin directly into my ear like a spiritual GPS. Every fight felt like I was starring in a one‑man crossover event: stunt driver, philosopher, and demolition crew all rolled into one wandering swordsman.

The graphics? It’s like Zhang Yimou’s Hero collided with Breath of the Wild and then got baptized in Unreal Engine 5. Every mountain looks like it was painted by a drunk poet, every temple feels like it was designed by a feng shui master who moonlights as a rave DJ. The sunsets? Bro, they’re so gorgeous I half-expected a fortune cookie to pop up saying “Your destiny awaits.”

The progression? Think Karate Kid montage but on steroids. I started as a barefoot villager who couldn’t swing a stick without hitting myself. By the end, I was basically Bruce Lee with a glaive, punching Mongol invaders so hard they respawned in the tutorial zone. Even the skill tree felt like unlocking cheat codes from a Shaw Brothers film.

PvP? Haven’t touched it yet because I’m still busy living my best wuxia soap opera life. Why duel my bros when I can roleplay as a wandering philosopher who occasionally suplexes bandits?

Final Verdict:
This isn’t a game. This is a 12-episode drama directed by Ang Lee, choreographed by Jackie Chan, and scored by Hans Zimmer after he binge-watched Dynasty Warriors.

But considering how alive the world is with all the NPCs chattering and enemies also having their own conversations, I enjoyed it a lot more the way I played it.

The game is completely free, there is a stamina system to claim rewards from some challenges which is a bit of a drag considering how slowly it replenishes as well, but I've barely engaged with that system in my almost 80 hours of playing this game since we can also get the same loot (at a slower rate) from fighting enemies in the open world and exploring.

If you want to avoid the story out of pure spite for mmo-like games, you can skip it altogether just by playing in the coop mode, it's super streamlined and if you have friends to play with, you'll enjoy yourself if you think you'll enjoy any aspect of this game. (Coop also has some extra stuff in it that solo mode doesn't have in it's map)

Bottom line is - Game is great. I haven't been able to think about other games as much because I want to play this as much as I can as a lover of open-world adventure games with easy to understand combat mechanics and mmo-like features, without having to exclusively depend on daily logins like most other live service games.

There's a lot I'm missing from my review, like the 10 player raids, guild and cohort bonuses, as well as the outfit gacha (not worth it imo, unless you want to get them for personal reasons), but all of these are just side products you can choose to engage with if you feel like it, it won't affect your experience of the game in any way.

Amaaazing.

Seriously blown away that this game hasn't ignited bigger than it has. Its seriously such a beautiful game with clean combat and highly addictive story and exploration. Me and all of my friends have been obsessed since we first got into it. I am floored that this isnt a paid game. It plays better than a huge chunk of games Ive paid for throughout this year, even better than the majority of AAA games. 

Still on the fence about playing? Don't. You can legit ride a pack of geece as a mount, pet cats, teleport pick pocket, and throw lettuce/eggs at other players in jail in a pardon parade 😂

=Main Gameplay Loop=
I usually play games for the core loop, and this one splits pretty cleanly into combat and exploration.

=Combat=
The combat is basically Sekiro’s posture system, where most of your damage comes from breaking posture by parrying. The problem is that it does not really understand what makes Sekiro’s combat so good. There are a bunch of small quirks that make the fights feel off. The worst one is how enemies can randomly stun you and stop you from parrying at all. I will be mashing parry and my character just stands there doing nothing.

The game also does not encourage you to stay aggressive. Against the hardest bosses, the easiest strategy is to sit back and just parry everything. It works, but it is boring. Sure you can weave in attacks and abilities if you want, but for most people it is much easier to be a parry bot. In Sekiro, you feel cool mixing your attacks in while deflecting theirs. Here it is mostly waiting and reacting. Enemy telegraphs are also way less clear.

=Exploration=
Exploration is straight up Genshin style. Open chests, grab currency, XP, materials. Whether you enjoy this depends on how much you like that kind of exploration. The game pushes you to explore because you need “oddities” like bugs and plants to upgrade your character. There are also a ton of little minigames that raise exploration stats, and you will need those later.

=Social and MMO Stuff=
There is another side of the game that I did not interact much with. The world has two versions, one for solo play and one MMO style where you see other players running around. There are a lot of social systems built on top of this, like marriage, discipleship, sworn cohorts, and the usual guild stuff. Some rewards are tied to these systems, so if you avoid them you will miss some things.

=The Bad=
This is a free to play, always online game that relies heavily on whales. Because of that, most cosmetics are locked behind really pricey paywalls. Some sets cost something like 40 thousand dollars. There are free cosmetics that look good, but the high end prices are ridiculous. Though because of this, players are able to play this game for free.

The worst part of the whole game is the UI. It is genuinely awful. Even ignoring the obvious dark patterns, everything is buried under layers of menus. People call it “Where Menus Meet” for a reason. You dig five or six menus deep just to find basic stuff.

The game also has a janky feel. Movement feels weird at times, wallrunning only works half the time, and there are tons of little bugs. None of them are game breaking, but they stack up and get annoying after a while.

=Conclusion=
Even with all the problems, this is still one of the best free to play games I have tried. You can ignore all the cosmetic nonsense and still get a full scale open world with a solid story to play through.

OVERALL:
I'm putting this first because the game is free, and seriously, go play it. You don't need to read my review first, but if you insist, overall this game is an amazing game, I haven't really encountered anything about the game that detracts long-term from all the things that make it great though if you find yourself losing interest in the first couple of hours, stick with it as it gets a lot better.

THE (REALLY) GOOD:

Definitely one of the top free-to-play RPG games of all time. The game has amazing visuals, sound, and story for a game that not only costs nothing, but has no subscription. On top of this, the monetization in this game is entirely cosmetic, so there is nothing you need from the store unless you want to support the developers and get something cool. All these elements of the game do justice to the wuxia theme. the An absolute gem of a game.

THE (KINDA) BAD:

The story does start off a little slow and is a little confusing at the beginning but then when the pieces start coming together it's like a good book that is hard to put down. Ultimately the story is a pro and not a con, but people may lose interest in the early story missions (I found myself wandering and doing side quests a bit) though I suggest sticking with it until the plot begins to unfold. Gameplay itself does have a lot of moving parts that take some getting used to at first, and the menus are a bit convoluted so patience is key. It's not so bad as a game like Dark Souls that doesn't tell you what anything is or does.

THE NEUTRAL:

The game does use AI in limited areas. While the game isn't made with AI and doesn't use AI art, there are some NPCs that you can befriend and talk to that use an AI chatbot. These clearly state that the chat is handled by AI, and so far in my playthrough I haven't found it necessary to interact with them but they do seem to have some sort of reward for befriending them. I, personally, find it a little weird to try to make friends with an AI bot, I would rather interactions with them be limited to asking questions (like for directions to somewhere in game) or completing quests for them, but  everyone will feel different about this. Other than this, the game uses AI to generate a face for your character based on a picture you upload. This feature isn't even close to being accurate. You can do better with the sliders yourself.

Where Winds Meet is everything I ever wanted from a wuxia fantasy game. It delivers freedom, beauty, action, and storytelling in a way that completely pulled me in.

The combat is fast, stylish, and incredibly satisfying. Parries, deflects, weapon styles, martial arts techniques—every fight feels like a duel straight out of a classic wuxia movie.

The world is huge and alive. Forests, rivers, mountains, ancient temples, busy villages—every area feels handcrafted and full of small stories. NPCs act naturally, random events happen around you, and exploring never gets boring.

What hooked me the most is the freedom. You can climb anything, sprint across rooftops, glide through the wind, explore hidden caves, switch combat styles, and even shape your own moral path. It truly feels like living inside a wuxia novel.

I’ve played many ARPGs and open-world games, but Where Winds Meet gave me something rare: the feeling that “this is the game I’ve always wanted.”

If you love wuxia, open worlds, deep combat, or immersive storytelling, you should absolutely play this.

The game itself is a F2P Single player Open-World RPG set in the Wuxia universe, with optional Co-Op and Souls-like combat. Over 100 hours of gameplay.

[h3] The Good: [/h3]
- Combat is fun, graphics are great, building system is intuitive, and exploration is heavily encouraged. Game is free and can be played entirely solo. 

[h3] The Bad: [/h3]
- No Skimpy outfits. Cat and Fox Ears/Tails for $50, but nothing revealing.
- The UI. There's 15 different reward systems and they are all hidden behind 20 different menus.

[h3] The Ugly: [/h3]
- Game is incomplete, even in China. It's been out for over a year on PC and Mobile in China. Players seem to complain about lack of catch-up mechanics and lack of a true endgame.

I really wanted to like the game… but it kept throwing artificial roadblocks at me just to slow down my progression. I also really dislike how the game separates solo and multiplayer content. It would make the world feel so much more alive if I could do my solo quests with other players around instead of being isolated in my own instance.

The main story is also incredibly confusing in some aspects, I eventually gave up trying to understand it. Performance in the main city was another disappointment; even with a high-end PC, the game still runs poorly/stutters there. On top of that, I ran into issues where fast travel points I had already discovered became undiscovered the next time I logged in.

Overall, the game has potential, but the constant roadblocks, confusing story, technical issues, and unnecessary separation between solo and multiplayer made it hard for me to enjoy.

I hope they will improve in the future!

Pros:
 - Good graphics and well optimized
 - I was told atmosphere is very "Wuxia" (doesn't mean much to me, considering the cons)
 - It has a nice use of AI chat with NPCs
 - It has minigames (I didn't like any of them), and puzzles (those were interesting)

Cons:
 - UI is a horror and a nightmare to find or do anything in. First gameplay experience is horrendous (no settings or volume control until tutorial is finished). Character creation and appearance change is confusing at best. Buttons don't work when clicked, you have to use dedicated keys instead. I needed someone with experience in Asiatic games (Genshin Impact) to be able to host co-ops.
 - Very poorly implemented multiplayer (single player Elden Ring co-op mechanics on multiplayer marketed game)
 - Story and characters seem to have weird themes (too much accent on kids giving quests)
 - Cheap appearance mechanics: gear doesn't have any impact when equipped appearance-wise
 - Cheap XP implementation: looting gives XP (???)
 - Very few mob and miniboss types (went west across all allowed map and encountered only 2-3 types of enemies) + I think I encountered same miniboss 3 times; the other 1 miniboss I found was an enlarged normal version
 - Some consumables get auto-equipped on loot and auto-consummed; their use has to be disabled after each loot that contains consumables
 - Level gatekeeping: Level progress is limited by account age
 - Zone gatekeeping: Invisible wall when trying to leave main continent 
 - Horrible translations
 - There is no way to skip cutscenes
 - Some quest progress can be done in multiplayer without having prerequisites for it (my experience: [spoiler]you can insert a key in multiplayer for fan unlock quest before you get it in single player, then when you try to do the quest as single player some cinematics are skipped[/spoiler])
 - Some weapons are weird (umbrellas? fans? really?) and some are repetitive (3-4 types of katana), and some of them don't make any sense (ex: spears that have no "impale" basic attack, even if that's their main use; I mean nobody is going to try to slash with a spear....)
 - "free game"

Impression:
Seems like an attempt to cheaply copy Elden Ring by an Asiatic company, but with too much focus on quests and stories rather than combat mechanics and bosses (quests which can't be done in co-op). Character creation pushes very hard to take a picture of you and record your voice (???). Some quests are marked as "random encounters" probably to create a FOMO feeling, to not leave the area (I didn't see any other difference than any other quests). I tried this game to play with friends, but it's just impossible to really co-op this game.

It also has a feeling of lacking immersion: some npcs (kids appearing to give quests) have no backstory or explanation at all when you meet them (they seem to be completionist quests added as an afterthought), and advancing to the next [spoiler]sequence of levels (first group is 1-15, next is 15-20, third is 20-30 or so, etc)[/spoiler] teleports you to an arena, and the entire mechanic has no immersion at all.

Non-boss combat too easy to call it souls-like. Miniboss combat is facerollable with [spoiler]spear stun[/spoiler]. I didn't encounter any boss for my level in first 8h of gameplay.
Decent game but some boss rooms are a little annoying in design. There are invisible walls that keep you from walking into spaces that look open, making the fight unpredictable sometimes.

Incredible. This game is absolutely incredible. Now you might think that I'm glazing a little too much, but honestly I was blown away with how much there is to explore and discover in this game. Now the early game is a little bit generic when it comes to ARPGs but power through the first 3 hours and unlock the entire world and you will quickly understand how amazing this game actual is.

This is honestly the first game where I have found that the world truly feels alive. There are hundreds of NPCs to interact with and grinding for masteries, at my measly 11,800 rating leads you exploring the world, gathering resources to boost your stats just a little higher as you work your way towards the game cap.

Now I've heard a lot of people complain about the level cap, and although I don't agree with it, its necessary and I'm thankful that they have put it in place to save us from chinese players who know how to exploit the leveling system. The level cap also forces you to explore the world rather than just play main story until you hit max level which is something that keeps players coming back every day for their daily rewards and also to spam their sect quests, bounties and multiplayer modes to get adventure slips to go towards snagging some cool cosmetics.

The only downside for me is the limit on free cosmetics. The vibrant hair colour being locked behind a premium gacha system is a little sad but you can get free credits for the gacha by defeating wandering martial artists which are highlighted on your map and I was lucky enough to get myself a bright hairstyle which makes my character stand out in a crowd of players that weren't lucky enough to get a decent gacha roll. 

All in all I am eagerly awaiting future updates and I can't wait to see just how much content there is at end game.

Pro tip, if you get stuck and can't find any information on a certain quest or item you need to gather, use chatgpt. It takes information that chinese players have posted and fetches it for you in english or your language of choice.

I originally ignored Where Winds Meet because the trailers made it look like another flashy open-world game, but once I learned it was free, I gave it a shot—and instantly got hooked. 

The game offers a grounded, cinematic world without any gacha systems, skill-based combat heavily inspired by Sekiro, and a surprising amount of content, from arenas and raids to player bounties and even a battle-royale mode. 

For a free title, it feels incredibly polished and full of depth. It’s the first game in years that genuinely made me feel addicted again, and I’m glad I didn’t overlook it.

📝 **Review: Where Winds Meet**

⭐ **Rating: 4.5 / 5**

**Where Winds Meet** is one of those games that grabs you immediately with its atmosphere and refuses to let go. The world is *absolutely stunning* — sweeping landscapes, dense forests, ancient towns, and cinematic lighting that constantly makes you stop just to look around. Exploration feels rewarding, not because the game forces you to, but because the world itself invites you in.

Combat is stylish and fluid, with a strong wuxia vibe. Once you get used to the timing and movement, it becomes extremely satisfying to chain abilities together and dance around your enemies. The game does a fantastic job blending martial arts fantasy with grounded historical tone.

There *are* moments where pacing and tutorials feel uneven, and some systems can be a bit overwhelming at first. But once they click, the game opens up beautifully. The storytelling feels personal, emotional, and often surprisingly mature — moments of reflection, loss, and quiet mystery tie the whole adventure together.

If you’re into open-world RPGs with strong atmosphere, exploration, and martial-arts fantasy, this one is absolutely worth your time.

**✔ Pros**
- Gorgeous, atmospheric open world  
- Fluid wuxia-inspired combat  
- Strong storytelling and character moments  
- Great sense of adventure and exploration  

**✘ Cons**
- Some systems feel confusing early on  
- Occasional pacing bumps  

**Final Verdict:**  
A captivating, emotional wuxia RPG that rewards players who take their time. Beautiful, atmospheric, and deeply engaging.

Okay so listen… I’m that person who lives and breathes gacha worlds. Genshin? WuWa? Inject it straight into my veins.
But throw me into a Souls-like or anything Elden Ring-coded and I’m already crying on the floor.
So I went into Where Winds Meet expecting chaos… and somehow walked out obsessed.

This game is like someone took the elegance of an open-world wuxia dream, sprinkled in cozy gacha vibes, added a little “try-hard combat but make it friendly,” and blended it all into something that just works. Like an unexpected fusion playlist that somehow slaps.

Co-op? Absolutely delightful.
You can jump in with friends, do missions, fight stuff, flex your drip, or literally just wander and vibe. No pressure, no grind walls, no “git gud” energy chasing you. Just pure chill wind-in-your-hair freedom.

Combat in multiplayer? Surprisingly fun.
It’s flashy without being frustrating, stylish without punishing you for breathing wrong. It feels like wuxia parkour meets accessible action rpg — and that balance is rare.

Solo story? Lowkey fire.
And if you’re like me and your brain sometimes says “no thoughts, just fast-forward,” the game gets you.
You can speed the story up to x3 or even skip entire dialogues, and it still hands you a clean little recap so you never feel lost. Respectful. Considerate.

In short?
If you adore gacha aesthetics but fear Souls-borne trauma… this game feels like a bridge gently guiding you across. A perfect blend of chill, charm, action, and adventure.

The wind meets you where you are and somehow carries you further.

Game of the year for me. Bought the season pass and still think this game is a steal. Have no idea why this game isn't even more popular than it already is. This game is the standard bearer for what free games should be. The only real thing that people can buy is a horse that helps gather items or cosmetics. So, if you're okay gathering stuff like any other game then the horse is meaningless, especially since your character can get to various places much faster than the horse. People crash out over some bugs and the menu system. I think that is such a cope and it wouldn't surprise me if those people were xenophobic of China or industry plants afraid of how games will be judged going forward. This game is about as big, if not bigger than Skyrim, and has fewer bugs than when that game first came out. Skyrim is still adored and looked at through rose-tinted glasses to this day. The menu system is admittedly terrible. However if a menu system on a free game is the most troublesome point, than I genuinely don't care. A separate argument in favor of the menu system, has to do with the game's depth. Game depth necessitates a certain amount of menus and this game has more depth than most out there. 
But, back to the good points. The game has great visuals and some stunning artwork littered throughout. If you're looking for picturesque areas to litter your steam profile, then this is the game for you. If you want accessible combat or souls-like combat, it's in here. There are raids that you can do with bots to get the mechanics down, which should be industry standard at this point. They offer slightly lower rewards than the group up options but allow players to get the timing and mechanics. There is even a separate talent system for bossing which rewards players for getting certain mechanics throughout the fight down in order to make the boss fight quicker. If raiding isn't your thing, there is plenty of solo content and exploration that you can easily spend a two hundred hours in. Given the price tag, this game is absurdly good  and I would've gladly paid 60 dollars and got the season passes for it.

Where Winds Meet is one of those rare games that captures both the spirit of classic wuxia and the excitement of modern open-world design. The world feels alive in a way that’s hard to describe  from quiet villages and sweeping fields to bustling cities full of stories waiting to unfold. Every corner has something to discover, whether it’s a hidden shrine, a heartfelt side quest, or a breath-taking view that makes you stop just to take it in.

The combat blends style and technique beautifully, turning every fight into a smooth and satisfying dance of martial arts. Whether you prefer fast blades, graceful movement, or powerful skills, the game lets you shape your own path. The freedom in exploration, traversal, and character growth keeps every moment fresh.

What surprised me most is how emotional and meaningful the world feels. The music is calming, the atmosphere is rich, and the characters carry real depth. It has that timeless feeling a reminder of how adventure games used to make us feel, while still moving boldly forward with new ideas and modern polish.

It’s also a place that’s fun to enjoy with friends or simply wander alone. The community has been warm and helpful, which only adds to the experience.

Overall, Where Winds Meet isn’t just a game it’s a journey worth taking. A beautiful blend of tradition, innovation, and heart.

Seriously, this game is the Wuxia experience I've been waiting for! It's such a relief to finally have a proper, expansive game in this genre, especially for us Western fans it truly fills a void, I haven't play a game like this since Age of Wushu. My first impressions were overwhelmingly positive, and honestly, I think this is a total must-play for fans of deep narrative and character-driven fantasy. Also for FREE.

What instantly grabbed me was the incredible story development and the level of freedom you get. The extensive character creation is deep, and the way the narrative branches means your entire journey feels 100% authentic and immersive. I didn't just feel like I was playing a character; I felt like I was forging my own martial destiny in the turbulent Jianghu.

Aesthetically, the game is a treat. The music is absolutely stellar—it perfectly nails that epic, sweeping Wuxia vibe. Visually, it's stunning, but I should mention that to see those incredible, high-fidelity graphics at their best, you'll definitely need a powerful graphics card. The good news is that even when I dropped the settings to low, the world still looked visually amazing, which is a huge credit to the artists.

As for the gameplay, the core experience is solid and engaging. I'll admit, the combat can feel a little clumsy in spots, but this minor friction is easily overlooked when you consider the depth of content and narrative quality provided.

My Verdict: If you're looking for an authentic Wuxia adventure, stop waiting and dive in. I'm hooked on the deep character focus, unique setting, and massive world-building. This game is an easy recommendation from me.

This game has sooo much but it's giving 'quantity over quality' vibes.

The visuals are epic, especially the lighting. Some stunning vistas and magical lands. This and the boss fights are my two big positives.

Strangely, time quickly ceases to mean anything. Time of day will change four times during a ten minute quest, scripted to react to who knows. It heavily undermines the feeling of being in a 'world'.

Sooo many things to pick up in the wild, but it feels like too much. No sense of accomplishment from finding things.

Boss fights are epic and my main reason for continuing to play. Even the early fights are like mid to end game Souls bosses. It gives the game big dynamics, going from flute music to yelling at your screen on your fifth death to the same unrelenting combo. But the challange is great. The devs spent a lot of time on nailing the different fight physics.

Other Enemy AI is 6/10. Melee fights are varied (depending on enemy and location) and sometimes challenging. Decent fun. Ranged enemies have very little AI. I've had many battles where I've killed everyone, then I hear weird thunking noises, which are three archers standing behind a wall shooting at me... but into the wall, or standing underneath a ledge below me shooting into the ceiling. You can also snipe enemies with impunity because once you're a certain distance away (not far at all) the enemy reverts to its patrol script, no matter how much damage you're doing to it.
Also, often nearby enemies won't notice you fighting their mates, especially if they're facing away from you.

Everyone's been saying it, but the menus are chaotic and non-sensical. So many redundant systems buried in oddly named sub-menus.

The game will shower you with 'achievements' and it becomes oppressive. An onslaught of notification icons.

The group events are a fever dream. Very weird, kinda funny, mostly broken. Most are to promote engagement, with no applicability to the game world.

Apparently you can build houses and decorate them? 42 hours in and I've no idea why. It's not a home base you can store stuff in.

Overall the game is 8/10, mainly propped up by the boss battles. Without those it'd be 7/10.

Where Winds Meet is a rare kind of open-world experience, one that doesn’t simply give you a map to explore, but a world that feels alive, breathing, and dramatically shaped by the philosophies that guide its characters. It’s a game that blends "wuxia" romanticism with grounded political tension, presenting a landscape where beauty and brutality constantly coexist.
What struck me most is how the game treats freedom. Almost everything is interactable, not in a shallow, checkbox-style “open world” way, but in a manner that feels intentional. Scaling mountains, drifting across bamboo forests, dueling under moonlight, every mechanic invokes a larger theme, a person in search of identity navigating a fractured world.
Combat is both art and discipline. It rewards precision, patience, and creativity, and you can feel the design philosophy drawn from traditional martial arts, every stance, counter, and dodge reflects a worldview where mastery is born from harmony between body and environment.
Narratively, the game invites you to reflect. Every quest feels like a moral question disguised as a simple mission. Even the smallest encounters like beggars, wanderers, healers, corrupt officials, carry weight. You’re not just completing tasks, you’re participating in the emotional and cultural fabric of a turbulent era. Visually, the game is breathtaking. But its beauty isn’t just aesthetic, it’s symbolic. Light and shadow reflect the tension of an empire in collapse. Ruins tell stories. Temples whisper forgotten truths. Nature acts almost like a silent narrator. Ultimately, Where Winds Meet excels not only as a game, but as an invitation to wander, question, and discover. It is a world that respects the player’s intelligence and imagination, a place where every quiet valley and every violent confrontation reveals something about the world and, surprisingly, about yourself.

If Steam had a neutral option, I would pick it immediately and peacefully.  
But since I must choose, this review exists.

“Not Recommended” (but only for players like me — explanation below)  

I really wanted to recommend this game. And honestly, I tried.

[h3] PREFACE [/h3]
I normally don’t write reviews. I prefer to mind my business quietly, struggling with dignity like a wandering wuxia extra who refuses to admit she’s lost.  

But after tonight’s experience (coincidentally, the Steam Awards), I felt morally obligated to leave something honest, balanced, and hopefully helpful for players like me.

So, here we are.

But not out of dislike, just a lack of a middle ground.

[h3] GAMEPLAY EXPERIENCE (solo, story mode) [/h3]
“Where Winds Meet” is beautiful and ambitious.  

It is thrilling to create a character, explore, find treasures, and solve open-world puzzles.  
But unfortunately, it also has the genre’s typical (and expected) trappings:  
• hard time gates for raising level caps  
• multiple currency types for price obfuscation  
• event grind loops with low reward rates  
• systems that quietly funnel you toward spending real cash  

None of these surprised me — but they do stack.

The early shimmer begins to fade the longer you play.

I started noticing cracks: one NPC literally said the word “sigh” out loud instead of actually sighing — which immediately made me suspect AI-generated voice lines. Later, when I saw the built-in AI chat feature that lets you “talk” to NPCs, it all made sense. The responses felt like scrambled fortune-cookie wisdom.

Even in character creation, the “upload image → custom character” feature shows signs of heavy AI assistance.  
Some players won’t care. I do.

And while I do appreciate the attempt at interactivity (the AI chat, AI-assisted facial generation, and AI voice), I also can’t ignore the quiet concern under it.  
These features ask for voice input or photo uploads. And while I personally didn’t use them, nor did I feel pressured to, the very idea still raises questions about privacy and transparency.  

Even if the system seems not to retain anything, AI is still machine learning. And, ethical clarity matters. Especially in a game that wants to feel like a living world.

And, there’s also a strange disconnect between English spoken dialogue and subtitles — sometimes they don’t even match remotely. It is immersion-breaking when a dramatic cutscene is happening, the character says one thing, and the subtitles display something entirely different.

It makes you wonder:  
If the dialogue is AI, what else is?  
Textures? Models? Scene scripting?

It [i] looks [/i] like a lot of work was put into this game — but the more I saw, the more I questioned whether that effort was spent in the places that truly matter.

Then come the technical issues:  
• framerate drops in larger cities  
• occasional texture flicker and corruption  
• getting stuck inside collision during traversal  
• dialogue audio not playing despite subtitles  
• camera bugs during long-distance transitions (especially cat “Meow Meow” puzzles)

Even so, these will likely be fixed in time. It is still early days. 
The AI integration, however, feels fundamental — and it genuinely detracts from what could’ve been an exceptional, fully human experience.

And, there is a real tension between the game’s business decisions and the world it tries to immerse you in.  
The moment you start thinking about the [i] production [/i] instead of the [i] story, [/i] the spell breaks.

Still, to be fair:  
[b] Where Winds Meet absolutely scratches the classic MMORPG itch. [/b] 
The world is stunning, the designs are elegant, and the character creator alone made me believe I would become a legendary swordswoman by the end of the tutorial.

Then the actual gameplay began.

The biggest issue is not difficulty —  
[b] it’s how unintuitive everything feels. [/b]

And, the ironic part?

[b] I am an intuitive player. [/b]  
I like exploring at my own pace, reading things carefully, learning systems naturally and gradually. 

Most games reward that. 

This one… it punished it.

Every 30 seconds another system unlocked. 
Then another. And another.

Currency → sub-currency → alternate currency → system menu → hidden submenu → reward screens → tooltips → unskippable tutorials → a mechanic I did not ask for →  
and suddenly, a boss fight.

Not optional.  
Not foreshadowed.  
Just violence at my doorstep.

And, I read everything carefully, but the UI avalanche drained me faster than any boss fight. There’s just [i] too much [/i] happening too early, and the sheer number of currencies + unlockables made me feel like I’d accidentally walked into an advanced accounting class.

And, combat itself is fun… when the buttons work. Sometimes they ignored me like I was an NPC they owed money to. Half the time I’m parrying like a wuxia protagonist. The other half I maintained a deadpan face while mashing buttons in silent panic imaginable — but somehow survived. Zero deaths. I should get a flower basket.

(And somehow — somehow — I still didn’t die. I am as surprised as you.)

But the reality is this:

Even though [i] I personally enjoy slow exploration, [/i]  
this game felt like [b] more work than play. [/b]

It overwhelmed me long before it let me breathe.

And getting thrown into a boss fight immediately, before I even acclimated to the controls or pacing, wasn’t enjoyable for me.  
I like slow immersion, not urgent survival.

[b] THE MOMENT I STOPPED [/b]

Full honesty:

When the game threw me into [i] another [/i] boss fight — immediately after the last — I simply paused, stared, and chose peace.

“No.”

I exited the game mid-boss-fight.  
Not even defeated — just spiritually done.

I wrote this review right after closing.  
And I may never return… or maybe I will, in years, after forgetting everything, only to re-log and get instantly one-shot because I re-entered directly into the boss I abandoned. That is my prophecy. A fitting ending. A poetic fate.

[b] THE GOOD: [/b]
• Gorgeous visual world  
• Surprisingly fun combat foundation  
• Rich content for players who love complexity  
• Unexpected, community-driven guidance from supportive player signposts
• Being a cat magnet  
• Beautiful character creation  
• Many activities and systems to dive into  
• Generous F2P cosmetics model  
• Clear developer passion
• It’s free   

[b] THE NOT-FOR-ME: [/b]
• UI/UX is overwhelming, unintuitive, and disorienting
 - low learnability and is hard to build muscle memory for.
• Too many menus, currencies, and systems introduced too fast  
• Very little breathing room for new or slower-paced players  
• Story pacing feels sudden and disjointed early on  
• Occasional input inconsistencies in combat  
• Difficulty spikes thrown cold without buildup  
• Game feels like homework sometimes
 - Overwhelm > enjoyment  
• I just want to explore and breathe, not fight bosses at breakfast  

[h3] VERDICT [/h3]
This [i] is [/i] a good game — just not good [i] for my type of mind. [/i]
If you are new, easily overstimulated, or prefer clean UI and gradual progression, this may feel more exhausting than enjoyable.

If you love complexity, depth, constant systems, and always having something to do?  
→ You might love it.

If you’re solo, intuitive, overstimulated easily, or like quiet immersion (like me)?  
→ Approach with caution.

I can fully understand why people love this game — and I respect it a lot. But as someone who gets overstimulated and prefers clean, simple UI and gradual introduction of mechanics, this title just wasn’t a fit.

Still, respect to the devs — and congrats on the style and ambition.

I’ll continue cheering from the sidelines as someone who nominated it for [b] “Best Game You Suck At” [/b] …because never have I been so impressed and exhausted at the same time.

Where Winds Meet is basically the latest and only game I've recently seen where you get to play a Wuxia MMO that doesn't look like it's basically trying to be Mabinogi with some numbers filed off. As a warning of course you should know that the game has a few instances of AI usage that are very obvious and you will know them when you see them. 1) The game will give you the option of letting it see a picture of you (doesn't actually have to be you) or hear your voice (doesn't have to be your voice) to create a character from its customization tools to be your character. 2) The game has a large amount of NPCs you can befriend for random items that have an AI Chatbot Piloted minigame to gain their friendship.

With that out of the way, the game is entertaining enough. Of course this still comes with the caveat that it expects your computer to be able to run decently intense graphics before being able to access the settings menu and change the game to medium/low. And that the game is 100 gbs (currently before any of the other content from China comes in).

If you want a game where you can engage in some Wuxia combat that is challenging while having the ability to adjust it to your preference, with a decent overworld to explore with a large amount of side activities you will probably enjoy this one as much as anything mihoyo has splatted out. Do be aware that it intends on selling you cosmetics through a gacha system if you feel you wouldn't be able to resist the urge to spend on costumes.

I do recommend it but it's absolutely [i]not for everybody[/i]. If you're looking for a tight single-player experience, this isn't for you. This might be for you if you like open world adventure games with lots of faffing about.

Basically if you don't like spending a lot of time exploring and getting sidetracked from main quests, this isn't for you.

The game can be played almost fully solo, co-op, or mostly in this quasi-MMO multiplayer mode. For now let's do a basic pros and cons thing.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Fun combat.[/b] It's sorta like Dark Souls or Sekiro in that there's dodging and timed parries. The enemies are really difficult compared to most non Souls-like action RPGs, but for the most part they're well-designed and you can "git gud" relatively easily. A lot of the bosses I beat in 2-3 tries after learning some of the basic attack patterns, and some I even beat on my first try. This is on the medium "Recommended" difficulty. There's good enemy variety among regular enemies too. Even the humanoids have various types of attacks.

[*][b]Gorgeous visuals.[/b] The scenery is very lovely. Open fields of grass or flowers, bamboo forests, rocky mountains and hills, sea and lakeside and riverside views, the bustling city of Kaifeng, the quaint little villages, the depressing ruins and mysterious locations, dungeons, etc., all look great.

Kaifeng gets a special mention as it's one of the most believable cities I've ever seen in any game. Not only is it large and with lots of people, but the layout of the districts and the houses and other buildings all make you believe that people could actually live there. Compare to cities designed for spectacle, like those in most MMORPGs with unnecessarily large structures, sparse actual housing and confusing layouts.

The smaller villages also for the most part make you feel like people live there, though some of the smaller ones feel like there aren't enough houses for everybody. Kaifeng looks like it has enough houses. Small details that really help with immersion.

The character models are beautiful for the most part. I don't just mean being attractive. I mean they're very well-made. Even the uglier or more grotesque bosses have interesting designs.

[*][b]Cosmetics that fit the theme.[/b] So far the game isn't "Fortnite-ified". All the outfits, even the premium ones, could conceivably fit a Chinese wuxia fantasy thing, though some are a bit more fantastic than others, both in terms of magical qualities as well as things like short skirts, which you wouldn't really see in like a wuxia film for example. But it all still fits. No T-shirts and jeans, bodysuits, or costumes from other IP's or anything like that.

[*][b]Fun and rewarding exploration.[/b] If you like exploration, just wandering around and stumbling on things (looking at you Skyrim players), you're gonna love this. You actually do need to explore as progression is tied to going around and doing all the little things you can do. There's various activities from side quests to long puzzles, to shorter puzzles and challenges, chests in various places, hunting and gathering. Cats to pet, but weirdly you can't pet any of the dogs. And bandit camps of course.

[*][b]Lots of other activities.[/b] Sorta tied to the above point, there's a whole lot of minigames that can be played even in multiplayer. There's archery target shooting, a music/rhythm game, a poker-like card game, minigames for healing and debates, fishing, etc.

[*][b]Adjustable difficulty.[/b] Whether you're a more casual player who just wants to chill out, or you really want a challenge, the game can cater to you. Mostly only available in solo mode though, but that's typically where it matters.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Live service.[/b] This will absolutely be a con for a lot of people. It's very, very live service. Lots of currencies, gacha/random draws for cosmetic rewards, battle pass, and so on. And because it's a live service, almost certainly the story will never truly end or will likely have an open-ended "ending" so that when they add a new chapter or expansion, it'll slot right in. So yeah, if you were looking for a tight single-player narrative experience, this ain't it.

[*][b]INCOMPREHENSIBLE STORY.[/b] The story is extremely confusing, with lots of plot holes, missing info, and strange actions by characters. Some people try to say it's localization issues, and while I think that is certainly a factor, I don't think it's the main one. The way the main story is written leaves so many questions as well as baffling decisions by the characters. A lot of scenes seem meaningless, and a lot of events are left unanswered, in a bad way. It's as if the writers forgot about some things and later on just go, "oh yeah I forgot about that" and then just shoehorn it back in. I can't spoil too much here but even if you just glance over at online discussions, it's a whole bunch of people trying to figure out wtf is going on. This is true for both the main quest and almost all of the side stories, at least the ones that have actual story.

[*][b]Confusing UI.[/b] Oh man. Trying to find something in this game's UI can take forever without looking it up or asking in the global chat. There's menus upon menus for everything. Nested menus, and stuff that keeps calling your attention. You learned some lore from a note on the ground? Menu notification with minor inconsequential reward. You met a new NPC? Menu with notification. You had an achievement? Two menu notifications. You're trying to find which of the various menus sold the thing you wanted? Good luck.

[*][b]You [i]must[/i] explore.[/b] This is only a con if you don't like "wasting time" on exploration and just wanna get through the story ASAP. But you really must explore in this game. Progression is directly tied to how much of the world you've explored. Not just with gathering materials or finding new martial arts but also direct increases to strength and other stats tied to finding certain items. Sometimes if you're too weak, you need to spend some time upgrading your equipment, skills and attributes through exploration. I personally like exploration but I can see some players being turned off by this.
[/list]

[h1]Multiplayer? MMO?[/h1]
It's not quite an MMORPG. It's sorta like one though. The main mode is definitely the Solo mode. You start out in that and can't even join the multiplayer until a certain level. As far as I can tell, you can't play the story at all in full multiplayer, which is different from co-op. In multiplayer, you run instanced content, world bosses, minigames, and hang out with other players, and also various PvP things.

The story is largely played in Solo mode, with some Dark Souls style multiplayer aspects where you can invite people to your world in co-op, or temporarily to fight a boss or to heal you if you've got some kind of illness or injury. If you play co-op with a friend, the host's world progression is used, but both players apparently will get credited for quest progression. In fact, both of you can and will trigger cutscenes if you're in the same area, which can get a bit confusing if both of you are doing a quest of looking for clues for example, as both characters will be speaking at once.

Take note however that co-op seems to be peer-to-peer, and the game's netcode is... weird. I tried playing with a friend from across globe and it was only 203 ms ping but utterly unplayable for me as he was hosting. Strangely it works a bit better in full multiplayer, likely because the multiplayer servers are properly hosted at a datacenter rather than somebody's PC.

[h1]Final Thoughts/Conclusion[/h1]
I like it more than I thought I would tbh. This game is absolutely my cup of tea. I love open world sandboxy exploration games. It's got microtransactions and some of them are pretty expensive, but you can live without them. No P2W really. And that's good.

One of the features I thought was really weird to have in-game was chatting with the AI bots / npc's. It's like talking to chat GPT and having a conversation with it. But I took the time to communicate with a monk that lost his daughter and it was kind of interesting talking to him and confiding in him telling him I had lost someone close to me too (ominous foreshadow for those who played the story so far). Then I talked to another npc and how he wanted to punish his wife and he couldn't see eye to eye with me because I kept telling him he was wrong. Haha. Honestly as I said before, it is an interesting game and honestly that portion of alone is refreshing to see in a game. Yes, it uses AI and you can hear it (at least in the English voices) in some of the NPC's but it's nothing that completely breaks immersion or makes the game unplayable. I have only caught an AI voice by an NPC like twice so far.

Professions are really fun and keep the game healthy and can make players go out of there way to help other players. For the core portion of the game, the Co-Op and Solo mode though, the game feels fully fleshed out. Movement is extremely fun through lightness skills/movement and exploring the map is extremely fun for me.

Again, it amazes me that this game is free. try it out at the minimum for a couple of hours.

This game really surprised me with how good the combat is, how well-designed the side quest stories and locations are, the graphics, and the customization. 

The combat/gameplay is obviously heavily inspired by FromSoft games, specifically Sekiro, with a bit of Bloodborne, via parrying, dodging, and weapon switching similar to Bloodborne. (Not visually, it's just swapping to another weapon.)

There are difficulty options ranging from normal to "Legend". I play on Legend and would recommend it, really makes me feel the "Souls-like" aspect (I would not recommend if you dislike that.). I will say, though, enemies can be spongy, and some bosses are just not that hard, but I still enjoy it as of level 55.

Parrying is very important (Though the timing is forgiving) to break enemy stance (or "Qi" in this case), and dodging some unblockable attacks is a must.
 You also have two weapons you can switch between via an ability that does an attack and swaps to your other weapon (Or just using the swap weapon button :P), as well as a bow. 
Healing items are similar to Bloodborne in that they are finite items that you have to buy or craft.
 The abilities are similar to an RPG, using a special attack with a cooldown, and a low-cooldown attack that uses an energy gauge. You also have up to 8 abilities that use the same energy. (Though they are kinda gimmicky and you probably won't use them too much against bosses.) 
There is also stealth, but it isn't that crazy.

The open world is really well designed, mixing incredible graphics with finely tuned locations for a basically AAA experience. Side quests are no different, having weirdly detailed lore and area's that have love and emotion put into them, like a cave with a blind swordswoman with half packed bags and notes showing what she did or has done, hobbies, relationships, and combined with the music and visuals, tell a sad story of someone with a life they don't want anymore.

The customization is also detailed, giving you a lot of control over your face, and lots of clothing and hairstyles are also available, some even being dyeable. 

It's a free gacha game, so obviously, there are microtransactions, but they are 100% cosmetic only, no characters, weapons, etc. The only things in the shop are visual effects, mounts, clothing, and hairstyles. However, you can unlock a decent amount of outfits and hairstyles by just playing. 

There is also a lot of multiplayer content, like PVP co-op missions, bounties, minigames, etc. I haven't delved very far into that, so I can't say much, but it seems pretty fun.

The only catch so far is the shop prices. Gacha rolls are ridiculously expensive, like, 100's of dollars expensive. On top of that, apparently, the Chinese version doesn't have Gacha mechanics and is not even half as expensive, which is unfair, and they have barely "fixed" it. 
Also, there is a boat that, from what I know, is basically an online hangout that some people can buy that costs thousands to maybe even tens of thousands of real U.S dollars.

Also, the English dub is terrible, like, most world bosses have no voice, terrible audio mixing, repeated dialogue, lines just straight up read wrong, etc.

So all in all, if you don't care about the Gacha or shop, you don't have to; the whole game is free, and the items in the shop (As of writing) are all kinda... bad anyway, having visual effects and a lot of ridiculous accessories (In my opinion.). 

I would highly recommend it, as you can just uninstall it later anyway :)

Where Winds Meet strikes me as one of the most ambitious wuxia open-world games in recent years—beautiful, atmospheric, and overflowing with things to do—yet also unmistakably weighed down by its own excess. The combat feels genuinely satisfying, with a sharp focus on timing, parries, and stylish martial-arts techniques that make even ordinary encounters feel cinematic, and the world itself is lush, detailed, and clearly crafted with love for classic Chinese sword-hero storytelling. But at the same time, the game sometimes tries to do too much for its own good: menus are dense, systems overlap in ways that can feel confusing, and the free-to-play structure occasionally casts a shadow over long-term progression. Still, despite the bloat and the occasional technical quirks, I think the game has a rare charm—there’s a sense of discovery, spectacle, and playfulness (sometimes unintentionally, given the infamous goose incidents) that keeps the experience memorable. For players who enjoy wuxia aesthetics, large worlds, and fast, reactive combat, I genuinely believe Where Winds Meet is worth diving into, especially if you’re willing to embrace its quirks as part of its personality rather than flaws.👍👍

Where Winds Meet honestly caught me off guard in a good way. The first thing that really pulled me in was the atmosphere—it’s calm and almost poetic, but when combat starts, it suddenly feels sharp and intense. The world itself is beautiful and feels alive, especially with the flowing landscapes and strong wuxia vibe. It’s the kind of game that makes you slow down, take in the scenery, and explore instead of just sprinting from quest to quest.

Combat feels smooth and stylish, with a good mix of skill and freedom. It never feels too restrictive, and trying out different moves and playstyles is actually fun instead of confusing. I also appreciate that the game focuses more on mood and storytelling rather than nonstop action—it gives everything more weight.

That said, the game can feel overwhelming at the start. There are a lot of systems thrown at you early on, and some things aren’t very clear right away. But once it clicks, the experience becomes much more rewarding.

Overall, Where Winds Meet feels like a game made for players who enjoy immersion, exploration, and a slower, more thoughtful pace. It’s not perfect, but it has a strong personality—and that’s what makes it stick with you.

This game has had such a grasp on me since I've started playing it. The story by itself has had me excited and teary eyed within the same day. This game is more than just a Wuxia RPG; it’s a detailed, living, breathing world set in 10th-century China that lets you define your own legend—whether you’re a noble protector, a cunning rogue, or a traveling physician. Yes, the English localization is a bit janky in spots, and the UI is dense, but the core experience is a stunningly generous package that absolutely deserves your time. It is the Wuxia dream made digital.

I love Asian culture, have recently visited, read many Chinese web novels, and watched quite a few donghuas, and playing this game feels like stepping directly into the worlds I’ve imagined for years. 

From the way healing and scholarship are implemented, to the martial arts they used, stories, and quests.. everything fits with what I’ve always dreamed of. The missions are out of this world, and I really love the story and the open world feel. They even balanced the freedom that comes with open world perfectly.

I would have loved a cultivation system instead of the traditional leveling up (Er-Gen style: Qi Condensation > Foundation Establishment > Core Formation, etc). It was a perfect opportunity to implement such a mechanic, but even with the standard leveling system, the game is still fantastic.

- The graphics are stunning. 
- The quests (both main and side quests) are out of this world. 
- I really love the story line 
- Open world feel is implemented nicely.
- The stat/skill mechanics can be a bit confusing and need some polish, but I believe they are working on it. 
- There are way too many currencies in the game, so simplifying them could make the experience even smoother.
- I have around 50 hours of gameplay so far, and I haven’t noticed any pay to win content. On the other hand, some of the in game costumes you can buy look absolutely gorgeous! (Ngl the basic costume looks amazing too) 
- The end game haven't been reached yet, level cap is unknown, but I can easily tell that there will be some serious grind.
- Ohh finally.. well.. IT IS A FREE GAME!
