Read somewhere that this was originally intended to be a single player game. If that's true, you can definitely see how that could be the case. The solo game play is pretty great, for the most part. The story is interesting enough. The gameplay is pretty fun and exploration/leveling is genuinely rewarding. 

What I hate is that certain injuries require me to deal with other players to get them healed since the NPC healer can't handle certain levels of ailment. So then I get stuck waiting forever to find a player to fix my stuff, unless of course you play with friends (which luckily my boyfriend also plays and takes care of me but before he ranked up healer it was excruciating.) I also feel like they wanted scholar to be as gameplay involved as healer was as far as being multiplayer applied, and I absolutely hate how they integrated it. The jail system is stupid. Other than having the badge of (dis)honor for being jailed for over 160 hours as a joke, this just kills gameplay. (which, what? You want me to be in game jail for a realtime 160 hours for an achievement? ♥♥♥♥ you.) You have to get a player to be your lawyer (scholar) and you need in-game bounty tokens to even get them, which makes an already inconvenient feature even more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying. Not to mention you can just get falsely accused of crimes by NPCs even in solo-mode, and then get your ass beat by a player who's taking in your bounty because you didn't even know there was a bounty board system to hire a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lawyer. 

Multiplayer co-op is also genuinely horrendous. About 1/10th of the time were my friends able to actually join me in the heartseeker combat. There was no understandable reason as to why that was. They were the same level as me, same progression rate as me, in my party, in my team, in my guild, in every possible thing you can imagine, and still it wouldn't let them join. They would get locked out of the arena. And to make it more confusing -- sometimes it DID work and let them join the fight. So I legit don't know what arbitrary function was not functioning. And then on top of all of that, it would sometimes glitch out when we WERE able to fight heartseeker together and say we were both still in the dungeon when we left that could only be resolved by going into online mode, then back into solo mode. Nothing else worked, not even leaving the party/team.

A personal complaint of mine, which again is with a grain of salt because I don't even like playing online mode: I went to online mode to do the disciple/partnership ceremonies, and got killed at random by other players. Legit don't even know how. Was in the screen doing my thing, and when I finished setting up the partnership, was just dead. So that was great!

Also, just a petty grievance: SIGN POSTS WERE A PLAGUE. It works in dark souls because it limits the amount of bloodstain messages and doesn't get in the way when you're trying to interact with other things. This game is littered with them so much that I had to just turn them all off in general so it wouldn't bog my ♥♥♥♥ down.

And aside from my gripes about multiplayer shenanigans: The game is just broken at times. There is a quest at one point where you need to board a warship, and to do so you need to get on a lift. I did that, then fell of the lift because it doesn't keep your character in place while you're riding the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing. So I fell off, and into the water. Was like, whatever no big deal, sure I can call the lift back. Nope. Had to redo the whole quest from the beginning, and honestly didn't even want to at that point.

Combat is weird. Sometimes my Q ability with the spear will lock onto targets and not pop off until I'm in range, or forces me to walk toward a targeted enemy to set off the ability, and then other times it just goes off no problem. Don't know what that's about but it's annoying as ♥♥♥♥. Some stairways are insanely annoying to walk down because your character auto grapples to the banisters in front of you instead of just GOING DOWN. It has driven me to madness on more than one occasion. The wall running is janky as well. I also love having my stamina exhaust because I get caught on a rock that doesn't even make sense getting caught on? I also constantly break my legs and get sprains, even though I always hit my Q to do the safe drop with the bonus to mitigate/remove fall damage. Yay spending 10K coins, because otherwise to "self-heal" you have to just not do anything for an hour in game. 

Also, the puzzles are terribly translated for english speaking users. The first main fortress has a puzzle you legit can't solve unless you understand chinese, as well as at least one of the meow meow puzzles (the lantern puzzle in kaifeng specifically. From the very start, when Where Winds Meet drops you into its extensive, wind-swept world, one thing instantly becomes clear: this is not just a game; this is a love letter to everything that I adore about murim. It holds that perfect blend of honor, martial spirit, ancient philosophy, and sky-splitting swordsmanship that makes it so addictive.

A world that feels like peak Murim fantasy

Every location feels like it was sculpted straight from a legendary wuxia epic: towering cliffs, lonely temples, whispering bamboo forests. As someone who loves murim stories, I instantly felt at home. The world is alive, breathing with that fierce, noble energy, where every breeze feels like it carries the echoes of warriors past.

Pure Art Combat

The swordplay is basically a murim fever dream brought to life.
It's not just combat; its moving poetry.

Every strike, every dodge, every rooftop sprint feels like reading a martial arts novel where the protagonist grows stronger not just in skills, but in spirit. It's that kind of fighting system wherein you do not simply battle with enemies, but you duel their philosophies.

A Story That Cuts Deep

The plot is heavy with emotional weight, reflecting everything I love about murim:

the push and pull between fate and self-determination.

the tension between honor and survival.

the quiet, aching loneliness of a wandering swordsman.

It's beautifully written, never melodramatic, and full of those moments when your heart just stops for a second.

Characters Who Feel Like They Walked Out of a Cultivation Classic

You meet warriors with tragic pasts, sages with cryptic wisdom, rivals who push you to be better, and companions who feel etched into your memory. Every character feels like they belong in the highest tier of murim storytelling: complex, flawed, and unforgettable.

Visuals That Redefine "Beautiful"

It doesn’t just represent a martial world; it pays homage to it.

The flowing robes, the drifting petals, the silent snowfall on temple roofs… all speak volumes. The wind is nearly a character in its own right.

Music That Moves You

Soft flutes, heart-stirring vocals, and melodies that feel like wandering through ancient mountains with nothing but your thoughts and your sword. It's atmospheric in the most emotional of ways.

Final Verdict: Full Marks 10/10
Being a person who loves murim with my whole heart, Where Winds Meet didn't just meet expectations; it shattered them, rebuilt them, and sent them soaring on a gust of wind.

This game is a true masterpiece.

A journey. A feeling. 10/10 would be a must-play for anyone who ever loved the spirit of murim. Soar away, my friends! This review is inspired by bugdouglas

The quality of games emerging from China these days is genuinely impressive. As a long-time fan of Wuxia literature, I can say this game absolutely excels at immersing you in that fantastical world.

It features a massive, truly open world that is packed with compelling side activities. It's clear the developers poured a tremendous amount of effort into crafting this beautiful, detailed world, making the exploration fantastic. Visually, the game is stunning—I haven't spent this much time taking glam shots since my days in FFXIV.

I highly recommend this title to anyone seeking a deep dive, whether you love the exploration loop of Genshin Impact or the rich progression of an MMO.

Personal Complaints

- The sheer volume of side quests delivered to you when traveling quickly across the map can be overwhelming. As an anxious 100% gamer dude, this is compounded by the worrying possibility (as I've read) that progressing certain story/campaign elements might cause you to permanently lose access to specific side quests. I have low tolerance for P2W and I'm surprised how little there is. I'd put it in line with Path of Exile's monetization, which IMO is the gold standard for F2P games.

All that said, gameplay/combat is great. Very challenging if you play on harder modes. Fluid animations and interesting build/weapon diversity. Visuals and audio are TOP NOTCH!!! Better than a lot of AAA games I've seen. The lighting and ambience in the game are tremendous and immersive as hell.

**UPDATE** - The second chapter is WAY better than the first! Kaifeng's storyline is compelling and dark so I wanted to update this review.

The only real downside is the story and VA (some of which is poorly done AI voicing). The story is really pretty mediocre and most dialog is stilted and doesn't feel natural. It's a passable story though so far and even had some really cool moments/chapters but don't go into this expecting a gripping narrative. As for side quest and events it's standard MMO-ish content. Some writing is ok, some not so much.

Let me be clear though, the world-building and lore are actually pretty cool. The "Wuxia" time period is interesting and handled fairly well, unlike the main quest narrative.

Oh and the systems and menus are a lot to wrap your head around at first. I'd recommend to explore a lot in the first zone and don't just rush the main story. Learn about the basics of upgrading your weapons/skills/passives to keep them in line with your character and solo mode level. There's multiple layers of gear/skill progression in the "DEVELOP" menu. Do it ALL to feel powerful and don't forget the things called "Oddities" which are essential permanent passives. Do just those things and you'll be ok. Learn the other 10 million menus later. LOL

Definitely try the game out. And if you choose "Legend" difficulty at character select (and you can only do it then or you miss it forever), remember if you drop it down to Expert or Normal you CANNOT go back to LEGEND ever again.

Where Winds Meet is the only game where I’ve been able to:
🐈 Pet stray cats like I’m running an ancient Chinese cat café,
🤏 Accidentally steal something worth 2 coins,
🚨 Get hunted down like a war criminal,
🔒 And spend the night in prison reflecting on my life choices.

The world is gorgeous — the kind of scenery that makes you stop and say, “Wow.” Then you press the wrong button, steal a turnip, and suddenly it’s Les Misérables but with better architecture.

And of course… the legend… the myth… the $40,000 ship. 🚤💸
Some brave, financially fearless soul dropped forty. thousand. dollars. on a digital boat. A boat that does approximately:
• Nothing ⚪
• Nada ⚪
• Jack squat ⚪

It exists purely as an expensive floating monument to impulsive spending. Honestly, this boat is the real final boss of the game.

Combat? It’s fine. It’s flashy. It’s dramatic. It’s the sort of thing where you mash buttons and hope nobody notices you’re actually terrible. ✨⚔️
Story? It’s there… somewhere… drifting like a leaf in the wind, probably meeting itself occasionally.

But hey — there are cats. So many cats. 🐱❤️
If the devs added nothing but 200% more cats, I’d bump my review to Overwhelmingly Positive immediately.

Pros:

🌄 Stunning visuals
🐈 Lots of cats
🐈‍⬛ Even more cats
🔒 Prison roleplay (accidental or otherwise)
😌 Immersive wuxia vibes

Cons:

🤺 Combat that feels like a midlife crisis in animation form
🚫 Story pacing powered by fortune cookies
🚤 A $40k boat that does less than a real rubber duck
💸 Monetization that politely asks for your wallet… then elbows you in the ribs

Final Verdict:

Play it if you like wuxia worlds, cats, and mild legal trouble.
Avoid the ship store unless you have the financial self-control of a monk.

This game is supremely janky in myriad ways. 

Kaifeng city is presumably best translated as Single Digit Framerate city. There are about thirty(?) random minigames that have nothing to do with anything. Gacha slots don't seem terribly generous, and you had best enjoy the riveting depth of 10th century politics because a many an NPC is happy to weigh in at length about such topics as the illegitimate minting of iron coins against the far superior copper, where to buy and sell quality grains, and so on and so forth.

However, unlike most other 2025 games, this one is not only fun to play, but actually interesting. The jank facilitates imagination. The boss fights are challenging and require you to try, co-op is very social, and side quests are unique enough that they don't feel much like an Assassin's Creed style endless checklist to nowhere. The main campaign is also entertaining, provided you don't mind fantasy drama, and of course, reading subtitles. 

If nothing else, Where Winds Meet proves that western game devs especially are risk-adverse to a terrible fault. In turn, I'd recommend this game to pretty much anyone. It's reminded me that I don't hate open-world games, I just hate the way most are made.

(Be warned that changing the difficulty will lock you out from going back.

My personal opinion about the game is ultimately good, but I seem to have a problem having friends who also enjoy this Wuxia genre. I am more of a multiplayer person but there are moments in this game where after beating a difficult boss makes you get chills and excited. My personal favorite was the "Black Rogue" in Keifang, she was difficult, especially when I had 16k Strength when the recommended was around 20k+. For Wuxia fans or for Manhua fans, this is one to check out.

However the good is soo good, there are some cons to this game. The outfits in this game can be expensive and cheap depending on what you look at. Like in a car dealership, there will be the nice 2026 Dodge Chargers and then the used Honda Accord. Some outfits here are about 600 pearls, or roughly 6 USD, and some other outfits are around 2.6k Pearls, which goes about 26 dollars. This game pays with pearls so you will ultimately spend 10 USD or 30 USD for either, and thats just the tip of the ice berg.

If you wish to pull a Gatcha, the pity system kind of scams you. If you hit Pity, which will happen a lot, it'll cost about 150 USD. The Pity doesn't give you a chance for the outfit, it just straight up gives you a "orb". This beautiful gem is a type of currency that can be used at an exchange shop. (Keep in mind, this "orb" costs about 150 USD). The outfit you want costs about 2 orbs, but its okay because you can buy previous draw outfits for the same amount. 

Now the bigger one is if you decide to spend that "orb" for a sword which costs 1 "orb" i believe. You get a pretty weapon (Not for me cause it breaks the immersion). I have seen youtubers and fellow players spend up to 1000 USD to max it out with its cool effects and style, and its randomized so you dont get the one you want unless you keep rerolling which costs even more money.

Then ofc, there is the expensive ship which we wont get into cause thats straight up 20k USD, which is can literally buy you or your mom a brand new Kia K5. 

So do I recommend this game after writing all this.... Yeah, but dont spend all your money in this and wait for LOTM to come out, then spend your 20k on whatever is in that.

I walked into [b]Where Winds Meet[/b] expecting nothing more than another stylish wuxia RPG—fun martial arts, pretty scenery, maybe a dramatic cutscene or two. It isn’t even a fully polished one.

Some villages blend together.
Some regions feel too large and underused.
Certain NPCs loop the same lines as if they’ve forgotten who they are.

There were moments where I stopped and thought:

[i]“This world deserves more stories.”[/i]

And yet… despite the emptiness in spots, I kept exploring.
Not for rewards — but because the world simply felt [u]alive[/u].

[h3]A Personal Example[/h3]
At one point, I wandered off a main path and ended up on a lonely cliff during sunrise. Nothing happened—no quest, no cutscene, no reward.
But it was one of my favorite moments in the entire game.

That’s the magic of this world.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]⚔️ COMBAT: WHEN IT’S GOOD, IT’S ART. WHEN IT’S BAD, IT’S CHAOS.[/h2]

Let me be brutally honest: combat is both a [b]masterpiece[/b] and a [strike]disaster[/strike] (at times).

[h3]The Beautiful Side[/h3]
One-on-one duels feel like choreographed martial-arts films:

• Perfect parries
• Aerial flips
• Internal-energy bursts
• Finishers that hit with emotional weight

When everything aligns, the combat isn’t just good — it’s art.

[h3]The Chaotic Side[/h3]
But then you get into group battles and suddenly:

• The camera panics
• Lock-on jumps between enemies
• You get stunned in the middle of long animations
• The screen becomes a storm of flashing lights and numbers

Sometimes it’s glorious.
Sometimes it’s a mess.
Sometimes it’s both at once.

But when the system works, it reminds you why the frustrations are worth enduring.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]🎭 STORY: EMOTIONAL POTENTIAL WITH RUSHED EXECUTION[/h2]

The game begins with mystery, loneliness, and a sense of drifting purpose.
You are a swordsman shaped by tragedy in a collapsing world.

I love stories like this — stories about lost souls wandering through broken landscapes.

Some characters grabbed my heart instantly:

• The general torn between peace and ambition
• The traumatized assassin shaped by war
• The merchant girl desperate for freedom
• The scholar trying to preserve philosophy as everything burns

These characters deserved more time.
More depth.
More breathing room.

[h3]Where It Hurts[/h3]
Some arcs end too suddenly.
Some emotions don’t get to fully bloom.
Some plot twists feel rushed.

And the protagonist — despite being interesting — sometimes feels too expressionless in scenes that beg for more emotion.

But make no mistake: the game succeeds in delivering moments that hit hard.

[spoiler]A certain mid-game revelation about a companion’s past genuinely surprised me emotionally.[/spoiler]

The story is uneven, but its emotional core is real.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]🎎 SIDE ACTIVITIES: FREEDOM THAT SOMETIMES OUTSHINES THE MAIN GAME[/h2]

One thing the game absolutely nails is the sense of being a true wandering wuxia hero.

You can:

• Heal people as a doctor
• Judge village disputes
• Explore ruins
• Pick up random jobs
• Learn rare martial arts
• Craft, trade, hunt, meditate
• Or simply walk with no destination

This freedom is intoxicating.

But…

[h3]The Downside[/h3]
Some side quests feel deep, emotional, even poetic.
Others feel rushed, shallow, or unfinished.

The inconsistency is the only thing holding this brilliant system back.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]🎨 VISUALS & SOUND: THE HEART AND SOUL OF THE EXPERIENCE[/h2]

The art direction is stunning.
The lighting, the clothing physics, the particle effects — everything feels handcrafted.

The soundtrack?
A masterpiece of traditional Chinese instruments blended with modern cinematic style.

There were moments when I stood on a mountain peak and simply let the music wash over me.
[b]This is a game made by artists, not technicians — and you can feel it.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]🧩 PERFORMANCE: BEAUTIFUL, BUT CRACKED[/h2]

Even though my performance was mostly smooth, the issues are real:

• Frame drops in crowded cities
• Texture pop-in
• Quest progression bugs
• Animation clipping
• Occasional dialogue glitches
• Rare crashes

Its ambition exceeds its stability.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]❤️ OVERALL: AN IMPERFECT MASTERPIECE WITH A WARRIOR’S HEART[/h2]

Where Winds Meet is flawed.
Where Winds Meet is inconsistent.
Where Winds Meet is sometimes frustrating.

And despite all that…

[b]Where Winds Meet is unforgettable.[/b]

It made me feel:

• Peace during quiet travels
• Sadness during reflective moments
• Awe at its landscapes
• Nostalgia for a world I never knew
• Adrenaline in duels
• Wonder in its artistic vision

It’s rare to find a game this ambitious, this emotional, this willing to take risks even when it stumbles.

[b]When it falters, it frustrates me.
When it shines, it moves me.
And I will remember it for a long time.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]⭐ Final Personal Score: 8.5/10[/h2]

Not perfect.
Not polished.
But incredibly emotional, artistic, ambitious — and unforgettable.
[b]I Recommend You To Play This Game![/b]

This is a masterpiece. In a very shallow way I could say it's like The Witcher, Skyrim and Guild Wars 2 had a child in ancient China, but it's so much more. It has quirky quests, one of the most amazing storylines, in a beautiful setting (not only visuals but the whole thing - music, voice acting, the works). It has random NPCs with more personality than a lot of recent RPG main characters. The world is believable even with it's fantasy flair (in fact it contributes to that effect). There is SO MUCH to do, without it feeling like a chore. I could go on and on with praising it but honestly? Go play it. Of course there are some annoyances (feels like there is a separate game of ... game menus) but the most painful one is the translation. There is a lot of subtlety involved pretty much everywhere and unless you have some knowledge of Chinese lore a lot of what you do and what you're doing is going to be lost. And about the monetization, it's there but it doesn't impact a free player in any way, it's just (gorgeous) cosmetics.
All in all, this game made me dream, made me cry, and I'm all the more grateful for its existence. Hope it will continue up this lane.

This is the best free to play game I've ever played hands down. It is a brilliant combination of a soulslike singleplayer RPG with a massive wuxia MMO like Age of Wushu. But inherently it is better because not only can players choose their own challenge difficulty, they have the option to progress by themselves or with others. The best thing about this game is there is absolutely NO pay to win aspects. There are only cosmetics in the cash shop and everything in the battle pass is pay for convenience. There is no daily grind routine that you have to worry about. They have a perfect system based on weekly activity so you can play as much or as little as you want each day. There is a catch up mechanism that allows players to cheaply buy materials with earned in-game currency. Because the gear power resets every 90 days, new players never fall permanently behind veterans. The devs want to ensure that even if you take a break, you can jump back in next season without any penalties. I could continue writing about how beautiful the seamless open world is or how satisfying it is to beat the well designed bosses. But don't just take my word for it, try it out yourself. You don't need me or others to convince you. If you don't like the style or the theme of the game, that's totally okay. But I can almost guarentee that something about Where Winds Meet will capture your heart and you will realize that your experience in Jianghu will become an unforgettable memory.

I went into this game a bit skeptical, to often trailers and demos look better then a game plays, but I was pleasantly surprised, the game performs very well and looks stunning, after a little getting used to things, rebinding a few controls I'm solidly hooked, there is enough variety to keep many people busy from exploration, to combat, to casual games. Considering its free its definitely worth a go to see if it scratches an itch.

Aside from the most common things to be expected it is worth noting that this martial arts themed game has a very enjoyable story with terrific cinematics and in the Chinese language the voice acting is super solid, its basically just like watching a Wuxia film except you get to play the part of one of the heroes in the story, it has tension, levity and drama all mixed together.

The movement once you get used to it is very polished feeling, you are very soon jumping over buildings springing off trees and running across water or flying through the sky on a spear like martial artist from Crouching tiger hidden dragon! And there is a component of skill involved in the movement as you get better you can navigate to places like a true master. It also translates into the PVP very smoothly.

Another important factor for me is the Co-Op mode, I've been trying to find a fun game to play with friends that allows for a variety of skill and times between us and is still fun and this game provides this, when we get together the fun is in sharing the story and scenes, solving puzzles, and trying not to get smashed fighting bosses, and others we just chill and play the mini-games and hang out. They did a really good job at providing different types of players to play and have fun together.

To add more to the puzzle part, most things in the world have a puzzle or mechanic or adventure involved in learning , you want to learn a new skill you sneak into a base and steal it from a master in that skill, you want to get through a dungeon you have to pay attention to what is around you and then solve problems based on the clues the devs provided along the way, it really does reward players who enjoying puzzles, and for those that don't just read the answer from someone's Sign Post. 

Some people might be put off by the Wuxia aspect but I think if given a chance it will grow on people as it fits perfectly with the style of game and provides a cohesive narrative behind the mechanics making it more engaging.

The only issues I would present are very technical in nature, things to do with lighting transitions, sliding monsters at times in coop if not properly sync'd with the host client, and items popping up too closely when coming into view or distance. These are momentary and more surprising then problematic it would be a perfect experience if not for these little issues which is amazing for a free game.

Most F2P games are very much pay to win but this game is heavy on the cosmetics, and it can get super expensive to buy some of the outifits but even if you don't spend a dime you get gifted many great outfits for free and there are plenty of low cost items and most importantly you can not purchase power ups or equipment that effects your stats, I think the only advantage you can get is some resources which you can easily grind out. 

In regards to pvp there is a lot of potential variety in the dual weapons, and martial arts skills you choose to equipment, along with the internal arts that will provide bonuses on top of that, you can create a lot of valid builds and most importantly it still comes down to player skill to be able to time and execute actions that matter the most. It is a ton fun! 

There are so many different systems, the menu and build of things can be overwhelming but just take your time and have fun.

I would highly recommend playing it even just for the open section and the initial battle and story, you will have a good grasp of whether the game is for you pretty quickly, just keep in mind you start off like a young martial artist who is not very trained, and slowly you get introduced to dual weapons, new martial arts, and inner arts, along the way as you gain access to more game play modes, online modes, guilds, sects, and challenges. Don't think you will have the game figured out in a few hours, or days, or weeks. There is a ton of content in this game, and the Chinese version is a year ahead so a ton more to come.

Please go into it open minded and understand the game does have strong Asian vibe and style, it is showing off in a fantastical way some of the beauty and mysticism of the Chinese culture, that is part of its charm, it has a different vibe and pacing and I would encourage you to embrace it as part of the experience. 

One last thing, for any parents, I think the rating is 12+ is a bit borderline, there is lots of combat, and while its not gore, there is death and more mature themes presented in the game. But there is also a lot of wonderful stories besides those, it is not all that, but worth mentioning.

8/10

The World & Visuals

The strongest part of the game. Environments feel alive misty mountains, lantern lit towns, bamboo forests that react to wind. The art direction is outstanding. Exploring the world is genuinely peaceful, and sometimes I just stop to take screenshots.

Movement & Exploration

Parkour and wuxia mobility are smooth and fun. Wall running, gliding, water walking, rooftop jumps it sells the fantasy extremely well. Traveling never feels boring.

Combat

Combat is fast, stylish, and varies a lot depending on the weapon you pick. Swords feel sharp and responsive, spears have great reach, and even “utility” tools like umbrellas feel surprisingly viable.
Boss fights can be flashy and satisfying, though sometimes inconsistent in difficulty.

Story & Characters

The main story is serviceable not groundbreaking, but interesting enough to keep you moving forward. Some side quests are surprisingly heartfelt, blending folklore with personal drama.
Character facial animation could be better, but voice acting (especially in Chinese) is solid. And for the love of god PLEASE play in Chinese dub.

Audio

The OST is beautiful. Traditional instruments, calm ambience, and dramatic battle themes help strengthen the wuxia mood.

Multiplayer

Works, but still feels a bit experimental. Coop is fun for roaming the world or doing bosses together, but some activities can be chaotic. Netcode is mostly stable.

Issues

-Occasional fps drop in Kaifeng city

-Minor bugs and NPC clipping

-Some quests feel formulaic

-UI could be more polished

None of these are deal breakers, but they do remind you the game is still evolving. 😉

A truly inspiring game. It is hard to believe that it is free. Yes, there is paid content in-game, but you may fully enjoy the game without buying it, it's mostly for character design. Though there are a lot of free items, anyway.

I love that you may fully customise your character: starting from appeareance and ending with skill customisation. You may pick one of 7 types of weapons. For some of them there are different martial arts styles available, so you may choose how to wield your spear, for example. It's easy to get used to fight mechanics. I personally prefer infernal twin blades and panacea fan as my weapon pair: for shift attacks and quick heal.
Very important info for all stealthy rogues: rope darts are available in this game!

The overall experience is positive: you may just enjoy open-world exploration. There is already a lot of content. For exploration you may pick one of the modes:
— Solo: you travel alone in your own world, completing the quests;
— Co-op: you travel with your friend(s) in yours or their world, fight together;
— Online: you walk around with all the other wanderers. May interract with them.

Another interesting detail: there are different ways to be included in a social group: guilds, sects and professions.
Guilds are created by players, and you may pick the type that suits you the most:
— combat guilds (fight together);
— leisure guilds (just chill with friends, play guzheng and chat);
— exploration guilds (explore the world together).
[b]Btw, join my guild Horangi![/b] I help with fights and can heal injuries.

Sects are also a nice addition, that's more like a plot content, each sect is linked to certain weapon mastery and certain type of activity. Like fan users healing, rope darts stealing, all good.

One more plus: you can play guzheng, learn how to play Chinese chess and much more.
Main plot is quite interesting, side quests sometimes heartbreaking.

Only problems: sometimes game is lagging in co-op + English translation is probably AI, sometimes looks weird.

Overall experience is great. That's one of the best games with open-world exploration, rich lore and a lot of activities: both social and mini games.

i cant believe this game is free, Where the Winds Meet is one of those rare open-world titles that actually feels alive. It blends wuxia fantasy, historical drama, and player freedom in a way that’s refreshing if you’ve been craving something beyond the usual Western RPG formula.

The world is the star here. Villages, forests, rivers, and bustling cities all feel handcrafted, and the verticality of the environments makes traversal genuinely fun. Whether you’re sprinting across rooftops, riding across sweeping grasslands, or diving into duels straight out of a classic martial-arts film, the game constantly rewards exploration.

Combat is fast, stylish, and surprisingly flexible. You can approach situations with stealth, swordsmanship, magic-like martial abilities, or even nonviolent solutions. The variety of stances and special techniques makes every fight feel like a choreographed moment, especially when facing elite enemies.

Storytelling leans into choices and consequences, and while not every narrative beat lands perfectly, the characters and their moral dilemmas feel grounded in the era. The game lets you role-play meaningfully—sometimes through dialogue, sometimes through action, and sometimes through what you choose not to do.

Performance is decent, though not flawless. Expect the occasional dip in crowded areas and some rough edges typical of a large open-world RPG. None of it breaks the experience, but optimization patches will help.

If you enjoy wuxia, open-world discovery, or RPGs that prioritize player agency, Where the Winds Meet is absolutely worth your time. It’s ambitious, atmospheric, and packed with moments that feel uniquely its own.
i like it !!!

Honestly, Where Winds Meet caught me off guard in the best way. I went in expecting some super generic wuxia game with copy-paste combat and a “Genshin but more realistic” vibe. But after putting about 15 hours in and hitting level 32, I can say it’s way better than I thought it’d be.

The combat is the first thing that surprised me. I thought it’d be a button-mashy snoozefest, but it actually takes skill. You have to pay attention to timing, spacing, and reactions,it feels way more like a real wuxia duel than I expected from a free game. Landing perfect counters or chaining styles together is honestly addicting.

Movement is wild too. You get that classic wuxia freedom, running up walls, gliding across rooftops, zipping around like you’re straight out of a martial arts movie. Traversing the world feels fun all by itself.

And the story? It’s actually rich. I’m still early in, so there’s a lot I haven’t seen yet, but even so, the worldbuilding and quests feel more polished than most free-to-play titles. It gives you enough mystery and drama to keep you curious without feeling overwhelming.

Overall, this is a genuinely good game,not “good for free,” but good-good. I still have a ton to explore, but if the rest of the game keeps this quality, I can see myself sinking a lot more hours into it.

If you’re into wuxia, open-world games, or just want something fresh to try, this one’s honestly worth a shot.

This is the game that literally does everything, and does it well. This is an immense and lively open world Action RPG. Many of the systems of this game are reminiscent of Genshin, Where Genshin tends to include a lot of different systems/minigames though, many of them tend to be very shallow almost tech demos of what they would like to include. The many systems and minigames in Where Winds Meet are very fleshed out and engaging.

The game features full building mechanics where you can place homes and items practically anywhere in the world you please. This will soon be expanded to allow building guild towns in the shared guild space as well as a full town management system where you recruit NPCs to harvest resources and live in spaces you build for them.

They crammed GTA in here as well. You can commit crimes by stealing from or hurting other NPCs, as well as breaking things that aren't yours. Bounties can be placed on your head before long and you can be arrested and thrown in jail for your crimes.

The combat also feels amazing with a parry system and satisfying movement and timing to your attacks. Bosses are challenging and offer variety in their mechanics. Every boss also has a solo mode version with a more souls-like fighting pattern, and an online mode version that require full teams of players to take down with MMO style patterns and mechanics.

You get this all for free with monetization that is purely cosmetic. This game is an absolute must play that I would recommend to anyone that likes some meat to their game's bones.

Where Winds Meet stands out as a rare blend of beauty, emotion, and dynamic gameplay. Its world is crafted with breathtaking detail, offering peaceful landscapes filled with sunlight, ancient architecture, and flowing rivers. Yet beneath its beauty lies an unsettling edge—misty forests, abandoned ruins, and haunting supernatural elements that add layers of tension and mystery. This balance between serene and eerie environments makes exploration constantly engaging.

Gameplay is fluid and expressive, allowing players to embrace the freedom of wuxia movement and combat. Every battle feels like a dance, combining martial-arts agility, strategic choices, and creative approaches to challenges. The many features—from parkour-like traversal to varied combat stances—make each moment feel fresh and rewarding.

Multiplayer adds another enjoyable dimension. Sharing the world with friends turns exploration into a lively adventure, where teamwork, sudden chaos, and shared discoveries build unforgettable experiences. It feels natural, enhancing the game without overshadowing its core design.

At its heart, the game’s story gives it emotional weight. It explores themes of identity, conflict, and personal struggle, presenting characters with depth and motivations that feel real. The narrative is touching, memorable, and elevates the entire journey.

In the end, Where Winds Meet is more than just an action RPG—it is a beautifully crafted experience that blends heartfelt storytelling with thrilling gameplay and stunning scenery.
Visuals, storytelling and gameplay are absolutely magnificent! Lets just hope that the developer doesn't give up with this.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
If you like reading those wuxia novels or manhua, specifically the martial arts genre and hoping to see a big enough studio to make a decent game about it. This will be your dream game for a couple weeks or maybe even longer depending on how they want to approach the updates for this game. That is at the cost, you're patient enough to understand and endure the convoluted UI/UX designs and buggy multiplayer experiences that is.

There's a quite a bit of stuff you can do in this game, they made a lot of gameplay systems to entertain the players other than combat. From fishing, debating, wrestling, healer, etc. Pretty much most of them you'll be doing since it progress your combat skills, gears and add quite a decent amount of buffs and mechanics that you will need. Don't expect them to have a lot of depth, since they're pretty much just mini-games and quick little activities you can do all over the world. It's not the main focus, but it really enhanced the overall experiences and vibes of the wuxia world. For me, exploring the world and finding all sorts of events, fights and stories that is happening in this crafted world is the main point of this game.

The combat itself is satisfying and fluid enough to make it feel nice to play with, there's quite a bit of weapons and skills to choose from that you can mix and match to make your own, of course there's still optimal sets, but you can use whatever you prefer and still do well enough. The enemies other than the small mobs is pretty engaging to make you keep an eye and don't lose focus (as long as you don't turn on the auto-parry, it pretty much trivialize and ruin the combat engagement, so I advise to turn it off even when playing on a easier difficulty. If you want a real challenge that will make you consider inviting friends or matchmaking for help, do legend difficulty, besides it's only hard for the first time fighting new bosses and they get easier after) The amount of combat content "for now", seems to be enough since they limit all players level-up based on real-time days, some may be fan of it, some may not like it at all (I personally like it as long as it's done properly, it keep things fresh without quickly getting stale) but I can't say how it will do after we can max our level later on.

For the story itself, it's nothing mind breaking or disappointing, right now it feels like the story is focusing more of the beginning of our character's journey. So, I can't judge too much about it, the executions for the voice actor (I'm using Chinese dub), cutscenes, flow of the story, the humor/comedy or serious moment of the game and pretty much how entertaining it is, is mid with some high point that I will not spoil, at the very least the story will amuse you if you're not the skip everything kinda person. We'll have to wait and see how will the story progress later on.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
Now, for the negative, I mentioned before the convoluted UI/UX and buggy multiplayer/co-op. Let me explain more in detail, the game sucks at showing you how stuff works and where it is, there's a lot of menus inside menus with a lot of stuff begging to be click one by one. You will be fighting with the UI and the lack of proper information. Stuff missing or not loading correctly and a whole lot more. They need to simplify and organize the whole thing. Because right now, you'll be dependent on clicking the item you want or need, then just click the button beside it to automatically be navigated to the right menu. Not to mention how weird and confusing it is to create your team to do co-op contents and what button do what.

The co-op experiences itself is buggy and cumbersome, sometimes players got kicked out from the boss battle and now you need to invite them back to the boss arena or they just couldn't at all. A lot of times the loading screen sucks and the battle already begun and the boss managed to hit you first with no way to defend yourself. The lack of information about how co-op works and the effect of it to the boss and how things will be affected. Lastly, the most annoying thing is how only the host could progress the quests on co-op. So, if you helped your friend finished a certain quest and finally killed the boss, when you get back to your own world, you STILL have to do it again yourself. Your friends can claim chests on your world that progress both of you, but the quest itself is separated and that SUCKS. period. It discourage friends to play together and make things boring since you need to do quests multiple times. It's just main quests and side missions you'll do once anyway, you're not going to be suddenly over/under-powered just because you got helped or finished this with your friends, it's nothing game breaking to allow progressions between players, let us progress together with the missions. So many games like this sucks at making a nice enjoyable co-op experiences on the world and main/side missions, be unique and come up with some ways to change this.


There's a lot more negatives and positives I haven't mentioned yet in detail or at all, for example the monetization, the battle royale mode, level scaling, gear system, etc. But the game itself is definitely worth a try, especially for the wuxia fans out there.

Update : I have to put an emphasis on the fighting the UI and menus, because wow, there are times I have to restart the game because of black screen, menus not appearing/missing (from combat, other player profile, minigames, etc), glitched UI and many more. The "Concealer"/Guessing Word minigame often turned my screen black and now I can't interact or do anything other than to close the game and restart it. (This is still valid till this day, at least for me. More over, I don't know why but quite a bit of times, I have to load the game two or three times for the loading bar to appear after clicking the continue button on the start menu)

This game brings the world of Wuxia to life. It captures many amazing elements of Chinese lore and storytelling to the west and it's completely free to play. The only paid elements is for costumes but in-game unlocks already features plenty of amazing outfits and hairs. 

The main story of this game has been captivating and touching so far and I really appreciate the visual storytelling it provides with its cutscenes and build up. The side content is also engaging, there's some misses with weird puzzles but most of them are fun and more importantly they are unique from one another. The side stories and dungeons do not feel reptitive as they all feature different types of puzzles and stories and feature fun boss fights as well.

The game also does a good job of pacing the population with IRL timers for breakthroughs of levels / story quests. Although it may feel too long at times, it helps people catch up and, more importantly, gives them incentive and time to explore the world and take their time enjoying the dialogue and content in the vast open world.

A couple downsides in the game currently that they could fix are with Sects (ranking up) and UI/UX design. For sects, there are various exploits that lead to a feeling of not wanting to "properly" progress to rank up (as its competitive with other people in your "shard") and also some Sects like Silver Needle have very annoying upkeep week-to-week when including the exploits of other people in the shard. The game also just has WAY too many menus/hidden buttons and often times, even as an experienced gamer, it can be difficult to find the menu I was just at moments ago. Keeping track of everything and weeklies is an annoyance for sure.

Overall though, I think the game is amazing and worthwhile playthrough even as just a singleplayer experience, especially since its free to play.

Wow.

I felt compelled to write this after my experience this morning—because it perfectly captures what Where Winds Meet feels like.

I opened my map, noticed a quest, and headed in. It took me into a small dungeon filled with puzzles, minor fights, chests, clues… the whole thing probably took 20 minutes before I reached the final boss. He was tough—took me four tries. After beating him, I explored the area and noticed a creek running out into a waterfall that seamlessly dropped me right back into the open world.

Then I saw a massive stone pillar out in the ocean, connected to the mountains by a rope bridge. So of course I went to investigate. I climbed the mountain, fought a few roaming groups, found some rundown temples and chests, and eventually crossed the rope bridge—while four archers and a ballista lit me up the entire way. Barely survived that. At the top was another group guarding a small chest. A little disappointing… until I read a player marker pointing down a cliff face to an eagle’s nest. I climbed down, fed the eggs with meat I’d stolen from a sleeping bear earlier, and that let me track the eagle’s flight and steal a new skill from it.

I climbed down the pillar, explored the shore, saw a cave indicator below me, and realized the entrance was on the opposite side—so now I’m at the entrance of an entirely new dungeon. All of this because I decided to “check out that rock.”

This is what the game does constantly. You head somewhere with a purpose and end up stumbling into five other adventures: mini-games, fishing, archery trials, oddities, horse taming, stealth missions, random AI-driven NPC events. The world just feels alive. You never know what’s around the next corner.

The game is overwhelming at first—there are a ton of systems, and I’m still digging through menus after a week of play. My build and gear aren’t optimized and I don’t care. Take it slow. Pay attention. Explore. That’s where the magic is.

And best of all: no pay-to-win. The battle pass gives some convenience, but nothing you can’t get just by playing. I haven’t bought anything yet—cosmetics haven’t tempted me—but honestly, I want to support this game. It’s easily worth a full AAA price tag. I’d have no problem paying $80 for this.

But it’s free-to-play.

Surprisingly amazing game with huge depth and variety.
I didn’t have high expectations, but the game turned out to be incredibly complex and immersive.

+ Pros:
Highly detailed world full of exploration, stories, and NPCs that feel alive.
Rich content: play solo, co-op with specific players, or jump into the MMO world packed with people.
Unique health system: you can get injured, treated by NPCs or other players, and some clans are focused entirely on healing others.
GTA-style freedom: rob NPCs, fight them, escape from the police, get imprisoned (even for real-time days!) and place bounties on players.
Minecraft elements: build bases, craft materials, and even “cheese” some bosses with clever tricks.
Extensive PVP options: 1v1, 2v2, 5v5, battle-royale modes, plus fun competitions like fishing, sumo, archery, mahjong, etc.
Many NPCs can chat using AI, and friendships with them can unlock gifts.

– Cons:
Lots of content means key missions only appear while exploring, which can make progression feel a bit unorganized.
Defensive mechanics (block/dodge/relive force) are tough on higher difficulties; bosses hit hard and require precise timing.
Most guides and player info are on Chinese platforms, so international players might miss important details.

Verdict:
A fantastic, deeply immersive game with a living, interconnected world. It’s rare to see a game create such a believable and atmospheric environment.

Wuxia has been part of my life since childhood. I grew up watching countless TV shows and playing video games in the genre. But no game has captured that magic quite like this one. It delivers everything I love about Wuxia, and best of all, it's not pay-to-win. The world is stunning, the story is engaging, many unexpected moments, and there's so much content that I never find myself getting bored.

Where Winds Meet isn’t perfect. There’s a lot of AI, the movement and animations feel a bit rough, and the UI is honestly a mess with way too many menus and rewards popping up. It’s very easy to get lost.

But the game also does a lot right. The gameplay loop is fun, and the combat gives you plenty of freedom to play your own way. There are different classes, lots of weapon choices, and good customization so your character really feels personal. The world is huge, the setting is great, and the Chinese mythology adds a lot of charm. Combat can be challenging, but you can adjust the difficulty if you need to. You can play solo or with friends, and joining a guild actually affects the way you play.

Monetization is cosmetic-only. It’s pricey, but since the game is free, that’s honestly the best outcome. Anyone can try it without spending a cent and see for themselves, so why not give it a try?

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ – A Phenomenal Open-World Experience With A Few Rough Edges

Where Winds Meet is an absolutely phenomenal game that delivers a rich, emotional story wrapped in a gorgeous open world. Whether you're playing online with others or immersing yourself fully in solo mode, the game shines with its incredible flexibility. There are so many ways to play: combat, exploration, professions, social systems and each path feels rewarding and thoughtfully designed.

The social aspects are especially impressive. Jumping between online interactions and solo gameplay feels seamless, and the world feels alive because of it. It’s one of the few games where I genuinely enjoy both modes for different reasons and I am primarily a cozy gamer. I've put in almost 40 hours in the last 4 days.

That said, I do have a couple of frustrations. Profession bounties are extremely hard to complete because they’re often claimed the moment they appear, leaving you staring at empty boards or a full board where they've already been claimed more often than not. Healing is also a bit too saturated right now, which makes leveling certain abilities and roles harder than it should be.

Even with those issues, Where Winds Meet is a fantastic experience with huge potential, and I’m excited to see how it evolves. Highly recommended for anyone who loves open-world adventures with depth, style, and community.

[Where Winds Meet] is a game set in the Song Dynasty period of ancient China of Wuxia genre. You are playing as a lone wanderer that ventures through the "Jianghu" seeking fame, mythical arts, and riches. It's an epic story and experience infused with chinese culture and its unique style of martial art "Wuxia". It is a free-to-play game with Gacha for the cosmetics. 

Gameplayer [8] - is somewhat similar to the Genshin Impact style where you will find the usual mechanics such as exploration, collectables, random events and NPC quests. The leveling process are also really similar as you will need to breakthrough on multiple level cap. If you have played some of the hoyoverse game before you will be very familiar with the game from the get go. There are still innovation in this MMO lite co op system as you have dozens of mini games to play with friends. Join a "Sect" that reflects your traits and behavior in the world for more activities. Or role play as a doctor or lawyer cure illness for the villagers and peasants. Or you can just log on and play instruments and Marjong with friends. That are plenty of things to do!

Story [7] - I will give it a 7 for all the efforts with the voice over cutscene. It tells a very fragmented story that some of the part seems missing or completely not explained. Leaves you wonder whether you are missing a major cutscene or something. But overall the story delivers and leaves you care about the characters around you. 

Graphics [10] - The graphic is amazing. It has probably the best photo mode in any game i've played. You WILL want to take a moment during your adventure and quest to slow down and enjoy the view. Some of the scenery is simply breathtaking and the weather system is immersive! When you arrives at the "Kaifeng" city in the 2nd chapter. You will be amazed with this beautiful city as it offers a huge variety of scene.

Combat [7] - Combat and bosses is probably something that I am not too fond of. The whole system is revolving around the weapon of your choice. Each weapon offers a different role or play style. When combining two sets of weapons, and mythical arts. You are opened with many possibilities to build your unique character. Though I am not a fame of switching weapon as the Wuxia fantasy rarely talks about switching weapon. I play on Legendary difficulties. The highlight of the combat is its bosses. I do feel some of the boss or mobs requires more attention of its attack pattern as often there are always on the offensive and leaves the player no room to attack and leaves too much emphasis on the "Parry" mechanics that leaves everything else kinda pointless. 

Overall [8.5] - Overall this game deserves to be one of the best game released this year. I've played for 70 hours and I am still hooked and wanting to see more of what it can offers me. It does keep you engaged either for it's single player story or co op gameplay. This is a title that you don't want to miss!

Very early game review, but I'd say, the game is worth checking for RPG and gacha players alike. The blend of the two might put off some people, but if you don't mind either too much, I think the game strikes a fair balance. 

One of the things that has to be noted is that the gacha mechanics themselves are largely tied to cosmetics in this game. you don't pull characters or weapons, mainly cosmetics. of course, there's various subscriptions you can adhere to that will give you more chances at high tier gear drops, cosmetic drops, and crafting/upgrading materials, however, the game does a good job of making the in-game activities for these interesting and varied enough for most players to enjoy the content, provided they don't mind some grinding.

It's far too early for me to evaluate endgame content and balance, however, I feel that the gameplay systems are solid and well balanced. combat is fun, side activities are relaxing, and the story is not particularly exciting so far but not bad either. overall I feel the game manages to capture the wuxia aesthetic pretty well, so if that's something of interest you won't be disappointed. 

As always, it remains to be seen how monetization will evolve over time, if the amount of grind necessary to participate in endgame content will be sensible, and if the story will remain interesting, but these are risks one incurs with every live service game and I feel this one is off to a very good start.

Where Winds Meet is a fairly interesting game given its premise and design. While this is a bit premature considering no one has made it to endgame yet (due to story/level time gates), after 72 hours, I think I can at least give a preliminary review of the game as it's played out so far up to level 55.

As usual, my specs:
- 13900k CPU
- 7900XTX GPU
- 64gb RAM
- Linux Mint Cinnamon


### Linux Performance

Honestly, it ran OOTB with no tinkering beyond finding an appropriate Proton version. I'm at a stable 60fps unless I'm loading into Kaifeng for the first time. No crashes that I remember. Game runs fine. Nice job!


### Graphics

The graphics are actually really pretty. There's a lot of signposts of people taking very cinematic screenshots. There are a lot of visually distinct areas and nothing really seemed out of place to me. From toxic underground caverns to beautiful fields of violet flowers to a grassy field with a river cutting through it, the presentation of the game does not slouch.

As for characters and enemies/NPCs, they all look fine to me. No attacks felt like they came out weird, things seem to be well telegraphed, parryable and non-parryable attacks are adequately conveyed. Honestly, no complaints.

This game does also offer a decent character creator and a wide array of cosmetics, both free and paid. They seem fine enough to me. However, the lack of barefoot options is a bit disappointing. Then again, female characters have the feet of a middle-aged slavic factory worker so I guess it's not so disappointing after all.


### Sound

I play with Chinese audio and English subtitles. This is a Chinese game taking place in a Chinese setting so it seemed the most appropriate. I do not understand a lick of Chinese but I do appreciate how this feels like older Chinese wuxia/xianxia/martial arts films from back in the day. With all that said, I don't really have any complaints.

As for enemies and combat, attacks generally have audio cues to let you know when a red/golden attack is coming. The soundtrack sounds very appropriate, and I appreciate the authentic Chinese aesthetic.


### Gameplay

This is what I meant when I said this game was interesting. If I had to describe this game using a few words, it'd be "Wo Long-lite MMO". I'm sure many of us have had the thought of "What if Dark Souls but MMO" and this seems to be the answer. You have a light and heavy attack, both of which can have chained options or charged options. You have up to 8 martial art skills equipped at any given time. Each weapon has two unique skills and a third skill to aggressively swap to your other weapon.
In addition to this, weapons seem to operate in pairs. Meaning that one weapon has synergy with the other weapon in its given class. For example, Strategic Sword has a Spear counterpart. The sword is good at inflicting and consuming stacks of bleed. The Spear boosts damage and also has synergy with bleed stacks. The Tank weapons are similar, where one is focused on shields and aggro while the other is focused on damage reduction and CC.

With that aside, enemies litter the world and can range from common bandits to elites to world bosses to campaign bosses. The entire world seems to scale to your level so when you're lvl 1, the bandits are lvl 1, and when you're lvl 55, the bandits are of a relevant level. Enemies have the equivalent of a stamina meter. When the meter is drained, the enemy goes into an exhausted state that allows you to pile on the damage. You can end the exhausted state with a finisher that does ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of damage. Enemies have normal attacks, unblockable (red) attacks that can only be parried or dodged, and golden attacks that can't be parried and must be dodged. This game adopts the Sekiro mechanic where successful parries (especially on red attacks) deplete the enemy's stamina bar.

Honestly, this game has a lot to do. There's so many side quests, side stories, outposts, world bosses, and other random things to do that I can't adequately cover it all here.


### Progression

As previously mentioned, the story and levels are time gated. After reaching certain levels, you need to perform a breakthrough to raise the level cap. The breakthroughs are just combat trials with extra rewards. After a breakthrough, all your stored exp is applied up to the next level cap. Good time to point out that, yes, the game does bank exp gained when at the level cap. So, if you were to bank enough exp at lvl 20, you could immediately jump to lvl 30 after performing the required breakthrough.
You will, however, encounter a time gate after a certain point. As of the time of writing, I'm lvl 55 and have to wait another 7 days to raise the cap to 60. Story quests are also gated for a few days.

As for gear, it seems fine enough for now but endgame is going to be the real indication of how painful it will be. You have two weapons, a bow, 4 pieces of armor, two trinkets, and one other item that I don't remember the name of. Almost all items can roll with an equipment set that has different bonuses depending on the 2/4 equipped set items. Weapon levels are tied to the level of your style. So, for example, every Strategic Sword I equip is automatically lvl 55 since that's the level of my style. You can Tune equipment, which gives bonuses, but Tuning is tied to the weapon itself so be wise on how you spend resources for now.


### Cash Shop

To get this out of the way immediately: No, the game is not P2W.
From browsing the shop, all there seems to be are cosmetics which offer no stat boosts and horse armors. I have not personally found anything that would give you an advantage over others. The prices seem to range from cheap to expensive and, of course, the game has a gacha for certain items. Personally, I don't partake in gacha. If I wanted to gamble, I'd go tap some Kharazad accessories in BDO.

However, this game is monetized differently in Global than it is in China. I have no personal experience with the Chinese version but from reading around, they have lower prices and the option to outright buy items since there are gambling laws in China. For Global, they're effectively testing the waters to see what they can get away with.


### tl;dr

Game is fun. Give it a try. There's a lot of things to do and plenty of community interactions. You can even screw around with NPC chat AI for some hilarious outcomes. We're not at endgame yet so I can't really give a final determination but so far it's been fun. Go be a jade-like Chinese princess.

It takes a while to understand everything, but this game is worth the effort. I have to admit, that I do not prefer F2P games, especially those with a gatcha component. I have tried Genshin, Wurthering Waves, Zenless Zone Zero, and Honkai Star Rail. None of them really resonated with me.

When I saw the trailer for this game, I was immediately drawn in by the atmosphere. I am in my late 40s and grew up watching kung-fu theatre reruns in the 80s and awesome films like Iron Monkey, House of Flying Daggers, Hero, and of course, Crouching Tiger/Hidden dragon in the 90s. If you like those those movies and aesthetics, I can almost guarantee you are going to like this game.

First of all, there is a lot of content. I love just wandering around and finding so many quests or mini-games, chests, collectibles, you name it, they have it. Second, the graphics for this game are well-done, but even better is the atmosphere. While the writing leaves a lot to be desired, I like the gist of the stories that are being told. I will be honest, I am only a PVE player and the few times I've tried PVP the lag is so bad I just stop trying and only do PVP to do my weekly guild or battle pass quests.

The combat for each weapon and how you obtain that weapon or skills is done through "stealing techniques" which is fun. There's even some light stealth sections and the ability to do ambush kills. You get mounts, plentiful waypoints, and can even unlock wuxia-style flying, eventually. The music in the game is wonderful as well.

Now, onto the gatcha. Honestly, it's only cosmetic, but its pretty bad. Global players are getting shafted when compared to CN players. However, I won't gamble in this game. Since I've put in over 20 hours already, I want to give some money to the devs and the best value I saw were the monthly pass ($4.99 US) and the battle passes if you are going  to play frequently.

Another element that I am not too fond of is all of the systems and currencies - it is a lot to remember and I have had to use videos a few times just to understand everything.

Overall, I give this game a solid 8/10 and am looking forward to future updates.

Note: I have only been enjoying this game solo so far:
Summary: Got SSD space? try it! Have played sekiro? try it! Like Wuxia media? try it!

I gotta say. this was an amazing surprise. I thought that it would be just like any online game that focuses on grinding and power scaling. The reality is quite different and quite refreshing. If you've watched or read wuxia/manhwa/chinese shows, there are moments that make you go, "HEY! I understood that reference" or the moments plays out like in any wuxia centered media. From the start of me playing until now, none of them has fallen flat for me yet. 

The gameplay is quite fun as well, I did not expect to play a sekiro-esque game that you can play co-op or as an MMORPG at that. But they did add another touch of hogwarts legacy spells mechanics in here as well. Sometimes you need to use the right skills for the right enemies and for the right occasion. And to be prepared for situations like that feels very rewarding. 

You can also build your character for any archetype from Healer, DPS and more as you would any MMORPG. But on top of that you have the roles in the world as well. not sure about the rest but the big profession right now is healers.  You're the doc that gets called by other plays if they get a debilitating condition or after they got stung by a bee.

Then they have the interesting techno additions to the game as incorporating a chatbot as npc. As far as I know some NPC's you can befriend via the chat funct. It's nice as it is but not yet to the point that it is groundbreaking , but hey it is new for me and it serves as a fun downtime activity for me in-game to get rewards.

Now the graphics and presentation I think is where it shines bright. From the trivial moments to the important cutscenes, it presents it to you beautifully. Cutscenes are beautifully animated(so far for me) and the graphics are ridiculously great for a free game such as this (reminds me of GoT/GoY). And it also helps that there are just random quests/encounters that happen in-game which feels like something out of RDR2. NPC's also have their own routines and schedules, and so this makes the world look very colorful and feel almost alive. 

In conclusion, this was an absolute treat and was deceptively fun. This may take some time for rookies to get into as the game tries to hold your hand but most of the time their hands are kinda soapy and slippery. But when you get into it, it reels you in with everything it has to offer and its not limited to what I have mentioned.

The world is filled with beautiful landscapes, detailed villages, and hidden secrets that reward curiosity. The movement and parkour system feel fluid and satisfying, especially when combined with martial-arts abilities.

Combat is dynamic and stylish, offering a good mix of swordplay, special techniques, and evasive maneuvers. While some animations and balance issues could use refinement, the overall experience is fun and engaging. The story has an intriguing foundation, and the side quests add personality to the world.

The game still has some rough edges—occasional bugs, performance drops on certain systems, and UI quirks—but none of them were deal-breakers for me. The developers seem committed to improving the experience, and the potential here is huge.

If you enjoy wuxia themes, open-world exploration, and cinematic action, Where Winds Meet is definitely worth trying.

I really want to love this game. A beautiful world, wonderful music, decent combat, interesting exploration, and decent quests. What more could you want from a game? But in this barrel of honey, there are a few spoonfuls of disgusting substance.
1) The main spoonful is restrictions. Oh, the developers love restrictions and have taken care to impose them on everything possible. Want to level up another 5? Wait 9 days. Want to level up your skills? Wait until you're allowed to level up. Want to play through another small part of the story? Wait 5 days. Want to earn cult currency to buy a suit for 8,000 currency? 1,500 currency per week. You just want to earn some currency, and the developers have smilingly imposed restrictions on you.
2) Some quests simply don't have the required NPC where they should be. Someone call it a bug? But in my opinion, this is intentional, as the developers are doing everything they can to prevent you from fully enjoying their game by imposing restrictions on everything.
3) There's no Pay-To-Win in the game, only cosmetics and convenience features. But firstly, getting anything truly interesting is gacha at its worst, where you first have to acquire a resource and only then save it up to buy what you need. And the chances are, well, tenths to thousandths of a percent.
4) The Battle Pass is absolute garbage, costing between $12 and $20.

So (Tuesday, restrictions reset overnight from Sunday to Monday) - I still want to play the game, but for the next nine days (or more accurately, seven at the time of writing), there's absolutely no point in logging in, as I'm currently at the maximum possible level (restrictions), the story quest has been completed to the maximum (again, restrictions), and all side missions have been completed. There's no point in doing any activity on the map (again, restrictions). Log in for another day to farm more cult currency (15 minutes), and that too will be restricted. After 9 days, you'll be allowed to play a little more, and then you'll be back to waiting for the restrictions to be lifted.

Then think for yourself, decide for yourself.

In this review, I’ll talk about High Ping, the Combat System, P2W vs F2P, and finally what I liked and disliked.

Right now, the only real issue. at least for me, is the high ping for EU players. Maybe other regions have the same problem, but I can only speak for myself. The devs promised they’re working on it, so fingers crossed.

P2W vs F2P:

The game is free to download and free to play. Money buys cosmetics, and for $20 you can purchase a game pass that gives a very small amount of extra energy for claiming boss rewards. The same energy regenerates for free, so it’s not a big deal, just an option if you don’t want to wait.

As far as I know, that’s the only gameplay-related advantage whales can get, and even that is limited. All the expensive stuff is purely cosmetic and gives nothing but flexing points xD

Combat + Early Game Confusion

The first few hours were rough. If you don’t enjoy games with Elden Ring / Wukong / Sekiro-style combat, the early fights might overwhelm you. But that’s not all.

The game throws so many menus, notifications, unlocks, achievements, and systems at you that you feel completely lost. I genuinely struggled to find my attribute page or figure out how to upgrade gear xD

But that confusion disappears after your first 10 hours or so, and the game really grows on you.

What looked like a 7/10 at first now feels like a 9/10, and if they fix the ping issues, I might even call it 10/10.

The combat feels rewarding. Learning parry/dodge timings makes boss fights so much easier, and the time you invest into mastering the mechanics feels worth it. The fighting styles are also beautifully animated.

So far I’ve tried:

Umbrella + Fan hybrid build for ranged DPS and healing, I've also tried full healing build and now sword + spear for melee DPS

The hybrid build was more fun than pure DPS/heal, but switching to sword and spear has been amazing even if I lost my sustain. Something about slashing bosses and mobs feels different XD

Non-Combat Content

I’ve focused a lot on combat, but the game offers so much more:

You can be a doctor curing diseases, a scholar arguing legal cases to save players from jail, or compete in archery, fishing, drinking contests, card games, trivia and a bunch more.

There’s also a building system, letting you construct your own house or other structures.

Guilds & Sects

Right now, the guild and sect systems feel a bit underwhelming. They’re missing some features like being able to post announcements that don’t disappear the moment someone closes the game and the chat is too limited with only one channel for guild.

That pretty much covers it. If you are still hesitating, don't!

I like it a lot.
Pros:
* Fun world to explore. There is a lot to see and do in the world and the visuals are often stunning.
* Combat feels fun. Decent amount of options to build your character around.
* Nice character customization, lots of sliders for your face and stuff.
* Boss fights have fun mechanics. They can be challenging if you want them to be.
* Lots of side activities that are enjoyable.
* Decent Photo Mode. It's easy to use but could have some more options for sure.
* No Power in the cash shop. Though there are some overprized comsetics (see cons)
* A lot of content for F2P.
* The setting is nice. At least I like the Wuxia style world. The main story is kind of the expected quality for these types of games. Nothing to write home about but it's not too bad and less important to me than the general feel of the world that is solid.

Cons:
* There are too many menus making it an at best cumbersome and at worst confusing experience to navigate through them and since a lot of menus are where you claim rewards for activities you will need to learn to navigate them.
* Gacha mechanics - They are cosmetic only but I'll always say that gacha mechanics suck.
* Some shop items are way too expensive. Sure, it's optional and cosmetic only but there's some stuff that will cost you 100+ bucks.

A game with a lot of potential, not to mention that it contains one of my favorite genres Wuxia and it's free, but despite all this, it would be even nicer if in the future they moved more towards the Xuanhuan style. In any case, it's a very fun game with lots of things to do and places to explore and an interesting story.

It gets a 9/10 from me, there's still room for improvement.
