Absolutely gorgeous game. The controls are a bit janky and the UI is a nightmare to work around, I’m still having trouble trying to find certain submenus, but I actually enjoy the story! Several cutscene in the game are done in real time and the full blown cutscenes are so stunning visually.

Movement in the game is insane. You can triple jump, dash, run up walls, use special skills to travers across the world quicker, and even horses have their own abilities. The map is HUGE and I’m still discovering new places. On top of exploration, you’ll also come across player sign posts which can either help you find hidden items or hurt you and have you dying or clipped in a wall somewhere (you can turn these off thankfully). You can also call other players to help you take down hard bosses which is nice. You can change your difficulty at any time even during bosses. 

There is a progression system level wise that does limit you by actual days. So if you reach level 20 and your experience is capped, you’ll have to wait a real day (or until the day resets at a certain time) and complete some side quests like do a few trials or do “x, y, z”. However once you reach progression level 6 there’s no longer a time limit and you can catch up to other players. I found this really odd as I’ve never came across this in other games I’ve played before, but thankfully the experience you earn while at your max level does get saved and stored until you hit the next progression level, which increases your skills and abilities but also increases the difficulty of bosses and enemies. Now you don’t have to progress your level, but there will be a lot of things locked from skill level, so you kinda have to (Like you can’t redeem x2 or x3 the rewards from a boss if not at a certain prestige level). 

This game offers several things to do like: bounties, side quests, a build mode, trials, leisure activities in online (cross platform btw, only with ps5 as that’s the other way to play this game atm), marriage (only with other players, no npcs), healing games, dye and post outfits, boss fights, dance, obviously the main quest, sects, guilds, filling out the compendium, explore hidden dungeons and so much more.

I love how lively the game is from npcs riding horses along a road to seeing two bucks wrestling with each other. However it can be off putting as when talking to npcs to form a relationship with you’re chatting to an AI bot. That’s something I’m not personally fond of, I’d rather there be set dialogue options (IMO).

Yes there is a gatcha system, yes it is outrageous. However it ONLY AFFECTS COSMETICS! There are people who’ve dropped 40k+ (yes $40,000+ USD) for an in-game boat with a set of clothes. You must be wary as on the Chinese server there are skins that were purchased directly from the store with NO gatcha and on the Global servers they’ve began releasing new gatcha’s with these same skins (Veiled Edge, I’m looking at you) not to mention terrible luck rates (this game came out over a year ago in China and is now accessible with Global servers). There IS a pity system, but please be careful of how much you’re spending and confront yourself if you have gambling addiction and get help. Don’t go broke over a game (or any game) that can easily be removed from servers and platforms. If you really want to support the game but avoid going broke, buy some of the guaranteed cheaper skins in the shop. 

One way to circumvent spending real money on gatcha are the in-game items you receive which can be exchanged for tickets for gatchas, however some banners are only premium currency which require real money. So you can still be f2p in the game and earn several outfits and cosmetics, some just require real money. 

Combat is pretty fun but can be hard to get used to at first. There are several systems you have to remember which you can use to benefit from while against a boss or enemy. You can however turn off the hud in a boss fight or just in general and it makes things far more cinematic.

I almost forgot to mention the soundtrack for this game which is beyond beautiful. It changes from town themes to travel themes, and more. I mentioned dancing earlier and yes you can dance along to several songs in the game as well as play instruments! In online you’ll often come across players on the guqin doing renditions of popular songs from several genres. 

Keep in mind, this game is completely free! You don’t have anything to lose and I highly recommend you to at least try it out! Hopefully this was in-depth enough. :)

"i'll be adding stuff to this review as i go deeper into the game, as 23h for an mmo isnt enough imo to review"

The goods:
- Game runs smooth 60fps,1080p on directx12, my rig is an old DDR3 setup with a gtx1080/I7-4790k so this is great

- combat is amazing, combos almost in too big a number and there is many ways to build your character.

- There is a multiplayer and a solo mode.... SOLO MODE IN AN MMO GUYS, you can be the SOLOLEVELING™! 

- Chiness type of setting almost too perfect, also feels nice being the chiness anime character that goes anywhere it wants and does whatever it wants.

- The world and graphical beauty is just on equal footing with expedition33, to the point where you'd ask yourself why the color palettes are now being used to "force" certain emotions, psychological response ect, yes this is a thing btw, i sadly studied both art and psychology...

- Parcours!, Parcours! Horse of skyrim type of thing where, if you see it, you can climb it, man, this feels amazing.

- I'm a big advocate of AI art and it being used in video games and do think there is always a balance, may it be humanmade or AImade, and this game, it just does it perfectly imo. You can tchat with AIbots to build relationship points lol, use AI to search or open menus, you can even voice command these things too. At the character creation there is even a way to use your photo or one of your portrait artwork to make a character...bruh wuuut.

-Healing people and most job related stuff is build around some roguelike type of card game which is nice and so inovative in an mmo. there is sooooooo many minigames too and they build your character's stats too which gives the game an almost DnD feeling of being alive in a miniworld that you can always chose what to do.

The Neutrals:
- Story is meh most of the time, sometimes soooo engaging and the next it's sooo bad i'd want to just mute the voiceover...like cmon it ain't that hard to find good voices or use ai at this point, most female characters make me cringe tbh, some male ones are truly not on the spot ( middle aged man talking like he's 80years old or smoked weed for as much as snoop dog does... ( found out today the chiness voiceover is WAY BETTER, so this is a anime rule type of thing here ) 

- Mounts, most of the time i find myself not even using it, even tho i got the drop from the draws it just doesnt feel needed tbh, if it's too far you'll want to tp anyways even more after fully exploring a zone....

- Pay to win vs Play to win ratio is neutral here, there is a lot of go faster transactions if we're being honest here but it doesnt affect my experience as of yet and i'm lvl 50 ( capped for a day )

- Capping Solo mode progression level is neutral, i get why you'd need that, but it just feels like a big bandaid for something bigger, it's nice that the exp still stacks up tho.

- Bosses in solo mode are meh, once you get the timing they're easily managable without being hit once, and i'm at the hardest difficulty so no i don't have the autothing mechanics... idc about them anyways i'm a souls game/ARPG addict. 

The bads:
- UI and Menu optimization is so bad i have to use the ai to look for what i want, it is designed in a way to keep players interacting through psychological "abuse" of their brains to make them want to find out which menu has the shiny reward red dot on it just so it keeps you playing for a bit more time everytime, a bit more dopamine and anticipation here and there and pop you're gone for a day, almost like a casino here.
I thought playing poe was bad for my wrist but maaaaan this game's UI makes me wanna buy athlete gear just for it, hence why i'm now using the ai tool lol. Btw i do most of this as work so yeah i do know what i'm talking about.

- The factional stuff is tedious as hell, yeah sure you can be factionless but it does build a FOMO kinda thing.

- Exploration, yup, don't get me wrong i love the open world genshin of the elden ring thing, but man, the collectoton of platitudes you have to get in this game for exploration advancement is tedious, tho rewarded if there is any good point to it....

- PvP is jacked and hacked too, i won my first battleroyale thing by using 100% uptime powerarmor skills and spamming the switch for healing too, comboed that with a poison buff and reflect and there we go, everybody was dying by hitting me.... so dumb. Another guy from the next match was flying around the map one shotting everybody. The last one i did made me wanna quit pvp forever, there was an afk invincible guy on the map that Won the BR cause the miasma killed 2 of us trying to hit him....WE HAD TO WAIT THE WHOLE MATCH TIMER LOL K.

- Most Story mode dungeons have this weirld debuff that prevents you from parkour abilities... which sucks let's be honest and is the reason i will never be playing hardcore on this game. Yes i fell into that damn pit the village trying to capture flame moths... 

- i'd say data collection is crazy but then again netease probably knows more about me than the government does lol. Still has to be pointed out tho.

As of now, i'd say this game is a solid 88/100.

Yet another F2P gacha with mobile-style gameplay.

Okay, the game does have a fairly nice art direction, mainly thanks to the Wuxia aesthetic, but nothing truly outstanding, and the graphics are pretty mid-tier for 2025.

Combat feels straight out of a mobile game: it may give the illusion at first, but there is basically no real feedback.

It will probably satisfy people who enjoy Genshin-style gacha "games" or mobile games, which are ultimately casinos disguised as games more than anything else, even if in this case the casino aspect seems a lot softer.

In the end, I'm starting to think these games are the fast food of our era: they look good, they taste good at first, but everything is extremely artificial and they will never compare to a real chef's dish.

As for the "but it's free" argument: sure, but your time is not, and what you end up spending on this kind of game, even if it's "only cosmetic", will almost always end up exceeding the price of a genuinely good game, even second-hand.

And never forget: when something is free, you're the product.

A very good free-to-play game with some flaws.

I’ll start first with the combat:
It feels like Naraka combat with Sekiro’s posture break and Wukong’s talent/weapon system, which is a good thing.
There are some issues, though.

The feedback on deflecting isn’t satisfying enough for me, purely in terms of audio and visual.
I can’t even tell sometimes if I successfully deflected because the audio and visual feedback aren’t that good.
The visual cue is passable, but the audio cue for attacks is nowhere to be found.
If you want a good example of perfect audio and visual cues/feedback, I highly recommend checking out E33 or Sekiro (GOAT).

Visuals are good.
The introduction of the story is cinema.

Last thing: dark patterns.
The game’s login rewards counts the day you missed, but the cap for your level doesn't.
So I’ve gotta wait for some days to level up. It should be a global cap, not a player cap.
If someone who started the game earlier can hit level 50 today, then someone who also started today should be able to hit that level too.

Monetization so far seems to be purely cosmetics.

Overall, it’s enjoyable and a great game. I would recommend checking it out.

This game is a blast with so much content, so many systems and a good bit of depth. Not sure calling it an ARPG is really accurate since it's a blend of different things - almost a life sim in some respects only not at all - go watch someone review or play it and you'll see what I mean (ignore the IGN review - nonsense). I've been pleasantly surprised by the exploration, the build crafting, the variety of the weapons and marshal arts, the amount of side stories and encounters (some great, some bad) and how smooth the animations are.

You can build a house, you can mainline the story and beat up the bosses or get ripped a new one by them (me), you can wrestle, you can get drunk and throw arrows into jars against an NPC......bounties, boss replays, secret bosses, medical profession, scholar profession, get sent to jail........the list goes on.

They even have systems in place to help noobs like the parry assist or being able to revert your world level to reduce the level of the mobs and bosses, after you've already geared to the max inside that world level bracket. Heck, there's probably more systems that I don't even know about.

Is it a perfect game? Of course not, those don't exist - there's some cutscenes where the voice lines aren't spoken or interactions where they same thing twice or not at all related to what the subtitles say and I've had some ping issues causing the group boss fight to become a chore but I rate those things as minor because there's so much here. The single biggest issue are the menus - it's maze of menus and sub menus to find reward and information in some cases.

However, I would recommend this game - it is free after all and a lot of fun and if you don't enjoy then you can move on.

Basically, it’s a jack-of-all-trades.

There are so many things packed into this 100 GB free-to-play game. Besides its large, vast world, it also has lots of lore, mini-games, miscellaneous content, points of interest (POIs), activities, and more. That being said, I can’t say it really excels at everything it adds, but it’s still enjoyable overall, hence why I called it a jack of all trades at the beginning.

The game also gives you the freedom to decide what you want to be. You can be a lone wolf if you don’t really want to socialize, you can be a doctor who heals players out in the world (not to be confused with a healer in a combat role), you can even be a scammer who tricks people, a drunkard, and many more things. All of this is tied to its Sect system, although I think some parts of that system are still lacking.

First off, a disclaimer: a bunch of the early bad reviews are either bots, people with mysterious grudges, or folks who simply woke up in a bad mood. Sure, not everyone will love this game, but it’s definitely worth trying before believing Chad_1997’s one-star rant.

Now the important part: the game is awesome. Imagine Elden Ring and Assassin’s Creed had a baby, and that baby decided it wanted to grow up to be an MMO. Some people argue it’s not a “real MMO,” but honestly, if I can run into strangers in the open world and accidentally ruin their screenshots, that counts.

Combat? Fantastic. Elden Ring is a 10/10, untouchable martial arts god. This game is a solid 7 or higher, which is basically “still better than most things you’ve dated.”

Performance? Smooth. No crashes. Only minor screen tearing—like the game occasionally blinks weirdly at you.

Pay-to-win? Nope. It’s free, and somehow not a psychological trap designed to steal your wallet. All the paid stuff is cosmetic, so if you want to look fabulous, go ahead, but you’re not forced. There is a gacha system, but you can ignore it like that one cousin who only texts when he needs money.

The world? Huge, pretty, and full of things to do. You’ll get distracted every five minutes—sometimes on purpose.

Story? Shockingly good. I usually skip MMO storylines like they're unskippable ads, but this one is actually worth listening to. Voice acting is “mostly fine,” like your friend who’s not a singer but still tries karaoke.

Graphics and sound? Beautiful visuals, great music, juicy sound effects. Not the best-looking game ever, but it definitely showered, combed its hair, and put effort in.

In short: this game slaps. If you like action RPGs even a little, you should try it. It’s like Elden Ring, Assassin’s Creed, and Ghost of Tsushima tossed into a blender and somehow made something delicious. If the future MMO content keeps up this quality, I might be here for a long, long time.

For a game that is free, the sheer volume of content is absolutely staggering. This isn't just a basic action RPG; it's a world that demands countless hours, offering immense value from the moment you step in.

The implementation of conversational AI with NPCs. This is a game-changer for world immersion. Instead of simple dialogue trees, you can actually have dynamic, natural conversations, making the world feel genuinely reactive and alive. It's a fantastic touch that elevates the entire experience.

The depth of content is so extensive that even with the phased progression (where capped levels unlock over time), you still have an overwhelming amount of things to discover and complete. The world is packed with activities, hidden lore, and challenging missions that make the level cap feel secondary to the exploration and journey.

It successfully combines three essential pillars: a deep, engaging Solo experience; effective Cooperative play (think of the satisfying, small-group instanced content found in games like Genshin Impact); and dedicated Online features where you can team up for major activities with other players. This combination gives you total flexibility in how you approach the game.

If you are looking for a title with incredible value, beautiful presentation, and true innovation in NPC interaction, look no further. This is a must-play.

Where Winds Meet is one of those rare games that grabs you from the first moment and doesn’t let go. The visuals are absolutely breathtaking — from the sweeping mountains to the lively villages, everything feels like it was painted with love. The world is full of atmosphere, and the Chinese aesthetic is captured beautifully, from the architecture to the clothing to the smallest environmental details.

The gameplay is where it truly shines. Combat is fluid, responsive, and stylish, with tons of ways to approach each encounter. Whether you prefer swordplay, martial arts, stealth, or mystical abilities, the game gives you room to express yourself. The amount of customization available is insane — outfits, abilities, builds, even how you role-play your character. It feels like your story from start to finish.

One feature I absolutely adore is the signboard system. Players can leave notes, warnings, jokes, or helpful tips all over the world, and it creates this amazing sense of community. It genuinely feels like everyone is adventuring together, helping each other through danger or just sharing a funny moment. It makes the world feel alive in a way few games manage to achieve.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a stunning, immersive experience that blends gorgeous visuals, deep gameplay, and a unique, heartfelt community element. If you love open-world adventures, Chinese culture, or just beautifully crafted games, this one is a must-play.

Highly recommended.

⭐ Where Winds Meet – Steam Review

Where Winds Meet is an impressive open-world wuxia RPG that blends fast-paced martial-arts combat with beautiful world design and rich storytelling. The game captures the feeling of classic Chinese martial-arts fantasy, giving players the freedom to explore, fight, and master unique abilities across a massive landscape.

🌄 Graphics & World Design

The visuals are one of the strongest points of the game. Landscapes look stunning, environments feel alive, and character animations are smooth and cinematic. The world feels handcrafted, and exploring it never gets boring.

⚔️ Combat & Gameplay

Combat is fast, fluid, and stylish. You can combine martial arts, parkour, weapon skills, and special abilities to create your own fighting style. Boss fights are intense and rewarding, and the mobility options make every encounter dynamic.

Started playing Where Winds Meet and the first thing that hit me was the atmosphere. The world looks genuinely beautiful detailed cities, calm villages, forests, mountains, all of it feels alive. You can tell they put a lot of effort into the environment. Sometimes I catch myself just riding around for no reason other than enjoying the view.

Combat feels smooth and satisfying. The weapons, the skill combos, the dodges, the animations everything connects nicely, and fights have a really good rhythm. 

The story is interesting so far, and the world building pulls you in more than you’d expect. Main quests are solid, but the side quests surprised me too  they’re not just filler, and a lot of them have small touches that make exploring actually worth it.

Co-op still has ping issues, and at this point it’s honestly pretty frustrating. It’s especially bad during fights, and it really shouldn’t be taking this long to fix. The devs say they’re working on it, but they seriously need to sort it out soon. And on top of that, I still don’t understand why we can’t play the main story in co-op  it makes no sense for a game like this.

And yes, the game is completely free to play. No hidden fees, no forced purchases. For a world this big and detailed, that’s honestly impressive. You can just jump in and enjoy without worrying about anything.

Overall, if you like open world exploration, wuxia themes, and atmospheric games, this one is definitely worth checking out. It has tons of potential and already looks great. The menu takes a bit of time to get used to, but once you figure things out, everything becomes much easier and smoother. 

Even after 80 hours, I’m barely into the second map and there’s still tons to explore, and it keeps me hooked.

Where Winds Meet - A Personal Take
So I finally got my hands on Where Winds Meet, and honestly? It's a mixed bag that somehow keeps pulling me back in.

The Good Stuff

The world is absolutely gorgeous. Like, I found myself just wandering around ancient China, getting distracted by misty mountains and little villages instead of doing actual quests. The wuxia combat feels pretty satisfying too - there's something really cool about grappling onto rooftops and having these flowing sword fights that actually make you feel like you're in a martial arts movie.

The Not-So-Great

The story can be a bit all over the place. Sometimes I'm invested, other times I'm just button-mashing through dialogue to get back to the action. And yeah, there are some performance hiccups here and there - nothing game-breaking, but noticeable.

Bottom Line

If you're into open-world games and have any love for wuxia or Chinese historical settings, it's worth checking out. It's not perfect, but it scratches that itch for exploration and martial arts fantasy that not many games do. I'd say wait for a sale if you're on the fence, but if the setting speaks to you, dive in.

Rating: 7/10 - Flawed but charming, with enough personality to stand out.

I rarely write Steam reviews. I'm usually the quiet "play and move on" type, but Where Winds Meet is so good that it genuinely deserves one.

I honestly wasn’t even sure I wanted to try it at first. So many games in the same genre released around the same time that I almost skipped this one entirely, but I'm incredibly glad I didn’t.

From the very first moment, the world pulled me in. It's breathtaking, alive, and full of little details that made me stop more than once just to soak everything in. The atmosphere is beautiful, the music is gorgeous, and the combat is some of the most fun I've had in years. It's fluid, stylish and incredibly satisfying without being needlessly complicated.

What surprised me the most is the feeling the game gives. It captures the sense of freedom and adventure that so many modern open world titles try to deliver but rarely do. Whether I'm exploring ancient temples, flying across huge landscapes or experimenting with all the unique abilities, I keep thinking to myself, "This is something special."

The story and characters are genuinely engaging as well. It's rare for me to actually care about the story instead of rushing to the next fight, but here I'm fully invested.

To put it simply:
Where Winds Meet is magical. It's polished. It's heartfelt. And it absolutely deserves your time. If you're unsure, do yourself a favor and jump in. This is one of those rare games that reminds you why gaming is amazing.

And again, I rarely write reviews.
But this one earned it.

This game is great.
Strong solo player/coop/multiplayer game. While some may not agree that it is an MMO, it has all the important parts. The big difference between this is a more traditional MMO is that there is not an open world with everyone doing quests but instead you have your own world and then you can group up for content. The world in this game feels really lived in, with NPCs having their own little stories and conversations. Buildings are open to be walked into and the world just feels so much more fleshed out than anything else.

Lots of games have little minigames that are meant to be a distraction while you wait in town but in WWM the minigames are expansive. There's a lot to do besides just grind main story and gear up. Guilds have stuff to do, Sects are like clubs that get you to do stuff that aligns with their values like: pvp, make currency (separate from the normal gold everyone wants), heal people (this is a minigame), and more.

Combat is good even if it can be a bit of a deflect session. PvP is decent too, I recently hit the top rank in 1v1, and is more than just spamming left click. There's also a Battle Royale game that's fun too.

Boss fights are good and instead of being a one and done you learn to master them. Group bosses feel different and have normal multiplayer mechanics that are easy to pickup.

There's just so much to do, even after 160hrs I'm not very far into 100%'ing either of the first two zones and having a lot of fun.

“Go touch that dangerous thing. No reason.”

The parkour is smooth, as long as you enjoy overshooting every jump like you’re auditioning for a wuxia-themed circus. And the wind physics? Amazing. They even blow away my hopes and dreams.

Story is deep and emotional, from what I gather between my frequent unconsciousness.

Would I recommend it?
Totally.

This game has an action RPG feel to the combat like Genshin, or Wuthering Waves. It's art style is more realistic, and the only Gacha is fashion. It has a deflection system that is really satisfying to use and master. I recommend anyone comfortable with Souls games to play on Legendary first, you can always tone that down later. It is styled after mystical Chinese martial arts (Wuxia), if you've seen any kind of Chinese wire-fu movies then you know what to expect. I am really happy the genre is coming West in such a well put together game. I can't wait for more games like this type to become popular and hopefully some Xianxia style games come over as well.

It is a F2P game obviously with a single player story. Once you reach level 10 to can kick the world into MMO mode if you want. Lots of fun new things to learn in the world. Lots of minigames. Just having a weapon type is not enough you must seek out a way to learn that weapon style. Also you can learn Tai Chi from a literal bear++

NPCs that you find can frequently be talked to again after a quest or their written dialogue is exhausted, where you can get the option to chat with them to raise your affection. This is done through AI chat. You are given a hint and prompt, and then can try to help that NPC with suggestions on what to do. Sometimes it feels smooth, and sometimes clunky, but it is important to do. You can summon these NPCs if you have problems during boss fights for instance.

If you’re into open worlds with a strong wuxia vibe, Where Winds Meet is basically a playground you’ll want to get lost in.

The world-building is absolutely fantastic — the atmosphere feels alive and full of energy. NPCs are everywhere, doing their thing, giving you stuff to do. No matter where I wandered, there was always something waiting: a collectible, a side activity, a random minigame (and the game has a lot of them). Exploration never felt empty or repetitive.

Combat on Legendary mode hits that sweet spot: demanding, but intuitive. There’s a lot happening on the screen —  yet it never becomes chaotic I never felt overwhelmed or lost. Every clash feels weighty and satisfying.

I’m still early in the story, so I can’t say much there — mostly because exploration keeps distracting me every five minutes. But one thing that really surprised me is the bond system with NPCs. You can actually “chat” with your own words with side characters via an AI-driven system. You can tell they have prompt-based anwsers and not fully natural, but it’s still charming in a weird, cozy way.

Performance-wise, the game runs flawlessly on a strong PC. The only hiccups I noticed were occasional stutters when overlay apps (like Discord) kicked in — but that's probably an engine issue.

Overall? Between the combat, the exploration, and the surprisingly pleasant NPC interactions, Where Winds Meet feels like a world worth diving into.
Would I recommend it? Absolutely

First of all, I want to start by saying that the initial reviews, which brought the game to the Mixed score, rather shocked me. I was honestly worried that there's something very wrong with this game and I'm happy it didn't turn out that way at all.

I was quite fascinated with the premise of WWM, as it seemed rather unique. At the time, I didn't even know that it was going to be free, so it pleasantly surprised me with that. At the same time, I was worried about p2w elements, as it comes with free games 90% of the time BUT this game is one of those rare exceptions where paid stuff is only cosmetic. There's some things to be said about this too, but this will come later.

What I really like about this game:
- Visual style. It is beautiful. The surroundings are absolutely gorgeous. I keep making tons of screenshots during sunrise/sunset. 
- Interesting and lived in world. There are some many NPCs everywhere you go (especially in the city), and they all have their own life. You can talk to many of them to find out more about the world and the regular life of people.
- Unique/historical setting. The setting is fantastic and as far as I know it is based on real peoples that lived long time ago. Really cool.
- Fast paced/fun combat. Some people have negative opinion of this and I am rather baffled as due to why, the combat is fluent and responsive. I personally love it.
- TONS of stuff to do. Fishing, stealing, talking your way out of the fights, discovering new locations by accident, "grinding" your currency, doing your weekly/daily tasks for the rewards, you name it. There is just so much to do and you never feel bored.
- Boss encounters are unique and interesting. You have to learn the mechanics to actually beat it (depending on the difficulty you chose of course).
- Difficulty options - there's something for everyone. I personally picked recommended because I'm no tryhard, I like to enjoy my games without having to be stuck at some boss for hours. The recommended setting is actually well balanced, as it is not too hard and neither easy - it is just right. I tried legend in multiplayer and it is BRUTAL. For those who like challenges, they have a choice to have it right there.
- Multiplayer done right. There's no tedious multiplayer aspects such as having to go grind some mobs together. People can invite you to do any tasks but you can also do everything alone, including beating bosses or trials with fellow NPCs. You can also do it with real people - you can choose. I really like how they implemented healer/scholar mechanics - both parties can get benefits by doing healing, for example, which makes it a cool mechanic in my opinion.
- None of the side quests are fetch quests - they are rather elaborate and contained stories you discover while travelling around the world.

Neutral:
- Story. It has SO much depth in it but I think a lot of elements get lost... in translation.
- Progression systems. While it is satisfying uncovering more and more new systems as you level/breakthough, they are not very meaningful. The world also becomes stronger so you never feel like you are actually much stronger. Even simple mobs take sometime to kill. I am not sure how I feel about this, so I put it in neutral.
- Daily/weekly caps. On one hand, it kind of sucks that you are limited and can't "finish" the game as you please. However, it allows you to take a slower pace and explore the world and discover more things you otherwise might have skipped.

Disliked:
- Translation/localisation is absolutely horrible. It's obvious they used AI for many of the (side) NPCs to be voiced (which I generally don't mind) but the outcome in some of those cases is that you simply can't understand what it is being talked about. This also includes the names of locations/people: not only are they pronounced differently from time to time, but descriptions of certain stats (I believe it was vitality) can also differ depending where they are seem, for example, stat description page vs item description.
- Sound. Lip sync doesn't always match, some dialogue lines are completely skipped so it ends up only half voiced in some cases. The dialogue sound loudness does not always match from line to line too, which makes it rather bizarre. Music itself is beautiful though.
- Menus are absolutely confusing and a real abomination. They simply need to redo them. After 92 hours in the game, I STILL constantly get confused which menu do I need to do certain things and how to find them.
- Gacha (this is rather optional critique). I obviously dislike gacha mechanics because I do believe them to be extremely predatory. However, everything is just cosmetics and completely optional. I'd like them to sell cosmetics without gacha mechanics. I got a couple of skins that cost me 1.5 euro and I'm rather satisfied with them.
- Chests are rather meaningless, all you get is some currencies most of the time. I'd like to see some rare drops sometimes at least.

Conclusion:

Alright, so Where Winds Meet is basically the game I dreamed about as a kid. Huge open world, tons of stuff to do, mysteries everywhere—you just hop in and play exactly the way you want. Solo, with friends, wandering off for hours… it’s all fair game. And honestly? The amount of love poured into the world and environments is wild. Exploration actually feels rewarding, not like busywork.

Combat starts simple, but it opens up fast. The Inner Ways system adds new follow-ups and variations, and there are plenty of different builds and weapon types so everyone can find something they like. Plus, you can adjust the difficulty however you want. Sometimes the fights really keep you on your toes—in a fun way.

Now, heads up: there is a lot of content. Like, almost “I need to sit down for a second” levels of stuff. If you get overwhelmed when games throw everything at you at once, you might feel that here. My tip? Just pick one thing to focus on and follow that thread. The game won’t punish you for not doing everything at once.

Exploration is where the game really shines, though. Not only does it reward you constantly, but it actually gives you new movement abilities and talent upgrades to make exploring even better. It’s that good.

Content-wise, there’s something for literally everyone.

You’ve got:

A cinematic main story

Stranger/side missions that feel very Red Dead Redemption

Mysteries on both small and large scales that you solve without quest markers—just clues, logs, and your own brain

Chests and collectibles tucked away everywhere

And that’s just the single-player side.

There’s also this whole MMO layer where you can jump online, chat, hang out, and do more social stuff. Tons of minigames, exploration challenges, leisure activities like dancing or drunken shenanigans—seriously, it just keeps going. Then you’ve got group fights, outposts to clear, and bosses with actual mechanics that feel like mini raid encounters. There’s way too much to list here, but it’s genuinely impressive.

Best part? The game is free, and the quality is kind of crazy for something you don’t have to pay for.

The cash shop is purely cosmetic, so no pay-to-win worries. Just… avoid the gacha. The rates are rough. If you really love the game, buy an outfit or two and you’ll get your money’s worth easily. And if you’re someone who gets tempted to spend too much, keep an eye on your wallet—it can drain you if you’re not careful(maybe even avoid this game and this genre completely).
Luckily, there are solid lock functions in the settings, which is great if you’re a parent or just want to limit purchases.

Honestly? Give the game a shot. It’s free, it’s huge, and there’s something in it for everyone.

A great and enjoyable free wuxia game that has some obvious strengths and flaws.

[b]Pros:[/b]

1.  A wuxia game with modern graphics, which is very rare. The game delivers artistically great visuals of an explorable map with plenty of interesting side quests. Although there are also some boring ones, most of the quests are enjoyable from at least one aspect (stories, fights, or explorations).

2.  Free with no p2w mechanics. The real currency shop is mostly for cosmetics.

3.  Single player game with optional multiplayer content. Players are allowed to play fully single player without being forced to enter the multiplayer mode at all. Multiplayer elements still slightly affect the single player experience though, which will be mentioned in flaws.

[b]Flaws:[/b]

1.  Character strength growth and weapon upgrades are slightly ruined by the underlying "multiplayer PVE elements". Similar to common MMOs, the upgrades are usually minor and not immediately noticeable. The upgrades are confusing and not straightforward. There are countless currencies and upgrade materials in the game, and usually you are rewarded with these materials after most quests and bosses. No matter how strong the boss or how difficult the quests are, you will never obtain some mind-blowing or interesting rewards. This might be acceptable in a live service game, but really feels unrewarding in a single player experience.

2.  Some boss fights are unbearable, especially with the bad counter/dodge timing. The timing feels off and inconsistent. Sometimes you need to counter early, sometimes late—not enjoyable.

3.  A lot of repetitive collectibles, but still bearable.

Overall I still think this game is definitely worth a try, especially with its free price tag. There is not really a modern day alternative that can provide an authentic wuxia experience.

Overview & Core Strengths

Where Winds Meet is an open-world wuxia action-adventure RPG set in ancient China, praised for its stunning visuals, expansive world, and deep martial arts combat. It features a robust mix of campaign missions, side quests, guild systems, and varied PvP modes, creating a blend of single-player and multiplayer experiences.​

What Makes It Outstanding

Combat System: The game offers fast-paced, engaging martial arts combat with the ability to chain skills and manage buffs, feeling more MMO-like than typical action games. Movement through the world is fluid—wall-running, acrobatics, and diverse weapon choices echo classic martial arts fantasies.​

Open World: The environments are beautifully designed, from lush fields to bustling villages. The game encourages exploration, with Wandering Tales requiring players to find clues without heavy guidance, enhancing immersion and re-playability.​​

Content Volume & Variety: Players have access to a packed campaign, lengthy side quests (some can last an hour or more), and a range of smaller tasks. The PvP options extend beyond combat to mini-games, offering longevity for different playstyles.​

Downsides & Criticisms

Cluttered/Overwhelming Menus & UI: Many players report the game’s menus feeling like “menus inside menus”—there’s a lot to take in, with frequent notifications and blinking icons. It’s easy to get lost or distracted by the sheer volume of rewards and options, leading to a cluttered experience, especially for new players.​​

Handholding & Guidance: While main story quests provide clear direction, much of the game’s content (side quests, Wandering Tales, certain progression systems) deliberately avoids holding your hand. This can make progression confusing and difficult for those used to clearer guidance. Some side quests lack excitement and can feel like simple fetch missions.​

Bot/A.I. Interactions: Instead of traditional menus, some systems use AI bot interactions, which can feel bland or repetitive, missing the depth and personality of classic NPC dialogue. This new approach isn’t universally loved, and many suggest it needs refinement.​

Technical & Economic Issues: While the game is visually stunning, there are complaints about technical polish (character models, lip-sync) and a confusing in-game economy, particularly regarding currencies and rewards. Some progression is grind-heavy, especially at higher difficulties or for end-game PvP content.​

Where Winds Meet is an impressive and atmospheric action RPG that blends Chinese martial arts, mythology, and open-world exploration into a truly unique experience. Set during a turbulent period of ancient China, the game draws you in immediately with its rich cultural identity and beautifully crafted world.

The combat is one of the game’s strongest aspects. Inspired by wuxia martial arts, battles feel fluid, fast, and cinematic, with a wide variety of weapons and techniques that encourage experimentation. Movement is especially satisfying—running across rooftops, gliding through the air, and chaining attacks together makes every encounter feel dynamic and stylish.

Visually, Where Winds Meet is stunning. The landscapes range from peaceful villages to vast wilderness and war-torn areas, all brought to life with striking art direction and detailed environments. The use of weather, lighting, and music creates a strong sense of atmosphere that enhances both exploration and combat.

The story focuses on identity, loyalty, and survival in a world shaped by political conflict. Rather than holding your hand, the game allows players to uncover the narrative at their own pace, making choices that shape their journey and how others perceive them.

Overall, Where Winds Meet stands out as an ambitious and refreshing RPG. It respects its cultural roots while delivering exciting gameplay and a deep, immersive world. For players looking for something different from traditional fantasy RPGs, this is an experience well worth diving into.

🌬️ Where Winds Meet – Detailed Review 🌬️
⛰️ Wuxia • Open World • Martial Arts Fantasy

✨ OVERALL RATING:
⭐ 8.3/10 (I'm loving it 😍)

🌄 FIRST IMPRESSIONS:
Where Winds Meet immediately impresses with its gorgeous world and atmosphere. The visuals and environmental detail feel surprisingly high-quality for a free-to-play title. The opening hours set a strong tone and make the world feel alive and expansive.

🗡️ COMBAT & MARTIAL ARTS:
Combat is stylish and fun, with a great focus on parries, dodges, martial-arts skills, and flashy finishing moves. Weapon variety and ability sets keep battles interesting. Some animations could use extra polish, but overall, solo combat feels satisfying and responsive.
However, co-op introduces problems.
When playing with friends, there is a noticeable lag, delayed reactions, and desynced enemy positions. Parries in particular become unreliable: timing windows don’t match visuals, making defensive play frustrating. Co-op is still playable, but it currently feels inconsistent and needs optimization.

🌏 OPEN WORLD EXPLORATION:
The world is huge, lively, and fun to explore. There’s a ton to do, puzzles, quests, mini-games, parkour, side events, treasures, and it never feels empty.
On the downside, the UI is cluttered and overloaded with menus, currencies, and popups, which can be overwhelming in the early game.

📖 STORY & CHARACTERS:
The wuxia setting is engaging and rich in atmosphere. The main story is decent, though not groundbreaking, and the world’s lore is one of its strongest points. Character creation is very deep to the point that you can even upload your own photo into it to create a character out of it.

🎨 GRAPHICS & PERFORMANCE:
Graphically, the game is beautiful, landscapes, lighting, and character designs are all impressive.
Performance is reasonable but not perfect: occasional stutters, some low-res textures, and a few rough combat animations show the game still needs refinement.

🎵 AUDIO & MUSIC:
The soundtrack fits the world perfectly and enhances exploration. Voice acting quality varies across languages, and there are occasional lip-sync issues, but nothing game-breaking.

🔍 PROS & CONS:
✔️ Pros:
1. Gorgeous open world with great atmosphere
2. Fluid and stylish solo combat
3. Tons of content for a free-to-play game
4. Engaging exploration and activities
5. Strong character customization

❌ Cons:
1. Co-op lag and desync affect combat, especially parries
2. Cluttered and overwhelming UI
3. Some animation and texture inconsistencies
4. Occasional performance hiccups
5. Mixed localization and voice acting quality

🧭 FINAL VERDICT:
Where Winds Meet is a visually striking, content-rich wuxia adventure with satisfying solo combat and a massive world to explore. While its UI can feel bloated and co-op suffers from lag and desync, especially hurting parry timing, the overall experience is still enjoyable and impressive for a free-to-play release.
Recommended, especially for solo players and fans of open-world martial-arts RPGs.

I genuinely love the game, like actually love it. The graphics are insane for a free game; you won’t find anything better unless you prefer a different art style. The music is great, and while there are a few minor bugs (like NPCs or story moments missing voice lines), it still all works out because the game is a masterpiece.

BUT the chat moderation is honestly a pain. My first message in two days was simply the word “diddle,” and I got muted for twenty four hours—24 HOURS—instead of something reasonable like ten minutes. Meanwhile, other players are openly talking about grooming, sexual activity, shooting dogs for being loud, and masturbation. I’m not even mad about my mute, because this really feels like a “get gud” situation, but it’s strange that the people saying much worse stuff aren’t touched while I’m muted for something so tame.

Yeah, technically “diddle” can be taken the wrong way, but let’s be honest: compared to what others are saying, it’s extremely mild on the same level as a parent saying “don’t play violent games because violence is bad” even though the game itself contains violence. It just seems inconsistent.

If the goal is to stop certain terms from being used in world chat, then fine I’m okay with being muted from that specific channel. But the mute currently affects every channel: co-op requests, envelope sending, assist requests, boss requests, private messaging, everything. And for twenty-four hours over a silly, non-slur word.

It would be much better to:
Apply mutes to the specific channel where the issue happened, not the entire game.
Use shorter and more reasonable mute durations.
Keep moderation consistent, so mild words aren’t punished harder than actual inappropriate content.

If “diddle” gets a 24-hour mute, then what happens if I make a joke to a friend like “shut up your ahh”? Am I banned for a week? The punishment system just feels disproportionate and unclear.

Where Winds Meet is a visually stunning, ambitious Wuxia-inspired open-world RPG that dazzles with its combat and scale, but struggles under the weight of overwhelming systems and uneven pacing.

🌏 Setting & Story
The game is set in 10th-century China during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era, immersing players in martial arts traditions and factional conflicts.

You begin as a young martial arts student whose pendant is stolen, sparking a journey across a politically unstable land.

The narrative mixes grand sagas with countless side stories, creating a collage of fables that range in quality.

⚔️ Combat & Gameplay
Combat is described as stylish yet tactical, slower than it looks but rewarding once mastered.

Boss fights are praised for their intensity and spectacle, showcasing the game’s mechanical depth.

The game includes mini-games, stealth systems, puzzles, and exploration, though some feel bloated or under-polished.

Fighting mechanics are fun but take time to get used to, with martial arts moves even applied to quirky tasks like fishing.

🌄 World & Design
The open world is massive and beautiful, filled with natural landscapes and vibrant characters.

Players can run up walls, glide through the air, and explore a jaw-droppingly large map.

The sheer scale is both exciting and daunting, often making the game feel like it’s trying to do everything at once.

💰 Systems & Progression
As a free-to-play game, it incorporates gacha mechanics and a complex economy system that can feel overwhelming.

Progression pacing becomes jarring in the late game, with excessive micromanagement that bogs down the RPG systems.

Co-op modes exist but are locked behind significant progression, limiting accessibility.

🎭 Overall Impressions
Strengths: Gorgeous visuals, thrilling combat, rich Wuxia atmosphere, and enormous content variety.

Weaknesses: Overloaded systems, uneven storytelling, grind-heavy progression, and a lack of cohesion in design.

Critics agree it’s a game of extremes—incredible highs in combat and exploration, but frustrating lows in pacing and system management.

👉 In short: Where Winds Meet is a bold attempt to merge martial arts fantasy with sprawling open-world RPG design. It’s breathtaking at times, but its ambition often outweighs its execution.

[h1]Where Winds Meet: A 90+ Hour Review That Will Surprise You![/h1]

[h2]The TL;DR (Too Long; Didn't Read)[/h2]
Stop what you are doing and download this game! This is the first review I've ever written, and I had to do it because this game is an incredible, massive open-world Wuxia RPG. The best part? It's [b]Free-to-Play![/b] I've spent over 90 hours on both PC and PS5. This game is a true masterpiece of its genre.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]What I Loved[/h2]

[b]100% Free-to-Play (F2P):[/b] This is the game's biggest strength. You get a beautiful and polished experience, including a narrative that provides over 150 hours of content, without spending a single penny. The monetization is fair, focusing purely on cosmetics, such as outfits and mounts. This is the perfect model.

[b]The World is Stunning:[/b] The visuals are breathtaking, especially on the PS5. Running around the map feels like stepping into a historical painting. It’s vast but packed with content.

[b]Combat is Next-Level:[/b] It's fast, fluid, and deeply rewarding. The Wuxia martial arts are implemented brilliantly, making every parry, dodge, and special move feel epic.

[b]The Story & Lore:[/b] The writing is surprisingly good. It offers a complex narrative about identity and honor that goes far beyond a simple backdrop for fighting.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Developer Support & Constant Improvement[/h2]
The ongoing commitment from the team is exceptional and makes spending your time in this game worthwhile:

[list]
[*] [b]Responsive and Open:[/b] The Customer Support team is genuinely helpful and quick to respond. They clearly listen to the community.
[*] [b]Feedback-Driven:[/b] They often send out surveys and are very open to feedback on how to improve the game's systems and quality.
[*] [b]Near-Daily Updates:[/b] The game gets updates and patches almost every day. Their commitment to fixing bugs and refining the experience after launch is exactly what you want to see from a live-service open-world RPG.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]A Wish for the Future (Language Support!)[/h2]
To make this game truly perfect and globally accessible, I have one main request:

I sincerely hope the developers consider adding support for [b]more global languages, especially Arabic[/b]. Text-only support is sufficient; there’s no need for voice acting.

Expanding the language options will help the game reach a larger player base and make the rich, deep lore accessible to more gamers worldwide. This will create an even more beautiful and enriching experience for everyone.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Verdict after 90+ Hours[/h2]
Where Winds Meet is clearly a passion project with a dedicated development team. It delivers a huge, authentic, and enjoyable open-world experience that has kept me hooked for almost 100 hours. The fact that it is a [b]Free-to-Play[/b] title with a clear [b]no pay-to-win[/b] policy makes it an easy [b]must-play[/b] recommendation.

TLDR: Its good, but lots of menus and lots of different currencies bring it down a bit for me.

This game is genuinely fun to play and I have enjoyed my time with it thus far. 
Positives:
- My favorite part of the game so far has been the amazing bosses and combat system. 
- Traversal is fun and the exploration aspect of the game is great. 
- Lots to do and so far a good story
- It's FREE as long as you don't spend on the battle pass or cosmetic stuff.
- You can get some pretty good cosmetics for free through progression.

Nuetral: 
-Time-gating progression is not my favorite, but it isn't terrible. 
-PVP: haven't played it yet, and its not why I tried it.
-Performance overall has been serviceable. Boss fights at consistent 120fps 2k res, but I have been experiencing pop-in stutter from assets loading in on a semi-frequent basis while in the open world.

Negatives:
- There are a lot of resources to keep track of, and many are not explained too well. 
- My biggest gripe so far is the menu system. They really need to make it easier to navigate and make it less confusing. I'm sure I'll get used to it, but I can easily see someone dropping the game because of how confusing it is. 
- There are some really annoying uses of AI in this game. Having to interact with AI chatbots to "befriend" an npc in order to complete the exploration of areas is pretty annoying and tedious. Really immersion breaking and just bad. 
- some quests are really finicky and broken. An example being a quest at the General's Shrine where you have to encounter a man in a well at night, but getting him to appear may just not happen even if you meet the conditions for it.


Overall, good experience thus far, but there is definitely room for improvement. I would recommend the game to people who enjoy souls-likes if they aren't playing any at the moment as this does scratch that itch and is free, but due to some of the above issues I would not say it is an amazing experience.

This game has shocked me with how good it is. It's a Genshin-esk open world with all the camps, chests, oddities. without the character Gacha as you just play as a character you make. It's got action combat with parry and dodge, but it's very forgiving and has an easy mode which auto parries with a CD. The weps all have diff movement sets, animation and determine your 'class' if you want to call it that. It has mini games out the wazoo. The story and quests are solo mode, but it has the activites of an MMO, where you can queue up for dungones, raids, PvP and a BR mode. Traditional Tank, Heal, DPS roles.  It has professions doctor and solicitor which are utilised online to heal other players or get them out of legal trouble. It has a full criminal system which a star rating like a GTA, if you get caught you go to prison for RL hours and you can have friends raid the prison to break you out or go through a walk of shame in online mode where other players throw veggies and eggs at you for a reduced sentence. If you don't get caught you get a bounty and other players can go into your solo world and kill you to collect it. You can also just play as a Bounty Hunter, ganking fools. It's got a few eastern tropes, progression time-gating, energy/stamina, gear is stated items you can't visually see and you wear costumes. You do get plenty of in-game costumes through the story/game play. It's a 'freemium model' where it's free to play but they have a cash shop for cosmetics some direct, some on gacha pulls, and it has an optional monthly sub $5 and a battle pass $15 which give mats, which is basically a minor advantage to your progression ie; iron for weps, leather for armour, stones for upgrading gear, etc.

[h2]If I had to describe this game, it would be if Dark Souls and Infinity Nikki had a baby.[/h2]

Overall, I'm really enjoying this. Much like a lot of games in this style, however, there are... SO many menus. SO MANY. I still sometimes stumble across some other menu with MORE things to collect from, more tasks, and I'm not sure I even remember how I get to most of them. It can be a little overwhelming, if I'm completely honest, but most MMO's kind of suffer from that. 

The story is really good fun. The translations are honestly pretty good, and while I'd love to listen to the Chinese voice acting, sometimes the dialogue goes so fast that I can't read and play the game at the same time, so I've had to forfeit that sadly. 

The gameplay is excellent. There's tons of customization so you can play the way you want to. Want a Dark Souls challenge? You can have that. Want just enough challenge that you can still reasonably progress but also feel really good about yourself? Absolutely. Want to just hurry up and get to the next part of the story? You can do that, too.

There's so much to do. I spent like two hours the other day just messing around and learning Wuji from the Untamed on the guqin, in free play. Maybe at some point I'll feel brave enough to go and play that for giggle in multiplayer, but I go in, see people running around, panic, and go back to solo play.

That's the other thing, if you're just wanting to solo play, you can absolutely do that. You don't HAVE to play with other people, though of course there's a special currency tied into if you play with others. I still have 4 of that currency, and stuff you can buy with it generally costs like... 400. >.> Pretty sure I got those 4 tickets for free, lol.

Eventually, I'll try it out. 

I'm probably not going to be doing the banners very much. Maybe a risk here and there, but to be honest, I have very little faith in trying to complete banners, lol. It costs... a LOT LOT LOT of money to actually obtain what you want to get from banners in these sorts of games. Infinity Nikki has made me wary.

That said, I probably will snag the battle pass, and the monthly stuff. I like the game a lot, and I'll support where and how I can, but I'm definitely no whale, lol. Even so, you can DEFINITELY enjoy this game without Whaling. For those who don't know: "Whaling" refers to players who drop obscene amounts of money to earn and win the items off of banners. I'm talking thousands of dollars on ONE banner, let alone all of them.

This game is absolutely enjoyable without being a whale. It is beautiful, serene, and just the right amount of panic-inducing challenge.

Where Winds Meet is the kind of game that makes you stop mid-fight, pan the camera, and think, “Wow… I should quit my job and go live in a misty bamboo forest.” The world is stunning, the combat animations make you feel like a gravity-defying kung-fu legend, and the soundtrack whispers ancient wisdom directly into your eardrums. The story has that mystical, wandering-hero energy that makes you feel simultaneously enlightened and slightly confused, in the best way. And I love that it works equally well as a solo, peaceful pilgrimage, or as a wild co-op adventure if you want to bring friends along to destroy all serenity immediately.

That said, I swear the menus were put together by a council of immortals arguing for 600 years. There are menus inside menus, on top of sub-menus hiding beneath secondary tabs. You don’t “open inventory,” you embark on a spiritual pilgrimage to the UI realm. And occasionally the English dub translations shift depending on the gender or body type you select at the start, sometimes leading to lines that are… incorrect, but hopefully fixable. It’s immersive, in a very unintentional way.

But despite the menu labyrinth, the translation hiccups, and a few performance issues here and there, Where Winds Meet is genuinely enchanting. It’s ambitious, poetic, dramatic, and surprisingly funny when you play co-op. If the devs simplify just half of the interface, the gaming universe will rejoice. Until then, I’ll be wandering the breathtaking wilderness alone, occasionally joined by friends, all of us lost, confused by settings, but having a great time.

The monetization is a complete non-issue, as there is zero pay2win unlike 90% of other free games like this. The in-app purchases are solely cosmetic. There are some crazy skins at exorbitant prices (like 700 USD if unlucky with the gacha), but I think the normal buyable skins are just as stylish (around 20-40 USD). You can also get plenty of cosmetics for free just by playing.

The combat is very deflection/parry heavy with weapons having very ability-based kits, like a blend of Sekiro and Nioh/Granblue Relink. I won't pretend the combat is quite as tight as those titles, but it completely makes up for it with the multiplayer content and freedom of the open world.

Exploration is reminiscent of Genshin or Wuwa, but much more refined and with a crazy amount of QoL. Those games feel like a chore to explore, while this game is hard to put down. I hit level cap before doing the first story quest, that's how easy it is to get lost and dive down rabbit holes.

The Co-op aspect is pretty decent, but could be improved a bit. You can do a majority of the exploration content in Co-op with friends and progression will be shared, which is awesome and kind of rare for this type of game. You just can't do Main quests and certain special dungeons (but it's easy to drop out, complete it, and re-join).

There's a completely optional MMO mode, where you can join an instance of the world with tons of players running around for social activities. There are also MMO-style raid bosses you can fight with either 5 or 10 people. The game has roles like Tank, Healer, Melee-DPS, and Ranged-DPS. All can clear the campaign just fine, except maybe healer which you'd want to bring a secondary DPS weapon for.

The story is quite good so far, but I would play in Chinese as the English dub is pretty bad. There are an insane amount of side quests, and they're pretty decent for the most part (and often comedic).

Overall, even if it's not a mind-blowing game in any one category, it does everything very well and really gives you a reason to keep playing with the multiplayer aspect and constant flow of content that comes with live service games. I think I'll play this game for quite a long time.

I'm a huge fan of the stories of ancient china, wuxia, the immortals etc and this game delivers it perfectly. It's a genre that's not really been tapped into much at all in gaming and a few of the ones that did try weren't even chinese. So it's really cool to see it done with some authenticity and a lot of passion, there's also a bunch of references from movies like kung fu hustle which are fun easter eggs.

Atm it's more mmo-like than an actual mmo or more similar to older ones like vindictus where you have player hubs and instances. But there is a LOT of co-op orientated stuff like guilds, sects and sect challenges, sworn co-horts (like mini gangs), taking disciples, marriage, boat parties, minigames, professions etc.

Cash shop as far as I can tell is purely cosmetic, there's no p2w in this. They will also randomly do offers and give stuff out for free, 90% discounts or do reward milestones for draws. You can also grind out free draws through season quests, quests in the world like martial challenges or use currency you can grind out to buy them.

So honestly, this is my first real review on Steam, and I’m writing it because I truly believe this game is a masterpiece. After years of stagnation, it finally pushes the boundaries of gaming again. We gamers have been very lenient with Western studios releasing unpolished games with little content. Where Winds Meet raises the bar back to where it should be. I’ll try to summarize:

The Good

Single-player experience on par with the best games ever made - KCD2, Cyberpunk, and The Witcher, just to name few while also being an online game.

Beautiful graphics and sound design.

Huge world with an insane amount of interactions and polished content with almost no bugs.

Combat system is simple to learn but deep, rewarding skill, timing, and strategy. Button-mashing gets punished; parries and dodges feel tight and responsive.

Large variety of bosses, all with different fighting styles.

Kaufeng – one of the best cities ever made in a game, with incredible scale and interactions.

Completely F2P, and no pay-to-win elements.

Tons of collectibles, customization options, outfits, and accessories, most of which you can earn without paying.

Strong amount of co-op and online content at launch.

Unmatched release cadence – new locations, bosses, equipment, and level caps every few days instead of waiting months.

Group content from 5–30 players available from day one.

Fully playable solo or with a party/guild.

First real use of AI NPC implementation, even if it still has a few issues.

The Bad

One of the worst UIs I’ve ever experienced.

Optimization needs work – boss fights run well, but cities (especially Kaufeng) can melt even a 5090 with low FPS.

Multiplayer content could be better (it’s in the pipeline) and can be laggy at times.

The game expects you to know Wuxia. If you’re unfamiliar with the genre, some questlines may feel confusing—like playing a Star Wars game without knowing what Star Wars is.

Can feel grindy for some players.

Final Thoughts

This is a dream come true for gamers. If you can, please support this game. It’s free and truly deserves it.

[h2]Where Winds Meet brought the fun back into gaming for me.[/h2]

I haven't been this hooked on a game in a long time, and with that many hours already played, it's clear this one hit differently.​

[h3]So Much To Do[/h3]

The best part is [b]how much there is to actually do[/b]. Between main story, side quests, exploration, martial arts collecting, sect activities, guild content, and maxing out gear and companions, you're never short on things to work toward. The world feels packed with content that matters, not just filler, and there's always something meaningful to chip away at whether you have 20 minutes or 4 hours to play.​

[h3]The Level Cap System (It's Actually Smart)[/h3]

The level cap system gets a lot of complaints, but honestly, [i]I think it's one of the smarter design choices[/i]. Yes, it's time-gated through Exploration Days and Breakthrough quests, but instead of feeling frustrating, it gives you [u]natural stopping points[/u] and encourages you to actually engage with all the side content instead of just blasting through the main story.​

You can:
[list]
[] Max out your gear
[] Finish entire side quest chains
[] Collect Martial Arts from different sects
[] Work on your companions
[*] Just explore and mess around without feeling like you're falling behind
[/list]

It also means any extra XP you earn gets stored so that means nothing goes to waste and you get to progress faster when future levels unlock.​

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Combat & World Design[/h3]

The combat is [b]fluid and skill-based[/b], the world is gorgeous, and the wuxia setting is refreshing compared to the usual fantasy MMO fare. There's real depth here if you want to dig into builds, weapon combos, and mastering different fighting styles, but it's also accessible enough that you can just enjoy the ride.​

[h3]Final Verdict[/h3]

For a [b]free-to-play[/b] game, this is an absolute steal. The monetization is mostly cosmetic, and progression isn't paywalled, so you can play at your own pace without feeling pressured to spend. If you've been burned out on gaming lately, this might be the one to pull you back in. [b]Highly recommend giving it a shot![/b]​

In all honesty, I did not expect to enjoy my time with this game (85 hours as of writing this) but I have had an absolute blast, mostly in solo expert mode. There is far more content to get caught up in than I imagined, for a free to play game especially. I only recently purchased the battle pass because I feel I spent more than enough time in game to justify it.

The Pros
Traversal is S Tier when you get to that point in game.

Combat is crisp. Blocking can have it's issues but it's often just my skill issue.

Quests are enjoyable. Some can be repetitive, but you can't really get away from that in such a huge world. I never really found myself sick of doing something more than once or even 10 times.

Exploration is outstanding. So many times I find myself looking in every nook and cranny for side quest items.

Cons.
The menu/menus. WAY TO MANY. You get so many unlocks that constantly trying to search for which of the 40 some odd tabs has the unlock you need to "collect" is just way to over complicated.

Performance in some of the later zones was worse for me than the starting area, but given there is way more to interact with in those later areas, it's a very small con.

The time gated content. It didn't really bother me all that much because it gave me time to go explore other areas and find cool interactions, but I get why some are not a fan of it. I think the time between could be lowered.

I know some will not agree, but for me, a gamer dad that plays later in the evenings when the family is asleep. 
This is my game of the year. Right now. (of games I've played)

This game is so good it'll make you want to cultivate immortality until you ascend to the upper realm.

Joke aside, the ambiance and atmosphere is amazing. It truly feels like Murim, and at a time when most mmorpg follow the same boring recipe witht he same mechanics, WMM is a breath of fresh air. The world is alive, and you'll often find yourself wandering to explore your surroundings, even if you were in the middle of the main quest.

Just something as simple as finding a cave entrance under a random rock in the middle of nowhere is something that most rpg lack nowadays. They don't do this anymore, which is a shame because that's what made games like skyrim or the witcher 3 special when they came out. And that's what makes WWM so good now.

The NPCs all have their own personality, and the quests they give aren't the repetitive "go kill this thing x times", or "go gather that thing x times". Even the smallest side quests are real missions, and while some quests are similar, they're never 100% the same. Most of the time they feel unique.

Another very good point too, especially for an asian mmorpg, is that it's not P2W. If anything, the devs made sure that the micro transactions would be as little impactful and intrusive as possible. You can buy skins, or try your luck in the usual gacha pulls if you have money to waste, but those are cosmetics only. And even then, the gacha pity system seems very forgiving compared to other gacha games. 

You can't artificially boost your strength by buying a sht ton of materials for weapons either. After each season the weapons upgrades are reset and everyone starts from scratch, both f2p players and whales. You keep your skills though so it's not a complete reset, just enough so everyone starts fresh.

Even the grind is casual friendly ; you don't need to log in and play for hours every day. You don't need to farm days for x item. The game lets you play at your rythm, and doesn't punish you for it which is extremely rare for an asian mmorpg.

The combat system is very good. It feels like a mix of souls like with dodge/parry like other arpg, and classic mmorpg with skills, weapon combos, talent points, etc.

You can play alone or online, and you're not penalized for either. The game doesn't force you into one mode either. And if you play solo, you can still interact with other players by putting signs (think of darks ouls) that other players can see, which more often than not pushes players to be helpful toward each other. You'll often see signs near secret entrances hiding a chest for example, tips to complete missions, or just a small message in hard to reach location that have a good scenery to enjoy. 

I could list all the pros here, but the review would be way too long, so I'll just end with the few cons instead : 

1. The english VO is terrible, and many lines are missing. You're better off using chinese voices with subtitle.

2. The UI is beautiful, but an absolute pain to navigate. Too many menus, with menus inside menus. You need to spend a couple of minutes every hour clicking around just to claim your rewards, and it can get frustrating very fast.

3. This is not so much about the original studio itself, but rather whoever was in charge of the localization : as you may expect from a western localizer team, they gave themself the liberty to change some translations that weren't politcaly correct, such as male/female for body type 1/2

4. While the game isn't P2W, for some reason the devs decided to increase the price of MTX for the global version compared to the chinese version. Same stuff you can buy in the shop, but more expensive for no reason. Idk if they take us for fools or not, but apparently they don't mind raising the price for the global version, and I doubt they'll ever change it unless people are vocal about it.

5. And lastly, the movements can feel a bit junky sometimes because of the animations. I understand they put a lot of care on the movement animations, especially for a game that takes place in Murim which revolve entirely around martial arts, but this should really be fixed. For example, if you turn at 180°, your character will waste some frames on place before turning. It's even worse on the horse. The jump has a delay too. All in all, movement don't feel as responsive as they should.

Anyway, WMM is definitely an amazing game. They're setting up new standards for mmorpg.

nt. : oh and also, it's one of the rare game (if not the only one) that makes a great use of AI. No bs AI art, but instead, some NPCs used an AI to answer to you, and it's extremely well done. It's free by itself and is entertaining enough to pass the "I'll quit in an hour... Oh ♥♥♥♥ it's been 3 hours" test.

That said I feel like the UI was designed by someone who's never played an MMO and didn't bother looking at any of the UIs of other popular games, it can take 3-4 different menus following red dots to find a Daily Login Reward because it's part of a sub-event of a battlepass event of a holiday event. 

There's quite a bit of options for in game feedback at least, as attested to by the number of world events(?) that seem to only exist in menus with comment sections full of people asking what it even is in 2-3 different languages.

The control scheme is a bit unusual as well but actually does work once you manage to reprogram yourself from the usual souls like controls with mouse being little more than enemy lock and sometimes camera control.

The positives: As I said at the start, even with $0 investment I found myself losing track of time to a significant degree, there is a LOT of content to the point of being a bit daunting but it's free and as far as I can tell will let you get away with damn near any build to the point where I'm genuinely surprised by how many dead player markers in boss rooms I come across where I end up with an Ace. 

The Shop so far seems to be mostly cosmetic with healing potion and inventory capacity boosters, there isn't any pvp as far as I've seen and there isn't any real inventory usage aside from crafting materials so these advantages are useful and possibly worthwhile, but not in a directly competitive way. Maybe someone with the Battlepass will find it easier to clutch in a raid or skip some trips in resource gathering but nothing major.

- Good combat with difficulty options. Unless you pick Legendary mode, you can freely switch between difficulties. If you didn't start with Legendary mode you cannot switch to it. If you picked it but then switch off of it, you also cannot switch back.
- Very engaging and interesting bosses - boss difficulty also varies.
- Lots of exploration. The two regions we have on Global server as of now are huge. The city of Kaifeng is huge, and you can even walk into every single building. I also love reading signposts left by other players. Most of the time, Chinese players tend to be helpful, and there's been a mix of helpful, funny, or trolling ones in English. 
- Touching stories (including short sidequests) - Love the lore given to bosses and exploring their respective locations. IMO: I liked the prologue, but after that the main quest felt kinda boring at first until towards the end of Qinghe. Kaifeng is immediately very interesting though.
- All the emotional moments in this game do really well at drawing me in.
- Nice OST, I especially love the menu music.
- Great graphics with well-crafted environments
- You have the option to play this game completely solo if you want. Even in multiplayer, there is never any pressure to talk in chat. In leisure multiplayer hangouts, everyone just chills and minds their own business.
- Outside of a few specific areas in Kaifeng (where there's a ton of NPCs in one area), the game is optimized well. If you are struggling to run the Steam version I heard there's also a Lite version on the official website you can download that has a bit lower system requirements.
- No P2W. You pay to play dress up with your character.

Cons: 
- Menu UI is just horrendous. Menus within menus that are painful to navigate, although once you get used to it it isn't as bad - still needs QOL.

The choice to translate a few characters' names into their English meaning (i.e. Ruby, Water Lady, etc.), while 99.9% of other names are in Pinyin, is odd to me. I would've preferred their name be kept in Pinyin with the option to click on their name to see their name's meaning.
