Where Winds Meet is a surprisingly polished open-world wuxia adventure that mixes stylish combat, great atmosphere, and some innovative features you don’t usually see in free-to-play games. It blends classic inspirations with new ideas, creating a unique experience right from the start.

Pros:

• Smooth and responsive combat with great parries and dodges

• Atmosphere reminiscent of Ghost of Tsushima and Sekiro

• Unique minigames (healing people, debating, solving social situations)

• The ability to chat with AI-driven NPCs and build relationships is genuinely fresh for this genre

• Highly detailed graphics, especially impressive for a free-to-play game

Cons:

• The menu is overly cluttered with events, rewards, and notifications

• New players may find it overwhelming to navigate at first

Personal Comment:
The game blends martial arts and exploration in a surprisingly effective way. The AI-driven NPC interactions are one of the most interesting innovations I’ve seen recently. The UI is definitely messy, but considering this is a free-to-play title with such strong visuals, it’s still an impressive experience overall.

Total Score: 8/10

I do recommend trying it out, and I played it on both PC/PS5, but I do caution about "the bad" listed below. For many it would be deal breaker regardless of the games "free to play" nature.

The good:
- The Wuxia world is great and really enjoyed the atmosphere/music of the Ghostlight Market (foggy or not)
- Graphics are pretty good, and the outfits, and weapons look great.
- The story and characters are enjoyable too, and some parts are funny while some are sad.
- The Sect's are interesting and unique, and you can swap between them, so you are not locked into one. (can only be 
   in one at a time, and you lose all progress when you leave with the exception of unlocked cosmetics).

The bad:
- Story is mostly a solo experience (or played on a Co-Op world which is not MMO scale)
- It is not truly an MMO, as there is a MMO like environment, but there isn't much to do there other than the points stuff below.
- Always behind Chinese servers (by like 6 months or something like that)
- Time Gates (want to progress, sorry... need to wait 5+ real life days)
- The game can be VERY time consuming with all the side stuff and they get really tedious and repetitive.
        - Scholar minigame for a kind of special points
        - Dancing in a field of animals for special points
        - Meditating in a field... for special points
        - Doing your Sect or Sectless quests... for special points (to gain rank it is a leaderboard based system, and top 
          ranks are left to player vote)
        - Defeating the bosses using points... for chests, and points
        - Doing PVP stuff (if that is your thing) for points
- Combat is kind of repetitive, and boss fights are fun (the first few times you fight a particular boss anyway)
- Performance issues (there were so many at launch that there is no way they tested the game before release)
- Cosmetics are ridiculously overpriced (yes, one outfit is $40,000 USD+ due to RNG (or Gacha-like mechanic with a pity system)), but comes with a boat that lets people... you guessed it.... idle for points BUT with everyone on the server)
- The menus are really clunky/slow, and there are like 500 of them (exaggerating, but there are lot)
- Not sure why this is, but most Chinese games always have input limits within so many seconds, so you almost need to deliberately put it a delay in between your button presses when navigating the menu. press... wait 1 sec... press... wait 1 sec...

Ok so here's a review. I am gonna treat this as a "Paid game" because there's really no F2P game that would be a fair comparison.

I'll try to keep glaze to a minimum but I love the chinese wuxia genre so be warned.

Content? Plenty.
Graphics? Beautiful.
Story line? I usually skip cutscenes, I didn't this time
AI usage? For once I can say usage of AI was made tasteful and added to the game, instead of using AI to generate slop storylines and terrible art, they let it help you create your own faces based on images and voice, and to actually talk to npcs
Gameplay? Absolutely great, each new skill makes you giddy

Now for the downsides.
I had to delete the game because the content was releasing too slowly and all I could do was grind bosses.
The AI npc conversations are very monotone and have no affect on the world, which I know are due to limitations but still kinda makes me not actually talk and just go *does whatever you need* till I get the affection.
The UI is terrible, seriously finding something twice is almost a miracle at this point, the glowing notifs are a life saver but the UI still suffers.
This isnt really a game fault but I couldn't find any matches for the 10 player raids except once, perhaps that was just me tho.

Will I download it again when more content exists? absolutely.

Do I think It should be nominated for game of the year? Absolutely.

Do I think it brings uniqueness and a tasteful innovative element that doesnt just mean "ai generated graphics" ? yes.

That said. if the bad parts are fixed I believe that this game would absolutely keep me engaged for hundreds of hours more and that's rare for me I usually am quit to hate a game.

The world map is vast and the regions are beautiful (with even better ones to come). Pretty much all genres of gameplay in an open world RPG are represented in this game, there's something for everyone and it doesn't feel forced on you.

Unfortunately, the main story (what was revealed so far) is mediocre at best. Some events feel forced and they don't tie into each other very well. The story wants you to take it (and the world) seriously, only to insert an extremely unrealistic interaction or plot point every couple of quests that wakes you up to how unserious and fantastical everything actually is, despite the serious themes. The characters (both main and side) are also very one dimensional and it's hard to develop any kind of emotional attachment to them. It's better to just pretend the main character has no story at all, and it's just you experiencing the world.

In summary: Play it for the gameplay, the visuals, or feel free to skip this one.

Where Winds Meet delivers a rich narrative paired with stunning visuals, excelling in both solo and multiplayer experiences. The combat system is the highlight: it is accessible but discourages simple button-mashing. Instead, it prioritizes defense and timing—landing a precise parry is often more rewarding than executing a long combo.

The game also features AI-driven NPCs that you can befriend. While not revolutionary, these interactions offer an interesting way to uncover deep lore through conversation. Note that the user interface has a slight learning curve, but once you get the hang of it, the experience is seamless

Where Winds Meet is truly one of the best games I’ve played in a long time. Everything is crafted with impressive attention to detail—from the gameplay flow to the breathtaking world design. The cultural elements woven throughout the game make the experience even more meaningful and immersive.

I grew up reading stories filled with ancient legends and martial arts fantasy, so the atmosphere of the game felt familiar and incredibly enjoyable. I understood every layer of the story and every message it tried to express, which made the journey even more special.

Overall Impression

Where Winds Meet genuinely surprised me in a good way. It’s clear a lot of thought went into the overall design. The game isn’t relying on mini-games, grinding, or combat-heavy padding — it’s the full package working together that makes it shine.

Gameplay & Combat

The combat system is sophisticated and deeper than expected. It took a bit of time to fully understand, but once it clicks, it feels rewarding and flexible. So far, I haven’t seen any pay-to-win elements, which is a massive plus.

World & Exploration

Exploration is top tier. The map feels alive, with small details, hidden treasures, and side quests that actually feel meaningful. Discovering things naturally in the world is one of the game’s biggest strengths.

Visuals & Atmosphere

Visually, the game is fantastic. The environments, lighting, and overall presentation look stunning and make every area feel handcrafted. It’s easily one of the game’s standout qualities.

Story

The story is good so far, though it’s not the main driver for me. It supports the experience without trying too hard to dominate it.

Bugs & Issues

There are some voiceover bugs — probably the most noticeable downside at the moment. Aside from that, I haven’t encountered major issues.

Final Verdict

8.5 to 9/10 — with a lot of potential to get even better. Where Winds Meet offers a cohesive, thoughtful experience that goes beyond typical open-world formulas.

The combat is VERY good, none of the weapons are really considered stronger than others, so you can use any build you'd like. The battlepass doesn't actually give you any advantage, and I'd only recommend it if you like the cosmetics. You have a fan and umbrella that can repeatedly heal you without potions. 

Going off the cosmetics, so far they're all super pretty and unique. They aren't overpriced compared to other mmos in my opinion, and people buy them to support the game. This game has triple A quality because of the cosmetics alone, so I don't really regret spending $5 here and there on something cute. 

I have no complaints so far, the game will only get better from here and I'm excited to see how.

Bad:
- The story and quests makes no sense for Western audience as in most cases they reference some extremely niche Chinese/Wuxia history and lore.
- Horrible translation make it even worse.

- Too many systems and subsystems, none of which is polished and added just for content padding.

- Can't play the story in co-op, only some side-activities

Overall, there are way too many annoying things to enjoy this game. Such a shame, since combat is actually fun.

Honestly, side quests tend to be engaging — a rarity in such games (and in games generally for quite some time). World design is stunning, and animations are generally excellent, although occasionally clunky — allowing little precision to movement. Bosses tend to skip frames and even cancel animations halfway through, which sometimes makes fights irritating.

Learned and took everything it could from other gacha, ARPG, MMOs etc and put it into this game and somehow executed it amazingly. Combat is challenging yet fun and rewarding, boss raids and real mechanics avoiding "bullet sponge" scenarios, easy/simple exploration from literally flying through the sky with martial skill with various styles and more, endless coop features including PVP and PVE with modes similar to battle royal and so much more, "job" progression such as healer or scholar that has both player interaction or environmental reactions meaning AI or jobs directly from players themselves, guilds/family/partner(marriage)/master/disciple all player-to-player focus from roleplaying to getting rewards, endless customization and outfits that look stunning and beautiful. There is so much more and most of these I am barely scratching the surface on.

Now for the negative. It does have a gacha system and for those who are unfamiliar with that it's basically a very expensive gambling system that operates on FOMO and eggs you on into keep going further to get something really cool, which in this case for this game it's mostly cosmetic/outfits or mounts. Meaning if you have terrible luck (they don't give out too many chances to pull for these exclusive items anyway) you could spend somewhere roughly 300-400$ or even more just to get the item you want. It goes even further for example a big/show-off skin to flaunt your money as of right now costs very roughly $35,000-$60,000. Yes that's correct you heard that right, there is a skin in-game that high. However, it is a free game and it's not really pay to win so keep that in mind. That's also not to say that it's the only good skin in the game at all, in fact most of the skins even the common ones you get are pretty good.

Last negative is more for newer players and the new player experience. Menu simulator/menu inception. Just SO MANY MENUS AND MENUS WITHIN MENUS AND OBSCURE BUTTONS TO TAKE YOU TO SOME OTHER RANDOM MENU. 95% of the time I was completely lost on finding anything and I knew if I clicked off that page I was never going to see it again. This took some actual effort in trying to be acquainted where stuff is and it's still confusing. This problem of course will fix itself with time as you continue to experience the game but it will probably be a struggle for a bit to navigate.

Conclusion: 2 small negatives does not outweigh the tremendous amount of positives this game is holding right now and has something for everyone of all variety from skill/playtime-availability/casual-hardcore and more. Give it a try since it's free and see if you can get past the hurdle of menus and you might find something you really like.

I can appreciate the suprisingly decent exploration and the sheer number of minigames with online interactions, I can excuse the typical 'mobile game' feature stank these types of game usually suffer from, but I'm deeply disappointed on how this game handles the arguably most important thing - combat. I've defeated multiple major bosses and a world boss solo on expert and if you're expecting soulsike gameplay - the comparisons to sekiro are definitely less than honest, as this game is more like Nioh and less like Souls. What I'm about to say will sound like common Fromsoftware shilling but these types of games have either really good and polished combat, or they fall flat in the deep ocean of mediocrity which is unfortunately the case both with Nioh (imo) and this game. Mobility is fast yet clunky, as the character usually takes a long time to react to inputs. Enemies are damage sponges which prolongs the fights unnecesarilly. Visual clarity is quite bad with tons of flashy effects spinning around you and your targets. Missing deflects on any part of a combo is severely punishing which is unfair at best, considering no proper alternative for defence in this game (blocking and dodging are definitely not meant to be used as a replacement for deflects). Feels like bosses have a lot of true combos (true, as in 'miss 1 deflect and watch your character get hit by the whole combo' feeling). Some hitboxes tied to some animations are questionable at best. 

All in all I played this game hoping to get a fun, funfilling combat. As many such cases, the game tries to copy Souls but fails to offer comparable level of polishness and things that 'just make sense' in terms of combat fluidity, fairness and challenge.

You might like it if you don't care or have more tolerance to wannabe soulslike experiences, especially since other features are genuinely interesting despite f2p-mobile-gacha aura this game reeks of. The most important thing for me turned out to be mediocre, so all these mechanics around combat lead to annoyance and frustration.

Review time.

First things first; it's fun. I'm having fun and there is a LOT to do in this game.
Some areas are a bit bland, some areas are like Blighttown. Some areas are like Siofra/Nokron.
Beautiful, misty, grassy things everywhere.

Pleasing to the eye.

I've heard some (not a lot) of people say they felt it was a bit clunky... No. Not at all. The combat is tight. Very tight.
It's also interesting, flashy and satisfying.
I mean, come on... you can master an UMBRELLA.

That's like threaded cane level Bloodborne swag.

The map doesn't feel empty. Quite the opposite; there's stuff everywhere.
The treasure chests may not always feel very rewarding, like "oh, cool... some more coins and other sh*t I don't know how to use". But the map is packed with stuff!

You also get XP for everything. Even picking up pebbles.
A pebble.

I just got XP because I picked up a rock.


So, that's all fine and dandy. Great stuff. Can't believe it's free, yadda yadda....
Then you open the menu.

Yeah, you... do that, and the game immediately shifts to "wtf am I even looking at... what is all this sh*t?"
It's a lot. It's overwhelming. Most of it is redundant.

There's like 4 ways of getting to the same thing via menus.
It's like those Russian dolls, where you open one up, just to find another smaller one. Only, in this case, the menus get larger and more extravagant as you go (and, ehem... more expensive, too).


Seriously, imagine you're playing Warframe for the first time.
You go through the opening cinematic, finally gain control of your character, and what's the first thing do you do?
Open the menu. You always open the menu, just to see what's what.

So, you're a new player in Warframe, you open the menu... and you are suddenly FLOODED with info. ALL KINDS OF INFO.

Pets, BPs, artist cosmetics, dev cosmetics, archwing, syndicates, plat, credits, forma, Index-tutorials, focus, Empyrean missions, archons, sorties, kitguns, EVERYTHING is right there. To a brand-new player.

It's all LOCKED, of course. But it's all there, menu upon menu upon menu... of just STUFF.

You look at it all, you see debt-bonds... and you're like "wtf is a debt-bond??"
"GRANDMOTHER TOKENS?? WTF IS A GRANDMOTHER TOKEN??"
"KURIA... WHAT IS A KURIA!?"

And you're lost.
This is initially what this game does to you with its menu.

I really think this game could have benefitted more from a "one bite at a time" approach, rather than trying to cram your mouth with the whole 23" pizza.


14 hours later, and I get what most of the stuff is, and where to find it.
But that first menu impression is rough, man.

Maybe they should revamp the new player experience a bit, like how WF and FF14 did a while ago.

PS: it’s very well optimized. Oh, and your double-jump/dash is disabled indoors and in dungeons… why? I don’t know…..

TLDR - it’s free so give it a try!

Absolutely love this game, but I wouldn't give it a 10/10... probably more of a 8.5 or 9. I did have a chance to take part in the beta, so I had a bit of a head start as to learning where to go and how to do certain things (Nothing carried over, so I had to remake my character from scratch). Haven't had any graphic or connection issues, so my list of pros and cons is more so about my average play experience.

Pros:
---- Free to Play (Money is mainly spent on cosmetics or a few extra chances to gain energy to fight bosses, etc.)
---- Detailed character creator (Can even use your voice or photos to generate a random character).
---- Open world that feels lived in (Full of npcs, enemies, quests and secrets that reward exploration and don't feel repetitive. You can actually follow the npcs to see them go through detailed full day routines with dialogue. And yes, you can be thrown into jail for committing crimes like attacking/killing villagers).
---- Swapping Solo & Multiplayer/Co Op Play (Very easy to pop into a friends world or the multiplayer lobby to adventure and hangout for fight/arena queues then pop back into your own game when you need a break from people or simply want to solo).
---- Rewarding Co Op (Unlike some F2P games, both players get the items you find when exploring co op instead of it just going to the world owner).
---- Interesting Relation System (You can marry other players regardless of gender, find a master/disciple, put together a team to adventure with, sworn cohorts/siblings, guilds, and an intimacy system, simple romantic and/or platonic, which can unlock cosmetics and emotes.
---- Not being forced into multiplayer (I enjoy playing solo with the occasionally hangout here and there, so not having the game push me to party up in order to do stuff is refreshing. Though sometimes injuries can only be healed by other players, which 99% of the time you just pop up the notification that you need a doctor and another player accepts, pops in your world, heals you up, then goes back to their own world.
---- Beautiful boss fights (Qianye's 2nd fight and Zheng E's fight are by far my favorites!).
---- Lots of things to do (If you want a break from the main story there is a ton of things to do: cards, mahjong, sumo wrestling, healing, scholar debate games, exploring, outpost takeovers, world bosses, world compendium discoveries, steal skills from different sects, play pranks on other players, disguise yourself as an npcs to cause mischief, and more!). 

Cons:
---- Real world time gates on progression (Kinda sucks having to wait a few real world days to move past a level cap, but I also see it as a chance to explore more since the exp gets stored).
---- Can't change most of the settings until after the tutorial fight, but luckily it doesn't last too long (They may update this later).
---- Chat can move very fast (So asking for help or information can be daunting if on a populated chat server, but this can be dealt with by swapping to a less populated one).
---- Lots of different in game currencies (Draw shop, general goods, bounties, guild jades, jade fish for activities, sect activity tokens, and even more. Can get overwhelming, but I feel the separation is simply to get people to try out different modes since most of the rewards are just cosmetics or background pieces).
---- Cosmetics can be expensive for some people ($20 average for big sets. But considering its F2P, they have to get their money from somewhere. Outfits and stuff can also be gifted to others players as well, so if you really want a cosmetic, find yourself a sugar daddy/momma in game. There are also in game coupons you can earn from battle passes and other events).

here Winds Meet is a bold, high-ambition open-world wuxia RPG that succeeds in many areas but trips in some due to its scope.

If you love: Wuxia / martial-arts stories, open-world exploration, deep character builds, and don’t mind a steep learning curve — this game is very compelling.

If you’re more casual or don’t like overly complex systems, the amount of menus, currencies, and features might feel overwhelming.

Technical requirements: You’ll want a reasonably good PC or PS5 to get the most out of its visuals and performance.

For a free-to-play game, Where Winds Meet delivers very strong value — the cosmetic monetization model is generally seen as fair, and the game offers a lot of content without forcing pay. But because of its technical and UI issues, it’s probably still a “work in progress” in some respects.

DETAILS:

---{ Graphics }---
The game looks amazing for its scope and size. There are plenty of spots where you will just stop, stare, and probably take a screenshot. The character creator is robust and transfers to the actual game well.
The only consideration is the skin tone may be slightly off, but this is very common in games, and easy to fix here.

---{ Gameplay }---
An explorer's dream! The game is absolutely choked full of distractions that are always worth it.  The fighting is fun and the many different weapons all feel wholly unique.  I read a comment left in game that I think best sums up the gameplay, "I can't stop playing this game for some reason."

*Important note: At first the multitude of game menus, play modes, and systems can seem overwhelming.  I felt this, but you must give it a chance.  I don't even have it all figured out yet, but I see this as a positive.  There's so much to see and do in this game!
Plus, they give you rewards for exploring the menus and interacting with the various systems.

---{ Audio }---
At first I thought the sound design was just "good", but yesterday when I loaded the game and the theme started playing, I realized how much the music has already stuck with me. Similar to how the Oblivion or Skyrim themes do. 
Regarding sound effects, they are on the high end of serviceable. I would like a bit more bass-based sounds, but that's a nitpick.
Sound direction works well, and even works on the pair of three-way speakers I typically use.

---{ Audience }---
I have seen conflicting ratings listed for the game. One was ages 12+ and the other 16+.
That said, I believe it is fine for ages 12+. Nothing overly adult and very little blood, gore, etc.

---{ PC Requirements }---
I have a decent setup (i9-11900K, RTX 4070TI, 64GB RAM, NVME) and the game runs like a dream!
There was one cave where you have to solve puzzles using automatons that I noticed some frame drops.
Other than that, it has run very smoothly everywhere.  Even multiplayer areas with lots of other players.
That said, I have just gotten to the major city in the game, so I cannot speak to performance there.

*I think what's important here is the game runs at Ultra settings on my PC.  Therefore, even if you have different specs, still give it a try.  I mean, it's free to do so!

---{ Game Size }---
Right now the game is about 100GB.  This will increase as the many planned updates are released.
for example, the Chinese version is up to 170GB currently.
Plan accordingly, but is anyone surprised by the size?

---{ Difficulty }---
The game can be as difficult or as challenging as you want it to be.
My wife is a gamer and loves playing on easier modes, they have that.
I like playing on standard difficulty. Where I go between Power Fantasy and Challenge based on the content, they have that too.
For players who want extra titles and things for a more brutal challenge, it's there.
There's even a permadeath option...

---{ Grind }---
Some of the content is quite grindy. Min/Maxing stats and some of the cosmetics.
However, I don't think this is a bad thing...
This game has a grind, but you do not need to participate in it to progress.
However, I will be!

---{ Story }---
Story is vital to me, and at first I thought it was a weak point.
Until I realized I had been exploring and completely ignoring the MSQ. Once I engaged with it, it got very good!  Especially during the quest that occurs between the two main areas.

The side quests are also very well done.  They can be funny and emotional.  I happened across one yesterday about spirits that really hit me hard in the feels.
Some of the voice acting does not match the mouth movement in cut scenes, but this is something they are very aware of and rapidly improving.  I have already noticed it.

---{ Game Time }---
I was wondering if this would be a situation where the game feels vast, but then before I knew it, I would be out of content.  However, given the updates and content the Chinese version has already received, and all of the MMO content I have hardly dabbled in, I expect the game to be as long as you want it to be.
That said, expect 150 hours of quality content realistically.
*If a game is good, I want it to be long.  If you like short games, this is not for you.

---{ Price }---
There's no way a Western studio would offer this much content for free!
It's an obvious play by China to take a big chunk out of the Western AAA video game industry.
And if Western game devs refuse to give us good games at a fair price, I say "Bring it on!"

Really, they could have charged full price AND had all the battle passes and such.  There is some gacha to attract whales or whatever, but I couldn't care less!  You don't have to engage with it at all, and there are plenty of cool outfits and ways to get premium draws for free.
*Frankly, anyone who complains about the pricing model here has no idea what they are talking about!

---{ Bugs }---
There's the voiceover issues that are being worked on.
Other than that, I haven't experienced bugs.  No floating items or glitches.
In fact, the few things I thought were bugs turned out to be me not reading the screen...

---{ 10 / 10 }---
If you can't tell already, I love this game!
*I can't stop playing the game, and I know precisely why!

The best advice I can give is to go slow, read the screens, and don't try to take it on all at once.
Hit the menu every once in a while and select anything with a red square or diamond.  That means you have a reward waiting to claim in that menu.
Start with the solo gameplay, and once you begin to feel comfortable, add in some multi-player elements.

Genre: The game is described as a hybrid between a single-player RPG and an MMO, which is quite unique. It is not a traditional action-adventure RPG but rather mimics MMO mechanics in a single-player environment.
Setting: The world is visually beautiful and rich in exploration opportunities, which is a strong positive for players who enjoy immersive environments.
2. Core Gameplay Mechanics
Time-Gated Progression:
The progression system is heavily time-gated, meaning players can only level up their character a limited number of times before needing to perform a "breakthrough" to the next tier.
Early breakthroughs occur daily, but by level 40, the waiting period extends to two days.
Experience points (XP) earned during the waiting period are stored but cannot be used until the breakthrough occurs.
This gating affects not only leveling but also quest progression and access to new story areas, which can feel restrictive and frustrating.
The reviewer notes that some players believe these time gates might be temporary, linked to the current game season.
3. Wuxia and Combat Elements
Cinematics and Combat:
The game features impressive cinematics that enhance the storytelling.
Combat is visually appealing but requires more dexterity, especially when using a controller.
The gameplay complexity is higher than initial previews suggest.
Flying Kung Fu and Mobility Skills:
Iconic Wuxia elements like flying kung fu are locked behind exploration milestones, which can be counterintuitive.
The flying mechanics are described as "janky" and lack precise control, limiting player satisfaction.
Other mobility skills (wall striding, running fast, running on water) are mostly restricted to exploration and disabled during quests, breaking immersion and fluidity.
This restriction creates a jarring experience when transitioning between free exploration and quest areas.
4. Game Complexity and Depth
Menu Simulator and MMO-Like Systems:
The game features an extensive array of menus and systems, reminiscent of MMOs.
Players must manage numerous progression layers: character level, gear, martial arts, mystic ways, inner ways, harmony, professions, profession skills, and even gear slots.
The complexity is likened to games like Warframe, known for their deep and sometimes overwhelming progression systems.
Despite the complexity, the game maintains a singular story arc focused on the player's character, justifying its RPG label.
5. Overall Impression and Value
Pros:
The game is free to play, which is a significant advantage.
Beautiful graphics and immersive cinematics, with emotionally impactful moments (e.g., Velvet Shade's Revelry Hall cinematic).
Offers a large amount of content and exploration.
Cons:
Time-gated progression can be frustrating and limit the pacing.
Mobility and combat mechanics have limitations and control issues.
The overwhelming number of menus and progression systems may intimidate or fatigue some players.
Reviewer’s Conclusion:
Despite its flaws, the game is enjoyable and offers substantial free content.
The reviewer appreciates the experience and the entertainment value it provides over many hours.

TL;DR - Worth it. Fun. In-depth. Beautiful. LOTS to do and explore. Yes, Chinese Free-to-Play so ya know - gambling (loot box type stuff), monetization cosmetics, battle pass system. But this game is MMO 2.0 and well worth the time and effort.

Before I begin I highly recommend watching Dalfang's youtube video ripping IGN's review of the game apart. Because it will give some cultural context to the game. And allow one to approach the game with a clear understanding of what is expected. Plus they are way more entertaining than me. 

Combat: Souls-like with stipulations. Patient, parry and dodge. Be smart. Use the mystic arts. It is in-depth and fun. The various weapon styles are beautiful, but also relevant. I really wanted to use a specific weapon, but my play style fits the Spear, so I had to adjust. I love the spear, it is fun, and fit with just my tempo. The fan is my second favorite. Overall, I have found the combat to be fun and engaging.

Professions: Engaging. Doctor and Scholar are interesting easy to learn card games. Plenty of npc open world moments to use them and Star Wars Galaxies style of healing and helping players as well. The Bounty Board system makes it quick and easy to engage in this. Or just going to the main online mode and people will often be willing to heal without prompting.

Building: A cool addition, needs work. Building in the game is easy enough. But the pieces don't always seem to line up. Once you explore it, build some custom blueprints, it eases, but this could use some work. I am not a major builder, No Man's Sky, Starfield, Fallout, these are my experiences to draw from. Still, I feel this area could be improved.

Advancement: I spent a lot of time exploring without advancing my level cap. I enjoy that. There are things locked behind specific levels and that encourages to continue that level progression. But not forcing the advancement and allowing open exploration with scaled enemies is a great addition I think. The Main Story and even some side ones have real-time timers on it. I am currently waiting for the main story to unlock and at first that bugged me a bit. Because I was engaged, I was in it and then brakes! But it forces you to stop and look around. Go explore. And I realized I hadn't been doing that as I was in the beginning. It was a reminder to go enjoy the world and spend time on other quests. Such as the Gold Leaf Warrior questline. Which was 100% worth it. So have a more positive view on this now.

Music: It is a big thing for me in games. I have loved the guqin for decades and to see it fully in-game. To be able to play it. Amazing. Not the hugest fan of the mechanics, but love that it is included. The various music in the game is great. Just journeying, the opening title song, the various musical challenges, all hit the perfect note.

Jack-of-All-Trades: "a master of none, is better than a master of none." People forget the rest of that saying too often. This game gives you options. You are not gate-kept on weapons, professions, or play. Solo, multi-player, exploration, main story. You'll have loops to jump through, but you are never fully stopped, and none of it is behind a paywall. I enjoy the various activities. I enjoy the chance to explore new things, try new systems, all of it. This isn't a weakness of the game, it is player freedom. 

Free-to-Play?: I played a majority of it free-to-play with no issues. I enjoyed the game so I purchased the battle pass, nice addition, but definitely wouldn't say needed at all. I didn't feel any difference. I just wanted to support the game because I was enjoying it so much. Definitely wouldn't say play-to-win, money is more about looking "cool" - but the game gives you plenty on its own. And earning them through quests gives the items weight and meaning. I wear the heck out my gold leaf trinket. The loot box drawing system is rigged as they always are, but you can still get cool stuff. Just be mindful as you could easily drop 150$ chasing a specific cosmetic (happened to a player I know - that is on him of course, but still, be mindful, wise money management). 

Overall: "A Jack of All Trades is a Master of None, which is still better than a Master of None." Player freedom. Exploration. The game has flaws for sure. Localization is still messy. Some game mechanics feel AI built, because no humanly way to complete certain challenges. But it feels the developers are addressing these concerns. Making these minor adjustments to polish the challenge and gameplay without sacrificing the difficulty. Voices can be weird. Still some hiccups on framerate at times (specifically with world bosses). It has rough edges, but we are going into week two of global launch. All games have rough edges, this one way less than most AAA games these days. 

But overall? This is a gem of a game - dynamic, grand, beautiful, engaging, interesting. A great introduction to a genre and culture I have enjoyed for some time. Explore it with an open mind and you'll have a ton of fun.

⭐ Where Winds Meet — Review
Where Winds Meet is an ambitious open-world action RPG set in a richly stylized version of ancient China during the final years of the Ten Kingdoms era. At its core, the game blends martial arts combat, narrative choice, and immersive exploration — all wrapped in stunning visuals inspired by traditional Chinese landscapes and wuxia fantasy.
From the very first moments, the game impresses with its worldbuilding. The environment feels alive: misty mountains stretch across the horizon, cherry blossoms fall from ancient trees, and villages breathe with culture and conflict. Whether you’re leaping across rooftops or gliding between mountain peaks, traversal feels fluid, cinematic, and deeply satisfying.
In terms of gameplay, Where Winds Meet offers a wide range of approaches. Players can fight as a wandering swordsman, practice different martial arts techniques, or even avoid combat altogether by picking paths of diplomacy or stealth. The combat system is fast and dynamic, sometimes reminiscent of titles like Ghost of Tsushima or Black Myth: Wukong, but with more emphasis on acrobatics, philosophy, and martial-arts mastery.
Narratively, the game gives players freedom: your decisions shape your character’s fate and influence the world around you. While not every storyline branch feels equally polished, the moral complexity and multiple endings give the game strong replay value.
Technically, Where Winds Meet is impressive but not perfect. The world is large and detailed, yet occasional bugs, animation inconsistencies, and pacing issues can break immersion. However, these rough edges feel like the result of ambition rather than laziness — and many players will find that the game’s artistry outweighs these flaws.

Verdict
Where Winds Meet is a captivating experience for fans of open-world RPGs and wuxia storytelling. It’s not flawless — but its heart, atmosphere, and creativity make it stand out from many recent releases. If you're looking for a game that offers emotional depth, freedom of playstyle, and breathtaking exploration, this one is worth your time.

Where Winds Meet delivers a visually striking wuxia world with exceptional atmosphere and freedom. The standout is its character customisation—easily one of the best in any RPG, with detailed sculpting, authentic faces, and outfits that genuinely match the setting. It’s a major reason I enjoyed the game so much.

Exploration feels rewarding, movement is fluid, and the wuxia abilities make traversal fun. Combat looks stylish and cinematic, though the hit detection and AI still need refinement. The story has strong moments but sometimes loses pacing.

Performance can be inconsistent depending on hardware, and some systems feel ambitious but not fully polished yet.

Overall: A bold, beautiful RPG with incredible customisation and great potential, held back slightly by technical issues and uneven balance. Still absolutely worth trying if you enjoy wuxia, exploration, and creating your own unique hero.

This is, by far, one of the best Action Combat MMO-lites out there, you might come for the outfits, for the lore, for the meme clips you see on tiktok and youtube but you will stay for the insanely cool and diverse environments and the addictive combat that strikes the right balance between challenging and easy to get used to.

Let's start with the cons bc that list is rather short:
-incredibly expensive microtransactions (if you consider upwards of 1000$ micro)
-sometimes lack of quality in translations (typos, wrong translations etc)
-some quests lack clear structure i.e. wait 1 real day to continue w/o explicitly stating that
-some NPC interactions esp the "make a friend/familiar faces" interactions can feel clunky as hell

Now on to the pros:
-combat, by far the strongest part of the game, it's souls-like but easier to pick up, you can mix and match any weapon and martial arts style freely, pick whatever you think is most stylish, easiest to play or whatever, everything goes
-genuinely no p2w, you can not buy progress, no timesavers, no weapons, no skills no nothing, every single purchase is cosmetic only, expensive yes, but no p2w
-some of the best outfits and mounts selection i've ever seen, the game has it all, goofy outfits and mounts, serious outfits, lore attire, some are rewarded by achievements others by progress etc. mounts outside of regular horses have to be purchased and come with skills that are helpful like collecting corpse loot automatically if summoned 
-the world is genuinely breathtaking, you have a vast desert area, a massive city, a large mountainous region, fields, rivers etc quests that lead you to different and hidden places which feels to discover and rivals in exploration games like Tomb Raider or Uncharted
-very in-depth story for those that care and fast forward options for those that just want the combat flow, the story is genuinely very interesting, obv the wuxia elements are deeply woven into the story but for those that like history, are interested in old chinese history especially will undoubtedly be hooked since the game does feature real historic events, figures, key moments in chinese history and while obv heavily stylized and interwoven with wuxia elements it still manages to teach you quite a lot about china, it's history, politics, legends etc. 
-boss fights, yes i have to list them independently from regular combat, boss fights in this game are just as satisfying as boss fights in fromsoft games, heavily stylized, well choreographed fights, at times throughout multiple phases, that feel just as rewarding as fights in regular souls-likes
-adjustable difficulty, for the ign reviewer among us, a story difficulty and parry assist can be enabled and for the biggest masochists among us, a mode where death means character wipe can be selected, the latter can only be switched to upon character creation other than that difficulty can be switched on the fly between story, recommended, expert
-amazing soundtrack, especially during combat but even just exploring, overall sounddesign is superb
-ability to play solo, co-op, or completely online with a bunch of random people, the balancing is amazing, no matter if you tackle stuff alone, with a single other mate, 2 mates, a full group or play through the game in the MMO mode, some things require you to be in one version or the other i.e. story content can not be experienced in the MMO section and some healing can not be done in the solo section and has to be performed by another player, other than that you're free to do whatever you want however you want
-no written or spoken interaction required whatsoever, like every asian MMO talking or writing is hardly required, just know what tf you're supposed to do in group content i.e. boss mechanics or how to traverse the battleroyale group pvp section etc and you'll never have to write or talk a word in the online mode, even if you have contracted an illness just join the online mode at the evercare clinic and wait a couple seconds for someone to heal you, don't forget to give them likes and be on your merry way, no need to write "need healer" or something like that
-the game respects your time, there is no other way of putting it, if you only have an hour or 2 to play each day the game respects that, no massive fomo and you still progress, if you spend a lot of time the game respects that too and rewards you with a seemingly endless amount of things to do, get chests, oddities, grind gear upgrades, grind martial ways, build your own home, do hidden quests and encounters and with every bit of time spent you get the feeling of understanding your build better, learn animation cancels, hidden features of skills or unique interactions between weapon styles etc. learn how to dodge, reflect, counter each and every attack thrown at you, the skill ceiling for the game is quite high but it feels like a natural growth and learning process instead of hitting a plateau and having to watch a 60min pro player guide on how to play properly

TL:DR worth? 1000% yes, hell it's free to play just load it up and see if it is for you, nothing lost except maybe a tiny bit of time during character creation.

Beneath some of the poor first impressions such as substandard English localization and the fact that the game is F2P (which conjures up an impression of being predatory junk), is a thoroughly mindblowing, triple A quality game. 

I came in not knowing what to expect (beyond the little that was shown at the initial Gamescom reveal trailer), and this game has thoroughly exceeded my expectations in every regard. The more you play and the more you progress, the more you discover content and gameplay system that just.. surprises you. 

I could possibly write an essay expanding on this, but honestly just give it a try yourself since it's F2P and risk free. At least for me, it compares extremely favorably whether it be to pure single player RPGs such as Assassin's Creed or Yakuza: Like a Dragon, as well as to games in the MMO genre whether it be WoW, ESO, GW2, etc... 

At the time of writing this review, I'm nearly a 100 hours in (with extremely minimal AFK time) and there is still SO MUCH content (unique, bespoke content even) to experience. We're also maybe halfway(?) through the time-gated progression systems. I don't know if the game eventually gets annoying with its systems - but a game that provides this quality and quantity of entertainment for FREE is absolutely worth your time, IMO.

Only thing is - you just have to get over the servicable but below-par localization quirks, as well as cultural terminology such as "Jianghu" which the game never explains (go look up Wikipedia for an explanation).

My dearest seekers of digital splendour,

Permit me, if you will, to recount my most recent sojourn into a land so breathtaking, so lavishly wrought, that it has left even my well-traveled gaming soul in a state of profound reverie. I speak, of course, of Where Winds Meet, a title that does not merely entertain; it enchants, enveloping the player in a world so majestically realized that one feels less like a gamer and more like a wandering poet adrift in a living painting.

From the very first moment my footsteps touched its boundless soil, I found myself utterly captivated by a realm that defies simple description. Imagine a world sculpted by the hands of celestial artisans: jade mountains that pierce the heavens, golden plains that shimmer like liquid sunlight, ancient forests whispering secrets to the breeze. Every vista is a masterpiece, every horizon a promise. The world is so staggeringly, impossibly beautiful that one is compelled to pause again and again simply to breathe it in. It is, without exaggeration, a seamless open world of such elegance that the word “map” feels crude; this is a continent, a tapestry of wonders without loading screen or limitation.

Yet beauty alone does not carry a game. Fortunately, Where Winds Meet wields combat that dances, strikes, and flourishes with the grace of a master swordsman. Each encounter is a choreographed duet of steel and sorcery, equal parts artistry and exhilaration. Battles feel weighty yet fluid, deliberate yet free, an intoxicating blend of martial prowess and cinematic delight that elevates every skirmish into a moment worth savoring.

And what abundance the world offers. One scarcely walks a dozen steps without stumbling into some enticing pursuit. Mountain shrines calling to be unveiled, arcane mysteries begging investigation, duels to be fought, treasures to be unearthed, challenges to be conquered, and quiet corners where serenity itself seems to dwell. Exploration is not a chore; it is a calling, a siren song that whispers, “Just one more peak, one more valley, one more secret.” Before long, hours vanish like mist beneath the morning sun.

As for companionship, the delights multiply tenfold in good company. Roaming this majestic land with friends transforms every adventure into a shared legend. Whether racing across wind-kissed fields, teaming up to challenge formidable foes, or simply reveling together in the grandeur of the world, camaraderie blooms effortlessly. Laughter echoes across mountaintops, triumphs are celebrated with gusto, and even simple travel feels like the beginning of a tale worth retelling.

And, dear reader, allow me one indulgent flourish: my husky dogs mount, a noble duo of frost-furred companions, elevates every journey into a spectacle of unrestrained joy. Gliding across the plains atop my faithful canine chariot, wind in my hair and horizon before me, I feel as though I have stepped into legend itself.

In closing, Where Winds Meet is no mere game; it is an odyssey woven of wonder, artistry, companionship, and adventure. It beckons the refined traveler to lose themselves in a world where beauty reigns supreme, freedom knows no bounds, and every breath feels like a verse of poetry.

Yours sincerely,
A Traveler Carried by the Wind

Here is a rephrased and slightly condensed version of your guide, using headings and lists to improve scannability while preserving all your key points and your authoritative, veteran voice.

⚔️ "Where Winds Meet" Veteran's Guide: 400 Hours from the Chinese Server 🇨🇳
Author's Note: This game is genuinely excellent, but I want to provide a transparent, critical perspective for players seeking the full picture. I have nearly 400 hours on the Chinese launch server (UID: 0105284840) and have created this guide to correct common international misunderstandings.

💰 Economics & Monetization: Is it P2W?
1. The P2W Question (Answer: No)
Healing Capacity: The Season Pass offers a small, non-significant boost to healing item capacity.

The Real Limit: Your core potion carry limit (currently 7 in the Chinese server) is increased by exchanging rewards from Stronghold First Clears, an in-game activity.

2. The Cash Shop & F2P Viability (Answer: Definitely Yes)
Obtaining Free Cosmetics: You absolutely can get high-value items without spending.

Cash Prize Pools: You regularly earn free draw tickets. With 6–8 months of play, you can obtain a top-tier $500 outfit for free (I have done this).

Seasonal Prize Pools: The green currency used for these tickets is acquired through all forms of standard gameplay (exploring, gathering, quests, chests). Progressing your exploration speed is key. (I have cleared this pool's contents twice for free).

Discounting Direct Purchases: Login rewards provide 10% discount coupons. You can stack up to five of these per item, allowing you to eventually purchase any item at half price.

The Need for Whales: The developers need support! Thank you to the big spenders who purchase luxury items—you help keep the game alive for everyone.

🎧 Quality of Life & Customization
3. Voice Acting
Strong Recommendation: Use the Chinese voice-over! It has better tone, lip-sync, and no bugs.

Story is King: Do not skip the story—it has a great plot. If you plan to skip everything, you might have more fun with a direct combat game like Naraka: Bladepoint.

4. Character Creation & Appearance
Second Character: The "Create New Character" function is currently missing because the international version is running an older client. It will be unlocked soon, mirroring the Chinese server's release schedule.

Appearance Change: You receive a free "Appearance Modification Voucher" during a main story quest (about 3 hours in) that takes you under the hospital.

11. The ESC Menu
A Known Issue: The ESC menu is notoriously complicated and may not be fixed soon (Chinese players have complained for a year).

Advice: Ignore the red notification dots. Only claim your rewards right before logging off to save time.

13. Road Signs & Chat
For a clean, uninterrupted solo experience, use the settings menu to customize the visibility of road signs, chat boxes, and scrolling messages.

14. Flight Adjustment
Crucial Tip: Go to the settings menu and choose a different camera mode for flight. This completely eliminates the annoying close-up animation and greatly improves the experience.

🗺️ Gameplay & Progression Insights
5. The Level Cap (It's Protection, Not Restriction)
Misconception: The cap is not to restrict you; it's to protect you and keep the player base together.

The Problem: I could reach max level in hours by farming Mahjong. But without exploration, you won't have the required exploration-level stats and equipment to keep up.

The Reality: The cap forces you to explore the map and acquire necessary gear sets, skill books, and weapon combinations. Trust me, you'll find this restriction reasonable in a few months.

6. Exploration
Mandatory: Explore More! Do not ignore any tasks. Every aspect of the game is directly tied to your exploration progress.

10. Multiple Currency Types
Historical Context: The different map currencies (beyond the store currency) reflect the game's setting during the tumultuous transition between the Tang and Song dynasties, a period when multiple currencies coexisted.

Narrative Depth: This detail shows how common people suffer during dynastic change, often having their life savings made worthless.

📜 Story & Lore (Deep Dive)
9. Tragedy and Historical Tide (SPOILER CONTEXT)
Character Deaths: Do not leave negative reviews because a character dies. The deaths reflect the game's brutal historical context (war, famine, and despair).

The Underground Hospital Quest: This quest explains the fate of assassins sent to reclaim the "Sixteen Prefectures." The unsuccessful, disfigured facial reconstruction surgery and their hopeless 430-year wait in the dungeons profoundly conveys the powerlessness of individuals against historical tides.

12. Quest Review System
Hidden Insights: After completing certain quests, a review system is available. Read the comments! Even I, as a Chinese player, gain deeper insight into the story's historical background from the messages left by history enthusiasts.

🌐 Server & Multiplayer Status
7. Game Longevity
No Doom-Saying: The game is doing very well in China and has even received national-level recognition. You can play with confidence.

15. Multiplayer Modes
Solo Mode: Supports up to 5-player co-op. Quest progress is individual, but exploration rewards are shared within the team.

Multiplayer mode: This is a separate mode with reduced NPC counts where quests cannot be completed. It includes exclusive content like cruise ship parties.

After playing for over 100 Hours with still so much stuff that I haven’t done or discovered, I surely do recommend this game very much.

Storywise; The story is A okay, nothing deeply mindblowing but also nothing bad, and since the game is complete for free that’s an amazing outcome.

Gameplay; The mechanics and Movements are a thing you need to get used to, but after you have, it’s actually a decent one. If something is not for your liking you simply can exchange the settings. The weapon system is also something you need to get used to but as said it’s actually pretty good, you can choose between DPS/Healer/Tank or just make a mix of it - Dungeon system is decent but could be better especially with coop. 

Graphics and world building; The graphics are very well done with a style I enjoy, same as the World design and the love of Detail everywhere - the NPCs commit jobs, most have dialogue, many encounters to discover, the animations are amazing for a free game like this, and the small mini games are fun too.

Coop; The Coop Overall is just about okay, it could be better if they would add a better shared progression system which rn there isn’t a very well done one. The online mode is fun to hang around with tho, bosses and mini games to do and play with your friends is good - PvP I haven’t really played so I will leave out this part.

The Gambling everybody talks about; Since everyone knows that this game includes Gacha: it is very optional to either waste you real Life money, play with Ingame Jade or grind long enough to buy the expensive gacha option for completely free. There is nothing „P2W“ stuff in there, only cosmetics or mounts - you can simply just play the game without needing to gamble on Gacha, the game works perfectly without it since it’s (as said) Optional. Same with buying cosmetics, you don’t have to buy them, you can play the game for free very fine.

Overall: it’s a game that is too good to be free for my opinion, it’s an amazing game for my love in games and the styles and categories of games I love. I shall recommend everyone to try it out who likes openworld and exploring in games. If you don’t like it, you didn’t lost much. Trying out never hurts.

The best way I can describe WWM is... It's a Banquet Hall. It's a free one, so everyone is invited, and it hosts a variety of foods for you to try out or feast upon. The decor is wonderful, fitting as well as the music playing (to the point where its hard to believe the game is free). The food is good, no doubt, and it looks gorgeous, tastes good, and it's a great time... But there's a lot of it. A Lot. If you eat too much, you're going to make yourself sick.

There's plenty of table space, but if you're like me and get anxious around other people, there are suitable tables that spaced apart and face a wall [Solo mode]... However, you're still going to be in the same room as others, and quite often you are going to detect signs of other guests within the Hall [Usually in the form of 'Signposts']. And if you're taking up bounties or obtain the Healer profession, you might get whispered by another player to help out.

Regardless, they can't keep hosting the hall for free forever, so of course there are going to be some fancy dishes that have a paywall to them- as in 'the actual dishes/cutlery', chairs, etc. [cosmetics]. This comes with the territory we're all too familiar with: Gacha mechanics, Fear Of Missing Out, everyday logins, etc. If this bothers you, yeah. The Banquet might not be for you, but I have seen them much much worse.

However, I'm a nerd for Martial Arts, high Chinese fantasy where people can run up/on walls, triple jump, and throw jerks off of cliffs with Tai Chi. And honestly, I'm a very picky eater. VERY. I'm not going to like every dish I come across, and I KNOW the ones I just will not enjoy [bloody Rhythm Games]. So I'm just taking my time with Where Winds Meet, occasionally going out of my comfort zone to try some things, but mostly sticking with what I enjoy. With that, I'm enjoying my sessions with the game. Not saying "do it like I do", but instead "Consume responsibly. You're driving home tonight."



Also, because I didn't really know where to put this in, the voice acting is kinda silly. It happens with translations to English and it's not Specifically that the VAs did a bad job, but more the editors had more than a few hiccups. There's been a few times where I've heard outtakes of lines or multiple line reads from the same subtitle x3

This game has no right being this good! Especially, being free-to-play!

Make no mistakes, despite its Action RPG label, this is an MMO package, with all the expected mechanics, dungeons, bosses, and activities you might expect. It might honestly get a bit overwhelming, with all the content and diverse mechanincs it offers, making it so that you have to understand the game, despite of its label.
But the fact that you can play this Solo or Co-Op from the start, is very interesting. Specially, because you can change at any point from one to the other.

What I find more interesting, is that 'even' as an Open-World Action RPG, I think it excels! 
The story is honestly compelling, with memorable characters throughout, but the world itself and everything in and around it is what makes this so deep and rewarding.
The fact that almost every NPC has unique voice or text lines and that basically every side quest has a narrative guiding it, sometimes emotional, while in the overall Co-Op/MMO package, is outstanding and something the more recent single-player AAA RPGs don't manage to do.
I find myself much of my time roaming around the open world, because of all the different things I can experience, and all the smaller and unexpected narratives I can encounter.

And let's not forget that there is a GTA-style wanted system; and that even some wounds have a permanent effect while not healed. For example, if you fall from a great height and break a bone, you'll remain unable to sprint until you heal. 
I heard a comparison to the immersive nature of [i][b]Red Dead Redemption 2[/b][/i], and it's an accurate example, as some of the same ideas for constructing a completely immersive experience definitely apply here, adapted to this beautiful culture.

It is, in fact, all the "side stuff" that makes this 'experience' (more than just a game) feel truly alive outside of your playthrough. The fact, for example, that another player can heal you at any point, if you ask, gives you the sense of the larger community outside of the familiar multiplayer tasks. You don't just fight with other players, you live with them in this compelling Wuxia universe and story.

This game also proves that artsyle is definitely more important than graphics per say. And this has definitely style in waves!
Specially when you're running through the vast fields of grass, and colorful flowers, and Bamboo trees, every single piece of your surroundings and your clothes blowing in the wind, with the sunlight shining trough. Also, the fact that every woosh of your sword affects these elements, with fire even burning the grass and ground around it, with the game continuously running so well, is impressive!
Be it the the vast plains and mountains of Qinghe, or the richly ornamented traditional chinese architecture of Kaifeng, you just want to stay in this world, and see it as immaculate as it is presented to you.

Simplifying this to a western standard might give you the wrong impression, because you might put your standards and expectations forefront, and not meet the game where he wants you. But if' you're willing to accept it, I'm sure you'll find a very deep, rewarding interactive narrative here.
This easily became one of my favorite games, just because it let's me experience the world, more than just play in it. That's called immersion, and [i][b]Where Winds Meet[/b][/i] is immersion at its core.

Initial review: 5/5 stars

Has everything for a free to play RPG game. Great story, great music, great graphics, rich character creation and customization, and the full assortment of in-game activities (instanced dungeons, open world bosses, puzzles, fishing, crafting, music, etc). 

The ancient (fantasy?) version of China is beautiful and well designed with plenty of POIs and activities across the map. It also features both Solo and MP/CoOp play. So if you're into the quiet exploration, you can literally turn off all other player activities (basically hiding them in your UI) and stick with an isolated story. However, you can dip into CO/MP mode at any time and get more achievements and currencies (there is a LOT of in-game currency).

The martial arts styles are fun and the combat mechanics are tricky, but do-able on a keyboard/mouse. The ancient Chinese culture and story is rich and the AI interactions are really fun. The AI NPC dialogue is a great feature and adds a unique element of immersion to the world. You can keep asking a PC questions and if you hit on their topics in the dialogue you have a chance to befriend them, which provides in game benefits. 

It's truly unique in a lot of aspects; but for overall playstyle, I'd say it's a mix of Skyrim, Genshin Impact, and quite a bit of Elden Ring. I say Elden Ring because the open world bosses are handled very much like Elden Ring where you can try to handle them solo (and get murdered), or you can request online assistance from co-op/multiplayer (or get more powerful and come back later). 

Speaking of CO/MP...I've only been Online/MP in the social areas and as long as you turn off voice comms; it's a fun activity. You gain XP by participating on group activities or contests; the longer you stay (avg. 10-20mins); the more XP you earn. This nets you some additional currencies you need for advancing your build. 

For solo activities, you are free to explore and participate up until a certain point, then you get restricted until you have enough currency (in the form of upgrades) and the right skills to best the "breakthrough" challenge; which allows you to advance to the next tier (every five levels). The breakthrough challenges are fun and challenging; but not overly so. There's a bit of a twitch element to them, it is an action-rpg afterall; but you feel rewarded for succeeding. 

My main criticism is the quantity of in-game currencies is staggering...too many to keep track of and it's setup like a lot of tablet based free-to-play/pay-to-advance games. Every activity is associated with a currency and those currencies are used to advance different elements of the game (and not always the same activity the currency was generated from). The most important ones, like pearls, (for actually advancing your character and improving your avatars look and costume) are very rare and costly. Drop rate is like 1/hr and it takes 600-1200 to purchase a new costume. Most do drop in the world in some quantity; but never enough to actually purchase anything of value. 

For the pay-to-play, there's a lot to buy. Mostly in terms of very detailed costumes, cosmetics and vanity gear; but also with interesting mounts and personal vessels. If you make it past the first 2 hours; get the BattlePass for the bonus advancement rewards...it helps. 

 It's an amazing game and well worth it for the free-to-play aspect; though I'm dubious for the long game with so many activities being gated or restricted by specific currencies.

First of all, I really want to highlight how beautiful this game is. Not only does it have amazing graphics, but the art direction is genuinely outstanding. I constantly feel the urge to take screenshots because so many moments look like actual paintings. The combat, the story, the exploration, the cutscenes, the music, the minigames, and even the building mode all have an incredibly high level of quality, and honestly, for a game that costs 0€, it’s absurd how good it is. Sure, there are a few things that could be polished, but complaining would feel pointless when there are 60–70€ AAA games that don’t even come close. And if you’re thinking there must be some catch because it’s free, there really isn’t: the shop is purely cosmetic, plus a battle pass and a monthly material boost. No pay-to-win at all, which is a huge win.

The story is engaging and keeps you wanting to see what happens next, the bosses are extremely well designed, and if you enjoy Sekiro-style deflection combat, you’re going to love this game. The world is full of lore, and the game gives you plenty of collectibles and information to dive into, which is a real treat for Wuxia fans.

About co-op: even though the main story can only be progressed by the host, the co-op mode is still amazing. There are side quests, exploration, and a ton of activities you can do together, so it honestly feels like a very well-made co-op experience despite the restrictions. The MMO-style area is more of a social space, basically the same map acting as a lobby with social events.

As for performance, the game runs fantastic on my setup (GTX 1070, i7-7700K, 32GB RAM, and an NVMe SSD). With the graphics set to High at 1080p, I’m getting a very stable 55–60 FPS almost everywhere, even in crowded areas. For a free game with this level of visual quality, the optimization is honestly impressive.

I’ve also seen genuine interest from the development team in continuing to improve the game, even offering materials in exchange for answering survey questions about your experience and what you’d like to see improved. Considering all of this, I can only recommend this game!

Where Winds Meet feels like stepping into a living Wuxia legend. From the moment you enter its reimagined 10th-century China, the world pulls you in with sweeping landscapes, misty mountains, and towns that feel alive with their own quiet stories. It’s the kind of game where you can lose track of time simply wandering — watching lanterns drift over rivers at night or climbing ancient ruins just to see the sun rise over a distant valley.

Combat is where the game truly shines. Every duel feels sharp and stylish, almost like acting out scenes from a martial arts film. Swords clash with weight, spears sweep with elegance, and the game lets you mix in fantastical martial arts abilities that make every fight feel cinematic. Whether you prefer a light-footed, agile style or heavy, crushing blows, the game gives you room to experiment and find your rhythm.

But it’s not just about fighting. Where Winds Meet constantly invites you to carve your own path. You can be a wandering doctor helping strangers, a merchant building influence, an assassin lurking in the shadows, or simply a traveler who lets curiosity decide the day. Decisions matter — sometimes subtly, sometimes dramatically — and the world reacts in ways that make you feel like your presence has weight.

The sheer size of the world is impressive, and it’s filled with small moments: hidden tombs tucked behind waterfalls, NPCs who surprise you with unpredictable conversations, and side activities like music, cooking, or joining festivals that make the world feel rich rather than empty.

Of course, it isn’t perfect. The interface can feel crowded, especially for newcomers, and the game throws a lot of systems at you early on. Performance can be uneven depending on your hardware, and online co-op isn’t always as smooth as it should be. Still, none of these issues overshadow how ambitious and generous the game feels — especially considering it’s free to play.

At its best, Where Winds Meet is a beautifully crafted martial arts epic that lets you live out your own Wuxia dream. It’s visually stunning, full of freedom, and packed with moments that feel genuinely magical. If you enjoy open-world adventures and the romanticism of classic Chinese martial arts tales, this game has a way of pulling you in and not letting go.

This game combine pieces of everything I like from several other games I played before:

1. Exploration like Zelda and Genshin Impact: Finding chest, clear enemy camp, puzzles, collectible, platformer challenges and many more

2. Sandbox like Skyrim and GTA: You can commit crime and gain wanted level, can kill many NPC, there is faction you can join, you can build homes, tons of minigames and many more

3. Combat like Sekiro and Stellar Blade: Big emphasize on parrying enemy attacks, there are perfect dodge too, distinct playstyle every weapon

4. MMO-lite endgame like FFXIV: many endgame fight demand holy trinity setup (at minimum healer and dps) and there is mechanic that need to be done correctly or it will end with party wipe

5. Social hub for people who like to interact with community with tons of casual activity like chess, wrestling, meditate, etc.

6. PvP: there is 1v1 mode, battle royale mode and in future team fight (2v2, 5v5) and guild fight

Keep in mind, there is a bit of everything means it not particulary best at anything especially if you compare it to AAA games that specialize in that one aspect (e.g. The sandbox while pretty open dont have same depth like skyrim, the endgame fight is not as hard as FFXIV savage or ultimates). Although for combat i heard on hardest difficulty (you can switch between 3 difficulty except hardest one called Legend where you can only pick at start of character creation) is on par with FromSoft game but don't quote me on that.

Monetization is strictly cosmetic and there are enough free cosmetic ingame that you dont really pressured into spend money.

NEGATIVE of this game: UI is stupidly complicated for no reason, bad on boarding experience: too many system thrown at players with no explanation, coop / pvp have unstable network atm (solo mode is fine), if you want to spend... cosmetic in this game is expensive af, especially if you do the cosmetic gacha.

All in all if you want play the "all in one game" cause you dont have time to juggle between multiple game genre that overlap with Where Winds Meet, this can scratch the itch.

I hoped this game would focus on a smooth combat flow, requiring you to master your own skills and learn from the enemies movements, but its rather a spam your keyboard/mouse as fast as possible and hopefully you'll win the stagger chain.

Where Winds Meet creates a fantasy world that feels like stepping directly into the pages of a high-stakes Wuxia novel. It isn’t a history lesson; it is a romanticized, supernatural martial arts fantasy. If you can tolerate a frustratingly poor translation and a cluttered UI, the combat system alone is worth the price of admission.
The Combat: 
This is the heart and soul of the game. Unlike RPGs that flood you with hundreds of useless skills, this game focuses on a smaller, tighter selection of weapon types and skills. The joy here isn't in unlocking a thousand buttons, but in mastering the few you have.
• Mastery over Variety: Because there aren't an infinite number of weapons, the depth comes from learning the distinct rhythm of the ones you have.
• Parry Mechanics: The parry system is incredibly satisfying. Getting the timing right, deflecting a fatal blow, and countering is an addictive loop if you hit it correctly that’s .It feels sharp, responsive, and fair. When you die, it’s because you missed a beat, not because the game cheated.
The World & Exploration:
Currently, the game opens up into two massive zones. They are dense, beautiful, and packed with content. This is a fantasy setting, so expect exaggerated landscapes and atmospheric lighting that fits the Wuxia vibe perfectly.
• Content Density: There is a lot to do. Between the fighting, the collectibles, and the side objectives, the map feels alive. Exploring these two zones is genuinely fun because the movement allows you to traverse the world with the agility of a martial arts master.
The Story & Sound
• Audio : The sound design does a lot of heavy lifting for the immersion. The environmental audio and combat effects are top-tier.
• Story: The narrative is just "Okay." It serves its purpose to move you from one fight to the next, but don't expect a masterpiece of storytelling. It’s a functional backdrop for the action.
The Issues (The "Cons")
While I recommend the game, you need to know what you are walking into:
1. Localization Nightmares: The translation is poor. It feels like a direct, literal translation that misses the context. This makes understanding mechanics difficult.
2. Riddles & Mini-Games: There are many puzzles and mini-games based on Chinese culture or language. Because the localization is weak, these are often baffling for a Western audience. They shouldn't have just translated these; they should have replaced them with puzzles that make sense logically to a global audience.
3. UI Clutter: There are way too many menus. Navigating the interface feels like administrative work.
4. Monetization: The shop is aggressive and items are expensive. However, it is not Pay-to-Win. You can ignore the shop and still dominate in combat if your skills are good enough.
Final Thoughts
If you are willing to struggle through some bad menus and confusing text to experience some of the best swordplay and martial arts mechanics on the market, get this game. The fighting carries the experience.
