[b]UPDATE[/b] The developers have now fixes my issues with Gen AI by disclosing it on the Steam page (shown at the bottom of the description right above the system specs). [b]Review has thus been changed to a positive and the negative points have been removed.[/b]

[h1]Preface[/h1]
First off, the game itself if you know that it's a gacha and enjoy those kind of games, is very good. The reviews of 84% positive as of writing is deserved and it's a number I believe should be up there if not higher. The game is very polished, and I wish to play it more when I have a chance. For now there's only positives that I can think of, but not too many that are worth pointing out yet.

[h1]The Review[/h1]
My usual reviews feature 2 sections, positives and negatives. However due to the nature of the game itself, it's hard to find negatives that are worth pointing out. Thus this review only feature positives. I know I've only played for 2 hours at review time, but it's 2 hours which let me see the first intro boss, get into the "home" village, and then a tiny little bit after that. I will play more of this and maybe update some of the review if I feel like there needs to be further changes that reflect my new experience.

[h3]Positives[/h3]
I'm not gonna cover too many points, mainly because I haven't played it enough yet. But there are some first impressions I genuinely want to point out.

[b]Controller Support[/b]
This should come at no surprise. I've played some of NetEase's other games they've published, and generally since their games are also mobile first, their controller support is always top notch. If you come from Dark Souls, Sekiro, or particularly Elden Ring, while there are some differences, the general experience should just click for you immediately and straight up get you going. They really nailed this part of the game.

[b]Performance[/b]
A bit surprised about this one honestly. I didn't tweak any settings going into this, and playing on a 180Hz 1440p monitor with an RTX 4070, Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 96GB 6000MHz CL32, a lot of other bigger games recently has run at dramatically lower FPS than I would have expected in a just previous gen GPU. While I only really reach half of the refresh-rate, I do still get the frames at a stable rate with little to no stutters. And this is while the game has defaulted to everything on max settings, with any form of upscaling turned off completely. (I know my setup is hella scuffed too with the CPU + GPU combo that I have, but it shouldn't change the review in any way).

[b]Combat & Story[/b]
I'm putting this in the same category because I have similar experiences with both, even if they generally should be split. I just wouldn't need to write the same thing twice this way. Both the Combat and Story feels better than I expected. Coming from both Genshin Impact and Zenless Zone Zero, but particularly the former, I feel that Where Winds Meet's story make sense in a way that is different than the other two games in a very positive way. With the combat in Genshin Impact, I often found myself repeatedly dashing through enemies when attacking normally, which doesn't happen here, and Story wise, the story in Genshin Impact felt very "forced" and "complex". I'm sure this could change with Where Winds Meet when I keep playing, but so far for my first impressions, the intro sequence at least make sense and I feel it could realistically happen. At least compared to the other two games I've played as I mentioned.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
The game is quite good. Gacha? Yes. But it doesn't take away from the game. You find a lot of games that is a real cash grab, but this one so far doesn't seem like it. Or at least not compared to other Gacha games I've played that force you to spend money. I know the prison system in the game first felt a bit rough, but after looking it up on YouTube I noticed the prison system is actually pretty complex and has interesting depth in it. I had that as a negative at first, but I have since embraced it as a quite a cool way of going about lawfullness in an MMORPG. The overall experience from the gameplay, combat, performance and story mixed with the difficulty level, flexibility and just the core concepts that piece it together, I'm definitely giving this a recommendation.

Where Winds Meet is a truly remarkable free-to-play game. And I say this as someone who rarely enjoys free games. It's baffling how IGN gave this game a 6/10 rating, when it's truly incredibly polished, with engaging gameplay and stunning visuals. But in retrospect, it's not really surprising, as IGN isn't a benchmark for game reviews anymore (they gave Concord a 7, and many other terrible games a 8 or 9!). So, what makes this game worth trying and playing?

First, let's talk about the free-to-play system. Usually, free games are filled with pay-to-win nonsense or restrict free users from certain things, such as slower gameplay progression compared to paid users. Where Winds Meet doesn't implement that, as it focuses more on making money by purchasing cosmetics. Therefore, you can enjoy this game without having to spend a dime! (Although, if you have the money, I recommend purchasing some cosmetics or the battle pass to support the developer.) Additionally, as a free player, you can even earn quite a few cosmetics by completing missions or fighting bosses.

Second, even though this is an online game, you can choose single-player mode, allowing you to play alone. You can also choose online mode if you want to interact with other players in boss fights or minigames (of which there are many and they're fun!). So, you could consider this a single-player action-RPG.

Third, in terms of visuals, I think this game is absolutely stunning! I've long wanted a game set in ancient Chinese history, and this game, set in the Song Dynasty, does it brilliantly. The soldier armor, the city visuals, and the environment are all truly stunning. Sometimes I just decided to wander around the city to take in the sights.

Fourth, I think the game's combat system is quite good and not too difficult; it's not a soul likes game. So, if you're not used to playing action games, I think the controls will be quite easy to master. And if you're a fan of kung fu films or wuxia novels (like me), you'll definitely love this game. Unfortunately, I don't think this game has many kung fu moves, and we'll be using weapons more (there are six weapons, and each weapon has its own distinct style, so even if the weapon is the same, we can choose a different "school" of weapon).

Those are some of the good sides. So, what are the weaknesses? As a fan of RPGs or games with deep stories, I think the main weakness of this game is the story pacing. Don't get me wrong, this game has an interesting story, and in some parts, it's incredibly well-presented and can make players feel emotional. Unfortunately, as I said, the pacing can sometimes feel odd. For example, after playing the intro, the game opens with a cutscene of our character losing to a warrior who stole our jade necklace. Instead of worrying about how to get it back, we're instead accompanying a little girl on a walk and serving customers at a pub. How can our character not think about the necklace anymore? Fortunately in general the main story is quite engaging.

And what is the other weakness of this game? The English dub. In my opinion, some characters feels off. That's why I decided to play with the original Chinese voice over. I think playing like this is good, because the Chinese setting feels more real.

So that's my take on this game. In short, I think if you're curious, don't hesitate to give this game a try, considering it's free. Personally, I think Where Winds Meet is one of the games I've enjoyed most this year. I hope you enjoy it as much as I do.

A weird mix of Black Desert, Ghost of Tsushima, Elden Ring and The Witcher. 

Can be played as a solo story driven game and an MMO, crazy how much content they give you for free. It has some absolutely stunning areas, easily throwing punches with the best that 'AAA' gaming has to offer. Not only that but it runs extremely well on low end systems too. 

It has some spectacular boss fights (up there with From Software in terms of visuals and musical scoring). Combat difficulty can be adjusted with features such as auto parrying, general difficulty sliders. You can make this play like an ARPG or a 'Souls Like'.

It contains a lot of quality of life features for MMO players, such as a robust help guide with an AI chat assistant that you can converse with - giving you instructions and tips for quests. Makes finding NPC's and crafting materials a breeze. 

If you're interested in Wuxia or Chinese culture in general, this is a no brainer. 

The only negatives i've come across so far are a few wonky translations, and some very expensive cosmetics. However, the game throws a lot of cool looking ones at you for free and you don't have to engage with the shop if you don't want to.

As long as they don't bring in any crazy grinds or P2W, then they could be on to a winner here. If this sort of quality keeps coming out of China, its going to be a wakeup call for western game dev's.

Where Wind Meets – A Stunning Blend of Wuxia, Freedom, and Emotional Storytelling

Where Wind Meets is one of those rare open-world RPGs that doesn’t just invite you into its world—it pulls you in with the force of a hurricane. Set in a beautifully reimagined Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era, the game blends traditional Wuxia fantasy with grounded historical detail, creating a world that feels both mythical and authentic.

🌄 World & Atmosphere

The environment is nothing short of breathtaking. Rolling bamboo forests, misty mountain temples, lively markets, and war-torn plains all flow seamlessly into each other. Every location feels handcrafted and lived-in, making exploration not just enjoyable but deeply immersive.

⚔️ Combat & Gameplay

Combat is the game’s beating heart. It’s fluid, flashy, and strategic—striking a perfect balance between martial-arts fantasy and realistic weapon play. Whether you’re clashing blades, deflecting arrows mid-air, or sprinting across rooftops, the game nails the feeling of being a Wuxia hero.

But what truly sets Where Wind Meets apart is freedom.
You can choose to be a swordsman, doctor, merchant, wanderer, or even something morally grey. The open-ended systems encourage creativity rather than forcing you down a rigid story path.

📖 Story & Characters

The narrative is deeply emotional, driven by themes of loyalty, loss, political turmoil, and the blurred lines between right and wrong. Characters are memorable and layered—each one shaped by the chaos of the era. Your choices genuinely influence how the world responds to you, making your journey feel personal.

🎶 Music & Cinematics

The soundtrack is phenomenal, mixing traditional instrumentation with modern dramatic scoring. Cinematics feel like scenes from a high-budget historical drama, adding weight to both major battles and quiet, reflective moments.

💬 Final Verdict

Where Wind Meets is an exceptional fusion of art, storytelling, and freedom of play.
If you love open-world exploration, Wuxia fantasies, deep narratives, or simply beautifully crafted games, this title is an absolute must-play.

⭐ 9.5/10 – A masterpiece of martial-arts worldbuilding and emotional storytelling.

WWM - Gorgeous Wuxia Shell With No Spine
3 / 10 – Not Recommended

WWM feels less like an MMO and more like an expensive tech demo wearing an MMO costume.

Pros

Beautiful environments and lighting. The world is often screenshot tier.
Some boss fights, like Qianye, have excellent animation and staging.
The main story has emotional moments and avoids the worst bargain bin wuxia writing.
Visual fidelity and animation quality are far above a lot of older martial arts MMOs.


Cons


Mystic skills feel half implemented and poorly explained. They sit on the UI instead of being integrated into boss mechanics or real build identity.

Core systems are shallow. Exploration is just the same few encounter templates repeated hundreds of times with different icons. Once you notice the pattern, the world feels hollow.

Gear progression is bland. It is basically level breakpoints and reskinned versions of the same weapon with slightly different set bonuses. No real buildcraft, no satisfying chase.

World leveling kills any sense of power growth. Returning to early zones only to find level 5 wolves now scaled to your level feels fake and demotivating.

Movement completely undersells the wuxia fantasy. Flight is gated behind a long animation and a very short glide window. It feels stingy, not liberating.

The economy is a mess of overlapping currencies, tokens, and shops. It feels like a mobile monetization skeleton, not a coherent RPG system, and it buries simple upgrades under layers of clutter.

Huge missed opportunity on visual identity. You get flashy cloaks, but no real character auras or cultivation visuals that would sell the fantasy.

Guild missions often feel like chores instead of social content. Being told to spam a dual emote twenty times a week is not engaging design. It is padding.

Verdict:

If you want a pretty world to run through once for the story and screenshots, WWM can deliver that. If you want a deep wuxia MMO with real systems, progression, and long term replay value, it feels like a promise that never made it past the concept art stage. Not recommended in its current state.

The combat is very Elden Ring-like, loose dodges, tight parries and blocks as well as good flowing combat, maybe more flowy than Elden Ring. I like it much better. Good weapon combos and RPG system and it does have a holy trinity for groups. Tanks, healers and DPS. But it also plays a lot like other action MMOs that don't have a holy trinity. It has put me in groups with only healers and dps and no tanks. There isn't a lot of provokes but the boss does tend to go after the tank if you have one, but can be done without one. I think it's a solid hybrid system. As someone who heals in all MMOs, I LOVE the healing here with the heal fan. The DPS weapons also feel good. 

That being said, despite how amazing the game is it isn't perfect. The translation, localization and voices on our end could use some work. The subtitles sometimes say the wrong thing, sometimes worded poorly, differently or what have you. It doesn't ruin the game by any means, but combined with the voice lines and subtitles sometimes skipping or doubling up, it can be a bit frustration. The devs have already fixed a lot in the first zone and are working quickly to get everything in order but it's worth noting.

The monetization is good in general. You get so many outfits and general mounts for free, and the game is F2P, so there's nothing to complain about there. The shop ranged from $1 skins all the way to $43 skins, not to mention the gacha loot box-only skins, which can cost anywhere from $20 to $42k. That wasn't a mistype, ONE skin is really rare and costs around $42k. There is also a party boat that isn't important to the game at all, but costs $42k-65k as well. Big whale stuff, 

So, overall, the game is both generous and greedy with the shop, nothing wrong with that, however, there is troubling potential. One of the Chinese skins (the game launched in China for over a year now, it's only new to us) has a $40 skin in the shop, they cut the parts of it up and put it in a limited draw gacha with scaling draws, so you need to spend anywhere from $40 to $125 to get it guaranteed in the global version we play. So in general, the pricing and shop is great, but it seems like they are trying to screw over the global people COMPARED to the Chinese version. Keep that in mind.

Overall, I wanna say it's a 9/10 game ACROSS THE BOARD. I would dare say it's damn near a 10/10 if it wasn't for frustrations with subtitles, voices and even some of the mini-games being quite hard and obnoxious. I don't want to do some of them, but they are kind of important for stats. I soldier on through, but it is frustrating at times and lowers the score.

親愛的各位玩家，尊敬的武林弟子，以及熱愛開放世界武俠體驗的各位高貴追求者：

我懷著對中國古代武術傳統和探索精神的崇敬之情，鄭重宣布：

《風雲變幻》堪稱當代互動武俠藝術的傑作，值得江湖讚譽。

這款傑作呈現了一個廣袤無垠、美輪美奐的中原，每一座山峰、每一片雲霧繚繞的竹林、每一座燈火通明的古城，都在召喚著有誌之士前來自由探索。從潺潺流淌的黃河到險峻險峻的聖峰，整個世界都充滿了鮮活的生命力，為玩家提供了無窮無盡的探索機會、神秘的洞穴傳承以及與隱居高手的邂逅。

遊戲中的武術戰鬥，尤其是與傳奇宗主、墮落仙人和魔族強者的宏大對決，都展現出精湛的技藝和令人熱血沸騰的深度。每一場首領戰都要求玩家精通八大宗門的深奧技法，精準把握輕功的時機，並巧妙運用內力——這才是真正區分浪人與天之驕子之間的考驗。

此外，遊戲也為玩家精心打造了豐富多彩的人生道路：精於醫術的醫師，以銀針和珍稀草藥療傷；鍛造神兵的鐵匠，鍛造出無與倫比的神兵；潛心鑽研書法和古琴的學者；以及經營茶館或四處奔波的商人。就連烹飪、煉丹和馴獸等技藝也都展現得細緻入微，並提供了豐厚的成長獎勵。

This game is shockingly good. I know, I know, a Chinesium game for western audiences has a lot of cultural baggage, but genuinely this is the gold standard for how these games should be brought the the West. The cash shop appears to be completely cosmetic only from what I can see after digging around in there for a while, and while the game does have the customary battlepass and gatcha for fluff, I'm willing to give them a pass on that because there is a truly massive amount of very high quality content here. The game looks and runs superb, the wuxia setting is really fun to get immersed in, and it's such an interesting mix of ideas that really hasn't been done quite like this before. You have the combat system of a souls-like, the cultivation and lifeskill type stuff you'd expect from something like black desert, minigames like you'd see in ESO, and a questing and party system most similar in my mind to the original Guild Wars. There's so much to do and see and it's all at a level of polish that would take Ubisoft, EA or Activision multiple pants ♥♥♥♥♥, restarts and hundreds of millions of dollars to accomplish. 

If Chinese game developers keep throwing haymakers like this, I think Western AAA game devs might be genuinely cooked. Give it a try and see if you agree!

I've only about 4 hours in, but so far it's been perfect. If you have ever played  Wuthering Waves, Sekiro, Elden Ring, Nioh, it somehow did a great job actually blending those disparate styles of game (Gacha and Soulslike/traditional highly customizable ARPG) into one package. The open world is incredible and very lived in, and while not being an MMO (very important to note, in case anyone thought it would be) . The character you make can be built in several ways and there are tons of different abilities and styles to learn. The story starts slow but gets far more interesting the more you play. The combat is simply perfect and easy to pick up. I would also highly suggest turning off auto-assist parry and switching the total parry button on your mouse with the defend (damage reduction). It'll make your life a lot easier, trust me. Difficulty options are also plentiful, if you aren't a souls-like gamer and just want to play casually, you can. The game is also extremely well-optimized and despite looking so good runs really well. 

Those are all the pros. 

Cons: Minor cons are just just minor bugs and graphical ticks here and there, and a rare mini-freeze in menus and loading stuff. 


There is only one major con, the out of combat UI and Menus are an absolutely confusing hodgepodge mess. It will take you a long time before you can actually figure out where everything is and where the important stuff for upgrades and such are, but they at least do let you go straight to relevant stuff when upgrades are available with hotkeys. That being said, it is still the biggest flaw in the game, the menus have submenus and it can be incredibly overwhelming for a new player.  The only negative I've experienced so far in an otherwise excellent game, having the menus be more easily understandable  would definitely be one piece of constructive criticism I would give this title. Tip: Use the search function, its probably the fastest way instead of trying to remember how to get to what you're looking for. 


Despite that I still rate this a solid 9/10 so far, I only can't play more because I'm too busy to commit a large amount of time.

This game is unreasonably amazing for what it is. There is a ridiculous amount of stuff to do in this game, the fights are beautiful, the story is actually really well done, and its all free. You won't find many free games that will be this fun. I've had this game for a few days and ive already sunk around 30 hrs into it. That being said I will give advice for anyone who decides to give this game a chance. This game is going to throw a massive amount of information at you without a whole lot of handholding, don't get me wrong it will give you quick tutorials on a lot of the important menu trees and such, but a lot of it you will also be forced to figure out on your own. All this to say, do NOT be afraid to google how to do something if you get stuck or don't understand something. It doesn't take away from the game, I promise you. And to clarify something a lot of people worry about, yes, this is a free game. Yes, there is an in game store with lootboxes and cosmetics you can buy. No, there is not a single pay-to-win mechanic in the game whatsoever. Nothing that you can pay for can enhance anything about your character, every purchase is strictly cosmetic. As for the MMO elephant in the room. You have essentially 3 options while playing this game. The main storyline is going to be SinglePlayer with the option to invite friends or anyone really to help you with certain bosses and such. There is also a Co-Op mode which has its own quests and little things you can do. And yes there is also technically an MMO mode where you essentially join an MMO server. I don't know what all can be done in this mode as I have not explored it that much, but the community in this game is very welcoming for the most part and you can usually find someone to show you the ropes. I hope someone finds this review helpful, this is a gem of a game and I hope no one misses out. If i missed anything do feel free to comment below this to correct or add on.

Amazing quality and a lot of content for a free to play game. The only other F2P game I can compare it to is Path of Exile with only cosmetics and season passes being the money earner. There's no pay to win, but there are many issues I have with the game.

Mini Games: They are fun pretty early on, then they get near impossible with the AI reading you and reacting accordingly. Pretty much a waste of time after the first zone.

There's a lot of nice systems and not so nice systems in place. I kind of like the healer system, but the legal system kind of threw me for a loop. Being falsely accused by NPC's is weird and not welcome.

There's very little hand holding, maybe due to poor translations. You'll be thrown into a massive world without much guidance. My advice is to just do what you feel like doing, forget all of these YouTube videos, it's better to discover things for yourself because in the end, everything evens out anyways.

There's a lot of time-gated portions of this game. Beyond level 41 you will be waiting days for the opportunity to get to the next level cap. I understand this to a point, the developers probably wish for you to stay as long in the game as possible for their benefit and yours. Although grinding for items below max level is pretty much a waste of time, because you'll likely be doing it all over again when you raise the cap.

Grinding is massive in this game. It's to be expected, but you're also time-gated on grinding as you must spend points that you acquire over time in order to farm chances that enhance your character. It's not a very fun experience, especially when you get so little for your efforts every time.

The gacha and rewards are a mess and definitely feel like a mobile game, and with it comes the ridiculous amount of currencies. There's like 100 different places through menus upon menus where you can claim rewards or spin to win stuff. It's easy to constantly overlook things to claim, or spend way too much time combing through the menus to claim items.

Signposts. Just like a souls game. There's tons, with many being helpful while others being an annoyance. Remember to report the annoying ones.

This game is, without exaggeration, one of the most impressive experiences I’ve ever had. Visually, it’s breathtaking—its graphics feel a generation ahead, even compared to many major Triple-A releases.

What truly sets it apart is the sheer breadth of its systems. You can gather resources, farm mobs, and grind materials to upgrade your gear—with guaranteed upgrade success, meaning no frustrating RNG-based failures. The world is populated with dynamic NPCs whose AI-driven interactions feel surprisingly natural, creating moments that are far more engaging than any other game I've played.

On top of that, the game’s social systems let you form genuine bonds with other players, progressing from simple friendships to commitments, vows, and possibly marriage if you choose to pursue it. The world itself is fully explorable: follow butterflies to find chests, uncover oddities, stumble into random events, dive into cave systems and dungeons, break through hidden walls to find treasure, or hunt down journal entries for side-quest achievements.

I honestly struggle to convey just how much this game offers. And the best part? There’s virtually no pay-to-win. While you can purchase jade coins for the rotating shop, you earn them easily through normal gameplay. The only real incentive to buy is for cosmetic “melodies,” and even those are completely optional.

Ultimately, the experience is built around playing, exploring, collecting a huge variety of earnable cosmetics, and mastering the weapon styles you enjoy most. It’s the ARPG/MMO I’ve been searching for, and after nearly three decades of gaming, it’s genuinely one of the best titles I’ve ever played.

Push through the learning curve, take a shot at legend difficulty, and wander the world with everyone else. I can’t recommend it highly enough—and I hope to see you in-game! :D

In the vast world of indie games, few titles manage to blend beauty, storytelling, and gameplay mechanics as seamlessly as Where Wind Meets. Developed by the small, but talented team at Windfall Studios, the game offers an experience that is both atmospheric and thought-provoking. It invites players to step into an ancient land, shaped by wind, myth, and the power of elemental forces. But is this game more than just a beautiful world to explore, or does it offer depth and substance to match its striking visuals?

Setting and Story

Set in a sprawling, mythical landscape inspired by East Asian folklore, Where Wind Meets crafts a world where wind itself has the power to shape the fate of its people. Players take on the role of a wandering warrior, gifted—or cursed—with the ability to commune with the wind. The game draws heavily on themes of nature, spirit, and the ongoing clash between tradition and progress, as players uncover long-buried secrets in a land on the brink of change.

What stands out in the game’s story is the rich, yet understated narrative. Unlike many open-world games where quests are delivered in overwhelming amounts, Where Wind Meets employs a subtle approach, allowing the player to piece together the lore and history of the land through exploration, dialogue, and encounters. It’s a slow-burn story that rewards patience, a narrative that blooms organically as you interact with the world rather than rush toward predetermined objectives.

The protagonist’s journey is one of self-discovery, as they learn more about their powers and the ancient conflict between the elemental spirits. But unlike many games of this genre, Where Wind Meets focuses not just on the heroic side of this struggle, but also on the costs of wielding such power. It’s a narrative that makes you question your role in the world—not just as a savior, but as a participant in a larger, more complex ecosystem.

Gameplay Mechanics and Combat

At the heart of Where Wind Meets is a blend of exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat. The wind is not just a thematic element; it plays a crucial role in gameplay mechanics. Players can harness the wind to traverse difficult terrain, solve environmental puzzles, and even manipulate enemies. Combat, though, is perhaps the most dynamic aspect of the game. It’s a fluid, fast-paced system that focuses on timing and elemental strategy rather than sheer strength. Your character can tap into the wind to execute swift, graceful attacks, or use gusts to disorient and defeat foes in a dance of nature.

The combat system is deeply satisfying, though it might feel overwhelming at first. The wind powers allow for a variety of attack styles, but mastering them requires patience. There's a rhythm to it—a certain elegance that complements the game’s overall tone. The use of wind-based abilities feels natural and intuitive, giving the player an empowered sense of fluidity as they engage with both enemies and the environment.

Exploration is equally rewarding. The world is vast and filled with hidden corners, where the wind can guide you toward secrets or treasures. The landscapes themselves are rich with detail, from the towering mountains to the tranquil rivers, and each environment feels distinct. The wind’s role in traversal is fascinating: players might need to use gusts to propel themselves across cliffs, or ride currents to unlock hidden areas. It's not just about combat—it's about using your powers to interact with the world in meaningful ways.

Visuals and Sound Design

One of the standout features of Where Wind Meets is its breathtaking visual design. The game takes full advantage of its mythical setting, blending lush, vibrant landscapes with traditional East Asian architecture and natural elements. The world feels alive, thanks to dynamic weather systems, realistic foliage movement, and the way the wind interacts with the environment. The art direction clearly draws inspiration from ancient Chinese and Japanese art, making each scene feel like a living painting.

The attention to detail extends beyond the world itself. Animations are smooth, and the character design is equally impressive. The protagonist moves gracefully through the environment, with each action, whether it’s combat or exploration, being fluid and deliberate.

Accompanying the stunning visuals is an immersive soundscape. The score is tranquil yet emotive, perfectly underscoring the game’s themes of nature and introspection. Sound plays an important role in gameplay, too—subtle audio cues alert players to the presence of wind currents or hidden objects. The environmental sounds—from the rustling of trees to the whispering winds—add to the atmosphere, making it feel as if you’ve truly entered a living, breathing world.

Thematic Depth

While many games of this genre focus on heroism, Where Wind Meets delves deeper into the philosophical aspects of power, nature, and balance. The wind, as a central motif, represents change and fluidity. The game constantly asks the player to consider their relationship with the forces they manipulate. Are you a force for good, or is there a danger in harnessing power without understanding the consequences?

The theme of balance is further explored through the interactions with various factions and spiritual beings. These entities, each representing different aspects of the natural world, offer guidance and challenges that test the player’s understanding of harmony. The story never forces morality onto the player; rather, it presents choices and consequences that feel meaningful.

Challenges and Pacing

The game isn’t without its challenges, though. Some players may find the pacing to be slow, especially in the early stages when the narrative takes time to unfold. There are moments when the game’s lack of clear objectives can feel disorienting, but for those who enjoy piecing together stories through exploration and subtle clues, this may feel more rewarding than detrimental.

Combat, while fluid, can become repetitive if you’re not actively engaging with the elemental mechanics. There’s a steep learning curve in mastering wind powers, but once the rhythm clicks, it becomes an incredibly satisfying experience. The game also suffers from occasional pacing issues, particularly during long stretches of dialogue or environmental puzzles that can feel a bit tedious.

Conclusion

In conclusion, Where Wind Meets is a breathtakingly beautiful and thoughtfully crafted game that offers an experience that is both meditative and engaging. Its stunning visuals, intuitive combat system, and deep narrative themes make it stand out as a unique entry in the indie game landscape. While it might not appeal to everyone due to its slower pacing and emphasis on exploration over immediate action, those who take the time to immerse themselves in its world will find a game that is both rewarding and memorable.

Where Wind Meets isn’t just a game about controlling the elements—it’s about understanding them. And in doing so, it offers players not just an adventure, but a reflection on the forces that shape our world, both seen and unseen.

Literally the most impressed I've ever been by a game.  

As someone who has been enjoying wuxia/xainxa novels for several years now. I came into this game with extremely high standards but very low expectations, especially considering that its f2p. I was enjoying the first couple of hours but was constantly waiting for a slap in the face, some kind of disappointing moment that would make the fact that it was free make sense. However, that slap never came, each encounter I had, system I came across and mechanic I discovered truly impressed me. 

The fighting feels incredible, once you realize that you just gotta be as badass as possible, you start chaining together normal attacks, deflects/dodges and special moves in a way that makes you feel like a martial arts master. After playing for a while, I found out that the reason that this game is f2p is not due to a lack of quality but due to the game having confidence in being good enough to get your money anyway. From what I've seen so far, the cash shop is entirely cosmetic, with some some of the best looking outfits and items I've ever seen. 

The characters are compelling, with exposition weaved naturally into their dialogues, it hasn't felt forced at all. The AI NPCs truly shocked me, you can talk and befriend these characters and get to discuss their fears and motivations while giving advice, helping guide them through whatever problems they are facing, allowing you to form a far deeper and more memorable bond with characters than in any game I've played so far. 

While I'm not too far into the story, I've come across a couple of twists and mysterious that lead me wanting to know more. The whole world feel incredibly alive, with npca talking and giving subtle bits of information while they converse and there constantly being things to do.

This games whole goal is to make you look and feel as cool as possible. As such, it has a character creator with so many features that it borders on excessive. Thankfully it also has the option to load characters that the community has made and tweak them to suit your preference.  

Overall this game perfect encapsulates the wuxia genre, I'm so glad that I picked this up. I fully expect to be playing it for quite some time.

Where Winds Meet is one of those rare RPGs that feels like stepping into a living world rather than just playing through a checklist. The game blends breathtaking exploration with a combat system that rewards skill, timing, and creativity.
• World & Atmosphere: From Qinghe’s flower fields to underwater caves, every region feels alive with secrets. Spirit Vision, hidden puzzles, and lore‑rich NPCs make exploration endlessly rewarding.
• Combat: Fluid, cinematic, and versatile. Whether you’re parrying red telegraphs, chaining Lightness Skills across rooftops, or diving into underwater battles against alligators, fights feel dynamic and satisfying.
• Progression: The permanent consequence design makes choices matter. Planting seeds, solving riddles, or failing quests all shape your Jianghu journey in ways that feel personal.
• Guild & Community: The Seasons guild system adds another layer of depth. Building titles, sharing lore, and tracking exploration together makes the game feel collaborative even in solo play.
• Mystic Arts & Gifts: Unlocking arts like Meteor Flight or experimenting with curios and gifts adds flavor beyond combat — it’s about living in the world, not just surviving it.

Verdict: If you enjoy open‑world RPGs that reward curiosity, skill, and storytelling, Where Winds Meet is a must‑play. It’s not just a game — it’s a journey through seasons, choices, and legends.

About a week or so ago, I was really craving a MMO game. I've played stuff like Metin, Lost Ark, Kritika, Black Desert before, but they all died pretty soon for me. Then, Where Winds Meet came out, and oh boy.

I currently have about 25 hours in the game, and I can say I've been captivated like nothing else. I got my girlfriend to play it, my sister and a few of my friends, this is something that barely ever happens. 

I could stay and write words of appreciation and say how much I like the game, but obviously everyone is already doing so, as this is an insanely good game. However, I want to say a few things.

I think that if we look beside the fact that the game is free, and yes, whaling is a big part of the funding for the game, the game seriously needs some more cosmetics. Especially for weapons. Why do I mean by this? Well, I don't necessarily have a problem with an in-game item costing 40.000USD, nor do I have a problem with people paying around 200-400USD for a text to appear for about 5-10 seconds during a firework event. However, I do have a problem with the fact that, from a free-to-play player to a whaling player, there's barely an in-between. Sure, there's a battlepass, there are a few cosmetics that don't cost a fortune, but even they cost around 20USD per set. I think pricing them lower would really benefit the game and open the market for more of the playerbase. Also, we desperately need weapon cosmetics. There's barely a few skins for weapons, and they're either bad or straight up expensive. I would love to play this game for months to come, but the updates that come out next are what will either keep me or push me away, and I think that will be the case with many other players. As honestly, I really appreciate the free-to-play aspect of the game, and I'm often left in awe at just how much detail and gameplay / possibilities are available for free, but then again, I'd also like to spend some money, get some cosmetics, get some cool stuff. I've already gotten the basic pass and the monthly 4USD little pass for some pearls. But for the money, it's barely any content, if you look at what you could get for the same money on games like Fortnite or League.

This is everything I ever wanted an open world game to be. Terrific and deep combat that's animation based like Monster Hunter (No, it's not SoUlSlIkE, Souls is Monster Hunter like since Demons Souls was literally Monster Hunter at home with the core combat don't @ me) aloong with a vibrant world full of just stuff to do, things unlocking organically and not being on rails, a world where you have way more things to do than just combat. 

It feels like with every situation, and every combat scenario, you as the player have like at least 3 ways, always, to approach it, this game just makes me feel like I'm actually PLAYING a GAME and not an onrails simulator. 

The fact that this also just feels like GTA in the major city is also incredible. 

I see this game as GTA + Batman + Dragon's Dogma + Genshin Impact all in one. 

I LOVE how this FEELS like a wuxia TV shows with the martial arts and skills that you just get random in the open world. 

The sidequests are also executed so well. They are short and sweet, with dense production value and they make me feel like I'm going on an adventure all the time. 

The story also surprised me, the Qinghe chapter made me cry like crazy. 

The way you acquire power in this game to make your character stronger is so non-linear and so exploratory, like old PS2 games before everything became ubisoftified and linear, where 99% of your power can't be missed. Here, I'm making a conscious effort to look for insanely cool new abilities including but not limited to LITERALLY SHOOTING THROUGH THE SKY LIKE AN EFFING METEOR, in the world, and it feels so satisfying when you meet a random fisherman who turns out to be a kung fu master in hiding who teaches you this stuff. 

I also just love how goofy this game is too. There is so much just silly stuff  in it that shows the developers don't take themselves so seriously, and these silly stuff really make me laugh. 

I don't know, this game has a lot of jankiness, and the company that actually owns this game, Netease, is greedy trash, but the developers who made this game has in my opinion, made a masterpiece. After platinuming elden ring (I platinumed every soulsbourne game), I griped for ages about how Elden Ring basically made a pointless open world that just looks pretty but gives you not much else. The dream game I imagined Elden Ring could've been IS this game, and this game has surpassed my imagination in every way.

This isn't a bad game, but it does have a few draw backs. I tend to go with the bad first. Multiplayer is a hard sell. So I started early on and have been playing awhile. But recently my friend took my recommendation and joined in as well. I thought it'd be cool to journey with them, even if I get no rewards. Well it turns out they wouldn't either since you don't scale down to their world. Which I get...so I figured ya know what, let me roll back my breakthrough and that should scale me down right? Not even in the slightest. I was one shot killing everything so I had to stop. There are multiplayer games, the mmo style one is a prime example. But I'm a bit disgruntled that I can't journey with my friend without being the dues machina. 
Second point, character creation. I get why they want you to use the cash shop or rewards to buy cosmetic ticket to change your look...but you can't make a second character, there is no character deletion and your gender is perma locked at creation. Even if I wanted to change, not that I would mind you, there is no way to do so.
Another is matchmaking. There have been a few bosses that've beat my ass like a drum. People leave assistance markers there but I've never had anyone respond to one. The companion can be a little useful, but a real player is better. Matchmaking is another option but you HAVE to be the host or progress doesn't count...trust me, thought I killed a boss only to find out it reset once the other player left so I had to fight them again. That and you might have a level vastly lower than yours try to join...my 50 boss fight with a level 20 trying to get in.
Another low point, translation. Sometimes it works well, but there are some times where dialog gets repeated twice. Lines said and written are two wholly different animals. Sometimes the dialog just kills out altogether. Especially once you learn that nearly all the NPC's and I think your own character, are just voiced by AI. You can even have chats with an AI both npc, which is funny as hell.
That being said the things I do like. Combat is satisfying and has a good level of difficulty. There is a lot, and I mean a LOT to do in this game. Some are a bit harder to learn...gift of gab being one...but ones like medicine can be satisfying once you learn how it all works. The MMO style of it has no solo progress obviously, but there are plenty of social activities you can do. And you can build nearly everywhere. You can't build in cities obviously, but the world is wide open to build on. Music is pretty good, even have some mini games involving music that sounds really good.
Not sure what else I can add here. But my overall score...since steam doesn't do scores...personally is 7 out of 10. Not bad, but not great.

I've been playing "Where winds Meet." It's not without it's fair share of controversy. but we won't be focusing on that. Instead my Review will only Score the game Based on Gameplay & User experience. 

I've dropped the games score from my previous of 6 to a 4.5 out of 10. 

Previously I gave it a 6 because It was lacking but felt like the game had potential. After delving into the game for 75hrs I've come to the conclusion the game is an incomplete Mess. I do not reccommend the game at it's current state. 

Here is a Small list of issues.
[list]
[*] Each Weapon art attacks deal Different Amounts of damage with the Same Attack damage on your character. This information is nowhere to be found. as an example. Spear light attack deals about 123 damage with a Weapon attack damage range of 284-494. While Mo Blade deals about 359 damage. Their Damage is clearly different, and so is their attack speed. But such information is not avilible. Instead you have to go through the Tedious work of Recording each attack. Check the MS of each attack in the video. Type it out. Then attack the same enemy 100+ Times and write down the damage of each attack done. Adding all together and dividing by the amount of attacks done. to get the Avarage damage of each hit. Then Divide That value with your Characters attack damage to get the % of the attacks damage. Multiply that value based on the Attack speed of the attack. Repeat for every weapon and All their attacks and attack chains. Compare with each weapon. This damage info is missing on the weapon arts but is availible for Mystic Arts. Which are a different set of abilites players can use on Number 1 - 4.
[*] Each Weapon arts Element has 2 Different Symbols Aswell as a unintuitive Name you need to learn, That are only used in Different screens. Some of these symbols are used to describe a weakness. The other to describe the Type of element. Both mean the same thing. a example of a Element would be "Stone Split". [url=https://imgur.com/a/uawic29] Link to a image i made.[/url] Its in swedish. but icons are still the same as in game.
[*] Equipment Mod Descriptions reference things by name Yet those things have Icons also representing them. Making it harder for 
[*] Not all Keybinds are rebindable. ALT displays the 2nd set of Mystic Arts. Can not be rebound on ARPG camera. 
[*] This point has multiple issues. Please read all of it. Deflection/Parry Can be Done by Holding RMB then pressing LMB. which is highlighted by the LMB icon changing. This information is never given in game. Instead the game has a Dedicated Button. [E] By default. as the Parry button. I figured that I can rebind my [~] Special skill to [E] Instead. But you can't. Because the Dedicated Parry button works differently then the RMB + LMB one. It both has a Longer Parry window, But also, you are able to spam it with almost no delay with the Dedicated Button. While the RMB + LMB Changes the Parry function on LMB while you hold RMB with a Light attack while the Parry animation plays. So you can't chain parries. Because the Game Stops reading your RMB & will instead Do a basic attack. 
[*] Movement Is like Driving a Car. So finer movement is not possible. Even when standing still. 
[*] Standing next to a fence, and you want your Character to turn towards the fence. No. You'll vault over it instead. 
[*] Movement have you grab anything you can climb when running past it. If you are just a little bit too close your character will do a Quarter Turn and start climbing. As you progress you unlock some "Winds" something running. Where the distance you keep from object is now Double what it was before Or you will Randomly run up a object or get stuck in a Loop which your only way to stop is to Stop running.

Did the game ever Teach you that or ask? no. it will ruin your food just cause.

[*] Weapon art ability descriptions are unintuitive & Hard to follow.
[*] Weapon art Ability Descriptions may have multiple tabs, Depending on your Resolution these are hidden. Press E to cycle to next one if you are unsure. I play on 1080p. I can barely see some tabs. Mostly notice because the [E] Prompt isn't greyed out.
[*] Multiple times during the story VA stops.

[*] A lot of Scenes are Drawn out to emphesis. But instead they often did the oposite. Just left me thinking "wtf!?".

Where Winds Meet is a visually appealing open-world action role-playing game related to the culture of ancient China. The world feels vibrant, featuring gorgeous vistas, active weather, and beautiful environments that constantly immerse you into the world and experience. Combat is precise, fun, and stylish, allowing you to combine martial arts, swordplay, and special abilities seamlessly and in a way that feels like it is in between modernity and antiquity.

The narrative is full of mystery, emotional impact and enticing side quests that reward players for exploring. Parkour, gliding, horseback travel, and free movement, make traveling an enjoyable rather than unpleasant experience. It mixes true history with fantasy elements that feel new and engaging.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a deep open-world action role-playing game with beautiful visuals, great combat, and an engaging story. This title will appeal to players who enjoy immersive worlds, and the gameplay lends itself to martial arts themed games.

Pros:
-Graphics a stunning and the English voices are not the worst I've seen
- Story is 10/10 honestly gives most AAA a run for its money
- Gameplay is incredible and the skill floor is very low
- Classes are pretty well balanced
- Exploration is actually fun and well worth your time
- Bosses are cinematic master pieces and will give you a challenge

Cons:
- The multiplayer aspect of the game needs some heavy work to make it feel more like a multiplayer game/campaign and not just solo mode but friends are standing there too
- There is a bit of a learning curve for certain classes that can make them hard choices for early players
- The Tank class is a bit odd compared to other titles since you don't really face tank like I would expect at least till you get much farther into the game and with very specific gear. Id like to see it more like new world where the tank high high sustain and low damage, with the role to keep aggro off the team
- The game does stutter from time to time and likely will not run well on lower end PCs
- There needs to be some polish with the animation canceling both with weapons and the movement options. I found myself jumping off cliffs, running past objectives pretty frequently

Overall:
- The game is incredible and more so with it being free. I would gladly pay $60 for it if the campaign missions were full multiplayer. But since the loot, missions, objectives, are for the most part solo only its a big missed opportunity in my eyes especially since there is so much multiplayer features baked in already. Most of them are pretty boring IMO though since they are things like the healing circles or group meditation. Also the difficulty really doesn't seem different no matter what I do. I can turn it all the way up or down and it makes very little difference in terms of damage output or input but maybe this isn't fully finished yet or its a bug I am not sure

Disclaimer: Spent about 5 bucks on the pass because I wanted to support development. 

TLDR: Very good game, a lot of different things for all sorts of players. 100% does not require money to access all game mechanics. 


♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, what a game! 

They've somehow taken the open-world feel of: 
--Red Dead Redemption 2 (think main story arc, with hundreds of side missions AND little non-missions (no markers, but narrative quest: "I dropped my bag over the cliff, could you find it?")) All set in ~10th century 
--Eldin Ring with boss fight mechanics, stamina management, and timed parry (lower difficulties can slow time and other helpful mechanics)

...and blended it to an optional MMO style game with raid like mechanics, boss fights, pvp duels, and fun online healing mini games like chi-healing, throwing food at penance wagons, chess like games and other party style games.

The combat is surprisingly complex for being so simple. There's light/heavy attack, 2 weapon skills and your usual jump/sprint/etc attack. But using the parry system can result in some very epic fights. Some enemies are weak to a certain attack type (other games do this as elemental weakness) you can still power through with just one or two weapon types, but keep this in mind when equping main hand and secondary weapon. 

All of this, absolutely free with (from what I've seen) 100% of the content accessible without spending any money. 

Yes, they have cosmetics behind gatcha, but they provide a wide variety of outfits and accessories through gameplay. If you don't like the gatcha mechanic, there are several outfits that allow you to pay X amount and get them. 

Speaking of outfits, they have AMAZING detail and physics. There is a wide range from elegant to cool to simple. Most all the paid outfits can be dyed, some of the earned currency outfits can be dyed too, but the outfits given during the main story usually aren't dyeable. outfits are separated by head, head accessories, outfit, outfit accessories, so unfortunately when it comes to the main outfit, you can't mix and match between feet/legs/torso.

Pretty meh. This review will ignore all the monetization issue and will just judge it as a game. It's not bad, but the more I play, the more flaws I start to see. 

For a game about precision parry and fast paced combat, the controls can be extremely unresponsive, even when outside of combat. I'm not even joking when I'm saying there are times it takes the game a whole 3 second to register my inputs. My imputs to jump, my imputs to use an ability, my inputs to drink a potion. I'm not even locked in an animation or anything, I'm just spamming the button while my character just stands still doing nothing. No lag or stutter, just the game staring blankly at me while I spam my healing potion only to take several seconds to register and start drinking.

The game also has very inconsistent hitboxes and hit registration, or just attacks in general. Projectiles that are nowhere near you will hit you. Enemies can shoot you even if they aren't facing you, sometimes even if their backs are turned. Enemy hits can happen a split second before/after their attack animation

Then there's the translation being complete ass. Dialogue and subtitles don't match. Descriptions are weird and often don't make sense. Some voicelines sound like they used AI for voiceover so it feels stilted and emotionless. Also, sometimes a character is voiced, sometimes they aren't. They'd be voiced in 1 scene, be mute in another, then magically become voiced again in the next. It's weird and takes away from the experience.

EDIT : Also, in multiplayer, latency makes it almost impossible to parry. I don't know if it's the connection that's bad, or is the netcode just terrible, but if you're helping other people with bosses, you're going to have a miserable time. If you thought hit registration was bad in SP, it's 100x worse in MP. 
But even worse though, if just 1 person has a faster computer than you, you will get hit before your game even loaded. Because while you're loading, if just 1 other player loaded it, it will spawn your character and it will get hit, even if you're still loading in. I've been killed several times in multi-stage bosses because of that.

Where Winds Meet is one of the rare free-to-play games that immediately feels like it belongs in the same conversation as big budget, premium titles. From the moment you step into the world, it's clear the developers aimed higher than typical F2P formula. Instead of relying on repetitive zones or mobile style design, the game delivers a fully open, handcrafted world inspired by ancient China lush landscapes, busy villages, dense forests, and towering mountains that invite you to explore at your own pace. It feels alive, and more importantly, it feels deliberately made, something you almost never see in a game that doesn't cost money upfront.

The combat system is another major reason the game stands out. Most F2P titles stick to simple, spam heavy combat. Here, every fight feels like a choreographed wuxia duel. The gameplay leans heavily into fluid swordplay, parries, counters, acrobatics, and flashy martial arts techniques that make every encounter feel dynamic. You're rewarded for timing and precision, not just mashing skills on cooldown. It's action heavy, stylish, and surprisingly deep closer to something you'd expect in a paid action RPG.

What also separates Where Winds Meet from its competitors is how much freedom it gives the player. You're not funneled into one playstyle or forced into a grind loop. instead, you can approach the experience however you want whether that's focusing on combat, sneaking through missions with stealth, exploring the world like a wanderer, or diving into side professions like medicine, hunting, trading or bounty hunting. You can glide across cliffs, run across rooftops, swim through rivers, tame horses, craft gear, or simply wander from village to village taking in the scenery. It offers the kind of sandbox freedom you rarely see in a F2P environment.

The narrative also aims higher than expected. The story is grounded in political tension, personal conflict, and mystery, and it's presented with a level of cinematography and emotional weight that gives it real presence. F2P games usually treat story as an afterthought, but this one tries to make you care about the world and the people in it allowing the storytelling to feel surprisingly premium.

Finally and maybe most importantly Where Winds Meet is one of the few F2P games that doesn't feel predatory. There's no energy system cutting off your playtime, no gacha walls stopping your progress, and no pay to win mechanics that give paying players unfair advantages. Monetization focuses mostly on cosmetics and optional conveniences, which makes the experience feel respectful instead of exploitative. In a gaming landscape full of aggressive microtransactions, the fairness of this system alone makes the game refreshing.

Game has awesome concepts, but there's just too many things I have issues with that took several hours to hit. First thing, time-gating. Many people defend this mess but I think they only do it out of a sunk cost fallacy. They have invested time and money into this game and they will defend it no matter what. You are limited to 500 energy that takes three real time days to recharge. You use that energy to kill bosses or outposts. Killing bosses is objectively the best way to get these chests. You then have an RNG chance to get your specific weapon, specific tier, and specific trait for your build. If you get lucky to get all of these, the level cap just increases in ten days and then you will have to farm it all again. Not fun at all.

Invading someone's world and taking them out when they have a bounty sounds awesome. That is until you realize you rarely ever will see an actual player with a bounty, it's mostly NPCs. When you finally do see a player you will hardly ever actually get in their game. The game will tell you someone else has already taken it, or that the host is in a specific cutscene therefore you can't join. 

Same with healing. You want to heal people with an illness? Good luck, even though they post on the healing board that they need healing, you will rarely ever get in their game. They have friend only invites, afk, in a certain area, or just reject your invite completely. It's so aggravating.

The gacha gambling bs is here. Outfits are very expensive, people that say "I can't believe this game is free!" well you simply have no understanding how these f2p gacha games work. Yes, this is a gacha game, it has gacha in it, get over it. Gacha is a cancer and should be illegal in games. Outfits on the CN version are much cheaper and available to straight up purchase, meanwhile in the western version they lock them behind a massive paywall that's three times more expensive. 

The graphics, sound, and world are all good but I just can't get behind these mobile gambling systems. You can't experiment with different builds on the fly because each weapon takes a lot of time and investment and if you haven't got the resources or gear locked behind time gates, well you just can't play a specific way until you wait it out in real time. 

When I play a game, I want to play how I want when I want. I have a life and don't want to feel pressured about not logging in to get awards every day, or dealing with these stupid time mechanics. It's also quite astonishing at how many idiots can't figure out why this game is free. If you have made that stupid comment "How is this game free?" you really need to look up the statistics on these gacha games and understand the game is actually playing you.

My early journey in this beautifully chaotic game:

I began by sculpting a character so disturbingly misshapen that any divine being would request a refund, then immediately had to watch my monstrosity share screen time with flawless, idol-tier NPCs.

Witnessed a bear attempting a mystical t’ai chi routine to nab a beehive, learned the same move, punted the bear into orbit, nearly died from bees and bruises, accidentally stole a horse, and got my skull rattled by its furious owner — leaving me with a collection of painful injuries.

Out of nowhere, a stranger with a Chinese username — essentially Asian John Wick — joined my world, purged my ailments with a chakra battle straight out of a shonen anime, then politely asked to duel and proceeded to fold me like laundry before bowing and disappearing.

Spiritually defeated, I swore to train as a healer, unlocked basic poison remedies, and practiced on a wounded goose because I wasn’t competent enough to treat actual players.

Started experimenting on my guildmates with the chakra healing mechanic, slowly building expertise until I could mend everything from fractures to full-blown emotional collapse.

Took on healing requests from random adventurers, entered their sessions, cured them, challenged them to honorable combat, and vanished like a wandering sage.

Eventually reached such absurd medical proficiency that I could bypass the mini-game entirely and instantly fix even the nastiest conditions — still insisting on duels afterward out of ritual.

Climbed to the top of the healer leaderboard, gained the nickname “the green-faced dueling physician” in world chat, and began receiving requests at a constant, almost comical pace.

After more than a hundred successful healings — and zero duel losses — I got a message for a level 4 Soul Bind, one of the hardest afflictions in the game. The sender? Asian John Wick.

I cured him once more, we clashed in an incredibly tight duel, I survived with literally 1 HP, and he knelt, offered a deep, respectful bow, said “GG,” and departed — confirming that I had officially become the game’s supreme healer.

Where Winds Meet an Open world Wuxia game, and probably my new home, this game makes me feel like I'm at home like I was with TERA ONLINE when the Enmasse servers were online. So lets dive in.

CONS FIRST to get them out the way!

100GBs, bit on the Cruiser weight bracket for File size.

Learning curve – PREPARE TO NITPICK IT ALL, you'll want to slow down, and literally walk away for 5 minutes while thinking what you missed for progression.

Online PvP dynamics – mainly people invading other's instances, but feels like a toggle for invaders/bounty hunters in a Grace period (Never toggle always temporary) to allow some grief relief.

Not fully open world – sections are locked behind story mode. I was in starter zone for almost 4 days.

Lack of information and context due to Translations mismatching Simplified, Traditional Mandarin into English, and causing confusion.

PRO!

ACTION RPG – Just like classics and prototypes of Yore, WWM is Action combat based not Tab target/assist so if you whiff not because of RNG stat rolls, you missed because SKILL ISSUES!

Open world – Makes my brain happy!

Character creation – So they got clever here and used what feels like "AI assistance" here so you can use a real photo of yourself, if you want, or some character you like, and the game gives you a rough draft to work with; Works with voice too, I can hear my own Iberian Lisp escape some the lines.

WEAPONS – ok we got all the classic Wuxia and some few the Heng dao is actually a 9ring Staff-Saber meant for anti-calvary, than we got the Classy Jian, Tieshans, Rope Darts, Qiangs (Spear!), and so many more and more on the way.

Progression – Once you get a basic grasp you'll understand that this world is about "Practice makes perfect if you go slowly," and it works well.

Notes:
To me this is my second home, TERA where I learned to react and understand twitch reaction mechanics, BDO and EVE taught me to be wary of Gankers, Blade and Soul couldn't match what I truly desired and for me as a Martial Artist and Student-Teacher in the ways of Kung Fu myself this feels proper, though there are issues I agree I will be wary, Observant and a touch hopeful this games proves it can do better than the rest that failed.

[h1] overall a great experience [/h1]
gameplay-wise, think Assassin's Creed meets Elden Ring meets Infinity Nikki, but make it wuxia.

[h3] pros: [/h3]
+ absolutely breathtaking visuals. you think the first area is as beautiful as a game can get, then you see the second one.
+ large and complex open world
+ engaging and challenging combat
+ very good character customisation options
+ a great way to learn about historical chinese culture
+ unique sect mechanic, which is a separate system to guilds
+ the gacha is only for cosmetics so very free to play friendly
+ excellent chinese voice acting
+ robust multiplayer mode with marriage option
+ freedom to play single- or multiplayer

[h3] cons [/h3]
- the first area is somewhat weak narratively. it seems a vague story was woven around the insane environments and bosses, not vice versa.
- busy and somewhat confusing interface with stores and rewards hidden in all different places.
- for one mode of getting cosmetics, it's gacha for global users while CN users can pay for it outright.
- some players like to troll with signpost placement, but you can turn this feature off
- it costs irl money to change from male to female and vice versa, so customisation is only half as fun to play with as it could be if you're f2p.
- minor hiccups with the English localisation, particularly in puzzles based around chinese characters.

[b] some personal points of contention: [/b]
- it seems the army must have conscripted all of the older ladies in the countryside, because in the first area, there are none. (this was fixed in the second area)
- in the first area, all but 3 female NPCs have the exact same douyin influencer face. even those referred to as aunty. also an immersion killer. 
- during the universal furnace quest, in the space of 3 minutes, a male gay couple are introduced out of nowhere, every homophobic trope known to man is whipped out at once, unfortunate things happen, then they never come up again. i hadn't expected representation, but that was... something.
- the cat models in this game are really ugly. (you can pet them, fortunately)
- you can't pet the dogs.

all said, it's a great experience. so much was improved on in the second area, which is promising. i definitely recommend.

The game offers a little bit of many different things. Its story unfolds within the extremely complex social and historical context of China. As a result, the underlying lore can be difficult to fully understand, although this limited accessibility also gives it a certain sense of mystery. That said, there were quite a few moments when I wished the lore had been built from the ground up, allowing the player to discover it gradually, rather than relying on such a vast pre-existing context that requires prior historical and cultural knowledge.

Aside from this, and the frustrating menus, another weakness is the lack of variety in clothing and visual styles. Everything is strictly Chinese in design. After a while, this aesthetic can become tiring.

Nevertheless, the game excels in areas that I have rarely seen blended together so successfully in any other title. The combat is highly enjoyable and more than satisfying for me, especially thanks to the adjustable difficulty settings. Exploration is equally rewarding, with exceptionally beautiful and varied environments. It is the kind of game where you can frequently stop progressing altogether and simply admire your surroundings.

The story itself is presented exceptionally well. The game portrays it without compromise and with very little censorship, depicting numerous dark aspects of the period and even artistically intensifying them in order to achieve the intended emotional effect. Although the broader context can sometimes make the narrative confusing, and the limited artistic variety may occasionally lead to disengagement, the story remains remarkably well constructed and presented.

The aesthetics of certain dungeons and areas affected me visually and emotionally in ways that very few games ever have. From the beauty and quiet mystery of the immortalized Lunar Goddess to the semi-horror experience of the Mist-Shrouded Prison, with its red candles and ritualistic atmosphere, these elements strongly appeal to my personal taste and, in my opinion, are essential to creating a complete experience.

More precisely, what is truly necessary is contrast; a contrast that allows the intended artistic direction to stand out properly. The game moves from extraordinary, vividly colored landscapes to areas completely enveloped in fog, darkness, and mystery.

Artistically, the game offers almost everything that a title so deeply rooted in Chinese aesthetics possibly could. Unfortunately, the Chinese influence dominates the design too heavily, and I would have preferred greater variety. I am also not a fan of gacha systems, although I can mostly ignore that aspect.

Once you get past the endless cascades of menus and red notification markers that absolutely refuse to disappear unless you spend more time dealing with them than actually accomplishing something meaningful in the game, it remains one of the finest experiences in terms of exploration, artistic direction, and the stories it chooses to tell.

Overall I'd say this is positive. Combat is fun and you can easily feel very cool while also having some strategy. Basically you can just throw yourself into any fight and feel like you can handle it but also you're given a couple of panic skills making you realize you might want to be a bit more careful if you constantly see them popping up.

You also have like a lot to discover. Usually you'd essentially be forced to just power level for content and abilities but here you just need to actively find certain spots and exploration is highly recommended and rewarded. Feels incredibly satisfying to both stumble into something very awesome and getting some new skills often just asks you to to search the map.

Biggest issue is its formatted like an MMO. The menus are a hassle to work through, you're getting slapped with "If you give us money you'd get more". Progression isn't locked behind paywalls, thankfully, but some times seemingly arbitrary time caps. Like I reach a level cap and sometimes I just need to face a trial to advance but other times seems like I got there too fast and the game wanted me to wait like three actual literal days before I could advance again. A bunch of times I'd log in and see five different things telling me I needed to check something but after like an actual ten or twenty minutes of trying to navigate screens I just gave up. Like I got to around lvl 40 which needs like four separate advancements and upgrades of weapons until I ended up finding one thing that was on screen saying I had a reward yet unclaimed. Dailies are also a significant chore as well. Normally they'd take like a few minutes but here its closer to like 30 mins to an hour. Everything just feels like I'm getting FOMO but instead of advancing the story and more actual content I'm getting told because I couldn't navigate one screen I missed a log in reward and I'm also not maximizing my gear or upgrade materials. Its just too much, even shaving half of this is still a bit too excessive.

Can be extremely metaphorical and steeped in historical context which makes it challenging to follow along at times. Exceptional storytelling, nonetheless.

Normally, I'd argue that if a player is left feeling confused and unclear on the storyline, it's typically due to flaws in the game's design, but in this case I'm holding back on this judgement simply because the complexity is a beautiful one.

The game seeks to tell multiple deep, thought-provoking tales that are interwoven with so much real history that it would be difficult and even counterproductive to the devs' intentions to simplify. History has always been ridiculously nuanced and convoluted, after all, so props to the studio for daring to tackle such a challenge.

Now, I still believe the delivery to players can be made clearer and more efficient (especially in terms of suggesting the order of recommended quests to make for the most chronological sense), but given the ambitious scope and the devs' apparent passion, I can't find it in myself to be too hard on them. This is my own flaw as a player, haha.

Of course, a byproduct is players drawing back from the game because of this complexity. When something is not easily grasped or understood by the player, the player is very likely to look over it and even deem it shallow/redundant, which is sadly already happening. Intricacies of translating aside, it doesn't help that the English translation feels noticeably poorer compared to the original text in Mandarin Chinese. This is something I hope to see improved in future patches. 

I personally recommend players take the time to look up explanation/summary videos on the side to better appreciate the game and its whole multi-layered shebang. Obviously the game has its other issues, but its narrative core (at least so far) is proving itself to be very well thought out.

If you're someone who loves a good story and/or are a history fan, please do give WWM a chance.

[h1]Is this the Wuxia game we've been waiting for?[/h1]

[b]The Short Version:[/b]
If you loved [i]Ghost of Tsushima[/i] for the world but wanted the flashiness of [i]Sekiro[/i] or [i]Naraka: Bladepoint[/i], this is it. It has some jank, but the freedom of movement is unmatched.

[hr][/hr]

[b]The Good:[/b]
[list]
[*] [b]Movement:[/b] Running on water, scaling walls, and the Qinggong mechanics feel incredible. It flows better than almost any other open-world game.
[*] [b]The World:[/b] Period-accurate China looks stunning. The environmental storytelling is top-tier.
[*] [b]Combat Depth:[/b] It’s not just button mashing. The martial arts system allows for different playstyles (Tai Chi vs. aggressive swordplay).
[*] [b]Roleplaying:[/b] You can actually be a doctor, architect, or merchant. It adds a "life sim" layer that I didn't expect.
[/list]

[b]The Bad:[/b]
[list]
[*] [b]Optimization:[/b] Frame drops in large cities are noticeable. Be prepared to tweak settings even on good hardware.
[*] [b]UI Clutter:[/b] The menus can be overwhelming at first, and the translation is occasionally a bit rough.
[*] [b]Camera:[/b] Like many action games, the camera is sometimes the hardest boss fight in tight spaces.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h1]The Verdict: 8/10[/h1]
It scratches that Wuxia itch perfectly. Recommended if you like action RPGs with a steep learning curve.
