TLDR: Not a straightforward recommendation but more of a 'it is free so check it out'. 

First things first AI and potentially generative AI is at work here, I'm not sure of the full extent but there is an LLM basically built into the game for a dialogue system used with generic NPCs, I don't like LLMs out of principle but they don't cross a redline for me so long as they stay stripped down, non-invasive and don't make use of any generative functions, obviously that's hard to ascertain precisely but it is walking the line for me at the moment. In terms of generative stuff, I've heard whispers but haven't been able to pinpoint anything, some loading screen art might be slightly retouched but I have no way to know for sure, it makes me uneasy but until I know for sure, I'll let it slide. 

Now for the actual game - in the growing tradition of ambitious and convoluted projects to come out of the recent Chinese (and to a lesser extent Korean) development boo, WWM is a game packed so full of mechanics and systems that it becomes hard to give you an elevator pitch for what it actually is. It is probably easiest to start with the baseline structure and theming, this is an open-world third person action 'rpg' (whatever that term means at this point) with a beautifully rendered Wuxia setting. The points of comparison I come to are the recent Assassin's Creed games (Origins onward), as well as a clear influence from Sekiro and Team Ninja's soulslike output (Wo Long and Nioh 2 especially). The core gameplay loops are comprised of a mix of exploration and combat; completing side content, clearing outposts, gathering resources, engaging with minigames, challenge checklists etc. The side content ranges from simplistic and fairly boring to genuinely really engaging, a lot of the side stories are full fledged 'campaigns', complete with lengthy dungeons and elaborate and beautifully presented boss fights ,that you unlock for replay at endgame challenge difficulties (and associated rewards) once you beat. 

The main story too is fairly engaging, the English translation is currently kind of messy and if you are familiar with the modern body of Wuxia ('Cultivation') media across manhua, games and the like, then you won't be particularly surprised by anything Winds is doing with its narrative, but the production value, and consistently excellent presentation (both in art design, cutscene direction and music) keeps everything entertaining no matter how predictable it is. I really do wish the translation was a little better because it is clear that there is extensive worldbuilding and character writing going on here, but it can be a little hard to parse (thankfully the game has a hilariously extensive internal wiki system). 

So if at the core of Winds there is a kind of souls/ubisoft action rpg mashup thing going on, what else is layered on top of it? In short - just about whatever you could possibly imagine. Some people are erroneously calling this game an MMO, in actuality it is a lot closer to the kind of MMO-Lite experiences that have popped up over the last 10 years - think Destiny. There is a large focus on multiplayer gameplay, social interaction and community building, with systems upon systems to support each aspect. There is a Guild system, which is separate from the Sect system, there is a Profession system which is separate from the Class system and interacts with the Sect system; there are numerous multiplayer minigames (there is a fully-fledged rhythm game with multiple instruments that you can freely mess around with), there is a range of PVE and PVP activities that all interact with a variety of other gameplay and progression systems. I physically do not have the character limit to convey the sheer breadth of gameplay on offer here, it is frequently overwhelming and a little absurd and all of it works just well enough to keep me playing. 

I have some pretty clear concerns from a content ethics perspective and I do think that most of the systems here aren't exceptional on their own, most ranging from passable to 'pretty good', however the sum of the parts currently on offer for the low low price of completely free (microtransactions are wholly cosmetic) make it pretty hard not to tell you to at least give it a try.

From the very first minutes, Where Winds Meet failed to draw me in. Despite being built on Unreal Engine, the game’s artistic direction and visuals feel surprisingly bland, lacking the impact and polish you would expect from the engine.

The characters and voice acting fall flat, offering little emotional depth or personality. The young girl you meet at the beginning is, frankly, more irritating than endearing — and that’s saying something considering even Paimon from Genshin Impact manages to be annoying in a fun way.

The early gameplay segments don’t do much to raise the bar either. Combat and movement feel average at best, with nothing particularly memorable or exciting to hold onto. One positive note is the character customization system, which is fairly robust — though similar features are becoming increasingly common across comparable games.

In the end, the strongest argument in its favor is that it’s free. Without that, I doubt it would stand out enough to avoid being forgotten as yet another unremarkable title.

[b]Edit : [/b] After looking deeper into what the game actually offers (maybe I judged it too quickly), I’m even more confused to see that many of these elements are apparently praised. The game throws in a massive mix of gameplay systems, blending concepts without ever committing to a clear direction.
There’s building, MMO elements, solo/co-op action-adventure RPG mechanics, bits of realism (from what I understand, even the healing and prison systems)… and I have absolutely no idea where to place this game now. But hey — everyone has their own taste in games.

A massive Wuxia surprise – stunning world, fair monetization, but drowning in menus.

I was genuinely surprised by the sheer depth and polish of Where Winds Meet. For a Free-to-Play title, the quality here is staggering. It offers a massive, rich experience that doesn't try to empty your wallet, though it does try to overwhelm you with its interface.
Here is my breakdown:
PROS:
Breathtaking Open World: The world is not just huge; it’s dense, beautiful, and packed with secrets and activities. Exploring feels genuinely rewarding.
Combat & Progression: The combat system is engaging and fun to master. Character progression feels meaningful and offers plenty of depth.
Unique Mechanics: The minigames are plentiful, and I have to highlight the Healer profession—it is approached in a very original way compared to other MMOs.
Fair Monetization: Despite being F2P, I felt absolutely no pressure to pay. The cash shop is strictly for skins and cosmetics that do not affect gameplay. A rare and welcome sight.
CONS:
UI & Menu Bloat: This is the game's biggest flaw. There are simply too many menus nested within other menus. It feels like "playing a game within the menus" rather than enjoying the world.
Tedious Reward Systems: Similar to the issue in Delta Force, the game constantly makes you manually claim rewards for every minor action (like just entering a new cave). It interrupts the flow of gameplay unnecessarily. I don’t understand why developers think this manual clicking is rewarding; it’s just exhausting.
VERDICT:
Despite the frustrating UI design choices, Where Winds Meet is an incredible experience. The world and gameplay are top-tier, and the fair business model makes it easy to recommend.

Where Winds Meet has huge potential, but I really think the game needs to become more player-friendly and deeper long-term. First, the gacha/skin prices should be lowered, and skins should be shared across the account. If I buy an outfit, I should be able to use it on all my characters. That alone would make people more willing to spend.

But the real game changer would be life skills and economy systems. Imagine a BDO-style marketplace mixed with Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 realism: alchemy, crafting, trading, hunting, fishing, cooking, investing, professions, and real supply/demand. Players could buy goods cheap in one region, travel by Viking-style ships or caravans, sell them somewhere else, and slowly become rich through smart trading.

Owning businesses would also be amazing: shops, inns, workshops, trading companies, medicine/alchemy stores, weapon factories, or even investment houses. Add an in-game stock market using in-game currency, where player actions and regional demand affect prices. That would make the world feel alive.

They could also add chess, Go, leadership ranks, guild politics, professions like alchemist, merchant, investor, strategist, and more meaningful social/economy systems. Where Winds Meet should not only be a martial arts game — it should become a living world where players can fight, trade, build wealth, own businesses, and rise in society.

If WWM embraces deep life skills, realistic economy, and capitalism-style progression, it could become something much bigger than just another open-world RPG.

I'm not someone that can write details about game but here goes my impression of the game and its pros and cons

Impression:
The grind system feels like your typical modern gacha arpg game with limited stamina per week/day and capped important currencies/resource for progression so that no one can overgrind in a day (example, you can overgrind the craft materials but you cant overgrind the coins/money to craft it since it is capped 175k daily iirc). 

the UI and its system made it feels like genshin/wuwa but i guess thats just the standard nowaydays. However, the battle is more like the fast souls game like nioh/sekiro (people say its more like wukong than soulslike, i cant confirm since i dont play wukong).

Pros:
1.  wide/varied character customization (i don't do that but there are many character custom from other player that are very unique)

2. difficulty selection and difficulty accessibility (it doesn't gatekeep people but you still need do your fair amount of job to do some action)

3. fun and solid gameplay (battle, exploration, social) with no major bug/glitch. fun is subjective so you need to play it yourself.

4. story driven game and world that feels "alive" with how they handled sub-quest, their AI npc, and the npc-to-npc interaction.

5. high potential of RP-ing in game and sandbox experience.

6. Last but not least. it is an F2P game with no heavy P2W progression (battle pass give you a little bit more stamina to grind resource but doesn't give significant edge against F2P)

Cons:
1. high ping in online/multiplayer, specially in arena/pvp. and people also say imbalance pvp/invasion content.

2. greedy monetization in Global server. I wont say predatory since they do not shove it on your face and pops up on your windows every now and then like many other gacha games.  So why greedy? because the price is higher than CN server (up to 3-4x price) and it was suppose to be direct purchase but in global they made it gacha step up.

it is not predatory because by the end of the day, predator is actively (be it patient or rushingly) trying to eat you (banner pops up/deal pops up every now and then so that you got eaten (buy the stuff)) while this game doesn't do that to you and let you game for hours and hours and can even forget that the cash shop even exist.

3. by far the most horrible and confusing UI design i have ever seen and experience in any online game. menus upon menus and it is confusing since everything is all over the places. it is difficult to navigate the menu. 

4. what i heard from people there are problems with localization/translation for the narrative and the game description. what i also notice is that, in CN, there is a particular male villain that was voices by man that was changed into female voice actress because the guy dressed feminine. 

5. i read that many people are confused with the story and doesnt like the pacing of the story or how it unfolds. but i will attribute this because they arent familiar with wuxia trope since the story feels like one of those typical wuxia trope tv drama and even the light novels.

6. continuing no.5, since many people arent familiar with wuxia trope, there are many wuxia terms that is confusing for people.

7. my own personal dislike about this game, much  like genshin/wuwa or other similar, is that they tied character progression and important resource with exploration and i hate that exploration feels like a chore instead of natural. there are too many of them and i hate to play with a guides and checklisting things that i missed but thats just me personally.


final verdict:
Since this is a review about the game itself, REGARDLESS of how greedy/predatory/bad they are in handling the monetization, i personally recommended this game for anyone that wanted to jump or be introduced to wuxia theme game. although its soulslike and action heavy, the difficulty mode will help but again you still need to stand on your own feet and play the game with your own skill. i hope that you will feel a fresh experience in playing games again in times where it is hard to find good and solid game without their money price shenanigans, especially since this is an F2P game and again, with little to no significant P2W progression. Ill be borrowing what people say that the game, at its core, is a single player game with multiplayer/online world feature. So you can enjoy the game with your own pace.

Regarding the monetization, i do not condone their ways of handling the cash grab. it is a damn shame really, i hope they will reflect and follows marvel rivals monetization plan both game handled by same company and marvel rivals itself is a huge success. so it should be the most rational thing to do, follow your other successful global game monetization.

STORYLINE
When I first started playing this game, I expected to laugh and have fun because of the many funny memes (Kung Fu Hustle, etc.) and the typical xianxia storyline (young master this and that, etc.). And it turned out I was right.

Even the main story in the next province (God of Avarice) made me cry again, but it turned out to be a trolling (d**n you storyline writers).

GAMEPLAY
The combat style is basically similar to Skyrim and their friend-friend.
It involves lots of parries, light attacks, heavy attacks, and weapon combinations to suit your preferences.
So, if you want to roleplay as anything, you can (wannabe ninja, young master with fan, etc).
If you have autistic-like tendency, you can play solo at most, just online for a while to find a healer and a lawyer, or during dungeons that require a party. It's a relaxed experience, not a battle power-hungry game like other free-to-play games. High battle power doesn't matter when fighting bosses. So, just be smart about parrying, dodging, and understand boss battle pattern.

The world is gorgeous, from calm villages to dramatic mountain views, and the movement system is the star of the whole game. Combat is stylish but not perfect. It looks great, and the martial-arts abilities feel powerful, but the hit detection and timing can be a bit inconsistent at times. The story is decent and has some emotional moments, though it may feel a little slow in the beginning.

Overall, it’s a visually impressive game with a fresh setting, amazing traversal, and some rough edges. If you like open-world action with a strong wuxia vibe, it’s worth trying.

I've only played a few hours so far, but I’m genuinely loving Where Winds Meet, especially the main story. The writing is surprisingly bittersweet and emotional, and I love how deeply Chinese culture is woven into every part of the world. The game is packed with beautiful details, side stories, and activities that make the world feel alive.

The wuxia atmosphere, the characters, and the storytelling have really drawn me in, and I’m excited to keep playing. If anything changes as I progress, I’ll update this review, but so far, this journey has been wonderful.

That said, the game can feel overwhelming for new players. Whether you're in solo mode or online mode, the amount of systems, menus, currencies, and bonus features hits you all at once. A slower introduction or clearer guidance would help a lot.

My only other issue is the red alert notification system. Sometimes UI icons don’t match where the alert is coming from, which leads to opening menus and still not finding the source of the red dot. It can get a bit annoying and confusing.

But overall, I’m really enjoying the game. The story, world, and cultural atmosphere make it absolutely worth playing, and I look forward to diving deeper into it.

[h1] CHARACTER CREATION VARIETY IS GOOD? [/h1]
Character creation is quite detailed and good; in fact, it's not just about letting you create beautiful characters, it lets you create complete abominations as well. And it even has a feature letting you create characters from pictures or sounds, and they are fun to use for sure, and somehow accurate.


[h1] HOW ABOUT STORY, QUESTS? [/h1]
Story & the quests are mostly boring, and time for time confusing for no reason as well, at a lot of parts the story feels like it's disconnected, and not really fluid, and since the game is a bit too chill at a lot of parts, that doesn't really help this case either, and makes the whole experience really boring.


[h1] HOW ABOUT THE GAMEPLAY & COMBAT? [/h1]
Movement feels a bit heavy and unnatural; it's not as fluid as it should be. Meanwhile, core combat is better than the movement, and variety-wise, it's not bad. I can't say it's amazing or anything; it's rather mediocre.


[h1] HOW ABOUT CLASSES & SKILLS? [/h1]
There are no classes; there are weapons, martial arts, and mystical skills. Some of these are learned by leveling up with using that weapon or martial art; meanwhile, some of them are learned by literally stealing/copying from NPCS, which is a kind of interesting mechanic, I do say, and variety-wise they are not that bad.


[h1] HOW ABOUT THE ENEMY & THE BOSS VARIETY? [/h1]
Enemy & BOSS variety is not great, in fact, open world mostly don't even have that many enemies, focus is mostly NPC interactions, learning some side stuff from them, doing some side activities, etc, and honestly, this is one of the things that makes this game chill, but at the same time, really boring.


[h1] HOW ABOUT THE GROUP CONTENT? [/h1]
The game gives you option to play solo or with other people, and I can say this game has a lot of intereactions with other people, and there are some interesting stuff like marriage system, master/disciple system or healing system where you need to seek other players to heal the sicknesses you got from your encounters, and all of these makes the socialization part somehow alive.


[h1] HOW ABOUT THE WORLD? [/h1]
The open world is full of people to interact with, and even though the world feels somewhat alive since their dialogues are mostly boring, and stuff you can't even relate to, it makes things even worse, because on one side you want to explore, learn, and listen to them more, but on the other side, you really don't wanna since they are not enjoyable at all.


[h1] VISUAL STYLE IS GOOD?[/h1]
Visually, the game looks great, open-world design, character models, colors, optimization, etc, all are really good, and this is the strongest part of the game, or more like the only thing it does well...


[h1] VERDICT [/h1]
In the end the game has good quality for a F2P game for sure, and at least worth trying, but you will found enjoyable or not is up to your tastes, especially if you are looking something chill at most parts, with good visualls it could be your game, if not, then you might be bored like me, eitherway give a try, and see yourself.


[h1] RATINGS [/h1]
[*]Main Story, Quests & Story-Telling = 3
[*]Combat Mechanics  = 6
[*]Weapon & Armor Variety = 7
[*]Skill Variety = 7
[*]Enemy/BOSS Variety & Design = 6
[*]Open World Design = 8
[*]Visual Style & Quality = 9

[*]General Rating = 6.6

Pros: 
1. Action combat feels good.

Cons:

All in all if you aren’t big into solo questing or heavy questing at all and looking for PvP or just fighting bosses in a group I’d wait a few months to play this so you can pass all the locked walls. -Comat: Souls like with easy modes, actually fun with unique weapons
-Environment: look at the screenshots, say no more
-Multiplayer: a bit buggy sometimes, but honestly the vast range of activities you can do with other people has been fun, i enjoy the mahjong and leaf version of "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" card game the most. And I ended up with two disciples now calling me their master that was so hilarious.

Cons:
-Menu is a lot, i am level 51 but still sometimes still learning to process where i need to click
-Some collection items and side quests require actually exploring or looking at the cues left by other players
-if you want to understand the lore and history you probably have to look up many references

Overall this is not even an mmorpg with gacha, it is a real action RPG with amazing graphics and story. Multiplayer and gacha is just like a bonus. Despite how hard some western game critic websites try to smear this, players know the truth by experiencing it themselves.

25 hours in and I just can't quite believe this is a free game. Moment-to-moment, it plays like AssCreed Odyssey mixed with Red Dead 2, with a greater number of more elaborate minigames and an incredibly content-dense environment... There is so much going on at any given time with the absurd number of categories of activity that are being constantly tracked, that it feels like every step you take provides free rewards to claim buried in some menu screen or another, mostly in the form of various in-game currencies, items, materials, etc. Combat is fairly deep and engaging, difficulty options are highly customizable, the story is decent epic wuxia with a truly massive open world and vast number of interactive NPCs, and the open world itself is beautiful and well-realized through an art-style obviously meant to evoke the kind of far-eastern mystic realism that we're all here for in the first place.

The only real problem with the game is the labyrInthine UI - there are a ridiculous number of menus to click through to get to any one of dozens upon dozens of different screens that might let you claim a reward or see some new information or what have you. It's asinine and completely unnecessary (in the sense that many of the menus could be folded into one another, and rewards could simply be claimed from the main gameplay screen as they appear with a simple prompt and button-press), and takes away from time I would rather spend, you know, actually playing the game. 

In short, it's good enough that most of the early complaints are not about bugs or gameplay, but instead are from PvPers and cosmetics whales who are upset that there are things available for purchase on the chinese server that are not available on global, or only available through lootbox gambling, or whatever.  The only other issue I've encountered so far is relatively high ping in PvP, but a lot of people seem to be getting by and playing PvP despite that. Some minority is complaining about cosmetics pricing in general, but who cares? Just don't buy it then? The outfits and titles you can get from doing difficult in-game achievements are better anyways. 

Speaking as a free game connoisseur - Still can't believe it's free.

⭐ My Steam Review for Where Winds Meet 

After spending a good amount of time in Where Winds Meet, I can honestly say this game surprised me in ways I didn’t expect. It’s absolutely packed with content far more than I thought a game like this would offer.

✔ What I loved:

A huge variety of board games and mini-games

Interesting quests with fun NPC interactions

Great boss fights with unique designs

Beautiful world-building and a stunning environment

Surprisingly solid PvP

Excellent sound design

Tons of skills, abilities and systems to explore

There’s always something to do, and the world feels alive and full of surprises.
I’ve genuinely enjoyed my time so far.

✔ But here’s my concern:

As much as I enjoyed the first dozens of hours, I can’t shake the feeling that after 100–200 hours, once you’ve done most activities and everyone hits level 50, the game may not have enough long term depth to keep players engaged.

Some systems already feel like they’re becoming unnecessarily complicated
for example, having to go to specific places and do several steps just to earn one item needed to unlock a certain skill.
It reminds me a bit of how Lost Ark eventually felt: lots of tiny chores stacked on top of each other.

I really want the game’s surprises to continue, and I hope the devs expand content in meaningful ways, but my gut tells me I might not stick around for more than ~500 hours unless they keep the experience fresh and not overly grindy.

⭐ Final Score: 8/10

A great game with amazing content and an impressive start
I just hope it stays fun in the long run.

So, I will be upfront; this is an incredible level of quality for a free-to-play game, and while I do not recommend it, it's only because it doesn't suit *my* needs. The following is just my opinions, and by no mean should you base your decision of playing a free-to-play game on my opinion.

+Beautiful : The game is just... wow. Very pretty. It's not over the top, so you can still play it on a medium-end PC rather comfortably. The character models are nice, and you do feel like you are part of a wuxia story with the art direction.

+Combat: The combat is really satisfying once you get the hang of it. Parrying becomes a fun challenge instead of an awkward "will it won't it connect" situation. Every enemy has a rhythm that is clear, and while it is not always easy to follow, once you understand the movement and auditive cues, even very quick enemies become just a matter of keeping the rhythm.

+No Pay to win: The good side of it, and one of the reason I played it, was because everything in terms of gacha is for customization. No weapon is locked behind it, and you can progress easily without using it.

But those are my three good points. Then...

- Localization: Buddha, give me patience, because the Tao definitely isn't balanced in me. English translation is terrible. I don't know if it's because AI has been used, or if because the developers and translators didn't really care, but the translation is hacky. A lot of times, you aren't 100% sure of what you just heard, and other times, the dialogues makes no sense. I've been in wuxia stories for a while now, and I've never been this confused about the terminology.

-Character: Your character is a dumbass. It makes doing side quests and following some stories a bit of a pain. I know I would say the same for FFXIV, but... Yes. Dumbass.

-Pricing : Everything is overpriced for the international community compared to the china market. Price shouldn't change based off where you are from, especially non-tangible currency and merchandise. I *never* spend money on games beyond the licence purchase, and I never will, but for everyone who do invest in games (as we are want to do with our hobbies), I find this despicable.

-Difficulty: Legend is challenging in the sense that it makes combats last **so much longer**. Your enemies are damage sponges, and you never feel any progress by optimizing your character because... well... you can't. It's less an increase in difficulty as it is an increase in the amount of time you are going to have to spend on each boss or group of enemies (which becomes manageable once you know some tai-chi to throw them off a ledge).

-Coop : This is 2025, and this is an online game. How the f*ck is coop not seamless?

-Bugs : *so many f*cking bugs*. Graphical, sure, but input bugs, movement bugs, enemy teleportation bugs, character getting stuck bugs, invisible wall bugs. I think most of my defeats on boss battles was over collison bugs and attacks connecting when they shouldn't because of a latency between animation and action.

Where Winds Meet completely blew me away. The world is huge, beautiful, and very alive, with an atmosphere that takes all the good parts of game like GoT and BnS. The level of detail in the landscapes, villages, and forests makes exploration feel rewarding, and the day-to-day life happening around you helps the world feel grounded instead of empty. There are an incredible amount of instances and NPCs in the world. Even turning off the MMO mode, the game feels very full.

The combat is fast and fun, especially once you start unlocking more martial arts abilities. It strikes a nice balance between feeling skill-based without being frustrating. Boss fights feel cinematic, and pulling off counterattacks or combining abilities is super satisfying. The weapon combos are forgiving and you can try out a number of different playstyles. Love that you aren't locked into a Dark Souls difficulty and they respect the solo story focus playstyle.

The story is engaging, and I love how much freedom the game gives you. Whether you want to focus on the main quest, wander off to help random NPCs, or just climb mountains and see what’s on the other side, the game never rushes you. I've spent 5 hours on the main story, and 10 hours just looking behind every rock and tree in the FIRST area. 20 hours in the first area is amazing value (the game is FREE).

Performance is so smooth. I never have frame drops and combat is flawless for me. The visuals seem graphically demanding but the optimization is so good, I feel like you could run this on a pretty outdated PC with no issues.

I have not even touched the MMO side of the game yet. If you are worried that it is just another MMORPG, please take the plunge. It's a free to play Ghost of Tsushima with better difficulty sliders. It's changing the standard of this genre of game. It's reinventing this genre really. I hope to see it continue to grow and get more attention because it is very deserving.

After sinking over 100 hours into Where Winds Meet, I’ve got a pretty solid grasp of what this game actually is — the highs that hooked me, and the flaws that annoyed the hell out of me.

First off, the world is the star here. Huge, beautiful, constantly surprising. Even after dozens of hours, I kept finding new areas, hidden routes, and set-pieces that actually felt handcrafted. The wuxia atmosphere is what carries the whole experience — the music, the landscapes, the martial-arts theme… it’s all immersive as hell.

Combat is another strong point. Fast, sharp, timing-focused. Once you get used to parrying and weapon switching, it becomes addictive. Rope darts, swords, umbrellas — everything has a unique rhythm, and it keeps the game interesting long-term.

Now for the annoying parts. The UI is honestly bloated. Too many menus, too many currencies, too much unnecessary clutter. It doesn’t ruin the game, but it definitely slows things down. And the technical issues? They aren’t just little glitches — the real problem is when the game randomly refuses to let you interact with anything. No picking up items, no talking to NPCs, nothing. The only fix? Restarting or backing out to the main menu and logging in again. I had to do that more times than I should in a 2025 game.

On the bright side, there aren’t harsh progression walls or grind traps. You can play at your pace without the game forcing you to hit some power threshold or time gate. And for a free-to-play title, the value is honestly impressive. Monetization is mostly cosmetic, and you can enjoy practically everything without spending a cent.

In short: the game isn’t flawless, and the interaction bug alone deserves a slap — but the world, the combat, and the whole wuxia fantasy make the 100 hours absolutely worth it.

tldr: very good f2p mmorpg that can be enjoyed solo, with friends, or online, with an abundance of content to explore and enjoy!

[h1]Comentario Analítico: "Where Winds Meet" (燕云十六声)[/h1]

Desarrollado por Everstone Studios y publicado por NetEase estrenó en Noviembre del 2025 este ARPG de mundo abierto y tematizado al más puro estilo Wuxia (武俠).

El creador de personajes quizá no sea de lo más versátil, pero el juego per se da una sorprendente cantidad de libertades al jugador, en mi caso al principio quise ver qué ocurría si ignoraba las primeras quests tras el tutorial y arranqué a explorar las áreas cercanas, hacer quests secundarias y enfrentar jefes contra los que no estaba preparado.

Esto da lugar a partidas totalmente únicas para distintos perfiles de jugadores, en especial de cara a cuán versátil es el combate y movimiento y de cuántas formas es posible afrontar una adversidad. Cada escenario está repleto de secretos con los que alentar al jugador a explorar y recompensarlo por tomarse el tiempo de aprender a controlar a su personaje en tanto movimiento como combate.

Es fundamentalmente un MMORPG Offline pero Online (...si es que eso tiene sentido), y si bien es inicialmente Singleplayer, podés dejar que un jugador entre a tu mundo o vos entrar al suyo si es que así lo deseás. No es totalmente co-op, la progresión ocurre únicamente en la partida del host; pensalo como si estuvieras invocando a alguien en Dark Souls.

Es gratuito y cuanto menos hasta la fecha la monetización radica en su mayoría en los cosméticos, de modo que quienes no se vean interesados en éstos no van a verse opacados por los jugadores más adinerados. En donde sí se vuelve molesto es cuando tenés que esperar un día (en tiempo real) para poder convertir en niveles a la experiencia acumulada (Aparentemente esto es algo que sólo va a ocurrir en esta temporada, iremos viendo).

Me dejó sorprendido, no tenía tan altas expectativas y acabé encontrándome con un excelente juego (Cuanto menos en ésta, su primera temporada). Además los personajes femeninos son preciosos, lo que es habitual en productos Orientales pero que voy a continuar aplaudiendo en vista de lo mucho que esto se perdió en títulos Occidentales.

[b]¿En conclusión?[/b] Una muy grata sorpresa.

Where Winds Meet is a really mixed bag. It certainly scratches the same itch that early Genshin had for me. It's fun to create a character, run around and explore, look for treasures, and solve open world puzzles. Unfortunately, It also has the typical and somewhat expected genre trappings too: hard time gates for raising level caps, multiple currency types for price obfuscation, event combat grind/low reward chances to incentivize and funnel you into spending real cash for goods. 

Unfortunately, the early game shimmer begins to fade the further along you get in the game. The more I played, the more cracks I would find in the facade. At one point, an NPC audibly said the word "Sigh" at the beginning of a sentence, and my suspicions that AI was being used for NPC dialogue was immediately confirmed, but that's not all. AI is all over this thing; they have an AI tool where you can 'talk' to NPCs by typing or recording your voice in a clip and it generates NPC dialogue, and It sucks. It also appears that there is a distinct disconnect between spoken dialogue and subtitles on the screen when playing in English; It's amazing to hear a character say one thing and read something entirely different right there on the screen, which is an indicator that either the subtitles are being AI generated, or the cutscene dialogue is, even for important, primary campaign cutscenes involving major characters.

You begin to wonder what else is made with AI. Textures? Models? Scenarios? It certainly looks like a lot of time and effort was put into this thing on the surface, but the more you see, the more you begin to wonder if that statement is actually true. Corners are obviously being cut in areas like NPC dialogue, menu and dialogue text, dialogue delivery timing, and at first I just figured it was a rocky translation, right up until NPCs started literally saying garbage to my face, so really who could say? It breaks the immersion of playing in a fantasy world in a very stark manner which I do not appreciate. If time and effort isn't being put into the product, why should I invest my time and effort into the game (not to mention, my money)?

The game has other technical issues as well, the game's frame rate, especially in large cities like Keifeng, is not stable by any means. I've run into multiple bugs such as getting stuck inside collision during standard traversal, seen flickering textures in obvious places, graphical corruption when camera switching over long distances (which happens during certain open-world traversal puzzles involving cats), dialogue not playing when subtitles are on screen during voiced cutscenes, and a few others. 

It's early days and I expect that the more technical issues will eventually be addressed, however the AI integration is poor to say the least and ruins what could've been an interesting game, There is a tension between the business decisions made during development that make the game appear the way it is, and what is communicated to the player over the course of playing the game...having to stop and think about it while playing the game is a detriment to the experience as a whole. There is a broader conversation to be had about the AI integration of this style, in this specific type of game, but the review is getting long enough as it is. I imagine there are plenty of players out there who simply do not care, they just want the shiny new thing... but I do care, and it very much feels like the developers don't

Where Winds Meet is one of those games where you start with a simple quest, and an hour later you’re standing on top of a mountain you don’t remember climbing, holding five screenshots of a random tree, and wondering when exactly your life went off-track. That’s how pretty the game is, it constantly distracts you on purpose.

The story and characters are charming too. At one point an NPC told me something deep and philosophical, and all I could think was: “Yes, wise elder, very inspiring, but could you also point me in the right direction? I’ve been lost since the tutorial.”

Exploration is where the game really shines. You start walking, notice a shiny rock, go to check it out, then find a hidden pond, then chase a butterfly, then somehow end up on top of a hill you weren’t supposed to reach yet. The game doesn’t stop you, it just silently approves your chaos.

You can interact with cats in the world, and sometimes they even pretend to like you. It’s a small, charming detail that makes wandering around even more fun, especially when they completely ignore you in the middle of a serious quest.

There are a few quirks: the pacing slows down occasionally, some objectives are explained with the confidence of someone giving directions while half-asleep, and I had a couple of small performance snags, nothing major, just small pauses for dramatic effect.

Overall though, it’s a lovely, relaxing adventure. If you enjoy exploring, getting (very) lost, and accidentally creating your own side stories, you’ll love it.

Still early in the game, but I find myself deeply impressed by what the developers have achieved here. Where Winds Meet is basically a single-player game with the full scope of an MMO that somehow manages to ALSO be an MMO at the same time. What's more, the elements that are usually sidelined in favor of MMO scale, namely graphics, storytelling, general presentation, etc, are genuinely really impressive.

This game at its core is an action RPG with a focus on medieval Chinese history. But it's also got fishing mini-games, stealth mechanics, soulslike checkpoints, musical instruments, base building, cooking, deep character customization, gear progression, dungeons, world bosses, puzzles, collectibles, and on and on. It even has some risky but ambitious additions like cosmetic gacha (which I don't like) as well as being able to freeform chat with AI NPCs and even befriend them (which is interesting but not as revolutionary as some would make it seem).

Normally in a game this crowded with content, it would feel like the devs are just throwing everything at the wall and seeing what sticks, and the result would be a sloppy, half-assed mess. But that's not the case so far in this game. It's got solid mechanics, a good story, beautiful visuals, and a rewarding gameplay loop. I keep hunting around waiting for the other shoe to fall, but so far I haven't found it.

[h1] Changing from a positive review to a negative review after 450 hours, here’s why: [/h1]

First, let me be clear: the combat, art style, graphics, and overall quality of this game are awesome. It’s literally better than most AAA games out there. The campaign, side quests, and MMO-style multiplayer are all fun. The guild system and openworld online activities are really enjoyable. They nailed the casual multiplayer aspect, you never feel alone, and there’s a good balance between PvP, boss farming, and other activities.

I also don’t mind the gacha gambling. It’s a free game, and you have free will. You don’t HAVE TO gamble, because there’s no pay2win whatsoever, it’s just cosmetics. People leaving negative reviews for that reason are being silly. It’s like CS: your gun does the same damage, no matter how expensive your skin is.

[h2] So why am I changing my review to negative? [/h2]

The ceiling is too low. The game forces you to repeat 1–2 bosses for weeks. It caps your level, caps the item level you can get, and makes grinding unrewarding. Why bother getting better than anyone else? Why learn boss mechanics or improve your playstyle, only to be forced to wait weeks for everyone else to catch up, while the available content no longer rewards you?

This is exactly why millions still play WoW. In WoW, you can always improve, get stronger gear, attempt harder content, and even fail. In Where Winds Meet, after an update and the first 1–2 days, you already know there’s no challenge left. Locking progression like this might come from a fear of not having enough players at the same level, but ironically, that’s exactly what’s killing the game.

I really wish the developers would learn something from WoW. WoW would die within weeks if its progression were capped the way it is in Where Winds Meet. like a casual mobile game.

[b]Where Winds Meet[/b] (WWM) is simply gorgeous. Just look through the Community screenshots. Character models are well made, especially faces and hairs (which is rare) and that not only apply to Player toons, but to NPCs and mobs as well.
Performance wise - I probably could dust off my 10y old PC and still play it.
Game is smooth like a butter. Here are some raw numbers for you, after few 4h game sessions - overall median of usages for: CPU=20% | RAM=11GB | Swap=15GB | GPU=60% | GRAM=6GB.*
*[i]PC specs in my Profile info[/i]

Character creator is great at what it allow you to modify, and would be perfect ...if they would allow for modifications not limited to face and hair, but the rest of the body as well.

Gameplay is [strike]great[/strike] fun at the beginning.
You can almost instantly switch between Social / Co-op / Single-player modes by a simple push of a button. There's always something to do no matter of your play style.
You can interact with environment and NPCs. Combat is smooth, interactive, and engaging. You can adjust the combat difficulty level and enable/disable assistance ...if you're [i]THAT[/i] good.
Oh, did I mentioned that you can climb anywhere, fly, swim, dive, run on the water ? Cuz you can. And you should.
Also, there are puzzles, public humiliation, magic boat rides, group meditation, PvP arena, Bosses, etc.

Where Winds Meet have progression points though. In order to do some things - you have to first complete certain quests / meet certain goals. Which mean that if you're a free spirit, a wanderer like me and on level 5 going through half of a map to finish some random quick-time side-quest ...there's a chance that you will not have a required abilities (like Tai-chi for the cave bear). So, yeah - I had to back-track a lot.

WWM have also a few flaws in the gameplay.
First of them is the key-re-binding that does not allow for a total re-bind, and even that my interaction key is E and environment interaction is R ...I am still forced to press F for interactions (skill-steal, select, etc.) in some quests. Oh, and you can do so only AFTER the tutorial **[i]facepalm[/i]**.
Second being the mini-games and puzzles in the world that have a brief tutorial set to like 500% speed so you blink and miss it and you have no idea what to do, so you have to try to figure it out, and you fail and you re-do, until you will get it right.
And third one is the signs / markers that Players can set up in the CRUCIAL points, like in the middle of the mob-pack, at a spawn point of NPC, etc. which will activate once you press your interaction key (required for speaking to NPC / finishing moves in combat / etc.) ...and *[i]F[/i]* your day up.

Quests are quite interesting and I often did find myself doing a side-quests instead of MSQ. I have found the storyline to be engaging and written quite well. If you like and know Asian cinema, I think you will like that too; if not - there's a skip button.

I can not say a bad word about music and sound effects in this game. This is a personal taste, but I love it and it is one of a very few games where I have it not muted.

It is free, with a CashShop, which will give you some better rewards than other F2P Players. Though, I wouldn't say it's required or P2W.
In comparison to BDO ([i]which I love and still play[/i]) ? - it REALLY is not.
I know that I will use it - just yesterday I had found out that they have [i]Cat Ears[/i] as a hair ornament there.

[/spoiler]

★ ★ ★ ★ ☆ (3.5 / 5)

I went into Where Winds Meet expecting absolutely nothing… and somehow walked away wondering how the hell this much content is FREE. Like genuinely, no joke — this is one of the most beautiful MMORPGs out there. It looks like an Unreal Engine showcase while not being Unreal Engine, which means it’s gorgeous and ridiculously optimized. A rare combo these days.

Gameplay-wise, this isn’t your usual tab-target snoozefest MMO. It’s way more in line with Sekiro / Souls-lite combat systems, and honestly? It’s addicting. The timing, the parries, the movement — it all feels clean.
Plus, the character customization? Bro… it’s deep. Like “I spent an hour adjusting my eyebrows and I’m not ashamed” deep. The game actually encourages you to look pretty, even if you're a dude rocking silk robes and the sharpest cheekbones in the province.

This is the kind of game you install once, leave on your drive forever, and jump back into every few months because they keep stacking on new content like it’s a buffet.

But now… the pain.

Multiplayer?
Technically?
Garbage.
My ping is permanently living in the 200–300ms realm, input delay hits harder than any boss, and eventually I just said screw it and switched to healer because at least healing can be done on a 2-second delay without me screaming.

And the monetization…
Look, I get it. It’s free-to-play. But GOOD LORD. The gacha draws are just cosmetics, sure, but they’re also stupidly expensive. I’m begging Asian devs at this point: just let us BUY the thing. Show me the item, show me the price, I click buy. Charge me $10, $50, $500, hell $10,000 — at least I know exactly what I get instead of playing RNG casino in a bamboo forest.

And for the love of all martial arts traditions, remove the daily cap on boss farming. If you wanna cap cosmetics, fine. But limiting gear progression in an MMO is insane.

Overall?
A legitimately impressive MMO with insane potential, gorgeous visuals, great combat… held back by netcode and monetization sins.

3.5 out of 5.
Still worth checking out — especially if you like looking sexy while parrying like a budget Sekiro.

Decided to try this game because the graphics and combat system seemed promising in the trailers.
The opening cinematics were pretty cool with smooth transitions and the main story's goal was clear right from the beginning. After 30 minutes of progressing though, many new terms and lore drops still left me confused and it felt like the pacing was a bit too quick.
I like the idea that the game offers so much more than just combat and makes the game feel alive, especially with the options you have during online gameplay, but a lot still feels buggy and could use some fixing.
Now to address the elephant in the room - the combat feels a little.... off. It feels fun to switch between weapon classes depending on your situation and tinker with their unique skills but some of the visual execution feels lackluster. Aside from that, the dodges feel awkward (at least with keyboard controls) and enemy visual cues are sometimes very subtle or far too quick to react to compared to other soulslike games which also makes it harder to manually parry and i seriously don't want to rely on the automatic parry timeframe the entire time. 
Lastly, the tabs for various activities like missions and events feel hard to navigate through and upon unlocking various modes, it feels like too much is thrown at you to start up and I'm sure that it also may feel a bit overwhelming for other players as well.
In summary, pretty cool concept of a game and delivers in a lot of aspects but is still in the rough as of release and I'll probably change my mind when the game gets some more polish. The monetization is almost well executed so I'd consider this a W if not for the fact that, as far as I know, I can't change my darn username without spending 5€ of real money for it. That's why the game is getting a no from me until anything changes.

Normally, when devs brainstorm ideas for things to include in their game, they pick and choose of the ideas on the board when they're done. These guys just decided to include it all. It's gloriously chaotic, and an honestly incredible experience. I don't think I've even tried half the stuff this game has to offer yet.

Oof, this one stings. Not even big on wuxia or the whole Chinese fantasy vibe, but the multiplayer and some art direction hooked me enuf to sink 35ish hours in (+10 afk). And frankly, the game does have $hit loads of "content." Though most of it feels like DeepSeek-generated mobile sludge, mindless chores you can clear with a single functioning neuron.

Don't fall for the usual surface-level praise like "combat is fluid" or "the only issue is the gacha." Those takes usually come from ppl perfectly content to mash the same 2 buttons for 500 hours and grind their life away for one gachafit a year. Yeah, I can see how an average joe might tolerate all that, but for anyone expecting depth and variety of fighting styles, you quickly realize just how amateurish the systems really are. High-level and endgame progression is so shallow that even with every MA (martial art) and IW (inner way) unlocked, your combat loop never evolves aka "spam your 2 buttons sextillion times, only now they deal maybe 5% more damage, yay!" Your in-game personality? Nope. Everyone ends up playing the same homogenized setup, and somehow, in a martial arts game they didn't even bother adding a katana..

And to make things even more depressing for the game's future, it turns out WWM got saddled with terrible devs who straight-up cannot be trusted (super shady NetEase on top of that). They promise critical fixes one day and ghost the community the next, pretending none of it was ever said. They completely botched global servers and tons of accounts, leaving most players sitting at 300+ ping with input lag even in solo mode (!), then quietly swept the whole disaster under the rug while proudly patching... f**ckin pixels and random trees (!!) on the map. Deadass.

Their "compensation" for this mess is a whole 10 premium gacha pulls, yay! Each with a near-guaranteed chance (99.96%) of spitting out total garbage. You literally burn premium currency to pull a clump of dough or a chunk of bread that can be found anywhere in the game lol. It's comical if it weren't so insulting.

And yet, there is / was a trace of something genuinely enjoyable. But it just keeps [i]meeting[/i] head-on with the ppl in charge whose incompetence is only matched by how blatantly dismissive they are of any real feedback.

Old Review:

It's rough in many places, but once you get through the fixed keybind tutorial and adjust to the messy mess of a UI, you'll find a solid game underneath, one that's fun as hell.

Don't listen to the game media, the game is FREE TO PLAY, so try it out for yourself. Clear the first part and get into the open world, spend an hour or two getting lost.

Despite never buying BP's, I purchased one in the first 10 hours of gameplay because I needed to give something back to the devs.

Things I didn't like:
- Energy.  I get it, you need a hard cap on earning gear otherwise people would be geared out on day 1, but it's more of an instinctual hate reflex than anything.
- No Aussie servers. Pinging 250ms online makes it unplayable and there doesn't seem to be a peer2peer co-op mode (according to my sister, because I'm a loner who hasn't tried it yet).
- Menus - Nothing like hunting for 5 minutes to get rid of the red dot, only to discover it's in a sub-menu with a button that blends into the background...
- Sometimes the AI NPC's are a bit sketchy with understanding, like they're running on a 3B param model or something. Would be nicer if the NPC's were a bit less 'tarded, since even older Llama 3 8B models are more intelligent.
- Localisation is iffy in places, but still functional.
- Some event markers are unclear about what they actually mean (A bear sleeping next to meat? WTF is the icon the same as the guy from earlier, who I cured from itching?!)

Things I like:
- Pretty world. I've read Wuxia novels online for years and it's nice to have stuff in this genre.
- Free2Play. Nuff said.
- Lots of people.
- Fun combat. Difficulty is scalable for challengers of all level.
- Being a doctor is fun. Sending messages like "Stop eating food off the ground..." after curing someone's indigestion is a good laugh.
- Lots of cats. Petting them even gives you stats!
- Drop in / Drop out MP and Co-op.

Con's
-Movement can be clunky sometimes (Getting stuck on trees and buildings that you didn't plan on climbing when sprinting due to auto-climb feature)

I'd say if you think you'd like it, give it a try but if you're on the fence it just isn't worth it.

Want to use a weapon you just found? Too bad you need to do a quest in a completely different map first. Want to level up? Too bad you need to do breakthrough challenges. Want to use the flying skill you just unlocked? Too bad you need to max out your exploration level on each map separately to use it. Want to claim the rewards you earned from playing the game? Not to mention the AI slop infesting the world. NPCs will attempt to have AI chat bot conversations with you, immediately killing any immersion or world building. Even the initial prompts feel out of place with the setting and talk as if they are from 2025, not the 900s ce. And you can convince them to talk about cars or cell phones or any modern technology. How are you supposed to believe the world if there are walking AI bots spewing nonsense at every corner. If this is how AI will "revolutionize" gaming, count me out. It exists solely to pad the game with meaningless dribble, an insult to the beautifully handcrafted areas of the game.

[u]Great F2P[/u] game. Some guy with his $40k USD boat keeping the servers up for the rest of us. 

Devs aren't using UE5 but their own engine (Messiah) and it shows - the optimization is amazing. 
Able to run no problem on GTX 1080.
Only experience is with M&K on MMORPG controls, so no experience with controller.
English subtitles + CN audio.

Can play entirely solo and adjust difficulty to your liking. The highest as of release is Legend difficulty, that can only be tuned down once selected. No real incentive to play it; only a badge on in-game profile displaying bosses slain, as far as I can see since you can play bosses through a separate instance on the highest difficulty if you want to. [u]Easier difficulties and adjustable assistance[/u] allows a lot of people to make this [b]baby's first souls-like[/b]. There are signposts (such as in dark souls) where people are guiding others (helpful and troll), sharing experiences, and taking amazing photos. 

The coop is a little weird in that only the MSQ progress is not shared between players. All other side quests, as well as chests and collectibles (oddities), are shared with everyone. You are able to sync these coop quests to even experience cutscenes at the same time. Can just run around with the host.

There are plenty of activities you can play with friends, random people. Some include Maidiao cards (think Liar's Bar, BS), Mahjong God, Graceful Melody (rhythm game). 

There are a variety of social systems you can involve your friends or random people with.
Increasing intimacy through partaking in activities or sending them in-game messages allows the ability to ask for a partnership. There are master-disciple relationships or cohort creation. Any of these funds currency that allows you to buy some more cosmetics from the shop. There is of course a guild system (80 person cap I think), and a sect system where you can unlock exclusive cosmetics and unlock weapons, and jump around more-or-less as you please. 

Some funny systems include the [spoiler]public jail[/spoiler] and [spoiler]talking with AI bots to gain their trust[/spoiler]

Energy system for end-game content - increases as you level up your solo world level. 
Late-game seems to revolve around inner ways, gear tuning, and gear sets that you can grind for using the energy system.
Have only played in 5 person raids and they add mechanics to bosses. 10 player raids should arrive soon.

Weekly reset is Sunday @ 1 PM PST/4 PM EST.

No experience with the PvP but there is a 1v1 and battle royale queue active as of now. I know guilds will eventually have 30v30 as well. Sparring is not equalized so don't see the point for it.

Major cons include the menu clutter and some monetization. 
Even with hours of time spent in-game (~25 hrs actually doing stuff, 15 hrs sitting around+char customization) I have trouble trying to remember how to navigate to get to what I'm looking for (high learning curve here). I think atm there is some backlash regarding a banner that costs 3x more for global over the CN version. There is no true P2W monetization (there is a battlepass but can grind for the same items, and everyone is restricted by world cap anyway). Make sure you note that some gachas that [u]pulls with pearls increase the price/pull every pull.[/u]

Lots of cool content to uncover, environments to admire, and bosses to study. 
Looking forward to spending a lot of time in Wuxia.

First of all, there is no reason to not recommend this game since it's completely free. Cash shop is pretty predatory with gachas, but it's cosmetics only and completely ignorable (there are some pretty cool looking cloths/hair ingame already).

The game itself is pretty fun:
* the main story has full English dub and it's pretty high quality
* The combat is very snappy. Characters can block, dodge, parry with increasing tighter window, but parry doesn't consume any resources and will decrease enemy's stagger guage so that's the recommended gameplay style. What I really like is there are no animation locks i.e. your character will interrupt their current action and parry as soon as your press the button, so if I get hit, it feels like it's my fault, not the game being unfair.
* Multiplayer is well integrated e.g. I did something stupid and got afflicted with a "Mental Illness" debuff XD. The healer NPC told me that she can't heal it, redirects me to multiplayer instead (the toggle appeared right on the NPC's dialog window). I clicked on it, a huge crowed of healers appeared and I immediatelly got offered for healing. 

Now for the flaws.. there are a lot:
* the biggest annoyance is the game's mountain of menus. At the end of every game session, I have to go through dozens of them to claim rewards ...
* there are some audio editing mistakes e.g. some lines are repeated twice
* character progression started out pretty straigh forward, but are getting a lot more complicated as the game progresses, similarly to rewards, I have to go through multiple menus to check my current character build

Honestly, it's 'fine', if a bit lacking.

Has some really strong qualities, but it's mostly just a grindfest of various activities, your average gacha-style game only with 100x the production value. The game's gorgeous and the art design is clearly a work of love, but it's also cluttered with so much jank and unnecessary stuff that it's a bit overwhelming and made me lose focuse almost immediately.

Besides, there are glaring issues with the main focus of the game: the combat. Like so many others, it tries to mimic Sekiro without actually taking the best from it; you're supposed to focus on combine attacking and parrying, but the former feels weightless and the later is confusing due to the lack of proper tells for enemy attacks. Besides, most enemies are braindead and you can just kill them with relative ease by keeping a safe distance and kiting.

In Sekiro, you're in a duel based on rhythm where you and your opponent exchange blows and pressure each other until one breaks.

In Where Winds Meet, you slam the attack button and abuse a ton of skills, then run around or parry 2/3 of all attacks and repeat until the enemy's dead.

In true Wuxia fashion, the story's all over the place, feels disconnected and characters just interact with each other with zero natural feel to it. This is not a mistake, it's the way the genre works. I don't mind it, but it can be jarring to those that aren't used to it.

On another note, the use of LLMs for certain interactable characters is an abomination and I hope it doesn't become the norm. Stop shoving the damn thing down our throats; if you add characters, hire and pay an actual human to write their dialogues.

If you have nothing else to do with your time, then I guess it's fine, but I tend to prefer my games to have a purpose besides accumulating resources endlessly with no proper objective in sight. There's a lot to do, but it feels pointless.

I’ve spent years searching for an open world that gives me the same “escape from real-life stress” feeling I got from RDR2. I played Red Dead Online for 850+ hours because I love worlds that feel alive, beautiful, and endless. But after a point, even that world started feeling familiar, and I wanted something new — not fantasy-heavy, not empty, not repetitive. Just a world I could disappear into again.

Surprisingly, Where Winds Meet is exactly that.
Yes, it has some wuxia/chi-powered martial arts, but it never overdoes the fantasy. It still feels grounded, logical, and atmospheric — like a believable alternate world where you can actually live for a while. That’s the kind of realism I want. Not “physics realism,” but world logic realism. The places feel lived-in, the people feel active, and wherever I go, something is happening. That’s what gives me the same comfort that Witcher 3 and RDR2 gave me.

And the craziest part? This huge, lively, beautiful world is FREE.
Honestly, this feels like a proper AAA title disguised as a free game. With 40 hours already spent, I still haven’t run out of things to do. As someone who avoids heavy fantasy and prefers grounded worlds, Where Winds Meet hits the perfect sweet spot — a bit of magic sprinkled in, but not so much that I disconnect from the world.

Review: 9/10

This game delivers an incredible open world with visuals that immediately impress. The amount of customization is almost unbelievable, to the point where it feels like you could spend hours just shaping your character and playstyle without ever running out of options.

The gameplay itself is a lot of fun, although it starts out a bit slow for my taste. There’s so much to learn right from the beginning that it can feel overwhelming at first, but it also makes it clear that the game has enough depth to keep me busy for a very long time.

The part I struggle with the most is the story. I find it hard to follow and could use more guidance to help me understand what’s really going on. Other players might love the freedom, but for me it’s the weakest part. The rest of the world, though, feels incredibly alive. NPCs follow their own routines, have personalities, and you can actually make friends with them through real conversations powered by AI. It adds a surprising amount of immersion.

The gameplay feels like a mix of Soulslike combat and Assassin’s Creed exploration. Choices seem to matter, the world responds to you, and the combat, even though it feels a little slow to me, is extremely well done.

Overall, this is a game that becomes whatever you want it to be. It’s massive, detailed, and packed with things to discover. Even with my issues following the story, I’d still give it a solid 9 out of 10.

Ignore my playtime — I play on the official launcher, and Steam is only there because I needed to use my wallet to get a dumb $1 horse and a $1 stick sword. Just play this game. It really has something for everyone. Want a challenge? Pick Legend mode and earn a badge that counts how many bosses you’ve beaten — then get destroyed by the scythe lady. Want something more relaxed? Go Easy mode and turn on Parry Assist.

The story is amazing, but the English localization doesn’t fully convey the original meaning from Chinese. I recommend using the Chinese voice acting because it sounds better and the lip sync actually matches.

Combat feels smooth and satisfying. You get different weapon types and martial skills to try, and parrying, dodging, and countering all feel responsive. Bosses are varied, tough, and usually have multiple phases, so fights never get boring.

The open world is fun to explore, with side quests, puzzles, hidden spots, and plenty to do. NPCs can even chat with you through an AI system, which makes the world feel more alive. The game also looks great — characters, environments, effects, everything is very pleasing to the eye.

Performance is solid, with good optimization and smooth framerates on decent hardware.

You can also turn on multiplayer and interact with other players: place bounties, hunt wanted targets, heal others, join co-op dungeons, complete missions together, or just hang out and enjoy side activities. It adds variety and makes the world feel less lonely.

Best of all, the game is completely free-to-play. The only thing you can spend real money on is cosmetics — there’s no pay-to-win.

If you want challenge, story, exploration, multiplayer, or just something fun to play, this game delivers and is easy to recommend.

✅ Tried to meditate but got kicked by a goat
✅ NPCs called me a legendary hero even though I fell off a roof 6 times
✅ Horse controls me instead of me controlling horse
✅ Accidentally challenged a guard to a duel while trying to open the menu

Combat feels like Ghost of Tsushima, if Jin Sakai had slipped on oil and used TikTok filters.

Exploration? Beautiful.
Parkour? Stunning.
Story? I have no idea, I was too busy getting blown off cliffs by “dynamic wind physics”.

At one point I tried to stealth… but the wind literally betrayed me and blew a pot over.
Ghost of Yotei would be ashamed.

This game is an ABSOLUTE MASTERCLASS in everything fun and exciting about gaming. I thought I was bored to death with open worlds and RPGs. Now, I can't wait to get back into this unbelievably engrossing game. 

Where Winds Meet is probably the most beautiful game I've ever played...and it runs well on my 6-year-old potato. The story is gripping and the cinematic cutscenes are a testament to the profound history of Chinese Action Cinema. Without a doubt, the cultural presentation is one of the best aspects of the game...you go on a journey deep into a time and a culture and a way of living that absolutely drips with authenticity. 

Even side quests involve immersive stories that can take you in completely unexpected directions. Sure, there is usually fighting, but there is also an abundance of beauty and high-quality writing interwoven throughout.

Combat is complex and fast-paced, and the game gives you an ABUNDANCE of different weapons, skills, and talents to use. You can join a sect and follow their path, or you can follow the pathless path and find out what works best for you. Best of all, you can develop your own style and teach it to others. 

On the negative side, this game is COMPLICATED. There are TONS of different methods and materials and skill-trees used to upgrade your character as you go along, and it can definitely get overwhelming to try to max your build or figure out how to accomplish certain goals. 

Another unusual issue is that you cannot make more than one saved game/character per account on Steam and another one per account on PS. If you want to link your Steam and PS accounts, you have to do that before you make different saves/characters...and then you will share the single character between Steam and PS for cross-play. 

Added bonus: I was expecting to have to play using my keyboard. I tried my X-box controller, and it worked perfectly.

I cannot recommend this game enough. For free, there is no reason not to give it a try.

Where Winds Meet: The Best Free Game I Have Ever Played

Where Winds Meet is, without exaggeration, the best free game I have ever played in my life. It puts many expensive triple-A titles to shame the moment you realise just how polished and generous this game truly is. The graphics, the gameplay, the combat systems, the world design, everything feels on another level. I still can’t fathom how a game of this quality is being offered for free.

One of the biggest surprises is how unannoying the game is. There’s no nonsense like limited inventory space or weight restrictions forcing you to pay real money just to expand it. You can actually play and enjoy the game without being nickel-and-dimed, which is extremely rare nowadays.

There is no pay-to-win here. Yes, there are mounts that offer small conveniences like auto-looting or auto-gathering flowers, but that’s about it. They don’t give you unfair power or advantages, just quality-of-life options. The core gameplay remains fair and balanced for everyone.

Speaking of quality of life, it’s top-notch overall. The game is well optimised, smooth, and most importantly, it respects your time. Some content is time-gated, but in a good way. As someone with real-life commitments, I can still progress and enjoy the game without feeling left behind, while hardcore grinders still have plenty to do while waiting for level caps and new updates.

I also fully understand how the developers earn money, and honestly, I don’t mind spending more here than I ever did on triple-A games. When a game delivers this much value, supporting it feels natural.

To put it simply: this game is better than Ghost of Yotei, it feels like a more refined and enjoyable version of Dark Souls, and it easily surpasses every Assassin’s Creed title for me. You have to play it to believe it.

I cannot recommend Where Winds Meet enough.

Unpolished, buggy, unresponsive at the weirdest of times.
Bad localization, voice lines run multiple times in succession often in conversation.
The aim of the game is fashion; you don't do gacha for gear or characters, but outfits, hairstyles, horses, props for picture taking and such.

Drop rates are abysmal. If a chest you get from a boss says it has a "probability" to give something, that probability is so low as to be non-existent. I've defeat the boss of Still Shores (drops Chasing Red hairstyle and outfit) 120 times in a row now. Used up all my energy (it takes 3.3 days for energy to fully recharge) and all my energy-regaining items to do it this much. I've yet to get hairstyle or outfit.

Main quest is mainly incomprehensible. The game throws a new concept at you every 1.2 seconds (translated in a very flowery way, of course, because this is China we're talking about) then expects you to know what they mean. For instance, I am in the second area of the game, Kaifeng, and I have no idea why I went there. They just never actually told me why I'd ever go there.

Combat is a clutter of special effects that obscure everything. Most enemies stand in front of you and the developers didn't pan the camera a little off-the-shoulder so you could see the enemy you're fighting clearly, meaning you cannot see their attack cues most of the time. The parry and dodge assistance system helps here a bit, luckily.

Gacha system is fully for the rich Chinese whales. Only way to pull on premium banner is to buy in-game currency; otherwise the game gives you about one "ticket" to pull per heavens knows how long. I've managed to do a full 25 pulls of the premium banner; pity is at 150 pulls, which is too high by about 100 for cosmetics.
The basic banner is better; you get the jade echoes needed to buy the "tickets" for that from pretty much everywhere a little at a time. 150 for pity in that as well.

It's pretty, though. That's most of what it has going on for it, really. Cannot recommend.

⭐ Review of Where the Wind Meets — From an Older Black Nerd & Kung Fu Lover ⭐

Man… Where the Wind Meets hit me in a place I didn’t even know a game could still reach. As an older Black nerd who grew up on Saturday-morning kung fu flicks, wire-fu epics, and Dreamcast-era wuxia games, this title feels like somebody reached into my memories, dusted them off, and polished them with next-gen shine.

First off, the martial arts choreography? Smooth. Fluid. Thoughtful. This ain’t button-mashing — it’s form, rhythm, and respect. Every stance feels like it was crafted by someone who actually studies the philosophy behind kung fu, not just the aesthetics. It reminds me of the old Shaw Brothers mindset: your technique tells your story.

The world-building is a whole other love letter. Rolling misty mountains, ancient villages, wandering swordsmen with tragic poetry in their voices… it brings back that feeling I had watching Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon for the first time — that mix of beauty, danger, and destiny. And as an older gamer, I appreciate how the game lets you breathe in its world instead of rushing you from fight to fight. It respects your time and your curiosity.

Also, let me say this as plainly as I can:
It feels GOOD seeing a game honor Eastern philosophy and martial traditions without watering them down. The meditative pacing, the moral choices, the quiet moments where your character sits and reflects — those are the touches that make this more than just a game. It’s a vibe.

And the combat? Whew. When you finally nail that perfect parry after studying your opponent — not spamming, not panicking, but flowing — it gives that same satisfaction I get watching Donnie Yen dismantle somebody with pure skill and discipline.

If you’re an older gamer who loves kung fu cinema, lore, or philosophy?
If you’re a Black nerd who grew up mixing anime with Wu-Tang albums, absorbing Eastern wisdom right alongside superhero comics?

Where the Wind Meets is the game that reminds you your passions never got old — they just needed the right world to grow in.

Absolutely worth diving into.

Where Winds Meet is honestly one of the most impressive free games I have ever played. From the moment you enter the world you feel like you’ve stepped into a living Wuxia story filled with beauty, detail, and an unbelievable amount of freedom. The open world is massive, full of mountains, rivers, ancient towns, hidden places, and so many moments where you just stop and admire how much love and effort the developers put into the game. The combat feels exciting, fluid, and stylish with so many different weapons and martial arts to choose from, and the fact that you can play solo or jump in with friends makes the experience even better. The game offers so many professions, activities, side stories, and ways to build your character that it’s honestly hard to believe all of this is completely free. No paywalls, no forced purchases, just a huge world that you can explore however you want. The amount of content almost feels like a full-price game but they just give it to everyone for free, which in today’s world is something you don’t see often. I also love how the game supports every type of player: if you want to play alone you can, if you want to play with others the multiplayer is amazing, if you want to explore or fight or just relax in the world, everything is possible. The visuals are stunning, the animations are cinematic, and the whole atmosphere makes you forget time while playing. I have to mention one important thing though: the game is very demanding on computers. It really eats resources, so players with low-end PCs might struggle or not get the best experience. But honestly, the game is so good and offers so much value for free that it’s totally worth upgrading your PC at some point because this kind of quality is rare, and you don’t have to pay anything to enjoy it. In short, Where Winds Meet is a masterpiece of free Wuxia adventure, and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a deep, beautiful, and rewarding open-world experience.

I wish I could give a 'neutral' review. This game is gorgeous. The animations, visual aspects, combat are all great.

My two gripes that make me struggle to keep jumping back in:

- There is like a 20:1 ratio of dialog to combat. As a non-Chinese I can't determine if this lore is accurate to folklore or history, and if it is, I'm really not versed in it enough to be able to relate to it.
- The UI surrounding the inventory and skill system is the most confusing I've ever played in a game. I have no idea what anything is for, what it's doing, how to find specific views, and have no idea how to even gauge my progress or what I *can* do. It is far and away the worst UI system I've ever had the misfortune of using. I still have no idea how to find my inventory, 9 hours in. There's a menagerie of hotkeys that do things but they seem to change depending on what's being shown.

Please, devs, "depth" isn't achieved by "complexity". It's an extremely confusing play experience with a beautiful art style and combat system at its core.

我真希望可以给出“中立”的评价。这款游戏画面精美绝伦，动画、视觉效果和战斗系统都无可挑剔。

然而，有两点让我难以坚持玩下去：

- 对话和战斗的比例大概是20:1。这让人非常厌烦，主要是因为游戏里充斥着大量的背景故事，不断冒出新名字，却没有任何连贯的剧情线索可以让人真正理解。作为一名非中国人，我无法判断这些背景故事是否符合民间传说或历史，即便符合，我也对此知之甚少，难以产生共鸣。

- 物品栏和技能系统的用户界面是我玩过的所有游戏中最令人困惑的。我完全不知道这些东西是干什么用的，它们的作用是什么，如何找到特定的视图，甚至不知道如何衡量自己的进度或自己能做什么。这绝对是我用过的最糟糕的用户界面系统。玩了9个小时了，我还是不知道怎么找到我的物品栏。游戏里有一大堆快捷键，但它们的功能似乎会根据当前显示的内容而改变。

拜托各位开发者，“深度”并非靠“复杂”来实现的。这游戏画面精美，战斗系统也很棒，但玩起来却极其混乱。
