You live the life of a ninja/samurai and everything that goes along with that. You learn new skills, hone those you have already learned, find new gear and weapons, learn new fighting styles and magic, you can take on bounties to help cure other players or absolve them of their crimes - there really is so much content that it does make it feel like you're a part of a living world with countless opportunities for exploration and progression in different aspects of your life.

This isn't a questing system like WoW where you have a yellow marker, you go to it and complete the quest. A lot of the side quests are heavily reliant on your talking to people, reading the clues and searching things down for yourself. The game doesn't hand hold you and this makes exploring and solving mysteries all the more satisfying.

The story feels engaging, the movement and combat is solid, even with the slight input lag depending on where you live and considering there feels like an unlimited amount of things you can do each day the game is somehow completely free without any items that you can pay to progress with. 

You can't go wrong by giving this game a try, just do it.

The UI is a bit of a mess, but you get used to it after 2–3 hours of playing.

The localization and voice acting are mediocre (but still tolerable).

The boss fights. I’m playing on Legend, I’ve done all currently available bosses in the game, and compared to many soulslikes, the boss fights here feel extremely repetitive. The Deeply Authentic Wuxia Combat System
This is the game's greatest strength.

Diverse Martial Arts: Combat goes beyond simple slashing and blocking. You can utilize Tai Chi for powerful parries, employ Acupoint Pressing to temporarily paralyze enemies, and master a variety of weapons (swords, spears, fans, umbrellas).

Qinggong (Lightness Skill) Mechanics: The game truly allows you to master movement. You can run on water, scale vertical walls, and glide through the air with incredible fluidity. The sense of movement and freedom is superior to typical open-world titles like Assassin's Creed.

Skill Absorption: You have the ability to learn techniques from your enemies during combat, providing a gratifying sense of progression akin to a martial arts master learning new forms.

True Sandbox Freedom and Roleplaying
The game doesn't restrict you to being just a hero saving the world.

The Profession System: This is highly unique. You can choose to be a Physician (healing NPCs or other players), an Architect (building your own structures), or even a Ferryman. This depth offers robust role-playing opportunities.

Environmental Interaction: You can use wind to spread fire, destroy objects, or use your Qinggong to approach objectives from any direction, rewarding clever exploration.

Visuals and Sound
The graphics are impressive, capturing the details of ancient China beautifully. Weather effects, lighting, and especially the animation of the character's robes while using Qinggong are captivating.

The music is appropriately epic and melancholic, perfectly setting the historical and martial mood.

2. The Drawbacks (Cons)
The "Floaty" Combat Feel
This is a common issue in some Chinese-developed action games. While the animations are gorgeous, the impact and weight when striking an enemy often feel lacking. Sometimes, hitting an opponent feels less satisfying and less visceral compared to the heavy feedback found in titles like Ghost of Tsushima or Sekiro.

Cluttered UI and Steep Learning Curve
Due to the integration of too many systems (martial arts, Meridian points, professions, building...), the game's interface (UI) can feel overwhelming and chaotic, leaning more towards an older PC MMORPG than a modern streamlined AAA title.

New players are easily flooded with information and mechanics, making the initial hours quite challenging to navigate.

Optimization Issues
In past beta tests, the game occasionally struggled with inconsistent frame rates (FPS) in crowded areas or when complex visual effects were being deployed. This remains a point of concern for players with less powerful hardware.

Niche Narrative
The Ten Kingdoms and Five Dynasties period is historically complex and politically intricate. Players unfamiliar with Chinese history or traditional Wuxia literature may find the main storyline difficult to follow or feel disjointed.

I wasn’t really impressed with the game at first. The story felt light and too spread out, and I couldn’t quite figure out what the game wanted from me. But after passing the 100-hour mark, I started to understand: the game isn’t trying to guide you—it’s truly open. And that was the problem. I’m not used to that level of freedom in an RPG.

Few games actually let you go wherever you want and do whatever you want, with so little handholding. It’s massive, and there’s so much to do—but without understanding how to navigate it, I was just drifting. I spent over ten days before I even opened the J-Quest Journal. That was a turning point. I realized I had tons of quests still in progress that I thought I’d finished. Once I started working through them methodically, the structure clicked. The game communicates clearly—when you finish a quest line, it literally says “END” on screen.

The storylines are epic. One arc nearly brought me to tears—and then, much later, a side quest revisits that same emotional wound, pouring salt and lemon juice into it. It’s brutal, but brilliant.

This game is amazing, but it’s built very differently from Western RPGs. It takes time to adjust to its flow, but once you do, it’s phenomenal. Easily the best Wuxia game I’ve ever played.

It's basically Wuxia version of Genshin Impact / Wuthering Waves, but with WAY worse localization, and the gacha is cosmetic instead of characters.

The story is incomprehensible, there many places that are left in simplified Chinese, including puzzles, and there's UI text that you can't even read in English because it's cut off.

You may wonder, why do I have so many hours if the game is bad?  Anyone who has played Genshin Impact or any of its clones will understand.  It's just an addictive dopamine box.

As a person who enjoys character customization and tends to buy cosmetics in all the games I play, here they have chosen some very suspicious and predatory tactics that I'm NOT willing to support.

The current newest costume is sold in a gacha for potentially up to 7440 cash shop currency (about 130€). HOWEVER the pricing is veiled by making the first pull only 60 pearls (1€) and the cost goes up significantly with each draw until you have the full set. The only way to see this information is by clicking a small button that says "Intro" in the bottom left corner. I felt the price suspicious immediately so I looked carefully, but they did manage to scam multiple people with what appears to be a good deal at first, until you see the fine print.

That same costume is (as mentioned in some other reviews) sold in China straight away in the cash shop for cheaper, it was not a gacha release over there.

Global version also did not get the marketplace system at the Ghost Market to buy and sell items to other players, which the Chinese version has.

Not to mention all hair colors except black and muddied tones cost up to 800€, if you're unlucky (and the rates are abysmally low) and have to hit pity twice for the hair dye, which also only dyes a single hairstyle of yours. I can play just about any other game and simply color my character's hair in the customization screen. Disgusting pricing.

The gacha is also filled with trash 99% of the time (fireworks and other junk that has little to no use), so 10 pulls worth of about 27€ is going to end up giving you nothing at all and you need 150 pulls to guarantee a pity, which is potentially only one pity orb, and you need 2 for the costume set. I've never seen a cosmetic gacha as pathetic as this, but the pay piggies will keep paying and we will see this sort of pricing become the norm.

Now obviously the game has more issues than just that. Quest text occasionally goes by so quickly you can't read it before it already vanishes and same goes for some boss mechanic information. Sometimes it even cuts out without showing full text like in the Wolf Maiden boss when she reaches half health.

The translations are sometimes bizarre, like in the chess minigame when you make a "Check" it instead calls it a "Checkmate" and obviously the information buttons being called "Intro" for example. Maybe they will eventually fix these translation issues at least, time will tell.

Coming from normal MMO's I have to admit this game caught me off guard in all the best ways. Despite the thousands of Menus all leading to the same menus or slight bugs, the game has a great way of presenting so much to distract you from the Menus long enough to keep playing for a few more hours.

Originally I was thinking it would be another Throne and Liberty able to buy power or sell a guilds bank for real money but only having Cosmetics is a breath of fresh air... HOWEVER. The Pulls are something that cannot be ignored nor can I say to bother spending real money UNLESS you REALLY want to support the game. Just be warned, it can cost hundreds to complete all the pulls with just how low the probabilities are. I get its a F2P game with so much going on it feels like a 10th Century Chinese Martial Arts movie had a baby with GTA and Elden Ring but still, It would be nice to have cheaper looking free options to play around with.

The Solo Game story is decent (better than a ton of KR mmo's like BDO) and the voice acting is better on the Chinese version compared to English but it IS a Chinese Game. I would've like to have Co-Op for the Story Missions but the world is huge, immersive, and forces you to get lost in the environment. The music is beautiful and the sounds help keeps attention which is a plus and PLAYER MUSIC (BDO and LOTRO players eats your hearts out) 

Co-op comes with a few bugs at times with Bosses but for the most part jumping into and out of a co-op session is smooth, not confusing, and even rewards you if you don't do much (me and friend bugged a Boss and had to end the session. I hope they add more to do for Co-op because this aspect of the game is really fun.

The Online part leaves more to be desired for coming from any MMO but not in a deal breaking way. While there is a lot to do in the Social Hub, Guild or PvP. Until more is Localized, its just the barebones of what the Chinese version has but they ARE 11 months ahead. The mini games help break up the grinds and even makes friends. The healing Profession is a great surprise IF players would stop denying being diagnosed for 3 broken bones, mental break, and bee venom in their wounds but hey its a different kind of job most game don't bother with.

Ooooh the PvP.. as a Casual Gatherer Crafter kinda player, the combat in PVP has me blown away. I didn't think I'd want to hunt down players for fun before. That's not to say Combat is wonky and could use some slight changes to make it less jumbled for Keyboard and Mouse (skill issue mainly) I will say though, the battlefield and arena is a lot better than Black Desert even if the combat still falls short.

At the end of the day I'll still reccommend this game to all my friends 8/10 and glad to see a free Chinese game competing with the AAA titles

The Good game
Stunning World and Atmosphere The game is widely praised for its gorgeous, massive open world, which beautifully captures the Wuxia aesthetic of ancient China with bustling cities, serene bamboo forests, and snowy mountains.
Deep, Satisfying Combat The combat system, which draws inspiration from games like Sekiro and Team Ninja titles, is a major highlight. Where Winds Meet is a mixed bag of both highly incumbering and very intuitive systems that make you wonder both "Why isnt everyone else doing this" and then in your encounter with another system moments later, you think about how everyone else did it better.

For starters, there shouldn't be an autoplay mode that automatically deflects/counters for you, what's the point of playing normally if that exists? it makes otherwise difficult challenges often trivial.

Second, the cash shop is hilariously overpriced, they want 30, 40 and 50 dollars for cash shop outfits bought outright, and that's not even accounting for the gachapon systems.

But there's another special one in between those 2 systems, a semi-guaranteed gacha system where you pull 1 of 10 items, with 10 pulls being the maximum required to obtain everything, however the cost to pull each time increases exponentially, according to a reddit post, the outfit in question at the time of this review was purchasable outright in the chinese version, biased marketing leaves a bad taste in the mouth.

Another is that in PVP, there is unlimited use of regeneration tools, during a bounty, I had to fight through atleast 7 health bars to kill someone. That's ridiculous, and a waste of time. There's also no punishment for using them mid combat, a lot of games which feature a system like this will nerf the amount regenerated by food/potions if they're used during combat to prevent this kind of 30 minute battle type of thing.

All of that said, as is common in the not-so-common Wuxia MMO space, there's a lot of great systems here, the music system is wonderful, the bounty system is fun and even though the actual feel of an MMO is missing here, with it mostly just feeling like a lobby where you throw a needle into people to fix their broken bone or afk in a regeneration field and then turn into a deer, the framework for a good MMO style system is all mostly there, but purposefully fragmented, likely for the reason of profit.

I don't see Where Winds Meet lasting a very long time, the market for a wuxia game is there, but its not big enough to keep this boat afloat past its hype phase with people like Asmongold playing it, I'll check back in a year to see how it's doing, but I have no expectations because I feel as if most of these systems will be greatly offputting to the average person.

The progression system is initially extremely complicated and overwhelming. It is easy to accidentally sink all of your materials into various specialties without knowing what you are doing, so caution is advised. This is, at heart, a gacha game, so there are shadows of predatory practices dancing along the edges of the UI. However, with the latest patch, they devs are clearly showing that improving localization is one of their top priorities. A lot of issues from launch have been addressed, but it is far from perfect.

The combat is VERY good, especially if you are a fan of souls-like systems. Many people have compared it to Sekiro, where defense and reaction is paramount. There is a high skill ceiling here, and a system that helps us plebs deflect as well so everyone can progress.

The story is difficult to understand. There is a massive glossary, which reminds me of AC, and i truly appreciate that while im chowing and want some context. But the localization is really bad, so a few carefully-planned youtube videos may be required to get the proper background/avoid spoilers for a western audience.

Starting out I will note that this game in my opinion could use some work before reaching it's full potential. 

It is in a playable state as it is, and it's not bad. There are several things that don't really hit the mark. Things like combat. Combat seems a bit basic and very simple. 

Something I really enjoyed in this game was NPCs that use an Ai to talk to you. You can use a chat box to say whatever you want to them and they will respond accordingly. It's fun to have conversations with the different NPCs that allow it (not all NPCs use Ai chat), but they can't interact with physical things in the world based on what you discuss through the Ai system, which is something I think needs to change and this game will be ultimately fun without limits to what you can do. Right now the Ai system just RPs with you. For example i asked a woodcutter if he happened to have a pickaxe I could buy from him, and he told me he could part with it if I did some work for him cutting down trees in the area. I told him it was a reasonable deal so i went and cut down some trees as promised. Then when I returned to him. He told me good job and the Ai said (he drops a pickaxe on the ground by your feet). There was no physical item in the world it just roleplayed that whole scenario with me. I could have not even cut the trees and said that I did and the wood cutter would have been equally impressed and still would have "dropped a pickaxe for me" an imaginary one. So I think if there are physical things in the world that you could obtain through quickly created on the fly quests it should be possible to obtain them form Ai NPCs. That's my personal opinion. That being said I have still spent time just chatting with the Ai NPCs and trying to build good rapport with them. I have been able to sneak up on enemies several times only to be disappointed by the fact that You can't do any kind of stealth attack or takedowns. 

There is a crafting system but you are not allowed to use it until you are level 25. boooooo. lol.

Honestly though, the game is free, it's fun to mess around in for a few hours. Check it out. You have nothing to lose. 

Rating: 7/10.  The game could do with a few improvements; A stealth system, Ai enhancements, Crafting should be available from the start, combat needs an upgrade (it's mid)

I do agree with what most here are complaining about: The menus-within-menus, the lack of communication for certain tasks due to either poor Translation (or simply not telling you how at all), the honestly downright comedic levels of both Gacha & Microtransactions/Monetization of Cosmetics (it is very close to Diablo Immortal in terms of how expensive Cosmetics can get); Though at the very least, nothing in the game is Pay2Win. No true Co-Op is another huge downside, so prepare for one of the longest Single-Player Games of your life, with some occasional Online Guild Events, an Online Overworld Hub you can visit for random Quests and see other Players, and the occasional ability to Invite in a Friend or join a Friend in their World to help with menial tasks, but no Main Quests or NPC's. The Story itself is so Titanically-Massive in both size & scope, that simply keeping up with even the absolute base-line Plot of the game requires either a Photographic Memory, or a Degree in Chinese Literature & History; And perhaps worst of all: The hilarious but still just honestly awful English Voice Acting.

NOW... If you either ignore ^ all of this, don't mind any of it, or in-fact love the sound of it? Then I have to be equally honest here as well: For a free game? I have never been remotely close to this impressed when it comes to how absurdly massive, deep, and visually-impressive this game has turned out to be at multiple points. I played Warframe for years but was never once truly wowed by not just their Art-Direction & Storytelling, but I also hated their Monetization-Practices as well; So far there have already been numerous points in Where Winds Meet that have genuinely made me soyjack unintentionally just from how visually-striking everything can be out of nowhere, even if I didn't fully understand the Plot or what was/is going on (I still don't)... To me though? That's very rare now when so many games are so heavily focused on visuals; Combat is also incredibly fluid, simple, and satisfying to both learn, yet equally challenging to master; Which is also rare to see everything nailed so well in Combat Games now oddly, yet here we have an incredibly solid Combat System that's just downright fun. Also another huge positive for the game is oodles upon oodles of Kung-Fu Hustle & Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon references (among countless others).

TLDR: HIGHLY recommended - BUT it comes with the known-caveat of it definitely not being perfect by any standard, primarily being Single Player, having Gacha & Microtransactioned Cosmetics from hell, confusing/convoluted Story, and honestly quite hilariously bad English VA.

This is a decent Wuxia Open-World ARPG with interesting quest design, a story I am enjoying, and multiple reasons to go explore the decently sized (for now!) open world. The fact that a game of this high quality being published by NetEase was allowed to be Free is astounding. The microtransactions aren't predatory and solely focused on unlocking wild and outlandish outfits for your character to wear, on top of skill effects and mounts with equally outlandish effects.

Combat is smooth and responsive (when the servers aren't overloaded) and has an exhilarating feel to it when you're able to successfully chain multiple parries. That's where it falls short at moments though. There's a delay on parry input when missing (which is fine), and because of the online pseudo-MMO nature, latency and input registration can and WILL cause you to fail or miss timings. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but when it comes to the boss fights...man. Eighty percent of the bosses in this game are what I would consider reasonably well designed...but then you get to the other 20%. 

Some of the bosses are asinine and frustrating to deal with due to the latency based parry system, and it shows. These bosses will have attack strings with multiple hits, purposeful attack delays (Elden Ring) and just an absurdly fast output time. When you do hit the parry, you don't have that input delay for the next one to come out, so you're reasonably able to deflect these bosses to good success. When you miss though, or get told "No" by the server, you WILL be punished into a stun-lock that will continue until the boss delays an attack or finishes the string. It's irritating, and really doesn't make those specific bosses enjoyable, but I've overcome them eventually.

Despite that glaring complaint for me personally, this is a good game. It's a good free to play game, and the monetization isn't necessary or required. Try it out, make your own opinions. I definitely recommend it.

I just saw this game for free on Steam and it looked too good so I had to read what I'm getting into and what I'm going to accept, as they don't let you play if you don't accept their Terms of Use AND Privacy Policy.
This post is not done to judge or give a bad review, but it is purely informative (at least I hope so).

Here are the points that I find interesting and if you are ok with it, then this game is legit for you:
1. Purchases are non-refundable and non-cancellable (10.1, 10.3(a))
Almost everything you buy is final, even if it was a mistake, unless local law forces them to refund.

2. Auto-renewal without notice (10.2)
Subscriptions automatically renew without alerting you when the free trial ends or when billing restarts.

3. Up-front 12-month payment authorization (10.2)
Your payment method can be pre-authorized for up to a year of service immediately when you sign up, which may reduce your available balance.

4. No refunds for partially used subscription periods (10.2)
If you cancel after renewal, you still pay the full period. No partial refunds.

5. Digital content refunds require waiving your rights (10.3(b))
In the EU/UK, you only get the 14-day refund for digital content if you haven’t started downloading AND you waived your right to cancel, otherwise no refund.

6. Virtual goods are always final (10.3(b)(2))
Anything like virtual currency or in-game items is non-refundable, even in Europe.

7. Arbitration required (11.3)
Almost all disputes must go to private arbitration, not court. This is generally bad for consumers.

8. Confidential arbitration (11.3(c))
You must keep the entire arbitration secret, which protects the company and hides patterns of abuse.

9. Mass arbitration limitations (11.4(c))
If many users file similar claims, they force a “batch” process that can weaken individual cases.

10. No class actions (11.9)
You cannot join or start a class action lawsuit.

11. No jury trial (11.10)
You give up your right to a jury trial completely.

12. Opt-out window is only 30 days (11.11)
You must opt out of arbitration within 30 days or lose the right permanently.

13. They can modify arbitration terms (11.12)
They can change the arbitration rules later, and you’re bound unless you opt out again in 30 days.

14. They can assign the contract, you cannot (12.2)
They can transfer your contract to another company without consent; you’re not allowed to do the same.
====================================================================
On the Privacy Policy side:
1. They can collect government-issued ID
Even though it’s “only if needed,” having an option to request passport, ID card, or similar is a major red flag for a gaming service.

2. They gather precise technical and diagnostic data
Including:
Core dumps & crash reports containing memory snapshots
CPU/memory usage, device identifiers, MAC address
This can sometimes unintentionally include sensitive data.

3. They track your gameplay chats and screen captures
They collect:
Chat logs
Gameplay screen captures
Social connections
These are often used for moderation but are also a huge privacy intrusion.

4. They can link social media profiles & friend lists
If you log in with a platform (e.g., Steam, Xbox, Facebook, etc.), they may access:
Friend lists
Profile pictures
Email, age, country
This creates deep cross-platform tracking.

5. They get advertising & marketing engagement data
They track:
How you interact with their marketing in emails, websites, or ads.
Cross-site tracking for targeted ads.

6. They collect location through IP, Wi-Fi, and cell ID
This can reveal:
Your city and region
Sometimes approximate movement patterns (with Wi-Fi/cell ID).

7. They warn you not to send sensitive data, but they collect a lot already
The fact they explicitly warn you suggests their system could accidentally ingest sensitive data through logs or uploads.

8. “Legitimate interest” is used as a catch-all
They justify a huge range of processing using: "our legitimate interests"
This is very broad and means they can process data beyond what you explicitly agreed to.

9. They tie legal compliance to things that enable more data collection
Legal obligations are used to justify:
identity verification
age assurance
KYC requirements
This can force you to give more personal info than you'd expect for a game.

10. They warn you that internet transmissions aren’t secure
This is basically a passive disclaimer that:
your data could be intercepted or leaked
they aren’t fully responsible for “errors” in transmission.

11. They track your engagement across third-party platforms
Interacting with their:
Facebook page
Discord
Social posts
gives them access to identification, profile, communication, and activity information.
This means cross-platform tracking.

12. “We don’t sell your information”… but they share it widely anyway
They reassure you they “don’t sell” data, but they still share it with:
advertisers
social media platforms
subsidiaries
service providers
companies involved in mergers/acquisitions
That’s basically everyone except literal strangers.

13. Data travels globally, including to countries with weak privacy protection
Your data can be stored or processed in:
countries with lower privacy standards
jurisdictions with weaker oversight
They rely on Standard Contractual Clauses. Legally acceptable, but practically weak.

14. Business transfers = your data gets handed to new owners
If NetEase is ever:
bought
merged
reorganized
your full profile becomes part of the transferred assets.

15. ID verification required to exercise your privacy rights
To request deletion or access, they can ask for:
identity verification
Further information about your account
They can refuse your request and make you appeal.

16. They explicitly don’t honor Do Not Track signals
Your browser’s privacy settings telling companies not to track you are ignored.

17. They use cookies and similar tracking without a real opt-out
You cannot disable “necessary” cookies (often the ones used for tracking authentication, device identity, and behavior.)

18. They can profile and track children (with parental consent)
Even for children:
they collect and process personal data
they require parental documents to verify age
The system still retains a child’s identifiable data, just “limited.”

19. Rewards program uses your personal info as part of a “financial incentive”
They admit:
They collect extra personal data for rewards
That your data has a calculated monetary value
This is essentially: your data = payment.

20. Global Privacy Control only works if you’re NOT logged in
If you’re logged out → GPC opt-out works.
If logged in → they ignore it because they “can’t link your browser to your account.”
This undermines the entire privacy signal.

21. They allow third-party “authorized agents” but require heavy verification
This makes opting out or deleting data more difficult than necessary.

22. They keep minors’ content even if deletion is requested
If you posted something under 18:
They might not fully remove it
Because other users “may have reposted it”
Meaning: child content = permanently stuck online.

Do what you want with what you read above.

AMAZING GAME
Diverse & Fluid Wuxia Combat: The game emphasizes timing, parrying, dodging, and counters in real-time combat. Players can switch between various weapons (swords, spears, twin blades, fans, umbrellas, etc.), each with unique skills and combos that can be customized into a build.

Skill Theft System: Instead of just finding skill books, players can learn martial arts by observing and successfully "stealing" techniques from practicing NPCs through a specialized mini-game.

Deep Profession System: Beyond the main story and combat, players can choose from a wide range of civilian "Identities" or jobs, such as being a doctor, architect, merchant, or bodyguard, which allows for different styles of gameplay and progression.

Moral Alignment & Consequences: Player choices in quests and interactions influence their character's moral alignment (justice, chaos, or neutrality), which in turn affects world reactions, available quests, and NPC interactions.

Sandbox Freedom: Players have immense freedom to ignore the main quest entirely and spend their time exploring, crafting, taking photos, or focusing on their chosen profession.

Dynamic Injury & Self-Healing: Injuries like sprains are not just solved with a simple item; they can be healed by visiting an in-game doctor, having a co-op partner heal you, or by "self-healing" through specific world interactions (e.g., avoiding fall damage for a set amount of real-world time).

Optional Multiplayer: The game can be played entirely solo, cooperatively with up to four friends in the campaign, or as part of a persistent online world with guild systems and large-scale events.

There is glitching, sometimes shaders take longer to load entirely, NPC respawns can be janky (specifically horses, I captured all the ones in an area, and none respawned despite me leaving the area for extended periods or restarting the game), and there can be delays in sound. All in all, Id give the game a try, yes its a larger game but, for it being free there is a lot this game does currently offer. Surprisingly good. If you want another Genshin — interestingly, without any big agressive “buy power” paywall and with a brilliant combat system [despite 20 hours of play, I still feel like there's a trick somewhere] — but you're bored with the anime style and plot for kids, this game is for you.

However, as everyone expected from a Genshin-type game, the multiplayer is terribly weak. Don't expect great co-op with your friends, as exploring together is pointless. You can't do practically any quests together, and the game even kicks you out of the area where the host is doing the quest. It's a shame about the wasted potential, as a lot of the mechanics look like they were made for fun in co-op, but well... it is what it is. (arena is fun tho)

Overall
If you liked slashers such as Stellar Blade, if you liked gacha games with a monetization system straight out of mobile games (this time it's not that bad) such as ToF or Genshin, if you're into Tsushima vibes, then this game is for you. If you're expecting a co-op game, skip it.

WWM is a fantastic game. The amount of interactability is insane for such a free game. The bosses are fun on the highest difficulty, parrying and learning their patterns can be satisfying, and the story itself is made with passion and actually quite hilarious.

I'd say gear optimization and the energy system are holding this game back for me, because it's constantly fighting you to get the "good rolls" for your gear, which, by the way, you have to invest a lot of time to get better. 

And while having god rolls is not really necessary to complete the game, not being able to create a variety of builds because you can't spread your resources thin by investing in multiple weapon and gear sets, is probably the reason why I think it's kinda boring for me.

A solid game sadly crushed under the weight of its predatory and exploitative take on gacha mechanics. This is supplemented by the addition of manipulative tactics to trick players into spending ever increasing amounts for mostly little to no return on investment. You can spend hundreds of dollars and walk away with items that are completely useless, like fireworks or meals that heal you. These are once off items that offer no further benefit.

They double down on the aggressive monetization with thinly-veiled nickel-and-diming that quickly spiral down into more aggressive tactics to extract ridiculous amounts of cash from the player. On top of this they have an item shop where a single item can cost the price of a full Triple-A game. That's right. For the price of one outfit you can purchase and entire AAA game. 

Then they have a battle-pass; another carefully constructed "feature" that hides its malicious design intent behind the guise of "you can earn everything". Sure, except that progress is tuned to a crawl. You need to grind and grind some more, or you know, purchase one of the "convenient" packages that will skip ahead slightly on the progress bar. Only by a little bit, to ensure you come back for more.

I wish I could say that these are the only monetization hurdles to overcome. You will need to spends tens- to hundreds of dollars if you want to change your hair colour to anything remotely acceptable. Surely you can dye your armor? Nope - that's a "premium" feature that comes with a price tag to match. We're not talking about a few bucks here - these things are monetized so aggressively that I truly can't see anyone other than whales getting the cosmetic look they desire. In case you missed it, you have to purchase the outfit and then purchase several dyes and then there are even more purchases which allow you to slightly modify certain parts of an outfit. 

In good conscience I cannot recommend a game that blatantly take advantage of human beings and exploit their vulnerability for monetary gain. Is there a good game here? Sure, they made it appealing enough so you would want to play more and spend an even greater amount. The game literally reads like a to-do list of things that feed into player's dopamine addiction.

If you can control your impulses, and don't care for cosmetics (aka, looking badass), then give this game a whirl, but I beg all of you, don't give these guys your hard-earned money. Don't let them take advantage of you (by design).

Gotta say, this is one mixed bag and that's why it's good. If you played these games: Genshin Impact, Soulslikes, any new modern asian MMORPG, action RPG games and Ghost of Tsushima. Yeah, take those and mix it in one pot and you get Where Winds Meet. It is so good that it's stupid. Free to play game shouldn't be this good. There's currently 200 hours content for solo mode only and that is a lot. 

How does the game work? You can freely change from your solo world to the MMORPG-lite world and create your own co-op world where anyone can join freely. There's tons of activities. World bosses, public dungeons, matchmaking bosses and trials. Campaign bosses like in Genshin Impact, you just do the story boss again for loot and use the daily stamina points on it. All the content use this but it generates fairly quickly during the day and max cap is 400. 

How is it this good and free to play? Yeah, it has gacha but only cosmetics. There is ZERO pay to win mechanics on this. You can't skip anything by paying but you can literally buy the sickest and coolest cosmetics. The amount of effort they have put in these is sick. Details are so amazing. 

Combat is like Sekiro but much easier. You can even select your difficulty for this game how easy you want your world to be and assisted deflections etc. It is very casual friendly that anyone can pick up. All the martial arts are absolutely unique and different. There's dps, heal and tank weapons that give different mythic skills and martial arts. It's sick, there's so much depth in the mechanics that it feels overwhelming and can make many new players not interested. It's easy to just pick up the 1h sword + heal fan combo. Can do almost anything solo when you learn to play the style. Professions are sick. So far I have only leveled up the healing professions and it works that you heal npcs in the world or other players. It is a whole mini game itself and insanely unique one too. Scholarship I haven't tried yet but will pick up that eventually. 

There's just so much I could write about this game and I suggest trying it out. It's free. Graphics and audio absolutely gorgeous looking. Story so far has been ok but I have side tracked a lot due to exploring so much and doing different quests, got myself that strategic sword which is insanely good 1h sword art. Learning about the sect guilds that are in the game and started doing co-op content and events. 

Game can't be perfect tho. It will exhaust you since the UI is absolute garbage and confusing. It will take a couple of hours to learn from which you can do the thing you want. Lip syncing is bad, you can't adjust the chat window size and with higher resolutions it looks like complete ant crap. It suffers from few choices that only are used in asian multiplayer games. The chat is garbage and until they give way to adjust the size, opacity and other stuff you might miss a lot of stuff what players are saying. English voice acting is pretty horrible, they should hire much better ones. Chinese one is good but since you can't adjust the dialogue opacity or subtitles size you can miss a lot of stuff. The subtitles tend to overlap some UI parts totally making it a huge mess. There's been lots of complaining about the UI so I bet it will receive overhauls at some point.

I can't speak anything bad about the performance since for me the game runs on ultra, capped 120 (averaging  between 60-100) fps, 2560x1440p with DLSS and frame gen. You'd think the game would be a huge performance mess with how the game looks but it works really well. 

I recommend this game, check it out if you like action RPGs. You can play solo the whole story and about the whole content. You don't ever have to touch the multiplayer side if you don't want to. Switching between the modes is so easy and simple.

This game is mostly a f2p single player wuxia RPG game with dozens of hours of story, side quests, exploration & collecting. The environments are neat and the clothing aesthetics are dope - lots of flowy robes, long hair etc. It's one of the few games I think where the male outfits have parity with female outfits and even look better sometimes. I also appreciate that it didn't devolve immediately into the women running around in thong bikinis in a cynical "sex sells" kind of way. I find that incredibly boring nowadays so a game that has a strong visual identity without delving into that is pretty cool.

You can't really co-op the main story, and it's not really an MMO in that you can't see other people run around in your world, so some people might find that disappointing. There are co-op aspects like beating bosses or just social stuff like standing around chatting or playing mahjong. Speaking of, the combat for bosses is a bit souls-like with lots of deflecting/parrying going on, and it's pretty fun.

As mentioned earlier the environments look good, but for a game that I'm running at ultra/high settings on a pretty beefy rig, it feels like the engine often forgets to bother with lighting and a lot of stuff looks flat and low-res. I don't know if they'll fix this down the line but it sometimes takes me out of the game with a bit when it happens, and I've played f2p live service games that legitimately don't really drop in quality at high settings (like infinity nikki).

Localization - hit or miss, I think. I actually thought the first story arc was emotionally charged and pretty well-done. I have heard a lot of people complain but I think people also expect a bit too much. In the west many people don't have the cultural/historical experience with this genre (but no better way than to just... start experiencing it, lol) and many things absolutely won't translate 1-to-1, either the idioms or the symbolic (but compact) way that chinese works as a language. I think they did a decent job in some places but not others. I mean, opening a treasure chest is labeled as "enable". I play on CN dub but I've heard the EN dub is mediocre and even uses AI voice acting (which is definitely not great), so I would not be surprised if a lot of the translation was also done via LLM.

The UI/UX is absolutely terrible. I've been playing live service, mobile, and/or gacha games for close to two decades now  so I am totally used to all the freemium nested menus, red dots everywhere etc. But this game is like 4 steps beyond that. I do not normally get overwhelmed or confused when gaming but the UI here is absolutely annoying, sometimes overwhelming, and I even had cases where I *knew* a menu existed but could not figure out how to get back to it. I think that the hundreds of menus in this game is going to be a big hurdle, especially to a lot of casual gamers who aren't used to navigating that type of thing. 

The monetization is primarily cosmetics. I am fine with that. My favorite live service games follow a similar model, and I've spent hundreds if not thousands on games like path of exile and warframe. HOWEVER... and [b]this is the primary reason this gets a "don't recommend"[/b] review. I do not mind paid cosmetics, especially a variety of pricing tiers (there's a boat you can buy that costs $40-60k US dollars btw lol), but what I do mind is when [b]global is treated like a second class citizen[/b] to the game's home country.

Recently an outfit came out that can cost over 7000 pearls (over $100) in a gacha, which was a 2580 pearl direct purchase shop outfit in CN (about $40). There is nothing different about this outfit and no reason for them to have changed it for our version other than pure greed. When i saw this, it knocked the wind right out of my sails. I don't play games to be reminded that all I'm there for is my wallet, and that my money is somehow worse than someone else's. I just want equal treatment between the global and CN clients, and I don't think that's too much to ask. It's 2025 and it's the digital age - we can just see what is happening in CN and see how they're treated, so I don't know why I'd put up with being treated worse for no reason. On top of this pricing change, we're also missing an in-game marketplace that CN has that would have allowed f2p players to slowly earn pearls/cosmetics using in-game currency (think of gold/WoW tokens or trading for plat in warframe).

I don't take the time to review games very often. Like many other people, I find this game to be overall fun. It doesn't take much for me to enjoy a game, and this one has many flaws. The localization is poor, there's no way to slow down unspoken dialogue progression so I regularly miss large sections of conversations, navigating the various menus is extremely painful and half the time I don't know where something is in the UI. But the combat is fun, bosses are challenging, there's tons to explore, it's all beautiful. That's usually good enough for me.

But I can't in good conscience recommend a game with business practices this predatory. We have the normal gacha dark patterns - currencies for currency, a sense of being flooded with rewards from the myriad different systems, timed events and daily log-in bonuses. But the "free" or low cost options for draws are few and far between, the rewards for bad draws are really, really bad, the "reward flood" is typically a flood of miniscule amounts or worthless items.

And, of course, there is the first draw special event that everyone is upset about. An event with an item pool of 7-8, and with each draw, that item is removed for better chances at the others. Unfortunately they don't clearly mention that the cost of each subsequent draw is almost exponentially more than the last, until the last three draws cost roughly $15, $30, and $50 respectively. Imagine paying $50 for a single draw. All the while luring the less-wary by concepts like "there's only two draws left to finish the set!"

No. This is absurd. I'm ashamed that I even dropped $30 on the special event. Be extremely careful if you play this game, and I would recommend withholding support - either verbally or monetarily - until (or if) these practices change.

Best Open world Free game I have played in a long time, if not ever. I maybe slightly biased as I enjoy Murim  Manhwa but this really scratches an itch.
However, despite my bias opinion and as a gamer I have to say that this beats many Games, even the paid For Triple A titles. 
It has a soul like feel, MMO-Like Wrap to it with a style near to Genshin or similar Titles. However, it actually Stands Far out from these and blends a nice mixture of each with something for everybody. It has its own take on things and i really like what they have done to try and truly immerse you in the games content. I love How you have to Watch NPCS in order to learn new Skills and Use other weapons and the various ways to to boost Dmg and really Make it For your Playstyle. I mean... What else can i say about the game. You Can even get married to other players and if they cheat you can put bounties on them or Go to prison and have Veggies thrown at you. 

A Few Points to make: 

Is it pay to win? 
-No, not at all. 

Is it AI Slop Like some claim it to be? 
- No... It uses an AI Chat system so you can actually have conversations with NPC's in the game and You have to use your own words to Convince, Cheer up or Help NPC's so they become your friends and you can summon them to help in Boss fights or They Send you Gifts every so often to Help You. That's Basically it to my Knowledge. 

Combat
- Very Nice and smooth in my Opinion, Though I play in the ARPG Control mode I believe so I'm not sure about the MMO Style mode. 

Can I play this Alone?
-I am very Anti-social for the most part and I can Honestly say this game really thought about solo Players. Of course Some content Requires Some Social activity but you don't have to say a word and its only for some Events or Quests for little rewards to help you. Completely up to you how many toes You Dip into the online mode. 

Side note
- Visuals, Graphics and optimization are Honestly Really Good or at least from My Experience and PC build which is a top Mid Tier Build or maybe just mid tier Build now. So I have no issues, I run a Rtx 3060 with a Crappy Ryzen 5 3600x  (Seriously Need Updating) But I've had 0 issues and the game is Stunning.

Overall - 9/10 Game So Far. Really Shocked me and I wasn't expecting it.

Where Winds Meet is a surprisingly impressive game, especially considering that it’s completely free. Set during the last years of the Ten Kingdoms era, it drops you into a world full of wandering warriors, political intrigue, and scenic landscapes that feel pulled straight out of classic wuxia stories.

      The open world is easily the highlight. One moment you’re climbing mist-covered cliffs, the next you’re wandering through quiet villages or weaving through busy market streets. There’s always something happening nearby—random encounters, small side stories, or hidden spots that reward exploration. For a free title, the world feels unusually detailed and lively.

      Combat embraces full wuxia fantasy, and it’s a lot of fun. You can sprint across rooftops, parry arrows, use flashy sword techniques, and chain together abilities in a way that feels stylish without being overly complicated. Character growth is flexible too, letting you mix stealth, martial arts, and other skills depending on how you want to play.

      The story takes a bit to pick up, but once it does, it balances personal moments with larger political tension. Many of the side quests feel handcrafted rather than filler, which is another pleasant surprise.

      There are still some rough edges—occasional performance dips and the odd stiff animation—but given that the game doesn’t cost anything, it’s hard to complain too much. The overall experience is far above what you’d expect from a free-to-play open-world RPG.

Conclusion:
      Where Winds Meet delivers a rich world, stylish combat, and a true wuxia atmosphere—without asking for a dime. For a free game, it’s impressively polished and absolutely worth trying.

After spending over 50 hours with Where Winds Meet, I’m truly impressed by the skill and ambition shown in this evolving open-world wuxia experience. The game offers a great sense of freedom, letting players shape their own martial-arts journey without pushing a specific playstyle. I’ve enjoyed using a balanced mix of combat styles, switching between fluid close-range swordplay, ranged encounters, and unique martial techniques. This variety makes each battle feel dynamic and rewarding.

World exploration is a major highlight. From lively towns to stunning mountains and ancient buildings, every area feels carefully designed and full of detail. Whether you’re discovering hidden secrets, making moral decisions, or just enjoying the view, there’s always a good reason to stray from the main path.

Narratively, the game blends history, mythology, and personal storytelling well, making sure quests feel engaging rather than repetitive. The progression system encourages experimentation and rewards players who take the time to master different skills and explore various role-playing options.

Overall, Where Winds Meet offers a captivating and beautifully crafted adventure that keeps growing in depth the more you play. I highly recommend this title to friends and fellow gamers who appreciate freedom in gameplay, stylish combat, and immersive world-building.

I was extremely hesitant because of Net Ease being the publisher, they normally have extremely greedy and aggressive monetisation practices but I thought: Hey, the game is free, might as well give it a try.

The gacha is purely for cosmetics so far and as someone who has actually played predatory gachas that actually straight up block or impede your progression if you don't pull for the newer stuff (Looking at you, Hoyoverse) I'm ok with this. I believe that the paid mounts do have some exploration advantages? They're able to auto follow roads, you can have other players ride with you and they can point out resources in the world so it makes it a bit easier to find. Whenever that's a deal breaker for you or not is up to you.

We've all played genshin during the pandemic; the exploration + solo world is a lot like it. Imo it's more immersive since there's a befriend NPC mechanic, if you're into role play. The game implements an AI chatbot that you can converse with which is a beautiful implementation of AI in a video game that isn't just stealing other people's hard work. All the NPC's are unique, you can talk with most of them [strike] You can commit crimes, have bounty hunters (Players or NPC) hunt you and be sent to jail [/strike]. There's people walking on the roads, bandits that will trick you into helping them only to steal your horse. You can duel NPC's with the sheer power of yapping or heal people by hitting their broken bones.

You experience the story in this purely solo exploration world as if the game was just an rpg and once you reach level 10, you have access to the coop/multiplayer aspect of the game. You can either invite friends to your world to make it a 4 player coop or go Online.
There is no story available in the Online part of the world, only multiplayer activities. You can wrestle other players, participate in a shame parade and throw eggs and vegetables at the players who are exiting jail. Beg for money and have players hand over a few coins. Play a music rhythm game against other players. There's more but then this review would get too long.
There are guilds, brotherhoods, discipleship, marriages (if you're part of the Harem sect, you can have up to 5 spouses!)

Overall, I'm having so much more fun than I expected and if the raiding content is interesting (if there are raids at all) I might just drop FFXIV for good :O

I’m one of the players who have been following the game since the beta and who supported the arrival of Where Winds Meet with a lot of enthusiasm — but I was disappointed by the latest update (after only one week since the global launch, I know).

For me, WWM had the perfect balance between the free part of the game and the paid aspect, which relied entirely on cosmetics. Despite a few differences compared to the Chinese version — like the gacha banner containing two gacha elements, which prevents us from focusing on the cosmetic we actually want and pushes us to pull more, or the pearl prices with no regional adjustment depending on the country, and the overall higher cost — I still told myself it was “fair game” as long as the rest of the shop stayed consistent with the CN version’s philosophy.

Nothing more. Not asking for special treatment. Just equal products for the global players and the CN servers.

Well, that wish lasted… a week. We’re already seeing unjustified price increases for the global version and a sad x10 token “compensation” used as a shut-up ring.

What shocks me the most is how comfortable NetEase felt pulling something like this just one week after the server launched.
What’s next?
Tripling the prices was already bad enough; removing NPCs that allowed us to earn in-game outfit tokens was the breaking point.

We will be taken advantage of — even though we support the game with our time and our investment. I dont want to be seen and treated as a second class player.

A GOOD F2P GAME WITH PREDATORY MONETISATION :

After playing this game for hours on end since release, I can confidently say that this is one of the best free-to-play titles to land on Steam in recent years.
This ARPG/MMO hybrid is rooted in wuxia fantasy and set in a stunning world where every region feels intentional, alive, and rewarding to explore.

⚔️ Combat & Gameplay

The combat system and movement are insane — fluid, expressive, and deeply satisfying in both PvE and PvP.
If there’s one drawback, it’s the “Legendary” difficulty: the encounters are exactly the same as Expert, just with comically inflated health bars. Boss fights and even casual open-world encounters can drag on for minutes — sometimes for nearly an hour, as with Tian Ying and its three phases.

🌏 Exploration & Variety

Exploration, mini-games, and mission diversity genuinely enrich the experience. They don’t just give you something fun to do — they help you progress by unlocking new Inner Ways, martial arts, and stat points. After 60 hours spent just in Qinghe, I still have more to uncover.

💸 Monetisation

This is where the game stumbles.
The battle pass barely adds value; you get more loot from a single outpost than from five BP levels. Skins in the shop are priced similarly to other NetEase titles (e.g., Marvel Rivals), but the premium system raises questions like:

Why does a skin cost 50,000?

Why are reforged weapons 2,000?

Why does the flagship banner skin require TWO pitties?

Most banner pulls (99% of them) are items you can find for free just by playing normally.
The monetisation runs very deep, and it feels predatory. I would strongly recommend that the average player avoid engaging with it altogether.

✅ Final Verdict

As a free-to-play game, Where Winds Meet is fantastic — generous, fun, and filled with content.
But once you factor in the monetisation, it becomes hard to ignore how scammy the premium systems feel.

Great game, bad monetisation. If you can enjoy it without spending, you’ll have an amazing time.

Was expecting gacha slop. Instead I got a grand Wuxia adventure.

Game looks incredible, but runs well. Combat is good, but don't go in expecting Devil May Cry.
Chinese voice acting is good (there's English too), sound design is good, music is good.
Story is good. It's not Final Fantasy X level or anything, but it's no slouch either.
The world is gorgeous and has an absolute truckload of stuff to do.

At its core, it plays somewhat similarly to if Elden Ring and Skyrim had a secret child.
Combat (at least on expert difficulty) is fun and challenging. It forces you to use all the tools at your disposal and learn to parry. If you're after something more casual, the lower difficulties give you the option of using an auto parry that requires its own meter.
The rewards for diving into caves and dungeons are very good too.
You can run up and along walls, dive underwater or even run on the water's surface. You can also get some very over-the-top skills that allow you to soar through the air.
You can learn to be a doctor and cure other players (or NPCs) ailments. There are a lot of minigames and each of them are actually fun. You can sneak into Wushu sects and steal their skills by observing them.

Despite the game being free, there's no P2W and there's an obscene amount of things to do.
There is an outfit gacha, unfortunately, but you can get lots of nice outfits, hairstyles and accessories for free just by playing (you can get gacha currency for free too, of course).
The game either plays as a solo adventure with optional co-op, or as essentially an MMO-lite.
You can equip two weapon types at once, each with multiple different martial art styles, and switch between them freely on the fly.

Edit: I honestly forgot some gripes. Currently the co-op is incredibly laggy. It's nice that you can play with friends and actually do quests together. The person joining goes directly into the hosts world, no special co-op world where you can do basically nothing, but main story quests are single player only and the lag is honestly quite shocking. It's still servicable, but I don't see end game raiding online being possible.
The game can also be quite buggy at times and the translation, while decent, is far from perfect.
I'm also not sure if it's impressive or infuriating that the enemy AI is smart enough to capitalise on buggyness and surround you while you're caught on geometry or an invisible wall and absolutely pummel you.
On higher difficulties basic enemies can also feel very tanky. It would probably be more fun if they had less health and were more aggressive. It can be very annoying when a random group of enemies is smart enough to harass you with melee units while archers sit in the back and you're stuck on a rock and the random archer has more health than you do.

It's the only game, aside from TLoZ Breath of the Wild, that got me to truly enjoy an open world.
Game is free, so there's no reason not to at least try it.

[h1]Singleplayer Game with Co-op – Why I Don’t Recommend It[/h1]

The game itself is a single-player game with a co-op option; it has NOTHING to do with an MMORPG. It plays VERY much like Assassin’s Creed, with tons of small mini-games and challenges on the map that give you small rewards. I can’t recommend the game – here are the details:

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Positives[/h2]

It’s great that you really get a feeling of being rewarded for exploring the world, because there’s so much cool stuff to see everywhere, though over time it also gets a bit sluggish.

The side quests are small tasks from citizens that often involve their lives a bit, which lets you dive more into the world, if that’s important to you.

Combat feels good in terms of handling.

The world is relatively large and feels really cool in terms of layout and visuals.

The graphics are genuinely awesome.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Negatives[/h2]

Way too many menus and weird rewards that you get for every little bit of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

You can only have one character and you can’t delete that character. That means if you want to switch the difficulty to Legendary, you can’t – you have to create a new account.

You always level up to the next 10-level threshold and then you have to play Breakout, which is only available every 24 hours. That means you can gain at most 10 levels per day.

Gearing and leveling feel super useless, because you don’t actually get any stronger. The enemies always scale with your level, so it’s completely pointless.

The flying skill is pretty cool at the start, but the animation massively sucks after the third time, because it drags everything out unnecessarily.

Combat is well done, but it gets boring really fast. The trash mobs all work the same and are positioned the same way in the open world, so it’s just boring.

Boss fights also become dead boring after 2–3 bosses, because all you do is throw out a few attacks, then pop your E for the parry on the boss’s attacks, and keep repeating that until you can finally use F for the finisher to deal more damage. Then that rotation starts all over again. It’s super annoying and works exactly the same for every boss. Once you’ve beaten one, you just have to pay attention to the animation on the next one, but apart from that there is zero “logic” to the bosses.

Mini-games suck.

The drinking game, for example: you have to maneuver an icon with keyboard and mouse into a moving circle, keep it there for a set time and then click – just annoying.
The speech duel with cards isn’t turn-based, which sucks a bit because it’s so hectic.
The mini-game with the barrels and shooting arrows often only starts after talking to the NPC several times – totally unnecessary.
The mini-games themselves are just repetitive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They’re boring after the second time because there’s no variety at all.

When you’re in an open-world dungeon, you often can’t use your agility skills like wall-running, double jump, etc. That massively breaks immersion.

On top of that, when you die in such a dungeon, you get teleported out – sometimes even directly to the boss, even though you were still at the beginning. I was even teleported once to the wrong boss of another dungeon that I had already killed. Also, when you get teleported out, you sometimes can’t even find the dungeon entrance again because it’s not shown on the map.
The boss area in some dungeons is placed so badly that if you explore the boss room to see whether there are treasure chests and then run back into the boss’s spawn area, the boss just keeps respawning every ~30 seconds. That basically gives you zero chance to actually explore the room.
Some dungeons are so badly designed that you often get stuck and have to use the unstuck function, which ultimately also means you get teleported outside and then have to find and run back in again. That happened to me at least four times, because as a curious explorer you want to look at everything.

Some dialogues can be skipped with Space, others can’t. Feels totally arbitrary.

Speeding up dialogue with R to 1.25x etc. is more annoying than helpful.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Overall[/h2]

Overall, I think the game is well made, but I still can’t recommend it, because it’s never clear what the game actually wants to be. I personally find the story boring, the characters are poorly staged, and there’s no real tension curve or anything like that.

The open world is useless to explore, because even if you get “stronger”, it has zero impact on your actual power in the world – the mobs scale with you. So you never feel like you’re making any real progress, which is also missing visually on the character. You do have costumes you can equip, which is cool, but in the context of the world it’s all Chinese-style clothing. That means it mostly looks like everyday clothes and nothing about it feels imposing or epic.

If you just want to kill some time, it’s a great game – especially since it’s free. But:

if you’re into MMORPGs – this is not one;

if you’re into story – it’s dull;

and if you’re into awesome fights – everything here is way too routine and repetitive to really be a challenge.

🌄 A World That Feels Alive

Where Winds Meet delivers one of the most immersive open worlds I’ve experienced in years.
From the golden fields of Huainan to the mist-covered mountains of Jiangnan, every location feels hand-crafted with heart.

NPCs live believable lives, random events feel organic, and the world constantly rewards wandering. I found myself exploring for hours without touching the main quest, simply because everything invites curiosity. The atmosphere alone makes this game worth playing.

⚔️ Combat That Flows Like Poetry

Combat is fast, fluid, stylish, and deeply satisfying.
Whether you're:

parrying a warlord’s flaming spear,

running across bamboo stalks mid-fight, or

performing a perfect wuxia aerial finisher…

…you feel like the hero of your own martial arts epic.

Multiple disciplines, seamless weapon swapping, and skill combos give you the freedom to fight in your own style. Every duel feels like a cinematic moment.

🎭 A Story Full of Mystery, Emotion, and Depth

The narrative surprised me in the best way.
It begins quietly, but slowly pulls you into a tangled mystery involving:

your missing Uncle Jiang,

the secrets surrounding Aunt Han,

political tensions,

hidden identities,

and an undercurrent of supernatural intrigue.

The world may look peaceful, but everyone wears a mask — literally and figuratively. The storytelling feels like a beautiful blend of wuxia legends and emotional drama.

I genuinely care about these characters… maybe too much.

🧭 Freedom to Live Your Wuxia Life

This isn’t just a combat RPG. It’s a living wuxia life simulator.

You can…

hunt, fish, cook,

become a doctor, musician, or blacksmith,

free prisoners, help strangers, solve crimes,

or simply travel as a wandering swordsman.

The freedom is incredible. The game respects your pace and your playstyle.

🎨 Visuals & Music — A Work of Art

The visuals are breathtaking.
Character animations feel weighty and natural, lighting is gorgeous, and scenery often looks like paintings from classical Chinese art.

The soundtrack deserves special praise. The calm flute melodies and emotional orchestral themes make every moment feel cinematic.

🐉 Performance & Polish

For such a massive world, the performance is surprisingly good.
Smooth combat, stable framerate, and almost no immersion-breaking bugs across my 100 hours.

Considering the scale and ambition, this is impressive.

⭐ Final Verdict

Where Winds Meet is the most refreshing game I’ve played in years.
It recaptures that old feeling of discovering a world full of wonder — something many modern games forgot.

If you love:
✔ wuxia
✔ open-world exploration
✔ emotional storytelling
✔ stylish combat
✔ beautiful art direction

…then this game will steal your heart like it did mine.

I played 100 hours in 6 days, and every minute was worth it.

👉 10/10 — A modern wuxia masterpiece.

TLDR: This game is for you if you like character customization, open world exploration with a wuxia theme, occassionally co-oping with friends, and MMO socialization. 

This game scratches the itch of playing an open world game where I can complete on my own and also occasionally co-op with friends and do quests together. I really like the ancient Chinese wuxia theme, it brings me back to the old HK dramas I used to watch as a kid. For those who like MMOs, there are a lot of activities you can do in the multiplayer rooms; you can hang out in the main hub, throw veggies at players who are being paraded as prisoners, you can play minigames such as mahjong, madiao, Chinese chess, there is a handful of combat activites like 1v1, and battle royale too. 

As for the monetary side of things, I like that it's not [i]as[/i] predatory as the other F2P games I've played. The gacha and outfit shop are all cosmetics only and doesn't affect gameplay mechanics. You don't need to pull on the banners for "the latest and greatest" to chase the meta. The least expensive outfit is 60 pearls which equate to $1.39 CAD plus tax, and the most expensive sets go for 2580 pearls which will need the 3000 pearl pack for $70 CAD plus tax. Again, the spending is only for cosmetic appearances, whether or not you purchase anything will not affect how you progress through the game. There are still plenty of outfits and accessories to obtain through regular gameplay and they all look really appealing, including some of the sillier sets like the one rewarded from Path of the Strong. 

So far, my only gripe with this game is the amount of menus hidden within menus. It makes it difficult to find what I'm looking for especially when I was just starting out and figuring out what are martial skills and mystic skills, how to level up my gear, etc. There are also a lot of different reward lists and events going on and it feels like everything is all over the place and disorganized. Each time I think I'm done with finding reward lists, another one shows up later!! Hopefully the devs can figure out a better way to organize the menu UIs.

🌟 Final Thoughts
Where Winds Meet is a rare blend of compelling storytelling, refined gameplay, and gorgeous visuals. Whether you're a fan of open world adventures, wuxia-style action, or simply enjoy immersive storytelling, this game is absolutely worth playing. It delivers not just entertainment, but an experience.

Okay, so, the game is great. It's a lot of fun, the world is immersive, the story doesn't suck, combat's weighty and a bit more involved than mindless mashing and there's a massive amount of content even for a paid game. For a free one? It's mindblowing. I highly recommend at least trying it out. There are issues with localization and the UI is atrocious, but those problems do nor overshadow how strong the core game is.

So. Why the negative review?

Because of treatment of global players as paypigs. Yesterday (20.11), a new outfit was added to the game. Not a big deal, right? It is a f2p game after all, they gotta make their money somewhere. On CN server, the outfit was easily buyable in the shop just like the rest of the outfits. It costed ~2.5k of premium currency there. On global server, however, they made an idiotic decision to include it via a special draw event. A large banner will appear when first launching the game after update, inviting you to check it out. Once you click it, you are transported to a screen where 7 rollable components are visible, and you are encouraged to roll at a rate of 60 premium currency per roll. Hey, that's cheap! 60*7=420, much less than in CN! 
Only, it's not 60*7. The cost increases sharply after each pull, ultimately making the whole 7 element set cost 7440(!) of premium currency, almost 3x as much as on CN server. It is also the only way to get the outfit, which brings us to our second point...

All evidence points to the player skin trading system, present in CN version, being completely removed from the global version. Meaning that while a dedicated F2P player in CN would, eventually, be able to get a few of the more expensive cosmetics for just playing the game, global players have no such opportunity.

Therefore, I strongly implore you - play the game. If you like Tsushima, Sekiro, newer AC games or Wuxia vibes, chances are you will greatly enjoy it.
But do not spend a single cent. Such treatment of Global players is unacceptable and the only thing we can do is vote with our wallets. I was planning on getting the battle + monthly pass for the game, not because I need it, but because I wanted to support the devs at least a little, but now I will not spend a dime until global gets full financial parity with CN.

Blah:
- Too many currencies.
- Everything seems to have it's own way to upgrade.
- Too many things to keep track of and where to find it, okay, I don't HAVE to...
- Multiplayer exists, but you still have to complete the story in solo.
- I'm not a fan of having to wait on progressing the game; breakthroughs take a day, two, or more before you can progress.  Although, this probably won't be a big deal for new players, just those of us that started on release.
- I don't understand the manual parry/deflection system, I always seem to do it wrong.
- There isn't always an trigger for automatic deflection system and I suck at the manual system.
- How many of the bounties are already taken or no longer exist.  I should only see ones that exist.
- When running and then getting stuck in a tree.  Happens about once every couple hours?
- Some quests are either buggy or too difficult to complete.  Just in-case, log out and back in when you get stuck.

Hate:
- I felt locked in on the intro/tutorial of the game.  It would have been nice to be able to open my settings during that.
- I know it's a free game and I don't have to buy anything, but I despise expensive cosmetics.  Don't waste your money on cosmetics, it's a gotcha!  Spend responsibly.
- I hate not knowing the purchase rules, for instance, the new set of items says it's 80 pearls to try your luck at getting an item.  It doesn't say that the cost is going to go up to 160 for your second try.  Seems like a trick!  It probably goes up even more on future tries?
- I suck at the PvP arena combat.  That's on me though, not the game.  :p
- Make it a MMORPG like one of it's labels and allow co-op in the story rather than restricting it to solo.
- The archery quests that have you shooting explosive barrels, they suck.
- Fishing challenges are horrible or I'm doing something wrong.  I may need to try a controller for it b/c it doesn't work great with my trackball mouse.

I recommend the game.  Feel free to stop by and ask me questions about it when I'm streaming on Twitch.tv/Sarcoth.

Tried this completely on a whim. Kind of figured it would be typical mobile gatcha slop. But damn was I wrong, the world has a huge amount of lore and depth to it. It has a huge sense of immersion as the world is gorgeous and throws all sorts of random emergent events at you, that happen organically as you explore. One minute I'm yeeting a bear off a cliff to kill it, the next I am fighting for my life against a daoist on a donkey as he chucks boulders at me in a dreamscape fighting arena. The game constantly surprises you in the coolest of ways. The combat feels really smooth and responsive but has depth, as deflection timing, weapon swapping, and dodge timing are all needed to survive. You also can sneak into rival sects and steal their techniques to learn different martial arts disciplines, which is a cool bit of world building.  The shear amount of things to explore is massive, I've dumped 40 hours into it thus far and I'm only 42% done with the first zone, so needless to say the content is definitely there. But I have to say the biggest issue this game has is it's menus, tutorials, and quest journal. For one there are way too many menus and their lay outs are convoluted as all hell, I spent the better part of the first 10 hours learning what they all did. Which brings to the next problem, the tutorials are way too brief and quite often kind of useless, as they don't functionally explain what you are supposed to do. This brevity leads into the issues with quest journal, the game only allows you like 20 seconds to track the quest, otherwise you have to slog through the multi menus within the quest journal, and if you didn't catch the quest text good luck with finding it in that mess of a journal. The frequency of having to deal with this can be grating as hell at times, and can take away from the otherwise wonderful immersion of this game. Overall the game is great in a majority of aspects, if not standout in a couple areas, and while the obtuse menus and system bloat can grate at times, it's never been enough to detract from the huge amount of fun I'm having with this game. Would definitely recommend the game, was probably the most pleasant surprise game, of the year for me thus far. Also Infernal Twin Blades are dope AF.
