Have you ever been really enjoying a game and then hit an event that took the wind out of your sails completely? That was me at the end of the first story arc. 

The open-world, the gameplay, and the character creator had me invested. I dumped some ten hours into the game before reaching the point of no return for the first story arc, Heaven has no Pier. I didn't love the story, it was neigh incomprehensible to me at quite a few parts and tbh I couldn't tell you what the main plot was even now. There's a few moments where it seems to shift almost comically in tone, but I tried to push past it in the hopes that something was lost in translation. The monetization wasn't something I loved about the game but it didn't bother me enough to stop, it's mostly just gacha gimmicks.

What really stuck in my craw though was playing the entire game up until the final boss fight at their recommended difficulty and having 0 issues. Then after the final boss starts for the Heaven has no Pier story arc the game floors it off a cliff. The first phase you get helped by an NPC who does almost all the hard work for you, you can't learn anything about the boss from this phase because chucklehead is literally tanking and out dpsing you and it's mostly on autopilot. Then the game stops, stares you right in face and asks "Got all that? Good." It rips the floaties off and throws you into a deep-end infested with sharks. The boss now is using moves you haven't ever had to fight against while dealing damage you can't protect against, and not leaving any breathing room for you to attack back. When all of that overwhelms you and your character lies dead on the floor the game will tell you you didn't level up your abilities enough. Ok let's do that and try again. Fast forward and you're dead again, the game will now tell you you're not blocking the right attacks, or you didn't dodge at the right time. Ok let's try again but I'll lookout for the parry and dodge call-outs. Fast forward and you're dead again. Now the game says ok champ lower the difficulty and we'll pause time to hold your hand through the combat. What follows is the most brainless combat I've ever slogged through, not only can you not get hurt, the prompt for the parry is slowed down and emphasized and to a mocking degree, then you get to button mash her to death. I still couldn't tell you what the timing was for any of the parry mechanics, I couldn't even tell you which of her flurry of attacks was the one the parry and which to dodge. And I sure couldn't tell you where I got the materials to level up my talents, my gear or my character. 

After "defeating" the boss you get to watch a gruelingly long cut scene that's another tonal departure from what came before showcasing you and the aforementioned NPC kicking ass and drinking together doing things you wish you could have done moments ago in the boss fight. Then the tone shifts again, you get knocked out and... now you're a horse. Finally realizing I would not only never understand the combat of this game, but I also would never understand the story I signed-off and uninstalled. I guess... thanks for the free 11 hours of gameplay?

Yes, it's actually [b]free[/b]. Progression is not made unfairly difficult—it doesn't force you to buy packs or materials. Most of the real-money purchases are purely cosmetic. You can find and earn materials, and/or use in-game currency (which you earn naturally just by playing), to get everything you need in order to get stronger.

Yes, there are some minor bugs and localization issues, but the team has been faithfully updating and fixing problems throughout these first few days of global release. The game is beautiful, vast, and filled with content. The combat is fun once you get the hang of the controls, and there are a good number of options for diversifying your build.

The biggest issue for me is navigating the layers upon layers of menus, getting lost in the different UI systems and not finding what I'm looking for. But the more you use it, the more familiar you become with it—even if it's painful for a while. The other peeve is having story quests locked behind a time-wall that makes you wait real life days before accessing them. The "saving grace" here is that there's a ton of side-quests, activities, events, and exploration to be done in the meantime.

Overall, I'm really enjoying my experience and would recommend this game.

There are three things I despise in video games.

1: Janky movement. No, I do not want to climb the tree next to me. No, I do not want to be stuck between 2 mooks and a damn pebble, or ledge. No, I did not say I wanted to jump in that direction.

In theory the movement looks like it would be really smooth. In practice, it is definitely not. Any game that hampers my ability to move as I input downright pisses me off.

2: Fighting mooks feels like a slog. I'd rather fight any boss than a pack of 5+ enemies. ESPECIALLY if there are 2 or more archers. So many generic enemies can, and will, super armor you. They can, and will, combo you. You can not perfect parry 5 people at the same time.

I played on expert, turned it down to recommended, and the mooks still feel tedious to deal with. They're not fun to fight. They're not exciting to do fancy combos against. They just suck to deal with when they're almost always in packs of 4+. And like I said, when you start getting mobs of 5+, it's just downright awful.

3: UI navigation. The menus, shops, inventory, event tab, other event tab, other event tab, collections tab, 5 other collection tabs, season tab, other shop tab, other shop tab in a different season tab, cosmetic tab, gear tab, ability tab in your gear tab, other gear tab, other ability tab, talent page, etc. etc.. You can get used to it, but that does not make it "good". In this case, it is not good -- it's straight up bad.

Now, the above withstanding, there are great elements to this game. The graphics are amazing, and the music honestly goes so well. The voice actors for the Chinese dub are superb. Even without being able to understand the words (though you can with the subtitles) you can feel the emotions in their voice. Additionally, the story is also rather enjoyable. Not the most amazing, but it's easily a solid 7.5/10.

tl;dr - non-bias review I would rate this game a 7.5/10. Good story, excellent graphics and the combat is fairly decent. The combat has a nice flow when fighting bosses in particular. Exploration is pretty cool, and honestly does feel rather enjoyable (movement issues not-withstanding. UI is bad, no sugar coating that bit.

Overall I am really enjoying the game, but these are the "bad" things:
* The menus are a damn mess (very mobile like)
* I don't really enjoy the style nor the story.
* The game pretty much tells you exactly what to do, so the puzzles are rarely (ever?) actual "puzzles".
* Even in "Exploration Mode" the interface is way too cluttered. (You can disable the interface entirely, but I'd like a middle ground.)
* There's a huge annoying notification whenever you walk or stroll.
* I'd like to disable the shimmer highlights on world items altogether and things like the XP bar and ID in the corner.
* The cutscenes somehow look worse than the actual game...
* The world feels kind of "small", or rather, the scale of everything seems small and compact.
* The game runs great overall, but there's a ton of stuttering when entering populated areas, especially in DX12, but I still run DX12 for DLSS and Frame Genertion.
* If you walk while entering bow/aim mode, the character keeps moving in the direction you were going until you release the left gamepad stick, meaning you have to stop first to strafe while aiming. (this also happens in some cutscenes and the photo mode too)
* Using mouse & keyboard, the mouse sensitivity is too high even on the lowest setting.
* The icon that tells me to right click to exit out of menus rarely works (but the gamepad 'press B/O' works)
* There's smoothing on the mouse camera, but only in some modes, and jumping between modes is quite jarring.
* There is no "Aim Camera Sensitivity" option when using mouse & keyboard, and the aiming speed is way too high even on the lowest setting.
* "Visual Styles" gets disabled during any cutscene or interaction, then re-enabled a second later, which is extremely jarring.
* The adaptive triggers on the PS5 controller sometimes gets stuck.
* There's very little feedback when switching between arrow types.
* The game displays pretty well overall in 32:9! The main complaint is that the interface can't be locked to something like 16:9, meaning things like the mini-map end up way off to the sides. Other issues like some pre-rendered movies being stretched weirdly I can live with.

Alright, I’ve been playing "Where Winds Meet" for a while now, and I gotta say—this game blew me away. For a free-to-play title, it’s absolutely packed with content. If you’re into open-world exploration, martial arts, and just vibing in a beautiful world, this one’s a rare legendary gem every gamer must play once in their lifetime.

🎭 Character Creation (THE BEST)
I think this is the only game with best character creation any FREE video game has ever given.
you can make your own character just with a good looking picture and give your own voice! seriously! you own voice in the game! and thousands of brilliant customizations you can possibly imagine.
- face sculpting is exceptional, you can literally adjust every bone in your face lol.
- great initial costumes, accessoreis (you get more in game as you play)
- just one word (too many options to build your own character as you like)

🌏 Exploration is Next-Level
This is hands down the best part of the game. You can literally lose hours just wandering around. The world feels alive—especially Keifang City, which is full of life, shops, NPCs, and random stuff to do. I found myself doing so many side activites right in the first few hours of the gameplay doing:
- 🎣 Fishing by rivers
- 🎼 Playing the guqin or harp (yes, you can actually play music! all by yourself with free tuning)
- 🍜 Buying food from vendors (eat them, cook yourself some tender meet you hunted, eggs and more)
- 🎯 Doing mini-games and random challenges (play chess, mini cat challenges, drunk pot games, more)
- 🧩 Stumbling into side quests that actually feel meaningful (ever npc has a quest or you can chat with them freely if green option pops up)
There’s always something to discover, and it never feels like filler. It’s the kind of game where you go to do one thing and end up doing ten others. (stay away from that goose boss, you better don't)

🤝 Multiplayer is Wildly Fun
This game is stacked with multiplayer content. You’ve got:
- PvP battles if you’re into that
- Chill stuff like Tiger Ring Battles, harp challenges, funny (group dances) dance emotes, group events, and co-op challenges and more (spoilers so not telling do discover for yourself).
- Tons of daily rewards just for doing checklist stuff or seasonal challenges
- And the best part? It does not have the so called "pay-to-win" we all hate. You can just enjoy the game and still get rewarded at your own pace and you will enjoy doing it.

📊 Performance? Surprisingly Great!
I’m running this on a old GTX 1060, and it still hits a smooth 60 FPS. That’s rare these days, especially for a game that looks this good. Super optimized, barely any stutters (turn Vsync on please)—even in crowded areas.

📖 Story & Quests
The main story is actually really solid. I didn’t expect much from a free game, but it’s got crazy depth, exceptionally super cool characters (Ruby my fav heroine 💌), and a lot of emotional moments. Plus, there are tons of side quests—some are super funny, some are very touching, and some are just plain superly unexpectedly weird (in a good way).

⚠️ A Few Things That Bug Me (because it just launched so not a major thing)
Okay, not everything is perfect:
- You need 100 GB of SSD space, which is a lot.
- It’s always online, even for solo play. If your internet drops, you get kicked out.
- You can’t restart the game with the same account. So if you want to start fresh, you’re out of luck unless you make a new account. (devs, please! allow us mere gamers to restart our journey we can't keep making 100s of accounts to play the game from the beginning, pretty please 🙏).
- There’s a subtitle/audio mismatch bug in some cutscenes. Not game-breaking, but definitely annoying and sometimes the subtitles just speed up before you even finish reading it.

👑 Final Verdict
If you love open-world games with tons of stuff to do, Where Winds Meet is a must-try. It’s beautiful, fun, and surprisingly deep for a free-to-play title. Yeah, it’s got a few flaws and (hundres of menus😵‍💫) but nothing that ruins the experience. Epic Boss battles, silly npcs, helpful community, you can also go to doctor for that illness or ask a player online to fix you up! plus you have a horse! you can throw the bear, you can jump and fly, crafting and also (you can build your own house and decorate it like a heaven anywhere on the map) you can craft basically anything. you can recycle items and get cash coins. Oh there is so much. I can't summ it up here! Just do me a favour and please go and PLAY THIS GAME!

Like the Pitch Pot game super easy to under stand, click the mouse while drunk when  the icon lights up while keeping the mouse in the middle of the circle, easy enough to under stand. Then they add a second moving blue circle some times, and a keyboard icon. No explaination of either or of when to use them or what key the entire keyboard icon should mean. There are also puzzles to solve but they only have chinese characters on them, I do not speak or read chinese so guess what more fumbling along.
The character progression is linear no branching skill tree just dump points in and follow a straight line. You upgrade equipment slots, the equipment its self, the skills, the sub skills and most of it makes zero difference other then number go up.
There is an auto parry or assist feature but if you turn it on enemies just turbo spam attacks and you just sit there mashing E waiting for them to all to finish. Its pretty lame and not really recommended to play with it on. However if you turn it off good luck with dodging or parrying giant sweeping attacks that have little to no way of gauging the depth perception since the camera keeps pitching up when target locked.
Bosses have a slim chance of dropping a cosmetic, very slim it would seem, killed 75 of them and got the same token every time. That could just be RNGess hating me but who knows.
Their are no pay to win buys on the shop good points there. However the gacha is massively over priced and odds are not listed in game. Most cosmetics are very exspensive as well, 25-50 usd on average for skins and mounts. Most are saying 400-600 on some of the gacha junk.
The coop is pretty lame, you are just a helper for the host any progression you make  if your not the host doesn't stick, the loot does but kinda defeats the point of coop. The open multiplayer part is very timmed down, not much to do. Go to an outpost that is full of enemies on single or coop and its empty on multi. The game very much feels like it was made as a single play and tacked multi player on. 
There is plenty to keep you busy for a while but if you are looking for new main game this is very much not it.
Other little naggles all start adding up over time leading to a unpleasant experience. Oh game also uses a lot AI in the form of chat bots for npcs and some voices and does NOT disclaim that on the store page on steam like they are suppose to do. 
Over all for free its a worth a try, just play the first act and quit before going to Kaifeng as it just gets worse over time. Honestly, the idea of time-gated progression isn’t bad on paper. Slowing people down so they don’t blast to endgame? Sure, whatever. The problem starts the moment you realize that entire weapon abilities are locked behind those same gates. Want to use two weapons that both require three real-world days and level 32+ just to function? That kills the vibe instantly.

What makes it worse is how the game hands you every weapon at the start like a buffet, then quietly tells you, “Oh, by the way, none of these actually work yet.” You can swing them, but you don’t get the abilities that make them worthwhile. So you spend half the game stuck using whatever scraps the system allows instead of the styles you actually want.

It just feels bad. The time gates and level gates don’t create meaningful progression; they just block you from playing the way you actually want to play.

At the present, this game is amazing. The combat system is fun, exploration is plentyfull and the visuals are breathtaking.

However, if you are like me and wish to buy skins to support the devs, then frankly you are out of luck. Normally a skin would be 2.8k Pearls. That would cost roughly around 30-40 bucks.

The "newest" skin released was put into a gacha pool and raised the price from 2.8k to 7.4k pearls. So from 40 bucks to 140 bucks. Meanwhile in CN, the same skin can be brought directly, without gacha, for 2.8k.

Now, a lot of smoothbrained induviduals will say its because the price difference is the same as CN, because CN is poor, while global is rich.

Yet every other skin is priced the same as CN. If they cared about price power, they'd increase all skins to 7.4k. But they didn't. 

And yes, I am fully aware that itd a free to play game and no one is forcing you to buy skins. Normally, I'd see the price and say "well, its not for me because its out of my price range". But the problem lays that if the skin was priced like it was in CN, it would have been in my price range. 

A lot of people are "poor" shaming people for this, calling them names for being stupid enough to buy skins in the first place. 

I want my character to look cool/pretty. I immerse myself in these types of games. If I want to splurge for a new cute/cool outfit, I will. But not if I learn that I have to pay 4x the price that CN did. 

I don't care if they release new skins for whales, but it had to been for whales in the first place. At 40 dollars, that seems to me like it was intended for everyone, but on global they increased it to 140 so that only whales can afford it. 

If you don't plan on spending money, then this is a great game. But if you are like me, then your time is best spent with your wallet shut.

First of all WWM is a good game. It's got a cool Wuxia setting, action based combat with a lots of weapons to choose from, and an interesting system to drive players to interact with each other. 

However the microtransaction practices has so many predatory things about it that I can't whole heartedly recommend. It's got a lot of the red flags, multiple premium currency, you can't buy the specific amount of currency you need and different gacha with different rules that can easily mislead you. On top of all of it they're retroactively release outfits from the CN version at a far higher cost and putting it behind a misleading Gacha.'

I don't care if people don't like this review because they think I'm attacking the game. I like the game and want to support the game without feeling mislead by shady tactic. This review is here to warn people so they do not end up falling for misleading gacha tactics like many others did. To future players, especially those that never played a gacha games you should follow these rules.

- Read the details and rule of the gacha banners so you can make an informed decision. I know this sounds extremely obvious but most who don't play gacha are used to pricing transparency. Most do not expect a sudden change in rules especially between banners. 

- If a deal looks too good to be true it probably is. Check if there is something else is going on.

- Don't fall for sunk cost fallacy or fomo. They almost always bring time-limited stuff back and often easier to obtain later. 
 
For those who don't know, recently they released a new scratch (Unseen Veil) that appears to be cheap. However the price of the gacha actually jumps significantly with every scratch and many only found out after already invested a lot of money into.

Only the first scratch is 60 pearl. The price jumps significantly with every scratch. It actually adds up to 7440 pearl (over 100 USD, jumping from 60 to 180, 400, 800 all the way to 2600 pearl). It's not 7 scratch at 60 pearls each like a lot of people were mislead into thinking. You would not know this if you did not see the extremely easy to miss information in the details.

The rule is a tiny icon down near the corner for you to click on and it's even misspelled as "intro" not "info". This resulted in a lot of people to spend money on the scratch only to find out that its far more expensive than their initial price point. At lot of the time people would have already spend 30 50 dollars without said costume and will fall for sunk cost fallacy trying to finish the scratch. 

This is extremely concerning as the outfit in question CAN BE PURCHASED DIRECTLY on the Chinese server and significantly lower price too at 2580 pearl for the entire set. Meaning they made this outfit retroactively more expensive and put it behind gacha for the international release. I do not know what Netease is trying to pull but its nothing good for the long term health of the game. 

Netease is notorious for it's microtransaction practice but this was a first for me. There is more than a fair share of players who just want to enjoy the game on a budget fell for this. Why not just make the price upfront? Why resort to misleading people? You got whales spending over 40k on a ship on the 5th day of release, this isn't even about keep a game alive, your game is alive and well. Did you really have to start using this kind of tactic so soon?

You already have the legendary banner that cost over 300 dollar to hit pity (Not even the specific item you want, it's double if you want to costume), regular costumes reaching 40 USD and a bunch of other weapons skins and animation changes. Did you really have to make an existing outfit that sold for 2580 pearls and lock it behind a 7440 Gacha instead?

This is on top of the fact that the NPC for f2p or budget players to earn cosmetics is not in the international version as well as coupons being cut back from 2 a month to 1 through the login bonus. The currency for the monthly pass do not give a player to player trading currency but rather regular coins. 

Why are so many features missing and items being cut back? You can't even access some existing multiplayer function because of the missing currency.

I want to love this game, the combat is great, the world is great, the story is great, but it's this kind of practice that cause people to leave games in the first place. Most don't mind spending money on games they enjoy, most don't want to feel like they're being tricked into it.

TL;DR

Where Winds Meet is gorgeous and fun to play, but the extreme monetization and lack of meaningful rewards make it hard to recommend.

Review

Where Winds Meet nails the fundamentals: the world is stunning, the combat feels great, and the early progression is genuinely enjoyable. Most players agree that gameplay-wise, this could’ve been one of the best wuxia titles in years. 

But the biggest complaints online match my own:

The Battlepass is good, but completing it offers no currency toward the next one as is traditionally done, so you have to buy the battle pass every round. 

Now, understand, you receive a few starter weapons, but there are very few actual "upgrades". Instead, you hop into one of the 250 menu's and use money and resources to "upgrade" your weapon. SO you have the same weapons for most of the games with, usually, only one per class accessible at a time. Also, gear has no visuals, so your character has a few options, otherwise looks the same unless you pay real money for cosmetics. Additional cosmetics cost $40+ with almost nothing earnable in-game. 
(side note- You CAN buy a couple of things off the ingame currency store, but at 2-10 jade rings per quest/activity, and items costing up to 50,000... well, you do the math on how much life that will cost you in RL). 

Game wise, you have the unique ability to repeat boss fights and dungeons at higher levels, but they hide almost all loot or weapons behind a "Probability" (RNG with low probability) flag, and the RNG is brutal, with boss drops so low that many players report dozens of runs with absolutely nothing to show for it.

Events reward tiny amounts of currency, nowhere near the 5,000–10,000+ needed for cosmetic shop items.

Progression eventually dries up, making leveling feel pointless with no rewards or goals to work toward. Also, time-gated farming (like jade fish currency- limited farming per week) slows everything down unless you pay.

This mirrors what many players are saying: the game feels like a free-to-play title that refuses to reward actual playtime or progress. You are only rewarded if you pay money to the company.

Where Winds Meet has an incredible foundation, but the heavy paywalls and stingy reward structure drain the fun fast. Until the monetization and RNG systems are reworked, I can’t recommend it.

This game is incredible. The best F2P experience I've ever had. Important to note: unless you count the membership and battle pass cost (the same price as a sub to any other MMO) it has absolutely no P2W.

Pros:
- Incredibly fun combat with a Soulslike and ARPG base that blends with traditional MMO elements
- Immersive, beautiful, giant open world with lots of activities/minigames and things to do
- Story is actually very good, especially considering the game's genre. This is including main quests, side quests, and small quests
- Lots of very different, interesting skills to play around with ranging from combat skills to utility skills to RP skills and everything in-between. Including both actives and passives
- Movement is very fun and extremely stylish
- Power progression is great
- Character customization is top notch and cosmetics are both cool and varied for players of differing tastes. There's a lot here. You can download others' uploaded appearances and use them or tweak them to your liking. You can save different presets for your character so you can change how you look, including entirely different faces, or even just have different make-up presets (I have a 'battle paint' preset and my normal look). There's a ton of different emotes, there's character profile backgrounds you can fully customize with unlocked decorations. There's a bunch of different cosmetic slots where you can put things like a guqin (instrument), harp, daggers, farming tools, bags of fruit, etc. It is not one slot, it is many, so you can look entirely goofy if you want.
-You can build a home in the open world
-You can master songs from different musicians and then play the songs
-It's not P2W (unless you count the membership and battle pass cost, which again, is the same price as a sub for any other MMO, $15)
-Can play completely solo, in your own world, or in multiplayer, in a shared world or an instanced area. As of making this review I've been almost entirely solo but the group activities seem fun and range from traditional bosses and dungeons to participating together in the MANY minigames in the game (seriously, there's a ton, they put a lot of love into this).
-Fresh take on professions that other players will surely, without a doubt, rely on you for.

Cons:
-There's a huge number of currencies and it's not very clear what you should and shouldn't spend the currency on. Again, not P2W, all free currencies, but you can spend them poorly and set your build far behind. 
-The UI is pretty and looks great in combat, but navigating it is a complete mess and super annoying. I'm almost 70 hours in and I'm still getting lost in the UI all the time.

Neutral:
-The only thing I'm iffy on is the gacha system. The game has plenty of great cosmetics that you can buy right out of the shop, but the "top tier" cosmetics come out of the gacha system. Again, the game has no P2W, but hiding cool stuff behind a gacha system still leaves a bad taste in my mouth. The only reason this is neutral and not a con is because they give regular players enough 'draws' to eventually get something cool.

The game is F2P and you lose nothing by trying it. But I'm completely hooked and I recommend everyone who is considering this game to give it a go to see if they feel the same. In my opinion, the game is a borderline masterpiece. 9.25/10.

I love the wuxia genre in books and games, so I gave this a try.  And...after banging my head against the wall for an afternoon I deleted the game.

Basically, my frustrations boiled down to the controls feeling clunky and several being impossible to change, the initial appearance customization being...granular in a good way, but also several buttons having no description so you can't know what they do until they wreck your character and you are forced to start over, and others being in nonsensical locations.  (why is iris color under makeup?!)  Lastly, as I opted out of all multiplayer options, I was surprised when I typed in a character name and got hit with "name taken, please choose another".  I was playing a solo campaign, who took the name?  The imaginary hamster in my PC?

So I spent over an hour typing in different names in three different languages and hitting "enter the jianghu" only to get told my name was already taken.  So in annoyance I typed a few gibberish strings of letters to only get told that, once again, my name was already taken.  -.-

At last, I mashed a few keys at random, convinced the game was bugged and simply rejecting all inputs, hit enter, and was shocked as it launched the opening cutscene without so much as a, "this cannot be changed, are you sure?" confirmation screen or anything. (Which is standard in games both online and offline, so I'm not sure where that went)

I sighed in frustration and thought, 'well, it said map markers, combat difficulty, and appearance can all be changed at any time in-game, so surely I can just fix my name after the cutscene'.

And you can, if you pay $5.  You know, to change your name that only you ever see.  Because you turned off multiplayer.  Which still requires your name to be unique - for some reason.

Next I thought, 'well, I'll just delete this character and start over.  Annoying, but whatever'.

You can only delete a character by emailing a petition to the developer stating why you should be allowed to do so.  And the developer says they reserve the right to just refuse, and also says they can't estimate how long it will take to get a verdict.  Meaning you are just STUCK if you have any sort of problem and want to restart, or if you just want your character deleted because you don't want to play anymore then too bad.

So yeah, I'd love to try the game out, see it grow, figure out the ins and outs of the combat system, and experience the story.  But I'm not paying money to rename my character that only got a stupid name because the system rejected literally anything I, a multilingual l person could think of (I tried dozens of names in THREE LANGUAGES), rejected multiple gibberish names, then instantly accepted the final one and finalized it without any confirmation screen.  And I'm also not going to beg in an email for the right of deleting MY character save and starting over.

Game deleted.  Not worth the frustration nor the predatory microtransation necessary to fix something that is only even possible because of bad game design.

A Love Letter to a Wild and Beautiful Wuxia World
If you have ever dreamed of being a wandering swordmaster—sprinting across water, leaping between ancient pavilion rooftops, and existing in an era of poetic chaos—Where Winds Meet is that dream realized. Developed by Everstone Studio, this open-world action RPG is not merely a follower of Ghost of Tsushima or Sekiro; it is a distinct entity that elevates the spirit of Chinese legends (Wuxia) to breathtaking new heights.

Here is a deep dive into why this game deserves your attention:

1. Breathtaking Art Direction
The first thing that will capture your soul is the visual aesthetic. Set during the tumultuous Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era, Everstone has successfully blended next-gen graphical realism with the artistic touch of traditional Chinese ink paintings.

Lighting & Weather: From sunlight piercing through bamboo forests to rain splashing on muddy streets, the atmosphere is incredibly immersive.

Environmental Design: Whether it’s a moss-covered giant Buddha statue or a bustling city lit by lanterns, every corner feels like a frame from a colossal cinematic masterpiece.

2. Limitless Freedom of Movement
While many open-world games restrict you with rigid stamina bars during traversal, Where Winds Meet offers absolute freedom through the Qinggong system (martial arts lightness skill).

You can run vertically up city walls.

Glide through the air with acrobatic grace.

Sprint effortlessly across the surface of the water. The transition between exploration and combat feels remarkably fluid, making the simple act of moving from point A to point B a joyful experience in itself.

3. Fast-Paced and Tactical Wuxia Combat
The combat system is not mindless hack-and-slash; it is a "dance of death" that requires strategy.

Tai Chi Combat: You can utilize "soft" fighting styles to deflect enemy attacks or use their own force against them.

Weapon Variety: From the straight sword (Jian) and spears to iron fans, every weapon boasts a unique move-set.

Environmental Interaction: You can kick objects at enemies or use the surrounding elements to gain a tactical advantage.

4. True "Role-Playing" Mechanics
This is perhaps the game's strongest selling point. You are not forced to be a killer forever. The game features a deep Identity System.

Want to retire from violence? You can become a Doctor and heal NPCs.

Love design? You can become an Architect and build structures (the game features a complex building system with over 600 antique components).

You can even become a Merchant or a Bodyguard. The world reacts to the role you choose.

5. Narrative: History Meets Mythology
The story tackles themes of moral choice during wartime. You play as a swordsman whose fate is determined by your decisions. Will you uphold justice with your blade, or save the people through medicine? The dialogue is poetic and steeped in Eastern philosophy.

Edit: I initially gave this a negative review because the intro to this game is honestly awful. 
- The tutorialization sucks, it both patronizes you (you know healing heals right?) and simultaneously neglects to mention critical information. Not to mention the sheer amount of spamming of popups is insane.
- Theres an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of systems and menus to dig through to understand how all the different mechanics and minigames and upgrades and progressions work.
- There are about 5 billion different reward track scattered everywhere in the UI that show up as red dots in your main menu that you need to dig through to claim and get rid of the dot. These then give you 10 different currencies spent in 10 different shops that you need to find by going through 100 other menus. Its tiring to say the least.
- The story starts off confusing as hell. Theres about 100 different names of people and places and events mentioned and you got no idea how any of it fits together or why you should care.
- Translation leaves much to be desired. E.g. you dont "open" chests, you "enable" them. Voiceover performances are so bad you should immediately swap to chinese VO and read the subs instead.

So why the positive review now? Well, once you power through all that crap, learn the systems, swap the VO, skip most dialogue cause you know its crap, find the comedy in the bad story, learn to navigate the spiderweb of ♥♥♥♥ UI, theres a pretty beautiful game underneath it all.

The good:
- Animations. Combat animations are absolutely fantastic, movement has some jank (wallrunning and "windstriding" specifically) but is mostly very satisfying, cutscenes are very well crafted (mostly), it just all looks very good.
- Combat feel. Sound, impact, FX, enemy reactions to attacks, its satisfying and addicting.
- World aesthetics. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this world looks beautiful. Level design and lighting is S tier. You cant move 5 meters without stopping to awe at the scenery.
- Sound design. Very good and very stolen :D They take some very obvious "inspiration" from ghost of tsushima and breath of the wild on this front. But yeah, no matter how blatantly ripped off it is, its good.
- Bosses. If you enjoy the Dark Souls series, you got a lot of challenging boss fights to dig in to here. Combined with the satisfying combat systems based around dodges and parries and committing to attacks in openings youll feel right at home here. Just make sure you start the game on "Legend" difficulty cause you cant switch to it later and the game is ridiculously easy without it
- Minigame variety. Theres quite a few minigames and theyre all pretty fun. Though they really need to take a balancing pass on them. Some are ridiculously hard (pitch pot) while others are stupidly easy (gift of gab and healing) to the point of you being able to randomly press buttons and get through them. The mechanics are there but the difficulty needs to encourage understanding and usage of them.

All in all, the game is pretty rough but is also a very unique blend that makes it stand out and keep your interest even though theres so much ♥♥♥♥ you have to tolerate :D

Pro's:
> Free - For the price, the game is amazing. Are there Microtransactions? Yes. Battlepass? Yes
Am I considering buying the battlepass just to support the game developers for a great product? Yes.  

> Graphics are awesome. Cutting edge, near movie like cut scenes. 

> Story is imersive, interesting, engaging.  I normally hit skip skip skip, but I have not found myself doing that for any part of the main story.  

> Gameplay / Exploration - I'm walking everywhere (even though you get a horse) so as to explore and enjoy the beauty of the world. Quests are fine, basically, what you would expect of any RPG/MMO.  

>  Combat - If you like general ARPG combat, you'll enjoy this. Lots of abilities to utilize. Combat is fun (I am playing on basically easy mode.  

> No Agenda - This is a traditional game and it doesn't feel like they're trying to push any agenda or idealogy onto the player like some western developers are currently doing with other games. I appreciate this.  


CONs:
> Complexity (Menus, Menu Navigation, Abilitiy/Item Upgrades, - there's a lot of stuff going on behind the scenes, all of which seem to matter.  Thankfully there's a bot that kind of helps you understand what you kind of need to do to upgrade, etc, but after about 10h I still find navigation and understanding of the various abilities, upgrades, etc, super complicated.  

> Some of the combat can feel a bit repetative and it feels like maybe it takes a long time to kill a common enemy.  I assume this is because I do not understand the game systems that well yet and probably do not have the best itemization, abilities, etc and am not really min/maxed, but that's okay - I guess it's a good think that I can still progress in the game (so a bit of a pro as well).

Anyhow, great game.  I never would have tried it had there been a cost to it, so "free" was perfect and I will likely support the game for the battlepass because I want to support developers who have made a really fun experience.  Thank you, keep up the great work!

3. The NPC Ai Chat System is surprised me. I didn't expect to care about the npc at starting but later when i get it i spend time on chatting and its really fun.

I picked the Doctor profession. I thought it would be a side gimmick, but I literally spent a 3-hour session just diagnosing NPCs in a village, mixing herbs, and curing them.

It adds this layer of roleplay that Ghost of Tsushima or Elden Ring doesn't have. You aren't just a killer; you’re a person living in this era.

The "Real Talk" Negatives
It’s not perfect. If you’re 30 hours in, the cracks start to show.

UI Overload: The screen is busy. There are so many menus, sub-menus, and currency types. It feels very "MMO-lite" sometimes, even though it plays like a single-player action game. I still get lost looking for the skill tree sometimes.

The Story is Dense: Unless you are a history buff regarding the Ten Kingdoms era of China, you are going to get confused. There are a lot of names, a lot of factions, and a lot of politics thrown at you very fast. I honestly started skipping some dialogue around hour 20 because I just wanted to get back to the action.

 It’s beautiful, but it bugs out. I’ve clipped through floors. I’ve had enemies freeze in T-poses. But its free to play after all so can't complain on everything.

The Verdict after 30 Hours

Pros

To elaborate on this the weapon hit boxes for enemies are really clunky missing when they should hit so it throws off your timing and then hitting when they should miss things like a bear diving at the ground with randomly kill you and a lot of the bosses red attacks (the attacks you want to parry) will either miss u completely if your two close or punish you because the red flash comes so early it may as well have not been there. I understand its a Chinese game and to be honest the voice acting in English is not that bad but the game will randomly pause some times and the dialog or subtitles will either vanish or stop completely leaving you watch gestures and hearing some dialog or nothing.

You can run out its not hard to make but there should be a notice if you run low a few times i was trying a boss fight and running out of healing before an attempt and just had to die to the boss and make more after its not a huge deal but really annoying.

A lot of these could be skill issues to most people and i half agree getting used to combat and learning a fight after losing a bunch is what i enjoy but to lose to the games issues is more of a what could i do situation rather than a get good situation but that is open to everyone's interpretation i suppose.

I recommend going into the game with an open mind and giving it a try and hopefully in the next coming years if this game gets enough funding and attention I hope they'll polish the many things that need improvement such as the minor lag/delay playing in co-op, the audio from cut scenes and random dialogue cutting out or not being voiced when it feels like it should, the clunkiness of certain mini games, and certain translation issues that make reading skill tooltips and other things a bit confusing.

As a Chinese American, I'm deeply in love with Where Winds Meet. I think its the Assassin's Creed ancient China I've been waiting for combined with my favorite elements of Wuxia C-dramas and movies. The game is genuinely stunning and the cat puzzles are my favorite aspects of the game. As well as the evil geese in the game, I can tell the devs have a sense of humor and have been emotionally harmed by mean geese. :D The hanfu is beautiful and I appreciate the codex informing people of the historical aspects of the Song dynasty as well as Chinese culture, I think its important for players not well-versed in Chinese history and culture. The music is lovely as well, and Chapter one was genuinely amazing from start to finish and was deeply cinematic. I think one of the best part's of the game IS the main story quest.

Having said that, I think the English localization for text could be much MUCH better, some of the grammar is easily fixable and also not exactly accurate compared to the Chinese audio. I really think Netease could hire proper translators to fix this, there are parts of the main story where the subtitle translations don't show up at all.  I use English subtitles and have Chinese audio so I'm not sure on the quality of the English dubbing, but the Chinese voice acting is very good. 

As for the AI "controversy" (not sure if there is a controversy besides some folks making a stink on bluesky), I'm not a big fan of the feature and think its unnecessary. Personally I am against AI, however I don't think its that big of a deal though, its just a chatbot. But I've played the game solo so far without doing any of the AI chatbot features and think I'm better off for it. and the game doesn't need it. I hope the devs reconsider the use of AI in this game since it is a polarizing subject and I don't think adds to the experience either. Players would much prefer writing and storytelling written by actual humans instead of AI/LLM where there is no soul in it. Wuxia was invented by humans after all and it would not be what it is without centuries and centuries of human thought and philosophy combined with elements of Chinese history, Buddhism, and Daoism. 

I'll edit this review more as I play along but so far these are the things that stand out to me. What I do see however, are the daily hotpatch fixes so its nice to see the devs being aware of all the bugs and mistranslations and updating the game.

All-in-all, Where Winds Meet is another open world eye candy game with lackluster combat and a confusing narrative.

I'll give you the short breakdown first, more details below.
IF you want to "EXPERIENCE" a game with friends, you'll enjoy this.
IF you want to "PLAY" a game with friends, find another game.

What do I mean by that?

Where Winds Meet is a “Theme’d game” during a particular era in China. Meaning you go in with the “intent” to immerse yourself into the weeaboo culture of China and become this Asian themed hero with your magic skills and abilities.

It’s designed around playing “open world” with your fellow LARP buddies to role play your hearts out to immerse yourself into your chosen weeb. Then you do guild ♥♥♥♥ like WoW or FF to fight world bosses or other guilds in competitions to keep the weeb energy alive.

All the while you can fly around the world, admire the scenery, take group photo’s, go on digital dating sims, etc. Just to “experience” it together, both exploring, collecting goodies and doing mini-games and events. (Even some PVP in the guild battles.)

But as far as “gaming” goes. It is a single player game. You explore it while having its core intent in mind, knowing that to improve your basic combat skills, you are going to need to do as many as the aforementioned mini games and fetch quests to level up to make your individual gaming experience more balanced with the skills you gain along the way.

Just going thru the story mode only leaves you at a disadvantage, you need to do side missions and other things to help get you geared up to take on the next challenges. 

So for the 66 hours I’ve put into the game so far. How will I rate it?

As a solo player game? 6/10. just above average in quality and movement controls with decent combat mechanics and exploratory value. Why it’s not higher is because there is no “direction” that helps you find out what to do next outside of the direct main story.

As it’s “intended” design of an open world MMO roleplay game. Maybe 4/10 (for me) but at 8/10 in execution. As intended, they made it so many people can “experience” the world together. 

But overall 3/10 in execution as a “game with friends” is concerned.

So if you want to play a Souls like, Assassin creed wannabe with no clear plot directive and plenty of mini-games and side quests with no clear direction that are nearly mandatory to the overall character development, this is a great solo game. But if you are looking to find a game to play with friends? Nope. Better luck next time chief. 

The Dev's wanted to make a game that "had something for everyone" but in doing so, they made a whole lot of nothing for everyone as well. If you only take advantage of 2 or 3 aspects of the game instead of the full MMO experience, you'll be severely disappointed with all the fetch quests and lack of direction. But if you let your asian weeb heart cultivate hard enough, this will be a good experience for you.

Overall, its a free game, just a pay to look pretty. So you don't lose anything except a time sink into leveling up a character. Try it out, you might like it. But do so with the right mindset of you are "playing a solo game with world experiencing / exploration co-op" not a multiplayer game.

Where Winds Meet is a gorgeous Wuxia open-world RPG where you can soar across rooftops, duel like a martial arts legend, and accidentally punt a goose off a bridge because the physics engine was feeling spicy that day.

Combat? Awesome. World? Stunning. Character customization? I spent 40 minutes giving myself the jawline of a guy who definitely skips leg day.

But let’s talk about the story.
Playing the solo story starts strong… then very suddenly drops you into a desert of side quests where time slows down, your enthusiasm fades, and you begin to question whether you are actually the forgotten identity the plot keeps hinting at, because you’ve lost all memory of what’s going on.

It’s not bad—it’s just lonely. Wandering this giant world solo feels like being the only kid who showed up to field trip day. Beautiful scenery, but no one to share the chaos with.

And here’s the kicker:
The current co-op? Fun, chaotic, and great for messing around with friends…
…but it has nothing to do with the actual story.
No shared quests, no co-op narrative, no “let’s uncover our mysterious past together while accidentally setting an entire village on fire.” Nothing.

This game desperately needs a co-op story mode. The world is built for adventure with people, not as a quiet pilgrimage of one lonely sword master contemplating every rock on every mountain.

TL;DR:

Stunning world

Great Wuxia combat

Solo story gets boring fast

Co-op is fun but disconnected

Please, Everstone… let me suffer or triumph with my friends

If they ever add true co-op story progression, this might become one of the best open-world Wuxia adventures out there. Until then, I’ll be in the corner practicing Tai Chi and waiting for my friends to finish a dungeon that has nothing to do with the plot.

Verdict:
A sweeping Wuxia adventure with the colorful whimsy of a hero’s journey and the painterly look of prestige open worlds. It doesn’t always match the polish of its inspirations, but it’s a beautiful, generous game that I’m happy to recommend.

What it does well

World & Atmosphere:
The scenery is stunning—sunlit rice fields, misty peaks, lively towns. Exploration feels rewarding thanks to playful, puzzle-tinged dungeons and lots of tucked-away secrets.

Combat:
Responsive dodge and counter mechanics form the core, layered with multiple weapon types and distinct styles. Some weapons even let you pick between roles like damage, sturdiness, or team support, which adds variety without overcomplicating things.

Modes & Flexibility:
It’s primarily a single-player experience, yet it lets you tackle dungeons in co-op and features a lightweight “MMO-style” social space. Think of it as a lively hub where you can do almost everything the world offers—just not the main campaign.

Progression & Loot:
Gear is straightforward but satisfying to upgrade. Materials come in familiar rarity tiers, and chasing rarer components for higher-level upgrades gives exploration a steady pull.

Story:
So far, the narrative lands well—classic Wuxia melodrama with a steady rhythm of set-pieces. I’m genuinely excited to see where it goes.

Extras players will care about

Ranged options:
A bow is part of the toolkit, and it integrates smoothly with close-quarters combat rather than feeling like a bolt-on.

Co-op dungeons:
Bite-sized, replayable runs that fit neatly between solo story sessions.

AI-driven NPC chatter (optional):
You can have free-form conversations with certain NPCs. It’s novel and sometimes charming, though not everyone will want it switched on all the time.

Monetization:
Leans cosmetic. Progress hinges on playing—collecting, crafting, upgrading—rather than on purchases.

Where it can stumble

Feature flood:
The game throws a lot at you—minigames, side systems, little distractions. It’s fun, but newcomers may need a moment to find their rhythm.

Tone swings:
The mix of earnest drama and playful side activities can feel a bit jumpy from scene to scene.

Tech odds and ends:
Big install size and plenty of graphics options to tune. Once set up, performance is solid, but the first hour on PC may be spent tweaking.

Final thoughts

If you want a lavishly realized world to roam, brisk timing-based combat, and the freedom to bounce between solo storytelling and co-op dungeon runs, Where Winds Meet delivers. Its sheer abundance can be a little much in the early going, but once it clicks, it’s a delight. I fully recommend it.

Pretends to be an MMO/action game, is actually just a predatory time sink.

I've played 25 hours on legend difficulty.  Killed 10 bosses including some un-nerfed world bosses.  The game makes the cardinal sin of thinking raw HP=difficulty, which makes every encounter take about 50% longer than it needs to.  

The game has a block system which is worthless, because you still take damage and healing is in short supply. The game expects you to use a parry system, which on every other difficulty besides legend is a qte, resulting in parries doing basically nothing.  The frame window is sekiro level of tight, and when you stagger the enemy you get to do like....25% of its health pool on a good hit.  Some bosses will do 50% of your hp in a single hit as a wakeup attack from a stagger.
This is where pay to win comes in.  Some of the smoothbrains will tell you to just use the fan for infinite healing. This is technically correct for some bosses and farm bosses which you've already beaten. For new bosses you're progging, most of them give you an 80% healing taken reduction meaning the only effective way to heal is via consumable.   Buying the battle pass gives you up to 2 extra healing consumable slots. This is by definition pay to win.

The voice acting is fiverr tier bad.  Localization to english is pathetic. This really wouldn't matter much if the game actually let you skip dialogue  and cutscenes.  It lets you fast forward, and skip one line at a time with a delayed input. The cutscene skip isn't active for a good 3-4 seconds in every cutscene (then has a 3 second confirmation delay that resets if you hit the button too many times) and the game LOVES areas where you walk slowly and someone yaps at you for 10 minutes.   Find your favorite LLM and turn on the robot voice, you'll get the same experience and level of quality.

Now for the predatory portion.  Previously, I mentioned pay to win, already a negative.  This game has EVERY dark pattern manipulation tactic to separate you from your wallet.  Daily login rewards, battle pass. Daily reminders to upgrade your battle pass. 7000 different menus to collect 5 currency at a time from "achievements". Multiple in game currencies, a gacha draw system, an in game shop.  If you want to buy a cosmetic in the shop it costs 2580 "Pearls"(In game premium currency that can only be purchased for IRL money).  They sell pearls in 1800 packs for 30 dollars and 3000 packs for 50 dollars.  Prime scumbag developer tactic.

a genuinely enjoyable open world game to play! it reminds me a lot of black desert but with the choice to play solo (as in you only see your character and it is effectively a singleplayer RPG) or with others, and with a heavy focus on spiritualism and the arts. it has nice character customization, the open world is beautiful and full of stuff to collect, people to interact with, and different puzzles to complete. you can play instruments, go fishing, catch and ride horses, debate NPCs in a minigame and upgrade your skills, pet cats, you can become a healer and heal other players or NPCs that have afflictions, you can even kill NPCs and steal their horses and other items using skills you learn. the combat is alright, definitely not black desert levels of combos, but there is a pretty good range of weapons you can use (umbrellas, war fans, swords, spears, bows) each with their own martial arts styles. there is base building too, but i dont know too much about it outside of discovering different architectural designs as i explore. i have only played solo, but there is definitely a lot of co op aspects to the game that i havent personally gotten into if that is more your style: you can join guilds, make friends, PVP, even find romantic interests and earn rewards. THIS GAME DOES HAVE A GACHA SYSTEM, however it is only (as of now) for appearances, and you can earn resources for spins FOR FREE. i have seen some reviews complaining about paying for this feature, and while it is a bit slow, you absolutely do not need to pay for spins!! you CAN pay for appearances, and i will say some outfit prices are steep, but you can get and stack up to 5 10% coupons, and it seems they put certain outfits on sale, as well as all of the free outfits, accessories, and hairstyles you get from just playing the game. there is also a battlepass system, with the usual free battlepass vs. paid battlepass ($10 for regular elite, 20$ for elite+) you find in most games. overall this game has been pretty fun to play, the quests have been engaging, even spooky and silly at some points, which is right up my ally. absolutely recommend.

Pro:
- Nice graphics, all characters and technique look spectacular and feel Wuxia like
- Horizontal Progression : Lots of side activities to do to grow in various way that are not level dependant. As a friend said, you look at a quest that is 100 meters away from you, but it will take you 5 hours to reach it if you do all the content.
- Massive amount of interesting content
- Some world exploration copies genshin and the like, but with their own touch that doesn't make them a genshin clone.

- No power monetization (the day this change, this review will automatically change and I will quit), monetization is cosmetic only. And contrarely to some western games, you do not look like a garbadge bag if you do not roll in the gacha.

- Love the diversity of activities

Cons:
- The UI is very hard to navigate, there is a lot of sub sub sub categories.
- Bonus currency (Jade) is spread across a lot of different menu, having a 'claim all' button would be nice.
- Too many currencies
- Items that are important are sometimes mixed with items such as consumable and others which makes parsing inventory more annoying. I wish there was a dedicated inventory for important items such as martial art books and chests. (read once and done)

Overall, if they can make some optimisation on the UI side I feel this game will do very well in the future, its  a great game and I suggest trying it.

[h3][b]TL;DR:[/b][/h3] Better than what I expected. I was pleasantly surprised. Some input delay but not sure where it comes from. Visually beautiful. Plays good enough through Proton.

[h2]Monetization[/h2]
Although they do not really force you to pay to play since most monetized stuff are cosmetic, they do time-gate you when you start reaching higher levels. Also they have so much currencies everywhere that is overwhelming. I think they should reduce the amount of different currencies.

[h2]UI/UX[/h2]
The main UI it's OK, clean enough to let the game shine, the problem is the rest. Menus inside menus inside  sub-menus with a bunch of tabs each. It gets confusing and tedious to navigate through the. They really should streamline them and make them friendlier to keyboard/mouse.

[h2]Movement and Combat[/h2]
Moving around the world is fun you get as you progress abilities to access other parts of the map and to travel faster and more efficiently around it and they are fun.
The combat at times feels sluggish and clanky, the animation needs to play to completion most of the time before you are able to use another move or ability with only exception it seems to be the parry button and not always. Some abilities when you chain them one after the other flow nice but other times they look weird or lose their target when NPC desides to do 2 steps to the side even if you are locked on them and you are not in the middle of the animation (meaning the ability haven't fired yet).
But the biggest problem of all is the delay, there is a noticeable delay most of the time that the movements, abilities and other interaction will need a few fractions of a second to execute, which can make it really annoying when you fight stronger enemies or bosses.

[h2]Graphics and Performance[/h2]
The worlds looks wonderful, the art-style is spot on and the player and NPC models are detailed and beautiful. My problem is with the effects, especially the bosses attack effects many times obscure their models which can make it hard to see their movement/animations this combined with the delay that I mentioned previously it makes the difficult fights more annoying. I would prefer if the attack effects especially from enemies where a little more subtle.
The performance is decent even on a lower end gaming PC running through Proton most of the time just works fine.

[h2]Proton/Wine compatibility[/h2]
Had some problems running through Proton 10 and GE 10-25 but it seems to work with Proton Experimental. 
I had a couple of crashes and freezes after a few hours and also it seems the performance drops after playing a few hours so I would suggest to restart the game every few hours or so.

[h3]Not tried yet:[/h3]
Most of the multiplayer features.

Game was okay for a while, but then you realize all the boss design is a hotpot of the worst combat decisions made in gaming from about the last decade.

Some attacks are arbitrarily delayed for 5 seconds, some attacks come out instantly. Some attacks have a fixed range and others will cause the enemy to move across half the arena and do a 180 degree flip just to make absolutely sure positioning doesnt matter. Sometimes you get hit once and then are unavoidably hit 5 more times as part of some combo. Grabs last like 10 unskippable seconds, just to waste more time I will never get back. The block works maybe 40% of the time, and for the other 60 you take damage and elemental dots right through it and might as well not bother.

At first I thought the devs had accounted for this by just giving you a generous amount of health, so as long as you dodged or deflected here and there you could get through. But very quickly that disappears and we are right back in the usual hardslop "Do it perfect or die in 2 hits" land, and I'm genuinely so tired of games insisting on being this way.

There is a "Story" difficulty, but that point you go from dying in 2 hits to the boss unironically needs to hit you 20 times before you even have to heal. So you have your pick between outright no challenge or all of the above.

The rest of the game is varying degrees of alright. The graphics are incredible, the exploration is your standard open world you've played 20 times before, the dialogue is very stilted and often badly translated but has cute moments. Puzzles are generally above average for the genre, and as for the Free to Play, I didnt feel like pay to win was a factor at any point for the duration that I played. Make of that what you will, it might get worse later.

Very pretty presentation and it has a lot of potential. But the countless menus, with no clear explanations, along with what seems like a couple dozen different currencies and items whose use is never clearly explained, make it impossible to recommend at this time. The AI-driven NPCs are cool and can give a pretty convincing semblance of a real conversation in many cases. But half of the ones I talked to, where you are explicitly told you can establish a relationship with them, were impossible to make progress with, even after 10 minutes of conversation that was thoroughly in keeping with what they were looking to hear. The English translation can also be very confusing at times, but overall seems pretty good. The multiplayer aspect of the game is even more confusing and unexplained, causing me to abandon any attempts to play with other people, which is a major issue for an MMO.

I hope they can work through some of these issues, especially the overload of menus and poorly explained game progression mechanics. As it stands now, you are asking for a lot of wasted time and frustration playing this game.

Edit: I forgot to add that after my first day playing, more often than not, I can't log in. I get an "account authorization failed" sort of message, and the only option is to quit the game and try again. The log-in screen of the game has an option to "repair" things, so I always try that first. But most of the time, it doesn't help. There doesn't seem to be any pattern to why logging in works or fails. But it has taken up to a dozen tries spread out over 20 minutes to successfully play in the 3 days since I started playing.

Edit 2: After playing longer, I've decided to change my review to positive. That said, most of what I said above still stands. The log-in issues seem to be gone in the past 24 hours, and the combat gets better as you level up. But the extremely confusing menu systems, the innumerable different things to level up and/or claim, the unexplained/confusing game mechanics and the absurd number of currencies are still major problems that need to be addressed.

Pleasantly surprised by this game. With it being free-to-play, my expectations were kind of low, I wont lie.
But this game is absolute cinema! The whole design of the world, characters and story does not feel like a F2P game.
Combat is fun, exploration is interesting, the lore is amazing, the graphics are beautiful and I'm just loving my time so far! But it's not without it's flaws:

Translations are not the best, at times the English voice acting cuts out or repeats, or the translation isn't correct at all, but it doesn't hinder any gameplay. I've seen a lot say play it in Chinese VA instead, so I would recommend that if the translations bother you.
Co-op is fun but, seems buggy to me. If I am not the host, it feels like I am on a delay, enemies will teleport and look like they're moving in 10 FPS. I believe the Devs are looking into this though so, here's hoping this gets addressed soon. Also, I've had issues were I, or whom I am playing with, will be locked out of a boss fight, stuck behind an invisible wall. Only way to fix this was to die so it respawns us back in the arena.
In solo mode, I've had an issue where I couldn't use any abilities or even use my weapon. I was a sitting duck and it got me killed, even spawning back in I was still stuck. I had to reload the game to fix this.
And finally, this is a personal gripe but, I'm not a fan of content being time-gated. Having to wait days to be able to increase my level cap is frustrating but, it does stop people flying ahead and running out of things to do quickly so I guess I can't complain. Weekly caps for everything, like battle pass XP, guild activity etc., is minorly annoying - but again, this is a personal gripe and doesn't hinder any gameplay at all.

I do recommend the game despite the bugs I've come across. It's so much fun, plenty to do in-between the level caps, and I am enjoying everything so far. I love the Wuxia open-world here and it has thoroughly sucked me in at the moment. I can't wait for more content to see where this goes!

Big Review!

First up, English isn't my native language and I am hella sleep deprived right now, so I apologize for any grammar mistakes!

This Game came at the right time, while I was sitting there, not having anything to play and boom, I am hooked. I didn't expect much from the game and went in with 0 expectations but now that I have played for a while, I can safely say, this game is a massive hit. I yet want to address some things. 

The gacha experience: Yes, this game has a pulling feature like Genshin or WUWA etc. BUT it is NOT P2W. It rather gives you cosmetics or "social items" which will not impact the difficulty of the game or make you any stronger. 

I would say the biggest P2W feature is the battle pass. The battle pass can reward you with an item that replenishes 60 "Stamina" like the resin from Genshin Impact. But the free battle pass still rewards you quite handsomely with pretty decent items as well so it is definitely NOT a must have. 

The English va: I totally agree that after testing it myself, the English voice acting is a bit off and definitely not as polished as the Chinese one. If you don't mind it for yourself, go with the Chinese voice acting and lip syncing as well as the overall quality of the experience will be heavily improved. 

The Co-Op: Finally. For the first time I feel like one of those games got the Co-Op experience right. Here it is not only being marketed to engage with a wider audience but instead you can actually explore, fight and quest together in this game. It feels exactly how a Co-Op experience should be. Also, this game has quite a few aspects that almost force you to have at least some kind of interaction with other players. You can claim bounties of people who broke the law, let other players heal you when you have an illness or broken bones, aid players who call for help and so on... Overall this game feels even more alive due to the interactions that you share with other players. 

The optimization of this game: This game looks stunning and is still super well optimized. This game is running S M O O T H. I recommend to run the game on DX12, since it offers an even better performance in my case and also unlocks more graphical settings. If in your case DX12 might cause issues, just go with the standard launch option :). 

Endgame: Usually it has always been the same with those kind of games, you do the story, you explore the world and then... then what? While I have not reached the endgame yet myself, I can only talk about what I have seen and heard. This game seems to have tackled exactly that problem and still gives you many things to grind and go for, even after you are done with the story & exploration. So, you don't have to be worried about being left with nothing to do after finishing the story. 

The world building: This is probably one of the things that I am most impressed with. The visuals, the npcs, the random encounters, the side missions that are not just boring but often offer a deep story as well, the scenery... it feels like no matter where you go, there will always be something to do around you. The world feels complete and is absolutely stunning and beautiful. 

While I also feel like there is much more to say and address about this game, I do not intend on making this too long so that people might actually come across this review and still take their time to read it :). Have a lovely day y'all!

As someone who grew up watching/being exposed to East Asian shows, movies, and stories, this game is a dream come true. While yes, one can find similarly themed games in the Chinese market, there are plenty of people with Chinese or East Asian ethnicities living in the western world.

The game itself is a lot of fun. So many things to do, so many beautiful sights to see. You won't find yourself lacking in activities to do, from solo stuff to the multiplayer features. The combat feels great and responsive, combining the typical souls-like experience with certain elements of MMO-ARPG systems.

The main story is surprisingly very engaging and immersive. I find that the plot is so much better than most other AAA games. It's a rollercoaster of emotions. Some cutscenes aren't the best, but the ones that are great - they aren't far off from what you'd watch in a typical wuxia/xianxia drama series.

There are downsides, of course. Lots of currency/resources to keep track of, confusing UI (although I think it's because it is mainly derived from the same UI layout that most Chinese gamers are already used to). But for a free-2-play game?? I am absolutely okay with that.

Try it for yourself! It's free, so it doesn't cost you a dime to experience it. You might not like and that's fine. But if you do, welcome to the world of Jianghu :)
